profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-17T09:28:24.49+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Běnjì No. 1: Gāo Dì, Part 1
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì, personal name Dàochéng,
courtesy name Shàobó,
surname Xiāo.
His childhood name was Dòujiāng.
He was the twenty-fourth-generation descendant of Xiāo Hé, the Chancellor of Hàn.
Xiāo Hé's son, Zāndìng Hóu Yán, begat Shìzhōng Biāo.
Biāo begat Gōngfǔ Yuàn Zhāng.
Zhāng begat Hào.
Hào begat Yǎng.
Yǎng begat Yùshǐ Dàfū Wàngzhī.
Wàngzhī begat Guānglù Dàfū Yù.
Yù begat Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shào.
Shào begat Guānglù Xūn Hóng.
Hóng begat Jìyīn Tàishǒu Chǎn.
Chǎn begat Wújùn Tàishǒu Yǒng.
Yǒng begat Zhōngshān Xiàng Bāo.
Bāo begat Bóshì Zhōu.
Zhōu begat Shéqiū Zhǎng Jiǎo.
Jiǎo begat Zhōu Cóngshì Kuí.
Kuí begat Xiàolián Xiū.
Xiū begat Guǎnglíng Fǔchéng Bào.
Bào begat Tàizhōng Dàfū Yì.
Yì begat Huái'yīn Lìng Zhěng.
Zhěng begat Jíqiū Lìng Jùn.
Jùn begat Fǔguó Cānjūn Yuèzǐ.
In the ninth month of the second year of Shēngmíng of Sòng, he was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng.
He begat the Imperial Father.
Xiāo Hé resided in Pèi.
Shìzhōng Biāo, after being dismissed from office, resided in Zhōngdū Township, Zhōngdū Village, Lánlíng County, Dōnghǎi.
In the first year of Yuánkāng of Jìn,
Dōnghǎi was divided to form Lánlíng Commandery.
During the chaos in the central court,
Huái'yīn Lìng Zhěng, courtesy name Gōngqí,
crossed the river and resided in Dōngchéng Village, Wǔjìn County, Jìnlíng.
Those who temporarily resided south of the Yangtze River
were all given a "qiaozhi" (transferred) designation of their original homeland,
and a "southern" prefix was added.
Thus, he became a native of Nán Lánlíng (Southern Lánlíng).
The Imperial Father, personal name Chéngzhī,
courtesy name Sìbó.
From a young age, he harbored great ambitions,
and his talent and strength surpassed ordinary men.
His kinsmen, Dānyáng Yǐn Múzhī and Běi Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ Yuánzhī, both held him in high regard.
Initially, he served as Cānjūn of the Jiànwēi Palace.
During the Yìxī reign,
after the initial pacification of the Shu bandit Qiáo Zòng,
the Imperial Father was promoted to Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Āngù and Wènshān.
He was skilled in pacification and administration.
In the early Yuánjiā reign,
he was transferred to be Wēiliè Jiāngjūn
and Jìnán Tàishǒu.
In the seventh year,
Yòu Jiāngjūn Dào Yànzhī's northern expedition suffered a great defeat,
and the barbarians, taking advantage of their victory, ravaged various commanderies and states in the Qīng region.
A separate chieftain, Ānpíng Gōng Yǐzhān Juàn, plundered Jìnán.
The Imperial Father led several hundred men to resist the attack,
and repelled them.
When the barbarian forces gathered in large numbers,
the Imperial Father ordered his troops to lay down their arms and opened the city gates.
The multitude advised,
"The enemy is numerous, and we are few.
Why are you so dismissive of the enemy!"
The Imperial Father said,
"Today, we are isolated, defending an impoverished city.
The situation is already perilous.
If we again show weakness,
we will surely be massacred.
We can only confront them with a display of strength."
The barbarians, suspecting an ambush,
then withdrew.
Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Sīhuà intended to abandon the garrison and secure a safer position,
but the Imperial Father firmly advised against it, and his advice was not heeded.
Sīhuà lost his footing and fled in disarray.
The following year,
Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Tán Dàojì, after battling his way back from Shòuzhāng, returned with his army.
Huátái fell,
and Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhú Língxiù was punished.
Emperor Wén of Sòng, acknowledging the Imperial Father's achievement in preserving the city,
personally wrote to Dūdū Chángshā Wáng Yìxīn, saying,
"Chéngzhī's governance of the people is not inferior to his military prowess.
I now propose him for Yùnzhōu.
... Tán Zhēngnán should consider this carefully."
The Imperial Father had no prior acquaintance with Dàojì,
so the matter was dropped.
He was transferred to be Fǔguó Zhènběi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn and Yuánwàiláng.
In the tenth year,
Xiāo Sīhuà became Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and the Imperial Father served as his Héngyě Fǔ Sīmǎ and Hànzhōng Tàishǒu.
The Dī chieftain Yáng Nándāng plundered Hanchuan,
and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhēn Fǎhù abandoned the city and fled.
Sīhuà arrived at Xiāngyáng but did not advance.
The Imperial Father advanced with light troops,
attacking the Dī's self-proclaimed Wèixīng Tàishǒu Xuē Jiàn at Huángjīnshān,
and captured him.
Huángjīnshān was
an old garrison of Zhāng Lǔ,
bordering Hanchuan to the south
and leaning against the post road to the north,
extremely steep and fortified.
After Jiàn's forces were scattered,
the Imperial Father immediately occupied it.
The Dī's self-proclaimed Liáng and Qín Two Prefectures Cìshǐ Zhào Wēn had previously occupied the prefectural city.
Hearing of the Imperial Father's arrival,
he retreated to a small city.
Xuē Jiàn retreated and encamped at Xiàtáochéng,
setting up a palisade camp.
The Imperial Father led his army and arrayed them opposite,
two *lǐ* apart.
Jiàn and the self-proclaimed Féngyì Tàishǒu Pú Zǐ (or Zǎo) exerted all their strength in battle,
and the Imperial Father thoroughly defeated them.
Jiàn and others closed their camp and defended themselves, not daring to sally forth.
Sīhuà arrived subsequently,
and the bandits then gradually retreated.
The Imperial Father advanced to Égōngshān,
where he was besieged for several days by the large army of Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn and Shāzhōu Cìshǐ Lǚ Píng.
Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Xiāo Wāngzhī and Píngxī Dūhù Duàn Qiú and others arrived,
and fought fiercely,
greatly defeating them.
Nándāng again sent his son Hé, leading over ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
along both banks of the Hànshǔi,
to reinforce Zhào Wēn
and attack the Imperial Father.
They resisted each other for over forty days.
The bandits all wore rhinoceros-hide armor,
which swords and arrows could not penetrate.
The Imperial Father ordered his troops to cut their spears to several *chǐ* long,
and to strike their rear with large axes.
The bandits could not withstand this
and then burned their camps and retreated.
The Imperial Father pursued them to Nánchéng.
All the armies advanced from the rear,
winning consecutive battles,
and Liángzhōu was pacified.
An imperial edict stated:
"Chéngzhī, receiving orders to lead the vanguard,
braved dangers and penetrated deep,
preserving his army and repeatedly achieving victory,
demonstrating loyalty and courage.
He may be appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn."
He subsequently transferred with the palace to be Níngshuò Sīmǎ,
his role as Tàishǒu remaining as before.
He entered the court to become Tàizǐ Túnqí Xiàowèi.
Emperor Wén, recognizing his efforts in pacifying the Dī,
and with a vacancy in Qīngzhōu,
intended to appoint him.
However, Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng held power,
and the Imperial Father did not attach himself to him.
Instead, he was transferred to be Jiāngxià Wáng Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, and Nán Tàishān Tàishǒu,
and enfeoffed as a fifth-rank male (nán) of Jìnxīng County,
with three hundred forty households.
He was promoted to Yòu Jūn Jiāngjūn.
In the twenty-fourth year of Yuánjiā, he passed away,
at the age of sixty-four.
The people of Liáng region missed him
and erected a temple at Égōngshān to offer sacrifices.
In the second year of Shēngmíng, he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Tàizǔ was born in the *dīngmǎo* year, the fourth year of Yuánjiā (427 CE).
His appearance was extraordinary and distinguished,
with a dragon-like forehead and a resonant voice,
and scales纹 covering his body.
The scholar Léi Cìzōng established a school on Jīlóng Shān.
Tàizǔ, at thirteen years old,
began his studies there,
focusing on the *Lǐjì* and *Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū*.
In the seventeenth year (440 CE),
Sòng Grand General Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng was dismissed
and garrisoned in Yùzhāng.
His Imperial Father led troops to defend.
Tàizǔ abandoned his studies and traveled south.
In the nineteenth year (442 CE),
the Jìnglíng barbarians became restless.
Emperor Wén dispatched Tàizǔ to lead a detachment to attack the barbarians north of Miǎn.
In the twenty-first year (444 CE),
he attacked the *Suǒlǔ*,
reaching Qiūkǎn Shān,
and utterly defeated them.
In the twenty-third year (446 CE),
the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Xiāo Sīhuà, was stationed in Xiāngyáng.
He invited Tàizǔ to accompany him,
to guard north of Miǎn,
and to suppress the barbarians in the mountains of Fán and Dèng,
breaking their settlements.
He was initially appointed Zhōngbīng Cānjūn of the Left Army.
In the twenty-seventh year (450 CE),
the *Suǒlǔ* besieged Chén Xiàn, the garrison commander of Rǔnán.
The court dispatched Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Zāng Zhì and Ānmán Sīmǎ Liú Kāngzǔ to rescue him.
Emperor Wén ordered Tàizǔ to convey his decree
and grant the *jié dù*.
Hearing that the *Lǔ* ruler Tuòbá Tào was approaching Péngchéng,
Zāng Zhì and others turned their army to rescue it.
Upon reaching Xūyí,
Tàizǔ, along with Zāng Zhì's other army commanders Hú Zōngzhī and others, totaling five armies,
with several thousand infantry and cavalry, advanced as a vanguard.
Tuòbá Tào had already secretly crossed the Huái,
and they unexpectedly met at the foot of Guǎn Shān.
They engaged in battle and suffered a defeat,
retreating along the Huái.
Hú Zōngzhī and others were all captured or killed.
Tàizǔ returned to Zāng Zhì and held their ground.
They were besieged by the *Lǔ*,
and were in great peril.
Once the situation stabilized,
he returned to the capital.
In the twenty-ninth year (452 CE),
he led a detachment to conquer Qiúchí.
In the western border of Liángzhōu, there was an old Wǔxīng garrison,
which during the Lóng'ān era of Jìn fell under the control of the Dī.
Northwest of Wǔxīng was the Lángāo garrison,
two hundred *lǐ* from Qiúchí.
Tàizǔ attacked these two strongholds,
and broke them both.
He then entered the pass through Gǔkǒu,
and was eighty *lǐ* from Cháng'ān when
Liángzhōu Inspector Liú Xiùzhī sent Sīmǎ Mǎ Zhù to assist Tàizǔ in attacking Tántí Chéng.
They captured it,
and the *Lǔ* pretender Héjiān Gōng fled.
When the *Lǔ* relief forces arrived,
Tàizǔ's army was fatigued and small in number.
He also heard that Emperor Wén had died.
So he burned the city and returned to Nánzhèng.
He inherited the title of JìnXīng Xiàn Wǔ Děng Nán.
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn (454 CE),
he was appointed Dàsīmǎ Cānjūn for Jiāngxià Wáng.
Following the prince's transfer, he became Tàizǎi.
He was successively promoted to Yuánwàiláng, Zhíhé Zhōngshū Shèrén, Xīyáng Wáng Fǔjūn Cānjūn,
and Jiànkāng Lìng.
Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán enjoyed great favor,
and Tàizǔ was chosen as his aide, becoming Běi Zhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
[一０] When Empress Dà Chén died,
he was appointed Wǔliè Jiāngjūn.
He again became Jiànkāng Lìng,
retaining his post as Zhōngbīng as before.
During the Jǐnghé era (465 CE),
he was appointed Hòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Upon Emperor Míng's enthronement,
he became Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
At that time, rebellions erupted in all four directions.
The Administrator of Kuàijī, Xúnyáng Wáng Zǐfáng, and all the eastern commanderies raised troops.
Emperor Míng conferred the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn upon Tàizǔ,
and he led his troops to suppress the rebellion in the east.
Reaching Jìnlíng,
he battled the enemy vanguard commanders Chéng Hàn and Sūn Tán Guàn and others.
In one day, he broke twelve enemy strongholds.
He divided his forces to pacify the various counties.
Jìnlíng Administrator Yuán Biāo abandoned the city and fled.
The cities in the eastern region successively dispersed.
Xúzhōu Inspector Xuē Āndū rebelled in Péngchéng.
His nephew Suǒ'ér attacked Huáinán.
Shānyáng Administrator Chéng Tiānzuò surrendered the city and rebelled.
Xúzhōu Inspector Shēn Lìngsūn also surrendered.
Tàizǔ was summoned to suppress them.
At that time, Tàizǔ had returned from pacifying the eastern rebels,
and was about to campaign in the south.
He camped at Xīntíng.
The vanguard had already departed,
when Suǒ'ér crossed the Huái from Suīlíng,
with over ten thousand cavalry and infantry.
He attacked and killed the court commander Sūn Gěng.
He deployed his troops to press against the vanguard's camp of Zhāng Yǒng,
who sent an urgent message for help.
Emperor Míng, hearing of the enemy crossing,
quickly recalled Tàizǔ to rescue them,
and he encamped at Pòfǔ.
Suǒ'ér advanced towards Zhōnglí.
Zhāng Yǒng sent Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wáng Kuān to hold Xūyí,
blocking his return path.
Suǒ'ér attacked and defeated the court commander Gāo Dàoqìng,
chasing him to Shíbiē,
and was preparing to return west.
Wáng Kuān and army commander Rèn Nóngfū had already occupied Báihú Jiàn.
Zhāng Yǒng dispatched Tàizǔ to swiftly supervise Wáng Kuān.
Suǒ'ér ambushed Tàizǔ from the east,
preventing him from advancing.
Tàizǔ advanced with drums beating, forming his ranks,
and marched directly into Wáng Kuān's stronghold.
Suǒ'ér saw this and dared not attack.
After several days,
Suǒ'ér led his army and halted at Shíliáng.
Tàizǔ pursued him to Gězhǒng.
His scouts returned reporting the arrival of the enemy.
Tàizǔ then halted his army and withdrew to a defensive position,
deploying two cavalry units on either side of the camp to await them.
Soon after,
the enemy cavalry and infantry arrived unexpectedly,
and also pushed several fire carts to attack.
They fought for an entire day.
Then Tàizǔ sent light troops to attack the enemy's west flank,
and had the cavalry attack their rear.
The enemy forces were greatly defeated,
and in pursuit, captured their weapons.
He then advanced and encamped north of Shíliáng Jiàn.
Suǒ'ér sent a thousand men to raid the camp at night.
The camp was alarmed,
but Tàizǔ remained lying down, not getting up.
He ordered his左右 to keep their positions and not move.
In a short while, the raiders dispersed.
Tàizǔ discussed building a stronghold on the high ground southwest of Shíliáng to open a southern route,
cutting off the enemy's escape path.
Suǒ'ér indeed came to contest it.
Tàizǔ led his army to attack and defeat him.
The enemy's horses trampled each other to death.
Suǒ'ér fled towards Zhōnglí.
Tàizǔ pursued him until darkness fell, then returned.
He was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Xīyáng Xiàn Hóu,
with six hundred households.
He was promoted to Bālíng Wáng Wèijūn Sīmǎ,
and followed him to guard Kuàijī.
Jiāngzhōu Inspector Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn sent Línchuān Nèishǐ Zhāng Yān to enter Sānwú via the Qíyáo pass from Póyáng.
Court commander Shěn Sīrén, along with the pretender Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Rèn Huáng and Zhènxī Cānjūn Liú Yuèxù, each held strategic points.
Emperor Míng dispatched Tàizǔ to lead three thousand men to attack them.
At that time, all the court's armor and weapons were used for the southern campaign.
Tàizǔ's forces were ill-equipped and lacking.
So he wove palm fiber into horse armor,
and split bamboo to make "parasites" (probably spiked traps or shields).
[一一] He advanced his army at night with torches.
The enemy, seeing this, were terrified
and fled without fighting.
Upon his return, he was appointed Guìyáng Wáng Zhēngběi Sīmǎ, Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu, and acted as the administrator for Nán Xúzhōu.
Earlier,
Emperor Míng had sent Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī with troops to persuade Xuē Āndū to surrender.
He said to Tàizǔ:
"I am now going to campaign north.
What do you think of this?"
Tàizǔ replied:
"Āndū's talent and discernment are insufficient,
but he is cunning and treacherous.
If he is loosely controlled with a long rein,
he will surely send his son to court.
But if he is pressed with troops,
he will be afraid and make his own plans,
which I fear will not be beneficial to the state."
The Emperor said:
"Our armies are fierce and sharp,
there is nowhere they cannot conquer.
You always rely on stratagems,
but fortunately, do not speak too much."
When Āndū saw the troops arrive,
he indeed brought in the *Suǒlǔ*.
Zhāng Yǒng and others were defeated at Péngchéng.
Huáinán was isolated and weak.
Tàizǔ was appointed Jiǎ GuānJūn Jiāngjūn, with *jí* and *dūdū* over all vanguard forces for the northern campaign,
stationed in Huáinán.
In the third year of Tàishǐ (467 CE),
Shěn Yōuzhī and Wú Xǐ were defeated in the north at Suīkǒu.
All the large and small garrisons in the various cities fled back.
The barbarians then advanced to the north of the Huái River,
[一二] besieging Jiǎojiǎochéng.
The garrison commander, Jiǎ Fǎdù, was weak and could not resist.
The generals advised Tài Zǔ to cross the river to rescue them,
but Tài Zǔ refused.
He dispatched Army Commander Gāo Dàoqìng, leading several hundred crossbowmen on floating ships into the Huái River,
to shoot from a distance at the barbarians outside the city.
When a crossbow was fired, several hundred arrows went forth simultaneously,
and the barbarian cavalry withdrew to avoid them.
He then ordered an advance to engage in battle,
and the city's siege was immediately lifted.
He was promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nánxǔ and Xú Prefectures, and Governor of Nánxǔ Prefecture,
retaining his imperial credentials, acting title of General of Agile Cavalry, and his previous duty of supervising the northern campaigns.
In the fifth year (469 CE),
he was promoted to Supervisor of Xǔ, Qīng, and Jì Prefectures.
In the sixth year (470 CE),
he was appointed Huangmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant),
and concurrently commanded the Yuèqí Xiàowèi (Commander of the Elite Cavalry),
but did not take up the post.
He was again awarded the title of General of Agile Cavalry,
remaining in his original position.
Emperor Míng often suspected Tài Zǔ of not having the appearance of a loyal subject,
and rumors circulated among the populace,
saying,
"Xiāo Dàochéng will become the Son of Heaven."
Emperor Míng grew even more suspicious.
He sent General of Agile Cavalry Wú Xǐ with three thousand men on a northern mission,
ordering Xǐ to leave his troops and smash their cooking pots (as a sign of determination),
and personally carry a silver pot of wine, sealed, to bestow upon Tài Zǔ.
Tài Zǔ, in military attire, came out to welcome him
and immediately poured and drank it.
When Xǐ returned,
the Emperor's mind was then pleased.
In the seventh year (471 CE),
he was summoned back to the capital.
His subordinates advised him not to comply with the summons.
Tài Zǔ said,
"Gentlemen, you are ignorant of the current situation.
The emperor himself has executed his younger brothers
and, due to the crown prince's youth and weakness,
is making plans for after his death.
What does this concern other clans?
One should only depart quickly;
if the matter is delayed, suspicion will surely arise.
Now, with kin harming kin,
unless it is a time of divine longevity,
disaster will surely arise.
Then, I shall exert my strength with you, my lords."
He was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Attendant-in-Ordinary) and Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ (Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince).
At that time, Shìzǔ was due to be separately enfeoffed as Gànxiàn for his achievements.
Tài Zǔ, considering two enfeoffments for one family,
firmly declined,
and the imperial edict granted his request.
He was given an additional two hundred households.
When Emperor Míng died,
his dying edict appointed Tài Zǔ as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
concurrently Wèiwèi (Commander of the Palace Guard),
and added five hundred soldiers to his command.

He was to manage crucial state affairs together with Shàngshū Lìng (President of the Department of State Affairs) Yuán Càn, Hùjūn (Protector-General) Chǔ Yuān, Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Central Army) Liú Miǎn.
He also separately oversaw the selection of officials in the northeast.
Soon after, he was relieved of the Wèiwèi post,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
and concurrently commanded the forces at Shítou.
Emperor Míng had executed imperial kinsmen,
but Gùiyáng Wáng Xiūfàn, the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, was the only one who survived.
When Cāngwú Wáng was enthroned,
Xiūfàn harbored further ambitions of usurping power.
He secretly practiced horse riding with his eunuchs and close associates in the rear hall
and gathered fugitives.
[一三]In the fifth month of the second year of Yuánhuī (474 CE),
he raised an army in Xúnyáng,
collecting officials and commoners.
In a few days, he had prepared
an army of twenty thousand men
[一四] and five hundred cavalry.
Departing from Pénkǒu,
they all rode on merchant ships and boats.
[一五]The garrison commander of Dàléi, Dù Dàoxīn, and the garrison commander of Quèhóu, Liú Qiānqī, reported the rebellion,
and the imperial court was terrified.

Tài Zǔ, along with Hùjūn Chǔ Yuān, Zhēngběi Zhāng Yǒng, Lǐngjūn Liú Miǎn, Púshè Liú Bǐng, Yóují Jiāngjūn Dài Míngbǎo, Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Ruǎn Tiánfū, Yòujūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Dàolóng, Zhōngshū Shèrén Sūn Qiānlíng, and Yuánwàiláng Yáng Yùncháng, gathered in the Central Secretariat to deliberate.
No one spoke.
Tài Zǔ said,
"In the past, rebellions from the upper reaches [of the river] were always due to delay and slowness,
leading to their downfall.
Xiūfàn will surely learn from these past mistakes,
descend rapidly with light troops,
and take advantage of our unpreparedness.
The current strategy for adapting to the situation
should not consider distant factors.
If even a detached force suffers a defeat,
it will greatly dampen the morale of the army.
It is advisable to station troops at Xīntíng and Báixià,
and firmly defend the imperial palace, Dōngfǔ, and Shítou to await them.
The rebels, an isolated army a thousand *lǐ* away,
with no supplies in the rear,
will naturally disintegrate if they cannot force a battle.
I request to be stationed at Xīntíng to meet their vanguard;
Zhēngběi can guard Báixià with his armored troops;
the central hall was historically a place for stationing troops,
so the Lǐngjūn should be stationed at Xuānyángmén to command the various armies;
the nobles should remain seated in the palace.
The Yòujūn and others do not need to rush out.
I will lead the vanguard myself;
we will surely defeat the rebels."
He then asked for a brush to write down his proposal,
and all noted their agreement.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Sūn Qiānlíng, who had a secret agreement with Xiūfàn,
alone said,
"It is advisable to send troops as before to occupy the area between Liángshān and Lǔxiǎn.
If the Right Guard does not go out to Báixià,
then they should advance and station at Nánzhōu."
Tài Zǔ, with a stern expression, said,
"The rebels are now close.
How can we reach Liángshān?
Xīntíng is a strategic point for battle;
that is why I wish to sacrifice my life for the country.
Normally, one might be able to comply flexibly,
but not now."
He rose from his seat.
Tài Zǔ looked at Liú Miǎn and said,
"The Lǐngjūn has agreed to my humble proposal;
it cannot be changed."
He then departed for Xīntíng in a plain carriage and white clothes.
Tài Zǔ was granted the title of Imperial Envoy with Credential, Overall Commander of the Punitive Expeditionary Forces, [一六] and General Quelling the South,
along with a set of drums and pipes.
Before the fortifications at Xīntíng were complete,
the rebel vanguard had already arrived.
Tài Zǔ then undressed and lay down calmly,
to reassure the troops.
He then called for the White Tiger Banner
and ascended the western wall.
He ordered General of Ning朔 Gāo Dàoqìng, Yǔlín Jiān (Supervisor of the Imperial Guard) Chén Xiǎndá, and Yuánwàiláng Wáng Jìngzé to float small boats to engage the rebels in a naval battle.
From Xīnlín to Chì’àn,
they utterly routed them,
burning their ships and boats,
and causing numerous casualties.
The rebel infantry advanced on Xīnlín.
Tài Zǔ swiftly sent a messenger to Liú Miǎn,
ordering him to quickly open the large and small pontoons,
and move the boats in the Huái River
to all cross to the north bank.
Xiūfàn, riding a shoulder litter, led his troops to the south of the rampart.
The emperor sent General of Ning朔 Huáng Huí and Cavalry Commander Zhōu Pánlóng to lead infantry and cavalry out of the rampart to array for battle.
Xiūfàn divided his forces to attack the east of the rampart.
They engaged in close combat.
From *sì* (9-11 AM) to *wǔ* (11 AM-1 PM),
all the troops turned pale.
Tài Zǔ said,
"Although the rebels are numerous, they are disorderly;
they will soon be broken."
Yáng Yùncháng led seven hundred archers from Sānqí,
drawing their strong bows and hitting their targets,
thus preventing the rebels from approaching the city.
At *wèi* (1-3 PM),
Zhāng Jìng'ér beheaded Xiūfàn.
Tài Zǔ dispatched Team Leader Chén Língbǎo to send the head back to the imperial court.
Língbǎo encountered rebel troops on the way
and buried the head by the roadside.
[一七]The imperial troops did not see Xiūfàn's head,
and grew even more suspicious and fearful.
The rebel forces also did not know that Xiūfàn was dead.
Another commander, Dù Hēilǐ, fiercely attacked the east of the rampart.
[一八]Sīkōng Zhǔbù (Secretary to the Minister of Works) Xiāo Huìlǎng, with several hundred men, rushed into the east gate,
shouting and clamoring to the foot of the hall.
The gate guards on the city wall retreated.
Tài Zǔ bravely mounted his horse
and led several hundred men out to battle.
The rebels all advanced pushing their shields,
a few *zhang* away from each other.
Dividing his forces, he shot horizontally.
When Tài Zǔ drew his bow to full tension, about to shoot,
his attendant Jiāng Dài Zhòngxù raised a shield to protect him,
and an arrow struck the shield, embedding its feathers.
Over a hundred men were wounded,
and the rebels, fighting desperately, could not withstand the attack
and retreated.
The imperial army once again secured the city
and resisted Dù Hēilǐ's attack.
From *bū* (3-5 PM) until dawn the next day,
arrows and stones rained down without ceasing.
That night, there was a heavy rain;
the sound of drums and shouts could no longer be heard.
The generals and soldiers had not slept or eaten for days.
At night, the horses in the camp were startled,
running wildly within the city.
Tài Zǔ, holding a candle, sat upright
and loudly shouted to stop them.
This happened several times.
The rebel leader Dīng Wénháo (丁文豪) set an ambush and defeated the imperial army at Zàojiáqiáo (皁莢橋),
reaching Zhūquèlìng (朱雀桁).
Liú Miǎn (劉勔) wanted to open the pontoon bridge,
but Wáng Dàolóng (王道隆) refused to follow.
Miǎn and Dàolóng both died in battle.
Initially,
Miǎn held lofty ideals,
pretending to build a garden and residence,
naming it
"Dōngshān" (東山),
and was quite negligent in worldly affairs.
Tàizǔ (太祖) said to him:
"General, entrusted with the weighty dying wishes of the emperor,
your responsibilities encompass both internal and external affairs.
The emperor is young,
and all the princes are mere infants.
Rumors are circulating upstream,
heard far and wide.
These are days of hardship for the General,
yet the General deeply cherishes ease,
neglecting his 'wings' [i.e., supporters/preparations].
Should an event occur one day,
it will be too late to regret. "
〔一九〕Miǎn ultimately did not heed him.
The rebels advanced to Dùmǔzhái (杜姥宅).
Chēqí Diǎnqiān (車騎典籤) Máo Tián (茅恬) opened the Eastern Palace and admitted the rebels.
〔二０〕Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) Shěn Huáimíng (沈懷明) fled in disarray at Shítou (石頭),
Zhāng Yǒng (張永) was routed at Báixià (白下),
and the new pavilion within the palace was also captured.
The Empress Dowager held Cāngwú Wáng's (蒼梧王) hand and wept, saying:
"The empire is lost!"
Tàizǔ dispatched military commanders Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達), Rèn Nóngfū (任農夫), Zhāng Jìng'ér (張敬兒), Zhōu Pánlóng (周盤龍) and others,
who crossed the Huái River (淮) from Shítou,
and took a secret path through Chéngmíngmén (承明門) to guard the palace.
After Xiūfàn (休範) had died,
Diǎnqiān (典籤) Xǔ Gōngyǔ (許公與) falsely claimed that Xiūfàn was in Xīntíng (新亭).
The officials and common people were terrified and confused,
and thousands came to the camp to submit their names.
Tàizǔ immediately burned all the names he received.
Then he arrayed his troops and ascended the north city wall,
saying:
"Liú Xiūfàn (劉休範) and his son were both executed yesterday,
their bodies lie beneath Nángāng (南岡).
I am Xiāo Píngnán (蕭平南).
Gentlemen, look closely!
All your names have already been burned,
so have no fear."
The court then sent various armies to attack the rebels at Dùmǔzhái and Xuānyángmén (宣陽門),
defeating and pacifying them all.
Tàizǔ triumphantly returned with his army,
and the common people gathered along the road to watch,
saying:
"This is the man who saved the nation."
Tàizǔ, Yuán Càn (袁粲), Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), and Liú Bǐng (劉秉) attributed blame to themselves and requested to resign their posts,
but this was not permitted.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍), Dūdū Nán Xú Jì Wǔzhōu Jūnshì (都督南徐冀五州軍事), Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍), Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史),
retaining his status as a Jié (節) holder.
His noble rank was advanced to Duke (公),
and his fief was increased by two thousand households.
Tàizǔ wished to share his merits,
requesting to increase the households of Càn and others,
and that they should take turns on duty daily to make decisions,
they were called
"Sì Guì" (四貴, Four Nobles).
During the Qín (秦) dynasty, there were the Empress Dowager, Ráng Hóu (穰侯), Jīngyáng Jūn (涇陽君), and Gāolíng Jūn (高陵君),
who were known as
"Sì Guì,"
and now they reappeared.
In the fourth year,
Tàizǔ was additionally appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射),
his original posts remaining unchanged.
After Xiūfàn was pacified,
Cāngwú Wáng (蒼梧王) gradually became violent and cruel.
Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史) Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù (建平王景素) was young and had a good reputation,
and the court and common people turned their hearts to him.
Jǐngsù also secretly planned for his own safety,
expressing sincerity to Tàizǔ,
but Tàizǔ refused to accept him.
In the seventh month,
Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監) Yuán Zhī (袁祗) fled to Jǐngsù,
〔二一〕who then raised an army.
Tàizǔ moved his troops to Xuánwǔhú (玄武湖),
dispatched armies to campaign in the north,
and returned after the matter was settled.
As Tàizǔ's prestige and fame grew,
Cāngwú Wáng deeply suspected and resented him,
almost bringing great disaster.
Chén Tàifēi (陳太妃) scolded him, saying:
"Xiāo Dàochéng (蕭道成) has rendered meritorious service to the state.
If you harm him now,
who will exert effort for you in the future?"
He then stopped.
Tàizǔ secretly plotted to depose and enthrone a new emperor.
On the Wùzǐ (戊子) day of the seventh month of the fifth year,
the Emperor went out in disguise to Běihú (北湖),
often riding alone ahead.
His guards followed closely behind,
trampling over each other on the embankment.
Zhāng Hù'ér (張互兒), one of his attendants, fell into the lake with his horse.
〔二二〕The Emperor was enraged,
had the horse taken and placed in front of Guāngmíng Tíng (光明亭),
then personally rode over and stabbed it to death.
He then had it butchered,
and enjoyed himself with his attendants performing Qiānghú (羌胡) dances.
He also gambled on jumping at Mángāng (蠻岡).
〔二三〕At dusk, he returned to sleep in the felt tent east of Rénshòu Diàn (仁壽殿).
He told his attendant Yáng Yùfū (楊玉夫):
"Watch for the Weaver Girl's crossing,
and report to me."
At this time, killings were frequent and unpredictable,
and people were filled with fear.
Yùfū and his associates, including Chén Fèngbó (陳奉伯), a total of twenty-five people, conspired together.
In the felt tent, they took a Qiānniú Dāo (千牛刀) and killed Cāngwú Wáng.
They claimed it was an imperial edict,
ordered the musicians below the corridor to perform,
then took the head out and gave it to Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則).
Jìngzé sent it to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ entered at night through Chéngmíngmén, riding his usual red horse.
Those in the palace were terrified,
but upon learning of Cāngwú Wáng's death,
they all shouted "Long live!"
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he named this horse
"Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn" (龍驤將軍, General Dragon Gallop),
and it was commonly called
"Lóngxiáng Chì" (龍驤赤, Dragon Gallop Red).
The next day,
Tàizǔ, in military attire, appeared beneath the locust tree in the palace courtyard,
and summoned the Sì Guì for a meeting.
Tàizǔ said to Liú Bǐng:
"The Liú (劉) family of Dānyáng (丹陽) is a significant relative of the state.
Today's matter [of imperial succession]
should have a proper claimant."
Bǐng declined, feeling unworthy.
Tàizǔ then offered it to Yuán Càn,
who also refused.
Tàizǔ then proceeded with the discussion,
prepared the imperial procession, and went to Dōngchéng (東城),
to welcome and enthrone Shùn Dì (順帝).
Thereupon, men with long swords blocked Càn, Bǐng, and others,
who all paled and departed.
On the Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
Tàizǔ moved his garrison to the Eastern Palace,
and with Yuán Càn, Chǔ Yuān, and Liú Bǐng, each with fifty armed guards, entered the main hall.
On the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中), Sīkōng (司空), Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事), Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍),
retaining his status as Jié holder, Dūdū, and Cìshǐ.
He was enfeoffed as Jìnglíng Jùn Gōng (竟陵郡公),
with five thousand households,
and granted an oiled carriage with tassels,
and a guard of thirty men with ceremonial swords.
Tàizǔ firmly declined the highest official posts,
〔二四〕and instead held the titles of Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
On the Gēngxū (庚戌) day,
he was additionally appointed Dūdū Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (都督南徐州刺史).
Yáng Yùfū and twenty-five others were enfeoffed with noble ranks and lands according to their respective contributions.
On the Wùchén (戊辰) day of the tenth month,
he was again additionally appointed Dūdū Yù Sī Èrshōu (都督豫司二州).
Initially,
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) and Tàizǔ served together in the palace during the Jǐnghé (景和) era,
establishing a friendly relationship,
and Tàizǔ married his eldest daughter, Yìxīng Gōngzhǔ (義興公主), to Yōuzhī's third son, Yuánhé (元和).
〔二五〕When Yōuzhī was at Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
during the later years of Míng Dì's (明帝) reign,
he secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
After being transferred from Yǐngzhōu to Jīngzhōu,
he amassed military strength.
If officers and soldiers deserted,
he would immediately punish their neighbors and relatives as guarantors.
He raised over two thousand horses,
distributing them among the garrison soldiers and officers,
and had them cultivate fields for food,
while all tax revenues were stored in granaries.
The Jīngzhōu arsenal annually sent several thousand weapons,
but Yōuzhī retained them,
recording them as provisions for suppressing the Four Mountain Barbarians.
He equipped and prepared several hundred thousand warships,
sinking them in Língxī Ào (靈溪𩹉).
His stores of money, silk, and weaponry were immense,
and the court feared him.
Gāo Dàoqìng's (高道慶) family was in Huáróng (華容).
When he was granted leave to return home, he passed through Jiānglíng (江陵).
Dàoqìng was skilled at horsemanship.
Yōuzhī hosted a banquet for him,
and they practiced horse-lancing in front of the audience hall.
Dàoqìng's lance broke Yōuzhī's saddle.
Yōuzhī was enraged,
demanded a sharp lance,
but Dàoqìng rode away.
Upon returning to the capital,
Dàoqìng reported Yōuzhī's rebellious behavior,
and requested three thousand men to attack him.
The court deliberated, fearing the task would be difficult to accomplish,
and Tàizǔ also protected Yōuzhī and did not permit it.
After Tàizǔ had deposed and enthroned the new emperor,
he sent Yōuzhī's son, Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史) Yuányǎn (元琰), with the various instruments of cruelty used by Cāngwú Wáng, to show them to Yōuzhī.
Yōuzhī was not yet able to immediately raise an army,
so he submitted a memorial expressing congratulations,
and also wrote to Tàizǔ to praise his achievements.
Shěn Yōuzhī had a plain letter of a dozen lines,
which he always kept concealed in the corner of his doublet.
He claimed it was a sworn covenant between him and Míngdì.
In the twelfth month,
he accordingly raised an army.
His concubines, Lady Cuī and Lady Xǔ, advised Shěn Yōuzhī, saying:
"Your Excellency is already old;
why do you not think of your entire family?"
Shěn Yōuzhī pointed to the corner of his doublet and showed it to them,
claiming that the Empress Dowager's order summoned him to the capital.
The capital was in a state of fear.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Tàizǔ entered and resided in the imperial hall,
〔二六〕ordering his generals to suppress the rebellion in the west.
General Píngxī, Huáng Huí, was appointed Dudū of the vanguard.
The former Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Wáng Yùn,
a nephew of the Empress Dowager,
had great courage and strength from a young age.
Because his father Wáng Kāi's official career had not advanced,
〔二七〕he wished to distinguish himself through military service.
Whenever he stroked his sword, he would say:
"Lóngyuān, Tà'ē,
you know me."
His uncle Jǐngwén admonished him, saying:
"Adá,
you will destroy our household!"
Wáng Yùn replied:
"Adá and Tóngwū are very different in status."
Tóngwū
was the pet name of Jǐngwén's son, Xuàn;
Adá
was Wáng Yùn's pet name.
Wáng Yùn, due to his mother's mourning, had resigned his post.
Returning to Bālíng,
he moored his boat for a month,
daily secretly conspiring with Shěn Yōuzhī.
At that time, Shěn Yōuzhī was not yet ready to raise an army,
so Wáng Yùn proceeded down to Yǐngzhōu.
Shìzǔ was the Administrator of Yǐngzhōu.
Wáng Yùn planned for Shìzǔ to come out for a condolence visit,
and then take advantage of the opportunity to cause a disturbance and seize Yǐngchéng.
Shìzǔ knew of this,
and did not go out.
Wáng Yùn returned to the front of Dōngfǔ,
and again waited for Tàizǔ to come out,
but Tàizǔ also did not go out for a condolence visit.
His second plan failed,
and his external conspiracy grew firmer.
Sītú Yuán Càn and Shàngshūlìng Liú Bǐng saw Tàizǔ's power and authority gradually strengthening,
and feared for their own safety.
They conspired with Wáng Yùn and Huáng Huí to start an uprising.
The main commanders of the palace guard
all agreed to cooperate.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion first broke out,
Tàizǔ went to Shítóu to consult with Yuán Càn,
but Yuán Càn feigned illness and refused to meet.
They planned to raise troops on the night of Rénshēn and occupy Shítóu.
Liú Bǐng was timid;
in the late afternoon,
he brought women from Dānyáng Commandery into Shítóu,
which the court did not know about.
That night,
Dānyáng Registrar Wáng Xùn reported the change.
Liú Bǐng's cousin, Lǐngjūn [Yùn],〔二八〕 and Zhíjiá Jiāngjūn Bǔ Bóxīng and others prepared their troops as internal collaborators.
Tàizǔ ordered Wáng Jìngzé to execute them within the palace.
He dispatched his generals to attack Shítóu.
Wáng Yùn led several hundred elite armed men to join Yuán Càn,
but the city gates were already closed,
and the government troops had also arrived,
so they dispersed.
The assembled troops attacked Shítóu,
and beheaded Yuán Càn.
Liú Bǐng fled to Luòyánhú,
〔二九〕 and Wáng Yùn escaped to the fields;
both were captured and executed.
Although Yuán Càn held an important position,
he lacked strategic vision for governing the world.
He was unrestrained and fond of wine,
often strolling in sandals in the suburbs of Báiyáng.
When he met a scholar-official on the road,
he would call him to drink heartily.
The next day,
this person, thinking he had been appreciated,
came to his gate seeking an audience.
Yuán Càn said:
"Yesterday I had no drinking companion,
so I merely invited you."
In the end, he did not meet him.
He once wrote a five-character poem which said:
"Though my footsteps explore the central realm,
my true refuge is in the azure state."
This was likely his aspiration.
Liú Bǐng was known from a young age for his purity and prudence as a member of the imperial clan.
During Xiàowǔ's reign,
Liú Bǐng's brother Xiá was implicated for having relations with his嫡母 Yīn's adopted daughter.
When Yīn died, blood came out of her mouth,
and many suspected she had been poisoned.
Xiàowǔ ordered Liú Bǐng's cousin Zhī to implicitly suggest that Liú Bǐng memorialize to confirm the matter.
Liú Bǐng said:
"Even a passerby should not do such a thing;
today, how can an entire family perish together?
I cannot accept the imperial decree."
Many praised him for this.
Therefore, he was trusted by Míngdì.
When Cāngwú was deposed,
Liú Bǐng went out to attend a deliberation.
On the way, he met his brother Liú Yùn.
Liú Yùn opened his carriage and asked Liú Bǐng:
"Today's matter,
should it properly fall to you, elder brother?"
Liú Bǐng replied:
"We have already yielded to the Lǐngjūn."
Liú Yùn pounded his chest and said:
"Is there blood in your flesh?!"
Yuán Càn's clerk Mò Sìzǔ knew of Yuán Càn's plot.
Tàizǔ summoned Mò Sìzǔ and asked:
"Yuán Càn plotted rebellion,
why did you not report it?"
Mò Sìzǔ said:
"A servant has no two hearts for his master;
even if I die, I dare not reveal it."
Wáng Yùn's favorite attendant Zhāng Chéngbó concealed Wáng Yùn.
Tàizǔ pardoned both and employed them.
Huáng Huí was stationed at Xīntíng.
When he heard the drums and shouts from Shítóu,
he led his troops to respond.
At Zhūquè'ěr there were garrison troops,
who,
receiving orders,
did not allow passage at night.
As Shítóu had already been pacified,
he then claimed to have come for reinforcement.
Tàizǔ knew but did not speak of it,
treating him even more generously,
and sent Huáng Huí westwards,
bidding him farewell with tears.
Tàizǔ stationed his troops at Yuèwǔtáng,
and swiftly organized his army.
On the Xīncǒu day of the intercalary month,
an edict granted him the Fúhuángyuè,
and ordered him to lead the large army to encamp at Zhōngxīngtáng in Xīntíng,
where he prepared defenses and built ramparts.
He issued an instruction saying:
"Hénán is called 'benevolent,'
presumably because it covers decaying bones;
Guǎnghàn flows with 'humanity,'
truly preserving the deceased.
Recently, when this camp was extensively constructed,
with deep ditches and excavated moats,
ancient ruins and former tunnels
were sometimes buried or relocated.
Dense pines and thick grass
were sometimes cut down.
Leaning on the railing, my heart is moved;
patrolling the city moat, my sorrow increases.
It is proper to collect and rebury them,
and also offer humble sacrifices."
In the first month of the second year,
Shěn Yōuzhī attacked Yǐngchéng but could not conquer it.
His troops dispersed,
and he hanged himself,
his head being sent to the capital.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Tàizǔ returned to garrison at Dōngfǔ.
On the Guǐwèi day of the second month,
Tàizǔ was promoted to Tàiwèi,
his enfeoffment increased by three thousand households,
and he was appointed Dudū of the military affairs of the sixteen prefectures: Nánxú, Nányùn, Xú, Yùn, Qīng, Jì, Sī, Yù, Jīng, Yōng, Xiāng, Yǐng, Liáng, Yì, Guǎng, and Yuè.
Tàizǔ resigned from Píyáojūn
and declined the Dudū appointment,
but it was not permitted.
So he submitted a memorial returning the Fúhuángyuè.
On the Jǐyǒu day of the third month,
the number of attendants with swords was increased to forty, and armed guards to one hundred, when entering the palace.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
he was granted Yǔbǎo Gǔchuī,
with all other privileges remaining as before.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Tàizǔ executed Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí.
From the Tàishǐ reign of the Great Míng [dynasty] onwards,
extravagance was passed down from generation to generation,
and became a custom among the common people.
When the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) assisted in government,
he abolished the imperial household storehouses,
and reduced the decorative items and curiosities from the two Imperial Workshops (Shàngfāng).
By this time, he again submitted a memorial to prohibit extravagant and counterfeit miscellaneous items among the people: it was forbidden to use gold or silver as foil;
horse-drawn carriages and their equipment were not to be plated with gold or silver;
it was forbidden to weave or embroider skirts;
〔三０〕it was forbidden to wear brocade shoes on the roads;
it was forbidden to use red for banners, canopies, or clothing;
it was forbidden to cut colorful silk into various flowers;
it was forbidden to use damask for various clothes or ornaments;
it was forbidden to make "deer-walk" brocade, or narrow-legged chēngbó beds, ivory boxes, cages, and other miscellaneous items, or screens made of colorful silk, or mats edged with brocade;
it was forbidden to privately make weapons;
it was forbidden to adorn musical instruments or other miscellaneous lacquerware with the seven precious gems;
〔三一〕it was forbidden to fashion flowers or beasts from gold or silver;
it was forbidden to arbitrarily cast gold or bronze into images.
All these required an imperial decree (mòchì),
totaling seventeen articles.
Regarding the attire worn by the inner court and the various princes,
though it followed old precedents,
he also requested a detailed review and moderation.
In the ninth month, on the day bǐngwǔ,

he was promoted to acting Grand Axe Bearer (Jiǎ Huángyuè), General-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnsì), Grand Tutor (Tàifù), and concurrently Governor of Yángzhōu (Lǐng Yángzhōumù).
〔三二〕He was allowed to enter the imperial hall with sword and shoes,
walk without hurrying in court,
and have his name not called when receiving the emperor's praise (zànbài bùmíng).
He was assigned four each of Left and Right Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ), Commanders (Sīmǎ), Attendant Officials (Cóngshì Zhōngláng), Clerks (Yuàn), and Subordinates (Shǔ).

His titles of Bearer of the Imperial Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Grand Commander (Tàiwèi), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū), and Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ) remained as before.
He firmly declined,
but an imperial edict dispatched an envoy to urge him,
whereupon he accepted the Grand Axe,
but declined the special courtesies.
On the day jiǎyín,
he was granted a three-pronged carriage.
In the first month of the third year, on the day yǐsì,
the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) memorialized to remit the debts of the common people.
On the day bǐngchén,
he was granted the feathered canopy and drum-and-wind music for his vanguard.
On the day dìngsì,
the Grand Tutor's (Tàifù) Residence was ordered to recruit officials as before.
On the day dìngmǎo,
the Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) was granted five hundred armed guards,
who would accompany him in and out of the palace.
On the day jiǎwǔ,
the previous command was reiterated:
〔三三〕he was allowed to enter the imperial hall with sword and shoes,
walk without hurrying in court,
and have his name not called when receiving the emperor's praise.
In the third month, on the day jiǎchén,
an imperial edict promoted him to Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
to preside over all governmental affairs (zǒng bǎikuí),
and enfeoffed him with ten commanderies as the Duke of Qí (Qígōng),
with the full rites of the Nine Bestowals (Jiǔxī),
and added an imperial seal and ribbon, and a far-roaming crown (Yuányóuguān),
his status above that of all feudal princes.
The Chancellor (Xiàngguó) was also given a green braided ribbon (lǜlì shòu).
His titles of General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōumù), and Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu (Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ) remained as before.
The Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) declined three times,
but the high officials and ministers strongly urged and implored him,
whereupon he accepted.
On the day jiǎyín,
a proclamation was made to the Chancellor (Xiàngguó) and Duke of Qí (Qígōng), saying:
Of the changes and transformations of Heaven and Earth,
none is greater than hot and cold;
of the visible and shining celestial bodies,
none is more revered than the sun and moon.
When severe winter spreads its chill,
the integrity of the steadfast pine stands tall;
when the light of the sun and moon
is at times obscured, the radiance of the Ruòhuá [tree] shines even brighter.
Therefore, the heroic and sagacious do not waver in times of chaos,
and the loyal and worthy fulfill their duty when facing danger.
Since the Jǐnghé era was dark and cruel,
the imperial order became chaotic and
disordered.
Tàizōng received the mandate,
restarting the restoration,
but fate belonged to hardship and difficulty,
with many fortifications in the four suburbs.
General Xiāo (Xiāo Jiāngjūn) manifested his awe-inspiring power over both Chinese and barbarians,
truly relying on his righteous valor.
To stabilize the country and relieve
the people,
it rests upon this.
I, being unworthy,
suffered early misfortune.
The successor ruler lost his virtue,
unrecorded in written history.
He defied the five elements,
massacring the nine provinces.
The spirits
ceased their reverence,
〔三四〕the seas surged and flocks of birds scattered,
the ritual vessels were covered in dust,
and who would preside over the ancestral sacrifices?
The peril of the hanging banners
is insufficient as a metaphor;
how can it be merely like the "Xiǎoyuàn" (Little Garden) ode expressing satire,
or "Shǔlí" (Millet Stalks)
being sung?
Heaven assisted the Imperial Sòng,
truly raising an enlightened minister.
Thereupon, I, the ignorant one, ascended
to inherit the great enterprise.
〔三五〕The grand lineage was re-established,
the magnificent foundation rebuilt.
Your high
merits and utmost virtue
are unparalleled throughout antiquity.
In the past, Bǎohéng aided the Yīn,
and Bólù rectified the Hàn;
compared to you, they are nothing.
Now I shall bestow upon you the rites;
listen respectfully to my
command.
Recently,
Yuán (Dèng) (the text has Yuán, but the correct character is Dèng) caused disaster,
〔三六〕with many followers.
Zǐfáng was disloyal,
raising troops and joining the rebellion.
He traversed the five lakes,
oppressing Wú and Yuè.
Pestilence spread,
and thick miasma obscured the sun.
Drums of war shook the imperial domain,
and weapons clashed in the capital.
Looking back at the palace,
it was about to become overgrown with weeds.
Thinking of the nation,
it was being cut into pieces by enemies.
At this time,
people had no firm resolve.
You threw yourself into the crisis,
standing out and bravely rising up.
Holding the golden tablet, you led the charge,
ascending the yínchē (battle chariot) and setting out on
the road.
Military governance was strict and orderly,
and the soldiers and chariots were united and harmonious.
With one deployment of your axe,
the rebellious faction scattered like ice.
This was the foundation of the hegemonic enterprise,
and the beginning of service to the emperor.
Āndū (An Du) rebelled,
usurping Xúfāng (Xuzhou region).
He dared to lead his dog-like barbarians,
oppressing the banks of the Huái River.
Suǒ'ér (Suo Er) was foolish and perverse,
joining forces with the wicked.
Heaven's blessing had no manifestation,
turning from righteousness to rebellion.
The common people of the northern frontier
suddenly plunged into misery,
with officials abandoning their posts,
and border armies reporting alarms.
You received the mandate from the ancestral temple,
your spirit piercing the morning sun.
Holding the imperial credentials at Hémén (He Gate),
your aura surpassed the heavens.
The victory at Pòfǔ (Pofu)
resulted in severed heads covering the fields.
In the Battle of Shíliáng (Shiliang),
you captured their chief.
You protected the border and saved the entire populace,
and Jiāngyáng (Jiangyang) was thereupon pacified.
This too is your achievement.
Zhāng Yān (Zhang Yan) was deluded
and disregarded the imperial court.
(He) (The text has shòu (receive), but the correct character is yuán (thereupon)) From the southern region,
〔三七〕he plotted to conquer the eastern parts of China.
His army stealthily entered,
secretly eyeing an opportune moment.
At that time, the Jiāngfú (Yangtze region) was not yet pacified,
and the imperial roads were frequently obstructed.
Your loyalty and sincerity were magnanimous,
shining brighter in danger.
You profoundly understood the nine changes,
and subtly perceived the five colors.
You used few to control many,
and wherever you went, your opponents crumbled like grass in the wind.
The court
had no worries from the east,
and Mǐn and Yuè enjoyed the blessing of revival.
This too is your achievement.
The Xiongnú, with their savage ambitions,
invaded and plundered the borders.
The vanguard army suffered a defeat,
and the king
Troops collapsed and twisted,
blood flowed into rivers,
corpses lay for a thousand *lǐ*.
The ugly Jié (羯) rebelled and spread,
their power shook Péng (彭) and Sì (泗),
they pressed on with their victory,
spying on the capital region.
The path of civilization
was about to be annihilated,
the appearance of disheveled hair was imminent.
You, Gōng (公), received the imperial mandate to punish the wicked,
and set forth at dawn.
When the chariots first engaged,
the ominous aura was dispelled.
You mourned the dead and comforted the wounded,
greatly spreading the imperial
benevolence,
so that our Huái (淮) and Féi (肥) regions
again received the flourishing transformation.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
Since then,
the Xiǎnyǔn (獫狁) grew rampant,
like wild boars and long snakes,
again eyeing the upper country.
But worldly circumstances continued,
the army grew old daily,
the warriors lacked the heart to face battle,
the soldiers harbored thoughts of returning home.
Because of this, the elite armor of Xiàpéi (下邳)
trembled with
fear at the sight of the enemy,
the high walls of Juéchéng (角城)
were destined to fall within days.
You, Gōng, thought of the affairs of the state,
and forgot to eat in your indignation.
You personally donned armor,
treating danger as ease.
As soon as the short weapons clashed,
the great
villains scattered like birds.
You divided territories and drew borders,
founding Qīngzhōu (青州) and Xúzhōu (徐州).
This is also your merit, Gōng.
At the end of Tàishǐ (泰始),
you joined the imperial guard,
concurrently holding military and state responsibilities,
your authority was like
that of a regent entrusted with a dying wish.
Guìyáng (桂陽) relied on his followers,
and presumptuously questioned the imperial authority,
breaking crowns and destroying ceremonial caps,
uprooting the foundation and blocking the source.
He led troops into the myriad-chariot nation,
and stationed his halberds below the Xiàngwèi (象魏) gates.
Fierce fires
burned in the royal city,
flying arrows gathered upon the ruler's house.
The sudden changes were swift,
unparalleled throughout history.
All the lords were anxious and afraid,
the commander-in-chief was without a leader.
You, Gōng, grasped your sword and focused your spirit,
then brilliant strategies penetrated the world.
You held the banner and commanded,
then cowards became brave.
It did not even take a full morning,
and a victory was presented at Xīntíng (新亭).
Within a few days,
Xuānyáng (宣陽) was pacified,
the clouds and mists
cleared,
and the whole realm enjoyed peace and order.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
The imperial household faced many difficulties,
strife arose among the imperial relatives and feudal lords.
Yú (邘), Jìn (晉), Yìng (應), Hán (韓)
turned into enemies.
Jiànpíng (建平)
lost his way,
and raised troops to commit internal aggression.
You, Gōng, again instructed the six armies,
righteousness showing on your face.
The campaign did not last more than ten days,
and Zhūfāng (朱方) was peaceful and settled.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
Cāngwú (蒼梧)
wreaked havoc,
all of Huáxià (華夏) was in turmoil.
Excessive punishments were enforced,
who was without guilt?
Fire burned Kūngāng (崐岡),
jade and stone were consumed together.
The common people mourned,
unable to plan for the next day.
The achievements of Gāozǔ (高祖)
had already fallen,
who would inherit the path of Wén (文) and Míng (明)?
[三八]You, Gōng, far examined the righteousness of the Yīn (殷) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,
and closely followed the precedents of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉).
Humbly with your insignificant
self,
you entered to uphold the ancestral temples.
The seven temples were purified and peaceful,
the nine regions returned to proper governance.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
Yuán Càn (袁粲) lacked integrity,
Liú Bǐng (劉秉) harbored disloyalty.
Yùn (韞) and Shù (述)
instigated each other,
[三九]creating this path to chaos.
An ugly plot was secretly conceived,
a crisis stealthily erupted.
They occupied Shítóu (石頭),
aiming to attack Yìng (應) and Lù (路).
You, Gōng, operated divine strategies internally,
and wielded frost-sharp blades
externally.
The evil and calamity were quelled,
the nation's path became joyful and harmonious.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) harbored disaster,
[四０]which grew more evident with years.
With蜂目豺聲 (fēngmùcháishēng) (bee-like eyes and jackal-like voice),
he resisted with his army
and was ruthless.
Pity the people of Jīnghàn (荊漢),
who alone became disloyal subjects.
They looked to the west,
distant as if in a foreign land.
But the state's foundation was just being laid,
the nine punitive expeditions had not yet been declared.
He continued in his wickedness,
and then indulged in fierce rebellion.
He gathered treacherous elements,
his power exceeding that of a roaring tiger.
The court and country were anxious and doubtful,
the three armies were dispirited.
You, Gōng, took up your battle-axe and left the pass,
projecting your might upon the Jiāng (江) region.
Your righteous character
was as bright as the midday sun,
your brilliant strategies competed with the autumn clouds.
Moved by ultimate righteousness,
people became a hundred times more courageous.
With one wave of the war drum,
Xiàshǒu (夏首) became peaceful.
Before the cloud ladders were even raised,
Lǔshān (魯山) was subdued.
Years of unpunished rebellion
were punished with a single execution.
Jǔpǔ (沮浦) flowed peacefully,
Zhāngtái (章臺) followed its course.
This is also your merit, Gōng.
You, Gōng, possessed the merit of aiding the world,
further enhanced by your sagacity.
Your principles protected the people,
your ambition rectified the universe.
You exerted your strength and heart,
toiled for the royal house.
From east to west,
there was no peace or ease.
Dangers
and difficulties,
you thoroughly experienced them all.
As for the diligence in establishing the imperial altars,
the grace of the creator at the beginning of creation,
spreading like clouds and dispersing like fog,
its light covering the six hidden realms,
assisting the one
person,
forever pacifying the four seas.
Therefore, fragrant *jùcǎo* (秬草) bloomed in the suburban gardens,
and auspicious stars cast their radiance upon the clear Milky Way.
Distant lands came to the passes admiring righteousness,
and wilderness regions came to
court through double interpretation.
How vast and distant it is!
[四一]It cannot be named.
I have heard that rewarding merit and recognizing virtue
was a grand tradition of former kings,
and establishing marquises and earls
was common among nations.
Thus, when Wénmìng (文命) achieved success,
the dark *guī* (珪) was conspicuously bestowed.
When Jī Dàn (姬旦)
held sagacity,
Qǔfù (曲阜) was established as a feudal state.
Some changed jade to extend influence,
some were enfeoffed with land to spread enlightenment.
Their rituals surpassed ordinary ranks,
their favor surpassed all lords.
Down to Huán (桓) and Wén (文),
their carriages and attire
an unusual number.
Only your [Gōng]'s achievements surpass those of the former worthies,
yet the commendations and rewards fall short of the old regulations.
How disparate
are the ways of ancient and modern times!
Reflecting, I admire and sigh,
truly there is a lack
therein.
Now, you are promoted to Grand Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
and with Qíjùn of Qīngzhōu,
Liángjùn of Xúzhōu,
Lánlíng, Lǔjùn, Lángyé, Dōnghǎi, Jìnlíng,
and Yìxīng of Nán Xúzhōu,
and Wújùn, Kuàijī of Yángzhōu,
a total of ten commanderies,
you are enfeoffed as Duke of Qí (Qígōng).
I bestow upon you this dark earth,
wrapped in white rushes,
to establish your state and family,
and thereby erect
the altars to the land and grain (zhǒngshè).
This is indeed the old fief of the Grand Tutor (Shàngfù),
which for generations served as the covenant leader,
governing the ducal domains,
following the old rules.
In the past, when Zhōu and Shào established their states,
they held concurrent roles as masters and protectors;
Máo and
Bì held their jade tablets,
entering the court as ministers.
The responsibilities both internal and external
〔四二〕were aligned in the past.

Now, I command the Bearer of the Imperial Seal (Shǐchíjié), concurrent Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshūjiān), Minister of Works (Sīkōng), General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn), Founding Marquis of Yúdū County (Yúdūxiàn Kāiguóhóu) Chǔ Yuān to present [you] the Grand Chancellor's official seal and ribbon,
〔四三〕and the Duke of Qí's seal and sash.
The Bearer of the Imperial Seal (Chíjié), concurrent Assistant Minister of Works (Sīkōng Fù),
〔四四〕and acting Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūlìng) Wáng Sēngqián, shall present the Duke of Qí with the Mao and Tu (茅土) for enfeoffment,
the gold tiger tallies (jīnhǔfú) numbers one to five (left halves),
and the bamboo tallies (zhúshǐfú) numbers one to ten (left halves).
The Grand Chancellor's position oversees all
officials,
its rank surpasses the Three Dukes (Sān Xuàn),
〔四五〕its functions are transferred by ritual,
its titles change with circumstances.
Therefore, with the Grand Chancellor overseeing all officials,
〔四六〕the title of "Recorder of the Department of State Affairs" (lù shàngshū) is removed.
Return the borrowed

credentials, the Palace Attendant's sable cicada ornament, the seals and ribbons of the Grand Director-General of Internal and External Military Affairs (Zhōngwài Dūdū Tàifù Tàiwèi), and the seal and tablet of the Duke of Jìnglíng.
Your titles of General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Mù), and Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu (Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ)
remain as before.
Moreover, I add to your [Gōng]'s honors the Nine Bestowals (Jiǔ Cī).
Please listen respectfully to the following commands: As you [Gōng] uphold ritual and promulgate regulations,
〔四七〕setting an example for the whole realm,
making far and near one body,
and the people without different
occupations,
therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] one grand carriage (dàlù) and one military carriage (rónglù) each,
and two teams of black stallions.
You [Gōng] have diligently cultivated the southern fields,
valuing grain above all else,
filling the royal granaries,
and enriching the common
people.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] the ceremonial robes of a monarch (gǔnmiǎn zhī fú),
with red slippers (chìxì) as an accessory.
You [Gōng] conduct yourself with humility,
and guide others with righteousness,
melting and molding all classes of people,
none are not harmonious and joyful.
Therefore I
bestow upon you [Gōng] the music of "Xuánxiàn" (xuánxiàn zhī yuè),
and the dance of "Lìuyì" (liùyì zhī wǔ).
You [Gōng] assist and support the royal plans,
your fame and teachings extend afar,
the barbarians exhaust their joy,
turning their heads to pledge allegiance internally.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] vermilion
doors for your residence.
You [Gōng] clearly discern human relations,
distinguishing the Jīng from the Wèi,
appointing officials according to their abilities,
and promoting outstanding talents.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] the royal ramp (nàbì) for ascending.
You [Gōng] protect and assist the imperial
court,
cultivating yourself and transforming your subordinates,
stopping insidious trends and preventing nascent dangers,
so that all living beings follow your example.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] three hundred Tiger Warriors (hǔbēn zhī shì).
You [Gōng] control the wicked with punishments,
and deter evildoers with
virtue.
None will rebel against their sovereign or parents;
those who rebel will surely be executed.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] one battle-axe (fū) and one hatchet (yuè).
You [Gōng] soar like a phoenix in the four directions,
and rise like a dragon across the eight extremities,
wherever your might and spirit reach,
foreign lands
share the same culture.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] one vermilion bow,
one hundred vermilion arrows,
ten black bows,
and one thousand black arrows.
You [Gōng] clearly express what you cherish,
and reverently perform sacrifices.
The weight of your filial piety and reverence
moves the spiritual deities.
Therefore I bestow upon you [Gōng] one jar of fragrant black millet wine (jùchàng),
with a jade goblet (guīzàn) as an accessory.
The State of Qí (Qíguó) shall establish a Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) and other officials
all in accordance with old regulations.
Go forth reverently!
You
shall respectfully obey my command,
ordering heaven and earth,
greatly expanding the grand enterprise,
magnificently manifesting your great virtue,
and proclaiming my high ancestor's excellent decree.
The Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) declined three times,
but the Dukes and Ministers (Gōngqīng) earnestly exhorted and firmly requested,
whereupon he accepted.
On the day Dīngsì,
an edict was issued to pardon all crimes in the state from capital punishment downwards,
before the dawn of the fifteenth day of this month,
all are to be pardoned.
The widowed, orphaned, and solitary who cannot sustain themselves
are granted five *hú* of grain.
Those under the jurisdiction of prefectures and provinces
are also treated with the same leniency.
Emperor Sòng (Sòng Dì) decreed that beyond the ten commanderies of the Duke of Qí,
appointments may be made as appropriate.
As the State of Qí was newly established,
five million cash,
five thousand bolts of cloth,
and five thousand bolts of silk were granted.
On the day Guǐyǒu of the fourth month,
an edict promoted the Duke of Qí's peerage to King,
with Nánliáng, Chénjùn, Yǐngchuān, and Chénliú of Yùzhōu,
and Xūyí, Shānyáng, Qínjùn, Guǎnglíng, Hǎilíng, and Nán Pèi of Nán Yǔnzhōu, ten commanderies, added to the enfeoffment.
The Bearer of the Imperial Seal (Shǐchíjié), Minister of Works (Sīkōng), General of the Guard (Wèijiāngjūn) Chǔ Yuān presented the imperial tablet and conferred the seal and sash,
the gold tiger tallies numbers one to five (left halves),
the bamboo tallies numbers one to ten (left halves),
bestowing this dark earth,
wrapped in white rushes,
〔四八〕and establishing the royal altars (wángshè).
The titles of Grand Chancellor (Xiàngguó), Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Mù), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), and Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu (Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ) remained as before.
On the day Bǐngxū,
it was ordered that the King of Qí's (Qí Wáng) crown (miǎn) should have twelve strings of beads (shíyǒuèr liú),
he should display the Emperor's banners and flags,
have an imperial escort when going out (chūjǐng) and an imperial clearance when entering (rùbì),
ride in a golden-rooted carriage (jīn gēn chē),
drawn by six horses,
be equipped with five seasonal auxiliary carriages,
have a Maotou (旄頭) and Yúnhǎn (雲罕) pennant,
have music with the eight-row dance (bāyì),
and set up bell-stands and palace chimes (zhōngjù gōngxuán).
The King's heir (Wáng shìzǐ) was to be Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
and the King's daughters and grandsons' peerages and appointments were all to follow old regulations.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Emperor Sòng abdicated,
issuing an edict that read: "Only virtue moves Heaven,
which is why the jade balance (yùhéng) carries order;
penetrating the divine and understanding transformation,
which is why the myriad people submit their hearts.
Thus one can order Heaven and Earth,
encompass the universe,
proclaim
grand achievements,
and greatly protect the living people.
From obscurity to brightness,
successive generations follow the same path;
former kings tread in their footsteps,
and generations must follow this.
Sòng's virtue has diminished and faded,
with ruin and decay succeeding one another.
Jǐnghé indulged in perversion in the past,
Yuánhuī unleashed tyranny later.
The Three Luminaries (Sān Guāng) were twice obscured,
and the Seven Ancestral Temples (Qī Miào) were about to fall.
The celestial pole (xuánjí) abandoned its chariot,
and all conscious beings knew of its demise.
The fortune of our civil and military
ancestors
was as precarious as a thread.
Reflecting on this disorder,
I am troubled day and night.
The Grand Chancellor, King of Qí (Xiàngguó Qí Wáng),
Heaven-born with sagely wisdom,
his divine essence illuminates rivers and mountains.
He rescued the fallen and uplifted the imperiled,
clearing away chaos and calming disorder,
rescuing the nation from difficulties,
his achievements equal to creation itself.
His grand strategies..."
Shuāngzhào,
bìmóu yún huí,
jīngpèi suǒ lín,
yī huī bì jié,
yīngfēng suǒ fú,
wú sī bù yǎn,
biǎolǐ qīngyí,
xiáyǐ níngmì.
Jì
ér guāngqǐ xiànzhāng,
hóngxuān lǐjiào,
jiānguǐ zhī lèi,
dǔ lóngwēi ér géqíng,
mùshàn zhī chóu,
yǎng huīyóu ér zēnglì.
Dào mài yú
Chónghuá,
xūn chāo hū Wénmìng,
dàngdàng hū wú dé ér chēng yān.
Shìyǐ biànfà zuǒrèn zhī qiú,
kuǎn guān qǐng lì,
mùyī huìfú zhī
zhǎng,
hánghǎi lái tíng,
qǐ wéi Sùshèn xiàn hú,

The ruler,
truly relies on the sagacious and enlightened,
to rectify and save from hardship and danger.
The King, embodying Heaven and patterning Earth,
sets forth vast and great radiance,
his brilliance rivals the sun and moon,
his benevolence equals the clouds and rain.
When the nation's progress is blocked,
his formidable might is displayed outwardly;
when royal strategies are not yet achieved,
his profound wisdom shines inwardly.
He rebuilt Mǐn and Wú,
and brought peace again to Huái and Jì.
He calmed the surging waves of the Jiǔ-Jiāng,
rolled back the miasma of Hǎi-Yí,
[五一] expelled the wicked and obscure,
preserved our ancestral sacrifices,
renewed the old order,
and changed the illumination of the three luminaries.
When favored ministers rebelled,
he managed them with strategic plans;
when Jīng and Hàn turned against him,
he shook them with thunder.
Wherever his banners and pennants arrived,
it was like the wind blowing over grass, making it bend;
wherever his divine calculations pointed,
dragons ascended and clouds gathered.
All of Xià was purified,
and the Róng and Dí longed for
righteousness.
He promoted culture and ceased military campaigns,
displaying his grand achievements.
He brightly protected the young and ignorant,
allowing them to roam in the fields of rites and music,
and gently nurtured the common people,
all of whom ascended to the
realm of benevolence and longevity.
[五二] From where frost and dew fall,
to where stars traverse,
where the calendar did not reach,
and human footprints were rare,
none failed to cross mountains and seas,
face north and declare vassalage,
knock at
the passes with double interpreters,
and fulfill their duties and tribute.
Therefore, auspicious omens appeared,
and the Left Scribe recorded their wonders;
celestial phenomena displayed their patterns,
and the Baǒzhāng (official) verified their measurements.
Phoenix writings indicated the operation of the four seasons,
and dragon diagrams revealed the timing of auspicious omens.
Furthermore, with his pearl-like brow and sun-like corner of the eye,
his divine bearing was especially prominent;
his principles as a ruler
were always manifest in his actions.
Does the Shu (Classic of Documents) not say:
"Heaven has no favorites,
it only aids the virtuous"?
The hearts of the people are not constant,
they only cherish benevolence.
The favor of the deities is like that,
and the desire of the common people is thus.
The sounds of sheng and guan changed,
and the tunes of bells and stones were altered.
This is why I hold the jade and balance,
earnestly awaiting the sagacious one.
In the past, when the Metal Virtue declined,
the mandate was transmitted to our Sòng;
the numerical count of reigns reached its end,
truly on this day,
just as the Water Virtue transmitted it to Qí.
Following the former
precedents,
and widely consulting public opinion,
the princes, dukes, ministers, and gentry,
all said it was most appropriate.
Now I dispatch the envoy holding the credentials, concurrently Grand Tutor, Palace Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, Minister of Works, General of the Guards, and Marquis of Yúdū, Yuān,
and concurrently Grand Commandant and Administrator of the Department of State Affairs, Sēngqián, to present the imperial seals and ribbons,
for the ceremony of abdication,
which will fully follow the precedents of Táng and Yú.
May the King
truly correspond to the seen and unseen,
ascend to the throne as the great sovereign,
bestow peace upon the eight directions,
to requite the auspicious mandate of August Heaven.
Taìzǔ declined three times,
but Emperor Sòng, the princes, dukes, and others below adamantly requested it.
Chén Wénjiàn, concurrently Director of the Grand Astrologer and Superintendent of Construction, presented a memorial on the auspicious prognostication, saying:
"Six,
is the亢 (kàng) position.
From Jiànwǔ of the Later Hàn to the 25th year of Jiàn'ān,
one hundred ninety-six years, then it ceded to Wèi;
[魏] from Huángchū of Wèi to the 2nd year of Xiánxī,
[五三] forty-six years, then it ceded to Jìn;
from Taìshǐ of Jìn to the 2nd year of Yuánxī,
one hundred fifty-six years, then it ceded to Sòng;
from the 1st year of Yǒngchū of Sòng to the 3rd year of Shēngmíng,
a total of sixty years: all ended and received according to six.
Six,
is the亢 (kàng) position.
Examining the past and measuring the present,
it is clearly evident like this.
I dare, by virtue of my office,
fully present my humble opinion.
I humbly wish that you follow the timing of Heaven,
and respond to the auspicious signs."
The officials of both courts again adamantly requested.
Wáng Jiǎn, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, memorialized:
"Having received the edict from Sòng to abdicate.
Your humble servants have deliberated,
and it is fitting to set a date for your carriage to receive the abdication,
and to prepare the ceremonial procedures."
Taìzǔ then consented.
The historian states: According to the Taìyī Jiǔgōng Zhān (Prognostication of the Nine Palaces of the Grand Monad), tracing back to the 5th year of Hàn Gāo (Gāozǔ),
Taìyī was in the 4th palace,
where both host and guest gained good fortune.
Calculating, the one who initiates the action first wins;
in that year, Gāozǔ defeated Chǔ.
In the 2nd year of Jìn Yuánxīng,
Taìyī was in the 7th palace,
Taìyī was the Emperor,
Tiānmù was the assistant,
pressing and threatening Taìyī;
in that year, Emperor Ān was forced out of the palace by Huán Xuán.
The Grand General was in the 1st palace,
and the Chancellor was in the 3rd palace,
opposing Taìyī.
The Classic says that one who opposes,
when political affairs are already established,
and superiors and inferiors oppose them,
it is unfavorable for action,
it is a time for peaceful dwelling,
and unfavorable for movement.
In the 3rd year of Yuánxīng,
Taìyī was in the 7th palace,
and Sòng Wǔ (Wǔdì) defeated Huán Xuán.
In the 1st year of Yuánjiā,
Taìyī was in the 6th palace,
unfavorable for action;
Xú and Fù deposed King Yíngyáng.
In the 7th year,
Taìyī was in the 8th palace,
indicating a year of imprisonment and misfortune,
both major and minor generals could not establish themselves;
in that year, Dào Yànzhī's northern expedition,
initially successful but later defeated,
was unfavorable for both guest and host.
In the 18th year,
Taìyī was in the 2nd palace,
unfavorable for both guest and host;
in that year, the Dī Yang Nándāng raided Liáng and Yì,
and in the following year, Qiúchí was defeated.
In the 19th year,
both major and minor generals were seen to be blocked and unable to establish themselves,
which was inauspicious;
in that year, Péi Fāngmíng attacked Qiúchí,
conquering Bǎiqǐng,
but lost it the next year.
In the 1st year of Taìshǐ,
Taìyī was in the 2nd palace,
being attacked by both major and minor generals;
in that year, Jǐnghé was deposed.
In the 2nd year,
Taìyī was in the 3rd palace,
unfavorable for initiating action,
the host wins;
in that year, Jìn Ān Wáng Zǐxūn rebelled.
In the 2nd year of Yuánhuī,
Taìyī was in the 6th palace,
the initiator loses;
in that year, King Guìyáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
and both were executed.
In the 4th year,
Taìyī was in the 7th palace,
the initiator is the guest,
fleeing to the northwest;
in that year, King Jiànpíng Jǐngsù was defeated.
In the 1st year of Shēngmíng,
Taìyī was in the 7th palace,
unfavorable for being the guest,
it is a time for peaceful dwelling,
initiating action makes one the host,
responding to an action makes one the guest;
Yuán Càn, Shěn Yōuzhī, and others rebelled,
and were executed.
In this year, Taìyī was in Dùmén,
overseeing the 8th palace,
Emperor Sòng abdicated,
unfavorable for being the guest,
it is a time for peaceful dwelling,
initiating action makes one the host,
this is the prognostication for abdication and succession.

In the summer, fourth month, on the *jiǎwǔ* day of the first year of Jiànyuán,
the Emperor ascended the imperial throne at the Southern Suburb.
He set up an altar, burned wood, and made a sacrifice to Heaven, saying:
“Your subject, Emperor Dàochéng, presumes to use a dark bull
to reverently inform the August Sovereign, Supreme Lord.
Emperor Sòng, having ascended to observe the order of Heaven,
reverently followed the bright mandate,
and bestowed it upon Dàochéng.
From the very beginning of human life,
shepherds were appointed
to clarify the ultimate principles of Heaven,
to inaugurate new beginnings and create all things,
thus extending this great Way.
The world is for the public,
and the mandate is not constant.
In ancient times, during the reigns of Yú and Xià,
the end of the previous era was received.
Then, from Hàn to Wèi,
the throne was yielded in the middle period.
All these are clearly recorded in the canons and plans,
preserved in the historical records.
When the Water Virtue became weak,
and successive generations faced many difficulties,
it truly relied on Dàochéng’s efforts to rectify and save,
to broadly assist in those crises.
The great creation had fallen,
and the realm was rebuilt.
Rites were proclaimed and laws made clear,
benevolence was established and righteousness cultivated.
The sun and stars formed images,
rivers and mountains manifested their numinous power.
Thus, Heaven and man
were all harmonized.
Therefore, bowing to the convergent destiny
and the support for the capable,
the great mandate was gathered here.
Though our virtue is insufficient to continue
the achievements of previous generations,
yet all the dukes, ministers, and officials,
the myriad magistrates and administrators,
as well as the common people,
and even the hundred tribes,
all said, ‘Heaven bestows its mandate,
and it cannot be steadfastly refused.
Gods and men have no one to rely on,
and the throne cannot be left empty.’
Fearing the majesty of Heaven,
how could we not respectfully follow the grand calendar?
Respectfully selecting an auspicious day,
we devoutly receive the imperial tally,
ascend the altar to accept the abdication,
and make a sacrifice to the Supreme Lord,
to forever respond to the people’s will
and widely spread it to the myriad states.
May the bright spirits accept this offering!”
After the ceremony,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The Emperor presided at the Front Hall of Tàijí.
An edict stated:
“The five virtues succeed each other,
which is why imperial reigns prosper in succession.
The three orthodoxies rise in turns,
which is why kingly ways shine anew.
The world has its simple and refined periods,
and times of continuity and reform.
Those who rely on the auspicious signs of the calendar
and govern the people through the Dao
