are certainly those who achieve the same goal through different methods,
and share a common thread despite diverse origins.
I, with my limited understanding,
happened to live in a difficult era.
By exerting diligent sincerity
and leveraging the principles of good governance,
the capable and virtuous devoted their hearts,
and the scholars and commoners exerted their efforts,
thus achieving the rescue from peril and the suppression of tyranny,
unifying the whole world.
My achievements do not yet rival those of antiquity,
but my merit is almost equal to the past.
The Sòng dynasty, with evident signs of decline
and the end of its destined reign,
wished to promote the peaceful transfer of power,
forever reflecting on the rise and fall,
and thus gathered the heavenly bounty upon my person.
Although my aspirations are humble
and my words cannot fully express it,
I respectfully follow Heaven and man,
and thus obey the glorious mandate,
reverently rectifying the calendar before the ancestral temple,
and offering pure sacrifices to the Supreme Lord.
Unworthily, with my meager virtue,
I am to brightly reside over the four seas,
continuing the legacy of a changed dynasty,
and being placed above kings and dukes.
It is like crossing a deep abyss,
not knowing how to succeed.
Now that the precious throne has just begun
and the grand celebration is new,
I wish to extend beneficial grace
and widely spread it to the myriad people.
Therefore, a general amnesty is granted to the entire realm.
The third year of Shēngmíng is changed to the first year of Jiànyuán.
The common people are granted two ranks of nobility.
Civil and military officials are promoted two grades.
Widows, widowers, orphans, and the solitary who cannot support themselves are each given five *hú* of grain.
Outstanding rents and old debts are no longer collected.
Those who have violated local public opinion,
or committed corruption, lewdness, or theft,
are all cleansed,
their previous records wiped clean,
and they are given a fresh start.
Prisoners serving long sentences or under strict detention
are all specially pardoned and released.
Those who lost their official positions or titles,
or were banned from office or deprived of their merits,
are all to be treated according to the old regulations.”
Emperor Sòng was enfeoffed as Rǔyīn Wáng.
A palace was built for him in the old administrative seat of Dānyáng Xiàn.
The Sòng calendar was used.
His carriages, banners, and attire
were all as before.
His memorials were not called “tables” (*biǎo*),
and replies to his memorials were not called “edicts” (*zhào*).
Xiè, Prince of Jìnxī of Sòng, was demoted to Yīn’ān Gōng.
Jī, Prince of Jiāngxià, was demoted to Shāyáng Gōng.
Huì, Prince of Suí, was demoted to Wǔyīn Gōng.
Sōng, Prince of Xīnxīng, was demoted to Dìngxiāng Gōng.
Xǐ, Prince of Jiàn’ān, was demoted to Lìpǔ Gōng.
The commandery princesses became county ladies (Xiànjūn).
The county princesses became village ladies (Xiāngjūn).
An edict stated:
“Succeeding generations and honoring the worthy
is a grand tradition of past dynasties.
Rewarding merit and inheriting excellence
is a fine plan from ancient records.
The Sòng *tōnghóu* (marquises of general rank)
should appropriately be reduced in rank with the change of destiny.
However, those who reverently cherished virtue and righteousness
still had their tombs and residences honored.
How much more so those whose achievements benefited the entire realm
and whose Dao enlightened the customs of the people?
The tradition of demotion
should follow past precedents.
The Nánkāng Xiàn Gōng and Huáróng Xiàn Gōng may be made *hóu* (marquises).
The Píngxiāng Xiàn Hóu may be made *bó* (earl).
Their household allowances are reduced accordingly,
to continue the line of Liú Mùzhī, Wáng Hóng, and Hé Wúyì.”
Sīkōng Chǔ Yuān was made Sītú.
Wú Jùn Tàishǒu Liǔ Shìlóng was made Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
An edict stated:
“As the imperial destiny begins and is newly established,
and the precious mandate is renewed,
it is appropriate to broadly extend grace and clemency,
and widely implement reforms and purges.
Remaining captives from rebellions who are held in government offices
are all pardoned and released.
Those who were exiled for crimes
are all permitted to return to their hometowns.”
Qí Guó Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá was made Zhōnghùjūn.
Zhōnglǐngjūn Wáng Jìngzé was made Nányùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Lǐ Ānmín was made Zhōnglǐngjūn.
On the *wùxū* day,
Yì, the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, was made Shàngshū Lìng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Yìng was made Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xī Zhōnglángjiāng Huàng was made Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Yuán Chóngzǔ was made Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Piàojì Sīmǎ Cuī Wénzhòng was made Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
The sending of congratulatory gifts from the four directions was stopped.
On the *jǐhài* day,
an edict stated:
“Since the destruction of the well-field system,
agriculture and sericulture have changed occupations.
Salt and iron have harmed the people,
and commercial trade has damaged governance.
These became customs over successive generations,
and their corrupting influence grew yearly.
To assist and rectify these lingering弊,
and revert from the secondary to the fundamental,
the government should not monopolize profits,
and the people should not lose their livelihoods.
The two palaces and all the princes
are strictly forbidden from establishing manorial estates
or enclosing mountains and lakes.
The Imperial Cuisine ponds
and palace tax revenues
are to be thoughtfully reduced or abolished.”
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
an edict
stated, “The tombs of Emperor Sòng and the princes of his lineage
should have guards.”
The officials concerned proposed that each imperial tomb be assigned one chief
and a varying number of soldiers;
royal tombs, five men;
and empress and concubine tombs, three men.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the fifth month,
Hé Nán Wáng Tǔyùhún Shíyīn was advanced to the title of Píwèi Dàjiāngjūn.
An imperial edict stated:
"The imperial fortune has brought about a revolution,
with dignities bestowed and fiefs changed.
Though the ranks and orders of the Sòng clan
ought to be reduced and abolished,
those who have rendered service in difficult times and at the frontier,
and exerted their efforts in establishing the enterprise,
shall all retain their original fiefs,
without any reduction or demotion."
The officials reported that sixty-two people, including Xiāngyáng Jùngōng Zhāng Jìng'ér, would be retained,
while 122 people, including Guǎngxīng Jùngōng Shěn Tánliàng, would be dismissed.
The Yuánjiā Calendar was changed to the Jiànyuán Calendar.
With the Wood Element flourishing from *mǎo* (rabbit) to *wèi* (goat),
the first month began with *mǎo* as the ancestor,
and the twelfth month concluded with *wèi* as the end of the year.
(*Xīn*)[*Dīng*]wèi,
an imperial edict stated:
"Recruiting generals and offering rewards for soldiers
was a matter of expediency,
not a permanent system.
In recent difficult and dangerous times,
it gradually became a custom,
further enabling escapees
and opening up crimes in mountains and lakes.
This means that tattooing as a punishment brings no disgrace,
and fleeing brings no fault.
From now on,
public recruitment is to be abolished."
Rénzǐ,
an imperial edict enfeoffed thirty-one civil and military meritorious officials who had assisted in the establishment of the dynasty, including the newly appointed Sītú Chǔ Yuān.
Their ranks were advanced and their households increased, each according to their circumstances.
(*Jǐ*)[*Yǐ*]mǎo,
Hé Nán Wáng Tǔyùhún Shíyīn presented a memorial and tribute.
Bǐngchén,
an imperial edict dispatched grand envoys to tour the four directions,
sending twelve *jiān Sànqí Chángshì* to conduct inspections.
As Jiāoníng was too distant,
no envoy was sent.
Jǐwèi,
the Rǔyīn Wáng passed away.
He was posthumously granted the title Sòng Shùndì,
and his funeral rites followed the precedents of Wèi Yuán and Jìn Gōngdì.
Xīnyǒu,
Yīn'ān Gōng Liú Xiè and others were executed.
The emperor's elder brother Dàodù was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title Héngyáng Yuánwáng,
and Dàoshēng as Shǐ'ān Zhēnwáng.
Bǐngyín,
the imperial father was posthumously honored as Xuānhuángdì,
the imperial mother as Xiàohòuhòu,
and the consort as Zhāohòuhòu.
On the *xīnwèi* day of the sixth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"The offices of Xiàngguó, Píwèi, and Zhōngjūn Sānfǔ
may be allotted to two officials based on their qualifications and service.
If an official's term limit is already met,
the remainder may be bestowed in full."
Rénshēn,
Yóují Jiāngjūn Zhōu Shāntú was appointed Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yǐhài,
an imperial edict stated:
"In the latter years of Sòng, there were frequent military raids,
and also natural disasters and diseases that caused devastation.
Some dried bones were not collected,
and ruined coffins not covered.
It is fitting to quickly issue an order to bury and inter them.
If the markers still exist,
and the names are recognizable,
they should be transported
and returned to their native villages.
The officials proposed sending four external supervisors of affairs
to travel within a thirty-five *lǐ* radius outside the capital gates.
The rest shall be assigned to the prefectures and commanderies.
For those without coffins, funerary vessels, or markers,
the funds for their purchase shall be provided by the imperial treasury."
Gēngchén,
the ancestral tablets of the Seven Temples were escorted by the imperial carriage to the Grand Ancestral Temple.
An imperial edict stated:
"All generals and guests
who exerted their efforts in difficult times,
and diligently guarded the emperor,
those who returned to the palace with the emperor
shall all be granted one rank."
Xīnsì,
the office of Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ was abolished.
Jiǎshēn,
Crown Prince Zé was established.
All celebratory ceremonies in the various prefectures and commanderies were forbidden.
Those who were currently imprisoned for serious crimes
were to be demoted by one degree,
and the previous amnesty grace was extended by one hundred days.
Imperial Prince Yí was established as Yùzhāng Wáng,
Yìng as Línchuān Wáng,
Huǎng as Chángshā Wáng,
Niàn as Wǔlíng Wáng,
Gǎo as Ānchéng Wáng,
Qiāng as Póyáng Wáng,
Shuò as Guìyáng Wáng,
Jiàn as Guǎnglíng Wáng,
and imperial grandson Chángmào as Nánjùn Wáng.
Yǐyǒu,
Sòng Shùndì was buried at Suìníng Líng.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *dīngwèi* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Jiāozhǐ and Bǐjǐng,
alone are cut off from imperial decrees.
This is because in the previous era, when the dynasty was in decline,
they were separated by the sea and did not pay tribute,
thus they continued in their error,
and had no means to return to allegiance.
A partial amnesty is granted to Lǐ Shūxiàn alone within the Jiāozhōu region,
who shall govern the southern lands,
and civil and military talents shall be carefully selected for employment.
Grand envoys shall also be dispatched to proclaim imperial grace."
Lǐ Shūxiàn, who was provisionally serving as Wǔpíng Tàishǒu and acting governor of Jiāozhōu, was appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
Bǐngchén,
the chieftain of the barbarian pseudostate Jiālú Garrison, Yīnpíng Gōng Yáng Guǎngxiāng, was appointed Shāzhōu Cìshǐ.
Dīngsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"For Nán Lánlíng, our ancestral home,
rent and cloth taxes shall be permanently remitted;
for Wǔjìn, the foundation of the imperial enterprise,
it shall be remitted for ten years."
In the ninth month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"As Èr Wú and Yìxīng three commanderies suffered from floods,
this year's land tax shall be reduced."
Yǐsì,
the newly appointed Shàngshūlìng and Píwèi Jiāngjūn, Yùzhāng Wáng Yí, was appointed Cìshǐ of Jīng and Xiāng two prefectures,
and Píngxī Jiāngjūn Línchuān Wáng Yìng was appointed Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
Bǐngwǔ,
Sīkōng Chǔ Yuān assumed the additional post of Shàngshūlìng.
Wùshēn,
the imperial carriage visited Xuānwǔ Táng for a banquet,
and an imperial edict commanded all princes and dukes and below to compose poems.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Liú Yìn of Péngchéng was established as Rǔyīn Wáng,
to carry on the line of the Sòng emperor.
Jǐmǎo,
the imperial carriage conducted an *yīn* sacrifice at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Xīnsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"I have been burdened with worldly affairs
for over thirty years,
and have experienced
all sorts of dangers and difficulties.
In these latter difficult times,
military chariots have been driven year after year,
truly relying on the opportune fortune
and indeed on the strength of the soldiers and people.
Since the second year of Sòng Yuánhuī,
those who have gained official positions through military service
have not all received their emoluments.
An urgent order should be issued to investigate,
and once confirmed, they should be immediately granted.
Those capable of other appointments
should be investigated, examined, and ranked.
If the gentry and commoners of the four prefectures
have had their native villages overrun and lost,
and their registers no longer exist,
making it impossible to verify,
they may be allowed to be vouched for by their prefectures and commanderies,
and promotions reported based on facts.
For remote areas lacking *zhōngzhèng* officials,
special permission is granted to report promotions based on military registers.
Or if they are garrisoned on border duty,
and have no means to return,
they may be allowed to form five mutual guarantee groups within the same army,
and the responsible officials shall report on their behalf from time to time."
Rǔyīn Tàifēi Wáng Shì passed away,
and was posthumously granted the title Sòng Gōnghòuhòu.
In the eleventh month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ Xiāo Jǐngxiān was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xīnhài,
Crown Prince Consort Péi Shì was established.
Jiǎshēn,
ten meritorious officials, including Píwèi Chángshǐ Jiāng Mì, were enfeoffed with varying ranks and households.
On the *wùxū* day, the first day of the first month of the second year of spring,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Sīkōng Shàngshūlìng Chǔ Yuān was appointed Sītú,
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Zhāng Jìng'ér was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn,
Zhōnglǐngjūn Lǐ Ānmín was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Zhōnghùjūn Chén Xiǎndá was appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
Xīnchǒu,
the imperial carriage personally performed a sacrifice in the southern suburbs.
Guǐmǎo,
an imperial edict stated that the Suǒ barbarians were invading Huái and Sì,
and dispatched all armies for a northern expedition,
with preparations made both inside and outside the capital.
In the second month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
the barbarians invaded Shòuyáng,
and the Governor of Yùzhōu, Yuán Chóngzǔ, defeated and repulsed them.
Bāzhōu was established.
On the day Rénshēn,
Míng Huìzhāo, the Commandant of Sānbā, was appointed Governor of Bāzhōu.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Xiāo Chìfǔ, the Commandant for Pacifying the Man, was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu,
and Cuī Huìjǐng, the Chief Clerk of Southern Man, was appointed Governor of Liángzhōu and Southern Qínzhōu.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
an edict declared a victory in the western border,
and the state of emergency was lifted.
On the day Guǐsì,
envoys were dispatched to tour and comfort the people of Huái and Féihé,
and those border residents of Xúzhōu and Yùzhōu who were particularly poor and had encountered difficulties.
The governors and officials of two thousand *shí* were instructed to provide relief as appropriate.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
an edict stated:
"The northern people of the area west of the Jiāng (Yangtze River) who have fled their homes due to hardship
are ordered to return to their native places,
and their rent and taxes for this year are remitted.
Those who are poor and alone, or elderly and unable to support themselves,
are permitted to be registered in the military rolls,
and the commanderies and counties shall take charge of them."
In the third month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Luán, Marquis of Xīchāng and Grandee-Secretary, was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
On the day Wùxū,
Chén Xiǎndá, General of the Guards, was appointed Governor of Nányǔnzhōu,
and Zhāng Dài, Grand Administrator of Wú County, was appointed Central Protector-General.
On the day Jǐhài,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the Lèyóu [Yuàn] for a banquet,
and princes, dukes, and officials below them composed poems.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Cuī Sīzǔ, General Who Conquers Barbarians, was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu.
In summer, fourth month, on the day Bǐngyín,
Gāo Lián, King of Gāolì and Duke of Lèlàng, was promoted to the title of General of Agile Cavalry.
In the fifth month,
the Six-Gate Capital Wall was erected.
In the sixth month, on the day Guǐwèi,
an edict stated:
"In the past year, due to floods and droughts,
a partial amnesty was granted to the four commanderies of Dānyáng, the two Wú, and Yìxīng, especially to the counties most severely affected by floods.
Regarding the unpaid three levies from before the first year [of this reign],
the vacant lists have been completed.
Apart from what the officials and clerks are obliged to pay and prepare,
the details of what is to be pardoned and remitted are to be investigated."
In autumn, seventh month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Lú Shàozhī, General Who Guards the State, was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Empress Pèi of the Crown Prince passed away.
In the intercalary month, on the day Xīnsì,
Lǐ Ānmín, General of the Palace Guard, was dispatched to tour Huái and Sì rivers.
On the day Gēngyín,
the Suǒ barbarians attacked Qúshān,
and Lú Shàozhī, Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu, and others defeated and repulsed them.
In winter, eleventh month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Yáng Hòuqǐ of the Dī people was appointed Governor of Qínzhōu.
In the twelfth month, on the day Wùxū,
Chǔ Yuān, Minister of Works, was appointed Grand Preceptor.
On the day Yǐsì,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the Central Hall to hear lawsuits.
On the day Rénzǐ,
Yúzhāng Wáng Yì, General of Agile Cavalry, was appointed Minister of Works,
and Línchuān Wáng Yìng, Governor of Yángzhōu and Former General, was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day Rénxū, the first day of the month,
an edict called upon princes, dukes, ministers, and scholars to recommend upright advice.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Chén Xiǎndá, General Who Pacifies the North, was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu,
Zhēnyáng Gōng Liǔ Shìlóng was appointed Governor of Nányǔnzhōu,
and Imperial Prince Fēng was enfeoffed as King of Jiāngxià.
Lǐ Ānmín, General of the Palace Guard, and others defeated the barbarians at Huáiyáng.
In summer, fourth month,
Shěn Jǐngdé, General Who Pacifies the North, was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
a great amnesty was proclaimed.
Overdue rents and old debts
were remitted or reduced in varying degrees.
In autumn, seventh month,
Yuán Róngzǔ, General of the Vanguard, was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu.
〔一一〕
In winter, tenth month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Tǔyùhún Dùyì Hóu, heir of the King of Hénán, was appointed Governor of Xīqínzhōu and Hézhōu, and King of Hénán.
〔一二〕
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the day Rénxū,
an edict stated:
"The institutions of schools
are foundational to human relations,
serving to attract and develop talent,
and to inspire one's nature.
They broadly nurture the common people
and guide them toward proper conduct.
Thus, the traces of the Five Rites can be transmitted,
and the forms of the Six Musics will not perish.
Since I received the mandate and the charts of destiny,
I have aspired to elucidate the classics and teachings.
And indeed, the officials and various administrators
have all submitted their proposals,
indicating that because military vehicles were constantly alert,
cultural education had not been propagated.
I have longed for the Pàngōng (Imperial College),
and often sighed over it.
Now, with no worries at the passes and beacons,
the times are harmonious and the year bountiful.
Near and far share the same customs,
and both Chinese and barbarians admire righteousness.
Therefore, it is appropriate to follow former precedents,
to restore and establish schools,
carefully select Confucian officials,
and widely invite the imperial relatives."
Wáng Yánzhī, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, was appointed Grand Master of Guanglu of the Right.
On the day Guǐhài,
an edict stated:
"In recent years, our might has been displayed in the northwest,
and brave volunteers have vied to be first,
perishing on the battlefield,
giving their lives in royal service.
While there are standing regulations for pardoning and remitting for those who died in battle,
those in charge, when following them,
have always been regrettably perfunctory.
For those who died in battle since the Jiànyuán era,
rewards and remission of rent and cloth will be granted for twenty years,
and of miscellaneous corvée for ten years.
For those whose bodies could not be recovered,
the army commanders shall guarantee and certify them,
and they shall also be treated according to this precedent."
Chángshā Wáng Huǎng, General of the Rear, was appointed General of the Palace Guard.
Nánjùn Wáng Chángmào, General of the Central Army, was appointed Governor of Nánsúzhōu.
Ānchéng Wáng Gǎo, General of the Vanguard, was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
In the second month, on the day Yǐwèi,
Huán Kāng, General of the Vanguard, was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu.
The Emperor was unwell.
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict pardoned prisoners in the capital to varying degrees,
and all outstanding debts from before the first year were pardoned and remitted.
In the third month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Grand Preceptor Chǔ Yuān and Left Chief Administrator Wáng Jiǎn were summoned, and the Emperor declared:
"I was originally a commoner of humble lineage,
and never expected to reach this position.
Through the opportunity of the times,
I achieved this great enterprise.
My influence has spread,
and an era of peace can be anticipated.
I have been struck by a lingering illness,
and now face death.
You gentlemen must serve the Crown Prince as you would serve me,
treat distant people kindly and those nearby well,
and maintain harmony within and without.
You must ensure that the Crown Prince cherishes his relatives,
entrusts matters to worthy and talented individuals,
upholds frugality,
and broadly promotes simplicity and benevolence.
Then the governance of the world will be complete.
Life and death are fated;
what more is there to say!"
On the day Rénxū,
the Emperor passed away in the Línguāng Hall,
aged fifty-six.
In the fourth month, on the day Gēngyín,
the Emperor was posthumously titled Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì.
His coffin was placed on a dragon boat in front of the eastern palace.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
he was interred in Tài'ān Líng at Wǔjìn.
The Emperor was deep and magnanimous in his youth,
both lenient and strict, pure and frugal,
showing no emotion in joy or anger.
He was broadly versed in classics and histories,
skilled in literary composition,
and proficient in cursive and clerical scripts;
he was a second-grade player of *yì* (Go).
Even when managing affairs in difficult or easy times,
he did not abandon his scholarly pursuits.
He listened to remonstrances and considered strategies,
gaining the masses through his imposing authority.
After his ascension,
he personally did not use fine or exquisite items.
He instructed Huán Jǐngzhēn, a Secretariat Aide, saying:
"It seems there is a jade *jièdǎo* in the imperial wardrobe.
This style originated at the end of Dàmíng,
and became even more splendid during Tàishǐ.
Keeping this in the imperial wardrobe
is precisely fostering the source of extravagance;
it should be immediately smashed.
And any other unusual items
should be dealt with accordingly."
Ornamental railings and other objects in the inner palace that were decorated with bronze
were all changed to iron.
Yellow gauze curtains were hung in the inner hall,
palace women wore purple leather shoes,
and the golden floral claws of the imperial canopy were removed
and replaced with iron rivets.
He often said:
"If I govern the world for ten years,
I will make gold as common as earth."
He wished to lead the world by example,
and transform customs.
The emperor's appearance, physique, and periodic fortunes and numbers of fate,
all corresponded to several dozens or hundreds of prophecies and portents,
a phenomenon unprecedented in previous dynasties.
Although his officials compiled records of these,
the emperor suppressed them and did not allow them to be publicized,
so grand was he.
The imperial historian says: Xún Qīng had a saying:
"When a sage possesses the world,
he receives it,
he does not seize it."
Hàn Gāo, with his divine martial spirit and outstanding sagacity,
when observing Qín Shì's eastern tours,
probably exaggerated greatly,
and did not initially know his heavenly mandate.
Guāng Wǔ, upon hearing Shǎo Gōng's discussion of prophecies,
also dismissed it as merely a temporary jest.
Wèi Wǔ, when he first raised his righteous army,
aimed
for "conquering the west"
as his ultimate goal.
Jìn Xuān, if not for the internal pressure on Cáo Shuǎng,
would he have established his dominance at Fúqiáo?
Sòng Shì rose from a commoner,
his army founded on righteousness. All of them were acclaimed as heroes of their age,
and eventually established the grand enterprise of a dynasty.
Sòng Shì, established by eight rulers,
lasting five *jì* (cycles/decades),
suffered four failures of the eldest heir,
and three instances of proclaimed restoration.
Internal strife and border anxieties,
military conflicts constantly plagued the generations.
When Tài Zǔ first established his mandate,
his military prowess was used subtly.
With the opening of the Tài Shǐ era,
he greatly relieved the difficulties of the time.
His dragon-virtue was in the field,
though he was suspected of seeking the clouds and rain (i.e., the throne).
When Cāng Wú became tyrannical,
enmity arose throughout the court and countryside.
The common people trembled in fear,
their lives hanging by a thread.
As the proper way was put into practice,
it benefited the entire realm.
His great achievements overshadowed the ruler;
a sharp weapon is difficult to lend to others.
Talented individuals worked together,
truly harboring hopes of even a small share.
Could it be that Heaven disliked the element of Water,
and people already yearned for the virtue of Wood?
Credit was given and ability was recognized;
matters reached this peak.
Although he was utterly impartial to the four seas,
his fortune indeed arrived at the opportune moment.
He harbored no intention for the imperial yellow chariot,
yet the Dao changed with circumstances.
He responded without acting,
this is why the imperial Qí gathered the great mandate.
A eulogy says: O, magnificent Tài Zǔ,
with a mandate from Heaven.
His measure encompassed the universe,
his capacity matched mountains and abysses.
Sòng's virtue was not continued,
the divine implement (throne) was transferred in vain.
He pacified chaos with military might,
dismissed tyrants and supported the worthy.
His efforts began in the western borderlands,
his achievements flourished in the north.
A detached force alone achieved victory,
a lone expedition struck like thunder.
He hoisted his banner in the eastern Huáxià,
his duty was to calm the chaos.
He directed his axe towards Xú Fāng,
it was time to punish the rebels.
He defied the capital's power,
and easily pacified Jiāng-Hàn.
Literary arts were his,
his fragrant dust (fame) filled the deep frontiers.
He used his talent to govern those below,
and calmed the people with his virtue.
Upright and majestically serene,
he reigned with dignity and silence.
He encompassed the four seas,
greatly creating the state and its lineage.
Collation Notes
Basic Annals, Volume 3: Emperor Wǔ
Shìzǔ, Emperor Wǔ, whose given name was Zé,
courtesy name Xuānyuǎn,
was Tài Zǔ's eldest son.
His childhood name was Lóng'ér.
He was born in the Qīngxī residence in Jiànkāng.
That night, Empress Chén Xiào and Empress Liú Zhāo both dreamed of a dragon perched on the roof,
hence his courtesy name.
Initially, he served as a Gentleman of Xúnyáng Commandery,
then was appointed Sī Xī Cáo Shūzuǒ for the province,
and later served as Magistrate of Gàn.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn, the Cǐshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, rebelled,
the emperor did not obey his command.
Shěn Sùzhī, the Prefect of Nánkāng, imprisoned the emperor in the commandery jail.
His clansman Xiāo Xīnzǔ and retainer Huán Kāng, among others, broke into the commandery and released the emperor.
Sùzhī led several hundred generals and officials in pursuit.
The emperor and his attendants resisted and fought,
capturing Sùzhī alive,
and beheading over a hundred others.
He then led his troops, numbering over a hundred, to raise an army of righteousness.
Yīn Fú, the Prefect of Shǐxīng, led ten thousand troops to join Zǐxūn at Xúnyáng.
Some advised the emperor to attack them,
but the emperor, considering the numerical disparity,
avoided them and encamped in the Jiēyáng Mountains,
gathering his forces to three thousand men.
Zǐxūn sent his general Dài Kǎizhī to be Prefect of Nánkāng,
along with army commander Zhāng Zōngzhī and over a thousand men to assist him.
The emperor led his troops towards the commandery,
attacking Kǎizhī's separate army commander Chéng Chāo and his several hundred men at Nánkāngkǒu.
He then advanced to attack Zōngzhī,
defeating and beheading him.
He then besieged the commandery city.
Kǎizhī, with several thousand men, held out firmly.
The emperor personally led his generals and soldiers in an all-day assault.
The city fell,
Kǎizhī fled,
and the false Magistrate of Gàn, Táo Chōngzhī, was killed.
The emperor immediately occupied the commandery city,
and dispatched army commanders Zhāng Yìngqī and Dèng Huìzhēn with three thousand men to attack Yùzhāng.
Zǐxūn sent army commander Tán Xiùzhī and others with seven thousand men,
who engaged Yìngqī at Xīchāng,
building camps and fortifications,
but the battle was indecisive.
Hearing that the emperor was coming down himself,
Xiùzhī and others dispersed and retreated.
After the matter was settled,
he was summoned to be Shàngshū Kùbù Láng,
then Zhēng Běi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
Xīyáng Xiànzǐ,
acting Nándōngguǎn Tàishǒu,
Yuèjì Xiàowèi,
Zhèngyuán Láng,
Liú Yùn Fǔjūn Chángshǐ,
Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu,
and separately enfeoffed as Gàn Xiànzǐ,
with an estate of three hundred households.
He firmly declined to accept.
He was transferred to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Guǎngxīng Xiàng.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
the emperor sent an army to attack Xúnyáng,
reaching Běijiào.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Jìn Xī Wáng Ānxī Zīyì,
but did not accept the post,
returning to the commandery.
He was transferred to Sī Yòu Chángshǐ and Huángmén Láng.
When Shěn Yōuzhī was in Jīngchǔ,
the Sòng court secretly prepared for him.
In Yuánhuī Year 4,
the emperor was appointed Jìn Xī Wáng Zhènxī Chángshǐ, Jiāngxià Nèishǐ, and acting Yǐngzhōu Shì.
Following the emperor's enthronement,
Jìn Xī Wáng Xiè was summoned to be Fǔjūn and Yángzhōu Cǐshǐ,
and the emperor was appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
assisting Xiè in proceeding south.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
and before the court's decision was made,
the emperor, believing that the middle reaches of the river could be used to await the enemy,
immediately occupied Póukǒu City to prepare for battle and defense.
Tài Zǔ, hearing of this,
joyfully exclaimed:
"This is truly my son!"
He submitted a memorial requesting to march west,
but was not permitted.
Instead, a detached army was sent to aid Yǐng.
Píngxī Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí and others all received the emperor's command.
He was additionally appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and given the *jié* (credentials).
In Shēngmíng Year 2,
after the matter was settled,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu Zhī Xīncài Jìnxī Èr Jùn Jūnshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cǐshǐ,
retaining his *jié* as before.
He was enfeoffed as Wénxǐ Xiànhóu,
with an estate of two thousand households.
In the same year,
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
He was granted a set of drums and pipes.
A staff was established for his residence.
He commanded the troops at Shítóu Garrison.
Soon after, he was again granted the *jié* and appointed Dūdū Jīngjī Zhū Jūnshì.
In Year 3,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū Púyè, Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
advanced in rank to Gōng,
retaining his *jié*, Dūdū, and Lǐngjūn as before.
He was granted twenty honor guards with ceremonial swords.
When the state of Qí was established,
he was made the Crown Prince of Qí.
His titles were changed and augmented to Shìzhōng and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
he was granted an oil-decorated carriage,
a feather canopy and drum and wind instruments,
and the number of guards with drawn swords was increased to forty.
Shítóu was made the Crown Prince's palace,
and officials, from the two commandants downwards, were appointed.
The regulations for clothing and insignia
were all the same as for the Eastern Palace.
His peerage was advanced to Crown Prince (Wáng Tàizǐ).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he became the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
In the third month, on the day Rénxū, of the fourth year of Jiànyuán,
Tàizǔ passed away.
The emperor (shàng) ascended the throne
and issued a great amnesty.
The commandants and chiefs of various prefectures and commanderies, and the military garrisons and camps,
were each to observe three days of mourning,
and were not allowed to leave their posts.
The city defenders and defense units of the capital and cities
were likewise not allowed to return.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
citing the late emperor's (Xiāndì) posthumous edict,
Sītú Chǔ Yuān was appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Jiǎn was made Shàngshū Lìng,
and Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhāng Jìng'ér was made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
An edict stated:
"Although there are fixed rules for mourning rites,
the late emperor's wishes always emphasized simplicity.
Inner officials may return to mourn every three days,
while outer officials may return every other day.
All future grand mourning rites shall follow this."
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Lǚ Ānguó was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Sīkōng Yùzhāng Wáng Yí was appointed Tàiwèi.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
an edict stated:
"The system of city taxes
should remain consistent through generations.
In recent years, the arrears have accumulated
to tens of thousands.
Although it should be punished according to law,
their original intentions are understandable.
The accumulated city tax arrears
may all be forgiven and cleared.
From now on,
the old regulations shall be reaffirmed,
and any violations will be rectified."
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict stated:
"The recent years have not been abundant,
and there are many poor people.
Both banks of the capital
suffer greatly from this.
Zhōngshū Shèrén shall be dispatched to assess and provide relief."
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Bǐngwǔ,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhāng Ní was appointed Xúyùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Mù Fēi was posthumously honored as Empress.
In the fifth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
Dānyáng Yǐn Wénxǐ Gōngzǐ Liáng was appointed Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the newly appointed Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Yuán Chóngzǔ was made Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Guǐwèi,
an edict stated:
"Recently, rain and floods have frequently descended,
and the tides have repeatedly swelled,
inundating
many residents on both banks.
Zhōngshū Shèrén shall be dispatched with officials from both counties to assess and provide relief."
In the sixth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
Crown Prince Zhǎngmào was enthroned.
An edict extended the grace of the Rénxū amnesty by a hundred days.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Póyáng Wáng Qiāng was appointed Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Línrǔ Gōngzǐ Qīng was appointed Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Zāng Língzhì was appointed Yuèzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Crown Prince's consort, Wáng Shì, was established.
Wénxǐ Gōngzǐ Liáng was advanced to Jìnglíng Wáng,
Línrǔ Gōngzǐ Qīng to Lúlíng Wáng,
Yìngchéng Gōngzǐ Jìng to Ānlù Wáng,
Jiānglíng Gōngzǐ Mào to Jìn'ān Wáng,
Zhījiāng Gōngzǐ Lóng to Suíjùn Wáng,
Imperial Son Zǐzhēn to Jiàn'ān Wáng,
and Imperial Grandson Zhāoyè to Nánjùn Wáng.
On the day Wùxū,
an edict stated:
"Floods have caused calamity,
and the celestial order is out of alignment.
Prisoners in the capital
may be interrogated and judged on a set day;
as for distant prisons, the Cìshǐ shall be entrusted to investigate and judge in a timely manner.
Poor people in Jiànkāng and Mòlíng counties shall receive additional relief and grants,
ensuring thoroughness.
Wúxīng and Yìxīng counties, affected by floods,
shall be exempt from rent and taxes."
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Sītú Chǔ Yuān was appointed Sīkōng and Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Gēngshēn,
Wèiwèi Xiāo Shùnzhī was appointed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Rénxū,
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Yuán Róngzǔ was appointed Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì prefectures.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Sītú Chǔ Yuān passed away.
In the ninth month, on the day Dīngsì,
due to national mourning,
the Guózǐxué was suspended.
On the day Jǐsì,
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Jiāng Bóqǐ was appointed Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngqián was appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Shàngshū Yòupúyè Wáng Huàn was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
an edict stated:
"The frontier generals along the Huái River
have long endured hardships on the border.
As the three new year's days begin,
they should receive imperial favor and congratulations.
Zhōngshū Shèrén shall be dispatched to convey this decree and attend the gathering.
This shall be done every year thereafter."
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài Dài Sēngjìng was appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng, in spring, in the first month, on the day Xīnhài,
the imperial carriage offered sacrifices at the southern suburbs,
a great amnesty was issued,
and the era name was changed.
On the day Rénzǐ,
an edict ordered all internal and external officials to point out any imperial failings
and offer candid remonstrances.
Another edict ordered princes, dukes, ministers, and scholars
to recommend those they knew,
promoting them according to their abilities.
An edict stated:
"The heavy responsibility of governing the state
truly relies on administering the people.
The salaries and stipends of local administrators
have a consistent standard.
Previously, due to border alarms,
adjustments were made according to the times.
Now that the realm is peaceful,
all endeavors are flourishing.
Mindful of diligence and capable personnel,
they should be generously rewarded.
The county and prefecture assistant magistrates and lieutenants
may have their land and rank restored."
Tàiwèi Yùzhāng Wáng Yí was appointed concurrently Tàizǐ Tàifù,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Chángshā Wáng Huǎng was appointed Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Jìnglíng Zǐliáng was appointed Nányùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Shìzhōng Xiāo Jǐngxiān was appointed Zhōnglǐngjūn.
On the day Rénxū,
Imperial Brother Ruì was established as Nánpíng Wáng,
Kēng as Yídū Wáng,
Imperial Son Zǐmíng as Wǔchāng Wáng,
and Zǐhǎn as Nánhǎi Wáng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the old palace at Qīngxī was ordered to be rebuilt for him,
and an edict instructed the inspection of spears and weapons.
In the second month, on the day Xīnsì,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yáng Jiǒng was appointed Shāzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Lǒngxī Gōng Dàngchāng Wáng Liáng Míji was appointed Cìshǐ of Hé and Liáng prefectures,
and Dōngqiāng Wáng Xiàng Shūpéng was appointed Xīliángzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
an edict stated:
"The virtue of the Sòng [dynasty] is drawing to its close.
Its customs and norms have declined,
with feudal lords and common states
increasingly losing their proper order.
Successions and departures are swift,
and both public and private affairs are in decline.
The great [new] era has just begun,
starting from a state of chaos.
We wish to follow the precedents of our predecessors
to eternally solidify the roots of governance.
The tenure of officials overseeing the people
shall all be limited to Xiǎomǎn.
Those who achieve notable successes
shall be generously recognized and distinguished;
those whose administration is ineffective
shall be dismissed as the times require."
On the day Bǐngchén,
an edict stated:
"Since Our accession to this bitter and arduous position,
We have suddenly encountered the anniversary of [Our predecessor's] death.
Looking at the burden [of state],
it is as if We are falling into a deep abyss.
Yet, long-term plans are still obscure,
governance and laws are not yet in order,
the constellations are out of sequence,
and yin and yang are not in harmony.
We wish to spread the beneficence of Our predecessors,
and also to atone for Heaven's afflictions.
Therefore, the amnesty granted on Xīnhài may be extended for fifty days,
starting from its original expiration date.
All prisoners in the capital [Jīngshī]
shall be pardoned and released.
Military conscripts from the three agencies [Sānshǔ]
shall be leniently assessed and sent down [to their homes].
For the impoverished, widowed, and solitary in the capitals and cities [Dūyì],
thorough relief shall be provided."
On the day Wùyín,
an edict
"All prisoners in the four directions,
regardless of the severity of their crime,
as well as remaining brigands and those serving long sentences or ordered to be imprisoned,
are all pardoned and released.
Unpaid debts and outstanding stolen goods to be recovered,
from before the third month of the fourth year of Jiànchuán,
are all specially waived."
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
an edict stated:
"Wèi was generous to Yuán Shào,
and his benevolence extended to [his] grave.
Jìn honored its two kings,
and their glory reached their descendants.
These two generations showed great righteousness,
a fine story from previous times.
Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng, with the former court, jointly supported the Sòng house.
Shěn Yōuzhī, during the Jǐnghé era,
showed particular loyalty.
Though his final actions were not good,
his initial sincerity is commendable.
As years pass,
they should be specially favored and treated leniently.
Càn and Bǐng had their grave mounds reburied the previous year,
but the wooden coffins were not yet properly built.
Arrangements can be made for this,
to ensure they roughly meet the standards of the Rítuals of Zhōu.
For Yōuzhī and his sons whose coffins are in the west,
Jīngzhōu may be ordered to send them back to their old graves,
and provide for their burial there."
In the fifth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhāng Jìng'ér was executed.
In the sixth month, on the day Bǐngyín,
an edict
"All those involved in cases requiring review,
from before the third month of the fourth year of Jiànchuán,
are all pardoned."
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Wùxū,
the newly appointed Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Wáng Sēngqián was promoted to Tèjìn.
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Língchuán Wáng Yìng, was appointed Piàojí Jiāngjūn;
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, Lúlín Wáng Zǐqīng, was appointed Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ;
Wúqùn Tàishǒu, Ānlù Hóu Miǎn, was appointed Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year, spring, first month, on the day Yǐhài,
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Lǚ Ānguó was appointed Nán Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ;
Zhēngbèi Jiāngjūn, Jìnglín Wáng Zǐliáng, was appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn concurrently Sītú;
Zhēngbèi Chángshǐ Liú Quān was appointed Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yòu Guānglù Dàfū Wáng Yánzhī was appointed Tèjìn.
In the third month, on the day Yǐhài,
Wúxìng Tàishǒu Zhāng Dài was appointed Nán Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ;
Qián Jiāngjūn Wáng Huàn was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ;
Píngbèi Jiāngjūn Lǚ Ānguó was appointed Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Wùyín,
Shǎofǔ Zhào Jǐngyì was appointed Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
an edict
"All prisons within the five prefectures of Yáng, Nánxú, Nán Yùn, Xú, and Yù;
all current prisoners in the prefectural and provincial jails of Bìng, Yù, and Jiāng;
and those imprisoned in the two commanderies of Xúnyáng and Xīncài in Jiāngzhōu;
shall all be sent back to the capital [Tái] by their departments,
awaiting a set date to determine their guilt or innocence.
For distant commanderies along the river and other prefectures,
the Cìshǐ shall be entrusted with thorough investigation and inquiry."
〔一０〕On the day Jǐsì,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Chéng Fǎqín was appointed Níngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the sixth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the Central Hall [Zhōngtáng] to hear lawsuits.
On the day Yǐsì,
Ānlù Wáng Zǐjìng was appointed Nán Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Wùshēn,
Huángmén Shìláng Cuī Píngzhòng was appointed Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì prefectures.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Guǐwèi,
an edict stated:
"The origins of music,
the ancient sages have taught;
the rites do not forget their roots,
a common practice through generations.
Thus, Hàn Guāng lingered in Nányáng,
and Wèi Wén was diligent in Qiáoguó.
Qīngxī Gōng embodies the brilliance of Heaven,
where precious treasures reside on Earth.
The divine source of light is established,
and auspicious omens truly converge.
In ancient times, when the period of destiny first opened,
and grand schemes were still distant,
the labor of construction
was not yet something We had time for.
As time flows and events pass,
We constantly feel choked with emotion.
As We are of little virtue,
We have inherited this great foundation.
We contemplate establishing and building [a new palace],
to manifest the kingly achievements.
Consulting the stars to devise the plan,
and choosing the day to commence work,
the people have announced its completion,
and its scale is fully manifest.
It is fitting to perform the ritual of consecration [xīnlùo zhī lǐ],
to express Our feelings of gratitude and comfort.
A small gathering may be held on a set date."
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Imperial Prince Zǐlún was enfeoffed as Bālíng Wáng.
In the eighth month, on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the old palace for a small gathering,
where music of metal and stone instruments was performed,
and those present composed poems.
An edict extended
"For prisoners in the capital's [Jīngshī] jails and the three agencies [Sānshǔ],
the extent of pardon shall be leniently determined.
Officials holding palace positions [Lǐng Gōngzhí Sī]
shall be generously gifted silks and fabrics."
On the day Wùshēn,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Xuánwǔ Hú to review military exercises.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
an edict stated:
"Burying dry bones and covering skeletons
is a weighty matter, previously enjoined;
caring for the old, sorrowful, and infirm
is indeed a virtuous institution.
We constantly reflect on the suffering of the people,
never forgetting it even in sleep.
Though Our benevolent voice has not yet fully spread,
many things are still not in their proper place.
In the two districts of the capital [Jīngshī],
there may be old graves that have been destroyed or exposed;
these should be buried as appropriate.
For remains not yet coffined,
they shall all be collected and buried.
For those who are ill, impoverished, and unable to sustain themselves,
detailed regulations shall be formulated,
and they shall all receive assistance and gifts."
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Dīngsì,
Guìyáng Wáng Shuò was appointed Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eleventh month, on the day Dīnghài,
Shǐxīng Wáng Jiàn was appointed Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
〔一一〕
In the spring, the first month of the third year, on the day of Bǐngchén (丙辰),
Liú Kǎi (劉楷), Grand Minister of Agriculture, was appointed as the Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州).
Cuī Qìngxù (崔慶緒), Counselor to the General Who Guards the West, was appointed as the Inspector of the two prefectures of Liáng (梁) and Nánqín (南秦).
[一二]On the day of Jiǎshēn (甲申),
Zǐmào (子懋), Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安), was appointed as the Inspector of Nányùzhōu (南豫州).
On the day of Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
the imperial carriage performed a sacrifice at the southern suburb,
and a great amnesty was declared.
For those whose crimes would lead to severe punishment within three hundred *lǐ* (里) of the capital,
their penalty was reduced by one degree;
others followed the amnesty regulations.
Those under investigation and detention
had their cases reduced and dismissed with distinctions.
Relief was provided to the poor people of two counties.
An edict also stated:
“The *Chūnqiū Guóyǔ* (春秋國語) says: ‘The existence of learning and education among the people
is like the branches and leaves of a tree.’
Good conduct and the cultivation of virtue
all depend on this.
In the past, when the dynasty was founded,
and peace prevailed over Huáxià (華夏),
the grand codes and plans were greatly promoted,
and education and thought were robustly developed.
Officials were commanded
to establish academies and schools.
However, just as the initial plans were laid,
difficulties and old issues arose again.
Looking up to the glorious precedents,
the years have passed far away.
Now, with the near and far united,
and chariot tracks sharing the same script,
it is fitting to select highly qualified academic officials
and widely recruit talented students.”
Another edict stated:
“The essential duty of governors and magistrates who govern the people,
and the primary concern of inspectors when inspecting their regions,
is to strictly enforce the cultivation of agriculture and sericulture,
to survey the land and gauge the seasons,
and to fully exploit the land's potential.
If the number of farmers and silkworms significantly increases,
and those who are idle and neglectful are stimulated,
reports should be immediately submitted by the respective localities.
As for those who violate regulations, are arrogant and conceited,
or whose idleness hinders agriculture,
their names should also be reported.
Rewards and punishments will be clearly administered
to encourage diligence and curb idleness.
Performance will be evaluated and ranked,
and at the end of the year, assessments will be made,
to implement promotions and demotions.”
In the second month, on the day of Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
the imperial carriage performed a sacrifice at the northern suburb.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day of Wùxū (戊戌),
Zǐxiǎng (子響), heir of the Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章), who had just been appointed General of the Right Guard, was made Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州).
Huán Jìng (桓敬), General Who Assists the State, was made Inspector of Yǔnzhōu (允州).
In the fifth month, on the day of Yǐwèi (乙未),
an edict stated:
“The common people's livelihoods have been in decline
for a long time now.
Although the annual harvest has been timely,
scarcity and want are widespread in many households.
All single adult males, and the solitary and orphaned who are supported by stipends,
are hereby exempted from this year's land rent.”
In this month,
the Zǒngmíng Guān (總明觀) was abolished.
In the sixth month, on the day of Gēngxū (庚戌),
Dù Yìhóu (度易侯), Prince of Hénán (河南), was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
[一三]
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day of Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
an edict stated:
“All prisoners under the jurisdiction of Dānyáng (丹陽) and within two hundred *lǐ* (里) of the capital
shall be gathered in the capital.
Beyond this radius,
the authority to make decisions is entrusted to the prefectures and commanderies.”
On the day of Jiǎxū (甲戌),
Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔), Grand Master of Glorious Happiness of the Left with *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (開府儀同三司) rank, passed away.
On the day of Dīnghài (丁亥),
Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒), Staff Officer of the Central Army of the Agile Cavalry, was made Inspector of Níngzhōu (寧州).
[一四]
In the eighth month, on the day of Yǐwèi (乙未),
the imperial carriage went to the Central Hall to hear lawsuits.
On the day of Dīngsì (丁巳),
Liáng Míjié (梁彌頡), acting Prince of Dàngchāng (宕昌), was made Inspector of the two prefectures of Hé (河) and Liáng (涼).
On the day of Wùwǔ (戊午),
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉), Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, was made concurrently Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince.
Xiāo Shùnzhī (蕭順之), Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, was made General of the Leading Army.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day of Rénxū (壬戌),
an edict stated:
“Since the Imperial Crown Prince Chángmào (長懋) has completed his studies,
a *shìdiàn* (釋奠) ceremony shall be held.
Princes, dukes, and officials below them should all attend to observe the ceremony.”
In the eleventh month, on the day of Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Wáng Wénzhòng (王文仲), General of Champion Courage, was made Inspector of the two prefectures of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀).
[一五]
In the twelfth month, on the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
an edict stated:
“The nine grains are of utmost importance,
while the eight materials are secondary.
Therefore, when the sacrificial grains are abundant,
the祝 (priest) and史 (scribe) have no shame in their words.
It was not the lack of a thousand *mǔ* (畝) of land
that caused Zhōu Xuān (周宣) to be admonished.
In the past, when the dynasty first began,
and all government affairs were in their initial stages,
the ritual of the 'three plows'
was something we did not have time for.
I have inherited the grand foundation
and wish to promote the ancestral ways.
I shall personally carry the plow
and follow the old customs.
Therefore, in the early spring, at the beginning of the year,
a propitious day shall be respectfully chosen.
The green phoenixes will be sounded in the eastern suburb,
and wearing the vermillion cap, I shall preside over the ceremony,
offering sacrifices to the ancestors above,
and encouraging the common people below.
This will ensure that the granaries are full within,
and surplus grain overflows outside.
To enrich the people and then educate them,
this is where it lies.”
In this summer,
Lángyé (琅邪) Commandery suffered a drought.
The people cut down the withered sprouts,
and by autumn, the new shoots emerged, resulting in a great harvest.
In the spring, the first month of the fourth year, on the day of Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Zǐlóng (子隆), Prince of Suí (隨) Commandery and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánlángyé (南琅邪) and Péngchéng (彭城), was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Zhāng Guī (張瓌), Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers Barbarians, was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Xuē Yuān (薛淵), General Who Conquers Barbarians, was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州).
Zǐliáng (子良), Prince of Jìnglíng (竟陵), who was General of the Household Guard and concurrently Minister of Works, was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Táng Quèzhī (唐𧜛之) of Fùyáng (富陽) rebelled,
gathering a multitude in Tónglú (桐廬).
He attacked and took Fùyáng (富陽), Qiántáng (錢塘), and other counties,
and killed Xiāo Chóngzhī (蕭崇之), Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽).
Imperial guard troops were dispatched to suppress him,
and he was executed.
On the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Chén Tiānfú (陳天福), General of Champion Courage and commander of the cavalry, [一六]was executed in the marketplace
for plundering the common people while suppressing Táng Quèzhī (唐𧜛之).
On the day of Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
the imperial carriage went to the Central Hall to test talented scholars.
In the intercalary month, on the day of Guǐsì (癸巳),
the imperial prince Zǐzhēn (子貞) was enfeoffed as Prince of Shàolíng (邵陵),
and the imperial grandson Zhāowén (昭文) was enfeoffed as Duke of Línrǔ (臨汝).
On the day of Dīngwèi (丁未),
Yáng Jíshǐ (楊集始), Prince of Wǔdū (武都), was made Inspector of Běiqínzhōu (北秦州).
On the day of Xīnhài (辛亥),
the imperial carriage performed the ritual plowing (*jiètián* 藉田).
An edict stated:
“The ritual plowing is for demonstrating respect,
and personally undertaking it is to lead the people.
I emulate the former regulations,
personally wielding the good plow.
With all a thousand furrows cultivated,
a harvest of six *rèn* (稔) can be expected. [一七]The teachings and righteousness are fully proclaimed,
and sincerity and inspiration are both widespread.
Moreover, with divine omens and spiritual blessings,
and propitious signs accumulating year by year,
a precious cauldron opened, revealing the auspicious jade casket,
and auspicious grains produced ears of multiple stalks.
Sweet dew condensed brightly in the fields,
and divine sparrows soared and flew in the orchid garden.
These are the blessings of the ancestral temples and the state,
not something achieved by my meager virtues.
Wishing to extend harmony,
and spread it among the common people,
all prisoners whose crimes are punishable by death or less
are hereby pardoned.
All debts incurred three years ago or earlier by those who are especially poor
are completely remitted.
Those who are filial, fraternal, and diligent in farming
shall be carefully granted titles and ranks.
The orphaned, elderly, and poor
shall be granted ten *shí* (石) of grain.
All those who wish to engage in agriculture but lack food and seeds
shall be given loans,
with efforts made to be generous.”
On the day of Guǐchǒu (癸丑),
Liú Chì (劉勑), Inner Administrator of Shǐxīng (始興), was made Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
On the day of Jiǎyín (甲寅),
upon the completion of the ritual plowing ceremony,
the imperial carriage went to the Yuèwǔ Táng (閱武堂) for a small banquet to reward the troops.
An edict granted silk to princes, dukes, and officials below them, with different amounts.
On the day of Wùwǔ (戊午),
the imperial carriage went to the Xuānwǔ Táng (宣武堂) to review military exercises.
An edict stated:
“Today, I personally reviewed the six armies;
young and old alike observed the proper decorum.
The commanders who led the various groups
can be rewarded according to their ranks.”
In the second month, on the day of Jǐwèi (己未),
the imperial brother Qiú (銶) was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìnxī (晉熙),
and Xuàn (鉉) as Prince of Hédōng (河東).
On the day of Gēngyín (庚寅),
Wáng Xuánzài (王玄載), Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, was made Inspector of Yǔnzhōu (允州).
In the third month, on the day of Xīnhài (辛hài),
the Imperial Academy lectured on the *Xiàojīng* (孝經).
The imperial carriage went to the academy
and bestowed silk upon the Libationer, erudites, and assistant instructors of the Imperial Academy, with different amounts.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Dīnghài,
Liǔ Shìlóng, Left Attendant Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
In Línyí Xiàn, the wheat crop failed,
and was cut for horse fodder.
By summer, it sprouted and bloomed again.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"For the household taxes of Yángzhōu and Nán Xúzhōu this year,
two-thirds shall be collected in actual cloth,
and one-third in money.
From next year onward,
in all prefectures, near and far, where money is paid,
the value of cloth shall be uniformly reduced;
one bolt shall be set at 400 (cash),
and as before, half of this value shall be used,
to be made a permanent regulation."
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Luán, Marquis of Xīchāng and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, was appointed General of the Central Army.
In the autumn, eighth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Xiāo Huìxiū, Chief Clerk to the General Who Guards the South, was appointed Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Wáng Guǎngzhī, General Who Conquers the Barbarians, was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu.
In the winter, twelfth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Cuī Huìjǐng, Military Advisor to the General of the Central-East, was appointed Inspector of Sīzhōu.
In the fifth year, spring, first month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Xiāo Ní, Prince of Yùzhāng and Grand Commandant, was appointed Grand Minister of War;
Xiāo Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng and General of Chariots and Cavalry, was appointed Minister over the Masses;

Xiāo Yìng, Prince of Línchuān and General of Agile Cavalry, Wáng Jiǎn, General of the Guards, and Wáng Jìngzé, General of the Central Army, all retained their original titles and were granted the privileges of a Grand Minister, equal to the Three Ducal Ministers;
Shěn Wénjì, Minister of the Bureau of Supply, was appointed Inspector of Yǐngzhōu;
Xiāo Zǐjìng, Prince of Ānlù and General of the Left, was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu;
Xiāo Zǐmào, Prince of Jìn'ān and General Who Conquers the Barbarians, was appointed Inspector of Nán Yǔnzhōu;
Xiāo Zǐzhēn, Prince of Jiàn'ān and General Who Assists the State, was appointed Inspector of Nán Yùzhōu.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
"I rise at dawn and diligently govern,
contemplating the welfare of the people and their afflictions.
Although harvests are frequently abundant,
famines still occur alternately.
Now, as the year begins and the season commences,
and the warmth of spring announces its start,
it is fitting to align with this propitious season,
and extend it to the common people.
All orphans, elderly, poor, and sick,
shall all be granted provisions,
and envoys shall be sent to distribute them personally,
always ensuring fairness and universality."
The barbarians in Yōngzhōu and Sīzhōu repeatedly stirred up trouble.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Xiāo Jǐngxiān, Administrator of Dānyáng, was dispatched to Píngyáng,
and Chén Xiǎndá, General of the Protectorate Army, to Wǎn and Yè.
() In the third month, on the day Wùzǐ,
the imperial carriage visited Fānglín Yuán for a spring purification ritual banquet.
On the day Dīngwèi,
Chén Xiǎndá, General of the Protectorate Army, was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
〔一八〕
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
the imperial carriage offered solemn sacrifice at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
〔一九〕An imperial edict stated:
"Imprisoned criminals currently serving sentences of four years or less,
shall all be pardoned and released;
those with five-year sentences shall have them reduced to three years;
and offenders in the capital city who ought to be committed to hard labor,
shall have their punishment reduced by one degree."
In the sixth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
an imperial edict stated:
"Recently, the continuous rain has been excessive,
and floods have risen repeatedly.
The residents of the capital,
many have suffered from its ill effects.
Palace Writers and officials of the two counties shall be dispatched to distribute relief as appropriate."
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Wùshēn,
an imperial edict stated:
"The outstanding land taxes from the subordinate counties of Dānyáng from the fourth year of Jiànyuán to the third year of Yǒngmíng,
are indeed not a small amount.
Within the capital region,
special leniency should be granted.
For those not of moderate means,
all outstanding taxes may be pardoned and exempted."
In the eighth month, on the day Yǐhài,
an imperial edict stated:
"This summer's rainfall
has heavily damaged the farmlands in the two commanderies of Wúxīng and Yìxīng.
Their taxes and levies shall be carefully exempted."
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
an imperial edict stated:
"On the ninth day (of the ninth month), I shall go to Shāngbiāo Guǎn, ascend a height, and host a banquet for the assembled officials."
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage visited Shāngbiāo Guǎn.
The pavilion
was established by the Emperor,
located on Sūn Línggǎng,
and popularly known as
"Jiǔrì Tái"
by the people.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
an imperial edict stated:
"One who governs the state well
causes the people no harm,
and encourages agriculture.
Thus, by taxing one-eleventh,
the way of Zhōu flourished;
by establishing Ever-Normal Granaries,
the Hàn dynasty was peaceful.
Silk and hemp from the valleys of Mount Tài
flowed as tribute via the Wèn River;
leather from Shízǐ
surely travelled via Chǔ.
Since the Water Virtue is about to decline,
disasters and turmoil have become increasingly numerous;
〔二０〕armies have risen annually,
and famines have occurred alternately.
Poor households are exhausted by taxes and levies,
money flows out to distant regions.
Military and state supplies
constantly draw resources from all corners,
and without regard for local production,
all are obtained through various taxes.
Although there is the name of trade,
there is no actual benefit to the private sector,
and the people lament their misery;
this is truly the reason for it.
In the past, at the beginning of this reign,
the celestial cycle had not yet completed,
and remaining malpractices were still severe.
Agriculture and sericulture are not as prosperous as in former days,
and grain and silk are undervalued compared to previous years.
Artisans and merchants rarely accumulate wealth,
and common people suffer much from hunger and cold.
This is truly due to the long-standing neglect of the coinage system,
and the scarcity of high-value currency.
As it is said, when the people lose their resources,
how can they not be impoverished?
All households of the lowest poverty
may be exempted from three types of levies for two years.
The capital and all regions shall spend hundreds of millions (of cash)
to purchase grain, silk, and cotton, etc.,
at fair prices to benefit the common people.
Distant states that frequently traded miscellaneous goods,
if those goods are not produced locally,
shall all have their trade stopped.
If it is truly fitting for annual tribute
and needed by the capital,
it may be purchased at current market value,
without allowing arrears or exploitation."
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
Luán, Marquis of Xīchāng and General of the Central Army, was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu;
Xiāo Miǎn, Marquis of Ānlù and Palace Attendant, was appointed General of the Central Army.
Construction of Xīnlín Yuàn began.
In the sixth year, spring, first month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Xiāo Gǎo, Prince of Ānchéng and Minister of the Bureau of Rites, was appointed Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu.
An imperial edict stated:
"Prisoners from within 200 li shall all be gathered in the capital,
and on an appointed day, their cases shall be heard and reviewed.
Beyond this distance,
their cases shall be entrusted to the prefectures and commanderies for interrogation and investigation.
For the convicts and bondservants of the three departments,
details shall be compiled for their pardon and release."
In the third month, on the day Jǐhài,
Xiāo Zǐxiǎng, Heir Apparent to the Prince of Yùzhāng, was invested as Prince of Bādōng.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Zhōu Pánlóng, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, was appointed Acting Inspector of Yǔnzhōu.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Liáng Míchéng, King of Dàngchāng, was appointed Inspector of Hézhōu and Liángzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Shěn Jǐngdé, Palace Attendant Groomsman, was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Fáng Fǎchéng, Grand Administrator of Shǐxīng, was appointed Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Yǐsì,
Lǚ Ānguó, Minister of the Bureau of Supply, was appointed General Who Leads the Army.
In the eighth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
"Due to floods in Wúxīng and Yìxīng,
in the affected areas,
the chronically ill and severely infirm shall be granted two hú (of grain);
the elderly and infirm, one hú;
〔二一〕and children, five dǒu."
In the ninth month, on the day Rényín,
the imperial carriage visited Lángyá Chéng to review troops,
practising naval and infantry forces.
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Gēngshēn,
was the Start of Winter.
For the first time, he presided over Tàijí Diàn to read the seasonal ordinances.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Xiāo Niàn, Prince of Wǔlíng and Minister of the Bureau of Rites, was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the intercalary month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
"The eight prefectures of Běi Yǔn, Běi Xú, Yù, Sī, Qīng, and Jì,
〔二二〕border the frontiers,
and many people are destitute;
therefore, all taxes and levies outstanding from before the Yǒngmíng era are to be pardoned."
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Wáng Huàn, Attendant Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed General Who Leads the Army.
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Fèi Yánzōng, Supervisor of the Feathered Forest Guard, was appointed Inspector of Yuèzhōu.
On the day Gēngshēn,
Xiāo Zǐmào, Prince of Jìn'ān and General of the Rear, was appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu;
Xiāo Zǐmíng, Prince of Xīyáng, was appointed Inspector of Nán Yǔnzhōu.
In the seventh year [of the Jiànyuán era, 485 CE], spring, the first month, on the day bǐngwǔ,
Wáng Jìngzé, General of the Central Army, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yùzhōu.
Yīn Zhìbó, General of the Central Army, was appointed Grand Administrator of Liáng and Nánqín prefectures.
On the day wùshēn,
an imperial edict stated:
"Yōngzhōu has suffered from military campaigns for several years,
combined with the ravages of floods and droughts.
Therefore, all outstanding taxes from four years ago and earlier are remitted."
On the day xīnhài,
the imperial chariot performed sacrifices in the southern suburb,
and a general amnesty was declared.
Poor people in the capital
were universally granted relief and gifts.
Another imperial edict stated:
"Distributing in spring and collecting in autumn
is how all states are cherished;
pacifying the distant and bringing comfort to the near
is how the myriad people prosper.
When Zhèng Hún governed a city,
he established names based on surnames;
when Wáng Jùn received his imperial credentials,
the population flourished.
Currently, it is not uncommon for children to be born and not raised;
although there are clear standing prohibitions,
it is still heard
that this occurs in various places.
This is indeed due to poverty leading to infanticide according to rites,
or perhaps also due to feelings being diluted by custom.
It is fitting to regulate this with stern authority
and encourage it with generous beneficence.
The responsible officials should consult old regulations,
deliberate and settle on a plan,
ensuring that suitable exemptions and relief
are provided with utmost generosity."
On the day rénxū,
Wáng Yìng, Prince of Línchuān, Grand General of Cavalry, and Minister of the Household with the Same Rights as the Three Dukes, passed away.
On the day wùchén,
an imperial edict stated:
"All senior officials, though their ranks are elevated and their years advanced,
their salaries and support are notably meager.
How can this be called 'respecting the old upon dismounting from the chariot'
or 'revering the elderly when crossing a bridge'?
Their stipends should be increased,
and their current service thoroughly compensated."
In the second month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
Zǐ Xiǎng, Prince of Bādōng and General of the Left Guard, was appointed Protector-General of the Army.
On the day jǐchǒu,
an imperial edict stated:
"Xuánní (Confucius) extensively disseminated the civil virtues,
his greatness reaching to heaven.
He illuminated seven generations [of rulers],
and shaped the myriad things.
His heroic spirit stands alone;
who can compare with this 'uncrowned king'?
His achievements were hidden in his own time,
and his Way is deeper than the sun and moon.
Moved by the capture of the qílín, he tired of the world;
a thousand years have passed since then.
Rivers have dried up, valleys become empty,
hills leveled, and abysses filled.
Not only have the Zhū and Sì rivers been submerged,
but even his sacrificial rites lack a principal celebrant.
Previous kings revered him,
and reconstructed his shrines and temples;
but with the swift passage of time,
they have become overgrown with lush grass.
Now that schools are being established,
they truly derive from his grand principles.
As I reflect on these matters and remember the man,
my reverence and attachment only grow.
His ancestral temple should be rebuilt,
ensuring it is in a bright and elevated location.
Sacrificial provisions should be allocated
with rites equivalent to those for feudal lords,
and the title of 'Serving the Sage'
should be continually inherited at the proper times."
On the day rényín,
Wáng Yàn, Prefect of Dānyáng, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jiāngzhōu.
On the day guǐmǎo,
Zǐ Lún, Prince of Bālíng, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yùzhōu.
In the third month, on the day dīngwèi,
Wáng Xuánmiǎo, Director of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yùnzhōu.
On the day gēngxū,
Zǐ Xiǎng, Prince of Bādōng and Protector-General of the Army, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jiāngzhōu;
Zǐ Lóng, Prince of Suíjùn and Minister of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Protector-General of the Army.
On the day jiǎyín,
Imperial Prince Zǐyuè was invested as Prince of Línhè;
Zǐjùn as Prince of Guǎnghàn;
Zǐlín as Prince of Xuānchéng;
and Zǐmín as Prince of Yì'ān.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day wùyín,
an imperial edict stated:
"Marriage rites are widely practiced,
the beginning of human relations.
The Rites of Zhōu established the office of Matchmaker,
and the Classic of Poetry promoted timely weddings.
The four cups are arrayed within,
their meaning is not extravagance;
the three tripods are placed outside,
the matter is not about luxury.
Late customs have become ostentatious,
persisting for a long time.
I often consider reforming this,
but the people do not yet know the prohibitions.
It is heard that the expenses for the 'common feast'
are particularly excessive and grand.
Dishes and delicacies fill the tables,
exceeding those of kings and nobles.
The wealthy flaunt their extravagant customs,
while the poor feel ashamed of their inability to match them.
Sometimes, due to incomplete arrangements for banquets,
postponements are frequent,
the year does not return,
and the prime time passes quickly.
Regulations should be established
and promulgated among officials and commoners alike.
All should emulate the imperial court,
using square baskets for food presentation.
The rites of the 'nuptial cup' should not be diminished,
and the principle of frugality should be upheld.
If anyone still violates this,
they shall be punished by law."
In the fifth month, on the day yǐsì,
Wáng Jiǎn, Minister of the Secretariat, General of the Guards, and Minister of the Household with the Same Rights as the Three Dukes, passed away.
On the day jiǎzǐ,
Liǔ Shìlóng, newly appointed Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, was made Minister of the Secretariat.
In the sixth month, on the day dīnghài,
the imperial chariot proceeded to Lángyé.
Autumn, the eighth month, on the day gēngzǐ,
Zǐ Zhēn, Prince of Jiàn'ān and General of the Left Guard, was appointed Protector-General of the Army.
Winter, the tenth month, on the day jǐchǒu,
an imperial edict stated:
"During the last three dynasties, customs became shallow and decadent,
and old regulations fell into disuse.
Both auspicious and inauspicious ceremonies became extravagant,
often violating proper norms.
Some tore up silk and embroidery to compete in the ornamentation of chariots and clothing,
or applied gold and carved stone to maximize the splendor of burial grounds.
Even the elderly with white hair did not marry,
and coffins were left exposed for generations.
They merely sought to boast and show off,
disregarding important principles.
Clear regulations should be established
and strictly enforced everywhere,
making everything uniform.
If there are any further violations,
they shall be impeached according to the circumstances."
In the twelfth month, on the day jǐhài,
Zǐ Zhēn, Prince of Jiàn'ān and Protector-General of the Army, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yǐngzhōu;
Zǐ Xiǎng, Prince of Bādōng and Grand Administrator of Jiāngzhōu, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jīngzhōu;
Yuán Róngzǔ, former Military Advisor of the Pacify the West General, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yùnzhōu.
In the eighth year [of Jiànyuán, 486 CE], spring, the first month, on the day gēngzǐ,
Wáng Jìngzé, General who Conquers the West, was promoted to Grand General of Cavalry;
Shěn Wénjì, General of the Left, was appointed General of the Palace Army;
Qiāng, Prince of Póyáng and Prefect of Dānyáng, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jiāngzhōu.
An imperial edict ordered the release of captives from isolated cities,
allowing them to return to their native places.
[二三]
[Second month], on the day rénchén,
Sīmǎ Yàoshī, Prince of Línglíng, passed away.
[二四]
Summer, the fourth month, on the day wùchén,
an imperial edict stated,
"Ministers and officials below them should each recommend those they know,
who shall be appointed to office according to their talents.
Those who recommend suitable individuals
shall receive the reward for advancing the worthy;
those who recommend unsuitable talents
shall incur the penalty for indiscriminate recommendation."
Autumn, the seventh month, on the day xīncǒu,
Miǎn, Marquis of Ānlù and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, was appointed Grand Administrator of Yōngzhōu.
On the day guǐmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
"Yīn and Yáng are out of harmony,
and celestial phenomena deviate from their normal course.
The heir apparent has suffered from illness,
which has lasted for several weeks.
I contemplate reverently observing the celestial warnings
and alleviating the sufferings of the people.
A general amnesty should be proclaimed throughout the empire."
On the day guǐhài,
an imperial edict stated,
"The two prefectures of Sī and Yōng
have experienced poor harvests in recent years.
All outstanding taxes from Yōngzhōu before the eighth year and Sīzhōu before the seventh year are entirely remitted.
For the single commandery of Rǔnán, the period [for tax exemption] is further extended by five years."
Eighth month, on the day bǐngyín,
an imperial edict stated,
"As the continuous rain in the capital has passed,
and residents are affected by flooding,
Secretaries of the Central Secretariat and officials of the two counties are dispatched to provide relief."
On the day yǐyǒu,
Xiūliúchéng, acting Heir Apparent of the Prince of Hénán, was appointed Grand Administrator of Qín and Hé prefectures.
[二五] On the day rénchén,
Zǐ Lóng, Prince of Suíjùn and General of the Left Guard, was appointed Grand Administrator of Jīngzhōu.
Zǐ Xiǎng, Prince of Bādōng, was found guilty;
Xiāo Shùnzhī, Prefect of Dānyáng, was dispatched to lead troops to suppress him,
and Zǐ Xiǎng was executed.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
an edict
declared, "Wúxìng has suffered excessive flooding.
Open the local granaries to provide relief and grants."
On the *guǐsì* day,
arrears of rent from before the *Jiànyuán* era were waived.
In the eleventh month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Fú Dēngzhī, General of Jiànwǔ, was appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu.
In the twelfth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Chén Sēngshòu, General of Zhènwēi, was appointed Governor of Yuèzhōu.
On the *wùyín* day,
an edict
stated, "The duties of the Secretaries and Ministers of the Department of State Affairs are arduous and numerous,
yet their salaries are not generous enough.
They may be granted a measured increase in emolument."
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Imperial Prince Zǐjiàn was made Prince of Xiāngdōng.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Zhāng Chōng, Supervisor of Military Affairs for Qīng and Jì Two Provinces and acting Governor, was appointed Governor of Qīng and Jì Two Provinces.
In the ninth year, in spring, in the first month, on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Jiāngxiàwáng Fēng, Attendant-in-Chief, was appointed Governor of Nánxúzhōu,
and Liú Quān, General of Chāmpion, was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the imperial carriage performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb,
and an edict
declared, "Regarding current prisoners in the capital,
investigate and consider releasing them."
In the third month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Liú Kǎi, Southern Central Protector and Administrator, was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Liú Zǎn, Palace Guard Commander of the Heir Apparent, was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
the officials concerned memorialized,
"According to old regulations, there were two visits to the imperial tombs per year:
