on the fifteenth day of the third month, a small visit by junior officials from *Cáoláng* downwards;
on the fifteenth day of the ninth month, a grand visit by officials from *Sīkōng* downwards.
Now, the small visit will be permanently discontinued,
and only one grand visit for the two states will be held."
An imperial edict said,
"Approved."
In the sixth month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
Wáng Huàn, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
In autumn, in the ninth month, on the *wùchén* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Lángyéchéng to review the military.
Spectators filled the capital,
and wine and meat were universally distributed.
In the tenth year, in spring, in the first month, on the *wùwǔ* day,
an edict
declared, "All debts and numerous arrears from seven years ago and earlier
are to be completely waived.
Wealthy households are not included in this exemption.
are to be given five *hú* of grain per person.
Officials both within and outside the capital with official duties are to have their salaries and emoluments increased."
Nánpíngwáng Ruì, Minister of the Left for Civil Affairs, was appointed Governor of Xiāngzhōu;
Jìnglínwáng Zǐliáng, Minister of Works, was appointed Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs;
Wáng Xuánmiǎo, Right Guard General, was appointed Governor of Běixúzhōu;
Lúlínwáng Zǐqīng, Central Army General, was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry;
Nánhǎiwáng Zǐhǎn, Northern Central Protector, was appointed Governor of Yùnzhōu;
Zhāo Wén, Duke of Línrǔ and General of Fǔguó, was appointed Governor of Nányùzhōu;
Wáng Wénhé, General of Champion, was appointed Governor of Běiyùnzhōu.
In the second month, on the *rényín* day,
Chén Xiǎndá, General of Zhènjūn, was appointed Commander of the Central Army.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
Yùzhāngwáng Yì, Grand Minister of War, passed away.
In the fifth month, on the *jǐsì* day,
Jìnglínwáng Zǐliáng, Minister of Works, was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Guō Ānmíng, Prefect of Xīnchéng, was appointed Governor of Níngzhōu.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Xuánwǔhú to review the military.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the imperial carriage performed the *yīn* sacrifice at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
In the eleventh month, on the *wùwǔ* day,
an edict said:
"Recently, continuous rain
has caused firewood and provisions to become increasingly expensive,
and many residents of the capital
are suffering from this hardship.
Send the Secretariat Attendant and the officials of the two counties to distribute relief and grants."
In the eleventh year, in spring, in the first month, on the *guǐchǒu* day,
an edict
declared, "Regarding current prisoners in the capital,
investigate and release them."
Wáng Jìngzé, Grand General of Cavalry, was appointed Minister of Works;
Chén Xiǎndá, Grand General of Zhènjūn, was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu;
Cuī Huìjǐng, Right Guard General, was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Imperial Heir Apparent Chángmào passed away.
In the second month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
Lúlínwáng Zǐqīng, General of Chariots and Cavalry, was appointed General of Cavalry and Governor of Nányùzhōu;
Ānlùwáng Zǐjìng, General of the Guard, was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Cáo Hǔ, General of Fǔguó, was appointed Governor of Liáng and Nánqín Two Provinces.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Jìn'ānwáng Zǐmào, newly appointed Supervisor of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Wáng Wénhé, General of Champion, was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu.
In the third month, on the *yǐhài* day,
Wáng Huàn, Governor of Yōngzhōu, was executed.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict
declared, "All civil and military officials of the Eastern Palace
may be transferred to serve as officials of the Imperial Grandson."
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Imperial Grandson Zhāoyè and Grandson Consort Hé were established.
An edict
declared, "All throughout the empire who are heirs to their fathers are granted one rank of nobility;
filial sons, obedient grandsons, righteous men, and virtuous women are granted grain and silk according to their respective circumstances."
Liú Língzhé, General of Agile Cavalry, was appointed Governor of Yùnzhōu.
In the fifth month, on the *wùchén* day,
an edict said:
"Floods and droughts have caused disasters,
and crops are damaged.
All three kinds of taxes and numerous arrears
may be postponed until the autumn harvest.
For the two counties of the capital, Zhūfāng, and Gūshú,
the sale of alcohol may be temporarily prohibited."
Xiāo Huìxiū, General of Fǔguó, was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Yídūwáng Kēng, Minister of the Left for Civil Affairs, was appointed Governor of Nányùzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict
declared, "Since the continuous rain has passed,
send the Secretariat Attendant and the officials of the two counties to distribute relief and grants to the residents of the capital."
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the *dīngsì* day,
an edict said:
"Recently, wind and water have caused disasters,
and many residents on both banks
have suffered from these calamities.
Furthermore, the poor, the sick with six kinds of chronic illnesses,
orphans, the elderly, and the young and weak
are especially deserving of pity and care.
Send the Secretariat Attendant to personally visit and provide assistance."
Another edict said:
"Floods and droughts have caused disasters,
indeed harming agricultural harvests.
Between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
granaries are already empty,
leading to rampant petty theft,
mutual encroachment,
and reliance on mountains and lakes
to form this group of fugitives.
A partial amnesty is granted to the five provinces of Nányùn, Bīngyù, Sī, and Xú.
For the four commanderies of Lìyáng, Qiáo, Línjiāng, and Lújiāng in Nányùzhōu, the three kinds of taxes,
numerous arrears, and old debts
are all to be completely waived.
As for the *qiáomín* (migrants) along the Huái River and newly submitted ones in Qīng and Jì,
their tax exemptions have already ended,
but are now extended for another five years."
That month,
the Emperor was unwell.
He moved his residence to the Yánchāng Diàn.
When the imperial carriage first ascended the steps,
the palace roof groaned and creaked.
The Emperor disliked this.
The barbarians invaded the frontier.
On the day of Wùchén,
Chén Xiǎndá, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, was dispatched to govern Yōngzhōu and Fánchéng.
Fearing that the court and the populace would be worried and panicked,
the Emperor, despite his illness, summoned the Music Bureau to perform orthodox music and dances.
On the day of Wùyín,
his illness became critical.
An imperial edict stated:
“The ultimate end comes to all,
even the wise and the saints cannot escape it.
I am sixty years old,
what more regrets could I have?
However, the imperial enterprise is arduous,
and the myriad affairs of state are heavy,
so I cannot be entirely without lingering worries.
The Imperial Grandson's virtue grows daily,
and the altars of earth and grain have someone to rely on.
Let Zǐliáng assist him well,
and contemplate how to expand the path of governance.
All internal and external matters, great or small,
should be jointly deliberated and decided with Luán.
The fundamental duties of the Department of the Grand Secretariat
〔三二〕are entirely entrusted to Wáng Yàn and Xú Xiàosì.
Strategies for military campaigns and frontier defense
are entrusted to Wáng Jìngzé, Chén Xiǎndá, Wáng Guǎngzhī, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, Shěn Wénjì, Zhāng Guī, Xuē Yuān, and others.
All civil and military officials,
each uphold your duties,
serve the Imperial Grandson diligently,
and do not be remiss.
What more is there to say?”
Another edict stated:
“After my consciousness perishes,
my body should be dressed in summer clothes with painted heavenly garments,
and a pure black rhinoceros horn staff.
All ritual vessels should not use precious jewels or woven fabrics, etc.,
only one set of padded and lined garments, each (originally) simple.
〔三三〕The two iron-ringed knives, one long and one short, that I usually carried,
should accompany me into the coffin.
The ceremonies of sacrifice and reverence
are fundamentally based on sincerity.
A neighbor to the east who slaughters an ox
is not as good as a family to the west offering a simple seasonal sacrifice.
At my spirit altar, strictly do not use sacrificial animals.
Only offer cakes, tea drinks, dried rice, and dried meat with wine.
The noble and humble throughout the realm
shall all follow this regulation.
Before the construction of the imperial tomb,
offer vegetarian meals on the new moon and full moon.
The imperial tomb is the dwelling for ten thousand generations.
I have always regretted that the Xiū'ān Líng was not satisfactory.
Now, the easternmost of the three sites to the east can be used to bury me,
and it shall be named Jǐng'ān Líng.
Funeral rites should always be kept simple and economical,
without burdening the people.
Officials should cease the six daily mourning visits;
the new moon, full moon, and ancestral days can follow the old customs.
None of the ladies of the six palaces
need to follow to the imperial tomb.
The three inner palace areas, Fènghuá, Shòuchāng, and Yàolíng,
were designed and constructed by me.
For a ruler who possesses the realm
and is rich with the four seas,
his banquets, rest, and sleep
should not be simple and crude.
I consider these to be within the bounds of luxury and frugality;
strictly do not destroy them.
The jade statues of Buddhas and offerings in the Xiǎnyáng Diàn,
as detailed in a separate document,
should be wholeheartedly worshipped and offered to.
Any meritorious deeds
should be focused on this.
From now on, neither public nor private individuals are allowed to renounce the world to become monastics,
or to erect pagodas and temples,
or to convert residences into monasteries.
All these are strictly forbidden.
Only those aged sixty,
who definitely possess a heart for the Way,
may be selected and appointed by court officials,
as there is a separate edict for this.
For various small grants and requests,
and internal dispositions,
there is also a separate document.
The old commanders of the internal and external imperial guards and their attendants
are all entrusted to Xiāo Chén for him to assess and employ them well,
〔三四〕do not fail my last wishes.”
On that day, the Emperor passed away,
aged fifty-four.
The Emperor was resolute and decisive;
prioritizing enriching the state.
He generally disliked banquets, entertainment, and ornate affairs.
He often expressed regret about them,
he governed by focusing on the overall framework,
Just before his death, he further decreed:
“All extravagant expenses
should be ceased.
From now on, offerings from far and near
must be made with frugality in mind,
and no one should go beyond their boundaries to seek
to outdo others in luxury and splendor.
Gold, millet, silk, and floss
have already burdened many people;
pearls, jade, and precious trinkets
harm artisans even more severely.
Strictly prohibit and eliminate these,
and let no one violate these rules.”
In the ninth month, on the day of Bǐngyín,
he was buried in Jǐng'ān Líng.
The historiographer says: Shìzǔ ascended to the throne facing south, inheriting the imperial enterprise.
His achievements were comparable to founding the dynasty.
Although he was a successor,
the situation was indeed difficult.
Governing with his robes and ceremonial tassels,
he deeply upheld the political norms.
Military and civil appointments
did not alter previous regulations.
Clear punishments and generous benevolence
all originated from the Emperor,
his principles embracing both the long-term and the distant,
and everyone was solemn.
Outwardly, there was no dust;
inwardly, the court was mostly at ease.
State affairs were managed smoothly,
tribute was constant.
The treasuries were full,
and the people rarely suffered forced labor.
Palaces and gardens
were not enough to harm the finances.
Peace, joy, and longevity
were shared good fortune for the common people.
However, as for sacrificing personal affections,
like the common people in the countryside,
Tàizǔ's many descendants
were ranked after many of his brothers.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's affections lingered and he repented late,
regretting the Lì Yuán.
Marquis Wén of Wèi conquered Zhōngshān,
but did not grant it to his younger brother.
The inner thoughts of these heroes and sages
are not fully clear to your servant.
Eulogy: Emperor Wǔ's great display
earned him the noble title of 'halting war'.
At Sháolǐng, ill omens ceased;
at Péngpài, the waves calmed.
His might upheld the glorious reign,
he strictly governed by golden laws.
To the north, the Rong barbarians offered submission;
to the south, the Yi sang their songs.
Markets and courts were peaceful and leisurely,
the interior and exterior were harmonious.
〔三五〕Collated Notes
Annals Fourth: King Yùlín
Xiāo Zhāoyè, King Yùlín, courtesy name Yuánshàng,
was the eldest son of Crown Prince Wénhuì.
His childhood name was Fǎshēn.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as King of Nánjùn,
with two thousand households.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year of Yǒngmíng, on the day of Wùzǐ,
he was capped in the Chóngzhèng Diàn of the Eastern Palace.
On that day, a small gathering was held,
and princes and dukes and those below them were granted silk in varying amounts,
and Zhāo Yè was provided with two bearers.
In the seventh year,
the relevant authorities memorialized to grant him twenty sword-bearers,
and one set of drum and wind instruments,
and to select highly capable friends and tutors.
In the eleventh year,
he was granted a dark-wheeled chariot with three banners.
An edict commanded the selection of highly capable state officials.
When Crown Prince Wénhuì passed away,
Zhāo Yè was established as Imperial Grandson,
residing in the Eastern Palace.
When Shìzǔ passed away,
the Imperial Grandson ascended the throne.
In the eighth month, on the day of Rénwǔ,
an edict was issued, stating the late emperor's will,
appointing Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, the King of Wǔlíng, Xiāo Yè, as Wèijiāngjūn.
Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá retained his current title,
both receiving the concurrent title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, the Marquis of Xīchāng, Xiāo Luán, was made Shàngshū Lìng.
Tàisūn Zhānshì Shěn Wénjì was made Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
On the day of Guǐwèi,
Sītú, the King of Jìnglíng, Xiāo Zǐliáng, was made Tàifù.
The edict stated:
"I, being of slight virtue,
have inherited the precious rule,
facing the divine mandate with reverence,
and humbly following the precedents.
I contemplate how to respectfully uphold the established rules,
and respectfully defer to the various lords.
During the time of sorrow and desolation,
being ignorant of the great principles,
it is fitting to cultivate virtue and inspire the people,
illuminating the sagely example.
All arrears of the three levies and various debts,
incurred before the thirtieth day of the seventh month of this year,
are to be entirely remitted.
As for goods and properties designated for compensation, which were sold or unsold,
they are all to be returned to their owners.
The imperial storehouses, various offices, ponds, fields, estates, and smelters
— their establishment and abolition followed circumstances,
and were originally implemented for a time.
Those that are now useless,
are to be carefully reviewed for reduction or abolition.
Officials should temporarily ban [their use by the government]
and return them entirely to the people.
Tolls and taxes at customs and markets
are to be significantly reduced."
On the day of Bǐngxū,
an edict stated:
"Recently, the remaining captives from the north
were entirely assigned to military service.
Criminal cases, however minor,
were not pardoned.
To comfort the wronged and promote benevolence
is a profound matter of sagely example.
It is fitting to grant a general amnesty,
allowing them to start anew.
They shall all be released
and restored to their civilian household registers.
Those who have already been rewarded [with captives]
shall also redeem them."
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
an edict stated:
"In previous years, the Mán barbarians conspired,
intending to disturb the border regions.
The various commanders strategized,
and greatly annihilated the fierce evildoers.
At Gécchéng, a victory was achieved,
and at Wǔyīn, a strong defense was maintained.
The meritorious people from these two places
have not yet received titles or rewards.
Selected officials are to be dispatched
to arrange for their promotion and employment there."
In the ninth month, on the day of Guǐchǒu,
an edict stated:
"The elderly accumulated [wealth] in the eastern and western provinces, prefectures, and states,
but their resources are meager and their stipends few.
This is truly a cause for concern.
The selection bureau should identify talent and ability,
and examine their years [of service].
Prefects of states and magistrates of counties
should be appointed as appropriate,
with priority given to the poor."
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
the Crown Prince Wénhuì was posthumously honored as Shìzōng Wénhuángdì.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day of Rén'yín,
the Imperial Grandson's Grand Consort was honored as Huángtàihòu,
and Empress Hé was enthroned.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Xīnhài,
the Duke of Línrǔ, Xiāo Zhāowén, was enthroned as the King of Xīn'ān.
The Duke of Qújiāng, Xiāo Zhāoxiù, was enthroned as the King of Línhǎi.
The imperial younger brother, Xiāo Zhāocàn, was enthroned as the King of Yǒngjiā.
In the first year of Lóngchāng, spring, the first month, on the day of Dīngwèi,
the reign title was changed,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Tàifù, the King of Jìnglíng, Xiāo Zǐliáng, was granted special honors.
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, the King of Jìnxī, Xiāo Qiú, was made Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu.
Dānyáng Yǐn, the King of Ānlù, Xiāo Zǐjìng, was made Cìshǐ of Nánróngzhōu.
Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn, the King of Jìn'ān, Xiāo Zǐmào, was made Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
The King of Línhǎi, Xiāo Zhāoxiù, was made Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
The King of Yǒngjiā, Xiāo Zhāocàn, was made Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu.
Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá was promoted to Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn.
Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ, the King of Jiàn'ān, Xiāo Zǐzhēn, was made Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
An edict commanded all officials to frankly state their opinions on gains and losses.
Another edict commanded all, from kings and dukes downwards, to recommend those they knew.
On the day of Wùshēn,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Shěn Wénjì was made Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
former Jiāngjūn Cáohǔ was made Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Xuē Yuān was made Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Xiāo Yī was made Cìshǐ of Liáng and Nánqín two prefectures.
Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ Shēn Xīzǔ was made Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu.
On the day of Xīnhài,
the imperial carriage performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb.
An edict stated:
"Forgetting the plow for a moment,
bellies are empty in neighboring households;
those who hold the loom may be idle,
without clothes throughout the year.
Neither laziness nor neglect,
though it may be due to the kingly way,
no weeds, no wild grasses,
truly relies on popular harmony.
In recent years, harvests have been consistently good,
with surplus grain piled up.
Yet, the beauty of abundant harvests has not been fully realized,
and the foundation of prosperity is still distant.
Moreover, climates differ,
and the hundred peoples have different occupations.
Penal laws and governance,
may not all originate from the same source.
Hindering the fundamental and harming governance,
these matters are not uniform.
The emperor's mind is burdened,
never forgetting to rise early.
It should be strictly ordered to the prefectures and counties
to diligently promote cultivation,
measure and open up fields,
extensively develop land resources,
deeply establish the nation's foundation,
and enrich the people.
Also, investigate prisons and markets,
broadly listen to popular rumors,
and any practices that corrupt customs and harm transformation,
each shall be reported by item.
The relevant officials shall thoroughly draw up regulations."
On the day of Wùwǔ,
the imperial carriage paid homage at Chóng'ānlíng.
On the day of Jǐsì,
the newly appointed Huángmén Shìláng Zhōu Fèngshū was made Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
In the second month, on the day of Xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage performed sacrifices at the Míngtáng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day of Xīnsì,
Wèijiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, the King of Wǔlíng, Xiāo Yè, passed away.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
Tàifù, the King of Jìnglíng, Xiāo Zǐliáng, passed away.
On the day of Wùxū,
former Shāzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Jiǒng was made Cìshǐ of Shāzhōu.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
Piàojí Jiāngjūn, the King of Lúlíng, Xiāo Zǐqīng, was made Wèijiāngjūn.
Shàngshū Yòupúyè, the King of Póyáng, Xiāo Qiāng, was made Piàojí Jiāngjūn.
Both were concurrently granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the intercalary month, on the day of Yǐchǒu,
Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was made Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì two prefectures.
On the day of Dīngmǎo,
Zhènjūn Dàjiāngjūn Xiāo Luán retained his current title and was made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
On the day of Wùchén,
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn, the King of Xīn'ān, Xiāo Zhāowén, was made Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the day of Bǐngyín,
Huángmén Shìláng Wáng Sīyuǎn was made Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day of Gēngxū,
Zhōngshū Láng Xiāo Yáoxīn was made Cìshǐ of Róngzhōu.
Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu Zāng Língzhì was made Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu.
On the *Guǐsì* day,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:

“To the Zhèn Jūn (General Quelling the Army), Chē Qí (General of Chariots and Cavalry), Zuǒ Pú Shè (Left Director of the Department of State Affairs), Qián Jiāng Jūn (Former General), Lǐng Jūn (Commander of the Palace Guard), Zuǒ Wèi (Left Guard), Wèi Wèi (Minister of the Guards), and the Bā Zuò (Eight Seats): Since the establishment of Our imperial dynasty,
we received the Mandate from Sòng.
Sagely and wise rulers have continued the lineage,
with three generations shining brightly.
Tài Zǔ (Emperor Gāo) founded the enterprise with divine martial prowess,
bringing order to the chaos of Qū Xià.
Wǔ Huáng (Emperor Wǔ) ascended to the throne with brilliant wisdom,
managing the affairs of heaven and man.
Wén Dì (Emperor Wén), with his supreme sagely disposition,
embodied the gravity of a true heir.
Although his merits had not yet reached all beings,
his virtue was already among the people.
The favor of the three spirits is eternal,
and the foundation for seven hundred years is already solid.
The current sovereign, however, has been afflicted by an ill omen,
manifesting in his tender age.
His depravity was evident while still in the green carriage,
and his foolish stubbornness became apparent in Chóngzhèng.
He is fond of dogs and horses,
and addicted to wine and sex.
His pursuits are only base matters,
and his aversion is only to good people.
Shì Zǔ (Emperor Wǔ) had profound and compassionate love for him,
always covering up his faults,
hoping that with age his will would change,
and he would be able to uphold the divine instruments.
But since he ascended to the grand enterprise,
his wickedness has grown even more severe.
During mourning, he showed not a day of sorrow;
mourning attire became clothes for feasting and revelry.
Drunk and debauched through long nights,
all state affairs were blocked.
Orders and decrees were issued,
but no one knew their origin.
The eunuch Xú Lóngjū monopolized the privy council,
while Fèngshū and Zhēnzhī alternately held power.
He believed he had found the right people,
and that outward appearances would be orderly and harmonious,
surpassing Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān, and even more trustworthy than Xìn and Bù,
leaning on Mount Tài while sitting on a flat plain.
Thus, he indulged his passions and desires,
disregarding the manifest ways of Heaven.
The empresses and concubines of the two previous emperors
were all taken as his paramours.
The relics of the two palaces
were all brought into his play treasury.
Inside and outside became confused and disorderly,
with no distinction between men and women.
North of the crimson screen,
it became a place for selling wine.
Above the green rushes,
market stalls were opened like those of Sāngzhōng.
Moreover, he would travel incognito,
losing track of time and forgetting to return.
The court officials would stand in their formal robes before an empty throne,
and guards with halberds would stand before an empty palace for tens of days.
Loyal and virtuous chief ministers,
who sincerely served the ruler,
tried to eradicate the small-minded people,
hoping he would change and reform.
Yet he never restrained himself,
but instead harbored deeper resentment.
His chief ministers and close advisors,
if they were different from him, were put to death.
Civil and military officials, regardless of their seniority,
were suspected because of their virtue and reputation.
He indulged in outrageous speech,
intending to carry out a massacre.
The state is in peril,
more precarious than a single thread.
In the past, Tài Zōng (Emperor Xuān of Han) brought glory to the Hàn dynasty,
and Jiǎnwén Dì (Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jin) rose to power in the Jìn clan.
What happened in the past, if not forgotten,
can be a teacher for those who come later.
The Zhèn Jūn (General Quelling the Army) upholds righteousness and embodies the Way;
the family and the state rely on him.
The task of an Yī (Yī Yǐn) or an Huò (Huò Guāng)
is entrusted to his profound strategic judgment.
Therefore, he should thoroughly follow the old precedents
and depose him according to the rites.
The Zhōng Jūn Jiāng Jūn (General of the Central Army), Xīn'ān Wáng,
is a descendant of Wén Huáng (Emperor Wén).
He is sagacious and wise, and naturally outstanding.
He is fit to succeed to the grand enterprise
and eternally bring peace to the four seas.
Outside, he should be respectfully welcomed according to the rites.
This surviving widow, in these difficult times,
throws down her brush with increasing emotion.”
Zhāoyè was young, with a beautiful appearance and demeanor.
He was good at clerical script.
Shì Zǔ (Emperor Wǔ) ordered that the imperial grandson’s handwritten notes should not be carelessly circulated,
valuing them highly.
When he spoke in audience,
he had a very good reputation.
Although the princes and marquises greeted the emperor only once every five days,
Shì Zǔ (Emperor Wǔ) would often call Zhāoyè alone to his tent-seat,
and personally ask after him,
calling him ‘Fǎshēn’ (Dharmakāya),
and loved him dearly.
When Wénhuì Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince Wénhuì) died,
Zhāoyè would cry intensely every time he attended the mourning,
sobbing uncontrollably.
But shortly after returning to his chambers,
he would be laughing and enjoying himself immensely.
During Shì Zǔ’s (Emperor Wǔ’s) mourning,
after he finished crying,
he would enter the inner palace,
and often had two troupes of Hú (non-Chinese) female musicians arranged on either side of a corridor to perform for him.
When he was Nánjùn Wáng,
Crown Prince Wénhuì restricted his movements
and limited his expenses.
Zhāoyè said to Yùzhāng Wángfēi (Princess of Yùzhāng) Yǔ Shì:
“Grandma,
Buddhist teachings say
that those with blessings and virtue are born into imperial families.
Today, being an emperor
is a great sin.
My attendants and chief officers
constantly restrain me.
It’s a hundred times worse than being a rich butcher or wine seller in the marketplace.”
Upon his ascension,
he indulged in lavish rewards,
often spending hundreds of thousands.
Every time he saw money,
he would say:
“In the past, I longed for a single coin from you but could not get it.
Can I use you now?”
Within a year,
the several hundred million coins stored in Shì Zǔ’s (Emperor Wǔ’s) private treasury were almost exhausted.
He opened the main wardrobe treasury for the Empress and his favorite concubines to view.
He gave several eunuchs and servants to each,
allowing them to take as much as they wished,
freely carting things away.
They took various precious vessels and smashed them against each other,
finding amusement in it.
He often went about naked,
wearing red silk gauze underwear and undergarments of various colors.
He was fond of cockfighting,
secretly buying chickens worth several thousands.
Shì Zǔ’s (Emperor Wǔ’s) personal item, a licorice root cane,
was cut into pieces and used by the palace women.
He destroyed Shì Zǔ’s (Emperor Wǔ’s) Zhāowǎn Diàn (Hall of Bright Serenity),
asking the eunuch Xú Lóngjū to use it as a private residence.
Lóngjū was particularly favored and trusted,
serving as a privy chamberlain,
and was day and night in the chambers of the six palaces.
Zhāoyè had an illicit affair with Wén Dì’s (Emperor Wén’s) favored concubine, Huò Shì.
Lóngjū advised him to keep her in the palace for a long time,
claiming she was being ordained as a nun,
and replacing her with someone else.
He often advanced himself through flattery and deceit,
and would often say to people:
“In ancient times, there were also eunuchs who served as the Three Dukes.”
The Empress was also promiscuous and disorderly.
The inner chambers were open all night,
and inside and outside were mixed up,
with no distinction whatsoever.
Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretaries of the Central Secretariat) Qímǔ Zhēnzhī and Zhū Lóngzhī,
along with Zhí Gé Jiāng Jūn (General of the Inner Gate) Cáo Dàogāng and Zhōu Fèngshū,
all served as the Emperor’s trusted aides.
Gāo Zōng (Xiāo Lún) repeatedly advised him but was not heeded.
First, he initiated the execution of Lóngjū,
then the execution of Fèngshū and Zhēnzhī.
The Emperor could not prevent any of them.
After this, nuns and old women entered from outside,
spreading strange rumors,
leading him to suspect Gāo Zōng (Xiāo Lún) had ulterior motives.
Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat) Hé Yìn, being the Empress’s maternal uncle, was close to her.
He was made to serve in the Zhí Diàn Shěng.
The Emperor often followed the Empress in calling Yìn ‘Sān Fù’ (Third Uncle).
He plotted with Yìn to execute Gāo Zōng (Xiāo Lún),
ordering Yìn to take charge.
Yìn dared not accept,
and ambiguously resisted the suggestion.
The Emperor’s intention was then halted.
They then plotted to send Gāo Zōng (Xiāo Lún) out to Xīzhōu.
The imperial edict was carried out,
no longer consulting anyone.
Gāo Zōng (Xiāo Lún), fearing a coup,
decided to depose the Emperor.
On the twenty-second day, *rénchén*,
Xiao Chén and Tǎnzhī, among others, were sent to the Department of State Affairs to execute Cáo Daogāng, Zhū Lóngzhī, and others.
They led troops from the Department of State Affairs and entered through the Yúnlóngmén gate.
They wore military attire with a scarlet robe over it.
When they were about to enter the gate,
they lost their slippers three times.
Wáng Yàn, Xú Xiàosì, Xiāo Tǎnzhī, Chén Xiǎndá, Wáng Guǎngzhī, and Shěn Wénjì advanced.
The Emperor was in the Shòuchāngdiàn palace.
Hearing a disturbance outside,
he ordered all the inner palace rooms and corridors to be closed,
and eunuchs to climb the Xīngguānglóu tower to look.
They returned and reported:
"We saw one person in military attire,
with several hundred followers,
hastily armed,
below the Western Zhōnglóu tower."
A short while later,
Xiāo Chén led troops and entered the palace first,
cutting off the Shòuchānggé pavilion.
The Emperor ran to the room of his beloved consort, Lady Xú,
pulled out a sword and tried to stab himself but missed.
He wrapped a piece of silk around his neck.
He was then carried out to the Yándédéng palace.
When Chén first entered the palace,
the imperial guards and officers all held bows and shields, intending to resist.
Chén said to them:
"The one we seek is a specific person;
you all need not move!"
The imperial guards believed him.
When they saw the Emperor being led out,
they all wanted to exert themselves,
but the Emperor said not a single word.
He was led out through the western corridor
and killed.
He was twenty-two years old at the time.
His body was carried out to Xú Lóngjū's residence
and buried with the rites of a prince.
The remaining partisans were also executed.
The historian comments: Yùlínwáng's outward appearance was beautiful and brilliant,
deceiving everyone.
His hidden feelings and cunning were
difficult to fathom.
Appointing the eldest as heir-apparent,
without knowing his flaws and defects,
was the intention of Shìzǔ,
who did not deviate from the Way of Zhōu.
But then, villainy arose from within,
originating from the imperial harem.
Though the harm was not yet far-reaching,
it was sufficient to overturn the state.
The *Chūnqiū* records the transgression of Liáng Bó,
stating that he brought about his own ruin.
A eulogy says: With ten faults and one,
no state is not lost.
Yùlín bore the burden,
abandoning rites and neglecting laws.
Eastern and Western two provinces, prefecture, state, elders (one text writes 長 as 屯 (doubtful) - coll. note)
Annals V: Hǎilíngwáng
Hǎilíng Gōngwáng Zhāo Wén, courtesy name Jìshàng,
was the second son of Wénhuì Tàizǐ.
In the fourth year of Yǒngmíng,
he was enfeoffed as Línrǔ Gōng,
with an estate of one thousand five hundred households.
Initially, he served as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Jìyáng Tàishǒu.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to be Chíjíe, Dūdū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general title remaining as before.
In the eleventh year,
he was promoted to the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Wénhuì Tàizǐ died,
he returned to the capital.
When Yùlínwáng ascended the throne,
he became Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
commanding troops and establishing an advisory staff.
He was enfeoffed as Xīn'ān Wáng,
with an estate of two thousand households.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he became Shǐ Chíjíe, Dūdū Yáng Nánxú Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general title remaining as before.
In that same year,
Yùlínwáng was deposed.
Shàngshū Lìng, Xīchāng Hóu Lúan, deliberated and decided to enthrone Zhāo Wén as Emperor.
In the autumn, seventh month, *dīngyǒu* day, of the first year of Yánxīng,
he ascended the imperial throne.
Shàngshū Lìng, Zhènjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Xīchāng Hóu Lúan was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Lù Shàngshūshì, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Xuānchéng Jùngōng.
The imperial edict stated:
"Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì, with his brilliant and great schemes,
received the mandate to establish Qí;
Shìzǔ Wǔhuángdì, with his grand plans that surpassed the age,
continued the glory from below;
Shìzōng Wénhuángdì, with his clear and bright renown,
won the hearts of all within the four seas: all their virtues spread like flowing springs,
and their accomplishments shone like the constellations above.
Wherever their teachings reached,
there was no thought un-accorded.
The great foundation was firmly secured,
and the auspicious fortune was flourishing.
However, the path of Heaven encountered many obstacles,
and the era was beset by misfortune and decay.
The succeeding ruler was dim-witted and cruel,
increasing in violence and tyranny,
abandoning and insulting the heavenly canons,
and overturning human principles.
The court and commoners stood on tiptoe,
those far and near looked askance,
the people resented, the spirits grieved,
and the ancestral shrine was like a thread hanging by a thread.
Thanks to the solemn execution of loyal plans,
the sky was cleared.
This allowed the achievements of the three empresses
to be renewed after being severed,
and the seven hundred years of good fortune
to be restored after being in peril.
Though an insignificant person,
I have come to inherit the great enterprise.
I bear in mind the difficulty of ruling a decaying state,
as if falling into an abyss.
I wish to share with the common people
the peace and prosperity."
A general amnesty was granted,
and the era name was changed.
Civil and military officials were granted two ranks.
On the eighth month, *jiǎchén* day,
the newly appointed Wèiwèi, Xiāo Chén, was made Zhōnglǐngjūn.
Sīkōng Wáng Jìngzé was promoted to Tàiwèi.
The newly appointed Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, Chén Xiǎndá, was made Sīkōng.
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, Wáng Yàn, was made Shàngshū Lìng.
Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, Wáng Guǎngzhī, was made Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Póyáng Wáng Qiāng, was made Sītú.
An edict was issued to send grand envoys to tour and inspect local customs.
On *dīngwèi* day,
an edict stated:
"All officials of Xīn'ānguó from the fifth rank and above
shall be fully employed.
Those below this rank
are all permitted to resign and be dismissed.
Those who wish to serve
may choose according to their preferences."
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, Hédōng Wáng Xuàn, was made Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xīzhōnglángjiāng, Línhǎi Wáng Zhāoxiù, was made Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ, Yǒngjiā Wáng Zhāocàn, was made Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On *wùshēn* day,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Wáng Xǔ, was made Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zhōngshū Láng, Xiāo Yáoxīn, was made Yǔnzhōu Cìshǐ.
On *gēngxū* day,
Chēqí Bǎnxíng Cānjūn, Lǐ Qìngzōng, was made Níngzhōu Cìshǐ.
On *xīnhài* day,
Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, was made Zhōnghùjūn.
The newly appointed Hòujūn Sīmǎ, Xiāo Dàn, was made Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
On *rénzǐ* day,
Guānjūn Sīmǎ, Zāng Língzhì, was made Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
On *yǐmǎo* day,
the prohibitions on woven silks, gold leaf, colored flowers, and embroidered slippers were reiterated.
In the ninth month, on *guǐyǒu* day,
an edict stated:
"Recently, because of the arduous labor and hardship of frontier guards at the Huáiguān pass,
we have extended ranks of honor
to slightly reward their efforts.
However, records of merit have been delayed
and not yet collected by the imperial office,
which does not align with the urgent principle of granting titles
and quickly rewarding merits.
Therefore, envoys should be dispatched
to evaluate and employ them there."
On *xīnsì* day,
the former Jiǔzhēn Tàishǒu, Sòng Címíng, was made Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ.
On *guǐwèi* day,
the newly appointed Sītú, Póyáng Wáng Qiāng, and Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Suí Jùngōng Zǐlóng, were executed.
Píngxī Jiāngjūn, Wáng Guǎngzhī, was sent to execute Nányǔnzhōu Cìshǐ, Ānlù Zǐjìng.
Thereupon, Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Jìn'ān Zǐmào, raised an army.
Zhōnghùjūn, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, was sent to suppress him.
On *yǐwèi* day,
Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Lúan, was granted the yellow *yuè* axe,
and strict preparations were made both inside and outside the palace.
Furthermore, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, Nánpíng Wáng Ruì, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ, Jìnxī Wáng Qiú, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ, Yídū Wáng Kēng, were executed.
On *dīnghài* day,
Wèijiāngjūn, Lúlíng Zǐqīng, was made Sītú.
Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, Guìyáng Wáng Shuò, was made Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Guǐsì,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Zhōu established officials for matchmaking,
emphasizing the timely completion of marriages.
The Hàn prioritized light corvée labor,
following the principle of rest and recuperation.
This was how virtue was spread and teachings were propagated,
loosening customs and enriching the people.
I, the ruler, control the eight directions,
and my ambition is to spread the nine virtues.
However, the customs of society
have not yet reformed from their detrimental practices.
When I quietly reflect, I often feel sorrowful,
never forgetting the dusk and dawn.
The urging and encouragement of marriage
should be strictly re-emphasized,
ensuring that betrothal gifts are given in due season,
and the grievances of women of marriageable age are put to rest.
The various duties of the imperial kitchen
were formerly sourced from the zhōu and jùn,
conscripting officials and commoners to fulfill their numbers.
Public service took twenty days,
while private burdens accumulated for several months.
Moreover, Guǎnglíng used to send out a thousand people annually in rotation to assist the Huái border garrisons,
which was a troublesome burden,
and also fostered bribery.
Now, both can be permanently suspended,
and alternative arrangements for their supply shall be considered.
The practice in various xiàn of having village elders and road supervisors oversee city defenses and directly manage xiàn affairs,
which creates particularly severe hardship,
should also be prohibited."
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
the state of emergency was lifted.
The Pìyàoqí Dàjiàngjūn and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, Xuānchéng Gōng Luán, was promoted to Tàifù,
and was made Lǐng Dàjiàngjūn and Yángzhōu Mù,
granted special honors,
and advanced in peerage to Wáng.
On the day of Wùxū,

the newly appointed Zhōngjūn Jiàngjūn, Guìyáng Wáng Shuò; the Fǔjūn Jiàngjūn, Héngyáng Wáng Jūn; the Shìzhōng Mìshūjiān, Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng; the Zhènjūn Jiàngjūn, Jiàn'ān Zǐ Zhēn; and the Zuǒjiàngjūn, Bālíng Zǐ Lún, were executed.
On the day of Guǐmǎo,
Níngshuò Jiàngjūn Xiāo Yáoxīn was made Yùzhōu Cìshǐ;
the newly appointed Huángmén Láng Xiāo Yáochāng was made Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ;
and Fǔguó Jiàngjūn Xiāo Dàn was made Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xuānchéng Wáng assisted in governance,
and the emperor's daily activities all required consultation before proceeding.
The emperor desired to eat steamed fish and vegetables,
but the Tàiguān Lìng replied that there was no record of a public command,
and ultimately did not provide them.
On the day of Xīnhài,
the Huáng Tàihòu issued an edict saying:
"To the Sīkōng, Hòujiàngjūn, Dānyáng Yǐn, Yòupúyè, Zhōnglǐngjūn, and the Eight Chief Ministers: Indeed, brightness and darkness alternate,
and difficulty and peace succeed each other.
It is by this that the high spirits grant their mandate,
and by this that the myriad people place their trust.
Since the pure brilliance of the imperial house,
the sagely predecessors have followed in succession,
the feudal lords have held their official posts,
and the myriad deities have received their duties.
However, great sorrows have arisen from time to time,
and many difficulties have continuously accumulated.
Lóngchāng lost his virtue,
especially unsettling both humans and spirits.
Not only did the four seas disintegrate,
but even the nine tripods were about to shift.
Fortunately, Heaven sent forth an eminent assistant,
who greatly rectified the altars of soil and grain,
rebuilding the fallen foundation,
and reviving the lost principles.
The heir-apparent is young and immature,
and many state affairs are obscure to him.
Furthermore, he suffered illness early on,
and is unable to bear the heavy burden.
Thus, the imperial clan internally insulted him,
and the relatives and feudal lords rebelled externally.
Observing Heaven and surveying Earth,
each person had their own intentions.
Although the virtue of [two] ancestors resides in the people,
the danger to the seven ancestral temples was imminent.
Unless a mature ruler is established,
and one with profound capacity to stabilize the realm,
it will not satisfy the hopes of Heaven and man,
nor will it quell the schemes of villains.
Tàifù Xuānchéng Wáng has inherited the essence of Xuān Huáng,
and is endowed with the kindness of Tàizǔ.
His wisdom surpasses that of all living beings,
and his achievements are as great as those of the creator.
His auspicious signs have long been manifest,
and songs of praise exist for him.
It is fitting that he should enter to inherit the precious mandate,
and thus stabilize the imperial ancestral shrine.
The Emperor shall be demoted and enfeoffed as Hǎilíng Wáng,
and I shall retire to a separate residence in my old age.
In the past, Xuān Dì restored the Hàn dynasty,
and Jiǎnwén Dì greatly extended the Jìn sacrifices.
May our grand foundation
be eternally secured from this point forward.
When I think of the family and the state,
I am filled with both emotion and joy."
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
an edict stated:
"Hǎilíng Wáng shall, in accordance with the precedent of Hàn Dōnghǎi Wáng Qiáng,
be provided with Hǔbēn, Máotóu, and painted chariots,
and be supplied with bells, stands, palace musical instruments.
All necessary provisions
shall always be generously supplied."
In the eleventh month,
it was claimed that the King was ill,
and imperial physicians were repeatedly sent to examine him,
then he was killed.
He was given a Wēnmíng secret coffin and
one set of clothes,
and was interred in gǔnmiǎn robes.
The Dàhónglú supervised the funeral arrangements.
For the burial, a wēnláng carriage,
a nine-streamer grand chariot,
a yellow canopy with a left-hanging banner,
front and rear divisions with feather canopies and drums and flutes,
and two sections of dirges were provided,
following the precedent of Dōnghǎi Wáng.
His posthumous title was Gōng Wáng.
He was fifteen years old.
The historian stated: Guō Pú remarked that the name Yǒngchāng
bore the image of two suns,
and the appellation Lóngchāng was also similar.
Examining the six years of Hàn Zhōngpíng,
when Xiàn Dì ascended the throne,
the era name was immediately changed to Guāngxī.
After Zhāng Ràng and Duàn Guī were executed,
the era name was changed to Zhāoníng.
When Dǒng Zhuó assisted in governance,
the era name was changed to Yǒnghàn.
This was four different era names in one year.
In the second year of Jìn Huì Dì's Tàian reign,
after Chángshā Wáng's affairs failed,
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng changed the era name to Yǒng'ān.
When Yǐng was seized from Yè,
Héxián Wáng Yǒng again changed the era name to Yǒngxīng.
This was three different era names in one year.
Lóngchāng, Yánxīng, and Jiànwǔ
also represent three changes in era names.
Thus, it is known that the trajectory of chaos and disorder,
though a thousand years apart, will inevitably be similar.
A eulogy states: Solemn and dignified Hǎilíng,
rose to power as the dynasty perished.
Neither too early nor too late,
he met his destined fate.
Collator's Notes
Annals of Emperor Míng, Chapter Six
Emperor Gāozōng Míng's taboo name was Luán,
courtesy name Jǐngqī,
he was the son of Shǐ'ān Zhēnwáng Dàoshēng.
His childhood name was Xuándù.
Orphaned young,
Emperor Tàizǔ raised him,
with favor exceeding that shown to his own sons.
In the first year of Sòng Tàiyù (472 CE),
he became the Magistrate of Ānjí,
and earned a reputation for strict competence.
He was appointed Left Attendant-in-Ordinary to the King of Wǔlíng,
but did not accept the post.
In the second year of Yuánhuī (474 CE),
he became the Magistrate of Yǒngshì.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (478 CE),
he became Military Adviser and Recorder for the Pacifying South General to the King of Shàolíng.
Before taking office,
he was consequently promoted to General Who Pacifies the North and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Huáinán and Xuānchéng.
Soon after, his title was advanced to General Who Assists the State.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīchāng,
with a fief of one thousand households.
In the second year of Jiànyuán (480 CE),
he became Holder of a Tallies, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yìyáng in Yǐng and Sī Provinces, General of the Vanquishing Army, and Governor of Yǐng Province,
and his title was advanced to General Who Conquers the Barbarians.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Minister of Finance,
concurrently holding the post of General of the Right Army.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (483 CE),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
concurrently holding the post of General of Elite Cavalry.
Imperial princes and marquises traditionally rode in fully curtained carriages,
but Emperor Gāozōng alone rode in a half-curtained one,
with a retinue like that of an ordinary scholar.
When official matters became muddled and confused,
a food vendor carrying a stove accidentally burned an ox's nose,
and the King of Yùzhāng reported it to Emperor Shìzǔ,
whereupon Emperor Shìzǔ laughed.
He was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Left Guard,
and traveled with the way cleared.
The Emperor was very pleased.
In the second year (484 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Conquers the Barbarians and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
In the fourth year (486 CE),
he was promoted to Central Leader of the Army,
his Attendant-in-Ordinary post remaining as before.
In the fifth year (487 CE),
he became Holder of a Tallies, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xīyáng in Yù and Yǐng Provinces and Rǔnán in Sī Province, General of the Right, and Governor of Yù Province.
In the seventh year (489 CE),
he became Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In the eighth year (490 CE),
he was additionally appointed to concurrently hold the post of Commandant of the Palace Guard.
In the tenth year (492 CE),
he was transferred to Left Vice-Director.
In the eleventh year (493 CE),
he concurrently held the post of General of the Right Guard.
Emperor Shìzǔ's posthumous edict appointed him Palace Attendant and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and soon after he was additionally appointed General Who Guards the Army,
and granted twenty sword-bearers.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was made Grand General with his original rank,
granted a military band,
and five hundred personal guards.
Soon after, he was further additionally appointed Director of the Central Secretariat and granted the privilege of Establishing a Staff with Ceremonial Privileges Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers.
When the King of Yùlín was deposed,
and the King of Hǎilíng was enthroned,

he became Bearer of Imperial Tallies, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Yáng and Nánxú Provinces, General of Agile Cavalry, Director of Affairs of the Department of State Affairs, and Governor of Yáng Province,
his privilege of Establishing a Staff remaining as before.
The number of sword-bearers was increased to thirty men,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Xuānchéng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He garrisoned the Eastern Prefectural City.
He was granted five thousand soldiers,
two million coins,
and one thousand bolts of cloth.
When Jiǔjiāng caused trouble,
he was granted the yellow battle-axe.
After the matter was settled,
he memorialized to return it.
Soon after, he was additionally granted the yellow battle-axe, Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs, Internal and External, and Grand Tutor,
concurrently holding the posts of Grand General and Chief of Yáng Province.
The number of sword-bearers was increased to forty men,
he was granted a carriage with tasseled banners and three lookout points,
front and rear feathered canopy and military band,
the privilege of entering the imperial court with sword and shoes,
not needing to hurry when entering court,
having his audience announced by title instead of by name,
and the establishment of four each of Left and Right Chief Clerks, Registrars, Central Officers of the Executive, Clerks, and Subordinates.
He was enfeoffed as King of Xuānchéng,
with a fief of five thousand households.
His posts as Holder of a Tallies, Palace Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, and Director of Affairs of the Department of State Affairs all remained as before.
Before he could accept (these new titles),
the Empress Dowager issued an order to depose the King of Hǎilíng.
As he was to succeed Emperor Tàizǔ as his third son,
and all officials formally requested him three times,
he then accepted the mandate.
On the Guǐhài day of the tenth month in the winter of the first year of Jiànwǔ (494 CE),
he ascended the imperial throne.
An edict stated:
"The Imperial Qí received the end (of the previous dynasty's mandate) and established the ultimate standard,
grasping the mirror to preside over the imperial throne,
its divine martial power shining brightly again,
reverent and intelligent, splendid and grand.
It was meant to last seven hundred years,
as solid as a firm rock.
Yet the royal way stumbled,
the heavenly path repeatedly obstructed,
successors to the mandate often erred,
and the troubles among the feudatories were very critical.
The grand plan and magnificent mandate
were on the verge of falling into the abyss.
Empress Xuāndé, with foresight, observed the rise and fall (of states),
conformed to ancient canons,
consulted widely with the high officials,
and truly determined the divine plan,
thereby gathering the precious mandate upon Me, the Emperor.
Unworthily, with my humble and meager abilities,
I succeed to this great enterprise,
looking up to the grand foundation,
and looking down upon the myriad people.
I am forever mindful of the achievements of my predecessors,
as if treading on thin spring ice.
Anxious morning and cautious evening,
I know not how to succeed,
and wish to spread this renewal among all states.
A great amnesty is granted throughout the realm,
and the reign title is changed.
All palace guards are universally promoted one rank,
the rest of the civil and military officials
are granted two grades in rank.
Overdue taxes and old debts,
and government property owed through exchange,
that existed before the first year of Jiànwǔ,
are all pardoned and remitted.
Remaining family members of bandits who are residing in central government offices
may all be pardoned and released.
Those implicated in crimes and exiled
shall all be returned to their native places."
Grand Commandant Wáng Jìngzé became Grand Marshal;
Minister of Works Chén Xiǎndá became Grand Commandant;
Director of the Department of State Affairs Wáng Yàn was additionally appointed General of Agile Cavalry;
Central Leader of the Army Xiāo Chén became Leader of the Army General and Governor of Nánxú Province;
Imperial Prince Bǎoyì became Governor of Yáng Province;
Central Protector of the Army Wáng Xuánmiǎo became Governor of Nányù Province;
newly appointed General of the Right Zhāng Guī became Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness;
General Who Pacifies the North Wáng Guǎngzhī became Governor of Jiāng Province.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
an edict prohibited officials, near and far, from presenting gifts.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
an edict stated:
"From now on, elaborate carvings and seal inscriptions,
and seasonal renewals,
may all be ceased and abolished.
If regional supervisors or local administrators
have recommendations or offerings,
and the matter is unrelated to their local duties,
they shall be strictly prohibited."
Ānlù Zhāohóu Miǎn was posthumously granted the title of King of Ānlù.
On the Jǐsì day,
the son of the Marquis of Ānlù, Bǎozhì, was appointed Governor of Xiāng Province.
An edict stated:
"Recently, officials holding office
have often violated old regulations,
prioritizing private interest and harming public interest,
truly causing harm to the people.
Currently, taxes levied on merchants and travelers at Shítou's back islet, and forced labor and coerced loans,
shall all be ceased.
Everywhere, all appropriate public actions
should immediately be prohibited by decree.
The responsible officials shall carefully establish regulations for this,
and the censorate shall strictly hear and investigate."
On the *guǐyǒu* day of the eleventh month,
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng, Chief Clerk of the Western Central Army, was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
Wáng Hóngfàn, Grand Administrator of Jìnshòu, was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu.
Wáng Yàn, Director of the Department of State Affairs, concurrently served as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Grand Marshal Xúnyáng Gōng Wáng Jìngzé and thirteen others were promoted in peerage and emolument, each with a different grade.
An imperial edict ordered the closure of Xīnlín Yuàn.
This was formerly common land,
which was entirely returned to its owners,
with debts for its original value waived.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Imperial Prince Bǎoyì was enfeoffed as Jìn'ān Wáng,
Bǎoxuán as Jiāngxià Wáng,
Bǎoyuán as Lúlíng Wáng,
Bǎoyín as Jiàn'ān Wáng,
Bǎoróng as Suí Jùn Wáng,
and Bǎoyōu as Nánpíng Wáng.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The emoluments of district magistrates are meager and insufficient
to sustain their families without farming.
Although they are subject to local tribute,
it is also a burden.
From now on, all such tributes are abolished."
Another edict stated:
"For Xuānchéng Guó, all officials of the fifth rank and above
shall be granted full tenure.
Those below this rank
are all permitted to resign and depart.
If they wish to serve,
they may choose their preferred posting."
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the late Shǐ'ān Zhēn Wáng was posthumously honored as Jǐng Huáng,
and his consort as Yì Hòu.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wénxǐ Gōng Yáoxīn was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Fēngchéng Gōng Yáochāng was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"For the Fine Arts Department, Craftsmen, and Chariot Office,
all artisans
may be granted leave in shifts,
allowing them to rest in rotation."
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Crown Prince Bǎojuàn was established.
A one-rank promotion in peerage was granted to all in the realm who were successors to their fathers.
Filial sons and dutiful grandsons,
righteous husbands and chaste wives
were all granted special awards and publicly acclaimed.
Their residences were marked,
and they were presented with bolts of silk.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Eastern Palace has just been established,
and some from near and far may wish to offer celebratory gifts.
All such offerings are to be forbidden."
On the *rénchén* day,
the newly appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎoxuán, was made Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
Imperial Censor-in-Chief Shěn Yuān memorialized that all officials reaching seventy years of age
should be compelled to retire,
and many were impoverished in their private lives.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Recently, many aged officials in the various departments
were permitted to state their own cases.
The Eastern and Western Provinces [of the imperial secretariat] still enjoyed meager salaries,
but those who resigned from their duties to private life
were deprived of both honor and emolument.
Expressing concern for the elderly,
We truly harbor compassion.
Henceforth, for gentry who reach the age limit,
the regulations of appointment from before the seventh year of Yǒngmíng
may be entirely followed."
This month, the princes executed by the Emperor while he was Regent
were restored to the imperial clan register,
and their sons were each enfeoffed as marquises.
On the *rénzǐ* day of the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Those above may overlook much,
and the sentiments of those below are difficult to convey.
For this reason, the 'Sweet Pear Tree' was lauded,
and the 'Petition Stone' became famous in song.
From now on, once a month,
if anyone feels wronged and unable to state their case,
or holds a just grievance yet cannot bring it forth,
the officials overseeing the populace
shall all be held accountable for their failings."
In the first month of spring of the second year, on the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"For prisoners in the capital sentenced to death,
their sentences may be reduced to five years of imprisonment.
For those currently imprisoned in the three departments with sentences of five years or less,
all are to be pardoned and released.
From princes and dukes downwards,
each is to recommend those they know [to be virtuous].
From princes, dukes, ministers, and gentry,
both inside and outside the court,
each is to point out Our transgressions,
and offer extreme remonstrance wholeheartedly."
The Northern barbarians invaded the four provinces of Sīzhōu, Yùzhōu, Xúzhōu, and Liángzhōu.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Guǎngzhī was dispatched to supervise the punitive expedition in Sīzhōu,
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Xiāo Tǎnzhī to supervise the punitive expedition in Xúzhōu,
and Shàngshū Yòupúyè Shěn Wénjì to supervise the punitive expedition in Yùzhōu.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
an imperial edict ordered that for any damaged tombs and burial mounds in the two capital districts,
repairs should be carried out as appropriate.
Another edict stated:
"Food is the people's heaven,
its importance lauded since Jī's time.
Sericulture is the root of life,
its teaching stressed in Xuān's classics.
The great examples of past sages,
and the flourishing models of later kings,
issued decrees with careful deliberation,
all necessarily followed these principles.
We, reverently donning Our robes in the imperial palace,
contemplate extending virtuous instruction,
deeply committed to the eight policies,
ever vigilant in diligence.
Reflecting silently from dawn to dusk,
We never forget this in waking or sleeping.
Governors and magistrates, as the masters close to the people,
and provincial administrators, as the officials who regulate customs,
should strictly supervise farming and sericulture,
allowing none to be idle or remiss.
Measuring the sun's shadow to exert their strength,
they must thoroughly exploit the land's bounty.
They must firmly repair dykes and dams,
and diligently assess performance.
If farming and sericulture efforts are exceptionally strong,
their names should be fully reported.
If idleness harms productivity,
a memorial should be immediately submitted.
The responsible officials are to formulate detailed regulations."
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the barbarians attacked Zhōnglí,
and Xúzhōu Governor Xiāo Huìxiū defeated them.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Grand Commandant Chén Xiǎndá was additionally granted the title of Bearer of the Imperial Credentials and Regional Commander of all forces for the Northwest Expedition.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
a state of alert was declared both inside and outside the capital.
On the *wùshēn* day of the third month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Many of the native and immigrant commoners in Nánxúzhōu
have been conscripted into military service.
Their three taxes for this year are to be remitted."
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Sīzhōu Governor Xiāo Dàn and his forces attacked the barbarians,
and defeated them.
An imperial edict stated:
"For families in Yōngzhōu, Yùzhōu, Sīzhōu, Nán Yǎnzhōu, and Xúzhōu that have suffered from the invasion,
all taxes and levies for this year are suspended.
For those who communicated with the barbarians,
their past crimes are to be disregarded."
On the *bǐngyín* day,
wheat rents in Qīngzhōu were suspended.
The barbarians retreated from Shòuchūn.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the state of alert was lifted.
On the *jǐhài* day, the first day of the fourth month of summer,
an imperial edict stated:
"Lawsuits within three hundred *lǐ*
are to be gathered in the capital,
and heard on an appointed day.
Cases outside this area are to be entrusted to the prefectures and commanderies for investigation.
The prisoners and laborers in the three departments
are to be pardoned and released in varying degrees."
The Northern barbarians besieged Hànzhōng,
but Liángzhōu Governor Xiāo Yì repelled them.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
the newly appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Péi Shúyè was made Governor of Xúzhōu.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day of the fifth month,
the imperial ancestral temple was completed.
An imperial edict stated:
"The supervising officials and chief overseers of the construction
may be granted a one-rank promotion.
Those forced into labor are to be granted one year of leave,
and those not forced into labor are to have their rents remitted for the same duration as the leave."
On the *rénxū* day of the sixth month,
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Chén, Xīyáng Zǐ Míng, Nánhǎi Zǐ Hǎn, and Shàolíng Zǐ Zhēn were executed.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Xiāo Tǎnzhī was made Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
On the *xīnwèi* day of the seventh month of autumn,
Yòu Jiāngjūn Jìn'ān Wáng Bǎoyì was made Governor of Nánxúzhōu.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Liáng Wáng was made Governor of Sīzhōu.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Dī Yang Fùzhī was made Governor of Běiqínzhōu and Duke of Qiúchí.
On the *dīngwèi* day of the eighth month,
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Lúlíng Wáng Bǎoyuán was made Governor of Nán Yǎnzhōu.
On the *gēngxū* day,
the newly appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Shēn Xīzǔ was made Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
On the *jǐchǒu* day of the ninth month,
Nánpíng Wáng Bǎoyōu 蕭寶攸 was restyled Shàolíng Wáng 邵陵王;
Shǔjùn Wáng Zǐwén 蜀郡王子文 was restyled Xīyáng Wáng 西陽王;
Guǎnghàn Wáng Zǐjùn 廣漢王子峻 was restyled Héngyáng Wáng 衡陽王;
Línhǎi Wáng Zhāoxiù 臨海王昭秀 was restyled Bālíng Wáng 巴陵王;
Yǒngjiā Wáng Zhāocàn 永嘉王昭粲 was restyled Guìyáng Wáng 桂陽王.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Those who follow the ways of the world eschew extravagance.
When serving the sagely empress of the Yīn 殷 dynasty,
she taught the people frugality,
and managed by mirroring previous kings.
I am at the tail-end of declining customs,
inheriting a time of shallowness and superficiality.
Though I respectfully strive to spread transformative influence
and diligently seek to achieve great peace,
propriety and deference have not yet flourished,
and luxury and splendor are still fiercely competed for.
Reflecting deeply on the mysterious [heavenly] ways,
I feel profoundly ashamed by these words.
I contemplate how to restore sincerity and change customs,
returning to antiquity and transforming the people.
Therefore, the Eastern Fields (*Dōngtián*) are to be abolished,
and the Xīngguānglóu 興光樓 is to be demolished."
It was also decreed that the Water Bureau (*Shuǐhéng*) should reduce the number of imperial carriages.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the imperial crown prince's consort, the Chǔ 褚 clan, was received,
and a great amnesty was granted.
gifts were distributed in varying amounts.
Offerings from the four directions were prohibited.
In the twelfth month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The former capital cities and towns,
when one looks at them, fill one with sorrow.
Especially after having once faced south [as emperor],
and resided behind the screen,
some whose achievements benefited their time,
and whose virtue extended for a generation,
yet their tombs are overgrown with weeds,
and their burial trees are not maintained.
How can this merely be a deep sigh from a herdsman,
or a sorrow greater than that of Xìn líng 信陵?
In the past, when the central capital fell,
the imperial regalia moved east.
At the beginning of the founding of the Jìn Yuán 晉元 dynasty,
the lingering songs of Jiǎnwén 簡文 remained among the people.
Yet, the pine gates have fallen into disrepair,
and the burial paths are overgrown with thorns.
Though the years have passed,
reflecting on these matters stirs emotion.
All the imperial tombs of the Jìn 晉 dynasty are to be repaired,
and their guards increased.
For the regions of Wú 吳 and Jìnlíng 晉陵 that suffered from poor harvests,
the three taxes are to be exempted in varying degrees."
In the first month of spring of the third year, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
Yáng Jiǒng's 楊炅 son Chóngzǔ 崇祖, Prince of Yīnpíng 陰平, was appointed Governor of Shāzhōu 沙州,
Xiāo Bǎoyín 蕭寶夤, Prince of Jiàn'ān 建安 and Northern Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household, was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu 江州.
On the *jǐsì* day,
an edict was issued to re-emphasize the six-year term limit for local officials.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
an edict stated:
"Last year, the suǒlǔ 索虜 barbarians encroached on the border.
For those officers and soldiers in the border prefectures and commanderies who died in battle or from illness,
their bodies are all to be returned to their native lands."
In the third month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"Imperial carriages with gold and silver decorations in the Imperial Carriage Office (*Chēfǔ*)
are all to have them removed."
In the fourth month of summer,
the barbarians invaded Sīzhōu 司州,
and the garrison troops defeated them.
In the fifth month, on the *jǐsì* day,
Xiāo Yì 蕭懿, General Who Attacks Barbarians, was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu 益州;
Yīn Guǎngzōng 陰廣宗, General of the Vanguard, was appointed Governor of Liángzhōu 梁州 and Nánqínzhōu 南秦州;
Lǐ Qìngzōng 李慶宗, newly appointed Governor of Níngzhōu 寧州, was confirmed as Governor of Níngzhōu 寧州.
In the ninth month of autumn, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Xú Xuánqìng 徐玄慶, General Who Manifests Awe, was appointed Governor of Yǔnzhōu 兗州.
In the tenth month of winter,
Shēn Xīzǔ 申希祖, General Who Upholds the State, was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu 司州.
In the intercalary twelfth month, on the *wùyín* day,
the imperial crown prince came of age.
Kings, dukes, and others were granted silk in varying amounts,
and those who succeeded their fathers were granted one rank higher in peerage.
Offerings from near and far were prohibited.
An edict also stated:
"This year, new [luxurious] items are not required for celebration;
cash can be used to supply the hundred officials."
In the first month of spring of the fourth year, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
a great amnesty was granted.
"When fine dishes are placed on the table,
their deliciousness is certain to be appreciated;
when good jade is carved,
its brilliance as a *guīzhāng* 珪璋 tablet is manifested upon completion.
Therefore, in shaping all things,
emphasizing the root is primary;
in governing the nine regions,
learning is paramount.
Previously, due to peaceful times,
schools were established.
However, with repeated difficulties and anxieties,
they were temporarily reduced or abolished.
The sounds of recitation have been silent,
for many years.
Recalling antiquity,
I am never forgetful, even at dawn and dusk.
Now that China is at peace,
and the remote areas yearn for [our culture],
the reconstruction of the Eastern Academy (*Dōngxù*)
is truly appropriate for the times.
Let it be established according to old regulations,
widely extending [education to] the nation's noble children,
magnificently spreading this grand undertaking,
and gloriously covering future generations."
On the *rényín* day,
an edict stated:
"For commoners who bear children,
their parents' taxes and labor service are to be exempted for one year,
and they are also to be granted ten *hú* 斛 of rice.
For newly married couples,
the husband's labor service is to be exempted for one year."
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn 尚書令王晏 was executed.
In the second month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Xú Xiàosì 徐孝嗣, Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令;
Xiāo Jìchǎng 蕭季敞, General Who Attacks Barbarians, was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu 廣州.
In the third month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
Shěn Wénjì 沈文季, Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, assumed the concurrent post of Commander of the Household Guards (*Hùjūn Jiāngjūn*).
In the eighth month of autumn,
the Lady Wáng 王氏, mother of Jǐng Huáng 景皇, was posthumously honored as Gōng Tàihòu 恭太后.
The suǒlǔ 索虜 barbarians invaded Miǎnběi 沔北.
In the tenth month of winter,
they again invaded Sīzhōu 司州.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Liáng Wáng 梁王, Prince of the Crown Prince's Household and Zhāng Jì 張稷, Right Army Cavalry Commander, were dispatched to suppress them.
In the eleventh month, on the *bǐngchén* day,
the Dī 氐 ethnic group leader Yáng Língzhēn 楊靈珍 was appointed Governor of Běiqínzhōu 北秦州, Duke of Qiúchí 仇池, and Duke of Wǔdū 武都.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an edict stated:
"Regarding the calculation of taxes on houses, land, and mulberry trees in various locations,
the old valuations should be significantly reduced after careful consideration."
In the twelfth month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Péi Shúyè 裴叔業, General Who Manifests Awe, was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu 豫州;
Xú Xuánqìng 徐玄慶, General Who Manifests Awe, was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu 徐州;
Zuǒ Xīngshèng 左興盛, General Who Pacifies Distant Regions, was appointed Governor of Yǔnzhōu 兗州.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Cuī Huìjǐng 崔慧景, Director of the Department of State Affairs for Fiscal Affairs, was dispatched to lead troops to relieve Yōngzhōu 雍州.
On the *guǐwèi* day, the first day of the first month of spring of Yǒngtài 永泰 first year,
a great amnesty was granted.
Overdue taxes and old debts from before the fourth year [of Jiànwǔ 建武]
were all pardoned and canceled.
Xú Xiàosì 徐孝嗣, Grand General of the Central Army, was granted the privilege of establishing an administration with the same status as the Three Dukes (*Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*).
The various commanderies of Miǎnběi 沔北 were invaded by the barbarians,
and successively fell.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Chén Xiǎndá 陳顯達, Grand Commandant, was dispatched with a staff of authority to relieve Yōngzhōu 雍州.
On the *dīngwèi* day,

Hédōng Wáng Xuàn 河東王鉉, Línhé Wáng Zǐyuè 臨賀王子岳, Xīyáng Wáng Zǐwén 西陽王子文, Héngyáng Wáng Zǐjùn 衡陽王子峻, Nánkāng Wáng Zǐlín 南康王子琳, Yǒngyáng Wáng Zǐmín 永陽王子珉, Xiāngdōng Wáng Zǐjiàn 湘東王子建, Nánjùn Wáng Zǐxià 南郡王子夏, Guìyáng Wáng Zhāocàn 桂楊王昭粲, and Bālíng Wáng Zhāoxiù 巴陵王昭秀 were executed.
In the second month, on the *guǐchǒu* day,
Xiāo Huìxiū 蕭惠休, General of the Left Guards, was dispatched with a temporary staff of authority to reinforce Shòuyáng 壽陽.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
Péi Shúyè 裴叔業, Governor of Yùzhōu 豫州, attacked the barbarians north of the Huái 淮 River
and defeated them.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Xiāo Yáoxīn 蕭遙欣, General Who Pacifies the West, assumed the concurrent post of Governor of Yōngzhōu 雍州.
In the third month, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
taxes on land and cloth for the counties of Yōngzhōu 雍州 that had suffered barbarian attacks were exempted.
an imperial edict stated:
"Confucius (Zhòngní 仲尼) possessed brilliant sageliness,
truly illuminating the highest wisdom.
He propagated his refined Way,
greatly instructing the people,
serving as a model for a hundred kings,
and an exemplar for a thousand years.
He established humanity, which is revered,
and from him sprung loyalty and filial piety.
His profound achievements secretly spread,
and his ultimate virtue became even more manifest.
Though he has long since departed,
the ancestral sacrifices for him have not been lacking.
ranking with those for feudal lords.
However, in recent years,
the sacrificial rites have fallen into neglect,
the ritual vessels are empty,
and no animal offerings are made.
How can this properly manifest his glorious achievements
and forever uphold moral teachings?
Therefore, let the old regulations be followed,
and the sacrificial ranks be carefully restored,
so that the offerings of whole animals and cooked food are complete according to ritual,
and reverence and offerings are simultaneously expressed."
In the summer, fourth month, on the day *Jiǎyín*,
the reign title was changed.
Prisoners held in the three bureaus were pardoned, with various differences in their original punishments and reductions.
Civil and military officials were granted two grades in rank.
On *Bǐngxū*,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī, General of the Garrison Army, was made Grandee Remonstrant and Central Leader of the Army.
On *Jǐwèi*,
Zǐtǎn, son of Zhāowáng of Wǔlíng, was established as King of Héngyáng.
On *Bǐngyín*,
Liú Xuān, Long史 of the Western Commandant, was made Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
On *Dīngmǎo*,
Wáng Jìngzé, Grand Marshal and Administrator of Kuàijī, raised an army in rebellion.
〔一五〕
In the fifth month, on *Rénwǔ*,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Liú Shānyáng was dispatched to lead troops in an eastern campaign.
On *Yǐyǒu*,
Jìngzé was beheaded and his head sent forth.
A partial amnesty was granted to the seven commanderies of Zhèdōng, Wú, and Jìnlíng.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, Long史 of the Rear Army, was made Inspector of Nányùnzhōu.
On *Dīngyǒu*,
Sīmǎ Yuánhé, Northern Commandant, was made Inspector of Yùnzhōu.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Wáng Zhēnguó, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, was made Inspector of Qīng and Jì Prefectures.
On *Guǐmǎo*,
Liáng Wáng, Prince of the Heir Apparent's Household, was made Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
and Tàiwèi Chén Xiǎndá was made Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
On *Jǐyǒu*,
the Emperor passed away in the Zhèngfú Diàn,
〔一六〕aged forty-seven.
The imperial edict stated:
"Xú Lìng may be reiterated with eight commands;
Zhōngshū Jiān remains in his original post;
Shěn Wénjì may be Left Grandee Secretary;
Chángshì Hùjūn remains in his original post;
Jiāng Yòu may be Right Grandee Secretary;
Jiāng Sì may be Grandee Remonstrant;
Liú Xuān may be Commander of the Imperial Guards.
Military and political affairs are entrusted to Tàiwèi Chén.
All internal and external affairs, whether great or small, are entrusted to Xú Xiàosì, Yáoguāng, Tǎnzhī, and Jiāng Shí.
Major affairs should be discussed with Shěn Wénjì, Jiāng Sì, and Liú Xuān.
Crucial responsibilities
may be entrusted to Liú Quān, Xiāo Huìxiū, and Cuī Huìjǐng."
He was buried in Xīng'ān Líng.
The Emperor was discerning and possessed administrative talent,
enforcing laws without bias.
He strictly controlled his favored relatives and intimates,
keeping his officials solemn and clear.
〔一七〕He forbade commoners from using four-paneled parasols,
greatly practicing frugality.
He abolished the Xīnlín Yuàn built by Shìzǔ,
returning the land to the people.
He abolished the Eastern Field of the Heir Apparent built by Wéndì,
and sold it off.
During the Yǒngmíng era, the imperial carriages, palanquins, and boats
had all their gold and silver stripped and returned to the imperial wardrobe treasury.
When the Grand Steward presented imperial meals,
there was a wrapped steamed bun.
The Emperor said:
"I cannot finish this.
It can be cut into four pieces,
the remainder for dinner."
However, the palaces, robes, and utensils in the women's quarters of Shìzǔ
remained entirely unchanged.
He was suspicious by nature and prone to worry,
thus frequently resorting to executions.
He secretly believed in occult arts,
using calculations.
When undertaking imperial tours,
he would first divine their auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
If going south, he would announce it as a western journey;
if touring east, he would announce it as a northern visit.
He was sparing in his comings and goings,
never performing the southern sacrifice.
When the Emperor first fell ill,
he did not cease his deliberations,
keeping it secret and not divulging it.
When his illness became severe and prolonged,
he ordered the bureaus and departments to submit documents requesting whitefish for treatment,
only then did outsiders learn of it.
He wore a dark red robe,
and all his attire was red,
believing it to be an apotropaic charm.
Shamans said:
"The water from Hòuhú flows through the palace,
causing the Emperor's illness."
The Emperor then personally went to the Grand Steward's office to inspect the water ditch.
His attendants reported:
"If the Grand Steward's office has no water, it cannot function."
The Emperor was determined to block it,
intending to divert the Huái River southward.
He passed away before this happened,
and the matter was dropped.
The historian commented: "Gāozōng, as a collateral descendant, ascended the throne,
relying on a nephew and making arguments.
To reach this point overnight
was truly not his original intention.
The legacy he left,
he could not truly escape.
The act of killing and harming
has many motivations,
some arising from boldness and cruelty,
others from fear and apprehension.
If a relative with shared wealth,
〔一八〕is abandoned first by me,
and a beloved person I promoted
is judged to inevitably betray me.
〔一九〕When suspicion and timidity run deep,
one suspects others as outsiders.
Shedding tears while carrying out executions
cannot be called a righteous act.
If affairs merely seek tranquility,
how can one avoid inner shame?
After establishing his own roots,
his branches and descendants were isolated and weak.
His legacy did not flourish,
eventually overturning his clan and state.
If the 'Nǐu' [sign] of pressure
〔二０〕must be entrusted to Heaven's will,
the sacrifices of Pángēng
also succeeded Yángjiǎ.
If one relies on fate to push for fairness,
what is there to criticize?"
An encomium says: "Gāozōng rose from the side,
a blessing to the ancestral state.
He admired frugality and virtue,
and left behind written laws and decrees.
Cautious and meticulous,
he was clear and precise in governance.
Loss of land in Miǎnyáng,
the southern wind did not prevail."
Collation Notes
Annals 7: Dōnghūn Hóu
Dōnghūn Hóu Bǎojuàn, courtesy name Zhìzàng,
was Gāozōng's second son.
His original name was Míngxián,
changed after Gāozōng took power as regent.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
