he was established as Heir Apparent.
In the first year of Yǒngtài, seventh month, on *Jǐyǒu*,
Gāozōng passed away,
and the Heir Apparent ascended the throne.
In the eighth month, on *Dīngsì*,
an edict stated that soldiers and officers in Yōngzhōu who died fighting against the barbarians (rebels)
would have their taxes and duties remitted with various differences.
Another edict ordered the examination and selection of talents,
and the seeking out of the poor and oppressed.
On *Gēngshēn*,
Bǎoyì, Prince of Jìn'ān and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn, was promoted to Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn and Kàifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Bǎoyín, Prince of Jiàn'ān and Nánzhōnglángjiāng, was made Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
In the winter, tenth month, on *Jǐwèi*,
an edict ordered the revision and simplification of laws and statutes.
In the eleventh month, on *Wùzǐ*,
Empress Chǔ was established,
and princes, dukes, and officials below them were granted money with various differences.
In the spring, first month of the first year of Yǒngyuán, on *Wùyín*,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
An edict ordered the examination of *xiùcái* and *xiàolián* candidates,
and the evaluation of all officials.
On *Xīnmǎo*,
the imperial carriage performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb.
An edict stated that officials of the third rank and above, who were entitled to salaries,
and had two parents or grandparents aged seventy or above,
would all be given cash.
On *Guǐmǎo*,
Bǎoróng, Prince of Nánkāng and Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, was made Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In the second month, on *Guǐchǒu*,

In this month,

In the summer, fourth month, on *Jǐsì*,

On the *bǐngchén* day,

〔一０〕On the *bǐngchén* day,
Lǐ Jūshì battled the righteous army at Xīntíng,
and was defeated.
In the winter, tenth month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
Wáng Zhēnguó battled the righteous army at Zhūquèhéng,
and was defeated.
On the *wùyín* day,
Xú Yuányú, General of Níngshuò, surrendered with the city of Dōngfǔ.
Huán Hé, Governor of Qīng and Jì Prefectures, entered the imperial guard,
and encamped at the Eastern Palace.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
he surrendered with his troops.
〔一一〕Zhāng Guī, Grand Master of Guanglù, abandoned Shítóu and returned to the palace.
Thereupon, the palace city gates were closed for self-defense.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Hú Hǔyá, General of Xiāoqí, was appointed Governor of Xú Prefecture;
Xú Zhìyǒng, General of Zuǒjūn, was appointed Governor of Yì Prefecture;
Niú Píng, General of Yóujī, was appointed Governor of Liáng and Nánqín Prefectures.
Lǐ Jūshì surrendered with Xīntíng,
and Zhāng Mù, the lord of Lángyá city, also surrendered.
The righteous army built a long siege-work around the palace city.
In the twelfth month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
Wáng Zhēnguó, the newly appointed Governor of Yōng Prefecture, and Zhāng Jì, Attendant-in-ordinary, led troops into the hall and deposed the emperor,
〔一二〕who was nineteen *suì* at the time.
While in the Eastern Palace, the emperor was fond of amusement,
and disliked studying books.
Gāozōng also did not consider this a fault,
but merely urged him to conduct himself as a family member.
He ordered the Crown Prince to request an audience twice a day,
but an imperial edict was issued refusing this,
instead stipulating an audience every three days.
He once hunted mice all night until dawn,
finding it a source of laughter and amusement.
When Gāozōng was on his deathbed,
he entrusted him with future affairs,
and, taking Lóngchāng as a warning,
said:
“One must not lag behind others in one's actions!”
Therefore, he entrusted power to petty individuals,
and executed various chief ministers,
everything proceeded as he wished.
His nature was heavy, reserved, and he spoke little,
he did not associate with court officials,
only trusting eunuchs and those attendants on his left and right who bore knives and responded to his commands.
After Jiāng Shí and Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng were executed,
he gradually became adept at horse riding.
Day and night, he played with horses in the rear hall,
and engaged in singing and drumming with his close eunuchs and entertainers.
He often went to bed at the fifth watch (3-5 AM),
and did not rise until *bū* (3-5 PM).
When kings and marquises came for their seasonal court appearances,
they would only be admitted after *bū*,
or sometimes dismissed as darkness fell.
Memorials from the various ministries
would only be reported after several tens of days in a month,
or sometimes their whereabouts were unknown.
During the New Year's assembly in the second year,
he only appeared after the meal,
and as soon as the congratulations were barely finished,
he returned to sleep in the west wing of the hall,
from *sì* (9-11 AM) to *shēn* (3-5 PM).
The hundred officials waiting in attendance
were all stiff, exhausted, and pale.
When he finally gathered to preside over the assembly,
it ended abruptly and hastily.
After Chén Xiǎndá's affair was settled,
he gradually began to travel outside.
Along the roads he traveled,
residents were expelled and driven away.
From Wànchūn Mén, through the Eastern Palace to the east, and reaching the outskirts,
for several tens or hundreds of *lǐ*,
all homes were emptied and deserted.
The streets and alleys were hung with curtains to form high barriers,
and armed guards were stationed to defend them,
which was called
“píngchú” (clearing the way).
Sometimes he would pass by the houses of his favored relatives on the left side of the marketplace,
circling and winding,
covering the entire capital.
Every three or four watches of the night,
drum sounds emanated from all directions,
banners and halberds blocked the roads.
The common people rushed and ran together,
scholars and commoners alike could not distinguish what was happening.
When he went out, he never announced his destination,
north, south, east, west,
people were driven out everywhere.
Within the high barriers,
troops were arranged with feathered ceremonial attire,
and there were several other groups
all playing drum and wind music with Qiāng and Hú instruments,
and horizontal trumpets.
He went out at night and returned by day,
the firelight illuminating the sky.
He appointed his beloved concubine, Lady Pān, as Guìfēi.
She rode in a sleeping carriage,
while the emperor rode a horse behind her.
He wore woven patterned trousers and a jacket,
a gold foil cap,
and carried a seven-jeweled bound spear.
In military attire, ready for action,
he was unaffected by cold or heat,
braving rain and snow,
not avoiding pits and traps.
When galloping until thirsty and exhausted,
he would dismount, take out a shell-like vessel from his waist to scoop and drink water,
then remount and gallop away.
Where horse accoutrements were made of brocade,
he worried they would get wet in the rain,
so he had them woven with multicolored pearls as coverings,
exhausting all kinds of elaborate craftsmanship.
He taught fifty or sixty palace eunuchs to be cavalrymen,
and also selected unruly commoners who were good runners to be horse chasers.
Five hundred attendants on his left and right
constantly followed him,
running back and forth,
scarcely resting.
He set up two hundred ninety-six pheasant hunting grounds.
The screens, tents, and temporary barriers within them
were all lined with green and red brocade.
Crossbows were inlaid with gold and silver,
and arrows were tipped with ivory.
The four categories of people in the suburbs and city were all forced to abandon their livelihoods.
The roads for gathering firewood were cut off,
and auspicious and inauspicious occasions were missed.
Families with nursing mothers or weddings
had to move their belongings and stay elsewhere,
or carry the sick and abandon corpses,
unable to perform funerals.
There was one who abandoned a sick person by Qīngxī.
The officials, fearing interrogation by their superiors,
pushed him into the water,
covered his face with mud,
and he died in an instant,
his bones were then lost.
After the fire in the rear palace,
the Xiānhuá, Shénxiān, Yùshòu, and other halls were rebuilt.
Carved, painted, and adorned with various colors,
with blue and gold-mouthed sashes,
〔一三〕musk-scented walls,
brocade curtains, and pearl screens,
they reached the utmost in splendor.
Artisans were shackled and put to work,
from night until dawn,
yet it was still not fast enough.
So, they removed ceiling panels depicting immortals riding beasts from the coffered ceilings of Buddhist temples and monasteries to make up the numbers.
Shìzǔ's Xīngguāng Lóu had a green lacquer applied to its upper part,
which people at the time called
“Qīnglóu” (Green Tower).
The emperor said:
“Emperor Wǔ was not clever;
why didn't he just use pure *liúlí* (glazed tiles)?”
Lady Pān's attire and possessions
were chosen from the finest treasures.
The old items in the main clothing storehouse
were no longer sufficient for her use.
Gold, silver, and precious objects from the marketplace were bought at high prices,
all several times their value.
One amber bracelet
was worth 1.7 million.
All wine taxes in the capital
were commuted to payments in gold,
to be used for gold plating.
When this was still not enough,
the bridge timbers and causeways in Yáng and Nánxú Prefectures were assessed for their value,
and ready money was collected
to supply the expenses of the Great Music Bureau and the main clothing storehouse.
Consequently, many dikes and waterways everywhere
fell into disrepair.
He also ordered the procurement of pheasant-head cloaks, crane-feather cloaks, and egret-feather mourning clothes.
Favored individuals and petty people
used this as an opportunity for illicit gain,
taxing one and collecting ten,
and no one in the commanderies or counties dared to speak out.
In the summer of the third year,
the Fānglè Yuàn was built in the Yuèwǔ Táng.
The rocks and mountains were all painted in five colors.
Purple pavilions and various viewing towers were erected over the pond waters.
The walls were painted with images of men and women engaging in private acts.
Beautiful trees and fine bamboos were planted,
but in the intense heat of the season,
they withered and died
before even a day had passed.
Thereupon, commoners' homes were searched,
and trees were taken as soon as they were sighted.
Walls and houses were torn down to facilitate their relocation.
Planted in the morning and uprooted in the evening,
the roads were filled with them.
Flowers, medicinal herbs, and miscellaneous grasses
were all treated the same way.
Furthermore, a market was set up within the park.
The Grand Provisioner would deliver wine, meat, and various dishes every morning,
and palace women were made to butcher and sell them.
Lady Pān served as the market director,
and the emperor was the market chief,
enforcing penalties.
Disputants would go to Lady Pān for judgment.
The Emperor possessed great physical strength,
able to carry a _báihǔ tóng_ (white tiger spear-halberd).
adorned with gold flowers, jade mirrors, and various treasures,
displaying all sorts of poses.
The thirty-one minor officials and partisans he favored,
and ten eunuchs,
initially appointed Xú Shìbiāo (徐世檦) from Xīncài (新蔡) as the Director of the Palace Guard and General of Agile Cavalry.
Whenever there were executions,
he was the one who carried out the orders.
After killing Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣),
he was enfeoffed as the Sub-Prefectural Duke of Línrǔ (臨汝).
When Chén Xiǎndá's (陳顯達) rebellion occurred,
He personally designed and made elaborate, multi-colored brocade performance costumes,
Although the Defender-in-chief Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) was appointed as Commander-in-chief,
military authority actually rested with Shìbiāo.
When the rebellion was pacified,
Shìbiāo told people:
"A commander of five hundred men
can pacify a commander-in-chief of ten thousand!"
Shìbiāo also knew the Emperor was depraved and dissolute,
and secretly told his partisans Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍) and Méi Chóng'ér (梅蟲兒):
"No emperor in any generation needs important people;
it's just that the master is wicked."
Fǎzhēn (法珍) and others vied for power
and reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor gradually grew displeased with their ferocity and arrogance,
and in the first month of the second year,
dispatched imperial guards to kill Xú Shìbiāo (徐世檦).
Shìbiāo resisted and died in battle.
From then on, Fǎzhēn (法珍) and Chóng'ér (蟲兒) handled affairs,
both serving as external supervisors,
orally issuing imperial edicts;
Wáng Xuānzhī (王咺之), a Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretariat, was their close associate,
exclusively managing official documents.
The other twenty-odd people
all wielded influence.
After Cuī Huìjǐng's (崔慧景) pacification,
Fǎzhēn (法珍) was enfeoffed as a Sub-Prefectural Baron of Yúgān (餘干),
and Chóng'ér (蟲兒) as a Sub-Prefectural Baron of Jìnglíng (竟陵).
When the Righteous Army arose,
and the two garrisons of Jiāngzhōu (江州) and Yǐngzhōu (郢州) had already surrendered,
the Emperor still indulged in his usual pleasure trips,
saying to Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍):
"They must come to the front of Báimén (白門);
then we'll have a decisive battle."
When the Righteous Army reached the near suburbs,
he then gathered troops and planned a firm defense.
He summoned princes, marquises, and court nobles, assigning them positions in the Imperial Secretariat and palace offices.
He also believed in ghosts and spirits.
During Cuī Huìjǐng's (崔慧ǐng) affair,

he appointed Jiǎng Zǐwén (蔣子文) as Acting Imperial Axe-Bearer, Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Chancellor, Grand Preceptor, Grand General, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Administrator of Yángzhōu (揚州), and Prince of Zhōngshān (鍾山).
By this time, he further honored him as Emperor.
He brought the divine image and various miscellaneous gods from temples into the rear hall,
and had his trusted shaman Zhū Guāngshàng (朱光尚) perform sacrifices and prayers for blessings.
He ordered General of Champion 王珍國 (Wáng Zhēnguó) to lead thirty thousand men to hold Dàhéng (大桁),
He sent the Director of the Left and Right, the eunuch Wáng Bǎosūn (王寶孫), to supervise the battle,
calling him
"Wang the Elder Son."
Director of the Palace Guard Xí Háo (席豪) died rushing into the enemy lines in a fit of rage.
Háo (豪) was a brave general.
Once he was defeated,
the entire army immediately collapsed like earth,
and countless soldiers threw themselves from the Zhūquèguān (朱雀觀) tower or plunged into the Huái River to their deaths.
Thereupon, he closed the city gates and defended the city,
entrusting military affairs within the city to Wáng Zhēnguó (王珍國).
Zhāng Jì (張稷), the Prefect of Xǔnzhōu (許州), entered to defend the capital.
Jì (稷) was appointed as deputy,
with still seventy thousand armored soldiers.
The Emperor, wearing a black cap and military attire,
prepared his feathered imperial regalia
and ascended the Nányèmén (南掖門) to observe.
He also fictitiously set up a thousand armored cavalrymen with weapons,
all drawing bows and brandishing white blades,
exiting the Dōngyèmén (東掖門),
claiming that "King Jiǎng" (蔣王) was going out to clear the area.
He had always been fond of battle formations.
Initially, he used palace women as soldiers;
later, he used eunuchs.
He personally oversaw the formations,
feigning injury
and having people carry him away.
By this time, in the Yuèwǔtáng (閱武堂), he set up a vanguard army camp,
with strict vigilance every night.
The Emperor rode a horse within the palace, entering Huīmíngmén (徽明門) from Fèngzhuāngmén (鳳莊門).
The horse wore silver lotus-leaf full armor,
adorned with various feathers and kingfisher plumes.
Horsemen escorted him left and right.
He slept during the day and rose at night as usual.
Hearing the drums and shouts from outside,
he donned a large red robe and ascended to the rooftop of Jǐngyánglóu (景陽樓) to observe,
where a crossbow nearly struck him.
Everyone was lax and resentful,
not exerting themselves.
When troops were recruited to sally out,
they would go a few dozen paces outside the city gate
and then sit down in their armor and return.
Fearing ambushes outside the city,
he burned the various government offices adjacent to the city,
completely razing everything within the six gates.
Inside the city, near the elevated walkways and the Xīyèmén (西掖門),
people gathered to form a market,
selling meat from dead cattle and horses.
The Emperor initially discussed with his minor officials.
Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) was defeated in one battle,
and Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) besieged the city but retreated.
He believed that the Righteous Army, having come from afar,
would disperse within ten days
and ordered the Imperial Provisioning Department to prepare firewood and rice for only a hundred days' rations.
After the defeat at Dàhéng (大桁),
public morale was terrified and anxious.
Fǎzhēn (法珍) and others, fearing that the populace would flee in panic,
therefore closed the city and no longer sent out troops.
Soon, when the Righteous Army had established a long siege,
and their palisades were firm and strong,
they then sallied out to fight,
but repeatedly failed to achieve victory.
The Emperor especially cherished money
and was unwilling to bestow rewards.
Fǎzhēn (法珍) repeatedly bowed his head and pleaded for them.
The Emperor said:
"Will the rebels come and take only me?
Why do you ask me for things?"
There were hundreds of planks stored in the rear hall.
When asked to use them for city defenses,
the Emperor said they were intended for building a palace
and refused to give them.
He also urged the three hundred skilled craftsmen of the Imperial Arsenal to hastily produce refined weapons,
intending them for clearing out after the siege was lifted.
The production of carved gold and silver and miscellaneous items
was more urgent than usual.
Wáng Zhēnguó (王珍國) and Zhāng Jì (張稷), fearing disaster,
led troops into the palace.
A portion of the army also entered the inner palace from the Xīshànggé (西上閣) to cut off escape,
with the Imperial Guard Fēng Yǒngzhī (豐勇之) acting as an inside accomplice.
That night,
the Emperor was playing the sheng and singing a tune called "Daughter" (女兒子) in Hándé (含德) Palace,
not yet soundly asleep.
Hearing soldiers enter,
he rushed out the north door,
wanting to return to the inner palace.
Qīngyàogé (清曜閣) was already closed.
The eunuch in charge of defense, Huáng Tàipíng (黃泰平), wounded his knee with a knife,
and he fell to the ground.
He looked back and said:
"Are you a rebellious slave?"
The Imperial Bodyguard Zhāng Qí (張齊) then beheaded him and sent his head to the King of Liáng (梁).
Xuāndé Tàihòu issued an edict saying:
“The imperial house received its mandate to rule,
and the ancestors were all sagely.
Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì established the grand mandate,
receiving the auspicious charts and records.
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì continued the brilliant martial tradition,
and Gāozōng Míng Huángdì further invigorated the grand enterprise.
However, all their reigns were not long-lasting;
their imperial chariots departed prematurely.
〔一七〕The gravity of the imperial throne
rightfully belonged to the Crown Prince.
Yet, his nature was vicious and foolish,
manifesting from his tender years.
From the time of his wet nurse
until he reached adolescence,
his cruel and dim-witted disposition
was evident in every action.
Gāozōng was intent on establishing the rightful heir,
making the eldest son the Crown Prince,
supporting him with numerous talented individuals,
and assisting him with virtuous relatives.
With internal and external support,
he hoped to avert many difficulties.
But before a full year had passed,
he indulged in slaughter and massacre.
Close relatives and kinsmen,
founding ministers and good assistants,
had their families eradicated and their clans wiped out,
one after another, within weeks and months.
All those he relied upon
were wicked and utterly treacherous;
they were all military ruffians and butchers,
with sinister and ugly appearances.
They held court power
and determined the nation's fate with their own hands,
executing the innocent
and confiscating their property.
In a blink of an eye,
they slaughtered and destroyed entire neighborhoods.
Holding the highest office,
he delighted in vulgar activities.
Wearing a precarious cap and short clothes,
he sat and slept in them.
Leaving in the morning and returning at night,
there was no end to his excesses.
He expelled the common people,
leaving no residents in the alleys.
The old and young scurried about,
with nowhere to settle.
They moved east and shielded west,
went north and drove south,
carrying the sick and bearing corpses,
filling the streets and blocking the paths.
His construction and renovation projects
continued day and night without cease.
What was built in the morning was demolished in the evening,
and what was dug in the morning was filled in the evening.
Even if adorned with luminous pearls,
it would still be considered crude;
decorated with jade earrings,
it would hardly be worth mentioning.
In the scorching summer,
when metal flowed and stones melted,
he transplanted bamboo and cultivated fruits,
not by day but by night.
Before the roots were planted,
the leaves had already withered.
Shovels and hoes were constantly in use,
with endless toil and fatigue.
He squandered the national reserves
on frivolous decorations,
and forcibly seized the people's wealth,
from near to far.
The common people were terrified
and roamed the roads as exiles.
〔一八〕When the palace treasury was depleted,
he arbitrarily seized goods from the marketplaces.
Merchants and peddlers
cried out in the streets.
He, the lord of ten thousand chariots,
personally engaged in wrestling,
raising his head and shrugging his shoulders,
displaying his skills on a pole.
The spectators were like a solid wall,
yet he showed no shame.
Fānglè and Huálín
were established in the markets,
where he sat on stalls, wielded knives,
and personally weighed goods.
Clashes of weapons and shouts
continued without cease from dusk till dawn.
To build a city without war
— how can it be compared to this?
As for the transgressions of indulging in banquets during mourning,
the disgrace of playing for three years,
the offenses of acting contrary to principle and norm,
and the impropriety of a hen crowing at dawn—
these are minor matters,
and thus can be omitted.
Even if all the bamboos of Chǔ and Yuè were used,
they would not suffice to describe his actions.
Comparing him to the rulers Xīn and Guǐ,
who could possibly match him?
Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Zhōngwǔ rose in valor,
throwing his sleeves across ten thousand li,
brilliantly serving the enlightened sage,
and assisting in the restoration.
Taking advantage of victory, he swept through,
clearing the capital city.
Yet, the petty men, ignorant,
fortified the city and defended themselves,
delaying the executions and deferring the punishments.
Suddenly, weeks and months passed.
It is fitting to swiftly suppress and stabilize,
thereby bringing peace to our nation.
Let discreet envoys be dispatched
to secretly proclaim this decree.
Let the loyal and brave rise together,
swiftly launch an attack,
expel the dim-witted and vicious one,
and escort him to an outer residence.
This unfortunate widow,
suddenly afflicted with these myriad woes,
reflects on those who live and those who have passed,
and her heart feels as if it is being cut.
Alas!
Alas!”
Another edict followed the precedent of Hàn Hǎihūn Hóu,
posthumously enfeoffing him as Dōnghūn Hóu.
Rú Fǎzhēn, Méi Chóng'ér, Wáng Xuānzhī, and others were executed.
Fēng Yǒngzhī had already died.
The historian commented: During the reign of Hàn Xuāndì,
a white tiger was captured in Nánjùn.
The one who captured it was Zhāng Wǔ,
meaning that "Wǔ" (martial) "Zhāng" (displayed) enabled the fierce beast to be subdued.
Dōnghūn Hóu's lack of virtue led to chaos,
and the path of rescue returned to order.
His personal execution
indeed ushered in great peace.
Inferring from the names of the eunuchs,
it was also the will of Heaven.
A eulogy says: Dōnghūn disregarded the Way,
matching Guǐ and comparable to Xīn.
He destroyed the established norms,
and abandoned human ethics.
He indulged in military conflict and fire,
and ultimately perished by them.
Qīng Máo (doubtful)校勘記 (textual critical note)
Běnjì No. 8, Hédì
Hédì's personal name was Bǎoróng,
courtesy name Zhìzhāo,
and he was Gāozōng's eighth son.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was enfeoffed as Suíjùn Wáng,
with two thousand households.
In the third year,
he became Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
commanding the forces garrisoned at Shítou.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was re-enfeoffed as Nánkāng Wáng,
and became Chíjǐe, Dūdū Jīng Yōng Yì Níng Liáng Nánběi Qín Qī Zhōu Jūnshì, Xī Zhōnglángjiāng, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eleventh month of the second year, on the *jiǎyín* day,
Chief Clerk Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (蕭穎冑) killed Liú Shānyáng (劉山陽), General Who Aids the State and Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī (巴西) and Zǐtóng (梓潼).
He then supported the Prince of Liáng (梁王) in raising the banner of righteousness.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
an order was issued to prepare for war.
Another order stated:
“I will personally lead the army from Jìnyáng (晉陽)
to eliminate these treacherous villains.
As military affairs are pressing,
it is fitting to extend my benevolence.
All prisoners and convicts within my jurisdiction,
regardless of the severity of their crime,
from those deserving death downwards,
shall all be pardoned and released.
Those who previously held positions
shall be reinstated to their original posts.
Generals and officials shall be promoted by one rank.
Those accompanying the campaign whose families remain in their hometowns
shall be provided with rations.
All those currently serving in miscellaneous duties within the various armies who bear arms,
after peace is restored,
shall all be freed and made commoners.
As for their meritorious service and rewards,
there will be separate regulations.”
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Prince of Liáng, Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州), was appointed as Grand Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Supervisor of All Vanguards, and Left General.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was appointed as Right General and Supervisor of All Troops Remaining.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the Prince of Liáng submitted a memorial urging the emperor to ascend the throne.
In the twelfth month, on the *yǐhài* day,
all officials urged the emperor to ascend the throne,
but he did not permit it.
On the *rénchén* day,
General of Valiant Cavalry Xiàhóu Dǎn (夏侯亶) arrived in Jiānglíng (江陵) from the capital,
claiming to carry the order of Empress Dowager Xuāndé (宣德太后):
“The Prince of Nánkāng (南康王), Western Commander of the Gentlemen-at-Arms, should succeed to the imperial throne
and preside over the myriad people.
As the purification of the palace is still pending,
he should not immediately assume the grand title.

He may temporarily be enfeoffed as Prince of Xuānchéng (宣城王), encompassing the ten commanderies of Xuānchéng (宣城), Nánlángyá (南琅邪), Nándōnghǎi (南東海), Dōngyáng (東陽), Línhǎi (臨海), Xīn'ān (新安), Xúnyáng (尋陽), Nánjùn (南郡), Jìnglíng (竟陵), and Yídū (宜都).
He shall be Chancellor of State, Protector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
be granted the Yellow Axe,
establish his own officials,
and select his bureaucracy.
The Western Commander of the Gentlemen-at-Arms’ residence and the State of Nánkāng shall remain as before.
When the army approaches the capital,
the responsible officials shall carefully follow the old institutions
and respectfully welcome him with the imperial procession.”
In the first month of the third year, on the *yǐsì* day,
the Prince received the mandate,
and a general amnesty was declared,
except for Méi Chóng'ér (梅蟲兒), Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍), and others, who were not included.
Right General Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was appointed Left Chief Clerk and promoted to General Who Guards the Army.
The Prince of Liáng was promoted to General Who Conquers the East.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
General Who Manifests Valour Yáng Gōngzé (楊公則) was appointed Governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
On the *jiǎyín* day,
the imperial banner was erected south of the city.
In the second month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Chief Clerk of Manifest Valour Wáng Màoqiān (王茂先) was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
General Who Manifests Valour Cáo Jǐngzōng (曹景宗) was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Right General Shàolíng Wáng Bǎoyōu (邵陵王寶攸) was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
On the *jǐsì* day,
all officials presented the venerable title
and requested the establishment of ancestral temples and the northern and southern suburbs.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Prince of Liáng led a large army to encamp at Miǎnkǒu (沔口).
Zhāng Chōng (張沖), Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
resisted and defended.
In the third month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Zhāng Chōng died.
General of Agile Cavalry Xuē Yuánsì (薛元嗣) and others held the city firmly.
In the spring of the first year of Zhōngxīng (中興), on the *yǐsì* day of the third month,
he ascended the imperial throne,
declared a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
Civil and military officials were granted two ranks of promotion;
orphans, widows, and the lonely who could not support themselves
were given five *hú* of grain per person.
This was the third year of Yǒngyuán (永元).
Chancellor of State Left Chief Clerk Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Prince Bǎoyì (寶義) of Jìn'ān (晉安) was appointed Minister of Works.
Prince Bǎoyuán (寶源) of Lúlíng (廬陵) was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Granted the Privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Prince Bǎoyín (寶寅) of Jiàn'ān (建安) was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州).
Counsellor to the Emperor without Portfolio Xiàhóu Xiáng (夏侯詳) was appointed Central Leader of the Army.
General Leader of the Army Xiāo Wěi (蕭偉) was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the responsible officials proposed to enfeoff the commoner Bǎojuǎn (寶卷) as Marquis of Língyáng (零陽).
An imperial edict denied this.
They then proposed to make him Prince of Fúlíng (涪陵).
The edict approved this.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was appointed acting Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and the Prince of Liáng was granted the Yellow Axe.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
General Who Conquers Barbarians Liǔ Tán (柳惔) was appointed Governor of the two provinces of Yìzhōu (益州) and Níngzhōu (寧州).
On the *jǐwèi* day,
General Who Manifests Valour Zhuāngqiū Hēi (莊丘黑) was appointed Governor of the two provinces of Liángzhōu (梁州) and Nánqín (南秦).
General Who Manifests Valour Dèng Yuánqǐ (鄧元起) was appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
In the summer, in the fourth month, on the *wùchén* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“The righteous uprising in Jīng (荊) and Yōng (雍) was founded
on the true beginning of the royal path.
Gentlemen labored with their minds,
and commoners exerted their strength.
It is fitting to give them rewards
to match their sincerity.
All armies on the eastern expedition and all forces who answered the call of righteousness
shall be universally restored to their former positions and exempted from service.”
In the fifth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the imperial carriage visited the meditation room of Zhúlín Temple to entertain the officials.
Lǔ Xiūliè (魯休烈), Administrator of Bāxī, and Xiāo Huìxùn Zǐguī (蕭惠訓子璝), Administrator of Bādōng (巴東), resisted the righteous army.
In the autumn, in the seventh month,
Wú Zǐyáng (吳子陽), commander of the Eastern Army, led thirteen armies to rescue Yǐngzhōu,
encamping at Jiāhú (加湖).
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
General Who Conquers Barbarians Wáng Màoqiān defeated them.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Màoqiān was appointed Central Protector of the Army.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Sūn Lèzǔ (孫樂祖), lord of Lúshān (魯山) City, surrendered with his city.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Xuē Yuánsì, lord of Yǐngchéng (郢城), surrendered.
In the eighth month, on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
General Who Pacifies the West Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) surrendered.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Bózhī was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and his son Hǔyá (虎牙) was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu.
In the ninth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict instructed the Prince of Liáng that if he pacified the capital,
he should act as he deemed expedient.
In the winter, in the eleventh month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
General Who Aids the State Lǐ Yuánlǚ (李元履) was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州).
On the *rénchén* day,
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat and General Who Guards the Army Xiāo Yǐngzhòu died.
Xiāo Dàn (蕭澹), a Yellow Gate Retainer, was appointed acting official for the Jīngzhōu administration.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Xiāo Guī (蕭璝) and Lǔ Xiūliè surrendered.
In the twelfth month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
Jiànkāng (建康) City was pacified.
On the *jǐsì* day,
the Empress Dowager ordered that the Prince of Liáng be made Grand Minister of War, Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat, Grand General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州),
enfeoffed as Duke of Jiàn'ān Commandery,
and that, following the precedent of Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn (武陵王遵) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
all officials pay him respects.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Prince Bǎoyín of Jiàn'ān was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽).
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Prince Bǎoyì of Jìn'ān, Minister of the Masses and Governor of Yángzhōu, was appointed Grand Commandant,
also holding the post of Minister of the Masses.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Grand Minister of War was granted twenty million cash
and five thousand bolts each of cloth and silk.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
General Who Aids the State Xiāo Hóng (蕭宏) was appointed Central Protector of the Army.
In the spring of the second year, in the first month, on the *wùxū* day,
Empress Dowager Xuāndé held court,
moving into the inner palace.
Grand Minister of War Prince of Liáng relinquished his acting authority,
paying respects as before.
On the *jǐhài* day,
General Who Pacifies the North Xiāo Bǐng (蕭昺) was appointed Supervisor of Nánqīng (南青) Province.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Grand Minister of War was made Supervisor of All Armies, both central and external,
and granted extraordinary privileges.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Wáng Liàng (王亮), Chief Clerk of the Grand Minister of War, was appointed acting Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
an imperial edict promoted the Grand Minister of War, Prince of Liáng, to Chancellor of State,
overseeing all governmental affairs,
and Protector of Yángzhōu.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Liáng, encompassing ten commanderies,
granted the ceremonial Nine Bestowals,
wore the "Far-Journey" cap,
his rank was above all other princes,
and the Chancellor of State was granted a green and purple sash.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
the newly appointed Right General Cáo Jǐngzōng was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
In the second month, on the *rénxū* day,
Prince Bǎozhì (寶晊) of Xiāngdōng (湘東) was executed.
On the *wùchén* day,
an imperial edict promoted the Duke of Liáng to Prince of Liáng
and increased his enfeoffment by ten commanderies.
On the *yǐwèi* day of the third month,
the Empress Dowager ordered five million cash to be given to the state of Liáng,
five thousand bolts of cloth,
and one thousand bolts of silk.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
Pōyáng Wáng Bǎoyín fled to the虜,
while Shàolíng Wáng Bǎoyōu, Jìnxī Wáng Bǎosōng, and Guìyáng Wáng Bǎozhēn were executed.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Liáng Wáng was granted a twelve-streamer diadem,
allowed to erect the Son of Heaven's standards,
to have an escort when going out and a clearance when entering,
to ride in a golden carriage,
drawn by six horses,
to be attended by five seasonal副車,
to have *máotóu* and *yúnhǎn* banners,
eight rows of dancers,
and to set up *zhōngjù* and *gōngxuán* musical instruments.
The appointments and ranks of the princes and princesses were to be as before.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Xiāo Xiù, the *Chàngjūn Zhǎngshǐ*, was appointed *Nánsúzhōu Cìshǐ*,
and Cài Dàogōng, newly appointed *Zhōnglǐngjūn*, was appointed *Sīzhōu Cìshǐ*.
The imperial carriage returned east to Gūshú.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the throne was abdicated to Liáng Wáng.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Lúlíng Wáng Bǎoyuán died.
In the summer, on the *xīnyǒu* day of the fourth month,
the abdication edict arrived,
and the Empress Dowager moved to an outer palace.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Liáng Wáng honored the Emperor as Bālíng Wáng,
housed him in Gūshú,
and had him observe the Qí calendar and rituals,
all as was customary.
On the *wùchén* day,
he died,
at the age of fifteen.
He was posthumously honored as Qí Hédì
and buried in Gōng'ānlíng.
The historian states: The Xià perished with Jié,
the Yīn vanished with Zhòu;
changing the rites to Heaven and the calendar
offered no reason for prolonged reign.
Yet, where the imperial mandate gathered,
Xīchǔ was revitalized,
and the divine vessel briefly arrived;
though predetermined,
to attain such a grand title and glorious name
was indeed fortunate.
A eulogy says: Hédì rose late,
cleared difficulties and purified the palace.
He understood the opportune moment and recognized destiny,
his grand eulogy marking an eternal end.
校勘記 (Collation Notes)
Treatises (志) Volume One: Rites (禮) Part One
Rites and ceremonies are complex and extensive,
vast as Heaven and Earth,
establishing nations and setting up rulers,
the beginning of human relations.
The surviving texts from the Three Dynasties
are largely found in the classics and pronouncements,
with much having been lost during the Qín era.
In the early Hàn, Shūsūn Tōng established Hàn rituals,
but Bān Gù's treatise does not record them.
Arriving in the Eastern Capital,
Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng compiled old ceremonies,
and Left Central Commandant Cài Yōng created the *Dúdùan*.
Yìng Shào and Cài Zhì both recorded contemporary events,
but Sīmǎ Biāo's work did not include them.
The Wèi dynasty, due to the great chaos at the end of the Hàn,
saw old statutes obliterated.
Court Attendant Wáng Càn and Minister of Personnel Wèi Jì collaboratively established court ceremonies,
but Yú Huàn, Wáng Shěn, Chén Shòu, and Sūn Shèng did not detail them.
For Wú, Grand Astrologer Dīng Fú collected forgotten Hàn matters;
for Shǔ, Méng Guāng and Xǔ Cí drafted numerous canons.
In the early Jìn, Minister of Works Xún Jì, based on the previous affairs of the Wèi era,
compiled the Jìn Rites,
comparing ancient and modern practices,
and amending their regulations.
Yáng Hù, Rèn Kǎi, Yǔ Jùn, and Yìng Zhēn all collaboratively edited and compiled them,
completing one hundred and sixty-five chapters.
Later, Zhì Yú and Fù Xián continued this work,
but before its completion,
the Central Plains fell.
Zhì Yú's *Juéyí Zhù*
is a remnant of this work.
In the Eastern Jìn, Grand Secretariat Diāo Xié and Grand Minister of Rites Xún Sōng
supplemented and compiled old texts,
and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness Cài Mó further followed up and edited court precedents.
In the early Sòng, reforms were introduced based on existing practices,
with matters involving numerous scholars.
What was detailed in previous histories
will not be repeated.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
Crown Prince's Infantry Commandant Fú Mànyóng memorialized to fix the rites and music.
Thereupon, an edict ordered Minister of Personnel Wáng Jiǎn to formulate new rites,
establishing scholars of rites and music and their bureaus,
appointing four scholars of old learning,
six scholars of new learning,
one chief clerk and one assistant each,
and one executive,
with the Secretariat selecting two skilled scribes.
Consequently, they gathered from previous generations
and compiled the Five Rites:
auspicious, inauspicious, guest, military, and celebratory.
The text is extensive and not fully included.
As for the ceremonies of suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and schools,
and the regulations of capping, marriage, and mourning,
matters that have changed
and are suitable for recording current events
are reserved for this treatise.
As for carriages, banners, and standards,
those that differ from or are similar to previous eras
will be presented in separate chapters.
In the seventh month of the first year of Jiànyuán,
the relevant officials memorialized:
"Regarding the rites of *jiāo* and *yīn*,
it is unclear in which year the *jiāo* should be performed?
And which ancestor should be associated with the *jiāo*?
When should the *yīn* be performed?
Is it permissible to perform the *yīn* before the *jiāo*?
Should the *Míngtáng* sacrifices also be performed in the same year as the *jiāo*?
If they should be performed,
should there be associations or not?
For the sacrifices,
what are the arrangements for the halls, palaces, and officials?"
The eight ministries' *chéngláng* and *tōngguān bóshì* deliberated.
*Cáolángzhōng* Péi Zhāomíng and *Yícáolángzhōng* Kǒng Dì deliberated:
"This year, in the seventh month, the *yīn* sacrifice should be performed.
Next year, in the first month, the southern *jiāo* and *Míngtáng* should be performed,
both with sacrifices but without associations."
*Diànzhōngláng* Sīmǎ Xiàn deliberated:
"The southern *jiāo* should have no associations, and the sacrifices should be as before.
The *Míngtáng* should have no associations,
and thus its sacrifices should be abolished.
The *yīn* sacrifice should be performed in the tenth month of this year."
Right Grand Secretariat Wáng Jiǎn deliberated: According to the *Lǐjì* and *Wángzhì*,
the Son of Heaven performs the *xiá* sacrifice first, then seasonal sacrifices;
feudal lords perform seasonal sacrifices first, then *xiá*.
In the *Chūnqiū*, in the second year of Lǔ Xī, there was a *xiá*,
and in the spring of the following year, a *dì*.
From
then on,
a *yīn* was performed twice in five years.
The *Lǐwěi Jīmìngzhēng* says:
"A *xiá* every three years,
a *dì* every five years."
The discussions in the classics and records regarding *dì*, *xiá*, and seasonal sacrifices
are
detailed,
and never considered performing *yīn* before *jiāo* an issue.
As for the importance of *jiāo* associations,
it stems from the emperor's lineage.
Thus, Dù Lín deliberated, saying:
"The Hàn enterprise arose uniquely,
not inheriting from Yáo,
so Gāodì should be associated with Heaven."
Wèi's Gāo Tánglóng deliberated that Shùn should be associated with Heaven.
Jiǎng Jì said:
"In the Hàn era's memorials,
it was argued that Yáo had already abdicated to Shùn,
and thus could not be the ancestor of Hàn.
Shùn had also abdicated to Yǔ,
and thus
could not be the ancestor of Wèi.
Now, Wǔ Huángdì should be associated with Heaven."
Jìn and Sòng followed this,
making it a precedent.
Furthermore, the *Lǐ* and *Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì* both state:
"The *Míngtáng* has five chambers.
The Son of Heaven, monthly, in its chambers, hears the pronouncements and issues decrees,
sacrifices to the spirits of the Five Emperors,
and associates them with meritorious rulers."
The *Dàdài Lǐjì* says:
"The *Míngtáng*
is where the status of feudal lords is clarified."
Xǔ Shèn's *Wǔjīng Yìyì* says:
"The
palace for issuing governance,
hence called *Míngtáng* ('Bright Hall').
*Míngtáng* means grand appearance."
The *Zhōuguān Jiàngrén Zhí* states the *Míngtáng* has five chambers.
Zhèng Xuán said:
"The Zhōu people's *Míngtáng* had five
chambers,
with one chamber for the Emperor."
He never heard of Wén Wáng's bedchamber.
Zhèng Zhì Zhào Shāng asked:
"Some interpreters say that the Son of Heaven's ancestral temple system is like the *Míngtáng*;
does this mean the *Míngtáng* is
the Wén temple?"
Zhèng replied:
"The *Míngtáng* primarily sacrifices to the Lord on High,
with Wén Wáng associated,
just as Hòujì is associated with the *jiāo* sacrifice to Heaven."
Yuán Xiàoní
said:
“The Míngtáng 明堂, the palace that emulates Heaven,
is originally for sacrificing to the Tiāndì 天帝 (Heavenly Thearch).
To have Wénwáng 文王 as a co-sacrificed deity,
it is acceptable to assign one’s father a place in Heaven.
However, to drag the Tiāndì 天帝 down to be alongside human ghosts
is not
righteous.”
In the thirteenth year of Tàiyuán 太元 (388 CE),
Sūn Qízhī 孫耆之’s deliberation
stated:
“The jiāo 郊 (suburban sacrifice) is for sacrificing to Heaven,
hence Hòujì 后稷 is co-sacrificed with it.
The Míngtáng 明堂 is for sacrificing to the Dì 帝 (Thearch),
hence
Wénwáng 文王 is co-sacrificed with it.
From this perspective,
the jiāo 郊 is the seat of Huángtiān 皇天 (August Heaven),
and the Míngtáng 明堂 is the temple of Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High).”
Xú Mò 徐邈 said:
“The term ‘co-sacrificed’
necessarily implies a divine
principal deity.
If the jiāo 郊 is the Altar of Heaven,
then the Hall is not the Temple of Wénwáng 文王.”
The Shǐjì 史記 (Records of the Grand Historian) states that Zhào Wǎn 趙綰 and Wáng Zāng 王臧 desired to establish a Míngtáng 明堂,
but at that time, there was no co-sacrifice at the jiāo 郊.
The Hàn 漢 dynasty also sacrificed to
the Wǔzhì 五畤 (Five Altars) at Fén’yīn 汾陰,
which was a sacrifice to the Wǔdì 五帝 (Five Thearchs),
and likewise had no co-sacrifice at the jiāo 郊.
Some deliberators suggested that on the day of the Southern Jiāo 郊,
the Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High) had already been honored.
If the Míngtáng 明堂 were again specially sacrificed to without a co-sacrificed deity,
then two sacrifices on the same day
would be considered a defilement according to righteousness.
However, in antiquity, the jiāo 郊 and Míngtáng 明堂 were originally not on the same day.
Cài Yōng’s 蔡邕 Dúdùan 獨斷 says:
“After sacrificing at the Southern Jiāo 郊,
the sacrifice is concluded,
then followed by the Northern Jiāo 郊,
then the Míngtáng 明堂, Gāomiào 高廟 (High Temple), and Shìzǔmiào 世祖廟 (Temple of the Ancestor of the Dynasty),
which are
called the Wǔgòng 五供 (Five Offerings).”
Mǎ Róng 馬融 said:
“The sacrifices to Heaven at the jiāo 郊
were all performed in the Xià 夏 calendar’s first month.
As the Wǔqì 五氣 (Five Vapors) took their turn in office,
with some flourishing and others waning,
each according to its season,
they were manifested in the altars of the four jiāo 郊.
The four
seasons complete the year,
and their functions mutually support each other.
It was also in this month that the Míngtáng 明堂 was generally honored.”
This is evidence that the Southern Jiāo 郊 and Míngtáng 明堂 were on separate days.
In recent times, due to simplification,
it is
performed on the same day as the jiāo 郊,
yet there is no concern of defilement.
Why?
Although the nature of their sacrifice is the same,
the reason for making the sacrifice is different.
Kǒng Cháo 孔晁 said that
the Five Thearchs assist Heaven in
transformation and nurturing,
hence there is the rite of accompanying sacrifice,
which is the honoring of Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High).
As for the four jiāo 郊 and the Míngtáng 明堂,
these are places for the principal sacrifice.
It is like meritorious officials receiving accompanying offerings,
how could
their private temples then be abolished?
Moreover, at times when the Míngtáng 明堂 had a co-sacrificed deity,
the Southern Jiāo 郊 also honored Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High).
This then did not raise doubts about being on the same day.
Now, why is there an objection to being on the same
day?
Furthermore, the Lǐjì 禮記 (Book of Rites) says:
“The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the four directions, mountains and rivers, and the Wǔsì 五祀 (Five Sacrifices)
throughout the year.”
The Yáodiǎn 堯典 (Canon of Yáo) in the Shàngshū 尚書 (Book of Documents) says:
“All were regularly arranged and plain.”
The Shī 詩 (Book of Odes) says:
“Reverently serve the Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High),
thereby holding many blessings.”
Based on these various principles,
the four directions and mountains and rivers
must still receive offerings.
The Wǔdì 五帝 (Five Thearchs), great deities,
cannot be omitted by righteousness.
In the
first month of the second year of Huángchū 黃初 (221 CE) under Wèi Wéndì 魏文帝,
sacrifices were made to Heaven and Earth and the Míngtáng 明堂.
In the first month of the first year of Tàihé 太和 (227 CE) under Míngdì 明帝,
Wǔhuángdì 武皇帝 (Emperor Wǔ) was co-sacrificed with Heaven,
and Wénhuángdì 文皇帝 (Emperor Wén) was co-sacrificed with Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High).
Thus, during the Huángchū 黃初 period, the Southern Jiāo 郊 and Míngtáng 明堂
both had no co-sacrificed deity.
Furthermore, there are many differing opinions regarding the day of the jiāo 郊 sacrifice and the color of the sacrificial animals.
The Jiāotèshēng 郊特牲 (Single Victim at the Suburban Altar) says:
“The jiāo 郊 sacrifice uses the xīn 辛 day.
This was the beginning of the Zhōu 周 dynasty’s jiāo 郊 sacrifice.”
Lú Zhí 盧植 said:
“The word xīn 辛
means to renew and purify oneself.”
Zhèng Xuán 鄭玄 said:
“The use of the xīn 辛 day
is because people should fast, purify themselves, and be made anew and clean.”
Since the Hàn 漢 and Wèi 魏 dynasties,
sometimes dīng 丁 or jǐ 己 days were used,
but the use of
xīn 辛 was often more common.
Examining the classical references,
the xīn 辛 day is deemed appropriate.
The Jiāotèshēng 郊特牲 also says that
the sacrificial animals and silks for the jiāo 郊
should be of the correct color.
Miáo Xí 繆襲, citing the Jìfǎ 祭法 (Laws of Sacrifice),
said that for Heaven and Earth,
a red calf was used,
which was valued by the Zhōu 周 house.
As the Wèi 魏 dynasty took jiànchǒu 建丑 as its 正 (first month),
the sacrificial animals should preferably be white.
The Báihǔtōng 白虎通 (Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall) says that
the Three Kings sacrificed to Heaven,
all using the Xià 夏 calendar’s first month,
the reason
being
that the Xià 夏 calendar’s first month corresponds to Heaven’s numbers.
The Wèi 魏 dynasty used a different calendar,
hence the different colors for sacrificial animals.
Now, upon the Great Qí 齊 receiving the Mandate,
it established the jiànyín 建寅 (first month of the Yín 寅 branch) and created a new calendar.
The sacrificial animals for the jiāo 郊 and temples
will
all follow the precedent of Jìn 晉 and Sòng 宋.
It is appropriate to perform the yīn 殷 sacrifice to the ancestral temples in the tenth month of this year.
From now on,
the yīn 殷 sacrifice will be performed twice every five years.
Next year, on the first xīn 辛 day of the first month,
the rite will be performed at the Southern Jiāo 郊.
It is appropriate
to perform it on the same day,
and also sacrifice at the Míngtáng 明堂.
Then, on the next xīn 辛 day,
offer sacrifices at the Northern Jiāo 郊.
And neither will have a co-sacrificed deity.
The color of the sacrificial animals
will follow the old regulations.
The imperial edict said:
“Agreed.
The Míngtáng 明堂 should be further deliberated.”
The officials concerned again memorialized:
“Regarding the Míngtáng 明堂, there is no explicit text in the rites.
We only take the Xiàojīng 孝經 (Classic of Filial Piety) as the standard.
We humbly believe that the intention behind establishing sacrifices
is that if there is a principal deity with a co-sacrificed deity, then the sacrifice is performed;
if there is no co-sacrificed deity, then it ceases.
We foolishly believe that since it is already co-sacrificed with Shàngdì 上帝 (Lord on High),
then Shàngdì 上帝 is the principal deity.
Even if there is no co-sacrificed deity now,
the sacrifice should not be omitted.
Xú Mò 徐邈, a great scholar of recent times,
whose judgments were always fair and balanced,
said: ‘If the jiāo 郊 is the Altar of Heaven,
then the Hall is not the Temple of Wénwáng 文王.’
This is indeed clear evidence.
The various internal and external offices have already finalized their deliberations.
If we inquire further,
there will ultimately be no different opinions.
Other scholars, following historical records,
have exhausted their limited insights.
Since Your Sacred Majesty still has doubts,
and your subordinates dare not elaborate,
the appropriateness of establishing or abolishing it
awaits Your Majesty’s divine judgment.”
The imperial edict said:
“Follow the old practice.”
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán
Shìzǔ ascended the throne.
That autumn,
the officials concerned presented a memorial:
"Observing the succession to the throne in previous dynasties,
some have continued the sacrificial year of the previous reign,
while others have started anew.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
there has been no uniform practice.
This year, the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth (jiāo) were performed in the first month.
We are uncertain whether next year the northern and southern jiāo sacrifices should be offered and the Míngtáng worshipped or not?"
In accordance with old practice, the matter was widely submitted to the eight bureaus, the secretariat chiefs, and the erudites for deliberation.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn deliberated:
"According to records, Qín, when it was a feudal state,
performed mixed sacrifices to various zhǐ altars.
When Shǐhuáng unified all under Heaven,
there was no established system of sacrifices.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn, having received the mandate,
continued the four zhǐ altars in Yōng and established the northern zhǐ altar,
beginning the sacrifices to the Five Emperors,
but the jiāo altars were not yet fixed.
In the sixth year of Emperor Wén,
Xīnyuán Píng proposed establishing the Five Emperors' temple at Wèiyáng for the first time.
Emperor Wǔ, upon first reaching Yōng for the jiāo sacrifices, saw the five zhǐ altars.
Afterwards, he regularly performed jiāo sacrifices at Yōng once every three years.
In the fourth year of Yuándǐng,
the altar to Hòutǔ was first established at Fén’yīn.
The next year,
the altar to Tàiyī was established at Gānquán.
From then on,
jiāo sacrifices were performed every two years,
alternating with Yōng.
When Emperor Chéng first ascended the throne,
Prime Minister Kuāng Héng established the northern and southern jiāo altars in Cháng'ān.
During the reigns of Emperor Āi and Emperor Píng,
the Gānquán and Fén’yīn sacrifices were resumed.
In the fifth year of Yuánshǐ under Emperor Píng,
Wáng Mǎng memorialized to follow Kuāng Héng's deliberation,
restoring the northern and southern jiāo altars in Cháng'ān.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ under Emperor Guāngwǔ,
the site for jiāo sacrifices was established in Luòyáng.
Wèi and Jìn followed suit,
largely adhering to the Hàn precedents.
Although there were occasional discrepancies,
mostly they were performed in alternate years.
As for rulers who succeeded to the throne,
there was no consistent practice.
It is appropriate to establish a fixed system.
Examining the southern jiāo sacrifices in the third year of Tàiníng under Emperor Míng of Jìn,
he passed away in the ninth month of that year.
Emperor Chéng ascended the throne,
and the next year, upon changing the reign title, performed the jiāo sacrifices.
The southern jiāo sacrifices in the second year of Xián'ān under Emperor Jiǎnwén,
he passed away in the seventh month of that year.
Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
and the next year, upon changing the reign title, also performed the jiāo sacrifices.
The southern jiāo sacrifices in the first month of the thirtieth year of Yuánjiā under Sòng,
he passed away in the second month of that year.
Emperor Xiàowǔ succeeded to the throne,
and the next year, upon changing the reign title, also performed the jiāo sacrifices.
These are clear precedents from two dynasties,
which can be followed.
Therefore, it is appropriate to offer sacrifices at the two jiāo altars in the first month of next year,
and reverently sacrifice at the Míngtáng.
From then on,
it should follow the old practice of alternate years."
Shàngshū Lìng Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Zhāng Xù and seventeen others all agreed with Wáng Jiǎn's deliberation.
The imperial edict
read, "Approved."
In the first year of Yǒngmíng, when the southern jiāo sacrifice was due,
Lìchūn (Start of Spring) fell after the jiāo sacrifice,
and Shìzǔ wished to postpone the jiāo.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn memorialized:
"According to the Lǐjì, Jiāotèshēng says: 'The jiāo sacrifice
is to welcome the arrival of the longest day (winter solstice);
it is a great offering to Heaven and honors the sun.'
The Yìshuō says: 'The jiāo sacrifices of the Three Kings
all used the Xià calendar's first month.'
Lú Zhí said: 'The Xià calendar's first month is after the winter solstice.
The commentary says, "Sacrifice at jiāo when the hibernating insects stir," referring to this.'
Therefore, the Yuánqiū and jiāo sacrifices each proceed independently,
without conflict.
Zhèng Xuán said: 'In the month of jiànyín, day and night divide (equinox), and days lengthen.'
Wáng Sù said: 'The Zhōu dynasty performed sacrifices to Heaven at the Yuánqiū in winter,
and in the first month, again sacrificed to Heaven to pray for grain.'
The Jìfǎ states: 'Burning wood on the great altar,'
which refers to the Yuánqiū.
The Chūnqiūzhuàn says: 'Sacrifice at jiāo when the hibernating insects stir,'
which refers to praying for grain.
Carefully examining these two texts from the Lǐ and zhuàn,
each has its own meaning,
and the two explanations by Lú and Wáng
seem to correspond perfectly.
The central court simplified the two mounds by combining them with the two jiāo altars,
so the current jiāo ritual
is meant to give thanks to Heaven,
and also encompasses praying for grain.
Since it is not entirely for praying for agriculture,
why must one await the stirring of hibernating insects?
The court historians only saw the meaning from the zhuàn,
but did not fully grasp the purport of the Lǐ.
Furthermore, examining the southern jiāo sacrifice on Xīnchǒu, the third day of the first month in the first year of Jǐngpíng,
Lìchūn fell on the eleventh day of that month.
The southern jiāo sacrifice on Xīnwèi, the sixth day of the first month in the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā,
Lìchūn fell on the eighth day of that month.
These are clear recent precedents,
showing that an earlier jiāo sacrifice followed by Lìchūn was not considered problematic.
If anyone considers the new moon on the first day of the month as an impediment,
then in the first year of Xiánkāng under Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
he put on the ritual cap on the first day of the first month
and personally sacrificed at the southern jiāo on the second day.
The gravity of putting on the ritual cap,
with all officials arrayed,
was carried out without hesitation, even during the period of ritual fasting.
Now, the new moon falls within the fasting period;
this is a previous standard.
If the Sacred Heart is overly reverent,
preferring strict purity,
on the day of the new moon,
dispersed officials should be prepared,
and those not within the fasting period
should establish a separate tented enclosure outside the stopping-carriage gate.
If the sun's color appears unusual,
they should be arranged in front of the enclosure.
Observing this seems appropriate,
and there is no need to postpone the day."
This was followed.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
Cíbù Lángzhōng Cài Lǚ deliberated:
"The jiāo sacrifices and the Míngtáng
should originally be on different days.
The Hòu Hàn Dōngjīng Lǐyí Zhì states: 'After the southern jiāo ritual is completed,
it is followed by the northern jiāo, Míngtáng, Gāomiào, and Shìzǔmiào,
which are called the Five Offerings.'
Cài Yōng's source also states this.
In recent times, due to simplification,
the jiāo and Míngtáng are on the same day.
For next year's jiāo sacrifices,
a fixed standard should be established."
Tàixué Bóshì Wáng Yòu deliberated:
"In the first month of next year, on the first Xīn day,
the southern jiāo should be sacrificed.
On the next Xīn day,
rites should be performed at the Míngtáng.
On the subsequent Xīn day,
the northern jiāo should be worshipped."
Jiān Bóshì Liú Màn deliberated:
"In the fifth year of Yuándǐng of Hàn,
rites were performed on Xīnsì.
Afterwards, the jiāo day
rarely differed.
In the fourth month of Yuánfēng first year, on Guǐmǎo,
they ascended Mount Tài for the fēng ceremony
and sat in the Míngtáng.
In the fifth year, on Jiǎzǐ,
Emperor Gāozǔ was associated (with Heaven).
The Hàn imperial jiāo sacrifices
were not entirely in the emperor's direct domain,
hence the sacrificial month
varied.
Since Yǒngpíng of the Later Hàn,
the Míngtáng was located south of the capital,
and the jiāo was on the shàngdīng day.
Therefore, the three sacrifices
could all be performed in the first month.
Although the jiāo had a fixed day,
the Míngtáng still had no set date.
Why is this?
Jiāo on Dīng and shè on Jiǎ
can be followed if there is an explanation,
but without textual basis in the classics,
it is difficult to invent it.
Therefore, one must calculate an auspicious day,
and not sacrifice on Yín or Chǒu days.
Moreover, in the rituals of offerings,
there is no sharing of duties,
except that Hàn combined the morning sacrifice with giving thanks to Heaven.
If we follow the Five Offerings in the Hànshū,
then the northern jiāo should be sacrificed first,
and then the Míngtáng.
But this would mean Earth precedes Heaven in receiving offerings,
which is unacceptable."
Cài Zhòngxióng (蔡仲xióng), concurrently acting as Tàicháng丞 (太常丞), discussed:
"Zhèng Zhì (鄭志) says, 'On the first Xīn (辛) day of the first month,
sacrifice to Hòujì (后稷) in the southern suburb,
then return to the Míngtáng (明堂)
to make Wénwáng (文王) the co-sacrificed deity.'
Therefore, when the Sòng (宋) dynasty first established the Míngtáng,
they immediately performed the sacrifice upon returning from the suburban sacrifice;
this follows Zhèng Zhì's (鄭志) theory.
The compiler of the 'Zhì' (志) probably erred,
it was not Xuán's (玄) intention.
Xuán (玄) said, 'It is unclear which month the Zhōu (周) Míngtáng (明堂) used;
according to the Yuèlìng (月令), it was in the last month of autumn.'
Examining Xuán's (玄) commentary on the Yuèlìng (月令) regarding the great feast for the Emperor in the last month of autumn, it says, '
The great feast involves sacrificing to all Five Emperors.'
It also says, 'The great feast is held in the Míngtáng (明堂),
with Wén (文) and Wǔ (武) as co-sacrificed deities.'
That time is autumn,
far from the 'Awakening of Insects' (啟蟄).
Moreover, the Zhōulǐ (周禮) 'Dà Sī Yuè' (大司樂) states, 'For all great sacrifices,
the instruments are suspended the night before.'
The purpose of suspending instruments the night before
is because the ceremonies are performed at dawn;
if ceremonies were performed after dark,
there would be no need for pre-suspension.
If ceremonies are indeed performed at dawn,
how can one then wait for the return from the suburban sacrifice?
The Dōngjīng Lǐyí Zhì (東京禮儀志) does not record the exact time of the sacrifice,
but the 'Zhì' (志) states, 'On the night of the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
cooked offerings are presented when eight kès (刻) of the night watch remain;
on the night of the Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifice,
cooked offerings are presented when seven kès (刻) of the night watch remain.'
It implies that the Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifice occurs one kè (刻) before the suburban sacrifice,
yet the presentation of offerings and performance of music
still await the return from the suburban sacrifice.
Wèi (魏) Gāotáng Lóng (高堂隆) memorialized,
'The ninth day for the southern suburban sacrifice,
the tenth day for the northern suburban sacrifice,
the eleventh day for the Míngtáng (明堂),
and the twelfth day for the ancestral temple.'
According to Lóng's (隆) statement,
this was the established system at that time,
meaning that during the Zhōu (周) dynasty, the two Hàn (漢) dynasties, and Wèi (魏),
these ceremonies were not held on the same day.
The Lǐ (禮) prescribes Xīn (辛) for the suburban sacrifice,
while the Shū (書) prescribes Dīng (丁) for the sacrifice.
Both Xīn (辛) and Dīng (丁) are suitable;
it is appropriate to choose carefully at the time."
Gù Xiànzhī (顧憲之), Táishù (太尉) Aide-de-camp, discussed:
"The Chūnqiū Zhuàn (春秋傳) states that the suburban sacrifice is held on the first Xīn (辛) day of the first month,
and the Lǐjì (禮記) also says that Xīn (辛) is used for the suburban sacrifice,
while the Shàngshū (尚書) uniquely states that Dīngsì (丁巳) is used for sacrifices in the suburb.
Earlier scholars believed that Xīn (辛) is three days before Jiǎ (甲),
and Dīng (丁) is three days after Jiǎ (甲),
which can be used for ceremonies serving the celestial deities.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng (永平) of the Later Hàn (後漢), on the Xīnwèi (辛未) day of the first month,
Gūangwǔ Huángdì (光武皇帝) was sacrificed to in the Míngtáng (明堂).
Since Xīn (辛) is the usual day for the suburban sacrifice,
and the suburban sacrifice precedes the Míngtáng (明堂) ceremony,
it is impossible to have the Míngtáng (明堂) ceremony without the suburban sacrifice first.
Thus, it is logical that the suburban sacrifice precedes the Míngtáng (明堂)."
Liáng Wáng (梁王), Sītú (司徒) Xīgé Jìjiǔ (西閤祭酒), discussed:
"Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) commentary on the Xiàojīng (孝經) says, 'Shàngdì (上帝) is also another name for Tiān (天).'
According to Zhèng's (鄭) meaning,
the words Dì (帝) and Tiān (天) are not distinct.
That they have been performed on the same day in recent times
also has its basis.
In the first year of Tàihé (太和) of Wèi (魏), on the Dīngwèi (丁未) day of the first month,
Wǔ Huángdì (武皇帝) was sacrificed to in the suburb to match Heaven,
and Wén Huángdì (文皇帝) was sacrificed to in the Míngtáng (明堂) to match Shàngdì (上帝).
This serves as a precedent for what has been done."
Jiāng Yān (江淹), Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍), discussed:
"The suburban sacrifice is to Heaven,
the Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifice is to the Five Emperors.
This is not what is meant by 'repeated defilement in a single day,'
so there is no need for reform."
Lù Chéng (陸澄), Shàngshū (尚書), discussed:
"Remaining texts and past events
are preserved in old books.
The suburban sacrifice and ancestral sacrifice are geographically close,
making it possible to hold them on the same day.
However, not holding them on the same day
is based on the principle that they must be distinct.
In the fifth year of Yuánshǐ (元始), on the Xīnwèi (辛未) day of the sixth month of the first month,
Gāohuángdì (高皇帝) was sacrificed to in the suburb to match Heaven;
on the Dīnghài (丁亥) day of the twenty-second,
Xiàowén (孝文) was sacrificed to in the Míngtáng (明堂) to match Shàngdì (上帝).
In the second year of Yǒngpíng (永平), on the Xīnwèi (辛未) day of the first month,
the Five Emperors were sacrificed to in the Míngtáng (明堂),
with Gūangwǔ Huángdì (光武皇帝) as the co-sacrificed deity.
In the second year of Yuánhé (元和) of Zhāngdì (章帝),
he went on an inspection tour to Dàizōng (岱宗),
performed the chái (柴) sacrifice,
and the next day,
sacrificed to the Five Emperors in the Míngtáng (明堂).
The chái (柴) sacrifice to the mountain and the sacrifice to the earth
were still not held on the same day;
it is even clearer from this precedent that the suburban and Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifices should be distinct.
Chén Zhōng (陳忠) memorialized, 'In the third year of Yánguāng (延光), on the thirteenth day of the first month, the southern suburban sacrifice;
on the fourteenth day, the northern suburban sacrifice;
on the fifteenth day, the Míngtáng (明堂);
on the sixteenth day, the ancestral temple;
on the seventeenth day, the temple of Shìzǔ (世祖).'
Zhòngyuǎn's (仲遠) five sacrifices
and Shàotǒng's (紹統) five offerings
all align with Chén Zhōng's (陳忠) memorial.
Gāotáng Lóng's (高堂隆) memorial
assigned one day each for the two suburban sacrifices, the Míngtáng (明堂), and the ancestral temple.
Zhì Yú's (摯虞) new ritual proposal argued for three days between the Míngtáng (明堂) and the southern suburban sacrifice,
which is evidence that the yīn (禋) sacrifice to Heaven and the xiǎng (饗) sacrifice to the Emperor are not held on the same day.
Furthermore, it has been explained in detail by ancients
that Shàngdì (上帝) is not Tiān (天).
Therefore, the Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifice should now follow the ancient practice of being held after the northern suburban sacrifice.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, only the southern suburban sacrifice involved the grand imperial retinue (dàjià, 大駕);
from the northern suburban sacrifice downwards, the imperial retinue (chējià, 車駕) was reduced by two tenths.
Therefore, the current Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifice
should not involve the grand imperial retinue."
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉), Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), discussed:
"The Former Hàn (前漢) held them on separate days,
and the Later Hàn (後漢) also did not hold them on the same day.
The precedents of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) do not clarify the similarities or differences.
When Sòng (宋) established the Míngtáng (明堂),
they only based it on the meaning of 'proceeding from the suburban sacrifice to the palace,'
not fully understanding the intent of sacrificing to Heaven and feasting the Emperors.
Why?
The suburban altar sacrifice to Heaven
commences at dawn,
and the return to sacrifice in the Míngtáng (明堂)
would then be in the afternoon.
Although there is a reason for the sacrifice,
such frequent defilement is excessive.
The proposal for separate days
is thus more profound in principle.
The Chūnqiū Gǎnjīngfú (春秋感精符) states, 'The king takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother.'
Therefore, the northern suburban sacrifice
should precede the Míngtáng (明堂) ceremony.
During the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties, the northern suburban sacrifice
was also personally attended by the emperor.
In Tàiníng (泰寧) of Jìn (晉), there was an imperial edict,
but it was not yet followed.
In the eighth year of Xiánhé (咸和),
construction was finally completed,
and Gù Hé (顧和), the Tàicháng (太常), advocated for personal attendance.
During Kāng Huáng's (康皇) reign,
this was already put into practice.
The Sòng (宋) dynasty merely followed old customs,
not yet having time for reform.
Now, it is appropriate for the emperor to personally attend the northern suburban sacrifice.
Next year, on the first Xīn (辛) day of the first month, sacrifice to Hàotiān (昊天);
on the next Xīn (辛) day, sacrifice to Hòutǔ (后土);
on the following Xīn (辛) day, sacrifice in the Míngtáng (明堂).
The Emperor shall personally attend all these.
The ceremonies for chariots and attire
shall largely follow the Hàn (漢) system.
The southern suburban sacrifice shall use the grand imperial retinue (dàjià, 大駕),
while the northern suburban and Míngtáng (明堂) sacrifices shall be reduced to the ordinary imperial retinue (fǎjià, 法駕).
The ceremonial robes (gǔnmiǎn, 袞冕) shall be used for all sacrifices."
An imperial edict stated,
"Approved."
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Yǔ Tánlóng, a Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, memorialized:
"I humbly observe that inside and outside the mound on the Southern Altar,
during the Yǒngmíng reign, a tiled building was erected,
grand in scale and design.
Upon examining the classics and histories,
there is no basis or precedent for this.
According to the Zhōu Lǐ,
the sacrifice to Heaven is performed at the round mound (Yuánqiū),
taking the meaning of utilizing a high place.
The mound is made in the southern suburb
to occupy the yang position.
Therefore, it should be high and open,
emphasizing that it illuminates the bright Heaven above
and allows vital energy to flow all around.
From the Qín and Hàn dynasties onwards,
although the suburban sacrifices varied,
there was never any additional construction of palaces or chambers
within the altar area.
What was the reason for this?
It was precisely to show sincerity and reverence for Heaven,
not to exalt oneself by building structures,
and at the same time, to make the ceremony vast and open,
always striving to be expansive and far-reaching.
During the Yuánjiā period of Sòng, at the Southern Altar,
a small temporary tent was erected at the time for resting.
In the Tàishǐ period, it was slightly expanded and improved.
At the beginning of Yǒngmíng, it gradually became higher and more elaborate.
In recent years, artisans then proposed building a tiled house.
Did previous emperors
blindly undertake such constructions for the sacrifice to Heaven?
The reason they did not do so
was deeply rooted in sentiment and principle.
The records state: 'Sweeping the ground for sacrifice
is for its simplicity;
utensils of pottery and gourds
are for the nature of Heaven and Earth.'
Therefore, 'utmost reverence has no embellishment,'
and 'plainness is valued.'
I humbly submit that the suburban ceremony should emulate simplicity and rest,
without requiring tall and large structures,
to demonstrate the principle of humility, reverence, and solemnity.
Hopefully, this will be approved by the Great Spirit above
and satisfy the aspirations of the multitude below."
An imperial edict stated:
"Submit this to the relevant authorities for detailed deliberation."
Xú Jǐngsōng, an assistant instructor of the Guózǐ, deliberated:
"I humbly examine the Sānlǐ.
For the two sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
at the northern and southern suburbs,
it only specifies the use of sacrificial animals
and utensils of pottery and gourds.
It does not record the rites for the monarch's resting place.
Although the construction of tiled buildings now differs from (beams) [tents],
neither is a thousand-year-old precedent,
so it is advisable to adhere to established customs."
Hè Yáng, a professor of the Tàixué, deliberated:
The Zhōu Lǐ states, "When the king offers a sacrifice (lǚ) to the Supreme Lord (Shàngdì),
a felt mat is spread,
and an imperial couch (huángdí) is set up."
If the state has a reason for sacrifice,
it is also called lǚ.
A felt mat means
a felt bed within a tent.
I have not heard of palaces or structures being placed at the suburban altar.
Wáng Chī, concurrently Zuo Chéng, deliberated that
sweeping the ground for sacrifice at the suburb
implies there is no proposal to construct buildings.
All agreed with Tánlóng.
Yú Yán, a Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, deliberated,
believing that
"sincere devotion is expressed,
confined to a single altar.
During the Hàn dynasty's suburban sacrifice,
the emperor received offerings at Gānquán,
and the Son of Heaven prostrated himself from the bamboo palace.
The resting hall was far from the altar grounds.
After the suburban ritual was completed,
he would then proceed there.
Between a tiled hall and a curtained palace,
I believe there is no fundamental difference."
Lǐ Huī, a Cíbù Láng, deliberated:
The Zhōu Lǐ states, "For all sacrifices, their 'lǚmù' (traveling tents) are erected,
and the 'shīcì' (place for the representative of the deceased) is arranged."
The shī would have a tent.
Zhòngshī said: "Shīcì is
the changing tent where the shī for the sacrifice resides."
The text for "all sacrifices"
is not limited to suburban sacrifices.
The mention of establishing a shī
should logically pertain to ancestral temples.
In ancient times, tents were erected;
today, they are rooms and chambers.
If the "lǚmù" of ancestral temples
can be transformed into permanent structures,
why can't the "felt mats" of suburban sacrifices
be similarly transformed into eaves and roofs?
Tánlóng's proposal was not adopted.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ, there was a drought.
The officials discussed performing the Yú (雩) sacrifice at the Míngtáng.
Hé Tóngzhī (何佟之), the director of the Ministry of Rites, argued:
“The Zhōulǐ (周禮) states that the Sīwū (司巫) says, ‘If the state suffers a great drought,
then they lead the shamans and dance the yú (雩).’
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) commented, ‘Yú (雩)
is a sacrifice for drought.
The Son of Heaven performs it for the Shàngdì (上帝),
and feudal lords and those below them perform it for the spirits of the superior dukes.’
It also states that the Nǚwū (女巫) (female shamans) say, ‘In times of severe drought, they dance the yú (雩).’
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) commented, ‘Using female shamans to dance the drought sacrifice
is to honor the yin (陰).’
Zhèng Zhòng (鄭眾) commented, ‘One seeks rain with female shamans.’
The Lǐjì (禮記) ‘Yuèlíng’ (月令) says, ‘Officials are commanded to offer sacrifices for the people to the mountains, rivers, and hundred springs.
Then a great yú (雩) is offered to the Dì (帝),
using grand music.
Then all counties are commanded to offer yú (雩) sacrifices to the hundred lords, ministers, and officials who have benefited the people,
to pray for grain harvests.’
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) commented, ‘The yang (陽) energy is abundant, leading to constant drought.
Mountains, rivers, and hundred springs
are capable of raising clouds and bringing rain.
The sources of all waters are the hundred springs;
one must first sacrifice to their origins.
Yú (雩)
is a sacrifice of lamentation and prayer for rain.
Yú Dì (雩帝)
refers to constructing an altar beside the southern suburban altar,
sacrificing to the Five Elemental Dì (五精之帝),
and associating them with the Former Dì (先帝).
From the drums and chimes to the zhù (柷) and yú (敔) is grand music;
other yú (雩) rituals only use singing and dancing.
The hundred lords, ministers, and officials
were, in ancient times, from the superior dukes downwards,
referring to those like Gōulóng (勾龍) and Hòujì (后稷).
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn (春秋傳) says, “When the dragon appears, yú (雩) is performed.”
[The appropriate time for the yú (雩)] should be in the fourth month.’
is a sacrifice to pray for rain.
The commentary says, “When the dragon appears, yú (雩) is performed,”
referring to the fourth month.
If there is a great drought in the fifth or sixth month,
yú (雩) is also used;
the Lǐ (禮) explains the meaning of yú (雩) in the fifth month.’
In the Yǒnghé (永和) era of Jìn (晉),
the Censor-in-Chief submitted a memorial stating that
the yú (雩) ritual involved building an altar south of the capital,
praying to the Shàngdì (上帝) and the hundred lords,
with eight rows of sixty-four dancing children,
singing the ‘Yúnhàn’ (雲漢) poem,
all in the first month of summer.
If rain was obtained,
a grand sacrifice (tàiláo 太牢) was offered in thanks.
At that time, the Academicians discussed it,
stating that an altar already existed,
and the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties each sought their own precedents.
The ‘Yuèlíng’ (月令) says, ‘Officials are commanded to pray and sacrifice to the mountains, rivers, and hundred springs,
then perform the great yú (雩).’
It also says, ‘Then all counties are commanded to perform yú (雩) sacrifices to the hundred lords, ministers, and officials.’
Therefore, the objects of the great yú (雩) sacrifice
should only be the Five Elemental Dì (五精之帝).
Gōumáng (勾芒) and the other five deities,
