according to Zhèng Xuán’s (鄭玄) explanation,
should appropriately be associated in the offering at the courtyard.
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said, ‘The yú (雩) altar is beside the southern suburban altar,’
but did not specify east or west.
Considering that the earth's path honors the right,
and the yú (雩) altar is of lesser importance compared to the suburban altar,
it should reasonably be on the left.
It is appropriate to build the altar to the east of the suburban altar,
outside its domain.
Since the Five Dì (五帝) are sacrificed to,
the altar should be round.
Regarding the height and width of the yú (雩) altar,
there are no clear texts in the Lǐ (禮) or Zhuàn (傳).
Examining the Jìnlǐ (覲禮) where the Fāngmíng (方明) sacrifice is established,
the altar is built four feet high,
using six jade objects such as guī (珪) and zhāng (璋),
to honor the spirits of Heaven, Earth, and the Four Directions.
The king leads the feudal lords in personally performing the ritual,
which serves to teach reverence for the revered.
The yú (雩) sacrifice to the Five Dì (五帝)
can generally follow this precedent.
Therefore, the altar built now should appropriately be four feet high,
and its width and circumference should also be based on four as the standard,
with a diameter of four zhàng (丈),
a circumference of twelve zhàng (丈),
and four steps.
The positions of the Five Dì (五帝) should be arranged,
each according to its direction,
following the ceremonial rules of the Míngtáng.
Since Huáng Qí (皇齊) associated Shìzǔ (世祖) with the Five Elements at the Míngtáng,
it is now also appropriate to associate him in the offerings at the yú (雩) altar.
In ancient times, the suburban sacrifice in mid-spring prayed for good harvests,
and the yúyíng (雩禜) in mid-summer prayed for sweet rain.
their purpose is one.
The Lǐ (禮) only mentions reporting to Heaven at the winter solstice,
and there is no precedent for thanking the Dì (帝) after receiving rain.
Although the winter solstice sacrifice is currently omitted,
the southern suburban sacrifice already includes the rites of prayer and gratitude,
so there is no logical need for a separate act of thanksgiving.
The Lǐ (禮) states that when sacrificing to the Dì (帝) in the suburbs,
frugality is valued.
In the Zhōu (周) sacrifices to Língwēiyǎng (靈威仰) or Hòujì (后稷),
each used one sacrificial animal.
Now, in sacrificing to the Five Dì (五帝) and Shìzǔ (世祖),
it is also appropriate to use one calf for each.
Other than this, all should follow the rites of the southern suburban sacrifice.
As Wǔhuáng’s (武皇) period of mourning has not yet ended,
it is certainly permissible not to perform grand music.
As for the drought sacrifice and the yú (雩) dance,
it is an act of lamentation and entreaty.
this is considered not to cause suspicion.
For the rest, the invocations by the祝 (zhù) and 史 (shǐ) (invocators and scribes) are merely to pray for spiritual blessings.
The Lǐ (禮) mandates that the yú (雩) dance should not be omitted.
However, the current female shamans
are not proficient in singing and dancing.
If they are to be trained and tested now,

According to the Jìn (晉) dynasty’s discussion,
using children

Sīmǎ Biāo’s (司馬彪) Lǐyízhì (禮儀志) states that during the yú (雩) sacrifice, black clothing is worn,

Currently, all sacrificial garments are black,
so there is no need for change.
As for the poems to be sung
and all other necessary provisions,
the responsible officials are to be instructed to prepare them thoroughly.”

In the first year of Lóngchāng,
the officials submitted a memorial,

Xiè Tánjì (謝曇濟), an assistant instructor in the Guózǐ (國子), argued:

Assistant Instructor Xú Jǐngsōng (徐景嵩) and Grand Master of Guanglu Wáng Jūnzhī (王逡之) argued that it was appropriate to associate Shìzōng Wén Huángdì (世宗文皇帝).

Why limit it to just two?
it is truly appropriate for Shìzǔ (世祖) to be associated.
May the Wénmiào (文廟) (Temple of Culture) stand for a hundred generations without decay!”
An imperial edict
said, “Approved.”
By the second year of Yǒngyuán
Tóng Zhī again proposed, saying:

One person being associated with two offerings

Since Emperor Míng of Hàn,

Therefore, the Míngtáng should not have a sacrifice with dual associations.
I privately believe that the former emperor should place the two emperors at the Wén Zǔ [temple],

Wáng Chī, a scholar of the Guózǐ, deliberated:
"The 'Classic of Filial Piety' says, 'The Duke of Zhōu performed the *jiāo* sacrifice to Hòu Jì to associate him with Heaven,

It does not mention King Wǔ.
Also, the 'Zhōu Sòng' says, 'Sī Wén,
Hòu Jì is associated with Heaven.'
'Wǒ Jiāng,
sacrificing to King Wén in the Míngtáng.'

Tóng Zhī again deliberated:

Upon examining this principle,
could it be applied to King Chéng?

If Chī's deliberation is correct,
then these two chapters

Also, the 'Guó Yǔ' says, 'The Zhōu people performed the *dì* sacrifice to Kù, the *jiāo* sacrifice to Jì,

Upon reflection, King Wén, with his civil governance, became *zǔ*,

This is to clarify that civilian virtue also has great merit,

Therefore, Zhèng's commentary on the 'Rites of Sacrifices' says, 'Zǔ and Zōng are used interchangeably.'

The commentary says, 'The two monarchs are
King Wén and King Wǔ.'

'When offering to the Five Emperors in the Míngtáng,

The phrase 'generally'

Since the rites are grand,

The assembled officials considered Tóng Zhī's view acceptable.

"Granted."
When Tàizǔ was King of Qí,

and I fear it is not appropriate for the princes to replace him.
According to the old temple rites, princes can also perform the duties of the three high officials.
I consider this more convenient."

When [he] died,

Sòngtái initially established five temples,

Its meaning countered that of Zhèng,

From this point onwards,

According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),

From this, it can be said that
the ceremonies of court visits, diplomatic missions, and seasonal ancestral sacrifices

Their establishment and abolition, their success and failure,

after the 'crying until the end' ceremony is completed,

Once buried and the initial mourning released,

Donning the emperor's robes after the mourning attire,

Furthermore, relying on Fàn Xuān's challenge to Dù Yù

for high ministers and grandees,

the one below must be ‘fresh fish.’

tíng

Guózǐ Zhùjiào Sāng Huìdù proposed:

Hé Yīnzhī’s proposal was not adopted.
In the tenth year,

an imperial edict ordered that the six individuals: the late Tàizǎi Chǔ Yuān, the late Tàiwèi Wáng Jiǎn, the late Sīkōng Liǔ Shìlóng, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Wáng Jìngzé, Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn Chén Xiǎndá, [二二]and the late Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Ānmín,
be enshrined in the ancestral temple of Tàizǔ.
Cíbù Láng Hé Yīnzhī proposed:
“The enshrinement of meritorious officials
has been practiced continuously since the Sòng dynasty.
Examining the remaining records,
the seating arrangements were inscribed,
detailing their posthumous official titles, ranks, and names.
The text did not refer to them as ‘lords,’
which means they were presented on boards.
The Báihǔ Tōng states, ‘The sacrifice has a lord, to which a filial son ties his heart.’
Considering this,
when elevated to the temple,
it is not permissible to have a lord.
The dimensions of the Sòng-era boards
no longer exist.
The present system,
with its size and thickness resembling the boards for summoning officials in the Shàngshū,
would be most appropriate.”
The officials in charge of the Tàimiào also stated that they had seen the Sòng meritorious officials enshrined on boards,
which were similar to the boards for summoning officials in the Shàngshū.
The matter is recorded in the Yízhù.
In the eleventh year,
Yòupúshè Wáng Yàn, Lìbù Shàngshū Xú Xiàosì, and Shìzhōng Hé Yìn reported:
“There is no precedent
for the late crown prince to be enshrined in the Tàimiào.
[二三]Upon examining the precedents of Empress Yuán of Sòng,
when the Tàiwèi performed the ritual,
the crown prince bowed and prostrated together with the Tàiwèi.
Your subjects have consulted and agreed
to follow this previous example.
The Tàicháng will preside over the temple positions,
the Tàiwèi will conduct the enshrinement ritual,
and the crown prince’s grandson will bow and prostrate,
all together.
After the main ritual is completed,
during the sacrifice in the inner chamber,
the crown prince’s grandson should personally offer the libation.”
The emperor decreed,
“Granted.”
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
officials proposed the ceremonial carriage and attire for the relocation of Empress Jǐngyì to the new temple.
Cíbù Láng Hé Tóngzhī proposed:
“According to the Zhōu Lǐ, among the king’s six robes,
the dàqiú is supreme,
followed by the gǔnmiǎn.
Among the five carriages,
the yùlù is supreme,
followed by the jīnlù.
Among the empress’s six robes,
the huīyī is supreme,
followed by the yúzhái.
There are three types of headdresses,
with the fù as supreme,
followed by the biān.
Among the five carriages,
the zhòngzhái is supreme,
followed by the yànzhái.
While the shànggōng
does not have the dàqiú and yùlù, [二四]the shànggōng’s夫人 has the fù and huīyī.
This is why the Jìtǒng says, ‘The fūrén, in fù and huīyī, stands in the eastern chamber.’
Moreover, Zhèng says, ‘Among the empress’s six robes,
only the shànggōng’s fūrén also has the huīyī.’
The Shī says, ‘Adorned with zhái fú, she goes to court.’
Zhèng considers zhái fú to be yànzhái,
which the夫人 of marquises and earls rode when entering the temple.
Now, since the fù and huīyī of the shànggōng’s fūrén are the same,
then the zhòngzhái may not be different either.
Moreover, Empress Jǐngyì’s rites were elevated to the rank of jiǔmìng.
Furthermore, in the Jìn dynasty, the ceremonial attire of a tàifēi
was the same as that of a tàihòu.
In the Sòng dynasty, the huáng tàifēi differed only by not having the five-ox banner;
otherwise, her attending officials included two Shìzhōng, two Sànqí Chángshì, two Huángmén Shìláng, and two Sànqí Shìláng each,
divided into front and rear sections,
same as the emperor.
Her internal officials included two Nǚ Shàngshū and two Nǚ Chángyù,
and her qǐyǐn was the same as the tàihòu.
Moreover, the Jìn King in the Wèi dynasty,
and the Sòng King in the Jìn dynasty,
both appointed all civil and military officials,
emulating the imperial court.
As for King Wén of Jìn, his death was still referred to as hōng,
while a Tàishàng Huáng’s death was called bēng,
meaning the ritual was elevated beyond that of a king.
Therefore, the previous proposal for Empress Jǐngyì to entirely follow the rituals of modern huáng tàifēi
means that her attendants and accompanying carriages should not be different,
and her riding the zhòngzhái
is also not to be doubted.
Upon reviewing the relocation of the temple at the beginning of Qí,
Emperor Xuān’s spirit tablet rode in a jīnlù,
and the emperor personally escorted it,
also riding in a jīnlù.
He went ahead to complete the ritual,
then followed the spirit tablet to the new temple.
This is what should be followed and adopted now.”
It was adopted.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
the responsible officials debated whether there should be a temple visit (miàojiàn).
Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì deliberated:
“When a successor ruler ascends the throne,
there is no text regarding temple visits.
When a branch of the imperial family assumes the throne,
then there is the rite of pious worship.”
Zuǒ Chéng Xiāo Chēn deliberated:
“I have heard that reverently meeting one’s ancestors
is an principle evident in the Shāngshū,
and paying respects at Wǔgōng
is a deed that shines in the Jìn Cè.
How can one, having assumed the proper position and residing in honor,
continuing the imperial enterprise and receiving the mandate of Heaven,
not piously visit and pay respects to the ancestors,
presenting oneself in the great ancestral temple (Tàishì)?
The ‘Lièwén’ chapter of the Zhōu Sòng in the Máoshī says,
‘When Chéngwáng assumed government,
the feudal lords assisted in the sacrifice.’
Zhèng Zhù commented, ‘When a new king assumes government,
he must offer sacrifices to his ancestors with the rites of court worship (cháoxiǎng),
announcing his succession to the throne.’
Another chapter says, ‘Alas, I, the young son,
the successor to the king, went to the ancestral temple (cháomiào).’
Zhèng Zhù commented, ‘The successor king
refers to Chéngwáng.
After the mourning period for Wǔwáng,
he was about to assume government
and went to the ancestral temple.’
Thus, the grand institutions of the flourishing Zhōu dynasty
are brilliantly recorded in the classics.
In embodying the legitimate line and occupying the proper position,
none surpassed Chéngwáng.
Furthermore, among the two Hàn dynasties, those who succeeded to the throne as crown princes—
seven rulers in Xījīng
and four emperors in Dōngdū—
namely, Zhāo, Chéng, Āi, Hé, and Cóng (five rulers),
all made temple visits,
as recorded in the Hànshǐ.
For Huì, Jǐng, Wǔ, Yuán, Míng, and Zhāng (six rulers),
earlier histories do not record their temple visits.
Perhaps there are occasional omissions in the texts;
there is no reason for a different explanation.
Some debaters claim that since they were previously in the Eastern Palace (Chǔgōng),
they had already shown reverence,
and after the mourning rites of ‘ending tears’ (cùkū),
they personally offered seasonal sacrifices,
which constitutes the temple visit.
Therefore, there was no separate rite of visiting.
I humbly believe this is incorrect.
When the crown prince was in the palace,
he also participated in the suburban sacrifices.
If previous reverence could serve as later respect,
then at the beginning of the reign,
there would be no need for the renewed sacrifice to Heaven.
If personally offering seasonal sacrifices
is considered a temple visit,
then from Hàn to Jìn,
when collateral branches succeeded to the throne,
they all made temple visits.
Since they all performed the seasonal offerings (zhēngcháng),
why would they alone perform complex rites?
Moreover, in the first year of Xiánhé under Jìn Chéngdì, after the change of reign title,
he visited the temple.
In the first year of Xiánkāng, when he underwent the capping ceremony,
he visited again.
If during the same reign, when there was no change of ruler,
they did not doubt that the two rites were interdependent,
how much more so when the positions of sovereign and subject were separated,
to retrospectively combine reverence into a single visit?
It is appropriate to far follow the grand precedents of Zhōu and Hàn,
and near reject the divergent principles of Jìn and Sòng.
Let sincerity be extended to a single temple,
and the myriad states rush to participate.”
The memorial was approved.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
the responsible officials submitted a memorial:
“On the third day of this month,
the Là sacrifice to the Tàishè and Jì was performed.
On the first day, the new moon occurred,
and a solar eclipse took place during the period of abstention (zhìzhāi).
We are unsure whether there is any doubt concerning the she sacrifice.
The Cao staff found no prior precedent.”
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn deliberated:
“The Lǐjì, ‘Zēngzǐ Wèn’ chapter says, ‘The Son of Heaven performs the dì, xiāo, shè, and the five rites of sacrifice,
Only during a great mourning period are they suspended.
As for the day of the sacrifice,
if there is a fire or a solar eclipse, it is suspended.
has a long history,
but the initial arrangement of fǔ and guǐ
is beyond the scope of the question.
According to this,
if the first day of abstention
coincides with a partial eclipse,
then the sacrifice should not be suspended.
Furthermore, in the fourth year of Chūpíng,
Shìsūn Ruì proposed that a solar eclipse should suspend the capping ceremony but not the suburban sacrifice.
The king takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother,
This serves as a prior precedent,
and it is believed that it should not be suspended.”
The imperial edict said,
“Approved.”
In the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng,
Jiān Cíbù Láng Hé Tóngzhī deliberated:
“According to the Lǐjì, ‘Jiāo Tèshēng’ chapter, ‘The she sacrifice is to the earth and presides over the yin qi.
The ruler faces south, below the northern wall,
which is the meaning of responding to yin.’
Zhèng Xuán commented, ‘Dá is like duì (facing).’
‘Běiyǒng (northern wall)
is the northern [area] within the she altar.’
Wáng Sù commented, ‘The yin qi faces north,
so the ruler faces south to respond to it.
The word dá (respond) refers to a relative orientation.’
Thus, it is clear that in ancient she sacrifices,
the divine position faced north,
and the officiating official faced south.
In recent times, it has been passed down that
the imperial she altar faces south,
while the Tàishè and Jì altars both face east.
The position of the officiating official is north of the imperial she altar,
facing west,
performing rites behind the spirit.
Furthermore, calling Jì ‘Jìshè’
is very contrary to the meaning of the rites.
but it is presumed that this principle has not been in error for long.
I humbly believe that as the imperial Qí (dynasty) transforms things,
and rites and music are renewed,
among the gods of the Central Plain,
none is more noble than She.
If the previous errors are maintained,
I fear it will diminish the grand institutions.
Regarding the two she altars,
their meanings differ,
but their spirits are one;
their positions should both face north.
If Jì faces north,
it would become back-to-back.
Jì is the overall god of all grains,
not the master of yin qi,
so it should follow the previous eastward orientation.
The officiating official should stand northeast of the she altar,
facing south.
East is superior.
All assisting officials stand facing west,
south is superior.
According to the rites, Jì should not have a combined name.
If one now wishes to honor it,
it should simply be called Tàijì;
how can it be called Jìshè?
The Là sacrifice to the Tàishè is approaching;
I request that the regulations be revised based on this memorial.”
The Ceremonial Bureau (Yí Cáo) quoted the scholar of rites, saying:
“The Jiāo Tèshēng also says, ‘The ruler facing south
is to respond to yang;
the minister facing north
is to respond to the ruler.’
If yang qi is in the south,
then the position should face north;
if yin qi
is in the north,
Now, the southern and northern suburban altars,
one is restricted to facing south,
and the Emperor, with his black zàn (libation cup), stands facing east or west on the steps.
Therefore, it is known that the altars are not tied to yin and yang,
and the setting of positions is not restricted by north and south.
For minor sacrifices to various spirits,
they are generally restricted to facing south.
During offerings,
the rites are performed facing north,
presumably to emphasize the dignity of the spirits and manifest the meaning of seeking the profound.
In the Wèi dynasty, Qín Jìng suggested that the she and ji altars be built separately,
stating that since the Hàn dynasty,
it has been customary for them to face south.
The Hàn dynasty was not far removed from the Zhōu dynasty in terms of generations.
The dilapidated foundations at Hào
and the remaining trees at Shāngqiū
should still have existed.
Being confused about directions and losing positions
would not have gone so far.
Knowledgeable scholars
did not consider it wrong.
Yǔ Wèizhī previously had this same deliberation,
but later Xú Yuán and Zhōu Jǐngyuǎn both disagreed,
and it remained unchanged.”
Tóng Zhī's deliberation:
“When one comes, it is difficult to lead the lord to face south to respond to the yang;
the minister faces north to respond to the lord.
May I venture to ask what the phrase 'respond' means?
Is it facing each other?
Or is it facing away from each other?
If it is facing away, then the altar of the Shè faces south,
and the lord also faces south;
this would accord with the incoming proposition.
The 'Jiāo Tè Shēng' says, 'The minister faces north to respond to the lord.'
This again means the lord faces away from the minister.
Now, if it is said that the lord faces south and the minister faces north,
and they face each other to respond,
then the lord facing south would not be able to respond.
How could the 'Jì' (Records) say that when sacrificing at the Shè, the lord faces south to respond to the yin?
If the Shè indeed faces the same direction,
then the lord should also face west.
Why does he face south at the Shè?
And west at the suburban sacrifice?
My explanation is not so.
The 'Jì' says,
‘The lord faces south to respond to the yang.’
This indicates that during court assemblies,
the prosperous yang is in the south,
so the lord faces south to confront it,
just as the sage faces south to listen
and governs by facing the light.
How could this be on the day of praying and sacrificing to heaven and earth?
Knowing that the sacrifice to the Shè faces north,
the lord responds by facing south.
If the sacrifice to Heaven faces south,
then the lord should respond by facing north.
Now, His Majesty's black goblets on the east-west stairs
are probably for a separate position upon entry,
not for the time of facing and responding.
〔三一〕According to the 'Jì,' it says, 'The Shè is that by which the way of the earth is deified.'
It also says, 'The Shè sacrifices to the earth and presides over yin energy.'
It also says, 'Those who do not obey orders
are executed at the Shè.'
Kǒng Ānguó said, 'The Shè presides over yin,
and yin presides over killing.'
The 'Zhuàn' (Commentary) says, 'When there is a solar eclipse,
drums are beaten at the Shè.'
Dù Yù said, 'This is to reprimand the multitude of yin forces.'
The Shè presides over the flourishing of yin energy,
hence its position is set facing north,
to base it on this meaning.
Although other sacrifices are also for the venerated earth deities,
they do not preside over this meaning,
hence their positions and directions differ.
One cannot conclude that because other yin sacrifices do not face north,
the Shè should face south.
According to the 'Zhōu Lǐ,' the sacrifice to the Shè faces south, and the lord seeks the obscure,
so he should face north.
But the 'Jì' says the lord faces south,
which is the meaning of responding to yin.
Is the argument about seeking the obscure not contrary to this?"
〔三二〕“During the Wèi's seizure of the Hàn,
the Shè and Jì were constructed together with a common gate,
with the Jì altar north of the Shè altar,
all of which were not ancient systems.
Later, after moving the palace south,
it should naturally
conform to the rites.
〔三三〕If Jìng's words are taken thus,
they highlight that the Hàn Shè deviated from Zhōu practices
and reflect the old customs of the Hàn era.
At that time, sacrifices to the Shè faced south.
It is unclear which historical records confirm this.
Even if the deliberator Jìng's words are true, that the Shè's position and direction still follow old Hàn practices,
and Hàn inherited Zhōu's established rules
and did not change them,
then the three altars of Shè and Jì
should all face south.
Why then is the Dì Shè now changed to face south, while the Tài Shè and Jì both face east?”
The director of rites also challenged Tóng Zhī,
with three exchanges in total.
By the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the officials deliberated:
“The director of rites has no definite and clear evidence.”
Tóng Zhī's deliberation was then adopted.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Hé Tóngzhī, the director of the Ministry of Rites, memorialized:
“According to the 'Zhōu Lǐ,' the Grand Master of Rituals 'performs rites to Heaven with a dark jade bi,
and to Earth with a yellow jade cóng.'
Zhèng Xuán further said, 'Both have sacrificial animals and silks,
each corresponding to the color of its vessel.'
〔三四〕Thus, we know that rites to Heaven at the round mound use a dark calf,
and rites to Earth at the square pond use a yellow animal.
The 'Mù Rén' (Herdsman) says, 'All yang sacrifices use a reddish-brown animal,
and yin sacrifices use a black animal.'
Zhèng Xuán said, 'Xīn (reddish-brown) is red;
yǒu (black) is black.
Yang sacrifices are to Heaven at the southern suburban altar and the ancestral temples.
Yin sacrifices are to Earth at the northern suburban altar and the Shè and Jì.'
The 'Jì Fǎ' (Law of Sacrifices) says, 'Burning firewood at the Tài Tán
is a sacrifice to Heaven.
Burying at the Tài Zhé
is a sacrifice to Earth.
A reddish-brown calf is used.'
Zhèng said, 'Earth,
being a yin sacrifice,
uses a black animal,
but since it uses a calf like Heaven,
they are mentioned together.'
Thus, we know that these sacrifices to Heaven and Earth are the northern and southern suburban sacrifices.
Now, both northern and southern suburban sacrifices use black animals,
and the Míngtáng, ancestral temples, Shè, and Jì all use red,
which violates ancient canons.
Furthermore, Zhèng Xuán said, 'Sacrifice to the Five Thearchs at the Míngtáng,
with Gōumáng and others as co-sacrificers.'
Since the Jìn dynasty,
the round mound was merged with the southern suburban altar,
hence the suburban altar includes the Five Thearchs, Gōumáng, and others.
Now, the Míngtáng sacrifices to the Five Essences,
but lacks the positions for the Five Spirits.
The northern suburban altar sacrifices to the Earth Deities,
but sets up seats for Chóng and Lí.
These two or three discrepancies
are feared to diminish the grand principles.”
Liú Huì, the Administrator of the Former Army, deliberated:
“The saying goes, 'The son of a brindled ox is reddish-brown and horned;
though one might not wish to use it,
would the mountains and rivers reject it?'
It is not clear whether mountains and rivers are considered yin sacrifices.
If they are yin sacrifices,
then it contradicts the use of black animals.”
Tóng Zhī again deliberated:
“The 'Zhōu Lǐ' considers Heaven and Earth as grand sacrifices,
the four directions (sìwàng) as secondary sacrifices,
and mountains and rivers as minor sacrifices.
The Zhōu people esteemed red.
For sacrifices from the four directions upwards, the color of the sacrificial animal followed its direction,
because these were grand sacrifices,
and should follow the origin.
For mountains and rivers and below, where the color of the sacrificial animal is not specified,
it is because these were minor sacrifices,
and followed what was esteemed.
Thus, do not the two explanations of the 'Lún' (Analects) and the 'Lǐ' (Rites)
accord with each other?”
The participants in the deliberation deemed it acceptable.
It was followed.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Hé Tóngzhī, the Commandant of Infantry, deliberated, saying:
“It is heard that when sagely emperors and enlightened kings govern the world,
none fail to revere Heaven and Earth
and respect the Sun and Moon.
Therefore, at the Winter Solstice, they sacrifice to Heaven at the round mound (Yuánqiū);
at the Summer Solstice, they sacrifice to Earth at the square pond (Fāngzé);
at the Spring Equinox, they greet the morning sun (Cháorì);
and at the Autumn Equinox, they greet the evening moon (Xīyuè).
This is how they instruct the people in the Way of serving their ruler
and transform their subjects to revere their superiors.
Thus, the Lǐ says, ‘The king must treat Heaven as father and Earth as mother,
and the Sun as elder brother and the Moon as elder sister.’
The Diǎnyuì chapter of the Zhōu Lǐ says, ‘The king holds the great guī tablet (dà guī) in his belt
and grasps the zhèn guī tablet,
with a mat adorned with five colors in five layers, when greeting the morning sun.’
Mǎ Róng said, ‘The Son of Heaven greets the morning sun at the Spring Equinox
and the evening moon at the Autumn Equinox.’
The Jìn Lǐ states, ‘The Son of Heaven goes out to bow to the sun outside the eastern gate.’
Lú Zhí said, ‘Greeting the morning sun should be on the day of Lìchūn (Start of Spring).’
Zhèng Xuán said, ‘Duān should be miǎn (ceremonial cap),
and greeting the morning sun is at the time of the Spring Equinox.’
The Cháoshìyì chapter of the Lǐjì says, ‘The Son of Heaven, wearing a miǎn cap and holding a zhèn guī tablet,
one foot and two inches long,
leads the feudal lords to greet the morning sun in the eastern suburbs,
thus teaching respect for the esteemed.’
Therefore, Zhèng Xuán knew this duān meant miǎn.
The Bǎofù chapter of the Lǐjì says, ‘According to the rites of the Three Dynasties,
the Son of Heaven in spring greeted the morning sun
and in autumn greeted the evening moon,
thus demonstrating reverence.’
But it does not specify the fixed celestial time (chén) to be used.
Mǎ Róng and Zhèng Xuán said it should be at the time of the two equinoxes;
Lú Zhí said it should be on the day of Lìchūn.
Tóngzhī believes that the Sun is the essence of greater yang (tàiyáng)
and the Moon is the essence of greater yin (tàiyīn).
At the Spring Equinox, the yang qi is just beginning to flourish;
at the Autumn Equinox, the yin qi is beginning to grow.
Heaven and Earth are supremely revered, so their beginnings are used;
hence, sacrifices are made at the two solstices.
The rites for the Sun and Moon are secondary to those for Heaven and Earth,
(（敬）)【therefore】 greetings are made at the two equinoxes.
〔三五〕If the discrepancy has a reasonable basis,
then the words of Róng and Xuán obtain their meaning.
During the Hàn era, the morning sun was greeted in the morning
and the evening moon in the evening.
Emperor Wén of Wèi decreed, ‘The Jìn Lǐ states that the Son of Heaven bows to the sun outside the eastern gate,
and the Fǎn Lǐ (Return Rites) is then clearly defined.
The Cháoshìyì states that the Son of Heaven, wearing a miǎn cap and holding a zhèn guī tablet,
leads the feudal lords to greet the morning sun in the eastern suburbs.
From this, it can be said
that perhaps the feudal lords perform the morning greetings,
and the Son of Heaven performs the sacrifice at the square pond (Fāngmíng),
and thus leads the greeting of the morning sun.
The Hàn dynasty altered the Zhōu regulations,
so the myriad dukes (qún gōng) did not have the affairs of the four morning greetings.
Therefore, they no longer performed morning greetings in the eastern suburbs,
which was a change in ritual.
However, bowing to the sun facing east in the hall morning and evening was
too troublesome a rite.
Now, adopting the Zhōu Spring Equinox rite,
reducing the Hàn daily bowing ceremony,
and also lacking the affairs involving feudal lords,
there is no reason to go to the eastern suburbs.
Today, the main hall itself is also the court for morning assemblies and performing rites,
so it is proper to regularly bow to the sun in the main hall courtyard at the Spring Equinox.
The text regarding the evening moon is not clear;
let a deliberation be submitted.’
Xūe Xún, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Mìshūjiān) of Wèi, requested a discussion, saying, ‘According to old precedents, the morning sun was greeted at the Spring Equinox
and the evening moon at the Autumn Equinox.
Examining the Zhōu Lǐ, there is no fixed day for greeting the morning sun.
Zhèng Xuán said to use the two equinoxes,
so it was carried out.
On the evening of the Autumn Equinox,
the moon often sinks in the east,
but bowing to it facing west
is truly turning one's back to it.
I suggest that greeting the morning sun should be on the first day of the second spring month (zhòngchūn zhī shuò),
and greeting the evening moon should be on the first day of the second autumn month (zhòngqiū zhī shuò).’
Chúnyú Ruì rebutted this,
citing the Lǐjì, which says, ‘Sacrifice to the sun in the east,
and sacrifice to the moon in the west,
to establish their proper positions.’
The Zhōu Lǐ’s greeting of the evening moon at the Autumn Equinox
was practiced in ancient times.
Bowing to the moon facing west,
even if it seems like turning one's back,
is still like sacrificing to the moon when it is in the sky but performing the sacrifice in a pit,
one would not speak of turning one's back to the moon.
Tóngzhī examined the Lǐqì, which states, ‘For morning and evening, one must emulate the sun and moon.’
Zhèng Xuán said, ‘The sun rises in the east,
and the moon is in the west.’
He also said, ‘The great light (dàmíng) is born in the east,
and the moon is born in the west;
this is the distinction of yin and yang,
and the positions of husband and wife.’
Zhèng Xuán said, ‘Dàmíng is
the sun.’
Knowing that greeting the morning sun faces east
and greeting the evening moon faces west,
this is likely based on the location of each.
Just as when the Son of Heaven travels east or west,
officials in the court and those being appointed
still face north to make their obeisance,
how can one take 'turning one's back' as a reason for doubt?
Tóngzhī believes that what was practiced in the Wèi era
skillfully grasped the essence of what to retain and what to discard.
At the beginning of the Jìn dynasty, the round mound (Yuánqiū) and square pond (Fāngzé) were abandoned,
and the rites at the two suburbs for the two solstices were suspended.
As for the morning greetings at the two equinoxes,
their cessation is without justification.
When the Jiāngzuǒ (Eastern Jìn) was first established,
many ancient regulations were missing.
The Sòng dynasty followed the old ways
and could not revert to antiquity.
I humbly suggest that as the imperial Qí responds to Heaven and rules the realm,
and its institutions and teachings are renewed,
it is fitting that these grand ceremonies be performed in this flourishing age.
At the Spring Equinox, in the western part of the palace courtyard,
bow to the sun facing east.
At the Autumn Equinox, in the eastern part of the palace courtyard,
bow to the moon facing west.
This is what is meant by 'must emulate the sun and moon to establish their proper positions.'
This will cause observers of the transformation from all four directions
to joyfully praise its beauty.
【服無】The omission of the streamers (liú) and ornamentation (zǎo) on the robes
〔三六〕is probably based on the utmost simplicity of Heaven.
The greeting of the morning sun should not be identical to the rite of the utmost simplicity for August Heaven (Hàotiān);
thus, the dark ceremonial cap (xuánmiǎn) has three streamers.
In recent times, when sacrificing to Heaven,
the twelve-streamer gǔn robe is worn,
reaching the pinnacle of literary (wénzhāng) (（義）)【beauty】.
〔三七〕This is therefore a change in ancient and modern rites.
For the rites to Heaven and the greeting of the morning sun,
the attire should differ.
In recent generations, when the Son of Heaven holds minor court assemblies,
he wears a crimson gauze robe (jiàngshāpáo) and a crown with a golden bócshān (tōngtiān jīnbóshān guān).
This is the current court attire, secondary to the gǔnmiǎn.
I humbly suggest that the Sun and Moon should be bowed to in accordance with this,
〔三八〕as it achieves a very appropriate hierarchy.
Tóngzhī's position is not within the ritual bureau,
and to lightly propose such a grand ceremony
is truly an encroachment upon official duties.
I prostrate myself, ashamed and trembling.”
It was adopted.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
the relevant authorities reported:
“On the dìnghài day, the twenty-fifth day of the first month of next year,
it is suitable to sacrifice to the Former Farmer (Xiānnóng),
and on that day the imperial carriage should be driven for the emperor to personally plow.”
Since Yuánjiā and Dàmíng of Sòng,
it has always been the hài day after Lìchūn.
Wáng Jiǎn, the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūlìng), believed that there was no textual basis in classics or records for plowing the imperial field (jiètián) on a hài day,
and conveyed this for detailed discussion.
Liú Màn, concurrently a Doctor of the Imperial Academy (Tàixuédàbóshì), deliberated:
“The Lǐ states,
‘In the month of Mèngchūn (first month of spring),
Lìchūn is observed to welcome spring.
Also in this month, on the yuánrì (first day of the month), prayers for grain are offered,
and a yuánchén (propitious day) is chosen for the emperor to personally plow the imperial field.’
Lú Zhí’s commentary on the Lǐ explains that chéndì (celestial stems and earthly branches) refer to days.
‘Rì’ (day)
refers to jiǎ through guǐ (the ten celestial stems),
and ‘chén’ (branch)
refers to zǐ through hài (the twelve earthly branches).
The suburban sacrifice to Heaven (jiāotiān)
is yang,
thus a ‘rì’ (celestial stem day) is used.
Plowing the imperial field (jiètián)
is yin,
thus a ‘chén’ (earthly branch day) is used.
Yin rites are humble and follow,
they must be at the end.
Hài is the last of the earthly branches,
thus the records call it yuánchén,
and the
(（法）)【commentary】 says ‘auspicious hài.’
〔三九〕Furthermore, according to the theory of the Five Phases (Wǔxíng),
wood is born in hài,
so sacrificing to the Former Farmer on a hài day
also has its meaning.”
Hé Yīnhī, the Grand Master of Ceremonies Assistant (Tàichángchéng), deliberated:
“Zhèng Xuán’s commentary says, ‘Yuánchén
is likely the auspicious hài day after the suburban sacrifice.’
Hài
is the water branch.
Wherever cultivation takes place,
sprinkling moisture is always present.
The Wǔxíng theory states that the twelve earthly branches form six harmonies (liùhé);
yín and hài combine.
Plowing in the east in the month of jiànyín (first month)
takes the combination of the month’s principal branch and the day’s branch.”
Sāng Huìdù (桑惠dù), National University Assistant Instructor, deliberated:
"Upon examining Zhèng Xuán's (鄭玄) view that 'hài' (亥) is an auspicious 'chén' (辰):
'yáng' (陽) is born in 'zǐ' (子),
its 'yuán' (元) originates in 'hài' (亥).
Taking the 'yuán' of 'yáng' to produce living things,
'hài' is also water,
the month of October is established by it,
and all grains rely on its moistening to fully ripen."
Zhōu Shānwén (周山文), Assistant Instructor, deliberated:
"Lú Zhí (盧植) said, 'Yuán (元)
is goodness.
Suburban sacrifice to Heaven
is 'yáng,'
so a day is used.
Ceremonial plowing
is 'yīn,'
so a 'chén' is used.'
Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) 'Yuè Lìng Zhāng Jù' (月令章句) explains 'yuán chén' (元辰) saying, 'A day
is a 'gān' (幹).
[四０] A 'chén'
is a 'zhī' (支).
When there is an affair concerning Heaven,
a day is used.
When there is an affair concerning Earth,
a 'chén' is used.' "
Hé Tōngzhī (何佟之), Assistant Instructor, deliberated:
"The 'Shào Láo Kuì Shí Lǐ' (少牢饋食禮) says, 'Filial descendant (his) [某],
[四一] tomorrow Dīnghài (丁亥),
presents the annual sacrifice to August Ancestor Bó [某].'
The commentary says, 'Dīng (丁) is not necessarily Hài,
it merely picks a day to speak of it.
The 'Dì Tài Miào Lǐ' (禘太廟禮) always uses Dīnghài.
If it is not Dīnghài,
then Jǐhài (己亥) or Xīnhài (辛亥) is used.
Any Hài will do.'
Zhèng (鄭) also said, 'The necessity of using Dīng or Jǐ
[四二] is to take their auspicious names.
Dīng and Dīng change themselves,
all for reverence.'
Given this,
Dīnghài is naturally a day for sacrifices,
not exclusively applied to the First Farmer.
Hàn Wén (漢文) used this day for plowing, ceremonial plowing, and sacrificing to the First Farmer,
hence later kings continued to use it,
without any separate meaning."
Gù Hào (顧暠), Palace Aide, deliberated:
"Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) speaks of 'first suburban sacrifice, then auspicious 'chén','
but does not explain why it must be 'hài.'
Lú Zhí (盧植) clarified 'zǐ' and 'hài' as 'chén,'
but also had no proof for a fixed 'chén.'
In the Hàn (漢) era, personal plowing and ceremonial plowing
began with Hàn Wén (漢文).
The edict said, 'Agriculture
is the foundation of the empire. Therefore, open the ceremonial fields.'
This was merely an initial decree,
and no auspiciousness of personally carrying it out has been seen.
Emperor Zhāo (昭帝) plowed in Guōdùn (鉤盾) ceremonial fields on a Guǐhài (癸亥) day.
Emperor Míng (明帝) plowed in Xiàpī (下邳) on a Guǐhài day.
Emperor Zhāng (章帝) plowed in Dìngtáo (定陶) on an Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
and also plowed in Huái (懷) on a Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day.
The Illustrious Ancestor of Wèi (魏) actually recorded Xīnwèi (辛未),
not adhering to a single 'chén,'
which is proven in two dynasties.
Extending to the Jìn (晉) replacing the Wèi,
and the Sòng (宋) inheriting from the Jìn,
it was precisely their adherence to Kāngchéng (康成),
not that they had different views.
Bān Gù's (班固) explanation of the 'hài' position says, 'Yīn (陰) 'qì' (氣) should be absent from shooting,
containing all things,
while mixing with 'yáng' obstructs sowing.'
Moreover, 'hài' is a water 'chén,'
its nature is to contain and nurture.
Taking auspiciousness for sowing,
is it in this?
The explanation of the 'chǒu' (丑) position says, 'Great 'yīn' (陰) helps 'Huángzhōng' (黃鍾) to disseminate 'qì' and sprout things.'
The explanation of the 'wèi' (未) position says, 'Yīn 'qì' receives the appointment,
assisting Ruíbīn (蕤賓) to preside over planting things,
causing them to grow large and flourish.'
Thus, the Hàn (漢) dynasty selected alternately,
and the Wèi (魏) house moved it,
drawing from old practices and using 'chǒu,'
which indeed has basis."
The deliberators collectively proposed using Dīnghài.
The edict
said,
"Approved."
In the first month of the fourth year of Jiàn Yuán (建元),
an edict established the National Academy,
setting up one hundred fifty students.
Of these, fifty were those with positions who entered by privilege.
Students were aged fifteen or above,
and twenty or below.

They were selected from the descendants of kings and dukes down to the three generals, Chief Scribes, Court Stewards, Crown Prince's Household Administrators, and those in charge of protecting various prefectural司馬 and advisers who had been appointed by imperial decree, as well as Assistant Administrators and other officials from various prefectures, both those currently in office and those dismissed.
All were limited to families living within two thousand 'lǐ' (里) of the capital.
Upon the passing of Tàizǔ (太祖),
this ceased.
In the first month of the third year of Yǒng Míng (永明),
an edict established a school,
creating halls and residences,
summoning the sons of dukes and high officials, down to the descendants of Supernumerary Assistant Administrators.
In total, two hundred students were placed.
[四三] In the autumn of that year, all assembled.
The responsible officials memorialized:
"According to the old practice of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of the Sòng (宋),
when students arrive, a 'shìdiàn' (釋奠) ceremony is first performed for the Former Sages and Former Teachers.
The rites also include a 'shìcài' (釋菜) ceremony.
It is unclear what ceremony should be performed now?
What music and ritual vessels should be used?"
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉), Minister of Personnel, deliberated:
"The 'Zhōu Lǐ' (周禮) says, 'In spring, upon entering school,
offer vegetables and perform dances.'
The 'Jì' (記) says, 'At the beginning of teaching,
perform 'píbiàn jìcài' (皮弁祭菜),
to show respect for the Way.'
It also says, 'Upon first entering school,
one must sacrifice to the Former Sages and Former Teachers.'
Since the Middle Dynasties,
the 'shìcài' ceremony has been abolished.
What is performed now
is only the 'shìdiàn.'
For metal instruments, stone chimes, sacrificial vessels,
there is no clear text.
Comparing it to the seven ancestral temples, it is too light;
comparing it to the five rites, it is too heavy.
Lù Nà (陸納) and Chē Yìn (車胤) believed that the temple of Xuān Ní (宣尼) should follow the rank of a Marquis.
Fàn Níng (范寧) wished to follow the temple of Zhōu Gōng (周公),
using the ceremony of a king.
Fàn Xuān (范宣) said that when he was a teacher, he was not treated as a subject,
so on the 'shìdiàn' day,
the ritual music of emperors and kings should be fully prepared.
[四四] Thus, Chē (車) and Lù (陸) erred by being too light,
and the two Fàn (范)s erred by being too heavy.
Yù Xī (喻希) said, 'If a supreme king himself sets up ritual music,
then he bestows great rewards in a place of utmost reverence;
if one wishes to praise the Former Teacher,
then what is compared is not complete.'
Examining this statement,
it adheres to reason.
The Imperial Dynasty has humbly honored and greatly promoted education,
treating him as a teacher,
elevating him to the rank of a Duke,
which is just and fitting for the occasion.
When the academy was established in Yuánjiā,
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) deliberated that six rows of dancers should be used.
Since the suburban music was not yet complete,
the 'dēnggē' (登歌) was provisionally performed.
Now that metal instruments and stone chimes are ready,
the music of 'xuānxuán' (軒縣) and the dance of six rows
should be set up.
Sacrificial animals, offerings, and vessels
should all follow those of a Duke."
In that winter,
the Crown Prince lectured on the 'Xiào Jīng' (孝經),
personally presiding over the 'shìdiàn,'
with the imperial carriage attending to listen.
In the first month of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
an imperial edict ordered the establishment of schools.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
after the Dōnghūn Hóu ascended the throne,
Shàngshū Fú followed the old precedent from Yǒngmíng and abolished the schools.
Lǐng Guózǐ Zhùjiào Cáo Sīwén submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, those who established states and governed the people
always prioritized teaching and education,
to regulate their perverse emotions
and restrain their rampant desires.
Thus, they were able to transform the people and rectify customs,
making habits become second nature.
This is why loyalty and filial piety were cultivated,
trustworthiness and righteousness were perfected,
and etiquette and deference were practiced.
Respecting teaching and venerating learning
all led to the same outcome.
This is why Chéngjūn shone brightly in the classical texts,
and Hǔmén was illustrious in the former scriptures.
Your Majesty possesses sagely and pure divinity,
inheriting a grand enterprise.
Now that the imperial decree has been issued,
and the abolition of schools has been heard first,
I fear that those who observe the glory of the state
will have cause to deliberate and criticize.
If it is because of an imperial taboo that abolition is deemed appropriate,
then when the Han dynasty established schools,
from then until Yuánshǐ,
for over a hundred years,
they were never temporarily abolished,
even though there were imperial taboos during that period.
Moreover, when Jìn Wǔdì passed away,
his schools still existed.
These are clear precedents from previous generations that did not abolish schools due to imperial taboos.
The abolition in Yǒngmíng was due to there being no Crown Prince,
but this is not a classical precedent.
Examining the existence of schools in a state,
it is fundamentally to promote transformation and achieve good governance.
The Son of Heaven consults and plans there,
and performs rituals there.
The 'Record' says: 'When the Son of Heaven goes on an expedition,
he receives his mandate from his ancestors
and achieves completion through the school.
When he captures the guilty and returns,
he offers a sacrifice at the school.'
It also says: 'The Son of Heaven feeds the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng in the Tàixué,
uncovering his shoulder and cutting the sacrificial animal,
holding the cup and offering a toast,
to teach the feudal lords fraternal respect.'
Therefore, the school
is the foundation of the Son of Heaven's possession of the state,
and his teaching often depends on it.
All that has been mentioned pertains to the affairs of the Tàixué.
Citing the Tàixué now is not an irrelevant reference.
According to what your servant has observed,
the current Guóxué
is precisely the Tàixué of ancient times.
In the early Jìn dynasty, there were three thousand Tàixué students.
As they were numerous and mixed,
during the reign of Huìdì, wishing to distinguish the clear from the turbid,
the Guózǐxué was established in the third year of Yuánkāng.
Officials of the fifth rank and above were permitted to enter the Guóxué.
The Son of Heaven left the Tàixué and entered the Guóxué
to perform rituals.
The Crown Prince left the Tàixué and entered the Guóxué
to show deference to age.
As for the Tàixué and the Guóxué,
this was during the Jìn era when they distinguished between gentry and commoners,
and differentiated the noble from the humble.
However, both noble and humble, gentry and commoners,
all required teaching to be perfected.
Thus, both Guóxué and Tàixué were maintained,
not established specifically because of a Crown Prince.
Therefore, to link the rise and fall of schools to the Crown Prince
is a grave error of Yǒngmíng.
The Han dynasty revered Confucianism,
almost achieving a state where punishments could be laid aside,
yet it still fell short of the Sān and Wǔ.
This was because its methods of teaching were not sufficiently profound.
In ancient education,
families had Shú,
Dǎng had Xiáng,
Shù had Xù,
and states had Xué,
where people learned by recitation and mutual emulation.
Now, not only should schools not be abolished,
but their principles should be even more vigorously promoted.
Looking to antiquity as a guide,
let commanderies and counties have schools,
and villages establish education."
"I request that this be submitted to the Shàngshū and the two academies for detailed deliberation."
The authorities reported this.
It was adopted.
However, the schools were ultimately not established.
In the tenth month of the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
the authorities reported:
"Nánjùn Wáng Zhāoyè is coming of age.
We seek ritual precedents, but there are no previous standards."
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn deliberated:
"The coming-of-age ceremony for an imperial grandson
is unprecedented in previous dynasties.
Although the rites mention an嫡zǐ but not an嫡sūn,
〔四五〕yet he holds a position as a direct descendant,
extending down five generations.
Now, Nánjùn Wáng's body is of the imperial radiance,
truly a descendant of the state.
The ceremony of the first cap
should differ from that of ordinary feudal lords.
According to the 'Shì Guānlǐ' (Ritual for the Capping of a Scholar): 'The host wears a black cap and court attire;
the guest places the cap on the one being capped,
and the assistant ties the chin strap.'
Zhèng Xuán commented: 'The host is the father or elder brother of the one being capped.'
Examining his words 'father and elder brother,'
it is clear that if the grandfather is present,
the father does not act as host.
The 'Gōng Guān Piān' (Chapter on the Capping of a Duke) in the 'Dà Dài Lǐjì' says that a duke acts as his own host for his capping,
with four additions of a black ceremonial cap,
and a minister acts as the guest.
This applies to a monarch who succeeds to the throne, and the imperial sons who are not direct descendants and therefore cannot be called 'sons' in this context.
The 'Guān Yì' (Meaning of Capping) in the 'Xiǎo Dài Lǐjì' says: 'Capping is performed at the eastern steps (zù)
to show succession.
The libation is offered at the guest's position;
the three additions of the cap become progressively more honorable,
as the additions signify completion.'
The commentary states: 'The嫡zǐ is capped at the eastern steps,
the庶zǐ is capped in a room.'
The record also says: 'In ancient times, capping was highly regarded,
so it was performed in the ancestral temple,
thereby humbling oneself and honoring the ancestors.'
Based on this,
it aligns well with Zhèng's commentary on the 'Yílǐ.'
Therefore, since the Mid-Court era,
when a Crown Prince was capped, the Emperor would preside from his carriage,
the Sītú would place the cap,
and the Guānglù would assist.
For other princes, the Lángzhōng would place the cap,
and the Zhōngwèi would assist.
Now, equating him with the Crown Prince would be too grand,
while treating him like other princes would be too slight.
Moreover, according to the principle of 'Chūnqiū,'
'one does not disobey a grandfather's command based on a father's command.'
The 'Rites' say: 'When the father is alive, one is a son;
when the ruler is alive, one is a subject.'
The皇tàizǐ occupies the position of a subject and son;
he does not have the authority to act independently.
Although Nánjùn Wáng resides in a feudal state,
he is not among the ranks of collateral branches.
He should receive the mandate of the imperial court,
and slightly observe the ritual of capping at the eastern steps.
Jìn Wǔdì's edict stated that the Han and Wei dynasties dispatched envoys to cap princes,
which was not the correct ancient canon.
This likely refers to princely sons of collateral lines,
who should follow the principle of a duke acting as his own host for capping.
As for the state's eldest grandson, dispatching an envoy is indeed appropriate.
It is fitting to send the Tàicháng with a scepter to perform the capping,
〔四六〕with the Dàhónglú as the assistant.
The libation ritual
should also be handled by these two ministers.
The text for the blessing and libation
should be drafted separately,
following the principles of the scriptures and records,
and not adhere to the usual customs of feudal states.
Officials of the state who attend and offer congratulations
shall follow existing regulations.
On that day, inner and outer officials of the second rank and above,
shall proceed to Zhǐchējí to offer congratulations,
and also proceed to the southern gate of the Dōnggōng to submit memorials.
On another day, the ritual of offering respect
shall be performed, and palace officials shall also proceed to the gate to offer congratulations,
following the procedures for ascending to office.
After the capping,
a specific date shall be chosen for him to visit the ancestral temple,
to promote the principle of honoring ancestors.
Since this is a major ceremony,
it should be communicated to the Bāzuò Chéngláng and submitted to the two academies for detailed deliberation."
Púyè Wáng Huàn and fourteen others all agreed with the deliberation,
and drafted the two texts for assisting with the cap and the libation.
An imperial edict stated:
"Approved."
The blessing text said:
"The Emperor dispatches Gěishìzhōng, Tàicháng, Wǔ'ān Hóu Xiāo Huìjī to cap Nánjùn Wáng."
The blessing continued:
"Divining the day, divining the guest,
〔四七〕you now begin your first capping.
Cast aside your childish will,
follow your perfected virtue.
Befriend the virtuous and employ the capable,
thereby greatly accumulating good fortune."
The libation text said:
"The fine wine is clear,
the auspicious offerings are full.
Brothers are all present,
your demeanor is virtuous and careful.
May you forever attain longevity,
serene and tranquil."
During the Yǒngmíng reign,
Shìzǔ, considering the extravagance of marriage ceremonies,
issued an edict that when various princes took consorts,
the emperor's personal carriage and those of the six palaces should, in accordance with ritual, only stop for dates, chestnuts, and dried meat,
with the addition of scented oils, flowers, and powders.
All other clothing and items were to be stopped.
Only when a princess married into a family,
would she merely send gifts to her parents-in-law.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì deliberated, saying:
"Of the beginning of human relations,
none are more important than capping and marriage.
This is to honor the cultivation of virtue
and to unite two families in joy.
Ages rise and fall,
and ancient and modern practices differ.
The rituals of intricacy and simplicity
vary with the times.
The 'three additions' (of caps) have been abolished for commoners,
and the 'six rites' are limited to the imperial court.
Although this custom has not been long established,
it is difficult to change abruptly.
However, the essentials of these great ceremonies
are deeply suitable for modification.
According to the 'Capping Ritual for a Gentleman',
after the three additions are completed,
the capped person is offered *lǐ* (sweet wine).
The *lǐ* is offered only once,
hence the *lǐ* incantation has no alternative.
If *lǐ* is not offered,
then wine is offered with each addition,
hence there are three *jiào* (libation) incantations.
Wáng Sù said, 'The *lǐ* (sweet wine) is ancient,
and its ritual is weighty;
[four-eight] wine used according to seasonal taste,
its ritual is therefore lighter.'
Whether *lǐ* or *jiào*,
the meaning of two or three [incantations]
is detailed in the classic texts.
[four-nine] Currently, after the emperor or a king is capped,
only one drink is offered,
which can correspond to the ancient practice of offering *lǐ*.
[five-zero] Yet, *jiào* incantations are still used,
which is truly inappropriate.
In examining the wedding ritual, a basket is filled with four goblets,
and the 'sharing of a gourd ladle' is added.
This both upholds the principle of valuing simplicity
and symbolizes the meaning of union.
Therefore, three meals are completed,
and the *jǐn* (gourd ladle) is used for the second *yìn* (rinse).
Former scholars believed that rituals complete good unions,
and matters conclude with three,
then the *jǐn* is used for union.
The ceremonial notes put the *jǐn* *yìn* first,
with a second and third,
which deviates from the original intent.
Moreover, the 'Jiaotesheng' (Special Victim) chapter states: 'The Three Kings made offerings using earthen and gourd vessels.'
This means that in primeval times,
there was no ritual of shared offerings.
The Three Kings created it,
using primeval vessels,
to emphasize the beginning of husband and wife.
Although today square baskets are used to indicate frugality,
this increasingly deviates from ancient canons.
Furthermore, connecting gourd ladles with [⿰⺡⿱宀⿺元攵] (gold and silver)
is a product of recent custom.
And there are separate 'offering candles',
carved and adorned lavishly,
which also diminish the former system.
Currently, as sacred governance daily prospers,
and renown and teachings are harmonious,
then the ancient customs should be upheld,
and the 'living sheep' preserved to cherish the rites.
The established practices
are crucial to governance.
Auspicious rites are truly important,
and old chapters should be fully observed.
I propose that from now on, for kings and marquises and below, after capping, one cup of *lǐ* be offered,
to follow the ancient meaning.
The *lǐ* should use the old text,
which is appropriate for the matter.
Marriage should also follow ancient ways,
using the *jǐn* to drink the final *yìn* wine,
and eliminating all gold and silver connected [⿰⺡⿱宀⿺元攵].
All other miscellaneous vessels
should be made of fired clay.
Servants holding candles
are sufficient for beautiful illumination.
The elaborate 'offering candles'
should also be stopped and saved.
Thus, plainness can be expected,
and custom can be gradually changed."
The participating officials all agreed.
The memorial was approved.
In the second year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔ,
the officials reported that
it was customary for the empress's taboo name and the emperor's taboo name to be listed together.
The imperial edict stated:
According to ritual, taboo names should not leave the palace;
this is a modern taboo practice.
In the first year of Jiànnyuán,
the Tàicháng presented the taboo names for the morning court.
Púyè Wáng Jiǎn deliberated, saying:
"The empress's taboo name should, as before, not have an instruction.
According to ritual, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords taboo the names of their ancestors.
Since officials and subordinates have the duty to show reverence,
they should taboo the name of the Tàicháng Fǔjūn.
As for the imperial court's name boards,
they are fundamentally applied to the highest (ancestors).
Since this concerns [five-one] those whose veneration is beyond reach,
and the ritual descends from those 'in three' (immediate ancestors),
the Jìngzhào of Jìn
and the Dōng'ān of Sòng
were not listed on name boards.
Sūn Yù argued that Jìngzhào was listed in the principal ancestral temple,
and thus subordinates should observe the taboo,
but it should not be on a board.
At the beginning of Sòng, the erudite Sīmǎ Dàojìng argued that the Dōng'ān Fǔjūn's taboo name should be on a board,
but Hé Chéngtiān disagreed,
which serves as clear evidence."
Anyone whose personal name or place name violated the taboo names of the Tàicháng Fǔjūn and the emperor and empress
was to change them.
The taboo name of Xuāndì was to be treated similarly.
Two-character names were not partially tabooed,
which is why Chéngmíngmén was changed to Běiyè,
because the board had
the character
"zhī"
next to
"chéng."
The Dōnggōng Chénghuámén was also changed to Xuānhuá, it is said.
At the end of Hàn,
Cài Yōng compiled the 'Hàn Cháohuì Zhì' (Records of Hàn Court Assemblies),
but it was never completed.
The Qín people regarded the first day of the tenth month as the beginning of the year.
Early Hàn initially followed this with grand banquets.
Later, the Xìa calendar was adopted,
but the banquet on the first day of the tenth month was not abolished.
After the Eastern Capital period,
on New Year's Day, seven *kè* before the end of the night-watch,
bells rang for receiving congratulations.
Princes and marquises and below presented gifts in the courtyard.
Officials of two thousand *shí* and above ascended the hall to proclaim "Long Live!",
then music was played and a feast was held.
Zhāng Héng's *fù* states:
"The emperor's carriage is harnessed early,
ascending to the dawn light from Fúsāng."
Thus, although it says "harnessed early,"
it must have been performed at dawn.
When Wèi Wǔ was in Yè,
the main assembly was at Wénchāngdiàn,
following Hàn rituals,
and also setting up a hundred flower lamps.
Later, Wèi Wén repaired the Luòyáng palaces,
temporarily moving the capital to Xǔchāng.
The palaces were small,
so on the New Year's Day, a felt hall was erected south of the city,
with blue curtains for its gate,
and music was played for a banquet.
Later, returning to Luòyáng,
they followed the old Hàn practices.
At the beginning of Jìn Wǔdì's reign,
the court assembly rituals were revised.
Ten *kè* before the end of the night-watch,
courtyard torches were lit,
and officials gathered.
Fù Xuán's 'Cháohuì Fù' states:
"Magnificent lanterns like fiery trees,
a hundred branches blazing brightly."
This indicates that the Wèi ritual and courtyard torches were used together.
Seven *kè* before the end of the watch,
officials entered to offer congratulations.
Five *kè* before the end,
they took their positions.
When the watch ended,
the emperor appeared in the front hall.
All officials offered congratulations,
as in the Hàn ritual.
After the ritual, they withdrew.
Officials sat,
which was called 'Chénhè' (morning congratulations).
Three *kè* after the start of the day-watch, the emperor appeared again.
All officials presented longevity wine,
and a grand banquet with music was held,
called 'Zhàohuì' (day assembly).
Separately, thirty female musicians were placed outside the yellow tent,
playing 'Songs of the Inner Chamber'.
East of the Jiāng (Yangzi), there were many troubles,
so 'Chénhè' was no longer performed.
Ten *kè* before the end of the night-watch,
the Xuānyángmén was opened.
The main hall gates were only opened at dawn.
Five *kè* after the start of the day-watch,
the emperor then appeared to receive congratulations.
During the Sòng era, congratulations were received only at ten *kè* (after the start of the day-watch).
The rest of the rituals for ascending, descending, bowing, and prostrating,
as well as the establishment of ancestral temples for empresses, consorts, kings, dukes, and below, evening sacrifices, bowing, conferring, condolence rites, and funeral rites,
all had their respective ritual notes,
but the text is too extensive to be included.
On the third day of the third month, the Qūshuǐ (曲水) gathering
was an ancient Xìjì (禊祭) ceremony.
The Hàn (漢) Lǐyí Zhì (禮儀志) says:
"In the third month of spring, on the first Sǐ (巳) day,
officials and commoners alike would cleanse themselves in the eastward-flowing water,
washing themselves to ward off old illnesses, which was called a 'great cleansing' (dàjié, 大絜)."
It does not state what water was the eastward-flowing water.
The Jìn (晉) Zhōngcháo (中朝) says that
from high officials down to commoners,
all performed the Xì (褉) ceremony by the Luòshuǐ (洛水) river.
This is recorded in various Xì Fù (禊賦) and in the biography of Xià Zhòngyù (夏仲御).
When Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) usurped the throne,
on the third day,
he gathered at Tiānyuānchí (天淵池) to execute Zhāng Lín (張林).
Huái Dì (懷帝) also gathered at Tiānyuānchí (天淵池) to compose poems.
Lù Jī (陸機) said:
"To the south of Tiānyuānchí (天淵池) is a stone channel,
drawing water from the Yùgōu (御溝).
To the west of the pond, piled stones form the Xìtáng (禊堂),
spanning the water,
where cups were floated and wine was drunk."
This also does not mention Qūshuǐ (曲水).
Yuán Dì (元帝) later issued an edict to abolish the third day's entertainment devices.
Nowadays, these are continuously passed down as devices for various games (bǎifèi zhī jù, 百猆之具),
with intricate carvings and craftsmanship,
subject to constant additions and deletions.
The historian says: Examining Xì (禊) and Qūshuǐ (曲水),
their meanings are somewhat different.
It was formerly said that when the yang energy spread vigorously,
all things fully emerged,
and the Gūxǐ (姑洗) would cleanse them.
Sǐ (巳) means blessing (zhǐ, 祉),
indicating a prayer for great blessings.
Another theory says that
on the third day of the third month,
which is the Qīngmíng (清明) festival,
rituals would be performed by the water,
with prayers and sacrifices to request a bountiful year.
Yīng Shào (應劭) said:
"Xì (禊) means
cleansing (jié, 絜),
referring to self-purification.
Some say that in the Hàn (漢) era, there was Guō Yú (郭虞),
who had two daughters born on the third day of the third month's first Chén (辰) day,
and another daughter born on Shàngsǐ (上巳).
These frequent births on the two days all resulted in death.
At the time, this was considered a major taboo,
so every time that day came, people
would all go to the eastward-flowing water to pray for exorcism and self-purification,
floating and drinking from the clear stream.
Later, this developed into Qūshuǐ (曲水)."
It is recorded that Gāo Hòu (高后) performed exorcism at Bàshàng (霸上).
Mǎ Róng (馬融) and Liáng Jì (梁冀)'s Xīdǐ Fù (西第賦) says:
"In the northwest Xū-Hài (戌亥) direction,
dark stones support the transport.
Shrimp vomit and excrete,
in the Gēng-Xīn (庚辛) region."
This is an image of Qūshuǐ (曲水).
Now, based on Xì (禊) being the Qūshuǐ (曲水) event,
it should have existed before Yǒngshòu (永壽).
The exorcism (fúchú, 祓除) cannot have occurred after Gāo Hòu (高后),
and the theory of praying for agriculture (qínóng zhī shuō, 祈農之說) is appropriate for the matter.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, there was horse archery (mǎshè, 馬射).
Some say that
it was during the autumn metal season,
practicing military skills and archery,
imitating the Hàn (漢) ritual for the beginning of autumn.
The historian says: Examining the Jìn (晉) Zhōngcháo (中朝) grand assemblies,
there were performances of lying riding, inverted riding, and headstand riding (wòqí, dǎoqí, diānqí, 臥騎、倒騎、顛騎),
racing from Dōnghuá Mén (東華門) to Shénhǔ Mén (神虎門).
[五二] This also belongs to the category of wrestling and various performances (jiǎodǐ zá fěi zhī liú, 角抵雜猆之流).
When Sòng Wǔ (宋武) became Sòng Gōng (宋公),
he was in Péngchéng (彭城).
On the ninth day, he went out to Xiàng Yǔ (項羽)'s Xìmǎtái (戲馬臺).
This has been passed down to this day,
regarded as an old standard.
Collation Notes
Zhì (志) 2, Lǐ (禮) B
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán (建元),
when Gāo Dì (高帝)'s mausoleum was built,
Zhāo Huánghòu (昭皇后) should be moved and interred with him.
The Cíbù (祠部) wondered whether there should be an ancestral sacrifice and ceremonies for sending out invitations to various offerings and nine meals.
Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Jiǎn (左僕射王儉) deliberated:
"The offerings should be like the great shroud (dàliǎn, 大斂).
Hè Xún (賀循) said, 'Offerings should be made at all tombs from the main tomb,
like the rites for the ancestral temple and court before burial.'
Fàn Níng (范寧) said, 'Offerings are made when about to be interred.'
Although it is not called an ancestral sacrifice (zǔjì, 祖祭),
a sacrifice cannot be omitted."
This was followed.
The relevant officials then presented:
"Zhāo Huánghòu (昭皇后)'s spirit tablet is in the temple.
Now she is being moved for interment,
((廣)) the temple has the Yú (虞) ritual to appease the spirit.
Since the spirit is already in the temple, if it is reburied and the spirit tablet is taken out,
should the Yú (虞) ritual be performed?
Zhèng Zhù (鄭注) on reburial says, 'From the temple to the temple,
the rites should be the same as from the tomb to the tomb.'
How can the matter be different?
Previous generations said there should be no Yú (虞)."
Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Jiǎn (左僕射王儉) deliberated:
"Fàn Níng (范寧) said, 'A burial must have a spirit carriage (húnchē, 魂車).'
If there is no provision for its return, where will the spirit reside?
When reburials occur in the world,
offerings are immediately made at the tomb.
How can it be destroyed without sacrifice?
Hè Xún (賀循) said, 'After interment,
offerings are made at the tomb
to conclude the matter.'
Although it is not a proper Yú (虞),
it is roughly similar.
When the Jìn (晉) dynasty restored the five mausoleums,
and the Sòng (宋) dynasty's Jìng Hòu (敬后) was reburied,
both had the Yú (虞) ritual.
So, performing the Yú (虞) now is not questionable."
This was followed.
In the second year of Jiànyuán (建元),
the Crown Prince's Consort passed away.
The former palace officials were unsure what mourning attire to wear.
Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Jiǎn (左僕射王儉) deliberated:
"The Lǐ Jì (禮記)'s Wénwáng Shìzǐ (文王世子) says, 'When the father is alive, one is a son;
when the ruler is alive, one is a subject.'
Furthermore, since the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
palace officials have been fully staffed,
and the protocol for subjects and subordinates is clearly defined in three categories.
Formerly, when Yǔ Yì (庾翼)'s wife died,
Wáng Yǔn (王允) and Téng Hóng (滕弘) said that the prefectural officials should wear the mourning attire for a minor lord's wife (xiǎojūn zhī fú, 小君之服).
How much more so for the importance of a subject's duty?
It is proper to follow the rites and wear Qīcuī (齊衰) for three months for the former lord's wife.
Those holding official positions
should all request leave of absence,
mourning and weeping morning and evening,
all related to the Eastern Palace (dōnggōng, 東宮).
For those subjects who have not yet taken office and are far away,
at their place of residence, they should mourn for two and a half days,
and then observe the mourning rites and don the mourning attire,
sending memorials
instead of rushing to the capital."
This was followed.
The Crown Prince's Consort wore the Zhǎncǎo (斬草) and rode the Chénhuáng (乘黃).
They debated about erecting a míngjīng (銘旌).
Púyè Wáng Jiǎn (僕射王儉) deliberated:
"According to the rites,
after the coffin is plastered, the invocator takes the inscription and places it to the east of the bier.
After the great shroud is completed, it should be erected to the east of the western steps."
In the second year of Dàmíng (大明) of Sòng (宋),
the Crown Prince's Consort passed away,
and nine streamers (jiǔliú, 九旒) were erected.
The relevant officials also deliberated:
"Should streamers be erected on the day of Zhǎncǎo (斬草) or not?
If streamers are erected, how many should there be?
And how should the rising and descending dragons be painted?
Also, how many funeral fans (shà, 翣) should be used?"
Púyè Wáng Jiǎn (僕射王儉) deliberated:
"Streamers (liú, 旒) are originally part of official attire,
unrelated to inauspicious events.
Nowadays, from high officials downwards,
they cannot fully observe the rites in life,
so they only erect them during inauspicious events.
The Eastern Palace (dōnggōng, 東宮) has the same rank as a duke with nine appointments.
The consort is one body with the Crown Prince,
so there is no reason for difference.
There is no reason to deviate from the usual practice
and specially erect inauspicious streamers.
The Dàmíng (大明) precedent
was not carefully discussed,
but was simply acted upon hastily.
Now, we should examine it by the ritual canons
and not follow previous mistakes.
The auspicious procession has its own palanquin and carriage,
and the inauspicious procession has its own míngjīng (銘旌).
If streamers are erected again,
where would they be placed?
Eight funeral fans (shà, 翣) should be used."
This was followed.
The relevant officials presented:
"According to the Dàmíng (大明) precedent,
the Crown Prince's Consort's Xuan Palace (xuángōng, 玄宮) had a stone inscription (shízhì, 石誌).
It was deliberated that tomb inscriptions are not found in ritual canons.
Recently, during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) reign of Sòng (宋),
Yán Yán (顏延) wrote the stone inscription for Wáng Qiú (王球).
Common families did not have steles or records,
so this was used to record virtues.
Since then,
from princes and dukes downwards,
all have adopted this practice.
The Crown Prince's Consort holds a significant position,
and her rites are exceptional among the usual ranks.
Since there is an elegy (āicè, 哀策),
it is believed that a stone inscription is not necessary."
This was followed.
The officials reported:
"After Mù Fēi's (穆妃) ān-kū (安哭) ceremony,
her spirit tablet (靈) is still on its journey.
If it encounters the new moon (朔) or full moon (望),
should sacrifices be offered or not?"
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) deliberated:
"Since the ān-kū (安哭) has been performed,
and sacrifices are offered at the ancestral temple (廟),
this is fundamentally about arranging sacrifices according to seniority (昭穆).
It is not entirely the same as the four seasonal sacrifices (四時之祭) offered after the 'final auspicious ceremony' (卒吉).
Therefore, there are additional ceremonies (殷事) on the new moon and full moon.
In vassal states (蕃國), the special regulations are not applied.
After Sòng Jiāngxià Wángfēi (宋江夏王妃) performed her ān-kū (安哭),
sacrifices were offered on the new moon and full moon.
The imperial family, having concluded mourning (除喪) with the ān-kū (安哭),
has no reason to then have new moon and full moon sacrifices.
Although the spirit tablet (靈筵) has not yet been elevated to the ancestral hall (廟堂),
the boat itself serves as a temporary temple (行廟),
just like Huán Xuán (桓玄) and Sòng Gāozǔ's (宋高祖) two states of Chángshā (長沙) and Línchuān (臨川),
both had the ritual of moving the ancestral temple (移廟之禮).
How can it be said that since the spirit tablet (靈筵) is on its way,
additional ceremonies (殷事) should be performed?
Based on this,
sacrifices are no longer needed on the new moon and full moon.
The old customs during Sòng Yìhòu's (宋懿后) time did not extend to this,
which further clarifies the contemporary view."
This was adopted.
In the third year of Jiànyuán (建元) (481 CE),
the officials reported:
"Huáng Tàizǐ Mù Fēi (皇太子穆妃) passed away in the seventh month of last year (480 CE).
That year had an intercalary ninth month.
We are unsure whether the intercalary month should be counted within the number of months?
Or should the intercalary month be appended to the first month?
If the intercalary month is to be counted within the number of months,
then Nánjùn Wáng's (南郡王) brothers should perform their xiǎoxiáng (小祥) on the last day of this fourth month.
As for the month of xiáng (祥),
will there be any doubt or not?"
Zuǒ Púshè Wáng Jiǎn (左僕射王儉) deliberated:
"Three hundred and sixty days (三百六旬) is the clear meaning in the Shàngshū (尚書).
Gōng Wén (文公) accepting betrothal gifts (納幣) was criticized in the Chūnqiū (春秋).
Gǔliáng (穀梁) says, 'Months are formed by accumulating days.'
Gōngyáng (公羊) says, 'Heaven does not have such a month.'
However,
Zuǒ Shǐ (左氏) considered 'reporting the new moon' (告朔) to be proper ritual.
Therefore, earlier scholars (先儒) all said that for the three-year mourning period (三年朞喪),
the intercalary month is not counted in the year count,
but for Dàgōng (大功) and lesser mourning,
the intercalary month is counted in the month count.
An intercalary month (閏)
is the extra days of a year,
and a distinct new moon for a month.
Therefore, Wú Shāng (吳商) said, 'Including the intercalary month to correct the anniversary (朞)
truly accords with reason.'
Now, for the one-year mourning period (杖朞之喪),
even if the xiǎoxiáng (小祥) is in the eleventh month,
when it comes to the xiánggǎo (祥縞) ceremony,
a full year must be completed.
All rituals of 'condensed mourning' (厭屈之禮)
essentially take their symbolism from the main mourning attire.
The xiánggǎo (祥縞) are two months apart.
The earlier performance (厭降) of xiǎoxiáng (小祥) also follows this principle.
Furthermore, in terms of nomenclature,
xiǎoxiáng (小祥) is fundamentally based on the annual limit.
When examining the precedents,
there should necessarily be a gap of two months.
Now, by performing xiáng (祥) earlier due to 'condensed mourning' (厭屈),
it cannot be said that this matter is not a full year.
Since the matter is of the same category,
the sentiment is not different.
The principle of 'not counting the intercalary month' (沒閏之理)
naturally takes precedence.
Supposing the xiáng (祥) is on the last day of this month,
then it would be three months from xiánggǎo (縞),
which, according to the standard precedents,
would create even more obstacles.
It should be that the xiáng (祥) is performed on the last day of the fifth month.
This is a major ritual of the state,
and should be thoroughly deliberated upon.
All eight bureaus (八座) and their officials (丞郎) should be consulted
to fully explore similarities and differences."
Shàngshū Lìng Chǔ Yuān (尚書令褚淵) challenged Jiǎn's (儉) deliberation, saying:
"The rule of 'condensed mourning' (厭屈之典)
arises from the venerated one (所尊) overriding natural sentiment,
thus the xiánggǎo (祥縞) system is complete,
but the years and months are not extended.
Now, performing xiáng (祥) in the eleventh month
shows that it follows the one-year anniversary (朞).
Since it is calculated by the number of months,
then the intercalary month should be counted to complete the ritual.
If it is still included (含之),
how is it different from the xiánggǎo (縞) system?
The doubt arises precisely because xiáng (祥) falls in an intercalary month,
and the number of months differs.
Accumulated extra intercalary months (積分餘閏) is a principle widely established in calendrical astronomy (曆象).
Those who count by months (計月者) count the intercalary month (數閏), thus there are extra months (餘月).
Those who count by years (計年者) encompass it (苞含), thus reaching a full accumulation (盈積).
To follow the ritual according to reason,
what is unacceptable about that?"
Jiǎn (儉) again responded to Yuān's (淵) challenge, saying:
"The principle of 'including the intercalary month' (含閏之義) is questioned by knowledgeable scholars.
However, xiáng (祥) should originally correspond to a full year (朞),
but is abbreviated (屈) and not fully carried out.
In terms of the actual event, both the name and the substance exist.
In terms of sorrow, the sentiment is no different.
Although it seems to be several months,
in essence, it is calculated by years.
The intercalary month (閏) is the remaining portion of the year,
so it should be entirely encompassed.
A full year (朞) with two xiáng (祥) ceremonies is due to abbreviation (屈) for the sake of the venerated one (緣尊).
For xiáng (祥), the intercalary month is not counted (沒閏),
symbolizing the extension of the year.
Abbreviation (屈) and extension (申) are simultaneously evident, both paths are presented.
Is this not the meaning of the classics and records?
If xiǎoxiáng (小祥) were in the fifth month,
and the intercalary month were only in the sixth month,
then the interval between xiáng (祥) and xiánggǎo (縞) would be two months.
This would mean the eleventh month symbolizes the preceding full year (朞),
and the two months represent the following year (歲).
The names have their specific regions and cannot be intermixed.
In the twenty-eighth year of Lǔ Xiāng (魯襄) (545 BCE), it is recorded: 'In the twelfth month, on the day Yǐwèi (乙未), the Son of Chǔ (楚子) died.'
Only the month is recorded;
it does not mention an intercalary month.
This is another clear example of appending to the preceding.
Zhèng (鄭), Shè (射), Wáng (王), and Hè (賀) only said that for a full year (朞), the intercalary month is not counted (沒閏).
They did not further distinguish between xiáng (祥) within the one-year mourning (杖朞).
Perhaps they thought it unnecessary to state.
Chéng Xiūfǔ (成休甫) said, 'After dàxiáng (大祥) comes tǎn (禫); if there is an intercalary month, it should be counted separately.'
This clearly indicates that xiáng (祥) for the one-year mourning (杖朞)
cannot be equated with the end of the zīnyīn (綅縞) period.
If the grace is like that, then the precedent is like this."
