Yuān (淵) again cited old interpretations to challenge Jiǎn (儉) with more than ten questions,
and Jiǎn (儉) explained each point.
Cíbù Lángzhōng Wáng Guīzhī (祠部郎中王珪之) deliberated,
stating,
"Mourning is applied with intercalary months.
For Gōngshuāi (功衰) and lesser mourning, if xiǎoxiáng (小祥) falls on an intercalary month,
it is generally not mentioned.
Although it is 'condensed' (厭屈) now,
the name xiáng (祥) still remains,
differing from other mourning attire.
Calculating by months means counting them,
abbreviating the heart of longing
by making the distant near.
If days are extra fractions,
and months are not proper new moons,
then encompassing them to complete the system
is the only reasonable thing to do.
Púshè Jiǎn's (僕射儉) deliberation
is thoroughly and extensively supported by reason.
I respectfully agree with it.
Sītú Yuān (司徒淵), though initially raising doubts,
after repeated exchanges,
has not agreed with Jiǎn's (儉) deliberation.
It is appropriate to follow the old practice of involving all eight bureaus (八座) and their officials (丞郎) in a broad discussion.
Therefore, the xiǎoxiáng (小祥) should be on the last day of the fifth month,
and the xiáng (祥) and tǎn (禫) ceremonies should follow the usual limits.
The report was submitted to the emperor,
and issued to internal and external offices."
The imperial edict stated,
"Approved."
Regarding the mourning attire for Crown Prince Mùfēi,
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) and concurrently Zhùzuòláng (著作郎) Wáng Qūn (王逡) asked Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射) Wáng Jiǎn (王儉):
"For the Xiǎoxiáng (小祥) of Zhōngjūn Nánjùnwáng (中軍南郡王),
should it wait for Wénxǐ (聞喜) or not?
Mùfēi (穆妃) passed away on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month.
Wénxǐgōng (聞喜公) began mourning in the eighth month.
Calculating the eleven-month period,
it should fall in the sixth month.
If Nánjùnwáng (南郡王) were to likewise observe it in the sixth month,
then the Dàxiáng (大祥) would be extended by another month,
to the eighth month,
no longer the first month.
In the spirit of honoring one's kin,
if each were to observe their own Xiáng (祥),
then mourning huts and whitewashed walls would be interspersed,
black and white mixed together.
I am unsure if such a doubt should exist."
Jiǎn (儉) said:
"The sending off of the deceased has its completion,
and the rebirth (of the spirit) has its measure.
Boundless grief is not what the mourning system extends to.
The white mourning attire for Xiáng (祥) clearly marks the conclusion.
As for the principle of waiting for each other,
there is no mention in the classics or records.
Many people of the world believe that mourning huts and coarse hemp
should not differ,
and so for those separated by one or two months,
they are sometimes extended to be concluded together.
This is what is called acting solely on emotion,
without understanding the intent of the rites.
When I compiled the Sāngjì (喪記) in the past,
I already spoke of this.
A person returning from afar,
if they have an occasion (to mourn) but have not yet performed the sacrifice,
how can a son at home
offer any reason for not changing (his attire)?
The rites state that there are those who remove their mourning attire and return (home).
This is the surviving text in the classics and records,
clear evidence that one does not wait.
Supposing one should wait,
then if the separation is a whole year,
one should also certainly wait.
That would lead to wearing coarse hemp for mourning for the rest of one's life,
and the cessation of auspicious purification in the ancestral temple forever.
This is impossible.
If it is said to be inappropriate,
then even a period of ten days or a month
cannot be extended.
Why?
Rites have their order,
and principles are not established in vain.
If one does not wait when far,
but must wait when near,
then the ritual precedents are contradictory,
and the heart finds no basis.
If one worries about brothers living together,
with auspicious and inauspicious events mixed,
then ancient times had the principle of separate residences.
Even if there are no separate residences,
then a son returning from afar
should open a separate gate
to complete the mourning rites.
The spiritual mat and sacrificial offerings
follow the person at home,
ending after two full years.
The reason for this is
that the rites for rushing to mourning state, 'one establishes a position but does not offer sacrifices.'
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) commented, 'because their spirit is not present here.'
Not hearing of the grief in time
is truly due to being far away.
Establishing a position but not offering sacrifices
makes even more sense.
This is due to a specific circumstance,
and is not related to嫡庶 (díshù, principal wife's son vs. concubine's son).
A concubine's son at home
also does not wait for the principal wife's son.
Moreover, the Crown Princess is the legitimate body of the royal house,
and the Zhōngjūn (中軍) is the principal heir of great importance.
The imperial court also implements provisional regulations,
making the matter even less doubtful whether to advance or withdraw.
I say they should not wait for each other.
On the day of Zhōngjūn's (中軍) Xiáng (祥) mourning attire removal,
Wénxǐ (聞喜) should merely express condolences,
and not receive expressions of sympathy.
And when the忌辰 (jìchén, anniversary of death) passes and mourning is removed,
brothers should also meet to express their feelings to each other, but not face guests.
This is a great standard of the state,
and it is appropriate to inform the Bāzuò (八座) and Chéngláng (丞郎),
for all to fully discuss agreements and disagreements,
and [then] present it to the emperor."
Sītú (司徒) Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) and twenty others all agreed with Jiǎn's (儉) proposal as valid,
and requested it be made a permanent regulation.
An edict said,
"Approved."
In the third year of Jiànyuán (建元),
Crown Prince Mùfēi (穆妃) passed away.
The officials of Nánjùnwáng (南郡王) and Wénxǐgōng (聞喜公) doubted how to observe mourning for the 君母 (jūnmǔ, ruler's mother).
Jiǎn (儉) further argued:
"The rites state, 'Commoners wear Qīcuī (齊衰) for their ruler.'
Earlier scholars said, 'Commoners in office, such as clerks and scribes, are meant.'
Furthermore, the great wife of a feudal lord wore Suìcuī (繐衰) for seven months for the Fūrén (夫人).
Because this is minor and distant,
the full rites are not observed.
Now, the imperial grandson is himself a prince and duke of a vassal state,
and Crown Prince Mùfēi (穆妃) is the principal wife of the imperial court.
Palace officials may observe the rites for a Xiǎojūn (小君),
but how dare state officials show respect for a Fūrén (夫人)?
They should wear plain clothes, a white cap, and a plain sash, and weep outside the central gate.
Each time they approach (the funeral), they should enter,
together with the palace officials."
In the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
Crown Prince Wénhuì (文惠) passed away.
Yòu Púyè (右僕射) Wáng Yàn (王晏) and others reported:
"According to the Sāngfújīng (喪服經), 'For the father and eldest son of the ruler,
one observes Qīcuī (齊衰) for one year.'
Now, since His Majesty does not observe the three-year mourning,
but only the one-year period,
the officials should lower by one degree,
and thus observe Dàgōng (大功).
Jiǔyuègōngcuī (九月功衰) is the mourning for brothers,
and cannot be used for someone of higher status.
We have deliberated
and believe it is appropriate to make the mourning attire heavier,
but reduce the number of months,
all observing Qīcuī (齊衰) for three months.
As for the Grand Imperial Grandson, since the three-year period is observed,
the officials of the Nánjùn (南郡) state
should fully observe Qīcuī (齊衰) for one year.
Línrǔ (臨汝) and Qǔjiāng (曲江), not being the principal heirs,
may not take precedence over the former Crown Prince.
The officials of these two dukes
should not observe mourning."
An edict
approved their proposal.
They also reported:
"Although the Sāngfújīng (喪服經) states, 'A concubine follows the ruler in observing mourning for his eldest son,'
since the Hàn (漢) dynasties,
this rite has long been abolished.
We request to follow previous precedents,
and not revive its practice."
An edict said:
"Since it has long been abolished,
cease the practice."
They also reported:
"We humbly recall that during His Majesty's one-year mourning for Crown Prince Wénhuì (文惠), music was not performed.
Although the various princes originally observed one-year mourning,
the Crown Prince is the legitimate body of the ancestral temple,
and those observing mourning for him are treated the same.
Upon the removal of mourning attire,
the playing of music and marriages
should all be permitted.
We humbly believe that these two matters are indeed auspicious rites,
but differ in severity.
Marrying a wife for progeny is not an entirely auspicious affair.
'No music for three days' is explicitly stated in the rites.
During the Sòng (宋) era, for those whose one-year mourning was reduced to Dàgōng (大功),
music was suspended for weddings
to express private grief,
in accordance with earlier precedents."
An edict
said,
"Follow the proposal."
They also reported:
"According to the rites,
for both Xiáng (祥) and Chú (除), one changes clothes on the eve,
and then performs the sacrifice on the next morning.
We observe that in recent generations, mourning attire is changed only after approaching the funeral,
which conflicts with the rites.
Now, on the day of Dōnggōng's (東宮) public mourning removal,
if following the usual practice, the Imperial Grand Grandson would only change clothes after approaching the funeral.
We have deliberated
and believe that one should first weep at the funeral and then offer sacrifices.
Those who are to publicly remove mourning
should all change their clothes at their mansions,
and then come to the funeral,
performing the rite of offering condolences."
An edict
said,
"Approved."
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
during a court assembly,
as Shìzǔ's (世祖) period of complete silence had not yet ended,
the court debated whether to perform music.
Cíbùláng (祠部郎) Hé Tóngzhī (何佟之) argued:
"In ancient times, Shùn (舜) received the mandate from Wénzǔ (文祖),
although he was not the heir of Yáo (堯).
When Fàngxūn (放勛) passed away,
he observed three years of complete silence.
In recent times, Emperor Kāng of Jìn (晉康帝) succeeded Emperor Chéng (成帝),
and at that time, music was also not performed.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) during Emperor Huái's (懷帝) reign,
Emperor Huì's (惠帝) mourning period had not ended.
At that time, Jiāng Chōng (江充) argued,
'Ancient emperors succeeded each other,
and although the succession varied,
the importance and gravity of the rites were the same.'"
This was followed.
In the first month of the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the relevant authorities, noting that the second anniversary of the decease of Shìzōng Wén Huángdì would fall on the twenty-fourth day of the first month of this second year,
〔一一〕and the Dàxiáng (grand sacrifice) on the twenty-ninth day,
and the Xiángtán (end of mourning) on the twenty-ninth day of the third month,
determined that the ceremonies for His Majesty and the assembled officials to express grief
should be established.
This was sent down to the two academies, the eight ministries, and the Cchéngláng.
Bóshì Táo Sháo believed that
“names establish meanings,
this has been the system since ancient times.
Wén Dì is formally revered as Zǔzōng,
arranging the hierarchy of generations.
On the days of Xiáng and the anniversary of death (Jì), and Tán,
the emperor should wear sacrificial robes,
and go out to the Tàijí hall to express grief,
while all officials should also wear sacrificial robes and attend.”
Tàicháng Chéng Lǐ Huī debated, saying:
“Considering that the honorable title has been posthumously conferred,
the heavy mourning attire should be proper.
However, since a provisional system has been followed,
the plain staff was not used.
As for the rekindling of fire, since it is treated the same,
heaven and earth also change.
How can one avoid feeling the impact?
Moreover, when Jìn Jǐngxiàn Huánghòu died,
the officials all wore the attire for a minor consort.
For a posthumously honored empress,
there should be no deviation from the imperial empress’s rites.
For a posthumously honored emperor,
it is certainly appropriate to follow the emperor’s rites.
Although subjects and sons are one category,
the rites vary with the times.
His Majesty, ascending to the throne in the midst of restoration,
is not succeeding in the martial line,
so there is no reason for a change to deep robes.
However, as the king embodies the state,
he should also don mourning attire and proceed to the main hall to express grief,
and all officials should express deep sorrow,
following the usual custom.”
Gěishìzhōng Lǐng Guózǐ Zhùjiào Xiè Tánjì (formerly Xiè Mòjì) debated: 〔一二〕
“Funeral rites are a single system,
but their observance is divided into two phases.
The Yú and Fù sacrifices express the feeling of remembering the deceased,
while the Xiǎoxiáng ceremony moderates the rites for the living.
This is because extreme love can be extended,
but intense grief should be restrained.
Although Wén Huángdì’s virtue as a ruler was established early,
and his civilizing influence had not yet fully spread,
his posthumous elevation to the highest honor
was truly due to his nature.
Now, to speak of him as a subject would be without basis,
and to discuss it from a personal perspective would be empty.
The Sacred Emperor rules the world,
and further receives the favor of Heaven,
reverently performing rites at the Seven Ancestral Temples,
not following the Three Empresses.
Thus, for the Jì, Xiáng, and Tán ceremonies,
there is no basis for their establishment.”
Tàixué Bóshì Cuī Xiǎn agreed with Táo Sháo’s deliberation.
Tàicháng Shěn Tán agreed with Lǐ Huī’s deliberation.
〔一三〕Guózǐ Bóshì Liú Jǐng and others agreed with Xiè Tánjì’s (formerly Xiè Mòjì’s) deliberation.
Cíbù Láng Hé Tōngzhī debated, saying:
“The essence of the Spring and Autumn Annals is that
a subject succeeds his lord, and a son his parent.
Although the grace and righteousness differ,
the rites are one and the same.
This is to strengthen the feeling of respect,
and solidify the righteousness of mourning.
Although the Sovereign respectfully succeeded Gāo Huáng,
and once served under him,
now that the sacred reign controls the universe,
and endless teachings are imparted,
the grace of the three years [of mourning]
cannot reasonably be set aside.
I humbly believe that for Shìzōng’s Xiáng and Jì days,
His Majesty should wear mourning attire and ascend the hall,
and the assembled officials should together express sorrow and emotion.
After the ceremony,
all officials should proceed to Xuāndé Gōng to present memorials,
and then go to the imperial tomb to express grief,
thereby extending the yearning for the distant past.”
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn and nineteen others agreed with Tōngzhī’s deliberation.
An imperial edict declared:
“Approved.”
When Hǎilíng Wáng died,
officials gathered to express grief.
At that time, there was strict military discipline,
and the court debated whether to attend in military attire.
Cíbù Láng Hé Tōngzhī deliberated:
“Lambskin robes and black caps are not for mourning.
It is not permissible to attend a funeral in military attire.
In the second year of Tàishǐ of Sòng,
on the day of Xiàowǔ’s Dàxiáng,
all officials who entered to attend
changed out of their military attire at the palace gate,
donned civilian robes,
and after attending, they exited
and resumed their military attire.”
This was followed.
A eulogy states: The system of Jī and the work of Kǒng,
serve as guidance for a hundred kings.
Three thousand [rites] are enumerated,
the four cardinal principles are displayed.
They augment or diminish the classics,
abolish or uphold the statutes.
Military rites, state matters,
ancestral temples, suburban altars, schools.
Capping, marriage, court assemblies,
mourning attire and periods for misfortune.
To preserve them is a great virtue,
to abandon them is a warning of peril.
Collation Notes
Treatise Three: Music
The lyrics for the music and dance of the Southern Suburban Sacrifice,
were used in both Hàn dynasties.
They can be found in the Former Hàn Treatise,
and were alternately performed at the five suburban altars.
The Wèi song and dance are not seen,
presumably they used Hàn lyrics.
In the second year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
when performing the suburban sacrifice at the Míngtáng,
an edict commanded that the rites follow the principle of the Zhōu dynasty first referring to the Yīn sacrifices,
and provisionally use Wèi rituals.
Later, Fù Xuán was ordered to compose a poem for the evening sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and the five suburban altars,
and a poem for welcoming the spirits.
Sòng Wén Dì ordered Yán Yánzhī to compose three poems for the evening sacrifice to Heaven, welcoming and sending off spirits, and feasting spirits at the suburban altars.
This indicates that the early Sòng still followed the Jìn.
In the second year of Jiànchuán,
the relevant authorities memorialized,
saying that the ancient music lyrics for suburban and ancestral temples were previously compiled by scholars and bóshì,
who would search, select, and adopt them.
They requested an imperial decree that,
in addition to those outside, all scholars of righteousness be generally ordered to compose them.
The participants debated: The ascending songs for the Tàimiào should use Sītú Chǔ Yuān’s compositions;
all others should use Huángmén Láng Xiè Chāozōng’s compositions.
The works compiled by Chāozōng largely involved deleting parts of Yán Yánzhī’s and Xiè Zhuāng’s compositions to create new melodies,
and comprehensively changing the names of the musical pieces.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi Fú Mánróng submitted a memorial,
suggesting that
excellent scholars should be gathered
to compile and edit the refined music.
An imperial edict instructed the relevant department to deliberate,
but it was ultimately not implemented.

Ming táng Song Lyrics,
Sacrificing to the Wǔdì.
The Hàn suburban sacrificial songs are all in four-character lines.
Sòng Xiàowǔ ordered Xiè Zhuāng to compose the lyrics.
Zhuāng followed the numbers of the Wǔxíng:
Wood uses three,
Fire uses seven,
Earth uses five,
Metal uses nine,
Water uses six.
According to the Wǔxíng of Hóngfàn,
first is Water,
second is Fire,
third is Wood,
fourth is Metal,
fifth is Earth.
The Yuèlìng states that the number for Wood is eight,
Fire is seven,
Earth is five,
Metal is nine,
Water is six.
Cài Yōng said:
"The East has Wood (three) and Earth (five),
hence the number is eight;
the South has Fire (two) and Earth (five),
hence the number is seven;
the West has Metal (four) and Earth (five),
hence the number is nine;
the North has Water (one) and Earth (five),
hence the number is six."
Also, according to the Nàyīn numbers,
one word obtains Earth,
three words obtain Fire,
five words obtain Water,
seven words obtain Metal,
nine words obtain Wood.
If we follow the Hóngfàn, Wood uses three,
then Water should be one, Fire two, Metal four.
If we follow the Yuèlìng, Metal nine, Water six,
then Wood should be eight, Fire seven.
When the numbers one and two of Hóngfàn
are used, the words do not form a proper verse,
hence there is selection and omission,
resulting in both interpretations being violated.
It is unclear what basis was used for establishing the verses with these numbers.
The Zhōu Sòng "Wǒ Jiāng Sì Wénwáng"
mostly uses four-character lines,
with one line having five characters,
and one line having seven characters.
Xiè Zhuāng's songs for Sòng Tàizǔ also had no fixed line length.
In the first year of Jiàn'yuán,
an edict ordered the Huángménláng Xiè Chāozōng to compose lyrics for the Ming táng evening sacrifices, etc.,
all adopting Zhuāng's lyrics.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
during the Yú sacrifice at the Ming táng,
Xiè Tiǎo composed lyrics,
completely following Xiè Zhuāng,
only Shìzǔ's were in four-character lines.

In the third year of Yǒngpíng (AD 60),
Wáng Cāng, Prince of Dōngpíng, composed a "Dēnggē" (Ascension Song) of one chapter and twenty-six lines for the temple of Guāngwǔ,
its lyrics praising his achievements and virtues.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān (AD 213),
when the state of Wèi was first established,
Shìzhōng Wáng Càn composed the "Dēnggē Ānshì Shī",
explaining the intention of the spirits observing and accepting offerings.
During Emperor Míng's reign,
Shìzhōng Miào Xí reported:
"The 'Ānshì Shī' was originally the name of a song from the former Hàn dynasty.
The songs sung now
do not match the text of the former songs.
I, Xí, have examined the Zhōu Lǐ (（志）)【注】annotation, which states,
〔四三〕'Ānshì music is like the Zhōu Fángzhōng music.'
In the past, discussants believed
that Fángzhōng music praised the virtues of empresses and consorts,
and proposed changing the name 'Ānshì' to 'Zhèngshǐ' music.
Later, upon (（續）)【讀】reading the Hàn 'Ānshì Gē',
〔四四〕it also describes spirits coming to banquets and accepting offerings,
with no mention of empresses or consorts.
I reflect that those who in the past referred to Fángzhōng music as a song for empresses and consorts
might have misunderstood its meaning.
When performing sacrifices to entertain the spirits,
the 'Dēnggē' praises the achievements and virtues of the ancestors.
When singing banquets below the hall,
there is no need to sing about the influence of empresses and consorts."
Thereupon, the 'Ānshì' music was changed to 'Xiǎngshén Gē' (Song for Feasting the Spirits).
Sànqí Chángshì Wáng Sù composed twelve chapters of "Zōngmiào Shī Sòng" (Ancestral Temple Odes and Eulogies),
but they were not incorporated into the music.
During the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
Fù Xuán composed one chapter of "Mìao Xī Shēng Zhāo Xià Gē",
one chapter of "Yíng Sòng Shén Sì Xià Gē Shī",
and seven chapters of "Dēnggē" for the Seven Temples.
Fù Xuán said:
"The 'Dēnggē' sings of the glorious achievements and merits,
so the texts differ for each temple.
As for the 'Xiǎngshén',
it is like the Zhōu Sòng having 'Gǔ' and 'Yōng'.
It only describes the grandeur of the ritual music for sacrificing and feasting the spirits,
and all seven temples use it for 'Xiǎngshén'."
Xiàhóu Zhàn also composed thirteen chapters of "Zōngmiào Gē".
During the Sòng dynasty, Wáng Sháozhī composed seven chapters of "Qīmiào Dēnggē".
During the Shēngmíng era,
Tàizǔ, as King of Qí,
ordered Sīkōng Chǔ Yuān to compose two chapters of "Tàimìao Dēnggē".
At the beginning of Jiànyuán,
an imperial edict instructed Huángmén Shìláng Xiè Chāozōng to compose sixteen chapters of "Mìaolè Gē Shī".
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
the Shàngshū Diànzhōng Cáo reported:
"For the spirit chamber of Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì's temple, the dance 'Gāodé Xuānliè' is performed,
but there are no accompanying songs.
The suburban sacrifice also requires lyrics.
The spirit chamber of Mùhuánghòu's temple also lacks song lyrics.
According to Fù Xuán, 'the 'Dēnggē' differs in text for each temple,
while the 'Xiǎngshén'
texts are the same for the chambers.'
〔四五〕This proposal is valid.
Furthermore, examining the song chapters of the Hàn era,
their number was not fixed,
all texts were established according to the occasion,
mostly consisting of eight lines,
after which the rhyme would change.
Sometimes there were only two or three rhymes before a change,
but such instances were very rare.
Zhāng Huá and Xiàhóu Zhàn also followed the previous style.
Fù Xuán changed rhymes quite frequently,
which further impaired the beauty of conciseness.
In recent times, Wáng Sháozhī and Yán Yánzhī both changed rhymes after four lines,
achieving a balance between length and brevity.
Yán Yánzhī and Xiè Zhuāng composed songs for the three temples,
each with three chapters,
each chapter having eight lines.
This format is suitable for detailing the accomplishments and deeds with appropriate detail,
and it should be followed now.
On the day of the suburban sacrifice,
the practice of 'lowering the honored to act as host' is altered;
the ritual differs from that of the ancestral temple.
Mùhòu's maternal virtues and influence,
and the affairs of governance are distinct.
These two songs should each be one chapter of eight lines,
and be submitted separately for imperial approval and implementation."
The imperial edict stated
"Approved."

The Xuānliè Dance holds shields and battle-axes.
For suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
they wear flat crowns, black netted headscarves,
dark robes and skirts,

The Zhōu's Dàwǔ Dance,
the Qín changed it to the Wǔxíng.
Hàn Gāo created the Wǔdé Dance,
holding shields and battle-axes,
symbolizing the world's joy at the removal of chaos by him.
According to the Rítuals, it says,
"With crimson shields and jade battle-axes,
wearing a crown, one dances the Dàwǔ."
This means the Hàn adopted this dance and established it.
Wèi Wéndì changed the Wǔxíng back to Dàwǔ,
and the Wǔdé was called Wǔsòng Dance.
Míngdì re-created the Wǔshǐ Dance.
During the Jìn dynasty, the old system was maintained.
Fù Xuán's Liùdài Dance Songs contained military lyrics;
thus, there was more than one martial dance.
In the early Xiàojiàn era of the Sòng,
the court deliberated and made the Kǎiróng Dance the Sháo Dance,
and the Xuānliè Dance the Wǔ Dance.
Based on Sháo,
Xuānliè is the ancient Dàwǔ,
not Wǔdé.
Today, the common saying calls it Wǔwáng fázhòu.
Its crown and attire were
the Wǔshǐ Dance attire decided by the Grand Secretary during Wèi Míngdì's reign,
adopted by the Jìn and Sòng,
and maintained in the early Qí,
without changing the Sòng dance's name.
The dancers' crown and attire
are seen in the Wèi Grand Secretary's memorial,
and later generations continued to use them.
The Kǎiróng Dance holds feather flutes.
For suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
they wear pointed caps,
and robes as before.
For court assemblies,
they wear Jìnxián caps,
black netted headscarves,
plain yellow robes,
single garments,
white pleated trousers,
the rest as before.
Originally Shùn's Sháo Dance,
Hàn Gāo changed its name to Wénshǐ,
the Wèi renamed it Dàsháo.
They also created Xiánxī as a civil dance.
Jìn's Fù Xuán's Liùdài Dance has Yúsháo Dance lyrics.
The Sòng adopted Kǎiróng as the successor to Sháo as a civil dance.
They continued to use the Wèi's Xiánxī crown and attire.
The Front Dance and Later Dance
were created in the ninth year of Tàishǐ of the Jìn.
The Zhèngdé and Dàyù Dances,
Fù Xuán and Zhāng Huá each wrote lyrics for them.
In the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng,
Zhèngdé was changed to the Front Dance,
and Dàyù to the Later Dance.

and dance tunes
for the court assemblies mentioned above

Solar Eclipses
On the *jiǎwǔ* day, the first day of the ninth month of the second year of Jiànjuán,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *jǐwèi* day, the first day of the seventh month of the third year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *yǐsì* day, the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the tenth year, on the *guǐwèi* day, the first day of the twelfth month,
the calculated time was at the mid-point of *wǔ* hour.
At the beginning of *wèi* hour, the sun was first seen to be eclipsed.
The loss began from the northwest corner,
eclipsing four-tenths of its disc.
At *shēn* hour, its light and color were restored.
In the first year of Lóngchāng, on the *jiǎxū* day, the new moon conjunction occurred in the fifth month.
At *sì* hour, one-third of the sun was eclipsed.
At *wǔ* hour, the light was restored.
Lunar eclipses:
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán, on the *wùchén* day in the seventh month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Wēi mansion.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng, on the *dīngsì* day in the fourth month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Nándǒu mansion.
In the third year, on the *wùyín* day in the eleventh month,
the moon entered the empty space of Dōngjǐng,
and was consequently eclipsed by one-third.
In the fifth year, on the *gēngzǐ* day in the third month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Dī mansion.
In the ninth month, on the *wùxū* day,
the moon was eclipsed in the Wèi mansion.
In the sixth year, on the *guǐsì* day in the ninth month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Lóu mansion at nine degrees.
The calculated time was at the early weak part of *yín* hour.
The loss began from the northeast corner,
eclipsing eleven-fifteenths of its disc.
On the fifteenth day, at *zǐ* hour,
the eclipse began from the northeast.
By the end of *zǐ* hour, it was completely total.
By *chǒu* hour, its light and color were restored.
In the seventh year, on the *dīnghài* day in the eighth month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Kuí mansion.
In the tenth month, on the *gēngchén* day,
the moon occulted and eclipsed Yínghuò.
In the eighth year, on the *gēngyín* day in the sixth month,
the moon occulted and eclipsed the first star of the left leg of the Bì mansion.
In the tenth year, on the *dīngyǒu* day in the twelfth month,
the moon was eclipsed in the Liǔ degree.
The calculated time was at the early weak part of *yǒu* hour.
By *hài* hour, the moon began to be eclipsed from the east corner by two-sevenths.
By *zǐ* hour, its light and color were restored.
In the first year of Yǒngtài, on the *guǐhài* day in the fourth month,
the moon was eclipsed,
and its color was red like blood.
Three days later, the Grand Marshal Wáng Jìngzé raised an army.
The masses believed that Jìngzé was afflicted by the ominous omen.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán, on the *jǐwèi* day in the eighth month,
the moon was completely eclipsed,
and its color was all red.
That night,
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng was executed.
The historiographer says: The sun and moon shine in alternation,
truly important in the course of heaven.
An upper conjunction or a lower eclipse,
they obscure each other at the same degree.
According to old sayings,
"There are five types of solar eclipses,"
referring to those starting from above, below, left, right, or the center.
According to old methods of conjunction,
solar eclipses do not begin from the east,
because the moon moves from its west,
traveling eastward to reach the sun.
Within the conjunction:
If the conjunction enters from outside to inside,
the meeting occurs before the conjunction,
and the loss is from the southwest corner;
if the conjunction occurs before the meeting,
the loss is from the northwest corner.
If the conjunction emerges from inside,
the meeting occurs before the conjunction,
and the loss is from the northwest corner;
if the conjunction occurs before the meeting,
the loss is from the southwest corner.
If the sun is precisely within the conjunction,
the loss is from the west,
hence it never eclipses the east.
If there is a defect within the sun,
it is called a "black spot"
and not an eclipse.
Huáng Xiāng, the Minister of the Secretariat of Hàn, said:
"Solar eclipses always begin from the west,
and lunar eclipses always begin from the east,
with no cases from above, below, or the center."
In the *Chūnqiū*, in the third year of Rǔ Huán's reign, there was a solar eclipse,
which passed through the center, from bottom to top, completely black.
Skeptics believed that if the sun and moon are equal in size,
how could the moon be small and appear within the sun?
Zhèng Xuán said:
"The moon completely covers the sun,
and sunlight emerges from the four sides,
which is why it is said to begin from the center."
Wáng Yì believed:
"If the moon covers the sun,
it should eclipse the western part of the sun.
Since the moon's movement is swift,
it should pass the western edge and become total in an instant,
then subsequently eclipse the eastern edge.
However, when observing solar eclipses, the western edge is missing,
but the light has already passed the eastern edge and is not covered."
Wáng Yì's meaning here
is indeed a great doubt.
Earlier Confucians challenged:
"The moon is eclipsed at full moon,
being extremely far from the sun.
Who eclipses the moon?"
Those who explain say:
"The sun has a dark aura,
and heaven has an empty path,
always opposite to the sun's balance.
When the moon travels in the empty path,
it is covered by the aura,
thus the moon is eclipsed.
Even when the time is midnight,
and the sun and moon are at *zǐ* and *wǔ* (noon),
separated precisely by the earth,
they are still eclipsed by the dark aura,
because the celestial body is large and the terrestrial form is small.
The dark empty aura
is like placing a mirror under the sun,
its shining light reflects on the bright core,
and is seen in the darkness,
always opposite to the sun's balance.
Therefore, stars are lost when they should be,
and the moon is eclipsed when it should be."
Now I ask:
"Stars and the moon are of the same substance,
both manifest the sun's radiance.
When the moon is eclipsed,
stars are not necessarily lost.
If there is something else that should be obscured,
but stars are never eclipsed,
how is it that they share the same origin but suffer different losses?"
What is the reason for this?
The reply is:
"The moon is the master of yin,
occupying the yang position.
Its body and power interact,
naturally causing waxing and waning.
Although stars are of the same kind,
their essence and light are humble and narrow.
Even small damages cause them to disappear.
They have no place to be eclipsed.
Their subtle light can be full,
and they do not share the same form as the crescent and full moon."
Another challenge:
"When the sun is eclipsed at night,
it is verified by the disappearance of night stars.
When a daytime eclipse is total,
why do daytime stars not appear instead?"
The reply is:
"When we speak of light being impinged upon,
there is also light that is not impinged upon;
when we speak of something being covered,
there is also something not covered.
The degree of a night eclipse is distant,
and it sets together with what it covers;
the degree of a day eclipse is near,
thus it obtains brightness from what is not impinged upon."
Another question:
"When Tàibái passes through the sky,
it is indeed far from the sun.
Now it becomes brighter when closer;
to what can this be compared?"
The reply is:
"The discussion on the nature of the two eclipses
just now shows different circulations.
Whether it passes through or not depends on the star's speed.
It is difficult to apply eclipses to the classics,
and I fear it may not be accurate."

The historiographer said: The central stars for observing the dusk and dawn in the monthly ordinances
are all among the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions.
The space between Jī and Dǒu
is slightly wide and sparse.
Therefore, in mid-spring and early autumn,
Jiànxīng is used twice,
appearing alongside the mansion degrees.
Frequent encroachments
and the disasters they portend
have no existing interpretations.
The Shíshì Xīngjīng (Master Shi’s Star Classic) says:
"Dǒu governs爵祿 (ranks and emoluments)
and the commendation and promotion of scholars,
hence Jiànxīng is placed as its auxiliary.
If an anomaly encroaches upon Jiàn,
it is not the same as encroaching upon Dǒu."
Thus, interpreting the text,
it also refers to omens concerning prime ministers.

Astronomy, Part Two
The court historian said: The celestial phenomena are set up with images,
and should encompass both inner and outer palaces.
However, the location of disasters [bì]
does not necessarily extend throughout the celestial longitudes and latitudes.
The five planets, as the essence of celestial time, with the two luminaries, form the seven.
They are the masters of omens and portents,
and are governed by calendrical calculations.
This is indeed different from the fixed constellations.
If the Běichén does not move,
resting at the axis of the celestial pole,
the movement of all other stars
is actually connected to the celestial body.
The occultations and appearances of the five planets
are not related to the two luminaries.
Therefore, Xú Xiǎnsī considered the five planets to be "non-stars,"
and Yú Xǐ discussed this in detail.

Disasters of shooting stars
In the first year of Jiànyuán, tenth month, on the day of Guǐ-yǒu,
there was a shooting star as large as a three-shēng jar,
white in color,
with a tail five zhàng long.
It emerged two chǐ northeast of Nánhé,
traveled north, passing west of Yúguǐ,
and disappeared before reaching the rear star of Xuānyuán.
After it disappeared, a remnant remained in the center,
curved like a cartwheel,
which shortly transformed into a white cloud,
and then vanished after a long time.
A shooting star that rises from below
is called a "flying star."
In the third year, tenth month, on the day of Bǐng-wǔ,
there was a shooting star as large as the moon,
reddish-white in color,
with a tail seven zhàng long.
It traveled northwest into Zǐgōng,
its light illuminating walls and fences.
In the fourth year, first month, on the day of Xīn-wèi,
there was a shooting star as large as a three-shēng jar,
red in color.
It emerged one chǐ north of the second star of Běijí,
traveled north for one zhàng, and disappeared.
In the ninth month, on the day of Rén-zǐ,
a shooting star like a goose egg
emerged north of Liǔ
and entered Xuānyuán.
Another one, as large as a melon,
emerged and traveled west, disappearing in the sky.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng, sixth month, on the day of Jǐ-yǒu,
there was a shooting star like a two-shēng bowl.
It emerged from Zǐgōng
and traveled south, disappearing in Dī.
In the second year, third month, on the day of Gēng-chén,
there was a shooting star like a two-shēng bowl.
It emerged from the center of Tiānshì
and traveled south, behind Xīn.
In the fourth year, second month, on the day of Yǐ-chǒu,
there was a shooting star as large as a one-shēng vessel.
On the day of Wù-chén,
there was a shooting star as large as a five-shēng vessel.
In the fourth month, on the day of Dīng-mǎo,
there was a shooting star as large as a one-shēng vessel.
It emerged northeast of Nándǒu,
traveled west through Dǒu and entered Dī.
In the sixth month, on the day of Bǐng-xū,
there was a shooting star as large as a duck egg.
It emerged south of Páoguā
and entered when it reached Xū.
In the eighth month, on the day of Xīn-wèi,
there was a shooting star as large as a three-shēng jar.
It emerged south of the Zī star
and traveled southwest, disappearing into Tiānméng.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Wù-yín,
there was a shooting star as large as a two-shēng jar,
white in color.
It emerged northeast of Kàng
and traveled into Tiānshì.
In the twelfth month, on the day of Dīng-sì,
there was a shooting star as large as a three-shēng bowl,
white in color.
It emerged from Dìzuò in Tiānshì,
traveled northeast for one zhàng, and disappeared.
In the sixth month, on the *xīnwèi* day of the fifth year,

After it disappeared, there was a trace.
In the ninth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,

white in color,

yellowish-white in color,

It traveled over ten *chǐ* southwestward before disappearing.
In the third month, on the *guǐyǒu* day of the sixth year,

In the fourth month, on the *bǐngchén* day,

yellowish-white in color.
It emerged from inside the eastern fence of Zǐgōng,
traveled northeast for one zhàng and five chǐ,
and disappeared four chǐ northwest of the fifth star of Běijí.
In the ninth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
there was a meteor like a duck's egg,
yellowish-white in color.
It emerged one chǐ south of Lóu,
traveled east for two zhàng and disappeared.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
in the southwest there was a meteor like a three-shēng vessel,
yellowish-red in color,
without a tail.
It traveled southwest for about three zhàng and disappeared,
scattering like remnants of fire.
On a night in Yǒngyuán three years,
the sky opened with a yellowish light, illuminating brightly.
A moment later, a purplish-red object like a small jar appeared,
gradually growing as large as a granary.
Its sound was rumbling like thunder.
It fell into Tàihú.
All the wild pheasants crowed.
People of the time called it
"mùyāng".
The court historians observe that in the Chūnqiū Wěi it states:
"A Tiāngǒu is like a large, rushing star,
with sound,
appearing like fire when viewed.
When it appears, the four directions will attack each other."
The Hàn Shǐ says:
"In the northwest, there are three large stars,
like the sun,
named Tiāngǒu.
When Tiāngǒu appears, people will devour each other."
The Tiānguān says:
"Tiāngǒu looks like a large mirror star."
〔一九〕It also says:
"It is like a large meteor,
yellow in color,
with sound.
Its landing place resembles where a dog falls.
When viewed, it is like a flame,
blazing and reaching the sky.
Its top is sharp,
its bottom is round,
like several qǐng of fields.
When it appears, blood flows for a thousand lǐ,
armies are broken, and generals are killed."
The Hàn Shǐ also says:
"When a Zhāomíng descends, it becomes a Tiāngǒu,
where it lands, wars arise and blood flows."
Zhāomíng
is a star.
The Luòshū says:
"When Zhāomíng appears, a hegemon emerges."
The Yùn Dòu Shū says:
"Zhāomíng has rays and points;
it is a sign of war."
The Hétú says:
"Tàibái scatters to form Tiāngǒu."
The Hàn Shǐ also says:
"When a star appears,
its form is reddish-white with light,
it is then a Tiāngǒu.
Its lower part is small and without feet.
Where it lands, the nation's government changes."
The various accounts differ,
it is not clear which is correct.
Judging by the fate of chaos and destruction,
could this perhaps be a Tiāngǒu?
Lǎorénxīng
In the first year of Jiànyuán, in the eleventh month, on the day Wùchén,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
sacrifices were offered to Lǎorénxīng.
In Yǒngmíng three years, in the eighth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
In the sixth year, in the eighth month, on the day Rénxū,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
In the seventh year, in the seventh month, on the day Rénxū,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
In the ninth year, in the intercalary seventh month, on the day Wùyín,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
In the tenth year, in the eighth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
Lǎorénxīng was seen.
In the eleventh year, in the ninth month, on the day Bǐngyín,
Lǎorénxīng was seen in the south, above Bǐng.
White Rainbows and Cloud Vapors
In Jiànyuán four years, in the second month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
In Yǒngmíng ten years, in the seventh month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
there was a white rainbow in the west,
which disappeared shortly after.
In the eleventh year, in the ninth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
there was a white rainbow in the west,
its southern end pointing to Shēn,
its northern end pointing above Xū.
It slowly dissipated and vanished.
In Jiànyuán four years, in the second month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
two masses of black vapor, one large and one small,
extended from the east to Mǎo
and from the west to Yǒu,
five zhàng wide.
They slowly dissipated and vanished.
In Yǒngmíng two years, in the fourth month, on the day Dīngwèi,
there was a white vapor between the sixth and seventh stars of Běidǒu.
In the fourth year, in the first month, on the day Xīnwèi,
a yellowish-white vapor about one zhàng and five chǐ long
entered Táiwēi.
In Yǒngmíng four years, in the first month, on the day Guǐwèi,
there was a battle-array cloud about one zhàng long in the south.
In the fifth year, in the fourth month, on the day Jǐsì,
there was a black cloud,
five chǐ wide,
its eastern end pointing to Chǒu,
its western end pointing to Yǒu,
both reaching the ground.
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐsì,
there was a battle-array cloud in the southeast, one zhàng high,
extending north to Mǎo,
and southeast to Sì.
It slowly dispersed and scattered.
In the sixth year, in the second month, on the day Guǐhài,
there was a single obstructive cloud spanning half the sky from east to west,
curved towards the west,
bluish-white in color.
In the third month, on the day Gēngchén,
there was an obstructive cloud in the south,
black in color,
six cùn wide.
In the seventh year, in the tenth month, on the day Xīnwèi,
there was an obstructive cloud,
bluish-black in color,
its eastern end reaching Yín,
its western end pointing to Yǒu,
three chǐ wide.
It penetrated Zǐgōng,
and slowly dissipated and vanished.
In the eighth year, in the eleventh month, on the day Yǐwèi,
there was an obstructive cloud,
black in color,
about six chǐ long,
its eastern end reaching Mǎo,
its western end reaching Yǒu.
It slowly dispersed and scattered.
In the twelfth month, on the day Gēngchén,
there was a battle-array cloud in the south,
black in color,
about one zhàng high,
its eastern end reaching Sì,
its western end reaching Wèi.
It slowly dispersed and scattered.
In the eleventh year, in the seventh month, on the day Bǐngchén,
there was an obstructive cloud in the east,
bluish-white in color,
two chǐ and three cùn wide,
its southern end pointing to Sì, reaching the ground,
its northern end pointing to Zǐ, reaching the ground.
It slowly and gradually dispersed and scattered.
A eulogy states: The yang essence is a fire mirror,
the yin spirit is stored water.
Some are endowed, some are projected,
alternating between brightness and obscurity.
They shed light, filling the canopy,
arranging their forms to encircle the cosmos.
They are positioned as ministers and assistants,
their images complete at the celestial gates.
Disasters arise from falling and fading,
calamities start from flying and rushing.
May people not forget to fear,
distinguishing between flaws and virtues.
If one yields to the way of Heaven,
even the stove will speak often.
Collation Notes
Treatise Six: Prefectures and Commanderies, Upper. Yáng, Nánxú, Yù, Nányù, Nányǔn, Běiyǔn, Běixú, Qīng, Jì, Jiāngguǎng, Jiāo, Yuè.
Yángzhōu was the capital and sacred land.
During the Hàn and Wèi dynasties, the Provincial Governor (cǐshǐ) was stationed at Shòuchūn.
Wú established eight Banner-Holding Regional Governors (chíjié dūdū zhōumù),
but there is no record of where the Governor-General (dūdū) of Yángzhōu was based.
In the first year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty (280 CE),
after Wú was pacified,
the Provincial Governor Zhōu Jùn first garrisoned Jiāngnán.
When Emperor Yuán became Governor-General
and crossed the Jiāng (Yangtze River) to the left bank,
it then became the imperial domain,
and its prestige and importance grew.

Yùzhōu.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng of Emperor Yuán of Jìn (312 CE),
the Provincial Governor Zǔ Yuē, to avoid the Hú bandits,
returned from Qiáo to govern Shòuchūn.
Shòuchūn
was a major gathering point in Huáinán,
with an area of over a thousand lǐ,
rich in irrigated fields.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties, it was where the Provincial Governor of Yángzhōu was based,
blocking the Huái River to the north.
The Yǔgòng states:
"The Huái and the sea constitute Yángzhōu."
In the fourth year of Xiánhé (329 CE),
Zǔ Yuē surrendered the city to the Hú.
Yú Liàng was again made Provincial Governor
and governed Wúhú.
Wúhú
has the Pǔ River flowing into it from the south,
also making it a strategic and hidden place.
Liú Bèi said to Sūn Quán:
"Jiāngdōng first has Jiànyè,
then Wúhú."
Yú Liàng planned to recover the Central Plains,
making Máo Bǎo Provincial Governor,
governing Zhūchéng,
but he was defeated by the Hú.
Yú Yì, Provincial Governor of Jīngzhōu, took charge of the province
at Wǔchāng.
Several commanderies had lost their land, and thousands of destitute people had no means of livelihood.
Yì submitted a memorial requesting the transfer of the destitute people from Xīyáng and Xīncài commanderies to the irrigated fields in Xúnyáng.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù (349 CE),
Wáng Jiá, the Hú's self-proclaimed Provincial Governor of Yángzhōu, surrendered Shòuchūn.
The Provincial Governors sometimes governed Lìyáng,
advancing to Mǎtóu and Qiáo,
and no longer returned to the old garrison.
In the first year of Lónghé of Emperor Āi (362 CE),
Yuán Zhēn returned to Shòuchūn.
Zhēn was defeated by Huán Wēn,
who made his son Xī Provincial Governor
and garrisoned Lìyáng.
In the first year of Níngkāng of Emperor Xiàowǔ (373 CE),
Huán Chōng moved to Gūshú.
As the border invaders were not yet pacified,
he divided the existing populations of Qiáo and Liáng commanderies
and settled them in Huànchuān,
establishing Nánqiáo and Liáng Commanderies.
In the twelfth year (384 CE),
Huán Shíqián returned to Lìyáng.
Yú Zhǔn became Provincial Governor
and submitted a memorial to abolish all temporary establishments,
restoring them all to their original status.
In the second year of Yìxī (406 CE),
Liú Yì again garrisoned Gūshú.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"Though I am humbly entrusted with this province,
the land is not expansive.
Its western border is desolate and close to invaders,
its northern frontier is bleak,
the local people are strong and fierce,
not knowing righteousness,
only skilled in warfare.
Fugitives and lawless elements
do not plan for daily gatherings.
In recent years,
there has not been a month without war,
which is indeed not something that an empty and weak force can manage alone.
I request that the General Who Assists the State (fǔguó jiāngjūn), Zhāng Chàng, administer the three commanderies of Huáinán, Ānfēng, and Liángguó."
At that time, the border regions of Yùzhōu
were in such a state.
In the twelfth year (416 CE),
Liú Yìqìng garrisoned Shòuchūn,
which thereafter often served as the provincial capital.
He pacified distant and desolate areas
and defended the borders.

Nányùzhōu.
In the first year of Jìn Níngkāng (373 CE),
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Chōng first garrisoned Gūshú.
Later, it was moved.
(See Jìnshū).
In the second year of Sòng Yǒngchū (421 CE),
Huáidōng was separated to establish Nányùzhōu,
with its seat in Lìyáng,
while Huáixī became Yùzhōu.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā (430 CE), it was abolished and merged.
In the first year of Dàmíng (457 CE), it was re-established,
with its seat in Gūshú.
In the second year of Tàishǐ (466 CE), its seat was Lìyáng;
in the third year (467 CE), its seat was Xuānchéng;
in the fifth year (469 CE), it was abolished.
Huáixī was lost to the barbarians.
In the seventh year (471 CE),
Huáidōng was again separated to establish Nányù.
In the second year of Jiànyuán (480 CE),
Emperor Tàizǔ, seeing that the officials and people of Xīyù were few and harsh,
and that establishing two separate zhōu (provinces)
incurred significant costs,
abolished Nányù.
Zuǒ Púshè Wáng Jiǎn memorialized:
“My humble opinion is that the region west of the Yangtze connects to the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers;
the land is vast but the population sparse.
The Xiōngnú frequently raid and escape,
relying solely on Shòuchūn as a barrier.
If capable individuals are appointed to the zhōu,
and any movement of the barbarians is promptly reported,
with defenses pre-arranged,
then Nányù would not be needed.
Suppose, however, that a mistake is made,
and the vile Jie people arrive,
their approach not heard in advance.
When the barbarian cavalry arrive,
if Shòuyáng merely entrenches itself and holds fast,
unable to cut off their routes,
and the imperial court dispatches troops to Lìyáng,
it will certainly be too late to seize the initiative.
When war chariots are first marshaled,
everything is started from scratch.
How can this compare to a frontier garrison permanently stationed there,
with a military administration always in order?
Temporary reinforcements
provide truly little benefit.
‘In peace, remember danger,’
is a good policy of antiquity.
Therefore, Jiāngzuǒ repeatedly establishing Nányù,
its purpose is also understandable.
I hear that the labor service in Xīyù is still somewhat manageable.
Now, if Nánqiáo and other commanderies are acquired,
the population will become even thinner.
As for actual benefit,
what more can be said?”
Emperor Tàizǔ did not heed him.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (484 CE),
Xuānchéng and Huáinán commanderies from Yángzhōu,
and Lìyáng, Qiáo, Lújiāng, and Línjiāng commanderies from Yùzhōu – a total of six commanderies –
were separated to re-establish Nányùzhōu.
In the fourth year (486 CE),
Guànjūn Chángshǐ Shěn Xiàn memorialized:
“When the two Yùzhōu were separated,
Sāngkuòzǐ Tíng was used as the boundary.
Yǐngchuān and Rǔyáng commanderies, located within the borders of Nánqiáo and Lìyáng,
all belonged to Xīyù,
while Lújiāng, situated between Jìnxī and Rǔyīn,
belonged to Nányù.
I request that Yǐngchuān and Rǔyáng be assigned to Nányù,
and Lújiāng be returned to Xīyù.”
In the seventh year (489 CE),
Nányùzhōu Biéjià Yīn Mí stated:
“Yǐngchuān and Rǔyáng
have long been desolate and ruined.
Their displaced population is scattered across the territories of Qiáo and Lì.
Many have received tax exemptions,
and they retain commandery names,
but their tax revenue is minimal.
The prefectures and zhōu have absolutely no generals or officials.
They nominally administer,
but ultimately yield no real benefit.
However, being nominally administered from Qiáo and Lì,
it is appropriate for them to be partitioned;
they truly should belong to Nányù.
The two Yùzhōu have frequently been separated and established.
Lújiāng belongs to Nányù,
borders the Cháng Jiāng (Yangtze River),
and adjoins Nánqiáo.
Its people's tax in silk
can be conveniently transported to the zhōu by river,
which is truly convenient.
It is far more convenient than Xīyù,
which is not what they desire.
The commandery includes Qiánshū and Shǐxīn Zuǒxiàn.
The villages produce bamboo.
The prefectures and zhōu fell it,
which provides no small benefit.
The prefectures and zhōu are newly established,
different from old garrisons.
There is a great shortage of resources and labor.
It is truly hoped that Lújiāng can be retained.
I request to follow the former division.”
Shàngshū Cānyì commented:
“In previous years, it was feared that the border situation required stability,
hence the memorial to revert the arrangement.
Now the Huái and Sì rivers are peaceful,
so the request should be granted.”
An Imperial Edict
said, “Granted.”

Nán Yǎnzhōu was garrisoned at Guǎnglíng.
This was the former kingdom of the Hàn dynasty.
It had the Pǔ River of Jiāngdū.
When Wèi Wéndì campaigned against Wú, he came out from here.
Seeing the mighty waves of the Jiāng River,
he sighed, saying:
“This is how Heaven divides north and south.”
When Jìn Yuándì crossed the Jiāng River
in the fourth year of Jiànxīng,
he loudly announced a northern expedition.
He sent Xuānchéng Gōng Póu to supervise Xú and Yǎn provinces,
garrisoning Guǎnglíng.
Afterward, some returned south of the Jiāng River,
but the establishment of a garrison began from this point.
At that time, the common people suffered calamities
and migrated to this region.
Many displaced people sought refuge with prominent families as their retainers.
In the fourth year of Tàixīng of Yuándì,
an imperial edict was issued regarding the displaced people who had lost their registrations.
It ordered them to report their names to the authorities
to establish a system for providing retainers.
However, the area north of the Jiāng River was desolate and ruined,
making it impossible to verify the facts.
In the third year of Tàiníng of Míngdì,
Xī Jiàn became the governor of Yǎnzhōu,
garrisoning Guǎnglíng.
Later, he returned to Jīngkǒu.
Thereafter, Yǎnzhōu was sometimes administered from Xūyí,
sometimes from Shānyáng.
Huán Xuán appointed Huán Hóng as the governor of Qīngzhōu,
garrisoning Guǎnglíng.
In the second year of Yìxī,
Zhūgě Chángmín became the governor of Qīngzhōu,
moving to Shānyáng.
At that time, the Xiānbēi bordered the region.
Chángmín submitted a memorial stating:
“This frontier has suffered ten years of continuous conflict and old grievances.
Cities and walls have collapsed.
Desolate old settlements are scattered and hidden.
In the border garrisons,
one hears no chickens or dogs.
Moreover, barbarian attacks and plunder
have become increasingly severe.”
He then returned to garrison Jīngkǒu.
At the end of the Jìn dynasty, Guǎnglíng controlled and connected the three Qís.
Thus, Qīng and Yǎn provinces were garrisoned together.
In the first year of Yǒngchū of Sòng,
Qīngzhōu was abolished and merged into Yǎnzhōu.
In the third year,
Tán Dàojì first became the governor of Nán Yǎnzhōu,
and Guǎnglíng thenceforth served as a provincial garrison.
The land was very flat and expansive.
The governor often went to Hǎilíng in autumn to view the tides.
It was opposite Jīngkǒu,
at the widest part of the Jiāng River.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
the governor Liǔ Shìlóng submitted a memorial:
“The Shangshū has issued regulations for 'land survey and registration' and
the abolition of 'sojourner' commanderies and counties.
All those who have drifted and resided here
originally had no fixed residence.
Ten households here, five scattered there,
they were dispersed like stars.
The people of one county
were scattered throughout the province,
west to the banks of the Huái,
east to the sea-corner.
Now, you exclusively abolish the sojourner states
but do not abolish the desolate settlements,
so their mixed residences and mismatched locations
are no different from before.
Separating them into districts
does not eliminate the aimless wandering.
I believe they should all be abolished together
and merged and settled according to their actual boundaries.
If villages and hamlets,
with two or three hundred households,
can have their fields and residences restored and
their areas easily divided,
they should be separately considered for establishment.”
Thereupon, the six counties of Jìyīn Commandery,
the four counties of Xiàpéi Commandery,
the three counties of Huáiyáng Commandery,
and the four counties of Dōngguǎn Commandery,
because they were scattered residents without actual land,
and their officials had no offices,
residing in civilian villages,
were abolished upon the establishment of the provincial administration,
and their households
were attached to other jurisdictions.

The "Geography Treatise" states that Huáiyīn County belonged to Línhuái Commandery.

He said:
“Huáiyīn is an old garrison,
its terrain is strategically vital,
with convenient water and land transport,
easy for observing enemy movements.
The fertile fields offer advantages for cultivation,
and large boats can transport grain
without other obstacles.”
Thereupon, he built cities and walls.

It administered only the (Píng)yáng [Píng] Commandery.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng,
Guānglù Dàfū Lǚ Ānguó submitted a petition, stating:
“The sixty people, led by Dài Shàngbó, from Běi Yǎnzhōu complain:
‘Our old homeland is remote and separated,
we have drifted and lost our dwelling places.
Although Huáiyīn is now newly established,
Yángpíng Commandery
has no actual land within the province,
but is attached to the territory of Shānyáng.
We observe that Sī, Xú, and Qīng provinces
are all newly established,
and all have actual commanderies.
Dōngpíng is a renowned state,
to which gentry families are attached.
We hope that between the two borders of Shānyáng and Xūyí,
a small number of households can be allocated to establish this commandery,
and then gather the scattered and desolate people.
This would allow families from our original homeland
to have a place to return to.’
Your servant notes that Dōngpíng Commandery is indeed this province's original territory,
and your humble servant's family originates from this area.
We wish to establish this state.”
This was granted.

In the first year of Jìn Yuánkāng,
Emperor Huì issued an edict:
"The territories of Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu
are vast and extensive.
The officials propose to carve out Yùzhāng, Póyáng, Lúlíng, Línchuān, Nánkāng, Jiàn'ān, and Jìn'ān from Yángzhōu to form a new prefecture.
Xīn'ān, Dōngyáng, and Xuānchéng, which were formerly within Yùzhāng's borders,
and are in the northeast of Yùzhāng,
are quite distant;
they can remain under Yángzhōu as before.
Also, carve out Wǔchāng, Guìyáng, and Ānchéng from Jīngzhōu, a total of ten commanderies.
They can be named Jiāngzhōu after the Jiāng (river),
and its administration should be in Yùzhāng."
Yǔ Liàng, serving as Cìshǐ,
and overseeing six prefectures,
stated that with Jīng and Jiāng as the base,
comparing the households of the two prefectures,
though they were distant in terms of governance,
〔一三〕it was actually more than half,
and Jiāngzhōu was truly the foundation.
Before his death, he memorialized that Jiāngzhōu's administration should be in Xúnyáng,
as the prefecture oversaw Xīncài and Xīyáng two commanderies of Yùzhōu,
and its administration in Pénchéng
was close to the various commanderies on the eastern Jiāng,
making travel convenient.
Later, Yǔ Yì returned to Yùzhāng.
After Yìxī,

Hé Wújì memorialized:

and return Jìnglíng to Jīngzhōu.
Also, Hóngnóng of Sīzhōu and Sōngzī of Yángzhōu,
are situated in Xúnyáng,
their people mixed.
They should all be supervised."
Today, Jiǔjiāng is north of the prefectural garrison,
and Pénglǐ is to its east.

Jīngzhōu:
In the late Zhōngpíng period of Emperor Líng of Hàn, Cìshǐ Wáng Ruì first administered Jiānglíng.
During the Wú period, the Dū of Xīlíng garrisoned it.
In the first year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty, Wú was pacified,
and it was made the seat of the Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn, Cìshǐ Zhōu Yǐ fled from the bandit Dù Tāo to Jiànkāng.
Táo Kǎn became Cìshǐ,
administering Dùnkǒu.
Wáng Dūn administered Wǔchāng.
Afterwards, it was sometimes returned to Jiānglíng,
or sometimes in Xiàkǒu.
Huán Wēn pacified Shǔ,
administering Jiānglíng.
Due to the western boundary of Línjǔ,
with its winding and treacherous waterways and land routes,
the paths were barely passable.
It connected south to Bā and Wū,
and southeast to the prefectural seat.
The route was populated by Man and Dan tribes.
The land was fertile and beautiful,
so it was established as Wènyáng Jùn,
to resettle displaced people.
When the Dī captured Xiāngyáng,
Huán Chōng relocated to Shàngmíng,
stopping over forty *lǐ* from Lù Xùn's Lèxiāng City.
Because the land was fertile and good,
it could serve as resources for the military and populace,
and it was also close to the Three Gorges,
without fear of the western border.
Therefore, the south of the river was heavily guarded,
and the north of the river lightly guarded.
After Fú Jiān's defeat,
Xiāngyáng was recovered.
In the fourteenth year of Tàiyuán,
Wáng Chén returned to Jiānglíng.
Jiānglíng was five hundred *lǐ* by foot from Xiāngyáng.
Their situations were like lips and teeth;
without Xiāngyáng, Jiānglíng would be vulnerable to attack,
so it was not established there.
From Chén onwards,
it never moved again.
Within its territory,
it encompassed Man and Dan tribes.
The land was vast and sparsely populated,
known as an expansive wilderness.
Among the great administrative centers south of the Yangtze,
none surpassed Jīng and Yáng.
Shǎnxian in Hóngnóng Jùn:
During the Zhōu dynasty, the two paternal uncles jointly governed the feudal lords.
The Duke of Zhōu was in charge of east of Shǎn,
and the Duke of Zhào was in charge of west of Shǎn.
Therefore, Jīngzhōu was called west of Shǎn.
It governed the following commanderies:
Nán Jùn: Jiānglíng, Huáróng, Zhījiāng, Línjǔ, Biān, Dāngyáng.

Bāzhōu:
The Three Gorges were steep and narrow,
and mountain barbarians were raiders.
In the third year of Tàishǐ of the Sòng dynasty,
it was proposed to establish a Sānbā Xiàowèi to pacify them.
Later it was abolished.
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
it was re-established.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
Bādōng and Jiàn(píng) from Jīngzhōu,
and Bājùn from Yìzhōu were divided to form a prefecture.
A Cìshǐ was appointed,
who also governed the Administrator of Bādōng,
and Fúlíng Jùn was also assigned to it.
It was abolished in the first year of Yǒngmíng,
and each returned to its original affiliation.
Bādōng Jùn: Yúfù, Qúnánpǔ, Nièyáng, Bāqú, Xīnpǔ, Hànfēng.

Shāqú, Xīnxiāng.

Yǐngzhōu:
Its administrative seat was in Xiàkǒu,
which was an old strategic point.
Wú established a Dūjiāng for the Lǔkǒu屯,
facing the bank of Mount Lǔ,
hence the name.
In the Yǒngjiā period of the Jìn dynasty,
Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Jiǎn of Jīngzhōu fled from the bandits in Xiāngyáng to Xiàkǒu.
Yú Yì was Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
administering Xiàkǒu, both relying on the treacherous terrain.
In the Tàiyuán period,
Cìshǐ Huán Chōng of Jīngzhōu moved his garrison to Shàngmíng.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"On the day the Dī bandits rushed to their deaths,
north of old Yǐng,
strong fortifications faced each other,
waiting without engaging in battle.
Cìshǐ Huán Sì of Jiāngzhōu should advance and garrison Xiàkǒu,
occupying the middle ground between upper and lower,
which would be convenient for the situation."
In the first year of Yìxī,
Guànjūn Jiāngjūn Liú Yì considered Xiàkǒu to be between the two prefectures,
strategically located,
connecting to the Xiāng River,
and bordering the Yǐn and Miǎn rivers.
He requested that Cìshǐ Liú Dàoguī of Bìngzhōu garrison Xiàkǒu.
Xiàkǒu city was situated on Huánghú Jī.
It was traditionally said that the immortal Zǐ'ān rode a yellow crane over this place.
Its riverside was steep and perilous,
with high and precarious towers.
It overlooked the Miǎn and Hàn rivers,
and responded to the Sī Department.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng established a prefecture here,
to divide the power of Jīng and Chǔ.

Xiāochéng
Sīzhōu
was garrisoned at Yìyáng.
In the early Jǐngpíng era of Sòng,
the land of Hénán was lost.
In the [last years] of Yuánjiā (Sòng),
a provisional prefecture was established in Hù, Rǔnán County,
but it was soon abolished.
In the Tàishǐ period,
a prefecture was established in Yìyáng Commandery.
It controlled the strategic passes of the Three Gates,
bordered Chén and Rǔ to the north,
and commanded Xǔ and Luò.
From then on,
it was always a frontier garrison.
When Tàishǐ was moved,
it administered Yìyáng,
and provisionally established Rǔnán,
administering three commanderies.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
it also administered Ānlù, Suí, and Ānmán, three commanderies.

Yōngzhōu
was garrisoned at Xiāngyáng,
which was where the Jīngzhōu Military Governor in the early Jìn dynasty resided.
Emperor Yuán appointed Wèi Gāi as the governor of Yōngzhōu,
garrisoned at Cuóchéng,
while Xiāngyáng had a separate heavy garrison.
Yǔ Yì, as governor of Jīngzhōu,
planned a northern expedition,
and garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Since the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
the households of Xiāngyáng were scattered and barren.
In the eighth year of Xiánkāng,
Shàngshū Yīn Róng stated:
“Xiāngyáng and Shíchéng
are border territories,
facing wild enemies.
The remaining barbarian settlers are provisionally governed in commanderies and counties,
but the households are few;
they should be merged.”
Zhū Xù became governor of Yōngzhōu
and established provisional commanderies and counties in Xiāngyáng,
but it was conquered by the Fú clan.
After the Fú clan was defeated,
it was returned to the south,
and Zhū Xù was reinstated.
Around Xiāngyáng,
the fields are fertile and good,
and mulberry and catalpa trees, as well as marshlands,
are everywhere.
When Xī Huī was governor of Yōngzhōu,
there were very few old residents at that time,
but new households were gradually increasing.
In the Yuánjiā period of Sòng,
five commanderies of Jīngzhōu were separated and attached,
thus making it a major garrison.
It borders barbarians along the Miǎn River,
is blocked by high mountains,
adjoins Wǎn and Luò to the north,
with a flat road leading directly there,
and straddles Fán and Miǎn,
serving as the northern gate to Yānyǐng.
It commands the Man-Zuǒ people,
hence a separate Man-Zuǒ Bureau was established there.

Xiāngzhōu
was garrisoned at Chángshā Commandery.
It is the core of the Xiāng River region,
with abundant people and fertile land.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
it was separated from Jīngzhōu and established,
with Gǒu Tiào as its Inspector.
〔一三〕After this, it was abolished three times,
and then re-established.
It was established in the tenth
year of Yuánjiā,
〔一四〕and remains an old garrison to this day.
It connects to the south of the ridges
and serves as a protective barrier for the Jīng region.

Liángzhōu
was garrisoned at Nánzhèng.
It was established by Wèi in the fourth year of Jǐngyuán when Shuǐ was pacified.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
the Shuǐ bandits took Hànzhōng,
and Inspector Zhāng Guāng governed Wèixīng.
Three years later,
he returned to Hànzhōng.
In the first year of Jiànxīng,
it was again conquered by the Dī leader Yáng Nándí.
When Huán Wēn pacified Shuǐ,
it was restored to its former territory.
Later it was conquered by Qiáo Zòng;
when Zòng was pacified, it was restored.
Each time Hànzhōng was lost,
the Inspector would garrison Wèixīng.
Hànzhōng served as a shield for Bā and Shuǐ,
which is why Liú Bèi, upon gaining Hànzhōng,
said,
“Even if Cáo Gōng comes,
he will be powerless.”
Therefore, whenever Shuǐ faced difficulties,
Hànzhōng would often be lost.
Although it was sometimes recovered,
the households were severely depleted.
In the Yuánjiā period of Sòng,
Zhēn Fǎhù was attacked by the Dī,
and lost the defense.
Xiāo Sīhuà recovered Hànzhōng.
Later, the Dī barbarians frequently attacked each other,
and many refugees from Guānlǒng
sought refuge and assimilated,
thus the number of households gradually increased.
The provincial border was adjacent to the Dī and Hú,
and it also served as a garrison for military control.

Qín Province,
established in the 5th year of Tàishǐ by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Its old territory possessed the wealth of Qín,
spanning and encompassing the Longshan mountains and slopes.
Abolished during Tàikāng,
re-established in the 7th year of Yuánkāng by Emperor Huì.
When the Central Plains were in chaos,
it was lost to the Hú.

but was soon after defeated by Fú Jiàn.
In the 11th year,
Huán Wēn appointed Dī King Yáng Guó as Qín Province Inspector,
but there were no people or land (under his control).
By the 14th year of Tàiyuán,
Yōng Province Inspector Zhū Xù first took charge of Qín Province,
this was what Emperor Xiàowǔ had established.
Its provisional seat of government was in Xiāngyáng,
there was no Inspector,
thereafter, the Yōng Province Inspector always took charge of it.
In the 2nd year of Lóng'ān,
Guō Quán first became the Inspector of Liáng and Nán Qín Provinces,
the province's provisional seat was in Hànzhōng.
In the 4th year,
Huán Xuán oversaw seven provinces,
but only Qín Province was mentioned.
In the 1st year of Yuánxīng,
Fú Jiān's son Hóng was made Běiqín Province Inspector.
From then on, the Jīng Province Regional Commander always oversaw Qín Province,
and Liáng Province always included the Nán Qín Province Inspectorate.
In the 3rd year of Yìxī,
Dī King Yáng Guó was made Běiqín Province Inspector.
In the 14th year,
Dōngqín Province was established,
with Liú Yìzhēn as Inspector.
Guō Gōng was Liáng Province Inspector,
and Yǐn Yǎ was Qín Province Inspector.
Emperor Wén of Sòng was Jīng Province Regional Commander,
overseeing Qín Province,
and further oversaw Běiqín Province.
Province names appeared confusedly,
their abolition and establishment not clearly recorded.
The Yǒngmíng Records of Commanderies and States states Qín Province's provisional seat was in Hànzhōng Nánzhèng,
without specifying North or South.
The Yuánjiā Records of Taxation also mentions Qín Province,
but the Jīng Province Regional Commander always oversaw the two Qíns,
and Liáng and Nán Qín had one Inspector.
Thus, the Qín Province recorded in the records was Nán Qín,
and the Dī's was Běiqín.

Yì Province,
its administrative seat is Chéngdū,
dating from its administration established in the 4th year of Jǐngyuán by Wèi.
It opened up and developed barren barbarian lands,
gradually forming commanderies and counties,
like Yǒngchāng of Hàn,
or Yúnshān of Jìn, and so forth.
Since Shǔ Marquis Yùn Zhuàng,
hence Zhūgě Liàng said,
"Yì Province is strategically formidable,
its fertile plains are a 'heavenly storehouse'."
Liú Sòng also said,
"Chéngdū should be where imperial relatives and younger brothers reside,
to establish a kingdom."
Therefore, Chéngdū King Yǐng was established,
but he never went to his state.
The Three Gorges are perilous,
and the barbarians are greatly rampant.
To the west, it connects to Ruìruì and Hénán,
similar to Wǔwēi and Zhāngyè of Hàn,
serving as a route to the Western Regions.
Its territorial extent and garrisons,
extend over ten thousand *lǐ*,
During the Jìn dynasty, it was a posting for military officials.
During the Sòng dynasty, due to its perilous remoteness,
kings were not sent there to govern.
In the middle of Tàishǐ,
a small islet suddenly appeared by a market bridge in Chéngdū,
Shào Shuò from Shǐkāng, a master of divination,
saw it and said:
"An islet appearing near the market,
indicates that a noble king will soon arrive in this territory."
In the 2nd year of Yǒngmíng,
Shǐxīng King Zhèn became the Inspector.
The province's land is splendid and rich,
it is one of the capitals of the west.

Treatise, Chapter 8: Officials
The establishment of officials and setting up of offices
originated from Yán Hào.
By the time of the flourishing institutions of Zhōu,
they were manifest in the extensive records of the prosperous Hàn.
Existing, altered, and continuously followed,
they are fully documented across all dynasties.
Many ancient sages and past scholars
have diligently inscribed them.
As for Hú Guǎng's old ceremonies,
the matters were merely brief and concise.
Yīng Shào's official regulations,
however, left almost nothing to be desired.
Wáng Lǎng's memorials
belong to the early stages of a hegemonic state.
Chén Jiǎo's additions to the Cao system
were made to supplement military affairs.
Currently, there are the official regulations of the Wèi clan and Yú Huàn's central and external offices.
Shān Táo's discerning judgments of people
are not [missing characters].
Xún Xù wished to reduce burdensome tasks,
advocating only for consolidation and simplification.
The established regulations were codified
based on the Jìn ordinances.
Later generations, inheriting the system,
used them as precedents.
The categorization of officials
distinguishes ranks and qualifications.
Yù Zōng's selection records are a general outline,
while Qīn Míng's graded sequence is detailed and comprehensive.
Yú Tōng and Liú Yín, building on Xún's work,
corrected old practices and added new ones,
comparing the present with the past.
When Qí received the abdication from Sòng,
matters followed established norms.
Since officials were in place,
nothing was arbitrarily abandoned.
Other scattered references in historical commentaries
have largely been collected.
Readers can easily understand them,
so they will not be re-stated.
(For all officials from Láng and Lìshǐ of the various government agencies downwards,
see the official regulations of the Commander of Chángshuǐ, Wáng Guī.)
Xiàngguó.
Since Xiāo and Cáo,

During the Xiàojiàn era of Sòng, Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān held it.

All Dàfū (大夫) officials
were chosen from experienced elders.
Those of higher standing were granted twenty Qīnxìn (親信).
Wèiwèi (衞尉).
The fǔ (府) had one Céng (丞).
In charge of the palace city gates and keys.
Zhāng Héng's (張衡) Xījīng Fù (西京賦) states:
"Wèiwèi (衞尉) eight garrisons,
guarding at night and patrolling during the day."
On the watchtowers of the palace city's defensive walls, drums were originally placed.
Those on night watch would respond to the changing of the watches.
Tàizǔ (太祖) believed that the many drums disturbed sleep,
and changed them to iron chimes.
Tíngwèi (廷尉).
The fǔ (府) had one Céng (丞),
one Zhèng (正),
one Jiān (監),
one Píng (評),
and one Lǜ Bóshì (律博士).
Dàsīnóng (大司農).
The fǔ (府) had one Céng (丞).
The officials under its jurisdiction were as follows:
Tàicānglìng (太倉令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
Dǎoguānlìng (導官令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
Jìtiánlìng (藉田令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
Shàofǔ (少府).
The fǔ (府) had one Céng (丞).
The officials under its jurisdiction were as follows:
One Zuǒyòu Shàngfānglìng (左右尚方令) each,
one Céng (丞).
Duànshǔ Céng (鍛署丞) one person.

Yùfǔlìng (御府令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
Dōngyèlìng (東冶令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
Nányèlìng (南冶令) one person,

Píngzhǔnlìng (平准令) one person,

Shànglínlìng (上林令) one person,
Céng (丞) one person.
