Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng (將作大匠).
Tàipú (太僕).
Dàhónglú (大鴻臚).
These three Qīng (卿) were not permanently established.
Jiàngzuò (將作) was in charge of palace and temple construction.
Tàipú (太僕) was in charge of holding the reins during suburban rites.
Hónglú (鴻臚) was in charge of guiding, assisting, and announcing obeisance.
When there were affairs, concurrent officials were temporarily appointed,
and abolished once the matter was concluded.
Chénghuánglìng (乘黃令) one person.
In charge of the five carriages, comfortable carriages,
and the large hearse and burial carriage used for funerals.
Kèguǎnlìng (客館令).
In charge of guests from the four directions.
Xuāndé Wèiwèi (宣德衞尉), Shàofǔ (少府), Tàipú (太僕).
When Yùlínwáng (鬱林王) was enthroned,
Wén'ān Tàihòu (文安太后) assumed the honorary title,
and these were established named after the palace.
Dàchángqiū (大長秋).
Established when Yùlín (鬱林) established his empress.
Lùshàngshū (錄尚書).
Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
Overall head of the twenty divisions of the Shàngshūtái (尚書臺),
serving as the chief of the Inner Office.
When travelling, all below the various princes
were ordered to halt.
The Zuǒyòu Púshè (左右僕射) divided their duties.
If there was no Lìng (令),
the Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) was the chief of the office,
equivalent to the Lìng (令).
Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射).
In charge of the affairs of the Diànzhōng (殿中) and Zhǔkè (主客) divisions,

and the matters of the various divisions concerning suburban temples, imperial tombs, imperial travels, court ceremonies, internal misconduct in the office, and civil officials' appointments, illnesses, and leave;

regarding all auspicious celebrations, auspicious omens and collective congratulations, disasters and rebel outbreaks, collective changes, reverent obeisance at court, changes of reign titles and regulations, assuming office and selection,
all appointments, merit evaluations, enfeoffments, demotions, the Eight Deliberations, questionable judgments, and official documents,
the Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) was in charge,
the Yòu Púshè (右僕射) reviewed next.
For yellow documents,
the Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) and Yòu Púshè (右僕射) signed with a vermilion seal and visible character.
After passing through the Dūcéng (都丞),
the Yòu Púshè (右僕射) drew a horizontal line to indicate completion,
then the Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射) drew a line,
then the Lìng (令) drew a line.
If the right official was absent,
then the next in line would draw their line concurrently.
If there were neither left nor right,
then the Púshè (僕射) would be directly placed in the middle,
overseeing all left and right affairs.
Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
In charge of the four divisions: Lìbù (吏部), Shāndìng (刪定), Sāngōng (三公), and Bǐbù (比部).
Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
In charge of the four divisions: Dùzhī (度支), Jīnbù (金部), Cāngbù (倉部), and Qǐbù (起部).
Zuǒmín Shàngshū (左民尚書).
In charge of the two divisions: Zuǒmín (左民) and Jiàbù (駕部).
Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書).
In charge of the four divisions: Dūguān (都官), Shuǐbù (水部), Kùbù (庫部), and Gōnglùn (功論).
Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書).
In charge of the two divisions: Zhōngbīng (中兵) and Wàibīng (外兵).
Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書).
The Yòu Púshè (右僕射) held this concurrent post,
not separately established.
Qǐbù Shàngshū (起部尚書).
Temporarily established for the construction of palaces and temples,
and abolished upon completion of the work.
Zuǒcéng (左丞) one person.

In charge of ancestral temples and suburban sacrifices, auspicious celebrations and omens, disasters, establishing regulations, various documents and impeachments, selection and appointment, and the appointment, completion, dismissal, and transfer of officials.
Yòucéng (右丞) one person.

In charge of soldiers and all craftsmen's recruitment, death, rebellion, evaluations, replacements, old age, illness, and dismissal, as well as internal and external treasuries' grain and silk, criminal punishments, founding enterprises, disputes, land and boats, provisions for soldiers and craftsmen, deaths, rebellions, examinations, purges, recruitments, various assignments, military equipment, personnel in various camps, taxes and cloth from provinces and commanderies, migration of households,

merging of provinces and counties, assignment of city and household populations, recall and dismissal or gifts to Cìshǐ (刺史), officials of two thousand *dàn* of grain, Lìng (令), Zhǎng (長), Céng (丞), and Wèi (尉), and cases of civil and military officials being stripped of office.
For white documents,
the Yòucéng (右丞) signed first,
then the Zuǒcéng (左丞).
For yellow documents,
the Zuǒcéng (左丞) signed first,
then the Yòucéng (右丞).
For all established regulations and detailed deliberations on major affairs, ancestral temples, and court ceremonies,
the Zuǒcéng (左丞) signed first,
then the Yòucéng (右丞).
From the Lìng (令) and Pú (僕) down to the five Shàngshū (尚書), Eight Seats, and twenty divisions,
each established Lángzhōng (郎中), Lìngshǐ (令史), and below,
and also established Dūlìngshǐ (都令史) to manage them.
The Púshè (僕射) managed court regulations,
the Shàngshū (尚書) managed adjudications and memorials,
the Dūcéng (都丞) handled miscellaneous tasks,
including impeaching violations within the various divisions' routine matters and external detailed adjudications.
If a joint deliberation was required,
the Láng (郎) would first propose an idea.
For yellow documents and official correspondence that required memorialization,
the official who proposed the idea would be the lead deliberator.
For all petitions with vague directives,
the divisions would consult as before.
If there was a consultation directive,
then the one who proposed the idea would be the lead deliberator.
Wǔkùlìng (武庫令) one person.
Subordinate to the Kùbù (庫部).
Chēfǔlìng (車府令) one person,
one Céng (丞).
Subordinate to the Jiàbù (駕部).
Gōngchēlìng (公車令) one person.
Dàguānlìng (大官令) one person,
one Céng (丞).
One Grand Physician-in-chief (Dà Yī Lìng),
one Aide (Chéng).
One Palace Supervisor (Diànzhōng Jiān) each for the inner and outer palaces.
One Stallion Supervisor (Huá Liú Chéng) each for the inner and outer palaces.
One General of the Materiel Corps (Cáiguān Jiāngjūn),
one Cavalry Commander (Sīmǎ).
Subordinate to the Starting Department (Qǐ Bù),
also subordinate to the Palace Commander (Lǐngjūn).
Libationer of the Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ).
(Those of high merit are so called.)
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the Hàn era, this was a close attendant position.
During Wèi and Jìn, selections for it
gradually increased in grandeur and importance,
but the general meaning remained unchanged.
During the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Wáng Huá, Wáng Tánshǒu, Yīn Jǐngrén, and others
all served as Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng).
Their relationship was one of intimacy.
Their貂拂(diāo fú) would touch the Emperor's hand.
They would remove the 貂拂(diāo fú) and place it on the table.
After speaking, they would reinsert it into their hand.
In the time of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Hé Yǎn accompanied him in the chariot for the southern suburban sacrifice.
When the imperial chariot passed the threshold of Báimén,
but the Emperor held him and said:
"I am accompanying you."
In the Qí era's court assemblies,
many with handsome appearances were given concurrent offices.
In the third year of Yǒngyuán,
the Lord of Dōnghūn performed the southern suburban sacrifice.
Not wishing to be close to the court officials,
he made Zhǔxǐ accompany him in the chariot.
This had never happened in previous generations.
Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng) were called "Ménxià".
Secretaries (Lìshǐ) were also established.
The subordinate officials were as follows:
Attendant Yellow Gate Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
Also managed imperial edicts and commands.
The world called them "Little Ménxià".
Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sǎnqí Chángshì).
Universal Access Cavalry Regular Attendant (Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì).
Supernumerary Cavalry [Regular] Attendant (Yuánwài Sǎnqí [Cháng] Shì) (Láng).
The Universal Access (Tōngzhí) and Supernumerary (Yuánwài) positions
were given to aged and infirm persons,
thus their offices gradually declined.
During Sòng Dàmíng, though the selection was grand, comparable to Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng),
due to long-standing habit among the people,
it was ultimately not highly regarded,
and soon returned to its former state.
Cavalry Attendant (Sǎnqí Shìláng).
Universal Access Cavalry Attendant (Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Shìláng).
Supernumerary Cavalry Attendant (Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng).
Attendant-in-ordinary (Jǐshìzhōng).
Bearing Imperial Summons (Fèng Cháoqǐng).

The Bureau of Collected Books (Jíshū Shěng) established a Chief Secretary (Zhèngshū Lìshǐ).
The Court Attendant (Cháosàn) comprised the remnants of the gentry,
their numbers accumulated in great profusion.
During Yǒngmíng,
those bearing Imperial Summons (Fèng Cháoqǐng) numbered over six hundred.
One Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān),

one Aide (Chéng).
Attendant (Láng).
Junior Editor (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
The Jìn Imperial Library Pavilion (Mìshū Gé) had Secretaries (Lìshǐ)

One Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
In the Jìn era, south of the Jiāng, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Zhōngchéng) and the Capital Commandant (Sīlì) jointly supervised all officials.
This is what Fù Xián referred to as
"within and without the barriers."
Currently, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Zhōngchéng)
has no duty that is not investigated.
They proceed along their exclusive path,
their retinue clearing the way with shouts and warnings,
and they add their stern countenance.
When military generals encounter them,
they are immediately subjected to encroachment.
If there is a ceremonial guard,
it can even lead to physical altercations.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn of Sòng, a decree was issued
that the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Zhōngchéng) and the President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) should take separate routes.
Even if the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Zhōngchéng) encountered an Attendant (Láng) descending from court,
they could still halt them.
All other inner and outer officials
were subject to being stopped and delayed.
Two Supervising Censors (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ).
Ten Palace Censors (Shìyùshǐ).

One Prefect of the Palace Ushers (Yèzhě Púyè).
Ten Palace Ushers (Yèzhě).

was in charge of court audiences, receiving guests, and banquets.
General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn), Central Palace Guard (Zhōng Lǐngjūn).

Established a Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ), a Cavalry Commander (Sīmǎ), a Registrar of Merit (Wǔguān), a Registrar of Merit (Gōngcáo), and a Chief Scribe (Zhǔbù).

General of Light Cavalry (Yóují Jiāngjūn).

Left and Right Two Commanders of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household (Zuǒyòu Èr Zhōnglángjiāng).
General of the Van (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn), General of the Rear (Hòujūn Jiāngjūn), General of the Left (Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn), General of the Right (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn),

Five Colonels (Wǔ Xiàowèi) of Garrison Cavalry (Túnqí), Infantry (Bùbīng), Archer Corps (Shèshēng), Rapid Cavalry (Yuèqí), and Long Water (Chángshuǐ).
Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household, Tiger Braves (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng).
Gentleman-of-the-Household, Aide (Nǔcóng Púyè).
Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Jiān).
General of Massed Archers (Jīshè Jiāngjūn).

Palace General (Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn), Supernumerary Palace General (Yuánwài Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn).
Palace Cavalry Commander and Inspector (Diànzhōng Sīmǎ Dū).
General of Martial Guard (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn).
Martial Cavalry Regular Attendant (Wǔqí Chángshì).
From the two Imperial Guards (Èr Wèi), the Four Armies (Sìjūn), and the Five Colonels (Wǔ Xiàowèi) downwards,

Junior Tutor (Shǎofù).

Steward of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).

Crown Prince's Gentlemen-in-waiting (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
One Commander of the Left and Right Imperial Guards of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zuǒyòu Wèi Shuài) each.
Three Colonels (Sān Xiàowèi) of the Crown Prince's Auxiliary Army Infantry and Garrison Cavalry (Tàizǐ Yìjūn Bùbīng Túnqí).
One Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household, Crown Prince's Loyal Braves (Tàizǐ Lǚbēn Zhōnglángjiāng).
Left and Right Generals of the Crown Prince's Massed Crossbows (Tàizǐ Zuǒyòu Jīlǔ Jiāngjūn).
Crown Prince's Palace General (Tàizǐ Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn), Supernumerary Palace General (Yuánwài Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn).
Crown Prince's Granary Official (Tàizǐ Cāngguān Lìng).
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) often followed the Commandant of the Tiger-Like Gentlemen (Hǔbēn Dū).
The officials of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) on the right.
Provincial Governors (Zhōumù) and Inspectors (Cìshǐ).
In the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, Provincial Governors (Zhōumù) held great prestige.
Inspectors (Cìshǐ) who held heavy responsibilities served as Envoys with Insignia, Supervisors-General (Shǐchíjié Dūdū),
while those with lighter duties were Insignia-Holding Supervisors (Chíjié Dū).
This began in the Hàn dynasty during the time of Emperor (Dì);
supervising the military affairs of Yáng and Xú provinces.
However, Hé and Xú’s Sòng Zhì states it began when Wèi Wǔ (魏武) dispatched generals to various provinces to supervise armies,
and Wáng Guī (王珪)'s Zhí Yí states it began with Guāngwǔ (光武),
both of which are incorrect.
In the Tàikāng (太康) era of the Jìn dynasty,
Supervisors-General (Dūdū) managed military affairs,
and Inspectors (Cìshǐ) governed the people,
each appointing their own personnel.
In the late Huì Dì (惠帝) period,
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Féng Shè (御史中丞馮赦) attacked the thieves of Jiǔjiāng,
Unless it was a crucial province, one would simply be an Inspector (Cìshǐ).

Protector-General of the Southern Man (Hù Nánmán Xiàowèi).

Protector-General of Sanbā (Hù Sānbā Xiàowèi).

Pacifying Man-Peoples Commandant (Píngmán Xiàowèi).

Right and Left Palace Attendants (Zuǒyòu Chángshì) and Gentlemen of the Household (Shìláng).

Chief of Provisions (Shíguān), Chief of Stables and Pastures (Jiùmùzhǎng), and Usher (Yèzhě) and below.
For dukes and marquises, one Minister of the Household (Lángzhōnglìng) (one minister) was established.
Eulogy says: All offices are separately established,
only by the emperor's command are they given duties.
Like cloud masters and bird recorders,
each has its own pattern.
Collation Notes
Treatise Nine: Carriages and Apparel (Yúfú)
In ancient times, the Three Sovereigns (Sān Huáng) rode zhǐchē (祇車) out of Gǔkǒu.
The Xià (夏) clan had Xī Zhòng (奚仲) as the Rectifier of Carriages (chēzhèng).
The Yīn (殷) had auspicious carriages (ruìchē), such as shānchē (山車) and chuíjù (垂句).
In the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ), the artisan made carriages (yú)
to symbolize heaven and earth.
In the fourth year of Tiānhàn (天漢) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (Hàn Wǔ),
the feudal lords were received at Gānquán Palace,
and the system of carriages and apparel (yúfú zhì) was established,
promulgated throughout the empire.
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) of Guāngwǔ (光武),
Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述)'s precious carriages (bǎochē) were obtained,
and the imperial chariots (yúniǎn) began to be fully equipped.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) initiated this treatise,
and Mǎ Biāo (馬彪) completed the Hàn code.
Zhì Yú (摯虞) of Jìn governed the rites,
also discussing the system of five imperial chariots (wǔlù).
In the beginning of Jiāngzuǒ,
carriages and apparel were largely lacking,
with only gilded armaments,
and the ceremony of filling the court was omitted.
In the Tàixīng (太興) era,
when the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) attended school,
there were no high-canopied carriages.
Emperor Yuán (Yuán Dì) decreed the use of an'chē (安車).
During the Yuán and Míng (Yuán, Míng) eras,
there were only nine attendant carriages (shǔchē).
In the Yǒnghé (永和) era,
after Shí Hǔ (石虎) died,
old craftsmen fled and returned to the country,
gradually building carriages (chēyú).
In the Tàiyuán (太元) era,
after Fú Jiān (苻堅) was defeated,
his imitation imperial chariots (wěichēniǎn) were also obtained.
Thus, the attendant carriages (shǔchē) increased to twelve.
In the Yìxī (義熙) era,
when Sòng Wǔ (宋武) pacified Guān and Luò,
he obtained Yáo Xīng (姚興)'s imitation imperial chariots (wěichēniǎn).
During the Dàmíng (大明) era of Sòng, the imperial chariots (niǎn lù) were reformed and repaired,
exquisitely achieving the splendor of the time,
finally completing the pseudo-Dī (wěidī),
and again establishing the system of filling the court.
In the Yǒngmíng (永明) era,
further ornamentation was added,
surpassing that of previous times.
Comparing this with the Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Lǐ) and examining the Hàn Zhì,
the names and implements differ.
Jìn and Sòng reformed,
gradually differing from the customs of the age.
This record is merely of contemporary events.

In the early Yǒngmíng reign of Shìzǔ,
the Yùlù was augmented with a double canopy.
Also, Qílín heads were made,
painted in colors,
and placed on the horses' heads.
Jìnglíngwáng Zǐliáng submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject has heard that chariot banners have specific patterns,
as recorded in former histories,
and implements must conform to ritual,
with no deviation in attire.
Generally, the canopy's roundness symbolizes Heaven,
and the chariot bottom's squareness symbolizes Earth.
There should be no two heavens above,
nor decorations of two canopies below.
Seeking this in records,
I fear it is contrary to what is proper.
Furthermore, creating artificial Qílín heads
to place on horse heads
is not modeled on antiquity
and can rarely be implemented."
During the Jiànwǔ reign,
Míngdì then abolished the double canopy and other such additions.

Erecting the Dàhuī (Great Banner).
(It is a red banner.
The top is fitted with a flaming banner.
In the third year of Shēngmíng of the Sòng [dynasty],
the Qí Wáng was bestowed with a mùlù (wooden carriage) and a rónglù (military carriage), each one.
The Chénghuáng Wǔlù (five yellow carriages) [were used],
without a dàlù (grand carriage) or rónglù.
Zuǒ Chéng Wáng Qūzhī deliberated:
“The dàlù
was the sacrificial chariot of the Yīn [dynasty],
hence it was not listed among the names of the Zhōu chariots,
yet the Míngtáng Wèi says, ‘The dàlù
is the Yīn chariot.’
The commentary says, ‘The dàlù
is the mùlù.’
The Yuè Lìng says, ‘[The ruler of] the central earth [element]
rides the dàlù.’
The commentary says, ‘It is the Yīn chariot.’
The Lǐ Qì says, ‘The dàlù has a fán yīng (many-tasseled bridle) of one grade.’
The commentary says, ‘The dàlù
was the chariot for the Yīn [dynasty]'s sacrifice to Heaven.’
The Zhōu Lǐ lists five types of carriages (wǔlù):
the yùlù (jade carriage), jīnlù (gold carriage), xiànglù (elephant carriage), gélù (leather carriage), and mùlù (wooden carriage).
Thus, the mùlù of the Zhōu [dynasty]
was the dàlù of the Yīn [dynasty].
The Zhōu gélù bore a large white banner
for military campaigns;
this was therefore the rónglù.
It is thought that the great affairs of the state
are sacrifice and war.
Therefore, [the Qí Wáng] was bestowed with the Yīn chariot for sacrificing to Heaven,
and the Zhōu chariot for military campaigns.
That sacrifice was performed according to Yīn [rites],
while war was definitely conducted according to Zhōu [rites],
clarifies that the meaning of the suburban sacrifice to Heaven is profound,
and establishes the rites of a former dynasty.
Military affairs are more immediate,
hence the system of the current era is used.
The Míngtáng Wèi says, ‘In the first month of spring, the ruler of Lǔ rode the dàlù,
bearing a banner with twelve streamers, and the patterns of the sun and moon,
to sacrifice to Dì in the suburbs.’
[(15)] Surely, to bestow the dàlù upon a feudal lord
[(16)] had good reason.
Now, the mùlù
is precisely the dàlù.”
Tàiwèi Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ Wáng Jiǎn deliberated
that the jīnlù with nine streamers should be used.
At that time, the Chénghuáng had no attendant carriages;

The yùlù and jīnlù
bore green banners.
The xiànglù and mùlù
bore red banners.
In the early Yǒngmíng reign,
Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi Fú Mánróng deliberated,
believing that
“The virtue of Qí favors blue.
The wǔlù, five oxen, and five-colored banners
should all be ordered with blue first.
The carriages for military display and affairs of war,
and the sacrifices of silkworm cocoons presented,
should all adhere to the favored color.
The服色 (costume colors) of the Three Dynasties
were based on the sound of the surnames (xìngyīn);
the Hàn [dynasty] did not understand these sounds,
so they reverted to favoring the colors of their cyclical fortune.
Now, since there is no good master of pitch pipes,
the color favored by Dà Qí
should also follow the Hàn method.
If there were a good master of pitch pipes,
then one should revert to taking the surname as the favored [color].”
Tàizǐ Pú Zhōu Yōng deliberated:
“The xìngyīn of the Three Dynasties
have no ancient records;
the assigning of sounds to favored colors
originated with Mánróng.
If so, Mánróng is good at discerning surname sounds,
and there is no need to additionally resort to pitch pipes.
How can he discern the gōngshāng (musical notes) of distant eras,
yet be confused about the lǜlǚ (pitch pipes) of the imperial dynasty,
and say that currently there is no one who knows how to blow pitch pipes to determine the favored color,
and that one should rely on Hàn and make do with what is lacking?
The imperial dynasty originally favored colors based on cyclical fortune,
not because of inability to determine them by surname sound.
If this is the case,
even if there were a good master of pitch pipes who understood sounds,
it would not be appropriate to follow sounds as the favored [color].”
Sànqí Chángshì Liú Lǎngzhī and fifteen others all debated against him,
and the matter was not implemented.

Treatise Ten: Auspicious Omens
Heavenly signs and Mandates of Heaven,
how distant and profound!
Spiritual texts and secret diagrams
are surely stored in golden caskets and filled in stone chambers.
Those that illuminate prophecies and reveal *wěihòu*
have not yet been recorded in official documents.
To awaken the timing of heaven and man,
and to assist the fortune of emperors,
the sacred achievements of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
the great treasure of divine enlightenment,
and the coordinated support of two strategies,
none are without these.
Indeed, the falling fire and red sparrow
marked the reign of Zhōu.
Carved clouds and white spirits
brought prosperity to the Hàn clan.
When Guāngwǔ brought about the restoration,
imperial talismans were abundant.
Wèi received the prophecy of *dāngtú*,
and Jìn had the writing of stone omens.
What is detailed in historical writings
is also already old.
The Qí clan received the Mandate,
their affairs surpassing previous precedents.
The Yellow Gate Palace Attendant (*huángménláng*) Sū Kǎn compiled the *Shènghuáng Ruìyìng Jì*.
During the Yǒngmíng reign, Yǔ Wēn compiled the *Ruìyìng Tú*.
Other various categories
are recorded in historical notes.
Now, a detailed record has been compiled, taking and leaving
to form this treatise.

means jiǎn (to cut).
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says:
"It truly began by cutting down Shāng."
The song also says:
"If you want to know his surname, the grass is rustling.
The finest grain in the valley bows its head, ripe.
Scale-bodied and armored, long-lasting fortune."
Gǔ means dào (way);
shú means chéng (completion):
also a taboo name.
Tàizǔ had dragon scales on his body,
mottled patterns formed,
initially thought to be black marks.
Treatments were applied thoroughly, and the patterns became even clearer.
Fúxī also had a scale body.
Jīn Xióng Jì says:
"Smelting gold to make a knife in Lónglǐ,
a sleeping superior person is destined to rise."
It also says:
"There will be another 'sù' entering 'cǎo'."
This refers to the character Xiāo.
The Yì (Classic of Changes) says:
"The sages make them."
The Jì also says:
"The grass gate is pitiable, then it withers,
establishing a reign name fails, the destiny boils."
The Shī says bù shí (not timely),
which means shí (timely).
Bù chéng (not completed) means chéng (completed).
Jiànhào (establishing a reign name) refers to establishing a reign title.
Yìyùn (changing destiny) refers to revolution.
The Chèn (prophecy) says:
"King Wén of Zhōu received the mandate,
one thousand five hundred years,
a sage will emerge from the Hé and Luò rivers,
receiving the mandate in the Jǐwèi year,
up to the Bǐngzǐ year for eighteen cycles,
troops spread across six commanderies in the southeast corner,
the four states will be stable and long-lasting."
Upon examination, after Zhōu destroyed Yīn, seven hundred and eighty years passed,
Qín forty-nine years,
Hàn four hundred and twenty-five years,
Wèi forty-five years,
Jìn one hundred and fifty years,
Sòng sixty years,
up to the first year of Jiànyuán,
which is one thousand five hundred and nine years.
At Péngshān in Wǔjìn County,
the old burial ground was located there.
The mountain range of hills stretched for hundreds of *lǐ*,
with five-colored clouds above,
and a dragon emerged from it.
Sòng Míngdì disliked this,
and sent the tomb geomancer Gāo Língwén to observe it.
Língwén was already on good terms with Shìzǔ,
and upon returning,
he deceitfully replied:
"It will be nothing more than a regional governor."
He then privately told Shìzǔ:
"Your nobility is beyond words."
The emperor's apprehension did not cease,
so he sent people to hunt around the tomb,
and drove large iron nails, five or six *chǐ* long, into the four corners of the tomb,
as a protective charm.
Tàizǔ later changed the markers and pillars,
and the pillars suddenly roared like dragons,
the sound shaking the valleys.
The elders all recorded this.
At Kèshíshān in Shàn County, Kuàijī,
the name was passed down,
but the location of the inscription was unknown.
At the end of Shēngmíng,
Ér Xízǔ, a resident of the county, was hunting
when he suddenly saw inscriptions on the rocks in three places.
Moss grew on them,
and the characters were unreadable.
He removed the moss,
and the inscription on the large rock said:
"This Qí is
the transformed *qì* of Huánggōng."
The inscription on the standing rock said:
"Huáng Tiānxīng,
surname Xiāo, given name Mǒujiǎ,
will obtain a virtuous commander,
and the world will be at peace."
The inscription on the small rock said:
"Who carved this stone?
Lǐ Sī from Nánshān, Kuàijī, carved this inscription on Qínwàng."
At Qíhòushān in Yìzhōu,
the elders passed down the name,
but its origin was also unknown.
In the third year of Shēngmíng,
the *shāmén* Xuánchàng established a hermitage on the mountain hill.
On that day,
it was the day Tàizǔ received the abdication.
At Sōnggāoshān,
in the fourth month of the third year of Shēngmíng,
Yǐn Wǔ from Xíngyáng
saw stones raining from the sky in the southeast ravine of the mountain.
The stones split open upon falling to the ground,
and a seal was found inside,
three *cùn* square.
The inscription said:
"The person of Wù-Dīng accompanies the Dao,
solemnly enters the grass, responding to the heavenly tally."
It also said:
"The emperor's fortune rises."
Yǐn Wǔ presented the seal to Xiāo Chìfǔ, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
who then memorialized it.
The court historian comments: In ancient times, when giants were seen in Líntáo, bronze figures were cast.
When Dǒng Zhuó was born in Líntáo, the bronze figures were destroyed.
With Dǒng Zhuó, the world was in chaos;
when the world was in chaos, Dǒng Zhuó perished.
It seems similar.
At the end of the Jìn dynasty, thirty-two jade *bì* were unearthed from Sōnggāoshān,
which the Sòng clan took as an auspicious sign of receiving the mandate.
Now, this mountain produces a seal,
and the virtue of water is said to wane.
These are also similar omens of beginning and end.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
when Tàizǔ was at the southern suburban sacrifice,
Chén Ānbǎo, a *wàngqì* observer, saw yellow and purple *qì* extending to the sky from Tàizǔ's body.
Ānbǎo said to his close associate Wáng Hóngfàn:
"I have never seen such *qì* on a general since my youth."
When Tàizǔ was seventeen,
he dreamed of a ten-thousand-chariot blue dragon traveling west, chasing the sun.
The sun stopped as it was about to touch the mountain.
He woke up in fear,
and his family asked a fortune-teller,
who said
"It is an omen of extreme nobility."
Sū Kǎn said:
"Blue is
the color of wood.
The setting sun
signifies the end of the Sòng clan's fortune."
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ,
Emperor Míng sent Sūn Fèngbó, the former Administrator of Huáinán, to Huáiyīn to supervise Yuán Huì.
Fèngbó slept in the same bed as Tàizǔ,
and dreamed that the Emperor ascended to heaven riding a dragon,
but he (Fèngbó) could not grasp its feet from below.
When he awoke, he said to Tàizǔ:
"You, Yùnzhōu, are destined to greatly shelter the common people;
I will not live to see it."
Fèngbó died in Sòng.
Cuī Língyùn of Qīnghé, who was a staff officer in the Emperor's household,
dreamed that the Heavenly Emperor said to him:
"Xiāo Dàochéng is my nineteenth son;
last year I already bestowed upon him the position of Son of Heaven."
From the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to the monarch who received the Mandate of Qí,
there were exactly nineteen individuals.
During the Tàishǐ era of Sòng,
a children's rhyme said
"An Emperor will emerge from Dōngchéng,"
which led Emperor Míng to kill Xiū Rén, the King of Jiàn'ān.
Sū Kǎn said:
"Later, when the Emperor (Shìzǔ) ascended the throne from Dōngchéng,
commentators believed it was in response to this,
but it actually referred to Dōngchéng Lǐ, where he resided in Wǔjìn County."
Xióng Xiāng said:
"The Emperor's old hometown had a great road,
which was傳 said to have been traveled by Qín Shǐhuáng,
and was called 'Tiānzǐ Lù' (Emperor's Road),
and later it indeed became the Emperor's hometown."
Upon examination, the Emperor (Shìzǔ) was indeed destined to be supported and established,
like Huái and Mǐn of Jìn,
and there were also omens.
Since the Qí dynasty had no
imperial inspection routes with specific names,
it might be an old Qín name,
and I am uncertain if this can be detailed.
When Shìzǔ was thirteen,
he dreamed that his entire body grew hair,
and his head hair reached his feet.
He also dreamed that someone pointed at the ground he was treading on and said,
"This is King Wén of Zhōu's field."
He also dreamed of flying in the void.
He also dreamed of wearing a peacock feather robe.
Yǔ Wēn said:
"A sparrow (què)
is a homophone for official rank (jué)."
He also dreamed that a phoenix flew down from the sky to the front of his hermitage at the Qīngxī residence,
its two wings spanning over ten zhàng,
with purple clouds beneath its wings.
When he was in Xiāngyáng,
he dreamed of walking up the steps of the Tàijí Hall wearing mulberry clogs.
Yǔ Wēn said:
"Clogs (jī)
are an omen for the element Wood (mù)."
Your servant observes that the character sāng (桑, mulberry) can be interpreted as forty (sì shí) and two dots (èr diǎn),
and Shìzǔ ascended the throne after this age;
wearing clogs (jī) is interpreted as "wood walking" (mù xíng).
Clogs have two teeth and make a sound;
this means that at forty-two (míng liǎng zhī chǐ, literally 'bright two teeth') one will walk and truly ascend the throne.
When he was in Yǐngzhōu,
he dreamed that a person flew down from the sky,
with a brush tucked into their head, and drew on both sides of his robe,
then left without speaking.
Yǔ Wēn explained:
"The drawings
are mountain dragons and splendid insects."
Shìzǔ was born on the night of jǐwèi in the sixth month of the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng.
There was no fire,
but a maid blew on the ashes and fire spontaneously ignited.
When Shìzǔ was performing music in Nánkāng Commandery,
there were string instruments but no wind instruments,
yet suddenly there was the sound of a chí (flute) in the air,
its melody corresponding.
When Shìzǔ was the Chancellor of Guǎngxīng,
the area below the ridge experienced a prolonged drought, and the water dried up, preventing boats from passing.

the water suddenly rose dramatically.
Yǔ Wēn said:
"This is the meaning of the Yì (Book of Changes) line 'favorable to cross the great river'."
When Shìzǔ was stationed at Pénchéng,
there was no water in the city.
Wishing to dig and draw water from the Jiāng River,
he tried digging wells
and found nine underground springs,
all gushing forth.
In the fourth month of the first year of Jiànyuán,

He immediately dug,

East of that, there was suddenly a jingling sound,

From the spring, a silver wooden tablet was retrieved,

two cùn wide,
with raised characters saying 'Lúshān Dàorén Zhāng Líng respectfully bows and inquires about your well-being.'
The wood of the tablet was firm and white, but the characters were yellow in color."
We respectfully observe the Ruìyìng Tú (Diagram of Auspicious Omens), which says,

when the king is pure and tranquil,

Kǒng Shì Shìlù (Records of the Kǒng Clan) states:

In the twelfth month,
sweet dew fell on a pine tree on Péngshān (彭山),
and stopped on the ninth day.
In the ninth month of the first year of Jiànkē (建元),
sweet dew fell on two trees, a peach and a pomegranate, in Huáinán (淮南) Commandery.
The officials reported that sweet dew fell on the trees in Wáng Ānshì's (王安世) garden in Xīnjí (新汲) County.
In the fourth month of the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
sweet dew fell on a *tóng* (桐) tree in Nánjùn (南郡).
In the second month of the fourth year,
sweet dew fell on a plum tree in Línxiāng (臨湘) County.
In the third month,
sweet dew fell on a *tóng* (桐) tree in Nánjùn (南郡).
In the fourth month,
sweet dew fell on a peach tree in Suīyáng (睢陽) County.
In the fourth month of the fifth year,
sweet dew descended upon the parasol trees outside the central hall of the prefectural office in Jīngzhōu.
In the sixth year,
sweet dew descended upon the parasol trees of the old mountain hall in Fānglínyuán.
In the eighth month of the ninth year,
sweet dew descended upon the courtyard of the Buddha hall at Shàngdìnglín Sì,
filling the sky like rain,
covering the ground like snow.
Its aroma was fragrant,
its taste sweet.
It shimmered in the sun and danced in the wind,
only stopping at dusk.
Thereafter, it frequently descended upon the pine trees of Zhōngshān,
and ceased only after more than forty days.
In the tenth month,
sweet dew descended upon the trees of Tàianlíng.
〔一三〕
In the third month of Zhōngxīng second year,
sweet dew descended upon Máoshān,
spreading for several *lǐ*.
In the third month of Yuánhuī fourth year,
sweet spring water emerged from Báilùshān in Chāngguó,
its taste exceedingly sweet.
In the first month of Yǒngmíng first year,
auspicious grain, with
one stalk bearing five ears, was harvested in Gùshǐ County, Xīncài Prefecture.
In the eighth month,
auspicious grain was harvested in Xīncài County,
with two stalks bearing nine ears, and
one stalk bearing seven ears.
In the eleventh month,
auspicious grain, with
one stalk bearing nine ears, was harvested in Gùshǐ County.
In the eighth month of the second year,
auspicious grain, with
one stalk bearing twenty-three ears, was harvested in a field in the vicinity of Suīyáng County, Liáng Prefecture.
In the ninth month of the fifth year,
one stalk of auspicious grain was harvested in Jǔ County.
In the sixth month of the tenth year,
auspicious grain, with
one stalk bearing six ears, was harvested in Qíchāng County, Hǎilíng.
In the ninth month of the eleventh year,
one stalk of auspicious grain was harvested in a field in Suīyáng County.
In the ninth month of Shēngmíng second year,
a villager from Jiànchāng, Jiànníng County, was gathering herbs on Wànsuìshān,
when he suddenly heard a strange sound in the ravine.
He found one bronze bell,
two *chǐ* and one *cùn* long,
with ancient characters on its rim.
In the tenth month of Jiànyuán first year,
in the rock fissures where the Dàn people of Fúlíng Prefecture, led by Tián Jiàn, lived,
〔一四〕clouds often lingered,
and there were echoing sounds like a dragon's roar.
They searched for many years,
but no one saw anything.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month preceding,
suddenly two lights appeared at night a few *lǐ* from the rocks.
They went the next morning
and found one ancient bell
and another vessel named Chúnyú.
The Dàn people regarded them as divine objects and offered sacrifices to them.
In the fourth month of Yǒngmíng fourth year,
the mountains of Dōngchāng County had been emitting strange sounds for several years.
On the fifteenth day of the second month preceding,
a rock face collapsed.
A county resident, Fāng Yuántài, went to inspect it
and found one ancient bell at the foot of the rock.
In the third month of the fifth year,
one divine bell was found on Chánggǎngshān in Yùníng County.
In the eleventh month of the ninth year,
while tilling land in Níngshǔ Guǎnghàn County, at a depth of one *chǐ* and four *cùn*,
one ancient bell was found.
Its height was three *chǐ* and eight *cùn*,
its circumference four *chǐ* and seven *cùn*,
its handle one *chǐ* and two *cùn* long,
for a total height of five *chǐ*.
It had nine holes on each of its four sides.
Furthermore, a white light was seen among the tiles of a pottery workshop.
They searched but found nothing.
Thereafter, the light reappeared every night.
After ten days,
a villager, Zhāng Qìngxuan, was building a tile-roofed house
when he again saw light shining inside and out from within the house.
Qìngxuan was suspicious
and reported it to Kǒng Xiūxiān.
They then jointly dug and inspected
and found one jade seal.
The *bì* was eight *fēn* square,
with a knob on top,
and bore the inscription
"Dìzhēn".
To the left of the residence of Huáng Qìng in Qǔ'ā County was a garden.
The southeast part of the garden was four *zhàng* square.
Whenever vegetables were planted there,
they were always fresh and unusual.
Even when picked,
they would quickly regrow.
At night, there was a white light,
pure and bright, reaching the sky,
resembling a suspended silk banner.
They privately suspected it was extraordinary
and asked a master to divine it.
The Daoist Fù Dézhān had them dig,
and at a depth of three *chǐ*,
they found one jade seal,
with the inscription
"Cháng Chéng Wànfú".
In the first month of Yǒngmíng second year,
Zhōu Pǔsūn, General of Champion, saw an unusual light on the ground shining on the city battlements from a hall on the north side of Shítóu.
He went and found one jade seal,
seven *fēn* square,
with the inscription
"Míngxuán Jūn".
In the eleventh month,
Qí Xiáng, a captive citizen, returned and entered Língqiū Pass.
He heard a deep rumbling sound.
Looking up,
he saw a purple aura like a cloud on the mountainside,
with many birds circling within it.
Xiáng went to the location of the aura
and found a seal, one *cùn* and four *fēn* square,
with an animal knob,
and the inscription
"Kūnwéi Shèngdì Yǒngchāng".
He sent it to Huì Dù, the Daoist master of the captive Empress Dowager,
intending to present it to the captive ruler.
Huì Dù, upon seeing the inscription,
secretly said,
"The legitimate authority and orthodox calendar of the present day
reside with the state of Qí."
He then entrusted it to the Daoist Huì Zàng to send to the capital,
who then presented it through Yǔlín Supervisor Cuī Shìliàng.
In the seventh month of the third year,
Gōng Xuánxuān, a resident of Shǐxīng Prefecture, stated that
in the second month of the previous year,
a Daoist suddenly came begging for food.
He then pulled out from his bosom one roll of a genuine scripture in seal script,
six sheets,
and one sheet for memorializing the North Star,
and one sheet for transferring to the lay Buddhist Luóhàn.
He said he came down from the Dōushuài Tiāngōng
to deliver it to the Son of Heaven.
Thereafter, the Daoist's whereabouts were unknown.
In the first month of this year,
Xuánxuān also claimed that a divine person bestowed an emperor's seal upon him.
It was turtle-shaped,
five *cùn* long,
two *cùn* wide,
and two *cùn* and five *fēn* thick.
On it were the characters
"Tiāndì",
〔一五〕in the center the character
"Xiāo",
and below it the characters
"Wànshì".
〔一六〕
In the tenth year,
Qí Bóshēng, a resident of Lánlíng, found one golden seal on Liùhéshān,
with the inscription
"Nián Yú Zhǔ".
Shìzǔ, while governing Pénchéng,
obtained ten five-*chǐ* long swords.
〔一七〕This was within the period of Yǒngmíng.
In Shēngmíng third year,
villagers of Zuǒlǐ found two *yī* halberds in Gōngtínghú,
with ancient characters on the side,
whose writing was too distant to be legible.
During the Tàishǐ period,
Shìzǔ found one coin in his Qīngxī residence,
with the Big Dipper constellation and a double knot in its inscription,
〔一八〕and also a human figure carrying a sword.
And when he governed Pénchéng,
he again found a large coin,
with the inscription
"Tàipíng Bǎisuì".
In Yǒngmíng seventh year,
Liú Yuánbǎo, Administrator of Qíxīng, while governing the prefectural city,
found a million coins in the moat.
They were extremely large in shape,
and were presented to the court as an auspicious omen.
Shìzǔ distributed them to the court officials and below, each according to their rank.
In the tenth year,
Wáng Shè, a resident of Qí'ān Prefecture, digging in the ground, found twelve thousand seven hundred and ten large coins with four characters,
all of the same make and style.
In Jiànyuán first year,
the water of Tiānjǐnghú in Jiānlì County, Yǐngzhōu, suddenly became clear,
and produced cotton,
which the common people gathered to make wadding.
In Yǒngmíng second year,
one mulberry tree outside the gate of the Hùjūnfǔ had silkworm cocoons covering its branches and stems.
The historian observes: In the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ [光武] of Hàn, there were wild silkworms that produced silk,
enabling the common people to make clothes.
Now, with floating bubbles covering trees,
is this perhaps a similar phenomenon?

Shìzǔ [世祖] personally threw it into Tiānyuān Chí [天淵池] to test it,

In the second year,
an ancient tripod was found at the foot of a mountain in Yángdānshuǐ [陽丹水] County.

An encomium says: From heaven they descend, from earth they emerge;

The myriad creations of the world,
