Textual Notes
Memoir 11, line 5.
The "Biography of Wood" says:
"In the East,
the Yi Jing [易經] views wood on the earth as 'observation' (guān [觀]),
thus wood, for humans, signifies
dignified bearing and appearance.
Wood is
the beginning of the spring qi,
the foundation of agriculture.
If one does not seize the farming season,
allows the people to spend no more than three days a year [on corvée],
levies a tax of one-tenth,
and has no greedy desires,
then the wood qi will follow.
If a ruler loses their dignified bearing,
acts contrary to the wood element,
indulges in hunting and racing,
does not return to their palace,
is immoderate in eating and drinking,
disregards rites and regulations,
has excessive comings and goings,
dispatches many corvée laborers
to seize the people's time,
and commits deceitful acts
to seize the people's wealth,
then the wood will lose its nature.
This is like how artisans making wheels and arrows often cause damage,
hence it is said that wood is neither straight nor crooked."
In the first year of Tàiyù [泰豫] of Sòng [宋],
the honey locust trees at Zhīyuán Sì [祗垣寺] in the capital withered and died.
Towards the end of Shēngmíng [昇明],
they suddenly sprouted new flowers and leaves.
The Jīng Fáng [京房] Yi Zhuan [易傳] says:
"If trees wither in winter and then sprout,
within two years,
the state will suffer loss,
and a gentleman will perish."
The prognostication was the same.
The Sòng [宋] clan abdicated the throne.
In the first year of Jiànyuán [建元],
branches and leaves grew on the huábiǎo [華表] pillars of Zhūjué [朱爵] [untranscribable character].
In early Jiànyuán [建元],
plum seeds grew hair.
In the second year,
there was a mulberry tree at the headquarters of the Commandant of Yuántóu [沅頭] in Wǔlíng [武陵],
which grew leaves in winter.
The Jīng Fáng [京房] Yi Zhuan [易傳] says:
"If trees bloom in winter,
there will be mourning under heaven."
The prognostication was the same.
Two years later,
the imperial carriage passed away (the emperor died).
In the fourth year,
several-hundred-year-old cypress pillars at the base of an ancient tower west of Bāzhōu [巴州] city
suddenly flowered.
In the sixth year of Yǒngmíng [永明],
the cypress wood from Shízǐ Gǎng [石子崗],
measuring two feet four inches long
and four and a half inches wide,
transformed into stone.
At that time, the imperial carriage frequently went on excursions,
which corresponds to the main text's statement that "wood loses its nature."
During Yǒngmíng [永明],
a large boat [untranscribable character] inexplicably sank,
but there was no water in its hold.
In the first year of Lóngchāng [隆昌],
blood inexplicably flowed from the base of the pillars in the study of Prince Zǐqīng [子卿] of Lúlíng [廬陵].
In early Jiànwǔ [建武],
Prince Yáoguāng [遙光] of Shǐ'ān [始安] was constructing a temple;
he cut off part of the roof of Dōng'ān Sì [東安寺] to straighten the temple wall,
and when a beam was cut,
water flowed out like tears.
The "Biography of Appearance" says:
"To lose the regulations of dignified bearing,
to be negligent and arrogant,
is called madness,
and thus one is not stern.
If subordinates are not respectful,
then the superior will have no authority.
If the world is not respectful,
and also unrestrained in its arrogance,
then if it is indulged, it will not obey.
If one does not respect their ruler
and does not obey their government,
then yin qi will prevail,
hence it is said that 'its punishment is constant rain'."
In the fourth month of the eighth year of Yǒngmíng [永明],
on the jǐsì [己巳] day, continuous overcast and rainy weather began.
During the day it occasionally cleared,
and at night the stars and moon were sometimes visible.
The heavy rain continued
until the seventeenth day, when it stopped.
On the xīnsì [辛巳] day, the first day of the fourth month in the eleventh year,
starting from the wùyín [戊寅] day of the third month,
with brief periods of clear weather in between,
overcast and rainy weather began again on the first day of the fourth month.
During the day the sun was sometimes visible,
and at night the moon was sometimes seen,
but it returned to overcast and rainy conditions
until the seventh month, when it stopped.
On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month in the first year of Yǒngtài [永泰], it rained,
and it did not clear until the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the first year of Yǒngyuán [永元].
Jīng Fáng's [京房] prognostication says:
"Winter rain means
famine under heaven.
Spring rain means
small military conflicts."
At that time, barbarians invaded Yōngzhōu [雍州];
the rest corresponds to the main biography.
The "Biography" says:
"Heavy rain and snow are
like the constant rain among the various omens,
but even more severe.
Rain is
yin.
Heavy rain and snow mean
that the accumulation of yin is extreme.
One explanation is that it shares the same象 as great floods,
saying it is a 'violent attack' in the form of snow."
On the jǐchǒu [己丑] day of the intercalary month in the second year of Jiànyuán [建元],
there was rain and snow.
In the eleventh month of the third year,
there was rain and snow,
sometimes overcast, sometimes dark,
for over eighty days,
until the second month of the fourth year, when it stopped.
The "Biography" says:
"Thunder, among heaven and earth, is the eldest son,
because it initiates the growth of all things,
entering and exiting with them.
Therefore, when thunder emerges, all things emerge;
when thunder enters, all things enter.
Thunder is the symbol of the ruler.
When it enters, it eliminates harm;
when it emerges, it brings benefit.
The subtle qi of thunder emerges in the first month;
its audible sound emerges in the second month;
it enters in the eighth month;
its remaining subtle qi enters in the ninth month.
In the three winter months, thunder should not emerge.
If the yang does not close off the yin like this,
then it will emerge into danger and harm all things."
In the first year of Jiàn-yuán, in the tenth month, on the day Rén-wǔ,
at night, there was lightning,
followed by thunder.
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēng-xū,
there was lightning,
and after a moment, thunder,
which ceased after a long time.
In the fifth year of Yǒng-míng, in the first month, on the day Wù-shēn,
at night, thunder was heard in the northwest.
In the sixth year, in the tenth month, on the day Jiǎ-shēn,
at night, it was overcast with light rain,
and thunder was first heard from above the northwest.
In the seventh year, in the first month, on the day Jiǎ-zǐ,
at night, it was overcast,
and thunder rumbled in the southwest Kūn-gōng (palace),
stopping after a single rumbling sound.
In the eighth year, in the first month, on the day Gēng-xū,
at night, thunder arose from the Kǎn-gōng (palace) water gate,
its sound rumbling,
stopping after a single sound.
In the ninth year, in the second month, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
there was lightning in the northwest,
followed by rumbling thunder,
which continued for ten sounds before stopping.
In the tenth year, in the second month, on the day Gēng-xū,
at night, there was lightning in the south,
followed by continuous rumbling thunder,
stopping on the day Dīng-hài.
In the tenth month, on the day Gēng-zǐ,
lightning and thunder arose in the northwest.
In the eleventh month, on the day Dīng-chǒu,
there was light in the southwest,
followed by faint thunder,
stopping after two sounds.
This was in the southwest Kūn-gōng.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jiǎ-shēn,
it was overcast and rainy,
with lightning,
followed by thunder from the southwest and above the northwest,
continuing for three sounds.
On the day Bǐng-shēn,
at night, thunder was heard continuously for two sounds from above the northwest.
On the day Xīn-hài,
there was a thunderstorm.
The commentary says:
"Rain with hail
is an omen concerning the ruler and his ministers.
When the Yang energy is concentrated, it forms hail;
when the Yin energy is concentrated, it forms soft hail (sleet).
When Yang is concentrated and Yin is pressed,
Yin is abundant and Yang is weakened.
Hail
is an omen of Yin weakening Yang.
Soft hail
is a sign of Yang pressing Yin.
The *Chūn-qiū* does not record soft hail
just as it does not record lunar eclipses."
In the fourth year of Jiàn-yuán, in the fifth month, on the first day Wù-wǔ,
there was hail.
In the first year of Yǒng-míng, in the ninth month, on the day Yǐ-chǒu,
hailstones fell as large as garlic cloves,
stopping shortly thereafter.
In the eleventh year, in the fourth month, on the day Xīn-hài,
hailstones fell as large as garlic cloves,
disappearing in an instant.
The *Mào-zhuàn* also says:
"When those above lose their sense of measure and act wildly,
and those below are negligent and disrespectful,
when both above and below deviate from the Way,
lightly applying laws and infringing upon regulations,
disregarding their superiors,
famine consequently follows.
When the 'appearance energy' is corrupted,
then there are strange occurrences with chickens."
Another account says:
"In years of water (element), if many chickens die or become monstrous,
this is also the case.
When those above and below do not trust each other,
and high ministers commit treachery,
and the people become bandits and thieves,
it is said that 'their extreme wickedness' occurs."
Another account says:
"When many people are punished,
or their appearance is ugly and deformed,
and customs are wild and disrespectful,
and they change their principles and alter their standards,
then they wear light, frivolous, and strange clothes.
Therefore, it is said, 'at such times, there are fashion anomalies.'"
During the Yǒng-míng period,
the inner palace adopted clothing with hunting and archery brocade patterns,
featuring images of horse archery and weapons.
By the beginning of Jiàn-wǔ,
During the Yǒng-míng period,
Xiāo Chén initiated the style of opening the back of the *bó-fēng* hat,
creating the 'broken-back hat'.
the barbarians became a major scourge.
Chén brought about deposing and establishing rulers,
and exterminated various princes.
Towards the end of Yǒng-míng,
the common people created the *yǐ-quàn* hat.
When Hǎi-líng was deposed,
and Míng-dì was enthroned,
the act of 'urging advancement' (quàn-jìn)
was indeed expected.
During the Jiàn-wǔ period,
hats covered the top of the head.
During the time of Dōng-hūn,
it was thought that the hat should be low,
but now it was high,
which was inauspicious,
so it was cut.
This was an omen of the subordinates rebelling against their superiors.
During the Yǒng-yuán period,
the Marquis of Dōng-hūn personally created attire for banquets and excursions,
adorned with colorful brocade and embroidery,
the details of which are difficult to ascertain.
The small courtiers also created four types of hats,
named according to their 'potential' (shì).
One was called
"Magpies Returning to the Forest."
The *Shī-yún* (Book of Songs) says,
"The magpie's nest
is the virtue of a lady."
As Dōng-hūn favored his concubines and indulged in promiscuity,
the magpies returned to their woods and thickets.
The second was called
"Rabbit Crossing a Pit,"
meaning that Heaven's will indicated that there would be 'rabbit chasing' (i.e., contention for the throne) in the world.
The third was called
"Yellow Orioles Tied Backward,"
yellow-mouthed small birds.
"Tied backward"
corresponds to being tied with face to the back.
The fourth was called
"Phoenix Crossing Three Bridges."
The phoenix is an auspicious omen.
The 'three bridges'
are the dwelling place of the King of Liáng.
The *Mào-zhuàn* also says:
"When the beginning of danger and chaos appears,
then strange phenomena arise in heaven and earth.
Wood is green,
hence it is called 'green calamity' (qīng-shěng),
which is an evil omen.
Generally, when 'appearance' is harmed,
Metal afflicts Wood,
or Wood afflicts Metal,
and the opposing *qì* communicate."
In the first year of Yán-xīng,
when King Hǎi-líng was first enthroned,
above the tomb of Crown Prince Wén-huì, there was an object like a person,
several *zhàng* long,
green in color,
ascending straight to the sky,
with a sound like thunder.
Fire,
being southern,
emits brilliant light,
and produces fiery radiance to be illuminating.
A ruler governs by facing the light,
probably taking this as its image.
If people are distinguished,
slanderers are kept at a distance,
and worthy officials are in positions of power,
then there will be illumination, and the fire *qì* will follow.
If the ruler is indecisive,
abandons laws,
and does not punish slanderers and evildoers,
then slander will spread,
causing internal estrangement among relatives,
and external alienation of loyal ministers,
leading to the killing of the heir apparent,
the expulsion of meritorious officials,
and taking concubines as wives.
Then fire loses its nature,
calamity above affects the ancestral temple,
calamity below affects the mansions and pavilions,
internally burning the court,
externally burning the watchtowers.
Even if a great army is raised,
it cannot save them.
In the third year of Yǒng-míng, in the first month,
on the *jiǎ* night, there was a wildfire in the northwest,
and glowing essences emerged from the light,
four in the northwest,
one in the northeast,
all seven or eight *chǐ* long,
yellowish-red in color.
In the third month, on the day Gēng-wǔ,
on the *bǐng* night, there was a wildfire facing north,
and a glowing essence emerged from the light,
six *chǐ* long.
On the *wù* night, there was another one,
five *chǐ* long,
both yellowish-red in color.
In the fourth year, in the first month, on the *dīnghài* day,
at night, there were three locations of fire spirits.
In the intercalary month, on the *dīngsì* day,
at night, there were four locations of fire spirits.
In the twelfth month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
at night, to the southeast, there were two wild fire spirits.
In the fifth year, in the twelfth month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
at night, to the northwest, there was a wild fire,
from which a spirit was born,
one in number,
three *chǐ* long,
yellowish-white in color.
In the sixth year, in the eleventh month, on the *wùshēn* day,
at night, to the southwest and north, on three sides, there were wild fires,
from which spirits were born,
nine in number,
all two *chǐ* long,
yellowish-red in color.
In the ninth year, in the second month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
in the first watch of the night, to the north, there was a wild fire,
from which spirits were born,
two in number;
to the northwest, there was another one,
all three *chǐ* long,
disappearing in an instant.
In the eighth month of the second year of Yǒngyuán,
there was a fire inside the palace,
burning the western hall, the Xuányí Palace, and the Zhāoyáng and Xiǎnyáng Palaces, among others.
To the north, it reached the Huálín wall;
to the west, it reached the Mìgé.
In all, over three thousand rooms were burned.
The *Jīngfáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
"If the ruler does not contemplate the Way,
the calamity is fire burning the palace."
The Mìgé fire was the same as the fire at the *Chūnqiū Xuānxiè*.
Heaven's intention seems to be saying,
"Since there is no order and discipline,
what use are classical texts and documents?"
In the winter of the second year,
people in the capital were alarmed, saying
a fire disaster was imminent.
In households on the southern bank, people often found cloth wrapped in fire within their fences,
saying the government used this to ward off evil.
In the first month of the third year,
heavenly fire burned over three thousand households in Yùzhāng Commandery.
The *Jīngfáng Yì Zhān* says:
"When heavenly fire burns down people's homes,
this is called a chaotic reign where soldiers are raised."
In this year,
the imperial army and the righteous forces attacked each other with various factions in the southern Jiāng commanderies.
In the second month of the third year,
the western wing of the Qiánhé Palace caught fire,
burning thirty rooms.
At this time, since the western hall had already burned,
the Emperor moved to reside in the eastern hall,
which was the palace where Gāozōng had lived.
This was consistent with the divination for palace fires.
The *Zhuàn* also says:
"If those who offend superiors are not punished,
then grass will violate the frost and not die.
Or, if killing is not done at the proper time,
the matter lies in losing control over life and death,
hence it is called the calamity of grass."
Another account says:
"The calamity of grass
is an omen of losing the masses."
During the Yǒngyuán period,
at the residence of Yùdāo Huáng Wénjì, *chāngpú* was planted in front of the study.
Suddenly, flowers bloomed,
their light and shadows illuminating the wall,
forming five colors.
His son saw them,
but other people did not.
A short time later,
Wénjì was killed.
Liú Xīn's *Shì Zhuàn* contains "calamity of feathered insects,"
referring to a chicken misfortune.
Bān Gù, examining the *Yì*, states that chickens belong to Xùn.
Now, the calamity of feathered insects is analogous to this,
and according to Xīn's explanation, it is attached to the *Shì Zhuàn*.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
a large bird gathered in Jiàn'ān,
shaped like a young water buffalo.
That year,
the commandery experienced a great flood.
In the third year,
a large bird gathered in Dōngyáng Commandery.
The Grand Administrator, Shěn Yuē, reported:
"The bird's body exhibited all five colors,
with red being predominant."
An examination of the *Yuè Wěi Yè Tú Zhēng* states:
"The *Jiāomíng* bird is red in essence;
its arrival is a sign of water."
In the fourth month of the second year of Yǒngmíng,
crows nested on the eastern *chīwěi* of the inner palace.
In the third year,
a large bird gathered in Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
That year,
the county experienced a great flood.
The *Zhuàn* says:
"Water harms fire."
It also says:
"Red omens are auspicious."
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
in the curtained screen residence of Wáng Yànzi Démó,
without cause, blood was sprinkled upon it,
dispersing after a few days.
[Yàn was soon executed].
The *Sīxīn Zhuàn* says:
"The heart
is an image of earth.
If the mind contemplating is not discerning,
its fault lies in confusion and loss of order.
Wind, in the context of yang, represents the ruler;
in the context of yin, it represents the image of a high official,
who is autocratic and overbearing,
hence the punishment of constant wind.
The heart is the master of the five affairs,
just as earth is the master of the five elements."
Another account says:
"When yin and yang contend,
if the partial qi of yang is excessive, it becomes wind;
its severity is constant wind.
If the yin qi is excessive,
it becomes overcast but without rain;
its severity is constant overcast."
Another account says:
"If wind rises at night and the day is dim,
it corresponds to the same omen as constant overcast."
In the first year of Jiànzhāo, in the eleventh month, on the *gēngxū* day,
wind suddenly rose at night,
clouds and thunder merged into darkness,
coming from the direction of *xū-hài*.
In the fourth year, in the eleventh month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
at the *yǒu* hour, the wind rose slightly swiftly,
and by the second watch, snow fell;
the wind intensified violently.
In the second month of the fourth year of Yǒngmíng, on the *bǐngyín* day,
at the *sì* hour, the wind was swift and urgent.
In the eleventh month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
at the *xū* hour, the wind was swift and urgent,
coming from the northwest, from the *xū-hài* direction.
In the fifth year, in the fifth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
at the *zǐ* hour, the wind was swift and urgent,
coming from the northwest, from the *xū-hài* direction.
In the seventh year, in the first month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
a day of *yángzhēng yīncéi*,
the time was at *zǐ*.
The wind rose swiftly and urgently,
coming from the north, from the *zǐ-chǒu* direction,
violent and turbulent,
stopping at the *yín* hour.
In the eighth year, in the sixth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
the time was at *zǐ*.
The wind rose swiftly and urgently,
violent and turbulent,
unroofing houses and breaking trees,
with dust and sand,
coming from the southwest, from the *wèi* direction,
followed by thunder and rain.
In an instant,
the wind subsided and the rain stopped.
In the ninth year, in the seventh month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
a day of *yángyǔ liánzhēn*,
the time was at *hài*.
The wind rose swiftly and urgently,
coming from the east,
violent, surging, and turbulent.
By the *yǐmǎo yīncéi* hour, it gradually subsided,
named "feather stirring feather."
In the ninth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the time was at *wèi*.
There was thunder,
a sudden downpour,
and the wind rose swiftly and urgently,
violent and turbulent,
coming from the northwest, from the *xū* direction.
In the tenth month, on the *rénchén* day,
a day of *yángshāng kuāndà*,
the time was at *chǒu*.
The wind rose from the north, from the *zǐ-chǒu* direction,
violent and turbulent,
swift and urgent,
with dust.
On the fifth day, at the *yín* hour, it gradually subsided,
named "feather stirring palace."
In the tenth year, in the first month, on the *xīnsì* day,
a day of *yángshāng kuāndà*,
the time was at *yín*.
The wind came from the northwest,
violent and turbulent,
swift and urgent,
raising sand and breaking trees,
stopping at the *yǒu* hour.
On the *jiǎchén* day of the second month,
a day when *yángzhēng* indicates treachery and wickedness,
the hour was *chén*.
A strong and rapid wind arose,
coming from the northwest, from the direction of *hài*.
It was violent, swift, raging, and turbulent,
stopping at the *yǒu* hour.
On the *dīngyǒu* day of the third month,
a day when *yángzhēng* indicates integrity and honesty,
the hour was *wèi*.
A swift and rapid wind came from the north, from the directions of *zǐ* and *chǒu*.
It was swift and rapid,
violent, and turbulent,
stopping at the *xū* hour.
On the *gēngshēn* day of the seventh month,
a day when *yīnjiǎo* indicates avarice and greed,
the hour was *wǔ*.
A swift and rapid wind came from the northeast, from the direction of *chǒu*.
It was swift, rapid, and turbulent,
gradually subsiding at the *sì* hour on the *xīnyǒu* day.
In the second month of the eleventh year, on the *gēngyín* day,
a day when *yángjiǎo* indicates integrity and honesty,
the hour was *hài*.
A swift and rapid wind came from the northwest, from the direction of *hài*.
It was swift, rapid, and turbulent,
gradually subsiding at the *chǒu* hour.
This was "angle disturbing angle."
In the seventh month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
a day when *yángyǔ* indicates integrity and honesty,
the hour was *sì*.
A swift and rapid wind came from the northeast, from the direction of *yín*.
It was swift, rapid, and turbulent,
unroofing houses and breaking trees,
gradually subsiding at the *wù* hour of the night.
This was "wing disturbing *zhēng*."
On the *jǐsì* day,
a day when *yángjiǎo* indicates generosity and broadness,
the hour was *wèi*.
A violent wind came from the direction of *xū*.
It was violent and swift,
stopping after a long time.
This was "angle disturbing *shāng* and *gōng*."
In all cases, the timing was not arbitrary and unrestrained;
it was likely caused by the clashing of *yīn* and *yáng*.
In the third month of the first year of [Jiànwǔ (originally Jiànchāng)], on the *yǐyǒu* day,
a turbulent and violent wind arose at the *wèi* hour,
coming from the north.
This corresponded to the "obscurity and confusion" mentioned in the main commentary.
In the second, third, and fourth years of Jiànwǔ,
every autumn, in the seventh and eighth months,
there were always great winds,
especially severe in the Three Wú regions,
unroofing houses, breaking trees,
and killing people.
Jīng Fáng's prognostication stated:
"When prison officials are cruel,
wind harms people."
At that time, the emperor was severe and harsh.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngyuán,
there was a great wind.
In the capital, trees ten *wéi* in circumference and the roofs of official buildings and residents' houses were all uprooted and collapsed.
This corresponded to the main commentary.
The commentary also says:
"Mountains on the earth
are symbols of the ruler.
When mountains collapse,
the ruler's power diminishes.
When capitals and mausoleums change places,
the world will change.
When hills turn into marshes,
the noble will become base."
In the summer of the second year of Jiànyuán,
in Shíyáng County, Lúlín Commandery, the banks of the Cháng Xī river were eroded, causing a mountain to collapse.
It was six or seven *zhàng* long,
and over a thousand pillars were found beneath it,
all ten *wéi* in circumference.
The longest were one *zhàng*,
the shortest eight or nine *chǐ*.
Ancient characters were inscribed on their tops,
but they were indecipherable.
Jiāng Yān asked Wáng Jiǎn about them.
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"The people of Jiāngdōng are not familiar with clerical script.
These are pillars from the Qín and Hàn dynasties."
The following year, the imperial carriage stopped (*i.e.*, the emperor died),
which was an omen of changing times.
In the autumn of the second year of Yǒngmíng,
a mountain collapsed in Qǔjiāng County, Shǐxīng,
blocking the stream and forming a lake.
Jīng Fáng's prognostication stated:
"When a mountain collapses,
it is an evil omen for the human ruler."
The commentary also says:
"What is struck by thunder and lightning
is that which is affected.
All are caused by thoughts and feelings having an excess."
In the intercalary sixth month of the second year of Jiànyuán, on the *bǐngxū* day,
there was thunder and lightning in the *wù* hour of the night.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the fourth year,
clouds and hail darkened the capital.
Thunder struck at the Lèyóu Ānchāng Diàn,
and fire from lightning burned it all down.
On the sixth day of the fourth month of the eighth year of Yǒngmíng,
thunder struck.
At Bǎolín Sì on Shānyīn Mountain in Kuàijī, the top of the pagoda was split into four.
Lightning fire burned the pagoda,
but the windows below the Buddha's face were unaffected.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
thunder struck the south gate of the Eastern Palace,
causing no damage or destruction,
but killing one imperial food official.
In the third month of the eleventh year,
thunder struck at the Eastern Study,
and the ridgepole collapsed.
Those around him secretly wanted to repair it,
but Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng said:
"How can this be repaired?
Let it remain to remind me of my faults,
and moreover to show Heaven's love for me."
The following year,
Zǐliáng died.
The commentary also says:
"When the *tǔ* element is disordered,
the *mù*, *jīn*, *shuǐ*, and *huǒ* elements disorder it."
In the second month of the second year of Jiànwǔ, on the *dīngsì* day,
there was an earthquake.
In the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngyuán,
there were eighteen earthquakes day and night.
On the nineteenth day of the ninth month,
there were five earthquakes.
The *jīn* element is
the west,
where all things are fully formed,
and the *shāqì* (killing aura) begins.
In matters of the king,
it represents the way of military conflict and warfare.
When the king raises an army and mobilizes the populace,
establishes banners and drums,
wields pennants and axes,
to punish evildoers,
and stop violence and rebellion,
and the killing and punishment are righteous,
then the *jīn* element follows.
It is also the forging and casting of metals,
reforming shapes into tools.
If the ruler enjoys invading and infringing,
loves to attack and wage war,
covets cities and towns,
and disregards the lives of the common people,
causing the people to be restless,
and internal and external disturbances,
then the *jīn* element loses its nature.
If metallurgy fails to transform,
becoming frozen, stagnant, solid, and hard,
then it is said that *jīn* does not follow transformation,
and also, "wood harms metal."
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Míng went out of the old palace to send off the second daughter of the King of Yùzhāng, Princess Suī'ān, as a bride.
Upon returning to his imperial carriage,
the golden wings on the carriage inexplicably broke off and fell to the ground.
The commentary says:
"In the way of *yán yì* (spoken change),
the west is called *duì*,
representing the mouth.
If the ruler makes excessive mistakes without measure,
his laws are inconsistent,
taxes are collected too heavily,
or there are military expeditions,
the season of intense *yáng* (heat),
if the populace is mobilized and people are toiled,
this means that words are not followed.
If the ruler has lost the support of the people,
and his decrees are not followed,
he governs with isolated *yáng*.
The lower classes fear the ruler's severe punishments.
If the *yáng* energy is excessive, a drought omen appears,
hence it is said, 'Its punishment is constant *yáng* (drought).'"
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
there was a great drought,
and at that time there were barbarian invasions.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
there was a great drought.
The following year,
Táng Huì's uprising occurred.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
there was a great drought,
and at that time barbarian invasions were flourishing.
All these were manifestations of mobilizing the populace.
The commentary says:
"If the lower classes are saddened and embittered by the ruler's actions,
and also fear severe punishment and dare not speak truthfully,
then it will first manifest in songs and ballads.
Songs and ballads
are matters of the mouth.
If the *kǒuqì* (mouth's energy) is perverse, there will be malicious words,
or even strange rumors."
After the Sòng dynasty lost Péngchéng during the Tàishǐ era,
a new type of pear, called *zhǒngxiāolí* (種消梨), began to be propagated south of the Yangtze River.
It had not existed before,
and the common people eagerly contended to plant it.
Those with foresight said:
"There will be someone whose surname is Xiāo (蕭) who will come."
More than ten years later,
the Qí dynasty received the imperial abdication.
During the Yuánhuī era,
a children's rhyme said:
"A white-bronze hooves from Xiāngyáng,
a郎 (láng) kills the children of Jīngzhōu (荊州)."
Later, Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) rebelled,
and Zhāng Jìng'ér (張敬兒), the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), attacked Jiānglíng (江陵),
killing Shěn Yōuzhī's son Yuányǎn (元琰) and others.
On the New Year's Day of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
a commoner opened a *báihǔzūn* (白虎樽) (White Tiger wine vessel).
Having become drunk,
he was given a writing brush and a tablet,
but he did not know what to write;
he merely said,
"I remember Emperor Gāo (高帝)."
An edict pardoned his crime.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) built the old palace at Qīngxī (青溪),
people at the time reversed the saying,
saying, "The old palace
is a poor stable."
After the emperor passed away,
the palace women moved out and resided there.
In the early Yǒngmíng era,
the common people sang:
"A white horse cries towards the city,
desiring grass by the city walls."
The later line intermittently said,
"Táo Láng (陶郎) is coming."
"White" (白) refers to the color gold,
and "horse" (馬) refers to military affairs.
Three years later,
the wicked bandit Táng Cuìzhī (唐𧜛之) rose up,
indicating that Táng (唐) was coming to reward.
When Shìzǔ first completed the construction of Chánlíng Sì (禪靈寺),
the common people watched intently,
and some said:
"Chán (禪) means 'to abdicate,'
and Líng (靈) is not a good name;
the one to whom the abdication is made will certainly not be the right person."
Later, the Crown Imperial Grandson was established,
but was then deposed.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
all food eaten in the palace, apart from imperial meals,
was called *kèshí* (客食, 'guest food').
Shìzǔ considered *kè* (客) not to be a family name,
and changed it to *biéshí* (別食, 'separate food').
People at the time regarded this as an omen of separation.
Shortly thereafter,
the emperor passed away.
When Wénhuì Tàizǐ (文惠太子) was in the Eastern Palace,
he composed a poem with the lines "Both ends *jiāngjiāng* (畕畕),"
and the later line said,
"Layered and scattered, the jade mountain collapses."
From then on, high-ranking princes and chancellors successively died,
and both imperial palaces saw emperors pass away.
Wénhuì Tàizǐ composed a seven-character poem,
and the later line always said,
"Sorrow and truth."
Later, there indeed was Emperor Hé (和帝) who abdicated.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
a children's rhyme among the barbarians said:
"Black water flows north,
red fire enters Qí (齊)."
Soon after, fires suddenly broke out in homes in the capital,
redder than ordinary fires,
but with little heat.
The rich and poor vied to use them to treat illnesses.
The method was to cauterize a peach board seven times with this fire;
all were cured within seven days.
An edict forbade it,
but it could not be stopped.
There was a person in the capital suffering from a goiter,
who was cured after several days of cauterizing with the fire.
His neighbor laughed, saying:
"The illness cured itself by chance,
how could fire accomplish it?"
This person then felt an itch in his chin,
and the next day his goiter returned to its original state.
Later, the Liáng (梁) dynasty rose with the virtue of fire.
When Wénhuì Tàizǐ built Dōngtián (東田),
people at the time reversed the saying,
"Later, there will surely be a mad child."
This indeed came to pass when the Crown Imperial Grandson lost his position.
Since the Qí (齊) and Sòng (宋) dynasties,
a folk saying went,
"Turbulence ascends to Jiànwǔ (建武)."
In the early Míng (明) era,
relatives of the imperial clan were purged and harmed,
and the capital was in peril and fear.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
a children's rhyme said:
"Vast and flowing for a thousand *lǐ*,
the *chì* (翣) flows to the east city gate.
〔一一〕A black horse, black leather trousers,
at the third watch they tell each other.
Lame foot cannot rise,
mistakenly kills the old woman's son."
"Flowing for a thousand *lǐ*" refers to Jiāng Shí (江祏).
Dōngchéng (東城) refers to Yáo Guāng (遙光).
Yáo Guāng (遙光) initiated his action at night,
and Yuán Lìshēng (垣歷生), wearing black leather trousers, rushed to join him.
"Lame foot" also refers to Yáo Guāng (遙光).
"Old woman's son" is an image of the character *xiào* (孝),
referring to Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣).
During the Yǒngyuán era,
a children's rhyme said:
"Though the wild boars grunt loudly,
the colts wander aimlessly.
Unknowing of the dragon and tiger,
they feast on the ruins south of the river.
Seven nines are sixty-three,
in the vast wilderness no one remains.
Crows gather at the relay station,
now you may rest at ease.
Just look after three eights,
and Jǐngyáng Lóu (景陽樓) will be destroyed."
Those with foresight explained:
"Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) belongs to the pig,
Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) belongs to the horse,"
which is incorrect.
The Dōnghūn Hóu (東昏侯) belongs to the pig,
the colts are unknown.
The King of Liáng (梁王) belongs to the dragon,
and Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (蕭穎冑) belongs to the tiger.
Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) attacked the capital,
died at the Guǎngmò Mén (廣莫門),
at the age of sixty-three.
"Crows gather at the relay station"
is what is called,
"Where do the crows gather?
On whose house?"
Three eights are twenty-four,
starting from the first year of Jiànruán,
to the second year of Zhōngxīng,
which is twenty-four years.
"Jǐngyáng Lóu (景陽樓) will be destroyed"
also means the collapse of a high platform.
It means that when the empire is about to be lost,
then there will be rest.
During the Qí (齊) and Sòng (宋) transition,
a folk saying went,
"Hé (和) rises,"
meaning a change arises with a gentle countenance.
Later, Emperor Hé (和帝) was enthroned.
When Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) besieged Táichéng (臺城),
a five-colored banner
flew in the clouds,
and after half a day it disappeared.
Everyone was amazed and bewildered,
〔一二〕and said to each other:
"The banner indicates
that things will soon be overturned."
Several days later, Huìjǐng (慧景) was defeated.
A saying goes:
"If the *qì* (氣) of speech is harmed, then the people will have much gossip,
thus there will be the affliction of gossip.
Gold is white,
thus there will be white calamities,
or if white appears, it is an ill omen."
In the second year of Shēngmíng of Sòng (宋),
a whirlwind arose in Nántáng Lǐ (南塘里), Jiànkāng Xiàn (建康縣),
blowing a bolt of silk into the clouds.
When the wind stopped,
it fell on the imperial road.
Jì Sēngzhēn (紀僧真) informed Tàizǔ (太祖) that the one who would receive the abdication of the Sòng (宋) dynasty
would be a commoner.
Water,
in the north,
stores all things in winter.
Its *qì* is extremely *yīn*,
symbolizing ancestral temple sacrifices.
When the spirits of the deceased wander off and do not return,
therefore temples are established to collect their scattered essence,
and images are made to collect their souls and spirits,
so that filial children may fulfill their rites.
〔一三〕When reverence reaches its utmost,
the spirits will accept the offerings.
This means that the *qì* of extreme *yīn* follows,
and then the water *qì* follows through ditches and channels and flows away,
causing no harm to the people.
If the ruler does not pray and sacrifice,
neglects the ancestral temples,
abolishes sacrifices,
and acts contrary to the seasons,
then misty waters will burst forth violently,
river waters will overflow inversely,
destroying cities and submerging villages,
drowning the populace.
Therefore it is said that "water does not flow downwards to moisten."
In the second year of Jiànwán,
the three commanderies of Wú, Wúxīng, and Yìxīng experienced great floods.
In the summer of the second year,
the two commanderies of Dānyáng and Wú experienced great floods.
In the fourth year,
there was a great flood.
In the summer of the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
Wúxīng and Yìxīng suffered damage to their crops due to floods and rain.
In the sixth year,
the two commanderies of Wúxīng and Yìxīng experienced great floods.
In the winter of the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the two commanderies of Wú and Jìnlíng suffered damage to their crops due to floods and rain.
In the seventh month of the first year of Yǒngyuán,
the tide entered Shítóu,
drowning and killing residents along the Huái River.
This corresponds to the main biography.
There was a sand pond inside the city of Jīngzhōu
that constantly leaked water.
When Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was the Grand Administrator,
the water no longer leaked.
But after Yǐngzhòu's death,
it dried up again.
The commentary says:
"When the *qì* of extreme *yīn* moves,
therefore there are fish calamities.
Fish calamities
are always a sign of punishment by persistent cold."
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng,
at Shípǔ in Yángguān County, sea fish rode the tide in,
and could not leave when the water receded.
They were over thirty *zhàng* long,
black and scaleless.
They were not yet dead,
and made sounds like oxen.
The local people called them "sea swallows" (*hǎi yàn*),
and took their flesh to eat.
In the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngyuán,
twelve large fish entered the Shàngyú River in Kuàijī.
The largest were nearly twenty *zhàng* long,
the smaller ones over ten *zhàng* long.
One entered Chēngpǔ in Shānyīn,
and another entered Yǒngxīng River.
They all baked on the riverbanks,
and the common people took them to eat.
The commentary says:
"When the omen of not listening is seen,
then evil arises from the ears.
Things respond to each other by their kind,
therefore it is said there are drum calamities."
Another interpretation says,
sound belongs to drum calamities.
On the *guǐmǎo* day of the eleventh month of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
there was a sound in the northeast sky at night,
lasting until the night of *wù*.
The commentary says:
"When the emperor is not extreme,
this is called 'not established'.
The fault lies in obscurity, chaos, and loss of hearing,
therefore the calamity is obscurity.
The fault of a worried mind is also mist.
Heaven
sets the beginning for all things,
the king
sets the beginning for all affairs.
Losing the mean harms the *qì* of Heaven;
things respond to each other by their kind.
Heaven rotates below and moves above;
clouds rise from mountains and spread across the sky.
When the *qì* of Heaven moves, its omen responds,
therefore the punishment is persistent *yīn*.
If the king loses the mean,
and his ministers become powerful,
obscuring the lord's brightness,
then clouds and *yīn* will also be numerous and obscure the light of Heaven.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the tenth month of the fourth year of Jiànwán,
after sunset, the earth mist was abundant like fire smoke.
On the *jǐhài* day of the eleventh month of the second year of Yǒngmíng,
earth mist from all four directions entered people's eyes and noses,
stopping on the *xīnchǒu* day.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day of the eleventh month of the second year,
after sunrise and after sunset,
earth mist from all four directions was abundant like fire smoke.
On the *gēngxū* day of the eleventh month of the sixth year,
at night, earth mist filled the sky,
dark, dense, and thick.
It slightly cleared at the *wèi* hour on the sixth day,
but at night it remained thick and dense,
〔一四〕abundant like fire smoke,
and acridly entered people's eyes and noses.
On the *rénshēn* day of the tenth month of the eighth year,
at night, earth mist filled the sky,
dense and abundant like fire smoke.
Its *qì* entered people's eyes and noses,
clearing away at the *chén* hour on the ninth day.
On the *bǐngchén* day of the tenth month of the ninth year,
day and night were constantly dim with mist abundant like fire smoke.
Its *qì* acridly entered people's eyes and noses,
and the sun's color was reddish-yellow.
It cleared away at night on the fourth day.
On the *xīnyǒu* day of the first month of the tenth year,
at the beginning of the *yǒu* hour, earth mist from all four directions was abundant like fire smoke.
Its *qì* acridly entered people's eyes and noses.
The commentary says:
"The *Yì* says, 'Qián is the horse.'
Going against the *qì* of Heaven,
many horses die,
therefore it is called 'horse calamity'."
Another interpretation says,
horses
are symbols of war.
There will be affairs of invasion and warfare,
therefore horses become monstrous.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
〔一五〕Wáng Yàn went out to Cǎoshì.
His horse was startled and ran away.
He returned by beating the ground and following his carriage.
Over ten days later,
Yàn was executed.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
there was a dappled horse on the south bank
that chased a woman on the road.
The woman, in distress,
ran into a house and hid under a bed to avoid it.
The horse would not give up,
pushed away the bed, and ate all the flesh between the woman's thighs and legs.
The authorities reported this,
and an imperial order was issued to kill this horse.
After this, there were frequent bandit incursions.
The *Jīngfáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
"If a person gives birth to two or more children joined below the waist,
the people will plot against their lord.
If there are three or more hands,
ministers will plot against their lord.
If there are two or more mouths,
the state will be alarmed by soldiers.
If there are three or more ears,
this is called 'much listening,'
and state affairs will be unstable.
If there are two or more noses,
the ruler will be ill for a long time.
If there are three feet and three or more arms,
there will be warfare under Heaven."
There are many such categories,
generally interpreted by omens.
In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
a woman from Wú Xiū's family in Dōngqiān, Wúxīng, gave birth to twins
joined below the waist and above the navel.
The *Jīngfáng Yì Zhuàn* says:
"When wild beasts enter a city,
that city will be greatly emptied."
It also says:
"If wild beasts causelessly enter the gates of the city and court or the palace,
the city will be rebellious and empty."
During the Yǒngmíng era,
Zǐhǎn, Prince of Nánhǎi, was the Inspector of Nányùnzhōu.
A deer entered Guǎnglín city
and drowned itself in a well.
Also, an elephant arrived at Guǎnglín.
After this, the Inspector Ānlù Zǐjìng was killed at his post.
In the spring of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
when the suburban *yuánqiū* sacrifice was to be performed,
〔一六〕and the arrangements had been completed,
a tiger seized and injured a person at night.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
a deer entered the ancestral temple of Jǐng Huáng.
These all portended the emperor's collapse and the transfer of the throne.
All instances for which there is no interpretation
are considered not to correspond to the main biography.
A eulogy says: Wood is marvelous and monstrous;
Fire is the consort of water.
Earth truly carries all things;
Metal creates bright power.
Forms and sounds have distinct traces;
Shadows and echoes return to the same origin.
All derive from symbolic correspondences;
None are without analogical inference.
Collation Notes
Biographies, First: Empresses
The ranks and titles of the Six Palaces,
since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
have been inherited and augmented,
differing from one era to another.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
the officials concerned proposed establishing Guìpín, Fūrén, and Guìrén as the Sān Fūrén;
Xiūhuá, Xiūyí, Xiūróng, Shúfēi, Shúyuán, Shúyí, Jiéyú, Rónghuá, and Chōnghuá as the Jiǔpín;
Měirén, Zhōngcáirén, and Cáirén as scattered ranks.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
the officials concerned proposed that Guìfēi and Shúfēi both be granted a gold seal and purple ribbon,
and wear Yútián jade.
Shúfēi was previously ranked alongside the Jiǔjí,
with 'Shú' being a term for modesty and reverence,
and 'Fēi' being a name for a secondary empress.
She was advanced to the same rank as Guìfēi,
to be compared with the Sān Sī.
The title of Fūrén
was not distinguished from that of a vassal state.
Shúyuán was demoted to be compared with the Jiǔ Qīng.
In the seventh year,
Zháoróng was re-established,
her rank below the Jiǔpín.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
three internal posts were established in the Crown Prince's palace:
Liángdì was comparable to an open-territory Marquis;
Bǎolín was comparable to a fifth-rank Marquis;
Cáirén was comparable to a Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Empress Xuānhào Chén, personal name Dàozhǐ,
was a native of Dōngyáng, Línhuái.
She was a descendant of Chén Jiǎo, the Wèi Sītú.
Her father, Zhàozhī,
was a Jùn Xiàolián.
When the empress was young, her family was poor,
and she diligently wove and worked.
Her family pitied her toil
and sometimes stopped her,
but the empress never changed.
She married Emperor Xuān.
She was the foster mother of King Yuán Dàodù of Héngyáng and King Zhēn Dàoshēng of Shǐ'ān.
She was the birth mother of Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
When Tàizǔ was two years old,
his wet nurse lacked milk.
The empress dreamed someone gave her two bowls of sesame porridge.
Upon waking, her milk flowed abundantly,
and she found it extraordinary and was pleased.
When Emperor Xuān was serving abroad,
the empress often stayed home, managing affairs and teaching her children and grandchildren.
A physiognomist told the empress:
"Madam, you have noble sons, but I do not see them."
The empress sighed and said:
"Which of my three sons will fulfill this?"
She called Tàizǔ by his childhood name and said:
"It must be you."
After Emperor Xuān's death,
the empress personally managed affairs diligently.
If maids or servants made mistakes,
she forgave them without inquiry.
Although Tàizǔ was an official,
his family was originally poor.
When he was the magistrate of Jiànkāng,
Gāozōng and others still lacked silk floss in winter,
yet the provisions for her meals were very generous.
The empress often removed extra meat,
saying:
"For me, this is more than enough."
She died in the county residence
at the age of seventy-three.
In the third year of Shēngmíng,
she was posthumously granted the title of Tàifūrén of Jìnglíng Gōngguó,
with a phoenix seal,
a painted green ribbon,
and sacrifices with a grand offering.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
she was posthumously honored as Empress Xiào.
Her maternal grandfather, Zhàozhī, was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous epithet Jìng Hóu.
The empress's mother, Lady Hú, was honored as Jìngjūn of Yǒngchāng County.
Empress Gāozhāo Liú, personal name Zhìróng,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
Her grandfather, Xuánzhī,
and father, Shòuzhī,
were both Yuánwàiláng.
The empress's mother, Lady Huán, dreamed of swallowing a jade ornament and giving birth to the empress.
At that time, a purple light filled the room.
She told Shòuzhī,
who said:
"It's a pity it's not a boy."
Lady Huán replied:
"Even a girl
is enough to prosper the family."
Whenever the empress slept,
her family often saw cloud-like vapor above her.
At over ten years old,
she married Tàizǔ.
She was strict, upright, and observant of proper etiquette,
and the household was orderly.
She died in the first year of Tàiyù of Sòng,
at the age of fifty.
She was buried beside Emperor Xuān's tomb,
which is now Tà'ān Líng.
When Wáng Qīng, a student, and the tomb workers first struck the ground with a shovel,
a white rabbit leaped up.
They searched for it but could not find it.
When the tomb was completed,
the rabbit returned to nest upon it.
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
she was granted the title of Fūrén of Jìnglíng Gōngguó.
In the third year,
she was granted the title of Qí Guófēi,
with a seal and ribbon like a Tàifēi.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
she was honored with the posthumous epithet Empress Zhāo.
In the third year,
the empress's father was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and her mother, Lady Huán, was honored as Yú Dū Xiāngjūn;
Shòuzhī's son Xìngdào was Sītú Shǔ,
Wénwèi was Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
Yìhuī was Guānglù Dàfū,
and Yìlún was Tōngzhíláng.
Empress Wǔmù Péi, personal name Huìzhāo,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
Her grandfather, Pǔzhī,
was a Gěishìzhōng.
Her father, Jīzhī,
was a Zuǒjūn Cānjūn.
When the empress was young, she and Lady Yǔ, the consort of the Prince of Yùzhāng, were sisters-in-law.
Lady Yǔ was diligent in women's work
and served Tàizǔ and Empress Zhāo with respectful tireless dedication.
The empress could not match her,
and therefore was not highly regarded by her parents-in-law.
Shìzǔ's affection for her was also lukewarm.
She had a strong and strict nature.
When Lady Yuán, the consort of Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng, made a mistake while still a commoner,
the empress punished her with instruction.
In the third year of Shēngmíng,
she became the Consort of the Crown Prince of Qí.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
she became the Imperial Crown Princess.
In the third year,
the empress passed away.
She was posthumously named Mùfēi
and buried in Xiū'ān Líng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Empress.
Jīzhī was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and the empress's mother, Lady Tán, was honored as Yuánjūn of Guǎngchāng Xiāng, Yúháng.
The Xǐanyáng and Zhāoyáng
palaces
were where empress dowagers and empresses resided.
During the Yǒngmíng period, there were no empress dowagers or empresses.
Guìpín Yáng resided in the west of Zhāoyáng Palace;
Guìfēi Fàn resided in the east of Zhāoyáng Palace;
the favored concubine Zhāohuá Xún resided in Fènghuá Bǎidiàn.
In the south pavilion of Shòuchāng Huàdiàn, where the emperor resided within the palace,
two ensembles of white egret drum and wind instruments were placed;
at the east and west ends of Gān'guāngdiàn,
bells and chimes were placed in two wings: these were all places for banquets and entertainment.
The emperor frequently visited various imperial gardens and parks,
carrying palace women in follow-up carriages.
The interior of the palace was deeply secluded,
and the sound of the drum and water clock from Duānmén could not be heard.
A bell was placed atop Jǐngyánglóu.
When the palace women heard the bell,
they would rise early to adorn themselves.
To this day, this bell only sounds for the fifth and third watches.
The imperial carriage frequently visited Lángyá City,
and palace women often followed.
They would set out early and reach Húběi Dài
just as the roosters began to crow.
Hán Lìnyīng of Wújùn
was a woman of literary talent.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
she presented a 'Fù on Mid-Dynasty Revival,'
was rewarded, and entered the palace.
During the reign of Emperor Míng [of Sòng],
she was employed as a palace official.
Shìzǔ appointed her as a Bóshì
to teach calligraphy to the Six Palaces.
Due to her advanced age and extensive knowledge,
she was called
"Hán Gōng."
Empress Wén'ān Wáng, personal name Bǎomíng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
Her grandfather, Sháozhī,
was the Grand Administrator of Wúxìng.
Her father, Yèzhī,
was the Tàizǎi Jìjiǔ.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Tàizǔ (太祖) married a consort for Wénhuì Tàizǐ (文惠太子).
When bandits from Guìyáng (桂陽) arrived,
Tàizǔ (太祖) was at Xīntíng (新亭).
Rumors spread that he had already perished,
and his residence was again plundered by people.
Wénhuì Tàizǐ (文惠太子) and Jìnglín Wángzǐliáng (竟陵王子良) escorted Mù Hòu (穆后) and Yǔ Fēi (庾妃), and the consort herself, to the home of her elder brother Bǐng (昺).
They only emerged after the situation had stabilized.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元) (479 CE),
she became the Consort of Nánjùn Wáng (南郡王).
In the fourth year (482 CE),
she became the Crown Prince Consort,
but was not favored.
The Crown Prince made new and beautiful clothes and ornaments for palace women,
while the consort's bed curtains and furnishings were old and worn,
and her tweezers numbered over ten.
〔一０〕In the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (493 CE),
she became the Crown Grandson's Grand Consort.
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
she was honored as Empress Dowager,
and her residence was called Xuāndé Gōng (宣德宮).
Her father was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫),
and her mother, Lady Huán (桓氏), was granted the title of Fēng'ān Xiànjūn (豐安縣君).
In the twelfth month of that year,
she attended the Imperial Ancestral Temple with full imperial equipage.
When Gāozōng (高宗) ascended the throne,
she moved out to reside in the former residence of Póyáng Wáng (鄱陽王),
which was named Xuāndé Gōng (宣德宮).
In the third year of Yǒngyuán (永元) (501 CE),
Liáng Wáng (梁王) pacified the capital,
and welcomed the empress into the palace to assume regency
until the abdication.
In the eleventh year of Tiānjiān (天監) (512 CE),
she passed away
at the age of fifty-eight.
She was buried in Chóng'ān Líng (崇安陵).
Her posthumous title was Ān Hòu (安后).
Her elder brother Huǎng (晃) was the Grand Administrator of Yìxīng (義興).
Yùlín Wáng (鬱林王)'s consort, Lady Hé (何妃), was named Jìngyīng (婧英).
She was a native of Lújiāng (廬江),
and the daughter of the Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (撫軍將軍), Jí (戢).
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (484 CE),
she was taken as the Consort of Nánjùn Wáng (南郡王).
In the eleventh year (493 CE),
she became the Crown Grandson's Consort.
When Yùlín Wáng (鬱林王) ascended the throne,
she became empress.
Her legal mother, Lady Liú (劉氏), was made Gāochāng Xiàn Dūxiāngjūn (高昌縣都鄉君),
and her birth mother, Lady Sòng (宋氏),
was made Yúháng Guǎngchāng Xiāngjūn (餘杭廣昌鄉君).
As she was about to be officially installed,
a mirror on her bed inexplicably fell to the ground.
In that winter,
she visited the Imperial Ancestral Temple on the same day as the Empress Dowager.
The empress had a lewd and disorderly nature;
when she was a consort,
she already had illicit relations with outsiders.
In the inner palace,
she again had an affair with Yáng Mínzhī (楊珉之), one of the emperor's attendants,
and slept with him as if they were husband and wife.
Mínzhī (珉之) also had an intimate relationship with the emperor,
so the emperor indulged her.
She welcomed her relatives into the palace,
bestowing hundreds of thousands in rewards upon each person.
The family members of the empress were housed in Shìzǔ (世祖)'s Yàolíng Diàn (耀靈殿).
When the emperor was deposed,
the empress was demoted to a royal consort.
Hǎilíng Wáng (海陵王)'s consort, Lady Wáng (王妃), was named Sháomíng (韶明).
She was a native of Lángyá Línyí (琅邪臨沂),
and the daughter of Tàicháng (太常) Cí (慈).
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (490 CE),
she was taken as the Lady of Línrǔ Gōng (臨汝公).
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
she became the Consort of Xīn'ān Wáng (新安王).
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興) (494 CE),
she became empress.
In that same year,
she was demoted to Hǎilíng Wángfēi (海陵王妃).
Míngjìng Liú Huánghòu (明敬劉皇后), whose taboo name was Huìduān (惠端),
was a native of Péngchéng (彭城),
and the granddaughter of Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Dàohóng (道弘).
Tàizǔ (太祖) took her as consort for Gāozōng (高宗).
In the third year of Jiànyuán (建元) (481 CE),
she was appointed Lady of Xīchāng Hóu (西昌侯).
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (489 CE),
she died
and was buried at Zhāng Shān (張山) in Jiāngchéng Xiàn (江乘縣).
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興) (494 CE),
she was posthumously granted the title of Xuānchéng Wángfēi (宣城王妃).
When Gāozōng (高宗) ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Jìng Huánghòu (敬皇后).
Her father, Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎) Jǐngyóu (景猷), was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫),
and her mother, Lady Wáng (王氏), Píngyáng Xiāngjūn (平陽鄉君).
In the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰) (498 CE),
Gāozōng (高宗) died,
and she was reburied,
interred next to Xīng'ān Líng (興安陵).
Dōnghūn Chǔ Huánghòu (東昏褚皇后), whose name was Lìngqú (令璩),
was a native of Hénán Yángzhái (河南陽翟),
and the daughter of Tàicháng (太常) Chéng (澄).
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武) (495 CE),
she was taken as the Crown Prince Consort.
The following year,
she visited the temple of Jìng Hòu (敬后).
When Dōnghūn (東昏) ascended the throne,
she became empress.
The emperor favored Consort Pān (潘妃),
and the empress was not treated kindly.
Huang Shúyí (黃淑儀) gave birth to Crown Prince Sòng (誦).
When Dōnghūn (東昏) was deposed,
both were reduced to commoners.
〔一一〕
Hé Dì Wáng Huánghòu (和帝王皇后), whose name was Shùnhuá (蕣華),
was a native of Lángyá Línyí (琅邪臨沂),
and the granddaughter of Tàiwèi (太尉) Jiǎn (儉).
She was initially the Consort of Suí Wáng (隨王).
In the first year of Zhōngxīng (中興) (501 CE),
she became empress.
When the emperor abdicated,
the empress was demoted to a consort.
The historian says: The virtues of empresses and consorts
are recorded in folk songs.
Their righteousness begins in the inner chambers
and spreads transformative influence throughout the world.
Presenting silkworm cocoons and seeds,
they were invariably engaged in farming and weaving.
Wearing their pendants and rising at dawn,
they shared duties with their children.
They could illuminate the conduct of the inner court
and be fitting partners for dukes and marquises.
Empresses Xiào (孝) and Zhāo (昭)
both had virtuous and enlightened teachings,
but were unable to govern all nations as mothers.
When the auspicious mandate was flourishing,
the Phoenix Court remained vacant.
There were women who,
in vain, admired the rise of Zhōu (周),
and auspicious omens and wonders,
merely gathered renowned names.
If only the inner palace could have shared such prosperity,
〔一二〕and its feminine teachings spread far and wide,
then the refined styles of Mǎ (馬) and Dèng (鄧)
would have once again existed here.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) first established his reign,
the palace restrictions were modest;
he demolished the Zǐjí (紫極) palace of Sòng Míng (宋明),
and reformed the excessive luxury of previous generations.
Clothes were not embroidered,
colors had no red hues.
The imperial alleys were poor and empty,
like plain dwellings.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) succeeded to the throne,
the times were peaceful;
Shòuchāng (壽昌) was built early,
Fènghuá (鳳華) was constructed later.
Fragrant cypress and ornamented tamarisks,
painted beams and embroidered pillars,
carved gold and inlaid jewels,
were extensively used in the private quarters.
〔一三〕The zither of Zhào (趙) and the melodies of Wú (吳)
were played during leisure,
and annual expenses were generously bestowed,
sufficient to fill up everything.
These matters came from private savings,
without harming the national treasury.
Gāozōng (高宗) relied on cunning to feign sincerity,
〔一四〕outwardly practicing frugality and simplicity,
but inwardly indulging in palace affairs,
〔一五〕without ever changing.
Dōnghūn (東昏) lost the Way,
and the lavish trend greatly spread,
consuming the wealth of the realm
to provide for superficial decorations.
Wise women ruined cities,
mirroring the examples of Yīn (殷) and Xià (夏).
Alas!
This serves as a warning for future generations.
〔一六〕
A eulogy says: Xuānwǔ (宣武) followed the rules,
possessing foresight.
Gāozhāo (高昭) gave birth to a martial son,
a motherly example for generations.
Péi Mù (裴穆) was stored in the inner court,
her position also fell.
Míngjìng (明敬) was in the archives,
matched in the imperial lineage.
The autumn palace was also hasty,
the splendor of Xuān (軒) diminished before.
Wén'ān (文安) was the deposed sovereign,
already free from a hundred sorrows.
In Zhōngxīng (中興), she held regency,
abdicating with grand principles.

Biography Two: Wénhuì Tàizǐ (文惠太子)
Wénhuì Tàizǐ Chángmào, courtesy name Yúnqiáo,
was Shìzǔ's eldest son.
Shìzǔ was not yet twenty when the crown prince was born,
and he was beloved by Tàizǔ.
He had a full and handsome appearance,
and his pet name was Báizé.
Towards the end of Sòng Yuánhuī era,
he followed Shìzǔ to Yǐng.
When Shìzǔ returned to guard Pénchéng against Shěn Yōuzhī,
he made the crown prince entertain generals and commanders,
personally attending to military affairs.
He was appointed Mìshū Láng,
but did not take office.
He was granted the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to be the Fǔjūn Zhǔbù for Jìnxī Wáng.
When the affairs settled,
Shìzǔ sent the crown prince back to the capital.
Tàizǔ was then establishing his hegemonic enterprise,
with his mind set on an heir apparent.
He said to the crown prince:
"When you return,
my affairs will be settled."
He was housed in the eastern study of the residence,
and allowed to receive civil and military guests.
He instructed Xún Bóyù:
"On the days I am out,
all the troops in the city shall be under Chángmào's command.
Even [if I am not out,
the internal and external guards, as well as the armed forces at all gates,
shall all be inspected by Chángmào] from time to time."
He was promoted to Mìshū Chéng,
but as it shared a taboo character with Xuāndì's name,
he did not take the position,
and was instead appointed Zhōngshū Láng,
then promoted to Huángmén Shìláng,
but he had not yet taken office.
In Shēngmíng third year,
when Tàizǔ was about to accept the abdication,
Shìzǔ had already returned to the capital.
As Xiāngyáng was a vital military stronghold,
he did not wish to entrust it to other clansmen.
So he sent out the crown prince as Chíjié, Dūdū Yōng Liáng Èrzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu zhī Suíjùn Jūnjì, Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng, Níngmán Xiàowèi, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In Jiànyuán first year,
he was enfeoffed as Nánjùn Wáng,
with a fief of two thousand households.
There had been no imperial grandson of the principal consort enfeoffed as a prince in Jiāngzuǒ before this,
this was the first time.
He was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Earlier,
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Fàn Bǎinián had enticed the Jinshòu fugitives Lǐ Wūnú to surrender and subdue the Dī bandits Yáng Chéng and Sū Dàochì, etc.,
gaining considerable prestige.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion broke out,
Bǎinián sent his general Yīn Guǎngzōng to lead troops out of Wèixīng to support the capital,
while observing the situation.
When the rebellion was suppressed,
the court sent Wáng Xuánmiǎo to replace him.
Wūnú advised Bǎinián to hold Hánzhōng and refuse the appointment,
but Bǎinián was indecisive.
Xuánmiǎo had already arrived,
and Bǎinián hesitated in Wèixīng, unwilling to descend.
The crown prince feared he might cause trouble,
so he sent someone to persuade Bǎinián,
promising to recommend him as Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
Bǎinián then advanced to Xiāngyáng,
and was consequently arrested and executed.
Bǎinián was
from Zǐtóng,
but had moved to Huáyáng.
His family had been local gentry for generations,
well-known in the region.
In the Tàishǐ era of Sòng,
the Dī bandits cut off the Jìnshòu road.
Bǎinián, as Cāngbù Láng with temporary insignia, led several hundred men to comfort and clear the road,
reporting back via the Yìzhōu road.
He was appointed Jìnshòu Tàishǒu.
He subdued the Dī bandits, and thus gained Liángzhōu.
Bǎinián was strong and upright,
and skilled in speaking of affairs.
His retorts were known to Sòng Míngdì.
After his execution,
Bāxī Tàishǒu Liǔ Hóng wrote to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ's reply read:
"Bǎinián might not have acted that way,
I regret it deeply!"
At that time, there were grave robbers in Xiāngyáng
who dug up what was rumored to be the tomb of the King of Chǔ,
obtaining many treasures: jade clogs, jade screens, bamboo slips with writing, and blue silk bindings.
The slips were several fen wide
and two chi long,
with their outer knots like new.
The robbers used them to light their way.
Later, some people obtained more than ten slips
and showed them to Fǔjūn Wáng Sēngqián.
Sēngqián said they were蝌蚪書 Kēdǒu Shū (tadpole script) of the Kǎogōng Jì,
the missing text from Zhōuguān.
At that time, the province sent officials to investigate,
and some relics were recovered,
leading to discussions of similarities and differences.
It happened that the northern barbarians invaded south,
and the Emperor was concerned about moving through Fán and Miǎn.
In the second year,
he was recalled as Shìzhōng, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
established a residence,
and was stationed at Shítou.
When Mù Fēi passed away,
on the day of assuming mourning attire,
the imperial carriage came to attend the funeral.
The court debated whether the crown prince should go out to welcome it.
Zuǒ Púyè Wáng Jiǎn said:
"Consulting the Lǐjì Fúwèn (Book of Rites, Questions on Mourning Attire), it states,
'The lord of the state takes charge of the mourning for his wife, the crown prince, and the principal daughter-in-law.'
This means the ruler of the state acts as the chief mourner for these three persons.
Now the imperial carriage is arriving,
coming as the chief mourner itself.
Although it is a visit for comfort,
the meaning is not one of condolence.
Nánjùn and below should not go out to welcome it.
However, given the supreme dignity of the arrival,
rites can be adapted.
Temporarily removing the staff and mourning band,
and standing outside the gate,
is sufficient to show respect,
without needing to stop crying.
As the imperial crown prince is the master of his own palace,
he should, when the imperial carriage visits his palace,
receive it as usual.
Since it is the day of assuming mourning attire,
auspicious and inauspicious events should not interfere with each other.
It is appropriate to perform the rites in mourning cap.
Bowing and stopping crying should
follow established precedent.
As the esteemed carriage does not arrive for condolence,
the reception should be according to normal practice.
Considering both sentiment and ritual,
this seems appropriate."
He was relieved of the position of Shìzhōng.
The Emperor, seeing that the crown prince was grief-stricken and ill,
deemed it unsuitable for him to reside at Shítoushān Fortress,
and moved his garrison to Xīzhōu.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Nánxú Yùn Èrzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne, he became the Imperial Crown Prince.
Initially,
Tàizǔ was fond of the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū.
The Crown Prince, following his wishes, recited and chanted it,
making it a common topic of conversation.
Once he was officially established in the Eastern Palace,
he excelled at establishing a good reputation,
received literati with courtesy,
and maintained martial men.
All of them were close to him,
stationed throughout the ministries and palace.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 CE),
he lectured on the Xiàojīng in Chóngzhèngdiàn.
Shàofù Wáng Jiǎn assigned Tàizǐpú Zhōu Yǒng to compose an interpretive commentary by picking out key phrases.
In the winter of the fifth year (487 CE),
the Crown Prince visited the National Academy,
personally presiding over the examination of the students.
From his seat, he asked Shàofù Wáng Jiǎn:
“The Qūlǐ says, ‘there is nothing that should not be reverent.’
Considering that inferiors serving superiors
can indeed exhaust reverence,
but superiors receiving inferiors
is characterized by benevolence, not reverence.
Now, to collectively use the term ‘reverence’
will it not lead to obscurity?”
Wáng Jiǎn replied:
“Zhèng Xuán said, ‘Reverence is primary in rites,’
so it should naturally apply equally to both the esteemed and the humble.”
The Crown Prince said:
“If it is as you interpret,
then loyalty and benevolence could be called by one name,
and filiality and compassion would not need separate designations.”
Wáng Jiǎn said:
“The titles for the esteemed and the humble
cannot all be the same,
but the names for love and reverence
sometimes come together.
The distinction between loyalty and benevolence
is indeed based on the sage’s intent,
and the mutual mention of filiality and compassion
has some basis.
The Lǐ [jì] says, ‘One who does not overcome grief for mourning is comparable to one who is not compassionate or filial.’
This is its meaning.”
The Crown Prince said:
“To serve a ruler with reverence,
and to serve parents with love;
to combine these two paths
is only at one extreme.
Now, to shift reverence to receiving inferiors,
how can it still conform to the meaning of being ‘at three’?”
Wáng Jiǎn replied:
“To serve a ruler with reverence
must be to the utmost,
while extending reverence to inferiors
simply means not being disrespectful.”
The Crown Prince said:
“Although the name ‘reverence’ is the same,
the depth and shallowness are different,
yet the text makes no distinction,
which further increases my doubt.”
Wáng Jiǎn said:
“An elaborate text cannot provide for every detail;
the distinction between depth and shallowness is already evident in summary statements.
The Zhuàn says, ‘Do not forget respect and reverence,
for he is the master of the people.’
The Shū [jīng] says, ‘In serving ancestors, think of filiality;
in receiving inferiors, think of respect.’
These are explicit classical texts
that mutually illuminate each other.”
The Crown Prince asked Jīnzǐguānglù Dàfū Zhāng Xù.
Zhāng Xù replied:
“Your humble servant believes that respect and reverence are the foundation of establishing oneself,
which is why they are applicable to both the esteemed and the humble.”
The Crown Prince said:
“Although reverence is the foundation of establishing oneself,
it is certainly not a term for receiving inferiors.
The Shàngshū says, ‘Be benevolent and cherish the multitude,’
why does it not say ‘be respectful and reverent to the multitude’?”
Zhāng Xù replied:
“If we distinguish them now,
there is indeed a clear difference between respect and benevolence;
but when generally introducing the beginning of a record,
it is why they share this designation.”
Jìnglǐng Wáng Zǐliáng said:
“Rites are simply about reverence.
From superiors to inferiors,
your humble servant sees no objection.”
The Crown Prince said:
“I did not originally mean there was an objection;
I merely wish for words to match facts,
and for there to be a distinction between important and minor points.”
Línchuān Wáng Yìng said:
“Firstly stating ‘must be reverent’
is to clarify the general principle;
the specific matters of the esteemed and the humble
are fully listed in later chapters.
Thus, it should not be hindered by being a general summary.”
The Crown Prince also asked the students about this meaning,
and Xiè Jǐqīng and eleven others
all responded in writing.
The Crown Prince asked Wáng Jiǎn:
“The Qián hexagram of the Zhōu Yì originally represents the position of Heaven,
but the Shuō Guà says, ‘The Di comes forth from Zhèn.’
Zhèn is fundamentally not Heaven,
how can their meanings be primary to each other?”
Wáng Jiǎn replied:
“Qián is strong, Zhèn is movement.
Heaven takes movement as its virtue,
therefore it says, ‘The Dì comes forth from Zhèn.’”
The Crown Prince said:
“Heaven takes movement as its virtue,
and the ruler himself embodies Heaven and occupies the position.
If Zhèn (thunder) is an emblem,
how can it be what Heaven embodies and comes forth from?”
Wáng Jiǎn replied:
“Among those who preside over the sacrificial vessels, none is better than the eldest son,
hence it is received with Zhèn.
All things emerge from Zhèn,
hence the Dì is also associated with it.”
Wáng Jiǎn also consulted the Crown Prince, saying:
“The Xiàojīng says, ‘Zhòngní was at leisure,
Zēngzǐ was attending.’
The principle of filiality is profound and far-reaching;
only great worthies can fully comprehend its essence.
Why was it not imparted to Yán Zǐ,
but entrusted to Zēng Shēng?”
The Crown Prince replied:
“Although Zēng Shēng’s virtue was inferior to that of the two (Yán Huí and Mǐn Zǐqiān),
he exhausted the rites of nourishing his parents with a pleasant countenance.
He was still close to ordinary people,
making him approachable without obstruction.
The meaning of widely propagating these teachings
lies in this.”
Wáng Jiǎn said:
“Being approachable without obstruction,
while making propagation easier,
the further one is from the sage,
the lighter the matter becomes.
Since it says, ‘It is man that can make the Way great,’
I fear that if the man is light, the Way will fall into disuse.”
The Crown Prince said:
“Since the principle exists,
it cannot be abandoned because of the person.
Moreover, with the talent of a moderately worthy person
propagating the teachings of the supreme sage,
how could there be any suspicion of obstruction?”
Línchuān Wáng Yìng consulted, saying:
“Filiality as the root of virtue
is something I have always doubted.
Virtue extends to all good deeds,
while filiality comes from natural disposition,
a natural principle.
How can it be due to accumulated practice?”
The Crown Prince said:
“It is because it is not achieved through accumulated practice
that it can be the root of virtue.”
Yìng replied:
“If it is achieved spontaneously,
without waiting for luminous virtue,
and great filiality brings glory to parents,
all virtues shine brightly.
Considering this,
how can it be considered the root?”
The Crown Prince said:
“Filiality has its depths and shallows;
virtue has its small and great aspects.
It is the root according to its scope,
what is there to doubt?”
That the Crown Prince lectured at the academy for many years
was unprecedented in previous generations.
The following year,
the Emperor was about to interrogate prisoners in Dānyáng and the prisons within two hundred *lǐ* to the north and south.
He issued an edict saying:
“The gravity of lawsuits and imprisonments
is paramount to governance and transformation.
The Crown Prince, having reached the age for his appointment as assistant,
should examine these matters in due course.
This interrogation is entrusted to him for his personal decision.”
So the Crown Prince, in Xuánpǔ Yuán Xuānyóutáng,
recorded the prisoners from the three bureaus,
and granted pardons and remissions with varying degrees.
In his later years, the Emperor enjoyed excursions and feasts,
so administrative matters of the Shàngshū Cáo were also partially sent to the Crown Prince for review.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) and Xiāo Zǐliáng (竟陵王子良) of Jìnglín Commandery both favored Buddhism.
He established the Liùjí Guǎn (六疾館) to care for the poor.
His demeanor was very gentle,
but his nature was quite extravagant and beautiful.
The halls and palaces within his residence
were all exquisitely carved and decorated,
surpassing those of the main palace.
He expanded the Xuánpǔ Yuán (玄圃園) garden,
making it as wide as the northern moat of Tái Chéng (臺城).
Within it, there were numerous towers, pavilions, and pagodas,
many of which gathered exotic stones,
exquisitely mimicking mountains and waters.
Fearing that the main palace would be able to see them,
〔一０〕 he arranged tall bamboos alongside the gate,
and erected high screens within.
〔一一〕 He constructed several hundred bays of movable walls,
〔一二〕 employing various clever mechanisms.
When concealment was needed,
they could be erected in a moment.
If they needed to be dismantled [撤] (sā),
〔一三〕 they could be moved instantly.
He was skilled at making rare and precious objects.
He wove peacock feathers into a fur robe,
whose golden and verdant luster
surpassed that of pheasant feathers.
〔一四〕 Remembering that Jìn Míngdì (晉明帝) had established the Xī Chí (西池) when he was Crown Prince,
he petitioned Shìzǔ (世祖) to follow that precedent,
requesting the Dōng Tián (東田) to build a small park.
The Emperor granted it.
During the Yǒngmíng (永明) era,
the military strength of the two palaces was entirely substantial.
The Crown Prince ordered his palace generals and officials to take turns in the construction.
The grandeur of the palace walls, gardens, and alleys,
and the splendor of their design,
drew observers from across the capital.
Although the Emperor's nature was strict,
he had many informants,
but no one dared to report what the Crown Prince was doing.
Later, when the Emperor visited Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) [Xiāo] Yí's (嶷) residence,
he returned via the Crown Prince's Dōng Tián (東田).
Seeing its vast expanse and remote beauty,
and its magnificence stretching as far as the eye could see,
he became furious.
He arrested the chief construction overseer.
The Crown Prince, fearing punishment,
hid them all.
Because of this, he was reprimanded.
The Crown Prince had long been sickly,
and his physique was also excessively robust.
He usually stayed within the palace
and rarely ventured out for excursions.
He indulged in playing with ceremonial regalia,
often overstepping his bounds.
Although he was but a stone's throw from the imperial compound,
the Emperor never knew.
In the tenth year,
Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) [Xiāo] Yí (嶷) passed away.
The Crown Prince saw that the Emperor's fraternal affection was deep,
so he composed a stele inscription and presented it,
but it was not yet carved.
In the first month of spring in the eleventh year,
the Crown Prince fell ill.
The Emperor personally visited him,
showing a worried expression.
As his illness worsened,
he submitted a memorial which read:
"Your subject, though of the highest lineage,
has but meager virtue.
In establishing the Dao and fostering good customs,
I have been utterly deficient.
From dawn to dusk, I have been anxious,
as if on the brink of an abyss.
In preserving my health, I have erred and fallen ill.
My condition is critical,
and I await my final departure.
My body is difficult to preserve long,
and I shall soon cease to attend to your meals.
I look up with longing at your benevolent face,
and my heart is filled with emotion and grief.
I secretly consider that life and death are destined,
and there is no reason to mourn excessively.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will put aside endless sorrow,
and lessen your past grief,
protect your sacred person,
and share seven hundred years of prosperity.
Even if your subject perishes in the nine springs,
I shall have no regrets."
He was thirty-six years old at the time.
〔一五〕 The Crown Prince had just reached maturity
and had long resided in the Eastern Palace,
participating in governance.
All internal and external officials
believed he would succeed to the throne any day.
When he passed away,
the court and populace were astonished and saddened.
The Emperor went to the Eastern Palace,
wept with profound grief,
and decreed that he be interred in a ceremonial robe (gǔnmiǎn zhī fú).
He was given the posthumous title Wénhuì (文惠),
and buried at Chóng'ān Líng (崇安陵).
Shìzǔ (世祖) visited the Eastern Palace
and saw that the Crown Prince's clothes and playthings exceeded regulations.
He was greatly angered,
and ordered the officials to destroy them as appropriate.
He converted the halls of the Dōng Tián (東田) into the Chóngxū Guǎn (崇虛館).
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored him as Wéndì (文帝),
and his temple was called Shìzōng (世宗).
Originally, the Crown Prince harbored ill will towards Míngdì (明帝).
He secretly told Jìnglín Wángzǐliáng (竟陵王子良):
"My expression shows that I am truly displeased with this person.
This must be due to his shallow fortune and virtue."
Zǐliáng (子良) then tried hard to mediate and explain.
Later, when Míngdì (明帝) ascended,
he indeed greatly persecuted them.
The historian said: In ancient times,
a father did not weep for his son.
The length of life, long or short,
