was merely lamented as a common occurrence.
How much more so for the legitimate heir to the Eastern Palace,
who was just establishing his years of virtue,
upon a solid foundation accumulated over generations,
flourishing in the imperial house,
a ruler who was to inherit the vessel,
and was already experienced in governance.
Though gentle and accomplished,
extensively displaying glorious achievements,
the martial dynasty was nearing its end,
and he perished prematurely.
The succession was passed to a youth,
thus hastening collapse and danger.
Judging from this,
there was indeed a hidden destiny.
The eulogy says: The two luminaries set the pattern,
the three stars adorn the sky.
Establishing the eldest as heir
is a matter of principle, not seeking the virtuous.
He was about to inherit the vessel,
but his destined life was not extended.
Proofreading Notes
Biography Three: Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng (豫章文獻王) [Xiāo] Yí (嶷)
Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng (豫章文獻王) [Xiāo] Yí (嶷), courtesy name Xuānyǎn (宣儼),
was the second son of Tàizǔ (太祖).
He was generous, benevolent, broad-minded, and refined,
possessing the capacity for great accomplishments.
Tàizǔ (太祖) especially cherished him.
He began his career as a Tàixué Bóshì (太學博士) and Prefect of Chángchéng (長城),
then entered service as Shàngshū Zuǒmín Láng (尚書左民郎) and Prefect of Qiántáng (錢唐).
When Tàizǔ (太祖) defeated Xuē Suǒ'ér (薛索兒),
[Xiāo Yí] was re-enfeoffed as Xīyáng (西陽) and granted the earlier title of Jìnshòu Xiànhóu (晉壽縣侯).
He was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (通直散騎侍郎),
but resigned due to a partial mourning.
During the campaign in Guìyáng (桂陽),
Tàizǔ (太祖) encamped at Xīntíng Lěi (新亭壘),
and appointed [Xiāo] Yí (嶷) as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
leading troops to escort him.
[Yuán] Xiūfàn (休範) led his soldiers to attack the southern part of the fortress.
[Xiāo] Yí (嶷) held the white tiger banner and supervised the battle,
repeatedly repelling them.
After the incident settled,
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎).
Soon after, he became Ānyuǎn Hùjūn (安遠護軍) and Prefect of Wǔlíng (武陵).
At that time, Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) demanded ransoms,
attacking various indigenous tribes within the Jīngzhōu (荊州) region,
reaching as far as the Wǔxī (五溪),
and prohibiting fishing and salt collection.
The tribes were enraged.
The Wǔxī (酉溪) chieftain, Tián Tóunǐ (田頭擬), planned to kill Shěn Yōuzhī's (沈攸之) envoy.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) demanded ten million in ransom.
Tián Tóunǐ (頭擬) paid five million,
and then died of indignation.
His younger brother Lóuhóu (婁侯) usurped the position.
Tián Tóunǐ's (頭擬) son, Tián Dū (田都), fled into the tribal lands.
Consequently, the indigenous tribes fell into great disarray,
plundering common people
up to the city walls of the commandery.
[Xiāo] Yí (嶷) dispatched his captain Zhāng Mò'ér (張莫兒) to lead his officers and soldiers to defeat them.
Tián Dū (田都) requested to be installed from within the tribal lands.
Meanwhile, Lóuhóu (婁侯), in fear,
also surrendered.
[Xiāo] Yí (嶷) executed Lóuhóu (婁侯) in the commandery prison
and appointed Tián Dū (田都) to succeed his father.
Only then did the various tribes become peaceful.
He entered service as Cóng Dì Chējì Zīyì Cānjūn (宋從帝車騎諮議參軍) and Fǔyuàn (府掾) for Sòng (宋),
then transferred to Piàojì (驃騎),
and subsequently promoted to Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
He visited Sītú Yuán Càn (司徒袁粲).
Yuán Càn (粲) said to others:
"This is a fine vessel for the future."
Tài-zǔ was in the *Lǐngjūn Fǔ*,
Yí resided in the Qīngxī residence.
Cāngwú Wáng secretly traveled at night,
intending to ambush the residence.
Yí ordered his左右 (attendants) to wield knives in the central courtyard.
Cāngwú (Wáng) peeked from the side and saw this,
assuming (Yí) was prepared,
and so he left.
Tài-zǔ held the governorship of Nányùnzhōu,
and Xiāo Shùnzhī, the *zhèn jūn fǔ zhǎngshǐ*,
was in the garrison.
The urgency of the danger was pressing,
and he planned to cross the river north to raise an army.
Yí remonstrated, saying:
"The Emperor is cruel and tyrannical;
subordinates cannot protect themselves.
Traveling alone on the road
makes it easy to accomplish something.
Raising an army from an outer province
rarely succeeds.
People's sentiments would be suspicious and doubtful,
and you would surely be the first to suffer calamity.
Making a plan here (in the capital)
is absolutely not to be missed."
Cāngwú Wáng perished.
Tài-zǔ reported to Yí, saying:
"The great matter has been decided.
You can come in early tomorrow."
After Dì ascended the throne,
(Yí) was transferred to *shìzhōng*,
overseeing the palace's internal guards.
During Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion,
Tài-zǔ entered the imperial court,
and Yí was sent out to garrison the *Dōngfǔ*,
with the added title of *Guānjūn Jiāngjūn*.
On the evening Yuán Càn raised an army,
Dānyáng *chéng* Wáng Xùn reported the變 (treason).
He first arrived at the *Dōngfǔ*.
Yí dispatched *zhàngnèi jūnzhǔ* Dài Yuánsūn with two thousand men to go with Xuē Dàoyuān and others to Shítou.
Yuánsūn participated in the merit of burning the gate.
Previously, Wáng Yùn had recommended sixty of his private troops to help defend the city,
secretly intending them as internal agents.
Yí knew Yùn harbored disloyal intentions,
so he did not give them weapons,
but dispersed them in the outer annexes.
When the rebellion broke out and a search was made,
they had all fled.
He was promoted to *zhōnglǐngjūn*,
with the added title of *sànqí chángshì*.
After the upstream region was pacified,
Shìzǔ returned from Xúnyáng.
Yí was sent out as *shǐchíjié*, *dūdū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu zhī Xīncài Jìnxī èr Jùn Jūnshì*, *zuǒjiāngjūn*, *Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ*,
with *chángshì* as before.
He was granted one set of drums and pipes.
For his merit in establishing the succession,
he was restyled Yǒng'ān Xiàn Gōng,
with fifteen hundred households.
He was then transferred to *dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yōng Yì Liáng Níng Nán Běi Qín bāzhōu zhū Jūnshì*,
*Zhènxī Jiāngjūn*, *Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ*,
with *chíjié* and *chángshì* as before.
At that time, Tài-zǔ was assisting in governance.
Yí focused on frugality and economy,
stopping the customary welcome gifts for prefectures and provinces.
Initially,
Shěn Yōuzhī, wanting to gather a crowd,
encouraged people to denounce each other,
and many officials and commoners were conscripted into service.
When Yí arrived at the garrison,
he released over three thousand people in one day.
Prisoners sentenced to five years or less, who were not in continuous custody,
were all pardoned and released.
Finding market taxes heavy and excessive,
he re-established the pricing system,
returning taxes to the people.
He prohibited various market levies and seedling taxes.
Officials of the two-thousand-dan rank were not allowed to engage in trade with people.
Officials of all departments were permitted to take turns on leave.
The common people were very pleased.
During the period of abdication,
Shìzǔ wished to quickly complete the great enterprise.
Yí demurred on the matter,
remaining silent.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
Tài-zǔ ascended the throne.
Before the amnesty edict arrived,
Yí first issued an order to remit all outstanding debts within his jurisdiction from before the second year of Shēngmíng.
He was promoted to *shìzhōng*, *shàngshūlìng*, *dūdū Yáng Nán Xú èrzhōu zhū Jūnshì*, *piàoqí dàjiāngjūn*, *kāifǔyítóngsānsī*, *Yángzhōu Cìshǐ*,
with *chíjié* as before.
He was enfeoffed as Yùzhāng Jùn Wáng,
with three thousand households.
The *púyè* Wáng Jiǎn submitted a memorial, saying:
"The former Chǔ region is desolate,
having suffered many troubles for years.
The wilderness people have scattered and fled,
and it truly requires reorganization.
Your Excellency has just taken office,
and your heroic reputation is truly esteemed.
The people of Jiāng and Hàn have revived,
and the eight provinces admire your righteousness.
Since Yǔ Liàng's time,
Jīngchǔ has not seen such excellent governance again.
The ancients achieved success in a month,
but Your Excellency brought order in a matter of days.
Is this not splendid!"
At this time, the northern barbarians stirred,
and the Emperor considered making plans.
So he issued an edict, saying:
"The divine shepherd, overseeing the royal domain,
is truly essential for governance;
while Jīngchǔ, governing distant lands,
bears a heavy and important responsibility.
Lately, both public and private resources have been exhausted,
and the need for pacification and relief
is especially urgent."
He was again appointed *dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yōng Yì Liáng Níng Nán Běi Qín bāzhōu zhū Jūnshì*, *Nánmán Xiàowèi*, *Jīng Xiāng èrzhōu Cìshǐ*,
with *chíjié*, *shìzhōng*, *jiāngjūn*, and *kāifǔ* as before.
During the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
*cìshǐ* often did not concurrently hold the *Nánmán* title;
a separate important person was appointed to it.
By this time, (Yí) held two prefectures and two provinces.
Jīngzhōu's annual expenses were thirty million cash,
ten thousand bolts of cloth,
sixty thousand *hú* of rice.
Additionally, one hundred thousand *hú* of rice from Jiāng and Xiāng provinces were given to the garrison headquarters.
Xiāngzhōu's annual expenses were seven million cash,
three thousand bolts of cloth,
fifty thousand *hú* of rice.
Nánmán's annual expenses were three million cash,
ten thousand bolts of cloth,
one thousand *jīn* of cotton,
three hundred bolts of silk,
one thousand *hú* of rice.
Nothing in recent times could compare to this.
Soon after, he was granted an oil-canopied, side-viewing carriage.
In the spring of the second year,
the barbarians invaded Sī and Yù provinces.
Yí submitted a memorial dispatching *Nánmán Sīmǎ* Cuī Huìjǐng to campaign in the north.
He also dispatched *zhōngbīng cānjūn* Xiāo Huìlǎng to reinforce Sīzhōu,
garrisoning Xīguān.
The barbarian army crossed the Huái River to attack Shòuchūn.
Part of their cavalry was expected to come out through Suí and Dèng.
The multitude worried about this,
but Yí said:
"The barbarians enter in spring and summer,
which is not a time for mobilizing large armies.
Order Yù and Sī (provinces) to hold their defenses firmly and block their strategic points.
When they see strong and strict defenses,
they will naturally disperse.
They will certainly not dare to bypass the two garrisons and go south."
At this time, the defenses were tightened.
Yí, knowing that Jīngzhōu bordered the Man and Dan peoples,
feared they might stir up trouble,
so he ordered everyone in the garrison to wear relaxed clothing.
Subsequently, the barbarians indeed did not come out through Fán and Dèng,
and were defeated and fled at Shòuchūn.
Soon after, he was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords.
That summer,
he opened a school and established an academy southeast of the Nánmán garden,
submitting a memorial detailing the situation.
Forty students were appointed,
selected from old noble families whose fathers or grandfathers held positions as principal assistants or court officials,
aged between fifteen and twenty-five.
One *rú lín cānjūn* and
one *wénxué jìjiǔ* were appointed,
along with two *quàn xué cóngshì*,
and a ceremony of offering vegetables was performed.
As grain was excessively cheap,
people were allowed to pay the poll tax with rice,
with one *hú* valued at one hundred (cash).
Zhāng Qún, a bandit leader from Yìyáng, had been an outlaw for many years,
leading a gang of thieves.
The borders of the four prefectures of Yìyáng, Wǔlíng, Tiānmén, and Nánpíng
were devastated by him.
Shěn Yōuzhī repeatedly attacked but could not capture him,
so he resorted to employing him.
When Yōuzhī started his uprising,
Qún followed him downstream to Yǐng,
but rebelled first along the way,
setting up a stronghold at Sānxī,
relying on its deep and treacherous terrain.
Yí dispatched *zhōngbīng cānjūn* Yú Xīnzǔ as *Yìyáng Tàishǒu*,
ordering him to entice and recruit Qún with a conciliatory attitude,
and offer generous gifts.
(But instead,) he beheaded (Qún) during a meeting.
His several hundred followers dispersed,
and the four prefectures achieved peace.
Upon entering, he was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Yáng and Nánxú Prefectures, Zhōngshū Jiān, Sīkōng, and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
His position as Chíjié and Shìzhōng remained unchanged.
He was granted additional troops and aides.
The civil and military officials from the staff of the former Prince of Línchuān, Yìng, were transferred to the Sīkōng's staff.
Nì, intending to return to the capital,
repaired the official residences and roads.
His troops returning east were not permitted to take goods from the prefecture or province out of the city.
When he departed from Jiāngjīn,
thousands of men and women watched him off,
all weeping.
Nì fell ill upon departing from Jiānglíng,
and had not recovered by the time he reached the capital.
The Emperor was deeply worried
and granted a general amnesty because of it.
The amnesty decree of Rénzǐ in the sixth month of the third year is this.
When he recovered from his illness,
the Emperor visited his Eastern Palace and held a banquet with music from bells and stone chimes.
He was granted permission to use an imperial carriage to enter all six gates of the palace.
When Tàizǔ passed away,
Nì wailed in grief,
and blood flowed from his eyes and ears.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Nì was promoted to Tàiwèi,
granted troops and aides,
relieved of his duty as Shìzhōng,
and the number of guards with ceremonial swords was increased to thirty.
During the JiànYuán reign,
Shìzǔ, due to certain matters, had fallen out of favor with Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ somewhat harbored the intention of replacing the heir apparent.
However, Nì served Shìzǔ with utmost respect and courtesy,
never showing any disrespect or displeasure.
Therefore, Shìzǔ's fraternal love for him was also deep.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was appointed Prince Tàifù,
and relieved of his duty as Zhōngshū Jiān;
his other positions remained as before.
He personally submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your Majesty, with your sagacious filial piety, has taken up the imperial industry,
renewing everything.
Your younger brothers are in proper order.
I have repeatedly received immense favor,
and am presumptuously bestowed with the highest ministerial office.
I dare not decline,
but humbly accept the honor,
my heart and soul feeling lost.
To bear a heavy burden requires strength;
this has been a consistent principle throughout history.
My humble existence is like floating,
my character and conduct are utterly plain.
Residing in a position of such importance
has already shifted my vital energy.
Since some time ago,
my chronic illness has gradually entangled me,
my mind is hazy and confused,
which is evident in my appearance.
Looking at this condition,
I constantly fear that my life cannot bear such grace.
Furthermore, astrological phenomena have repeatedly shown signs of disaster,
and although life has its duration,
how can one not be anxious?
Recently, I wished to follow common practice
and request to be relieved of my current duties,
but expressing it in words felt vulgar,
perhaps incurring criticism.
Therefore, I decided to remain silent,
entrusting everything to fate,
but now more honor and glory are added,
increasing my risk of stumbling.
Moreover, the heavy responsibility of the Crown Prince's tutor
is truly not suitable for me.
This would cause the Crown Prince to always gird his robes when he sees me,
and all palace officials to prostrate twice.
How can such a person, worthy of such respect,
be me?
Your Majesty had more than ten uterine brothers,
and now only I remain.
How can the love between brothers
be solely concentrated on me, granting me such immense favor?
I will submit a separate memorial, humbly praying for your enlightened consideration.
I also recently spoke with the Crown Prince,
and conveyed my intentions to Zǐliáng,
fully explained through Wáng Jiǎn's memorial.
I do not know if it has reached Your Majesty's ears yet.
As good fortune and blessings are flourishing,
and the national destiny is beginning to be eternal,
if Heaven grants me more years,
and I can remain among the ranks of people,
I only wish to request the demotion of my official rank
to adorn my humble self,
and forever serve Your Majesty,
until the end of my life.
Wearing inappropriate attire
is still a calamity for the body,
how much more so for exalted titles!
For extraordinary honor and profound grace,
I must pledge my life to request this."
The Emperor replied:
"Concerning this matter, I fear your request cannot be granted."
Since the Sòng dynasty,
the official salaries and
miscellaneous provisions for prefectures and commanderies
often varied according to local produce, without a fixed standard.
Nì submitted a memorial, stating:
"To follow reforms, it is appropriate
to adjust income and expenditure.
Governance resides in
early equalization, and policies stem from a unified system.
I humbly observe that the system for the salaries of county magistrates and chiefs,
though having fixed regulations,
the remaining provisions
are still determined by local customs.
The northeast has different sources,
the southwest has separate arrangements.
This has become customary,
and thus remains unchanged.
If relaxed, none seem to violate common practice;
if scrutinized, all fall under culpability.
This is far from establishing clear laws
and the principle of 'first decree, then punish.'
I suggest that each locality should list all public expenditures, public land, official salaries, and provisions according to old regulations.
What supplies and levies have been passed down by successive governors and magistrates,
the Shàngshū should thoroughly review
to ensure fairness and appropriateness.
Matters that are reasonable
should be permitted as appropriate.
Those that harm the public and infringe upon the people
should all be
stopped.
Clear, fixed rules should be established,
promulgated to all four directions,
to serve as a permanent system."
This was adopted.
Nì did not participate in court affairs,
but his advice and confidential strategies
were often trusted and accepted.
After the mourning period was over,
he was given the additional title of Shìzhōng.
In the second year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Hàn's Liáng Xiào
was uniquely favored among the feudal princes.
Jìn's Wénxiàn
had a special rank and order.
How much more so now, when his territory matches previous standards,
and his merits surpass past examples?
Although familial relations are fundamental,
feelings are heightened by circumstances.
It is appropriate to expand his land and households
to express this gracious etiquette."
His enfeoffment was increased to four thousand households.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
when various princes entered the imperial inner chambers,
they were allowed to wear white robes and hats to see the emperor.
Only when they exited the Tàijí Sìxiāng
did they don full court attire.
〔二二〕From this time
〔二三〕onward, this practice was abolished.
The Emperor and Nì, being born of the same mother, were friendly and harmonious.
During private banquets within the palace,
Nì was permitted to follow the Yuánjiā precedent.
However, Nì firmly declined to obey the imperial decree,
and only when the imperial carriage visited his residence,
did he attend the banquet in white robes and a black gauze cap.
He sent a memorial stating:
“Since my return to court,
I have dispensed with the ceremonial saber,
and the ten or so saber-wielding guards at my side have also been dismissed.
Only when traveling far outside the city,
do I perhaps occasionally have them,
but upon entering the palace, they are also dismissed.
The personal guards I currently employ
include two xiágǔ
and two báizhí,
totaling seventy or eighty people.
Whether the matter is great or small,
I always wish to memorialize it,
fearing that Your Sacred Heart may not be fully informed,
or that there might be talk of their number,
which does not adhere to the facts.
I humbly hope for an immediate imperial decree.”
He also memorialized:
“The Governor of Yángzhōu used to have six white-collared folding fans
and two white whisks.
I might have doubts about this,
and I am unsure what should be done about it.
When moving within the imperial gardens, one rides in a litter.
When exiting beyond the fence gate, one rides in a litter with horns blowing.
All these practices have been customary,
not limited to those governing the Shénzhōu region.
I am unsure what should be done about this.
I will soon be traveling,
and it is essential not to err.”
The Emperor replied:
“Ceremonial sabers and saber-wielding guards
should not be dismissed.
As for xiágǔ and báizhí,
it is appropriate to have a total of one hundred forty or fifty, no more.
I have also never heard anyone question this.
I myself do not allow the princes to be without guards,
how much less you?
Riding in a litter within private gardens is not questionable.
As for blowing horns outside the city, and the folding fans and whisks,
they used to exist,
but are no longer used.
This change happened a long time ago.
Generally, those in frontier garrisons are different from those returning to the capital.
Previously, Guǎngzhōu even had drum and fife bands,
and various departments then had litter services.
These things change with the times,
but there are also some that can be retained as before.
If you have any doubts,
you may discuss them with Wáng Jiǎn and others to reach a consensus,
but simply ensure that the decorum of a subject is not lost when acting.”
He further memorialized:
“I am unskilled at conducting myself
and ignorant of what to question.
I have often seen common folk carrying imperial edicts, sometimes wearing cloth shoes,
without considering it unusual.
When I was enfeoffed as a prince in the western court,
my ceremonial attire and decorations all followed the precedents of Sòng Wǔlíng.
I had two zhàngshàn,
and these were brought to the capital,
perhaps not causing any doubts.
The young boys and servants
all wore blue cloth trousers and shirts.
I also have one such person in my private chambers,
thinking that this was what commoners wore,
not doubting that it resembled a sheep carriage.
I am deeply grateful for Your benevolent instruction,
and will now change everything.
When I was formerly in a frontier garrison,
I was not without winged guards.
Since my return to court,
I have gradually dismissed them.
Xiágǔ and báizhí,
were fixed at around three hundred people,
but the number I currently employ
does not exceed one hundred.
I always believed that princes in the capital did not need to employ guards,
but this does not apply to long journeys outside the city.
I am not the only one with guards,
which is why it is not appropriate for me to make a detailed memorial about their dismissal,
and I have also had Wáng Jiǎn fully convey my situation.
My comings and goings are grand and conspicuous,
my ceremonial appearance is generous and relaxed,
and my residence is spacious and magnificent.
These matters deviate from simple frugality,
and although they are legacies of the Sòng dynasty,
and there is imperial favor involved,
I still feel deeply ashamed of not being dressed appropriately.
Regarding the request for imperial guards,
I humbly hope for Your kind consideration.”
The Emperor replied:
“The imperial edict bearers are merely household servants,
there is no need to suspect anything.
As for the zhàngshàn,
I have not seen them since I can remember,
hence the decree.
The young boys and servants
were not originally a cause for concern.
I had heard something,
how could I not inform you,
lest people criticize it?
I have already issued an edict;
you alone should not dismiss your xiágǔ,
just keep them.
Yesterday I was not clear about the guard matter;
Jiǎn has already spoken of it,
and I will respond immediately,
so there is no need for this memorial.
If you need to speak privately,
we can discuss it again one or two times.”
He again submitted a memorial, saying:
“It has been
more than a *jì* (cycle of twelve years)
since I was far away from attending your banquets.
Between sorrow and bitterness,
I have only recently been able to smile.
Recently, attending your presence frequently,
I cannot contain my mixed feelings of sorrow and joy.
Drinking excessively,
I genuinely wished to show my reliance on your affectionate familiarity,
to make those below understand and be aware,
and thereby block rumors.
Your Majesty extends your grace to your sons and nephews;
how is this feeling different?
External things naturally produce differences in their strength and weakness,
giving rise to their reputations.
I humbly surmise that this may not yet have been brought to your attention.
Previously, when I was in Dōngtián,
I was overly drunk from your grace.
I truly pondered and sighed about the slanders of the previous autumn,
hence my memorial was extremely earnest,
also to let all subjects hear of it.
I humbly wish that you have already illuminated this heart of mine.
Previously, when attending the imperial visit to Shùnzhī’s residence,
I customarily rode my carriage to the rear of the imperial retinue.
The supervising guards were unable to indicate to me whether it was permissible or not,
and then they competed to submit reports,
saying that my carriage was pressing upon the imperial canopy and banners as if intending to strike them.
Considering this intention,
how could it be easily dismissed?
I relied on your benevolent understanding
and immediately received an imperial edict.
Otherwise,
I would never have known of this secret accumulation of trouble.
Recently, restrictions have been strict and meticulous.
This is a common principle.
However, external rumors claim that the strictness intensified
because when I was in Huálín,
I dared to grasp an imperial sword.
Judging by the circumstances and reasoning,
this is certainly not possible.
I am simply reporting it to Your Majesty for your information.
But rumors easily arise,
and harmony is truly difficult to achieve.
I humbly wish that you still remember what I memorialized at Shítou,
so that no rifts may arise.
Recently, as I have attended without a fixed schedule,
I briefly conveyed my message through Rú Liàng.
My humble origins
have already been fully presented to Your Majesty.
Though I always wish to preserve my true feelings,
my thoughts and considerations are often incomplete,
or sometimes inappropriate.
Furthermore, I am fifty years old;
how many years do I have left to enjoy?
For this reason, I cannot control myself with reason.
The northern residence, my old dwelling,
was originally very splendid.
I merely renovated it,
and its minor arrangements
have already been submitted to Your Majesty.
Last year, I collected some miscellaneous materials,
and also received some old planks by imperial grace.
I requested and was internally permitted to build a small sleeping study.
Just as it was about to be completed,
everything was made from patched-up materials,
without violating the regulations.
It was merely splendid with tamarisk and cypress,
new and clean for a time.
The eastern residence also has a study,
which is also a splendid house.
Yet, I suddenly have two places of residence,
which deep down I feel uneasy about.
I inquired about the Xuánpǔ in the Eastern Palace
and found that there is a cypress house there,
whose construction is very ancient and rustic.
There is no such study within it.
I then wished to dismantle it and offer it to the Crown Prince.
However, not only would it be lost from its previous location,
but as it is mostly patched up,
it cannot be moved.
I also fear that external parties might raise different opinions.
I wonder if I may be granted permission to send the study from the eastern residence to be set up?
As for my public residence,
it is generally quite comfortable.
My current memorial
has no ulterior motive,
nor has anyone prompted me.
The Crown Prince also does not know I have this house.
It is simply because the Eastern Palace has none,
and I occupy one myself,
which is simply not proper.
If my request is granted,
I will then dare to complete the mansion and settle there without doubt.
If Your Majesty does not understand my feelings,
I will then permanently abandon and not repair it.
I believe that this memorial is not only about my own propriety,
but truly for the past matters of your humble servant.
I humbly wish that you will surely grant permission.
I humbly observe that due to the princes' commercial activities,
severe edicts have been repeatedly issued.
My modest attempts at earning a living
should have already been brought to your attention.
The official residences in the prefectures, districts, and commanderies
are not my private property.
Now, all that is needed, great or small,
comes from public funds.
My private debts are not few.
I do not know if, after I am dismissed from the province in the future,
I might not be forced to try learning how to manage affairs to support myself.
After years of severe illness,
I am but a lone shadow.
I have no desire to accumulate wealth;
I only seek pleasure as it comes.”
The Emperor replied:
“Rú Liàng has conveyed your thoughts in this memorial, and I have seen the separate paper.
How can you not be affected by your weary illness?
Why do you bother to write such a long and troublesome memorial?
All general edicts—
their meaning can be understood—
do not concern you alone.
If there is an edict specifically for you,
I will certainly state it.
Recently, I have seen you become more meticulous yourself;
I do not wish to write too much.
Regarding the house matter, be careful not to stubbornly force this idea.
Even Báizé would not understand your intention.”
In the third year,
when Crown Prince Wénhuì finished lecturing on the *Xiàojīng*,
Yí sought to resign as Grand Tutor.
This was not granted.
After the imperial grandson's marriage,
he again presented his resignation.
An imperial edict stated:
“Your Excellency's virtue and conduct
leave no room for criticism.
As eminent as Lǔ and Wèi,
who can rival you?
You serve as a model and example for your time,
and your reputation flows through historical records.
How can you repeatedly display humility
and go against expectations?”
Yí always worried about reaching the peak of prosperity.
Also, during a palace banquet,
he sought to resign from Yángzhōu and have it granted to Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng.
The Emperor ultimately did not permit it,
saying:
“Live out your life;
there is no need for many words.”
After Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he repeatedly issued edicts for Yí to visit the imperial tombs,
but he did not carry them out.
He then dispatched Yí to visit the imperial tombs.
On his return, he passed by the temple of Yánlíng Jìzǐ.
Observing the boiling well,
a water buffalo suddenly charged into the ranks.
The soldiers seized the buffalo and questioned its owner,
but Yí did not permit it.
He took a bolt of silk, tied it horizontally to the buffalo's horns,
and released it to return to its home.
His governance was characterized by magnanimity,
and thus he earned the affection of both the court and the common people.
In the fourth year,
when the rebels of Táng Yù rose,
he memorialized the Emperor, saying:
“This small band of brigands,
arises from their ferocity and foolishness.
Heaven’s net broadly covers [all],
so in principle, it's not worth discussing.
But Your Sagely Brilliance governs the world,
and fortunately, it need not be so.
Recently, relying on what I've heard,
〔三一〕everyone says there are reasons for it.
How can I not respectfully present what is in my heart,
and briefly lay out my thoughts?
Though mountains and seas are vast and deep,
your servant enjoys peace and contentment.
The sentiments of both public and private [life]
can be seen in this.
Qí possesses the empire,
but the years and months are not yet long.
Its beneficence has reached the myriad people,
but in reality, not much.
The common people are still precarious,
〔三二〕and those with ill intent are many.
Your Majesty graciously extends your love,
and always maintains generous decrees.
But recently, both high and low officials and commoners,
often serve the public for small gains,
not considering that the harm caused is great.
【擿】Exposing records and checking artisans,
〔三三〕overseeing and regulating small ponds,
concealing adult males and hiding household members,
all these regulations and systems,
truly foster resentment.
These are immediate, mutually beneficial [measures],
not a grand strategy for the empire.
Within a single room,
[things] still cannot be perfectly precise.
Within the Yǔzhòu,
how can [everything] be thoroughly 【洗】scrutinized?
〔三四〕How could the government ever not know that the people are full of deceit and trickery?
Governments, ancient and modern, because [affairs] cannot be meticulously dealt with,
therefore did not do this.
This is truly not contrary to reason.
But among a hundred, scarcely one understands reason.
Your Majesty's younger brothers and sons, and high ministers,
still cannot all submit to reason.
How much more so the vast multitude of people in the empire?
Resentment accumulates, forming factions.
The fierce and deluded gather together.
If confined to one place,
why wouldn't they be eradicated?
But if they are numerous and widespread,
they will become chaotic.
I have long wanted to present this memorial,
but leisure and opportunity to serve have been lacking.
I respectfully present my humble opinion,
humbly hoping Your Majesty will particularly ponder it.”
The Emperor replied:
“How can deceit and trickery be tolerated!
The Sòng era was chaotic,
do you think this is [right]?
What cause for worry are mere mosquitoes and ants?
They have already been defeated by the righteous volunteers.
The government troops arrived yesterday.
By now, they should all be scattered and annihilated.
I only regret that they didn't accomplish more.
When have there ever been no fugitives?”
Afterwards, an edict was issued to allow the resumption of registration and annotation.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to the position of Dàsīmǎ.
In the eighth year,
he was granted a black-wheeled carriage.
Soon after, he was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Jiān,
but he firmly declined.
Nì was seven *chǐ* and eight *cùn* tall.
He was skilled at maintaining a dignified demeanor.
Civil and military attendants followed him.
His decorum surpassed all officials.
Whenever he entered or exited the palace halls or departments,
all looked upon him with solemn respect.
Considering his high and weighty position,
he deeply cherished a desire for a life of retirement and simplicity.
His old Běizhái had beautiful gardens and fields,
so he extensively renovated it.
In the seventh year,
he memorialized requesting to return to his private residence.
The Emperor ordered his heir-apparent, Zǐlián, to take his place in governing the Dōngfǔ.
The Emperor frequently visited Nì's residence.
The main path from the Sòng's Chángníng Líng passed in front of his residence.
The Emperor said:
“I am practically entering his tomb to find him.”
So, he moved the monumental pillars and *qílín* statues to Dōnggāng.
The *qílín* and pillars,
were remarkably skillfully shaped.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng had them brought from Xiāngyáng.
Later, all imperial mausoleums imitated them but none could equal them.
Towards the end of the Yǒngmíng era,
the imperial carriage frequently went on excursions.
Only Nì accompanied [the Emperor].
The Emperor went out to Xīnlín Yuàn.
They returned at night in the same carriage.
Upon reaching the palace gate,
Nì dismounted from the carriage and bade farewell.
The Emperor said:
“Traveling tonight,
do not let the garrison officers reprimand you.”
Nì replied:
“Within the capital,
all belongs to your servant's jurisdiction.
I beg Your Majesty not to be overly concerned.”
The Emperor laughed heartily.
The Emperor planned a northern expedition.
He bestowed upon Nì the felt carriage presented by the captives.
Whenever [he] visited Nì's residence, it was cleared.
The Emperor no longer dismissed his attendants.
The Emperor commanded his outer attendants, saying:
“When I go to the Dàsīmǎ's residence,
it is like returning home.”
Consort Yǔ often suffered from illness.
When she recovered,
the Emperor visited Nì's mansion.
〔三五〕In the rear hall, music of metal and stone instruments was performed.
All palace women arrived.
Whenever [the Emperor] visited,
he would always make the most of the day, indulging in utmost merriment.
Nì said to the Emperor:
“In ancient times, people said, 'May Your Majesty's lifespan be as boundless as the Southern Mountains,'
or 'May you live ten thousand years.'
This is probably mere superficial flattery.
As for what your servant truly feels,
I genuinely wish Your Majesty would live to a hundred years; that would be enough.”
The Emperor said:
“How can a hundred years be attained?
If I merely attain a hundred [years of activity], encompassing east and west,
that would suffice for affairs.”
In the tenth year,
the Emperor enfeoffed Nì's sons.
The old regulation was a thousand households [per enfeoffment].
Nì wanted all five of his sons to be enfeoffed.
He memorialized requesting to reduce each [fief] by five hundred households.
That year, he became gravely ill.
He memorialized to resign his post.
It was not granted.
He was granted a million coins to perform virtuous deeds.
Nì again memorialized, saying:
“Since your servant contracted this current illness,
Your Majesty has frequently descended to visit.
Physicians have been moved (assigned) by officials,
〔三六〕the imperial treasury has been opened.
Your benevolent favor and generosity
have been fully extended to a human subject.
My remaining years are pressed by illness,
and my journey to the shades will be swift and not long.
I wish Your Majesty to discern the worthy and bestow goodness,
and live to the utmost age of the azure heaven,
strengthen virtue and embrace harmony,
and rule over the myriad people.
Your servant's fate has gone against the prosperous decree,
suddenly deprived of your grace and pity.
I take my long leave of this bright world,
prostrate, weeping and choking.”
He passed away,
age forty-nine.
On that day,
the Emperor visited him twice more,
until his death,
then returned to the palace.
An imperial edict stated:
“Nì was enlightened and wise, my closest relative.
His accomplishments were lofty from the beginning of his career.
His virtue flourished in the imperial court.
His influence enlightened districts and counties.
His sudden passing,
is a cruel agony that tears at my heart.
I cannot bear it.
Alas, alas!
I shall now personally attend the mourning.
The rites for the nine ranks of nobility
should be fully implemented for his ceremony.
He shall be encoffined in imperial robes and a ceremonial cap,
a warm bright secret vessel,
one set of ceremonial robes [of his rank],
and one suit of clothes.
His funeral affairs shall entirely follow the precedent of the King of Dōngpíng in Hàn.
The Dàhónglú, bearing credentials, shall oversee the funeral arrangements.
High officials shall offer sacrifices morning and evening.
All civil and military officials of the Dàsīmǎ's and Tàifù's establishments shall cease their duties for the funeral.”
Jìngláng Wáng Zǐliáng (竟陵王子良) petitioned the Emperor, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the 'Spring and Autumn Annals' so highly praised the Emperor's maternal younger brother
to honor what the Emperor esteemed.
Therefore, in terms of ritual ranks, there were distinctions;
in titles and appointments, there were elevated differences.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the King of Liáng (梁王) was granted the full ceremonial escort for entering and exiting;
in the Jìn (晉) dynasty, the King of Qí (齊王) received the special attire and the nine grants.
Since the Jiāngzuǒ (江左) era,
this reverence for kin has been lacking,
leading to the discontinuance of the elaborate ceremonial robes
and their failure to be passed down.
This is truly due to individuals failing to occupy their positions,
not due to a deficiency in the rites.
The past practices regarding the King of Qí (齊王)
are not dissimilar to the present.
In establishing the royal enterprise,
the merits and achievements are no different.
Any reforms or adjustments to suit the times
arise precisely because emotions have varying degrees of lightness and weight,
and virtues have varying degrees of thickness and thinness.
If one were to consider previous precedents,
the rites would have no different rules.
Moreover, the Kings of Liáng (梁) and Qí (齊), despite lacking the virtue of a good end,
still enjoyed the honor of commendation and bestowal.
How much more so the late Grand Marshal (大司馬) Rén Hè (仁和), whose innate kindness was renowned,
whose filial piety and brotherly respect persisted throughout his life,
whose integrity and righteousness were manifest in serving the Emperor,
and whose magnanimity and severity were evident in his governance of affairs.
He showed no signs of difficulty or weariness in serving his superiors,
and no signs of harm or injury in dealing with his subordinates.
He was tranquil and pure,
showing no signs of joy or anger.
He was calm and quiet,
free from the noise of competition.
The 'Odes' say, 'Few can end as they began.'
Truly, to persist to the end
is indeed difficult.
In the present conduct,
this virtue was not abandoned.
Dōngpíng (東平) delighted in small good deeds,
Héjiān (河閒) took pleasure in poetry and books;
their achievements were unheard of,
their involvement in peril was nil,
yet they still achieved outstanding distinction,
and a glorious reputation for ten thousand generations.
How much more so this individual, who assisted in establishing the imperial foundation,
and managed the beginning of the hegemony!
His accomplishments are lofty and prominent,
his pure reputation shines even brighter,
his wealth and status are eminent,
and his integrity is even more unyielding.
Comparing ancient times to the present,
who can be likened to this excellence?
Your servant, in his humble estimation,
believes there is no such precedent.
Among common families, where even blood relatives
have little love and harmony,
how could one find anyone who looks up to Your Majesty's fraternal nature with such admiration?
Rising from humble origins together,
both attaining heavenly nobility,
what in their daily lives
and interactions was not shared?
What delicacies
or flavors were not equally enjoyed?
Never was his countenance seen without Your Majesty's heart being gladdened,
nor his form beheld without the imperial demeanor being pleased.
When it came to facing danger and sacrificing his life,
Your Majesty personally witnessed his last breaths.
At that critical moment,
he passed away before Your sacred eyes.
The wailing moved heaven and earth,
the grief startled ghosts and gods.
Even to the extent of forgoing meals and changing sleeping quarters,
weeping from dawn till dusk,
the imperial countenance was diminished and worn,
changing in appearance overnight.
Beholding the imperial face,
who was not filled with sorrow and awe?
This is unheard of in ancient history,
and unrecorded in records.
Since there is such great virtue as this,
it is truly unacceptable for the bestowal of ceremonial robes not to be glorified.
[三七] If it were to be forgotten,
subsequent rectification would be troublesome,
lest ten thousand generations hence
harbor regret over this matter.
Even those whose virtues were not entirely perfect
still received the command of commendation and elevation.
How then could one who shines brighter than his predecessors
be deprived of this grand ceremony?
Your servant fears that discerning people
may offer their opinions.
Moreover, in recent times, commoners like Huán Wēn (桓溫) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮)
also received special appointments.
Your servant humbly believes that the imperial heart
must already have this in mind."
Again, an edict stated:
"Honored commendations are for manifesting virtue,
and ritual ranks are for recording merits.
Careful observance of the end and remembrance of the distant past
are grand strategies of former kings.
Accumulating good deeds and comparing achievements
are common pronouncements throughout generations.

Therefore, the former Commissioner with Staff (使持節), Grand Commandant of Military Affairs of Yáng (揚) and Southern Xú (徐) Provinces (都督揚南徐二州諸軍事), Grand Marshal (大司馬), concurrently Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (領太子太傅), Governor of Yáng Province (揚州刺史), newly appointed Palace Grandee Secretary (中書監), Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章王) Yí (嶷),
embodied the Way and possessed wisdom,
managed benevolence and governed righteousness.
He established a pure reputation in his youth,
and displayed a magnificent character in his early days.
He laid the foundation of the hegemonic enterprise,
and assisted in the establishment of the imperial foundation.
His filial piety and harmony were known in his village,
and his loyalty and integrity were evident in his state.
When he held virtue and discussed the Way,
and governed the imperial domain,
the seven teachings were certainly upheld,
and the six treasuries were all well-managed.
The wind and rain were harmonized,
without error in their seasons.
He cared for the people and saved living beings,
with profound compassion.
His dignified presence adorned the court,
and his exemplary conduct was a spectacle in the various commanderies.
His spirit was calmly distant,
and all eyes truly gathered upon him.
The depth of Our fraternal affection for him
encompassed both family and state.
We were about to entrust him with the divine plan,
and commit to him the strategic victories,
to bring harmony to the nine regions,
and to accompany Us in sacrificial rites on the Five Sacred Mountains.
Heaven did not spare him,
and he suddenly passed away.
Our sorrow and regret
shook Our heart with grief.
Now, the auspicious date for the distant funeral rites has been determined through divination.
It is fitting to add to his noble honors,
in accordance with these glorious plans.
He is to be posthumously granted the title of Acting Imperial Battle-Ax (假黃鉞), Grand Commandant of All Military Affairs (都督中外諸軍事), Chancellor (丞相), and Governor of Yáng Province (揚州牧).
He shall receive the green and black silk cord and tassel,
and the full rites of the nine grants of appointment.
His titles of Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中), Grand Marshal (大司馬), Grand Tutor (太傅), and Prince (王) remain as before.
He shall be granted a nine-streamer carriage with luan bird decorations,
a yellow canopy with a left-side banner,
one hundred imperial guards with ceremonial swords,
a funerary carriage,
and front and rear military bands with feather-decorated banners and drums.
The funeral ceremonies shall follow the precedents of the Prince of Dōngpíng (東平王)."
Héng Nì, near his end,
summoned his sons Zǐlián and Zǐkè and said:
"Human life in this world
is inherently uncertain.
My years are already old;
how much road lies ahead?
Being in this position today
was beyond what my heart had hoped for.
My nature is not to covet accumulation;
this has been my disposition since youth.
It is precisely because you, my brothers, accumulated much
that it damaged my ambition in my later years.
Without my desire,
you should all encourage each other
and prioritize deep harmony.
Talent has its superior and inferior,
position has its smooth and obstructed,
fortune has its rich and poor—
these are natural principles,
and nothing to be used for mutual insult.
If the Way of Heaven has spiritual power,
you yourselves will each cultivate your character and establish yourselves,
and your clear destinies will not be lost.
Diligently pursue learning and conduct,
guard your family enterprise,
manage your household,
and value simplicity and quietude.
Doing so will be enough to be free from worry and trouble.
The sagely sovereign, the crown prince, and all the esteemed relatives and wise men
also ought not to change their feelings because of my death.
For three days, offer sacrifices:
only incense, water in a basin, rice in a bowl, wine and dried meat, and betel nuts will suffice.
On the first and fifteenth of the month, a plate of vegetarian food,
with the addition of sweet fruits.
All other things are to be omitted.
After the burial, when removing the sacrificial arrangements,
you may use the sedan chair, fan, and parasol I regularly used.
On the first and fifteenth of the month,
incense and fire placed on the ground, water in a basin, wine and dried meat, rice in a bowl, and betel nuts will be sufficient.
Although my talent shames the ancients,
my intentions are roughly present;
I do not wish to be burdened by leaving wealth.
Whatever remains from the main wardrobe,
my younger brother is not yet married,
and my sisters are not yet wed.
All that is needed for these expenses
is inherently uncertain.
You should assess your capabilities and act in time,
arranging whatever is feasible.
There are many, many things;
I will not list them one by one.
For the coffin and inside the tomb,
do not use extraneous items to cause future trouble.
Beyond the court robes,
only a single iron-ringed knife should be placed below.
Do not make the tomb deep.
Follow the regulations exactly,
and do not exceed them.
In the rear hall, a Buddha may be enshrined,
and two foreign monks supported.
All other things remain as before.
The boats and carriages we used to play with in the rear hall,
and the oxen and horses I rode,
are to be sent to the two palaces and the Sītú.
All garments and furs
are to be used for charitable merits."
Zǐlián and others wept and carried out his wishes.
Shìzǔ's grief and pain were particularly profound.
Not until winter did he hold a banquet with music for his court officials,
and he sighed and shed tears.
The residences of the various princes were not allowed to build towers overlooking the palace.
Later, when the Emperor ascended Jǐngyáng,
he saw the towers and was saddened,
so he ordered them demolished.
After his demise,
there was no cash in his residence's treasury.
Shìzǔ ordered the sale of various items and clothing, obtaining several million (cash),
with which the Jíshàn Temple was built.
The residence was given one million cash monthly,
which ceased only upon the Emperor's death.
Héng Nì's nature was to love broadly;
he disliked hearing of others' faults.
If attendants submitted letters to accuse someone,
he would place them in his shoe,
never read them,
and then take fire to burn them.
When the fasting treasury caught fire,
burning the refunded assets from Jīngzhōu,
valued at over thirty million,
the chief officers were merely flogged a few tens of times each.
Among the many officials, Yuè Ái of Nányáng, Liú Huì of Péngchéng, and Zhāng Jì of Wúchún were most favored with intimacy and courtesy.
Ái wrote a letter to Jìnglǐng Wáng Zǐliáng, saying:
"Morality allows for long-lasting renown,
and elegance spreads far with its reputation.
Although writing on bamboo slips can establish fragrance,
it is not as enduring as jade and stone.
Flying brushstrokes and painted patterns,
how can they compare to carved inscriptions that do not vanish?
The Prime Minister's purity and essence were manifest in his natural disposition,
his profound insight almost reaching the fundamental principles.
He was a model for governing the state and guiding the people,
a standard for embodying the nation and accomplishing tasks.
Thus, his achievements were abundant through his sagacity,
his merits high through his wisdom.
His divine radiance is ethereal and distant;
even sagely calculations cannot pursue it.
Grief grips the attendant charioteer;
I lament that I was so long delayed.
This humble official has long cherished a reputation for integrity,
and my gratitude and righteousness stir my admiration.
I look forward to uniting our sorrow,
and intend to lead the officials of the three prefectures of Jīng, Jiāng, and Xiāng
to erect a stele at the head of the tomb.
Thus, his splendid virtues may be recounted,
and his noble principles preserved.
In the past, Zǐxiāng, with his pure virtue,
left an inscription by the Jiāng River;
Jùpíng's remaining deeds
caused tears to fall south of the Hàn.
How much more so for one whose Way surpassed those preceding,
and whose benevolence accumulated endlessly!
This humble official is now returning on leave,
unable to personally oversee the carving.
I must wait until I reach Xīzhōu to gather the necessary resources,
and entrust Zhōngshū Shìláng Liú Huì with managing the arrangements."
Ài also wrote a letter to the Right Overseer, Shěn Yuē, saying:
"Indeed, the lingering glory of the Way,
sometimes the bamboo and silk decay first;
the trust in virtue and its legacy,
metal and stone will not perish afterwards.
The Grand Chancellor alone stands out among humankind,
his radiance shines upon the sun and moon.
He sets a standard of excellence even in quiet gardens,
his conduct is solemn in loyalty and righteousness.
His reputation merits splendid robes,
his achievements are evident in assisting and harmonizing.
There is nothing that can fully praise him,
the truth transcends records.
As for daily life, even if it is quiet and still,
though nothing can be gained from trifles,
the grand achievements of a lifetime,
indeed have a place in the scales of justice.
I have secretly heard that the gentry and common people of your province,
have erected steles to record his deeds,
causing us in Jīngnán,
to feel a profound sense of admiration with no place to express it.
Moreover, he established order in the Jiāng and Hàn regions,
the foundation of his Way spread across the land,
bringing order, rites, and music,
which have all benefited later generations.
If bowing before his stele with complete reverence,
is the old custom of our province,
then abandoning markets and overturning valuables,
is a legacy of our humble land.
[四三] Hopefully, his great achievements will not be lost.
In the three provinces of Jīng, Jiāng, and Xiāng, not a few have enrolled their names,
and all wish to contribute a small amount,
to express their deep admiration.
The task of this literary memorial,
after careful consideration, is uncertain.
It must await a man of profound literary skill, a master of rhetoric,
whose virtue and conduct are equally outstanding.
Who else but a man of such high caliber?
How can one employ inadequate words,
to answer the expectation of such reverence?
We, the humble scholars of Xīzhōu,
are solitary and obscure individuals.
His benevolence encompassed our honor,
his grace permeated our sustenance.
Constantly reflecting on his protective influence,
as the days and months grow distant,
and recalling his legacy,
our hearts break at every sight.
We always believed his good fortune would be as boundless as Nánshān,
and his blessings would concentrate in benevolent longevity.
We, his humble servants,
would only bring dust to his canopy.
How could we have imagined this request would be made so suddenly?"
Yuē replied:
"The Grand Chancellor's magnanimous demeanor and Way,
uniquely stood out among humankind.
His established policies and grand achievements,
paralleled those of Yī and Dàn.
The sorrow of his passing,
is shared by the court and common people.
I understand that a stele is to be carved to record his merits,
to transmit his glory for a thousand years.
It certainly requires a grand inscription,
and your discussion is truly apt.
Guō Yǒudào was a commoner at the end of the Hàn dynasty;
without Cài Bójiē, he would not have been matched by the 'Three Perfections.'
Xiè Ānshí was a high official from an aristocratic family;
without beautiful prose at the time,
his stele remains without inscription to this day.
How much more so for King Wénxiàn, a paragon of the gentry,
whose example illuminated the realm!
Unless it is a literary master of his generation,
it would be difficult to achieve this.
I am a humble person from a common household,
my name is not listed among the elite.
To respond abruptly to this request now,
would be to rashly promise help.
Upon hearing your command, I am ashamed,
and cannot help but feel sweat soaking my back."
During the Jiànwǔ era,
his second son, Zǐkè, entrusted Yuē and the Crown Prince's Grand Master, Kǒng Zhìguī, with writing the inscription.
Zǐlián's courtesy name was Jǐng'ǎi.
Initially,
Yí adopted Fúhóu Zǐxiǎng as his heir.
Zǐlián was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yǒngxīn,
with one thousand households.
When Zǐxiǎng returned to his birth family,
Zǐlián became the heir.
He was appointed General of Níngshuò, Prefect of Huáilíng,
Palace Attendant in the Crown Prince's Secretariat,
[四四] and General of the Vanguard.
[四五] He was skilled at nurturing his younger disciples.
He died in the eleventh year,
and was posthumously granted the title of Attendant-in-ordinary,
and given the posthumous name Āi Shìzǐ.
The third son, Zǐcāo,
was the Marquis of Quánlíng.
The official positions for royal marquises were not fixed;
according to common practice, the eldest son of a Grand Chancellor from a common family would become a supernumerary official.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Zǐcāo began his career as an Attendant Officer,
and this became the precedent for all subsequent cases until the end of the Qí dynasty.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
the Marquis of Nánkāng, Zǐkè, was the Administrator of Wú County.
He fled to return home to avoid the rebellion of Wáng Jìngzé.
Zǐcāo was made General of Níngyuǎn and Administrator of Wú County.
During the Yǒngyuán era,
he served as a Yellow Gate Household Attendant.
When the righteous army besieged the city,
Zǐcāo and his younger brother, the Marquis of Yíyáng, Zǐguāng, died at the Ministry of Personnel's main office.
The fourth son, Zǐxíng,
was the Marquis of Táoyáng,
and died young.
Zǐyuánlín inherited his title.
[四六] When the present emperor received the abdication,
an edict stated:
"To honor and promote past generations,
is a principle clearly established in the canons.
I, in my present acceptance of this joyful succession,
desire to uphold ancient precedents.
Yùzhāng Prince Yuánlín, and the son of the late Bālíng Prince Zhāo(xiù)zǐ(tóng),
[四七] are of the Qí imperial clan,
direct descendants of Gāo and Wǔ.
They should be granted fiefs,
to continue their ancestral sacrifices for generations.
They are hereby demoted to Marquis of Xīngàn County,
with five hundred households."
The historian says: King Yuán of Chǔ, the younger brother of Gāozǔ,
achieved no merit in the Hàn era.
King Xiàn of Dōngpíng resigned his position in Yǒngpíng,
but could not compare to Gāngwǔ's achievements.
[四八] Emperor Xiào of Liáng was misled by Shèng and Guǐ,
and Ānpíng was estranged from the Jìn dynasty's fate.
Feudal princes, though noble and powerful,
held positions that were truly high and perilous.
Few were able to preserve their virtue by being content and guarding against arrogance.
[一三八] [豫章] the Grand Chancellor possessed the capacity
of true heavenly sincerity.
His actions were from the heart, without pretense,
guided by far-reaching foresight.
Thus, he was able to brilliantly assist the two ancestors,
and bring harmony within the nine clans.
This was truly like the beginning of the Zhōu dynasty;
since the Duke of Zhōu,
his equal is unknown.
A eulogy says: Majestic was the esteemed father,
his virtue surpassed predecessors.
He transformed loyalty into filial piety,
cultivated friendships with utmost reverence.
When the imperial reign first began,
our king exerted himself.
When the state and family had deficiencies,
our king mended them.
His Way permeated daily life,
his affairs brought harmony to the people.
His love was passed down through lingering sacrifices,
his fame resonated like a great bell.
Collated Notes
Biographies, No. 4: Chǔ Yuān (Yuān's brother Chéng, Xú Sì), Wáng Jiǎn
Chǔ Yuān, courtesy name Yànhuí,
was from Yángzhái, Hénán.
His grandfather, Xiùzhī,
was Grand Master of Ceremonies during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Zhànzhī,
was a General of Cavalry,
and married the daughter of Sòng Emperor Wǔ, Princess Shǐ'ān Āi.
Yuān had a good reputation from a young age,
and also married the daughter of Emperor Wén, Princess Nánjùn Xiàn.
Aunt and niece were successively married across two generations.
He was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law,
and then Assistant in the Secretariat for the Heir Apparent,
Attendant to the Crown Prince,
Assistant to the Grand Tutor,
Riding Companion to the Crown Prince,
and Secretary of the Imperial Library.
When Zhànzhī died,
Yuān ceded his wealth to his younger brother,
keeping only several thousand scrolls of books.
He inherited the title Marquis of Dūxiāng.
[歷] He served as Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
Right Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Education,
and Director of the Bureau of Personnel.
When Sòng Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he was additionally granted the position of Commander of Cavalry for the Crown Prince,
but he refused it.
He was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary,
overseeing affairs of the Eastern Palace.
He was transferred to Minister of Personnel,
and soon after, was concurrently appointed Right Commandant of the Palace Guard for the Crown Prince,
which he firmly declined.
The Grand Minister of Education, Prince Jiàn'ān Xiūré, campaigned south against the Yìjiā rebels,
encamping at Quèwěi.
He sent Yuān to the army,
giving him sole authority to select generals and above based on their merits.
After the rebellion was pacified,
he was additionally granted the title General of Valiant Cavalry.
Xuē Āndū (薛安都) rebelled with Xúzhōu (徐州).
Barbarians frequently raided Huái (淮) and Sì (泗).
Yuān (淵) was dispatched to console and reward the northern expeditionary forces.
Upon his return, Yuān (淵) reported to the Emperor, saying:
“West of Xūyí (盱眙),
military preparedness is insufficient.
It is advisable to redistribute soldiers.
Rǔyīn (汝陰) and Jīngtíng (荊亭) are already under siege,
and Ānfēng (安豐) is no longer defensible.
The forces in Shòuchūn (壽春)
are only sufficient for self-preservation.
If cavalry harasses Shòuyáng (壽陽),
then Jiāngwài (江外) will be in dire peril.
Lìyáng (歷陽), Guābù (瓜步), Zhōnglí (鍾離), and Yìyáng (義陽) all require significant forces and heavy garrisons,
with capable individuals chosen to command them.”
When the Emperor was still a prince,
he and Yuān (淵) were well acquainted due to their long-standing friendship.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he deeply entrusted Yuān (淵) with important matters,
and all his suggestions were adopted.
He was granted the altered title of Count of Yúdū (雩都) County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中),
and concurrently served as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍).
Soon after, he was transferred to Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
He was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Wúxìng (吳興),
retaining his position as Chángshì (常侍).
His rank was increased by a thousand dàn (石) of grain,
but he firmly declined the increased rank.
When Emperor Míng (明) became gravely ill,
he urgently sent for Yuān (淵)
and entrusted him with the affairs after his death.
The Emperor planned to execute Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén (建安王休仁),
but Yuān (淵) strongly remonstrated against it,
though his advice was not heeded.
He was again appointed Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書),
concurrently holding his former positions as Chángshì (常侍) and Wèiwèi (衞尉).
He declined the appointment,
so he was then appointed Yòu Púshè (右僕射),
retaining his position as Wèiwèi (衞尉).
Because his mother was elderly and infirm,
requiring care morning and night, Yuān (淵)
firmly declined the position of Wèiwèi (衞尉),
but his request was not granted.
When Emperor Míng (明) passed away,
the imperial will appointed him Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令) and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍),
with the additional title of Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and together with Shàngshū Lìng Yuán Càn (尚書令袁粲), he received the deathbed commission
to assist the young emperor.
Yuān (淵) wholeheartedly worked to manage all state affairs.
After a period of extravagance,
he diligently promoted frugality,
which benefited the common people.
He received guests and visitors
without ever showing arrogance or weariness.
When Wáng Dàolóng (王道隆) and Ruǎn Tiánfū (阮佃夫) held power,
bribery was rampant,
which Yuān (淵) was unable to stop.
He suffered the loss of his stepmother, Guō (郭) clan.
His filial piety was profound;
for several days,
he was so emaciated that he was unrecognizable.
For a full year, he did not wash his hair or comb it,
and only when tears flowed could his true countenance be seen.
An imperial edict ordered him to cease mourning,
and forbade guests from offering condolences.
After the funeral,
he was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍),
retaining his original positions.
In the second year of Yuánhuī (元徽) (474 CE),
Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範) rebelled.
Yuān (淵) and Wèi Jiāngjūn Yuán Càn (衞將軍袁粲) entered to defend the imperial palace
and stabilize the morale of the people.
When Yuān (淵) was first Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹),
he rode out with his younger cousin Zhào (炤).
On the road, they encountered Tàizǔ (太祖).
Yuān (淵) pointed to Tàizǔ’s (太祖) carriage and said to Zhào (炤):
“This is no ordinary person.”
When he was appointed Grand Administrator of Wúxìng (吳興),
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent him a special gift.
Yuān (淵) again said of him:
“This man’s talent and appearance are extraordinary;
his future is unfathomable.”
And at the time of the deathbed commission,
he brought Tàizǔ (太祖) into the process.
After Tài-zǔ had pacified Guìyáng,
he was transferred to Central Army Commander (Zhōng-lǐng-jūn),
concurrently Governor of Southern Yùn Province (Nán Yùn-zhōu),
and his enfeoffment was increased.
Tài-zǔ firmly declined,
and wrote a letter to Yuān and the Army Protector Yuán Càn, saying:
"This humble official is an ordinary man,
whose ambitions do not reach far.
Driven by circumstances,
I have improperly stepped into positions beyond my capacity.
My talent is meager, but my responsibility is heavy;
I am constantly fearful and vigilant.
Recently, when the state was in peril,
all sentient beings rallied together;
how much more so for this humble official?
How could I begrudge my life?
Treading on swords and hot coals,
repaying with loyalty is only natural.
Yet the ceremonies of commendation and reward
have singled me out for grace,
raising me to the highest military ranks,
and adding to my official title and lands.
Looking up to the celestial path,
my soul and spirit tremble and fall.
This humble official serves his superiors with sincerity,
acting according to his nature without pretense.
Though I have been undeservedly burdened before and since,
I have never firmly declined.
However, regarding the current appointment,
I am particularly deeply apprehensive.
This is truly because, having previously received the imperial favor,
my duty extended to avenging the throne.
But my understanding was obscured, failing to prevent the sprouts of trouble,
and my clansmen instigated disaster.
I have already brought reproach upon myself and taken the blame.
Since I have already shown a shameless face,
how can I again take advantage of misfortune to seek good fortune,
and leverage chaos to gain nobility?
This is truly a disgrace to the state,
and not something a loyal subject can endure.
Moreover, honor must not be abused,
and favor must not be obscured.
I beg to be excused from the Central Guard position,
and request to halt the increase in my enfeoffment.
Thus, I hope to maintain contentment,
and contribute my efforts on the banks of the Huái River.
If I were to lead an expedition against the Xiōngnú,
and return victorious with banners unfurled,
then I would accept the爵 title,
and no longer firmly decline."
Yuān and Càn replied:
"Your recent message is truly insightful;
we respect it endlessly.
Your humility is sincere,
and we deeply perceive it to be unadorned.
This sincerity and this intention
have long been evident beyond your words.
How much more so now, as you lay open your heart and express your thoughts in writing,
projecting your feelings and considering yourself,
it is indeed worthy of being inscribed on one's sash.
However, what needs to be deliberated upon now
must be weighed by its importance.
The world is plagued by many difficulties,
and affairs are dilapidated.
The four cardinal virtues are in disarray,
and the border people are not at peace.
The state's expenditures are vast,
and the treasuries need to be replenished.
The northern barbarians invade the borders,
and worries and anxieties press upon us.
All sentient beings within the realm
are still anxious for the safety of the world.
Given that we share such a heavy responsibility and trust,
can we still pursue honesty and retreat?
Looking into our hearts,
we truly believe it is impossible.
Understanding its impossibility,
there is no reason to stubbornly adhere to it.
Moreover, the powerful enemy is utterly vicious,
their momentum is like a prairie fire.
The suddenness of the transgression
is unprecedented throughout history.
In times of constant fear and confusion,
we must plan ahead.
Building strongholds at Xīntíng,
and sleeping on our spears awaiting the enemy,
such decisive strategies
had their profound reasons.
As soon as blades clashed,
the chief culprit was brought to justice.
Your leadership and ingenious strategies
were decisively proven by this action.
To enfeoff you with ten thousand households
and elevate you to the highest ranks
is hardly a sufficient reward for your merits and labors,
or even to roughly satisfy public opinion.
Now, as a close attendant and commander of the imperial guards,
to be promoted to Central Guard (Zhōng-hòu),
riding on the pacification of the realm and following the official dispatch,
this acquisition is not excessive.
Jǐ and Hé were previously your pastures (domain),
but your rank as Garrison General (Zhèn-jūn) did not exceed your original one.
Upon careful examination of the ranks,
we are ashamed that it is not yet superior enough.
Adding to it, even with reduction,
would particularly diminish the court's system.
Having served in office for several years,
few of us were in the same boat.
Liú Lǐng-jūn's integrity was as clear as frost;
he faced danger without hesitation.
His voice and traces have not yet faded,
yet he is already gone into history.
Lost without a companion,
our grief is beyond sorrow.
The critical military responsibilities entrusted to you
are now doubly urgent.
If you cling to your integrity and decline honors,
to whom shall these responsibilities be entrusted?
Indeed, the military command relies on what is expected,
and naturally enhances the nation's integrity.
Even a commoner's pledge
should be honored.
The ruler's command must be carried out;
what path is there for hesitation?
Generally, those who stand at the head of the people
and whose achievements are foremost among the multitude,
their proper actions regarding advancement and retreat
should be shared with the multitude.
If you merely pursue personal virtue,
how can you manage affairs?
To accept without selfishness
further reveals your utmost impartiality.
We have thoroughly investigated your memorial,
and it is impossible without it.
We hope you will consider the extraordinary circumstances
and deeply reflect, then accept it."
Tài-zǔ then accepted the command.
In that year,
Yuān was additionally appointed President of the Board of Civil Office (Shàngshū-lìng) and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords.
He firmly declined the presidency.
Three years later,
he was promoted to the rank of Marquis (Hóu),
and his enfeoffment was increased by a thousand households.
After the mourning period ended,
he was reassigned as Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū-jiān),
with his positions as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Army Protector (Hù-jūn) remaining as before,
and was granted one set of drum and wind instruments.
The following year,
Yuān's late stepmother, Princess Wújùn, passed away.
He became emaciated as before.
After the funeral,
an imperial edict ordered him to resume his duties,
but he firmly declined.
Later, as the first anniversary of mourning approached,
he again submitted a memorial to resign his posts,
but neither request was granted.
As Cāngwú's tyranny grew increasingly severe,
Tài-zǔ discussed current affairs with Yuān and Yuán Càn.
Càn said:
"The young emperor's minor faults are easy to rectify.
The affairs of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng
are not suitable for a declining era.
Even if such a feat were accomplished,
there would ultimately be no safe place."
Yuān remained silent,
and inclined his heart towards Tài-zǔ.
When Cāngwú was finally deposed,
the high officials gathered for a discussion.
As Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng refused to take responsibility,
Yuān said:
"Without Duke Xiāo, this matter cannot be settled."
He personally took a document and handed it to Tài-zǔ.
Tài-zǔ said:
"If you two refuse,
how can I decline?"
Thus the matter was settled.
Upon Emperor Shùn's ascension,
he was reappointed as Grand General of the Guards (Wèi-jiāngjūn) with the privileges of opening a mansion and establishing staff (kāi-fǔ-yí-tóng-sān-sī),
his position as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) remaining as before.
Fifty armed guards entered the palace.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
Yuán Càn harbored dissent.
Tài-zǔ summoned Yuān for consultation,
and Yuān said:
"The conflict and difficulties in Xī Xià
will surely fail.
You should first prepare for internal matters."
Tài-zǔ secretly made preparations.
When the matter was settled,
he was promoted to Central Secretariat Supervisor (Zhōngshū-jiān) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
his original posts remaining as before.
When Qí Tái was established,
Chǔ Yuān, to Tàizǔ, cited Hé Céng being transferred from Wèi Sìtú to Jìn Chéngxiàng,
and requested to be a Qí official.
Tàizǔ humbly declined.
In the first year of Jiàn yuán,
he was promoted to Sìtú,
with Shìzhōng and Zhōngshūjiān as before.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Nánkāng Commandery,
with an estate of three thousand households.
Chǔ Yuān firmly declined the Sìtú position.
He wrote a letter to Púyè Wáng Jiǎn,
wishing to follow Cài Mó's precedent.
Wáng Jiǎn deemed it inappropriate for Chǔ Yuān to say such a thing,
and advised Chǔ Yuān to accept the appointment.
Chǔ Yuān ultimately did not take it.
Chǔ Yuān had a beautiful appearance,
and a graceful demeanor.
His every movement, whether bowing, rising, advancing, or retreating,
was full of elegance.
Whenever there was a court assembly,
officials and envoys from distant lands [使] all craned their necks to watch him depart.
[一二]Sòng Míngdì once sighed,
"Chǔ Yuān can walk slowly and deliberately,
and with this alone, he can become a prime minister."
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshūlìng,
with his previous offices remaining.
In the second year,
the former decree was reiterated for him to be Sìtú,
but he again firmly declined.
In that year, the barbarians became restless.
The Emperor wanted to conscript all officials from dukes and princes downwards who held no office into the army.
[一三]Chǔ Yuān advised that this would be of no practical use,
and would only cause disturbance.
The Emperor then stopped.
Regarding crucial matters of the court,
he was often consulted,
and his advice was usually adopted.
He was treated with great respect.
When the Emperor held a grand banquet,
he said to his ministers after drinking,
"You are all dukes and ministers from the Sòng era;
surely you wouldn't say that I deserve to be Son of Heaven."
Before Wáng Jiǎn and others could reply,
Chǔ Yuān straightened his tablet and said,
"Your Majesty must not say that I did not recognize the dragon's face early."
[一四]The Emperor laughed and said,
"I am ashamed before Wénshú,
as I have known you to be Zhū Yòu [祜] for a long time."
[一五]
Chǔ Yuān was widely read and skilled in discussion,
and adept at playing the pípa.
When Shìzǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he bestowed upon Chǔ Yuān a pípa with a gold-inlaid handle and silver pegs.
His nature was gentle and refined, with great magnanimity.
He acted cautiously,
once his residence caught fire,
and the smoke and flames were very close,
his attendants were alarmed and flustered,
but Chǔ Yuān remained serene,
summoned his palanquin, and calmly departed.
Some frivolous individuals criticized him regarding his reputation and integrity.
Because Chǔ Yuān had a lot of white in his eyes,
they called him
"A white rainbow piercing the sun,"
implying it was an omen for the Sòng dynasty's demise.
When Tàizǔ died,
his dying edict appointed Chǔ Yuān as Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Since the time of the Eastern Jìn,
no one had been solely appointed as Lù,
so officials debated whether to establish a special decree.
Shàngshū Wáng Jiǎn deliberated,
believing that
"Given he already holds an official position,
and is separately appointed as Lù,
logically there should be an official document (cèshū),
but old records do not contain such a precedent.
Since the Central Dynasties,
for the Sān Gōng, princes, and marquises,
both 'excellent decree' (yōucè) and 'decree' (cè) are issued.
For officials of the second rank,
only 'decree' is issued, not 'excellent decree'.
'Excellent decree' praises virtues,
while 'decree' also clarifies the entrustment.
The office of Shàngshū is a heavenly office,
the foundation of government and transformation.
[故]Therefore, although Shàngshūlìng is of the third rank,
[一六]an appointment must come with a 'decree'.
The rank of Lù Shàngshū is not explicitly stated,
yet its overall responsibility is extremely important.
In previous dynasties, it was often conferred together with another official position,
thus no separate 'decree' was issued.
Considering the circumstances and sentiments,
it should not be treated the same as ordinary officials.
An official document (cèshū) is appropriate
to express the grand entrustment.
Since it differs from princes and marquises,
an 'excellent decree' is unnecessary."
This was followed.
Soon after, Chǔ Yuān's retinue of sword-bearers was increased to thirty,
and he was to attend court once every five days.
After some time, he fell ill.
The Emperor observed unusual stellar phenomena,
which worried Chǔ Yuān,
so he submitted a memorial to resign his position.
He also had Wáng Jiǎn and Shìzhōng Wáng Yàn verbally convey his request to Shìzǔ,
but Shìzǔ did not permit it.
He then submitted another memorial, saying:
"I, considering my humble and insignificant self,
find that excessive blessings lead to disaster.
I am unable to find peace with a righteous mind,
and feel deeply ashamed before Yànfǔ.
Since I harbor such a profound reservation,
I feel that every moment is difficult to endure.
I have not held this position for long,
yet at the beginning of the year, I fell seriously ill.
Since then, I have been chronically ill,
repeatedly experiencing critical situations,
which deepens my anxiety and fear.
Your Majesty's compassionate hesitation,
or perhaps the differing opinions of the assembly,
stems from excessive benevolence and love, wishing for my glory.
I am forty-eight years old,
and have been undeservedly honored thus.
To resign due to illness,
how could it alarm Your Majesty's keen observation?
The office of Zǒnglù [Recorder-General]
has been rarely bestowed in the South since the Eastern Jìn,
it ranks close to the Vice-Prime Minister,
its rise and fall are indeed subtle.
[一七]Now, I do not decline to receive the emoluments,
but my wish is to retire.
For my reputation and position,
this cannot be called a degradation.
All eyes and ears
clearly see this.
How can I presume to prolong Your Majesty's consideration,
and slightly indulge in pity?
If I were to internally adorn myself with a reputation for integrity,
and externally follow the path of modesty and humility,
[一八]then the imperial censors would impeach me,
and the legal system would enforce discipline.
[一九]My true sincerity cannot be denied;
neither the seen nor the unseen would forgive me.
With my humble heart,
I submit this memorial truthfully.
I begrudge every moment,
and sincerely wish for a time twice as long as the age of Yáo.
[二０]In the past, Wáng Hóng earnestly requested to resign,
and was transferred from Sìtú to Wèi Jiāngjūn.
The Sòng dynasty carried this out without hesitation,
