and at the time, no one had any differing opinions.
Compared to me,
what is there to say?
I humbly wish Your Majesty to expand upon your grand vision,
and graciously grant this request,
then the day of my death
would be like the years of my life."
He was then reassigned to Sīkōng,
and concurrently held Pìyào Jìangjūn,
with Shìzhōng and Lù Shàngshū as before.
The Emperor sent Shìzhōng Wáng Yàn and Huángmén Láng Wáng Xiùzhī to inquire about his illness.
He passed away.
His family had no surplus wealth,
and owed hundreds of thousands in debt.
An imperial edict stated:
"The Sìtú suddenly passed away.
I am deeply pained and sorrowful.
Although recently ill,
I will force myself to go and mourn him.
Grant him the secret funerary items from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
two hundred thousand coins,
two hundred rolls of cloth,
and two hundred catties of wax."
At that time, the clerks of the Sīkōng office wondered, since Chǔ Yuān had not yet officially assumed office,
whether they should observe the proper courtesies for an official.
Wáng Jiǎn deliberated:
"According to ritual,
if a wife on her way to her husband's home
hears of a death in his family,
she changes her clothes before entering.
Now, although the clerks have not yet performed service,
their official conduct is derived from the imperial court,
so they should observe ritual courtesies."
The staff of the Sìtú mansion also questioned whether, since Chǔ Yuān had resigned from his post,
and had not yet formally accepted the new appointment,
the mansion should still observe mourning attire.
Wáng Jiǎn again deliberated:
"According to the precedent of Shìsūn Dézǔ from the Central Dynasties, who was transferred from Lèlíng to Chénliú,
but died [卒]
before reaching the border,
[二一]the officials of Lèlíng Commandery observed mourning as for an existing lord,
while the welcoming officials of Chénliú observed the rites for a daughter married on an auspicious day, which is 'zícuī' (mourning clothes of uneven edges) for mourning.
Thus, the Sìtú mansion should observe the mourning rites as for an incumbent official."
Furthermore, an edict stated:
"To commend virtue is to set a standard for the people,
and to be careful in the end is to restore generosity.
The grand customs of former kings
[二二] must all be followed.

Therefore, the Attendant-in-ordinary, Grand Minister of Works, Recorder of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat, newly appointed Grand Minister of Works, [二三] concurrently General of Agile Cavalry, and Duke of Nánkāng, Yuān,
trod the path of virtue and upheld wisdom,
with broad and far-reaching insight.
From his earliest tender years,
his pure reputation was already established.
When called to office and public service,
he commanded universal respect.
Filial piety and fraternity were manifest in his family and state,
and loyalty and integrity shone in his bright character.
He assisted in the founding of the previous dynasty,
managing the royal administration,
in times of hardship and peace,
from beginning to end.
He oversaw the crucial affairs of government,
ensuring harmony throughout the realm,
truly aligning with the rules of antiquity,
serving as a model for the present.
His humility was profound and far-reaching,
repeatedly offering to decline and withdraw,
yet forced to comply with the imperial will,
thereby causing a deficit in his grand plans.
He was about to ascend to the highest ranks,
forever supporting the voice of instruction.
Heaven did not grant him a longer life,
and he suddenly passed away,
which has deeply grieved Our heart.
Let him be posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor,
with his Attendant-in-ordinary and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat titles retained as before.
He shall be granted the ceremonial staff,
with the addition of feathered parasols and drum and fife music,
and the retinue of sword-bearing guards increased to sixty men.
The funeral rites
shall entirely follow the precedent of Wáng Hóng, the Grand Protector of Sòng.
His posthumous title shall be Wénjiǎn."
Before this, the carriages for the three ducal ministers from commoner families
had no fixed regulations.
Wáng Jiǎn proposed that all officials of the first rank
should be adorned with banners and streamers,
and this began with Yuān.
Furthermore, an edict stated that Yuān's wife, Sòng Gù Baxī Zhǔ, whose tomb had been temporarily opened,
should be posthumously granted the title of Lady of Nánkāng Commandery.
His eldest son, Bēn,
courtesy name Wèixiān.
He began his official career as a Secretary of the Imperial Library.
During the Shēngmíng era,
he served as Aide-de-camp and Middle Administrator to Grand Ancestor's Grand Commandant,
Right Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Works,
Household Staff Officer to the Grand Tutor,
Yellow Gate Attendant,
concurrently Supervisor of the Imperial Forest Guards,
Middle Administrator to the Qi Crown Prince,
concurrently Commander of the Aiding Army.
In the early Jiànyuán era,
he continued as a palace official,
successively serving as Attendant-in-ordinary.
When Yuān passed away,
after the period of mourning ended,
Bēn had an audience with Shìzǔ,
weeping uncontrollably.
The Emperor greatly praised him,
appointing him Attendant-in-ordinary,
concurrently Commander of the Infantry,
Left Minister of the Common People, [二四]
Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
Supervisor of the Imperial Library,
but he did not accept the appointment.
Six years later,
he submitted a memorial citing illness,
ceding his enfeoffment to his younger brother Zhēn.
The world believed that Bēn resented Yuān's failure to uphold integrity towards the Sòng dynasty,
and therefore refused to serve again.
He died in the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (489 CE),
and an edict granted him thirty thousand coins
and fifty bolts of cloth.
Zhēn, courtesy name Màoxù.
In the Yǒngmíng era,
he began his career as a supernumerary official,
then served as Governor of Yìxīng. [二五]
In the eighth year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Bādōng Commandery. [二六]
The following year,
he memorialized to cede his enfeoffment back to Bēn's son, Jì,
which the edict permitted.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ era,
he served as Palace Grandee to the Crown Prince,
Minister of Revenue,
and General of the Imperial Army.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (499 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
with the posthumous name Mù.
Yuān's younger brother was Chéng.
Chéng, courtesy name Yàndào.
Initially, Zhànzhī married Princess Shǐ'ān,
but after her death,
he took a concubine, Lady Guō,
who bore Yuān.
Later, he married Princess Wúqùn,
who bore Chéng.
Yuān served the Princess with filial piety and reverence,
and she loved him.
When Zhànzhī died,
the Princess memorialized to establish Yuān as the legitimate heir.
Chéng married Princess Lújiāng, daughter of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
He held various prominent and prestigious official positions.
He was skilled in medicine.
During the Jiànyuán era,
he served as Governor of Wúqùn Commandery.
When the Prince of Yùzhāng fell ill,
Grand Ancestor summoned Chéng to treat him,
and he recovered immediately.
Soon after, he was promoted to Left Minister of the Common People.
When Yuān died,
Chéng spent eleven thousand coins
to redeem the white sable mat that Grand Ancestor had given Yuān from Zhāotí Monastery,
and had it made into a fur coat and a cap string.
He also redeemed Yuān's rhinoceros-horn-decorated head-covering and the yellow ox Yuān usually rode.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (483 CE),
he was impeached by Yuán Tuàn, the Censor-in-chief,
removed from office and prohibited from holding public service,
but later pardoned.
He was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary,
concurrently General of the Right Army,
and was known for his diligence and circumspection.
He died that same year.
Chéng's daughter became Empress of Dōnghūn.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (499 CE),

At that time, Xú Sì from Dōngyáng

There was a commoner suffering from a cold illness for many years,
using multiple layers of bedding and mats,
with a brazier fire under his bed,
yet he did not recover.
Sì treated him by,
in the depth of winter,
ordering the commoner to sit naked on a stone,
and pouring a hundred bottles of water
over his head.
Initially, after a few dozen bottles,
he shivered severely, almost dying,
and his sons and younger brothers watched him, weeping.
Sì ordered them to complete the full number.
After seventy or eighty bottles,
his entire body emitted vapor like steaming clouds.
Sì ordered the bed to be removed and the covers taken away.
The next day, he was immediately able to get up and walk,
saying, "This was a severe fever."
Another time, in spring, when he went out of the south bamboo gate to relieve himself,
he heard groaning from a thatched hut.
Sì said:
"This illness is very serious;
if not treated in two more days,
he will surely die."
So he went to examine the person.
An old woman complained of pain all over her body,
and there were countless festering black spots everywhere.
Sì returned, boiled over a sheng of broth, and sent it for her to drink.
After the old woman drank it,
the pain became even more intense,
and she repeatedly jumped onto the bed.
In a short while,
all the festering spots were pulled out, about an inch long. [一八]
Then he applied ointment to all the sores,
and in three days, she recovered,
saying, "This is called a nail carbuncle."
There were many such verified cases,
surpassing Chéng's abilities.
Wáng Jiǎn, courtesy name Zhòngbǎo,

His grandfather, Tánshǒu,

His father, Sēngzhuó,

Jiǎn was born when Sēngzhuó was murdered,

At several years old,

As a child, he possessed divine intelligence,

Yuán Càn, the Administrator of Dānyáng, heard of his reputation

He married Princess Yángxiàn

The Emperor considered that Jiǎn's legitimate mother, Princess Wǔkāng, was involved in the witchcraft incident of Tàichū,

He was appointed Mìshū Láng

In the first year of Jiànyuán,

The Emperor ordered the dismantling of Emperor Míng of Sòng’s Zǐjí Diàn,

Jiǎn, Chǔ Yuān, and his paternal uncle Sēngqín jointly submitted a memorial advising against it, stating:

Those two rulers,

If our humble petition is deemed correct,

The Emperor responded with an imperial rescript, accepting their advice.
During the Sòng dynasty, the outer six gates had bamboo fences.
Early this year,

and changed to erecting a dúfāng (wooden palisade).
Jiǎn again remonstrated,

The court was in its initial stages,

Jiǎn was knowledgeable about old affairs,

In that year,

He was given the additional title of Shìzhōng,

The Emperor (Shàng) held a banquet for several officials,

Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) played the pípa,
Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔) played the qín,
Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) sang "Zǐyè" (子夜),

Jiǎn (儉) said:

He then knelt before the Emperor and recited Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's (司馬相如) "Fēngshàn Shū" (封禪書).
The Emperor laughed and said:

how can I be worthy of it?"
Later, the Emperor ordered Lù Chéng (陸澄) to recite the Xiàojīng (孝經),
starting
from "Zhòngní jū" (仲尼居).
Jiǎn (儉) said:

He then recited
the chapter "Jūnzǐ zhī shì shàng" (君子之事上).
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!
Zhāng Zǐbù (張子布) is indeed extraordinary."
Soon after, he was appointed太子詹事 (tàizǐ zhānshì) in his current official capacity,

[四０] When the Emperor (Shàng) passed away,
his will appointed Jiǎn (儉) as Shìzhōng (侍中), Shàngshūlìng (尚書令), and Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍).
[四一] When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was granted twenty attendants with ceremonial swords.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (永明) [483 CE],
he was promoted to Wèi Jūn Jiāngjūn (衞軍將軍),
[四二] and participated in overseeing official selections.
In the second year [484 CE],

He was granted a set of ceremonial music (gǔchuī).
In the third year [485 CE],
he was again appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒).
When his paternal uncle Sēngqián (僧虔) passed away,
Jiǎn (儉) submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post,

He was also appointed Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅) and Běnzhōu Zhōngzhèng (本州中正),

Previously, the Tàizǐ's (太子) two grand tutors (Jìng Èr Fù) were treated equally;

In this year,
the Zǒngmíng Guān (總明觀) was abolished,
and a school for scholars (xuèshì guǎn) was established at Jiǎn's (儉) residence.
All the books of the four divisions were moved to Jiǎn's (儉) home,
and an edict also ordered Jiǎn (儉) to make his home a government office (fǔ).
In the fourth year [486 CE],
he was appointed Lìbù (吏部) in his existing capacity.
Jiǎn (儉) excelled in ritual studies
and was thoroughly versed in court ceremonies.
Whenever there was a broad discussion,
he would cite and provide evidence from earlier Confucians,
a rare occurrence.
The eight high-ranking officials and their assistants
could not surpass him.
When clerks consulted him on affairs,
and guests filled his seats,
Jiǎn (儉) handled and arranged them,
leaving no one waiting on the side.
Every ten days, he would return to the school,
supervise the examinations of the students.
With his cap and scrolls in the courtyard,
and his sword-wielding guards and clerks, his demeanor was very imposing.
He wore his hair in a loose bun,
with his hair-pin inserted diagonally into his head-wrap (zé).
Both the court and the common people admired him
and imitated his style.
Jiǎn (儉) often said to people:
"Among the elegant prime ministers south of the Yangtze,
only Xiè Ān (謝安) stands out."
He was, in fact, comparing himself to Xiè Ān (謝安).
Shìzǔ (世祖) deeply trusted and relied on him,
and his recommendations for the selection and appointment of scholars
were never rejected.
In the fifth year [487 CE],
he was granted the title and status of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) in his current position,
but he firmly declined.
In the sixth year [488 CE],
the previous order was reiterated.
Earlier, an edict ordered Jiǎn (儉) to return to court every three days.
When Shàngshū (尚書) clerks went out to consult him on affairs,

again ordered Jiǎn (儉) to return to the Shàngshū Xiàshěng (尚書下省),
allowing him to go out for ten days each month.
Jiǎn (儉) petitioned to be released from the selection duties,
but it was not granted.
In the seventh year [489 CE],
he then submitted a memorial, stating:
"For several years I have resigned from selection duties,
fully explaining to Your Sagacious Majesty,
[四三] my heartfelt words manifest in my service,
my sincere loyalty spread throughout the court and the land.
Public opinion does not deem it wrong,
yet Your Sacred Heart has not seen fit to accept it.
I have heard that wisdom is not as good as opportune times;
seeking this in my humble self,
it truly aligns with this meaning.
An arrogant and mediocre person,
floating without merit,
by chance encountered peace and prosperity,
and thus walked on the broad path.
Autumn leaves fall from branches
without the force of a strong wind;
the sun rises to its height
without waiting for the glow of a firefly.
Darkness departs, brightness arrives,
the Five Virtues (wǔdé) rotate;
the sage does not rule alone,
the Eight Primal Talents (bāyuán) shine forth.
I encountered this era,
and usurped this position,
constantly overseeing the central government,
frequently managing selections and evaluations.
My service spans two reigns,
extending over twelve years.
My prime years have passed,
my grandsons are now of age to wear caps.
People change and pass on,
nearly half of those who were have departed.
Three evaluations have yielded no renown,
the nine streams of thought (jiǔliú) are silent.
The praise for capable officials
has ceased in this time;
the satire of the 'Great Carriage' (dàchē)
will only arise in the future.
As for the nobility of wearing貂 (diāo) and衮 (gǔn) robes,
and the splendor of the Four Assistants and Six Teachers (sìfǔ liùjiào),
I sincerely know I am unworthy.
Although duties may be simpler,
and the position of prime minister heavy,
I could still exert myself.
However, for the responsibility of evaluating and classifying,
I especially fear my inadequacy.
From dawn to dusk I have exhausted myself,
repeatedly tried without success.
The length of time
is rarely matched in recent generations.
Not only are there regrets and faults in myself,
but this has also brought dust and burden to the nation.
Currently, numerous scholars fill the court,
and all talents compete brilliantly.
Who in ancient times chose from such a multitude and appointed them?
I presumptuously present this humble petition,
earnestly hoping for Your Heavenly Illumination.
The utmost reverence has no need for florid words;
I dare not trouble or defile."
His request was granted.
He was reassigned as Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監),
participating in the management of selections.
In that year, he fell ill.
The Emperor (Shàng) personally visited him.
He died

Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Wáng Yàn (王晏) presented a memorial regarding Jiǎn's (儉) death,
to which the Emperor (Shàng) replied:
"Jiǎn (儉) was rich in years and virtue,

How could I have expected a sudden illness,

so suddenly like this?
My grief is even deeper.
His hardships and difficult fortune,
his profound loyalty, I always held dear.
As I speak, sadness overwhelms me,
I cannot control myself.
Ah, how painful!
Ah, he is gone! "
An edict ordered that all military and civil officials of the Wèi Jūn (衞軍) and the troops from the Imperial Secretariat (Tái suǒ bīngzhàng) were to remain on standby for the funeral.
[四四]
Again, an imperial edict stated:
"Being mindful of the end and reverent towards ancestors

embodied the Way and possessed sagely wisdom;
his bearing was profound and expansive.
From his tender years,
his pure principles shone forth.
When he ascended to court to manage affairs,

He established the imperial foundation in its nascent stages,
helping to prosper the dynastic rule.
His grand strategies and glorious achievements
are inscribed in enduring records.
And when he assisted Our person,
his admirable merits were resplendent and abundant.
His loyal plans and excellent models
were evident in every action.
The four quarters were truly harmonious,
and all affairs were in their proper order.
As a prominent minister,
Our trust in him was extraordinary.
He was about to assume a high position to discuss the Way,
and forever bring order to the affairs of government,
assisting in this magnificent transformation,
to aid in a flourishing peace.
Heaven did not pity and leave him to us,
but suddenly he passed away.
We are deeply grieved in Our heart.
He is posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi (太尉).
His titles of Sīzhōng (侍中), Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), and Duke remain as before.
He is granted the jié (節),
and additionally bestowed with feather canopies and military music (yǔbǎo gǔchuī 鼓吹).
The number of attendant swordsmen (bānjiàn 班劒) is increased to sixty.
His funeral rites shall follow the precedent of the late Tàizǎi Wénjiǎn Gōng (太宰文簡公) Chǔ Yuān (褚淵).
The construction of his tomb and grave materials shall be handled by government officials.
His posthumous title is Wénxiàn Gōng (文憲公)."
Jiǎn (儉) had few desires,
devoting himself solely to affairs of state.
His carriages and clothes were plain,
and his household had no surplus wealth.
His calligraphy and literary style were exemplary,
and highly valued at the time.
In his youth, he compiled the Gǔjīn Sāngfú Jí Jì (古今喪服集記) and a collection of his own writings (wénjí 文集),
both of which circulated in the world.
When the present emperor received the abdication,
he issued an edict to erect a stele for Jiǎn (儉),
and downgraded his peerage to marquis,
with a thousand households.
Jiǎn's (儉) younger brother, Xùn (遜),
during the Shēngmíng (昇明) era,
served as Dānyáng Céng (丹陽丞).
He reported Liú Bǐng's (劉秉) affairs,
but received no enfeoffment or reward.
In the early Jiàn Yuán (建元) era,
he became the Prefect of Jìnlíng (晉陵 Tàishǒu 太守).
He uttered resentful words.
Jiǎn (儉) worried this would lead to trouble,
and so reported it through Chǔ Yuān's (褚淵) memorial.
The Zhōngchéng (中丞) Lù Chéng (陸澄) impeached him according to the facts.
An imperial edict stated:
"Jiǎn's (儉) family has for generations upheld virtue
and wholeheartedly assisted Our mandate.
Therefore, the penal code is specially mitigated,
pardoning Xùn (遜) with exile."
He was exiled to Yǒngjiā (永嘉) Commandery,
but was executed on the way.
The historian remarks: Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) and Yuán Càn (袁粲)
were both entrusted by Emperor Míng (明帝) of Sòng (宋).
Càn (粲) died a loyal death for the Sòng (宋) clan,
while Yuān (淵) encountered the rising fortunes of the new dynasty.
Many people in the world blame Yuān (淵).
I request to discuss this: The paths of Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武)
differed from those of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜);
the intentions of Yī (伊) and Lǚ (呂)
were also not those of Jì (稷) and Xiè (契).
Therefore, these historical precedents
are not sufficient to serve as proof.
From the prominent families of Jīn (金) and Zhāng (張),
and the esteemed Yuán (袁) and Yáng (楊),
who pledged their allegiance and served righteousness, all of whom derived from the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
their prominence and wealth
arose from this.
When the Wèi (魏) clan reigned,
their dynastic lifespan was short.
Some served the previous dynasty in humble attire,
and achieved officialdom in the succeeding court.
When the Jìn (晉) clan ascended to power,
they engaged with them.
Though nominally ministers of Wèi (魏),
they were in reality possessed by Jìn (晉).
Thus, though the sovereign's position changed,
the minister's duties remained as before.
From this, the prosperity of hereditary salaries
became a customary norm.
Those whose prominence was exalted
were admired by people,
and the principle of loyalty between ruler and minister
became merely an empty name.
Noble appointments and wealth
all came from family blessings.
Those who advanced smoothly
rose to high positions as dukes and ministers merely by sitting.
Thus, the sentiment of dying for one's country had no cause,
and the thought of preserving one's family was naturally more pressing.
Courts and marketplaces frequently changed,
while favor and wealth arrived steadily.
Though the imperial palaces differed,
their gazes were unchanged.
Zhōng Háng (中行) and Zhì Bó (智伯)
did not experience different treatment.
Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), in the early years of Tàishǐ (泰始),
already had a clear path to prominence.
Within a few years,
he had no fear of being without position.
Since he was drawn in by popular expectation,
he also departed with popular expectation.
Indeed, rank and salary are trivial,
and are common choices for those with a country.
Grace is not exclusive to oneself.
To demand death from others
is a common fallacy of rulers,
and an excessive error of worldly sentiment.
A eulogy says: Oh, Master Chǔ (褚)!
His virtue was internally abundant.
His popular reputation was unfailing,
his family's renown was well-established.
Calmly he assisted the world,
his advice was not self-serving.
Wénxiàn (文憲) was dignified and poised,
a model of an assisting minister.
He praised kings and hegemons,
maintaining the order of rites and laws.
His hopes were placed in both dynasties,
entwined with the imperial palace.

Liǔ Shìlóng (柳世隆), courtesy name Yànxù (彥緒),
was a native of Xiè (解), Hédōng (河東).
His grandfather, Píng (憑),
was the Prefect of Féngyì (馮翊).
His father, Shú Zōng (叔宗),
died young.
Shìlóng (世隆) was talented and dignified from a young age.
His paternal uncle, Yuán Jǐng (元景),
was the Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) during the Dàmíng (大明) era of Sòng (宋),
and admired him uniquely,
more than his own sons.
He spoke to Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝),
and Shìlóng (世隆) was granted an audience.
The emperor said:
"He will be one of the Three Dukes (Sāngōng 三公)
in the future."
When Hǎilíng Wáng (海陵王) Xiūmào (休茂) was in Yōngzhōu (雍州),
he appointed Shìlóng (世隆) as Yíng Zhǔbù (迎主簿).
He was appointed as Fǔjūn Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn (撫軍法曹行參軍) for Xīyáng Wáng (西陽王),
then went out to serve as Hǔwēi Jiāngjūn (虎威將軍)
and Prefect of Shàngyǒng (上庸 Tàishǒu 太守).
The emperor said to Yuán Jǐng (元景):
"You were once given the title 'Hǔwēi' (虎威) and served in Suí Jùn (隨郡);
now it is given again to Shìlóng (世隆),
so that your family's line of dukes may not be cut off."
Yuán Jǐng (元景) was killed by Jǐng Hé (景和),
but Shìlóng (世隆) escaped because he was far away.
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
when various prefectures rebelled,
Shìlóng (世隆) found an opportunity to redeem his family's misfortune,
an affair initiated by Emperor Míng (明帝).
He therefore held his commandery and raised an army,
sending envoys to respond to the imperial court.
Liú Sēnglín (劉僧驎) of Hóngnóng (弘農) also gathered a multitude to respond to him.
He amassed ten thousand men
and suddenly arrived at Wàn Shān (萬山) in Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
but was defeated by Kǒng Dàocún (孔道存).
His forces all scattered,
and he barely escaped with his life,
hiding among the common people.
He emerged when the situation was pacified.
He returned to serve as Shàngshū Yícáo Láng (尚書儀曹郎).
Emperor Míng (明帝) praised his righteous heart
and issued an edict promoting him to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬).
He then went out to serve as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (寧遠將軍)
and Prefect of Bāxī Zǐtóng (巴西梓潼 Tàishǒu 太守).
He returned to serve as Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉),
then transferred to Jiànpíng Wáng Zhènběi Zīyì Cānjūn (建平王鎮北諮議參軍),
concurrently Nán Tàishān Tàishǒu (南泰山太守),
then transferred to Sīmǎ (司馬) and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu (東海太守),
and entered to serve as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍).
Soon after, he became Jìn Xīwáng Ānxī Sīmǎ (晉熙王安西司馬),
and was given the additional title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍).
At this time, Shìzǔ (世祖) was a Chángshǐ (長史),
and he and Shìlóng (世隆) met with great joy.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) planned to cross to Guǎnglíng (廣陵),
he ordered Shìzǔ (世祖) to lead his troops down,
to gather together in Jīngyì (京邑).
Shìlóng (世隆) and the Chángliú (長流) Xiāo Jǐngxiān (蕭景先) and others prepared for war and awaited the appointed time,
but the plan was not carried out.
At this time, the imperial court suspected and feared Shěn Yōuzhī,
secretly preparing defenses against him.
The tools and weapons of the prefectural and state administrations
had all been prepared in advance.
When Shìzǔ was about to go down to the capital,
Liú Huáizhēn advised Tàizǔ, saying:
"Xiàkǒu is a strategically important military location;
it needs a suitable person."
Tàizǔ accepted this,
and wrote to Shìzǔ, saying:
"Since you are entering the court,
you must find someone who is both civil and military and whose intentions align with yours,
to entrust with future matters.
Shìlóng is that person."
Shìzǔ nominated Shìlóng to replace him.
He was transferred to be the Prefect of Wǔlíng Wáng’s Vanguard, Administrator of Jiāngxià, and acting Prefect of Yǐngzhōu.
In the winter of Shēngmíng元年 (the first year of Shēngmíng),
Yōuzhī rebelled,

sending Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Central Army Adjutant) Sūn Tóng, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wǔ Bǎo, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (Dragon Soaring General) and Qíbīng Cānjūn (Cavalry Adjutant) Zhū Jūnbá, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Shěn Huìzhēn, and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Qíbīng Cānjūn Wáng Dào with thirty thousand men as the vanguard.

He also sent Sīmǎ (Military Administrator) and Guānjūn (Champion Army) Liú Rǎngbīng, leading Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Wàibīng Cānjūn (Outer Army Adjutant) Gōngsūn Fāngpíng, Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Qíbīng Cānjūn Zhū Língzhēn,
Shěn Sēngjìng, and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Gāo Mào with twenty thousand men to follow.
He further dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wáng Língxiù,
Dīng Zhēndōng, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wáng Mízhī,
and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Wàibīng Cānjūn Yáng Jǐngmù with two thousand cavalry to split off and emerge from Xiàkǒu,
occupying Lǔshān.
Yōuzhī took a light skiff with several hundred men, going ahead of the main army to stay at Báiluózhōu,
sitting on a camp stool to watch his troops,
displaying an air of arrogance.
Upon arriving at Yǐng,
thinking the city of Yǐng was small and not worth attacking,
he sent someone to inform Shìlóng, saying:
"By order of the Grand Empress Dowager,
I must briefly return to the capital.
Since we both serve the state,
I trust you understand this."
Shìlóng sent a reply, saying:
"The army heading east
has been renowned for a long time.
Yǐngchéng is a small town,
merely defending itself."
When Yōuzhī was about to leave,
Shìlóng sent troops to challenge him at Xīzhǔ.
Yōuzhī indeed grew angry,
ordering his armies to land and burn the outer city and settlements,
building a long siege line to attack the road.
He turned to his men and said:
"With this, what city
cannot be conquered!"
They attacked day and night,
and Shìlóng responded appropriately,
repelling all their advances.
When Shìzǔ first descended,
he parted with Shìlóng,
saying:
"If Yōuzhī suddenly rebels,
burns the boats at Xiàkǒu, and goes east along the current,
then sitting and defending an empty city
will be uncontrollable.
Even if he stays to attack the city,
it cannot be taken quickly.
If you are on the inside,
and I am on the outside,
then there will be no worries."
At this point, Shìzǔ sent eight armies, including Jūnjǔ (Army Commander) Huán Jìng, Chén Yìnshū, and Gǒu Yuánbīn, to occupy Xīsài,
ordering them to fortify their positions and await the enemy's exhaustion.
Fearing Shìlóng's extreme danger,
he sent his trusted confidant Hú Yuánzhí to secretly enter Yǐngchéng to convey news of the relief forces,
which brought joy both inside and outside.
The Shàngshū (Minister) memorialized: Shěn Yōuzhī came from the common fields,
his family having been obscure for generations.
The late Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Shěn Gōng,
out of familial affection for a cousin,
loved him like a son,
protecting and promoting him,
allowing him to
rise through official ranks.
During the chaos and perversity of Jǐnghé,
the emperor was suspicious and afraid of his key ministers,
and Yōuzhī, being fierce and cruel,
pursued gain and delighted in disaster,
claiming to act on imperial edicts
to personally betray them.
Moreover, Yōuzhī,
along with Tán Jīn and Tóng Tàiyī, were favored excessively and were wild in court,
all serving as his confidants,
sharing achievements and bodies;
at the time they were called
"The Three Marquises."
At that time, their intimacy
surpassed that of Guǎn and Bào.
When the revolution occurred,
the treacherous faction feared execution,
but Yōuzhī turned good and sought to preserve himself,
thereby escaping.
He killed his cousin,
and also abused his good friends.
Although Lǚ Bù sold out his lord,
and Lì Jì betrayed his friend,
compared to this man,
they were not as cruel.
When Tàishǐ began,
the net was cast wide enough for a whale to escape;
overlooking his viciousness
and taking advantage of his ruthlessness,
he thus survived the chaos
and turned misfortune into fortune.
Yōuzhī's nature is shallow and empty,
impetuous and without strategy.
The collapse of Nónghú
was not due to his own strength.
At Péngchéng and Xiàpī,
he fled by night at the sight of the enemy banners.
Twice he (紹) [abandoned]
the imperial army,
and should have been executed long ago.
He happened to encounter the late emperor pardoning him for the shame of Huíxī,
hoping for a victory at Fēngxiáo.
Thus he was fortunate to be promoted and transferred,
repeatedly receiving prominent appointments.
Internally, he enforced military prohibitions;
externally, he pacified ten thousand *lǐ*.
When the sagely emperor passed away,
a distant dying command was issued,
entrusting him with profound responsibilities,
an obligation that moved even metal and stone.
Yet Yōuzhī, upon receiving news of the national mourning,
showed joy on his face;
while the whole world grieved,
he considered it a celebration.
He successively climbed to the position of Fān Yuè (Border Prince),
moving from Yǐng to Jīng.
When Jìn Xī Wáng (Prince of Jìn Xī) was to replace him as regional governor, as an imperial brother,
his status was honored and his prestige
weighty.
Yōuzhī arbitrarily restricted his reception,
acting wantonly and insultingly.
He selected soldiers and horses,
counted weapons and equipment,
and transferred elite troops,
taking them all for himself.
Of what was left in Yǐngchéng,
not one in ten remained.
He acted with complete willfulness and plunder,
disregarding national laws.
Since his arrival in Jīng,
he constantly employed treacherous schemes,
having harbored perverse intentions
and caused endless troubles.
He oppressed
the various Man tribes,
disturbing the mountains and valleys,
loudly proclaiming campaigns against them,
drafting all able-bodied men from every household.
He gathered them like ants in the cities and towns,
watching for the state's rise or decline,
continuing this for years,
demanding they not lay down
their armor.
there were no men on the roads;
plowing fields and carrying grain
were all done by women and the weak.
Such cruelty from ancient times
has never been heard of.
Last year, Guìyáng suffered internal strife,
and the imperial ancestral temple was in peril.
Yōuzhī, holding office in the upper reaches of the river,
with strong armies and vast territory,
should have fully exerted himself in the cause of loyal service.
Instead, he
merely sent
weak and feeble troops,
fewer than three thousand,
to Yǐngzhōu to receive orders,
intending that when the day of decision came,
the blame would fall on Jìn Xī.
He enticed swordsmen,
bound up travelers,
and harbored
fugitives entering his territory,
always protecting them.
If they escaped his jurisdiction,
he would certainly send out a relentless pursuit.
He regarded officials as enemies,
treated the people like grass,
imposed heavy taxes of more than half,
and inflicted brutal punishments
like those of barbarians.
He flogged state officials,
using only barbarian laws.
If one person fled,
his entire family would be arrested.
the imperial edicts of pardon;
the vast benefits [of the emperor's benevolence] were long
Across that zhōu,
people harbored resentment and grievances,
nine out of ten households.
Now, he raises an army to internally insult,
with treachery and deceit rampant outside.
This is truly the moment when evil ripens and crimes are consummated,
the day to lance a carbuncle and drain
a boil.
The Mùfǔ, having excessively borne the court's trust,
is righteously indignant beyond measure.
Controlling the grand army,
it performs Heaven's punishment.

Now, we dispatch the newly appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Military Commissioner of Yǐngzhōu, Sīzhōu, and Yìyáng, General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Yǐngzhōu, Founding Hou of Wénxǐ County, Huáng Huí;
Supernumerary Cavalry Attendant, General Who Assists the State, General of骁騎, Founding Zi of Chóng'ān County, Military Commander Wáng Jìngzé; Colonel of Cavalry, Founding Nan of Chángshòu County,

Military Commander Wáng Yíyǔ; Colonel of Cavalry Chén Chéngshū; General of the Right Army, Founding Nan of Gáyáng County, Péng Wénzhī; Staff Officer to the General of Agile Cavalry, General Who Manifests Martial Might,
Tái Zǎi;
with twenty thousand elite armored troops,
to charge their vanguard.
We also dispatch Cavalry Attendant, General of Roaming Cavalry, Founding Nan of Xiāng County, Lǚ Ānguó;

Envoy with Imperial Credentials, General Who Quells the North, Governor of Yuèzhōu, Sūn Tánguàn; Colonel of Cavalry, General Who Quells the North, Cuī Huìjǐng; General Who Quells the North, General of the Left Army, Hou of Xīntíng, Rèn Hòubó; General Who Soars like a Dragon, Colonel of the Tiger Guard, Yǐn Lüè; Colonel of Cavalry, Magistrate of Nánchéng, Cáo Hǔtóu; General Who Assists the State, General of Agile Cavalry,
Xiāo Shùnzhī;
with twenty thousand ships,
marching continuously in succession.

We also dispatch Colonel of Cavalry Gǒu Yuánbīn; Staff Officer to the General Who Guards the Army, Guō Wénkǎo; Staff Officer to the General Who Guards the Army and Central Army, Chéng Yǐnjùn; Court Gentleman for Consultation Zhū Xíguāng, and others;
with ten thousand light
boats,
to cut off their vital strategic points.
General of Agile Cavalry Zhōu Pánlóng, General of the Rear Army Chéng Mǎi, General Who Assists the State Wáng Chìqín, Colonel of Cavalry
Wáng Hóngfàn, and others;
with five thousand cavalry,
advancing by road in succession,
first to occupy the land routes,
and cut off their escape and concealment.
Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, Jìnglíng of Yǐngzhōu,
Suí Jùn of Sīzhōu, General Who Conquers Barbarians, Colonel Who Pacifies Barbarians, Governor of Yōngzhōu, Founding Hou of Xiāngyáng County, newly appointed General Who Guards the Army Zhāng
Jìnger;
with resolute and fervent spirit,
will roll up his armor at Fán and Dèng,
advancing by both water and land,
to destroy their strongholds.
Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Sīzhōu, General Who Conquers Barbarians, Governor of
Sīzhōu, concurrently Grand Administrator of Yìyáng, Hou of Fànyáng County, Yáo Dàohé;
with righteous valor and fortitude,
will throw off his robes and hasten to the designated area,
like the wind and lightning,
to attack their baggage train.
Banners are raised for ten thousand
li,
flags fly in all four directions.
All will lead their armies,
soaring like clouds and thundering like dragons.
Both men and gods are indignant,
near and far are united in heart.
Now, His Majesty is sagely and brilliant,
the chancellors and generals are benevolent and loving.
Laws are simplified to three chapters,
punishments are lenient, and taxes are eased.
Years are abundant and harvests plentiful,
households are self-sufficient, and people are content.
Above, there is the favor and
blessing of the people,
below, there is no desire for chaos.
Yōuzhī, ignorant of the opportune moment,
falsely plots a great rebellion,
raising an unjustified army,
and driving a multitude of enemies and resentful people.
Therefore, the court and common people are convinced
of his easy defeat,
and all intelligent beings deem him a captive.
The people of that land,
having suffered hardship for a long time,
are now again forced and pressured,
to throw themselves upon the sharp blades.
On the day of battle,
it will be difficult to distinguish
between orchids and mugwort.
Whether to stay or go is in the hands of fate.
It is hoped that you will understand this beforehand.
Do not let a single person be confused or in doubt,
and bring disaster upon their entire clan.
The principle of expansive forgiveness
is as clear as the shining sun.
Yǐngchéng could not be attacked,
and General Who Pacifies the West Huáng Huí's army arrived at Xīyáng.
Riding triple-decked warships,
performing Qiāng-Hú music,
they advanced upstream.
Yōuzhī had always lost popular support,
originally compelling people with power and might.
When he first departed Jiānglíng,
there were already deserters,
and by this time, they had grown in number.
Yōuzhī rode his horse day and night through the camps to comfort them,
but the deserters did not cease.
Yōuzhī was furious and
summoned his military commanders, saying:
"I received the Empress Dowager's order
to initiate this righteous cause and march on the capital.
If this great undertaking succeeds, we will all wear white gauze caps together;
if it fails,
the court will execute my hundred relatives,
it does not concern others.
The soldiers have been deserting and scattering.
You all do not take this seriously.
I also cannot question the deserters themselves.
From now on, if there are deserters in the army,
the military commander will bear their crime."
Thereupon, when one person deserted,
ten people were sent to pursue him,
and they all left and did not return.
No one dared to reveal this,
and all had different plans.
Liú Rǎngbīng shot a letter to Shìlóng, offering to surrender.
Shìlóng opened the gates and admitted him.
Rǎngbīng burned the camp and left,
and the fire starting was the only way it was discovered.
Yōuzhī was enraged,
biting and chewing his beard.
He arrested Rǎngbīng's nephew Tiāncì and son-in-law Zhāng Pínglǔ and executed them.
The army
largely dispersed.
Yōuzhī crossed to the shore of Lǔshān,
still with several dozen horsemen following him.
He announced to the army:
"There is a great deal of money in the city of Jīngzhōu.
We can go back and take it,
to serve as provisions."
Yǐngchéng had no pursuing army,
but the scattered soldiers, fearing barbarian raids,
gathered together again,
about twenty thousand men.
They followed Yōuzhī,
and dispersed when they were about to reach Jiānglíng.
Shìlóng then dispatched Army Deputy Liú Sēnglín to pursue him on the road.
Yōuzhī had already died,
and was posthumously appointed Shìzhōng.
Later, he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
and enfeoffed as Founding Hou of Zhēnyáng County,
with two thousand households.
He was appointed as General of the Left and Grand Administrator of Wújùn,
with an additional salary of two thousand dàn.
He observed mourning for his mother.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányùzhōu and Sīzhōu, General Who Pacifies the South, Governor of Nányùzhōu,
and his noble title was advanced to Duke.
The Emperor
personally wrote a decree to Sītú Chǔ Yuān, saying:
"I recently saw Shìlóng, emaciated to an excessive degree,
almost beyond recognition.
Not only does it make one feel compassion,
he is truly a treasure of the age and a gem of the nation."
Yuān replied:
"Shìlóng's innate nature is pure and profound,
his grief exceeds the proper rites.
He served Your Majesty faithfully in times of danger,
and in mourning his parent, he relies on a staff to rise.
These two principles, the foundation of human conduct,
have reached their utmost.
Increasing his honors and favors
is sufficient to encourage customs and strengthen morals."
In Jiànyuán second year,
he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South.
At this time, the barbarians invaded Shòuyáng.
The Emperor ordered Shìlóng, saying:
"Lìyáng city is large;
I fear it cannot be easily fortified.
It is appropriate to isolate and divide it,
to ensure its deep security.
Instruct the common people
that if they do not defend the city with their families,
a single person cannot be reliably trusted."
Soon after, he again decreed:
"I will inspect the outer city of
Lìyáng again.
If there is a bandit attack,
I will immediately order the common people to defend it.
Therefore, it should be protected rather than abandoned."
After Yuán Chóngzǔ defeated the barbarians,
the Emperor wished to merge the two Yùzhōu provinces.
He ordered Shìlóng, saying:
"I have been thinking that the area west of the Jiāng is desolate,
and managing two Yùzhōu provinces is difficult.
Many advisors say that reducing one would suffice,
which would be convenient for affairs.
I think this is not erroneous.
What do you think?
Please fully inform me."
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Rear Army and Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
but he declined the appointment.
Shìlóng enjoyed extensive reading.
He petitioned Tàizǔ to borrow books from the imperial library,
and the Emperor granted him two thousand volumes.
Three years later,

he was dispatched as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the military affairs of the five prefectures of Nányùn, Qīng, and Jì, General of the Pacified North, and Governor of Nányùn Prefecture.
The region north of the Jiāng River feared barbarian incursions,
causing unrest.
The Emperor commanded Shìlóng, saying:
“Recently there has been news from the north:
the bandits are still drilling troops in Péngchéng.
The year is already almost over,
so perhaps they will not necessarily come to their doom.
However, wolves cannot be reasoned with;
preparations must not be slackened.
Since their outer city walls are not strategically important,
it would be advisable to clear them away,
leaving them thirty zhàng from Jīnchéng would be best.
Mobilize the people to manage this,
there is no cause for concern.
If we are to prepare food for three thousand men,
how much rice do we have already?
Please write a dispatch and send it back with the messenger.
If there are many able-bodied men but few dependants among the populace,
order them all to garrison;
this is not a matter for doubt.”
He further commanded:
“Last night I received a memorial from the northern envoy.
The bandits in Zhōnglí have already crossed the Huái River.
Since we are certain they are coming to their doom,
we must immediately organize a full-scale suppression.
You should pay close attention to the situation.
If there is an emergency, order all the small garrisons to return to their posts;
we must not be unaware of the bandits’ arrival.
Since the bandits have crossed the Huái,
it is impossible for them to retreat and disperse nearby.
〔一七〕They must have a place where they will meet their doom.
They will certainly attack Shòuyáng;
I will send reinforcements.”
He also sent troops to assist Shìlóng,
and supplied military provisions.
When the barbarians retreated,
the Emperor wished to establish a permanent territorial division north of the Jiāng River.
He again commanded Shìlóng, saying:
“Lǚ Ānguó was recently in the west,
where he established territorial divisions for the mixed populace on the borders of Yǐng and Sī.
It was excellent,
the people were hardly alarmed or frightened.
Recently, I also ordered Yuán Yùzhōu to establish divisions within his prefecture.
I received a memorial from Chóngzǔ reporting on the matter,
which has already been completed.
There has been no recent complaints,
and it is greatly praised as an ancient practice.
Can you see if this matter can be carried out in the Nányùn department?
If it causes no disturbance,
we will begin in the spring.”
Such was the Emperor’s trust in him.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was given the added title of Palace Attendant.
Shìlóng was skilled in divination,
especially in distinguishing tortoise shells,
with a value of up to ten thousand.
When Yǒngmíng was established as an era name,
Shìlóng inscribed on the wall of the prefectural office, saying:
“Yǒngmíng eleventh year.”
He said to the clerk Lǐ Dǎng:
“I will not see it.”
He entered the court as Palace Attendant and General of the Household Guard.
He was promoted to Right Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and concurrently held the position of Right Commandant of the Crown Prince’s Household.
He was also Grand Neutral of Yōng Prefecture,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was instead appointed Palace Attendant,
Left Director of the Department of State Affairs,
with the position of Grand Neutral as before.
When the Mán tribes in Xiāng Prefecture revolted,
Shìlóng was dispatched with his original official title to command all armies for the suppression of the Mán,
and was concurrently appointed Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the military affairs of Xiāng Prefecture, General of the Pacified South, and Governor of Xiāng Prefecture,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
Upon arriving at his post,
Shìlóng pacified them with strategies.
While in the prefecture, he established a residence for business,
which was impeached by the Central Inspector Yǔ Gǎozhī.
The imperial edict pardoned him without inquiry.
He again entered the court as Left Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and concurrently held the position of Grand Commandant,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was then transferred to Minister of the Department of State Affairs.
Shìlóng established merits and fame in his youth,
and in his later years devoted himself solely to scholarly discussions.
He was skilled at playing the qín,
and was known by his contemporaries as Liǔ Gōng’s “double jades,”
ranking first among scholars.
He often said of himself: “My horsemanship is first,
my pure conversation is second,
and my qín playing is third.”
While in court, he did not interfere with worldly affairs,
but would lower the curtain and play the qín.
His music was clear and distant in its melody,
earning him great contemporary praise.
Due to illness, he resigned his position.
He was re-appointed Palace Attendant and
General of the Guards,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was then transferred to Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness of the Left,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
In the ninth year,
he died,
at the age of fifty.
An imperial edict granted him secret funerary items from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court attire,
one set of robes,
one hundred thousand coins,
three hundred bolts of cloth,
and three hundred catties of wax.
Another imperial edict stated:
“The late Palace Attendant and Grand Master of Brilliant Happiness of the Left, Zhēnyáng Gōng Shìlóng,
upheld virtue and established his career,
possessing both literary and military talents.
In his youth, he spread a pure reputation;
in adulthood, he cultivated great renown.
He entered the inner court as a participant,
and went out to assist the western regional commander.
He was entrusted with the region of Yǐng,
where he defeated powerful villains,
surpassing previous achievements,
his accomplishments making their mark on an era.
When he took charge of a regional prefecture,
the people praised his magnanimous virtue,
he assisted in promoting education from the grand gate,
and the court praised him as a prime minister.
His loyal strategies and excellent counsel
were clear in Our heart.
His elegant aspirations and pure conduct
were unsurpassed.
He was about to ascend to a crucial position,
to assist in the great transformation,
but unexpectedly met his demise.
Our grief is profound.
He is posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works,
thirty ceremonial sword-bearers,
〔一八〕one set of drums and pipes,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
His posthumous title is Zhōngwǔ.”
The Emperor further commanded Wáng Yàn, Minister of Personnel, saying:
“Although Shìlóng had been ill for years,
his spirit was not diminished.
We hoped that medicine would be effective,
and recovery could be expected.
Unexpectedly, he passed away in an instant.
The depth of this pain
cannot be expressed.
When he was in Yǐng,
his sincere loyalty was early established,
〔一九〕preserving a whole region,
and his achievements were remarkable.
Recalling our separation,
Our tears and sorrow increase.
You, sharing in this sentiment,
must also feel endless grief!”
Shìlóng understood numerology.
He established a tomb at Nítáng.
He would walk there with guests,
ten or five times,
always sitting in one spot.
When he died,
his tomb was precisely placed where he used to sit.
〔二０〕He authored two juan of the *Guī Jīng Mì Yào*, which circulated in the world.
His eldest son, Yuè,
died young.
Zhāng Guī,
courtesy name Zǔyì,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Prefecture.
His grandfather, Yù,
was Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Yǒng,
was Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
He understood music theory.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng asked Yǒng why the bell in front of the Tàijí Hall sounded hoarse.
Yǒng replied,
“The bell has copper impurities.”
He then struck the bell to locate the spot,
chiseled it out and removed it,
and the sound became clear and resonant.
Guī began his career as an aide-de-camp to the Grand Commandant, the Prince of Jiāngxià,
and was appointed to the external military section.
Following the transfer of the prince’s residence, he became an official in the Grand Tutor’s office,
and was well-regarded by Yìgōng.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Crown Prince’s Household,
then Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
then Executive Assistant to the General of Agile Cavalry,
then Right Senior Clerk to the Minister of Education.
Earlier,
Yǒng had resisted the bandits from Guìyáng at Báixià,
but scattered.
Ruǎn Diànfū and others wanted to punish him,
but Tàizǔ steadfastly defended and clarified his position.
Guī was grateful for this and became loyal.
He was then transferred to Straight-Corridor Palace Attendant,
and General of Agile Cavalry.
After his father’s death, he returned to Wú to observe mourning.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
Liú Bǐng harbored rebellious intentions.
His younger brother, Xiá, was the governor of Wú Jùn,
and they secretly influenced each other.
Taking advantage of Shěn Yōuzhī's difficulties,
they gathered three thousand men
and prepared siege equipment.
Tài Zǔ secretly dispatched Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Biàn Báilóng to order [person's name missing in original text, assumed to be Zhāng] Guī to capture Xiá.
The Zhāng clan had a history of heroism;
Guī's residence always housed several hundred old retainers from his father's time.
Xiá summoned Guī,
who feigned compliance with the order.
He and his uncle Shù led eighteen soldiers into the commandery,
and, with the commandery defense leader Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn Guō Luóyún, advanced into the central hall to seize Xiá.
Xiá escaped by climbing out a window,
but Guī's subordinate Gù Xiànzǐ personally beheaded him.
Within the commandery, no one dared to move.
When the victory was reported,
Tài Zǔ informed Lǐngjūn Zhāng Chōng.
〔二一〕Chōng said:
“Guī staked a hundred lives on one throw,
and drew a winning cast.”
He was immediately appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu,
and Guī was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yìchéng Xiàn,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Tài Zǔ thus bestowed upon him an auspicious title.
He was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Dōnghǎi and Dōngguǎn Commanderies,
but did not accept the appointments.
In the first year of Jiàn Yuán,
his stipend was increased by two hundred households.
〔二二〕Soon after, his enfeoffment was changed to Píngdū.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
and additionally appointed Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū,
retaining his position as Lǐng Xiàowèi.
He was then sent out as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
In the third year,
Wūchéng Lìng Gù Chāngxuán committed a crime,
and Guī was implicated for failing to rectify it,
and was dismissed from office.
The following year,
he became Dùzhī Shàngshū.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Póyáng Wáng Běizhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ, Xiāngyáng Xiāng, and Acting Yōngzhōu Fǔzhōushì,
and then, following the administration, was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
In the fourth year,
he was again appointed Chíjíe, Dū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sì Zhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suí Jùn Jūnshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and soon after, Lǐng Níngmán Xiàowèi.
He returned to serve as Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and Lǐng Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
then promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Dàsīmǎ Zhǎngshǐ.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to Tàicháng.
He pleaded illness and old age,
wishing to retire to a life of leisure.
The following year,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū.
Shortly thereafter,
the Emperor wished to re-employ Guī,
and so appointed him Hòujiāngjūn and Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
with a salary of two thousand dàn,
and Acting Nánxúzhōu Fǔzhōushì,
and also Acting Hédōng Wángguóshì.
Upon reaching his post,
he again claimed illness,
and returned to serve as Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū.
When Hǎilín ascended the throne,
he was granted a gold seal and purple ribbon.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was granted twenty personal attendants.
When Hǎilín was deposed,
the court officials went to the palace gate to pay respects to Gāozōng,
but Guī pleaded a foot ailment and did not dismount.
〔二三〕When Hǎilíng was established,
he was granted Yòujiāngjūn.
Gāozōng suspected that external lords would raise troops,
and so positioned Guī at Shítou,
to supervise all military affairs.
Guī, seeing the court beset by many difficulties,
then constantly feigned illness.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was transferred to Gěishìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū,
with his personal attendants as before.
He was given an additional twenty thousand coins monthly.
In the second year,
when the barbarians became formidable,
an imperial edict ordered Guī, in his original post, to provisionally hold a jié, supervise all military affairs in Guǎnglíng, and act as Nányǔnzhōu governor.
He returned only after the barbarians retreated.
Guī's residence was lavish and wealthy,
with a room full of courtesans and concubines.
He had over ten sons,
and often said,
“Surely there must be some good ones among them.”
At the end of Jiànwǔ,
he repeatedly petitioned Gāozōng to return to Wú,
and was granted permission.
He enjoyed a leisurely life.
Some criticized Guī for keeping concubines in his old age,
to which Guī said:
“I loved music when I was young,
but only now in my old age do I truly understand it.
Of my lifelong desires,
none remain
except for this one thing which I cannot relinquish.”
When Gāozōng became gravely ill,
he suspected Dàsīmǎ Wáng Jìngzé,
and knowing Guī was known for his strategy and foresight,
appointed him Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu,
to prepare for him.
When Jìngzé rebelled,
Guī dispatched three thousand officers and soldiers to intercept him at Sōngjiāng.
Hearing the drums of Jìngzé's army,
they scattered and fled at once.
Guī abandoned the commandery and escaped among the common people.
After the matter was settled,
Guī returned to the commandery,
but was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and stripped of his office and爵 (rank/title).
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán,
he became Guānglù Dàfū.
Soon after, he was granted Qiánjiāngjūn,
with a gold seal and purple ribbon.
In the third year,
when the righteous army advanced,
Dōnghūn provisionally granted Guī a jié,
and stationed him at Shítou.
When the righteous army reached Xīntíng,
Guī abandoned the city and fled back to the palace.
At the beginning of Liáng, he was again appointed Guānglù.
He died in the fourth year of Tiānjiān.
The court historian remarks: Civil administration for gathering the populace,
military might for establishing authority—
the talent of a grand marshal,
known as a pillar of the state.
Shěn Yōuzhī spent ten years preparing his troops,
launched his campaign in his old age,
with the upper reaches of Jīngchǔ,
facing the lower reaches of Jiāngdōng.
This was an enormous difficulty to overcome,
a great enemy to emperors.
Liǔ Shìlóng, whose power was centered in Zhōngxià,
was young and held a minor position,
yet he was the first to resist with his entire army,
challenging the attack with a solitary city.
He gave counsel from atop the ramparts,
without a single horse breaking a sweat.
The formidable enemy was disheartened and frustrated,
their strength exhausted at the high walls,
their scattered chariots vying to flee first,
surrendering and rushing towards the Yǐng road.
〔二四〕Even Lù Xùn's defeat of Xuándé
was no greater than this.
When the world became clear and peaceful,
he served as an external governor and internal assistant,
embodying integrity and simplicity,
and conducting himself with refined virtue.
This indeed was the great beauty that brought prosperity to his family.
A eulogy states: Loyal and martial, aiding and assisting,
truly possessing both talents.
He deliberated in the ancestral temple,
and captured banners from high fortifications.
He excelled in various arts and skills,
tuning strings and divining with tortoise shells.
Yìchéng established his lineage on earth,
his merits foundational to the imperial enterprise.
