Biographies, Chapter 6: Yuán Chóngzǔ, Zhāng Jìng'ér
Yuán Chóngzǔ, courtesy name Jìngyuǎn,
was a native of Xiàpī.
His clan was powerful and influential.
During Shí Hǔ's reign, they were moved from Luèyáng to Yè.
His great-grandfather, Chǎng,
served as a伪 (pretender's) minister of personnel for Mùróng Dé.
His grandfather, Miáo,
when Sòng Wǔ conquered Guǎnggù,
led his retainers to surrender.
They then settled in Xiàpī,
and he rose to the office of Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Rǔnán and Xīncài.
His father, Xún,
was Jīshè Jiāngjūn,
and died in service during Sòng Xiàowǔ's reign,
posthumously granted Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Chóngzǔ, at fourteen,
possessed talent and strategy.
His paternal uncle, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Hùzhī, said to his clansmen:
“This child will surely greatly prosper our family;
you all cannot compare to him.”
Cìshǐ Liú Dàolóng appointed him Master of Records,
and treated him generously.
He was appointed Shījiāngjūn of Xīn'ān Wángguó.
During the Jǐnghé era,
Dàolóng sought to be appointed governor of Liángzhōu,
and petitioned to transfer Chóngzǔ to Yìyáng Wáng Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn.
Chóngzǔ traveled with Dàolóng,
and was sent back to Xiàpī to recruit soldiers.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
Dào Lóng was executed.
Xuē Āndū rebelled,
and Míngdì dispatched Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī to campaign north.
Āndū sent his generals Péi Zǔlóng and Lǐ Shìxióng to hold Xiàpī.
Zǔlóng led Chóngzǔ to jointly resist the attack.
It so happened that Liú Mízhī, the commander of the reinforcing army from Qīngzhōu, mutinied and surrendered.
Zǔlóng's troops were dispirited and defeated.
Chóngzǔ and several tens of his close followers rescued Zǔlóng by night,
and together they fled back to Péngchéng.
After the Tartars had already captured Xúzhōu,
Chóngzǔ remained active as a Tartar general, roaming around Lángyá, and did not return.
The Tartars could not control him.
He secretly sent someone to Péngchéng to fetch his mother,
intending to flee south.
The matter was discovered,
and the Tartars seized his mother as a hostage.
Chóngzǔ's sister's husband, Huángfǔ Sù's elder brother's wife,
was Xuē Āndū's daughter,
which is why the Tartars trusted them.
Sù then took his family and Chóngzǔ's mother to Qúshān.
Chóngzǔ consequently took his troops and occupied it,
sending an envoy to pledge allegiance.
Tàizǔ was in Huái'yīn,
and appointed him as the commander of the Qúshān garrison.
He sent Chóngzǔ's mother back to the capital,
and Míngdì accepted her.
Qúshān was isolated and dangerous by the sea,
and the people were not yet settled.
Chóngzǔ often kept boats moored by the water,
so that in an emergency he could escape to the sea.
A general who had committed a crime and absconded
reported everything to the Tartars.
The Tartar's pseudo-Dūjiāng of Chéng, the Inspector of Dōngxúzhōu, Chénggù Gōng, had just acquired Qīngzhōu.
Hearing the defector's words,
he dispatched twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Chóngzǔ,
stationing them at Luòyào,
twenty *lǐ* from Qúshān city.
Chóngzǔ had gone out to see off a guest and had not returned.
Those in the city were alarmed and fearful,
and all went down to the boats, intending to leave.
When Chóngzǔ returned,
he said to his trusted followers:
"The enemy's recent approach
was not a major offensive;
it was merely in response to a single report,
and can easily be tricked.
If we can now gather a hundred or so men,
the matter will surely succeed.
But once people are startled,
they cannot be gathered.
You all should quickly go about two *lǐ* from here, shout loudly as you approach,
and cry, 'The righteous men of Àitáng have already defeated the Tartars!
The garrison troops must hurry to assist them in driving the enemy back!' "
The people in the boats were indeed pleased,
and scrambled ashore.
Chóngzǔ led them into the city to defend it,
and sent the weak into the island.
He ordered men to hold two torches and beat drums on the mountain.
The Tartar cavalry scout thought that their military preparations were very strong,
and so retreated.
Chóngzǔ memorialized Míngdì, saying:
"The scholars and common people north of the Huái River,
though their strength is broken by the barbarians,
yearn day and night to turn south.
My father and uncles were all governors of prefectures and commanderies north of the Huái,
and my clan is spread throughout the northern border.
The people trust me;
with a single rallying cry,
great achievements can be established.
However,
my rank and position are still low,
insufficient to awe the multitude.
I beg to be granted an official title,
to show to those near and far."
Míngdì appointed him as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Upholds the State) and Taìshǒu of the two commanderies of Běilángyá and Lánlíng.
A refugee Sīmǎ plotted with him to attack the commandery.
Chóngzǔ attacked, captured, and executed him.
He repeatedly presented calculations
to recover the Huái River region.
At that time, there were rumors that the Tartars would raid Huáinán.
Míngdì consulted Chóngzǔ about this,
and Chóngzǔ consequently proposed,
"It is advisable to penetrate deep with light troops,
catching them by surprise.
Advancing, one can achieve unparalleled merits;
retreating, one can cut off their threat of encroachment."
The emperor agreed.
Chóngzǔ led several hundred men into Tartar territory seven hundred *lǐ* deep,
occupied Nánchéng,
fortified Méngshān,
and agitated the commanderies and counties.
The Tartars led a large force to attack him.
His separate general, Liáng Zhàn, had his mother in Tartar hands.
The Tartars seized his mother
and made Zhàn tell his troops:
"The main army has already left,
why are you staying alone?"
Thereupon, the morale of the troops fractured,
and they fled all at once.
Chóngzǔ said to his attendants:
"If we all retreat now,
we will certainly not escape."
He then stayed behind and fought fiercely,
decisively defeating the pursuers before returning.
Due to his prolonged service,
he was enfeoffed as the Zǐ of Xiàpī County.
In the first year of Tàiyù,
he acted as the governor of Xúzhōu,
and was transferred to garrison Lóngjǔ,
south of Qúshān.
Chóngzǔ proposed cutting off the water to the plain,
to block the Tartar horses.
The emperor asked Liú Huáizhēn about it,
who said it could be done.
Chóngzǔ led his officers and men to dam it,
but it was not yet completed.
The Tartar ruler said to the pseudo-Péngchéng garrison commander, Píngyáng Gōng:
"If Lóngjǔ is fortified,
it will be a disgrace to our state.
Fight to the death for it."
Several tens of thousands of cavalry suddenly arrived.
Chóngzǔ, with his horse and spear, was unable to withstand the formation,
so he built a city to defend himself.
It happened to rain for more than ten days,
and the Tartars then retreated.
Lóngjǔ was ultimately not fortified.
He successively served as Taìshǒu of Xūyí, Píngyáng, and Dōnghǎi commanderies,
with his general title remaining as before.
He was transferred to be the Sīmǎ of Shàolíng Wáng's Nánzhōngláng.
He again served as Taìshǒu of Dōnghǎi.
Previously,
Chóngzǔ met Tàizǔ in Huái'yīn.
Tàizǔ, impressed by his martial bravery,
treated him well.
Chóngzǔ said to Huángfǔ Sù:
"This is truly my lord!
I have found my master now,
a once-in-a-thousand-year opportunity!"
He then secretly pledged his loyalty.
At the end of Yuánhuī,
Tàizǔ was worried,
and ordered Chóngzǔ to immediately entrust his family to Huángfǔ Sù upon receiving instructions,
and to lead several hundred men into Tartar territory,
awaiting further orders.
When Cāngwú was deposed,
Tàizǔ summoned Chóngzǔ to lead his troops back to the capital,
and appointed him Yóujī Jiāngjūn (General of Roaming Cavalry).
After Shěn Yōuzhī's affair was settled,
Chóngzǔ was made Chíjié, Dū Qīng, Jì, Yǔ Sānzhōu Zhū Jūshì (Bearer of a Staff of Authority, Overseer of Military Affairs of Qīng, Jì, and Yǔ Provinces),
and successively promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Army) and Yǔzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Yǔ Province).
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he said to Chóngzǔ:
"I have just come to possess the world.
The barbarians, ignorant of the Mandate of Heaven,
will surely stir up their vast hordes,
using the escort of Liú Chǎng as a pretext.
The place where the enemy will strike
will surely be Shòuchūn.
No one but you can repel this invasion."

He was transferred to be Shǐ Chíjié, Jiān Yù, Sī Èrzhōu Zhū Jūshì (Envoy Bearing a Staff of Authority, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yù and Sī Provinces), and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Yù Province),
with his general title remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as Wàngcài Xiànhóu,
with seven hundred households.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
the barbarians dispatched the false King of Liáng, Yùdòu Juàn, and Líu Chǎng,
with a cavalry and infantry force numbering two hundred thousand,
to invade Shòuchūn.
Chóngzǔ summoned his civil and military officials to a council and said:
“The enemy is numerous, and we are few.
We must use stratagem to control them.
We should repair the outer city walls to await the enemy.
The city is broad and spacious; it cannot be made secure without water.
Now I intend to dam the Féishuǐ River, flooding it to create a three-sided natural barrier.
What do you gentlemen think?”
The眾 (assembly) replied:
“In the past, when Fólí invaded our territory,
Sòng’s Prince Nánpíng, with a full complement of soldiers,
deemed the outer city difficult to defend,
and retreated to hold the inner city.
The situation today
is ten times more severe than before.
From ancient times, it has been customary
not to build a Féiyàn (Féi River dam),
always because the terrain is inconvenient,
and accumulated water is useless.
If we must proceed with this,
we fear it is not advisable.”
Chóngzǔ said:
“You see one aspect,
but you do not understand the other.
If we abandon the outer city,
the enemy will surely occupy it.
They will repair the watchtowers outside,
and build long siege lines within,
with no obstructions on any side,
leaving our inner city exposed to attack.
This is to allow ourselves to be captured.
Defending the outer city and building a dam
is my unwavering strategy.”
Thereupon, a dam was built northwest of the city to block the Féishuǐ River.
A small city was erected north of the dam,
surrounded by a deep moat,
and several thousand men were assigned to defend it.
Chóngzǔ said to his Chief Clerk, Fēng Yánbó:
“The barbarians are greedy and lack foresight.
They will certainly exert all their strength to attack the small city,
intending to break this dam.
Seeing the moat is narrow and the city small,
they will assume it can be overcome in one go,
and will attack it like ants clinging to a wall.
When the water is released with a single surge,
it will rush faster than the Three Gorges.
Their situation will become desperate, and they will flee,
naturally drowning.
Is this not little effort for great gain?”
The barbarian forces gathered south of the dam via the western road,
and a division of their army attacked the small city from the eastern path, pressing close.
Chóngzǔ, wearing a white gauze cap,
was carried on a shoulder litter up to the city wall,
personally directing the operations.
By dusk,
the Xiǎoshǐ Dam was breached.
The water rushed down,
and the barbarian troops attacking the city
were swept into the moat,
thousands of men and horses drowning.
The entire host retreated.
Initially,
when Chóngzǔ was in Huái’yīn
and met the Emperor,
he compared himself to Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
No one believed him,
except the Emperor alone who agreed with him.
Chóngzǔ bowed twice and accepted the imperial decree.
When the report of defeating the barbarians arrived,
the Emperor said to his court officials:
“Chóngzǔ promised me he would control the barbarians,
and it has indeed happened as he said.
He constantly likened himself to Hán and Bái,
and now he truly is such a man.”
He was promoted to Dūdū (Area Commander) with the title Píngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West),
and his fief was increased to one thousand five hundred households.
Chóngzǔ heard that Chén Xiǎndá and Lǐ Ānmín had both been granted additional military honors,
and memorialized the Emperor to request a drum-and-pipe band and a transverse flute band.
The Emperor decreed:
“How can Hán and Bái not be distinguished from the masses?”
A drum-and-pipe band was granted.
Chóngzǔ, fearing that the barbarians would again raid north of the Huái River,
memorialized for the relocation of the Xiàcài garrison to east of the Huái.
That winter,
the barbarians indeed intended to attack Xiàcài.
Having heard of the relocation,
they declared they would level the old city.
The populace suspected the barbarians would establish a garrison in the old city,
but Chóngzǔ said:
“Xiàcài is but a stone's throw from the garrison;
how would the barbarians dare to station troops there?
They genuinely wish to clear this old city.
I only fear that even if we chase and kill them, we won't get them all.”
The barbarian army indeed razed and dug up the city of Xiàcài.
Chóngzǔ personally led his troops across the Huái to engage them in battle,
and thoroughly defeated them,
pursuing the fleeing enemy for dozens of lǐ,
〔一一〕killing and capturing thousands.
The Emperor sent an envoy into the pass to gather intelligence on the barbarians. Upon his return,
the Emperor decreed to Chóngzǔ:
“Do you see me as merely a defender of Jiāngdōng?
What we lack is food.
You need only diligently manage the fields,
and naturally, the remaining scoundrels will be pacified and annihilated.”
The Emperor ordered Chóngzǔ to repair and cultivate the fields of Sháopí.
〔一二〕
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Chóngzǔ was summoned to serve as Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Shortly after, an edict ordered him to remain in his original post,
and he was given the additional title Ānxī.
He was then promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
and concurrently served as Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Initially,
the Prince of Yùzhāng enjoyed great imperial favor.
When Shìzǔ was still the Crown Prince,
Chóngzǔ did not align himself with him.
After the defeat of the barbarians,
an edict ordered him to return to court,
and he secretly discussed matters with Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ, suspicious of him,
treated him with extraordinary courtesy.
After drinking, he said to Chóngzǔ:
“The rumors in the world
I have already cleared from my mind.
From now on,
wealth and nobility will be entrusted to you.”
Chóngzǔ bowed and expressed his gratitude.
After Chóngzǔ departed,
the Emperor again sent Xún Bóyù with an oral decree,
stating that due to border affairs, he had received an imperial order to depart that night,
and could not take leave of the Crown Prince.
Shìzǔ, considering Chóngzǔ to be insincere,
〔一三〕held a grudge against him.
When Tàizǔ died,
fearing Chóngzǔ would cause trouble,
he ordered him to be transferred to an internal post.
On the ninth day of the fourth month of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
an edict stated:
“Yuán Chóngzǔ is vicious, abusive, treacherous, and impetuous,
and in his youth, he had no proper conduct.
In the past, due to the many difficulties faced by the state and military,
his singular usefulness was employed.
When the great destiny shone brightly,
he was frequently promoted,
but his ambition was never satisfied,
〔一四〕and only grew wider.
Last year, while in the west,
he conspired with those beyond the borders.
His disloyal heart
has become apparent far and wide.
He was given special care and nurture,
hoping he might reform.
However, his suspicion and disloyalty only intensified,
and he harbored intentions to foment rebellion,
colluding with Xún Bóyù and other malcontents,
peeking and coveting illicit gains,
inciting trouble in the borderlands,
acting as mutual supporters.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Sūn Jǐngyù thoroughly investigated his sinister plot,
and fully reported it.
To eliminate evil, one must get to the root;
punishment for this is without pardon.
He shall be arrested immediately,
to uphold the law and clarify justice.”
He died at the age of forty-four.
His son, Huìlóng,
was exiled to Pānyú and died there.
Zhāng Jìng'ér was a native of Guànjūn in Nányáng.
His original name was Gǒu'ér.
Sòng Míngdì, finding his name vulgar,
changed it.
His father, Chǒu,
served as a commander for the commandery, and his highest official post was Cānjūn in the Jiéfǔ.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) was young but skilled in archery and horsemanship.
He was brave
and liked to shoot tigers,
never missing a shot.
The customs of Nányáng (南陽) and Xīnyě (新野) fostered equestrian archery,
and Jìng'ér (敬兒) was particularly strong.
He sought to join the army and became a general at Qū'ā (曲阿)戍驛 (shùyì).
The prefecture appointed him as a prefectural general,
then he returned as Deputy Commander of the county's cavalry,
and was later promoted to Commander.
He gradually became an Acting Staff Officer (xíngcānjūn 行參軍) in the Níngmán (寧蠻) Prefecture.
[一五] He followed fellow county-man Liú Hú (劉胡) to lead troops to campaign against the Mán (蠻) tribes in the various mountains of Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
They penetrated deep into dangerous and remote areas,
and wherever they went, they were victorious.
He also attacked the Húyáng (湖陽) Mán (蠻) tribes.
[一六] When the government forces retreated,
several thousand Mán (蠻) bandits pursued them.
Jìng'ér (敬兒), alone on horseback, stayed behind
and charged into the bandit army.
After dozens of engagements,
he killed dozens of men.
An arrow hit his left armpit,
but the bandits could not resist him.
Píngxī Jiāngjūn (平西將軍) Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu (山陽王休祐) garrisoned Shòuyáng (壽陽)
and sought skilled archers and horsemen.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) offered his services and gained favor,
becoming a Chángshǐ (長史) [一七] and Acting Staff Officer (xíngcānjūn 行參軍) concurrently,
leading the Báizhí (白直) corps.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍).
He followed the prefecture to become a Staff Officer (cānjūn 參軍) under the Piàojì (驃騎) General
and was appointed Zhōngbīng (中兵).
He led troops to suppress the Yìjiā (義嘉) rebels.
He and Liú Hú (劉胡) confronted each other at Quèwěi Zhōu (鵲尾洲).
He petitioned Emperor Míng (明帝) for his home county.
After the matter was settled,
he became Nányáng Tàishǒu (南陽太守),
with his generalship as before.
Earlier,
when Wáng Xuánmó (王玄謨) was Yōngzhōu (雍州),
he registered Jìng'ér's (敬兒) family in Wǔyīn (舞陰) based on their actual residence.
When Jìng'ér (敬兒) arrived at the commandery,
he moved them back to Guānjūn (冠軍).
In the third year,
Xuē Āndū's (薛安都) sons, Bǎilìng (柏令) and Huánlóng (環龍), illegally occupied Shùnyáng (順陽) and Guǎngpíng (廣平),
[一八] raiding the borders of Yìchéng (義成) and Fúfēng (扶風).
The Inspector (cǐshǐ 刺史), Bālíng Wáng Xiūruò (巴陵王休若), dispatched Jìng'ér (敬兒) and Xīnyě Tàishǒu (新野太守) Liú Rǎngbīng (劉攘兵) to attack them.
They engaged in battle
and defeated them.
He was transferred to be Shùnyáng Tàishǒu (順陽太守),
with his generalship as before.
When the Nányáng (南陽) Mán (蠻) tribes caused unrest,
Jìng'ér (敬兒) was again appointed Nányáng Tàishǒu (南陽太守).
He returned home for his mother's mourning period.
The imperial court, suspecting Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn (桂陽王休範),
secretly made preparations for him,
and thus appointed Jìng'ér (敬兒) as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉).
When the Guìyáng (桂陽) incident occurred,
he was assigned to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) who was stationed at Xīntíng (新亭).
When arrows and stones were exchanged by the rebels,
Xiūfàn (休範), dressed in white, rode in a carriage to inspect the area below the walls.
Seeing from inside the city that he had few guards,
Jìng'ér (敬兒) and Huáng Huí (黃回) told Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖):
"Where Guìyáng (桂yáng) is,
the defenses are weak and lacking.
If we feign surrender and seize him,
he can surely be captured."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) said:
"If you can accomplish this,
I will reward you with your home province."
Jìng'ér (敬兒) and Huáng Huí (黃回) went out of the south gate of the city,
threw down their weapons,
and loudly declared their surrender.
Xiūfàn (休範) was pleased and
summoned them to his carriage.
Huí (回) feigned conveying Grand Ancestor's (Tàizǔ 太祖) secret message,
and Xiūfàn (休範) believed him.
Huí (回) winked at Jìng'ér (敬兒).
Jìng'ér (敬兒) seized Xiūfàn's (休範) self-defense knife
and cut off Xiūfàn's (休範) head.
Xiūfàn's (休範) hundreds of attendants scattered in shock.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) galloped back to Xīntíng (新亭) with the head.
He was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍)
and given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍).
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖), considering Jìng'ér's (敬兒) rank to be light,
[一九] did not want to immediately appoint him to the important garrison of Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Jìng'ér (敬兒) kept asking for it,
and then subtly moved Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖), saying:
"Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) is in Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Do you know what he intends to do?
If you do not send Jìng'ér (敬兒) to guard against him,
I fear it will not be to your benefit."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) smiled and said nothing,
but then appointed Jìng'ér (敬兒) as Chíjié (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng (雍) and Liáng (梁) Prefectures and Yǐng (郢) and Sī (司) Commanderies, Yōngzhōu Cǐshǐ (雍州刺史),
[二０] with his generalship as before,
and enfeoffed him as Xiāngyáng Xiàn Hóu (襄陽縣侯),
with two thousand households.
His troops were moored at Miǎnkǒu (沔口).
Jìng'ér (敬兒) crossed the river in a small boat (zé měng 舴艋)
to visit Jìnxī Wáng Xiè (晉熙王燮).
In the middle of the river, the boat capsized in a storm.
His strong attendants each swam away,
leaving two junior officials submerged below.
They cried out,
"Officer!"
Jìng'ér (敬兒) held them under his armpits.
As the boat flipped over and righted itself,
he always managed to stay above the water.
After such repeated overturning for dozens of li,
he was finally rescued.
Having lost his ceremonial staff (jié 節),
he was given a new one.
When Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) heard that Jìng'ér (敬兒) had arrived,
he sent men to scout.
Seeing that the welcoming ceremony for Yōngzhōu (雍州) was very grand,
he feared a surprise attack
and secretly made preparations.
When Jìng'ér (敬兒) arrived at his post,
he greatly befriended Yōuzhī (攸之),
sending constant letters and gifts.
He obtained information about his affairs
and secretly reported it to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖).
Yōuzhī (攸之) received letters from Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖)
discussing confidential matters about selecting and employing provincial governors (fāngbó 方伯),
and he often showed them to Jìng'ér (敬兒),
thinking he was a double agent,
but Jìng'ér (敬兒) never had a second thought.
Towards the end of Yuánhuī (元徽) era,
Xiāngyáng (襄陽) suffered a great flood,
with flat ground several *zhang* deep in water.
The people's assets were all swept away,
and Xiāngyáng (襄陽) was devastated.
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) wrote to Yōuzhī (攸之),
ordering him to provide relief loans,
but Yōuzhī (攸之) paid no attention.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) had a close relationship with Yōuzhī's (攸之) Sīmǎ (司馬) Liú Rǎngbīng (劉攘兵).
When Cāngwú (蒼梧) was deposed,
Jìng'ér (敬兒) suspected Yōuzhī (攸之) would consequently raise an army.
He secretly asked Rǎngbīng (攘兵) about it.
Rǎngbīng (攘兵) said nothing,
but sent Jìng'ér (敬兒) one stirrup.
Jìng'ér (敬兒) then made preparations.
In the winter of Shēngmíng (昇明) first year,
Yōuzhī (攸之) rebelled
and sent an envoy to inform Jìng'ér (敬兒).
Jìng'ér (敬兒) received him courteously and completely,
prepared food and wine for him,
and said to him:
"Why did Duke Shěn (沈公) suddenly send you, sir?
Sir, you are quite capable of giving orders."
Then he lined up his guards in front of the hall and beheaded him.
He assembled his troops
to spy on Yōuzhī's (攸之) movements below.
[二一] They were to attack Jiānglíng (江陵).
At this time, Yōuzhī (攸之) sent a letter to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖), saying: "I have heard that fish forget each other in rivers and lakes,
and people forget each other in the Way.
You and I can be said to have understood this.
During Dàmíng (大明) era,
I mistakenly served the sacred lord,
and was unworthy to be among
the attendants.
Our feelings were of shared hardship,
and our loyalty was as firm as cutting metal.
We shared silk for clothes,
and rations for food.
When Jǐnghé (景和) was corrupt and violent,
my heart was scorched and my body withered.
Such
suffering
cannot be fully expressed.
I resigned myself to having my head shattered at the pavilion,
and you too feared the extermination of your clan at the hand of the palace attendants.
At that time, our hearts were as firm as a rock,
and we had no
second thoughts.
Pressured by the difficult times,
we sought to preserve ourselves together.
Heaven pities the good,
and this principle is not in vain.
The beginning of our bond through marriage
truly concerned deep affection.
When Emperor Míng (明帝) ascended the
throne,
everyone else was gone.
You and I
received great grace,
our intimacy surpassed former friendships,
and we were treated as substitute officials.
Considering our deeds and hearts,
I was again unworthy to be employed.
On the day of his demise,
I was included in his last wishes,
receiving honor and favor,
with deep benevolence and high position.
Although my feelings are lacking compared to ancient worthies,
I vaguely understand loyalty and integrity.
I swore to repay him,
expecting
would surely die.
This indeed means that my aspirations were never realized;
the former emperor ascended to the heavens,
and my humble wishes were forever taken away.
Since then,
my verbal and face-to-face interactions with Your Excellency have almost ceased.
It is not merely that
we are separated physically,
but it naturally came to this.
Should you ever send a letter,
I never fail to shed tears upon reading it.
How could I wish to reproach you now?
If I harbor something in my heart,
I cannot
but disclose it.
Initially, I received a letter from your worthy son, Zé,
〔二二〕saying he got a family letter,
which stated that Your Excellency was involved in the matter of deposing and establishing a ruler.
To pacify the country and secure the people—
this achievement is immense,
something ordinary people
like us cannot comprehend.
Soon after, I received an imperial edict from the Empress Dowager,
stating that Your Excellency secretly conceived a profound strategy,
making decisions independently.
How bold!
But though a hat may be worn out,
it cannot
be used to wipe one's feet.
This is because it is universally honored.
Your Excellency cultivated connections with those around you,
personally committed acts of murder and rebellion,
to avoid personal misfortune.
You must think Lóngfèng and Bǐgān
were fools.
In matters of such great importance as deposition and establishment,
one should not widely consult.
However, Yuán and Chǔ left behind their legacies,
and Liú was a close relative of the state.
Several ministers had real, fertile landholdings,
and their positions
held contemporary prestige.
If these people were not consulted,
then with whom could one share one's heart?
The changing of darkness and light (rulers)
has existed since ancient times.
Why should the great Sòng
alone be exempt from this misfortune?
The grand ceremonies of previous dynasties
are brilliantly recorded in history.
Allow me to speak of them for Your Excellency.
The assembled officials deliberated together,
deeming it appropriate to appeal to the Empress Dowager,
and to act according to her decree.
The ruler should be sent
out of the palace with royal rites.
How can Your Excellency fail to understand this great principle,
and insist on listening to the words of a jūnzi?
How can you disregard heavenly principles
to such an extent?
The Xiàojīng says:
“Serve one's father
to serve one's lord.”
Even if it were for the great plan of the ancestral altars,
and not for this reason,
do you not understand the meaning of having a lord and a parent?
Instead, you consider the danger to your family,
and tempt with titles and rewards.
A base person,
acting without propriety,
then commits regicide.
Though I have limited knowledge,
I secretly sought ancient comparisons.
How could a minister ever have committed such recent acts?
To suddenly inflict suffering,
separating
body and head.
The living are hateful,
but what crime did the dead commit?
Furthermore, there is the reward for ascending the hall.
From what text does this rule originate?
All officials and subordinates,
who among them is not shocked and dismayed?
Both Chinese and barbarians strike their chests in grief,
and travelers weep blood.
To not even grant a funeral,
allowing maggots to infest the house—
since ancient times,
how many such instances have there been?
The state of Wèi was small,
yet it had
Hóngyǎn.
I did not expect that our Sòng,
alone, would have no such person.
I beat my chest in sorrow,
unable to control myself.
How is Your Excellency different from those who committed murder in the past?
Human nature easily turns;
it will revert to lamentation and sorrow.
For one who acts as a son to the ruler,
is this not difficult?
The analogy of trespassing on a field,
how is this any different?
Guǎnd Zhòng said,
"A ruler's good deeds are never unadmonished."
Your
Excellency, no remonstrance is heard from you,
willingly accepting the crime of Cuī Zhù.
〔二三〕What evil and rebellious suffering!
〔二四〕In the past, Tàijiǎ returned to his position,
and Yī did not doubt himself.
The faults of Chāngyì
were innumerable,
yet Huò Guāng, entrusted with the task,
still discussed it with the court officials
before deposing
him.
Because of the benefits of his imperial stipend,
〔二五〕commentators did not accuse him of coercing the ruler.
Huán Wēn's heart
had not forgotten usurpation.
Hǎixī lost the Way,
and human relations were
completely ruined.
Yet, when he was deposed publicly,
he was still treated with ceremony.
When Wēn was powerful and strong,
who could resist him?
Yet he still feared appearances,
and the whole world was not pleased.
There was never anyone who willingly supported
him.
Yīyǐn and Huò Guāng
are renowned for their loyalty as ministers.
The Huán clan also escaped the charge of coercion and usurpation.
All these matters
are recorded in books and documents.
They are so easy to understand,
they don't need pointing out.
You often said you followed in the footsteps of Yí and Shú.
How then can you suddenly surpass Jié and Zhí in wickedness?
A sage and enlightened ruler initiated a new era,
and the common people were remade.
Throughout the land,
who does not sing and clap?
This is truly a day for baring one's heart, exhausting one's loyalty, dedicating oneself to public service, and forgetting private interests.
Yet Your Excellency
lavishly acquired palace women,
plundered the imperial treasury,
and surely filled your private chambers with weapons and precious jewels.
You replaced old officials at court
and installed your private partisans.
Wearing armor, you entered the palace,
and all inner and outer palace gates,
locks, and keys
are controlled by your household members.
I do not know if Zǐmèng and Kǒngmíng's teachings were like this.
Did Wáng, Xiè, Táo, and Yǔ act in this manner?
Moreover, Zhūfāng is the imperial capital;
it is not conferred upon non-relatives.
Your Excellency is not an imperial kinsman,
yet you suddenly act presumptuously and establish yourself.
You say your son guards the imperial city,
and your father resides in the Eastern Residence.
Two positions in one family—
how is this any different?
I know that Your Excellency's defenses are strong and redundant,
and your suspicions and fears are manifold.
You speak of defending against external threats,
but in reality, you are guarding against internal ones.
If your virtue matches the people's expectations,
even barbarians would be willing to share their hearts with you.
If you deviate from reason and the Dao,
then fortified cities and moats are useless.
Wéncháng protected himself with spears and halberds,
but how did he escape destruction?
Wú Qǐ said:
“If righteousness and propriety are not cultivated,
all those in the same boat become enemies.”
Your Excellency has neither Wǔ Yuán's pain,
but if you harbor greed
and have the heart to harm Sòng,
would I rather discard the integrity of Shēn Bāo?
It is said that those who seek loyal ministers must come from the gates of filial sons.
Your loyalty and filial piety are now exhausted!
Now you secretly steal gold and silks from the imperial treasury to bestow illicit favors,
and usurp state power and titles
to win over people.
Moreover, these appointments are not rightful.
Those who align with me are rewarded.
This method cannot be used forever.
Once it has been used up,
I fear it is not a loyal strategy.
Furthermore, those who receive it
unfeeling.
Those who knew (me) did not understand (me).
Unable to prevent villainy or thwart schemes,
I am sincerely moved to indignation and regret.
Separated by thousands of *lǐ*,
I have no means to confront you directly.
I cannot know what your expression or countenance is like now,
nor if you
still recall our old friendship.
I have heard that former sages, when breaking off a friendship,
spoke no ill words.
But I merely declare my reputation and integrity within my heart,
and thus bid farewell for a thousand years.
As I lay down my brush, I sigh repeatedly;
publicly and privately, my tears stream down.
I imagine you will not take too deep offense at my past words.
However, the eyes and ears of the world,
how can they be deceived?
Moreover, you should know that once you cast your staff without limit,
it will inevitably be the first thing to reach its target.
Tài Zǔ (Emperor Gāo of Southern Qí) set up camp at Xīntíng.
His letter in reply to Yōu (meaning Wáng Yōu) said: "I am humbled by your critical letter.
That our friendship did not last to the end
is shame enough.
If you wish to descend, then come.
Why do you deceive gentlemen so often?
When I first tied my hair and entered officialdom,
did I ever expect great things?
I was simply moved by the words of Zǐ Lù,
and never chose an office based on its prestige.
When Emperor Wén was on the throne,
I was first recognized and
appreciated by the sagely and enlightened ruler.
And in the reign of Emperor Xiào Wǔ,
I again received the kind regard of the brilliant sovereign.
Moved by this gratitude,
I was unable to withdraw myself.
When I folded my sleeves and established friendship with you,
our affection and
bond were firm.
Did I not always encourage the aspiration for the heart of a national hero, like the ancients,
and strive to honor the loyal and steadfast integrity of excellent predecessors?
As for our intimate cups of wine,
our earnest hand-in-hand strolls,
the recommendation of my daughter for
marriage,
our shared resolve and promises –
the depth of our righteousness and trust,
who could come between it?
Moreover, during the tyranny of Jǐng Hé,
when affairs were urgent and fearsome,
Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
and our fortunes rose together in glory.
We opened our hearts and discussed our thoughts;
how could our views on security and danger differ?
In the late period of Yuán Huī,
he listened to the wicked words of Gāo Dàoqìng,
wishing to launch an attack against you.
He issued decrees and orders,
which had already been circulated internally and externally.
At that time,
officials and subjects were silenced,
and people communicated with their eyes on the roads.
Because of our deep friendship and weighty righteousness,
and that we should share hardships equally,
I braved drawn blades
to vouch for and protect you.
The imperial decree from the perverse ruler
is now
sealed and sent for you to see.
Was it not out of fear of his authority,
but rather out of consideration for the righteousness of our association?
Considering this hidden kindness,
how could I be ashamed of my innermost feelings?
I do not say that you maliciously harbored harmful bias.
Previously,
when I sent Wáng Sīwén with a report on court affairs,
it was because my feelings were like those for family and country,
to jointly examine what was appropriate or not.
With an open mind, whether in small matters or large,
I would always inform you first.
When asked on what
day Zhāng Yōngzhōu would be transferred,
who I intended to nominate?
This was originally a presumptuous discussion of future events,
not an attempt to replace Zhāng.
Instead, I sealed and showed this to Zhāng,
to provoke him into anger.
If Zhāng were confused by a single word
and indeed harbored
resentment,
it would be contrary to our refined principles,
something a gentleman would not do.
Moreover, Zhāng's service to the state
is based on loyalty and integrity.
How could the affection given to him,
and the shared understanding of our intentions, be unswerving?
Furthermore, Zhāng
Yōngzhōu reported
that there was unrest among the barbarians there,
and that the people were suffering from floods.
You were commanded to devise a plan to save them.
I also reported,
discussing the state as if it were my home,
expressing
my feelings frankly,
always hoping for clear communication.
Yet, in our interactions,
there was always suspicion and estrangement.
You, in turn, said that I sent messages for no reason,
and that this was espionage.
With a fair and open mind,
our actions always
obstructed each other,
harming and betraying our original intentions.
Who caused this?
Earlier, when you sent a message,
renewing our covenant and strengthening our old friendship,
and urged steadfastness to the end,
I merely replied,
fully expressing my
original feelings,
hoping our agreement would be far-reaching
and as solid as metal and stone.
Today's actions and mistakes,
who is truly ashamed of our long-standing words?
At the end of Yuán Huī's virtue,
his power was lost, and sacrifices ceased.
[二六]You are well aware of this,
there is no need to elaborate.
The Empress Dowager, solely concerned,
acted in accordance with previous admonitions.
The strategy of ending and establishing
fell to my humble self.
Deposing the dark and establishing the bright
was truly in line with previous precedents.
To stabilize the state for the new sovereign,
how is it inferior to the achievements of predecessors?
The removal and establishment had clear procedures,
which you sanctioned.
The criticism of 'worn-out cap,'
what will you
say to that?
To be enfeoffed as a princely county,
is that a breach of etiquette?
Jǐng Hé was nameless;
is it not worse than that?
Lóng Fēng was merely an excellent commoner,
while Yī (Yī Yǐn) and
Huò (Huò Guāng) were ministers of the state.
To conflate the similar and the different,
that is not what I accept.
Those who ascend the platform receive rewards;
Shòu Jì (Shòu Jìshī) already received this previously.
Those who conspire together and achieve merit;
Emperor Míng
also did this in the past.
These are instances where achievements followed one another;
who would dare to dispute them?
You said that I greatly took palace women,
and robbed the imperial treasury,

must fill my private chambers.
If it were a fabricated 'tiger in the marketplace,'
it would not be limited to
these words.
If I used this to deceive the people,
how could the world be without eyes?
If my heart is without flaw,
this is not what troubles me.
The granting of armor and weapons,
this matter is an old institution.
How can one who is
entrusted with governing the nation,
whose merits have established the ruler,
be allowed to come and go lightly and unescorted,
without relying on imperial guards?
This concern and apprehension

To respectfully receive this favor

The governorship of Zhūfāng,
the dukes and ministers all agreed,
and I also thought that, given my minor achievements,
it would not bring shame upon a province.
Moreover, according to old affairs of Wèi and Jìn,
in the imperial capital's vassal posts,
when was it ever

To break glue and receive a pillar (meaning to break an old bond and take on a new responsibility),

Yuán Càn held Shítóu;
you had no objection to that.
My defense of the East
the prefecture,
when they came to report, he declared them wrong.
His countenance betrayed his resentment,
his frequent laughter concealed his malevolence.
Is it really like this?
Yuán Càn and Líu Bǐng,
who received profound and weighty favor,
once the state and family were secure,
did not consider how to stabilize and pacify them,
but instead, with Your Excellency, secretly conspired and plotted,
on the night of seizing the city,
how could they have cared for
the altars of soil and grain (the state)?
Fortunately, Heaven did not prolong the chaos,

so I immediately joined with Chǔ Wèijūn in a righteous and decisive plan,

I imagine that upon hearing this, Your Excellency
was disheartened and
discouraged.
Your young son, who was humbly serving as a Shìzhōng,

To speak without choosing one's words,

As for my innermost
feelings,
the ancients and all spoke of them.

To compare my conduct to that of Yí [Yì] and [Bó] Shū,

To say that I do not attend court,

whether I attend court or not,

Your Excellency received the benevolent favor of the late emperor,

On the day of the Dǐnghú [incident]

When the Jìnxī Diànxià [Prince of Jìnxī]

(originally Zhì, corrected to)

Good horses and strong soldiers,

Fortunately, the Heavenly reign was immediate,
〔三０〕and your unwarranted ambition also dissipated.
Moreover, you gathered fugitives,

Even to the extent of not obeying imperial decrees,

(Yōu Zhī and his adjutants, Senior Clerk Jiāng Yì and Palace Clerk Fù Xuān, defended Jiānglíng city. Jìng’ér’s army strongly supported him. This served as a farewell.) Jìng’ér reported the rebellion and sent an envoy.
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
and promoted him to Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn,
added Sànqí Chángshì,
changed his title to Dūdū,
and bestowed a set of drum and wind instruments.
〔三一〕Yōu Zhī was defeated and fled from Yǐngchéng.
His son Yuán Yǎn 【along with Senior Clerk Jiāng Yì and Palace Clerk Fù Xuān defended Jiānglíng city.
Jìng’ér’s】 army reached Báishuǐ.
〔三二〕Yuán Yǎn heard cranes cry outside the city,
mistaking them for shouts,
and his heart was seized with fear, wanting to flee.
That night,
Yì and Xuān opened the city gates and fled.
The city collapsed.
Yuán Yǎn fled to Chǒngzhōu
and was killed.
The common people plundered each other.
When Jìng’ér arrived in Jiānglíng,
he executed Yōu Zhī’s close associates,
confiscated hundreds of thousands of their properties,
and appropriated all of it for himself.
Yōu Zhī hanged himself in Tāngzhǔ village.
The residents sent his head to Jīngzhōu.
Jìng’ér had it carried on a shield,
covered with a blue umbrella,
paraded through the markets and towns,
and then sent to the capital.
He was promoted to Zhēng Xī Jiāngjūn,
ennobled as a Gōng,
and his fief was increased to four thousand households.
Jìng’ér built a residence west of Xiāngyáng city,
and amassed wealth.
He also wanted to move Yáng Shúzi’s ‘Tears Stele’
and erect a platform in its place.
His officials admonished him, saying:
“Grand Tutor Yáng’s lasting virtue
should not be disturbed.”
Jìng’ér said:
“Who is the Grand Tutor?
I don’t know him.”
Jìng’ér’s younger brother, Gōng’ér,
refused to take up official posts,
and always lived in Shàngbǎo village,
no different from the local residents.
Jìng’ér invited him and treated him very generously,
but Gōng’ér would visit Jìng’ér once a month
and then leave again.
Gōng’ér’s original name was Zhū’ér,
and he changed his name following Jìng’ér.
Initially,
Jìng'ér, having already executed Shěn Yōuzhī,
sent a report to Liú Dàozōng, the Grand Administrator of Suí Commandery,
who gathered over a thousand men
and set up a camp.
Yáo Dàohé, the Inspector of Sì Prefecture, did not kill Yōuzhī’s envoy,
and secretly ordered Dàozōng to dismiss his troops.
When Yōuzhī besieged Yǐng,
Dàohé dispatched troops to Jǐnchéng to relieve Yǐng.
When the matter was settled,
he was rewarded with titles and honors according to precedent.
Jìng'ér reported all of this in a memorial.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
Tàizǔ ordered the relevant authorities to impeach Dàohé,
and he was executed.
Dàohé, courtesy name Jìngyǒng,
was the grandson of the Qiāng chieftain Yáo Xīng.
His father, Wànshòu,
was the pseudo-Grand General Who Guards the East,
who surrendered to Emperor Wǔ of Sòng
and died as a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
Dàohé began his career as a staff officer for the Administrator of Ānběi under Emperor Xiàowǔ,
had a renowned family name,
and read quite a bit of history.
He often deceived people by saying:
"My grandfather was an emperor,
my father was an emperor,
and I myself was once a Crown Prince."
In the Yuánhuī period, he served as a General of Cavalry,
and rendered meritorious service with Tàizǔ in defeating the Guìyáng bandits at Xīntíng,
serving as an Army-Protecting Sīmǎ.
He was then sent out as Inspector of Sì Prefecture.
He was timid and indecisive,
which led to his execution.
In the third year,
Jìng'ér was recalled to serve as General of the Household,
retaining his position as Attendant-in-ordinary.
Jìng'ér was a military general,
unfamiliar with court etiquette.
When he heard he was to be transferred to the capital,
he secluded himself in a private room, dismissed his attendants, and practiced bowing, yielding, and answering,
moving his body up and down in the air
like this all day.
His concubine and maids secretly peeped and laughed at him.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary and General of the Central Army.
As Jìng'ér had already reached the highest rank among the five classes of officials,
his former enfeoffment
remained unchanged.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary and
General of Agile Cavalry,
and was given staff officers.
When Tàizǔ passed away,
Jìng'ér secretly wept at home, saying:
"The imperial family’s great old emperor,
what a pity!
The Crown Prince is young,
not someone I can match."
The posthumous edict added the title of Ceremonial Director with Authority to Open a Mansion to Jìng'ér.
As he was about to be invested,
he said to his courtesans and concubines:
"After I am invested,
the yellow gates should open."
He then imitated the sound of drums with his mouth.
After his investiture,
Wáng Jìngzé mocked him,
calling him Chǔ Yuān.
Jìng'ér replied:
"What I obtained on horseback,
I can never turn into the merits of Huálín Pavilion."
Jìngzé was very resentful.
Jìng'ér initially could not read,
but in his later years, after becoming a regional governor,
he began to study the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects.
At the Címǔ Temple in Xīnlín, he had a shaman cast spells for his concubine's son,
and called himself one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
However, he knew how to be content.
When he first received drum and fife music,
he was too shy to have it played immediately.
He first married his former wife, Lady Máo,
who bore him a son, Dàowén.
Later he married Lady Shàng.
Lady Shàng was very beautiful,
and Jìng'ér abandoned his former wife to marry her.
Lady Shàng remained in her Xiāngyáng residence and did not accompany him,
and Jìng'ér feared he would not go out again,
so he had his whole family brought down to the capital.
He submitted a memorial to Shìzǔ,
but received no commendation or inquiry,
which made Jìng'ér suspicious.
When Yuán Chóngzǔ died,
he became even more afraid.
His wife said to Jìng'ér:
"Once I dreamt my hands were hot as fire,
and you gained Nányáng Commandery.
During the Yuánhuī period,
I dreamt half my body was hot,
and you gained your home prefecture.
Now I have dreamt my whole body is hot."
A eunuch overheard her words
and reported them.
The matter reached Shìzǔ.
Jìng'ér also sent envoys to establish contact with the aboriginal tribes,
making Shìzǔ suspect he harbored ulterior motives.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
an imperial edict ordered court officials to participate in the Huálín Eight-Precepts Fast.
Jìng'ér was arrested at the assembly.
Léi Zhòngxiǎn, one of Jìng'ér’s attendants, knowing a change was occurring,
embraced Jìng'ér and wept.
Jìng'ér removed his cap and sable, throwing them to the ground, saying:
"It is these things that have misled me."
A few days later,
he was executed.
The imperial edict stated:
"Jìng'ér, this stupid barbarian from the frontier,
was confused and uncultivated.
Having experienced the many difficulties of the late Sòng,
he gained some strength in battle.
He rose from the ranks of soldiers,
and ascended beyond his station.
Yet his foolish impulsiveness was endless,
and his boasting grew deep.
When he previously governed his home prefecture,
he long harbored ulterior motives.
In the past, we were magnanimous,
hoping he might reform.
His position was among the Three Ducal Ministers,
his rank reached the highest of the five classes,
yet no sound of gratitude was heard,
and treachery was repeatedly plotted.
From last year to now,
his disloyalty has deepened.
General Who Guards the East, Jìngzé, and the Administrator of Dānyáng, Ānmín, always at every meeting with him,
reported his vicious cunning,
and that he would surely turn and bite back.
I still believed that he would be moved by grace and righteousness,
and his original nature could be changed.
But recently,
his rebellious tendencies have become manifest.
He believes that with his sons and younger brothers in the west,
he can incite foreign tribes,
and rally the various barbarian groups
to disturb Fán and Xià.
He has resorted to sorcerers and witches
to bewilder others,
falsely fabricating auspicious signs,
and secretly plotting to usurp the throne.
Frost appeared at the time of the founding of the dynasty,
and hard ice formed in the era of succession.
If this can be endured,
what cannot be tolerated!
Heaven's way brings disaster upon the wicked,
and his rebellious plot has been exposed.
Tāng Tiānhuò, a merchant from Jiànkāng, traveled into the barbarian lands,
witnessed the entire conspiracy,
and through swift letters,
provided clear and undeniable evidence.
He should therefore be arrested
and punished according to the law;
those implicated as accomplices
are all specially pardoned."
His son Dàowén,
who was the Administrator of Wǔlíng,
Dàochàng,
who was the Meritorious Officer for the General Who Quells the Barbarians,
Dàogù, and his younger brother Dàoxiū,
were all executed.
His youngest son, Dàoqìng,
was spared.
Several years later,
the Emperor and Prince Yùzhāng, Yí, held a three-day Qúshuǐ banquet indoors.
A skiff drifted to the imperial seat and overturned.
Because of this, the Emperor spoke of Jìng'ér,
and regretted having killed him.
Gōng'ér’s official position reached Member of the Staff of the Secretariat.
In Xiāngyáng,
he heard of Jìng'ér’s defeat,
and fled with dozens of cavalry into the barbarian lands.
He could not be captured.
Later he gave himself up,
and the Emperor pardoned his crime.
The historiographer says: "For military officials in times of peace,
there is an art to establishing oneself.
If not foolish to gain trust,
then one should be wise to save oneself.
When one's intentions and actions are unobstructed,
then one receives leniency.
Chóngzǔ harbored resentment at the Eastern Court,
Jìng'ér feared the proverb 'when the birds are gone, the bow is put away,'
and when the new dynasty had just begun,
they surrendered their lives to the strict law.
If one's feelings are not expressed with indignation,
and one's actions lack profound conviction,
then between glory and disgrace,
there is nothing to be achieved."
A eulogy states: Wáng Chóngzǔ was a general;
his ambition was to chase after victory.
He strategized to trouble the Huái region,
and established meritorious service as the Governor of Yù.
Wáng Jìng'ér oversaw Yōng,
and deeply focused on defending against Chǔ.
Were they not toiling and weary?
Indeed, they raised armies.
They cooked dogs and hid bows,
returning home with different fortunes.
"Lài Yuán is Dàshì,"
doubtful.)
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 7: Wáng Jìngzé, Chén Xiǎndá
Wáng Jìngzé,
was a native of Nánshā, Jìnlíng.
His mother was a shamaness.
When Jìngzé was born, his amniotic sac was purple.
She told people,
"This child has the physiognomy of drums and horns [indicating a general]."
When Jìngzé grew older,
milk glands grew several inches long under both his armpits.
He dreamed of riding a five-colored lion.
At over twenty years old,
he was skilled at "patting and opening" (a type of acrobatics or martial art).
He was appointed as a cavalry guard.
Jǐnghé ordered Jìngzé to jump with a knife,
as high as the White Tiger Banner,
doing this five or six times,
and he never missed when catching it.
He was appointed as the Leader of the Xiá Gǔ Troops,
commanding the fine-armored guards.
He and Shòu Jìzhī together killed Jǐnghé.
Upon Emperor Míng's ascension,
Jìngzé was made a Zhíhé General.
For bringing a knife into the palace to report an affair,
he was imprisoned in the imperial guard for over ten days,
before being reinstated as Zhíhé.
He was appointed Fènwǔ General,
and enfeoffed as a Viscount of Chóng'ān County,
with an income of three hundred fifty households.
When Jìngzé was young, while hunting in the grass,
worms like black beans gathered on his body.
When he picked them off, they detached,
and blood flowed from those spots.
Jìngzé found this disturbing.
He went to a Daoist priest to divine.
The Daoist priest said,
"You need not worry.
This is an auspicious sign for being enfeoffed as a marquis."
Jìngzé was pleased to hear this,
and thus he went to the capital to offer his services,
and it came true as predicted.
In the early days of Tàishǐ,
Jìngzé was made Lóngxiáng General and Army Commander,
and followed Níngshuò General Liú Huáizhēn to conquer Shòuchūn.
Yīn Yǎn dispatched General Liú Cóng to build four forts at Sǐhǔ.
Huáizhēn sent Jìngzé with a thousand men to go around the rear,
advancing directly to Héngtáng.
The bandit troops were surprised and retreated.
He was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng,
and then assigned as Magistrate of Jìyáng (Dōngwǔ).
When Jìngzé first left the capital,
he arrived at the foot of Lùzhǔ Mountain.
Over ten boats of his companions departed together,
but Jìngzé's boat alone would not move forward.
He then ordered his younger brother to go into the water and push it.
They saw a black lacquered coffin.
Jìngzé said,
"You are no ordinary vessel.
If this is a good omen,
make my boat advance quickly.
When I become wealthy and honored,
I will rebury you."
The boat moved forward shortly after.
Once Jìngzé arrived in the county,
he collected this coffin and buried it.
After the period of military desolation,
a group of bandits in the county had fled into Zǐ Mountain, causing trouble for the people.
Jìngzé sent someone to convey his message to the bandit leader,
saying that if they would all surrender,
he would plead their case.
The local temple deity was very severe,
and the people believed in it.
Jìngzé swore an oath by the deity,
promising not to break his word.
Once the bandit leader came out,
Jìngzé set up a feast in the temple.
During the feast, he seized and bound them,
saying,
"I first appealed to the deity,
and if I broke my oath,
I would return ten oxen to the deity.
Now, I have not violated my oath."
He immediately killed ten oxen to appease the deity,
and simultaneously executed all the bandits.
The people were pleased.
He was promoted to Yuánwàiláng.
In the second year of Yuánhuī,
he followed Grand Ancestor (Xiāo Dàoichéng) to resist the Guìyáng bandits at Xīntíng.
Jìngzé, along with Yǔlín Supervisor Chén Xiǎndá and Níngshuò General Gāo Dàoqìng, went by boat to engage the enemy in the middle of the river,
severely defeating the bandit navy
and burning their ships.
After the affair was settled,
he concurrently held the position of Grand Administrator of Nántàishān,
Right Xiá Gǔ Commander,
was transferred to Yuèqí Commandant,
and then Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary to the Prince of Ānchéng.
When the Prince of Cāngwú was cruel and tyrannical,
his attendants could not protect themselves.
Jìngzé, knowing of Grand Ancestor's prestige,
sincerely pledged allegiance and served him.
Every time he finished his shift,
he would go to the commander's residence.
At night, dressed in green clothes,
he would crawl along the roads,
spying on Cāngwú's movements for Grand Ancestor.
Grand Ancestor ordered Jìngzé to await an opportunity inside the palace,
but no definite date was set.
Later, Yáng Yùfū and others, in dire straits, killed the emperor.
Jìngzé was at home at the time.
Yùfū brought the head and threw it to Jìngzé.
Jìngzé immediately rushed to Grand Ancestor.
Grand Ancestor feared he was being deceived by Cāngwú
and did not open the gate.
Jìngzé shouted loudly from outside the gate,
"It's Jìngzé!"
The gate still did not open.
So, he threw the head over the wall.
Grand Ancestor asked for water to wash and examine it.
After examining it,
he put on his military attire and came out.
Jìngzé followed him into the palace.
Upon reaching Chéngmíng Gate,
the gate guards suspected that it was not Cāngwú returning.
Jìngzé, fearing someone might peek and see,
used a sword pommel to block the peephole,
and urgently shouted for the gate to be opened.
The Imperial Guard Aide, Yán Língbǎo, secretly saw Grand Ancestor riding a horse outside
and whispered to a close relative,
"If we don't open the gate for the Commander of the Imperial Army now,
the world will surely fall into chaos."
The gate opened,
and Jìngzé followed Grand Ancestor into the palace.
The next morning,
the four high-ranking officials gathered for a discussion.
Jìngzé drew a white blade and leaped beside the bed, saying,
"The officials should make their decisions;
who dares to have a different opinion!"
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
he was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, Fǔguó General, Xiāoqí General, and concurrently Grand Administrator of Línhuái,
with an increased enfeoffment of one thousand three hundred households,
and was in charge of the palace guard's military affairs.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's incident arose,
Jìngzé was given the title of Guānjūn General.
Grand Ancestor entered and guarded the imperial court.
On the evening Yuán Càn raised troops,
Commander Liú Yùn, Zhíhé General Bǔ Bóxīng, and others in the palace conspired,
preparing to mobilize.
Jìngzé opened the gate, launched a surprise attack,
and killed them all.
All the secret uprisings within the palace were quelled,
which was due to Jìngzé's efforts.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi General,
with his Chángshì title remaining as before.
His enfeoffment was increased to two thousand five hundred households,
and shortly thereafter, another five hundred households were added.
Furthermore, Jìngzé's son, Yuánqiān, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngxiāng,
with an income of three hundred seventy households.
When the Qí dynasty was established,
he became Zhōnglǐngjūn.
When Grand Ancestor was about to receive the abdication,
the artisans recommended replacing the columns of the Tàijí Hall.
The emperor wanted to avoid the bad omen of the "earth" element,
and refused to leave the palace to abdicate.
The next day,
he was supposed to appear before the imperial carriage, but
the emperor again fled into the palace.
Jìngzé brought a carriage to welcome the emperor,
and patiently persuaded him to come out.
The emperor patted Jìngzé's hand and said,
"There is certainly no need to worry;
I will reward Fǔguó with a hundred thousand coins."
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials, Sànqí Chángshì, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of the Five Prefectures of Nánxǔ, Qīng, and Jì, Píngběi General, and Inspector of Nánxǔ Prefecture,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Xúnyáng Commandery,
with an income of three thousand households.
Jìngzé's wife, Lady Huái, was given the noble title of Lady of Xúnyáng State.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Ānběi General.
When the barbarians invaded Huái and Sì,
Jìngzé was afraid
and abandoned his post to return to the capital.
The common people were all frightened and scattered, fleeing.
The emperor, considering him a meritorious minister,
did not question him,
and appointed him Dūguān Shàngshū and Fǔjūn.
Soon after, Táo Qīnjiān was appointed bearer of the imperial credential, palace attendant, General of the Pacified East, and Administrator of Wúxīng Commandery.
The commandery had previously suffered much from banditry.
When a ten-year-old boy picked up a lost item on the road,
Táo Qīnjiān had him executed as a warning,
and from then on, nothing was picked up on the roads,
and there were no robberies in the commandery.
He also apprehended a thief,
summoned his relatives and flogged him in front of them,
and made the thief personally sweep the streets for a long time.
After a long period, he ordered the thief to find another former thief to replace him.
The thieves, fearing being recognized by him,
all fled,
and the entire region became orderly.
While on an outing,
passing through the market,
he saw a butcher's block for meat
and sighed,
"Wúxīng had no such block in the past;
this is what I made here when I was young."
Táo Qīnjiān was promoted to General of the Household Guard,
his position as palace attendant remained as before,
and his household was made into a headquarters.
Three years later,
he resigned due to a reburial.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred the title of Grand Madam of Xúnyáng Principality on Jìngzé’s mother.
He was then appointed Attendant Counselor and General of the Garrison.
The Grand Ancestor's dying wish was for Jìngzé to lead Dānyáng Prefecture with his current rank.

Soon after, he was transferred to bearer of the imperial credential, palace attendant, Inspector of Military Affairs of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā Five Commanderies, General Who Guards the East, and Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he was granted a set of drums and pipes.
The region of Kuàijī bordered lakes and seas,
and all commoners, regardless of status, were compelled to work on the embankments.
Jìngzé, seeing that there was a surplus of labor,
assessed and collected the value in money,
sending it to the imperial treasury, considering it convenient.
The Emperor assented to this.
Wáng Ziliáng, Prince of Jìnglín, submitted a memorial, saying: "I humbly reflect that the Three Wú region is inland,
the key stronghold of the state,
and a source of all resources.
The common people are suffering and scattered,
day by day they face hardship and destitution.
Silk farming and agriculture yield little,
and hunger and cold are especially severe.
The wealthy gradually increase their riches,
while the poor become increasingly burdened by their miseries.
This is truly heartbreaking
and impossible to fully describe.
Recently, money has become expensive and goods cheap,
almost doubling in disparity.
All
classes
are affected this way.
Farming is difficult and laborious,
with a bushel costing only a few tens of coins;
now, despite diligent work on looms, a bolt of cloth fetches only three hundred.
The reason for this
is truly not without cause.
The annual taxes and levies
have a fixed schedule,
and what is submitted by the commoners
is always based on actual value.
In the eastern region, much of the money is clipped and cut,
with few intact coins remaining.
What the government accepts
must be whole and substantial,
so two are taken for one.
This distresses those who trade,
and floggings and imprisonment
only increase their misery.
When I formerly served in Kuàijī,
I was somewhat familiar with the local customs.
What was submitted by the embankment laborers
was originally not sent to the government.
This was because reservoirs and lakes needed to be dammed,
and bridges and roads needed to be clear.
Labor was allocated
and valued,
for the people's own use.
If a section was damaged,
it was repaired once a year;
if a section remained strong and intact,
then there was no labor throughout the year.
Now, the commandery universally levies this payment
and sends it all back to the imperial court.
Beyond the regular rents and taxes,
another levy is imposed.
This causes embankments and roads to collapse and become overgrown,
and lake sources to leak and dissipate.
This truly causes harm to the people and damages governance more severely than anything else.
In the early Jiàn​yuán period,
cunning barbarians roamed,
and military expenditures were vast.
In the five commanderies of eastern Zhèjiāng,
a poll tax of one thousand coins was imposed,
leading some to sell their wives and children
to meet this obligation.
The
roads were filled with sorrow and poverty,
a sight unbearable to witness.
Much remained unpaid,
and collection efforts ceased.
I then fully reported this,
and it was immediately pardoned.
However, for this year's rents and levies,
one-third
remains unpaid.
It is clear that this merely harasses the people
and truly harms the state.
I humbly suggest that the embankment labor levy
should be restored to its old system.
Any arrears
should be generously pardoned.
For all payments due,
regardless of amount,
the local authorities
should be instructed to exchange them for cloth and silk.
If the people have sundry goods
that are needed by the military or the state,
they should be allowed to exchange them at their market value,
not necessarily required to send money.
This would not diminish the government's use,
and would greatly benefit the private sector.
In the early days when the Jìn dynasty relocated,
the area south of the Yángzi River was newly established,
and the value of silk and cloth
was ten times what it is today.
The amount of tribute and levies
was increased or decreased according to the times.
In the Yǒngchū period,
a bolt of official cloth
was valued at one thousand coins,
but what the people paid
was allowed to be nine hundred.
Gradually, by the Yuánjiā period,
commodity prices had further fallen.
A bundle of private goods would fetch six thousand,
while the government would accept a bolt for five hundred.
Thus, whenever they wished to favor the people,
they would always lower the amount.
Now, a bolt of good cloth accepted by the government
is worth over one hundred coins,
yet what the common people send
still
follows the old system.
In the past, this was a benefit to the payers;
now, it is a burden.
Is not the poverty and scarcity among the common people
caused by this?
To save the people and remedy this malady,
nothing is better than reducing taxes.
Even in times of peace and good harvests,
there is still such emptiness and lack.
Should there be floods or droughts,
how can we even bear to think of it?
Moreover, when the Western Capital flourished and was strong,
it was truly based on the Three Fǔ;
when the Eastern Capital was completely secure,
it truly relied on the Three Hé.
This has been consistent throughout dynasties,
an unchanging principle from ancient times to the present.
Beyond Shítou,
it is barely enough to supply the prefectures and commanderies themselves;
east of Fāngshān,
it deeply concerns the very foundation of the imperial court.
These vital areas are crucial
and must not be neglected.
They ought to receive lenient policies
and a bit more generous care.
Neglecting the small immediate profits
for the long-term great benefits
would ensure that the people's wealth is not meager
and the national treasury not small.
High-ranking officials, entrusted with great responsibilities,
all speak of benefiting the state.
But my humble opinion
is that I do not see how this
can bring peace.
The Emperor did not accept it."
Three years later,
he was promoted to the title of Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn.
Wáng Yì's concubine, Lady Lù, the son of the Sòng governor of Guǎngzhōu,
was violent
and frequently killed maids.
Wáng Yì's son, Fǎmíng, reported her to Jìngzé.
[一七]Jìngzé had her imprisoned in Shānyīn and executed.
Lady Lù's family appealed,
and Jìngzé was impeached by the judicial authorities.
Liú Dài, the magistrate of Shānyīn, was condemned to public execution.
When Jìngzé had an audience with the emperor,
the emperor said to Jìngzé,
"Human life is of utmost importance.
Who gave the order to kill her?
And why was it not reported to me?"
Jìngzé replied,
"It was my foolish decision.
I do not know the intricacies of the law,
but I saw that there was a precedent,
so I concluded she deserved to be killed."
Liú Dài also admitted his guilt,
whereupon the emperor pardoned him.
Jìngzé was dismissed from his official post,
but retained his command over the district as a duke.
The following year,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng and Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he and Wáng Jiǎn were both appointed to their original titles, with the honor of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
As Wáng Jiǎn firmly declined,
Jìngzé also did not immediately accept.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Yùzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Xīyáng Sīzhōu zhī Rǔnán Èr Jùn Jūnshì, Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
His Kāifǔ status remained as before.
He was promoted to Píqí.
In the eleventh year,
he was transferred to Sīkōng,
with his Chángshì position remaining unchanged.
When Shìzǔ died,
the imperial edict added the title of Shìzhōng.
When Gāozōng assisted in governance,
he secretly harbored intentions of deposition and establishment.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
Jìngzé was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Kuàijī Dōngyáng Línhǎi Yǒngjiā Xīn'ān Wǔ Jùn Jūnshì, and Kuàijī Tàishǒu.
His original official post remained unchanged.
When Hǎilíng Wáng ascended the throne,
Jìngzé was promoted to Tàiwèi.
Although Jìngzé had achieved high status,
he did not indulge in wealth and honor,
but remained vigilant and cautious,
seldom sitting down.
[一八]He conversed with both scholars and commoners in the Wú dialect,
and was always diligent and thorough.
Initially, when he served as Sànqí and was sent as an envoy to the barbarians,
he planted willows at the northern lodge.
Later, when Yuánwàiláng Yú Chángyào returned from his mission to the north,
Jìngzé asked,
"The willows I planted long ago,
how big are they now?"
Chángyào replied,
"The barbarians consider them sweet pear trees."
Jìngzé smiled without answering.
When Shìzǔ composed poetry on his imperial seat,
Jìngzé, holding a piece of paper, said,
"I almost fell into the trap of this fellow's design."
Shìzǔ asked,
"What do you mean by that?"
Jìngzé said,
"If I had been educated,
I would at most have become a Shàngshū Dū Lìngshǐ;
how could I be where I am today?"
Although Jìngzé was not highly literate,
he was very astute and intelligent.
When he governed a prefecture or commandery,
he would have his clerks read out the documents,
and his edicts and judgments
were always sound.
Upon Míngdì's ascension,
Jìngzé was promoted to Dàsīmǎ,
and his stipend was increased by a thousand households.
On the day the imperial envoy came to confer the title,
there was a heavy downpour.
Jìngzé's civil and military officials all turned pale,
but a guest nearby said,
"Your Excellency has always been like this;
it was the same when you were appointed to Dānyáng and Wúxīng."
Jìngzé was delighted,
saying,
"My fate must be to have rain."
So, he arranged his ceremonial guard,
donned his court robes,
and was led out to the listening hall to receive the appointment.
He still felt uneasy,
sticking out his tongue for a long time
until the ceremony was over.
Since the emperor had killed many people,
Jìngzé, being an old minister of Gāo and Wǔ,
felt apprehensive and anxious.
Although the emperor showed him great respect outwardly,
he harbored suspicion and caution inwardly.
He frequently inquired about Jìngzé's diet and physical condition,
and hearing of his aging and
that he resided in the interior,
he felt somewhat relieved.
In the third year,
he sent Xiāo Tǎnzhī with five hundred imperial guards
to visit Wǔjìn Líng.
Jìngzé's sons, who were in the capital,
were distraught and helpless.
The emperor, knowing this,
sent Jìngzé's eldest son, Zhòngxióng, to the East to comfort him.
Zhòngxióng was skilled at playing the qín,
but at that time, his skill was newly surpassed.
The famous "Jiāowěi qín" of Cài Yōng was in the imperial wardrobe,
and the emperor ordered it to be given to Zhòngxióng every five days.
Zhòngxióng played the qín before the emperor, performing the "Àonóng Qǔ" and singing:
"I always lament the unfaithful lover,
and now my lord indeed acts like that!"
The emperor grew more suspicious and embarrassed.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
the emperor fell ill
and repeatedly faced critical danger.
He appointed Zhāng Guī as Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu,
stationing troops and assistants
to secretly guard against Jìngzé.
Rumors circulated both inside and outside the court that there would be a different arrangement.
Jìngzé heard this
and secretly said,
"Who is there in the East now?
It's just that he wants to pacify me!"
His sons were terrified.
His fifth son, Yòulóng, sent Zhèngyuán Jiāngjūn Xú Yuè to secretly inform Xúzhōu Xíngshì Xiè Tiǎo of the situation
and ask for advice.
If Tiǎo agreed, he would report back to Jìngzé.
Tiǎo seized Yuè and rushed to inform the emperor.
Xú Shù, Jìngzé's Chéngjú Cānjūn, whose family was in Jīngkǒu,
had his son secretly inform Shù,
and Shù then told Jìngzé's Wǔguān Wáng Gōnglín.
Gōnglín,
a clansman of Jìngzé,
was always trusted by him.
Gōnglín urged Jìngzé to quickly send a memorial requesting permission for his sons to die,
and return to the capital by single boat overnight.
Jìngzé ordered Sīmǎ Zhāng Sīzǔ to draft the memorial,
but then said,
"If so,
the young lords in the capital
should send some news.
Let's wait for one night."
That night,
he called his civil and military subordinates to play chūpú for money,
and said to the crowd,
"What do you all think I should do?"
No one dared to answer first.
Fánggé Dīng Xīnghuái said,
"Your Excellency should just act."
Jìngzé remained silent.
The next morning,
he summoned Shānyīn magistrate Wáng Xún and Imperial Censor Zhōnglí Zǔyuàn
[一九] (侍, [傳]御史).
Jìngzé sat cross-legged with his sword drawn,
and asked Xún and others,
"How many men can be conscripted?
How much money and goods are in the treasury?"
Xún replied,
"The county's able-bodied men cannot be immediately mobilized."
Zǔyuàn stated,
"Most of the treasury's goods have not yet been transported in."
Jìngzé was enraged
and was about to have them executed.
Wáng Gōnglín again admonished Jìngzé, saying,
"Your Excellency, all other matters can be regretted,
but this matter cannot be regretted!
Why do you not reconsider?"
Jìngzé spat in his face and said,
"You brat!
What I do
is none of your business, you brat!"
Then he raised an army.
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
“Xiè Tiǎo’s (謝朓) memorial to Teng Xú (騰徐) and Yuè Liè (嶽列) is as stated on the right.
Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則) possessed a nature that was fierce and cunning,
fundamentally contrary to human morality.
It was precisely because the late Sòng (宋) dynasty faced many difficulties
that he had some use for his physical strength;
encouragement and promotion led him
to rise to glory and prominence.
When the imperial dynasty was first established,
he was privy to the last discussions;
his achievements were not in aiding the state,
but his rewards truly startled the sovereign.
His rank surpassed those holding ceremonial jade,
and he himself ascended to wearing imperial robes;
this already caused refined gentlemen to feel slighted,
〔二０〕and officials to look askance.
Yet, a valley is easily filled,
and an owl’s nature is hard to change;
suspicion brewed within him,
and ugly words were spread externally.
In the reign of Yǒngmíng (永明),
the treading on frost had its gradual beginnings;
in the era of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
the solid ice was about to form;
he idly joined in,
and We also had a hand in it.
When the imperial calendar was renewed,
We extended sincerity and full courtesy;
imperial envoys were seen one after another,
and high officials were numerous.
Yet, his suspicion grew with prosperity,
and schemes of disaster were thus conceived.
He gathered fugitives,
formed factions and groups,
externally watching for border alarms,
internally seeking national weaknesses.
Yuánqiān (元遷) and his brothers
were gathered in his den;
treacherous agreements were secretly made,
planning a stealthy uprising.
Tiǎo (朓) is his relative by marriage,
and Yuè (嶽) is also a man from his district;
the evidence is not from elsewhere,
but clearly credible.
The virtues of Fāng (方) and Shào (邵) are unheard of,
while the animosities of Hán (韓) and Péng (彭) have already accumulated.
If such a person can be tolerated,
who then needs the legal code!
He should immediately be dispatched for arrest and apprehension,
to solemnly clarify the state’s laws.
Capital punishment shall be applied
only to him and his sons;
all others who were mistakenly involved
shall be completely pardoned.”
Wáng Jìngzé’s (王敬則) sons, Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) Shìxióng (世雄),
〔二一〕Jìshì Cānjūn (記室參軍) Jìzhé (季哲), Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬) Yòulóng (幼隆), and Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人) Shǎo'ān (少安), etc., were arrested
and killed at their residence. His eldest son, Huángménláng (黃門郎) Yuánqiān (元遷),
who was Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍)
and commanded a thousand men in Xúzhōu (徐州) to attack the barbarians,
was ordered by edict to be killed by Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Xú Xuánqìng (徐玄慶).
Jìngzé (敬則) gathered his armed followers
and launched his rebellion within two or three days.
He wanted to abduct the former Zhōngshūlìng (中書令) Hé Yìn (何胤) to return and serve as Shàngshūlìng (尚書令),
but Chángshǐ (長史) Wáng Nòngzhāng (王弄璋) and Sīmǎ (司馬) Zhāng Sīzǔ (張思祖) stopped him.
He then led ten thousand armed soldiers across the Zhèjiāng (浙江) River,
and said to Sīzǔ (思祖):
“We should prepare an announcement.”
Sīzǔ (思祖) replied:
“You are now returning to court yourself,
what need is there for such a thing?”
Jìngzé (敬則) then ceased.

The imperial court dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Qiánjūn Sīmǎ (前軍司馬) Zuǒ Xīngshèng (左興盛), Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (後軍將軍) Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍) Cuī Gōngzǔ (崔恭祖), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Liú Shānyáng (劉山陽), Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將jūn) Mǎjūnzhǔ (馬軍主) Hú Sōng (胡松) with over three thousand men,
to build a fortified camp on Qǔ'ā Chánggāng (曲阿長岡).
Yòupúyè (右僕射) Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) was appointed Chíjǐe Dūdū (持節都督)
and stationed at Hútóu (湖頭),
to guard the Jīngkǒu (京口) road.
Jìngzé (敬則),
〔二二〕being a veteran general, launched his uprising.
The common people, carrying poles and hoes, followed him, amounting to over one hundred thousand people.
When he reached Jìnlíng (晉陵),
Fàn Xiūhuà (范脩化) from Nánshā (南沙) killed Xiànlìng (縣令) Gōngshàng Yánsūn (公上延孫) in response to him.
Jìngzé (敬則) arrived at Wǔjìn Língkǒu (武進陵口),
weeping bitterly as he advanced in a shoulder-borne carriage.
He encountered the two camps of Xīngshèng (興盛) and Shānyáng (山陽),
and attacked them with all his might.
Xīngshèng (興盛) had his soldiers shout to Jìngzé (敬則) from a distance:
“Your sons are all dead,
what are you holding onto this for?”
The government troops were outnumbered and wanted to retreat,
but the encirclement did not open,
so they each fought to the death.
Hú Sōng (胡松) led his cavalry to charge from behind them;
the unarmed commoners scattered in panic,
and Jìngzé’s (敬則) army suffered a great defeat.
Jìngzé (敬則) sought a horse,
tried twice but could not mount it.
Yuán Wénkuàng (袁文曠), a retainer in Xīngshèng’s (興盛) army,
〔二三〕beheaded him
and sent his head.
At this time, the Emperor's illness was already severe;
Jìngzé’s (敬則) hasty uprising in the east
caused alarm and fear at court.
Dōnghūn Hóu (東昏侯), who was in the Eastern Palace,
considered rebelling.
He sent people to climb onto the roof to look,
and seeing fire at the Zhēnglǔ Tíng (征虜亭),
thought Jìngzé (敬則) had arrived,
and hastily packed to flee.
Someone informed Jìngzé (敬則),
who said:
“Tán Gōng’s (檀公) thirty-six strategies,
fleeing is the best plan.
You and your sons should only flee quickly.”
When Jìngzé (敬則) came,
his momentum was very strong,
but he was defeated in just a few days.
He was over seventy years old at the time.
〔二四〕
Zuǒ Xīngshèng (左興盛) was enfeoffed as Xīnwú Xiànnán (新吳縣男),
Cuī Gōngzǔ (崔恭祖) as Suìxīng Xiànnán (遂興縣男),
Liú Shānyáng (劉山陽) as Xiāngyīn Xiànnán (湘陰縣男),
Hú Sōng (胡松) as Shāyáng Xiànnán (沙陽縣男),
each with four hundred households,
as a reward for pacifying Jìngzé (敬則).
Gōngshàng Yánsūn (公上延孫) was posthumously granted the title of Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉).
Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達)
