was a native of Nánpéngchéng (南彭城).
During the reign of Sòng Xiàowǔ (宋孝武),
he served as Zhāng Yǒng’s (張永) Qiánjūn Zhuàngzhǔ (前軍幢主).
During the Jǐnghé (景和) period,
he was promoted for his diligence in service.
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) period,
〔二五〕as a Jūnzhǔ (軍主), he was subordinate to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Liú Huáizhēn (劉懷珍) in the northern campaign,
and successively rose to Dōnghǎi Wáng Bǎnxíng Cānjūn (東海王板行參軍)
and Yuánwàiláng (員外郎).
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he was enfeoffed as Péngzé Xiànzǐ (彭澤縣子)
with three hundred households.
He successively served as Tàishǒu (太守) of the two commanderies of Mǎtóu (馬頭) and Yìyáng (義陽),
Yǔlín Jiān (羽林監),
and Púyáng Tàishǒu (濮陽太守).
He was subordinate to Tàizǔ (太祖) in suppressing the Guìyáng (桂陽) bandits at Xīntíng Lěi (新亭壘).
When Liú Miǎn (劉勔) was defeated at Dàhéng (大桁),
the bandits advanced to Dùmǔ Zhái (杜姥宅).
After Xiūfàn’s (休範) death,
Tàizǔ (太祖) wanted to return to guard the imperial city,
but someone advised Tàizǔ (太祖), saying:
“Although Guìyáng (桂陽) is dead,
the bandit faction is still strong,
public sentiment is difficult to secure,
so you must not move lightly.”
Tàizǔ (太祖) then stopped.
He sent Xiǎndá (顯達) to lead Sīkōng Cānjūn (司空參軍) Gāo Jìngzǔ (高敬祖) to cross the Huái (淮) River from Zhāpǔ (查浦) along the northern road of Shítóu (石頭) to enter the Chéngmíng Mén (承明門)
and garrison at Dōngtáng (東堂).
The palace was in fear and commotion;
upon Xiǎndá’s (顯達) arrival,
it gradually stabilized.
〔二六〕Xiǎndá (顯達) went out to Dùmǔ Zhái (杜姥宅),
fought a great battle, and defeated the bandits.
An arrow struck his left eye,
and he pulled out the arrow, but the arrowhead remained.
Pān Yù (潘嫗) from Dìhuáng Cūn (地黃村) was skilled in incantations;
she first drove a nail into a pillar.
When the old woman performed her Yǔ (禹) steps and chanted,
the nail immediately came out.
She then used her incantation to remove the arrowhead from Xiǎndá’s (顯達) eye.
He was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Xiànhóu (豐城縣侯)
with a thousand households.
He was transferred to Yóují Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍).

Soon after, he was appointed Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander of Guǎng, Jiāo, Yuè, and Guǎngxīng Military Affairs in Xiāng Prefecture, Auxiliary General of the State, General Who Pacifies Yuè, and Governor of Guǎng Prefecture.
His title was advanced to General of the Champions.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
Xiǎndá dispatched troops to reinforce the capital.
His Chief Clerk, Dào Dùn, and Staff Officer, Zhūgě Dǎo, said to Xiǎndá:
"Shěn Yōuzhī commands an army of a million.
The outcome of victory or defeat is yet unknown.
It is better to secure our borders and accumulate troops,
sending trusted messengers
to maintain secret communication between us."
Xiǎndá personally beheaded them at the seat
and sent a memorial expressing loyalty to Tàizǔ.
He was promoted to Bearer of the Staff and Left General.
The army reached Bāqiū
when Shěn Yōuzhī was pacified.
He was appointed Palace Attendant, General of the Left Guard,
then transferred to Front General, and Tàizǔ's Grand Commandant's Left Staff Officer.
When the Qí court was established,
he became Palace Attendant,
General of the Left Guard,
and concurrently Superintendent of the Guards.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Central Protector-General,
his emolument was increased by 1,600 households,
and he was transferred to Protector-General.
Xiǎndá submitted a petition to decline,
to which the Emperor replied:
"The court confers titles according to order.
Your loyalty shone forth from a myriad li away,
your solemn vows were kept as promised.
Even the merit of razing cities and annihilating states
cannot surpass yours.
If this is not rewarded,
where are the ancient statutes?
If you truly believe it is not appropriate,
I would certainly not grant it arbitrarily.
Among the few officials like you,
my feelings are like those for family members.
How can it be limited to just ruler and subject?
Early tomorrow,
come to court with Wáng and Lǐ."
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
the imperial meals did not involve slaughtering animals.
Xiǎndá presented a plate of steamed bear paw,
and the Emperor immediately consumed it as part of his meal.
In the second year of Jiànwán,
barbarians invaded Shòuyáng,
causing unrest among the common people in Huáinán and north of the Jiāng River.

The Emperor appointed Xiǎndá as Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Area Commander of the Military Affairs of Nányùn, Xú, Qīng, Jì, and Wǔ Prefectures, General Who Pacifies the North, and Governor of Nányùn Prefecture.
Upon his arrival at the garrison,
the barbarians retreated.
The Emperor issued an edict to Xiǎndá, saying:
"After the barbarians were routed and dispersed,
they should no longer dare to violate the passes.
However, the state's border defenses
should naturally be overly prepared.
After the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā of the Sòng,
the Prince of Jiāngxià made Nányùn his base,
moving his garrison to Xūyí.
Shěn Sīkōng also garrisoned there at the beginning of Xiàojiàn.
The administration was focused on the importance of the Huái River area over Guǎnglíng.
What do you think of this arrangement by previous generations?
Now, everyone's consensus is that you should occupy that area,
but I cannot yet decide.
This would cause trouble and labor for both civil and military officials.
If it is for the public good,
one must not shrink from it."
The plan was ultimately not carried out.
He was promoted to Area Commander of Yì and Níng Prefectures, General Who Pacifies the West, and Governor of Yì Prefecture,
concurrently serving as Prefect of Sòngníng,
with his Bearer of the Staff and Palace Attendant titles remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
his title was advanced to General Who Guards the West.
The mountainous terrain of Yìbù was treacherous,
and many people were not submissive.
The Dàdù village Man (Láo) tribes,
which previous governors could not control,
Xiǎndá sent envoys to demand their rents and ransoms.
The tribal chief said:
"Even the two-eyed governors dared not demand taxes from us!"
Thereupon, he killed the envoy.
Xiǎndá divided his generals and officials,
announcing that he would go hunting.
That night, he launched a surprise attack,
slaying all, young and old, men and women.
From then on, the mountain barbarians were awed and submitted.
The bandit Sīmǎ Lóngjū of Guǎnghàn revolted by seizing the commandery.
Xiǎndá again suppressed him.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he was summoned to serve as Attendant-in-ordinary and Protector-General.
Xiǎndá had served in various external posts,
and having experienced the distress of Tàizǔ's passing,
when he saw Shìzǔ,
he wept and choked with sobs.
The Emperor also wept
and greatly appreciated him.
In the fifth year,
the bandit Huán Tiānshēng, claiming to be a descendant of Huán Xuán,
incited the Man (Lǔ) tribes on the borders of Yōng and Sī Prefectures,
occupying the old city of Nányáng.
The Emperor sent Xiǎndá, bearing a假節 (jiǎjié) staff,
to lead General Who Conquers Barbarians Dài Sēngjìng and other naval forces towards Wǎn and Yè.
The armies of Yōng and Sī Prefectures were placed under Xiǎndá's command.
The garrison commander of Wǔyīn, Auxiliary General Yīn Gōngmǐn, attacked and killed his deputy, Zhāng Qílín.
Tiānshēng was wounded and retreated.

Subsequently, Xiǎndá was appointed Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Area Commander of Yōng, Liáng, North Qín, South Qín, and Yǐng Prefectures' Jìnglín Commandery, and Sī Prefecture's Suí Commandery Military Affairs, General Who Guards the North,
concurrently serving as Colonel Who Pacifies the Man (Mán), and Governor of Yōng Prefecture.
Xiǎndá advanced to occupy Wǔyáng City,
sending Sēngjìng and others to advance first.
They re-engaged Tiānshēng and the barbarians,
thoroughly defeating them,
and the government forces returned.
Several months later,
Tiānshēng again emerged to attack Wǔyīn.
Yīn Gōngmǐn defeated him,
and Tiānshēng fled back into the wilderness.
The bandits of Suìchéng, Píngshì, and Báitǔ three cities gradually surrendered and dispersed.
In the eighth year,
his title was advanced to General Who Conquers the North.
In the same year,
he was transferred to Attendant-in-ordinary and General of the Garrison,
and soon after, was given the additional title of Central Commander of the Guards.
He was dispatched as Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Area Commander of Jiāng Prefecture Military Affairs, Grand General Who Conquers the South, and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture,
and was granted a complete set of drums and pipes.
Xiǎndá was humble, generous, and had strategic acumen.
Believing himself to be of humble origin yet holding a high position,
each time he was promoted,
he always showed a look of shame and apprehension.
He had over ten sons,
whom he admonished, saying:
"My original ambition did not reach this far.
You must not use your wealth and high status to lord over others!"
his sons, along with the sons of Wáng Jìngzé,
all rode splendid carriages drawn by oxen
and wore magnificent clothes.
The swift oxen of the time were known as Chén Shìzǐ's Qīng,
Wáng Sānláng's Wū,
Lǚ Wénxiǎn's Zhéjiǎo,
and Jiāng Qúntán's Báibí.
Xiǎndá said to his sons:
"The deer-tail whisk is a possession of the Wáng and Xiè families.
In the autumn of the eleventh year,
with barbarian movements,
an edict ordered him to garrison at Fánchéng.
Shìzǔ's dying edict commanded that he be granted the privilege of establishing a government office with the same rank as the Three Ducal Ministers, maintaining his existing title.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary and General of Cavalry and Chariots,
retaining the privilege of establishing a government office,
and was allowed to appoint military assistants.
In anticipation of his merit in the dethronement of Yùlín,
in the first year of Yánxīng,
he was appointed Minister of Works,
advanced to the rank of Duke,
his emolument increased by one thousand households,
and fifty armored guards were permitted to enter the palace.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant,
with his Attendant-in-ordinary title remaining as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Póyáng Commandery,
with three thousand households,
an additional two hundred soldiers,
and was granted an oiled carriage.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians attacked Xú and Sī Prefectures.
An edict ordered Xiǎndá to go out and encamp,
moving between Xīntíng and Báixià,
to project an impression of strength.
The Emperor wished to eliminate all the descendants of Gāo and Wǔ.
He subtly mentioned this to Xiǎndá,
who replied:
"Are these people worth bothering about?"
The Emperor then stopped.
During the Jiànwǔ era, Xiǎndá felt uneasy,
deeply humbled and concealed himself.
His carriages and vehicles were old and worn,
and his retinue of attendants
all used feeble and small ones,
numbering no more than ten.
While attending a banquet,
after drinking, he respectfully said to the Emperor:
"Your subject is old,
and already has enough wealth and status.
All I lack is a peaceful death in my bed.
I specifically beg this from Your Majesty."
The Emperor changed color and said:
"You are drunk, Duke."
He requested to retire on account of his age,
At this time, the captives frequently invaded Yōngzhōu,
and the various armies were unsuccessful,
losing five commanderies north of Miǎnhu.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
Xiǎndá was dispatched to campaign north.
An imperial edict stated:
"When the Jìn clan was in decline,
and Sòng's virtue was about to wane,
vassal ministers rebelled externally,
and the wild frontiers encroached internally.
Heaven has not yet repented of the calamity,
and the 'left-lapel' barbarians have brought disorder to Huá,
nesting in Shénzhōu,
reversing the years and seasons.
I, who have inherited the grand enterprise,
following in the footsteps of previous kings,
reflect on rise and fall,
and ponder how to govern the central land.
But difficulties have just subsided,
and benevolent rule has just begun to spread.
Raising an army to disturb the populace
is not a priority of government.
Thus, distant plans were curbed,
and the northern campaign was temporarily delayed,
hoping that the barbarians would understand righteousness
and embrace our good tidings.
Yet the fierce and cunning brigands
exclusively engage in invasion and plunder,
inciting different tribes,
gathering like ants in the western regions.
Seize this opportunity of their self-inflicted coming,
and embrace this chance of their heaven-ordained demise.
The army will not be deployed twice,
nor the people burdened again.
A proclamation will suffice to pacify Sānqín,
and a single wave of the banner will subdue Yǔjì.
This is the moment for this endeavor.
Moreover, the gentry and commoners of the Central Plains
have long awaited imperial might,
begging for troops and requesting aid,
their carts filling the imperial roads.
Trust cannot be lost,
nor time prolonged.
It is fitting to issue orders to the regional governors,
based on this great mandate.
Attendant Counselor, Grand Commandant Xiǎndá,
may temporarily cease his duties under the huái trees,
and direct the various commanders."
The inner and outer courts were arrayed in solemnity.
Xiǎndá was further granted the title of Bearer of the Imperial Insignia,
heading towards Xiāngyáng.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Xiǎndá commanded a force of 40,000 men, including General Píngběi Cuī Huìjǐng,
and besieged Mǎquān City in Nánxiāngjì,
three hundred lǐ from Xiāngyáng.
After forty days of attack,
the captives ran out of food,
eating the flesh of the dead and tree bark.
As the outer siege became urgent,
the captives burst out and fled.
Thousands were captured or beheaded.
The government troops eagerly seized the silk in the city,
and did not pursue further.
Xiǎndá entered and occupied the city,
dispatching Army Commander Zhuāngqiū Léi to take Nánxiāng County,
which was formerly the seat of Cóngyáng Commandery.
The captive ruler Yuán Hóng personally led over 100,000 cavalry and arrived suddenly.
Xiǎndá led his army across the river, established a fortress on Yīngzishān to the west,
but morale was low.
The enemy's attack was very fierce.
Army Commanders Cuī Gōngzǔ and Hú Sōng wrapped Xiǎndá in a black cloth curtain,
and several men carried him on their shoulders,
taking a direct route from Fēnqíshān to Jūnshuǐkǒu.
The imperial troops fled in disarray along the road,
with over 30,000 casualties.
Left Army General Zhāng Qiān died in battle,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of Agile Cavalry.
Xiǎndá had always enjoyed a reputation for military prowess,
known among the barbarians,
but this occasion resulted in a great loss.
Censor-in-chief Fàn Xiù submitted a memorial requesting Xiǎndá's dismissal.
The court deliberated, and the emperor's gracious reply stated:
"In ancient times, Wèi and Huò campaigned beyond the passes,
often without success;
Féng and Dèng entered the passes,
sometimes suffering losses.
How much more so for the Duke, whose plans were solemnly executed,
whose hopes were deep, and who clearly faced difficulties?
This does not diminish his prestige or strategy.
He is still destined to carry out distant plans,
and clear the northern lands.
Although constitutional law has its regular procedures,
this is not a matter for such discussion."
Xiǎndá memorialized to resign his post,
but it was not permitted.
He requested a reduction in his rank,
which was also not permitted.
Xiǎndá was appointed Governor of Jīangzhōu Military Affairs, Governor of Jīangzhōu,
garrisoned at Pénchéng,
with his imperial insignia and original office remaining as before.
Originally,
when Wáng Jìngzé's rebellion arose,
Prince Shǐ'ān Yáoguāng memorialized to Emperor Míng, expressing concern that Xiǎndá might rebel,
and wished to recall the army.
The matter was soon settled,
and the plan was dropped.
Xiǎndá himself also felt apprehension.
When Dōnghūn came to power,
he was even more unwilling to return to the capital,
and was greatly pleased by this appointment.
He was soon promoted to lead as Grand General Zhēngnán,
and granted a carriage with three pennants.
Xiǎndá heard that there was widespread killing in the capital,
and also learned that Xú Xiàosì and others had all died.
Rumors spread that troops would be sent to attack Jīangzhōu.
Fearing disaster, Xiǎndá
raised an army on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month.
He ordered his Chief Clerk, Yǔ Hóngyuǎn, and Administrator, Xú Hǔlóng, to write to the court nobles, saying: "To all gentlemen: Our Great Ancestor, Emperor Gāohuang, was sagacious and wise by nature,
surpassing others and becoming a sage.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
the imperial order was broken.
He responded to the will of the people for abdication,
and established this foundation.
Our World Ancestor, Emperor Wǔ, was brilliant and far-sighted,
succeeding in the great inheritance.
The four passes were secured,
and the three rivers became peaceful.
Yùlín and Hǎilíng
completely failed to bear their responsibility.
Emperor Míng was heroic and sagacious,
inaugurating a restoration.
But when it came to the Last Ruler,
his actions violated the three cardinal virtues.
Zither playing filled the mats,
embroidered fabrics piled up on hemp cushions.
He committed adultery with former imperial consorts,
and defilement arose in the women's quarters.
The imperial palace became a marketplace,
and decorated chambers gave way to battlements.
Important positions were not given to the illustrious,
and favor was bestowed only upon low-ranking ruffians.
The brothers of Minister Jiāng
offered loyal advice and recommendations,
and righteous remonstrances repeatedly arose,
but the punishment of family extermination
arrived at this point.
Thus, the punishment of being devoured by beasts
was carried out four times by sea routes,
and the calamity for families
arose in the central capital.
Xiāo and Liú, the two commanders,
both ascended the imperial throne,
jointly accepting the late emperor's will.
The suffering of the imperial clan
is truly not worth
mentioning.
The sorrow of Wèiyáng,
why did it come to this undeservedly?
Vice Grand Commandant Xú,
loyal and illustrious through generations,
pure and simple, famous throughout the world,
his merits of assistance were not yet manifest,
but the punishment of family ruin was already clear.
Minister Shěn,
at an age for retirement,
about to consider his staff and chair,
singing happily in his garden retreat,
completely absent from the court gates,
suddenly incurred the punishment of being insulted and killed.
What a sorrow through the ages!
This has caused
the path to the purple palace
to be cut off for the gentry and officials;
the chambers of official caps and seals
to be emptied of descendants of Jīn and Zhāng.
How tragic!
The cicada-wing cap has become the attire of base favorites.
Alas!
The imperial palace is filled with seats for robbers.
Moreover, heaven and man share a common grievance,
and the celestial phenomena are in disarray.
Last year, blood flowed in three provinces,
and now five regions move spontaneously.
In the past, the Hànchí lake changed color,
and King Xū saw this as a sign.
deposed.
Wú Jùn experienced a slight earthquake,
which Bù Shēng regarded as an omen of treacherous prosperity.
Now the situation is more egregious than past anomalies,
and the treachery is more severe than previous cruelties.
If this is not overthrown,
what cannot be revived?
Wáng Púshè, Wáng Lǐngjūn, and Cuī Hùjūn
maintain integrity in the central government,
with thoughts of dissecting the hearts of rebels.
Xiāo Wèiwèi, Cài Zhānshì, and Shěn Zuǒwèi
each uphold their respectable
families,
united in sorrow over the perilous times.
The veterans of the former dynasty,
whose aspiration lies in reputation and integrity,
will collectively sign a declaration,
resolved to join this righteous cause.
Jiàn'ān Diànxià possesses outstanding virtue and far-reaching influence,
and is truly worthy
of the divine artifact (the imperial throne).
The choice between light and darkness,
is a teaching passed down by ancient sages.
Now, I am humbly performing military duties,
and urgently request permission to clear the path.
Once the dust in the capital settles,
we will welcome the imperial carriage from the west,
singing and dancing in great
peace.
Would this not be wonderful!
Péi Yùzhōu has long sent sincere words,
and has harbored noble aspirations for a long time.
Counting his strong troops,
they have already reached the Huái Road;
Shēn Sīzhōu's aspirations are firm and clear,
and he is clearly in agreement,
leading his auxiliary forces,
advancing behind me;
Xiāo Yōngzhōu and Fáng Sēngjì have both made great progress,
their banners and drums will soon arrive;
The Administrator of Nán Yǔn Zhōu, Sīmǎ Cuī
Gōngzǔ, is valorous and exceptional,
with frequent good news from his messengers.
Awaiting news of beacons and spies,
[三五] we will together form a strong alliance.
The provincial officials of Jīng and Yǐng, the two worthies Xiāo and Zhāng,
all draw their swords and face
the wind,
holding their halberds, awaiting the signal;
Among the frontier guardians of the capital region,
who is not a righteous companion?
Our Tàiwèi Gōng embodies the Dao and aligns with the sages,
relying on virtue to cultivate culture.
His divine martial prowess spans across the seven punitive expeditions,
and his heroic strategy shakes the nine divisions.
Thus, he will follow that sequence of heroes,
to restore
the state.
Originally, we intended to sound bugles and offer light tribute,
without needing weapons.
But loyal partisans are resolved,
and their integrity is hard to dismiss.
Within a few days,
a dense army of 100,000 will gather.
Flying banners will darken the Jiǔ Pài,
and lined ships will fill the Sān Chuān.
This is like pouring an ocean on a firefly,
or a raging fire melting ice.
My son, choose what is good and follow it,
do not let
history become a laughingstock for future generations.
The imperial court dispatched Hú Sōng, General of the Rear Army, and Lǐ Shūxiàn, General of Agile Cavalry, with a naval force to occupy Liáng Shān;
Zuǒ Xīngshèng, General of the Left Guard, was granted a staff of authority,
promoted to General of Pacifying Barbarians,
and appointed supervisor of the vanguard army,
to garrison Xīntíng;
Xú Shìbiāo, General of Supporting the State and General of Agile Cavalry, led troops to garrison Dù Mǔzhái.
Xiǎn Dá led several thousand troops from Xúnyáng,
and engaged Hú Sōng in battle at Cǎishí,
thoroughly defeating him,
causing panic in the capital.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month,
Xiǎn Dá arrived at Xīnlín and built fortifications.
Zuǒ Xīngshèng led his forces to prepare for battle.
That night,
Xiǎn Dá placed many signal fires along the riverbank,
secretly crossed the river with his army to attack the palace city from the north of Shítóu.
Due to wind, he lost the advantage of surprise.
At dawn on the fourteenth day,
several thousand men ascended Luòxīng Gǎng.
The Xīntíng army, seeing the fires,
believed Xiǎn Dá was still there.
Soon after, they rushed back to provide aid,
garrisoning the south of the city.
The palace was greatly alarmed,
and closed its gates for defense.
Xiǎn Dá, with his cavalry spear and several hundred infantry,
fought against the imperial troops in front of Xīzhōu.
After two engagements,
he won a great victory,
personally killing several people.
His spear broke.
Imperial troops continued to arrive,
and Xiǎn Dá could not resist.
He retreated to Wūbǎng Cūn behind Xīzhōu.
[三六] There, the cavalry officer Zhào Tán thrust his spear, causing him to fall from his horse.
He was beheaded by the fence,
his blood gushed and drenched the fence,
like Chúnyú Bó being executed.
He was seventy-two years old at the time.
While Xiǎn Dá was in Jiāngzhōu,
he suffered from an illness that was untreatable,
but then recovered spontaneously,
which made him very displeased.
That winter, there was continuous heavy snow.
His head was displayed at Zhūquè,
but the snow did not accumulate on it.
All his sons were executed.
The historian says: The reason why Emperor Guāngwǔ's meritorious officials were able to end their lives with their reputations intact
was not only because they were not entrusted with too many responsibilities,
but also because they consecutively served Míng and Zhāng,
respecting the legitimate heir in their hearts.
The ruler was at peace above,
and the ministers were content below.
When Wáng and Chén rose up and soared,
it was the era of Jiàn Yuán and Yǒng Míng;
when they reached the pinnacle of generalship,
it was the courts of Jiàn Wǔ and Yǒng Yuán.
Their achievements were not like those of former times,
and their positions exceeded their previous ranks.
Although the bestowed rites were grand,
their personal feelings were not intertwined.
Furthermore, the ruler was suspicious and the government chaotic,
and the threat of ruin was imminent.
Everyone raised their hands to protect their heads,
each thinking of saving themselves.
Once weapons were used,
it certainly became an act of rebellion against the superior.
An enemy state arose from those in the same boat,
how much more so for those less closely related?
The encomium says: Stern and upright Jìngzé,
unwavering in times of difficulty.
His achievements secured the palace,
eradicating our pests and thieves.
Xiǎn Dá, with his isolated roots,
responded to righteousness from the south.
His might was displayed, his favor abundant,
enjoying grand banquets and high status.
Wáng humbled Hé and Yǔn,
Chén defeated Xiāng and Fán.
Playing bugles and offering light tribute (doubtful)
Liú Huáizhēn, Lǐ Ānmín, Wáng Xuánzài (younger brother Xuánmiǎo)
Liú Huáizhēn, courtesy name Dàoyù,
was a native of Píngyuán.
He was a descendant of Kāng Wáng of Jiāodōng of the Hàn dynasty.
His grandfather, Chǎng,
when Emperor Wǔ of Sòng pacified Qí, appointed him as Zhìzhōng of Qīngzhōu,
and he rose to Yuánwài Chángshì.
His paternal uncle, Fèngbó,
served as Administrator of Chén and Nándùn commanderies during the Sòng era.
When Huáizhēn was young, he accompanied Fèngbó to Shòuyáng.
When Zhào Bófú, Inspector of Yùzhōu, went hunting,
the common people gathered to watch.
Huáizhēn alone avoided watching,
which Fèngbó found unusual,
saying:
"This child will revive our clan."
He was appointed Mùbù by his home province.
In the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā,
the outlaw Sīmǎ Shùnzé gathered a party in Dōngyáng.
The province dispatched Huáizhēn with several thousand men to secretly attack and pacify them.
Emperor Wén of Sòng summoned him to inquire about the details of defeating the rebels.
Huáizhēn declined the credit and refused to accept it.
His relatives were puzzled and asked him why,
to which Huáizhēn replied:
"In ancient times, Guózǐ Ní was ashamed of the rank of Chén Héxián,
how could I discuss the victory of a region!"
People at the time praised him.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng was stationed in Xūyí.
He met Huáizhēn on the road,
and was greatly impressed by his responses,
taking him as Pàoxí Zhǎngjiān Mòcáo Xíngcānjūn.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Chángguǎng.
In the early Xiàojiàn period,
he became Yìgōng's Dàsīmǎ Cānjūn and Zhíhé Jiāngjūn.
Huáizhēn was from an old prominent family in the northern provinces,
with numerous attached retainers.
He memorialized to the emperor that a thousand of his retainers be used as imperial guards.
Emperor Xiàowǔ was greatly surprised
and recruited several thousand local gentry and their private retainers from Qīng and Jì provinces,
which the scholars resented.
He transferred with the office to become Tàizǎi Cānjūn.
In Dàmíng二年,
the barbarians besieged Sìkǒu城.
Yán Shībó, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, requested aid.
Xiàowǔ dispatched Huái Zhēn with several thousand infantry and cavalry to respond.
They fought the barbarians at Mígōu湖,
and broke seven camps.
He was appointed Jiànwǔ General and Grand Administrator of Lèlíng and Héxián Commanderies,
and granted the peerage of Guǎngjìn Earl.
The following year,
Huái Zhēn petitioned to return.
Xiàowǔ replied,
"The frontier requires talent;
it is not appropriate to resign yet."
When the Prince of Jìnglíng, Tán, rebelled,
the local powerful gentry, Wáng Bì, urged Huái Zhēn to join him.
Huái Zhēn beheaded Bì and reported it.
Xiàowǔ was greatly pleased,
and appointed him Attendant Officer to the Chariots and Cavalry of the Prince of Yùzhāng, Zǐshàng,
and additionally Longxiáng General.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he was appointed Níngshuò General and Grand Administrator of Dōng'ān and Dōngguǎn Commanderies.
He led Longxiáng General Wáng Jìngzé and Jiāng Chǎn with five thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Shòuyáng.
Wáng Zhòngzǐ, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, fled south.
The rebels sent the伪Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, Liú Dàowèi, with five thousand men to station at Jiànwǔjiàn,
where they built three forts.
Huái Zhēn sent Army Commander Duàn Sēng'ài and others with over three hundred cavalry and infantry to surprise attack and decapitate them.
He led his army to Jìnxī,
where the 伪Grand Administrator Yán Zhàn resisted.
Liú Zǐxūn sent his general Wáng Zhòngqiú with ten thousand foot soldiers to relieve him.
Huái Zhēn sent three thousand cavalry and infantry to ambush Zhòngqiú,
and utterly defeated them at Mòyéshān.
He then advanced to Shòuyáng.
He also sent Wáng Jìngzé to defeat Yīn Yǎn's general Liú Cóng and others at four strongholds in Héngtáng Sǐhǔ.
Huái Zhēn and others, seizing the victory, pursued the routed enemy,
and encamped at Shòuchūn Chángluó Gate.
Emperor Míng of Sòng commended his achievements,
appointing him Yǔlín Supervisor and Túnqí Commandant.
His general title remained as before.
Huái Zhēn requested to first pacify the rebels
and declined the appointment.
When the Prince of Jiàn'ān, Xiūér, was stalemated with the rebels at Nónghú,
the situation remained unresolved for a long time.
Emperor Míng summoned Huái Zhēn back,
appointed him Qián General,
additionally Fǔguó General,
and led his army towards Qīngshān to assist in attacking Liú Hú.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Yóujī General,
with his Fǔguó General title remaining as before.
When Shěn Wénxiù, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, defied orders,
Emperor Míng sent his younger brother Wénbǐng to convey the imperial decree,
and ordered Huái Zhēn to lead three thousand cavalry and infantry to accompany Wénbǐng.
Before they arrived,
Xuē Āndū led the barbarians,
and Xú- and Yùnzhōu had already fallen.
Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī suffered a great defeat at Péngchéng.
An imperial order commanded Huái Zhēn's infantry to proceed from Xūyí, cross the Huái River from Huái'yīn, and rescue Yǒng and others.
However, the imperial army was pursued by the barbarians,
and successively fled back.
Huái Zhēn then returned.
In the spring of the third year,
an imperial edict commanded Huái Zhēn to temporarily garrison Shānyáng.
Previously, Emperor Míng had sent Míng Sēnggǎo, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, on a northern expedition.
Sēnggǎo sent a general to build a fort at Wángchéng
to threaten Shěn Wénxiù.
Before the wall was completed,
it was broken by Wénxiù,
who then advanced to attack Sēnggǎo.
The Emperor ordered Huái Zhēn to lead Longxiáng General Wáng Guǎngzhī with five hundred cavalry
and two thousand foot soldiers
to relieve them along the coast.
Upon reaching Dōnghǎi,
Sēnggǎo had already retreated to defend Dōnglái.
Huái Zhēn advanced to occupy Qúchéng.
The troops were terrified,
some even wishing to temporarily hold Yùzhōu.
Huái Zhēn said to the troops,
"You say Wénxiù has heavily bribed the Hú armies
to seek external aid.
Observing his partisans,
how can they necessarily join the barbarians?
When the gentry and commoners of Qí perceive righteousness as paramount,
and their reputation spreads,
Dōnglái can be taken with a flying dispatch.
How can we be hindered and slow our advance by stopping here?"
He then advanced to Qiánzōu.
The 伪Grand Administrators of Gāomì and Píngchāng Commanderies fled in disarray.
Huái Zhēn conveyed the court's intention,
and sent Wénbǐng.
Wénxiù ultimately refused to obey,
and burned the outer city.
When the common people heard that Huái Zhēn had arrived,
they were all joyful.
The 伪Grand Administrator of Chángguǎng, Liú Táogén, led several thousand men to garrison Bùqíchéng.
Huái Zhēn led his army to Yángshuǐ.
Everyone said,
"Wénxiù's light cavalry now fills the territory.
It is advisable to fortify our position and await an opportune moment."
Huái Zhēn said,
"Now our troops are few and our provisions scarce.
We are suspended while they are entrenched.
It is precisely appropriate to select elite troops
and surprise them when they are unprepared."
He sent Wáng Guǎngzhī to lead one hundred cavalry to attack and capture the city.
Táogén fled.
Jú Yánsēng, the 伪Grand Administrator of Dōnglái, with several hundred men, occupied the city
and forcibly detained the Gāolì envoys.
Huái Zhēn again sent Níngshuò General Míng Qìngfú and Guǎngzhī to attack and force Yánsēng to surrender,
and sent the Gāolì envoys to the capital.
When Wénxiù heard that all the cities had fallen,
he sent an envoy, Zhāng Língshuò, to request surrender.
Huái Zhēn then returned.
That autumn,
the barbarians invaded Qí,
besieging Lìchéng and Liángzōu cities.
Their light cavalry reached Dōngyáng,
disturbing the common people.
Cuī Dàogù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, and Liú Xiūbīn, the Inspector of Yùnzhōu, reported the emergency.
Xiūbīn
was Huái Zhēn's cousin.
The court appointed Huái Zhēn as Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the armies of Xú and Yùn Commanderies, Fǔguó General, Pínghú Zhongláng General, and Inspector of Xúzhōu,
ennobling him as Earl of Ài County,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
He commanded over forty thousand naval and infantry troops to go to their rescue.
As the two cities had already fallen,
they stopped.
He was reassigned as Níngshuò General and Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng,
then transferred to Simǎ to the Prince of Bālíng's Zhēngxī General,
additionally Grand Administrator of Nányìyáng.
When the Prince of Jiànpíng, Jǐngsù, was in Jīngzhōu,
he was then transferred to Yòujūn Simǎ,
promoted to Grand Administrator of Nánjùn,
and additionally Níngshuò General.
Emperor Míng personally wrote an edict to Huái Zhēn, saying,
"Your nature is loyal and upright,
which I have always relied upon.
When you are there working with young men,
you must not deeply seek personal gain.
Jǐngsù is indeed good,
but he cannot interact with others
and sometimes neglects his duties.
You must always admonish him."
Huái Zhēn received the order.
When the Emperor was seriously ill,
he again issued an edict to Huái Zhēn, saying,
"You should not have become Jǐngsù's assistant.
Your talent and old loyalty are what I rely on.
I now summon you to serve in the two imperial guards."
Coincidentally, the Emperor passed away,
so he became Fǔjūn Simǎ to the Prince of Ānchéng,
additionally Grand Administrator of Nángāopíng.
The court was suspicious of the Prince of Guìyáng, Xiūfàn.
Wáng Dàolóng, a Secretary of the Central Secretariat, conveyed an imperial decree,
appointing Huái Zhēn as Guànjūn General and Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Huái Zhēn said,
"Although Xiūfàn harbors seeds of disaster,
how dare he immediately act?
If he ultimately becomes a bandit,
I will certainly request to enforce the law and eliminate him.
Now this grant of an envoy
I fear will cause suspicion and coercion."
He firmly declined,
and was then appointed Huángménláng,
additionally Hǔbēn Zhongláng General and Grand Arbiter of Qīngzhōu.
When Guìyáng rebelled,
Huái Zhēn was additionally Qián General,
and defended Shítou.
He was made Bearer of Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of the armies of Yù and Sī Commanderies and Xīyáng within Yǐngzhōu, Guànjūn General, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
When the Prince of Jiànpíng, Jǐngsù, rebelled,
Huái Zhēn sent his son Língzhé to lead troops to the capital.
In Shēngmíng元年,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ General.
When Shěn Yōuzhī was in Jīngchǔ,
the court council was apprehensive.
Huáizhēn dispatched his Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison, Zhāng Hù, as an envoy to Yǐng,
expressing loyalty to Shìzǔ,
and presenting strategic plans.
When Yōuzhī raised an army,
the public believed he would sail straight downriver.
Huáizhēn said to his subordinates:
"Yōuzhī's arrogance and impetuousness have long been known;
he has inflicted cruelty upon Chǔfú.
He will surely block the army in the middle of the river,
and try to intimidate the young ruler with a show of force,
not daring to drive straight to victory, this is clear."
He sent his son, Língzhé, to lead several thousand cavalry and infantry to guard the capital.
Yōuzhī sent his envoy Xǔ Tiānbǎo to persuade Huáizhēn to ally with him.
Huáizhēn executed him,
and sent his head to Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ sent it to Yōuzhī to show him.
Huáizhēn was promoted to the title of General of the Left,
transferred his enfeoffment to Marquis of Zhōngsù County,
and his stipend increased by six hundred households.
Yōuzhī besieged Yǐngchéng.
Huáizhēn dispatched the Grand Administrator of Jiànníng, Zhāng Mó, and the Mobile General Péi Zhòngmù, leading ten thousand indigenous and Hàn troops, to emerge from Xīyáng,
seizing their weapons and armor.
He was promoted to General Quelling the South,
given additional oversight of Nányù and Běixú two prefectures,
and his stipend increased to one thousand households.
Initially,
during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign,
Tàizǔ was a Palace Attendant,
and Huáizhēn was a Palace Gate Guardian.
They met early and were old acquaintances.
When Huáizhēn was granted leave to return to Qīngzhōu,
the emperor had a white-maned horse
that bit people
and could not be ridden,
so he sent it to Huáizhēn as a parting gift.
Huáizhēn reciprocated with a hundred bolts of silk.
Someone said to Huáizhēn:
"This horse of Lord Xiāo is unridable,
which is why he gave it to you.
Your repayment of a hundred bolts,
is that not too much?"
Huáizhēn said:
"Lord Xiāo's magnanimity is grand and dignified;
how could he possibly owe anyone this silk?
I intend to entrust my person and reputation to him;
why should I care about the amount of money or goods?"
When Tàizǔ assumed regency,
because Huáizhēn's internal contributions were not yet numerous,
in the winter of the second year,
he was summoned to be Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
also serving as General of the Vanguard.
His fourth son, Huàng, General of Ning朔, was appointed to succeed him as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Some suspected Huáizhēn would not accept the replacement.
Tàizǔ said:
"When I was a commoner,
Huáizhēn already embraced me and showed his sincerity.
How much more so today?
How could he possibly be different?"
Days after Huàng departed,
the doubts did not cease.
The emperor then sent the Army Commander Fáng Língmín with a hundred cavalry to escort Huàng,
and said to Língmín:
"Those who argue say Huáizhēn will surely act differently,
but I have known his character for a long time;
he will certainly not do so.
You are from his hometown,
so I send you.
This is not only to guard the new appointee,
but also to welcome the old one."
When Huáizhēn returned,
he was immediately appointed Right Chief Clerk to the Chancellor.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he was transferred to General of the Left Guard,
and granted the additional title of Attendant Official.
His marquisate was changed to Marquis of Xiāochéng,
[增] with an additional two hundred households.
he was given the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
When the barbarians invaded Huái and Féi,
he was given the additional title of General Quelling the West, while retaining his original office.
He was granted a ceremonial axe,
and stationed in the west at Cháohú,
to provide support for Shòuchūn.
He returned only after the barbarians retreated.
Huáizhēn was old,
and finding the imperial guard duties arduous,
he requested a leisurely post.
He was transferred to Grand Master of Guanglu,
and his position as Attendant-in-Ordinary remained as before.
That winter,
when the barbarians invaded Qúshān,
he was appointed Bearer of Credential, General Pacifying the North,
retaining his original office,
and led troops to provide relief.
Before he arrived,
the situation was resolved,
and he was relieved of the titles of Pacifying the North and Bearer of Credential.
In the fourth year,
he became seriously ill,
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post.
The emperor graciously replied, granting his request,
and indicating that another appointment would be considered.
That summer,
he died.
He was sixty-three years old.
He left instructions for a simple burial.
Shìzǔ posthumously conferred upon him the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Guarding the North, and Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
and gave him the posthumous title of Marquis Jìng.
His son Língzhé,
courtesy name Wénmíng.
He began his career as a Kingdom Attendant-in-Ordinary, Acting Staff Officer,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He served as Colonel of Infantry at the Qí Court.
In early Jiànyuán,
he successively held the posts of General of Níngshuò,
Military Consultant to the Prince of Línchuān,
Administrator of Lúlíng,
Grand Administrator of Qí Commandery,
and General of the Vanguard.
Língzhé's birth mother once fell ill.
Língzhé personally prayed,
and dreamt he saw an old man in yellow clothes who said:
"You can take bamboo shoots from Mount Nán and eat them;
the illness will immediately be cured."
Língzhé awoke in surprise,
and as he said, the illness was cured.
His stepmother Cuī Shì and his elder brother's son Jǐnghuàn were captured by barbarians in the Tàishǐ period.
Língzhé wore commoner's clothes
and refrained from listening to music.
When Huáizhēn died,
it was his turn to inherit the noble title.
Língzhé firmly declined, stating that his elder brother's son was among the barbarians,
his fate unknown,
and there was no reason for him to bypass the rightful heir to the feudal land.
The court considered this righteous.
Língzhé expended his family's wealth to privately ransom his stepmother and Jǐnghuàn,
but for many years he could not succeed.
Shìzǔ pitied him
and ordered an envoy to the north to inform the barbarian ruler.
The barbarian ruler sent them back to the south.
Língzhé then inherited Huáizhēn's enfeoffment and noble title.
In early Yǒngmíng, Língzhé successively held the posts of Chief Clerk to the Protector-General,
Consultant to the Eastern Central Leader,
and Commander of the Central Palace Guard.
He was sent out as General of Níngshuò,
Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng,
and Right Military Supervisor to the Prince of Xīyáng.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he died,
aged forty-nine.
Lǐ Ānmín,
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Yí,
His father, Qīnzhī,
was General of the Palace,
and was appointed Magistrate of Xuē.
Ānmín followed his father to the county.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā, he was captured by barbarians.
He led his personal retinue to escape and return south.
During the early rebellion of Tàichū,
He surrendered to the righteous army,
was appointed General Establishing Might,
and became a staff officer to Lǔ Shuǎng's Left Army.
When Shuǎng rebelled,
Ānmín fled back to the capital,
and was appointed Acting Staff Officer to the Commander of the Army,
then promoted to General of the Left Guard's Palace.
During the Dàmíng period,
when barbarians invaded Xú and Yǔn,
Ānmín was made Military Supervisor of the Jianwei Command, and Magistrate of Wúyán.
He was then appointed General of the Palace, and led troops to suppress the mutually hostile bandits in Hànchuān.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn 反 revolted,
Emperor Míng appointed Ānmín as Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn and leader of the navy,
and assigned him as Sītú Chéngjú Cānjūn for Jiàn'ān Wáng.
He attacked Zhěqí Hú, Báidí Pǔ, and Tàkū,
achieving victory in all engagements.
He was appointed Jīshè Jiāngjūn and Jūnzhǔ.
Zhāng Xìngshì was entrenched at Qiánxī.
His provisions ran out,
and he was pressed by the enemy.
Ānmín led several hundred ships and boats,
bypassed the enemy's five strongholds,
and delivered rice to Xìngshì.
The false jūnzhǔ Shěn Zhòng and Wáng Zhāng led their troops from [⿰黹⺙]kǒu, intending to cut off the river.
Ānmín advanced his army, joined battle, and defeated them.
He also attacked Quèwěi and Jiāngchéng,
achieving merit in both.
When the matter was settled,
Emperor Míng held a grand assembly at Xīntíng,
where he entertained and honored the various jūnzhǔs.
During a game of chūpú with official stakes,
Ānmín made five successive lú throws.
The emperor was greatly astonished,
and gazed at Ānmín, saying:
"Your face is as square as a field;
this is the visage of one destined to be enfeoffed as a Marquis."
When Ānmín was young, he was poor.
A man passing by his gate
examined his features and said:
"You will later become extremely wealthy and noble,
and will play games with the Son of Heaven, hand in hand."
At this point, Ānmín sought this man,
but did not know his whereabouts.
He followed Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī in campaigning against Xuē Āndū at Péngchéng.
When the army was defeated,
Ānmín held the rear to resist,
and returned to defend Xiàpī.
He was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn
and garrisoned Huáiyáng Chéng.
For his merit at [⿰黹⺙]kǒu,
he was enfeoffed as the Zǐ of Shàowǔ Xiàn,
with an income of four hundred households.
He again followed Wú Xǐ and Shěn Yōuzhī to attack the barbarians,
reaching Suīkǒu.
They were defeated in battle
and returned to defend Sùyù.
After Huáiběi was lost,
Emperor Míng commanded Ānmín to garrison [角]chéng.
[一九] He was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Róngcóng Púyè.
He garrisoned Sìkǒu,
leading the naval forces to patrol along the Huái River,
reaching Shòuchūn.
The barbarians sent their false Chángshè Gōng, who established camps stretching over ten li to raid Rǔyīn.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Miǎn repelled them.
The barbarian garrison commander of Jīngtíng, Shēng Qǐnú, abandoned the city and surrendered.
[二０] Ānmín led the naval forces to attack the front,
conquered Jīngtíng,
and cut off their crossing routes.
He was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Guànjūn Sīmǎ, Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu, and acting Nányǔnzhōu Shì.
When Tàizǔ was in Huáiyīn,
[二一] Ānmín secretly allied with him.
Emperor Míng suspected this,
and transferred Ānmín to be Liú Yùn's Guànjūn Sīmǎ, Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhào Tàishǒu.
He was then appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently serving as Yìyáng Tàishǒu,
but he did not accept any of these appointments.
His original post was offered again,
but he still did not accept.
He was then appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Shānyáng Tàishǒu.
Towards the end of the Tàishǐ reign,
the people north of the Huái River rose in revolt, wishing to return south.
Ānmín was appointed supervisor of the vanguard forces.
He also requested reinforcements,
but was unsuccessful
and returned.
He was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
and then again Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Shānyáng Tàishǒu.
When the Sānbā region was in turmoil,
Tàishǒu Zhāng Dàn abandoned Fúchéng and fled.
Ānmín was given Jǐajié, Dudū Tǎoshǔ Jūnshì, and Fǔshī Jiāngjūn.
When the Wǔliáo tribes caused disturbances in Hànzhōng,
Ānmín was ordered to turn his army back to Wèixīng.
When the situation was settled,
he returned to Xiàkǒu.
In the early Yuánhuī period,
he was appointed Dūdū Sīzhōu Jūnshì, Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Yìyáng Tàishǒu,
with Jǐajié and his general title remaining as before.
A separate imperial decree to Ānmín stated:
"Jiǔjiāng requires defense,
and border preparations should be strengthened.
This appointment is now given
to augment the power of Yān-Yǐng,
so there is no room for refusal."
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
Ānmín moved out and took up position,
sending troops to reinforce the capital.
He was summoned and appointed Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
[二二] with the additional title of Jǐshìzhōng.
When Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù caused trouble,
Guànjūn Huáng Huí, Yóujī Jiāngjūn Gāo Dàoqìng, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Cáo Xīnzhī and others all secretly sent their allegiance.
However, Yóujī Jiāngjūn Gāo Dàoqìng led his troops out to campaign.
Tàizǔ feared he might defect,
and dispatched Ānmín and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Fórong to guard against him.
Ānmín reached Jīngkǒu
[二三] and defeated Jǐngsù's army at Géqiáo.
After Jǐngsù was executed,
Ānmín was left in charge as acting Nánxúzhōu Shì.
Chéngjú Cānjūn Wáng Jǐngsù was a close confidant of Ānmín.
[二四] When he stole two bolts of silk,
Ānmín wept and said to him:
"You and I have shared many hardships.
Today you have violated the state law,
and this is indeed you letting me down."
He had him executed at the army gate,
and then provided a generous funeral and offerings.
The entire military administration was awed and submitted.
He was appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
then Xiāowèi Jiāngjūn,
[二五] but did not accept.
He was then transferred to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Dōngzhōngláng Sīmǎ, and acting Huìjī Jùnshì.
When Ānmín was about to head east,
Tàizǔ held a farewell banquet and conversed with him,
lingering day and night.
Ānmín secretly presented his view that the Sòng dynasty's mandate was ending,
and that the Heavenly mandate had found a new home.
As Cāngwú was tyrannical,
Tàizǔ was anxious and distressed, without a plan.
Ānmín proposed to Tàizǔ that he would raise troops in the east with Jiāngxià Wáng Jī.
Tàizǔ did not permit it,
so he stopped.
When Cāngwú was deposed,
Tàizǔ summoned Ānmín as Shǐchíjié Dūdū Běitǎo Jūnshì, Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nányǔnzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
Tàizǔ recalled Ānmín to garrison Báixià with his original post,
and to repair the city walls.
He was given the additional title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
He advanced his army westward to campaign,
and was further promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn.
When he reached Pénchéng,
Shěn Yōuzhī was pacified.
He was then appointed Dūdū Yǐngzhōu Sīzhōu Zhī Yìyáng Zhūjūnshì, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with Jǐajié and his general title remaining as before.
In the third year of Shēngmíng,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Wèiwèi.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Zhōnglǐngjūn,
enfeoffed as Kānglè Hóu,
with an income of a thousand households.
Since the Tàishǐ period of Sòng,
there had been frequent internal and external rebellions.
Generals and their subordinates
each recruited personal troops,
gathering and encamping in the capital.
Ānmín submitted a memorial explaining this,
stating
"Except for the permanent garrisons north of the Huái River,
all other troops
should be dismissed and sent away.
If close attendants are needed as personal guards,
a limit should be placed on their numbers."
The emperor accepted this,
and thus issued an edict to abolish private recruitment.
At that time, Wáng Jìngzé was favored for his meritorious loyalty.
Regarding confidential matters of the state and imperial family,
the emperor only discussed with Ānmín,
saying to Ānmín:
"When your name is on the document,
I no longer scrutinize it in detail."
He was soon made Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the barbarians raided Shòuchūn,
reaching Mǎtóu,
an edict ordered Ānmín to campaign,
and he was granted a set of drums and pipes.
The barbarians retreated,
and Ānmín advanced along the Huái River to Shòuchūn.
Previously, during the Sòng era, the outlaw Wáng Yuánchū had gathered a faction on Liùhé Shān, usurping a title,
and claimed that his arms hung down past his knees.
The commanderies and prefectures could not capture him,
which lasted for over ten years.
Ānmín sent troops to reconnoiter,
captured Yuánchū alive,
and executed him in the market of Jiànkāng.
He was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
That year,
the barbarians again invaded the south.
Anmín was commanded to hold the staff of authority and inspect the garrisons along the Huái and Qīng-Sì Rivers.
The barbarians attacked Qúshān, Liánkǒu, and Jiǎochéng.
Anmín stationed his troops at Sìkǒu,
and divided his forces to respond.
In the third year,
he led the combined navy and army into the Qīng River,
and fought the barbarians at Huáiyáng,
defeating them.
The barbarians retreated.
Anmín knew there were ambushing troops,
so he sent his kinsman, the cavalry commander Chángwén, with two hundred horsemen as the vanguard.
He himself, with the army deputies Zhōu Pánlóng and Cuī Wénzhòng, followed behind them,
and a portion of the army was concealed in the woods.
When Chángwén reached Sùyù,
the barbarians, seeing his small numbers,
sent several thousand cavalry to intercept him.
Chángwén retreated and fought,
luring the enemy towards the main army.
Anmín, leading Pánlóng and others, quickly arrived with his troops,
and they engaged in battle at Sūnxīzhǔ, near Zhànfùwān.
The barbarian army suffered a great defeat,
and countless numbers plunged into the Qīng River and died.
The barbarians sent their Tútóu Gōng to deliver siege engine materials to Bùqiū.
The Left Army General Sūn Wénxiǎn attacked, defeated, and routed him,
burning his siege engine materials.
The four prefectures north of the Huái River, hearing that Tàizǔ had received the Mandate,
all wished to return south.
At this time, Huán Biāozhī from Xúzhōu, Xú Měngzi from Yùnzhōu, and others,
gathered tens of thousands of righteous volunteers,
fortified dangerous positions, and sought assistance.
Tàizǔ issued an edict saying:
“The four prefectures of Qīng and Xú
have risen in righteous cause like gathering clouds.
Anmín may take a long rein and drive far,
directing the various commanders.”
Anmín's relief effort was delayed,
and the barbarians, with urgent forces, attacked and subdued Biāozhī and the others.
The Emperor greatly reproached him for this.
When Tàizǔ passed away,
his dying edict added the title of Shìzhōng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
In Yǒngmíng second year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè,
with his general title remaining as before.
Anmín frequently submitted confidential plans which were praised,
and he also formed a good relationship with Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn.
Thus, it was commonly believed that Jiǎn’s recommendation led to this appointment.
Soon after, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to age and illness.
He was re-appointed as Sànqí Chángshì and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with his general title remaining as before.
In the fourth year,
he became Āndōng Jiāngjūn and Wúxīng Tàishǒu,
with his Chángshì title remaining as before.
He died in office
at the age of fifty-eight.
He was granted a posthumous gift of one hundred thousand coins
and one hundred bolts of cloth.
In Wúxīng, there was a spirit of Xiàng Yǔ guarding the prefectural government office,
and the prefects were not allowed to ascend it.
When a prefect arrived at the prefecture,
he had to sacrifice a bull with a yoke beneath it.
Anmín, being a devout Buddhist,
did not offer a divine bull.
He wore clogs and ascended the government office.
He also held the Eight Precepts fast in the office.
Soon after, the bull died
and was buried by the side of the temple.
Today, it is called
“Lǐgōngniúzhǒng” (Tomb of Lord Lǐ's Bull).
When Anmín died,
people at the time believed it was caused by the spirit.
An edict stated:
“Anmín has held various positions, both internal and external,
and his achievements are prominent.
His sincerity and loyalty
have always been clear to my heart.
He was administering governance in the nearby region,
and I was just about to entrust him with important responsibilities.
His sudden death
causes great sorrow in my heart.
He is posthumously granted the title of Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
with one set of drum and fife music.
His titles of Chángshì and Tàishǒu remain as before.
His posthumous title is Sù Hóu.”
Wáng Xuánzài,
courtesy name Yànxiū,
was a native of Xiàpī.
His grandfather, Zǎi,
was a self-proclaimed Northland Prefect.
His father, Ruí,
was Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu.
Xuánzài began his career as the Administrator for the Prince of Jiāngxià Kingdom and Aide-de-camp to the Grand Tutor.
In the early days of Tàishǐ,
he became Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
He followed Zhāng Yǒng to conquer Péngchéng,
and when the imperial army suffered a great defeat,
Xuánzài preserved his army and held Xiàpī city against the barbarians.
He was granted the title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn.
As the imperial army had just been defeated,
people were terrified.
Given Xuánzài's reputation among the gentry,
he was appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, and held the staff of authority, supervising military affairs of Xúzhōu, Yùzhōu, and Liángjùn, and given the titles Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Pínghú Zhōnglángjiàng.
Soon after, he also concurrently held the titles of Shānyáng and Dōnghǎi Prefects.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Overseer of the Cìshǐ of Qīng and Yùn Prefectures,
with his general title and Dōnghǎi Commandery title remaining as before.
In the seventh year,
he was again appointed Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
Overseer of Xú and Yùn Prefectures, and Zhōnglí Tàishǒu,
with his general and lángjiàng titles remaining as before.
He was promoted to Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Then he became Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Lìyáng Tàishǒu,
and was re-appointed with the staff of authority, Supervisor of the two Yù prefectures, Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Tàishǒu title remaining as before.
He was promoted to Fǔjūn Sīmǎ.

He went out to serve as the holder of the staff of authority, Supervisor of military affairs of Liáng, Southern Qín, and Northern Qín Prefectures, Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, Xīróng Xiàowèi, and Cìshǐ of Liáng and Qín Prefectures.
He was advanced to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Supervisor of Yì and Níng Prefectures, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ, and Jiànníng Tàishǒu,
with his general and staff-holding titles remaining as before.
During Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion,
Xuánzài rose in righteousness and demonstrated his loyalty.
He was advanced to the title of Hòujūn Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as the Viscount of Èxiàn.
He was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì
and concurrently Hòujūn.
Before he could be formally appointed,
in Jiànyuán first year,
he became Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
with his title of Viscount of Èxiàn remaining as before.
At that time, the barbarians became active,
and the Nányùnzhōu Cìshǐ, Wáng Jìngzé, fled to the capital.
The Emperor sent Xuánzài to command Guǎnglíng,
and added the titles Píngběi Jiāngjūn and provisional Jiǎjié, acting in charge of Nányùnzhōu affairs,
with his original office remaining as before.
When the situation was settled,
he became Guānglù Dàfū and Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
In Yǒngmíng fourth year,
he became holder of the staff of authority, Supervisor of military affairs along the Huái River in Yùnzhōu, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the sixth year,
he passed away
at the age of seventy-six.
His posthumous title was Liè Zǐ.
Xuánzài was modest and elegant, fond of recondite discussions,
and cultivated the conduct of a scholar.
In Liáng and Yì, he had a reputation for integrity,
and the people of the western regions still remember him fondly today.
His paternal cousin, Xuánmó, also known as Zǐzhān,
during the reign of Sòng Míngdì,
was Huángmén Láng.
He had always slighted Shìzǔ.
When Shìzǔ was lying on a large bed,
Zǐzhān said to the Prince of Yùzhāng:
“That thing behind the curtains also sleeps and wakes with people.”
Shìzǔ held a grudge,
but never showed it.
In Jiànyuán first year,
he became Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu.
When he paid respects at the palace, he did not perform the kowtow according to ritual,
and was impeached by the palace guards.
The officials reported this to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ summoned Zǐzhān into the Eastern Palace,
and then sent him to the Tíngwèi to be executed.
He sent his attendants to relay a message to the Emperor, saying:
“The father was disgraced, the son dies.
Wáng Zǐzhān was arrogant towards the imperial court,
and I have taken it upon myself to arrest and punish him.”
Tàizǔ said:
“Tell the young man,
what is there to fuss about this!”
When he heard that Zǐzhān was already dead,
he then remained silent.
Zhān's brother, Kuān,
during the Sòng era, was a regional governor alongside Zhān.
At this point, although Zhān was implicated in an incident,
Kuān's position and treatment remained as before.
In the early Tàishǐ period, Kuān was the Administrator of Suí Commandery.
When the west rebelled,
his father, Xuánmó, was in the capital.
Kuān abandoned the commandery and returned.
Emperor Míng awarded him and
sent him to follow Zhāng Yǒng to suppress Xuē Āndū.
Kuān declined, stating that his mother was still alive
and had been captured by the rebels in the west.
He requested permission to go west.
He then attacked and captured Suí Commandery,
beheaded the pseudo-Grand Administrator Liú Shīniàn,
and rescued his mother.
When the matter was settled,
Emperor Míng praised him
and ordered his portrait to be painted.
In the early Jiànyuán period,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently holding the position of Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he became Tàicháng.
He was dismissed from office
for slaughtering an ox in his residence.
Later, he became Guānglù Dàfū.
In the third year,
he died.
Xuánzài's younger brother, Xuánmiǎo,
whose courtesy name was Yàn yuǎn,
initially served as Piàojí Xíngjūn Cānjūn,
Tàizǐ Zuǒ Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn,
and Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
In the early Tàishǐ period,
he was promoted to Fúguó Jiāngjūn, Grand Administrator of Qīnghé and Guǎng[chuān] Commanderies,
When Shěn Wénxiù, the Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ, rebelled,
Xuánmiǎo wanted to report to the imperial court,
but fearing ambush,
he went to Wénxiù to request a secure encampment.
Wénxiù ordered him to encamp outside the city.
Xuánmiǎo immediately set up a camp
and at night led his troops south to answer the call of righteousness.
By dawn,
Wénxiù's pursuit was unsuccessful.
Emperor Míng appointed him as Chíjíe, Dūdū Qīngzhōu, and Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general's title unchanged.
When Tàizǔ was stationed at Huái yīn,
he was suspected by the emperor,
and sent a letter to Xuánmiǎo to establish a connection.
Xuánmiǎo's Chángshǐ, Fáng Shū'ān, advised Xuánmiǎo not to respond.
Upon returning from his provincial post,
Tàizǔ sent someone to waylay him on his route.
he then led his army straight through without stopping,
returned to the capital, and reported to the emperor,
stating that Tàizǔ harbored intentions of rebellion.
Tàizǔ did not resent him.
During the Shēngmíng period,
Tàizǔ invited him to serve as Piàojí Sīmǎ, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Tàishān Tàishǒu.
Xuánmiǎo was very afraid,
but Tàizǔ treated him as before.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
with his Guānjūn title unchanged.
He was sent out as Chíjíe, Dūdū Liáng Nán Qín Èrzhōu Jūnshì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Xīróng Xiàowèi, and Liáng Nán Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
The brothers served as regional governors simultaneously.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Héyáng County.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn,
with his marquisate unchanged.
The fugitive Lǐ Wūnú created disturbances in the Liáng region,
capturing Báimǎ Fort.
Xuánmiǎo led seven or eight hundred men from the east to suppress him,
but was unsuccessful.
Fearing he could not hold his position,
he sent someone to feign surrender to Wūnú,
telling him:
"Governor Wáng's troops are weak,
he has abandoned his concubines and servants in the city,
and has left with his two beloved concubines several days ago."
Wūnú was pleased,
and led light troops to attack the provincial capital.
Xuánmiǎo set an ambush and defeated them,
Wūnú barely escaped with his life.
When Tàizǔ heard of this,
he said:
"Xuánmiǎo indeed did not betray my trust and treatment."
He returned to serve as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Chángshā Wáng Hòujūn Sīmǎ, and Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
He was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Yòujiāngjūn, Yùzhāng Wáng Tàiwèi Sīmǎ,
and then sent out as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Línchuān Nèishǐ,
with a salary of two thousand dàn.
He returned to serve as Qiánjūn Sītú Sīmǎ, Sànqí Chángshì, and Tàizǐ Yòulǜ.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng,
he was appointed Chíjíe, Dūdū Yǒngzhōu Yuánhuái Jūnshì, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Before he could take up the post,
he was transferred to Dàsīmǎ,
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to Tàicháng,
then promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and sent out as Chíjíe, Jiān Xúzhōu Jūnshì, Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
In the eleventh year,
the Buddhist monk Shì Fǎzhì from Liánhuá Temple in Jiànkāng and the provincial commoner Zhōu Pánlóng and others rebelled.
Four hundred men attacked the west gate of the provincial capital at night,
climbed ladders onto the city wall,
shot and killed the Chéngjú Cānjūn Táng Yǐng,
and then entered the city.
Jūnjǔ Gěng Hǔ, Xú Sīqìng, Dǒng Wéndìng, and others resisted.
By dawn,
Xuánmiǎo led over a hundred men to ascend the city's side gate,
fiercely attacked,
and captured Fǎzhì and Pánlóng alive.
Xuánmiǎo was dismissed from office for this.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was appointed Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and then promoted to Shǐ Chíjíe, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, and Grand Administrator of Lìyáng and Nánqiáo Commanderies.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
and soon after transferred to Zhōnghùjūn.
Gāozōng sent Xuánmiǎo to Jiāngzhōu to kill Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐmào.
Xuánmiǎo strenuously declined to go.
When Wáng Guǎngzhī was sent to Guǎnglíng to take Ānlù Wáng Zǐjìng,
Xuánmiǎo had no choice but to obey the imperial decree.
He was granted drums and wind instruments and assigned staff.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was promoted to Chíjíe, Dūdū Nán Yǒng Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu Jūnshì, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Nán Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
In the fourth year,
he died,
at the age of seventy-two.
He was posthumously granted Ānběi Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His posthumous title was Zhuànghóu.
The kinsman Wáng Wénhé
was the grandson of Zhòngdé, the Sòng Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn.
During the Jǐnghé period,
he served as the Zhēngběi Fǔ Zhǔbù for Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng.
When Chǎng fled to Pénchéng from the captives,
all his troops scattered.
Wénhé alone escorted him to the border.
Chǎng said to him:
"Everyone else has left.
You have an elderly mother;
why do you not leave?"
Wénhé then left.
During the Shēngmíng period,
he was Bālíng Nèishǐ.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's incident arose,
Wénhé beheaded his envoy,
galloped to Shìzǔ to report the change,
and abandoned the commandery to flee to Yǐngchéng.
During the Yǒngmíng period,
he successively served as Cìshǐ of Qīng, Jì, Yǒng, and Yì four provinces,
and Píngběi Jiāngjūn.
The court historian says: When the Sòng clan's end was near,
disorder was daily manifesting.
Families harbored ambitions for the throne,
and individuals had different designs.
Thus, the opportunity for frontier governors to raise armies arose,
and for commanderies and prefectures to observe the opportune moment.
These several individuals were all veteran generals with old merits,
serving as regional governors alongside Tàizǔ.
In terms of age and position,
some were their seniors.
Yet they offered their sincerity to the ruler,
upholding righteousness from afar.
From this, one knows that the willing support was not baseless,
and trusts that the people's hearts had a rallying point.
Xuánzài's brothers and kinsmen,
generation after generation, upheld sincerity and loyalty.
They were not resented by the ruling house.
These are the Gěng clan of today.
Eulogy says: Xīaochen reported,
righteousness was the first to be championed.
Língzhé upheld modesty,
alongside Dīng and Wéi.
Lǐ aided the eastern lands,
his plans divinely inspired.
Wáng governed with purity,
his virtue never waning.
Xuánmiǎo was selected by the emperor,
early turning away from the common path.
Collation Notes
Biographies Nine: Cuī Zǔsī, Liú Shànmíng, Sū Kǎn, Yuán Róngzǔ.
Cuī Zǔsī, courtesy name Jìngyuán,
was from Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Cuī Yǎn.
His grandfather, Yīn,
was the Sòng Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
His father, Sēnghù,
was a Xiùcái from the province.
Zǔsī 少 (shǎo) had aspirations;
he loved to read histories.
Initially, the prefecture appointed him Chief Clerk (zhǔbù).
He and the Regional Inspector (cìshǐ), Liú Huáizhēn, offered sacrifices to the gods at Yáo (Yáo) Temple.
The temple had a statue of Sū Hóu (Sū Hóu).
Huáizhēn (Huáizhēn) said:
"Yáo (Yáo) was a sage,
yet he is placed among miscellaneous gods.
I want to remove them,
what do you think?"
Zǔsī (Zǔsī) said:
"Sū Jùn (Sū Jùn) today can be called the fifth of the Four Fiends."
Huáizhēn (Huáizhēn) then ordered the removal of all miscellaneous gods.
When Tài Zǔ (Tài Zǔ) was in Huáin (Huáin),
Zǔsī (Zǔsī) heard of his reputation and attached himself to him,
serving as His Majesty’s Chief Clerk (zhǔbù) of Auxiliary State (fǔguó).
He was greatly trusted and favored,
participating in plans and deliberations.
He was appointed Attendant on Summons (fèngcháoqǐng),
Acting Military Counselor (xíngcānjūn) to the Administrator of Anchéng (Ānchéng) Prince’s (wáng) Household (fǔjūn),
Supernumerary Regular Gentleman (yuánwàizhèngyuánláng),
and Middle Judge (zhōngzhèng) of Jì (Jì) Province.
When the Sòng (Sòng) court first deliberated on enfeoffing Tài Zǔ (Tài Zǔ) as Duke of Liáng (Liáng),
Zǔsī (Zǔsī) memorialized Tài Zǔ (Tài Zǔ), saying:
"The prophecy books say, 'The golden knife and sharp blade will cleave them evenly.'
It is now fitting to be called Qí (Qí),
truly responding to the mandate of Heaven."
This was followed.
He was transferred to Administrator of State (xiàngguó) Attendant Gentleman of the Interior (cóngshìzhōngláng),
and then promoted to Grand Administrator (nèishǐ) of Qí (Qí) Commandery.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (Jiànyuán),
he was transferred to concurrently serve as Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Attendant (gěishìhuángménshìláng).
When His Majesty first ascended the throne,
Zǔsī (Zǔsī) memorialized on government affairs, saying:
"Rites and admonitions
are the collars and crowns of human relations,
and the pivot and handle of emperors and kings.
From ancient times, the creation of things and the accomplishment of tasks
have always prioritized teaching and learning.
If the world does not practice learning,
the people forget their aspirations and righteousness,
and rebellion and contention arise from this,
with disaster and chaos then ensuing.
Therefore, to solidify customs and flourish governance,
nothing precedes the Way and teachings.
One must not change one's thoughts due to a change in circumstances (yíxiǎn gélǜ)
or shift one's profession due to poverty or prosperity.
Currently, there are officials without fixed posts,
who idly receive salaries and exert no effort.
After three years, there are no results from evaluations,
and after nine years, the order of promotion and demotion is absent.
The national treasury is thus depleted,
and the people's strength is scattered and exhausted.
Ability and inability are undifferentiated,
the Jīng (Jīng) and Wèi (Wèi) rivers flow mixed.
It is fitting that south of the Grand Ancestral Temple (dàmiào),
literary schools should be greatly re-established;
north of the Grand Minister of Agriculture (sīnóng),
military academies should be widely opened.
For officials outside the quota in the capital (tái),
inquire about their preferences,
and assign them to study according to their inclinations,
so that each may exhaust their abilities.
Monthly provisions for servants and laborers
should be supplied as before.
If there is idleness or negligence,
they should be sent back to their original commanderies.
Those with unique skills and extraordinary talents
should be treated exceptionally.
If scholars cultivate their studies,
there will certainly be exceptional individuals;
if the people recognize its benefits,
how can they not be encouraged? "
He also said:
"Emperor Wén (Wén) of Hàn (Hàn) collected written memorials to make curtains for his palace,
wore coarse silk garments,
and carried a sword with a leather belt.
His consort, Shèn Fūren (Shèn Fūren), wore clothes that did not trail on the ground.
He valued the wealth of ten middle-class (zhōngrén) families
and did not build a grand terrace.
Liú Bèi (Liú Bèi) took tent hooks and copper to mint coins for national use.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ) of Wèi (Wèi), when marrying off his daughter,
only provided a black curtain
and ten maidservants.
A woman from Dōng'ā (Dōng'ā) was given death for wearing embroidered clothes.
Wáng Jǐngxīng (Wáng Jǐngxīng) was ridiculed for washing rice.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ) of Sòng (Sòng) was extraordinarily frugal.
Zhāng Fēi's (Zhāng Fēi) chamber only had a green silk mosquito net,
a simple mat of 'three Qí (Qí)' reeds,
and a meal of peach blossom rice served in five small dishes.
Yīn Zhòngwén (Yīn Zhòngwén) urged him to keep entertainers,
to which he replied, 'I do not understand music.'
Zhòngwén (Zhòngwén) said, 'Just keep them, and you will understand yourself.'
He replied again, 'I fear understanding,
hence I do not keep them.'
Looking back at all emperors and kings,
none failed to rise through frugality and simplicity,
and perish through extravagance and splendor.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty
embodies the frugality of Táng (Táng) and
follows the simplicity of Yú (Yú).
Your sleeping quarters are constructed simply of plain wood,
and your dining utensils consist of pottery gourds.
Jade hairpins and chopsticks
are shattered into dust,
and precious furs and embroidered garments
are burned like grass.
This indeed sets a high standard for former ages,
and the people of later generations will submit to it.
However, although the teachings are believed,
the common people's habits have not yet changed.
It is fitting to further distinguish and clarify,
to quickly return to benevolence.
Carefully examine court officials:
those with simple carts and humble dwellings
should be honored with special ranks;
those with carved carriages and ornate wheels
should have their titles lowered.
Those who pursue hunting and extravagant pleasures
should be permanently removed from the pure ranks;
those who indulge in music and wine
should not be allowed to remain in office.
If all realize the path of righteousness,
they will both fear and be encouraged,
then the customs will be rectified and transformed
without waiting an entire day."
He also said:
"The importance of laws and regulations
has long been established.
Therefore, when Cáo Cān (Cáo Cān) left Qí (Qí),
he only entrusted the prisons and markets,
saying nothing else.
Lù Wēnshū (Lù Wēnshū) said,
and one still remains:
it is the officials who administer justice.'
It is truly fitting to appoint upright judges to the Court of Judicial Review (tíngwèi),
carefully select officials for the three judicial bureaus,
and greatly emphasize the selection of Temple Secretaries (sìchéng) and Prison Wardens (yùzhǔ).
They should diligently study the laws and statutes
and abolish cumbersome and harsh provisions.
Imperial prisons and the two county (liǎngxiàn) prisons
should conduct interrogations three times a month.
Observe appearances and scrutinize circumstances,
and any deception or injustice will surely be uncovered.
This will ensure that punishments are administered with clarity and caution,
not disgracing the 'Great Change' [of the Yìjīng],
rather erring on the side of leniency than impropriety,
and never shaming the 'Book of Zhōu (Zhōu).'
Since the Hàn (Hàn) dynasty, there have been families specialized in law,
whose descendants have continually pursued this profession,
gathering disciples and lecturing,
sometimes numbering several hundred.
Thus, the two families Zhāng (Zhāng) and Yú (Yú)
earned high praise in the reigns of Wén (Wén) and Xuān (Xuān);
the two clans Chén (Chén) and Guō (Guō)
were renowned in the courts of Wǔ (Wǔ) and Míng (Míng).
When judgments were without injustice,
their descendants flourished,
inheriting the highest offices,
and their cicada-wing purple robes radiated brilliance.
Now, the legal scholars of the Court of Judicial Review (tíngwèi)
are merely the household of petty clerks.
Their families are not like Xián (Xián) and Hóng (Hóng),
and their courts lack the guidance of Yú (Yú).
The neglect of punishment
stems from this.
If upright and magnanimous scholars are carefully selected,
and then tested for verification,
they should be promoted to the staff of the Court of Judicial Review (tíngwèi).
If an official's family holds office generation after generation
it is rare;
to abolish their positions yet wish for success in their affairs
has never happened.
If Liú Lèi (Liú Lèi) transmits his profession generation after generation,
the cook will not lack dragon liver dishes;
this is certainly understandable."
He also said:
"Music moves heaven and earth,
affects ghosts and spirits,
rectifies human emotions and nature,
and establishes human relationships.
Its significance is profound.
According to the Former Hàn dynasty, with millions of registered households,
the Grand Music Bureau (Tàiyùe Língguān) had eight hundred and twenty-nine officials.
Kǒng Guāng and others memorialized to dismiss four hundred and forty-one persons who did not conform to the classical norms.
To rectify the music and fix the establishment,
only three hundred and eighty-eight persons were retained.
Now, the population is less than a million,
yet the Grand Music Bureau (Tàiyùe) for Yǎ and Zhèng music,
during the Yuánhuī era, had more than a thousand people tested and selected;
the miscellaneous performers (zájì) in the rear hall
were not included in this count.
This wastes labor and resources,
〔一二〕 and corrupts public morals.
Now, if we wish to cast out evil and return to the right path,
there is nothing better than to abolish the miscellaneous performers.
In the royal court, only the zhǒngjù, yǔqī, and dēnggē should be retained.
If this is done,
then officials will be adequately provided for,
and the nation will revert to its pure customs."
He also said:
"Confucian scholars consider moral transformation as the foundation;
Legalists view strict regulation as the essence.
Moral education (dàojiào) is the sustenance for governing a world of order,
while penal laws (xíngxiàn) are the medicine for a disordered world.
Therefore, moral education (jiàohuà) is likened to rain and dew,
and laws and regulations (míngfǎ) are compared to wind and frost.
Thus, having a sense of shame and integrity
is the key to respect and humility;
enforcing commands and prohibitions
is the crucial foundation for the state.
Therefore, for the world to be well-governed,
it relies solely on rewards and punishments.
Rewards need not be abundant,
what is vexing is their unfairness;
punishments need not be heavy,
what is troublesome is their inappropriateness.
If, for example, person Jiǎ has few merits,
and person Yǐ has many achievements,
but Jiǎ is rewarded and Yǐ is neglected,
then the world will surely not be encouraged;
if person Bǐng has committed a serious crime,
and person Dīng a minor transgression,
but Dīng is punished and Bǐng is pardoned,
then the world will surely not [be] reformed.
〔一三〕 Thus, rewards and punishments are carried out in vain,
without effectively encouraging or deterring.
May those who are punished be favored and familiar officials,
and those who are rewarded be enemies and adversaries.
Execute one person, and the myriad states will fear;
reward one commoner, and all within the four seas will rejoice."
He also said:
"If taxes are relied upon to enrich the state,
the state becomes empty and the people poor;
if fields are expanded to fill granaries,
the state becomes rich and the people are well-provided for.
Yáo relied on the reserves from Heaven's bounty
to truly relieve the people afflicted by floods.
〔一四〕 Tāng relied on accumulated stores from the divided land
to overcome the crisis of scorching heat.
In recent times, Wèi established agricultural officials (diǎnnóng),
and the Central Capital (Zhōngdū) had sufficient food;
Jìn opened up the Rú and Yǐng rivers,
and the Biànhé River received stored provisions.
