Now, as we are about to clear and open up areas around Xián and Huá mountains,
and inscribe our achievements in the Dragon Desert (Lóngmò),
it is advisable to simplify labor service and encourage agriculture,
opening up fields and expanding cultivation.
At the same time, abolish the prohibitions on mountain and pond resources,
and deeply suppress the monopolistic land grabbing by powerful families.
Then both soldiers and civilians will be well-provided for,
making it possible to deploy armies."
He also said:
"In ancient times, the Left Historian recorded words,
and the Right Historian recorded events.
Therefore, whenever the ruler acted, it was necessarily written down,
using honest brushes without prevarication;
the superior would not act rashly,
knowing that words, like silk threads, would form a record.
Nowadays, the officials of the Bureau of Writing (Zhùzuò) merely record daily activities (qǐjū);
the scribes who narrate events
make praise and flattery their main task.
The world lacks a Dǒng Hú,
so the methods of historical writing are necessarily concealed;
the times lack a Nán Shǐ,
so straightforward writing is unheard of."
He also [said]:
"If the remonstrance officials (jiànguān) are abolished,
then there will be no one to rely on for hearing and accepting advice.
〔一五〕 Although one may urge and encourage court officials,
and seek out opinions from common people,
it is better to recommend honest and straightforward individuals
whose duty it is to consider their worries.
For exceeding one's office in matters,
speaking out is difficult;
when holding office and acting,
expressing criticism might be easy.
If public opinion expects nothing but silence from oneself,
then one should also be ashamed of being silent.
Although the Censor-in-Chief (Zhōngchéng) may be inferior to Xián or Xuán,
there has never been a complete abolition of impeachment and selection;
though the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) may not be Shì Zhī,
how could there be no interrogation documents at all?
Thus, it is known that rather than mislead people,
it is better not to neglect one's duty,
which is a clear lesson before our eyes.
Hàn Wǔdì appointed Gòng Yǔ as Grand Remonstrance Official (Jiàndàifū),
who spoke forthrightly in his initial memorials.
Xiàhóu Shèng, for his blunt honesty, was imprisoned,
then released and appointed to a position of admonishment.
Cutting an axe handle is not far-fetched;
practicing it is simply good.
He also said:
"Heaven and Earth have no mind,
imparting qi impartially.
How can it be that talent flourished in ancient times,
but this generation alone is desolate?
It lies in whether one knows or does not know,
employs or does not employ.
Indeed, having worthy individuals but not knowing them,
knowing worthy individuals but not employing them,
employing worthy individuals but not entrusting them,
and entrusting worthy individuals but not trusting them –
these four [factors]
are common ailments throughout history.
If now we genuinely value Guō Kuí to attract Jì Xīn,
and appoint Bào Shú to seek Yí Wú,
then the scholars of the world
will come by themselves without being summoned."
The emperor responded with a gracious edict.
Soon after, he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Marshal of the Champion Army (Guànjūn Sīmǎ),
concurrently holding the position of Administrator of Qí Commandery (Qíjùn Tàishǒu), his original post remaining unchanged.
In this winter,
the foreign tribes stirred.
He was promoted to General of the Champion Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Army Commander (Jūzhǔ),
stationed along the Huái River.
In the second year,
he was advanced to the title of General Who Subdues the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
with his position as Army Commander remaining unchanged.
Subsequently, he was transferred to Acting Imperial Commissioner (Jiǎjié) and Inspector of Qīng and Jì provinces (Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ),
his general's title remaining unchanged.
A short while later,
he died.
The emperor sighed, saying:
"I was just about to employ Zǔ Sī.
Unfortunate,
what a pity!"
An edict granted thirty thousand coins
and fifty bolts of cloth for his funeral.
Zǔ Sīzōng Rén Zhòngwén,
initially served as a Commendatory Official in the prefecture.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
he became Northern Pacification Principal Scribe for Xuē Āndū.
He escaped disaster and returned to the country.
In the early Yuánhuī era,
he followed Tài Zǔ at Xīntíng to resist the Guìyáng bandits,
demonstrating sincerity and effectiveness.
He was appointed as a Guerrilla General.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
he assisted the Prince of Yùzhāng in defending the Eastern Mansion.
He successively served as a Consultative Counselor to the Agile Cavalry General,
and was appointed as the Inspector of Xúzhōu.
In the early Jiànyuán era,
he was enfeoffed as the Sub-Marquis of Jiànyáng County,
with three hundred households.
In the second year,
the barbarians attacked Zhōnglí,
and Zhòngwén defeated them.
He also dispatched Army Commander Cuī Xiàobó and others to cross the Huái River and attack and capture the barbarian Chámei Garrison,
killing the garrison commander Lóng Déhóu and the false Administrator of Yángpíng, Guō Dùdī,
the Magistrate of Guǎntáo, Zhāng Dé,
and the Magistrate of Púyáng, Wáng Míng.
At that time, the barbarians attacked and killed the Administrator of Mǎtóu, Liú Cóng.
[一六] The Emperor said:
"Defeating Chámei
is sufficient to compensate."
Wénzhòng also dispatched Army Commander Chén Jìng to attack the barbarian Zhúyì Garrison commander Bái Zhòngdū,
and also dispatched Army Commander Cuī Yánshū to attack the false Administrator of Huáiyáng, Liáng È.
Both were killed.
In the third year,
the loyal people of Huáiběi, Huán Lěilěi, fought the barbarians at Bàodú Gù,
and thoroughly defeated them.
Zhòngwén quickly reported this,
and the Emperor issued an edict saying:
"Many righteous individuals have risen in the north.
I deeply fear that such a good opportunity will not come again.
You should strongly encourage the people of Pèi.
If they can unanimously take action,
I will dispatch an excellent general to advance directly."
While Wénzhòng was in office,
he was held in awe by the common people.
He was appointed as a Palace Attendant,
leading the Agile Cavalry Commander,
and was re-enfeoffed to Suí County.
He once presented Tài Zǔ with a beard-binding rope,
which the Emperor accepted.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he became the Left Commander of the Crown Prince,
and was successively promoted to General Who Conquers the Barbarians, General of the Champion Army's Grand Scribe, and Administrator of Rǔyīn.
In the fourth year,
he passed away.
He was posthumously granted General of the Rear Army and Inspector of Xúzhōu.
His posthumous title was Xiāngzǐ.
Liú Shànmíng,
was a man from Píngyuán.
He was a cousin of the Northern Pacification General, Huái Zhē.
His father, Huái Mín,
served as Administrator of the two commanderies of Qí and Běihǎi during the Sòng dynasty.
Towards the end of the Yuánjiā era,
Qīngzhōu suffered from famine,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
Shànmíng's family had stored grain;
he personally ate thin gruel,
opened his granary to rescue his fellow villagers,
and many were saved.
The common people called his family's fields
"Life-Extending Fields."
From a young age, he quietly dedicated himself to studying.
The Inspector Dù Jì, hearing of his reputation, called upon him,
but he declined to meet.
At the age of forty,
Inspector Liú Dàolóng appointed him as a Chief Administrator.
His father, Huái Mín, said to Shànmíng:
"I already know you have established yourself as a person;
now I wish to see you establish yourself in office."
Shànmíng accepted the appointment.
He was subsequently recommended as a Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent).
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng was greatly impressed by his strong and upright policy proposals.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
the Inspector of Xúzhōu, Xuē Āndū, rebelled,
and the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Shěn Wénxiù, responded to him.
At that time, the provincial capital was Dōngyáng City,
and Shànmíng's family was inside the city walls,
unable to extricate themselves.
His paternal uncle, Mízhī, cunningly persuaded Wénxiù to seek to prove his loyalty,
and Wénxiù sent Commander Zhāng Língqìng and others with five thousand men to reinforce Āndū.
Mízhī, upon leaving the gate,
secretly told his troops:
"We have just escaped the pit of disaster."
When they reached Xiàpī,
they revolted and betrayed Wénxiù.
Shànmíng's paternal cousin, Huái Gōng, was Administrator of Běihǎi,
and held the commandery in response.
Shànmíng secretly gathered his clan members and troops,
obtaining three thousand men.
That night, he broke through the gates and rushed to Běihǎi.
His clan elder brother, Chéngmín, also gathered a multitude in Bóhǎi to respond to the imperial court.
However, Mízhī
was soon killed by Xuē Āndū.
Emperor Míng posthumously granted him General Who Aids the State and Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Chéngmín was made General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Shànmíng was made Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of Běihǎi,
and was appointed as a Gold Department Director of the Secretariat.
Chéngmín fell ill and died.
[一七] Shànmíng was then appointed as General Who Pacifies from Afar and Inspector of Jìzhōu.
After Wénxiù surrendered,
Shànmíng was appointed as Commander of the Agile Cavalry,
and was dispatched as Administrator of Hǎilíng.
The commandery bordered the sea and
had no trees.
Shànmíng instructed the people to plant elm, Chinese toon, and various fruit trees,
and they subsequently reaped the benefits.
He returned to serve as General of the Rear Army and Palace Attendant.
In the fifth year,
Qīngzhōu was lost to the barbarians,
and Shànmíng's mother was trapped in the north.
The barbarians relocated her to Sānggān.
Shànmíng wore plain clothes and ate vegetarian food,
grieving as if observing mourning rites.
Each time Emperor Míng saw him,
he sighed in sympathy for him.
People at the time praised him.
He was transferred to General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng.
Shànmíng, with his mother among the barbarians,
did not wish to travel west,
and tearfully pleaded firmly,
which was granted.
The court greatly sympathized with Shànmíng's heartfelt wishes.
In the early Yuánhuī era,
an envoy was dispatched north.
The court deliberated and instructed Shànmíng to recommend someone.
Shànmíng recommended Tián Huìshào, a native of Běipíng from his prefecture, to be the envoy to the barbarians,
and was able to ransom his mother back.
When the young emperor was newly enthroned,
the various dukes held power.
Shànmíng alone forged ties with Tài Zǔ,
entrusting himself and offering loyalty.
In the second year,
he was dispatched as General Who Aids the State, Administrator of Xīhǎi, and Acting Inspector of Qīng and Jì Prefectures.
Upon reaching his post,
he submitted a memorial requesting a northern expedition,
but the court disagreed.
Shànmíng's younger cousin, Sēngfù,
was renowned alongside Shànmíng in their prefecture.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
the barbarians rampaged north of the Huái River.
Sēngfù led two thousand troops eastward, relying on Hǎi.
Tài Zǔ, then in Huái Yīn,
admired his actions,
summoned him for an audience,
and appointed him as Staff Officer to the Pacification Army for the Prince of Ānchéng.
[一八] When Cāngwú engaged in tyranny,
Tài Zǔ was worried and fearful.
He often ordered Sēngfù to travel secretly to observe public opinion.
He had Sēngfù secretly inform Shànmíng and the Administrator of Dōnghǎi, Yuán Chóngzǔ, saying:
"Many people urge me to fortify Guǎnglíng in the north.
I fear that if I move suddenly,
it may not be a long-term plan.
Now, the autumn winds are beginning to stir.
If you and Yuán, the Administrator of Dōnghǎi, can subtly provoke the barbarians,
then all my plans can be established."
Shànmíng replied:
"The Sòng dynasty is about to perish,
a fact discernible to both the foolish and the wise.
Therefore, if the barbarians were to move,
it would instead become a problem for Your Excellency.
Your Excellency possesses divine martial prowess, unmatched in your generation.
You should simply wait quietly,
seize the opportune moment to act,
and your achievements will naturally be established.
You must not distance yourself from your foundation
and bring about your own ruin."
[一九] He dispatched dozens of brave soldiers from his unit to return with Sēngfù to the Commander's Residence,
and Tài Zǔ accepted them.
After Cāngwú was deposed,
Shànmíng was summoned to be General of the Champion Army, Consultative Counselor to Tài Zǔ's Agile Cavalry, Administrator of Southern Dōnghǎi, and Acting Governor of Southern Xúzhōu.
When Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
Tàizǔ was deeply worried about it.
Shànmíng offered a plan, saying:
"Shěn Yōuzhī controls and draws upon eight prefectures,
indulging his desires and accumulating wealth,
gathering troops and cavalry,
building boats and armaments.
He has harbored rebellious intentions
for ten years now.
His nature is treacherous and impetuous,
his talent not suited for weighty matters.
Yet he has started this rebellion for several weeks,
hesitating and not advancing.
How could he be waiting for anything?
Firstly, he is ignorant of military strategy;
secondly, popular sentiment is alienated and resentful;
thirdly, there is the affliction of being restrained;
fourthly, Heaven has taken away his spirit.
Originally, we worried about his valor,
and his skill in a single battle,
fearing his swiftness,
and that he might strike before we were prepared.
Now, the six armies are all advancing vigorously,
and the various lords are rising together.
In the past, Xiè Huì lost his reason
and disintegrated without a fight;
Lú Lóng deviated from the Dao,
and though numerous, what could they achieve?
Moreover, Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng
are the very roots of the rebels.
With the roots destroyed,
how can the branches and leaves last long?
These are merely birds already trapped in a cage!"
When the matter was settled,
Tàizǔ summoned Shànmíng back to the capital,
and said to him:
"Your strategy concerning Shěn Yōuzhī,
even Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng
could only achieve something like this."
He was then promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
appointed commander of the Chángshuǐ Garrison,
Huángmén Láng,
and concurrently General of the Rear Army and Right Sīmǎ of the Tàiwèi.
When the Qí dynasty was established,
he was made Right Wèijiāngjūn,
but declined due to illness.
Sīkōng Chǔ Yuān said to Shànmíng:
"The pursuit of noble ideals
has always been your underlying intention.
But now the imperial court relies heavily on you,
how can you suddenly aspire to emulate Sōng and Qiáo?"
Shànmíng replied:
"I originally had no desire for officialdom,
[二０]but encountering a kindred spirit,
I therefore exerted all my strength and effort,
wishing to fulfill my aspirations.
Now that the world is pacified,
the court is full of able men.
[二一]Since my humble aspirations have been fulfilled,
I dare not covet wealth and honor."
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
in recognition of Shànmíng's merits and sincerity,
he wished to bestow emoluments upon Shànmíng,
and summoned him, saying:
"Huáinán is near the capital,
a strategic point of the state.
[二二]Unless it is a trusted and worthy person,
I would not let them reside there.
You shall govern it for me even while at rest!"
He replaced Gāozōng as General of the Expeditionary Army, and Governor of the two prefectures of Huáinán and Xuānchéng.
An envoy was sent to confer the appointment,
and he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Xīngàn,
[二三]with a five hundred household stipend.
Shànmíng至jùn,
上表陳事曰：
“The Zhōu dynasty relied on three sages to assist each other,
and only with repeated efforts did it succeed.
The Hàn dynasty, when the empire had no master,
only ascended after many defeats.
The Wèi dynasty, holding the emperor in its sway to issue commands,
effectively lasted more than two ji.
The Jìn dynasty, by deposing and enthroning to wield power,
continued for four generations.
The collection of propitious fortune
was thus difficult.
Your Majesty’s brilliance condenses from heaven,
shining brightly to the divine ultimate,
with wisdom encompassing myriad things,
and virtue pervading without limit.
Thus, you could sing loudly from a quiet carriage,
and the powerful enemies were self-eliminated;
you could rule with folded hands under the cloud canopy,
and the nine regions became tranquil.
There was no toil of a single battle,
nor the urgency of half a zhen,
encompassing the jiānghǎi like a pool,
and embracing Sōngdài like a garden.
Gods and spirits joyfully supported you,
and the whole world submitted.
Within two or three years,
you truly received the precious mandate,
presiding over the imperial calendar,
and occupying the imperial seat.
Since the beginning of heaven and earth,
there has been no such prosperity as this.
Indeed, those who always win have no worries,
and those who achieve tend to be complacent.
Therefore, even if at rest, do not rest,
as Jī Dàn issued a solemn declaration;
in peace, do not forget danger,
as Nífù set an example.
Now the imperial destiny is just beginning,
and the myriad transformations are starting.
Taking advantage of the late Sòng dynasty,
whose governance was largely harsh and cruel,
the countless people were in dire straits,
looking up to Qí to relieve them.
I have long received exceptional nurture,
and my ambition is to offer my liver and blood.
Though I have the sincerity,
I have fallen short in providing even a speck of dust or dew.
Night and day, I am ashamed and anxious,
as if falling into a deep valley.
Disregarding taboos,
I respectfully present my humble views,
blind words and rustic suggestions,
awaiting the axe.”
The matters he presented totaled eleven articles: The first,
was that
“When heaven and earth were established,
and gods and humans rejoiced,
it is appropriate to inquire about distant lands,
and proclaim broad benevolence.”
The second,
was that
“The capital is vast,
a destination for near and far.
It is appropriate to send medicine,
and inquire about their ailments and sufferings.
Those aged ninety and above, and those with six infirmities who cannot support themselves,
should be granted appropriate provisions.”
The third,
was that
“The Sòng clan’s amnesty decrees
pardoned few.
I humbly suggest that [now] when issuing amnesty decrees,
[二四] the facts should be made to match.”
The fourth,
was that
“The Xiongnú are not yet destroyed,
Liú Chǎng still exists.
When the autumn wind stirs up dust,
they might be able to bring about death.
The border cities
should be strictly prepared,
specially selecting brave strategists
to await opportunities.
All necessary resources and provisions
should be prepared in advance.”
The fifth,
was that
“It is appropriate to abolish the Sòng clan’s oppressive policies and minor regulations since Dàmíng and Tàishǐ,
[二五] to promote simplicity.”
The sixth,
was that
“All expenses for construction projects
should temporarily be suspended.”
The seventh,
was that
“Imperial princes and princesses
should cultivate frugality.”
The eighth,
was that
“It is appropriate to issue an edict to all officials, and to fǔ, zhōu, jùn, and xiàn,
to each contribute sincere words,
to propagate the beauty of Táng and Yú.”
The ninth,
was that
“Loyal, steadfast, filial, and brotherly individuals
should be promoted to special ranks;
those who are pure, frugal, and endure hardship
should be appointed to civil administration.”
The tenth,
was that
“As the revolution has just begun,
and heaven and earth greatly rejoice,
it is appropriate to timely select talented and eloquent individuals,
to send as envoys north to the Xiongnú.”
The eleventh,
was that
“Jiāozhōu is treacherous and distant,
beyond the crucial wilds.
The Sòng dynasty’s late harsh governance
led to resentment and rebellion.
Now that the great transformation has just begun,
it is appropriate to win them over with grace and virtue,
and not to trouble the generals and soldiers to distant places,
disturbing the border people.
Furthermore, the products of that land
are only pearls and treasures,
which are not urgently needed by the sacred court.
The matter of military expeditions,
I suggest should be temporarily halted.”
He also compiled a collection of wise and sagely sayings and presented it,
using it for veiled remonstrance.
The emperor replied:
“I have read the collection of sayings you presented,
which are all the clear guidelines of past sages,
and the profound principles of many wise men.
You are able to follow the precedents of the ancients,
and inscribe your feelings and insights.
Your loyalty and sincerity are already manifest,
and your profound sincerity is clearly evident.
I shall act upon them,
and not forget to listen and observe.”
He also remonstrated against building the Xuānyáng Mén;
presented a memorial suggesting clear rewards and punishments for local administrators;
establishing schools,
and formulating ritual regulations;
extensively opening guesthouses,
to receive people from remote areas.
[二六] The emperor again replied:
“I fully understand your loyal and upright sentiments.
Indeed, rewards and punishments to admonish local administrators,
and decorating guesthouses to receive people from afar.
These are all good policies of antiquity,
which I should strive for.
Formulating new rituals,
however, might not be easy to establish.
Regarding the excellence of national academies,
I have already instructed the gōngqīng.
The Xuānyáng Mén construction is now ordered to be halted.
I have little virtue and many shortcomings,
and I hope to hear more.”
Shànmíng's body was seven *chǐ* and nine *cùn* tall.
He was simple and unadorned, disliking lavish sights and sounds.
His dwelling was merely a thatched hut built from unhewn timber.
His bed, couch, table, and desk
were not smoothed or carved.
When young, he was close friends with Cuī Zǔsī.
When Zǔsī left to serve as governor of Qīng and Jì prefectures,
Shànmíng sent him a letter saying:
"Our past excursions
are now distant memories.
Sometimes we walked hand in hand in the spring woods,
sometimes leaned on staffs by autumn streams,
chasing the clear breeze among the treetops,
pursuing the pale moon at the garden's edge.
How is it that our old friends
have nearly all passed away?
You are now holding a banner, serving in the northern regions,
while I manage a district in the southern territories.
Separated by a thousand *lǐ*,
with rivers and mountains between us,
life is but a temporary stay;
when will we meet again?
I have often perused historical texts,
and the events of several millennia
have largely passed before my eyes.
Successive dynasties have been diverse,
and ten thousand principles have been similar and different.
The契 (contract/understanding) of dragons and tigers with wind and clouds,
the opportunity for chaos to invariably turn to peace,
how could ancient and modern times be different?
This is indeed one constant.
Lately, Shěn Yōuzhī marshalled his forces externally,
while Càn and Bǐng were again pushed by differing opinions.
[二七]Only the capital and its garrisons
formed the foundation for the sacred enterprise.
Consequently, I was promoted to chief aide,
appointed to a major commandery,
entrusted with Guānzhōng,
and given a retained post.
Since I lacked the ability to draw a sword to protect two cities,
or to wield a spear and capture banners,
it was merely with my limited wisdom,
that my name was counted among those who aided in establishing the dynasty.
I constantly fear that once the morning dew descends,
such profound kindness will not be repaid.
My worries are deep and my responsibilities heavy,
making me increasingly insecure.
Looking back at my life,
it feels even more disordered.
Living on bean soup and wearing cloth blankets
still firmly adheres to my simple preferences.
I abhor colorful sights and dislike sounds,
even more so in my old age.
When leaving the frontier, I did not bid farewell to the high officials;
when entering the capital, I did not socialize with dukes and ministers.
Standing alone between heaven and earth,
without suspicion or reliance,
I only know to serve my lord with loyalty,
to serve my parents with filial piety,
to govern the people with integrity,
and to manage my household with frugality.
You are now sounding your bugle in your old hometown,
wearing embroidered robes in your native land.
The suffering and misery of the late Sòng dynasty have already found relief and peace.
The hardship of the people in the area north of the Yellow River, hanging upside down, now urgently needs saving.
Send eloquent and persuasive gentlemen
to act as local guides and envoys,
to travel lightly and set forth,
to manage the old territories,
to [令]the people by the Sì River to return to their occupations,
[二八]and to restore the customs of Jìxià.
Whom do you wish to decline?
I offer these thoughts from my heart,
respectfully presenting this humble gift."
He died in the second year of Jiàn yuán (480 CE)
at the age of forty-nine.
His will stipulated a simple funeral.
He was granted thirty thousand *qián*
and fifty bolts of cloth.
An imperial edict also stated:
"Shànmíng was loyal and upright from an early age,
with both competence and diligence.
He endured dangers and difficulties,
and his meritorious achievements are manifest.
It is unfortunate that he has passed away;
my heart is filled with sorrow.
He is posthumously granted the titles of Left General and Inspector of Yù Prefecture,
and his posthumous name is Lièbó."
His son, Dí, inherited his position.
Shànmíng's household had no remaining savings,
only eight thousand scrolls of books.
Tàizǔ, hearing of his incorruptibility and poverty,
bestowed upon Dí's family five hundred *hú* of grain from Gétángtún.
Shànmíng's cousin, Sēngfù,
rose to the rank of Front General,
and was enfeoffed as the Baron of Fēngyáng,
with three hundred households.
In the fourth year of Yǒngmíng (486 CE),
he served as the Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng,
[二九]and then died.
Sū Kǎn, courtesy name Xiūliè,
[三０]was a native of Wǔyì.
His grandfather, Hù,
was the Administrator of their home commandery.
His father, Duān,
was a Secretary to the Inspector of the prefecture.
Kǎn was widely read in historical texts and commentaries,
and began his career as a General of the Regular Retainers,
then appointed Magistrate of Chángchéng.
When Xuē Āndū rebelled,
he enlisted Kǎn as his staff officer,
and made him responsible for managing documents.
When Āndū surrendered to the captives (Northern Wei),
Kǎn extricated himself and returned south.
He was appointed General of Archers.
When he encountered Tàizǔ by the Huái River,
he immediately pledged his loyalty.
When Tàizǔ garrisoned at Huái'yīn,
he recognized Kǎn's meticulousness
and appointed him as Recorder-General of the Champion General.
At this time, after Zhāng Yǒng and Shěn Yōuzhī's defeat,
[三一]the area north of the Huái River had just been lost.
Initially, Tàizǔ was sent north with less than a thousand men to guard the border.
Every autumn and winter,
the border along the Huái River was in turmoil,
fearing attacks from the "captives."
Tàizǔ widely dispatched scouts,
settled the desolate remnants,
and also repaired the city walls and government offices.
Tàizǔ had been involved in military affairs for a long time,
and was viewed with suspicion by some contemporaries.
So he wrote "Sài Kè Yín" (Song of the Frontier Traveler) to express his aspirations, saying:
"The precious order is in disarray,
the divine threads are out of sequence.
Virtue has faded in Hé and Jìn,
power prevails in Jiāng and Chǔ.
Clouds and thunder signify strength,
Heaven and mountains indicate martial prowess.
My hair stands on end, pointing to Qín Pass,
my spirit condenses, transcending Hànzhǔ.
Autumn winds rise,
frontier grass withers,
[三二]eagles and swans yearn,
border horses grieve.
Looking back a thousand *lǐ* across the plains,
I only see tumbleweeds flying.
Stars are solemn, the sea is clear,
the moon is bright, the river is distinct.
Clear radiance reflects on the tents,
pale liquid condenses in the courtyard.
Golden *jiā* (pipes) sound shrill at night,
feathered chariots set out at dawn.
I mourn by the clear pond and sigh for the Sì River,
paddle among the pine islets and lament my feelings.
Orchids are infused with wind, scattering their beauty,
chrysanthemums enclose springs, dispersing their fragrance.
The tune echoes the lament of the 'first swallows,'
the blowing stirs the sound of 'cutting through Yuè.'
I sigh at the lone plucking of the garden *qín*,
and imagine the lingering scent of the courtyard basil.
Qīng Pass is gazed at until it vanishes,
the white sun sets in the west.
Peaceful springs and serene mists,
the hilltops shimmer with twilight glow.
The *yì* (boats) are readied to turn,
leaping back into the waves.
My emotions are long and distant,
my thoughts are subtle and numerous.
I strike the *zhú* (zither) of Qínzhōng,
and then compose a song of the frontier.
The song says: Starting in the morning from the river springs,
by evening on the mountain hills.
Startling gusts rage and churn,
the Huái River flows gently.
Barbarian dust gathers like clouds,
Chǔ banners hang like stars.
Sorrow fills the city walls, longing for home,
how can I express such melancholy?
I will establish a clear mirror in the world,
and discern the lost spring in Diāolíng.
I realize that the cage of worldly ties may cause entanglement,
and sigh with a distant heart, seeking solace in the profound."
Kǎn understood Tàizǔ's intention in this,
and became even more diligent.
He was entrusted with matters of the administration,
and was deeply appreciated and trusted.
Early in the Yuánhuī reign,
Lǐ Chéngmíng from Bāxī rebelled.
Tàizǔ discussed sending Kǎn as an envoy to console the region.
Upon his return, he was appointed Yǔlín Jiān,
and promoted to Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
During the disaster of Guìyáng,
the Emperor again appointed Kǎn as Píngnán Lùshì,
and Lǐng Jūzhǔ,
following to Dùn Xīntíng,
tasked with distributing gold and silver as rewards to the various generals.
When the affair was settled,
he was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
and later Sūilǔ Jiāngjūn and Shānyáng Tàishǒu.
He governed with integrity and order,
and the common people cherished him.
He was promoted to the title Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
and appointed Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
Kǎn was appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to Tàizǔ Piàojì Zīyì,
and Lǐng Lùshì.
He was appointed Huángmén Láng,
and again Tàizǔ Tàiwèi Zīyì.
Kǎn had served the Emperor for a long time,
being thoroughly familiar with his daily life.
Thus, he, along with Qiū Jùyuán, compiled the Xiāo Tàiwèi Jì,
recording the Emperor's achievements in campaigns.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Xīnjiàn Xiàn Hóu,
with five hundred households.
When the Qí Court was established,
he became Huángmén Láng,
and Lǐng Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
entrusted with confidential matters.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Kǎn compiled one scroll of the Shèng Huáng Ruìmìng Jì and presented it.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (479),
he died
at the age of fifty-three.
The Emperor deeply lamented his loss,
and posthumously granted him the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Liángnán and Qín Èrzhōu,
with the posthumous name Zhì Hóu.
His younger brother, Liè,
courtesy name Xiūwén,
was initially the magistrate of Dōngguǎn.
Zhāng Yǒng served as Zhènjūn Zhōngbīng,
〔三三〕and he progressively rose to Shānyáng Tàishǒu,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
When Yuán Càn started his uprising,
Tàizǔ first sent Liè to assist in defending the city,
then he followed the generals to pacify Shítou,
and was enfeoffed as Jíyáng Xiàn Nán.
During the Jiànyuán period,
he was appointed Jiǎjié, Dū Bāzhōu Jūnjì, Bāzhōu Cìshǐ, and Bādōng Tàishǒu,
with the title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn remaining as before.
During the Yǒngmíng period,
he reached Píngxī Sīmǎ and Chénliú Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
Yuán Róngzǔ, courtesy name Huáxiān,
〔三四〕was from Xiàpī,
a paternal cousin of Wǔbīng Shàngshū Chóngzǔ.
His father, Liàngzhī,
was a Cānjūn in the Sòng Běizhōngláng Fǔ.
Róngzǔ studied horsemanship and archery from a young age.
Someone said to him:
“Martial arts are fearsome, why not study books?”
Róngzǔ replied:
“In ancient times, Cáo Cāo and Cáo Pī rode horses with lances,
and dismounted to discuss.
This way, they would not have wasted their food and drink in the world.
You gentlemen have no skill to protect yourselves,
how are you different from dogs and sheep!”
During the Xiàojiàn period of Sòng,
he was appointed Zhǔbù by the province,
and then Hòujūn Cānjūn.
〔三五〕His paternal uncle, Hùzhī, the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu, had a son, Xíqì, who was Huáiyáng Tàishǒu.
Sòng Xiàowǔ, for some matter, exiled him to Lǐngnán,
and Hùzhī died of starvation.
When the Emperor was gravely ill,
he sent an envoy to kill Xíqì.
Before his death, Xíqì
wrote to Róngzǔ, saying:
“My brother often advised me to act cautiously and speak humbly,
and now I have indeed failed.”
When Míngdì first ascended the throne,
the four quarters revolted.
Róngzǔ was appointed Rǒngcóng Púyè,
and sent back to Xúzhōu to persuade Cìshǐ Xuē Āndū, saying:
“Whom Heaven abandons,
who can revive?
Your Excellency is not like the eight hundred feudal lords now.
As the common people see it,
this is not a wise plan.”
Āndū said:
“Heaven's mandate has its place.
Now the capital has less than a hundred *lǐ* of territory.
There is no need to discuss attacking and winning;
we can simply clap our hands and laugh until they die.
Moreover, I do not wish to betray Xiàowǔ.”
Róngzǔ said:
“Xiàowǔ's actions
are enough to bring lingering calamities.
Although the whole world is now in accord with the rebellion,
this is merely hastening death,
and you can do nothing.”
Āndū said:
“I don't know what others say,
but I am not afraid of this.
The large-hoofed horses are near;
we must make plans quickly.”
Róngzǔ was detained and could not return.
Consequently, he gathered his troops
and became a commander for Āndū.
He was temporarily appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
Āndū brought the barbarians into Péngchéng.
Róngzǔ took his family and fled south to Qúshān,
but the barbarians' cavalry pursuing him could not catch up.
Fearing punishment, Róngzǔ
then hid along the Huái River.
When Tàizǔ was in Huáiyīn,
Róngzǔ defected to him,
and the Emperor protected him.
When Míngdì died,
Tàizǔ sent a letter with Róngzǔ to Púyè Chǔ Yuān,
and he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
Yuān said to him:
“Duke Xiāo praises your talent and strategy,
thus he grants you this commandery.”
Róngzǔ was skilled at slingshots;
he could shoot birds until their feathers were gone, but the birds would not die.
When sea gulls flew in flocks,
Róngzǔ ascended the western tower of the city and shot at them,
and none failed to fall with broken wings.
He was appointed Jìnxī Wáng Zhēnglǔ, Ānchéng Wáng Chējì Zhōngbīng,
and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
Late in the Yuánhuī reign,
Tàizǔ wished to cross to Guǎnglíng.
Róngzǔ advised against it, saying:
“The Administrator's residence is a hundred paces from the palace.
If you flee,
how could people not know?
If you go alone with light cavalry,
and the people of Guǎnglíng suddenly close their gates and refuse to admit you,
where would you go?
If you now even move your foot off the bed,
I fear someone will immediately knock on the palace gate,
and your cause will be lost.”
When Cāngwú was deposed,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Huáinán Tàishǒu,
promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn, Tàizǔ Piàojì Zīyì,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Xīzhōngláng Sīmǎ, Rǔyīn Tàishǒu,
appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
Jǐshì Zhōng,
and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He participated in the founding merits,
and was enfeoffed as Jiānglè Xiàn Zǐ,
with three hundred households,
enfeoffed with his ancestor's former fief.
〔三六〕He was sent out as Chíjié, Dū Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ,
with Guānjūn as before.
He was transferred to Huángmén Láng.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (484),
he became Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Xúnyáng Xiàng, and Nánxīncài Tàishǒu.
He made a large coffin to hold his weapons,
〔三七〕and had local men Tián Tiānshēng and Wáng Dàoqī carry it across the river to the north.
His supervisor slave committed a crime
and reported him.
The authorities submitted a memorial to dismiss him from office, strip his title, and hand him over to Dōngyě,
but the investigation found no truth, and he was acquitted.
He served as Ānlù Wáng Píngxī Zīyì,
concurrently Jiānglíng Lìng,
then transferred to Sīmǎ and Hédōng Nèishǐ.
He was transferred to Chíjié, Dū Yuán Huái Zhū Jūnjì, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Yǔnzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Lǐng Dōngpíng Tàishǒu, Yǔnzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
When Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng revolted,
all regional commanders memorialized, calling Zǐxiǎng a rebel.
Róngzǔ said:
“This is not what should be said.
One should rather say that Liú Yín and others betrayed the imperial favor
and pressured Bādōng,
leading to this situation.”
At that time, none of the memorials were accepted.
After the affair was settled,
the Emperor reviewed them
and considered Róngzǔ to have spoken wisely.
In the ninth year,
he died
at the age of fifty-seven.
His paternal uncle,
Cui Hóng,
was appointed General Weiyuǎn and Administrator of Rǔnán and Xīncài during the early Xiàojiàn reign of Sòng.
He held Liángshān against the rebel Chancellor Yìxuān,
and for his merit, he was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Xīdū County.
He successively rose to General Lóngxiáng and Inspector of Sīzhōu.
When the Yìjiā incident broke out,
Emperor Míng sent Hóng to guard Xūyí
and lead troops north to suppress Xuē Biāo,
whom he defeated.
He was enfeoffed as a Baron of Lèxiāng County
with three hundred households.
At the beginning of the Shēngmíng reign,
he became a Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
He shared duty in the palace with the Prince of Yùzhāng,
and was promoted to Right Guard General.
When Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) ascended the throne,
he retained Hóng's title due to his sincerity,
and added Gěishì Zhōng,
concurrently leading as General Xiāoqí.
He successively rose to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
At the age of seventy-six,
in the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
he passed away,
and was posthumously named Dìng.
Róngzǔ's cousin, Lìshēng,
also served as General Xiāoqí.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ reign of Sòng,
when Xuē Āndū rebelled,
he made his son-in-law Péi Zǔlóng the Administrator of Xiàpī.
Lìshēng, at that time, requested leave to return north,
planning to assassinate Zǔlóng
and surrender the city to the imperial court.
The plot was discovered, and he fled.
He successively held the post of Right Rate of the Crown Prince.
He was harsh and cruel by nature,
and fond of flogging.
He rebelled with Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng,
and was executed.
The Imperial Historian states: Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) served as governor of Huái and Yùn,
laying the foundation for his hegemonic enterprise.
His benevolence and prestige spread northward,
moving the three Qí regions.
The powerful clans of Qīng and Jì,
and the prominent families of Cuī and Liú,
first recognized the heroic figure,
and sought to form alliances with him.
The counsel concerning the strategy for Jiāngdū
was similar to the words of Rèn Guāng;
though the proposal did not arise independently,
reason made it a perfect fit.
These were indeed ministers behind the curtains.
A eulogy says: The Huái garrison in the northern prefectures,
found its strength in Cuī and Liú.
They presented memorials and discussed strategies,
the Emperor remembered their loyal schemes.
Kǎn presented his plans,
and auspicious omens gathered.
Yuán Fāng was like a garter and sash,
removing baseless accusations.
Collation Notes
Biography 10: Lǚ Ānguó (Quán Jǐngwén), Zhōu Shāntú, Zhōu Pánlóng, Wáng Guǎngzhī.
Lǚ Ānguó,
was a native of Guǎnglíng, Guǎnglíng.
In the late Dàmíng reign of Sòng,
Ānguó was appointed as a general,
known for his profound composure and organizational ability, and was praised by Liú Miǎn.
In the second year of Tàishǐ,
when Miǎn campaigned against Yīn Yàn at Shòuchūn,
Ānguó served as Miǎn's deputy general with the title of General Jiànwēi.
The combined forces defeated Yàn's Chief Clerk Dù Shūbǎo's army at Héngtáng.
Ānguó cut off the enemy's supply route,
burned their transport carts,
and inflicted heavy casualties.
Yàn's forces retreated.
Miǎn sent Ānguó in pursuit,
who arrived first at Shòuchūn.
Yàn closed the gates and defended himself.
Ānguó and General Fǔguó Yuán Hóng were stationed south of the city,
and soon, the main army arrived.
Ānguó's merit was paramount,
and he was enfeoffed as a Baron of Péngzé County.
Before accepting the title,
the following year,
his enfeoffment was changed to Zhōngwǔ County,
and his number of households was increased to four hundred.
He successively rose to General Níngshuò and Administrator of Yìyáng.
In the fourth year,
he was again enfeoffed as a Baron of Xiāngnán County.
When the barbarians captured Rǔnán
and Sīzhōu fell,
Ānguó was appointed Supervising Military Affairs of Sīzhōu, General Níngshuò, and Inspector of Sīzhōu.
In the sixth year,
Yìyáng established its prefectural seat,
and he continued to serve as Administrator of Yìyáng.
He was gradually promoted to Right Army General,
and was provisionally appointed General Fǔshī.
In the second year of Yuánhuī,
he became Conquest-Rear Admiral for the Prince of Jìnxī,
with the title of General Fǔshī remaining unchanged.
He was transferred to General Yóují.
In the third year,
he was sent out as Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander of the Front-line Armies of Qīng, Yùn, and Jì three prefectures along the Huái River, General Fǔshī, and Inspector of Yùnzhōu.
The following year,
he was promoted to General Guànjūn,
then returned as General Yóují,
and was granted Sànqí Chángshì and General Zhēnglǔ.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's incident occurred,
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) appointed Ānguó as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
with the title of General Zhēnglǔ remaining unchanged.
Previously, after Wáng Yùn had left the prefecture,
the Nánzhōngláng Jiāng, Prince of Nányáng Huì, had not yet arrived to take up his post.
Yùn's Níngshuò Chief Clerk Yǔ Pèiyù temporarily managed prefectural affairs.
The imperial court had initially sent Hán Yòuzōng, Nánzhōngláng Jiāng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn and Prefect of Línxiāng, to lead troops to defend the prefecture.
During Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion,
the two men (Pèiyù and Yòuzōng) became mutually suspicious.
Pèiyù summarily killed Yòuzōng.
When General Píngxī Huáng Huí arrived at Yǐngzhōu,
he sent his Military Aide Hòu Bó to act as Administrator of Xiāngzhōu.
Hòu Bó then killed Pèiyù.
Hòu Bó and Huí conspired with General Yuán Càn regarding the affair at Shítóu.
Huí ordered Hòu Bó's naval forces to proceed by boat to the rendezvous,
but by then, the main army had already arrived,
and they could not enter.
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) ordered Ānguó to proceed to the garrison
and apprehend Hòu Bó for execution.
Soon after, he was promoted to General Qián.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he was further ennobled,
and his number of households was increased by six hundred.
He was transferred to Right Guard General,
and granted Gěishì Zhōng.
In the second year,
when the barbarians encroached upon the border,
the Emperor sent Ānguó to Sīzhōu
to settle the populace.
An edict stated:
"Between Yǐng and Sī,
the mixed population is vast and numerous.
They should all be categorized and assigned their proper affiliations.
Consult with both prefectures;
since there is no one specifically in charge of this matter,
Ānguó may temporarily go to manage it."
With his current office, he was appointed Bearer of Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expeditionary Forces of Jīng and Yǐng,
and stationed at Yìyáng's West Pass.
Before the barbarians arrived,
Ānguó moved his garrison to Miǎnkǒu to await reinforcements.
His enfeoffment was changed to Xiāngxiāng.
When World Ancestor (Shìzǔ) ascended the throne,
he was granted Bearer of Credentials, Sànqí Chángshì, General Píngxī, and Inspector of Sīzhōu,
concurrently serving as Administrator of Yìyáng.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he was transferred to Area Commander of the Armies of Nányùn, Qīng, and Jì five prefectures, General Píngběi, and Inspector of Nányùnzhōu,
and continued to serve as Area Commander and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
In the fourth year,
when the Man people of Xiāngchuān stirred,
Ānguó commanded the prefectural troops to suppress them.
While ill,
he was summoned to be Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
Ānguó was pleased by the literary appointment,
and said to his son:
"After my time, you must not be a mere servant in trousers and folded garment.
Even a single-layered garment would be regrettably inadequate for you.
You should become an official in scarlet robes!"
The Emperor dispatched Rú Fǎliàng, Palace Secretary (Zhōngshū Shèrén), to issue an edict to Ānguó, saying:
"I am concerned about your illness.
If there is anything you require,
do not hesitate to ask."
The following year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Dūguān Shàngshū),
and concurrently served as Left Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard (Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài).
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Ānguó successively held positions of commander,
and was treated as an old acquaintance at court.

Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū), and Central Corrector of Yǒngzhōu (Yǒngzhōu Zhōngzhèng),
and was granted the privilege of being supported.
The Emperor again issued an edict to Rú Fǎliàng, saying:
"I have observed Lü Ānguó's illness.
It is truly not suitable for him to exert himself.
Moreover, his legs are already bad,
and for him to be supported to my presence
would be a considerable breach of etiquette.
I find it difficult to issue an edict regarding this.
He is very sensitive about his illness.
You should express it as your private opinion,
that if he recovers well and no longer needs support,
he should enter according to custom.
Please do not force him."
In the eighth year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Envoy with Imperial Credentials (Shǐchíjié), General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Southern Yǒngzhōu (Nányǒngzhōu Cìshǐ),
with his title of Palace Attendant remaining as before.
He was provided with one set of drum and wind instruments.
His posthumous title was Sù Hóu.
At that time, among the old generals and commanders, there was also Quán Jǐngwén from Wújun,
whose courtesy name was Hóngdá.
From a young age, he possessed vigor and strength.
He traveled to the capital with Shěn Yōuzhī in the same carriage.
Upon reaching Bēnniú Tàidài,
they rested on the bank.
A fortune-teller observed them and said:
"You gentlemen are all destined to be regional governors,
and will soon become rich and noble."
Jǐngwén said to Yōuzhī:
"Perhaps only one of us can become rich and noble.
Now he says all of us;
this is surely nonsense."
Jǐngwén later obtained a command and became a Military Chief (Jūzhǔ).
At the beginning of Xiàojiàn era,
he became a Cavalry Adjutant to the Prince of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn).
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hànshuǐ (Hànshuǐ Hóu).
He was appointed Supernumerary Gentleman (Yuánwàiláng)
and General of Accumulated Archery (Jīshè Jiāngjūn).
In the second year of Tàishǐ era,
he became Acting Imperial Credential Holder (Jiǎjié), General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), Attendant at the Imperial Palaces (Rǒngcóng Púyè), and Military Chief (Jūzhǔ).
He followed General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn) Liú Liàng to suppress and defeat the eastern rebels at Jìnlíng.
He was appointed Colonel of the Long Water (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi)
and granted the title of Acting General Who Upholds the State (Jiǎfǔguó Jiāngjūn).
He campaigned north against Xuē Suǒ'ér at Pòfǔ,
leading the naval forces to cut off the enemy's supply lines.
He then followed Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) at Gězhǒng Shíliáng,
and distinguished himself in both battles.
When the southern rebels were still locked in an indecisive struggle,
Jǐngwén was ordered to join Liú Liàng in resisting Liú Hú.
He fought bravely in the siege,
sustaining dozens of wounds.
He was appointed General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiàoníng County (Xiàoníng Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of six hundred households.
He was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn),
General of Roaming Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn),
Acting General Who Assists the Army (Jiǎfǔshī Jiāngjūn),
Administrator of Gāopíng (Gāopíng Tàishǒu),
Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) of both the General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn) and General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī) establishments,
and General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
At the end of Yuánhuī era,
he was appointed Governor of Nányùzhōu (Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ) and Administrator of Lìyáng (Lìyáng Tàishǒu),
with his title of General Who Upholds the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) remaining as before.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), Administrator of both Southern Lángxié and Jìyīn Commanderies (Nán Lángxié Jìyīn Èr Jùn Tàishǒu), and Military Chief (Jūzhǔ).
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
In the first year of Jiànyuán era,
because he did not participate in the founding of the dynasty,
his marquisate was abolished.
He was appointed Administrator of Southern Lángxié (Nán Lángxié Tàishǒu),
with his titles of Palace Attendant (Chángshì) and General (Jiāngjūn) remaining as before.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), Western Pacifying Chief Clerk (Zhēngxī Sīmǎ) to the Prince of Línchuān, and Administrator of Nánjùn (Nánjùn Tàishǒu).
Upon his return,
he was successively promoted to Palace Attendant (Gěishì Zhōng)
and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng era,
he died.
Zhōu Shāntú, whose courtesy name was Jìjì,
was a native of Yìxiāng in Yìxīng.
From a young age, he was poor and humble,
earning a living by copying books.
He possessed vigor and capability,
and served as a Company Commander (Duìzhǔ) for the Wújun Jìnlíng defense commandery.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng campaigned against Tàichū,
Shāntú participated in the meritorious service,
and was granted the noble title of Marquis of Guānzhōng (Guānzhōng Hóu).
Shěn Sēngróng, the Governor of Yǒngzhōu (Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ), was stationed at Xiáqiū.
Having a prior acquaintance with Shāntú,
he appointed him an Adjutant (Cānjūn) in his Jiànwǔ establishment.
When Prince Dàn of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng Dàn) rebelled, taking up position in Guǎnglíng,
Sēngróng dispatched Shāntú with two hundred men to Shěn Qìngzhī to receive orders.
After the matter was settled and merits were evaluated,
he was suppressed by Dài Míngbǎo, Palace Secretary (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
At the beginning of Tàishǐ era,
he became General of the Palace (Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn).
As rebellions broke out in all directions,
Wáng Yù, Attendant at the Imperial Palaces (Púyè), recommended Shāntú for a command.
He summoned him for a conversation,
was very pleased,
and had him lead a hundred boats as a vanguard.
Along with Military Chief (Jūzhǔ) Jiǎo Chángshēng and others, he attacked and captured the enemy's two cities of Húbái and Zhěqí.
He was appointed Supernumerary Gentleman (Yuánwàiláng)
and given the additional title of General Who Shakes Awe (Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn).
He participated in pacifying Nónghú,
pursuing the rebels to Xīyáng before returning.
Emperor Míng rewarded him,
bestowing upon him a residence in the western garden.
When General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn) Zhāng Yǒng campaigned against Xuē Āndū at Péngchéng,
Shāntú led two thousand men to escort supplies to Wǔyuán.
He was pursued by barbarian cavalry.
In the ensuing battle,
many were wounded and killed.
As the barbarian siege became increasingly urgent,
Shāntú held the city and defended himself.
Then he regrouped his forces and fought to the death,
breaking through the encirclement.
The barbarians scattered and could not stop him.
The masses praised his bravery,
calling him
"General of Wǔyuán."
When Yǒng's army was utterly defeated,
Shāntú gathered over a thousand scattered soldiers
and defended the city of Xiàpéi.
Upon returning, he was appointed Palace Attendant (Gěishì Zhōng), Attendant at the Imperial Palaces (Rǒngcóng Púyè), and General of the Direct Guard (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn).
Shāntú was fond of wine and made many mistakes.
Emperor Míng frequently expressed his anger and reproached him,
but he later reformed himself.
He was sent out to guard Qiántáng Xīnchéng.
At that time, the Huáixī region of Yùzhōu had recently fallen to the barbarians.
A new garrison was established at Lìyáng.
In the fifth year,
Shāntú was appointed General of the Dragon Stratagem (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Magistrate of Lìyáng (Lìyáng Lìng),
leading troops to defend the city.
Initially,
Tián Liú, a fugitive from Línhǎi,
proclaimed himself
"King of Dōnghǎi."
He hid in the coastal mountains and valleys of Yínxiàn, Kuàijī.
He established camps,
and distributed his forces in strategic locations,
which the government army could not suppress.
Emperor Míng sent Wénrén Xí, a Direct Attendant (Zhíhòu), to persuade him to surrender.
Liú was granted the title of General of the Dragon Stratagem (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn).
Liú accepted the command,
and led his followers out.
Upon reaching Hǎiyán,
he released his troops to plunder extensively and then returned.
That winter,
he killed Gěng Yóu, the Magistrate of Yín,
causing great alarm in the eastern region.
In the sixth year,
an edict ordered Shāntú to lead troops to garrison Jiákoǔ in the east,
and widely offer rewards for information.
Liú was killed by his deputy Jì Nú.
Separate commanders Dù Lián and Méi Luòshēng each gathered their own followers and held their positions.
By the following year,
Shāntú divided his troops and launched a surprise attack,
subduing them all.
In Yùzhāng, the bandit Zhāng Fèng
gathered a multitude on Kānglè Shān,
cutting off the river and plundering.
The capital's military commanders, Lǐ Shuāng and Cài Bǎo, repeatedly dispatched troops to attack him,
but for years they could not capture him.
By this time, the military commander Máo Jìshēng fought Fèng on the Yùzhāng Jiāng,
and was utterly defeated.
Emperor Míng then again dispatched Shān Tú to suppress him.
When Shān Tú arrived,
he first made his troops appear weak and his forces few,
then sent his chuángzhǔ, Páng Sìhòu, to offer Fèng generous gifts,
inviting him to a meeting,
allowing him to bring his own armed escort for self-defense.
Fèng trusted him.
When they reached Wàngcài,
Shān Tú set up an ambush by the water,
struck and decapitated Fèng,
and over a hundred of his followers surrendered.
He was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Liánkǒu Shùzhǔ.
Shān Tú dammed the Lián Shuǐ and built Xīchéng,
blocking the barbarian cavalry's path
and also using it to irrigate fields.
In Yuánhuī year 3 (485 CE),
he was promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi
and additionally awarded the title of Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He was transferred to Dūd Gāopíng Xiàpī Huáiyáng Huáixī Sìjùn Zhūjūnshì, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Huáinán Tàishǒu.
Thieves broke into Huán Wēn’s tomb
and obtained many treasures.
A retainer secretly took some and offered them to Shān Tú,
but Shān Tú refused them
and registered them to be returned to the officials.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng.
When Tàizǔ assumed regency,
Shān Tú secretly advised him, saying:
"Shěn Yōuzhī has long harbored rebellious intentions;
Your Excellency should prepare thoroughly for this."
Tàizǔ smiled and accepted his advice.
When Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn was made Yǐngzhōu,
Tàizǔ ordered Shān Tú to lead troops to escort him.
When Shìzǔ and Jìnxī Wáng Xiè descended from Yǐng,
they appointed Shān Tú as the rear guard.
When Yōuzhī's affair erupted,
Shìzǔ became the Xītǎo Dūdū
and recommended Shān Tú as his military deputy.
When Shìzǔ stayed to hold Pénchéng,
the general consensus was that Pénchéng's small size made it difficult to defend,
and it would be better to return to the capital.
Shān Tú said:
"We now hold the middle course of the river,
providing strategic support for all directions.
If the entire army exerts itself,
rivers and mountains can be overcome.
The size of the city wall is a minor matter
and not a difficulty."
Shìzǔ ordered the Chéngjú Cānjūn Liú Jiē and Chén Yuān to entrust Shān Tú with all arrangements.
Shān Tú seized planks from passing boats
to construct watchtowers,
and erected a water stockade,
all completed within ten days.
Shìzǔ greatly praised him.
He was appointed Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn,
additionally awarded Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and his title was advanced to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
When Yōuzhī attacked Yǐngchéng,
Shìzǔ ordered Shān Tú to assess the situation.
Shān Tú said:
"Yōuzhī has been our neighbor,
and we have frequently campaigned together;
I know his character fully.
His nature is treacherous and cruel,
with nothing to secure the loyalty of his officers and men.
If he keeps his troops stalled beneath a strong city,
it will only hasten their dispersion."
After Yōuzhī was defeated,
Píngxī Jiāngjūn Huáng Huí, in a light boat with over a hundred men in plain clothes, descended the stream shouting in front of the army.
Panic arose in Pénchéng,
but in a moment they realized it was Huí returning victorious,
and peace was restored.
Shìzǔ said to Shān Tú:
"Zhōugōng's earlier words
can be called clear-sighted in discerning affairs."
Upon returning to the capital,
Tàizǔ dispatched Shān Tú to lead his personal troops
to guard the capital city,
and all frontier garrisons
were subject to his command.
He was promoted to Yóují Jiāngjūn,
with Fǔguó as before.
In Jiànyuán year 1 (479 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Nán of Guǎngjìn Xiàn,
with three hundred households.
He was sent out as Jiǎjié, Dū Yǔnqīngjì Sānzhōu Xúzhōu Dōnghǎi Qúshān Jūnshì, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Yǔnzhōu Cìshǐ.
The common people were devoted to him.
In year 2 (480 CE),
his title was advanced to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
That autumn,
when the barbarians stirred,
the Emperor speculated that the barbarians would surely not emerge from Huáiyīn,
and thus issued an edict to Shān Tú, saying:
"I know that you pacify the border and treat the barbarians
with great orderliness.
I fully entrust to you
the strategies and calculations for responding to change.
I fear that the various enemies may not be willing to fight to the death;
you, as a true man, will have no means to achieve your goals."
The barbarians indeed attacked Qúshān,
but were defeated by Xuán Yuándù and Lú Shàozhī.
〔一０〕The barbarians were in Huáiyáng.
〔一一〕At this time, uprisings broke out in the four prefectures north of the Huái.
The Emperor ordered Shān Tú to enter Qīng from the Huái
and march rapidly to their aid.
The Emperor decreed to Shān Tú:
"You must fully lead and manage your forces,
always maintaining complete seriousness.
In affairs of the world,
only with a united effort
can mountains be shattered.
However, when deploying troops, one must ensure there are no worries behind;
if there is no unexpected trouble from the rear,
you can fight fiercely with closed eyes,
and nothing will not be crushed.
I should now cast a golden statue
awaiting your achievements.
If you do not take this opportunity to pacify the four prefectures,
you are no true man.
Strive to act on your own initiative,
and do not let others take the credit."
However, the righteous masses had already been overwhelmed by the barbarians,
and Shān Tú evacuated three hundred families back to Huáiyīn.
He submitted a memorial requesting to move the Dōnghǎi Jùn administration to Liánkǒu,
and also to establish Yángpíng Jùn at Shíbiē,
both of which were accepted.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Jìnglǐng Wáng Zhènběi Sīmǎ,
concurrently Nánpíngchāng Tàishǒu,
with his general title as before.
Due to his old connection with Pénchéng,
he frequently entered and exited the palace,
and was greatly trusted.
The god of Fēngmiào Temple in Yìxiāng Xiàn, surnamed Dèng,
had previously served as a xiànlìng,
and upon his death, his spirit became potent.
Shān Tú memorialized requesting to add Fǔguó Jiāngjūn to the god's title.
The Emperor replied:
"Simply having dog meat will suffice;
why bother with ranks?"
He was transferred to Huángmén Láng,
leading the Yǔlín Sìxiāng Zhíwèi.
Shān Tú built a villa in Xīnlín and commuted morning and night.
The Emperor said to him:
"You, the Dūd of ten thousand men,
travel lightly in the suburbs.
From now on, when you go to your villa,
you should have bodyguards with you
to guard against the unexpected."
When he fell ill,
the Emperor personally issued edicts inquiring about his health
and sent doctors and medicine.
In Yǒngmíng year 1 (483 CE),
he died
at the age of sixty-four.
An imperial edict granted him one set of court robes
and one suit of clothes.
Zhōu Pánlóng,
a native of Lánlíng, Běi Lánlíng.
During the Sòng dynasty, the land was re-surveyed,
and it belonged to Dōngpíng Commandery.
〔一二〕Pánlóng had extraordinary courage
and was especially skilled with bow and horse.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
he followed the army to suppress the Zhěqí bandits.
He personally engaged in fierce combat,
breaking through enemy lines and being the first to ascend the ramparts.
He was successively promoted to Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn
and Jīshè Jiāngjūn,
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Jìn'ān County,
with an estate of four hundred households.
In the second year of Yuánhuī,
the Guìyáng bandits rose.
Pánlóng was then Rǒngcóng Púyè, Qíjūn Zhǔ, and Lǐngmǎjūn Zhǔ.
He accompanied Tàizǔ to camp at Xīntíng,
and, with Tún Qí Xiàowèi Huáng Huí, went out to the south of the city.
〔一三〕They arrayed against the bandits,
then quickly retreated into the city,
combining their strength to resist the attack.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Nán Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu,
and additionally given the title Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
He gradually rose to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
he was sent out as Jiǎjié, Dūdū Jiāo Guǎng Èrzhōu Jūnjì, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Before taking up his post,
he participated in pacifying Shítou.
In the second year,
after Shěn Yōuzhī was suppressed,
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Yáo Dàohé, harboring disloyal intentions, was recalled.
Pánlóng was appointed Dūdū Sīzhōu Jūnjì, Sīzhōu Cìshǐ, and Jiǎjié,
〔一四〕with his general title remaining as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as the County of Dùnyáng.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title Yòujiāngjūn.
〔一五〕
In the second year of Jiànchuán,
when the barbarians raided Shòuchūn,
Pánlóng was appointed Jūnzhu and Jiǎjié,
to assist Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Chóngzǔ in diverting water to flood the area.
〔一六〕Pánlóng led Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhāng Ní’s cavalry and infantry to fiercely attack in the western marsh,
killing and wounding tens of thousands of people,
and capturing cattle, horses, and baggage trains.
When the emperor heard of it, he was pleased,
and issued an edict saying:
“The ugly barbarians court death,
daring to invade Shòuchūn.
Chóngzǔ and Pánlóng, having rightly commanded their righteous warriors,
seized the opportunity and swiftly fought.
They engaged in cutting and striking by land and water,
filling the rivers and covering the fields.
The army did not linger for long,
and the western border was pacified.
This is truly the merit of the generals and commanders who devoted themselves to their tasks,
and the efforts of both civil and military officials who competed to attack.
〔一七〕For all their distinguished services,
they should be promptly ranked and rewarded,
and their accomplishments should be inscribed.”
〔一八〕Pánlóng’s beloved concubine was Lady Dù.
The emperor sent her twenty golden hairpins and tweezers,
with a handwritten note that said,
“A gift for Zhōugōng’s Ā Dù.”
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài.
He was then appointed Chíjié,
with his Jūnzhu title remaining as before.
The following year,
the barbarians raided Huáiyáng,
and besieged Juéchéng.
〔一九〕Earlier, the emperor had sent Jūnzhu Chéng Mǎi to garrison Juéchéng,
〔二０〕saying to others:
“I am now garrisoning Juéchéng;
my son should have a son.”
Someone asked him the reason.
Mǎi said,
“Juéchéng is on the same bank as the barbarians,
and there are many dangers.
How can I make the barbarians dare not advance southward?
If I am not killed by the barbarians,
then I should defeat the barbarians.
If my son does not become a filial son,
he should become a crown prince.”
When the barbarians had besieged Mǎi multiple times,
the emperor sent Lǐ Ānmín, the Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, as Dūdū to relieve him.
He issued an edict to Pánlóng saying:
“At Juéchéng, at the mouth of the Lián,
the bandits have just advanced again.
〔二一〕The western road is clear of bandits;
you can lead your cavalry and infantry down to Huáiyīn to meet Lǐ Lǐngjūn.
〔二二〕There are few boats at Zhōnglí;
you can only bring clothes, weapons, and a few days' provisions.
The soldiers should proceed on foot along the Huái River.”
Mǎi fought the barbarians,
killing countless with his own hands.
One morning, waking early,
he suddenly saw several pints of blood in his hand,
and on that day, he died in battle.
Pánlóng's son, Fèngshū, leading just over two hundred men on a single horse, broke into the enemy lines.
More than ten thousand barbarian cavalry spread their wings left and right to surround him.
One cavalryman galloped back,
reporting that Fèngshū had fallen.
Pánlóng, who was eating at the time,
threw down his chopsticks,
rode his horse, wielded his spear,
and charged directly into the barbarian array,
proclaiming,
“Zhōugōng is here!”
The barbarians had always feared Pánlóng’s valiant reputation,
and immediately gave way.
By this time, Fèngshū had already killed many barbarians
and had gotten out.
Pánlóng did not know this,
and so he charged east, attacked west,
raced south, and surged north.
None of the bandit host dared to stand against him.
Fèngshū saw that his father had been gone for a long time
and again leaped on his horse to re-enter the array.
Father and son, on two horses,
entangled and stirred up tens of thousands of men,
and the barbarian host was utterly defeated.
Pánlóng and his son thus became famous throughout the northern country.
He was physically frail and reticent,
but when facing the army, he was brave and resolute,
surpassing all other generals.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Nán Lángxié Tàishǒu.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and additionally given the title Jǐshìzhōng.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Dàsīmǎ,
〔二四〕and additionally given Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Jìyáng Tàishǒu.
Shìzǔ frequently held military exercises,
and always ordered Pánlóng to command the cavalry,
with the military superintendents and cavalrymen practicing their spear skills.
〔二五〕Later, due to illness, he became Guānglù Dàfū.
Soon after, he was sent out as Chíjié, Dūdū Xǔ Yùnzhōu Yuán Huái Zhū Jūnjì, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Xǔ Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was promoted to the rank of Marquis.
〔二六〕
Zhāng Pú, the garrison commander of Juéchéng,
〔二七〕secretly conspired with the barbarians.
During a heavy fog, he took a boat into the Qīng River to gather firewood,
carrying over twenty barbarians.
He hid their weapons under the firewood
〔二八〕and headed straight for the east gate of the city.
The gate guard did not prohibit them.
They then disembarked and drew their white standards, fighting for control of the gate.
The garrison commander, Huángfǔ Zhòngxián, led Jūnzhu Mèng Língbǎo and over thirty others to resist at the gate,
killing three men.
The bandits were wounded and fell into the water.
By then, more than three thousand barbarian cavalry and infantry had arrived outside the city,
but were blocked by the moat and could not advance.
Huáiyīn Jūnzhu Wáng Sēngqìng and others led five hundred men to rescue them,
〔二九〕and the barbarian host then retreated.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and an imperial edict ordered him to perform his duties as a commoner.
The Eight Ministers soon memorialized for his reinstatement.
He was additionally given Lǐng Dōngpíng Tàishǒu.
Pánlóng memorialized that he was old and weak,
unsuitable for guarding the frontier,
and requested to resign his post.
His request was granted,
and he returned as Sànqí Chángshì and Guānglù Dàfū.
Shìzǔ jokingly said to him:
“How do your貂蟬 (diāochán, sable cicada hat) compare to a兜鍪 (dōumóu, helmet)?”
Pánlóng replied:
“These 貂蟬 came from the 兜鍪.”
In the eleventh year,
he died of illness
at the age of seventy-nine.
He was posthumously granted Ānběi Jiāngjūn and Xǔ Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zǐ Fèngshū
possessed strength that surpassed others.
He followed Pánlóng on campaigns,
committing acts of plunder wherever he went.
Shìzǔ sent him as Commander of the Army to campaign eastward against Táng Yáozhī.
Fèngshū, fearing the Emperor's majesty and strictness,
restrained his subordinates,
not daring to invade or expand.
He served as a Guard of the Eastern Palace.
When Yùlín was in Xīzhōu,
Fèngshū secretly presented himself.
When he ascended the throne,
he and Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Cáo Dàogāng became trusted confidants.
Dàogāng was made Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
with the added title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn;
Fèngshū was made Yóují Jiāngjūn,
with the added title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn: both supervising the palace guards.
A few days later,
Dàogāng was further promoted to Huángmén Láng.
Gāozōng vehemently remonstrated, but it was not accepted.
Fèngshū was skilled at horsemanship.
The Emperor learned riding and archery from him,
and he was especially favored and trusted,
being allowed into the inner palace.
Soon after, he was given the additional appointments of Administrator of Huáilíng and Zhōngzhèng of Yǔnzhōu.
Dàogāng was given the additional appointment of Administrator of Nánpúyáng.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was appointed Huángmén Láng.
Before he could accept the post,
he was instead sent out as Chíjié, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Qīng and Jì Provinces, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Qīng Province.
At this time, the Emperor planned to execute the grand counselors,
so he sent Fèngshū out as an external auxiliary.
Dàogāng was appointed Zhōngjūn Sīmǎ and Zhōngzhèng of Qīng and Jì Provinces,
retaining his original post.
Fèngshū asked the Emperor for a marquisate of a thousand households,
which was granted.
When Gāozōng assisted in government,
he deemed it inappropriate,
and instead enfeoffed him as a Baron of Qǔjiāng County,
with three hundred households.
Fèngshū was greatly enraged,
brandishing his sword and glaring fiercely in front of the crowd.
Gāozōng placated him,
and he then accepted.
Fèngshū concluded his farewells and was about to depart for his post,
his troops having already set out.
Gāozōng feared that once he left, he could not be controlled again.
He conspired with Xiāo Chén,
and under the guise of an imperial edict, summoned Fèngshū to the palace office and killed him.
Several brave warriors punched him for a long time before he died.
They reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Fèngshū showed disrespect to the court."
The Emperor, having no other choice,
approved their memorial.
On the day Gāozōng deposed the Emperor,
Dàogāng was at the Zhíhé office.
Xiāo Chén entered the room first,
as if to discuss matters,
and soldiers followed him, abruptly advancing,
stabbing him with knives,
killing him instantly.
Then they advanced into the palace to depose the Emperor.
Fèngshū's younger brother, Shìxióng,
during the Yǒngyuán period,
was the Protector of Xījiāng.
After Chén Xiǎndá's affair,
Shìxióng killed Xiāo Jìchǎng, the Inspector of Guǎng Province,
claiming Jìchǎng was complicit in the rebellion,
and sent his head to the capital.
Yán Fān, the Inspector of Guǎng Province, attacked and killed him.
Wáng Guǎngzhī, courtesy name Línzhī,
was a native of Pèijùn.
From a young age, he was fond of archery and horsemanship,
and was agile and brave.
Initially, he was a cavalry leader.
During the Dàmíng period of the Sòng dynasty,
he was appointed Magistrate of his home county for his merits,
then Diànzhōng,
Lóngxiáng,
Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn,
Piàojí Zhōngbīng,
and Administrator of Nánqiáo.
In the early Tàishǐ period,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Jūzhǔ,
subordinate to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Liú Huáizhēn in the campaign against Yīn Yǎn at Shòuchūn.
Yǎn's general Liú Cóng built a fort and resisted.
The imperial army besieged them for several days.
[三一] Yǎn sent his long history Dù Shúbǎo with five thousand men and five hundred supply wagons to reinforce Cóng.
Huáizhēn sent Guǎngzhī, along with army commanders Xīn Qìngzǔ, Huáng Huí, Qiān Dàolián, and others, to intercept them at Héngtáng.
Shúbǎo established a camp and resisted.
Guǎngzhī and the others launched a close-quarters assault on the camp.
From late afternoon until sunset,
they utterly defeated him,
killing and wounding over a thousand men,
then retreated
and burned his supply wagons.
Cóng heard of this,
abandoned his fort, and fled.
At that time, Héféi city rebelled.
The government forces were under attack from front and rear.
Commander Liú Miǎn called a meeting of the army commanders.
Guǎngzhī said:
"Please let me take the general's horse and go pacify them."
Miǎn gave his horse to Guǎngzhī.
Guǎngzhī left for three days
and attacked and captured the Héféi rebels.
He then followed Huáizhēn to suppress rebels north of the Huái River.
At that time, Emperor Míng sent Qīng Province Inspector Míng Sēnggǎo to campaign north to Sānchéng,
where he was attacked by Shěn Wénxiù.
Guǎngzhī led over three thousand infantry and cavalry
along the coast to rescue him,
and they both retreated.
Guǎngzhī then advanced and attacked Liú Táogēn, the Administrator of Chángguǎng appointed by Wénxiù.
Táogēn abandoned the city and fled.
Upon returning to the army,
he was enfeoffed as a Viscount of Ānmán County,
with three hundred households.
Soon, this was changed to Púqí.
He was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Nányáng,
but did not take up the post.
He was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn, and Administrator of Zhōnglí.
He was promoted to Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the added title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Gāopíng.
He was also appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn,
retaining Níngshuò as before.
He was given the added title of Jǐshìzhōng,
and Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the campaign against Sòng Jiànpíng,
he was the first to ascend Kǒukǒu,
and was re-enfeoffed as a Viscount of Níngdū County,
with five hundred households.
Tàizǔ deposed Cāngwú,
and sent Guǎngzhī out as Jiǎjié, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Xú Province, Inspector of Xú Province, and Administrator of Zhōnglí,
retaining Guānjūn as before.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
Guǎngzhī remained in the capital
and participated in pacifying Shítou.
He then followed Tàizǔ to camp at Xīntíng,
and was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Tàizǔ executed Huáng Huí.
Huí's younger brother Sī, along with his cousin Mǎ and nephew Nú, fled.
Tàizǔ wrote to Guǎngzhī, saying:
"Although Huáng Huí had minor merits,
his crimes became increasingly intolerable.
Recently, he even requested to use two imperial chariots, large and small, for his inspector's attire.
I would not begrudge reporting this for him,
but I fear that if he gets the chariots,
he will again ask for painted wheeled carriages.
Besides these, his crimes are too numerous to count;
you yourself know them all.
Now I am initiating action according to the law."
He ordered Guǎngzhī to search for Sī and the others in Jiāngxī.
In the first year of Jiànruán,
he was promoted to Marquis,
with a fief of a thousand households.
[三二] He was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
When the northern barbarians stirred,
the following year,
an edict granted Guǎngzhī the insignia of a commander,
and he was sent to the Huái River.
Guǎngzhī's home was in Péng and Pèi.
He memorialized, requesting to recruit his local villagers and troops
to take Péngchéng in the north,
and the Emperor approved it.
Guǎngzhī was appointed Shǐchíjié, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs North of the Huái River, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Xú Province.
Guǎngzhī led his army across the Huái,
but achieved nothing,
and was dismissed from office for this.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
with the added titles of Sànqí Chángshì and Tàizǐ Yòulǜ.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhènjūn Sīmǎ for the Prince of Chángshā,
Administrator of Nándōnghǎi,
Sītú Sīmǎ,
Prime Minister of Xúnyáng,
[三三] Administrator of Nánxīncài,
North Zhōngláng Zuǒjūn Sīmǎ for the Prince of Ānlù, and Administrator of Guǎnglíng,
retaining his general title.
He was sent out as Chíjié, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Xú Province, and Inspector of Xú Province,
retaining his general title.
Upon his return, he was made Guānglù Dàfū, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, and Sītú Sīmǎ.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
then transferred to Sànqí Chángshì,
and Qián Jiāngjūn.
[三四]
Shìzǔ saw that Guǎngzhī's son, Zhēnguó, was capable of great use,
and said to Guǎngzhī:
"You can be considered old."
Guǎngzhī replied:
"I dare not decline."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
He was appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn,
but did not accept the post.
In the eleventh year,
the barbarians made a move,
and he was granted Guǎngzhī's credentials
to recruit soldiers.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was promoted to Jǐshìzhōng and Zuǒwèijiāngjūn.
At that time, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Cuī Huìjǐng secretly communicated with the barbarians,
harboring ulterior motives.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
Guǎngzhī was appointed Chíjié, Dū Yùzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Xīyáng Sīzhōu zhī Rǔnán Èr Jùn Jūnjì, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
His pension from the Yùlín period was abolished,
and his enfeoffment was increased by three hundred households.
Gāozōng executed and harmed various princes,
and dispatched Guǎngzhī to suppress Ānlù Wáng Zǐjìng in Jiāngyáng,
granting him a set of drums and pipes.
When the matter was settled,
he was then re-appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdu Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was further enfeoffed as Yìngchéng Xiàn Gōng,
with an income fief of two thousand households.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians besieged Sīzhōu,
and Guǎngzhī was dispatched with credentials to oversee the campaign in Sīzhōu,
lifting the siege.
Before Guǎngzhī had arrived within a hundred *li*,
the barbarians retreated,
so he returned.
The following year,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted *fú* (a walking staff).
In the fourth year,
he died,
aged seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and given the posthumous title Zhuānggōng.
〔三五〕
The historiographer says: "Dukes and marquises guard cities,
which is what the state relies upon.
They must be long accustomed to military affairs,
not relying on the strength of a single battle.
Ānguó and others rendered service to successive dynasties,
their diligence and achievements were notable,
they all recognized the changes of the times,
and all knew whom to attach themselves to.
Pánlóng was fierce and brave,
alone topping the three armies;
the Xiongnu's fear of the Flying General
was not even comparable.
How magnificent!"
An encomium says: "Ānguó, an old general,
collaborated to move the altars,
together assisting Jiǔjiāng,
escorting and supporting Zhōngxià.
Pánlóng slew enemies,
piercing the barbarian cavalry.
In Guǎngzhī's later years,
he repeatedly held the commander's banners."
Collations:
Biographies, Chapter 11: Xuē Yuān, Dài Sēngjìng, Huán Kāng (Yǐn Lüè), Jiāo Dù, Cáo Hǔ
Xuē Yuān
was a native of Fényīn, Hédōng.
He was the nephew of Sòng Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Āndū.
His original name was Dàoyuān,
