but it was changed to avoid a taboo on Tàizǔ's given name.
As Āndū surrendered Péngchéng to the barbarians,
all his relatives entered the north.
When Tàizǔ was garrisoned in Huái’yīn,
Yuān fled south,
committing himself wholeheartedly.
He was indeed resolute and strong.
Tàizǔ assigned him to lead his personal troops,
to guard inside his tent,
and he followed on campaigns.
At the end of Yuánhuī,
due to his merits, he reached the offices of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, Jūnzhu,
and was enfeoffed as Jìnglíng Hóu.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion broke out,
Tàizǔ entered the imperial court,
and Yùzhāng Wáng Yí temporarily guarded the Eastern Palace.
He ordered Yuān to lead troops to garrison the Sītú Zuǒfǔ,
dividing forces to defend the capital.
When Yuán Càn occupied Shítóu,
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí climbed the West Gate at night and called out to Yuān from afar.
Yuān, startled, rose,
led his troops to respond to the crisis,
and was the first to arrive at Shítóu to burn the gate and attack.
When the matter was settled,
the next morning the various armies gathered back at Dùmǔzhái,
filling all the streets.
The palace gates were not opened.
Tàizǔ ascended the South Yè Gate tower to give orders for the various armies to return to their original camps.
After the meal,
the city gates opened,
and only then could Yuān enter to see Tàizǔ,
both happy and weeping.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
his fief was increased to two thousand five hundred households.
He was appointed Huáilíng Tàishǒu,
and given the additional title Níngsuò Jiāngjūn,
while Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn remained as before.
Soon after, he became Zhíhé Jiāngjūn,
and Guànjūn Jiāngjūn.
He was then transferred to Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài.
The barbarians dispatched their pseudo-general Xuē Dàobiāo to raid Shòuchūn.
Tàizǔ, knowing Dàobiāo was a close relative of Yuān,
ordered Qíjùn Tàishǒu Liú Huáiwèi, saying:
"I heard that Dàobiāo is definitely coming.
His wife and children are all in the capital,
and he has no brothers left alive.
For all such cases,
there is no reason not to try many ways to mislead them.
Even if they don't fully believe it,
it's enough to make the jackals and wolves suspicious."
He ordered a letter to be written by Yuān to Dàobiāo to show the intention of buying him over.
When the barbarians received the letter,
they indeed recalled Dàobiāo
and sent another general to replace him.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèijiāngjūn.
Originally,
when Yuān fled south,
his mother, née Suǒ, could not extricate herself
and remarried into the Yáng clan of Cháng'ān.
Yuān secretly sent someone to ransom her.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Cuī Huìjǐng reported to Yuān:
"Suǒ is at Jièshǒu.
I sent messengers to bring her,
and she has been rescued from hardship."
Yuān submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post to go to the border to welcome her,
which was granted.
He was re-appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
The matter of Yuān's mother returning south ultimately proved to be untrue.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
Yuān submitted a memorial to resign his post and return his official hat.
An imperial edict stated:
"Being separated by distant lands,
it is difficult to ascertain the news.
Yuān's deep anxiety and distress
make him firmly decline the court position.
In the past, the old customs of the Eastern Pass
still allowed for marriages and official positions;
how much more so when the mother's departure was ambiguous and news sometimes arrived!
Following previous precedents,
it is impermissible to grant this request.
The memorial should be rejected,
and the official attire promptly returned."
Since Yuān could not ransom his mother,
he again submitted a memorial requesting to resign,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
Later, when barbarian envoys arrived,
the emperor sent a letter from Yuān to his mother.
When the imperial carriage visited Ānlè Sì,
Yuān accompanied the retinue, riding a barbarian bridge (a type of carriage).
Previously, there was an order that barbarian bridges were not allowed in the imperial retinue.
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities,
dismissed from office,
but later pardoned.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Chíjié, Dū Xúzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
his general title remaining as before.
The following year,
he was promoted to Yòujūn Sīmǎ,
his general title remaining as before.
He was then transferred to Dàsīmǎ,
Jìyáng Tàishǒu,
his general title remaining as before.
In the seventh year,
he became Jǐshìzhōng and Yòuwèijiāngjūn,
but resigned due to illness.
Returning home,
he could not ride in a carriage,
so he removed the wheels of a carriage
and had people carry him.
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities
but later pardoned.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Right General and Grand Marshal,
leading an army to suppress Zǐxiǎng (子響), the Prince of Bādōng (巴東).
Zǐxiǎng's (子響) army commander, Liú Chāo (劉超), was in imminent danger of capture.
He bribed Yuān (淵) with over ten items, including sleeping mats and miscellaneous objects, to escape.
Yuān (淵) concealed him within the army.
He was impeached by the appropriate officials,
but an imperial edict pardoned him.
In the tenth year,
he became a Mounted Regular Attendant,
his generalship remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) passed away,
the imperial court feared a southern invasion by the barbarians.
Yuān (淵) was granted a staff of authority,
his army commander and original official post remaining as before.
Soon after, he was additionally appointed General of Valiant Cavalry,
his staff of authority and original official post remaining as before.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
he was sent out as one holding a staff of authority, supervising military affairs of Sīzhōu (司州) and serving as Governor of Sīzhōu (司州),
his position as Right General remaining as before.
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興),
he was promoted to the title of General Pacifying the North.
Before he could be formally installed,
he died.
When Míngdì (明帝) ascended the throne,
an edict was issued to bestow 50,000 cash
and 500 bolts of cloth,
and a day was set to observe mourning.
Dài Sēngjìng (戴僧靜)
was a native of Yǒngxīng (永興) in Kuàijī (會稽).
His grandfather, Shì (飾),
during the Jǐngpíng (景平) reign of Sòng (宋),
conspired to revolt with Sūn Fǎxiān (孫法先) of Fùyáng (富陽) and was executed,
and his family was exiled to Qīngzhōu (青州).
Sēngjìng (僧靜) was courageous and strong in his youth,
and skilled with bow and horse.
He served the Governor Shěn Wénxiù (沈文秀)
and was captured by the barbarians along with him.
Later, he led his family in rebellion and returned to Huáinán (淮南).
Tàizǔ (太祖) fostered and nurtured him,
and he was always at his side.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) was once carrying brocade out of the capital
when he was apprehended by Ōuyáng Shù (歐陽戍)
and imprisoned in Yǒngzhōu (永州).
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Xuē Yuān (薛淵) to bring wine and food to Sēngjìng (僧靜),
placing a knife inside the belly of a fish.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) drank with the prison guards.
Once they were drunk,
he used the knife to cut his shackles,
broke the [manacles] with his own hands,
and escaped by breaking through the roof.
Upon his return,
Tàizǔ (太祖) concealed him in his private chamber.
Because his family was poor,
he was given 1,000 *hú* of grain annually.
When the barbarians besieged Jiǎochéng (角城),
Sēngjìng (僧靜) was sent to fight and charge,
winning several victories.
He was appointed Commander of the Imperial Guard.
He followed them back to the capital,
his meritorious rank reaching General of Accumulated Archers and Director of the Feathered Forest.
When the affair of Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) arose,
Tàizǔ (太祖) entered the imperial court.
Sēngjìng (僧靜), as an army commander,
followed Yuán Càn (袁粲) to hold Shítóu (石頭).
Tàizǔ (太祖) sent Sēngjìng (僧靜) with trusted men to arrive at Shítóu (石頭) first.
At that time, Sū Liè (蘇烈) was holding Cāngchéng (倉城).
Sēngjìng (僧靜) shot an arrow with a letter to Liè (烈),
and was lowered into the city by rope at night.
Càn (粲) ascended the southwest gate of the city,
arranging [many] torches [for communication].
When the imperial army arrived,
they shot at them,
extinguishing the torches.
He then turned and ascended the east gate.
His confederate, General Fǔguó (輔國) Sūn Tán'guàn (孫曇瓘), was brave and skilled in combat.
Each time he engaged in battle,
he inflicted heavy casualties.
Over a hundred imperial soldiers died.
Army Commander Wáng Tiānshēng (王天生) fought desperately,
thus maintaining the standoff.
From *hài* (9-11 PM) to *chǒu* (1-3 AM),
a reddish meteor shone to the ground and fell into the city.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) led his forces to attack the Cāngmén (倉門) gate,
personally leading his soldiers.
The multitude collapsed,
and Sēngjìng (僧靜) personally beheaded Càn (粲).
Thereupon, the outer army burned down the gate and entered.
Originally,
during the Dàmíng (大明) reign, Càn (粲) was traveling in the same carriage with Xiāo Huìkāi (蕭惠開) and Zhōu Láng (周朗).
They encountered the Dàhéng (大桁) bridge open,
so they stopped their carriage and chatted.
Huìkāi (惠開) took out a mirror and looked at himself, saying:
"[I have] no more years left to serve."
Láng (朗) held the mirror for a long time and said:
"I view death as returning home."
Càn (粲) was the last to speak, saying:
"I shall reach the rank of the Three Dukes but will not see it through to the end."
Sēngjìng (僧靜) was appointed General of the Vanguard
and General Níngshuò (寧朔) for his achievements.
For the soldiers who died in battle,
Tàizǔ (太祖) arranged for their burials and sacrifices.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (昇明),
he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry.
After Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) was suppressed,
titles were conferred upon the generals for their contributions.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) was made Marquis of Xīngpíng (興平) County,
with a fief of a thousand households.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
his fief was increased by 1,200 households.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Southern Jìyīn (濟陰),
his original official post remaining as before.
He was appointed General Fǔguó (輔國)
and his enfeoffment was changed to Jiànchāng (建昌).
In the second year of Jiàn yuán (建元),
he was promoted to General of Valiant Cavalry,
additionally serving as an Attendant outside the Regular Establishment,
and transferred to Left Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was sent out as one holding a staff of authority, supervising military affairs of Xúzhōu (徐州) and serving as General Chàngjūn (冠軍) and Governor of Northern Xúzhōu (徐州).
He bought oxen for the poor to farm,
which was much appreciated in the desolate region.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant and Right Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard.
Soon after, he was additionally appointed General Attendant.
In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he was subordinate to Protector-General Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達)
to suppress the bandit Huán Tiānshēng (桓天生) at Bǐyáng (比陽).
Sēngjìng (僧靜), along with Han Mèngdù (韓孟度), the Sīmǎ (司馬) of General Pacifying the West, and Kāng Yuánlóng (康元隆), the Grand Administrator of Huàshān (華山), advanced.
Before reaching Bǐyáng (比陽) by forty *lǐ*,
they encamped at Shēnqiáo (深橋).
Tiānshēng (天生) led 100,000 barbarian infantry and cavalry in a sudden attack.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) engaged them in battle and inflicted a great defeat,
killing and capturing tens of thousands.
Tiānshēng (天生) retreated back to Bǐyáng (比陽),
and Sēngjìng (僧靜) advanced to besiege it.
Tiānshēng's (天生) army sallied out of the city,
and Sēngjìng (僧靜) again defeated them.
Tiānshēng (天生) closed the gates and did not come out again.
Sēngjìng (僧靜), exhausted, then retreated.
He was appointed General Pacifying the Barbarians, Sīmǎ (司馬) of the Central Director of the South, and Grand Administrator of Huáinán (淮南).
In the eighth year,
Zǐxiǎng (子響), the Prince of Bādōng (巴東), killed his subordinates.
Shìzǔ (世祖) summoned Sēngjìng (僧靜) and ordered him to lead an army towards Jiānglíng (江陵).
Sēngjìng (僧靜) respectfully said to the emperor in person:
"The Prince of Bādōng (巴東) is young.
His Chief Clerk pressed him too hard,
and he acted out of indignation without considering the consequences, that is all.
What great crime is it if the Emperor's son makes a mistake and kills someone?
If the court suddenly sends an army westward,
people will be terrified
and panic without limit.
Sēngjìng (僧靜) dare not obey this imperial decree."
The emperor did not respond
but inwardly approved of him.
He was transferred to Sīmǎ (司馬) of the Central Army of the Prince of Lúlíng (廬陵) and Grand Administrator of Gāopíng (高平),
his generalship remaining as before.
In the ninth year,
he died.
An imperial edict stated:
"Sēngjìng (僧靜) possessed a steadfast and resolute will,
his loyalty manifested in difficult times.
He decisively eliminated the Western ramparts,
his achievements shining at the beginning of our enterprise.
His sudden demise
fills us with sorrow and grief.
A gift of 50,000 cash
and 100 bolts of cloth is bestowed.
His posthumous title is Zhuànghóu (壯侯)."
Chén Yìnshū (陳胤叔), a native of Yúyáo (餘姚) in the same commandery as Sēngjìng (僧靜),
was originally named Chén Chéngshū (陳承叔),
but changed his name to avoid the taboo of Xuāndì's (宣帝) personal name.
He was eloquent, decisive, and agile,
and skilled with sword and shield.
Initially, he was a commander of the Left Chariot Guard.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he followed Tàizǔ (太祖) on his eastern campaign,
then committed himself to follow him in military expeditions.
He was careful and discreet in his duties,
and was rewarded for his achievements.
He was enfeoffed as Viscount of Dāngyáng (當陽) County.
His official post reached Left Commander of the Crown Prince's Guard.
He memorialized Shìzǔ (世祖) that forged arrowheads required too much iron
and that casting would be better.
The Eastern Foundry Prefect Zhāng Hòubó (張候伯) argued that cast arrowheads were blunt
and unsuitable for use,
so the proposal was not adopted.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he died.
Huán Kāng
was a native of Chéng in Běi Lánlíng.
He was brave, decisive, fierce, and skilled in combat.
During the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
he followed Tàizǔ as his military aide.
He served Shìzǔ in Gànxiàn.
In the early Tàishǐ era,
when Shìzǔ raised an army,
he was arrested by the prefecture.
His followers all scattered.
Kāng disguised himself as a peddler with a carrying pole,
storing Mù Hòu in one basket
and Wénhuì Tàizǐ and Jìnglín Wáng Zǐliáng in the other,
and carried them himself to the mountains.
He allied with over forty retainers, including Xiāo Xīnzǔ, Yáng Zhuànzhī, Gāo Fēnxǐ, Qián Sānnú, and Xiàng Sīnnú,
and broke into the prefectural prison to free Shìzǔ.
The prefectural pursuers were fierce,
but Kāng and his group fought desperately and defeated them.
He followed Shìzǔ in his uprising,
smashing fortifications and breaking through enemy lines.
His physical strength surpassed ordinary men.
Wherever his forces passed through villages and towns,
they indulged in violence and harm.
The people of Jiāngnán feared him,
using his name to frighten small children.
They drew his image to ward off malaria,
and everyone was immediately cured.
He was promoted to Cānjūn of Shìzǔ's Guānjūn Fǔ,
and appointed Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
Wǔqí Chángshì,
then sent out to serve as Xiāngbēn Lìng.
When the Guìyáng incident occurred,
Kāng abandoned his county and returned to the capital to join Tàizǔ.
When the matter was settled,
he was appointed Yuánwàiláng.
On the night of the sixth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of Yuánhuī,
the Shàodì made a secret excursion to the Lǐngjūn Fǔ.
The Emperor's attendants said:
"Everyone in the residence is asleep,
why not climb the wall and enter?"
The Emperor said:
"Tonight I wish to find a suitable place,
wait until tomorrow night."
Kāng, along with Lú Huāng and Xiàng Hēi, brave retainers of Tàizǔ, overheard their conversation at the gate.
The next evening,
Wáng Jìngzé arrived with the Emperor's head.
He knocked on the door.
Kāng thought it was an uprising,
and with Huāng and Hēi, he went downstairs in the dark,
drawing his sword, intending to go out.
[一一]He then followed into the palace.
[一二]Tàizǔ was stationed at Dōng Fǔ.
He appointed Kāng as Wǔlíng Wáng Zhōngbīng, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Lánlíng Tàishǒu,
always guarding his left and right.
When Tàizǔ executed Huáng Huí,
Huí was about to be made Nán Yuán Zhōu,
with several thousand troops under his command.
He was sent to be captured,
fearing he would cause rebellion.
[一三]He was summoned into the Dōng Fǔ,
and detained in the outer study.
Kāng was ordered to lead dozens of men to enumerate Huí's crimes,
and then kill him.
Huí had initially conspired with the Túqí Xiàowèi Wáng Yíyǔ at Shítóu.
[一四]Tàizǔ concealed the matter,
still entrusting Huí with heavy troops and assigning trusted confidantes to him.
Yíyǔ was agile and quick,
skilled in wielding swords and shields.
Huí once had more than ten men spray water on him from all directions,
but none could touch him.
Fearing that Yíyǔ would turn against him,
Huí first dismissed his military commanders.
Yíyǔ did not comply.
Huí became enraged, refused to follow orders,
and unilaterally beheaded him.
The generals then reported to Tàizǔ,
saying that since Huí commanded powerful troops,
he would inevitably rebel.
Kāng requested to go alone and assassinate him.
Tàizǔ said:
"Why are you [甚,
He] is incapable of doing anything."
[一五]When Huí was summoned and got into his carriage,
his favorite concubine saw a red light emanating from his head to his feet.
She desperately tried to hold him back,
but Huí refused to stop.
People at the time had a saying about him:
"If you want to be deceitful,
ask Huán Kāng."
He was appointed Hòujūn Jiāngjūn,
Zhíhé Jiāngjūn,
Nán Púyáng Tàishǒu,
with Níngshuò as before.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he was enfeoffed as the Bó of Wúpíng Xiàn,
[一六]with five hundred households.
He was transferred to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
Yóují Jiāngjūn,
with Tàishǒu as before.
Tàizǔ said to Kāng:
"You have followed me for a long time,
and have not yet become a provincial governor.
You must not understand my intention.
I simply wish to first eliminate the barbarians with you."
When the barbarians moved,
Kāng was sent to lead the army,
with temporary credentials (jiǎjié).
Soon after, he was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the spring of the third year,
he fought the barbarians at Huáiyáng,
inflicting a great defeat on them.
He then advanced and attacked and captured the barbarian's Fánxié Chéng.
Tàizǔ was delighted,
and ordered Kāng to welcome the righteous people north of the Huái River,
but he was unsuccessful.
The following year,
Kāng was appointed Chíjé, Dū Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Dōng Xú zhī Dōngguǎn Lángyá Èrjùn Qúshān Shù Běi Xú zhī Dōnghǎi Liánkǒu Shù Zhū Jūnjì, Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ,
with Guānjūn as before.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
and reinstated as Qiánjūn Jùn.
That year,
he died.
An imperial edict stated:
"Kāng previously participated in the Southern campaigns,
his righteousness was always cherished,
I am deeply saddened by his misfortune.
All necessities for his funeral
shall be generously provided for."
He was fifty-seven years old.
Yǐn Lüè, a native of Huáinán,
served Tàizǔ from a young age.
Later he practiced horsemanship and archery,
and was appointed a general due to his agility.
During the Shēngmíng era,
he served as Hǔbēn Zhōngláng and Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
In the early Jiànyuán era,
he was enfeoffed as the Nán of Pínggù,
[一七]with three hundred households.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng,
he served as Yóují Jiāngjūn,
and was killed
while suppressing Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng.
He was posthumously granted the titles Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiāo Dù, courtesy name Wénxù,
[一八]was a Dī from Nán'ān.
His grandfather, Wénkuī,
fled to Xiāngyáng during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
and was temporarily settled in Lüyáng Xiàn, Tiānshuǐ Jùn,
thus he belonged to it.
When Dù returned to the state,
he was appointed Běiguǎn Kè.
In the early Xiàowǔ era,
when Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yán Shībó was sent out to govern,
the imperial court dispatched Dù to lead a banner unit to escort him.
[一九]When the Suǒ barbarians invaded Qīngzhōu,
Shībó sent Dù to lead troops to fight the barbarians at Shāgōu Dùliáng.
Dù personally broke through the enemy lines,
achieving a great victory.
Shībó appointed him as Cānjūn of his Fǔguó Fǔ.
When the barbarians sent Qīngshuǐ Gōng Shíbēn Chìwén to raid Qīngkǒu,
Dù again led troops to reinforce them.
He stabbed the barbarian cavalry general Bàopí Gōng, who fell from his horse,
and captured his full set of armor and spear,
personally killing dozens of men.
Shībó reported to Xiàowǔ, praising Dù's strength, archery, and horsemanship as unsurpassed.
The Emperor summoned him back to serve as an imperial guard.
Seeing Dù's dark and strong physique,
he said to Shībó:
"He is truly a powerful man."
He was appointed Fǔjūn Cháng Jiānháng Cānjūn for Xīyáng Wáng,
and then Jǐahu Gǔduì Zhǔ for Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐxūn,
following him to guard Jiāngzhōu.
When Zǐxūn raised an army,
he appointed Dù as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
leading three thousand men as the vanguard,
stationed at Zhèqí.
Whenever he fought against the imperial army,
he always charged personally,
and was victorious in every direction he attacked.
When the rebellion failed,
he fled to the Gōngtíng Lake and became a bandit.
The imperial court, hearing of his bravery,
was very concerned about him.
They sent Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jǐngwén to entice Dù and others to surrender.
Dù led his troops to turn themselves in.
[二０]Jǐngwén appointed him as his Zhènnán Cānjūn,
and soon after, made him lead the Zhōngzhí Bīng,
treating him generously.
He followed Jǐngwén back to the capital,
always staying within the residence.
On the evening Jǐngwén was killed,
Dù was furious,
and urged Jǐngwén to resist the imperial order,
but Jǐngwén refused.
Emperor Míng did not know this.
to assess Wǔyǒng.
He was appointed Cānjūn (Staff Officer) of the Cǎocáo (Armory) of the Zhēnglǔ (General who Attacks the Captives),
and accompanied the garrison to Xiàkǒu.
When Prince Wǔlíng, Zàn, replaced Xiè as Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
Dù remained in the garrison,
serving as Zàn's Qiánjūn Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Vanguard).
Dù was transferred to Zhōngzhíbīng (Central Guards),
and was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General who Pacifies the North) and Jūnmǔ (Military Commander).
Tàizǔ also sent an envoy to provisionally appoint Dù as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General who Assists the State) and Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry).
Yōuzhī's large army reached Xiàkǒu,
intending to proceed directly to the capital,
leaving only a detachment to guard Yǐngchéng.
Dù, from atop the city wall, openly cursed and insulted Yōuzhī,
even exposing his own body to disgrace him.
and changed his plan to attack the city.
Dù personally fought with all his might.
Yōuzhī's troops, covered by shields, were about to ascend,
He was appointed to the staff of Prince Jìnxī, Xiè, guarding the inner palace.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair broke out,
Thus, Yōuzhī was enraged
"Jiāo Dù Lóu."
After the affair was settled,
Dù's merits were considerable.
He was transferred to Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army),
enfeoffed as the Viscoun of Dōngchāng County,
and Dōnggōng Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (General of the Eastern Palace Guards).
He was simple and somewhat awkward by nature.
He wanted to ask Tàizǔ for a province,
but by the time he saw him,
his expression had greatly changed,
and he could not utter a single word.
Tàizǔ, seeing that he was not skilled in civil administration,
ultimately did not employ him.
In the fourth year of Jiànzhāo,
he was appointed Huáilíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Huáilíng),
retaining his former official positions.
When Dù saw the court's prominent relatives,
revealing them as before.
He was fond of drinking alcohol,
and would become violently angry when drunk.
The Emperor often sent people to moderate him.
Although he was old,
his strength remained as before.
Soon after, he was appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Light Cavalry).
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he died
at the age of sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General who Assists the State) and Cìshǐ (Provincial Governor) of Liángzhōu and Qínzhōu.
His son, Shìróng,
served as Bādōng Wáng Fánghé (Guardsman for the Prince of Bādōng) during the Yǒngmíng period.
During the incident involving Prince Xiǎng,
Shìróng fled to Yōngzhōu.
Shìzǔ commended him,
appointing him Shǐxīng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army in Shǐxīng).
Cáo Hǔ, courtesy name Shìwēi,
was a native of Xiàpī in Xiàpī.
His original name was Hǔtóu.
At the end of Emperor Míng of Sòng's reign,
he was a Zhíxiāng (Guardsman).
When the rebels of Guìyáng rose,
he followed Tàizǔ out of Xīntíng Lěi (New Pavilion Fortress) to engage in battle.
He was the first to cut off a head and bring it back,
which is how Tàizǔ came to know him.
When Tàizǔ became Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Imperial Guards),
Hǔ recounted his merits,
and was appointed Fángdiàn Duìzhǔ (Captain of the Palace Guards),
stationed in the west wing.
The day after Cāngwú was deposed,
Hǔ wanted to go out to avoid the trouble,
and encountered Tàizǔ at Dōng Zhōnghuámén (East Central Grand Gate).
Tàizǔ asked Hǔ where he was going.
Hǔ replied,
"I merely wish to seek Your Excellency."
He then remained as a guard.
When Tàizǔ garrisoned at Dōngfǔ,
he appointed Hǔ and Dài Sēngjìng each to command three hundred Bái Zhí (White Guards).
He successively rose to Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry),
concurrently holding the position of Nánchéng Lìng (Magistrate of Nánchéng).
When Shítou was pacified,
he was enfeoffed as the Baron of Luójiāng County
and appointed Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard).
When the Emperor received the abdication,
his fief was increased to four hundred households.
He became Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (General of the Inner Palace Guards)
and commander of the Xiézhàng Zhǔ (Master of the Imperial Regalia).
Soon after, he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General who Pacifies the North) and Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dōngguǎn).
In the winter of the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Hǔ petitioned to be enfeoffed as a marquis in Hóuguān.
The Shangshū (Secretariat) reported that Hóuguān had a large population,
so he was instead enfeoffed in Jiānlì County.
In the second year,
he was appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Light Cavalry),
retaining his previous official positions.
When the righteous people of Péng and Pèi rose up,
Hǔ was sent to lead six thousand men into Wō.
Shěn Yōuzhī's Hengchui 部 (Hengchui division)
was cut off from the capital.
Hǔ petitioned to have them follow him.
As the righteous people were long in arriving,
His officers and soldiers, greedy for captives,
were instead defeated by the enemy,
with two thousand men dying.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Hǔ was appointed Yuánwài Chángshì (Extraordinary Chamberlain),
promoted to Nán Zhōngláng Sīmǎ (Commander of the Southern Central Army),
and additionally Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General who Pacifies the North) and Nán Xīncài Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nán Xīncài).
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was transferred to Ānchéng Wáng Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ (Commander of the Zhēnglǔ Army for the Prince of Ānchéng),
retaining his other official positions.
The following year,
when the Mán (barbarians) of Jiāngzhōu rebelled,
Hǔ was ordered to lead troops to garrison Xúnyáng,
was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General who Assists the State),
and Jūnmǔ (Military Commander) for the punitive expedition against the Mán.
He also served as Xúnyáng Xiāng (Chancellor of Xúnyáng).
Soon after, he was appointed Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Light Cavalry),
retaining Fǔguó and Jūnmǔ.
Shìzǔ considered the name Hǔtóu crude
and ordered it changed.
In the fourth month of the sixth year,
the bandit Huán Tiānshēng again led the enemy out to occupy Gécchéng.
Hǔ was sent to command several armies to suppress them.
Hǔ ordered Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhū Gōng'ēn to lead one hundred cavalry to scout ahead.
They encountered the enemy's roving patrol,
engaged them in battle, and defeated them.
They then advanced to Gécchéng.
The bandits resisted,
so Hǔ led his troops to besiege their palisades,
Shortly after,
scouting cavalry reported that enemy reinforcements had arrived.
Soon, Tiānshēng led over ten thousand cavalry and infantry to engage them.
Hǔ vigorously attacked and utterly defeated them,
capturing over two thousand people.
The next day,
they attacked Gécchéng and captured it,
beheading the pretender Hǔwēi Jiāngjūn (General who Awe-Inspires the Martial) and Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xiāngchéng) Bó Wūzhù,
and killing over two thousand more.
The bandits abandoned Píngshìchéng and fled.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General who Subdues the Army),
The following year,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài (Left Commander of the Crown Prince's Guards),
and transferred to Xīyáng Wáng Guānjūn Sīmǎ (Commander of the Guānjūn Army for the Prince of Xīyáng) and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Guǎnglíng).
The Emperor ordered Hǔ, saying,
"Guǎnglíng needs a confidant.
Unless it is someone I can entrust,
this responsibility cannot be held."
When Prince Zǐlóng of Suí County replaced Prince Zǐxiǎng of Bādōng as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
preparing his military retinue for the westward journey,
Hǔ was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General who Assists the State), Zhènxī Sīmǎ (Commander of the General who Guards the West), and Nánpíng Nèishǐ (Prefect of Nánpíng).
In the eleventh year,
when Wáng Huàn, Inspector of Yōngzhōu, was arrested,
Hǔ was ordered to lead several hundred cavalry and infantry
to take Xiāngyáng by land.

He was then appointed Chíjīe (Bearer of Imperial Insignia), Dū Liáng Nán Běi Qín Shā Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnmì (Military Commander of Liang, Southern and Northern Qin, and Sha Provinces), Xīróng Xiàowèi (Colonel who Pacifies the Western Barbarians), and Liáng Nán Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Liang and Southern Qin Provinces),
retaining his general title.
Soon after, he was advanced to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General who Attacks the Captives).
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title of Qián Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard).
In the first year of Lóngchāng,

he was promoted to Dū Yōngzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìngláng Sīzhōu zhī Suíjùn Jūnmì (Military Commander of Yongzhou, Jingling of Yingzhou, and Suijun of Sizhou), Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General who Subdues the Army), and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Yōngzhōu).
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was advanced to the title of Yòujiāngjūn (General of the Right).
In the second year,
his Dū (Supervising) title was changed to Jiān (Inspector),
enfeoffed as a Marquis,
and his fief was increased by three hundred households.
In the fourth year,
the invaders attacked the north of the Miǎn River.
Hǔ gathered troops at Xiāngyáng.
He was at odds with Fáng Bóyù, the Administrator of Nányáng,
and did not rush to the rescue.
Finally, he moved his camp to Fánchéng.
The barbarian lord, Yuán Hóng, sent Hǔ a letter, saying:
"The Emperor thanks the false Inspector of Yōngzhōu: Divine fortune aligns with the center,
and the imperial residence is established in Luòyáng.
Its transforming influence encompasses all under heaven,
extending to all eight directions.
Yet to the south there is the unsubmissive Wú,
creating a separation with two rulers.
The visible and invisible lament,
and human and spiritual energies are blocked (泰).
〔二九〕Moreover, the area north of the Hàn River and by the Jiāng River
is secretly becoming barren.
Therefore, I first mobilized the imperial chariot
to establish our divine capital.
You, in advancing, lack the wisdom of Chén Píng returning to Hàn,
and in retreating, lack the loyalty of Guān Yǔ dying for his cause.
Trapped within a besieged city,
and sorrowfully stalled by the long Miǎn River,
lacking both strategy and courage,
how lamentable!
I had intended to visit you recently,
but was prevented by urgent matters.
I shall return to the new capital,
to feast my six armies.
In the coming spring month,
I shall slowly unfurl my banners.
Improve your strategy well,
and await the arrival of righteousness."
Hǔ sent someone to reply, saying:
"Since the Golden Essence lost its way,
and the imperial residence moved afar,
the ancient trees stand empty,
and lush grass grows everywhere.
The Seven Dǐ barbarians invaded in succession,
and the Five Hú rose one after another.
Looking at the Central Plains,
I always feel sorrow.
I know you abandoned Gāolán,
and followed the waters of Chán and Jiàn.
The omen of Yīchuān
is upon us today.
An ancient person said: 'One does not choose a dwelling,
but chooses neighbors.'
Fánchéng and Hànshui are not spared;
though咫尺 apart, their customs differ.
The glue is broken when you enter the pass,
and you violate the border in autumn.
Relatives are utterly destroyed by slaughter,
and men and women are distressed by massacre.
You and those ignorant commoners
are like lips and teeth to each other.
Benevolence and righteousness are not heard,
but harsh tyranny is first revealed.
Then you changed your felt robes,
and arrogantly exalted yourselves.
Our emperor initiated the auspicious era,
brightly ruling the whole of Xià.
But you incite chaos among the fugitives,
abandoning the common and embracing the alien.
I always wished to deploy my armies,
to subdue the insubordinate.
I hoped that the shields and axes on the two steps
would make the rebellious come to terms.
But instead, the wandering spirits are not pacified,
and the cunning chaos (乾沒) becomes rampant.
〔三０〕I command the allied forces,
and the responsibility rests with Fāng Shào.
With a hundred thousand armored troops,
majestic like a thousand herds,
with these, I will overcome difficulties;
there is nowhere I cannot conquer.
Our lord always shows compassion to all under heaven,
pitying the common people,
enabling enemies to submit without battle,
and soldiers to shed no blood.
Therefore, I commanded a small garrison,
closed the city gates, and cleared the countryside.
I held my ground with dignity and nurtured them,
hoping they would be moved by our influence.
If you persist in your delusion,
knowing how to advance but forgetting how to retreat,
then the golden gongs will sound the warning on the road,
and the cloud banners will sweep north.
We will drive straight to Yān and Dài,
and capture all the famous kings,
making little lords disappear,
and Touman forgotten.
When armies clash, distance means nothing.
Let us have compassion for each other."
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
he was promoted to Gěishìzhōng
and Yòuwèijiāngjūn,
with a jié,
subordinated to Dūdū Chén Xiǎndá, who was stationed at Xiāngyáng to attack the barbarians.

Wáng Kūn,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
His grandfather, Huì,
was a General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) during the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Yì,
was unintelligent,
and a maidservant bore Kūn,
who was named Kūnlún.
Yì later married a woman from the Lè Xuán clan of Nányáng;
they had no son.
He changed Kūn's name
and established him as his heir.
Kūn was cautious and honest in his youth,
and was beloved by his paternal cousin, Minister of Works (Sītú) Mì.
During the Yǒngchū reign of Sòng,
Emperor Wǔ, because Kūn had married the daughter of Huán Xiū,
appointed him Director (Lángzhōng),
Cavalry Commandant (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
and Imperial Attendant (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
In the early Yuánjiā period,
his paternal cousin Huá, who was a Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), held power and favor.
Seeing their family's decline,
he treated Kūn as a close relative
and frequently recommended him.
Kūn served as Director of Ceremonial Protocol (Yí Cáo Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
and Central Administrator (Zhìzhōng) of the province.
He successively reached the position of Consultant to the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Zīyì),
and concurrently Registrar (Lùshì).
He was sent out as Administrator of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Tàishǒu),
then Middle Administrator to the Minister of Works (Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
and Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu).
He was incorruptible and frugal in all his successive appointments.
Returning to the capital, he became Chief Clerk to the General of the Northern Army (Běi Zhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ),
Palace Gentleman (Huángmén Láng),
General Who Pacifies Distant Regions (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn),
and Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
In the early Xiàojiàn period,
he was promoted to Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng),

additionally Administrator of Línhuái (Línhuái Tàishǒu),
then transferred to Director of Personnel (Lìbù Láng).
When the Personnel Department made selections,
many powerful and important figures sought favors.
Kūn set a precedent by appointing two protégés for everyone, from high officials to scholar-officials.
Prince Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, once asked Kūn to appoint two people.
Later, he sent another request to Kūn,
who replied by refusing it.

and transferred him to Chief Clerk to the General of the Eastern Army (Dōng Zhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ) for his beloved son, Prince Xīn'ān,
additionally General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
He was promoted to Right General of the Guards (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn),
and Minister of the Treasury (Dùzhī Shàngshū).
He was sent out as Chief Clerk to the General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Yǒngjiā, and Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ) for Prince Shǐ'ān—
additionally General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu).
These were all sons of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
In the first year of Tàishǐ (465 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Treasury (Dùzhī Shàngshū),
and soon after additionally Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
Initially,
his paternal cousin's son, Huá Sūncháng, inherited Huá's peerage as Marquis of Xīnjiàn.
He was fond of wine and made many mistakes.
Kūn submitted a memorial, saying:
"My nephew is not diligent.
My cousin's grandson, Cháng, is the son of the former Right General of the Guards.
He has little talent and is always common, yet I hoped he would improve late in life.
Recently, he has become more addicted to drink,
and has no self-control in his conduct.
The late General of the Guards, Huá, loyally and respectfully served the state,
and his goodness extended to his descendants.
But Cháng, bearing faults, inherited the enfeoffment,
and will likely ruin the family foundation.
His younger son, Tóng, lives leisurely and maintains a modest demeanor,
not deviating from the family's traditional style.
If he could be rescued and established,
then the living and the dead would be honored,
and private emoluments would be re-established."
He was sent out as General of the Champion Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu),
then promoted to Central Leader of the Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn).
He was impeached for using 360,000 in imperial funds while in the commandery to provision the two palaces' princes and to make crimson robes for military dedication.
He was [demoted to] Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
soon after additionally Grand Minister of the Court (Tàicháng) and Golden Purple,
and additionally Palace Counselor (Sànqí Chángshì).
Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi) Yú Hé argued that the altars of land and grain should be combined into one deity.
Kūn, based on old records, refuted him.
At the time, Hé was deeply favored and trusted,
so many in the court admired Kūn's strength and uprightness.
When Emperor Míng was nearing death,

Kūn was sent out as Military Governor of the five commanderies of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā (Dū Kuàijī Dōngyáng Xīn'ān Línhǎi Yǒngjiā Wǔjùn Jūnshì), General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn), and Administrator of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Tàishǒu),
with his position as Palace Counselor (Chángshì) unchanged.
He was impeached for an error and imprisoned,
and his title was reduced to General of the Champion Army (Guànjūn).
During the Yuánhuī period,
he was promoted to Golden Purple Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù),
Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (Hóngxùn Tàipú),
with his position as Palace Counselor (Chángshì) unchanged.
He became Censor of his native province (Běnzhōu Zhōngzhèng),
and additionally Special Advanced Official (Tèjìn).
After the emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
with his other positions as Palace Counselor (Chángshì) unchanged.
When the emperor abdicated,
Kūn attended the ceremony and paid respects at the ancestral temple, shedding tears throughout.
When Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) ascended the throne,
Kūn was appointed Grand Tutor of Prince Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng Wáng Shī),
additionally Attendant at the Imperial Gate (Shìzhōng),
and granted twenty trusted personal guards.
At that time, Wáng Jiǎn was Prime Minister (Zǎixiàng),
and he asked Kūn to appoint an officer to welcome him in Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Kūn said to his trusted men:
"Tell the gentleman [Jiǎn],
all the three platforms and five ministries [referring to the central government]
are places where the gentleman appoints people;
for small, remote commanderies,
he should let the poor and lowly have them.
How can the central government officials seize them again?"
So he did not comply with the request.
Kūn was by nature both old-fashioned and cautious,
and excessively frugal.
He personally handled all miscellaneous family affairs.
For official business and court assemblies,
he would always wake up early, before dawn,
carefully inspect his clothes,
and count his caps and headwear [repeatedly],
doing this several times.
The world laughed at him for this.
Soon after, he was relieved of his position as Grand Tutor (Wáng Shī).
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán (482 CE),
when Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) died,
Kūn heard the national mourning,
but his ox was not at home.
Being several li from the palace,
he walked into the palace.
All the court officials said to Kūn:
"You should have waited for a carriage;
this harms the national prestige."
Kūn said:
"Everyone rushing here today
should do the same."
He then fell ill
and died.
He was posthumously granted Left Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū),
with his other titles unchanged.
He was eighty-four years old.
Zhāng Dài (張岱), courtesy name Jǐngshān (景山),
was a native of Wújùn (吳郡).
His grandfather, Chǎng (敞),
was the Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū 戶支尚書) during the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
His father, Màodù (茂度),
was the Grand Master of Golden Purple Light (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫) during the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
When Dài (岱) was young, he and his elder brother, Yín (寅), who was a Palace Attendant in the Eastern Palace (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén 太子中舍人),

Jìng (鏡), who was the Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān (新安 Tàishǒu 太守), Yǒng (永), who was a General Who Attacks the North (Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn 征北將軍), and his younger brother, Biàn (辨), who was the Governor of Guǎngzhōu (廣州 Cìshǐ 刺史), were all well-known.
They were called the "Five Dragons of the Zhāng (張) Clan."
Jìng (鏡), when young, lived next to Yán Yánzhī (顏延之), a Grand Master of Light (Guānglù Dàfū 光祿大夫).
Yán (顏) would talk, debate, and drink,
with constant shouts and clamor.
But Jìng (鏡) was quiet, secluded, and had no sound of speech.
Later, Yánzhī (延之) heard him speaking with a guest by the fence,
took a folding stool, and sat to listen.
His words and meaning were clear and profound,
and Yánzhī (延之) was convinced.
He said to his guests,
"There is someone there."
From then on, he no longer shouted drunkenly.
Yín (寅) and Jìng (鏡) were the most famous;
Yǒng (永), Biàn (辨), and Dài (岱) did not reach their level.
The commandery nominated Dài (岱) as a Clerk for Imperial Accounts (Shàngjìyuán 上計掾),
but he did not accept.
The province appointed him an Attendant Official (Cóngshì 從事).
He was successively promoted to Aide to the Right General of Nánpíng (南平 Wáng Yòujūn Zhǔbù 王右軍主簿)
and Minister of Waterways (Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng 尚書水部郎).
He was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Dōngqiān (東遷 Lìng 令).
At that time, Yīn Chōng (殷沖) was the Governor of Wúxīng (吳興),
and he said to people,
"Zhāng (張) of Dōngqiān (東遷) is poor and needs to support his family,
which is why he is stranded in a lower office.
However, his reputation and talent will surely be revealed,
and he will eventually achieve great things."
When Suí Wáng Dàn (隨王誕) raised an army in Kuàijī (會稽),
he appointed Dài (岱) as General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn 建威將軍),
Assistant to the Grand Protector (Fǔguó Zhǎngxǐ 輔國長史),
and Acting Administrator of the Commandery (Xíng Xiànshì 行縣事).
After the matter was settled,
he became the Left Senior Clerk of the Minister of Works (Sītú Zuǒ Xīcáo 司徒左西曹).
His mother was eighty years old,
and her registration period for support had not yet expired.
Dài (岱) then resigned from his office and returned home to care for her.
The officials concerned considered Dài (岱) to have violated regulations
and intended to impeach him.
Sòng Xiàowǔ (宋孝武) said,
"Through his fault, we can know his benevolence;
there is no need to investigate."
He was successively promoted to Consulting Aide to the General of the Household (Fǔjūn Zīyì Cānjūn 撫軍諮議參軍),
concurrently serving as the Magistrate of Shānyīn (山陰 Lìng 令).
His official duties were relaxed and well-managed.
When Bālíng Wáng Xiūrùo (巴陵王休若) was the Governor of Běixúzhōu (北徐州),
he had not yet personally attended to governmental affairs.
He appointed Dài (岱) as Consulting Aide to the General of the Vanguard (Guānjūn Zīyì Cānjūn 冠軍諮議參軍),
concurrently serving as the Grand Administrator of Péngchéng (彭城 Tàishǒu 太守),
and acting on behalf of the regional administration, the province, and the state (Xíng Fǔ, Zhōu, Guóshì 行府、州、國事).
Later, when Línhǎi Wáng (臨海王) was the General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ 將軍) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) was the General of Agile Cavalry (Chēqí 將軍) of Yángzhōu (揚州),
and Jìn'ān Wáng (晉安王) was the General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ 將軍) of Nán Yǔnzhōu (南兗州),
Dài (岱) successively served as Consulting Aide for these three administrations (Sān Fǔ Zīyì 三府諮議) and acting official for the three princes (Sān Wáng Xíngshì 三王行事).
He worked with the Chief Clerks (Diǎnqiān Zhǔshuài 典籤主帥),
and his tasks were completed with harmony.
Someone asked Dài (岱),
"The princes are young,
and there are many people in charge of affairs,
yet you are always able to reconcile public and private matters.
How do you achieve this?"
Dài (岱) replied,
"The ancients said that with one mind, one can serve a hundred rulers.
I govern fairly and treat others with courtesy.
Matters of regret and difficulty
have no way to affect me.
The differences in intelligence and ability
merely indicate varying degrees of talent and usefulness."
He was appointed as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng 黃門郎),
then promoted to Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Zhǎngxǐ 驃騎長史),
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng (廣陵 Tàishǒu 太守).
Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán (新安王子鸞), due to his great favor, was made Governor of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州),
and Wújùn (吳郡) was ceded to his jurisdiction.
To select high-ranking assistants,
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) summoned Dài (岱) and said to him,
"Your excellent service has long been evident,
[一０] and you have held many official positions.
I now wish to appoint you as Aide-de-camp (Biéjià 別駕) to Zǐluán (子鸞),
to oversee the duties of the Governor.
Do not consider it a minor demotion;
you will eventually rise to great prominence."
After the Emperor's death,
he was successively promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Láng 吏部郎).
At the beginning of Emperor Míng's (明帝) reign,
rebellions broke out in all directions.
The Emperor, seeing Dài (岱) as a capable and experienced talent,

appointed him as Envoy with Imperial Insignia (Shǐ Chíjié 使持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xīyùzhōu (Xīdū Xīyùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 督西豫州諸軍事), General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍), and Governor of Xīyùzhōu (Xīyùzhōu Cìshǐ 西豫州刺史).
Soon after, he was transferred to General of the Vanguard (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍) and Governor of Běixúzhōu (北徐州 Cìshǐ 刺史),
and Supervisor of all armies for the Northern Expedition (Dū Dū Běitǎo Zhū Jūnshì 都督北討諸軍事),
but he did not assume these offices.
At the end of Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
he became Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興 Tàishǒu 太守).
In the Yuánhuī (元徽) era,

he was promoted to Envoy with Imperial Insignia (Shǐ Chíjié 使持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yì and Níng Prefectures (Dū Yì Níng Èrzhōu Jūnshì 督益寧二州軍事), General of the Vanguard (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn 冠軍將軍), and Governor of Yìzhōu (益州 Cìshǐ 刺史).
For several years,
the people of Yìzhōu (益州) were content with his governance.
He was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中),
concurrently serving as Commandant of Chángshuǐ (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi 長水校尉),
Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū 度支尚書),
concurrently serving as General of the Left (Zuǒjūn 左軍),
then promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書).
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) was Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Láng 吏部郎)
at the time and frequently made decisions in the Personnel Bureau (Cáoshì 曹事).
Dài (岱) often disagreed with him.
When Jiǎn (儉) became Prime Minister (Zǎixiàng 宰相),
they were thus not on good terms.
[一一]
His nephew, Guī (瓌), and younger brother, Shù (恕),
executed Liú Xiá (劉遐), the Grand Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡 Tàishǒu 太守).
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) wished to appoint Shù (恕) as the Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng (晉陵 Jùn 郡),
but Dài (岱) said,
"Shù (恕) is not yet skilled in administration.
Fine brocade should not be indiscriminately cut."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) said,
"I know Shù's (恕) character.
Moreover, he shares the same merit with Guī (瓌)
and should naturally be rewarded."
Dài (岱) said,
"If it is to bestow a salary because the family is poor,
that is not what is being discussed.
To speak of merit and claim positions
would be a disgrace to my family."
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍).
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元),
he was appointed General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn 左將軍) and Grand Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡 Tàishǒu 太守).
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ 太祖) knew Dài (岱) had always been upright and honest in his various posts.
Not long after he arrived at the commandery,
the Emperor personally issued an edict to Dài (岱), saying,
"The great state has heavy responsibilities,
and I did not wish to rotate you yet.
However, my military duties are urgent,
and I need someone with your reputation and ability.
I now appoint you as Protector-General (Hùjūn 護軍)."
He was also granted the additional title of Gentleman-in-Waiting (Jǐshì Zhōng 給事中).
After Dài (岱) bowed in acceptance,
an edict made his residence an official yamen.
He feigned illness.
The following year,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Golden Purple Light (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫),
concurrently serving as Tutor to the Prince of Póyáng (Póyáng Wáng Shī 鄱陽王師).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he again appointed Dài (岱) as Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍) and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興 Tàishǒu 太守),
with a salary of two thousand piculs (Zhì Zhōng Èrqiān Dàn 秩中二千石).
In his later years, Dài (岱) was in Wúxīng (吳興)
and became known for his leniency and magnanimity.

He was promoted to Envoy with Imperial Insignia (Shǐ Chíjié 使持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányǔn (南兗), Qīng (青), and Jì (冀) Prefectures (Jiān Nán Yǔn Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 監南兗青冀五州諸軍事), [一二] General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn 後將軍), and Governor of Nányǔnzhōu (南兗州 Cìshǐ 刺史).
His position as Palace Attendant (Chángshì 常侍) remained as before.
Before he could accept the appointment,
he passed away.
He was seventy-one years old.
Dài (岱) initially wrote his will,
distributing his family property,
sealing it in a box.
As the family's assets increased or decreased,
he would change it accordingly.
This happened over ten years.
He was posthumously granted his former office
and given the posthumous title Zhēnzǐ (貞子).
Chǔ Xuàn (褚炫), courtesy name Yànxù (彥緒),
was a native of Yángzhái (陽翟), Hénán (河南).
His grandfather, Xiùzhī (秀之),
was the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) during the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
His father, Fǎxiǎn (法顯), was the Grand Administrator of Póyáng (鄱陽 Tàishǒu 太守).
His elder brother, Zhào (炤),
courtesy name Yànxuān (彥宣),
upheld high principles from a young age.
Blind in one eye,
he rose to the position of Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士)
but did not accept the appointment.
He often criticized his cousin, Yuān (淵), for serving two dynasties.
Hearing that Yuān (淵) was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒),
he sighed,
"If Yuān (淵) had died as a Central Secretariat Secretary (Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎),
would he not have been a renowned scholar?
His virtue was not flourishing,
[一三] allowing him to live to such an old age."
Xuàn (炫) was clean and simple in his youth
and was recognized by his maternal cousin, Wáng Jǐngwén (王景文).
His cousin, Yuān (淵), said to people,
"My younger cousin is incorruptible, superior, and independent;
he is ten times better than me."
When Sòng Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng (宋義陽王昶) was the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常),
he appointed Xuàn (炫) as a Palace Attendant (Wǔguān 五官).
He was successively promoted to Gentleman of the Eastern Palace (Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人),
Recorder for the General of the Household and Agile Cavalry (Fǔjūn Chējì Jìshì 撫軍車騎記室),
and Regular Attendant (Zhèngyuán Láng 正員郎).
When [person: Sòng Míngdì] went hunting pheasants,
until midday,
he caught nothing.
The Emperor was very suspicious and ashamed,
and summoned his attendants, saying:
“I came out this morning as if to [place: Gāo],
but I’ve come back empty-handed.
It's laughable.”
No one in the audience responded.
[person: Xuàn] alone said:
“Although the season is suitable now,
the clouds and dew are still congealed,
〔一四〕thus these flying birds
have not yet been roused from their complacent hearts.
But merely having your divine carriage roam about
has already brought joy to the populace.”
The Emperor’s mood lightened,
and he then set up a banquet at the pheasant field.
He was promoted to [title: Zhōngshū Shìláng],
and [title: Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ].
In the early [era: Shēngmíng] period,
[person: Xuàn], due to his purity and lofty character,
along with [person: Liú Yǔ], [person: Xiè Fěi], and [person: Jiāng Jiào], entered the palace to assist with literary and intellectual matters,
and were known as
“The Four Friends.”
He was promoted to [title: Huángmén Láng],
then [title: Tàizǔ Piàojí Chángshǐ],
then [title: Shìzhōng],
and again [title: Chángshǐ].
When the [dynasty: Qí] court was established,
he again served as [title: Shìzhōng],
and concurrently held the position of [title: Bùbīng Xiàowèi].
Due to his family's poverty,
in the early [era: Jiànyuán] period,
he was appointed [title: Dōngyáng Tàishǒu],
and his rank was increased by [rank: Zhōng Èrqiān Shí].
Upon his return,
he again served as [title: Shìzhōng],
and concurrently held [title: Bùbīng].
In total, he served as [title: Shìzhōng] three times.
He was appointed [title: Jìnglíng Wáng Zhēng Běi Chángshǐ],
with the additional title of [title: Fǔguó Jiāngjūn].
Soon after, he was transferred to [title: Guānjūn Chángshǐ] and [title: Jiāngxià Nèishǐ],
with his general title remaining as before.
In the first year of [era: Yǒngmíng],
he became [title: Lìbù Shàngshū].
[person: Xuàn] maintained a pure and upright personal conduct;
he did not engage in miscellaneous social interactions except for visits of condolence,
which commentators regarded as commendable.
When he was in the selection department,
his home was desolate,
and few guests visited.
When he traveled,
his attendants carried a yellow paper hat box,
and the wind almost completely peeled off the paper.
After resigning from [place: Jiāngxià] and returning,
he received 170,000 cash,
which he distributed among his relatives at [place: Shítóu],
and he was too ill to buy medicine.
He submitted a memorial to resign,
and was reassigned as [title: Sànqí Chángshì],
concurrently serving as [title: Ānchéng Wáng Shī].
When the Imperial Academy was established,
he was appointed [title: Bóshì] in his original capacity,
but before he could assume the post,
he passed away,
with nothing to provide for his funeral.
He was forty-one years old at the time.
He was posthumously granted the title of [title: Tàicháng],
and given the posthumous name [posthumous_name: Zhēnzǐ].
[person: Hé Jí], courtesy name [courtesy_name: Huìjǐng],
was a native of [place: Qián], [place: Lújiāng].
His grandfather, [person: Shàngzhī],
was [title: Sòng Sīkōng].
His father, [person: Yǎn],
was [title: Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū],
and highly favored by [person: Sòng Wǔdì].
[person: Jí] was chosen to marry [title: Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ],
and was appointed [title: Fùmǎ Dūwèi].
He first served as [title: Mìshū Láng],
then [title: Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén],
then [title: Sītú Zhǔbù],
then [title: Xīn’ān Wáng Wénxué],
then [title: Mìshū Chéng],
then [title: Zhōngshū Láng].
During the [era: Jǐnghé] period,
Princess [title: Shānyīn] requested the Emperor to have [title: Lìbù Láng] [person: Chǔ Yuān] serve her intimately in her chambers.
[person: Yuān] felt constrained and pressured,
and ultimately refused to comply.
He resided with [person: Jí] for over a month,
and this led to a special friendship between them.
When [person: Míngdì] ascended the throne,
[person: Jí] was promoted to [title: Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng].
He accompanied [person: Jiàn’ān Wáng Xiūrén] on a campaign against [place: Zhěqí],
and was temporarily appointed [title: Sīmǎ].
He was then appointed [title: Huángmén Láng],
then [title: Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn] and [title: Dōngyáng Tàishǒu],
and [title: Lìbù Láng].
In the early [era: Yuánhuī] period,
[person: Chǔ Yuān] participated in court politics,
and recommended [person: Jí] as [title: Shìzhōng].
He was twenty-nine years old at the time.
[person: Jí], not yet thirty,
strongly declined the position of [title: Nèi Shì],
submitting repeated memorials,
and the prevailing opinion at the time permitted it.

Yánzhī and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Ruǎn Tāo

Yánzhī's family rules were strict and severe;

Tāo said:

Tāo and Hé Yǎn were another pair.
He often served as acting official.
At the end of Tàishǐ,
he was Zhēngnán Jiāngzhōu Chángshǐ.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn was in command,
he often went out on excursions.
Tāo, being upright and firm,
never followed him.
He reached Sànqí Chángshì,
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
and additionally held Shǐxīng Wáng Shī.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he died.
The historian comments: The internal attendants at the core of power
were traditionally noble selections,
their golden diadems shining brightly,
the splendid attire of the court.
For a long time, scholarly arts were forgotten,
and positions were exclusively given to prominent families.
Furthermore, selections were made with little regard for demeanor;
those who wore mink sables and ceremonial caps
were appointed through inherited influence.
Talent came after appearance.
The situation was similar to that of the chamberlains,
who held office based on their physique,
which deviated from ancient practice.
When Pìqiáng was in the Hàn court,
he possessed keen discernment in his youth.
When Zhòngxuān was in the Wèi state,
he was criticized for his plain appearance.
The concession made by Hé Jí,
though not a deep understanding of the beauty of ancient times,
was vastly different from those who merely occupied official positions with a shy demeanor!
What a difference in rank!
Praise: The Wànshí family was cautious and respectful;
Kūn became the paragon.
The Five Dragons were of one clan;
Zhāng also followed Xún.
Chú family's clarity shone;
Hé's lineage remained due to Jí.
Yánzhī lived simply;
his reputation as a royal official was lofty.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 14: Wáng Sēngqián, Zhāng Xù
Wáng Sēngqián was
from Lángyá Línyí.
His grandfather, Xún,
was a Jìn Sītú.
His paternal uncle, Tàibǎo Hóng,
was a prime minister during the Yuánjiā era of Sòng.
When guests were unsure of his taboo name,
Hóng said:
"My family's taboo name is the same as Sū Zǐgāo's."
His father, Tánshǒu,
was Yòuguānglù Dàfū.
When Tánshǒu and his brothers gathered their sons and grandsons,
Hóng's son Sēngdá was jumping and playing on the ground.
Sēngqián, who was several years old,
alone sat upright, picking candle beads to make a phoenix.
Hóng said:
"This child will surely become a senior."
Sēng-qián, at twenty (弱冠),
was magnanimous
and skilled in clerical script (隸書).
Sòng Wén-dì saw his writing on a plain fan
and sighed,
"Not only do his brushstrokes surpass Zǐ-jìng (王獻之),
but his character will also surely exceed his."
He was appointed Mì-shū-láng (祕書郎)
and Tài-zǐ Shě-rén (太子舍人).
He was reserved and had few social interactions,
but was good friends with Yuán Shú (袁淑) and Xiè Zhuāng (謝莊).
He was transferred to Yì-yáng-wáng Wén-xué (義陽王文學),
then Tài-zǐ Xǐ-mǎ (太子洗馬),
and later promoted to Sī-tú Zuǒ-xī-shǔ (司徒左西屬).
His elder brother, Sēng-chuò (僧綽),
was killed by Tài-chū (劉劭).
Relatives and friends all urged Sēng-qián to flee.
Sēng-qián wept and said,
"My brother served the country with loyalty and integrity,
and treated me with kindness and love.
Today's event
is painful because it didn't reach me as well.
If we return together to the Nine Springs (九泉),
it would be like ascending to immortality."
At the beginning of Xiào-wǔ's (宋孝武帝) reign,
he was sent out as Wǔ-líng Tài-shǒu (武陵太守).
His nephew, Jiǎn (儉), fell ill on the way.
Sēng-qián lost sleep and appetite because of it.
Fellow travelers consoled him.
Sēng-qián said,
"In the past, Mǎ Yuán (馬援) treated his sons and nephews with the same affection,
and Dèng Yōu (鄧攸) loved his younger brother's children even more than his own.
I truly harbor such feelings,
and am certainly no different from the ancients.
The offspring of my deceased brother
should not be neglected.
If this child cannot be saved,
I will turn my boat back, resign from my post,
and have no more desire for official life."
He returned as Zhōng-shū-láng (中書郎),
then transferred to Huáng-mén-láng (黃門郎),
and Tài-zǐ Zhōng-shù-zǐ (太子中庶子).
Xiào-wǔ wanted to monopolize fame in calligraphy,
so Sēng-qián dared not display his talent.
During the Dà-míng (大明) era,
he often used a worn brush to write,
thereby gaining tolerance.
He was sent out as Yù-zhāng-wáng Zǐ-shàng Fǔ-jūn Zhǎng-shǐ (豫章王子尚撫軍長史),
promoted to Sǎn-qí Cháng-shì (散騎常侍),
and again served as Xīn-ān-wáng Zǐ-luán Běi Zhōng-láng Zhǎng-shǐ (新安王子鸞北中郎長史) and Nán Dōng-hǎi Tài-shǒu (南東海太守),
acting as Nán Xú-zhōu Shì (南徐州事).
Both princes were beloved sons of the emperor.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yù-zhāng Nèi-shǐ (豫章內史).
He entered court as Shì-zhōng (侍中),
promoted to Yù-shǐ Zhōng-chéng (御史中丞),
and concurrently held Xiāo-qí Jiāng-jūn (驍騎將軍).
Traditionally, prominent families (甲族) often avoided residing in the Censorate (憲臺),
and those of the Wáng (王) clan who were cadet branches residing in Wū-yī (烏衣)
held slightly lower official positions.
When Sēng-qián took this office,
he said,
"This is where the young masters of Wū-yī sit;
I, too, can give it a try."
He again became Shì-zhōng (侍中),
concurrently holding Tún-qí Xiào-wèi (屯騎校尉).
During the Tài-shǐ (泰始) era,
he was sent out as Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn (輔國將軍) and Wú-xīng Tài-shǒu (吳興太守),
with a salary of two thousand *shí* (石) (中二千石).
Wáng Xiàn-zhī (王獻之) was skilled in calligraphy
and served as governor of Wú-xīng Commandery (吳興郡);
when Sēng-qián, also a skilled calligrapher,
also served as governor of the commandery,
commentators praised it.
He was transferred to Huì-jī Tài-shǒu (會稽太守),
with a salary of two thousand *shí* (中二千石),
and his general title remained as before.
Zhōng-shū Shě-rén Ruǎn Diàn-fū (阮佃夫) was from Huì-jī
and requested leave to return east.
Guests advised Sēng-qián that since Diàn-fū was a favorite of the emperor,
he should treat him with extra courtesy.
Sēng-qián said,
"I have always conducted myself with integrity;
how could I bend my will for such people?
If he holds ill will towards me,
I will simply brush off my robes and leave."
Diàn-fū spoke to Sòng Míng-dì (宋明帝),
who then ordered Yù-shǐ Zhōng-chéng Sūn Xiǒng (孫敻) to memorialize:
"Sēng-qián, during his previous tenure in Wú-xīng,
issued many erroneous appointments.
A review from his arrival at the commandery until his transfer showed that he appointed altogether
four hundred and forty-eight people to various posts, from Gōng-cáo (功曹) and Wǔ-guān Zhǔ-bù (五官主簿) to Er-lǐ (二禮) officials, scribes (署三傳), and those he personally recruited or his disciples (及度與弟子).
Furthermore, he allowed one hundred and ten households of commoners, such as Hé Xì-xiān (何係先), to be designated as 'old families' (舊門)."
The matter was entrusted to the province for investigation and revocation.
Consequently, he was dismissed from office.
Soon after, as a commoner (白衣), he concurrently served as Shì-zhōng (侍中),
and was sent out to supervise Wú-jùn Tài-shǒu (吳郡太守).
He was promoted to Shǐ Chí-jié (使持節), Dū-dū Xiāng-zhōu Zhū-jūn-shì (都督湘州諸軍事), Jiàn-wǔ Jiāng-jūn (建武將軍), and acting Xiāng-zhōu Shì (湘州事).
He then transferred to Fǔ-guó Jiāng-jūn (輔國將軍),
and Xiāng-zhōu Cì-shǐ (湘州刺史).
Wherever he served, he was known for his leniency and benevolence.
Many refugees from Bá-xiá (巴峽) lived in Xiāng-tǔ (湘土).
Sēng-qián memorialized to establish Xiāng-yīn County (湘陰縣) by carving out the riverside population from the three counties of Yì-yáng (益陽), Luó (羅), and Xiāng-xī (湘西),
which was approved.
During the Yuánhuī (元徽) reign,
he was transferred to the position of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書).
Tán Guī (檀珪) of Gāopíng (高平), having been dismissed as magistrate of Yuánnán (沅南),
Sēngqián (僧虔) appointed him as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn 參軍) in the Northern Expeditionary Army (Zhēngběi Bǎnxíng Cānjūn 征北板行參軍).
Guī (珪) sued Sēngqián (僧虔) for not granting him a proper salary,
and wrote a letter to Sēngqián (僧虔) saying:
“At the beginning of the Five Constants,
civil and military virtues are primary.
Civil virtue weaves the warp and weft of heaven and earth;
military virtue quells disorder and establishes the nation.
Although my family may be deficient in civil accomplishments,
we are nonetheless noted for military prowess.
Among my relatives,
three have married into the imperial family.
For two generations, my ancestors and elder brothers
sacrificed themselves for the nation,
only to have their nephews and grandnephews starve to death in the wilderness.
Last winter and this spring,
I repeatedly received imperial edicts.
However, having no intermediary,
I have repeatedly been deprived of opportunities.
After five months
and more than four fortnights,
twelve letters,
and six or seven interviews,
I have not received any favor,
but instead have been left to flounder.
The nine streams of government should be fair,
and it is surely inappropriate to torment one person alone.
My cicada belly and turtle intestines [i.e., extreme hunger] have long persisted.
A hungry tiger can frighten,
and people immediately give it meat;
a starving qílín (麒麟) does not bite,
so who would bother to pluck its hair?
Last winter, I begged for the post of Assistant Magistrate of Yùzhāng (豫章丞),
but it was contested by Mǎ Chāo (馬超).
This spring, I was granted the Nánchāng (南昌) county magistracy by imperial edict,
but it was seized by Shǐ Yǎn (史偃).
What superior merit, patronage, or talent
do these two men possess
that they should surpass me?
If it is a matter of wealth and poverty,
then my share is not inferior.
Though I am humble and insignificant,
my family has been national gentry for a hundred generations.
In terms of marriage and official position,
we are not inferior to others.
Your respected elder female cousin is the Princess of Jiāngxià (江夏 Wángfēi 王妃);
my respected elder female cousin is the Princess of Nánqiáo (南譙 Wángfēi 王妃).
Your wife is the daughter of the Prince of Jiāngxià (江夏 Wáng 王);
my paternal aunt was a consort of Prince Jǐng (景 Wáng 王) of Chángshā (長沙).
Your paternal uncle was a Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州);
my paternal grandfather was also a Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Your paternal cousin began his career as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn 參軍) in the Rear Army (Hòujūn 後軍);
my father also began his career as a Staff Officer (Cānjūn 參軍) in the Central Army (Zhōngjūn 中軍) after his first official appointment.
My social standing compared to yours
is fundamentally distant,
but regarding marriage and officialdom,
I refuse to be utterly dissimilar.
Now, although our fortunes differ,
we are still considered to be of the same class.
Why do you torment me so, Minister?
At the beginning of Tàishǐ (泰始),
when all eight directions were in rebellion,
my family, for two generations,
sacrificed themselves to protect the sovereign.
Our extraordinary merits and unique achievements
have not been recognized;
instead, our usual path
is once again obstructed and suppressed.”
Sēngqián (僧虔) replied in a letter:
“The Staff Officer (Zhēngběi Bǎnxíng 征北板行) position has had a slightly better lot in recent years.
Master Yīn (Yīn Zhǔbù 殷主簿) entered the崇禮 (Chónglǐ) from this very office;
Officer Hé (Hé Yícáo 何儀曹) immediately replaced Yīn (殷),
and he did not complain of hardship.
For you, Sir, to be promoted significantly after accumulating grievances
is truly a minor difficulty.
The diligence and suffering of the early Tàishǐ (泰始) period,
which have not yet seen their reward,
to suddenly demand recognition now
is simply not feasible.
You and I have no inherent grudges;
why should I cause you such suffering?
It is simply that my intentions are to help and assist others.”
Guī (珪) wrote another letter, saying:
“In ancient times, Xún Gōngdá (荀公達) was a meritorious minister of the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì 武帝) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty later bestowed titles upon his great-grandson.
Xiàhóu Dūn (夏侯惇) was a meritorious aide of the Wèi (魏) clan;
when the Golden Virtue first flourished,
he too began to be recognized and distinguished,
and his grandson was rewarded,
and his near relatives were enfeoffed.
Yáng Shúzi (羊叔子) proposed the strategy to conquer Wú (吳) during the Tàishǐ (泰始) reign of Jìn (晉);
it was not until the end of the Xiánníng (咸寧) reign
that he was greatly honored,
and his elder brother’s son was enfeoffed.
Biàn Wàngzhī (卞望之) died in the national crisis at the beginning of the Xiánhé (咸和) reign;
it was not until the end of the Xīngníng (興寧) reign
