After Xù was promoted,
the Emperor appointed Wáng Yánzhī to replace Xù as Zhōngshū Lìng.
People at the time considered this selection appropriate,
comparing it to the Jin dynasty's appointment of Wáng Zǐjìng and Wáng Jìyǎn.
Xù was skilled in the Zhōuyì,
and his interpretations were profound and subtle,
making him a leading authority of his time.
He often said that Hé Píngshū did not understand seven matters in the Yì,
[三三] and the timely significance present in all the hexagrams
was one of them.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
Sacrificial Libationer (Jìjiǔ) as before.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and concurrently held the position of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
The following year,
he was appointed tutor to the Prince of Nánjùn (Nánjùn Wáng Shī),
with the added title of Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng),
while his position as Grand Master of Ceremonies remained unchanged.
In the third year,
he was transferred to Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì),
his positions as tutor and Palace Attendant remaining unchanged.
Whenever Xù had an audience,
Shìzǔ would look after him as he left.
He said to Wáng Jiǎn:
“Xù respects me for my position,
but I value Xù for his virtue.”
He was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
his positions as Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, Gold and Purple, and tutor remaining unchanged.
He was granted twenty trusted attendants.
He again concurrently held the position of Central Justice (Zhōngzhèng).
Huáng, the Prince of Chángshā, wanted to appoint Wúxīng Wén Rén Yōng as the provincial judicial assistant (Zhōu Yìcáo),
but Xù, deeming his qualifications inappropriate,
insisted on not allowing it.
Huáng sent his secretarial assistant (Shūzuǒ) to earnestly plead for him,
but Xù, with a stern expression, said to Huáng’s envoy:
“This concerns my own home province,
how can Your Highness pressure me in this way!”
In the seventh year,
Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng, was appointed Sacrificial Libationer of the National University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
Shìzǔ ordered Wáng Yàn:
“I want to ask the Minister of Works (Sītú) to resign from Sacrificial Libationer and confer it upon Zhāng Xù.
What do people think of this?”
Zǐliáng ultimately did not accept the appointment.
Xù was appointed concurrently as Sacrificial Libationer of the National University,
his positions as Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, tutor, and Central Justice remaining unchanged.
Xù never spoke of profit,
and whenever he had wealth, he would immediately distribute it.
He would speak eloquently and sit upright,
sometimes without food for an entire day.
His disciples, seeing Xù hungry,
would prepare meals for him,
but he never asked for them.
He died at the age of sixty-eight.
His will stipulated that a reed-mat carriage be made,
and only a cup of water and incense be placed on his spirit altar,
without any sacrificial offerings.
His younger cousin Róng deeply respected Xù,
serving him as if he were his own elder brother.
He brought wine to Xù's spirit altar, poured and drank it,
and wailed:
“My elder brother’s elegance is utterly gone!”
He was posthumously granted the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Special Advance (Tèjìn), and Grand Master of Imperial Splendor, Gold and Purple.
His posthumous name was Jiǎnzǐ.
His son, Kè,
during the reign of Cāngwú,
was a Regular Palace Assistant (Zhèngyuán Láng).
He gained favor through dangerous conduct,
but was later dismissed and banned from office due to his transgressions.
Kè’s younger brother, Yǔn,
during the Yǒngmíng era,
was the Registrar of the General Who Guards the West (Ānxī Gōngcáo).
He was involved in debauchery, adultery, and murder,
and was executed.
Yǔn’s elder brother, Chōng,
in the first year of Yǒngmíng,
was the Friend of the Prince of Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng Wáng Yǒu).
He was impeached by Imperial Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) Dào Huī
for a letter he wrote to Minister of the Palace Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) Wáng Jiǎn,
the tone and words of which were inflammatory.
He was dismissed from office and banned.
Commentators believed he bore a grudge against Jiǎn.
According to records, at the beginning of the Jiàn Yuán era,
an imperial edict was issued to rank court officials.
It was intended to appoint the Right Executive Assistant (Yòu Púshè) to Zhāng Dài.
Chǔ Yuān said,
“This would be overly generous.
If there are others who have shown exceptional loyalty,
and are specifically promoted,
that would be a different matter.
It is up to Your Majesty to decide.”
The emperor decreed,
“Reconsider.”
Since opinions differed,
both accounts are recorded here.
The Grand Historian states: Wáng Sēngqián possessed the capacity for rare renown,
combined with artistic and scholarly accomplishments.
He guarded against excess and maintained moderation,
humbling himself to accommodate others.
He was on par with the various Dukes,
truly a fine chief minister in peaceful times.
Zhāng Xù possessed a tranquil and pure disposition,
with natural distinction.
He was a model of integrity among officials,
and the people looked up to him.
Such a man of Xù’s elegance,
how could he not be called a renowned official!
The eulogy says: A dignified and benevolent elder,
whose righteousness was broad and generous.
His expertise spanned poetry, calligraphy, and official documents,
and he harmonized and governed the three highest offices.
Sīmàn was incorruptible and tranquil,
distancing himself from worldly dust.
His mind delved into the Yáo lines of the Yìjīng,
and all recognized his pure talent.
Collation Notes
Biography Fifteen: Yú Wánzhī, Liú Xiū, Shěn Chōng, Yǔ Gǎozhī, Wáng Chén
Yú Wánzhī, courtesy name Màoyáo,
was from Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
His grandfather Zōng
was a Bureau Director of the Imperial Armory (Kùbù Láng) in the Jìn dynasty.
His father Méi
was a Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tōngzhí Chángshì).
Wánzhī was skilled in official documents and writing in his youth,
and broadly studied history.
He first served as a Provisional Military Assistant (Xíng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Dōnghǎi,
then as Magistrate of Wūchéng.
Zhū Rénmí, a maternal relative of Empress Dowager Lù, committed a crime,
and Wánzhī prosecuted him according to the law.
The Empress Dowager complained to Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and Wánzhī was dismissed from office.
During the Tàishǐ era,
he was appointed Langzhongling of Jìnxī Commandery (Jìnxī Guó Lángzhōnglìng),
then Bureau Director of the Imperial Construction (Shàngshū Qǐbù Láng),
and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tōngzhí Láng).
During the Yuánhuī era,
he became Right Assistant (Yòu Chéng).
At that time, Tàizǔ was involved in governance,
and wrote to Wánzhī, saying:
“Zhāng Huá was Minister of the Granaries (Dùzhī Shàngshū),
and his accomplishments were not by chance.
Now there is a shortage in the grain transport and storage;
as you, my worthy friend, hold the position of Right Assistant,
I already feel that golden grain can be accumulated.”
Wánzhī submitted a memorial, stating that the money and silk in the treasury,
the armaments, and the labor force
were increasingly in arrears,
and expenditures were growing,
fearing that they would not last the year.
The court deliberated and gave him an excellent commendation.
He was promoted to Recorder of the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Lùshì) to the Prince of Ānchéng,
then transferred to Court Steward (Shàofǔ).
When Tàizǔ was stationed in Dōngfǔ,
the court and commoners all paid their respects.
Wánzhī still wore his clogs when he called on him.
Tàizǔ took the clogs and examined them,
they were black and crooked, sharp at the ends,
and the straps were broken,
mended with straw.
He asked:
“How many years have you had these clogs, my lord?”
Wánzhī replied:
“I bought them when I first entered officialdom as a Provisional Assistant to the General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Xíngzuǒ).
I have worn them for twenty years.
A poor scholar cannot afford to replace them.”
Tàizǔ approved of him,
and appointed him as Consulting Aide to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn).
When the regent’s headquarters were first established,
guests flocked in.
Tàizǔ paid close attention to selecting and receiving them.
Wánzhī and Rèn Xiá from Yuè’ān
were both known for their excellent responses at gatherings,
and were equally renowned and highly regarded.
Xiá, courtesy name Jǐngyuǎn,
was fond of learning
and possessed righteous conduct.
He also had a long-standing friendship with Tàizǔ,
and was greatly cherished by Chǔ Yuān and Wáng Jiǎn.
His highest office was Grand Master of Imperial Splendor (Guānglù Dàfū),
and he died at the beginning of the Yǒngyuán era.
Wán zhī was promoted to the General of Agile Cavalry,
then a Yellow Gate Attendant,
and concurrently the Chief Judge of his own commandery.
The Emperor was concerned that the common people were being deceptive and cunning.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he ordered Wán zhī and the General of Agile Cavalry, Fù Jiānyì, to inspect and verify the registers.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
an imperial edict was issued to the court officials, saying:
"The yellow registers
are the great record of the people
and the foundation of the state's governance.
For some time, the common folk have been cunning and deceitful,
and this has been going on for a long time.
They even secretly record ranks and titles,
illegally alter dates,
add or subtract from the three declarations,
and exploit loopholes in countless ways.
Some households exist, but their documents have been terminated;
some people are alive but falsely reported as dead;
some cease private work but claim to be laborers;
and some are robust but claim to suffer from the six infirmities.
Among registered households and orderly families,
few are not like this.
These are all great parasites of governance
and deep blemishes on education.
Although registers have been rectified and records revised in recent years,
the truth has ultimately not been obtained.
If we constrain them with punishment,
the people's deceit is already deeply ingrained;
if we pacify them with virtue,
it is not easy to overcome their depravity.
You, gentlemen, are all deeply knowledgeable about the principles of governance;
you may each offer your excellent counsel
to revive this declining civilization.
Furthermore, as for the recruitment by the central and local government offices,
this system is not practical.
The preferential treatment is clearly stipulated,
and the distinction between busy and leisurely duties is constant.
Before the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
this service was always full.
After the Dàmíng era,
the desire for recruitment gradually ceased.
Perhaps due to frequent uprisings and banditry,
military exemptions became more common.
The common people followed their self-interest,
and few joined the offices.
However, the state's principles have not changed,
and the court's regulations still exist.
Comparing them,
how swift is the rise and fall!
This is the great source of urgent problems,
a pressing concern of the times.
How can we calculate
to eradicate this malpractice?"
Wán zhī submitted a memorial, stating:
"The eight articles for recruiting people in the 27th year of Yuánjiā of Sòng,
and the registers of the first year of Xiàojiàn,
were the beginning of many cunning practices.
During the Yuánjiā era,
the late Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Fù Lóng,
though over seventy years old,
still personally compiled the registers
and meticulously reviewed them himself.
Fù Lóng did not necessarily possess the caution of Shí Jiàn
or the diligence of Gāo Ròu,
but rather because the era was one of enlightened peace,
and people practiced the Way and cultivated themselves.
Now, Your Majesty, you forget to eat until late in the day
and seek your clothes before dawn.
I, a humble and foolish servant, am summoned by edict
and respectfully present my wild thoughts.
In ancient times, governing the world jointly
depended solely on good 'two-thousand-bushel' officials.
Now, if we wish to achieve good governance and rectify things,
it lies in diligent and enlightened prefects and magistrates.
Whenever registers are received,
if the county does not verify and combine them,
but merely seals and sends them to the province,
and the province, after verifying the facts,
then returns them to the county—
the officials become greedy for bribes,
and the people indulge their deception.
The deeper the deception, the more registers are returned;
the thicker the bribe, the slower the response.
From the third year of Tàishǐ to the fourth year of Yuánhuī,
the four issues of yellow registers for Yángzhōu and other nine commanderies
resulted in a total of over seventy-one thousand households being returned.
Eleven years have passed since then,
yet fewer than forty thousand have been rectified.
Even in the 'divine region,' the central area,
it is still like this.
As for the various departments along the Jiāng and Xiāng rivers,
it is even more inconceivable.
I humbly suggest that the registers of the 27th year of Yuánjiā be taken as the standard.
The people have been negligent of the law for a long time.
For the registers of the first year of Jiànyuán,
new clear regulations should be established.
Let there be one chance for people to regret and confess.
Those who are deluded and do not repent
shall be executed according to regulations.
Officials should carefully inspect and verify themselves,
ensuring a clear cleansing,
before submitting them to the province,
to serve as a permanent standard.
If there is any falsity or obscurity,
both provincial and county officials shall share the blame.
The current population size
is no less than in Yuánjiā,
yet the official registers are severely deficient.
There are reasons for this malpractice.
Since Xiàojiàn,
many have entered service through military merit.
Among them, those who actually wielded weapons to defend the state
are barely one-third.
Those who are listed in the merit registers
but fraudulently avoid service,
floating through the world's important positions,
not constrained or recorded by officials,
are also not few.
Recalling that after the suppression of Sū Jùn,
Yǔ Liàng asked Wēn Qiáo for the merit registers,
but Wēn Qiáo refused to give them,
believing that what Táo Kǎn had reported
was largely untrue.
It is found that people's self-serving motives
exist in every generation.
At the end of Sòng, when the state was falling apart,
such cunning became especially rampant.
Moreover, with many generals in positions,
offering relief became their salaries,
though the actual benefits were meager.
Yet individuals claimed tens of thousands.
With these two issues,
the bodies liable for service in the empire
have already been taken up by more than half.
Furthermore, some alter their registered status
and fraudulently enter officialdom.
Those who were once servants
now in turn command others.
Also, those who are born without long hair
are then called monks or Daoists,
filling streets and alleys;
this is everywhere.
Some live together with children
but are not registered as households,
moving about,
publicly violating the principle of local residency.
The conscripted service is never full,
and the wandering do not return.
They would rather lose their lives
or remain perpetually ill in bed.
If laws are strictly enforced,
they will naturally compete to return.
Furthermore, the garrisons and generals of the four frontiers
have names but little substance.
Their subordinates are organized based on talent,
without distinguishing brave from cowardly.
Appointments and allowances
are given to witches and old women alike,
filling mountains and seas,
all for private service.
Bribing to gain positions
is too easy a path.
Why would one volunteer for humble and arduous service?
This is why the government offices are depleted
and the hundred-li districts are vacant.
Now, if only the recruitment system is clear and trustworthy,
with a definite term of service,
and the people have no other way,
then the government offices can be filled instantly.
In governance, the lack of regulations is not the problem,
but their non-implementation.
And the non-implementation is not the problem,
but their short duration."
The Emperor reviewed Wán zhī's memorial
and accepted it.
He then established a separate office for registers,
and appointed clerks,
limiting the number of deceptive acts a person could commit in a day
to prevent idleness.
Consequently, due to bribes and connections,
even if the registration was correct,
it was still forcibly rejected
to meet the quota.
By the eighth year of Yǒngmíng during the reign of Shìzǔ,
those found to be deceptive were exiled to guard the Huái River for ten years,
which caused resentment among the common people.
Shìzǔ then issued an edict, saying:
"Indeed, distinguishing noble from base,
and discerning superior from inferior,
all rely on the authenticity of the yellow registers.
How can there be false pretensions and excessive honors,
or usurped positions beyond one's due?
Therefore, it is necessary to clarify and reform falsehoods,
and to conform to old statutes.
However, the faults arose in previous generations,
not recent errors.
Past transgressions
need not be pursued for blame."
Before the Shēngmíng [era] of Sòng,
all were permitted to return to their original registered residence.
Those who had been banished to serve in frontier garrisons
were all allowed to return to their hometowns.
After this, any offenders
were severely punished and purged."
Yú Wánzhī, due to long-standing official service (old age) and illness,
submitted a memorial to request retirement,
saying:
"I have heard that those who carry heavy burdens and travel far
will be exhausted when their strength gives out;
those who serve their lord with utmost sincerity
will surely fall when their wisdom is spent.
This is indeed a natural principle.
One enters officialdom at forty,
and retires at seventy.
One strives while strong,
and ought to rest in old age.
I was born in Jìn,
grew up in Sòng,
and aged in Qí.
I have lived through three dynasties,
and witnessed the capital change twice.
I became an attendant to the royal household in the twenty-eighth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng,
and it has been thirty years since then.
Recently,
my decline and debility have become severe.
By nature not lazy,
yet weariness suddenly overwhelms me.
My ears and eyes were originally keen,
but deafness and dimness have steadily increased.
My legs cannot support my body,
and I gasp for breath.
Time passes inexorably,
and I cannot guarantee to last from morning to noon.
Among my many brothers,
forty-two in total,
through prosperity and adversity, long life and short,
only I remain.
Like the last gleam of morning dew,
how can I endure for long?
Moreover, he who knows contentment suffers no disgrace;
I am already content.
Born into hunger and cold,
I did not seek wealth and honor.
Whether I obtain wealth or not depends on fate;
what regret do I have?
I have long been content with it.
Serving others with integrity,
I could not escape imprisonment,
but fortunately encountered an enlightened ruler
who knew it was not a crime.
This was my great good fortune.
Receiving my appointment during the decline of the Way,
and demonstrating my loyalty during a time of great governance,
this is the manifestation of my loyalty.
Fortune descended upon the beginning of civilization,
and I received blessings in this Heaven-sent era.
This is the coincidence of my fate.
Not planning for a clever career, yet rising to the position of a Nine Minister;
ashamed of my virtue compared to Lǐ Líng, yet occupying a position in the Household Department.
〔一０〕The virtue of Yáo and Shùn is endless;
I too have attained fulfillment.
To live beyond sixty is not considered an early death.
Róng Qī's three joys,
and Dōngpíng's one virtue,
I have fully experienced them all.
Having passed through periods of darkness and chaos,
and traversed difficulties and dangers,
I relied on the sagely virtue to preserve myself,
and depended on virtuous assistants to uphold my integrity.
I have never felt subservient to powerful figures,
nor feared drowning
among the cunning and deceitful.
The foundation of my character
has remained unblemished in this regard.
When I was strong,
I did not yield my office.
Now that I am old and infirm,
I have no means of support.
I humbly beg for your benevolent gaze,
and grant me my old bones.
It is not that I aspire to lofty ideals or admire the ancients,
nor that I love springs and forests.
It is specifically because I am orphaned and poor in this era,
and my filial duties are greatly lacking.
The sorrow of the 'wind and trees' [metaphor for filial regret]
has long entangled my heart.
I hope Heaven will grant me the time,
two or three years,
to sweep and guard the graves,
and thus achieve completeness.
Then my lifelong aspiration will be fulfilled."
The Emperor read Yú Wánzhī's memorial
and granted his request.
Yú Wánzhī was fond of judging people positively or negatively.
At the end of Sòng,
Wáng Jiǎn nominated Kuǒ Tì as a Yuánwàiláng to serve as an envoy to the barbarians.
Yú Wánzhī's opinions clashed with his,
and both Kǒng Tì and Wáng Jiǎn resented him.
By this time, when Yú Wánzhī returned east,
Wáng Jiǎn did not see him off,
and there was no farewell banquet from the imperial court.
Yú Wánzhī returned home and built a large residence,
and died a few years later.
Later, Yuánwàiláng Kǒng Xuān approached Wáng Jiǎn to request the position of Wǔguān in Kuàijī.
Wáng Jiǎn was washing his hands;
he threw a soap pod to the ground
and said:
"Your local customs are bad.
Yú Wánzhī bothered people until his death."
〔一一〕
Kǒng Tì, courtesy name Shìyuǎn,
was from the same commandery as Yú Wánzhī.
He was fond of historical precedents and learning.
He was a close friend of Wáng Jiǎn.
During the Shēngmíng [era],
he served as Shàngshū Yícáoláng in the Qí administration.
Tàizǔ said to him:
"You are a talent for the Yícáo."
When Wáng Jiǎn became Prime Minister,
Kǒng Tì often participated in planning within the inner chambers.
Whenever it came to selecting officials,
he somewhat neglected local sentiments.
Wáng Jiǎn casually remarked to the Emperor:
"I have Kǒng Tì,
just as Your Majesty has me."
During the Yǒngmíng [era],
he served as Tàizǐ Jiālìng [Household Administrator for the Crown Prince],
and died.
People at the time called Kǒng Tì and Hé Xiàn the 'Three Ducal Ministers of Wáng Jiǎn'.
Hé Xiàn, courtesy name Zǐsī,
was from Lújiāng.
He was known for his strong scholarship.
His mother was the daughter of Zhènběi Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Fū;
she was intelligent and had discerning judgment.
Hé Xiàn served as Biéjià for his home prefecture.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng,
he was sent as an envoy to the barbarians.
Liú Xiū, courtesy name Hóngmíng,
〔一二〕was from Pèijùn Xiāng.
His grandfather, Huī,
was Zhèngyuánláng.
His father, Chāo,
was Jiǔzhēn Tàishǒu.
Liú Xiū first served as Fùmǎ Dūwèi [Commander of the Emperor's Son-in-Law Escort],
and received imperial summons.
He was Sòng Míngdì's (Xiāng) Dōngguó Chángshì.
〔一三〕He was fond of learning and good at memorization,
but was not known to the Emperor.
He inherited his grandfather's title of Nánxiāng Hóu.
His friend Xiè Yǎn of Chénjùn rebelled with Prime Minister Yìxuān.
Liú Xiū was implicated for harboring him,
and was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng for seven years.
Upon Xiàowǔ's death,
he was finally released.
He followed his younger brother Qīn to Luóxiàn.
In the early days of Tàishǐ,
when various prefectures rebelled,
Liú Xiū divined that Míngdì would win,
and remained quiet, not participating in any dissenting plans.
Several years later,
he returned and joined Wú Xǐ as a Fǔshīfǔ Lùshì Cānjūn.
Wú Xǐ praised his talent
and recommended him to Míngdì,
allowing him to be at his side.
He was appointed Guìyángwáng Zhēngběi Cānjūn.
The Emperor was quite fond of certain things,
especially food and drink.
Xiū had many talents,
and when it came to culinary arts,
there was nothing he couldn't answer.
When women in the imperial harem became pregnant,
the Emperor would have their gender divined,
and it was always accurate.
The Emperor was naturally obese,
and impotent, unable to perform his marital duties.
When the concubines of the various princes became pregnant,
he secretly had them brought into the palace.
After they gave birth,
he would imprison their mothers in a hidden room.
This happened ten or more times.
Cóng Dì
was the son of Guìyángwáng Xiūfàn.
〔一四〕Cāngwúwáng was also not the Emperor's son.
Chén Tàifēi was formerly a concubine of Lǐ Dào'ér,
hence Cāngwúwáng, when traveling incognito,
often referred to himself as Lǐ Láng.
The Emperor hated jealous women.
When Shàngshū Yòuchéng Róng Yànquǎn
was injured on the face by his jealous wife,
the Emperor said:
"I will cure this for you,
how about that?"
Yànquǎn immediately replied:
"I obey Your Majesty's decree."
That evening,
he was granted medicine to kill his wife.
Xiū's wife, Wáng Shì, was also jealous.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he bestowed a concubine upon Xiū,
and ordered Wáng Shì to be given twenty strokes with a rod.
He ordered Xiū to open a small shop behind his residence,
and made Wáng Shì personally sell brooms and soap-beans to humiliate her.
Such was the closeness he showed.
Soon after, he was appointed Yuánwàiláng,
concurrently Fǔguó Sīmǎ and Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
and additionally Nánchéng Lìng.
He was appointed Shàngshū Zhōngbīng Láng,
Jǐshìzhōng,
with Shèrén and Lìng as before.
He was appointed Ānchéngwáng Fǔjūn Cānjūn,
〔一六〕then posted as Dōushuǐ Shǐzhě,
and Nánkāng Xiàng.
【Xiū】 was skilled in discussing the principles of governance,
〔一七〕yet showed no outstanding achievements in the commandery.
Returning, he became Zhèngyuán Láng,
Shàolíngwáng Nánzhōngláng Lùshì, Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn, and Xīncài Tàishǒu.
He was transferred to Zuǒjūnfǔ,
and given the additional title of Zhènmán Hùjūn,
with Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu remaining as before.
He was promoted to Zīyì,
Sīmǎ,
and further promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
with Zhènmán Hùjūn and Tàishǒu remaining as before.
He was transferred to Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
with Jiāngjūn and Sīmǎ remaining as before.
Later, he was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ.
During Shěn Yōuzhī's rebellion,
〔一八〕Shìzǔ, with the military garrisons of Jìnxī and Shàolíng, defended Pénchéng.
Xiū was responsible for the military expenses.
When the troubles ceased,
he was consequently promoted to Shàolíngwáng Ānnán Zhǎngshǐ,
appointed Huángmén Láng,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
Qiánjūn Zhǎngshǐ,
and Qítái Sànqí Chángshì.
At the beginning of Jiànyuán era,
he became Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
After some time,
Xiū reported:
"Since I took up this humble duty in the Southern Censorate,
the stars have crossed into spring,
and though my weak memorials have been heard by mistake,
there has not been a single month without an impeachment.
Not only have I been unable to make the vassal states submit,
or the powerful gentry hold their breath,
but I have even allowed notorious criminals to be heard,
and birds caught in the net to escape.
Yet, because of this,
harmony within villages and communities is lost,
〔一九〕and the court is devoid of mutual respect among peers.
Behind their backs, people loudly criticize me,
and military men sharpen their tongues.
Such accumulated resentment
is difficult to bear for long,
and when judgment is rendered,
who will find it acceptable?
I have quietly observed that during the sixty-year reign of the Sòng dynasty,
fifty-three individuals have held this office.
Comparing their tenures,
none exceeded a full year.
As I have held this position for too long,
I should request to retire."
The Emperor said:
"Your duty as a national official
is founded on awe and governance.
How can you suddenly fear worldly censure?
You should have resigned at the very beginning of your duties;
how can you seek to be lazy in your later years?"
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
the Emperor made a south-pointing chariot.
Because Xiū had an inquiring mind,
he was ordered to supervise and test it together with Wáng Sēngqián.
During the Yuánjiā era,
Yáng Xīn received the orthodox clerical script method from Zǐjìng,
which was universally revered.
The style of the Right General was slightly archaic,
and no longer esteemed.
Xiū was the first to favor this method,
and to this day, this style is widely practiced.
In the fourth year,
he was posted as Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
and given the additional title of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn.
He died
at the age of fifty-four.
Shěn Chōng, courtesy name Jǐngchuò,
was a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng.
His grandfather, Xuān,
was Xīn'ān Tàishǒu.
His father, Huáiwén,
【Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu】.
〔二０〕Chōng first served as Wèiwèi Wǔguān,
then transferred to Yángzhōu Zhǔbù.
During the Dàmíng era of Sòng,
Huáiwén had a literary reputation,
and Chōng also dabbled in literature.
He was transferred to Xīyángwáng Fǔjūn Fǎcáo Cānjūn,
then soon recommended as Xiùcái.
He returned to serve as Fǔjūn Zhèngzuǒ,
concurrently Jìshì.
When Huáiwén incurred a crime and was imprisoned,
Chōng and his brothers went to apologize,
their grief profound and their appearance sorrowful,
moving those who saw them.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng wanted to save Huáiwén,
and spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Shěn Huáiwén's three sons are in great distress and cannot be seen.
I wish Your Majesty would quickly mete out his punishment."
The Emperor eventually killed him.
Yuánjǐng sighed at this.
Chōng and his brothers became known for this.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ era,
due to his mother's old age and the family's poverty,
he memorialized Míng Dì and was appointed Yǒngxīng Lìng.
He was promoted to Bālíngwáng Zhǔbù,
and appointed Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng.
During the Yuánhuī era,
he was posted as Jìn'ānwáng Ānxī Jìshì Cānjūn,
then returned to serve as Sītú Zhǔbù,
Shānyīn Lìng,
and transferred to Sītú Lùshì Cānjūn.
When Shìzǔ was in Jiāngzhōu,
Chōng served as Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu,
and was greatly trusted and favored.
When Shìzǔ returned to the capital,
he made Chōng act as Fǔ and Zhōu affairs.
He was promoted to Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ.
At the beginning of Jiànyuán era,
he was transferred to Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn,
concurrently Lùshì.
Before he could take up the post,
he was transferred to Huángmén Láng,
and then promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Shìzǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he treated him with kindness and as an old acquaintance.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
he was transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
Shìzhōng.
When Guànjūn Lúlíngwáng Zǐqīng became Yǐngzhōu,
Chōng was appointed Zhǎngshǐ, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngxià Nèishǐ,
acting in Fǔ and Zhōu affairs.
With the transfer of the Fǔ, he was transferred to Ānxī Zhǎngshǐ and Nánjùn Nèishǐ,
acting in Jīngzhōu Fǔ affairs,
with his Jiāngjūn title remaining as before.
In the fourth year of Yǒngmíng,
he was summoned to be Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
Chōng, along with his elder brothers Dàn and Yuān, had reputations of varying quality.
The world called them
"bō gǔ brothers" (the brothers of the winnowing basket drum).
Dàn and Yuān both served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor-in-chief).
The three brothers
all became Sīzhí (Directors of Justice),
which was unprecedented in the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
The duty of a Zhōngchéng (Censor-in-chief) was to adjudicate cases,
and those who were subject to their constitutional scrutiny often bore grudges.
In the Yǒngmíng reign, Yuān impeached Yuán Tuàn, the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
In the Jiànwǔ reign,
Tuàn's younger cousin Áng became Zhōngchéng.
A few days after taking office,
he submitted a memorial impeaching Yuān's son, Huì, for having rented a white carriage cover while his father was still alive,
leading to Huì's dismissal from office and temporary confinement.
Chōng's mother, Lady Kǒng, was in the east.
A neighbor's house caught fire,
and it was suspected to have been intentionally set.
She cried out loudly:
"All three of my sons served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng!
How could they have been on good terms with anyone!"
Shìzǔ was about to appoint Chōng to a position,
but Chōng passed away while traveling west to Nánzhōu.
He was fifty-one years old at the time.
The Emperor deeply lamented his passing.
When his coffin returned,
an imperial edict stated:
"The arrival of Chōng's funeral coffin
fills Us with profound sorrow.
Remembering his past service in Nánfān,
We feel especially grieved and mournful."
The imperial carriage personally attended Chōng's funeral,
and an edict declared:
"Chōng was upright, discerning, and composed in his administration.
His aspirations and conduct were profound and just.
His sincerity was manifest in the provincial court,
and his achievements were evident both in and out of office.
[二一] It is unfortunate that he died young;
We deeply mourn him."
He was posthumously granted the title of Tài Cháng
[二二] and given the posthumous name Gōngzǐ (Reverent Son).
Yǔ Gǎozhī, courtesy name Jǐngxíng,
was a native of Xīnyě.
His grandfather, Shēnzhī,
was the Cìshǐ (Governor) of Yōngzhōu.
His father, Càn,
was a Cānjūn (Staff Officer) in the Sīkōng (Minister of Works) office.
Gǎozhī was upright and firm from a young age
and well-versed in literature and righteousness.
He began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng (Gentleman for Attendance at Court),
then became Bālíng Wáng Zhēngxī Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the King of Bālíng, General Quelling the West).
He was recommended as Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent) by Yǐngzhōu,
appointed JìnXī Wáng ZhènXī Wàibīng Cānjūn (External Military Staff Officer to the King of JìnXī, General Guarding the West),
then Shìzǔ Zhēnglǔ Fǔ Gōngcáo (Administrator in Shìzǔ's General Who Conquers the Barbarians' Headquarters),
and Shàngshū Jiàbù Láng (Secretary in the Ministry of Rites, Chariots Bureau).
He lived a life of integrity and poverty,
his only food being leek porridge, salted leeks, raw leeks, and various vegetables.
Someone once joked about him, saying:
"Who says Master Yǔ is poor?
He always has twenty-seven kinds of preserved fish!"
(Referring to three times nine, alluding to the various forms of leeks).
He then served as Shìzǔ Fǔjūn Zhōngjūn Jìshì (Secretary in the Central Army Headquarters of Shìzǔ's General Who Calms the Army),
then transferred to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Supernumerary Palace Attendant),
Zhèngyuán Láng (Regular Official),
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary in the Central Secretariat),
concurrently serving as Zhōngzhèng (Impartial Judge) for Jīng and Xiāng provinces.
He was transferred to Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng (Assistant Minister of the Left),
with Chángshì and Zhōngzhèng as before.
He was sent out to be Wáng Jiǎn Wèijūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to Wáng Jiǎn, General of the Guards).
People at the time called Jiǎn's residence "entering the hibiscus pond."
[二三] Jiǎn said to others:
"Previously, Duke Yuán served as Wèijūn and
wanted to appoint me as Zhǎngshǐ.
Although I was unable to take the position,
that was his intention.
Now, he should also need someone of my caliber."
So he appointed Gǎozhī.
Gǎozhī was promoted to Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and soon officially took the latter post.
Gǎozhī had a gentle and refined demeanor
and spoke eloquently.
Shìzǔ ordered him to receive the northern envoys,
also concurrently serving as Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
[二四] The Emperor often praised his graceful bearing,
and when Wáng Jiǎn was present,
he remarked:
"Gǎozhī, illuminated by the cicada-wing cap,
has an even more refined presence.
Your Majesty should truly grant him a substantial position."
The Emperor did not yet intend to use him in such a capacity.
During the Yǒngmíng reign,
the princes were young
and were not allowed to interact with people indiscriminately.
An imperial decree ordered Gǎozhī and Jiāng Yān from Jìyáng to visit the princes every five days
to foster good relations.
Soon after, he was transferred to Lúlíng Wáng Zhōngjūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Central Army Headquarters of the King of Lúlíng),
then transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel),
participating in important selection matters.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ (Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard),
with the added title of Tōngzhí Chángshì (Palace Attendant).
In the ninth year,
he died.
On his deathbed, he submitted a memorial stating:
"Last night and this morning, Your servant's illness has worsened.
I feel my chronic illness
is momentarily critical,
and I can no longer lie here.
Having held such a prominent position,
I have sullied this enlightened age.
I beg to be relieved of the post I have unworthily held,
so I may await my end in my private courtyard.
I, Your servant, am of ordinary ability,
yet by error, I encountered a prosperous fortune.
The generosity of Your promotions
is rarely seen in a thousand years.
Moreover, having passed the age of fifty,
with aspirations of glory and prominence,
longevity and early death are predetermined;
I have nothing to say.
If Heaven observes my humble sincerity
and temporarily grants me remaining years,
even if my clan perishes and my life ends,
my efforts will not be far-reaching.
Looking up at the imperial palace,
I lie on my pillow, choked with longing.
I send my貂蟬 (diāochán, sable cicada hat) and memorial."
An imperial edict did not grant his request.
Gǎozhī had served in high offices
and was favored for his literary talent.
The Emperor built the Chóngxū Guǎn (Hall of Exalted Vacuity)
and had him compose the stele inscription.
He died at the age of fifty-one,
and the Emperor deeply lamented his passing.
He was given the posthumous name Zhēnzǐ (Chaste Son).
At that time, Kǒng Guǎng from Kuàijī,
courtesy name Yānyuán,
also had a beautiful appearance and demeanor.
He served as Zhōu Zhōngzhòng (Administrator of the Province)
before he died.
Wáng Chén, courtesy name Zhònghé,
was a native of Tán in Dōnghǎi.
His grandfather, Wànqìng,
[二五] was Yuánwài Chángshì (Supernumerary Palace Attendant).
His father, Yuánmǐn,
was Hùjūn Sīmǎ (Military Advisor to the Protector-General).
During the Dàmíng reign of Sòng,
Shěn Tánqìng served as Xúzhōu,
and appointed Chén as Yíng Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk for Reception).
He also served as Zhōu Yíng Cóngshì (Attendant for Provincial Reception),
Xiāngdōng Wángguó Chángshì (Palace Attendant to the Kingdom of Xiāngdōng),
Zhènběi Xíng Cānjūn (Acting Staff Officer to the General Guarding the North).
The lords of the province, kingdom, and commandery were all Sòng Míngdì.
He was appointed Yìyáng Wáng Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn (Acting Staff Officer to the King of Yìyáng, General Conquering the North),
and also served in Dù Míngdì Wèijūn Fǔ (Emperor Míng's General of the Guards' Headquarters).
Chén was learned and righteous,
and repeatedly served as an assistant to the Emperor's imperial relatives.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Chén was appointed Sītú Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Minister of Education),
concurrently Xūlìng (Magistrate of Xū),
and concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretariat Imperial Clerk).
He was closely trusted
and always remained by the Emperor's side.
Seeing the Emperor's cruel and perverse actions,
Chén repeatedly remonstrated, but was not heeded.
He requested to retire,
for which he incurred the Emperor's wrath,
and was imprisoned in Shàngfāng (the Imperial Workshops/Prison).
He was released after a few days.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (Secretary in the Palace Bureau of the Ministry of Personnel),
transferred to Jìshì Cānjūn (Secretarial Staff Officer),
Zhèngyuán Láng (Regular Official),
and Xūlìng as before.
He was promoted to concurrent Zhōngshū Láng,
then Jìnpíng Wáng Piàojì Bǎnbù Zīyì (Consultant to the King of Jìnpíng, General of Agile Cavalry).
He was sent out as Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu (Grand Administrator of Xiāngdōng),
with a salary of two thousand shi.
Before he was formally installed,
he was dismissed due to a public matter.
He then served again as Guìyáng Wáng Piàojì Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant Staff Officer in the General of Agile Cavalry's Headquarters of the King of Guìyáng),
and Zhōngshū Láng.
Emperor Míng was fond of hunting grounds and established them in various provinces and cities.
He appointed Jiàn'ān Wáng Xiūrén as Wéizhōu Dūdà Zhōngzhèng (Chief Impartial Judge of the Hunting Ground Province).
Chén, along with Tàizǐ Yòulǜ Shěn Bó, Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng Yǔ Guīzhī, and Péngchéng Chéng Wáng Kàng, these four, were appointed Xiǎo Zhōngzhèng (Minor Impartial Judges).
Cháoqǐng Chǔ Sīzhuāng and Fù Chǔzhī were appointed Qīngdìng Fǎngwèn (Investigators for Clarity and Impartiality).
He was sent out as Grand Administrator of Línchuān.
He returned to serve as Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs.
Soon after, he was appointed Libationer of the Eastern Repository, holding his original office.
This was the Zǒngmíng Repository established by Emperor Míng.
He was promoted to Yellow Gate Attendant,
then transferred to Regular Attendant,
General Who Assists the State,
Chief Clerk of the Right Army for the Prince of Jiāngxià,
and General of the Vanguard.
He was transferred to Gentleman-in-Attendance,
then Minister of Justice,
but did not take up the appointment.
During the Jiànyuán era,
when Yè, the Prince of Wǔlíng, was Grand Warden of Kuàijī,
Chén was appointed Chief Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Captives, acting in that capacity,
his General of the Vanguard title remaining as before.
In the early Yǒngmíng era,
he was promoted to Cavalry Commander of the Grand Commandant for the Prince of Yùzhāng,
his general rank remaining as before.
Emperor Shìzǔ had met Chén during the reign of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
and wished to entrust him with important responsibilities.
〔二六〕He was appointed General Who Assists the State, Chief Clerk of the Southern Central Gentleman for the Prince of Jìn'ān, and Grand Warden of Huáinán,
acting in the capacity of both Administrator and Governor.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Yellow Gate Attendant,
and concurrently held the title of General of Agile Cavalry.
He was promoted to Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince,
his General of Agile Cavalry title remaining as before.
Chén was virtuous, upright, harmonious, and cautious;
the court called him a good person,
and many treated him with great generosity.
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to General of the Vanguard and Chief Clerk of the General of Chariots and Cavalry for the Prince of Chángshā.
He was then transferred to Chief Clerk of the Central Army for the Prince of Lúlíng,
his general rank remaining as before.
When Zǐmíng, the Prince of Xīyáng, was in Nányǎn Province,
and Chief Clerk Shěn Xiàn had retired from office,
the Emperor again transferred Chén to be Chief Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Captives,
acting in the capacity of Administrator and Governor of Nányǎn,
his general rank remaining as before.
Chén was poor in his youth
and once spun and wove cloth himself.
After he became prominent and esteemed,
he often spoke of this to others.
The world praised him for achieving his ambitions.
In the ninth year,
he passed away
at the age of sixty-nine.
The imperial historian says: "Like quails nesting and chicks drinking,
when rulers were first established,
and records began,
the people were not yet distinguished.
Thus, the meaning of 'cherishing the people' was profound,
and the intention to 'bring them out of danger' was weighty.
After later generations,
rulers sought to exhaust the people's strength,
assessing wealth and levying taxes
to support themselves.
The lower classes suffered, but the upper classes had no pity.
The world became corrupt, and affairs grew more changeable.
Hence there were those who secretly manipulated the census registers,
dared to harm their own bodies,
lived fraudulently, died defying,
and evaded the law's net.
This accumulation of falsehood and error
had continued for several decades.
Deception and concealment were tolerated,
shared by officials and commoners alike.
For the governance of the state,
it was indeed appropriate to rectify and reform.
If corvée labor were eased and levies lightened,
then this fraud would naturally cease.
If officials were clearly disciplined,
then this falsehood would not prevail.
Merely reviewing old documents
only provides the people with opportunities for evasion.
Thus, the censure of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi by Cuī Yǎn,
and Xiè Ān's discussions regarding the capital,
show that the difficulty of governing the people
is not merely a distant issue from the Zhōu dynasty era!"
〔二七〕
Encomium says: Wán's contentment,
his discourse was not yet illustrious.
Liú Xiū divined well,
and rested peacefully in Nánxiāng.
Chōng earned timely renown,
Gǎo believed in jade tokens.
Chén alone followed the old order,
and was used by the flourishing king.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 16: The Twelve Princes of Emperor Gāozǔ
Emperor Gāo had nineteen sons: Empress Zhāo gave birth to Emperor Wǔ and Yí, Prince Wénxiàn of Yùzhāng;
Honored Consort Xiè gave birth to Yìng, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, and Huǎng, Prince Wēi of Chángshā;
Grand Consort Luó gave birth to Niàn, Prince Zhāo of Wǔlíng;
Grand Consort Rén gave birth to Gǎo, Prince Gōng of Ānchéng;
Lady of Grace Lù gave birth to Qiāng, Prince of Póyáng, and Qiú, Prince of Jìnxī;
Lady of Composure Yuán gave birth to Shuò, Prince of Guìyáng;
Grand Consort Hé gave birth to Jiàn, Prince Jiǎn of Shǐxīng, and Kēng, Prince of Yídū;
Honored Lady Ōu gave birth to Jūn, Prince of Héngyáng;
Consort Zhāng gave birth to Fēng, Prince of Jiāngxià, and Xuàn, Prince of Hédōng;
Beauty Lǐ gave birth to Ruì, Prince of Nánpíng;
the ninth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and seventeenth imperial sons died young.
Jūn, Prince of Héngyáng, was adopted as the successor to Prince Yuán.
Yìng, Prince Xiàn of Línchuān, courtesy name Xuānguāng,
was the third son of Emperor Tàizǔ.
In the fourth year of Yuánhuī of Sòng,
he began his official career as Assistant Gentleman of the Bureau of Writing.
He was promoted to Acting Staff Officer of the General Who Soothes the Army,
and Literary Scholar for the Prince of Nányáng.
When Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
Emperor Tàizǔ then held the office of Governor of Nánxú Province,
and appointed Yìng as General Who Pacifies the North,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
When the rebellion was quelled,
he was appointed Consultant of the Central Army, Central Gentleman of Affairs, General Who Assists the State, and Grand Warden of the two commanderies of Huáinán and Xuānchéng,
but he did not take up any of these appointments.
He was then appointed Bearer of Insignia, Area Commander of the military affairs of five provinces, including Nányǎn, Qīng, and Jì, and acting Inspector of Nányǎn Province,
his general rank remaining as before.
Soon after, he was appointed Gentleman-in-Attendance and Yellow Gate Attendant,
and concurrently held the title of General of the Vanguard Army.
He was then again appointed General of the Vanguard and Inspector of Nányǎn Province,
Bearer of Insignia and Area Commander,
and again Army Supervisor,
commanding the five provinces as before.
When the Qí dynasty was established,
the Emperor of Sòng issued an edict to enfeoff Yìng and his brothers Huǎng, Niàn, Gǎo, Qiāng, Shuò, and Jiàn, all as Dukes of a Founding County,
each with a stipend of one thousand five hundred households.
Before their territories could be settled,
Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne.

Yìng was appointed Bearer of Imperial Insignia, Area Commander of the military affairs of eight provinces including Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, North Qín, and South Qín, General Who Pacifies the West, and Inspector of Jīng Province.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Línchuān,
with a customary stipend of two thousand households.
He also concurrently held the title of Inspector of Xiāng Province.
Since Yí, the Prince of Yùzhāng, had remained to guard Shǎnxī,
Yìng also did not take up his post.
He was reassigned as Cavalry Regular Attendant, Area Commander of the military affairs of the two provinces of Yáng and Nánxú, General of the Vanguard Army, and Inspector of Yáng Province,
his status as bearer of insignia remaining as before.
When the state was newly founded,
Yìng, though young, governed the Divine Land.
His administration was intelligent and keen,
and the officials in the prefectural and provincial bureaus
all stood respectfully to obey prohibitions.
Such efficiency had not been seen since Yìkāng, Prince of Péngchéng of Sòng.

He was sent out as Area Commander of the military affairs of nine provinces including Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Bā, Níng, North Qín, and South Qín, General Who Guards the West, and Inspector of Jīng Province,
his status as bearer of insignia and Regular Attendant remaining as before.
He was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
Due to national mourning, he resigned as Cavalry Regular Attendant,
and was promoted to the title of General Who Attacks the West.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he entered the court as Palace Attendant,
and General of Agile Cavalry.
In the second year,
he was granted an oil-painted carriage.
In the fifth year,
he was granted the right to establish a staff and held authority equal to the Three Ducal Ministers, maintaining his existing title.
In the seventh year,
he passed away.
Yìng was skilled in riding and archery.
He understood musical theory,
and was skilled at writing with both hands and shooting with both hands.
In receiving guests,
his demeanor was elegant and refined.
Everyone in court and country lamented his passing.
He was then thirty-two years old.
An imperial edict bestowed secret funerary objects from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothing.
He was posthumously appointed Minister of Works.
He had nine sons,
all enfeoffed as marquises.
His eldest son, Zǐjìn,
served successively as Grand Warden of the two commanderies of Dōngyáng and Wúxīng,
Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and concurrently held the title of General of the Rear Army.
In the early Yǒngyuán era,
he served as Palace Attendant,
and was promoted to Minister of the Left of the Bureau of Population.
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities
for failing to pay respects to his maternal grandmother on her birthday,
and the matter was held by the emperor.
Zǐjìn subsequently did not take up the appointment again.
When the Prince of Liáng captured the capital,
he still wore the robes of a Palace Attendant.
When he entered the Liáng court, he served as General Who Assists the State and Grand Warden of Gāopíng.
His second son, Zǐyóu,
was the Marquis of Zhōulíng.
He began his official career as Supernumerary Gentleman,
then Equerry to the Crown Prince,
and successively served as Grand Warden of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Jìnlíng,
and Yellow Gate Attendant.
He was fond of music,
and understood various arts of string and wind instruments.
In the early Liáng dynasty, he was impeached for licentious behavior within his household and murder.
The appropriate authorities memorialized
to deliberate on his permanent disqualification.
Zǐjìn later conspired to rebel,
and both brothers were executed.
Chángshā Wēiwáng Huǎng (晃), courtesy name Xuānmíng (宣明),
was Emperor Tàizǔ's (太祖) fourth son.
He was strong and brave in his youth,
and was loved by Emperor Tàizǔ.
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, he was appointed Mìshū Láng (祕書郎) and Shàolíng Wáng Yǒu (邵陵王友) but
did not take up the posts.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (昇明) (478 CE),
he replaced his elder brother Yìng (映) as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and governor of the two commanderies of Huáinán (淮南) and Xuānchéng (宣城).
Initially,
when Shěn Yōuzhí's (沈攸之) rebellion broke out,
Huǎng was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and often joined military exercises.
His magnificence shone throughout the capital's streets.
At the time, people made a saying about him:
"Brilliant, brilliant is Xiāo (蕭) the Fourth's parasol!"
In the same year,
he was promoted to Chíjié (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xīyáng (西陽) and other prefectures in the two provinces of Yù (豫) and Sī (司) (and Yǐngzhōu (郢州)),
Xīzhōngláng Jiāngjūn (西中郎將), and Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州).
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
Huǎng wanted to participate in state affairs,
but was always restrained by the Diǎnqiān (典籤).
Huǎng seized and killed the Diǎnqiān,
which greatly enraged the Emperor.
He personally issued an imperial edict granting him a beating with a staff.
Soon after, he was transferred to Shǐ Chíjié (使持節), Governor-General of Military Affairs of the two provinces of Nánxú (南徐) and Yǔn (袞), Hòujiāngjūn (後將軍), and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
When Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) was Crown Prince,
he paid respects at Wǔjìn Líng (武進陵),
and held a fighting display at Qū'ā (曲阿) Hòuhú (後湖).
He ordered Huǎng to lead the cavalry.
The Emperor heard of this
and was again displeased.
He was brought back to the capital as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍).
Due to national mourning,
he was relieved of his Shìzhōng (侍中) post
and given the added title of Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍).
When Emperor Tàizǔ was on his deathbed,
he entrusted Huǎng to Emperor Shìzǔ,
advising him to keep Huǎng in a close, important position
and not let him go out to distant posts.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (483 CE),
the Emperor transferred Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng (竟陵王子良), Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州), to Nányǔnzhōu (南兗州).
Huǎng was appointed Shǐ Chíjié (使持節), Governor-General of Military Affairs of the two provinces of Nánxú (南徐) and Yǔn (袞), Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍), and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
He was brought back to the capital as Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍)
and Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監).
Among the princes in the capital,
only forty personal guards with swords were allowed.
Huǎng, who loved military adornments,
privately brought back several hundred armed retainers to the capital
when he returned from Xúzhōu (徐州),
which was discovered by the security officials
who threw them into the Jiāng (江) river.
Emperor Shìzǔ forbade princes from keeping private retinues.
Hearing of this, he was greatly enraged
and intended to punish him according to the law.
Yùzhāng Wáng Yì (豫章王嶷) bowed before the Emperor, weeping, saying:
"Huǎng's crime truly cannot be excused.
Your Majesty should recall the late emperor's thoughts about Bái Xiàng (白象)."
[Bái Xiàng (白象)]
was Huǎng's childhood name.
When Emperor Tàizǔ was gravely ill,
he warned Emperor Shìzǔ, saying:
"If the Sòng (宋) clan had not plotted against each other,
how could other clans have taken advantage of their decline?
You must deeply heed this warning."
Therefore, Emperor Shìzǔ ultimately had no ill intentions.
However, Huǎng also did not receive imperial favor or trust.
Contemporary commentators considered Emperor Shìzǔ superior to Wèi Wén (魏文) (Emperor Wén of Wèi)
and inferior to Hàn Míng (漢明) (Emperor Míng of Hàn).
Soon, Huǎng was given the added title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍),
then transferred to Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹),
with his Chángshì (常侍) and Jiāngjūn (將軍) titles remaining as before.
He was also appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍),
with his Zhènjūn (鎮軍) title remaining as before.
Soon after, he was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
with his Shìzhōng (侍中) title remaining as before.
He was granted an oil-painted carriage
and a set of drum and wind instruments.
In the eighth year (490 CE),
he passed away
at the age of thirty-one.
He was bestowed with funerary objects from the eastern garden,
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
Keeping his original rank,
he was posthumously granted Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
Emperor Shìzǔ once visited Zhōngshān (鍾山).
Huǎng accompanied the imperial retinue,
and pierced a dead tree stump by the roadside with his horse spear.
The Emperor ordered several attendants to pull it out,
but the silver binding all crumpled up,
and the spear would not come out.
Then he ordered Huǎng to ride his horse and pull it out again,
and it came out immediately.
Whenever excellent horses were presented from distant prefectures,
the Emperor would always order Huǎng to test them in Huálín (華林) Garden.
Emperor Tàizǔ often said:
"This is my family's Rènmín (任城)."
Emperor Shìzǔ, following this sentiment,
therefore gave him the posthumous title Wēi (威).
Wǔlíng Zhāowáng Niàn (誾), courtesy name Xuānzhào (宣照),
His mother, Lady Luó (羅氏),
while accompanying Emperor Tàizǔ in Huáinán (淮南),
was executed for a crime.
[Niàn (誾) was four years old,
but his longing and remembrance were no different from an adult's],
which is why Niàn (誾) was loved.
then transferred to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍).
Niàn (誾) was naturally intelligent and outstanding,
skilled in Weiqi (弈).
He composed short poems with the other princes,
in the style of Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運),
and presented them to the Emperor.
The Emperor replied:
"Your twenty characters are the best among all the children's works.
However, Kānglè (康樂) (Xiè Língyùn) was uninhibited,
and his style lacked clear beginning and end.
Ānrén (安仁) (Pān Yuè) and Shìhéng (士衡) (Lù Jī) are deeply worthy of respect,
and Yán Yánzhī (顏延之) is next after them."
In the third year of Jiànyuán (建元) (481 CE),
with his Jiāngjūn (將軍) title remaining as before.
The Emperor sent the scholar Liú Huán (劉瓛) to the commandery
to lecture Niàn (誾) on the Five Classics.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍).
He was brought back to the capital as Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
with his Jiāngjūn (將軍) title remaining as before.
He was then transferred to Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍)
and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿).
He again served as Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
then transferred to Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書),
with his Chángshì (常侍) title remaining as before.
Niàn (誾) was not favored by Emperor Shìzǔ,
and never held a governorship in a distant region.
He often offended the Emperor with his words.
Emperor Shìzǔ once visited Yùzhāng Wáng Yì's (豫章王嶷) eastern garden to feast the princes,
but did not summon Niàn (誾).
Yì (嶷) said:
"The scenery is exceptionally beautiful today.
I deeply miss Wǔlíng (武陵)."
Niàn (誾) was skilled in archery,
often hitting the target.
He looked around at those present and said:
"How about my skill?"
The Emperor's expression changed greatly.
Yì (嶷) said:
"Fifth brother is usually not like this.
Today, one could say he relies on imperial majesty."
The Emperor's anger then dissipated.
Later, during an archery contest at Huálín (華林) Garden,
the Emperor commanded Niàn (誾) to hit the target consecutively.
He shot six arrows in total,
hitting the target five times and the skin once.
He was awarded fifty thousand coins.
Once, at an imperial banquet, the Emperor raised his cup to propose a toast to Niàn (誾).
Niàn (誾) said:
"Your Majesty has never granted this position to your servant."
The Emperor turned his face away without answering.
After a long time,
he was sent out as Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
with his Chángshì (常侍) title remaining as before.
As Niàn (誾) was about to leave to govern a distant region,
the Emperor requested Niàn's (誾) residence to give to the other imperial princes.
Niàn (誾) said:
"The late emperor bestowed this residence upon your servant,
so that your servant would have a place to sing and weep.
If Your Majesty wishes to exchange a province for a residence,
your servant requests not to exchange a residence for a province."
his Diǎnqiān (典籤) Zhào Wòzhī (趙渥之) reported Niàn's (誾) transgressions.
Thereupon, he was recalled to serve as Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū (左民尚書).
Shortly after, he was transferred to Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍)
and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿),
consistently failing to achieve his ambitions.
During the Winter Solstice greetings,
all the princes came out,
but Niàn (誾) arrived late.
The Emperor had already returned to the private hall.
Hearing of Niàn's (誾) arrival,
he granted him an audience and asked him about it.
Niàn (誾) claimed his ox was weak
and could not make good time.
The Emperor ordered the chariot office to provide him with an imperial ox.
He also ordered the supervisor of guests:
"From now on, if any princes who come do not follow the usual practice,
they are not to be announced again."
While on public duty, [Qiū] Niàn returned via the residence of Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglín.
One winter month, he encountered a beggar on the road,
and took off his jacket to give it to him.
Zǐliáng saw [Qiū] Niàn's clothes were thin,
and offered a jacket to [Qiū] Niàn.
[Qiū] Niàn said:
"How am I any different from that person I just helped?"
Shàngshūlìng Wáng Jiǎn visited [Qiū] Niàn.
[Qiū] Niàn kept Jiǎn and served a meal,
which consisted only of cabbage and fish on a plate.
He also named the mountain behind the hall
"Shǒuyáng,"
probably resenting his poverty.
Soon, he became Dānyáng Yǐn,
with the titles Chángshì and Jiāngjūn as before.
He no longer appointed a Xíngshì,
and was able to personally oversee government affairs.
He was transferred to Shìzhōng,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
He was granted an oil-canopied carriage.
He was also granted two attendants.
When Shìzǔ was on his deathbed,
an imperial edict appointed him Wèi Jiāngjūn,
with Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and granted a set of drums and wind instruments.
While the late emperor was in mourning,
Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglín was in the palace,
and the Grandson had not yet been enthroned.
Public opinion was noisy and uncertain.
[Qiū] Niàn spoke among the crowd:
"If the eldest is to be enthroned, then it should be me.
If the嫡 descendant is to be enthroned, then it should be the Grandson."
Once Yùlín was enthroned,
he relied heavily on him.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
at the age of twenty-eight,
he passed away.
He was granted the secret funerary items of the East Garden
and court attire.
He was posthumously granted Sīkōng,
with Shìzhōng as before.
He was granted a Jié,
and twenty swordsmen.
Ānchéng Gōngwáng Gǎo, courtesy name Xuānyào,
was the sixth son of Tàizǔ.
In the second year of Jiànkē,
he was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
garrisoned at Shítou Wèi,
and oversaw military affairs.
In the fourth year,
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Dū Jiāngzhōu Yùzhōu zhī Jìnxī Zhūjūnshì, Nán Zhōnglángjiāng, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
The following year,
he became Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Shìzhōng,
and concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was transferred to Zhōngshūlìng.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Cíbù Shàngshū,
and concurrently Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
In the sixth year,
he was sent out as Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì,
Mìshūjiān,
and concurrently oversaw Shítou Wèi affairs.
Gǎo was gentle, harmonious, and often ill.
He passed away that summer,
at the age of twenty-four.
He was posthumously granted Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
with Chángshì as before.
Póyángwáng Qiāng, courtesy name Xuānsháo,
was the seventh son of Tàizǔ.
In the fourth year of Jiànwú,
when Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Qiāng was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dū Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìnglín Sīzhōu zhī Suíjùn Jūnshì, Běi Zhōnglángjiāng, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year,
he became Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and was transferred to Shìzhōng,
and concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Soon after, he was granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and promoted to Fǔjūn.
He was sent out as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with Chángshì as before.
In the ninth year,
he began to personally handle affairs of the commandery and province.
He was granted Shǐchíjié, Dū Jiāngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Ānnán Jiāngjūn,
and established a staff,
with Chángshì as before.
Two years prior, the Jiāngzhōu commandery had been abolished,
and now it was restored.
In the eleventh year,
he became Lǐngjūn,
with Chángshì as before.
Qiāng was harmonious, fraternal, and well-behaved,
and was favored by Shìzǔ.
The appointment of Lǐngjūn
was unprecedented among the princes of the Qí dynasty.
Qiāng managed affairs in his office without obstruction,
and was praised at the time.
When the imperial carriage went on outings,
he often guarded and accompanied it,
and his favored treatment was second only to Prince Yùzhāng Yí.
That year,
he was granted an oil-canopied carriage.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè,
with Chángshì as before.
Shortly after, he was transferred to Shìzhōng, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and was allowed to command troops and establish a staff.
Qiāng was composed and understood people's sentiments,
and was trusted by Yùlínwáng.
Yùlín suspected Gāozōng,
and when the princes came to inquire,
he exclusively kept Qiāng and said to him:
"Have you heard about Luán, regarding the emperor's person?"
Qiāng said:
"Your subject Luán is the most senior among the imperial relatives,
and was entrusted by the late emperor.
We are all still young,
and the pillar of the court
is only Luán.
I hope Your Majesty will not worry about it."
Yùlín then told Xú Lóngjū:
"I wanted to plot with you to seize Luán,
but since you disagree,
I cannot do it alone,
so I will wait a little longer."
When Yùlín was deposed,
Qiāng was unaware of it.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
he was promoted to Sītú,
with Shìzhōng and Piàojì as before.
Gāozōng was garrisoned at Dōngfǔ,
and his power and influence gradually became distinct.
Whenever Qiāng visited,
Gāozōng would always rush out in slippers to greet Qiāng at his carriage.
When they spoke of family and state,
he wept tears.
Qiāng consequently trusted him.
However, within the palace and government offices, everyone turned their attention to Qiāng,
persuading Qiāng to enter the palace, raise troops, and assist in government.
Zhìjújiān Xiè Càn persuaded Qiāng and Prince Zǐlóng of Suí, saying:
"Your Highness just needs to ride an oil-canopied carriage into the palace,
bring the Son of Heaven out and place him in the court,
with the two princes flanking him to issue commands,
and we will close the city gates and arm ourselves.
Who would dare to disobey?
The people of the eastern city will simply bind and deliver Xiāo Lìng."
Zǐlóng wanted to finalize the plan,
but Qiāng considered that the palace and government troops had all been transferred to Dōngfǔ,
and also worried that the matter would be difficult to accomplish quickly.
He was very hesitant.
The cavalry commander Liú Jù,
an old associate from Shìzǔ's time,
approached Qiāng, requesting a private audience,
and repeatedly bowed his head, urging Qiāng to take action.
Qiāng ordered his carriage and was about to enter,
but turned back inside to bid farewell to his mother, Consort Lù Tàifēi.
Night fell, and he failed to depart.
A few days later,
Gāozōng sent two thousand men to surround Qiāng's residence and kill him.
Xiè Càn and others were also killed.
Qiāng was twenty-six years old at the time.
All the princes who were killed
were victims of troops sent at night to surround their residences,
who would chop down gates, smash walls, and storm in with shouts and clamor.
All their family property was sealed and registered.
Guìyáng Wáng Shuò 字 Xuānlǎng,
was the eighth son of Tài zǔ.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (484 CE),
he was dispatched as the Cìshǐ of Nánxú Zhōu,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
Throughout successive generations of garrison administrations,
it was only when Shuò was sent to a frontier command
that the military government was first reduced.
In the fourth year (486 CE),
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
In the sixth year (488 CE),
he was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng
and Dùzhī Shàngshū.
In the seventh year (489 CE),
he was again transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì.
At that time, Póyáng Wáng Qiāng was fond of literature,
while Shuò was fond of famous theories (or principles),
and people of the time referred to them as
"Pó-Guì".
In the tenth year (492 CE),
he was transferred to Tàicháng,
with his Chángshì position remaining as before.
Shuò was thin and frail, suffering from a chronic cold illness,
and was often lying on his pillow.
Shìzǔ personally visited him,
and bestowed upon him a bed, curtains, quilt, and mattress.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was additionally granted the title Qián Jiāngjūn.
He was given an oil-canopy carriage
and also two attendants.
When Hǎilíng was enthroned,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and given command of troops and a staff.
After Póyáng Wáng was murdered,
Shuò was transferred to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with the privilege of establishing an administration equivalent to the Sān Sī.
Shuò felt uneasy.
After returning from visiting Gāozōng at the Eastern Prefecture,
he said to his attendants,
"The Lù Gōng received me very warmly just now,
and kept me for a long time, unwilling to let me go,
but his face showed an expression of shame.
This certainly means he intends to kill me."
In the third watch of the night,
soldiers arrived and he was murdered.
He was twenty-five years old at the time.
Shǐxīng Jiǎn Wáng Jiàn 字 Xuānchè,
was the tenth son of Tài zǔ.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as Guǎngxīng Wáng,
and later his state was moved to Suí Jùn and his title changed.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (484 CE),
Shìzǔ first appointed Jiàn as Chíjíe, Dūdū Yì Níng Èr Zhōu Jūnjì, Qián Jiāngjūn, and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Duàn Zǔ, a commoner from Shífāng, Guǎnghàn, presented a chún yú to Jiàn.
It was an ancient ritual instrument.
It was three chi six cun six fen high,
with a circumference of two chi four cun,
round like a tube,
its bronze color was black like lacquer,
and very thin.
On top was a bronze horse.
If a rope was used to suspend the horse,
making it about one chi above the ground,
and water was poured into it,
and also a vessel of water was placed below it,
and a stalk of芒 (mang) grass was held at its center and knelt down to inject into the chún yú,
then by shaking the grass with one's hand,
its sound would be like thunder,
a clear resonance that would only cease after a long while.
This was anciently used to regulate music.
In the fifth year (487 CE),
Jiàn presented a dragon horn,
nine chi three cun long,
red in color,
with patterns.
In the eighth year (490 CE),
he was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
The following year (491 CE),
he became Sànqí Chángshì,
Mìshū Jiān,
and concurrently in charge of Shítóu Wù matters.
As the Emperor had been separated from Jiàn for a long time,
the imperial carriage went to Shítóu for a banquet and bestowed rewards.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
but before he could assume the post,
he fell ill.
When a new residence in Qīngyáng Xiàng was completed for Nánkāng Zǐ Lín,
the imperial carriage and the imperial concubines went to the residence for joyous feasting.
On that day, Jiàn's illness worsened.
The Emperor sent riders one after another to inquire about his health,
and issued an edict to stop the music for him.
He died
at the age of twenty-one.
He was posthumously granted Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his original and newly appointed official positions all remaining as before.
Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng 字 Xuānyǐng,
was the twelfth son of Tài zǔ.
〔一七〕In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng (487 CE),
he was Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng and Píngchāng.
He was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì.
In the seventh year (489 CE),
he was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
then again transferred to Shìzhōng,
and concurrently in charge of Shítóu Wù matters.
In the ninth year (491 CE),
he was dispatched as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Yùlín was enthroned,
he was additionally granted Sànqí Chángshì.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he entered the court as Shìzhōng,
and concurrently led Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
soon after additionally Mìshū Jiān.
Fēng was fond of zither and books,
and possessed martial prowess.
When Gāozōng massacred the various princes,
Fēng sent a letter reproaching him,
but his attendants did not deliver it.
Gāozōng deeply feared him.
He dared not arrest Fēng at his residence,
so he made him concurrently a sacrificial officer at the Tàimiào.
At night, he sent soldiers to arrest him within the temple.
When Fēng came out and boarded the carriage,
the soldiers wanted to get on the carriage to restrain him.
Fēng struck back several people with his hand,
all of whom fell to the ground immediately.
Thus, those who dared to approach him were then forced to harm him.
He was twenty years old at the time.
Nánpíng Wáng Ruì 字 Xuānyì,
was the fifteenth son of Tài zǔ.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (489 CE),
he became Sànqí Chángshì,
and soon after concurrently led Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
The following year (490 CE),
he became Zuǒmín Shàngshū.
He was diligent and attentive in his daily court duties,
and never suffered from illness.
The Emperor praised him for this.
In the tenth year (492 CE),
he was dispatched as Chíjíe, Dūdū Xiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Nánzhōngláng Jiāng, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
as a reward for Ruì.
When Yùlín was enthroned,
he was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
when the various princes were murdered,
Péi Shúyè was sent to pacify Xúnyáng,
and then advanced to Xiāngzhōu.
Ruì's defense officer Zhōu Bóyù urged Ruì to resist Shúyè,
but the strength of the prefecture and administration was too weak to act.
Ruì was murdered
at the age of nineteen.
