Sūn Láng'ér, a student who served Xiáng, reported: 'Xiáng has recently been drinking excessively,
his speech has been unrestrained and wild,
speaking of the imperial court,
and also using disrespectful language,
indeed, not avoiding those around him,
which cannot be put to paper.
His elder brother Zhěng was formerly at Guǎngzhōu,
and died while in office.
Last year, a request was made to retrieve the coffin.
On its return, when it reached Dàléi,
it was heard that Xiáng argued furiously with Zhěng's wife, Mèng, over property.
Xiáng then abandoned it and returned earlier.
Later, before it reached Quètóu,
that night, it was robbed.
All the female attendants were violated by the villains.'
What was reported matches the rumors.
We request that he be dismissed from office and handed over to the Tíngwèi. 」
The Emperor separately dispatched an edict to Xiáng, saying:
「You have always lacked moral conduct,
which is known throughout the court and the land.
You lightly abandoned your kin,
and disparaged your elder brother and sister-in-law.
This is a deficiency in your family conduct,
and concerns no one else.
As for your talent and knowledge,
what is there to discuss?
Your position involves a clean path (of officialdom),
and by your status, you are not wronged.
Why then do you carelessly vent your spleen,
maligning court officials,
standing at banquets to speak,
always taking criticism and judgment as your pretext?
I had hoped that as you are now advanced in years,
you would be able to rouse yourself to reform,
and I looked forward daily to your repentance and change.
However, what I hear now,
is that your behavior has only worsened,
tumultuously criticizing the imperial court,
not sparing high or low,
uttering extreme words without restraint,
publicly exposing your insolence to the ears of all.
Recently, I saw your "Shadow Connected Pearls,"
which conveys a rebellious and arrogant sentiment,
and this cannot be allowed to continue.
Have you not seen Xiè Chāozōng?
His talent is secondary,
so he was before you.
What happened to him is perhaps one in a hundred (compared to your misdeeds).
I shall spare your life,
and make you reflect on your transgressions from a thousand miles away.
If you can reform,
I shall allow you to return. 」
Xiáng's statement was interrogated in prison.
Xiáng replied:
「I was questioned, 'In youth, you practiced cunning and strangeness,
and in adulthood, you did not repent.
Recently, you have been drinking excessively,
carelessly criticizing the Emperor,
repeatedly disparaging revered officials,
always uttering foul words,
not sparing high or low.'
I humbly reply to the imperial decree.
I, your prisoner, entered officialdom from humble origins,
for over twenty years.
Dwelling in obscurity among the weeds,
without understanding the world.
At the beginning of the imperial reign,
I was fortunate to be promoted.
The Jìjiǔ and Zhǔbù posts,
were both from the previous dynasty's prime minister's residence.
Under the sacred and enlightened rule,
my honors and favors increased significantly.
As Zīyì Zhōngláng,
I received grace twice in one year.
At grand banquets and splendid feasts,
I always participated at the end of the
〔一一〕ranks, and during morning court, I offered inquiries,
occasionally receiving the Emperor's radiance.
Though I, your prisoner, am stubborn and foolish,
how could I not recognize such grace?
What grievances or resentments could I have,
that I would dare to make mocking comments?
Since I, your prisoner, served in various administrations,
I have served four princes: as Wǔlíng Gōngcáo,
for a total of two years;
as Chángshā Zīyì,
for a short period;
serving under the Dà Sīmǎ,
and receiving favor;
as Piàojì Zhōngláng,
directly serving for a few days;
His Highness of Línchuān did not forsake an insect or an ant like me,
and granted me participation in literary discussions.
His Highness the Sītú is brilliant in literary virtue,
and the whole realm inclines towards him.
I, your prisoner, did not limit myself by my low status or distance,
but inquired after him as was customary,
and paid respects at appropriate times,
also receiving his consideration and comments.
As for the other princes,
I have not yet paid respectful obeisance to them.
Since I have not served under them,
there is no reason for partiality.
Imperial edicts and proclamations,
command that if there are doubts, one should report them.
I, your prisoner, considered the Heavenly Sun (Emperor) to be far removed,
and did not dare to defile him.
For private matters of doubt,
Wèi Jiāngjūn Chén Jiǎn,
a prime minister of the sacred court,
and a respected figure of his time,
I, your prisoner, judging my own talent to be limited,
secretly consulted Jiǎn,
and Jiǎn provided a compromise (or mediated).
The written records still exist.
I do not understand how this could be construed as daring to 'repeatedly disparage revered officials.'
As for saying I, your prisoner, 'carelessly criticized the Emperor,'
to whom did I say it?
If I said it to someone,
then there should be a principal witness,
how could there be an event without a trace,
only to be falsely accused?
My nature, as known to my close acquaintances, cannot tolerate alcohol.
My close acquaintances all know this.
If I force myself to drink a sheng,
I am already confused and drunk."
He personally presented his defense for all other matters.
Thereupon, he was exiled to Guǎngzhōu.
When Xiáng arrived in Guǎngzhōu,
he was discontented,
drank excessively all day,
and died of illness a short while later,
at the age of thirty-nine.
Xiáng's paternal grand-cousin, Biāo,
was the rightful heir of Xiáng's great-grandfather, Mùzhī.
In the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
he was demoted and enfeoffed as the Duke of Nánkāng Xiàn,
〔一二〕and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was deprived of his title for failing to maintain the ancestral temple and tomb.
Later, he became Yǔlín Jiān.
In the ninth year,
he was again impeached for living separately from the mother of his deceased younger brother, Yáng,
and not taking care of her.
When Yáng died, she was not prepared for burial.
Huìshǒu, a nun from Chóngshèng Sì, shaved her head and became a nun,
used five hundred coins to buy a coffin,
and sent her for burial in the Liú tomb using a Nirvāṇa carriage.
This was reported by the relevant authorities,
but the matter was suppressed and not publicized.
The historian says: Emperor Wén of Wèi said,
"Literary men do not protect their minor conduct,"
which is the same in ancient and modern times.
It is because they know their feelings run deep,
and they have no contention in external matters,
beyond their person and fame,
everything else can be despised.
Since they follow this path,
its flaws spread further,
and wherever their reputation extends,
they incur opposition from the world.
That which they previously valued in themselves
instead turns into self-harm.
Therefore, enlightened people establish teachings,
performing them but not relying on them.
A eulogy says: Chāo Zōng harbored literature,
((coarse)) [Zǔ] structured remaining fragrance.
his words also stood out from the crowd.
He defied the court and lost proper conduct,
banished to the southern shore.

Biographies Volume 18: Dào Huī, Liú Qūn, Yú Cóng, Hú Xiézhī
Dào Huī, courtesy name Màoqiān,
was a native of Wǔyuán, Péngchéng.
His grandfather, Yànzhī,
was a General of Cavalry (Piaojì Jiāngjūn) during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Zhòngdù,
was a Cavalier Attendant Gentleman (Piaojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
Huī inherited the title of Duke of Jiànchāng.
He began his career as a Grand Academy Erudite (Tàixué Bóshì),
then was appointed Envoy-Escort Commandant (Fèngchē Dūwèi),
and provisionally served as Magistrate of Yánlíng.
Not finding this enjoyable,
he resigned from office.
He was appointed Northern Departmental Commandant (Běi Zhōngláng Xíngcānjūn) to the Prince of Xīn'ān,
but was dismissed due to official business.
He was appointed Pacifying Army Staff Officer (Fǔjūn Cānjūn) to the Prince of Xīn'ān.
Before he could take up the post,
Zǐluán, the Prince of Xīn'ān, was killed.
He was then appointed acting Supervising Secretary of the Left Bureau of the Ministry of Populace (Chángjiān Shàngshū Zuǒ Mínlángzhōng).
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
wishing to win popular support,
and as Huī was a descendant of meritorious officials,
he was promoted to Head of the Crown Prince's Household (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
He was appointed Pacifying South Consultant and Staff Officer (Ānnán Zīyì Cānjūn) to Wáng Jǐngwén.
Huī was of a wealthy and powerful family,
and maintained a luxurious lifestyle.
His mansion, gardens, and ponds
were the finest in the capital.
His courtesans and concubines were skilled
and all of the highest quality.
His talent and disposition were ample and refined,
and he was good at cultivating friendships.
His kitchens were abundant and lavish,
often hosting many guests.
Emperor Míng asked for his favorite courtesan, Chén Yùzhū,
but Huī did not give her up.
He was forced to surrender her,
and Huī harbored considerable resentment.
The Emperor ordered officials to falsely accuse Huī of a crime,
and he was handed over to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi),
intending to kill him.
After Huī was imprisoned,
his beard and hair turned white in a few nights.
He was spared death,
confined to the Imperial Arsenal (Shàngfāng),
and his enfeoffment was taken away and given to his younger brother, Bēn.
From then on, Huī rejected indulgence in luxury and pleasure,
and instead established himself through frugality and simplicity.
The Emperor appointed Huī as Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to Yáng Xīgōng's Garrison General Who Keeps the Peace (Níngshuòfǔ),
and transferred Liú Yùn to Assistant General (Fǔguó) and Wáng Jǐngwén to General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Cānjūn).
All declined due to illness and did not take up their posts.
Soon after, he was provisionally appointed General Who Spreads Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn)
and then Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to the Prince of Guìyáng's General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán).
He was transferred to Gentleman of the Palace (Tōngzhí Láng)
and then relieved of his duties.
After the Emperor's death,
his younger brother Bēn petitioned to yield his enfeoffment back to Huī,
and the court approved.
He was promoted to Senior Secretary of the Left (Zuǒ Xīshǔ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú),
but again did not take up the post.
He remained at home for several years.
His younger brother Dùn

served as General Who Establishes Distant Might (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk of the Assistant General (Fǔguó Chángshǐ), and Administrator of Nánhǎi (Nánhǎi Tàishǒu) in Guǎngzhōu during the Yuánhuī era.
In the first year of Shēngmíng (477 CE),
Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
and the Inspector (Cìshǐ), Chén Xiǎndá, raised an army to respond to the court.
Dùn, due to his hesitation, was killed.
Dùn's family, who were in the capital,
returned home from the countryside at night.
They saw two or three people using chalk to brush their family's gate.
In an instant, it vanished,
and the next day, news of Dùn's death arrived.
Huī was panic-stricken
and went to Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) to express his gratitude.
He was immediately appointed Consultant and Staff Officer (Zīyì Cānjūn) in the Central Army (Zhōngjūn) of Emperor Shìzǔ.
In the early Jiànyuán era (479 CE),
he was promoted to Senior Clerk of the Right (Yòuchángshǐ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú).
He went out to serve as Administrator of Yǒngjiā (Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu),
then became Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng),
and was relieved of his duties.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
but did not take up the post.
He was also appointed Chief Clerk of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ) to the Prince of Chángshā
and Senior Clerk of the Left (Zuǒchángshǐ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú).
During the Sòng era,
the Emperor frequently visited and held gatherings at Huī's home.
Once, he accompanied Emperor Míng hunting pheasants in the countryside.
Feeling thirsty and tired,
Huī obtained some early green cucumbers
and shared them with the Emperor, cutting them open and eating them together.
The Emperor remembered his old kindness,
and his regard for him was very warm.
By this time, he was promoted three times in one year.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (483 CE),
he was given the additional title of Assistant General (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn)
and transferred to Palace Remonstrant (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
When the Emperor's carriage visited Dānyáng Commandery for a banquet,
Huī, relying on his old relationship,
was rude to his colleagues after drinking,
and his speech and laughter were excessive.
He was impeached by Assistant Palace Remonstrant (Zuǒchéng) Yú Gǎozhī
and redeemed himself with a fine.
In the third year (485 CE),
he again became Senior Clerk of the Left (Zuǒchángshǐ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú)
and was transferred to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
When he accompanied Prince Zǐlóng, who held the post of Administrator of Péngchéng Commandery,
Huī visited him
but did not observe the proper respect for a civil official.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities
and dismissed from office.
After a long time,
he served as Palace Remonstrant (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) in plain clothes (bái yī).
He was transferred to Chief Clerk (Piaojì Chángshǐ) to the Prince of Línchuān's General of Cavalry (Piaojì),
then Senior Clerk of the Left (Zuǒchángshǐ) to the Minister of Works (Sītú),
promoted to Minister of Five Militias (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and then went out to serve as Assistant General (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ) to the Prince of Lúlíng.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
Before the mourning period ended,
he died in the eighth year (490 CE),
at the age of fifty-eight.
His younger brother, Bēn,
first served as Principal Scribe (Zhǔbù) to the Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi)
and Envoy-Escort Commandant (Fèngchē Dūwèi).
In the early Shēngmíng era,
he became Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Láng)
and Consultant (Zīyì) to Grand Ancestor's General of Cavalry (Piaojì).
In the Jiànyuán era,
he became Cavalier Attendant Gentleman (Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ)
and then died.
Bēn's younger brother, Tǎn,
first assumed office as Western Registrar (Xīcáo) in his home province.
In the second year of Shēngmíng (478 CE),
he also became Staff Officer (Cānjūn) to Grand Ancestor's General of Cavalry (Piaojì).
He successively served as Consultant (Zīyì) in the two administrations of the Prince of Yùzhāng's General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī) and General of Cavalry (Piaojì).
Tǎn had a beautiful beard,
and had an old relationship with Emperor Shìzǔ and the Prince of Yùzhāng.
Tǎn then followed the administration, being transferred to Staff Officer (Cānjūn) in the two administrations of Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
He went out to serve as Administrator of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Nèishǐ),
and after returning, he again became Consultant (Zīyì) to the Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ)
and Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōngshū Láng),
and then died.
Liú Qūn, courtesy name Shìcāo,
was a native of Ānshànglǐ, Péngchéng.
The Liú family of Péngchéng descended from King Yuán of Chǔ
and was divided into three hamlets (sānlǐ)
to distinguish them from the imperial clan of the Sòng dynasty.
His grandfather, Yǐngzhī,
was Administrator of the two commanderies of Rǔnán and Xīncài.
His father, Miǎn,
was Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
When Liú Yánsūn was Inspector of Nánxú Province,
he first appointed Qūn as Staff Officer (Cóngshì).
He accompanied his father Miǎn in campaigning against Prince Dàn of Jìnglíng in Guǎnglíng.
For his merits, he was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
He was transferred to Principal Scribe (Zhǔbù) of the Prince of Zōng's Pacifying Barbarians General (Níngmánfǔ)
and Cavalier Attendant Gentleman (Qíbīng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Jiàn'ān's Minister of Works (Sītú).
He again accompanied his father Miǎn in campaigning against Yīn Yǎn in Shòuchūn.
They won multiple battles at Héngtáng and Sǐhǔ.
He successively served as Supernumerary Gentleman (Yuánwàiláng)
and Staff Officer (Cānjūn) in the two administrations of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Minister of Works (Sītú).
He replaced Emperor Shìzǔ as Supervising Secretary of the Bureau of Treasury (Kùbù Láng) in the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū).
He was promoted to General Who Manifests Martial Might (Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Shǔ Commandery (Shǔjùn Tàishǒu).
Before he could take up this post,
he again accompanied his father Miǎn in campaigning.
He was provisionally appointed General Who Keeps the Peace (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn)
and granted the title of Heir Apparent to the Marquis of Póyáng County.
He was transferred to Mid-Army Staff Officer (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Guìyáng's General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi).
He served directly in the palace with Emperor Shìzǔ
and was favored and trusted by Emperor Míng.
Because of this, he became very close to Emperor Shìzǔ.
He was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng,
then sent out as Ānyuǎn Hùjūn and Wǔlíng Nèishǐ.
To the south of the commandery, an ancient levee on the river
had long been abandoned and unrepaired.
Liú Qūn began its repair but
before it was completed, the river water suddenly rose.
The common people abandoned their work and fled.
Liú Qūn personally led and encouraged them,
and thus it was completed.
Shào Róngxīng from Hànshòu, whose six generations lived under the same roof,
had his household recognized by imperial edict.
Liú Qūn was strong, resourceful, and followed the current trends,
excelling among common folk.
The Barbarian King Tián Tóng lived in the mountains,
aged over a hundred years.
When Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān was the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
Tián Tóng came out to pay respects.
At this time, he again came out to pay respects to Liú Qūn.
When Emperor Míng died,
he submitted a memorial rushing back to the capital,
and was ordered to return to the capital with his commandery.
Several thousand officials and common people saw him off.
Liú Qūn shook hands with each person,
and was moved to tears.
The common people were touched by this
and gave him generous gifts.
He was then appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
During the Guìyáng rebellion,
he was given the additional title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
to assist in defending Shítou.
His father, Liú Miǎn, died in battle at Dàhéng.
Liú Qūn was ill at the time,
and was carried along the roadside,
wailing and searching for Liú Miǎn's corpse.
Liú Miǎn's corpse
had a wound and was missing a piece from the back of the neck; Liú Qūn cut his hair to fill it.
He mourned
by the grave, not wearing padded clothes in winter.
Tàizǔ replaced Liú Miǎn as Lǐngjūn,
and had always been good friends with Liú Miǎn.
He wrote to admonish Liú Qūn, saying:
"I learn that your utmost filial piety has caused you to waste away,
and has turned into a dangerous worry,
which deeply saddens me.
To fully preserve life while mourning,
is the clear principle of the former kings.
How can one cast off silk floss,
remove warm mats,
and with such sorrowful wailing,
fully realize one's filial nature?
You should deeply consider the former teachings,
and restrain yourself a little."
When Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù rebelled,
Tàizǔ commanded all armies and encamped at Xuánwǔ Hú.
Liú Qūn had just completed his mourning period.
Tàizǔ wanted him to lead a branch army,
and summoned Liú Qūn and his brothers for an audience.
They were all emaciated and had changed in appearance,
so he stopped the plan.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Láng,
and acted as Sòng Nányáng Bā Wáng Shì.
He was then promoted to Nányáng Wáng Nán Zhōngláng Sīmǎ and Chángshā Nèishǐ,
acting as the Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Before he set out,
when the imperial enterprise was first established,
Liú Qūn was the first to show his sincerity and integrity.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
he was given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
Shìzǔ, garrisoned at Pénchéng,
submitted a memorial to campaign west,
requesting Liú Qūn to substitute for him.
Since Shìzǔ did not go,
Liú Qūn was appointed Huángmén Láng,
acting as the Governor of Wú Jùn.
Soon after, he was promoted to Jìn Xī Wáng Fǔjūn Zhōngjūn Èr Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ,
acting as the Governor of Yángzhōu.
He was then sent out as Chíjí, Dūdū Guǎngzhōu, Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general title as before.
He inherited the title of Póyáng Xiàn Hóu.
When Shìzǔ returned from Xúnyáng,
he met Liú Qūn on a boat by the riverbank.
They joyfully reminisced about old times,
and he stayed for over ten days before disembarking.
He sent Wénhuì Tàizǐ and Jìnglíng Wáng Ziliáng to adjust their attire and shoes
and show respect to his father's friend.
When Tàizǔ received the abdication,
his state title was abolished.
He was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
Xiàhóu Gōngshū, Píngxī Jìshì Cānjūn, submitted a memorial,
stating that Liú Yuánjǐng was a meritorious official of the restoration,
and Liú Miǎn died for the royal cause,
so their enfeoffments should be preserved.
The imperial edict said:
"The rise and fall with fate
has been so since ancient times;
the court's decision is already made,
and no further consideration is permissible."
Initially,
when Cāngwú was deposed,
Tàizǔ convened a meeting at the Zhōnghuámén.
He saw Liú Qūn
and asked him: "Were you on duty yesterday?"
Liú Qūn replied:
"I was indeed on duty yesterday,
but my words were urgently needed outside."
At this time, the Emperor said to Liú Qūn:
"The opportunity for fame and merit
is not forgotten by people.
When you answered me at the Zhōnghuámén,
why did you wish to decline worldly affairs so much?"
Liú Qūn said:
"Your servant's family has received the favor of Sòng for generations,
and our household is indebted to Qí's benevolence.
Extraordinary merits
are beyond my reach.
To not far resent the former dynasty,
and to not fail the sage and enlightened ruler,
how dare I not answer with the truth?"
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and concurrently held the position of Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
At that time, Shìzǔ was in the Eastern Palace.
He often
visited Liú Qūn's residence.
[一０]Their casual conversation lasted until evening.
He was bestowed with screens and bed curtains.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to be Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his Zhōngshùzǐ post as before.
Jìnglíng Wáng Ziliáng, General Zhēngběi, held the governorship of Nán Xǔ Zhōu.
Liú Qūn was appointed his Zhǎngshǐ,
with the additional titles of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu.
He was then promoted to Chíjí, Dūdū Sīzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general title as before.
Liú Qūn's father, Liú Miǎn, campaigned against Yīn Yǎn,
pacified Shòuyáng,
and committed no wrongdoing.
The common people appreciated him
and erected a stele in his honor.
Liú Qūn walked to his post in Shòuyáng,
passed Liú Miǎn's stele,
bowed respectfully and wept.
Initially,
Xià Bóyí from Yìyáng killed the commandant of the Gānglíng garrison, rebelled, and crossed the Huái River.
The Northern Wei appointed him as Yìyáng Tàishǒu.
Liú Qūn set up a campaign to entice him.
Xiè Jǐng, the Northern Wei's Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, killed Xià Bóyí and his brothers, and Lǐ Rónggōng, the Northern Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu, surrendered.
Liú Qūn established schools in the capital of his prefecture
and obtained two ancient ritual vessels: bronze léi, bronze zèng, mountain léi zūn, [一一]and bronze dòu zhōng.
He presented them.
He was promoted to Cháng Jiān Shìzhōng.
The imperial carriage often visited Liú Qūn's residence.
His residence featured elaborate gardens with hills and ponds,
and an "urn window" was built.
Shìzǔ wore a deerskin cap,
covered himself with Liú Qūn's rabbit-fur quilt,
and feasted merrily by the window.
He bestowed the cap upon Liú Qūn
and did not leave until night.
Later, Liú Qūn accompanied the Emperor on a climb up Jiǎng Shān.
The Emperor repeatedly sighed, saying:
"The friendship of the poor and humble should not be forgotten,
nor should the wife who shared hardships be dismissed from the hall."
He looked at Liú Qūn and said:
"This refers to you.
People say that the wealthy and noble often change their original sentiments.
Although I possess the four seas,
today I enjoy with you the camaraderie of commoners."
Liú Qūn rose and bowed in thanks.
He was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn
and Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ.
Soon after, he concurrently held his original post and acted as Dūdū Xǔzhōu Yuán Huái Zhū Jūnjì.
He was transferred to Shǐxīng Wáng Qiánjūn Zhǎngshǐ, Píngmán Xiàowèi, and Shǔjùn Tàishǒu,
with his general title as before,
acting as the Governor of Yìzhōu Prefecture and Yìzhōu.
The commandery was soon changed to Nèishǐ.
He was transferred along with the prefecture to Ānxī.
Liú Qūn managed affairs strictly and efficiently,
which accorded with the Emperor's will.
During the Sòng dynasty, Tàizǔ 宋太祖, when assisting in governance,
intended to cast coins.
However, at the time of the abdication,
he was unable to implement it.
In the fourth year of Jiànyuán 建元,
Kǒng Jì 孔覬, a Fèngcháoqǐng 奉朝請, submitted a memorial advocating for casting coins to stabilize currency,
〔一二〕which was extensively reasoned and supported by evidence.
Its gist was that
"food and currency being interlinked
is a natural principle and tendency.
Lǐ Kuí 李悝 said, 'When grain is excessively expensive, it harms the people;
when it is excessively cheap, it harms the farmers.'
If the people are harmed, they disperse;
if the farmers are harmed, the state is poor.
Excessive cheapness and excessive dearness
cause the same harm.
The Three Wú 三吳 region is the gateway to the state,
and in recent years, despite suffering from floods and waterlogging, grain prices have not risen.
This indicates a shortage of money in the realm,
not an abundance of cheap grain.
This cannot be overlooked.
The弊 of casting coins
lies in the frequent changes in their weight.
Heavy coins are problematic to use,
and their difficulty in use makes them seem too light;
light coins lead to illicit minting,
and illicit minting is a deep-seated calamity.
The reason why the people engage in illicit minting
despite strict laws is that
the authorities, when minting coins, are stingy with copper and labor.
Those who are stingy with copper and labor
consider money a useless instrument,
intended merely for facilitating transactions.
They strive to make coins light and numerous,
to save labor and facilitate their production,
without carefully considering the troubles they cause.
From the Hàn dynasty's minting of wǔzhūqián 五銖錢
until Sòng Wéndì 宋文帝,
over five hundred years passed.
Although the regulations regarding coins underwent periods of decline and resurgence,
the wǔzhūqián 五銖錢 remained unchanged.
This clearly shows that its weight was commendable
and appropriate for currency.
Therefore, it is advisable to establish mints (Quánfǔ 泉府),
for regional governors to contribute metal,
〔一三〕and to greatly increase smelting and casting.
The coins should weigh five zhū 銖,
entirely according to Hàn law.
When the state treasury is full
and national reserves are ample,
then salaries can be measured out,
and taxes lightened,
leading to sufficiency for families and prosperity for the people.
Currently, those who illicitly mint new coins
all imitate the practice of clipping and filing,
not minting large coins.
By rubbing, polishing, and dyeing,
they initially make them resemble old coins;
but after circulation,
they revert and become new again.
Honest people cannot all dye them,
〔一四〕and thus stop using them.
Those who sell goods
consequently lose their property in vain.
Illicit minters,
on the other hand, buy the new coins cheaply,
dye them, and use them again,
repeatedly creating fraud,
and continuously fostering wickedness.
This is precisely what an enlightened ruler should prohibit and not allow to proliferate.
If official coinage has already been widely distributed among the people,
(（使）)【便】then strict prohibitions should be imposed against clipping and filing.
〔一五〕Small, light, broken, or rimless coins
should all be disallowed from circulation.
As for small official coins,
they should be weighed to match the standard zhū 銖 or liǎng 兩,
and then melted down to make larger ones.
This would benefit the poor and honest people
and block the path of the cunning and fraudulent.
Once the currency is stabilized,
distance will make no difference,
the common people will enjoy their livelihoods,
and there will be no disputes in the markets,
and clothing and food will flourish."
At that time, many debaters thought that the currency was becoming scarce,
and it was advisable to expand minting,
and increase their weight in zhū 銖 and liǎng 兩,
to prevent illicit practices by the people.
Tàizǔ 太祖 ordered all prefectures and commanderies to extensively purchase copper 【炭】 (charcoal),
〔一六〕but the matter was suspended when he passed away.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng 永明,
Quān 悛 memorialized Shìzǔ 世祖, saying:
"Below Měng Shān 蒙山, within Nánguǎng Jùn 南廣郡,
there is a city named Měngchéng 蒙城,
about two qǐng 頃 in area.
It has four smelting furnaces,
one zhàng 丈 high
and one zhàng 丈 five chǐ 尺 wide.
About a hundred paces south across the water from Měngchéng 蒙城,
digging two chǐ 尺 deep on flat ground
yields copper.
There are also ancient copper mining pits,
two zhàng 丈 deep,
and residences still remain.
Dèng Tōng 鄧通,
a person from Nán'ān 南安,
was granted the copper mountain in Yándào Xiàn 嚴道縣 by Hàn Wéndì 漢文帝 to cast coins.
Today, Měng Shān 蒙山 is near the south of Qīngyī Shuǐ 青衣水,
and the left side of Qīngyī 青衣 is entirely the old territory of Yándào 嚴道 in Qín 秦.
〔一七〕Qīngyī Xiàn 青衣縣 was also renamed Hànjiā 漢嘉.
Furthermore, Měng Shān 蒙山 is two hundred lǐ 里 from Nán'ān 南安.
Based on this, it must be where Tōng 鄧通 cast coins.
Recently, when the Měng Shān Láo 蒙山獠 were summoned,
they said, 'It is very much worth exploiting.'
If this proposal is adopted,
the profits will be immense."
He also presented a piece of copper from Měng Shān 蒙山,
another piece of copper ore,
and an iron knife from Píngzhōu 平州.
The Emperor accepted his suggestion.
He dispatched envoys to Shǔ 蜀 to cast coins,
obtaining over ten million.
However, the costs were high,
so the operation was stopped.
Quān 悛 was then appointed to replace Shǐxīng Wáng Jiàn 始興王鑑 as Chíjíe Jiān Yì Níng Èr Zhōu Zhūjūnshì Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 持節、監益寧二州諸軍事、益州刺史,
his general title remaining as before.
Quān 悛, relying on past favors,
was particularly skilled at pleasing and attaching himself to the ruler,
and ingratiating himself with powerful officials.
His guests and private chambers
were lavishly supplied.
When he was dismissed from Guǎng 廣 and Sī 司 prefectures,
he exhausted his assets in contributions,
leaving nothing in his household.
While in Shǔ 蜀, he made a golden bathtub,
and other golden items were similarly extravagant.
Upon his dismissal,
he returned to the capital with his original title.
He wished to offer his tribute,
but Shìzǔ 世祖 passed away.
Yùlín 鬱林 was newly enthroned,
and Quān 悛 reduced his offerings.
Yùlín 鬱林, knowing this,
hinted to the appropriate officials to arrest Quān 悛 and hand him over to the Tíngwèi 廷尉,
intending to execute him.
Gāozōng 高宗 interceded for him,
and he was pardoned,
but confined for life.
Although he was disgraced and dismissed,
guests continued to visit him daily.
Quān 悛's wife's brother, Wáng Fǎxiǎn 王法顯, was involved in the affair of Sòng Guìyáng 宋桂陽,
so he requested to live separately
and never saw her again for the rest of his life.
When Hǎilíng Wáng 海陵王 ascended the throne,
he was appointed Jiān Zuǒmín Shàngshū 兼左民尚書 in plain clothes,
and soon after, as a full appointee.
When Gāozōng 高宗 was enthroned,
he was additionally given the title Lǐng Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 領驍騎將軍,
restored to his former office,
and made Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ 建武,
when the barbarian ruler invaded Shòuyáng 壽陽,
Quān 悛 was ordered, with his current office, to temporarily hold the jié 節 and be stationed at Cháohú 漅湖.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn 散騎常侍、右衞將軍.
As the barbarian incursions grew severe,
Quān 悛 was again stationed at Xīntíng 新亭 with his original office.
Quān 悛 was shown favor and trust throughout all reigns.
Tàizǔ 太祖 arranged for Póyáng Wáng Qiāng 鄱陽王鏘 to marry Quān 悛's younger sister as his consort.
Gāozōng 高宗 also arranged for Jìn'ān Wáng Bǎoyì 晉安王寶義 to marry Quān 悛's daughter as his consort.
From then on, he was related to the imperial family by marriage.
When Wáng Jìngzé 王敬則 rebelled,
Quān 悛 was sent to guard Lángyé Chéng 琅邪城.
He was then transferred to Wǔbīng Shàngshū 五兵尚書,
and simultaneously held the title of Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài 太子左衞率.
Before he could be formally appointed,
Míngdì 明帝 died.
Dōnghūn 東昏 was enthroned,
and Quān 悛 was re-appointed as Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
concurrently Lǐng Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 領驍騎將軍,
with his Shàngshū 尚書 title remaining as before.
He escorted the imperial coffin to the mausoleum,
where he died
at the age of sixty-one.
He was posthumously granted Tàicháng 太常,
with his Chángshì 常侍 and Dūwèi 都尉 titles remaining as before.
His posthumous name was Jìng 敬.
Yú Cóng 虞悰, courtesy name Jǐngyù 景豫,
was from Yúyáo 余姚 in Kuàijī 會稽.
His grandfather, Xiàofù 嘯父,
was Zuǒmín Shàngshū 左民尚書 during the Jìn 晉 dynasty.
His father, Xiùzhī 秀之,
was Huángmén Láng 黃門郎.
Cóng was careful and disciplined in his youth,
possessing a profound nature.
When Xiù died in the capital,
Cóng traveled east to mourn,
refusing to eat or drink.
The province appointed him as Zhǔbù,
then Staff Officer to Prince Jiànpíng,
Shàngshū Yícáo Láng,
Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
Lǐngjūn Chángshǐ,
Zhèngyuán Láng,
and progressively rose to Zhōu Zhìzhōng,
Biéjià,
and Huángmén Láng.
Initially,
when Shìzǔ first began his official career,
his family was still impoverished.
Cóng extended the kindness of a national scholar,
often sharing with him.
Whenever he traveled,
he would always call Shàng to ride with him.
Shàng greatly appreciated this.
During the Shēngmíng era,
when Shìzǔ was Zhōngjūn,
he appointed Cóng as Zīyì Cānjūn,
and sent Lìbù Láng Jiāng Mì with a handwritten letter to Cóng, saying:
"Today, I have something to tell you through Lìláng Jiāng.
Considering your affection and regard,
I wish to impose upon you."
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
then transferred to Hòujūn Chángshǐ (concurrently serving as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
〔一八〕Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
Zhènběi Chángshǐ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he became Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
with his general rank remaining as before.
Cóng managed his household to be prosperous and wealthy;
none of his servants were idle.
Although he was
in the southern lands, delicacies from Kuàijī and the sea were always fully supplied.
He was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Shǐxīngwáng Chángshǐ, Píngmán Xiàowèi, and Shǔjùn Tàishǒu.
Then transferred to Sītú Sīmǎ,
with his general rank remaining as before.
Cóng was skilled at preparing delicious food;
his seasonings and blends all had specific methods.
When Prince Yùzhāng, Yí, hosted a grand feast for guests,
he asked Cóng,
"Are there any dishes
we have missed today?"
Cóng replied,
"I regret that there is no huáng'àn [yángjìng],
which Hécéng's dining records describe."
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and
Tàizǐ Yòulǜ.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng,
there was a great flood.
All officials wore military attire to save the Grand Ancestral Temple,
but Cóng rode in a chariot in a vermillion robe with ceremonial escorts,
and at the Xuānyáng Mén Wài, he drove his carriage inside the horse barrier and struck people.
He was impeached by the appropriate authorities
but was pardoned.
Because Shàng cherished Cóng as an old friend from commoner days,
he casually said to Cóng,
"I shall make you restore your ancestral enterprise."
He was then promoted to Shìzhōng,
and the court was surprised by this honorable appointment.
He was promoted to Cíbù Shàngshū.
When Shìzǔ visited Fānglín Yuán,
he asked Cóng for biǎn mǐ tà.
Cóng offered tà and dozens of chariots of various dishes,
which even the Imperial Kitchen's best could not surpass.
Shàng asked Cóng for various food and drink recipes,
but Cóng kept them secret and refused to reveal them.
After Shàng was drunk and felt unwell,
Cóng then offered only one recipe for hangover-curing qíngzhǎ.
He was sent out as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
then Chēqí Chángshǐ,
then transferred to Dùzhī Shàngshū,
concurrently serving as Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was reassigned to Lǐng Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
Yángzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng,
and concurrently Dàjiàng Qīng.
When the Xiū'ānlíng tomb was being constructed,
he accepted beef and wine from the local people at the tomb site,
and was consequently dismissed from office.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was reinstated to office as a commoner.
When Yùlín was deposed,
Cóng secretly sighed, saying,
"Wáng and Xú have indeed bound the emperor in pants and deposed him.
How can there be such a principle in the world?"
In the first year of Tíngxīng,
he was again appointed Lǐng Yòujūn.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
Cóng claimed illness and did not attend the ceremony.
The emperor sent Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn to show Cóng the documents regarding the deposition and enthronement,
and, considering Cóng an old associate,
invited him to participate in the founding of the new reign.
Cóng said to Yàn,
"The emperor is sagely and brilliant,
and the high officials are working together.
Why would they need a decaying old man to assist in this new beginning?
I dare not accept the command."
The court discussed impeaching him,
but Púyè Xú Xiàosì said,
"This is also a remnant of ancient uprightness."
The general discussion then ceased.
Cóng claimed severe illness and returned east,
submitting a memorial that read:
"Your servant's clan is humble in the coastal region,
and I am of lowly status in Guījī.
(attaching) [猥] attached to the rise of the dynasty,
〔一九〕I have received undeserved private favors,
and merely passed through many years,
ultimately ashamed of being unable to repay them.
My health regimen has been improper,
and I am afflicted by persistent illness.
Since falling ill,
more than a month has passed,
and despite frequent medical treatments,
there has been no improvement.
Given this debilitated state,
it is truly difficult to recover.
I beg to be relieved of my duties,
to fully treat myself for the remainder of my days."
An imperial edict granted him a hundred days' leave.
He was transferred to Gěishìzhōng
and Guānglù Dàfū,
and soon after, promoted to Zhèngyuán Chángshì.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he passed away.
He was sixty-five years old at the time.
Cóng was sincere and practical by nature;
when he knew someone,
he would always visit and inquire after them.
His relationships, whether close or distant, always had a beginning and an end,
and the world praised him for this.
His younger cousin, Mà,
was determined not to serve as an official.
〔二０〕When Wáng Jìngzé rebelled,
he appointed Mà to oversee Kuàijī Jùn,
but all military affairs were entrusted to the commoner Zhāng Língbǎo.
The people of the commandery attacked the commandery and killed Língbǎo,
and Mà survived because he was not involved in the matter.
Hú Xiézhī was
a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
His grandfather, Liánzhī, was Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
His father, Yìzhī, was appointed by the province but did not take office.
Xiézhī was first appointed as Zhōu Cóngshì Zhǔbù,
then Línhè Wángguó Chángshì,
Yuánwàiláng,
Fǔjūn Xíngcānjūn,
Jìnxīwáng Ānxī Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and Nánliángjùn Tàishǒu.
He was praised for his capacity and demeanor.
He was transferred to Shàolíngwáng Nánzhōngláng Zhōngbīng,
concurrently Lǐng Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
but did not take the appointment.
He was appointed Shèshēng Xiàowèi
and Zhōu Biéjià.
He was appointed Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
but did not take the appointment.
He was then appointed Shàolíngwáng Zuǒjūn Zīyì.
When Shìzǔ was stationed at Pénchéng,
he ordered Xiézhī to guard Xúnyáng Chéng.
When Shìzǔ became Jiāngzhōu,
he again appointed Xiézhī as Biéjià,
entrusting him with important affairs.
When Wénhuì Tàizǐ was stationed at Xiāngyáng,
Shìzǔ, considering Xiézhī a trusted confidant,
appointed him as Běizhōngláng Zhēnglǔ Sīmǎ and Fúfēng Tàishǒu,
with the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
He provided great assistance at the post,
displaying much dedication and effort.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
he returned as Gěishìzhōng,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
Běnzhōu Zhōngzhèng,
then transferred to Huángmén Láng,
concurrently Lǐng Yǔlín Jiān.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was transferred to Shǒu Wèiwèi,
with his Zhōngzhèng position remaining as before.
The next year,
he was given the additional title of Gěishìzhōng.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì
and Tàizǐ Yòulǜ.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
given the additional title of Gěishìzhōng,
with his Zhōngzhèng position remaining as before.
Xiézhī's 蕭諧之 demeanor was graceful and refined,
and he was adept at managing his affairs.
Coupled with the favor he received due to old friendships,
many court officials befriended him.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū 都官尚書.
The Emperor wished to promote Xiézhī 蕭諧之,
and once leisurely said to Xiézhī 蕭諧之:
"How many Shìzhōng 侍中 are there from Jiāngzhōu 江州?"
Xiézhī 蕭諧之 replied:
"In recent times, there has only been Chéng Dàohuì 程道惠 alone."
The Emperor said:
"There should be two."
Later, he spoke of this to Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn 尚書令王儉.
Wáng Jiǎn's 王儉 opinion was different,
so Xiézhī 蕭諧之 was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子,
concurrently holding the position of Zuǒwèi Shuài 左衞率.
When Xiézhī's 蕭諧之 elder brother Mózhī 謨之 died,
Xiézhī 蕭諧之 submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant's private household has been afflicted with misfortune,
early suffering bitter hardships.
We three brothers
mutually nurtured and raised each other,
and though infants were plagued with illness,
we managed to reach adulthood.
My eldest brother, Chén Chénzhī 臣諶之,
also perished prematurely.
Together with my deceased second brother, Chén Mózhī 臣謨之, I bore sorrow in our household,
and was fortunate enough to receive his instruction and upbringing,
our feelings were like being under an immense shade.
How could I have imagined that in one day I would suddenly be abandoned,
with auspicious and inauspicious events separated,
unable to attend to him?
I beg to be relieved of my current post."
An imperial edict did not grant it.
He was reassigned as Wèiwèi 衞尉,
while his position as Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子 remained unchanged.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor sent Xiézhī 蕭諧之 to lead the imperial guards to suppress Wángzǐ Xiǎng 王子響 of Bādōng 巴東 in Jiānglíng 江陵,
also serving concurrently as Chángshǐ Xíngshì 長史行事.
The imperial army was defeated by Zǐxiǎng 子響.
The relevant officials memorialized for his dismissal,
but he temporarily retained his military authority as before.
He was again made Wèiwèi 衞尉,
concurrently Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
and Zhōngzhèng 中正 of his home prefecture.
Xiézhī 蕭諧之 had foresight and good judgment.
Whenever there was a vacancy in the court or a need for promotion and replacement,
he would secretly estimate the person the Emperor would use,
and his predictions always proved correct.
Yú Cóng 虞悰 praised and admired him for this.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to Dùzhī Shàngshū 度支尚書,
concurrently holding the position of Wèiwèi 衞尉.
The following year,
he died
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted the titles Yòu Jiāngjūn 右將軍 and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ 豫州刺史.
His posthumous name was Sù 肅.
The historiographer said: Sending two extra coins
means this will not be forgotten.
The sentiment of a single basket [of gifts]
was repaid with a Dūwèi 都尉.
A thousand gold pieces can be lost,
but what is precious is the human heart.
To be cautious and trustworthy,
and to love all broadly,
its benefit is indeed vast.
How much more so for a former discerning, latent dragon,
who formed deep bonds while still in humble circumstances.
To achieve high office according to one's talent,
this is naturally the case.
The eulogy says: Dào Jí's 到藉 extravagance and luxury,
later embraced simplicity.
Yú Shēng's 虞生 wealth and abundance,
his extravagance did not exceed the bounds.
Liú Shí's 劉實 court connections,
Hú Nǎi's 胡乃 numerous old acquaintances.
Striding proudly, with brilliant countenance,
galloping on the broad roads.
[Collations and Notes]
Biographies, Chapter 19: Xiāo Jǐngxiān 蕭景先, Xiāo Chìfǔ 蕭赤斧 (Zǐyǐng Zhòu 子穎冑)
Xiāo Jǐngxiān 蕭景先,
a native of Lánlíng 蘭陵 in Nán Lánlíng 南蘭陵,
was a cousin of Tàizǔ 太祖.
His grandfather, Yuánzhī 爰之, was Yuánwàiláng 員外郎.
His father, Jìngzōng 敬宗, was Zhōngjūn 中軍 of Shǐxīng Wángguó 始興王國.
Jǐngxiān 景先 suffered the loss of his father early,
and possessed extreme filial piety,
which Tàizǔ 太祖 admired.
When he later served as an official in Jīngyì 京邑,
Tàizǔ 太祖 often supported and guided him.
He was first appointed Shàngjūn Jiāngjūn 上軍將軍 of Hǎilíng Wángguó 海陵王國,
then made Jiànlíng Lìng 建陵令.
Returning, he became Shìláng 侍郎 of Xīn'ān Wángguó 新安王國,
and Yòu Chángshì 右常侍 of Guìyáng Guó 桂陽國.
When Tàizǔ 太祖 was stationed in Huái'yīn 淮陰,
Jǐngxiān 景先, in his original capacity, served as Jūnzǔ 軍主 accompanying him,
responsible for defending the city,
and was entrusted with confidential matters.
He was appointed Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn 後軍行參軍,
Qióngxiàn Lìng 卭縣令,
and Yuánwàiláng 員外郎.
He was intimate with Shìzǔ 世祖.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 was appointed to Guǎngxīng Jùn 廣興郡,
he petitioned Tàizǔ 太祖 to have Jǐngxiān 景先 accompany him.
Jǐngxiān 景先 was appointed Níngshuò Fǔ Sīmǎ 寧朔府司馬 under Shìzǔ 世祖,
and from then on, he always followed him.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 was Zhèn Xī Chángshǐ 鎮西長史,
he made Jǐngxiān 景先 Zhèn Xī Chángliú Cānjūn 鎮西長流參軍,
and appointed him Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍.
Following the move of the government, he was transferred to Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn 撫軍中兵參軍,
and soon after appointed Zīyì 諮議,
concurrently holding the position of Zhōngbīng 中兵 as before.
In the early part of Shēngmíng 昇明 era,
he became Shìzǔ's 世祖 Zhēnglǔ Fǔ Sīmǎ 征虜府司馬,
concurrently Xīncài Tàishǒu 新蔡太守,
accompanying the Emperor to station at Pénchéng 盆城.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's 沈攸之 affair was quelled,
and he returned to the capital,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍,
and concurrently Sīmǎ 司馬 of Shìzǔ's 世祖 Fǔjūn Zhōngjūn Èrfǔ 撫軍中軍二府,
also Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn 左衞將軍.
In the first year of Jiàn yuán 建元,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài 太子左衞率,
enfeoffed as Bó 伯 of Xīnwú Xiàn 新吳縣,
with an income of five hundred households.
Jǐngxiān's 景先 original name was Dàoxiān 道先,
which was changed to avoid the Emperor's tabooed name.
He was sent out as Chíjié Dū Sīzhōu Jūnshì 持節、督司州軍事,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍, Sīzhōu Cìshǐ 司州刺史,
concurrently Yìyáng Tàishǒu 義陽太守.
That winter,
the barbarians came out from Huái 淮 and Sì 泗 rivers,
increasing the border garrisons in the Sīzhōu 司州 region.
Xiè Tiāngài 謝天蓋, a person from Yìyáng 義陽, colluded with the barbarians.
Jǐngxiān 景先 reported this to the Dūfǔ 督府.
Piàojí Yùzhāngwáng 驃騎豫章王 sent Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Xiāo Huìlǎng 輔國將軍中兵參軍蕭惠朗 with two thousand men to assist Jǐngxiān 景先.
Huìlǎng 惠朗 built a fort along the mountain,
blocking the passes,
and attacked Tiāngài's 天蓋 faction.
The barbarians soon dispatched the false Nánbù Shàngshū Èbá 偽南部尚書頞跋 to garrison Rǔnán 汝南,
and Luòzhōu Cìshǐ Chānglí Wáng Fényuán Shā 洛州刺史昌黎王馮莎 to garrison Qīngqiū 清丘.
Jǐngxiān 景先 made strict preparations to await the enemy.

Yùzhāngwáng 豫章王 also sent Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngbǐng 寧朔將軍王僧炳, Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Yìngzhī 前軍將軍王應之, and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zhuāng Míng 龍驤將軍莊明 with three thousand men to garrison outside Yìyáng Guān 義陽關,
to serve as reinforcements.
When the barbarians retreated, he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍.
Jǐngxiān 景先 memorialized, praising the Emperor's excellent moral transformation.
The Emperor replied:
"The customs have been corrupted and ruined
for more than twenty years.
With me as the ruler,
how could it be swept clean all at once?
Fortunately, for several years I have exerted my strength to save the common people,
which must have brought benefit to all things.
Even a sage needs good assistants to govern the world.
If you all exert yourselves fully,
there will be no worry about misgovernance."
When Shìzǔ 世祖 ascended the throne,
he was summoned as Shìzhōng 侍中,
concurrently Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn 左軍將軍,
and soon after also Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn 領軍將軍.
Jǐngxiān 景先 served the Emperor with utmost devotion,
thus his favor and trust were especially close.
When he first returned from the west,
the Emperor sat in Jǐngyáng Lóu 景陽樓 and summoned Jǐngxiān 景先 to speak of old times,
with only Yùzhāngwáng 豫章王 also present at the table.
He was transferred to Zhōnglǐngjūn 中領軍.
When the imperial carriage went out to hunt pheasants in the countryside,
Jǐngxiān 景先 always followed in armor,
observing and inspecting his surroundings.
Soon after, he was advanced in rank to Hóu 侯.
He held the position of Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事,
and his original post remained unchanged.
Upon suffering the loss of his mother,
an imperial edict ordered his immediate reinstatement as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn 領軍將軍.
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍 and Dānyáng Yǐn 丹陽尹.
In the fifth year,
the wild people, led by Huán Tiānshēng, brought barbarian marauders to the borders of Yōngzhōu,
north of the Sībù commandery.
The populace was stirred with unrest.
The Emperor, considering Jǐngxiān's prior thorough understanding of the terrain,
issued an edict, saying:
"We have received a memorial from Zhāng Guī, the Administrator of Yōngzhōu,
stating that the barbarian marauders are inciting each other
and may invade.
These wasps and scorpions are venomous,
and it is fitting to promptly suppress them.
Let Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Dānyáng Yǐn Jǐngxiān be dispatched to command the infantry and cavalry,
marching directly to Yìyáng.
He shall be granted a jié (credentials),
and all forces in Sīzhōu shall be under his command."
When Jǐngxiān reached the garrison,
he camped his army north of the city.
The people were then at ease,
bringing oxen and wine to welcome him.
Before the army could return,
he fell ill,
leaving behind a final message:
"This illness,
different from previous ones,
makes me realize I will surely not recover.
However, having long borne deep imperial favor,
and now unworthily filling a military role,
my dim weakness has failed in every task,
making me ashamed before Your Majesty's kind intent.
To be forever parted from this sacred age
fills me with such sorrow that I know not what to say.
Please draft a memorial for me,
expressing my gratitude to His Most Honored Majesty,
and roughly conveying my foolish thoughts.
Although Yì has grown up,
he has always lacked proper instruction.
Zhēn and the others are too young
to understand anything yet.
They will still have to rely on Your Sagely Brilliance,
something this dying man is incapable of expressing thanks for.
Since experiencing this bitter distress,
many of my concubines have already been dispersed.
The remaining few, ugly and crude,
are not suitable for service.
Let Míngyuè, Fónǚ, Guìzhī, Fó'ér, Yùnǚ, and Měiyù be sent to the imperial court.
Měimǎn and Yànhuá should serve the Eastern Palace.
I have over twenty private horses
and several oxen.
Select ten good horses and two oxen to be sent to the imperial court.
Five horses and one ox should serve the Eastern Palace.
The Dàsīmǎ and Sītú should each be presented with two horses,
and the Piàojì and Zhènjūn each with one horse.
All private weapons and equipment
should also be submitted to the court.
Many of my close relatives have not yet been provided for;
they should be cared for as appropriate,
to slightly express my long-held intentions.
The large residence granted to me
is probably not suitable for Yì and the others to live in.
Once the mourning period is over,
it can be returned to the court.
I have long heard that the former Lú family residence
is for sale;
it can be collectively purchased.
If the price is too low,
a request can be made to the officials for a supplement.
The three plots of fertile land
are sufficient for self-sustenance.
For clothing and food, and due to a lack of labor,
buy some more coarse and ugly servants and maidservants as needed.
There is no need for other means of livelihood.
My retinue and military subordinates, returning to the capital,
should naturally be dispersed.
Those who have served long and diligently
should be provided for,
and a request for imperial grace should be made as appropriate."
He died
at the age of fifty.
The Emperor grieved for him,
issuing an edict that said:
"The western dispatch has just arrived;
Jǐngxiān has suddenly passed away.
My sorrow is so profound
that I cannot bear it.
I shall now observe mourning.
He shall be granted a funeral gift of 100,000 cash
and 200 bolts of cloth."
When Jǐngxiān's coffin returned,
an edict stated:
"The late Jiǎjié Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Dānyáng Yǐn Xīnwú Hóu Jǐngxiān
possessed an open and bright mind
and was capable and perceptive in his duties.
He was diligent from youth to maturity,
and his integrity encompassed both merit and kinship.
His sincerity was evident in both peace and peril,
and his achievements were outstanding in the offices he held.
He was on the verge of rising in honor
to fulfill a significant trust.
His sudden passing
causes deep sorrow.
He is posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, and Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ.
A set of drums and pipes shall be provided.
His jiǎjié and marquisate shall remain as before.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōng Hóu (Loyal Marquis)."
His son, Yì,
as the son of a meritorious relative,
held many prominent official positions from a young age.
He served as Tàizǐ Shèrén,
Xǐmǎ,
Suíwáng Yǒu,
Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu,
Dàsīmǎ Zīyì Cānjūn,
Nánkāng Tàishǒu,
and Zhōngshū Láng.
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ,
he was Fǔjūn Sīmǎ,
then promoted to Běizhōngláng Sīmǎ.
When the barbarians moved,
he led troops to guard Lángxié City.
Yì was extravagant and fond of archery and horses,
which made Gāozōng suspicious and wary of him.
When Wáng Yàn's plot failed,
Yì was also implicated and executed.
Troops were sent to surround his residence.
At that time, Yì was entertaining guests and enjoying performances.
Hearing of the change,
he sought a sword but could not find one.
The arresting soldiers burst in,
dragged Yì in to bid farewell to his mother,
and then brought him out and killed him.
Xiāo Chìfǔ,
a native of Nánlánlíng,
was a younger cousin of Tàizǔ from a collateral branch.
His grandfather, Lóngzǐ,
was Wèijūn Lùshì Cānjūn.
His father, Shǐzhī,
was Guānjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Chìfǔ's official career began as Fèngcháoqǐng.
He was known to Tàizǔ for his amiability and prudence.
At the beginning of Sòng Dàmíng era,
when Jìnglǐng Wáng Dàn rebelled in Guǎnglǐng,
Chìfǔ served as Jūnzhu,
subordinate to Shěn Qìngzhī.
They besieged Guǎnglǐng City,
and he distinguished himself in combat.
After the pacification,
he was enfeoffed as Yǒng'ān Tínghóu,
with an income of 370 households.
He was appointed Chēqí Xíng Cānjūn,
then dispatched to serve as Jìnlíng Lìng,
Yuánwàiláng,
and Dānyáng Lìng.
He returned to become Jìnxī Wáng Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
then went out as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Qiántáng Lìng.
He was promoted to Zhèngyuán Láng.
Chìfǔ's governance brought peace to the common people,
and officials and commoners requested his retention.
The court deliberation granted this,
and he was reappointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
When Tàizǔ assumed regency,
he appointed Chìfǔ as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Zuǒjūn Kuàijī Sīmǎ,
assisting in guarding the eastern frontier.
He was promoted to Huángmén Láng
and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
He followed the Emperor in his abdication,
and a palace was established in the former Dānyáng administrative seat.
The Emperor ordered Chìfǔ to assist in escorting him,
and he did not return until the Emperor's demise.
At the beginning of Jiànyuán,
he was promoted to Wǔlíng Wáng Guānjūn Chángshǐ,
Piàojì Sīmǎ,
and Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
with Fǔguó Jiāngjūn as before.
He was promoted to Chángjiān Shìzhōng,
but resigned due to the mourning for his paternal grandmother.
He was reinstated as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Níngmán Xiàowèi.
He was then appointed as Chíjí, Dū Yōng Liáng Nánběiqín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglǐng Sīzhōu Zhī Suí Jùn Jūnfǎ, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his original offices remaining as before.
While in the province,
he did not seek personal gain but was diligent in his public duties.
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
Shìzǔ treated him with personal favor, placing him on par with Xiāo Jǐngxiān.
He was enfeoffed as the Bó of Nánfēng County,
with a stipend of four hundred households.
He was promoted to Jǐshìzhōng,
and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Chìfǔ had long suffered from xialì (thirst and dysentery).
In the third year of Yǒngmíng, when
Shìzǔ summoned him with three contingents of armored guards,
Chìfǔ dared not decline.
His illness worsened,
and he died a few days later,
at the age of fifty-six.
His family had no savings;
they had no silk for a quilt.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he felt even greater sorrow.
An edict bestowed upon him fifty thousand cash,
one set of superior materials,
one hundred bolts of cloth,
and two hundred catties of wax.
He was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His posthumous name was Yìbó.
His son, Yǐngzhòu, inherited the peerage.
Yǐngzhòu, courtesy name Yúncháng,
was generous and inherited his father's demeanor.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng.
Tàizǔ said to Chìfǔ:
"Yǐngzhòu, though young, has a bearing that shows
his progress is becoming increasingly fine,
which is truly comforting."
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén.
After his father's funeral,
he suffered from a leg ailment,
and could only walk again after several years.
Shìzǔ issued an edict to console and encourage him,
and bestowed medicine.
He was appointed Jìnglíng Wáng Sītú Wàibīng Cānjūn,
and Jìnxī Wáng Wénxué.
Yǐngzhòu was fond of literature and righteousness,
while his younger brother, Yǐngjī, was fond of military prowess.
When Shìzǔ ascended the Fēnghuǒ Lóu (Beacon Tower),
he ordered his officials to compose poems.
Yǐngzhòu's poem matched the imperial intent.
The Emperor said to Yǐngzhòu:
"You are skilled in literature, and your brother in military arts;
the imperial clan will not lack talent."
He was appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Ānlù Nèishǐ.
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng.
Due to Yǐngzhòu being the son of an meritorious relative,
the Emperor appointed him Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
in charge of military and civil affairs within the palace,
and allowed him entry to the private chambers.
He was sent out as Xīn'ān Tàishǒu,
and the officials and common people cherished him.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
when Yǒngjiā Wáng Zhāocàn was the Governor of Nánxú Zhōu,
Yǐngzhòu was appointed Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
and acted concurrently as Governor of Nánxú Zhōu.
He was then transferred to be Chíjí, Dūdū Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Jūnshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
He did not take up the post,
but was appointed Huángmén Láng,
concurrently leading the Sìxiāng Zhí.
He was promoted to Wèiwèi.
During Gāozōng's deposition and enthronement,
Yǐngzhòu remained calm and did not take sides,
so he was included in the meritorious service.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was advanced to the rank of Hóu,
and his stipend was increased to six hundred households.
Yǐngzhòu was bestowed the white [⿰日門] (ox) that he usually rode.
The Emperor admired frugality,
and wished to melt down the silver wine spears used for imperial birthday toasts on Yuándàn (New Year's Day) in the Tàiguān (Grand Secretariat).
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn and others all praised this virtuous deed.
Yǐngzhòu said:
"Among the grand ceremonies of the court,
none surpasses the Sānyuán.
This particular vessel is an old item,
and not excessively extravagant."
The Emperor was displeased.
Later, at a private banquet,
silver vessels filled the tables.
Yǐngzhòu said:
"Your Majesty previously intended to melt down the wine spears;
perhaps it would be more appropriate to apply that intention to these vessels."
The Emperor showed great shame.
When Guānjūn Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎoxuán was stationed at Shítou,
Yǐngzhòu was appointed Chángshǐ,
and acted concurrently as Shítou Shùshì.
He again became Wèiwèi.
He was sent out as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Lúlíng Wáng Hòujūn Chángshǐ, Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu, and acted concurrently as Nán[gǔn] Zhōufǔ Zhōushì.
In that year, the barbarians made movements,
loudly proclaiming their intention to water their horses in the Changjiang.
The Emperor, fearing,
ordered Yǐngzhòu to move the residents into the city.
The common people were terrified,
and packed up their belongings, wishing to cross south.
Yǐngzhòu, judging the enemy's strength to be still distant,
did not immediately implement the order,
and the barbarians also soon retreated.
He was then appointed Chíjí, Dūdū Nán[gǔn] Xú Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Nán[gǔn] Zhōu Cìshǐ.
When Hé Dì was in Jīngzhōu,
Yǐngzhòu was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Xīzhōngláng Chángshǐ, Nánjùn Tàishǒu, and acted concurrently as Jīngzhōufǔ Zhōushì.
The Dōnghūnhóu executed many high officials,
entrusting power to the lowly.
After the defeat of Cuī and Chén,
the regional commanders each harbored different plans.
In the tenth month of the second year of Yǒngyuán,
Shàngshū Lìng Línxiāng Hóu Xiāo Yì and his younger brother Wèiwèi Chàng were killed.
Previously, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Bāxī Zǐtóng Èrjùn Tàishǒu Liú Shānyáng was dispatched with three thousand soldiers to receive imperial orders and take up his post,
in order to collaborate with Yǐngzhòu to attack Yōngzhōu.
The Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, Liáng Wáng, was about to raise an army of righteousness,
but feared that Yǐngzhòu might not recognize the opportune moment.
He sent an envoy, Wáng Tiānhǔ, to Jiānglíng,
proclaiming that Shānyáng was heading west,
and would attack both Jīng and Yōng.
He wrote to Yǐngzhòu,
encouraging him to join the righteous uprising.
Yǐngzhòu was still undecided.
Initially,
when Shānyáng departed for Nánzhōu,
he told people:
"Even if the court sends the white tiger banner to recall me,
I will not return."
He packed up his courtesans and concubines,
moving his entire household.
Arriving at Bālíng,
he hesitated for more than ten days without advancing.
Liáng Wáng again sent Tiānhǔ with a letter to Yǐngzhòu,
explaining his strategy.
At this time, some said that Shānyáng intended to kill Yǐngzhòu,
and would unite Jīngzhōu with the righteous uprising.
Yǐngzhòu then made a pact with Liáng Wáng,
beheaded Wáng Tiānhǔ,
and sent the head to Shānyáng as a warning.
He mobilized the common people's carts and oxen,
proclaiming he was raising an infantry army to campaign against Xiāngyáng.
On the eighteenth day of the eleventh month,
Shānyáng arrived at Jiāngjīn,
in a single carriage, dressed in white,
accompanied by dozens of attendants.
He went to Yǐngzhòu.

Yǐngzhòu had ordered the former Wényáng Tàishǒu Liú Xiàoqìng, the former Yǒngpíng Tàishǒu Liú Xīniàn, the Kǎicáo Cānjūn Xiāo Wénzhào, the former Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Chén Xiù, and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Sūn Mò to ambush him within the city.
As Shānyáng entered the gate,
he was immediately hacked to death in his carriage.
The deputy military commander Lǐ Yuánlǚ gathered the remaining followers and pledged allegiance.
An envoy, Cài Dáoyóu, was dispatched by express post to send Shānyáng's head to Liáng Wáng.
Yǐngzhòu then issued an order to prepare for war,
dividing up the troops and recruiting.
When the Dōnghūnhóu heard of Shānyáng's death,
he issued an edict to suppress Jīng and Yōng.
Shānyáng was posthumously granted Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yǐngzhòu had great capacity and resolve.
Having initiated the great affair,
he humbly entrusted himself,
and the hearts of the people turned to him.
Yǐngzhòu was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn,
Dūdū Xíngliú Zhū Jūnshì,
and was assigned assistant officials,
retaining his original titles.
Xīzhōngláng Sīmǎ Xiàhóu Xiáng was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wáng Fǎdù was dispatched towards Bālíng.
Yǐngzhòu donated two hundred thousand cash,
one thousand hú of rice,
and five hundred hú of salt.
Zīyì Zōng Sài and Biéjià Zōng Kuài donated two thousand hú of grain
Rich families were persuaded to lend their wealth
to aid military expenses.
The monks of Chángshā Temple were wealthy;
they had melted and cast several thousand liǎng of gold into dragons,
buried them in the earth,
and passed them down through generations,
referring to them as "yellow iron from below,"
unseen by anyone.
These dragons were then taken
to supply the army.
In the twelfth month,
a proclamation was issued by Xīzhōnglángfǔ Chángshǐ, Dūdū Xíngliú Zhū Jūnshì, Yòujūn Jiāngjūn, Nánjùn Tàishǒu, Nánfēng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu Xiāo Yǐngzhòu,
and Sīmǎ,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Xīnxīng Tàishǒu Xiàhóu Xiáng, addressed to the officials of the capital,
and the governors and prefects of all provinces and commanderies: "Indeed, fortune is not always constant and smooth;
it can sometimes be uneven.
Fate is not without reversals;
when misfortune reaches its extreme, prosperity will follow.
In ancient times, when the Shāng capital was in decline,
Péng and Wèi rose up;
when the Hàn dynasty was
in chaos,
Xū and Móu demonstrated their loyalty.
Thus, their fame was established forever,
and their generations endured for a long time.
In the past, our Tàizǔ Gāo Huángdì's virtuous example enlightened the people,
and his achievements reached heaven and earth."
Looking up, we see the crimson clouds;
looking down, we behold the purple zenith.
Emperor Shìzǔ continued to rise,
adding luster to the achievements of his predecessors.
Wherever the clouds and rain moistened the land,
wherever the sun and moon rose and set,
all peoples
came to pledge their allegiance,
offering tribute with joined arms.
However, Yùlín fell into confusion and delusion,
overthrowing the established order,
causing the prosperity of our great Qí dynasty
to be on the verge of collapse.
Gāozōng Míng Huángdì established the grand principles
of virtue and morality,
leaving behind the ultimate traces of benevolence and righteousness.
He continued the great foundation of the two ancestors,
succeeding to the interrupted enterprise of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
From dawn till night, he displayed great brilliance,
seeking out clothes before the light of day.
Thus, exceptional scholars
filled the court,
and extraordinary individuals converged like spokes to a hub.
As for the texts that weave rites and music,
the system of establishing the capital and making Luòyáng its center,
the auspicious omens of clouds like sweet wine,
and the auspicious signs of white patterns on a black background –
these were truly comparable to Heaven in their greatness;
no virtue could adequately describe them.
But the succeeding ruler lacked proper governance,
indulging in extreme tyranny and oppression.
All ten transgressions were committed,
and the three evil winds prevailed.
He showed no sorrow
at the beginning of mourning,

This deep regret,

Twenty. Liú Huán (劉瓛) (younger brother Jìn (璡)) Lù Chéng (陸澄)
Liú Huán (劉瓛), courtesy name Zǐguī (子珪), was from Pèiguó Xiàng (沛國相).
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹) Tàn (惔).
His grandfather, Hóngzhī (弘之), was a Gěishì Zhōng (給事中).
His father, Huì (惠), was a Zhìshū Yùshǐ (治書御史).
Huán (瓛) was initially appointed Jìjiǔ Zhǔbù (祭酒主簿) by the province.
In the fourth year of Dàmíng (大明) of Sòng (宋),
he was recommended as a *Xiùcái* (秀才).
His elder brother, Suī (璲), also had a reputation,
and had previously been nominated by the province.
At this time, the Biejia (別駕) Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuán (東海王元) wrote to Huán's (瓛) father, Huì (惠), saying:
"In recent years, your virtuous sons have been filling positions as *Xiùcái*,
and the province can truly be said to have found worthy individuals."
He was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請),
but did not take the post.
Shào was assiduous in his studies,
thoroughly mastering the Five Classics.
He gathered disciples and taught,
often having several tens of people.
Yuán Càn, the Administrator of Dānyáng, held a night gathering in his rear hall.
Huán was present.
Càn pointed to the willow tree in the courtyard and said to Huán:
"People say this tree dates from the time of Administrator Liú;
I often recall his noble character.
Now I again see your pure virtue,
which may be said to be undiminished."
He was recommended for the post of Mìshū Láng,
but was not employed.
He was appointed Shàolíng Wáng Jùn Zhǔbù,
Ānlù Wángguó Chángshì,
Ānchéng Wáng Fǔjūn Xíngcānjūn.
He was dismissed for official business.
Huán had always had no inclination for officialdom,
and from then on, he did not serve again.
He was appointed Chēqí Xíngcānjūn,
Nán Péngchéng Jùnchéng,
Shàngshū Cíbù Láng,
but declined all these appointments.
When Yuán Càn was executed,
Huán went to mourn him in disguise,
and also offered funeral contributions.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned Huán to talk in the Huálín Yuán.
He said to Huán:
"I have revolutionized in accordance with Heaven's will.
What do public opinions say about it?"
Huán replied:
"If Your Majesty heeds the mistakes of previous rulers
and adds leniency and generosity,
even a perilous situation can be made secure.
If you follow their old disastrous path,
even a secure situation will surely become perilous."
After he left,
the Emperor looked at Sītú Chǔ Yuān and said:
"How upright he is!
A scholar indeed surpasses ordinary people."
He commanded Huán to come often,
but Huán, unless summoned by imperial decree,
never reached the palace gate.
The Emperor wished to appoint Huán as Zhōngshū Láng,
and sent Lìbù Shàngshū Hé Jí to convey the imperial will.
Jí said to Huán:
"The Emperor intends to place you in the 'Phoenix Pool' (referring to the Zhongshu Sheng),
but regrets that your rank is low.
You can temporarily accept your current appointment;
in a few days, you will be transferred to Guózǐ Bóshì,
and then immediately appointed to the latter post."
Huán said:
"All my life I have had no desire for advancement.
If I were to accept the Zhōngshū Láng now,
would that be my original intention?"
Later, due to his elderly mother lacking care,
he was again appointed Péngchéng Jùnchéng.
He said to Sītú Chǔ Yuān:
"I realize I have no talent for the court,
my only wish is to retain the Péngchéng Jùnchéng post."
The Emperor also made Huán concurrently Zǒngmíngguān Jìjiǔ,
and appointed him Yùzhāng Wáng Piàojí Jìshì Cānjūn,
with his position as Cheng remaining the same,
but Huán ultimately did not accept.
When Wǔlíng Wáng Niàn became Huìjī Tàishǒu,
the Emperor wanted Huán to lecture for Niàn,
and appointed him Huìjī Jùnchéng.
The number of students following him increased.
In the early Yǒngmíng era,
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng invited him to be Zhēngběi Sītú Jìshì.
Huán wrote to Zhāng Róng and Wáng Sīyuǎn, saying:
"I received the order to be respectfully summoned.
I should stop my public duties,
but I reflect on my lifelong principles,
which are contrary to such favors.
My nature is clumsy in human affairs,
and I am unaccustomed to official advancement.
I once served as Xíngzuǒ,
but was dismissed for inability to handle official matters,
which all my acquaintances know.
Assessing myself and understanding my place,
I dare not expect honor.
I have long been afflicted by poverty,
and furthermore, I am lazy.
My clothing and hair
are enough to cause alarm.
In the middle of my life, for my elderly parents' support,
I pulled up my robes and walked on foot.
Suddenly, it has been from then until now,
two generations and one *jǐ* (12 years).
The former court ordered me to correct myself,
and to strive for advancement through the official ranks.
Seeing my threadbare clothes,
they sometimes bestowed clothing upon me.
Lords Yuán, Chǔ, and others all urged me on,
but I ultimately could not change myself.
If I did not do it once,
how can I do it again?
There was a person in the past who, having once removed his cap, would not put it on again.
I always believed this represented the proper manner of conduct.
In ancient times, worthiness determined rank,
and some would resign due to old age when their term expired.
Mediocrity determined salary,
and some [fell ill and sought to return home].
Looking back at excellent predecessors,
how am I to be compared?
Moreover, as my parents are old,
I am even less willing to hold official posts,
and thus neglect my morning and evening duties.
The previous court, for this reason,
graciously permitted my request,
so I was able to decline honorable appointments for consecutive years
and only hold minor, nominal positions with meager pay.
Since I have been accustomed to this for many years,
and am also old and afflicted by illness,
how can I preside over matters in the 'riverside' (referring to court affairs)
or join the ranks of the 'eastern plain' (referring to officials in the capital)?
I originally had no ambition to abandon the world,
nor was I capable of being aloof and esteemed.
This is what all discerning gentlemen should deeply observe.
Recently, upon receiving the initial summons,
I hoped to secure a position among the lesser guests,
but firmly declined the honorable rank.
What was the reason for this?
Because ancient kings and great lords
would sometimes use this to attract scholars from all directions.
The truly excellent ones would gather like spokes to the hub at Yān Lù,
admiring the righteousness of the kings,
or lift their reins at Wèi Què,
praising the benevolence of the noble sons.
Subsequently, there were those who followed Shēn and Bái into Chǔ,
and those who admired Zōu and Méi and traveled to Liáng.
I dare not presume to be like those former worthies,
but I hope to follow in the footsteps of the lesser ones.
Since I am not different from those who hear the Dao and gather in the academies,
and fortunately have no official duties to bind me,
I can serve my parents,
and pursue my private plans.
This is where my ambition lies."
He was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
but declined all such appointments.
Huán was slender and small in stature,
but his scholarship was unmatched in his time.
No scholar or noble youth in the capital would fail to lower their seats to receive his instruction.
His character was humble, straightforward, and of good reputation,
and he did not boast of his high reputation.
When visiting old friends,
only one student would follow him carrying a folding stool.
Before the host was informed,
he would sit down and engage in conversation.
He lived in Tánqiáo,
in a few tiled rooms,
all leaky above.
Students respected and admired him,
not daring to point this out,
and called him Qīngxī (Clear Stream).
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng personally went to visit him.
In the seventh year,
he memorialized Shìzǔ to establish a residence for Huán,
granting him the former mansion at Yánglièqiáo.
All the students congratulated him.
Huán said:
"A beautiful house brings disaster to its owner.
How can this magnificent dwelling be my home?
I would rather ask for it to be made into a lecture hall.
I still fear it might harm me."
Before he could move,
he fell ill.
Zǐliáng sent Liú Huì of Péngchéng and Fàn Zhěn of Chúyáng, who were students of Huán,
to bring a kitchen to Huán's residence to prepare meals.
When he passed away,
his disciples and students all wore mourning clothes and attended the funeral.
He was fifty-six years old at the time.

Jiǎn (儉) replied:

The divergent views of Shī (施) and Mèng (孟),

how can one rely solely on Xiǎo Wáng (小王)

Following tradition, Zhèng (鄭) is retained,

Yuán Kǎi’s (元凱) commentary on the *Zhuàn* (傳)

Jiǎ's (賈) annotations to the classics

The *Gǔliáng* (穀梁) is a minor text,

Retaining Mí (麋) and omitting Fàn (范)

All these principles
are in accord with refined discussions.
Regarding the doubt that the *Xiàojīng* (孝經) was not annotated by Zhèng (鄭),
I consider this book to elucidate the foremost of all virtues,
truly what human relationships prioritize.
The *Qīlǜe* (七略) and *Yìwénzhì* (藝文志) both categorize it among the Six Arts,
not in the same class as *Cāngjié* (蒼頡) or *Fánjiāng* (凡將).
Zhèng’s (鄭) annotations, whether factual or not,
were not questioned in previous generations.
I believe it can be maintained,
so it remains in its established place.”
Jiǎn (儉) considered himself widely learned and knowledgeable,

Chéng (澄) said:

After Chéng (澄) waited for Jiǎn (儉) to finish speaking,

The historian remarks: Confucian virtues prevailed in the world,

At the beginning of Jiànyuán's reign,

doubtful.

As Yín (寅) had his own troops,

"When the emperor goes out in the evening,
