Zǐqīng (子卿) was relieved of his supervisory duties.
〔二八〕
While Zǐqīng (子卿) was at his post,
he manufactured clothes and ornaments
that often violated regulations.
The Emperor issued an edict to him, saying:
"I have issued edicts before,
not just once or twice,
stating that princes are not allowed to make inappropriate styles of clothing and ornaments.
Why do you not recall my edicts at all?
Why did you suddenly make a set of tortoiseshell carriage fittings?
What was the meaning of that?
Since it's already made, there's no need to destroy it,
but you should send it down quickly.
As for the pure silver carriage fittings,
that might be acceptable,
but why are the stirrups also made of silver?
You must destroy them immediately.
Why did you suddenly wrap the arrow nocks with gold foil?
What was the meaning of that?
You must also destroy them quickly.
As for all official attire and ornaments,
from now on, if you dare to make them without informing me,
if I hear of it later,
you will again receive a painful beating."
He also said:
"When you were in the capital,
your studies did not progress.
As your age increases,
I daily hope for your improvement.
Do not let my edicts pass by your ears like the wind,
making me lose heart."
In the fifth year,
he entered the court as Palace Attendant and General Who Pacifies the Army,
but before he could take up the post,
he was retained as Central Protector of the Army,
with the Palace Attendant position as before.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat,
concurrently holding the post of General of the Right Guard.
Soon after, he was transferred to Central Army General,
with the Palace Attendant position as before.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.

Soon after, he was transferred to Bearer of Credentials, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of Nán Yù (南豫), 【豫】 and Sī (司) three prefectures,〔二九〕General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Nán Yù Zhōu (南豫州),
with the Palace Attendant position as before.
When Zǐqīng (子卿) took up his post,
he playfully arranged his troops into a naval force on the road.
The Emperor heard of it,
was greatly angered,
and executed his clerk.
He sent Kēng (鏗), Prince of Yídū (宜都), to replace him.
Zǐqīng (子卿) returned to his residence,
and until his death,
the Emperor did not see him.
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
he was again made Palace Attendant and General of Agile Cavalry.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was transferred to General of the Guards, with the ceremonial privilege of establishing an administration equal to the Three Excellencies,
and was allowed to recruit military assistants.
When Qiāng (鏘), Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽), was murdered,
Zǐqīng (子卿) was appointed to replace him as Minister of Education,
and was allowed to lead troops and establish assistants.
Soon after, he was also murdered,
at the age of twenty-seven.
Zǐxiǎng (子響), Marquis of Yúfù (魚復), courtesy name Yúnyīn (雲音),
was the fourth son of Shìzǔ (世祖).
Yí (嶷), Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章), had no son,
so he adopted Zǐxiǎng (子響).
Later, he had a son of his own,
but he memorialized to keep Zǐxiǎng (子響) as his heir.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was made General Who Assists the State and Administrator of the two prefectures of Southern Péngchéng (彭城) and Lín'huái (臨淮),
and he showed no respect to the other princes.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) was extraordinarily strong and brave;
he could draw a bow with a four-hú (斛) force.
He often galloped on horseback under bamboo trees in gardens and ponds,
without ever getting injured.
Since he was adopted as heir,
his carriages and attire differed from those of the other princes.
Every time he came to court,
he would become furious
and punch the walls of his carriage.
Shìzǔ (世祖) knew of this and ordered that his carriages and attire be the same as the imperial princes.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
he was transferred to be Right General of the Guards (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn).

Subsequently, he was sent out as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of Xīyáng Commandery in Yùzhōu and Yǐngzhōu, and Rǔnán Commandery [of Sīzhōu], General of the Champions (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu.
The following year,
he was promoted to the title of Right General (Yòu Jiāngjūn).
He was further [made] Area Commander-in-Chief (Dū) of Lìyáng, Huáinán, Yǐngchuān, and Rǔyáng Commanderies in Nányùzhōu.
and Right General of the Guards (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year,
the relevant authorities memorialized:
"Zǐxiǎng's (子響) body is endowed with sagely brilliance,
and he was sent out to inherit a ducal state.
Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Chén Yí (臣嶷) previously had no heir,
and so he adopted and raised him with his whole heart.
Your Majesty, with your great love for kinship,
and Chén Yí (臣嶷) with his deep affection for a nephew,
thus made him succeed to the line and flourish.
The imperial succession (shìzuò) was about to be altered,
the (symbols of) feudal authority were flourishing,
and the principal heir was not to be moved.
Truly, this is to delight in the custom of harmonious affection,
and to establish the teaching of succession by the legitimate son.
Your servants have deliberated,
and Zǐxiǎng (子響) should return to his original (family)."
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed as King of Bādōng Commandery,
transferred to be Central Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn),
and his position as Cavalier-in-Attendance (Chángshì) remained as before.
Soon after, he was sent out as Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu,
his position as Cavalier-in-Attendance (Chángshì) remaining as before.
In the seventh year,
He entered the court as Cavalier-in-Attendance (Sànqí Chángshì)
Zǐxiǎng (子響) had been fond of military matters since he was young.
When he was in Xīyù,
he personally selected sixty armed attendants,
all of whom were courageous and capable.
Upon reaching his post,
he frequently slaughtered cattle and prepared wine in his private chambers,
and enjoyed himself with them.
He ordered his female attendants to secretly make brocade robes and crimson jackets,
intending to give them to the indigenous tribes (mán) in exchange for weapons.
Liu Yín (劉寅), his Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ), and others jointly sent a secret memorial,
and the Emperor ordered a thorough investigation.
Yín (寅) and the others, fearful,
wished to keep it secret.
Zǐxiǎng (子響), hearing that the imperial envoy had arrived,
and not having seen the imperial order,

summoned Yín (寅), Army Supervisor (Sīmǎ) Xí Gōngmù (席恭穆), Consulting Adjutants (Zīyì Cānjūn) Jiāng Yù (江愈) and Yīn Táncàn (殷曇粲), Central Military Adjutant (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) Zhōu Yàn (周 Yàn), and Administrative Secretaries (Diǎnqiān) Wú Xiūzhī (吳脩之), Wáng Xiánzōng (王賢宗), and Wèi Jǐngyuān (魏景淵) to the terrace of the zither (Qíntái) and questioned them.
Yín (寅) and the others remained silent.
Xiūzhī (脩之) said:
"Since an imperial edict has arrived,
we should appropriately respond and explain."
Jǐngyuān (景淵) said:
"We should first conduct an inspection."
Zǐxiǎng (子響) was furious,
and seized Yín (寅) and the others, killing them in the rear hall.
Because Jiāng Yù's (江愈) name was not on the memorial,
he wanted to release him,
but those ordered to kill had already carried out the execution.
The Emperor, hearing of this, was enraged.

He dispatched Grand Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi) Hú Xiézhī (胡諧之), Guerrilla General (Yóujī Jiāngjūn) Yǐn Lüè (尹略), and Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Rú Fǎliàng (茹法亮) leading several hundred palace guards (zhāizhàng),
to arrest the various petty officials.
The imperial order stated:
"If Zǐxiǎng (子響) binds himself and surrenders,
his life may be spared."
Xiézhī (諧之) and others arrived at the Jiāngjīn (江津) ferry,
built a fortress at Yànwěizhōu (燕尾洲),
and sent the imperial messenger Shí Bó'ér (石伯兒) into the city to comfort and reassure him.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) said:
"I am not a rebel;
Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) and the others betrayed me.
Now I only deserve the crime of murder."
Thereupon, he slaughtered cattle and prepared food and wine,
sending them to the imperial army.
But Xiézhī (諧之) and the others were suspicious and afraid,
and arrested Zǐxiǎng's (子響) officials.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) was angered,
and sent several tens of his adopted men to collect weapons from the prefecture and commandery (fǔzhōu).
He ordered two thousand men to cross the river west of Língxī (靈溪),
planning to confront the imperial army on the south bank at dawn.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) himself, with over a hundred robed horsemen,
carrying three or four powerful crossbows (wànjūn nǔ),
camped on the river dike.
The next day,
the rebellious faction fought with the imperial army.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) fired crossbows from the dike,
and desperate men like Wáng Chōngtiān (王充天) advanced on the city with shields,
Yǐn Lüè (尹略) died,
and the government troops retreated.
The Emperor again dispatched Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn) Xiāo Shùnzhī (蕭順之) leading troops to follow up,
and scattered.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) then, in white mourning clothes, surrendered,
and was granted death.
At that time, he was twenty-two years old.
Before his death,
he memorialized the Emperor, saying:
"Liu Yín (劉寅) and others entered my chambers to inspect weapons,
as detailed in my previous memorial.
My crimes are as vast as mountains and seas,
Upon receiving the imperial order dispatching Hú Xiézhī (胡諧之) and Rú Fǎliàng (茹法亮) to bestow great favor,
when they arrived,
they did not proclaim the edict,
but instead erected banners and entered the ferry,
building a fort on the south bank opposite the city and defending it.
I repeatedly sent letters asking Fǎliàng (法亮) to cross over,
begging to see him in white mourning clothes,
but he absolutely refused.
My subordinates became terrified,
and thus led to the attack and battle.
This is my crime.
On the twenty-fifth of this month, I submitted myself to the army,
hoping to return to the Imperial Palace (Tiānquè),
stay in my residence for one month,
and I would then take my own life.
This would spare the Qí (齊) dynasty the criticism of killing a son,
and I would be free from the slander of being an unfilial son.
Since my wishes were not fulfilled,
my life now ends.
As I begin this memorial, I am choked with emotion;
I know not what more to say."
The relevant authorities memorialized to sever Zǐxiǎng's (子響) registration in the imperial clan,
strip him of his rank and land,
and hand him over to the Supreme Judge (Tíngwèi) for legal prosecution.
He was posthumously granted the surname Qiāo (蛸).
All those implicated
were separately investigated and judged.
Liu Yín (劉寅) was posthumously granted Attendant Counselor (Shìzhōng);
Xí Gōngmù (席恭穆) was posthumously granted General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu;
Jiāng Yù (江愈) and Yīn Táncàn (殷曇粲) were posthumously granted Palace Gate Yellow Gate Official (Huángmén Láng);
Yín's (寅) courtesy name was Jǐngrúi (景蕤),
and he was a native of Gāopíng.
He was learned in literature and meaning, but not skilled in worldly affairs.
Xí Gōngmù (席恭穆)
was from Yānshì (焉氏) in Āndìng,
a prominent clan in Guānlǒng.
The Emperor felt pity for Zǐxiǎng's (子響) death.
Later, when he visited Huálín Yuán (華林園),
he saw apes leaping and calling to their young.
The Emperor gazed for a long time,
and then sobbed and shed tears.
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí (豫章王嶷) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that killing those who commit grave offenses
has been manifest since the Spring and Autumn period,
carried out by the executioners,
and inscribed in the Rites.
Yet, there are still words of not bearing to do it,
and still the pain as if it were one's own kin.
Is it not that affairs proceed according to law,
but emotions remain due to grace?
Therefore, the commoner Qiāo Zǐxiǎng (蛸子響)
had no moral foundation in his heart,
and became lost in his misconduct,
giving vent to his anger for a day,
and falling into wicked behavior.
This caused his actions to border on unfilial conduct,
and his deeds to be close to disloyalty to his sovereign.
His body lies exposed in the wilderness,
and it cannot be said that the offense has been atoned for.
However, he sheathed his arrows and inverted his spears,
and surrendered to the executioners.
Considering the reason behind his actions,
he indeed went astray but knew how to return.
His bones are not collected,
and his guilty soul is not pardoned.
Reflecting on past events,
my heart and eyes are deeply wounded.
In the past, Mǐn Róng (閔榮) suffered punishment,
causing sorrow to his ancestral graveyard;
Sī Jīng (思荊) committed a crime and was executed,
evoking sympathy for his grave mound.
In both cases, these two officials committed offenses in an enlightened era,
and the two rulers deliberated on adding to their glorious age,
which generations have praised as virtuous,
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would extend heavenly compassion,
and issue an edict to the Qiāo (蛸) clan,
allowing him to be buried in the outer suburbs of the ancestral grave,
and laid to rest at the foot of the hill.
Let a humble hearse of reeds be permitted,
Is it only that this deceased body would receive grace?
Indeed, the whole world would attribute benevolence to you.
Your servant, though unworthy, is related by imperial lineage,
and holds special affection for his kin.
Because your servant's adopted lineage was not yet settled,
Zǐxiǎng (子響) was said to have been born of an imperial command.
I fostered and raised him,
and saw him grow into adulthood.
Although he ceased to be my adopted son and returned to his original family,
my attachment to him remains unchanged,
and my affection for nurturing him will never cease.
I dare to brave Your Majesty's sternness
to express this mournful plea."
The Emperor did not permit it.
Previously, he had been demoted to Marquis of Yúfù (Yúfù Hóu).
Ān Lùwáng Zǐjìng, courtesy name Yúnduān,
was the fifth son of Shìzǔ.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yìngchéng County.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (484),
he was appointed Chíjǐe, Jiān Nán Yǎn Xú Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu, Běizhōngláng Jiàng, and Nán Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fourth year (486),
he was promoted to Yòujūn.
〔三九〕The following year (487),
he was transferred to Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Liáng Yōng Nán Běi Qín Liùzhōu Jūnshì, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His Chíjǐe appointment remained as before.
Soon after, he was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
In the seventh year (489),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng
and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the tenth year (492),
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, and Dānyáng Yǐn.
In the eleventh year (493),
he was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was granted a set of gǔchuī.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494),
he was promoted to Shǐchíjǐe, Dūdū Nán Yǎn Xú Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu, Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn, and Nán Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494),
he was additionally appointed Shìzhōng.
Gāozōng eliminated all the feudal princes,
and sent Zhōnghùjūn Wáng Xuánmiǎo and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Guǎngzhī to attack and kill Zǐjìng.
〔四０〕He was twenty-three years old at the time.
Jìn'ānwáng Zǐmào, courtesy name Yúnchāng,
was the seventh son of Shìzǔ.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiānglíng.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485),
he was appointed Chíjǐe, Dūdū Nán Yù Yù Sī Sānzhōu, Nánzhōngláng Jiàng, and Nán Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Yúfùhóu Zǐxiǎng was appointed to Yùzhōu,
Zǐmào was relieved of his dūdū duties.
In the fourth year (486),
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
As Nán Yùzhōu was newly established
and had few laborers,
Zǐmào was additionally appointed to lead Xuānchéng Tàishǒu.
The following year (487),
he was appointed Jiān Nán Yǎn Xú Qīng Jì Wǔzhōu Jūnshì, Hòujiāngjūn, and Nán Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Chíjǐe appointment remaining as before.
In the sixth year (488),
he was transferred to Jiān Xiāngzhōu, Píngnán Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The following year (489),
he was additionally appointed Chíjǐe and Dūdū.
In the eighth year (490),
he was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn.
He compiled "Chūnqiū Lìyuàn" in thirty volumes and presented it.
Shìzǔ praised it
and ordered it to be stored in the Mìgé.
In the ninth year (491),
he personally managed the affairs of the fu and zhou.
In the tenth year (492),
he entered the court to serve as Shìzhōng
and lead Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the eleventh year (493),
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì
and Zhōngshū Jiān.
Before he could take up the post,
he was still appointed Shǐchíjǐe, Dūdū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu zhī Suíjùn Jūnshì, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and granted a set of gǔchuī.
As Yùzhāngwáng was still in mourning,
the Emperor, believing that border regions required prestige,
allowed him to make the memorial.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was appointed Dàjiāngjūn with his original title.
Zǐmào, seeing the young emperor newly enthroned,
secretly harbored a plan for self-preservation.
He ordered the manufacturing department to produce weapons and equipment.
Chén Xiǎndá, who was Zhēnglǔ at the time,
was stationed in Xiāngyáng, and Zǐmào wanted to coerce him into becoming his general.
Chén Xiǎndá secretly memorialized,
and Gāozōng summoned Xiǎndá back.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494),
Zǐmào was transferred to Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
leaving his troops from Xīchǔ to assist in guarding Xiāngyáng,
and only taking his personal guards and imperial carriage guards with him.
When Xiǎndá entered to bid farewell,
〔四一〕Zǐmào said to him:
"The court has ordered me to return alone,
but I am a royal prince,
how can I be so careless?
I still want to take two or three thousand men with me;
what do you think, Duke?"
Xiǎndá replied:
"If Your Highness does not leave your troops,
that would be a great disobedience to the imperial decree,
and the matter is not trivial.
Moreover, it is difficult to recruit people from this region for your use."
Zǐmào was silent,
and Xiǎndá then excused himself and departed.
Zǐmào's plan had not yet materialized,
so he returned to guard Xúnyáng.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494),
he was additionally appointed Shìzhōng.
Hearing that the two princes of Póyáng and Suíjùn had been killed,
he wished to raise an army to respond to the crisis.
His mother, Ruǎn, was in the capital,
and he sent a letter wishing to secretly welcome the Emperor.
Ruǎn
informed her brother Yú Yáozhī of the plan.
〔四二〕Yáozhī rushed to inform Gāozōng.
Thereupon, preparations were made,
and Píngxī Jiāngjūn Wáng Guǎngzhī was sent to attack the north and south.
Jūnzhu Péi Shúyè and Yáozhī were sent to first attack Xúnyáng,
claiming to be the Xíngsīmǎ of Yǐngzhōu.
〔四三〕Zǐmào, knowing this,
sent three hundred men to guard Pénchéng.
Shúyè sailed upstream,
〔四四〕and at night turned back to attack Pénchéng.
Chéngjú Cānjūn Yuè Bēn opened the gate and let them in.
Zǐmào gathered his administrative and military forces,
and had already prepared boats at Qíjǐng Zhǔ.
Hearing that Shúyè had taken Pénchéng,
he then held the zhou to defend himself.
Many of Zǐmào's troops were people from Yōng,
and they were all eager to fight.
Shúyè, fearing them,
sent Yú Yáozhī to persuade Zǐmào, saying:
"If you return to the capital now,
there will certainly be no excessive worries;
you will just become a sǎnguān
and will not lose your wealth and status."
Since Zǐmào did not send out troops to attack Shúyè,
〔四五〕the morale of his forces gradually dwindled.
Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Yú Línzhī,
who was Yáozhī's brother,
persuaded Zǐmào to heavily bribe Shúyè.
Zǐmào sent Línzhī to go.
Línzhī then persuaded Shúyè to take Zǐmào.
Shúyè sent Jūnzhu Xú Xuánqìng with four hundred men to follow Línzhī into the zhou city.
His subordinates all scattered and fled.
Línzhī, with two hundred men, burst into Zāi.
〔四六〕Zǐmào cursed, saying:
"How can such a petty person be so ruthless as to do this?"
Línzhī covered his face with his sleeve
and ordered someone to kill him.
He was twenty-three years old at the time.
Previously,
when Zǐmào was stationed in Yōng,
Shìzǔ instructed him with a border strategy, saying:
"I have recently received memorials from various places,
and what they say is consistent:
the barbarians will certainly not dare to send themselves to their deaths.
However, we must be prepared for them and cannot slacken even for a moment.
If these dog-and-sheep folk
are rampant this autumn,
it is a sign of their impending demise.
I am also secretly making preparations now,
and once there is a clear target,
there will be a major disposition.
I now generally order all garrison commanders
to mobilize commoners and able-bodied men.
If anything happens, they should immediately respond and transport supplies.
〔四七〕I have already issued an order to send more (men),
and I expect that they will arrive soon.
You should discuss with others
how many people can be sent to Nányáng Wǔyīn and other important places to scout.
〔四八〕Food is the most fundamental thing;
do not worry about personnel or weapons.
Always inspect the horses at the postal stations;
there must be no omissions or negligence.
Also, instruct all the zhou
to do the same within their respective jurisdictions.
If they fail to comply with the law,
they will be interrogated."
〔四九〕He also said:
"I have ordered the two garrisons of Jīng and Yǐng
to each form a five-thousand-man array,
originally intended to respond to them.
If the enemy sends themselves to their deaths,
then summon and capture them.
I have already ordered Zǐzhēn.
When Yú Jìzōng and Yīn Gōngmǐn arrive at the garrison,
〔五０〕Gōngmǐn can be made the city lord,
and three thousand men assigned to him will be sufficient.
You should carefully consider ranks and positions,
do not seek (them for) others,
or exceed three to five ranks.
As for essays, poetry, and writing,
〔五一〕these are fine accomplishments,
but worldly affairs are even more fundamental;
you should always remember this.
The weapons you requested in your memorial
are all my personal imperial guards' weapons;
how can you use them?
The regulations must not be violated.
I will arrange to send some of superior quality."
Previously, he had requested his favorite books in a memorial,
and the Emperor further said:
"Knowing that you always keep reading in your heart,
I am deeply pleased."
He bestowed upon Zǐmào Du Yù's hand-edited "Zuǒzhuàn" and "Gǔjīn Shànyán".
Suí-jùn Wáng Zǐlóng
(courtesy name Yúnxīng), was
Emperor Shìzǔ's eighth son.
He had literary talent.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhījiāng.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 CE),
he was appointed as Auxiliary General of the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn)
and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Lángxié and Péngchéng.
The following year,
he was promoted to Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
Before he could take up the post,
when the rebellion of Táng Qièzhī was quelled,
he was transferred to be a Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of the five commanderies of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, and Yǒngjiā,
General of the Central Guard (Dōngzhōngláng Jiāngjūn),
and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
He was then transferred to be an additional Censor-in-Chief (Zhǎngjiān Zhōngshū Lìng).
Zǐlóng married the daughter of the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìng) Wáng Jiǎn as his consort.
The Emperor, seeing Zǐlóng's literary ability,
said to Wáng Jiǎn,
"My family is of Dōng'ā lineage."
Wáng Jiǎn replied,
"Dōng'ā has emerged again,
truly serving as a bulwark for the imperial house."
Before he could take up this post,
he was again transferred to be Protector-General (Zhōnghùjūn),
then shifted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
In the eighth year,
he replaced the Marquis of Yúfù Zǐxiǎng as Bearer of Credentials (Shǐchíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of the six northern and southern prefectures of Jīng, Yōng, Liáng, Níng, and Qín,
General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn),
and Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
and was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
That year,
when Shǐxīng Wáng Jiàn was dismissed from Yìzhōu,
Zǐlóng was granted the additional title of Area Commander of Yìzhōu.
In the ninth year,
he personally managed the affairs of his headquarters and the prefecture.
In the eleventh year,
when Jìn'ān Wáng Zǐmào became Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
Zǐlóng again relinquished his Area Commander title.
When Yùlín was enthroned,
Zǐlóng was advanced to the title of General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he became Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
commanding troops and appointing his own staff.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
he was transferred to General-in-Chief of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn),
with his Palace Attendant position remaining as before.
Zǐlóng was twenty-one years old,
and his body was excessively robust.
He often took medicine to reduce his build.
When Gāozōng (Xiāo Luán) assisted in governing,
he plotted to harm the various princes.
Among Emperor Shìzǔ's sons,
Zǐlóng was most feared for his talent,
so he was killed on the same night as the King of Póyáng, Xiāo Qiāng.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Zǐzhēn
(courtesy name Yúnxiān), was
Emperor Shìzǔ's ninth son.
In the fourth year of Yǒngmíng (486 CE),
he was appointed Auxiliary General of the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn)
and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Lángxié and Péngchéng.
He was transferred to Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),

General of Exemplary Valor (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn),
and Inspector of Southern Yùzhōu,
additionally holding the post of Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
He was advanced to the title of General of the Southern Guard (Nánzhōngláng Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year,
seeing that his headquarters and prefecture were somewhat substantial,
he memorialized to relinquish his concurrent post as Grand Administrator.
In the seventh year,
he was advanced to the title of General of the Right (Yòujiāngjūn),
and transferred to Governor of Dānyáng,
with his general's title remaining as before.
He was then transferred to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to Protector-General (Zhōnghùjūn),
and then sent out as Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of military affairs of the two prefectures of Yǐng and Sī,

In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he became Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
he was transferred to General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn),
commanding troops and appointing his own staff,
with his Attendant-in-Ordinary position remaining as before.
He was killed that year,
at the age of nineteen.
Xīyáng Wáng Zǐmíng
(courtesy name Yúnguāng), was
Emperor Shìzǔ's tenth son.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (483 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the King of Wǔchāng.
In the third year,
having lost the state seal,
he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Xīyáng.
In the sixth year,
he became Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of military affairs of the five prefectures of Southern Xǔ, Qīng, Jì,
General of Exemplary Valor (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn),
and Inspector of Southern Xǔzhōu.
In the eighth year,
he was advanced to the title of General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn).
In the tenth year,
he was advanced to General of the Left (Zuǒjiāngjūn),
and also became Area Commander (Dūdú) of military affairs of the five commanderies of Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn'ān,
and Grand Administrator of Kuàijī,
with his general's title remaining as before.
Zǐmíng had a clear and pure demeanor and appearance;
men and women who observed him
all sighed in admiration.
At the beginning of Yùlín's reign,
he was advanced to the title of General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he became General of the Right (Yòujiāngjūn) and Censor-in-Chief (Zhōngshū Lìng).
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
he was transferred to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
concurrently holding the position of General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
with his Right General title remaining as before.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (494 CE),
he was transferred to General of the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn),
commanding troops and appointing his own staff.
In the second year (495 CE),
Xiāo Chén was executed.
Zǐmíng, his younger brother Zǐhǎn, and Zǐzhēn
were falsely accused of conspiring with Chén
and were killed,
at the age of seventeen.
Nánhǎi Wáng Zǐhǎn
(courtesy name Yúnhuá), was
Emperor Shìzǔ's eleventh son.
In the sixth year of Yǒngmíng (488 CE),
he became General of the Northern Guard (Běizhōngláng Jiāngjūn)
and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Lángxié and Péngchéng.
The Emperor initially considered Báixià to be connected by rivers and mountains,
so he moved the Lángxié Commandery to be governed from Jīnchéng.
Zǐhǎn was the first to guard this city.
In the tenth year,
he became Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of military affairs of the five prefectures of Southern Xǔ, Qīng, Jì,
General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and Inspector of Southern Xǔzhōu.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was advanced to the title of General of the Rear (Hòujiāngjūn).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì)
and General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (494 CE),
he was transferred to Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the second year (495 CE),
he was killed,
at the age of seventeen.
Bālíng Wáng Zǐlún
(courtesy name Yúnzōng), was
Emperor Shìzǔ's thirteenth son.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (489 CE),
he became Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié),
Area Commander (Dūdú) of military affairs of the two prefectures of Southern Yù and Sī,
General of the Southern Guard (Nánzhōngláng Jiāngjūn),
and Inspector of Southern Yùzhōu.
In the tenth year,
he was transferred to General of the Northern Guard (Běizhōngláng Jiāngjūn)
and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Southern Lángxié and Péngchéng.
[五二] When Yùlín ascended the throne,
considering the generous emoluments of Southern Péngchéng,
he took it from Zǐlún and gave it to the Palace Editor (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Qímǔ Zhēnzhī,
replacing it with Southern Lánlíng.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì)
and General of the Left (Zuǒjiāngjūn).
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
the Palace Editor (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Rú Fǎliàng was sent to kill Zǐlún.
Zǐlún, properly dressed, came out to receive the imperial edict,
and said:
"When a bird is about to die,
its cries are sorrowful;
when a man is about to die,
his words are good.
The previous dynasty once extinguished the Liú clan;
what happens today
is indeed a matter of fate and reason.
You are an old acquaintance of my family;
now, carrying out this mission,
it must be that circumstances leave you no choice."
Rú Fǎliàng did not dare to reply and withdrew.
Zǐlún was sixteen years old.

In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (489 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shǔjùn.
During the Jiànwǔ era (494 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng.

His mother, Lady Xún,

Xiāngdōng Wángzǐ Jiàn, courtesy name Yúnlì,

he ordered her to return to her son.
Zǐjiàn was killed in the first year of Yǒngtài (498 CE),
at the age of thirteen.
Nánjùn Wángzǐ Xià, courtesy name Yúnguǎng,

As the emperor was advanced in years,

Initially,
Shìzǔ dreamt of a golden-winged bird descending into the palace courtyard,
devouring countless small dragons,

In the first year of Yǒngtài (498 CE),

at the age of seven.

Zhāng Róng, courtesy name Sīguāng,
was a native of Wújùn, Wú.
His grandfather, Huī,
was the Lángzhōnglìng of the Principality of Lángxié in the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Chàng, was the Grand Administrator of Huìjī in the Sòng dynasty.
When Róng was a youth (twenty years old),
the Daoist Lù Xiūjìng, also from Wújùn,
gave Róng a whisk made of egret feathers,
saying:
"This is an unusual object,
bestowed upon an unusual person."
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng heard of Róng's early renown,
and appointed him without examination as the Cānjūn of the Beizhōngláng of the Prince of Xīn'ān.
When Xiàowǔ began building Xīn'ān Temple,
most of his subordinates donated money and silk,
but Róng alone donated one hundred coins.
The emperor said:
"Róng is exceptionally poor,
he should be promoted to a good position."
He was sent out as the Magistrate of Fēngxī.
His paternal uncle, Yǒng, saw him off at the rear sandbar,
saying:
"It seems I heard an imperial decree that
you will soon return."
Róng replied:
"I am not worried about not returning,
only about returning and then leaving again."
Guǎngyuè was steep and treacherous.
Barbarian bandits captured Róng,

Róng's expression remained calm;

The bandits found this extraordinary and did not harm him.

leaves clustered together, embracing each other.
Penetrating the clouds, brushing against each other,
connecting their sounds with the wind.
Shaking the islets and eroding the banks,
so that a thousand *lǐ* seem to collapse,
dashing against cliffs and inundating valleys,
so that ten thousand nations seem to be at war.
Shaking with majestic power to stir up thunder,
flying with heroic light to reverse lightning.
As for the rising clouds, they have no qi,
the flowing wind gathers its sound.
The patterned ripples move again,
the color of the waves startles anew.
How distant is the bright moon,
the sandy banks divide the stars.
As for its accumulation
of treasures, it is entirely remote;
its display of jewels speaks of depth.
Jade pools and jade ravines,
pearl-like peaks and towering summits.
Closing the day and opening the night,
unfurling the moon and dispelling the shade.
Corals unfold their patterns,
lapis lazuli lifts
its splendor.
Red patterns reflect colors,
various reflections like icy mists.
Vast and turbulent,
bathing the sun and moon.
Submerging the Milky Way's stellar regions,
permeating the Heavenly River's realm.
From what origin does the wind
arise by itself,
from where do clouds appear only to vanish?
Enveloping beautiful colors to brush away smoke,
〔一九〕mirroring the hanging radiance to illuminate snow.
Then, square and round depart from me,
blending together, emotions settle.
The *qi* is warm and turbid,
transformation to stillness naturally clears it.
The mind has no end, thus it does not stagnate;
the will does not fail, yet achieves nothing.
It overturns boats and carries boats,
it necessarily causes death and gives life.
It extends the straw dog to humans and beasts,
guiding to the fundamental to fill form.
Though all things are used daily,
how can
they be woven or strung together?
The Way is deep from the beginning of heaven,
its essence flourishes beyond form.
It exists without a reason for existing,
not adhering to existence at life's end.
It is non-existent without a reason for being non-existent,
truly
entering the Great Oneness without intention.
Not moving the moving causes mountains and peaks to collapse,
not sounding the sounding enables heaven and earth to be in harmony.
Action and concealment are empty in their use and abandonment,
response and sensation are truly in
their perfect union.
The benevolent see it and call it benevolence;
the discerning see it and call it discernment.
The talkative are close to the highest good,
I truly believe it to be great!
Róng's prose was strange and vehement,
unique and different from the crowd.
Later, returning to the capital,
he showed it to General Zhèn[jūn] Gù Jìzhī.
〔二０〕Gù Jìzhī said:
"Your *fù* is truly transcendent and profound,
but [it's a pity] it doesn't mention salt."
〔二一〕Róng immediately asked for a brush and added:
"Filtering sand produces white,
boiling waves yields pure white.
Accumulated snow in mid-spring,
flying frost on the summer road."
These four lines
were added later.
Gù Jìzhī had a good relationship with Róng's elder brother,
and when Gù Jìzhī died,
Róng personally carried earth for his grave.
While in the south, he had an old friendship with Biàn Zhǎn, the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ.
When Zhǎn was killed by someone in Lǐngnán,
Róng personally rushed to his aid.
He was recommended as Xiùcái,
and passed the examination with his policy proposals,
serving as Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng,
but did not take the position,
instead becoming Yícáo Láng.
〔二二〕In the fifth year of Tàishǐ (469 CE),
Emperor Míng recruited archers from the four provinces of Jīng, Yǐng, Xiāng, and Yōng.
Those who rebelled would be executed, along with their family heads,
and their family members would be enslaved by the Xīguān.
In the early Yuánhuī period (473 CE),
there were rebels among the Yǐng Province archers.
Róng argued that the families and family heads should not be implicated,
and that those who fled should be sentenced to five years.
Soon after, he requested leave to attend his uncle's funeral.
Along the way, he was punished by Gàn Qián Jìngdào with fifty lashes,
and was temporarily imprisoned in Yánlíng prison.
An edict from the fifth year of Dàmíng (461 CE) stipulated that
second-rank pure officials subjected to a servant's rod or cane
should not receive more than ten strokes.
He was impeached by Zuǒ Chéng Sūn Miǎn,
and dismissed from office.
He was soon reinstated,
taking charge of both Cícáo and Cāngbù departments.
When the commander Liú Miǎn died in battle,
〔二三〕Cícáo debated
"whether the Emperor should mourn Miǎn."
Róng argued
"that mourning was appropriate."
Thereupon, the mourning began.
Cāngcáo then asked,
"The first month is taboo for commoners,
should the imperial granary be opened or not?"
Róng argued
"that one should not be constrained by minor taboos."
Soon after, he concurrently managed the Zheng department.
When Róng witnessed a slaughter,
he turned his carriage and left directly,
personally memorializing to resign his post.
He served as Fǔjūn Cāngcáo Cānjūn for the Prince of Ānchéng,
then transferred to become the Friend of the Prince of Nányáng.
Róng's father, Chàng, had previously served as Prime Minister's Chief Clerk.
During Yìxuān's rebellion,
Chàng was captured by Wáng Xuánmó,
who was about to kill him.
Xuánmó's son, Zhān, was the Front Army Chief Clerk for the Prince of Nányáng.
Róng petitioned to resign his office,
but it was not granted.
Zhāng Róng (張融) was poor and wished to obtain an official salary.
He first wrote to his paternal uncle, Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn (征北將軍) Yǒng (永), saying:
"In the past, Róng (融) was known for his early studies,
and trained early in family traditions.
Although not keen,
I have generally formed my character accordingly.
Clothes of coarse cloth and a mat of reeds
were what I found peace in during my youth.
A single basket of food and a gourd of drink,
I felt no discomfort or unhappiness.
However, the family's traditional livelihood is pure poverty,
and people's lives require much sustenance.
Hazelnut, chestnut, jujube, and cured meat
are what daughters offer when they grow up;
bolts of silk and birds
are what sons offer as a great礼.
I strive to take up official positions,
serving seven times in ten years.
I do not wish to replace farming,
but why has it come to this matter?
In the past, I sought to be a Chief of Wú (吳),
though it repeatedly met with failure.
Now I hear that Nánkāng (南康) lacks a Prefect,
and I wish to take up that post.
Róng (融) does not know the hierarchy of ranks;
the hierarchy of ranks may also be unknown to me.
Róng (融) sought to be a Chief and did not get it,
which is why he sought a Commandery;
if he does not get a Commandery,
he can also seek to be a Chief again."
He also wrote to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔), saying:
"Róng (融)
is a hermit of heaven and earth.
When advancing, I do not distinguish nobility;
when retreating, I do not know baseness.
I am utterly natural, like a creation,
suddenly like grass and trees.
In reality, due to accumulated family poverty,
and the heartbreaking situation of orphans and widows,
with eight nephews all orphaned,
and two younger brothers quite weak,
I am moved when I comfort them,
which is what ancient people considered sorrow.
How can the paltry salary of mountains and seas
express Róng's (融) emotional burdens?
Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) loved the local customs of Dōngpíng (東平);
Róng (融) also delights in the tranquility beyond Jìnpíng (晉平)."
At the time, public opinion held that Róng (融) was not talented in governing the populace,
so he ultimately did not succeed.
He was appointed Tai Fù Yuàn (太傅掾) under Tàizǔ (太祖),
and served successively as Pīqí Yùzhāngwáng Sīkōng Cányì Cānjūn (驃騎豫章王司空諮議參軍),
then promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎).
This was not to his liking,
so he requested to be Zhōngsàn Dàfū (中散大夫),
but was not permitted.
Róng's (融) mannerisms were strange and eccentric;
he often sat with his knees up,
walked with a dragging step,
and leaned back with his head raised.
His self-imposed eccentricities were many.
When accompanying others according to custom,
he often lagged and did not advance.
Tàizǔ (太祖) had always held Róng (融) in high esteem and affection.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was Táiwèi (太尉),
he often spoke intimately with Róng (融).
Upon seeing Róng (融), he would often laugh and say:
"This person is indispensable as one,
but intolerable as two."
After Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
he personally issued an imperial edict to bestow clothes upon Róng (融), saying:
"I see your clothes are coarse and old.
This indeed stems from your usual disposition;
however, such shabbiness
is also a disgrace to the court.
I now send you a set of old clothes.
Although they are old,
I believe they are better than new ones.
These are what I have worn,
and I have ordered them to be tailored to fit your body.
Also, a pair of shoes."
Róng (融) was on good terms with Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Hé Jí (何戢).
Once, when he went to visit Jí (戢),
he mistakenly announced his arrival to Shàngshū (尚書) Liú Chéng (劉澄).
Róng (融) got out of his carriage and entered the gate,
then said:
"This is not him."
Upon reaching the doorway,
he looked at Chéng (澄) and
again said:
"This is not him."
When he finally reached the mat,
he looked at Chéng (澄) and said:
"It's all completely not him."
Then he left.
His eccentricity was like this.
He also served as Zhāngshāwáng Zhènjūn (長沙王鎮軍) and Jìnglǐngwáng Zhēngběi Cányì (竟陵王征北諮議),
simultaneously holding the position of Jìshì (記室),
and then Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng (司徒從事中郎).
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明) [484 CE],
a lecture was given at the Zǒngmíng Guān (總明觀),
and the court officials were ordered to gather and listen.
Róng (融) was helped in and sat on a couch,
secretly asking for wine to drink.
After the difficult questions were finished,
he let out a long sigh and said:
"Alas!
What kind of man was Zhòngní (仲尼)?"
He was impeached by Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Dào Huī (到撝),
dismissed from office,
but soon reinstated.
Róng (融) was short and ugly in appearance,
but his spirit was clear and sharp.
Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則) saw Róng's (融) leather belt hanging loosely,
almost reaching his crotch,
and said to him:
"Your leather belt is too tight."
Róng (融) said:
"Since I am not a footman,
why should my belt be tight?"
Róng (融) was granted leave to go east.
Shìzǔ (世祖) asked Róng (融) where he lived.
Róng (融) replied:
"Your servant has no house on land,
and no water for a boat dwelling."
The next day, the Emperor asked Róng's (融) cousin Xù (緒).
Xù (緒) said:
"Róng (融) recently went east,
but has no settled abode.
He temporarily pulled a small boat
and lives on the bank."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
When the barbarians heard Róng's (融) name,
the Emperor sent Róng (融) to receive the northern envoy Lǐ Dàogù (李道固).
As they sat down,
Dàogù (道固) looked at him and said:
"Is Zhāng Róng (張融) the son of Zhāng Chàng (張暢), Pénchéng Zhǎngshǐ (彭城長史) of Sòng (宋)?"
Róng (融) frowned for a long time,
and then said:
"My late father, unfortunately,
had his name reach the Six Barbarians."
When Yùzhāngwáng (豫章王) held a grand banquet for his retainers,
Róng (融) had just finished eating his roasted meat.
The person serving the roast then left.
Róng (融) wanted to ask for salt and garlic,
but could not bring himself to speak.
He just wiggled his index finger,
for half a day before stopping.
Whenever he entered or exited the court, people would wipe their eyes and stare at him in astonishment.
In the eighth year [of Yǒngmíng (永明), 490 CE],
court officials congratulated the emperor on auspicious omens in a public event.
Róng (融) was helped in to prostrate and rise,
but was again impeached by the appropriate officials,
and was pardoned.
He was promoted to Sītú Yòuzhǎngshǐ (司徒右長史).
Zhāng Xīnshí (張欣時) of Jìnglǐng (竟陵) was then Zhūjì Lìng (諸暨令)
and was condemned to death for a crime.
Xīnshí's (欣時) father, Xīngshì (興世), during the Sòng (宋) dynasty, attacked Nánqiáowáng Yìxuān (南譙王義宣).
The government troops wanted to kill Róng's (融) father Chàng (暢).
Xīngshì (興世) covered Chàng (暢) with his robe and sat on him,
thereby allowing him to escape death.
When Xīngshì (興世) died,
Róng (融) wore high shoes and carried earth to build his tomb.
Now, Róng (融) petitioned Jìnglǐng Wángzǐliáng (竟陵王子良),
asking to die in place of Xīnshí (欣時).
Zǐliáng (子良) replied:
"This is a noble deed for a Zhǎngshǐ (長史),
but I fear that the court has established laws,
and your wishes cannot be granted."
He was promoted to Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
and Sītú Zuǒzhǎngshǐ (司徒左長史).
Róng (融) was filial and righteous.
For three decades during the taboo month, he did not listen to music,
and served his sister-in-law with great respect.
When Sòng Chéngxiàng Yìxuān (宋丞相義宣) rebelled,
his father Chàng (暢) was almost killed for not joining him.
Sīmǎ (司馬) Zhú Chāomín (竺超民) advised against it and saved him.
Before his death, Chàng (暢) told his sons:
"In the past, during the Chancellor's rebellion,
I survived because of Sīmǎ (司馬) Zhú (竺).
You must repay his children and younger siblings."
Later, Chāomín's (超民) grandson Wēi (微) suffered his mother's death in winter,
and was poor.
Róng (融) went to offer condolences,
taking off all his clothes to give as a funeral gift,
and returned wearing only a cowhide blanket.
He always treated Wēi (微) as an elder brother.
When Yùzhāngwáng Yí (豫章王嶷) and Jìnglǐng Wángzǐliáng (竟陵王子良) died,
he considered himself a former subordinate official,
and wept uncontrollably each time.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he died of illness
at the age of fifty-four.
His dying instructions were to erect a plain white banner without streamers,
and to have someone hold a fly-whisk and climb onto the roof to recall his soul.
He said:
"What I have loved throughout my life
will naturally soar into the clouds with a smile."
Three thousand (cash) for a coffin,
no new shroud to be made.
In his left hand, he held the Xiàojīng and Lǎozǐ;
in his right hand, he held the Xiǎopǐn Fǎhuá Jīng.
His two concubines,
after the mourning rites were completed,
were each sent back to their homes.
He also said:
"Given my lifelong disposition and elegance,
how could I bear to have women weep and lose their voices?
They need not linger in the women's quarters."
Róng's profound interpretations were not based on any teacher's method,
yet his divine understanding surpassed others.
In debates, whether on white or black,
few could resist him.
In the Yǒngmíng period,
when he fell ill,
he wrote a preface to his own work, "Ménlǜ," saying:
often astonishes people of this world.
You may use your ears to learn with your heart,
but you must not let your ears be the teacher of your heart.
How can literature have a fixed style?
It is simply that having a style is taken as constant,
so it is precisely proper to always have a style.
A true man should abridge the Shī (Jīng) and Shū (Jīng),
and establish rites and music;
not to hold a sacrifice,
"The style of my writings
lacked variation in its fundamental structure;
it relied on small additions
to patch up old things.
How is my writing style different?
How could it ever confound warmth and coolness, or confuse heat and cold,
or mix sorrow and joy, or make singing and weeping crisscross?
It is simply that my choice of words is abundant,
my comparisons are unrestrained,
neither bounded nor confined,
neither a path nor a road.
However, its resonating sound and soaring spirit,
its rhythmic expression and uplifting cadence,
though perhaps not yet reaching the utmost,
have already reached their limit.
If you can find another style,
I will not restrict you.
My philosophy is also like my writing:
it may seem sudden and take hold of me,
but it does not fall into things by accident.
I have no teacher, no friends,
no set writing style, no fixed phrases;
I am quite solitary in spirit and unique.
The purpose of my philosophy
is to allow one's nature to enter clear waters,
and to cleanse the dust as if bathing.
Do not fish for fame while sharing profits,
or raise prices as if they were lofty,
thereby turning this spiritual ground
into a dangerous military road.
In the past, I delighted in the words of monks,
often engaging in Dharma debates.
These were all just playful exchanges of words and laughter,
and you yourselves have no such fortune."
He also said:
"The human mouth
is meant for discussing the Way and expounding righteousness,
and only for eating and drinking.
Beyond this, it is like a 'tree with nets.'
and you should uphold this principle."
When he was about to die,
he again admonished his son, saying:
"My handwritten works are here,
yet my father's books are unread!
Moreover, my father's sentiments
are elegantly expressed in his rhymes.
My intention is not so;
I leave you separate messages.
My writing style is exceptional and extraordinary,
constantly changing and often marvelous.
Since it cannot reach the distant Hán and Wèi dynasties,
there is no need to lament the Jìn and Sòng.
Is it due to my natural talent?
It is certainly not to disgrace my family name.
If you do not read them,
it is your father and grandfather's wish that you see them.
You may cry out loud and read them."
Róng named his collected works "Yùhǎi."
When Sītú Chǔ Yuān asked about the name "Yùhǎi,"
Róng replied:
"Jade is likened to virtue,
and the sea exalts supreme goodness."
His collected works, several tens of volumes, circulated in the world.
The Zhāng family was renowned,
with Fū, Yǎn, Jìng, Chàng before him,
and Chōng, Róng, Juǎn, Jì after him.
Zhōu Yóng, courtesy name Yànlún,
was a native of Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Jìn Zuǒguānglùdàfū Yǐ.
His grandfather, Hǔtóu,
was a Yuánwài Chángshì.
His father, Xún,
was Guīxiāng Xiàng.
Yóng was recognized as talented by his clan elder Lǎng in his youth.
He began his career as Hǎilíngguó Shìláng.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Huìkāi appreciated Yóng's uniqueness.
Upon entering Shǔ,
he was appointed Lìfēng Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently served as county magistrate for Féixiāng and Chéngdū.
retaining his titles of Jiāngjūn and magistrate.
He then became the Fǔ Zhǔbù.
He often considered Huìkāi's nature too harsh and severe,
and frequently offered remonstrances.
Huìkāi was displeased
and replied to Yóng:
"Heaven is dangerous, earth is dangerous;
kings and dukes set up dangers.
The only question is how one uses danger."
He returned to the capital with Huìkāi.
Sòng Míngdì was quite fond of discussing principles.
the emperor brought him into the palace,
keeping him close and on duty overnight.
When the emperor performed cruel and poisonous deeds,
Yóng dared not openly remonstrate,
but would recite Buddhist scriptures concerning the causes and conditions of sin and blessings.
The emperor would then somewhat curb his actions.
He was transferred to become Ānchéngwáng Fǔjūn Xíngcānjūn.
In the early Yuánhuī period,
he was sent out to be the magistrate of Shàn.
He showed kindness and beneficence,
and the common people missed him.
When Tàizǔ became regent,
he brought Yóng close.
Yóng was skilled at writing letters.
When Shěn Yōuzhī sent a letter severing ties,
Tàizǔ dictated to Yóng, instructing him to draft a reply.
He was transferred to become Qítái Diànzhōngláng.
In the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
Zhōu Yǒng served as Staff Officer for the Prince of Chángshā,
then Staff Officer of the Rear Army,
and Magistrate of Shānyīn.
The county previously levied *pāngmín*,
who were conscripted for various duties.
Zhōu Yǒng spoke to the Grand Protector, Wénxǐ Gōngzǐ Liáng, saying:
“I secretly observe the distress of the *pāngmín*,
their suffering is truly extreme.
Their conscription has no fixed term,
they are merely increasingly exhausted,
harassed, pressured, and driven,
unable to find peace in their homes.
Those in danger sometimes flee and hide in mountains and lakes,
while the desperate drown themselves in ditches.
There are also those who sever their arms or cut off their hands,
deliberately mutilating themselves,
selling their children into servitude,
temporarily responding to urgent needs.
Whenever the *pāng* duties are initiated,
the urgency of compliance is constant,
and there are always those who are beaten with cudgels and arrested,
〔四三〕bowing their heads on the steps,
weeping and lamenting their misery,
not knowing how to recover.
〔四四〕Your humble subordinate has never failed to lay down his chopsticks during meals,
or to pause his brush when writing,
pondering their plight for a long time,
unable to overcome the sorrow.
When tasks cannot be completed,
one cannot avoid being subjected to flogging and punishment;
witnessing such bitterness and sorrow,
this situation cannot be allowed to continue.
Shānyīn is a regional capital,
its affairs are twice as numerous as other cities;
however, I hear that in other counties too,
there are obstacles everywhere.
Only Shàngyú, with one *pāng* household for every hundred,
is greatly sufficient and well-off;
beyond this, among the other cities,
there is no lack of depletion and destitution.
It is fitting that there should be a universal rescue for those in dire straits,
to open a path and facilitate their relief,
then misfortune will turn into merit,
and how far away will that achievement be?”
He returned to serve as Central Army Registrar and Staff Officer for Crown Prince Wénhuì,
and followed the residence when it was reassigned to the Pacifying North General.
When Crown Prince Wénhuì was in the Eastern Palace,
Zhōu Yǒng returned to serve as Regular Attendant and Gentleman,
〔四五〕and Chief Military Advisor to the Prince of Shǐxīng.
He attended closely at the palace,
and was again highly esteemed.
Zhōu Yǒng’s voice and words were eloquent and beautiful,
his speech inexhaustible;
his words were perfectly structured,
forming sentences as soon as he spoke.
He broadly studied various schools of thought,
and was skilled in Buddhist philosophy.
He authored the *Sānzōng Lùn* (Treatise on the Three Doctrines).
He established the concept of "empty nominal existence" (*kōngjiǎmíng*)
and "non-empty nominal existence" (*bùkōngjiǎmíng*).
He proposed "non-empty nominal existence" to challenge "empty nominal existence,"
and proposed "empty nominal existence" to challenge "non-empty nominal existence."
As "nominal existence" and "emptiness" challenged these two doctrines,
he then established "nominal existence and emptiness" (*jiǎmíngkōng*).
Daoist Zhìlín from Xīliángzhōu sent a letter to Zhōu Yǒng saying:
“The gist of this teaching does not seem to be newly opened,
but its wondrous sound has been interrupted for sixty or seventy years.
When this humble Daoist was twenty,
I already grasped this meaning,
and secretly rejoiced,
but had no one to share it with.
When I was young, I met elders in Cháng’ān,
many of whom said that the highly virtuous in Guānzhōng already possessed this meaning,
but at the peak of Dharma assemblies,
there were not many who could deeply grasp this profound understanding.
Across the Yangtze River, there was almost none.
This humble Daoist has held a duster for over forty years,
lecturing in the east and west,
mistakenly highly regarded for a time;
other teachings were quite recorded and respected,
but for this path, absolutely no one understood it,
which caused me to fall ill.
Unexpectedly, this sound now enters my ears,
this is truly the first merit of practicing the Way.
His treatise was thus highly esteemed.
Zhōu Yǒng built a secluded dwelling on the western side of Zhōngshān,
and returned there during his days off.
He was transferred to Crown Prince’s Equerry,
concurrently serving as Historian,
and compiling the *Qǐjūzhù* (Diaries of Activity and Repose).
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Historian as before.
He often visited and attended the Eastern Palace.
When he was young, he learned the *wèisànlì* calligraphy from the family of his maternal relative, General of Cavalry Zāng Zhì,
and mastered it skillfully.
Crown Prince Wénhuì asked Zhōu Yǒng to write on the wall of the Xuánpǔ Máozhāi,
and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Hé Yìn sought to exchange it with his *dàoxièshū* (inverted seal script),
Zhōu Yǒng smiled and replied:
“When the Way prevails in the world,
Qiū (Confucius) would not exchange it.”
Whenever guests and friends gathered,
Zhōu Yǒng would engage in conversation with an open seat,
his words and rhymes flowing like a stream,
listeners forgetting their weariness.
He was also skilled in the teachings of Lǎozi and the *Yìjīng*,
and whenever he met Zhāng Róng,
they would become entangled in abstruse discussions,
unresolved for an entire day.
He was clean, poor, and had few desires,
eating vegetarian food all day long;
though he had a wife and children,
he lived alone in his mountain dwelling.
General of the Guards Wáng Jiǎn asked Zhōu Yǒng:
“What do you eat in the mountains, Sir?”
Zhōu Yǒng replied:
“Red rice and white salt,
green mallow and purple smartweed.”
Crown Prince Wénhuì asked Zhōu Yǒng:
“Among vegetarian dishes, which taste is the best?”
Zhōu Yǒng replied:
“Early chives in early spring,
late cabbage in late autumn.”
At that time, Hé Yìn also deeply believed in Buddhism,
and had no wife or concubines.
The Crown Prince again asked Zhōu Yǒng:
“How does your spiritual practice compare to Hé Yìn’s?”
Zhōu Yǒng replied:
“The three evil paths and eight difficulties,
are what we both have not escaped.
However, each has his own burdens.”
The Crown Prince said:
“What are these burdens?”
He replied:
“Zhōu’s wife and Hé’s meat.”
His eloquence and adaptability in speech
were all like this.
He was transferred to Doctor of the National Academy,
concurrently serving as Historian as before.
Students of the Imperial Academy admired his style,
and competed to engage in ornate debates.
Later, Hé Yìn declared that he would cease eating living creatures,
〔四六〕yet still wanted to eat white fish,
〔四七〕dried clams, and sugared crabs,
believing that these were not living creatures in his sight.
He was uncertain about eating oysters and mussels,
and asked his students to debate it.
Student Zhōng Guān said:
“When clams are processed into dried food,
they frequently contract and extend;
when crabs are sugared,
their struggles intensify.
A benevolent person, with good intentions,
feels deep compassion like a sharp pain.
As for mussels and oysters,
their eyes and brows are internally lacking,
ashamed of the marvel of Hundun;
their rough shells are externally sealed,
unlike the prudence of a metal figure.
They neither wither nor flourish,
inferior even to plants and trees;
they have neither fragrance nor stench,
what value do they hold compared to tiles and pebbles?
Therefore, it is fitting that they should perpetually fill the kitchen,
and forever be a food source.”
Jìnglíng Wángzǐ Liáng saw Zhōng Guān’s argument, and was greatly enraged.
Yǐn’s elder brother, Diǎn,
also embraced a pure and faithful ascetic life.
Yǒng wrote to him,
advising him to adopt a vegetarian diet.
He said:
“Perhaps the reason the venerable sir has not yet achieved the ultimate profound attainment
is because he does not adhere to a completely vegetarian diet?
The discussion of cutting and separating,
the rise of cauldrons, chopping boards, nets, and snares,
recorded in [之簡] ancient texts,
[four-eight] has a truly long history.
Who would dare to challenge it?
Observing how the Sages established their dietary provisions and practices,
they still set standards and regulations for them.
This is because eating raw meat and drinking blood
began concurrently with human civilization,
and if left unrestrained,
there would be no limits.
A good scholar,
how could he not embrace forgiveness towards himself?
Therefore, each keeps to their own boundaries,
and none encroach upon others.
[four-nine] Moreover, among the greatest transformations,
none surpasses life and death;
what is most valued in life
is nothing more than one's nature and life itself.
The nature and life of other beings are extremely precious to them,
while the taste in our mouths can be foregone.
Yet, morning and evening throughout our lives,
we sustain ourselves to prolong [歲] our years,
[five-zero] while they suffer unjust slaughter,
unable to defend themselves.
[five-one] Our karma endures for a long time;
alas, how fearful!
Furthermore, tiny, humble eggs,
fragile and easily pitied,
[five-two] and those panting, weak fawns,
their hesitant steps are worthy of compassion.
Watching them drink, peck, fly, and sink,
[five-three] makes people (beings) feel pity and sorrow.
[five-four] How can we repeatedly (心心) seize and strip them,
[five-five] and moreover, indulge in cruel gnawing and chewing?
[five-six] As for wild herds gathered in great numbers,
enclosed in heavy pens,
their flesh weighed, their fur estimated,
awaiting dismemberment,
[five-seven] like earth piled on the ground,
everyone considers it normal.
[可] It is a cause for sorrow and sighs.
[five-eight] Matters are not always one-sided.
If one says that the principle of the three ages is false,
then how fortunate and pleasant!
But if this path is indeed true,
and the [受] form one receives has not ceased,
[five-nine] then one going and one coming,
one life and one death,
reincarnation is a constant event.
[six-zero] Mixed retributions are like home,
humans and devas are like guests.
The days spent as guests are few,
the days spent at home are many.
Our accumulated karma
is not enough to guarantee long-term exemption,
so the anguish of heartbreak
will also (息念) [自及] eventually reach us.
[six-one] Although the venerable sir does not personally engage
in the slaughter of blood-and-flesh creatures,
as for the carp in the morning and night,
[six-two] he cannot avoid procuring them from the slaughterhouse.
Wealth and valuables
that pass through a thief's hands
[six-three] are still rejected by an honest gentleman;
how much less can the initiation of the phoenix knife into a living being
be tolerated by a compassionate heart?
Even the Zōuyú, though hungry,
does not eat grass that has not died on its own.
Hearing of its conduct, how can it not make people feel much shame?
[six-four] All sentient beings receive this form and body,
to accumulate flesh and fat,
all due to their accumulated ignorance and delusion,
sinking into the current, unable to return.
They receive defiled and turbid retribution,
enduring bitter and prolonged suffering.
This sweetness and richness
are all the accumulated retribution of ignorance.
Why then embrace such delicacies,
and defile one's own stomach and intestines?
The venerable sir has long understood this;
I merely offer these few words to awaken him.”
When Yǒng died in office,
it happened that Wáng Jiǎn had not finished lecturing on the Classic of Filial Piety,
and nominated Tánjì to take his place.
[six-five] Scholars considered this an honor.
His official position was Gěishì Zhōng.
The historian says: Hóngyì preserved his composure,
and extreme benevolence was evident in his appearance.
Jí Àn was resolute and blunt,
Cuī Yǎn had a commanding presence and voice,
and only then could they fearlessly challenge the powerful and eminent,
and frequently incur criticism.
Zhāng Róng set his heart and entrusted his purpose,
completely detached from the mundane world,
exhaling and inhaling with the winds and clouds,
disregarding people and matters.
Yet, when engaging with the monarch and meeting friends,
[six-six] he upheld righteousness and offered loyalty,
his grand conduct never exceeded proper bounds,
always conforming to the norms of moral teachings.
As for the epithet of extraordinary and magnificent,
then Yú Fān and Lù Jì could not exclusively claim it before him.
Eulogy says: Sīguāng was lofty and towering,
reaching ten thousand li and a thousand ren.
Promoted, he harmonized with the times;
demoted, he accepted his dismissal.
His efforts were focused on forming alliances,
not on dissolving seals of office.
Yànlún had eloquent rhetoric,
a rigorous ascetic life, and a pure character.
He captured the white horse across the field,
and uniquely shook the cloud ladder.
(Zhāng Róng’s Rhapsody on the Sea has many errors and omissions in the text,
which are consistent across various editions.)

Biographies, Chapter 23: Wáng Yàn, Xiāo Chén, Xiāo Tǎnzhī, Jiāng Shí
Wáng Yàn, courtesy name Shìyàn,
was a native of Línyí, Lángxié.
His grandfather, Hóngzhī, was Tōngzhí Chángshì.
His father, Pǔyào, was Mìshū Jiān.
Yàn,
at the end of Sòng Dàmíng era, began his career as Chángshì for Línhè Kingdom,
Yuánwàiláng,
Bālíngwáng Zhēngběi Bǎn Cānjūn,
Ānchéngwáng Fǔjūn Bǎn Xíngyù,
and transferred with the office to Chējì.
When Jìnxīwáng Xiè was Yǐngzhōu,
Yàn served as Ānxī Zhǔbù.
Shìzǔ became Chángshǐ,
and met Yàn.
The office transferred to Zhènxī,
appointing Yàn as Jìshì Zīyì.
During Shěn Yōuzhī’s rebellion,
all officials of the Zhènxī office followed Shìzǔ to guard Pénchéng.
Although the Emperor's (or 'His Majesty's') power and influence were great at that time,
there was still doubt among the populace.
Yàn, however, wholeheartedly served him,
and all military and literary matters were entrusted to him.
He was very accommodating by nature,
and gradually became close and trusted.
He was retained as the Emperor’s (or 'His Majesty's') Zhēnglǔ Fǔjūn Fǔ Bǎn Zīyì,
also overseeing Jìshì.
Following his return to the capital,
he was promoted to Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ,
and Zhōngjūn Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He was always in the Emperor’s (or 'His Majesty's') residence,
participating in discussions of confidential matters.
At the beginning of Jiàn Yuán era,
he was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Shìzǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he unilaterally made decisions on court affairs,
often without reporting them.
Yàn, fearing implication,
claimed illness to distance himself.
Soon after, he was appointed Lǐng Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
but did not take office.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Cháng Jiān Shìzhōng,
his trust and duties remaining as before.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he held the position of Commander of the Infantry (領步兵校尉).
He was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中祭酒).
His rank as commander remained unchanged.
He encountered a mother's funeral,
and was appointed General of the State Guard (輔國將軍) and Chief Clerk of the Left of the Minister of Works (司徒左長史).
Yàn's (晏) father, Pǔyào (普曜), used Yàn's influence to gain official positions,
serving in many high offices.
Yàn was soon promoted to General of the Left Guard (左衞將軍),
and given the additional title of Attendant Official (給事中).
Before he could be formally invested,
Pǔyào passed away.
He observed the mourning rites with distinction.
He was appointed General of the Champions (冠軍將軍), Chief Clerk of the Left of the Minister of Works (司徒左長史), and Administrator of Jìyáng (濟陽太守).
Before he could be formally invested,
he was promoted to Minister of the Guards (衞尉).
His rank as general remained unchanged.
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (太子詹事),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant (散騎常侍).
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Governor of Dānyáng (丹陽尹).
His title as Palace Attendant remained unchanged.
Yàn's (晏) position and responsibilities were intimate and weighty,
and he had daily audiences with the emperor,
discussing court affairs.
Even Prince Yí (嶷) of Yùzhāng (豫章) and Grand Secretary Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) lowered themselves to receive him.
However, Yàn (晏) was frequently admonished by the emperor for his oversights,
and he repeatedly claimed illness for a long time.
The emperor, considering that Yàn (晏) needed emoluments to support his family,
in the seventh year,
transferred him to Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州刺史).
Yàn (晏) firmly declined, unwilling to go out.
His request was granted,
and he was retained as Minister of Personnel (吏部尚書),
concurrently serving as Commander of the Right Guard of the Crown Prince (領太子右衞率).
He ultimately remained favored due to old kindness.
At that time, although Grand Secretary Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) was noble, he was estranged.
Since Yàn (晏) was in charge of selection,
his authority extended throughout the government offices.
He and Jiǎn (儉) were rather at odds.
When Jiǎn (儉) died,
the ritual officials debated his posthumous title.
The emperor wanted to follow Wáng Dǎo's (王導) posthumous title of
"Wénxiàn" (文獻).
Yàn (晏) memorialized the emperor, saying:
"Dǎo (導) indeed received this posthumous title,
but since the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
it has not been conferred upon common gentry."
He then went out and told his intimates:
"The 'Píngtóu Xiànshì' (平頭憲事) has already been carried out."
In the eighth year,
he was reappointed Commander of the Right Guard (右衞將軍),
and excused himself by feigning illness.
The emperor wished to have Gāozōng (高宗) replace Yàn (晏) in charge of selection,
and issued a personal decree to inquire about it.
Yàn (晏) memorialized, saying:
"Luán (鸞) has more than enough integrity and competence,
but he is not familiar with the various schools of thought,
and I fear he cannot hold this position."
The emperor then stopped.
The following year,
he was promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中),
concurrently serving as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (領太子詹事)
and Chief Justice of his home province (本州中正).
Again, he resigned due to illness.
In the tenth year,
he was reappointed Palace Attendant (散騎常侍) and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal (金紫光祿大夫).
He was granted twenty personal retainers,
and his position as Chief Justice remained unchanged.
In the eleventh year,
he was promoted to Right Director of the Palace Secretariat (右僕射),
concurrently serving as Commander of the Right Guard of the Grandson (領太孫右衞率).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) died,
his dying wish entrusted the affairs of the Secretariat (尚書事) to Yàn (晏) and Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣),
instructing them to remain in their positions for a long time.
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Left Director of the Palace Secretariat (左僕射).
His position as Chief Justice remained unchanged.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
he was given the additional title of Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中).
When Gāozōng (高宗) plotted to depose and enthrone,
Yàn (晏) immediately responded and supported him.
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興),
he was transferred to Grand Secretary (尚書令),

His titles as Attendant-in-ordinary (侍中) and Chief Justice (中正) remained unchanged.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qǔjiāng County (曲江縣侯),
with an estate of a thousand households.
He was granted a set of drums and pipes,
and fifty armed guards to enter the palace.
Gāozōng (高宗) and Yàn (晏) banqueted in the Eastern Palace.
When they discussed current affairs,
Yàn (晏) slapped his palm and said:
"You always said Yàn (晏) was timid,

In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
he was advanced to General of Agile Cavalry (驃騎大將軍).
He was granted twenty swordsmen to attend him,

He was also given an additional hundred soldiers,
concurrently serving as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (領太子少傅).
His noble rank was advanced to Duke,
and his estate was increased to two thousand households.
As the northern barbarians were active, he was granted a thousand soldiers.
Yàn was devoted to his family and old friends,
and was praised by Shìzǔ.
At this point, he considered himself a co-founder of the new dynasty,

Although Gāozōng needed Yàn due to circumstances,

He reviewed Shìzǔ's internal edicts

Initially, upon his ascension,

At that time, the Emperor often sent trusted confidantes like Chén Shìfàn and others into the streets to listen for dissenting opinions.

Yàn was frivolous and lacked foresight.

Since Lóngchāng,
when the times were difficult,

He was ennobled as a marquis,

The ravines may be filled,

He looked to the heavens and marked the earth,

He extensively sought divination and physiognomy,

He recommended and aligned with partisans,

He allowed his eldest son, Déyuán, to gather fugitives,

Messengers went back and forth,

We showed sincerity and entrusted him,

However, evil grew easily and spread even wider.
He conspired with Xiāo Yì, the Sīmǎ of the Northern Zhōngláng,

Míngdá's various statements are

“All involved are to be arrested and handed over to the Grand Minister of Justice,

Hòujūn Jiāngjūn,

When Shìzǔ was ill in bed at Yánchāng Diàn,

When Yùlín ascended the throne,

Whenever Xiāo Chén requested leave to stay out overnight for urgent matters,

When Gāozōng assisted in government,
he offered remonstrances.
Since the emperor stayed in the harem and did not come out,

could his words be heard and conveyed.
Xiāo Chén defected to Gāozōng,
advocating for the deposition and establishment of a new emperor.
He secretly summoned the clerks (diǎnqiān) of the various princes and instructed them,
forbidding the princes from interacting with people outside.
Xiāo Chén's influence and connections had been long-standing,

On the day Yùlín was deposed,
when he first heard of the disturbance outside,
