Xiāo Chén was inherently treacherous and ambitious, lacking strategy.
When the emperor was deposed,
he led troops and was the first to enter the inner palace.
The imperial guards in the inner chamber, who had always been subservient to Xiāo Chén,
did not make a move.
When Hǎilíng was enthroned,
he was transferred to Zhōnglǐngjūn,
elevated in peerage to Duke,
with two thousand households.
He was granted fifty armed guards.
He took turns on duty inside the palace,
returning to his residence ten days a month.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was transferred to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
granted Fú.
with a fief of three thousand households.
Gāozōng had initially promised to appoint Xiāo Chén as Governor of Yángzhōu after the matter was accomplished,
but when this appointment was made,
Xiāo Chén angrily said:
"When the cooked rice is ready,
it's pushed to someone else."
Wáng Yàn heard this and said:
"Who would still act as a utensil 【甌】 for Xiāo Chén?"
interfered in court affairs.
Whenever there were selections and appointments,
he would often instruct the Dìngyì Shàngshū to advocate for them.
The emperor, who had just ascended the throne,
sent trusted aides to listen and observe outside.
Fully aware of Xiāo Chén's words,
he became deeply suspicious and wary of him.
In the sixth month of the second year,
the emperor visited Huálín Yuán,
feasting with Xiāo Chén and Wáng Yàn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, and several others, enjoying themselves thoroughly.
After the banquet,
Xiāo Chén was detained and left late.
Upon reaching Huálín Gé,
the guards seized him and brought him back to the secretariat.
The emperor sent his aide Mò Zhìmíng to rebuke Xiāo Chén, saying:
"At the time of Lóngchāng,
without you, there would be no today.
Now, one family has two prefectures,
and three brothers have been enfeoffed.
The court's reward to you
can reach no higher than this.
Yet you harbor resentment and dissatisfaction,
saying, 'The cooked rice is ready,
but the pot is given to someone else'?
Today, I grant you death."
Xiāo Chén said to Mò Zhìmíng:
"Heaven is not far from man.
I, together with the emperor, killed the princes of Gāo and Wǔ.
You were the one who relayed messages back and forth.
When I die today,
I will come back for you."
He was killed in the secretariat.
By autumn, Mò Zhìmíng died,
haunted by Xiāo Chén's ghost.
An imperial edict stated:
"Xiāo Chén, elevated from common origins,
was light-minded and treacherous in his actions.
Relying on fortuitous circumstances,
he was early in rendering service.
In the late Yǒngmíng period,
he was specially favored and promoted.
When Yùlín was muddled and perverse,
he indeed rendered honest service.
His imperial favor and grace were abundant,
his expectations and encounters were both grand.
He controlled military power internally,
and abroad he enjoyed the prestige of a regional lord.
His brothers were honored and noble,
shining brilliantly throughout the court and country.
Yet he never felt grateful for the extraordinary favor,
nor did he repay even a fraction of it.
He considered his merits to be as high as Yī and Huò,
difficult to reward,
and his talent to be the foremost of his time,
ashamed to be behind others.
He usurped imperial authority,
giving and taking as he pleased.
Harboring baseless suspicions and fears,
he created animosity and distrust.
He spied on the inner palace,
hoping for what was beyond his proper aspirations.
His intention to deceive the emperor and mislead the people,
and his acts of slandering the sovereign and being disloyal,
were already openly known to the populace,
and spread widely.
He then secretly distributed gold and silk,
recruited unruly elements,
colluded with the imperial guards,
acting as their close allies,
and secretly conspired with relatives of the empress,
intending to commit treacherous rebellion.
Though We had entrusted him with heavy responsibilities,
and his noble rank was as enduring as mountains and rivers,
We always tried to cover up his faults,
and treated him with great trust,
hoping he would be touched,
and turn over a new leaf.
But his nature was like a wolf,
and his wicked schemes grew even more severe.
Disloyalty must be punished by death,
as clearly stated in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
How much more so when his crimes accumulated and his evil overflowed,
to such a great extent as this!
He is to be arrested and handed over to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi),
for the law to be swiftly enforced.
The blame stops with the principal offender;
the rest are not to be questioned."
Xiāo Chén was fond of heterodox practices.
Shěn Wényóu of Wúxìng, a physiognomist, once told Xiāo Chén:
"Your physiognomy is no less than Gāo Dì's."
"I appreciate your sentiment,
but don't tell anyone."
By this time, Shěn Wényóu was executed.
Xiāo Chén's elder brother, Xiāo Dàn,
courtesy name Yànwěi,
was initially a General of the Palace Guard.
During the Yǒngmíng period, he was the Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
He rode in the same carriage as Sīmǎ Dízhī, the Magistrate of Mòlíng,
with four soldiers guiding the carriage in front.
Zuǒ Chéng Shěn Zhāolüè memorialized:
"Officials with honor guards,
when sharing a carriage, should not concurrently display guards.
I request that Xiāo Dàn and others be dismissed from their posts."
An imperial edict ordered commutation of the punishment.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
from Fǔguó Xúzhōu, he became a Commissioner with credentials, Inspector of Sīzhōu,
with his general title as before.
When Míngdì was established,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Āndé,
He was promoted to General Guànjūn.
In the spring of the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians attacked Sīzhōu.
Xiāo Dàn resisted with all his might,
and the barbarians retreated.
His fief was increased by four hundred households.
He was summoned to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
The emperor wanted to kill Xiāo Chén,
but because Xiāo Dàn was defending the border against the barbarians,
the execution was delayed.
Sixty days after the barbarians retreated,
Xiāo Chén was executed.
The emperor sent Huángmén Láng Liáng Wáng to be Sīzhōu Biéjià,
to execute Xiāo Dàn.
He submitted himself to execution,
and his family members were imprisoned in the imperial workshops.
Xiāo Chén's (蕭諶) younger brother,
Xiāo Lǐ (蕭誄), participated with Xiāo Chén (蕭諶) in the dethronement and establishment (of emperors).
He served as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu (東莞太守).
He was transferred to Xīzhōngláng Sīmǎ (西中郎司馬).
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ (建武) reign,
he was enfeoffed as Xīchāng Hóu (西昌侯),
with one thousand households.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài (太子左率).
When Lǐngjūn (領軍) returned after relieving the siege of Sīzhōu (司州),
he was executed along with him.
Xiāo Chén's (蕭諶) paternal uncle, Xiāo Xiānmín (蕭仙民),
rose to the office of Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫),
and then died.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之),
was a man from Lánlíng (蘭陵), Nánlánlíng (南蘭陵).
His grandfather, Xiāo Dàojì (蕭道濟),
was a Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
His father, Xiāo Xīnzǔ (蕭欣祖),
rendered meritorious service to Shìzǔ (世祖),
rising to Wǔjìn Lìng (武進令).
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was of the same clan as Xiāo Chén (蕭諶).
Initially, he served as Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn (殿中將軍),
and was promoted repeatedly to Shìzǔ Zhōngjūn Bǎnxíngyù Cānjūn (世祖中軍板刑獄參軍).
He was employed due to his clan connections.
He was appointed Jìnglíng Wáng Zhènběi Zhēngběi Cānjūn (竟陵王鎮北征北參軍),
and Dōnggōng Zhíhé (東宮直閤),
and was known to Shìzǔ (世祖) for his diligence and uprightness.
[一四] He was appointed Jǐshìzhōng (給事中),
and Huáilíng Lìng (淮陵令).
He was again appointed Lánlíng Lìng (蘭陵令),
[一五] with the title of Jǐshìzhōng (給事中) as before.
He served as Shàngshū Qǐbùláng (尚書起部郎),
and Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (司徒中兵參軍).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) died,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) accompanied the Grandson (the future emperor) and Wǔwǔdù (文武度) to the imperial platform.
He was appointed Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉),
with his previous post remaining unchanged.
Before he was formally installed,
he was appointed Zhèngyuán Láng (正員郎) and Nánlǔjùn Tàishǒu (南魯郡太守).
The Young Emperor (Shǎo Dì) regarded Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) as an old retainer of Shìzǔ (世祖),
[一六] and trusted him intimately, keeping him close.
He was permitted to enter the inner palace to see the empress.
When the Emperor (Dì) was in the palace or went to the rear hall to play various mischievous games,
[一七] Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was always by his side.
Sometimes, when the Emperor (Dì) was drunk and naked,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) would assist him and remonstrate with him.
Seeing that the Emperor (Dì) was not worthy of support,
he changed his strategy and aligned himself with Gāozōng (高宗),
secretly acting as his eyes and ears.
He was appointed Jìn'ān Wáng Zhēngběi Zīyì (晉安王征北諮議).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
his father's merits were posthumously recognized,
and he was enfeoffed as Línrǔ Xiànnán (臨汝縣男),
with a stipend of three hundred households.
He was transferred to Zhēngnán Zīyì (征南諮議).
Gāozōng (高宗) planned to depose the Young Emperor (Shǎo Dì),
and finalized the plan with Xiāo Chén (蕭諶) and Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之).
Cáo Dàogāng (曹道剛), a trusted Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍) of the Emperor (Dì), suspected that there was something unusual outside,
and made secret arrangements.
Xiāo Chén (蕭諶) was unable to act.
Xiāo Jìchǎng (蕭季敞), the Shǐxīng Nèishǐ (始興內史), and Xiāo Yǐngjī (蕭頴基), the Nányáng Tàishǒu (南陽太守) (who was transferred to Dūwèi (都尉)), were to return to the capital.
[一八] Xiāo Chén (蕭諶) wanted to wait for the arrival of the two Xiāo (蕭) (men),
to leverage their power to execute the plan.
Gāozōng (高宗) worried about a change in the situation,
and informed Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之).
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) rushed to tell Xiāo Chén (蕭諶):
"Dethroning an emperor is a major event since ancient times.
I hear that Cáo Dàogāng (曹道剛) and Zhū Lóngzhī (朱隆之) are already suspicious.
If the Wèiwèi (衞尉) does not act tomorrow,
it will be too late.
You have a mother of a hundred years old,
how can you sit by and listen to disaster befall?
You should really make other plans!"
Xiāo Chén (蕭諶) was flustered,
and the next day, the Emperor (Dì) was deposed,
thanks to Xiāo Tǎnzhī's (蕭坦之) effort.
When Hǎilíng (海陵) ascended the throne,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was appointed Huángménláng (黃門郎), concurrently Wèiwèi Qīng (衞尉卿), and promoted to the rank of Bó (伯),
with his stipend increased to six hundred households.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍),
[一九] promoted to the rank of Hóu (侯),
with his stipend increased to one thousand five hundred households.
The following year,
when the barbarians stirred,
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was granted the jié (節) (an imperial staff),
and appointed Supervisor of military affairs for the punitive expedition in Xúzhōu (徐州).
When the barbarians besieged Zhōnglí (鍾離),
and cut off Huáizhōu (淮洲) in spring,
[二０] Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) attacked and defeated them.
Upon his return, he was additionally given the concurrent title of Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子).
Before he was formally installed,
he was transferred to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
In the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰),
he served as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Lǐngjūn (領軍).
When Dōnghūn (東昏) was established (as emperor),
he served as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍).
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
he suffered the loss of his mother,
but was reinstated to his post,
and additionally appointed Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍),
with his own establishment.
Jiāng Shí (江祏) and his brothers wanted to enthrone Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng (始安王遙光),
and secretly spoke to Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之).
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) said:
"Míng Dì (明帝) took the throne,
which was already out of proper succession,
and the people of the world are still not convinced.
If we do this again now,
I fear the whole world will fall apart.
I dare not speak of it."
He returned home to observe mourning.
His residence was east of Dōngfǔ Chéng (東府城).
When Yáoguāng (遙光) started his uprising,
he sent men to stealthily seize Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) at night.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之), bareheaded and in his underwear, climbed over the wall and fled.
From Dōngyě (東冶) he hired a boat to cross to the south,
and took a shortcut back to the palace.
He was granted the jié (節) and ordered to supervise the armies to suppress Yáoguāng (遙光),
and stationed them at Xiānggōng Sì (湘宮寺).
When the affair was settled,
he was transferred to Shàngshū Yòupúyè (尚書右僕射),
Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹),
with his title of Yòujiāngjūn (右將軍) as before.
[二一] He was promoted to the rank of Gōng (公),
with his stipend increased by one thousand households.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was fat, dark-skinned, and beardless,
with a hoarse voice.
People at the time called him
"Xiāo Yǎ" (蕭瘂) (meaning "Mute Xiāo").
He was stubborn and opinionated,
and minor officials feared and detested him.
About twenty days after Yáoguāng's (遙光) rebellion was quelled,
the Emperor (Dì) sent Yánmíng (延明) commander Huáng Wénjì (黃文濟) with troops to surround Xiāo Tǎnzhī's (蕭坦之) residence,
and killed him.
His son, Xiāo Shǎng (蕭賞),
a Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
was also executed.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī's (蕭坦之) cousin, Xiāo Yìzōng (蕭翼宗),
was in Hǎilíng Jùn (海陵郡),
and was about to set out.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) asked Huáng Wénjì (黃文濟):
"My cousin in Hǎilíng (海陵) should be fine, shouldn't he?"
Huáng Wénjì (黃文濟) asked:
"Where is the Hǎilíng (海陵) residence?"
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) told him.
Huáng Wénjì (黃文jì) said:
"He should be punished."
He then sent someone to arrest him.
Upon inspecting his home, it was found to be extremely poor,
with only a few hundred pawn tickets.
This was reported to the Emperor (Dì),
who pardoned him from death,
and imprisoned him in Shàngfāng (尚方).
In the first year of Hé Dì (和帝) Zhōngxīng (中興),
Xiāo Tǎnzhī (蕭坦之) was posthumously granted the title of Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) [二二] and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
Jiāng Shí (江祏), courtesy name Hóngyè (弘業),
was a man from Kǎochéng (考城), Jìyáng (濟陽).
His grandfather, Jiāng Zūn (江遵),
was a Níngshuò Cānjūn (寧朔參軍).
His father, Jiāng Délín (江德隣),
[二三] was a Sītú Yòuchángshǐ (司徒右長史).
Jiāng Shí's (江祏) paternal aunt was Jǐng Huánghòu (景皇后),
and he was favored by Gāozōng (高宗) from a young age,
with an affection like brothers.
At the end of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
he began his career as Jìnxī Guó Chángshì (晉熙國常侍),
then Tàizǔ Xúzhōu Xīcáo (太祖徐州西曹),
Yuánwàiláng (員外郎),
Gāozōng Guānjūn Cānjūn (高宗冠軍參軍),
concurrently acting as Shèyáng Lìng (灄陽令),
Jìnglíng Wáng Zhēngběi Cānjūn (竟陵王征北參軍),
and Shàngshū Shuǐbùláng (尚書水部郎).
When Gāozōng (高宗) was Wúxīng (吳興),
he appointed Jiāng Shí (江祏) as Jùnchéng (郡丞),
and additionally Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn (宣威將軍),
Lúlíng Wáng Zhōngjūn Gōngcáo Jìshì (廬陵王中軍功曹記室),
Ānlù Wáng Zuǒjūn Zīyì (安陸王左軍諮議),
concurrently Lùshì (錄事),
and concurrently Jīngzhào Tàishǒu (京兆太守).
He was appointed Tōngzhíláng (通直郎),
and assigned to Nánxúzhōu Biéjià (南徐州別駕).
Gāozōng 輔政
entrusted him as a close confidant.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was appointed Dānyáng丞 from a regular official,
and Zhōngshū Láng.
When Gāozōng became Piàojì
and governor of the Eastern Palace (Zhèndōng Fǔ),
he appointed Shí as Cīyì Cānjūn,
and acting Grand Administrator of Nánchāng.
〔二四〕He served with Xiāo Lěi directly within the Eastern Palace province.
At that time, Hǎilíng had just been enthroned,
and popular sentiment was not yet settled.
Gāozōng had a red mole on his shoulder blade,
which he always kept secret.
Shí advised the Emperor to reveal it to the people.
When Wáng Hóngfàn, the Grand Administrator of Jìnshòu, retired from office and returned,
the Emperor bared his shoulder to him
and said,
"Everyone says this is a sun-and-moon sign.
Please do not leak this information."
Hóngfàn replied,
"Your Excellency has the signs of the sun and moon on your body;
how can you hide it?
You should tell it to the high officials."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
At that time, Zhāng Bó and Yǐn Zàn, who were directly serving, repeatedly plotted a rebellion.
Shí and Lěi were anxious and had no strategy,
so every evening they would find an excuse to go out.
When the succession was settled,
Shí was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozōng was Wāng of Xuānchéng,
the Grand Astrologer secretly presented prophecies (túwěi) saying,
"One reign will last fourteen years."
Shí entered,
and the Emperor joyfully showed it to Shí, saying,
"With this, what more could I hope for?"
When he ascended the throne,
Shí was transferred to acting Wèiwèi,
his generalship remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānlù County,
with a thousand households.
Shí's grandfather, Zūn,
was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū as the empress's father;
his father, Délín,
was also posthumously granted Guānglù Dàfū as the emperor's maternal uncle.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
〔二五〕in charge of inspecting weapons and armaments.
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhànshì.
Due to his powerful position as an imperial relative,
Shí's influence surpassed everyone at the time.
He received gifts from afar,
and sometimes took famous writings and fine objects from the princes' residences.
However, his family conduct was very harmonious,
and he treated his nephews with kindness.
When the Emperor fell ill,
in the first year of Yǒngtài,
Shí was transferred to Shìzhōng and Zhōngshū Lìng,
with free access to the palace.
When the Emperor died,
the imperial edict appointed Shí as Yòu Púyè;
Shí's younger brother, Wèiwèi Sì, as Shìzhōng;
and Liú Xuān, the younger brother of Empress Jìng, as Wèiwèi.
When Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
they jointly managed selection affairs.
Although Gāozōng entrusted the grand officials with his dying wishes,
his true hopes largely rested with Shí's brothers.
From then on, they served directly in the inner palace,
and every action and movement required their consultation.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Shí served as acting Tàizǐ Zhànshì.
Liú Xuān was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì
and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Shí's brothers, Xuān, Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng, Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì, and Lǐngjūn Xiāo Tǎnzhī – these six individuals
took turns issuing imperial edicts daily.
They were then known as
"The Six Nobles."
The Emperor gradually wished to act on his own will.
Xiàosì could not restrain him,
and although Tǎnzhī sometimes differed,
Shí firmly insisted on his control,
which deeply resented the Emperor.
As the Emperor's misrule became apparent,
Shí considered enthroning Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎoxuán.
Liú Xuān had initially served Bǎoxuán as an acting official in Yǐngzhōu,
〔二六〕but his administration was overly harsh.
When someone presented a horse,
Bǎoxuán wanted to see it,
but Xuān said,
"Why bother looking at a horse?"
When the consort asked for a braised gizzard,
her attendants consulted Xuān,
who said,
"I've already cooked it this morning;
no need for more."
Bǎoxuán angrily said,
"My uncle truly lacks the affection of Wèiyáng."
Upon hearing this, Xuān was also displeased.
At this point, he disagreed with Shí's proposal
and wanted to enthrone Jiàn'ān Wáng Bǎoyín,
secretly plotting with Yáoguāng.
Yáoguāng, considering himself older,
felt it was his turn for the imperial mandate,
and hinted his intentions to Shí.
Shí's younger brother, Sì, believing it difficult to safeguard a young ruler,
persuaded Shí to enthrone Yáoguāng.
Xuān, fearing that if Yáoguāng were enthroned, he would lose his status as the senior maternal uncle,
refused to agree.
Therefore, Shí hesitated for a long time and could not decide.
Yáoguāng was furious and
sent his attendant Huáng Tánqìng to assassinate Xuān on the road at Qīngxī Qiáo.
Tánqìng saw that Xuān's retinue was large
and dared not strike.
When the plot was discovered,
Xuān reported Shí's conspiracy,
and the Emperor ordered the arrest of Shí's brothers.
Sì, who was on duty in the inner palace at the time,
suspecting something unusual,
sent a message to Shí saying,
"Liú Xuān seems to have a different plot.
What should we do now?"
Shí replied,
"We should simply remain calm and suppress it."
Soon after, Shí was summoned for an audience
and detained in the Zhōngshū Shěng.
Initially,
Yuán Wénkuàng, who was directly serving in the Zhāi, believed that Wáng Jìngzé's merits deserved enfeoffment,
but Shí refused to grant it.
The Emperor ordered Wénkuàng to seize Shí,
and with the pommel of a sword, struck his chest, saying,
"Can you still deny me enfeoffment?"
Shí and Sì were killed on the same day.
Sì, courtesy name Jǐngchāng,
initially served as Chángshì for the Kingdom of Nánjùn,
then successively as Gāozǔ's Piàojì Dōnggé Jìjiǔ,
Mìshū Chéng,
Jìn'ān Wáng's Zhènběi Zhǎngshǐ,
and Grand Administrator of Nán Dōnghǎi,
and acting prefect of the prefecture.
Under his administration, there was a temple to Xuānnǐ (Confucius)
which had long been dilapidated.
Sì renovated and rebuilt it.
Sì's younger brother, Xǐ,
died young while in mourning.
He had a son, Xīn,
courtesy name Wěiqīng,
who was twelve years old.
Upon hearing of the arrests,
he told his family,
"Since my uncle has come to this,
I have no mind to live alone."
He jumped into a well and died.
Later, the Emperor was riding a horse in the rear hall, enjoying himself,

Xuān, courtesy name Shìmù,

When Yáoguāng launched his uprising,

When the matter was settled,

In that same year,

In the first year of Hé Dì's Zhōngxīng era,

Xuān, Sànqí Chángshì and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn;

The historian says: "A scholar dies for his bosom friend"

Although there are two grades of wisdom and foolishness,

Indeed, to possess discernible talent,
to receive the discerning gaze of a knowing person,
and to feel no shame towards external things,

It is like hiding it in one's heart,

How much more so when the righteousness began early among subordinates,

surpassing oneself,
and disregarding previous generations,
abandoning sons as if nothing,

leading to the simile of "a dog that bites its master,"
earning the earlier censure of others,
with a heart filled with shame and guilt,
〔二七〕"I had no part in that."
Alas!
This is why Lù Jī composed "Fù Háo Shì" (Rhapsody on a Heroic Gentleman).
A eulogy states: Wáng Xiāo (王蕭) held the reins,

Yuè Yáng (樂羊) ate his son,
Lǐ Kè (里克) was not excused.
Jiāng (江) and Liú (劉) were imperial relatives,
maintaining the bright succession.
Their rise and fall occasioned differing opinions,

Later, when he held several palace positions,

he would say,
"It must have meaning."
After the game,
he returned to his study to sleep,
without inquiring about outside matters.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
Yán was again ill and did not attend to affairs.
Later, at an imperial banquet,
meritorious officials offered wine.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn and others rose from their seats,
but Yán alone did not rise.
He said:
"Your Majesty received the mandate,
responding to Heaven and following the people.
Wáng Yàn presumptuously claims heavenly merit as his own achievement."
The emperor laughed heartily and defused the situation.
After the banquet,
Yàn called Yán to ride with him back to the commandery office,
intending to console and please him.
Yán, however, sternly said:
"Where is your nest and den?"
When Yàn first received his rank and sword,
Yán said to him:
"Even the Grand Tutor's household only had six [attendants].
What did you do to achieve this overnight?"
Yàn greatly feared him.
He was additionally appointed Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
His brother Fěi, in Wúxīng,
was slow in submitting memorials on public affairs.
Yán would take his place in drafting them.
The emperor, seeing that it was not his handwriting,
inquired about it,
but excused him.
He was transferred to Shìzhōng,
concurrently Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and Yùzhōu Zhōngzhèng.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì,
and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
He died that year
at the age of forty-five.
He was posthumously granted Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with the posthumous title Jiǎnzǐ.
Initially,
Wúxīng
Xiè Fēi was sending off his elder brother Xiè Fěi at Zhēnglǔ Zhǔ.
Fěi pointed to Fēi’s mouth and said,
“This place is only suitable for drinking wine.”
In the early years of Jiànwǔ,
Fēi made prolonged heavy drinking his main pursuit.
He drank with Liú Tián and Shěn Zhāolüè,
each consuming several *dǒu*.
Emperor Shìzǔ once asked Wáng Jiǎn,
“Who among the present generation can compose five-character poems?”
Jiǎn replied,
“Xiè Fěi has inherited his father's essence;
Jiāng Yān has potential.”
The Emperor established Chánlíng Sì,
and ordered Fēi to compose the stele inscription.
Wáng Sīyuǎn was
a man from Línyí, Lángxié.
He was the younger cousin of Shàngshū Lìng Yàn.
His father, Luóyún,
was Píngxī Chángshǐ.
When Sīyuǎn was eight years old,
his father died.
His grandfather, Hóngzhī, and maternal grandfather, Xīn'ān Tàishǒu Yáng Jìngyuán,
〔一七〕both lived reclusively and were highly principled.
Therefore, Sīyuǎn had no desire for officialdom when he was young.
Sòng Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù appointed him Nánxúzhōu Zhǔbù,
and treated him with great respect.
When Jǐngsù was executed,
his attendants dispersed,
but Sīyuǎn personally supervised the burial,
and planted pine and cypress trees by hand.
He and Hé Chāngyū of Lújiāng and Liú Jìn of Pèi Jùn submitted a memorial to vindicate him,
which moved the imperial court.
Jǐngsù’s daughter was demoted to commoner status.
Sīyuǎn shared his clothing and food to support her.
When she grew up,
he prepared her hairpins and hair ties,
sought a suitable match,
and spent his family’s wealth to send her off.
He was appointed Jìnxī Wáng Fǔjūn Xíng Cānjūn,
and Ānchéng Wáng Chēqí Cānjūn.
In the early years of Jiànyuán,
he served as Chángshā Wáng Hòujūn Zhǔbù,
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng,
then was dispatched to serve as Jìnglíng Wáng Zhēngběi Jìshì Cānjūn.
he remained Lùshì Cānjūn.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén.
Wénhuì Tàizǐ and Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng had always favored scholars,
and both valued and received him.
Sīyuǎn requested to be dispatched to a distant commandery,
and was appointed Jiàn'ān Nèishǐ.
When his eldest brother Sīxuán died,
Sīyuǎn’s fraternal affection was profound.
He submitted a memorial requesting to resign,
but it was not granted.
On the anniversary of the death,
he again firmly stated his case,
and Emperor Shìzǔ finally permitted it.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Láng,
and Dàsīmǎ Zīyì.
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict to recommend talented individuals.
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng recommended Sīyuǎn, as well as Gù Gǎozhī of Wú Jùn and Yīn Ruì of Chén Jùn.
When Shàolíng Wáng Zǐzhēn became Wú Jùn,
Emperor Shìzǔ appointed Sīyuǎn as Wú Jùn Chéng,
and he managed the affairs of the commandery in his original capacity.
Commentators believed he was the right person for the job.
Due to illness, he resigned his post,
and returned to serve as Sītú Zīyì Cānjūn,
in charge of records,
then transferred to Huángmén Láng.
He was then dispatched to serve as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Guǎng Jiāo Yuè Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozōng became regent,
he did not appoint Sīyuǎn.
He was then transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Línhǎi Tàishǒu Shěn Zhāolüè was accused of corruption,
Sīyuǎn impeached him according to the facts.
Gāozōng, Sīyuǎn’s cousin Yàn, and Zhāolüè’s uncle Wénjì pleaded with him to stop,
but Sīyuǎn did not comply,
and investigated the case as before.
During the Jiànwǔ period,
he was promoted to Lìbù Láng.
Sīyuǎn, knowing that his cousin Yàn was Shàngshū Lìng,
did not want to simultaneously hold important positions in the inner court.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining the appointment.
It stated:
“Recently, I have frequently returned to report,
there is truly a slight matter.
Your Majesty’s generous treatment is rare in ancient and modern times.
If I were to betray your kindness,
who would then exert themselves?
Since I have sworn to disregard my life,
〔一八〕I no longer hesitate due to defilement.
〔一九〕It is precisely because I and Yàn are close relatives
that it is certainly inappropriate for us to both hold prominent and important positions.
My loyal and sincere heart
I will guard with my life.
I am truly mediocre and lowly,
unworthy of promotion.
Your Majesty’s intention to select and advance me
is ultimately to allow me a single act of integrity.
If I truly cannot uphold myself with reason,
I would deviate from the wisdom of discerning judgment.
The fault of transgression and offense
lies with me;
the impropriety of undue reward
would only tarnish the sagely gaze.
Weighing the gravity of the matter,
I would rather hold fast to my original intention.
Moreover, it is also because Your Majesty governs the subordinates with virtue
that I am able to advance and retreat with propriety.
I humbly wish that you would extend your saving grace
and not allow me to fall.
If I were to simply accept the position I am unworthily offered now,
the Three Ducal Ministers would not be enough to satisfy me;
after offending,
the Nine Springs would not be severe enough.
Yet, if I were to seek punishment
and abandon wealth and honor,
a foolish commoner would not do so,
and I, too, hope to be spared such a fate.
This heart, this will,
is lamentable and pitiable.
If, however, the imperial decree must be carried out,
and my request for punishment is deemed unreasonable,
and the imperial favor places me on the common path,
while I stubbornly seek rejection,
I pity and mourn myself,
and cannot help but shed tears.
I respectfully risk the axe
and earnestly make this plea.
When in distress, one calls upon Heaven;
I look up and pray for a single glance of understanding.”
〔二０〕The Emperor understood his intention,
and therefore reassigned him as Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
Initially,
during Gāozōng’s deposition and enthronement,
Sīyuǎn spoke privately with Yàn,
saying to Yàn:
“Brother, you bear the great kindness of Emperor Shìzǔ.
Now, to suddenly assist someone in such a matter,
he might temporarily need you for strategic reasons,
but I don't know how you will sustain yourself in the future.
If you were to make a decisive choice now,
you could still preserve your good name for posterity.”
Yàn did not accept this advice.
When he was appointed Piàojì,
he gathered his nephews and younger relatives,
and said to Sīyuǎn’s brother Sīwēi:
“At the end of Lóngchāng,
Āróng advised me to take my own life.
If I had followed his words,
how could I have achieved what I have today?”
Sīyuǎn immediately responded:
“According to Āróng’s view,
it is still not too late.”
When Yàn suffered defeat,
Sīyuǎn thus escaped harm.
Sīyuǎn was pure and cultivated,
and lived a simple and clean life.
His clothes and bed furnishings
were meticulously plain and clean.
When guests came to call,
he would always have someone secretly observe them first.
If their clothes were dirty or unkempt,
he would conveniently avoid meeting them.
If their appearance was fresh and neat,
then he would sit close to them.
Nevertheless,
after they left,
he would still order two servants to sweep and brush the place where they had sat.
The Emperor’s cousin Jìchǎng was very unrestrained,
and the Emperor secretly disapproved of him.
He said to Jìchǎng:
“You should frequently visit Wáng Sīyuǎn.”
After the Emperor executed Yàn,
Sīyuǎn was promoted to Shìzhōng,
in charge of imperial decrees and court records.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Before he could be formally appointed,
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
He was posthumously granted Tàicháng
and given the posthumous name Zhēnzǐ.
Sīyuǎn was good friends with Gù Gǎozhī.
After Gǎozhī’s death,
his family was poor,
so Sīyuǎn took in his son
〔二一〕and provided for him with great care.
Gǎo's courtesy name was Shì-Míng.
He was orphaned young,
loved learning, and had righteous conduct.
Initially, he was nominated as Xiù-Cái,
and served successively in various government offices.
At the end of Yǒng-Míng,
he became Táizi Zhōng-Shè-Rén,
concurrently Shàng-Shū Zuǒ-Chéng.
At the beginning of Lóng-Chāng,
he became Ān-Xī Zī-Yì,
concurrently Zhù-Zuò,
and, along with Sī-Yuǎn, was noted for his literary talent.
At the beginning of Jiàn-Wǔ,
he returned home due to illness.
Gāo-Zōng personally issued an edict to Sī-Yuǎn, saying:
"This person is truly regrettable."
He was then appointed Zhōng-Sàn Dà-Fū.
He died
at the age of forty-nine.
Sī-Wēi,
during the Yǒng-Yuán era, was Jiāng-Zhōu Zhǎng-Shǐ,
and was killed by Chén Bó-Zhī.
The historian says: Accomplishment in virtue is paramount,
accomplishment in art is secondary.
Observing how these few individuals conducted themselves,
it was not merely about purity and elegant pursuits
that established a grand foundation;
their adherence to ritual and treading the path of righteousness
could inspire others and serve as a model.
A gentleman's life in the world,
this is what is called beautiful!
Eulogy says: Jiāng Zuǎn's hereditary legacy,
was renowned at the time.
Hé Shēn served his former lord,
his words originated from righteousness.
Xiè Xiàn offered a toast,
expressing both joy and admonition.
Sī-Yuǎn retired from office,
his heart was calm and his trust profound.

Xú Xiào-Sì, courtesy name Shǐ-Chāng,
was from Tán, Dōng-Hǎi.
His grandfather, Zhàn-Zhī, was Sòng Sī-Kōng;
his father, Yù-Zhī, was Zhù-Zuò Láng:
both were killed by Tài-(Zǔ)【Chū】.
Xiào-Sì was spared because he was still in the womb.
He was outstanding from a young age,
with dignified and simple demeanor.
At eight years old,
he inherited the title of Zhī-Jiāng Xiàn-Gōng.
When he met Sòng Xiào-Wǔ,
he ascended the steps with tears streaming down,
until he reached his seat.
The Emperor greatly loved him.
He married Princess Kāng-Lè.
In the second year of Tài-Shǐ,
when the western campaign was concluded and the emperor's carriage returned to the palace,
Xiào-Sì ascended the hall without his hat.
He was impeached by Zhī-Shū Yù-Shǐ Cài Zhǔn
and fined two liǎng of gold.
He was appointed Fù-Mǎ Dū-Wèi,
and appointed Zhù-Zuò Láng.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
He served as Cān-Jūn in the two bureaus of Sī-Kōng and Tài-Wèi,
and Ān-Chéng-Wáng Wén-Xué.
Xiào-Sì's maternal aunt married Liú Shě of Dōng-Guǎn.
Shě's elder brother, Zàng, was Shàng-Shū Zuǒ-Chéng.
Xiào-Sì went to visit him.
Zàng retired and said to Shě:
"Xu Láng will certainly be a prime minister.
At over thirty, it is clear.
You should form a good bond with him."
During Shēng-Míng,
he was promoted to Tài-Zǔ Piào-Jì Cóng-Shì Zhōng-Láng,
concurrently Nán-Péng-Chéng Tài-Shǒu.
Following the chuyển from his yamen, he became Tài-Wèi Zī-Yì Cān-Jūn,
with his title of Tài-Shǒu remaining as before.
When Qí-Tái was established,
he became Shì-Zǐ Shù-Zǐ.
At the beginning of Jiàn-Yuán,
his hereditary state was abolished.
He went out to serve as Jìn-Líng Tài-Shǒu,
then returned to become Táizi Zhōng-Shù-Zǐ,
and concurrently Líng Cháng-Shuǐ Xiào-Wèi.
Before his appointment,
he became Níng-Shuò Jiāng-Jūn, Wén-Xǐ-Gōng-Zǐ Liáng Zhēng-Lǔ Zhǎng-Shǐ,
then promoted to Shàng-Shū Lì-Bù Láng,
Táizi Yòu-Wèi-Shuài,
then transferred to Zhǎng-Shǐ.
He was skilled in walking and at ease in his demeanor,
on par with Tài-Zǎi Chǔ Yuān.
Shì-Zǔ greatly favored and treated him.
Shàng-Shū-Lìng Wáng Jiǎn said to others:
"Xú Xiào-Sì will certainly become a prime minister in the future."
He was then transferred to Yù-Shǐ Zhōng-Chéng.
Shì-Zǔ asked Jiǎn:
"Who can succeed you?"
Jiǎn replied:
"When I was in Dōng-Dū,
it would be Xú Xiào-Sì!"
He went out to serve as Wú-Xīng Tài-Shǒu.
Jiǎn presented Xiào-Sì with a four-character poem, saying:
"His principles align with Shú-Mào,
he pursues the clarity of Yàn-Fǔ.
Soft, he does not (spit out)【swallow】,
hard, he does not (swallow)【spit out】."
People at the time compared his conduct to that of Cài Zǐ-Ní.
He earned a reputation for competence in the commandery.
When Wáng Jiǎn died,
the Emperor summoned Xiào-Sì to be Wǔ-Bīng Shàng-Shū.
That year,
the Emperor commanded the ceremonial officials Chén Shú, Wáng Jǐng-Zhī, Zhū Xuán-Zhēn, and Chén Yì-Mín to compile the ritual codes from the time of Jiāng-Zuǒ,
and instructed them to consult Xiào-Sì.
The following year,
he was promoted to Táizi Zhān-Shì.
He accompanied Shì-Zǔ to Fāng-Shān.
The Emperor said:
"I started construction south of this mountain,
to make it a site for a detached palace.
It should surpass Líng-Qiū."
Líng-Qiū Mountain Lake was originally Xīn-Lín Yuàn.
Xiào-Sì replied:
"Circumnavigating Huáng-Shān and reaching Niú-Shǒu
were great undertakings of the Hàn dynasty.
Now the area south of the river is not yet vast,
and the people are weary.
I wish Your Majesty would give it a little more thought."
The Emperor ultimately built nothing.
Jìng-Líng-Wáng Zǐ-Liáng greatly esteemed him.
Zǐ-Liáng was very fond of Buddhism,
and had Xiào-Sì and Hé Yìn of Lú-Jiāng oversee the vegetarian lectures and the assembly of monks.
He was transferred to Lì-Bù Shàng-Shū.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Yòu-Jūn Jiāng-Jūn,
then transferred to concurrently command Táizi Zuǒ-Wèi-Shuài.
Many affairs of the imperial court were entrusted to him.
When Shì-Zǔ died,
his dying edict transferred him to Yòu-Pú-Shè.
In the first year of Lóng-Chāng,
he was promoted to Sàn-Qí Cháng-Shì, Qián Jiāng-Jūn, Dān-Yáng Yǐn.
Gāo-Zōng planned to depose Yù-Lín
and informed Xiào-Sì.
Xiào-Sì received the order but offered no assistance or advice.
When Gāo-Zōng entered the hall,
Xiào-Sì, in military attire, followed behind.
After Yù-Lín was killed,
Gāo-Zōng needed the empress dowager's order.
Xiào-Sì produced it from his sleeve and presented it.
Gāo-Zōng was greatly pleased.
For his merit in the deposition and enthronement,
he was enfeoffed as Zhī-Jiāng Xiàn-Hóu,
with an income of a thousand households.
He was granted a set of drums and pipes,
and fifty armed guards to enter the palace.
He was transferred to Zuǒ-Pú-Shè,
with his position as Cháng-Shì remaining as before.
When Míng-Dì ascended the throne,
he was given the additional titles of Shì-Zhōng and Zhōng-Jūn Dà-Jiāng-Jūn.
For his meritorious service in establishing the new emperor,
he was advanced in rank to Gōng,
and his enfeoffment was increased by two thousand households.
He was granted twenty ceremonial sword-bearers
and an additional hundred soldiers.
Previously, one had to attend court to be appointed a Sān-Gōng.
At this time, the Emperor specifically decreed that he, Chén Xiǎn-Dá, and Wáng Yàn should all attend court to receive their appointments.
When the northern barbarians moved,
an edict commanded Xiào-Sì to temporarily hold the imperial insignia and be stationed at Xīn-Tíng.
At that time, Wáng Yàn was Shàng-Shū-Lìng,
but the public sentiment and popular expectation
did not match Xiào-Sì.
After Yàn was executed,
he was transferred to Shàng-Shū-Lìng,
concurrently leading the Zhōng-Zhèng of his home province,
with all other positions remaining as before.
Xiào-Sì loved literature
and appreciated refined discussions.
His capacity was broad and refined,
and he did not boast of his power or influence.
Thus, he was tolerated during the Jiàn-Wǔ era.
He maintained himself with humility and self-preservation,
and the court and common people praised him for this.
Initially,
Xú Xiàosì was in the Shuàifǔ (Commander's Office).
One day, he was sleeping against the northern wall of his study.
He dreamt that two youths suddenly said,
"Move the Duke's bed."
Xú Xiàosì awoke with a start.
He heard a sound from the wall,
walked a few steps, and then the wall collapsed onto the bed.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ (497 CE),
he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Government with the Same Privileges as the Three Excellencies) with his original title.
When Xú Xiàosì heard the imperial edict,
he composed himself and said to his attendants,
"My virtue shames the ancients,
yet I have attained the highest ministerial position.
How can I bear this?
A sagacious ruler can be persuaded by reason;
I must plead to decline, even to death.
If my plea is not accepted,
I shall simply wear a simple cap and retire to a garden,
awaiting punishment in my home alley."
He firmly declined the appointment.
At that time, barbarian invasions occurred year after year,
and the military and state were depleted.
Xú Xiàosì submitted a memorial advocating for the establishment of garrison farms, saying:
"Among the urgent affairs of the state,
soldiers and food are equally important.
If even one man ceases farming,
the matter becomes all the more critical.
Hence, in the days of the Zhōu dynasty, fields and borders were delineated,
and long chariots flourished.
When garrison farms were widely established,
weapons and wealth abounded in the Hàn court.
From then until now,
the details can be seen.
However, to seek precedents from ancient times,
the argument is too broad;
focusing on the present,
there should be essential methods.
I humbly observe that all the frontier garrisons along the Huái River
draw their supplies from the capital.
The expenditures are heavy,
and river transport is difficult.
Amassing grain to await the enemy
often suffers from insufficiency.
Among the foundations of benefit and harm,
nothing is more urgent than this.
I have recently inquired among old veterans and those who have served as officials there.
The old fields south of the Huái River
stretch as far as the eye can see.
However, the dikes and dams are not maintained,
and all have become overgrown with lush grass.
Flat plains and dry land
are especially abundant as far as the eye can reach.
Now, with frontier defenses strict
and the number of garrison troops increased,
we rely on distant transport for provisions,
while nearby fertile fields lie fallow.
Many soldiers show signs of hunger,
which is truly lamentable.
I foolishly suggest that the Cìshǐ (Provincial Governors) and Èrqiānshí (Magistrates receiving two thousand piculs) personally inspect the land,
reclaiming and cultivating it as appropriate.
They should carefully identify sources of irrigation
and skillfully assess the differences between fertile and barren land.
All officials, from the commander of the Zhōujùnxiànshù (Prefectural and County Garrisons) downwards,
should be divided into shifts to assist farmers.
Although it is late for paddy fields,
it is now time for soybeans and wheat.
Soybeans and wheat
are especially suited to the northern lands,
and the local people are accustomed to them,
finding them no less valuable than polished rice.
The benefits of initiating this
should be seized opportunely.
If my proposal is accepted,
please immediately send envoys to Xú, Yùn, Sī, Yù,
and also to Jīng and Yōng.
Each should survey their respective territories,
leaving nothing overlooked.
A special department should be established
to specifically manage this affair.
The court should carefully determine
the allocation of farming tools and plowing oxen.
At the end of the year, reports should be made on their performance,
and rewards and punishments clearly defined.
If this task can be accomplished,
it will surely yield great benefits.
If the border regions have sufficient food,
Jiāngnán will naturally be prosperous,
and the surplus
will be immeasurable."
His memorial was approved by the emperor.
At that time, the emperor was already gravely ill,
and military affairs were ongoing,
so it was never implemented.
When the emperor's illness worsened,
Xú Xiàosì entered and resided within the forbidden palace.
Upon the emperor's demise, he received a heavy entrustment in the will,
reiterating his appointment as Kāifǔ.
He was also appointed Zhōngshū Jiān (Palace Secretary).
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán (499 CE), when he assisted in governance,
he moved from the Shàngshū Xiàshěng (Lower Department of the Secretariat) to reside in a southern residence within the palace city,
and was unable to return home.
As the emperor's misconduct became increasingly apparent,
Xú Xiàosì dared not offer remonstrance.
When Jiāng Shí was executed,
he harbored internal anxieties and fears,
but never showed it on his face.
When the Prince of Shǐ'ān, Yáo Guāng, rebelled,
the populace was bewildered and alarmed.
When Xú Xiàosì entered,
the palace interior was then pacified.
However,
the small-minded officials held power, and he could not control them.
He was promoted to Sìkōng (Minister of Works),
but firmly declined.
He sought to resign as Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Dānyáng Commandery),
but was not permitted.
Xú Xiàosì was a literary man,
who did not openly show agreement or disagreement.
Although his position was high,
he thus avoided immediate disaster.
Xǔ Zhǔn, the Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (Commander of the Elite Cavalry), had courage and strength.
As Lǐngjūn (General of the Imperial Guard), he was subordinate to Xú Xiàosì.
He explained the opportune situation
and urged him to depose and enthrone.
Xú Xiàosì hesitated for a long time,
believing it absolutely unnecessary to resort to military force.
He waited for the young emperor to go on an excursion,
then planned to close the city gates, summon all officials to deliberate his deposition.
Although he harbored this intention,
he ultimately could not decide.
The small-minded officials also gradually resented Xú Xiàosì.
They advised the emperor to summon all officials for a meeting,
and then execute him.
In winter,
Xú Xiàosì was summoned to the Huálínshěng (Huálín Department).
Rú Fǎzhēn was sent to give him poison.
Xú Xiàosì's expression remained unchanged.
He could drink little wine,
but after drinking over a dou (roughly 2 liters) of the poison,
he finally died.
An imperial edict was then issued, stating:
"When the virtue of Zhōu was greatly flourishing,
the 'Three Overseers'
rebelled in delusion.
When the Hàn dynasty prospered for generations,
its chief ministers plotted treachery.
All had their bodies smeared by axes and halberds,
and their clans became like smoke and ashes.
Let these be a mirror from past ages,
a warning to future generations.
Xú Xiàosì, relying on his family's heritage,
received exceptional favor early on.
Through opportune circumstances, he rose through the ranks
to the highest official positions.
However, his sincerity in assisting the state was unheard of,
while his sycophantic and abusive conduct was repeatedly evident.
Shěn Wénjì's family lineage
Shěn Wénjì, courtesy name Zhòngdá,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His father, Qìngzhī,
was the Sìkōng of the Sòng dynasty.
Wénjì was known from a young age for his broad-mindedness, elegance, and uprightness.
In the second year of Xiàojiàn (455 CE),
he began his career as a Zhǔbù (Clerk),
and was summoned to be Mìshū Láng (Secretary of the Imperial Library).
Due to Qìngzhī's great merit,
in the fifth year of Dàmíng (461 CE),
Wénjì was enfeoffed as a Count of the Fifth Rank of Shānyáng County.
He was transferred to Taizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
then Běizhōngláng Zhǔbù (Clerk to the Northern Central Gendarme) for the Prince of Xīn'ān,
then Fǔjūn Gōngcáo (Military Registrar for the General Guarding the Army) for the Prince of Xīyáng,
then Tàiwèi Dōngcáoyuàn (Eastern Bureau Aide to the Grand Commandant) for the Prince of Jiāngxià,
and then promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (Palace Secretary).
When Qìngzhī was killed by Jǐnghé,
soldiers surrounded their residence,
arresting his sons.
Wénjì's elder brother, Wénshū, said to Wénjì,
"I can die,
you must seek revenge."
Thereupon, he hanged himself.
Wénjì brandished a knife and rode away on a horse.
The arresting officers dared not pursue him,
and he thus escaped.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
Wénjì was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), then promoted to Taizǐ Yòuwèilǜ (Right Guard Commander of the Crown Prince's Household),
and then Sītú Sīmǎ (Registrar to the Minister of Education) for the Prince of Jiàn'ān.
After Zhěqí was pacified,
he became Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe)
and Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant) for the Prince of Lújiāng.
He was sent out as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Zhēngběi Sīmǎ (Registrar to the General Who Conquers the North), and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Guǎnglíng Commandery).
He was then transferred to Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
and also held the position of Zhǎngshuǐ Xiàowèi (Commander of the Changshui Battalion).
When Emperor Míng hosted a banquet for court officials,
he appointed Hè Zàng, a Yùshǐ (Censor) from the Nántái (Southern Terrace), as Zhùxià Shǐ (Censor),
to monitor those who did not drink.
Wénjì refused to drink,
and was driven from the hall.
Jìn Píngwáng Xiūyòu (晉平王休祐) was the Administrator of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
The Emperor asked Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) to recommend a capable person as his chief assistant.
Yuān (淵) recommended Wénjì (文季).
He was transferred to General Níngshuò (寧朔將軍), Chief Clerk to the General of Agile Cavalry, and Administrator of Nán Dōnghǎi (南東海).
After Xiūyòu (休祐) was killed,
although a funeral ceremony for a prince was used,
most of his subordinates dared not attend.
Wénjì (文季) alone went to visit his tomb and express his sorrow.
He was later appointed Administrator of Línhǎi (臨海).
At the beginning of Yuánhuī (元徽) reign,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
concurrently serving as General of the Rear Army,
and then transferred to Director of the Imperial Library.
He was later appointed Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
Wénjì (文季) could drink up to five *dǒu* (五斗) of wine.
His wife, Wáng Shì (王氏),
a daughter of Wáng Xī (王錫),
could also drink up to three *dǒu* (三斗).
Wénjì (文季) would drink with her all day,
yet his official duties were not neglected.
In the first year of Shēngmíng (昇明),
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) rebelled.
Tàizǔ (太祖) appointed Wénjì (文季) as General Guànjūn (冠軍將軍),
overseeing military affairs in Wúxīng (吳興) and Qiántáng (錢塘).
Yōuzhī (攸之) had previously acted as Jǐnghé's (景和) envoy to kill Qìngzhī (慶之).
At this time, Wénjì (文季) apprehended and executed Dēngzhī (登之), Yōuzhī's (攸之) younger brother and Administrator of Xīn'ān (新安),
and exterminated his clan.
He was granted the *chíjié* (持節) privilege,
promoted to General Zhēnglǔ (征虜將軍),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lüèyáng Xiàn (略陽縣侯),
with a thousand households.
The following year,
he was transferred to Administrator of Dānyáng (丹陽 Yin),
with his generalship remaining as before.
When the Qí (齊) state was first established,
he served as Palace Attendant,
concurrently Director of the Imperial Library.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元),
he was transferred to Commandant of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
He was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīfēng Xiàn (西豐縣侯),
with an income of 1,200 households.
Wénjì (文季) had a resolute and distinguished bearing,
and was skilled in his conduct.
Sītú (司徒) Chǔ Yuān (褚淵), a noble and prominent figure of his time,
somewhat judged him by his family background,
but Wénjì (文季) would not yield to him.
While Shìzǔ (世祖) was in the Eastern Palace,
he held a banquet for his court officials at Xuánpǔ (玄圃).
Wénjì (文季) repeatedly urged Yuān (淵) to drink,
which greatly displeased Yuān (淵).
He memorialized Shìzǔ (世祖), saying:
"Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) believes that I, Yuān (淵), once served as an administrator in his commandery,
and thus he repeatedly forces wine upon me."
Wénjì (文季) said:
"As with the mulberry and catalpa,
one must show respect.
How can it be like Your Excellency, who lost his state and territory,
and does not recognize his own ancestral village?"
He then spoke of the barbarian movements.
Yuān (淵) said:
"Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) and Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) are the military strategists of today,
sufficient to be entrusted with frontier affairs."
Wénjì (文季) (文季) disliked being called a military family,
and became angry because of this.
He memorialized Shìzǔ (世祖), saying:
"Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) claims to be a loyal minister,
but I wonder on the day of his death,
how will he face Sòng Míngdì (宋明帝)?"
Shìzǔ (世祖) laughed and said:
"Commandant Shěn (沈率) is drunk."
The Censor-in-chief, Liú Xiū (劉休), reported the incident,
but he was pardoned.
Later, at a gathering in the back hall of Prince Yùzhāng's (豫章王) northern residence,
Wénjì (文季) and Yuān (淵) were both skilled at playing the *pípá* (琵琶).
As the banquet drew to a close,
Yuān (淵) took up an instrument
and played the "Song of the Enlightened Lord" (*Míngjūn qǔ* 明君曲).
Wénjì (文季) immediately rose from his seat and loudly declared:
"Shěn Wénjì (沈文季) cannot be an entertainer!"
Prince Yùzhāng (豫章王) Yí (嶷) again tried to smooth things over, saying:
"This surely will not diminish Zhòngróng's (仲容) virtue."
Yuān's (淵) expression remained unchanged;
he finished the song and stopped.
Wénjì (文季) was soon appointed General Zhēnglǔ (征虜將軍),
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant,
General of the Left Guard,
with his position as General Zhēnglǔ (征虜) remaining as before.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining as before.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he was appointed General of the Left and Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡).
In the third year,
he was promoted to General Píngdōng (平東將軍).
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
with his generalship remaining as before.
At this time, household registers were being checked for several consecutive years,
causing widespread resentment among the people.
Táng Jízhī (唐𧜛之) from Fùyáng (富陽) was a migrant living in Tónglú (桐廬).
His ancestors had traditionally made a living by geomancy of graves.
Jízhī (𧜛之) claimed that there was imperial *qì* (王氣) in his family graves
and that he had found a golden seal in the mountains,
spreading this delusion.
In the winter of the third year,
Jízhī (𧜛之) gathered a party of 400 people
and cut off merchant travel at Xīnchéng (新城) waterway.
His followers were distributed among nearby counties.
Lù Chìfèn (陸赤奮), Magistrate of Xīnchéng (新城), and Wáng Tiānmǐn (王天愍), Magistrate of Tónglú (桐廬), abandoned their counties and fled.
Jízhī (𧜛之) headed towards Fùyáng (富陽),
plundering the people.
Magistrate Hé Xún (何洵) reported to Cóng Xìgōng (從係公), chief of the Fú Pǔzǐ (魚浦子) patrol,
who mobilized male villagers from Yúpǔ (魚浦) to defend the county.
Yǒngxīng (永興) dispatched Xiàhóu Tánxiàn (夏侯曇羨), commander of the Xīlíng (西陵) garrison, to lead officers, soldiers, and people from the areas around the dikes to raise troops for rescue.
Jízhī (𧧜之) then captured Fùyáng (富陽).

Zhāng Sīzǔ (張思祖), Assistant Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽) Commandery, sent court envoys Kǒng Jīn (孔矜), Wáng Wànsuì (王萬歲), Zhāng Yáo (張繇), and others, equipped with weapons, officers, soldiers, and commoners,
to defend Yǒngxīng (永興) and ten other dependent areas.
Wénjì (文季) also dispatched weapons, officers, and soldiers to rescue Qiántáng (錢塘).
When Jízhī (𧜛之) reached Qiántáng (錢塘),
Liú Biāo (劉彪), Magistrate of Qiántáng (錢塘), and Niè Sēngguì (聶僧貴), garrison commander, sent company commander Zhāng Gān (張玕) to resist him at Xiǎoshān (小山).
Their strength was unequal,
and they were defeated.
Jízhī (𧜛之) advanced, landed at Yìpǔ (抑浦),
and burned the city and its settlements.
Biāo (彪) abandoned the county and fled.
Wénjì (文季) again mobilized civilian men from Wú (吳), Jiāxīng (嘉興), Hǎiyán (海鹽), and Yánguān (鹽官) to rescue them.
The bandits divided their troops and went out to various counties.
Xiāo Yuánwèi (蕭元蔚), Magistrate of Yánguān (鹽官), and Líng Jūzhī (陵琚之), Magistrate of Zhūjì (諸暨), both fled. Lè Yǎn (樂琰), Magistrate of Yúháng (餘杭), only fled after being defeated in battle.
That spring,
Jízhī (𧜛之) proclaimed himself emperor in Qiántáng (錢塘),
appointed a crown prince,
designated the Xīnchéng (新城) garrison as the emperor's palace,
and the county office as the crown prince's palace.
His younger brother, Shàozhī (紹之), was made Administrator of Yángzhōu (揚州).
Kē Lóng (柯隆), a rich man from Qiántáng (錢塘), was appointed Minister of the Left and Palace Secretary,
concurrently Director of the Imperial Kitchen.
He offered thousands of ingots for Jízhī (𧜛之) to make weapons,
and was additionally appointed Director of the Imperial Manufactories.
He dispatched his confederate Gāo Dàodù (高道度) to raid Dōngyáng (東陽).
Xiāo Chóngzhī (蕭崇之), Administrator of Dōngyáng (東陽), and Liú Guózhòng (劉國重), Magistrate of Chángshān (長山), resisted in battle but were killed.
Chóngzhī (崇之), courtesy name Mào Jìng (茂敬),
was a clan younger brother of Tàizǔ (太祖).
Faced with disaster,
he remained virtuous and decisive.
He was posthumously granted General Guànjūn (冠軍將軍),
with his position as Administrator remaining as before.
The bandits then occupied the commandery.
He also sent the false Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽), Sūn Hóng (孫泓), to take Shānyīn (山陰).
At that time, Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則), Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽), was attending court,
so Jízhī (𧜛之) thought it could be attacked by surprise.
When Hóng (泓) reached Púyáng Jiāng (浦陽江),
Zhāng Sīzǔ (張思祖), Assistant Administrator of the Commandery, sent Tāng Xiūwǔ (湯休武), commander of the Xiápkǒu (浹口) garrison, to resist in battle,
and greatly defeated him.
The Emperor was in the Lèyóu Yuàn (樂遊苑)
when he heard of Jízhī (𧜛之) the bandit.
He said to Prince Yùzhāng (豫章王) Yí (嶷):
"At the beginning of Sòng Míngdì's (宋明帝) reign,
the nine provinces rebelled together.
These small-time rogues just do their thing,
watch Xiāo Gōng (蕭公) strike them down."
He dispatched several thousand imperial guards
and several hundred horses to suppress the rebellion in the east.
The bandits, a motley crowd,
feared the horses.
When the government troops reached Qiántáng (錢塘),
they scattered after a single battle,
captured and beheaded Jízhī (𧜛之),
and then advanced to pacify the various commanderies and counties.
The imperial army pressed its advantage,
and the common people were considerably plundered.
When the army returned,
the Emperor heard of it
and had Chén Tiānfú (陳天福), the army commander and General of the Vanguard, executed in the marketplace.
Liú Míngchè (劉明徹), General of the Left Army and Viscount of Zhōngsù (中宿) County, was dismissed from office, stripped of his title, and handed over to the Dōngyě (東冶) prison.
Tiānfú (天福) was one of the Emperor's favored generals.
After he was executed,
everyone, inside and outside the court, was shocked and awed.
Tiānfú (天福) was skilled with the horse-spear, and to this day, all generals emulate him.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Xú Xiàosì played:
"I have heard reports that bandits in Shāndōng
have plundered various cities.
Although they were not immediately annihilated,
they did for a time obstruct the imperial strategy.
Counties and prefectures lacked proper defenses,
and granaries and treasuries suffered from numerous incursions and losses.
Rewarding good and punishing evil
should have a clear basis.
Xiāo Yuánwèi, the salt official of Wújùn Commandery, Wáng Tiānmǐn, the magistrate of Tónglú, Lù Chìfèn, the magistrate of Xīnchéng, and others,
had their counties plundered and destroyed by bandits.
[二一]They all did not engage in proper combat,
abandoning their posts and scattering.
[二二]Yuánwèi and Tiānmǐn returned to the imperial court,
while Chìfèn's whereabouts are unknown.
Furthermore, Liú Biāo, the magistrate of Qiántáng, and Hé Xún, the magistrate of Fùyáng,
led their officials and commoners to resist but were outmatched in battle.
[二三]They did not report back to the imperial court.
As for Jiàndé and Shòuchāng,
they were in the path of the bandits on the upper reaches [of the river],
it is unknown whether they were plundered or not.
Yúháng County, under the jurisdiction of Wúxīng, was plundered and destroyed.
Its magistrate, Lè Yǎn, led his officials and commoners to fight directly but was outmatched,
abandoning his post and fleeing to the capital.
Zhūjì County, under the jurisdiction of Kuàijī,
was destroyed by bandits.
Its magistrate, Líng Jūzhī, did not engage in proper combat,
abandoned the city and fled,
his whereabouts unknown.
Upon investigation, Yuánwèi and others, falsely relying on divine favor,
held office in the capital's vicinity,
but obscured their hidden depravity,
thereby inviting slaughter.
Zhāng Sīzǔ, the Assistant Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery, mistakenly filled the vacancy,
assuming the entire responsibility as a mere corpse,
his sincere efforts and contributions
ultimately amounting to nothing.
Píngdōng Jiāngjūn, Wújùn Tàishǒu Wénjì, and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Wúxīng Tàishǒu, Xīchāng Hóu Luán,
[二四] were entrusted with important responsibilities near the Guān and Hé rivers,
and their power and influence were relied upon.
I request that Biāo, Yǎn, and Xún be immediately prohibited [from official duties],
and Sīzǔ, Wénjì, continue their duties as before,
and Luán and others be subjected to a ransom judgment."
[二五]An imperial edict decreed that Yuánwèi and others be dismissed,
and Sīzǔ, Luán, and Wénjì be pardoned.
Wénjì firmly declined the appointment to Kuàijī,
and was transferred to Dūguān Shàngshū,
with the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
He was dispatched as Chíjié, Dū Yǐngzhōu Sīzhōu zhī Yìyáng Zhū Jūnshì, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn, Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Upon his return, he served as Sànqí Chángshì,
and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Shìzǔ said to Wénjì:
"The southern gentry have been without a Púyè
for many years."
Wénjì replied:
"The southern winds have not been strong,
and this has not been for just a day."
Although Wénjì was not learned,
his words always contained literary elegance,
and the people of his time praised his eloquent responses.
He was especially skilled at archery,
using five arrows.
Due to illness, he was transferred to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
with an additional twenty personal guards,
and his Chángshì title remained as before.
He was then transferred to Shìzhōng,
also serving as Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
then promoted to Zhōnghùjūn,
with his Shìzhōng title remaining as before.
His residence was made into a government office.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was again appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his Shìzhōng title remaining as before.
When Yùlín was to be deposed,
Gāozōng wanted to appoint Wénjì as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He sent his attendant Dān Jǐngjùn to convey the imperial edict.
Wénjì personally expressed his refusal,
stating that he was old and did not wish to go out [to a provincial post].
He then asked if there was anyone suitable for the Yòu Zhífǎ position.
Jǐngjùn returned and reported everything in detail.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Lǐng Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
and his stipend increased by five hundred households.
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn once jokingly called Wénjì "Wúxīng Púyè."
Wénjì replied:
"The Zhífǎ of Lángyá
seems to be someone from your family."
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì,
with his Púyè title remaining as before.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians attacked Shòuchūn.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ, Fēngchéng Gōng Yáo Chāng, defended the city stubbornly.
He repeatedly sent light troops to raid and attack them.
Míngdì was worried about this,
and ordered Wénjì to lead troops to garrison Shòuchūn.
Wénjì entered the city,
stopped the roving soldiers and forbade them from going out,
[二六] opened the city gates wide,
and greatly strengthened the defenses.
The barbarian army soon retreated,
and the common people suffered no harm.
His enfeoffment was increased to one thousand nine hundred households.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
with his Púyè and Chángshì titles remaining as before.
When Wáng Jìngzé rebelled,
an imperial edict ordered Wénjì to lead troops to garrison Hútóu,
to guard the capital's road.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng, Zuǒ Púyè,
with his Jiāngjūn title remaining as before.
When Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáo Guāng rebelled,
that night,
he sent three hundred men to Wénjì's residence to seize him,
intending to make him Dūdū,
but Wénjì had already returned to the imperial court.
The next day,
he and Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì guarded the imperial palace city,
sitting together in military attire on the southern Yèmén.
At that time, Dōng Hūn had already begun killing,
and Xiàosì was deeply worried.
He wanted to discuss current affairs with Wénjì,
[二七] but Wénjì always diverted the conversation to other topics,
and the matter could not be addressed.
After the situation stabilized,
he was given the additional title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted an official residence.
His Shìzhōng and Púyè titles remained as before.
Wénjì saw that the world was in chaos,
and, feigning old age and illness,
did not participate in court affairs.
His nephew Zhāolüè said to Wénjì:
"Father, you became a Yuánwài Púyè at sixty,
how can you expect to free yourself now?"
Wénjì smiled and did not reply.
[同]He was killed along with Xiàosì.
[二八]On that day, he had been summoned for an audience earlier.
Wénjì knew that he was doomed,
but acted as usual.
As he boarded the carriage, he looked back and said:
"This journey, I fear, will be a one-way trip."
He died in Huálín Shěng,
at the age of fifty-eight.
The court and common people mourned him.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Sīkōng,
and given the posthumous name Zhōngxiàn.
His nephew, Zhāolüè,
possessed a resolute spirit.
Towards the end of Shēngmíng,
he served as Xiàngguó Xīcáo Yuàn.
[二九]Tàizǔ appreciated him,
and upon ascending the throne,
said to Wáng Jiǎn:
"Among the southern gentry, there is Shěn Zhāolüè.
What position should he be given?"
Jiǎn replied:
"Your servant already has a nomination."
He then proposed transferring him to Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
The emperor did not wish to object,
and approved his proposal.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng.
In the early years of Yǒngmíng,
he successively served as Tàiwèi Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
Piàojí Sīmǎ,
and Huángmén Láng.
When Nánjùn Wáng wanted to select a friend and a scholar,
[三０] Zhāolüè was chosen as his friend.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Zuǒ Chéng.
In the first year,
he was dispatched as Línhǎi Tàishǒu,
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
In the Jiànwǔ era, Zhāolüè often became drunk to conceal himself.
He was on good terms with Xiè Tīng.
[三一] He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
and Fǔjūn Chángshǐ.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáo Guāng raised troops in Dōngfǔ,
and seized Zhāolüè within the city.
Zhāolüè [secretly escaped from the south,
crossed the Huái River and returned to the imperial court.
On this occasion, he was summoned into Huálín Shěng along with] Wénjì.
[三二] Rú Fǎzhēn and others offered poisoned wine.
Zhāolüè angrily cursed Xú Xiàosì, saying:
"To depose the ignorant and establish the enlightened
is a righteous principle of ancient and modern times.
The prime minister's lack of talent
has led to this day!"
He threw a cup at Xiàosì's face, breaking it,
and said:
"Become a broken-faced ghost!"
He died at the age of over forty.
His younger brother, Zhāo-Guāng,
upon hearing that he was to be captured,
was urged by his family to flee.
However, Zhāo-Guāng could not bear to abandon his mother,
and so he was captured
and executed.
In the first year of Zhōng-Xīng (499 CE),
Zhāo-Lüè was posthumously granted the title of Tài-Cháng,
and Zhāo-Guāng that of Tíng-Wèi.
The imperial historian says: In governing a state,
food is the people's heaven.
With sufficient food and troops,
the people will have faith.
〔三三〕The strategy of military agricultural colonies (túntián)
is truly important for both defense and offense.
For instance, Gōng Chōng-Guó's (充國) cultivation
was used to eliminate the Qiāng (羌) and Róng (戎).
Hán Hào (韓浩) and Zǎo Zhǐ (棗祇)
also established the office of diánnóng (典農) in Huá-Xià (華夏),
initiating the discussion of large-scale farming.
When Jīn-Chéng (金城) was strategically perilous,
with high ramparts extending far,
transporting provisions over long distances
was difficult to sustain.
If even one man did not farm,
there might be hunger and starvation.
Along the border, garrisons of soldiers
sat in their thousands, armored.
Therefore, it was advisable to fully utilize the land's bounty,
and provide food through military service.
During times of peace, they would personally farm;
during emergencies, they would go to war.
If there was surplus grain annually,
red meat could be expected.
The enlightened governance of previous generations
has already spoken of this in detail.
Since the time of the Eastern Jìn (江左),
there has been no time for far-reaching plans.
When the imperial army went out,
they were never fully fed.
The four suburbs were defended,
feared to be like firewood and straw.
The soldiers rescued by the counties
were delayed for months and days,
battling wind and waves,
with difficult and long transport of supplies.
Emptying the bottom of cellars
and exhausting the grain in granaries,
even the "flowing horses" (liúmǎ) and "wooden oxen" (mùniú)
still showed previous shortcomings.
The key to accumulating fields
lay only in the Jiāng-Huái (江淮) region.
Though commanderies and states might prosper together,
distant ones could not meet urgent needs.
Therefore, the Wú (吳) clan established garrisons on the southern bank
and agricultural colonies to the right of the water.
During the Wèi (魏) dynasty, large-scale farming was done north of the Huái (淮),
and Shí Héng (石橫) opened canals.
〔三四〕All these mutually supported each other like the parts of a carriage,
making it easy to confront the enemy.
〔三五〕When Xiào-Sì (孝嗣) faced the dawn of a besieged border,
he proposed a rarely-seen plan.
But the King had no foreign policy,
and the people were distressed by their leaders.
Observing the situation and acting accordingly,
this proposal was probably an empty gesture.
What a pity!
A eulogy says: Wén-Zhōng (文忠) served as prime minister,
his character and integrity were exemplary.
With tolerance and achievement,
he could establish a court.
He served through Fēng-Chéng (豐城),
〔三六〕his reputation and demeanor were widely known.
Like a boat encountering a storm,
in his fate, he perished along with others.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 26: Zōng-Shì Héng-Yáng Yuán-Wáng Dào-Dù; Shǐ-Ān Zhēn-Wáng Dào-Shēng (Yáo-Guāng, Yáo-Xīn, Yáo-Chāng); Ān-Lù Zhāo-Wáng Miǎn.
Héng-Yáng Yuán-Wáng Dào-Dù (衡陽元王道度)
was Tàizǔ's (太祖) elder brother.
He and Tàizǔ both studied under Léi Cì-Zōng (雷次宗).
When Xuān-Dì (宣帝) asked about the two sons' studies,
Cì-Zōng replied:
"The elder brother is outwardly bright,
while the younger brother is inwardly profound.
Both are excellent unpolished gems."
He followed Xuān-Dì on campaigns,
serving as the Grand Administrator of Ān-Dìng (安定),
and died during the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
In the second year of Jiàn-Yuán (480 CE),
he was posthumously enfeoffed and given a posthumous name.
Having no sons,
Tàizǔ had his eleventh son, Jūn (鈞), succeed Dào-Dù.
Jūn's courtesy name was Xuān-Lǐ (宣禮).
In the fourth year of Yǒng-Míng (486 CE),
he served as the Inspector of Jiāng-Zhōu (江州),
and was concurrently appointed Sàn-Qí Cháng-Shì (散騎常侍).
When his mother, Consort Qū (區貴人), died,
he observed the mourning rituals to the fullest.
In the sixth year (488 CE),
he was promoted to General of Conquering Captives (Zhēng-Lǔ Jiāng-Jūn).
In the eighth year (490 CE),
he was promoted to General of Elite Cavalry (Xiāo-Qí Jiāng-Jūn),
with Cháng-Shì as before.
He was then transferred to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ-Wèi Jiāng-Jūn).
Jūn had a good disposition
and was known by Shìzǔ (世祖).
Among his brothers, he was particularly close to Pō-Yáng-Wáng Qiāng (鄱陽王鏘).
In the tenth year (492 CE),
he was transferred to Central Secretariat Director (Zhōng-Shū Lìng),
and concurrently managed affairs at Shí-Tóu (石頭) outpost.
He was promoted to Sàn-Qí Cháng-Shì,
Secretary-General (Mì-Shū Jiān),
and concurrently Xiāo-Qí as before.
He did not take up the appointments.
In the first year of Lóng-Chāng (494 CE),
he was additionally appointed Grandee Remonstrant (Shì-Zhōng)
and given a扶 (fú) carriage.
When Hǎi-Líng (海陵) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to General of Protecting the Army (Fǔ-Jūn Jiāng-Jūn),
with Shì-Zhōng as before.
Soon after, he was murdered
at the age of twenty-two.
When Míng-Dì (明帝) ascended the throne,
he appointed Zǐ-Mín (子珉), son of Yǒng-Yáng-Wáng (永陽王), to retain his original state
and succeed the Yuán-Wáng (元王) as grandson.
Zǐ-Mín's courtesy name was Yún-Yú (雲璵),
and he was Shìzǔ's twentieth son.
In the seventh year of Yǒng-Míng (489 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Yì-Ān-Wáng (義安王),
later changed to Yǒng-Yáng.
In the first year of Yǒng-Tài (498 CE), he was murdered
at the age of fourteen.
Again, Zǐ-Tǎn (子坦), the third son of Wǔ-Líng Zhāo-Wáng Yè (武陵昭王曄), was appointed to inherit the Yuán-Wáng's line.
Shǐ-Ān Zhēn-Wáng Dào-Shēng (始安貞王道生), courtesy name Xiào-Bó (孝伯),
was Tàizǔ's second elder brother.
During the Sòng dynasty, he served as Féng-Cháo-Qǐng (奉朝請)
and died.
In the first year of Jiàn-Yuán (479 CE),
he was posthumously enfeoffed and given a posthumous name.
In the first year of Jiàn-Wǔ (494 CE),
he was posthumously honored as Jǐng-Huáng (景皇),
and his consort, Lady Jiāng (江氏), as Empress.
A memorial temple was established for him west of the imperial road,
and his tomb was called Xiū-Ān (脩安).
He had sons Fèng (鳳), Gāo-Zōng (高宗), and Ān-Lù Zhāo-Wáng Miǎn (安陸昭王緬).
Fèng, courtesy name Jǐng-Cí (景慈),
held the office of Zhèng-Yuán Láng (正員郎).
He died during the Sòng dynasty.
His posthumous name was Jìng Shì-Zǐ (靖世子).
In the first year of Jiàn-Wǔ (494 CE) of Míng-Dì,
he was posthumously granted Grandee Remonstrant, General of Agile Cavalry (Piào-Qí Jiāng-Jūn),
and granted the privilege of establishing an administration equal to the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāi-Fǔ Yí-Tóng Sān-Sī), as Shǐ-Ān Jìng-Wáng (始安靖王).
The Huá-Lín Fèng-Zhuāng Gate (華林鳳莊門) was renamed Wàng-Xián Gate (望賢門).
In the East Hall of Tài-Jí (太極東堂), (the character for "book" should be "painting") phoenixes were painted,
labeled "divine birds,"
and the luan bird was changed to "divine sparrow."
His son Yáo-Guāng (遙光) succeeded him.
Yáo-Guāng's courtesy name was Yuán-Huī (元暉).
He was born with a leg disability,
and Tàizǔ thought he was unfit to perform worship and sacrifices.
He wanted to enfeoff his younger brother,
but Shìzǔ remonstrated,
so Yáo-Guāng inherited the peerage.
He initially served as a Supernumerary Gentleman (Yuán-Wài Láng),
then transferred to Gentleman of the Palace (Jǐ-Shì Láng),
then Groom to the Imperial Grandson (Tài-Sūn Xǐ-Mǎ),
then transferred to Central Secretariat Gentleman (Zhōng-Shū Láng),
then Administrator of Yù-Zhāng (豫章內史),
but he did not take up these appointments.
When Gāo-Zōng (高宗) assisted in governance,
Yáo-Guāng, fond of astronomy and observing the Dao,
secretly planned and advised him.
In the first year of Lóng-Chāng (494 CE),
he was appointed General of Elite Cavalry, General of the Champion Army (Guàn-Jūn Jiāng-Jūn), and Grand Administrator of Southern Dōng-Hǎi (南東海太守),
and concurrently managed the affairs of Southern Xú-Zhōu (南徐州).
He was then appointed Grand Administrator of Southern Péng-Chéng (南彭城太守),
with his general title remaining.
He was also appointed General Assisting the State (Fǔ-Guó Jiāng-Jūn) and Grand Administrator of Wú-Xīng (吳興太守).
When Gāo-Zōng deposed Yù-Lín (鬱林),
he was again appointed General of the Champion Army, Commander of the Southern Man (Nán-Mán Xiào-Wèi), Senior Clerk to the Central Commandant (of Xī-Píng) (中郎長史),
and Grand Administrator of Nán-Jùn (南郡).
Within one year,
he was appointed five times,
but he did not take up any of them.
At this time, Gāo-Zōng intended to ascend the throne, and consulted only Yáo-Guāng on all matters of punishment and reward.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Chífú, Dūdū Yáng Nánxú Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Qiánjiāngjūn, and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
As Jìn'ān Wáng Bǎoyì was governor of Nánxúzhōu,
Yáoguāng remotely sought to be relieved of the督 (supervision),
and was granted permission.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Fǔjūnjiāngjūn,
and granted Sànqí Chángshì,
and provided with a tōngxiǎn carriage and drum music.
Yáoguāng was fond of official duties,
and was known for his clarity.
He was quite cruel and harmful.
Due to a leg ailment, he could not attend court with others (列),
and always entered through Wàngxiánmén in a carriage.
Whenever he had a long, quiet discussion with the Emperor,
after speaking,
the Emperor would ask for incense,
and the next day there would surely be an execution.
The Emperor, having few close relatives,
and resenting and fearing the descendants of Gāo and Wǔ,
wished to execute them all.
Yáoguāng planned and advised,
and it was to be carried out in sequence.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
he was appointed Dàjiāngjūn in his existing position,
and provided with an oil-lacquered carriage.
The Emperor was unwell,
and Yáoguāng frequently attended to him.
As the Emperor's condition worsened,
Hédōng Wáng Xuàn and seven other princes were killed overnight,
which was Yáoguāng's doing.
When the Emperor passed away,
his dying edict added Shìzhōng and Zhōngshūlìng to Yáoguāng's titles,
and granted him the fú (support/staff).
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was granted twenty ceremonial swordsmen,
and appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī under his existing title.
After Yáoguāng assisted in governance,
seeing the young ruler ascend the throne,
he secretly plotted with the Jiāng Shí brothers to establish himself.
His younger brother, Yáoxīn, was in Jīngchǔ,
commanding troops in the upper reaches of the river,
and they secretly influenced each other.
Yáoguāng was to take control of the Dōngfǔ and issue commands,
and have Yáoxīn immediately descend with urgency.
The secret plot was about to be launched,
but Yáoxīn fell ill and died.
When Jiāng Shí was executed,
Dōnghūn Hóu summoned Yáoguāng into the palace
to inform him of Shí's crime.
Yáoguāng was terrified,
returned to his residence and pretended to be mad, crying loudly.
From then on, he claimed illness and no longer entered the imperial court.
Earlier, when Yáoguāng returned and entered the city,
the wind blew his ceremonial parasol out of the city.
Yáoguāng's younger brother, Yáochāng, had previously died in Shòuchūn,
and all the troops of Yùzhōu returned to Yáoguāng.
When Yáoxīn's coffin was returned for burial in Wǔjìn,
it was parked in front of the Dōngfǔ (渚),
and the large number of escorts from Jīngzhōu was very impressive.
After the Emperor executed Jiāng Shí,
he feared Yáoguāng would not feel secure,
and wished to transfer him to Sītú and have him return to his residence,
so he summoned him to convey the decree.
Yáoguāng feared being killed.
At dusk on the twelfth day of the eighth month,
he gathered the troops from the two prefectures,
and assembled a crowd at the gate of the Dōngfǔ.
The streets and alleys were quite surprised by this unusual sight,
and no one knew its purpose.
Yáoguāng summoned his kinsman, Dānyáng Chéng Liú Fēng, and various Cāngchǔ (local strongmen),
intending to use "punishing Liú Xuān" as a pretext.
That night, he sent several hundred men to break into Dōngyě to release prisoners,
and to obtain weapons from Shàngfāng.
He also summoned Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Yuán Lìshēng.
Lìshēng immediately came upon receiving the message,
and advised Yáoguāng to lead the city's troops to attack the imperial court at night,
using bundles of straw to burn the city gates,
saying,
"You only need to follow in your carriage,
and it will be as easy as turning your hand."
Yáoguāng was hesitant and dared not go out.
As dawn approached,
Yáoguāng, in military attire, came out to the administrative office,
parked his carriage, and ordered weapons to be brought up to the city walls for distribution of rewards.
Lìshēng again urged him to dispatch troops,
but Yáoguāng refused,
hoping for a change within the imperial court itself.
By midday,
the imperial troops gradually arrived.
The Shàngshū issued a proclamation to Yáoguāng, saying:
"The numbers of success and failure [in rebellion]
are clearly evident.
To violate principles and disrupt order
is a crime for which there is no pardon.
Xiāo Yáoguāng, a distant relative of the imperial house, is foolish and incompetent,
and his talent and conduct are contemptible.
He can only hope for the status of a common woman;
how can he aspire to the imperial path?
He has been favored since olden times,
receiving grace as a nephew.
