His rituals surpassed those of an emperor,
and his favor exceeded that of an imperial prince.
His banners, carriages, and robes
reached the highest尊 (honor) of a thousand chariots;
his city walls and moats
exceeded the regulations of a hundred zhì (a unit of measure).
When the sagely Empress was in heaven,
he personally received her entrustment.
Her words are still in our ears,
and her virtuous voice remains.
Yet he scorns divine clarity,
and disregards injustice,
having harbored the heart of a regicide,
for a long time.
He then raised troops to invade within,
secretly launching an attack on the capital region.
Of all great evils throughout history,
none is worse than this.
Now, we shall dispatch the six armies,
and widely proclaim the nine punishments.
His Imperial Majesty will personally command the military chariots,
and carry out this strategic plan.
Rewards will be certain, and punishments unavoidable,
as sure as the great Jiāng (Yangtze River)."
Thereupon, a state of emergency was declared,
and a partial amnesty was granted to the capital.
Lǐngjūn Xiāo Tǎnzhī was stationed at Xiānggōng Sì,
Zhènjūn Sīmǎ Cáo Hǔ was stationed at Qīngxī Dàqiáo,
and Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ Zǐ Xīngshèng was stationed at the Dōngfǔ Dōnglí Mén.
The various armies surrounded the eastern city on three sides,
and burned down the two prefectural offices of the Sītú.
Yáoguāng sent Yuán Lìshēng to sally forth from the west gate,
and the imperial troops were repeatedly defeated,
killing Jūnjǔ Sāng Tiān'ài.
Initially,
when Yáoguāng raised his army,
he consulted Zīyì Cānjūn Xiāo Chàng.
Chàng sternly refused to comply.
On the fifteenth day,
Chàng and Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ Shěn Zhāolǜ secretly exited from the south,
crossed the Huái and returned to the imperial court.
Public morale was greatly depressed.
On the sixteenth day,
Yuán Lìshēng sallied forth from the south gate,
then abandoned his spear and surrendered to Cáo Hǔ's army.
Hǔ ordered him to be beheaded.
Yáoguāng was furious,
leapt up from his bed,
and had Lìshēng's son killed.
That evening,
the imperial troops shot fire arrows and burned the northeast corner tower.
By night, the city collapsed.
Yáoguāng returned to his small private room,
sat wearing his cap and robes,
holding a candle to illuminate himself,
and ordered his men to barricade the doors.
All the gates of the private rooms were double-locked.
His attendants all climbed over the roofs and fled.
Imperial army commanders Liú Guóbǎo and Shí Dāngbó were among the first to enter.
Yáoguāng heard the external troops approaching,
blew out the fire,
and stumbled off the bed.
〔一０〕The soldiers broke through the gates,
dragged him out in the dark, and beheaded him.
He was thirty-two years old at the time.
The night before Yáoguāng's defeat,
everyone in the city dreamed of monkeys climbing the city walls and spreading out,
and they all discussed it,
considering it very strange.
After the imperial troops entered the city,
they burned down almost all the houses.
Yáoguāng's aide, Sīmǎ Duān, served as Zhǎngshūjì.
Cáo Hǔ asked him,
"Are you a rebel or not?"
Duān replied,
"I received great kindness from Shǐ'ān.
I am content to die now."
Hǔ did not kill him,
but arrested him and sent him back to the imperial court.
Xú Shìzhú killed him.
Liú Fēng fled back to his home garden
and was killed by someone.
Duān was
from Hénèi.
Fēng was
from Nányáng,
known for his filial piety towards his stepmother,
and his younger brother Lián also served Fēng diligently.
An edict ordered the collection and burial of Yáoguāng's body,
and pardoned his sons.
Sāng Tiān'ài was posthumously granted Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiānglíng Gōng Bǎolǎn was appointed Shǐ'ān Wáng,
to succeed Jìng Wáng.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was appointed Chífú, Dū Xiāngzhōu, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiāo Chāng,
died in the first year of Yǒngtài.
The Emperor loved Xiāo Chāng and his brothers like his own sons,
and felt great pain and regret at his death.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) and Yítóng Sānsī (Grandee Remitted of the Three Callings).
The Emperor consulted Xú Xiàosì about this,
and Xú Xiàosì said:
"Fēngchéng's original status was rather low,
to posthumously grant him a position among the highest officials,
seems a slight overreach."
The Emperor said:
"You wish to preserve the standards for all generations,
but this is my orphaned nephew,
I cannot calculate with him."
His posthumous title was Xiàn Gōng.
Ānlù Zhāo Wáng Miǎn, courtesy name Jǐngyè.
He was good in appearance and demeanor.
Initially, he served as Mìshū Láng (Secretary of the Palace Library),
then Wénxué (Literary Tutor) to Sòng Shàolíng Wáng,
and Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary of the Central Secretariat).
In the first year of Jiàn yuán,
he was enfeoffed as Ānlù Hóu,
with a thousand households.
He was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
then promoted to Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū (Minister of Five Military Bureaus),
concurrently leading Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard),
and then sent out as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wú Commandery).
In a short time,
he greatly distinguished himself with his governance.
Jìnglíng Zǐliáng wrote to Miǎn, saying:
"I have secretly heard of your reputation,
such governance has not been seen for several decades."
Shìzǔ praised his ability,

and he was transferred to Chíjīe (bearer of credentials), Dūdū Yǐng Zhōu Sī Zhōu zhī Yìyáng Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yìyáng in Yǐng and Sī Provinces), Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Army), and Yǐng Zhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐng Province).
In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
he returned as Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
concurrently leading Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry),
then promoted to Zhōng Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Central Army).
The following year,
he was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì (Regular Palace Attendant),
Tàizǐ Zhànshì (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince).
He was sent out as Kuàijī Tàishǒu (Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery),
with his Chángshì title remaining as before.

He was promoted to Shǐchíjīe (envoy with credentials), Dūdū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sì Zhōu Jīng Zhōu zhī Jìnglíng Sī Zhōu zhī Suí Jùn Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, North and South Qín Provinces, Jìnglíng of Jīng Province, and Suí Commandery of Sī Province), Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (General of the Left), Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel for Pacifying the Barbarians), and Yōng Zhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yōng Province).
Miǎn paid close attention to legal disputes,
personally investigating hidden matters,
and for robbers who crossed borders,
he pardoned and released them, allowing them to reform,
only punishing them if they reoffended,
thus he was both feared and loved by the common people.
In the ninth year,
he died.
An imperial edict granted 100,000 coins and
200 bolts of cloth as a funeral gift.
When his coffin returned,
the common people lined the Miǎn River, weeping and offering sacrifices,
and built a shrine for him on Xiàn Shān.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guards),
with his Chíjīe (credentials), Dūdū (supervisor), and Cìshǐ (governor) titles remaining as before.
A military band was provided.
His posthumous title was Zhāo Hóu.
He was thirty-seven years old.
Gāozōng and Miǎn had been close friends since childhood,
and at that time, Gāozōng was Púyè (Director of the Department of State Affairs)
and concurrently Lǐng Wèiwèi (acting Grand Minister of the Guards).
He submitted a memorial requesting to resign from Wèiwèi
to mourn privately at his residence,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
Every time he faced Miǎn's spirit tablet,
he would weep uncontrollably, unable to utter a sound.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
Sītú (Minister of Education),
Ānlù Wáng (Prince of Ānlù),
with an additional two thousand households.
His son Bǎojì succeeded him,

and served as Chíjīe (bearer of credentials), Dū Xiāng Zhōu Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xiāng Province), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State), and Xiāng Zhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xiāng Province).
His younger brother Bǎolǎn was enfeoffed as Jiānglíng Gōng (Duke of Jiānglíng),
and Bǎohóng as Rǔnán Gōng (Duke of Rǔnán),
each with fifteen hundred households.
In the second year,
Bǎojì's title was advanced to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Army).
In the third year,
Bǎohóng's enfeoffment was changed to Xiāochéng.
[二０] In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
because Ānlù Commandery bordered the barbarians,
Bǎojì's enfeoffment was changed to Xiāngdōng Wáng (Prince of Xiāngdōng).
His title was advanced to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians).
In the second year,
he became Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard).
All the brothers of Gāozōng's family were skilled in official duties,
but Bǎojì was somewhat fond of literature.
When the righteous army advanced,
Bǎojì was inside the city.
After Dōnghūn was deposed,
Bǎojì expected the people to turn to him,
and waited sitting for the imperial carriage.
However, the people in the city instead presented his head to Liáng Wáng.
When Xuāndé Tàihòu presided over the court,
she appointed Bǎojì as Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies).
Bǎojì felt uneasy,
plotted rebellion,
and he and his brothers were all executed.
The historian remarks: Tàizǔ, having received the mandate to rule the world,
suffered the early deaths of his two elder brothers.
His auspicious destiny flowed to others,
thus he posthumously established feudal domains.
Ānlù Wáng Miǎn, as a collateral member of the imperial clan,
entered officialdom at a young age,
governed commanderies and provinces,
leaving behind a lasting legacy,
and his affection was remembered by the people.
This shows that one can move people with emotion,
and learn to govern;
this is not necessarily so.
A eulogy states: Tàizǔ's two elder brothers,
were posthumously granted dual feudal domains.
His descendants were established,
and their lineage flourished.
Both exercised power and authority,
and brought about their own rise and fall.
Ānlù was praised for his excellence,
his deeds recorded for the afterlife.
Collated notes
Biography Twenty-seven: Wáng Xiùzhī, Wáng Cí, Cài Yuē, Lù Huìxiǎo (Gù Xiànzhī), Xiāo Huìjī
Wáng Xiùzhī, courtesy name Bófèn,
was a native of Lángyá Línyí.
His grandfather Yù was Sòng Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Left of Splendid Happiness) and Yítóng Sānsī (Grandee Remitted of the Three Callings).
His father Zànzhī was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple).
When Xiùzhī was young,
Yù loved his demeanor.
He began his career as Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (Assistant in the Imperial Archives)
and Tàizǐ Shèrén (Gentleman of the Crown Prince's Household).
After his father died,
he built a hut by the grave and observed mourning,
returning to his post after the mourning period ended.
Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) Chǔ Yuān, seeing Xiùzhī's uprightness and purity,
wished to arrange a marriage with him,
but Xiùzhī refused,
and because of this, he was frequently transferred to Wàibīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer for External Military Affairs) in both major government departments.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Equerry to the Crown Prince),
Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ (Assistant in the Left West to the Minister of Education),
and Guìyáng Wáng Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Attendant Official to the Minister of Works for Prince Guìyáng).
Xiùzhī knew that Xiūfàn was about to rebel,
and resigned due to illness.
He was sent out as Jìnpíng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Jìnpíng Commandery).
After a year in the commandery,
he said to people:
"This region is fertile,
and my salary is always ample.
My personal wealth is already sufficient,
how can I remain here long and block the path of the worthy?"
He submitted a memorial requesting a replacement,
and people at the time said,
"Wáng Jìnpíng fears wealth and wishes to return."
He returned as Ānchéng Wáng Piàojì Zīyì (Adviser to the Cavalry General for Prince Ānchéng),
then transferred to Zhōngláng (Gentleman of the Household).
He also served as Tàizǔ Piàojì Zīyì (Adviser to the Cavalry General for Emperor Tàizǔ).
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
he was transferred to Zuǒjūn Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Left Army) and Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xúnyáng Commandery),
then followed the court and transferred to Zhènxī Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the General Who Guards the West) and Nán Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nán Commandery).
After the head of the department, Yùzhāng Wáng Yí, was enfeoffed as a prince,
Xiùzhī was promoted to Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk) and Hédōng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hédōng Commandery),
but he declined the commandery appointment.
He was given the additional title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North),
and appointed Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
but before he was invested,
he was again transferred to Yùzhāng Wáng Piàojì Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Cavalry General for Prince Yùzhāng).
[The Prince] established a school in Jīng Province,
and appointed Xiùzhī to lead Rúlín Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Confucian School).
He was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) and Nán Jùn Wáng Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nán Commandery).
He again served as Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
concurrently leading Yǔlín Jiān (Inspector of the Imperial Forest).
He was promoted to Chángshā Wáng Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Central Army for Prince Chángshā).
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he became Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
Lìbù Láng (Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel),
was sent out as Yìxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yìxīng Commandery),
promoted to Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the Palace Attendants),
and transferred to Dūguān Shàngshū (Minister of the Bureau of Prisons).
Initially,
Wáng Xiùzhī's (王秀之) ancestor, Wáng Yù (王裕),
was upright and principled.
When Xú Xiànzhī (徐羨之) and Fù Liàng (傅亮) were in power,
Yù (裕) did not associate with them.
When he retired to Wúxīng (吳興),
he wrote to his son, Wáng Zànzhī (王瓚之), saying:
"I wish for you to be in a place where there is no competition."
Zànzhī (瓚之) served successively as an official up to Wǔbīng Shàngshū (五兵尚書),
never once visiting an aristocratic official.
Jiāng Zhàn (江湛) said to Hé Yǎn (何偃):
"Wáng Zànzhī (王瓚之) is now effectively '隱於朝' (yǐn yú cháo, an 'hermit in the court')."
When Liǔ Yuánjǐng (柳元景) and Yán Shībó (顏師伯) became powerful as Lìng (令) and Pú (僕),
Zànzhī (瓚之) still did not call upon them.
When Xiùzhī (秀之) became Shàngshū (尚書),
he also did not associate with Lìng (令) Wáng Jiǎn (王儉).
For three generations, they did not serve the powerful and influential;
people of the time praised them for it.
He was transferred to Shìzhōng (侍中),
and concurrently held the position of Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉).
He was dispatched as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍), Suí Wáng Zhèn Xī Zhǎngshǐ (隨王鎮西長史), and Nánjùn Nèishǐ (南郡內史).
Gǒu Yí (苟顗), the Xīcáo (西曹) of the province,
sent Xiùzhī (秀之) a letter proposing friendship.
Xiùzhī (秀之) refused to reply.
Yí (顗) then sent another letter, saying:
"I have heard that remaining in a humble position
is already recorded in the Yì (易);
and that prosperity cannot last long,
which is clearly stated in the Lǐ (禮).
Thus, Xìnlíng (信陵) cultivated the righteousness of Yímén (夷門),
and Yàn Dān (燕丹) enlisted the loyalty of Jīng Qīng (荊卿);
all these were in accordance with Lǐ (禮).
How can a man, living in this world,
be content with obscurity and lack of honor,
and merely become a mound of earth for future generations?
Your Excellency's achievements shine brightly,
and your reputation ranks among the highest in the court.
If you do not cultivate deeds that transcend the age,
what will distinguish you from a common fool?
I, for my part, have been unyielding in my youth,
not conforming to the multitude.
Now, with a white head from hunger and cold,
I look at things and sigh.
To help others achieve their potential
is praised by the Chūnqiū (春秋).
To recommend my humble abilities,
and reveal your minor shortcomings,
is why I extend my aspirations and virtue,
aiming for mutual benefit.
Indeed, I am not a commonplace person seeking favor from Píngyuán (平原).
You and I,
are equally outstanding men of the realm.
For rise and fall to alternate
is the natural course of events.
Differences in rank and position
are due to the flow and blockage of fortune.
How can they be attributed to character and conduct?
The title of 'Dìwǔ (第五)'
is no different from that of 'Piàojì (驃騎)';
and the name 'Xīcáo (西曹)'
why should it yield to 'Zhǎngshǐ (長史)'?
Your Excellency has delayed answering my letter for a long time.
If your conduct is so unorthodox,
how can it be applied to a man of the state?
If you follow Lǐ (禮),
Lǐ (禮) dictates that there should be no unanswered letters.
I respectfully return this,
what offense could it be to '【逆】鱗' (nì lín, 'touch the dragon's scales')?
A gentleman treats others
by virtue, not by position.
Xiàngrú (相如) was not disgraced at Miǎnchí (澠池),
and Máosuì (毛遂) calmly endured no insult at Yǐngmén (郢門).
When facing an enemy or an urgent matter,
I will surely precede these two gentlemen.
I do not know if Your Excellency's nobility,
or Your Excellency's authority,
is comparable to the two kings of Qín (秦) and Chǔ (楚).
I consider virtue as my treasure;
Your Excellency considers position as your treasure.
Each treasures their own treasure,
and in this, we are respectfully alike.
I often hear that when ancient people broke off relations,
they did not speak ill.
I consider this vulgar.
Not to exchange gifts
is why I present the gift of a poor man."
Yí (顗)
was a native of Yǐngchuān (潁川).
When Yùzhāng Wáng Yí (豫章王嶷) was Jīngzhōu (荊州) governor,
Yí (顗) presented a letter advising him to reduce extravagance and luxury.
Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) responded with a generous and courteous reply.
When Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) was prominent in his generation,
Yí (顗) also wrote to Jiǎn (儉), saying:
"Your Excellency has established a name that transcends the age,
yet does not display deeds that transcend the age.
How then will you be recorded in the Qí Shǐ (齊史)?"
At this point, the secretariat of Nánjùn (南郡) initiated a request from Suí Wáng Zǐlóng (隨王子隆) to punish Yí (顗).
Yí (顗) submitted a memorial to defend himself.
Xiùzhī (秀之) was soon summoned back as Shìzhōng (侍中),
and concurrently held the position of Yóujī Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍).
Before he could be officially installed,
he was again made Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (吳興太守).
Xiùzhī (秀之) often said that reaching the position of Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (司徒左長史)
would be sufficient.
Wúxīng Jùn (吳興郡) was where his reclusive family estate was located,
and he wished to serve there.
Upon arrival at the commandery, he repaired his old mountain residence
and moved his baggage and supplies there.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌) (494 CE),
he died in office.
He was fifty-three years old.
His posthumous title was Jiǎnzǐ (簡子).
Xiùzhī's (秀之) clansman, Wáng Sēngyòu (王僧祐),
was Tàiwèi (太尉) Wáng Jiǎn's (王儉) paternal cousin.
His father, Wáng Yuǎn (王遠),
was Guānglù Xūn (光祿勳).
During the Sòng (宋) dynasty, there was a saying about him:
"Wáng Yuǎn (王遠) is like a folding screen;
he bends to custom
and can shield from wind and dew."
However, Sēngyòu (僧祐) was proud and independent.
Jiǎn (儉) often called on him,
but he declined to see him.
Shìzǔ (世祖) frequently reviewed the troops.
Sēngyòu (僧祐) presented a "Jiǎngwǔ Fù (講武賦)".
Jiǎn (儉) asked to read it,
but Sēngyòu (僧祐) refused to give it to him.
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng (竟陵王子良) heard that Sēngyòu (僧祐) was skilled at playing the guqin.
From his seat, he took a guqin and offered it to him,
but Sēngyòu (僧祐) refused to obey.
At the end of Yǒngmíng (永明) era,
he was Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人).
While on duty, he fell ill.
Before his replacement arrived,
Sēngyòu (僧祐) left without permission.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and fined.
His highest office was Huángmén Láng (黃門郎).
At that time, Kǒng Guàn (孔逭), a Wèijūn Yuán (衞軍掾), was also forthright.
He authored the Sān Wú Juélù (三吳決錄),
which is not extant.
Wáng Cí (王慈), courtesy name Bǎobǎo (伯寶),
a native of Lángyá Línyí (琅邪臨沂),
was the son of Sīkōng (司空) Wáng Sēngqián (王僧虔).
At the age of eight,
his maternal grandfather, Sòng Tàizǎi (宋太宰) Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭), invited him to his inner study.
He laid out treasures and allowed Cí (慈) to take whatever he wished.
Cí (慈) chose a plain guqin and a stone inkstone,
which Yìgōng (義恭) approved of.
As a youth, he and his cousin Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) studied calligraphy together.
He was appointed Mìshū Láng (祕書郎),
Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
Ānchéng Wáng Fǔjūn Zhǔbù (安成王撫軍主簿),
and then transferred to Jìshì (記室).
He was promoted to Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞),
Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ (司徒左西屬),
Yòu Zhǎngshǐ (右長史),
acting Xīn'ān Tàishǒu (新安太守),
Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
concurrently Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉),
Ānchéng Wáng Guānjūn (安成王冠軍),
Yùzhāng Wáng Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ (豫章王司空長史),
Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (司徒左長史),
and concurrently Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was dispatched as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Yùzhāng Nèishǐ (豫章內史).
He resigned due to his father's mourning.
He was reinstated as Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (建武將軍) and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (吳郡太守).
He was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍),
Dàsīmǎ Zhǎngshǐ (大司馬長史),
and again appointed Shìzhōng (侍中),
concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
Cí believed that the imperial court's bảng (榜) for taboo names
was not an ancient system,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"The virtues of emperors and empresses
intertwine with Heaven and Earth;
the brilliance of rulers
is like the continuous glow of the sun and moon.
As for the names of noble families not being clearly established,
they are revealed by the fāng cè (方策);
when posthumous titles are proclaimed,
they are recorded in books and treatises.
Thus, the Wèi (魏) minister relied on the zhòng (中) to propose,
and the Jìn (晉) ruler issued edicts according to the classics.
The practice of displaying taboo names on the court bảng (榜)
with characters openly exposed
is not deeply rooted in antiquity;
it became prevalent in the middle ages.
It merely forfeits the sentiment of reverence
and deviates from the way of solemn veneration.
As for meritorious and eminent officials,
and those who assist the common magistrates,
some are elevated due to their achievements,
while others are distinguished by their surnames.
Therefore, Kǒng Kuī (孔悝) was inscribed,
referred to as 'uncle of Biāo (標)';
Zǐ Mèng (子孟) appeared in illustrations,
called 'of the Huò (霍) clan'.
How much more so with the importance of 'holding the unique position,'
where a revered name stops benevolence;
and the nobility of 'having no peer,'
where a restrained character stops reverence.
In the past, when Dōngpíng (東平) passed away,
Xiàozhāng (孝章) visited his palace and wept;
when Xīnyě (新野) passed away,
Héxī (和熹) saw his likeness and shed tears.
To be moved by old customs
still evokes deep feelings;
how much more so when viewing their traces,
can one be without compassion?
Now the palace gates are deep and secluded,
and carriages often extend there.
If the imperial carriage were to leisurely view them,
and inspect them seasonally,
would it not greatly increase the sacred worries
and touch the imperial heart?
I foolishly believe that openly marking the tablets
〔一０〕is of no benefit to one's dedication;
directly stating names in the court hall
〔一一〕would not diminish one's vigilance.
I respectfully submit that Your Majesty, who protects and unites all nations
and brings order to all beings,
should abolish the harmful practices of former foundations
and initiate the filial principles of imperial Qí (齊)."
An edict was issued to the external officials for detailed discussion.
Doctor Bóshì (博士) Lǐ Huī (李撝) argued:
"According to the Zhōu Lǐ (周禮),
whenever there is a new decree,
a bell must be rung to alert the public,
then it is retired and displayed in the royal palace."
The commentary says, "'Xiàn (憲)'
means to display and hang it."
Tàicháng Céng (太常丞) Wáng Xiǎnzhī (王僩之) argued:
"The names of the highest尊 (zūn)
should be tabooed throughout the land.
They can be seen by the eye,
but cannot be spoken by the mouth.
If they cannot be spoken by the mouth,
then those who know them will be few,
and if those who know them are few,
then transgressions will be numerous."
Yícáo Láng (儀曹郎) Rèn Fǎng (任昉) argued:
"Huī (撝)'s proof texts are accurate,
and Xiǎn (僩)'s understanding of the sentiment is correct.
The practice of displaying taboo names
originated in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and continued down to the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
without deviation through the generations.
The current taboo bảng (榜),
which also clarifies the meaning of the instruction,
'bāng (邦)'
means 'guó (國)'
— this is indeed evidence of former practices.
The solemnity of taboo names
reaches its utmost in respectful sentiment.
Therefore, they are displayed in the court hall,
where high officials gather,
to ensure that, from dawn to dusk,
they are not absent from sight and hearing,
and the way of avoidance
is clear and easy to follow.
This is the profound meaning of reverence and respect;
how can such a practice be abolished?
〔一二〕To refer to the Huò (霍) clan with a respectful title
is an inappropriate analogy.
When one is in a lower position, a name is important,
so not naming is considered important;
when one is in a higher position, a name must be tabooed,
so displaying taboo names is considered honorable.
From the heart, there is no principle that is not at peace;
in practice, this custom has long been established.
It is advisable to respectfully follow it,
without any new innovations."
Cí's proposal was not adopted.
Cí suffered from a foot ailment,
and Shìzǔ (世祖) ordered Wáng Yàn (王晏) saying:
"Cí has not been in office long,
and now has a minor illness.
He is unable to attend court,
and also cannot ride a horse.
He is permitted to ride in a carriage behind the guards."
This was a rare exception since the migration to the south (Jiāng Zuǒ, 江左).
Due to illness, he was transferred to a leisurely position,
promoted to Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ (司徒左長史).
Cí's wife was Liú Bǐng (劉秉)'s daughter.
Their son Guān (觀)
married Shìzǔ (世祖)'s eldest daughter, Wúxiàn Gōngzhǔ (吳縣公主).
When performing the daughter-in-law's rites,
his mother-in-law never responded.
Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng (江夏王鋒) was governor of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州);
his consort,
Cí's daughter,
was made Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu (東海太守) by Cí,
with an added salary of two thousand dàn (石) of grain,
and was put in charge of the affairs of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州) prefecture.
〔一三〕He returned to be Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王)'s Zhōngjūn Chángshǐ (中軍長史).
Before being appointed,
in the ninth year of Yǒngmíng (永明) [491 AD],
he passed away.
He was forty-one years old.
Xiè Chāozōng (謝超宗) once said to Cí (慈):
"When will your calligraphy reach that of Qián Gōng (虔公)?"
Cí replied:
"My inability to look up to and reach him
is like a chicken's inability to reach a phoenix."
People at the time considered this a famous answer.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàicháng (太常)
and given the posthumous name Yìzǐ (懿子).
Cài Yuē (蔡約), courtesy name Jǐnghuī (景撝),
was a native of Kǎochéng (考城), Jìyáng (濟陽).
His grandfather, Guō (廓),
was Sòng (宋)'s Cíbù Shàngshū (祠部尚書).
His father, Xīngzōng (興宗),
was Zhēngxī (征西) and Yítóng (儀同).
Yuē (約) was young when he married Sòng Xiàowǔ (宋孝武)'s daughter, Ānjí Gōngzhǔ (安吉公主).
He was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) and Bìmì Shūláng (祕書郎),
but did not accept the latter.
He accompanied the emperor as Chēqí Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn (車騎驃騎行參軍),
〔一四〕Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
but did not take office.
He was promoted to Tàizǔ Sīkōng Dōnggé Jìjiǔ (太祖司空東閤祭酒)
and Tàiwèi Zhǔbù (太尉主簿).
When Qí (齊) was established,
he became the Shìzǐ Zhōngshèrén (世子中舍人),
and then accompanied him to the Eastern Palace.
He was transferred to Púyáng Wáng Yǒu (鄱陽王友),
then Jìnglíng Wáng (竟陵王)'s Zhèn Běi Zhēng Běi Zīyì (鎮北征北諮議),
and concurrently Jìshì (記室),
Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎),
Sītú Yòuchángshǐ (司徒右長史),
Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
and concurrently Zhōngzhèng (中正) of his native prefecture.
He was dispatched as Xīn'ān Tàishǒu (新安太守),
then again became Huángmén Láng (黃門郎),
concurrently Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉),
Tōngzhí Chángshì (通直常侍),
concurrently Xiāojì Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
and concurrently Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉).
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng (永明) [490 AD], eighth month, new moon,
Yuē (約) removed his military cap,
unbuckled his sword,
and slept in the provincial office.
He did not rise until the drum sounded for closing.
He was impeached by the appropriate officials
and fined.
When the Tàisūn (太孫) was established,
he retained his concurrent Xiàowèi (校尉) post.
He was dispatched as Yídū Wáng (宜都王)'s Guànjūn Chángshǐ (冠軍長史) and Huáinán Tàishǒu (淮南太守),
and performed the duties of the prefecture.
Shìzǔ (世祖) said to Yuē (約):
"Now I appoint you as a senior assistant to a close imperial relative;
I hope you will live up to my expectations."
Yuē (約) replied:
"Nányù (南豫) is close to the capital;
it governs itself without much effort.
What kind of person am I,
whose torch never goes out?"
At that time, many princes in office often interfered with each other;
however, Yuē (約), in his post,
maintained harmony between the lord and his assistants.
He was promoted to Left Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works [Sītú].
[xv] When Gāozōng acted as Assistant Regent for the Grand Secretariat,
all officials removed their shoes upon reaching his mat.
However, [he] persisted in wearing clogs.
[xvi] The Emperor said to Jiāng Shí:
"The Cài clan was indeed a house of propriety and etiquette,
and thus naturally admirable."
Shí replied:
"The Grand General had guests who bowed to him,
which we see again today."
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng].
The following year,
he was promoted to Army Administrator [Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ] for the Prince of Xīyáng,
with the added title of General Who Subdues the Army [Guànjūn Jiāngjūn].
He was then transferred to Right Army Administrator [Yòujūn Zhǎngshǐ] for the Prince of Lúlíng,
with his general title remaining as before.
He was transferred to Department Director of Revenue [Dūguān Shàngshū],
then promoted to Tutor [Shī] for the Prince of Shàolíng,
with the added title of Palace Aide with Special Powers [Jǐshìzhōng].
He was appointed Chariot and Cavalry Army Administrator [Chēqí Zhǎngshǐ] for the Prince of Jiāngxià,
with the added title of General Who Quells the Barbarians [Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn].
He did not accept any of these appointments.
He was fond of drinking wine,
and was aloof and did not mix with the world.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent [Tàizǐ Zhānshì].
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (originally Yǒngmíng),
he passed away.
[xvii] He was forty-four years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of Ceremonies [Tàicháng].
Lù Huìxiǎo, courtesy name Shūmíng,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
His grandfather, Lù Wànzài,
was a Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng].
His father, Lù Zǐzhēn,
served as Administrator of Hǎilíng during the Yuánjiā era.
At that time, Qiū Dāng, a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat [Zhōngshū Shèrén], was a favored confidant of the emperor.
His home was in Hǎilíng.
When he was granted leave to return and bury his father,
Zǐzhēn did not send condolences.
Dāng requested that commoners be dispatched to repair a bridge.
Zǐzhēn again refused, citing interference with farming.
Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng heard of this and admired him.
After returning home due to an eye illness while serving as Administrator of Línhaǐ,
he became a Grand Master of Remonstrance [Zhōngsàn Dàfū]
and then passed away.
Huìxiǎo was clear-minded, upright, and just,
and did not engage in casual socializing.
Zhāng Chàng, the Intendant of Kuàijī and a fellow townsman,
saw Huìxiǎo when he was a child and already found him remarkable.
Zhāng Xù praised him, saying:
"He is the Péi and Lè of the Jiāngdōng region."
Initially, he responded to calls from various commanderies and prefectures,
was nominated as an 'Outstanding Talent' [Xiùcái],
and served as a clerk in the Grand Master of Ceremonies' office.
He successively served as an acting staff officer in various governmental bureaus.
Due to his mother's old age, he returned home to care for her,
not holding office for over ten years.
When Tàizǔ became assistant regent,
he was appointed Palace Gentleman of the Grand Secretariat [Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng].
Relatives from his clan came to congratulate him.
Huìxiǎo raised his wine cup and said:
"Lù Huìxiǎo is over thirty,
and his wife's father is in charge of selections.
He is only now becoming a Department Director [Shàngshū Láng].
[xix] Are you really celebrating this?"
Tàizǔ submitted a memorial prohibiting extravagance.
Huìxiǎo drafted the reply edict,
which was praised by Tàizǔ.
He was then appointed Libationer of the Eastern Bureau of the Grand Tutor [Tàifù Dōnggē Jìjiǔ].
In the early Jiànyuán era,
he was subsequently promoted to Horseman of the Heir Apparent [Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ].
When Wǔlíng Wáng Niàn took office as Administrator of Kuàijī,
the emperor personally selected excellent officials for him.
Huìxiǎo was appointed Merits Registrar of the General Who Quells the Barbarians [Zhēnglǔ Gōngcáo],
and, along with Liú Jìn of Pèiguó, an army staff officer, he accompanied Niàn to report on his duties.
When they arrived in Wú,
Jìn said to others:
"I heard that Zhāng Róng and Lù Huìxiǎo live next to each other,
and there is a stream between their homes.
This stream must have an unusual flavor."
So he went,
drew water, and drank it.
Hé Diǎn of Lújiāng recommended Huìxiǎo to Yùzhāng Wáng Yí,
who appointed him Clerk to the Minister of Works [Sīkōng Yuàn]
and treated him with favor and courtesy.
He was transferred to Grand Marshal's Consultant and Staff Officer [Zhènjūn Zīyì Cānjūn] for the Prince of Chángshā.
When Ānlù Hóu Miǎn became Administrator of Wú Commandery,
he again treated Huìxiǎo with special respect.
Huìxiǎo sought to be appointed Consultant and Staff Officer [Zīyì Cānjūn] in Miǎn's bureau.
He was promoted to Consultant of the General of the Van [Qián Jiāngjūn] and General Who Guards the West [Ānxī] for the Prince of Shǐxīng,
also holding the position of Registrar and Staff Officer of the General Who Subdues the Army [Guànjūn Lùshì Cānjūn].
He was then transferred to Attendant Gentleman of the Minister of Works [Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng],
and promoted to Right Chief Clerk [Yòuzhǎngshǐ].
At that time, Xiè Fěi of Chén Commandery was Left Chief Clerk [Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ].
The bureau head, Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng, said to Wáng Róng:
"Of the two chief officials in my bureau,
if we look at previous generations,
who can compare to them?"
Róng replied:
"Two such worthies at the same time is indeed unprecedented."
Zǐliáng copied books in the Western Mansion,
and had Huìxiǎo participate in managing the affairs.

Soon after, he was promoted to Chief Clerk of three bureaus: General Who Quells the Barbarians [Zhēnglǔ] for the Prince of Xīyáng, General of the Rear Army [Hòujūn] for the Prince of Bālíng, and General Who Guards the State [Fǔguó] for the Duke of Línrǔ,
and acted in charge of the bureau and commandery affairs.
[xx] He again became Left Army Chief Clerk [Zuǒjūn Zhǎngshǐ] for the Prince of Xīyáng,
also holding the position of Assistant Administrator [Jùnchéng] of Kuàijī Commandery,
and acting in charge of commandery affairs.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was transferred to Chief Clerk of the General Who Subdues the Army [Guànjūn Zhǎngshǐ] for the Prince of Jìnxī and Intendant of Jiāngxià,
and acted in charge of Yǐng Province affairs.
Huìxiǎo served as aide in five administrations.
He maintained a clean and strict personal conduct.
When subordinate officials and staff visited,
he would promptly rise to see them off.
Someone once said to Huìxiǎo:
"Chief Clerk, you are highly esteemed;
it is not appropriate to be so overly humble."
He replied:
"It is my nature to detest those who are impolite,
so I cannot but treat people with courtesy."
He never addressed scholars and officials by their personal names (Qīng).
When asked the reason,
Huìxiǎo said:
"The noble cannot be addressed by their personal name,
but the humble can.
How can one establish such distinctions of importance in one's heart?"
Throughout his life, he always addressed people by their official titles.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he was appointed Chief Clerk of the General of the Central West [Xīzhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ],
with his acting and intendant duties remaining as before.
Soon after, he was summoned to be a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate [Huángmén Láng],
but before accepting,
he was promoted to Department Director of Personnel [Lìbù Láng].
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn selected his protégés to fill important internal and external positions.
Huìxiǎo used only a few of them and then stopped,
which Yàn resented.
Yàn sent a female entertainer,
wishing to establish a good relationship,
but Huìxiǎo did not accept her.
For generations, the Chief Clerk of the Personnel Department [Lìcáo Dūlìngshǐ] had been consulted on selection matters.
Huìxiǎo acted on his own initiative,
never speaking with him.
The Emperor sent Zuǒyòu Dān Jǐngjùn to question him about this matter with a reprimand.
Huìxiǎo said to Jǐngjùn:
"At sixty years of age,
I can no longer consult the Chief Clerk of the Personnel Department to be Department Director of Personnel.
If Your Majesty believes I am incompetent,
I shall simply brush my robes and retire."
The Emperor greatly feared him.
Later, he wanted to appoint him Palace Attendant [Shìzhōng],
but stopped due to his short stature.
He was appointed

General Who Guards the State [Fǔguó Jiāngjūn], [xxi] Marshal of the General Who Guards the North [Zhènběi Sīmǎ] for the Prince of Jìn'ān, Chief Clerk of the General Who Guards the North [Zhēngběi Zhǎngshǐ], and Administrator of Dōnghaǐ,
acting in charge of the bureau and commandery affairs.
He entered the court as Minister of the Five Bureaus [Wǔbīng Shàngshū],
acting in charge of Yáng Province affairs.
After Cuī Huìjǐng's
rebellion was pacified, [xxii] he was made General of the Right Army [Yòujūn Jiāngjūn],
then sent out to oversee Nán Xú Province.
A short time later,

he was again promoted to Bearer of Credential, Grand Administrator of Military Affairs of five provinces—Nányù, Qīng, and Jì—General Who Guards the State [Fǔguó Jiāngjūn], and Governor of Nányù Province.
Soon after arriving at his post,
he returned home due to illness
and passed away.
He was sixty-two years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Minister of Ceremonies [Tàicháng].
A fellow commandery man, Gù Xiànzhī,
whose courtesy name was Shìsī,
was the grandson of Sòng’s Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Kǎizhī.
〔二三〕His character was especially pure and upright.
In the sixth year of Yǒngmíng (488 CE),
he served as the Zhōngláng Chángshǐ to Suí Wáng and acted as the Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery.
At that time, Dù Yuányì, the commander of Xīlíng garrison, memorialized:
“Wúxīng has experienced a poor harvest,
while Kuàijī has had abundant yields.
The coming and going of merchants
is more than double that of a normal year.
The tax at Xīlíng niúdài
is officially set at 3,500 daily.
From what Yuányì has observed,
it could be doubled daily.
With increases and decreases combined,
it is estimated that the annual increase would be a million.
As for the northern and southern ferries of Púyáng and the four dài of Liǔpǔ,
I request that they be managed by the government.
This would yield an additional four hundred thousand and more per year.
The inspection of taxes in front of Xīlíng garrison
will not hinder military matters,
and the other three dài can be managed by trusted men.”
Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔ) issued an edict to Kuàijī Commandery:
“How can this be?
You should investigate and then memorialize.”
Xiànzhī deliberated: “The original intention of establishing the niúdài
was not to force people to pay taxes.
It was because of the swift and dangerous winds and waves,
the slowness of human effort,
and frequent capsizing and drowning.
It was to aid
and benefit the people.
Since both the public and private sectors enjoyed it,
there was no resentment in paying the fees.
The ferry crossings in the capital
are an example of this.
However, later supervisors
did not understand its
original purpose,
each pursuing their own achievements,
and mutually generating extraneous benefits.
Some prohibited alternative routes,
some imposed empty taxes on river travel,
some struck boats and charged double the price,
and some demanded payment even when assistance was complete.
All such
cases,
where people were troubled by the dài without actually using the cattle, were extensively reported to superiors,
and ten extra regulations were issued,
all of which were suspended.
The constant complaints
were finally temporarily quelled.
It is observed that Wúxīng has suffered
poor harvests for several years,
and this year is particularly severe.
Leaving it for places of abundance
〔二四〕is truly due to famine.
Some exchange goods for grain
〔二五〕to relieve their families.
Some
carry the elderly and the weak
〔二六〕to exert themselves for a living.
The dài officials demand taxes
according to the regulations without reduction.
The old regulations were recently reduced,
and there has been no discussion of increasing them.
How can extra charges be doubled
by what
means?
〔二七〕Imperial benevolence has compassion for the hidden suffering,
distributing grain and waiving taxes.
Yet Yuányì takes advantage of disaster to extort profit,
further increasing the suffering.
Such inhumanity
is abhorred by all, ancient and modern.
Furthermore,
those who were recently allowed to establish markets at the former rates
followed one after another.
Not only did the newly added ones yield no profit,
but the old rates also fell short.
I fear that Yuányì’s current memorial
will not be different.
If the facts do not match his words,
it will likely lead to censure,
and then he will employ every means to oppress and cause suffering,
earning public resentment for the state.
Yuányì’s nature is harsh and cruel,
which is already evident from his past actions.
Entrusting him with public resources
is like entrusting a wolf with sheep.
Those whom he wishes to appoint as his trusted men
would also be tigers wearing caps.
The Shu 書 (Book of Documents) says:
‘Rather have ministers who steal [for themselves] than ministers who accumulate [for the state at the expense of the people].’
This
means that stealing from the public causes slight harm,
while accumulating from the people causes great harm.
Now,
when peace and prosperity are in effect,
and even plants and trees receive moisture,
if it is not appropriate for the situation,
it is as per Your Majesty’s sacred will.
However,
those who hold such responsibilities
should be chosen for their integrity and fairness.
If they are incorruptible, they will not steal from the public;
if they are fair, they will not harm the people.
I also believe that what is expedient
means what is beneficial to the public
and suitable for the people.
I have recently noticed that those who speak of expediency
are not able to make use of natural resources beyond human labor.
〔二八〕Rather, they are
not suitable for the people on the day they are implemented,
and inconvenient for the public in the future.
The name and the reality are contradictory,
which deviates from proper governance.
All such matters
truly deserve thorough investigation.
In Shānyīn County alone,
there are 20,000 registered households.
Among them, those whose assets do not exceed 3,000 [cash]
almost constitute half.
Even after repeated taxation,
only a little over one-third remains.
Among
those who have assets,
many are scholars whose households are exempted.
〔二九〕The extremely poor
are all unprotected households subject to corvée labor.
Three to five subordinates,
it seems, are merely assigned,
while a hundred kinds of taxes and levies
are constant.
Currently, numerous bureaus inspect and verify,
continuously one after another,
and those who are mutually implicated and burdened
are also not few.
If one person is arrested,
ten
people are pursued;
if one sprout is pruned,
a thousand suckers emerge.
Sericulture makes people weary while agriculture is abandoned;
the poor are forced to take on menial labor while the rich are held accountable for debts.
They must supply public needs and support private affairs,
with no time
to spare.
How can they avoid wrongdoing
under such circumstances?
They do not even fear death,
let alone punishment;
they do not even cherish their own lives,
let alone their wives and children.
This is why previous inspections have not
fully solved the problems,
and new schemes have multiplied.
Even though the laws are strict,
they are still unable to repent.
I believe that the people’s widespread deceit
is actually due to the frequent military campaigns in the late Sòng dynasty,
which led to heavy taxes and corvée labor.
Unable
to endure the hardship,
they relied on cleverness to seek leniency,
and such practices became habitual,
so they forgot to change.
The world is vast,
and the common people are numerous.
Their minds and motivations vary,
making it difficult to quickly purify and unify them.
Transformation should be gradual,
not hastily demanded.
If we sincerely intend not to disturb them,
conceal their flaws and tolerate their impurities,
this will actually foster greater magnanimity.
If we focus on thoroughness, leniency, and simplicity,
they will gradually return to purity.
Furthermore, I have received orders
to review past records,
but the records from previous years are too old,
and complete information is unavailable.
〔三一〕Since the imperial decree is strict,
I dare not blindly believe.
The county reviews and sends to the commandery,
and the commandery reviews and presents to the envoy,
with various forms
and deceptive appearances,
constantly changing and multifaceted.
Those who hear of it are not surprised,
but those who see it are truly shocked and saddened.
Moreover, relatives and neighbors
wander on the roads,
often suffering from cold and hunger,"
The matter was not yet settled.
It was particularly difficult for
the scholars and women to find peace of mind.
If they were not interrogated, there was a suspicion of trickery;
if they were to be interrogated, it was unknown how to proceed safely.
I humbly suggest that for this matter,
it would be appropriate to entrust the county officials and baojia (local mutual responsibility units)
to outline the main points
and omit the trivial details,
just as a leaking bag
does not store anything within.
Then, those suffering from chronic illnesses
would
bear the grace of being given new life.
Furthermore, Yǒngxīng and Zhūjì, after being ravaged by the bandits of Tánglǜ,
have had both public and private resources completely depleted,
and are particularly severely affected.
If they were to encounter floods or droughts,
it would truly be a thought
not to be easily entertained.
A common saying goes:
"Kuàijī beats drums to send condolences,
while Wúxīng civil servants pace the eaves."
Kuàijī was formerly known as fertile land,
yet it is now like this;
Wúxīng was originally
barren soil,
so the situation is
understandable.
Therefore, these lingering弊 abuses should be sincerely reformed.
Following Yuán Yì's recent memorial,
I dare to present my humble opinion.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Shì) agreed with all of it.
From then on, he was deeply trusted for his uprightness.
He also served as the Administrator for Nányù and Nányǔn Prefectures,
and as a consultant for official matters.
He never showed any displeasure,
and always followed legal regulations.
He successively held the positions of Huángménláng and
Lìbùláng.
During the Yǒngyuán reign,
he served as Yùzhāng Nèishǐ.
Xiāo Huìjī was a native of
Lánlíng, Nánlánlíng.
His grandfather, Yuánzhī,
was a former general of Sòng.
His father, Sīhuà,
was a Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
As a child, Huìjī, being a maternal relative, met Jiāngxiàwáng Yìgōng,
who admired his meticulousness
and married his daughter to him.
He began his career as Zhuòzuò Zuǒláng, then
Zhēngběi Xíngcānjūn,
Shàngshū Shuǐbù, and
Zuǒmínláng.
He was then sent out as Xiāngdōng Nèishǐ,
appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi, and
Fǔjūn Chējì Zhǔbù.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ reign,
his elder brother, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Huìkāi, defied orders.
Míngdì sent Huìjī as an envoy to Shǔ
to convey the imperial decree and offer solace.
When Huìkāi surrendered, the local people of Yìzhōu rebelled,
leading Dī bandits to besiege the provincial capital.
Huìjī publicized the court's authority and rewards from outside,
whereupon the Dī people, Shào Hǔ and Hǎo Tiāncì, among others, beheaded the bandit leader Mǎ Xīnghuái and surrendered.
He returned to become Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén.
Huìjī had over a thousand troops under him during his western mission,
all of whom wished to claim功 merits.
Huìjī destroyed the records of their achievements,
so there was no way to use them.
Someone asked him his reasoning for this,
and Huìjī replied:
"If I were to acknowledge their efforts,
then the constant rush would never end.
Is this not against my original aspirations?"
He was then appointed Wǔlíng Nèishǐ and
Zhōngshū Huángménláng.
Huìjī was skilled in clerical script and Go.
Tàizǔ had a deep affection for him and esteemed him early on.
During the Gùiyáng campaign,
Huìjī's sister was Xiūfàn's consort.
Tàizǔ said to him:
"Your family in Gùiyáng has again become rebels."
Tàizǔ was stationed at Xīntíng Lěi,
and made Huìjī his military deputy.
Huìjī's younger brother, Huìlǎng, personally fought for Xiūfàn,
yet Huìjī in the city did not doubt himself at all.
He was then appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
Upon his return, he became Lìbùláng,
and then promoted to Chángjiān Shìzhōng.
On the evening of Yuán Càn and Liú Bǐng's uprising,
Tàizǔ, knowing that Bǐng was Huìjī's brother-in-law
and that Huìjī was then on duty in the Shìzhōng Shěng,
sent Wáng Jìngzé to observe his intentions.
Seeing Huìjī calm and not colluding with Bǐng,
Tàizǔ
then trusted him even more.
When suppressing Shěn Yōuzhī,
Huìjī was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and moved to Xīntíng.
After the matter was settled,
he was relieved of his military title
and took charge of Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
He resigned from office due to mourning his mother.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and
Wèiwèi.
Huìjī was in office for a short time
and repeatedly memorialized to resign,
which was granted.
After the mourning period ended,
he was made Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu,
and his salary was increased to two thousand shí.
He successively governed four commanderies
without accumulating any wealth.
He returned to become Dūguān Shàngshū,
and then transferred to oversee Lìbù.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
due to prolonged illness, he was transferred to Shìzhōng,
and led Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Shàngshūlìng Wáng Jiǎn was a noble and revered figure of the court.
When Huìjī was in the same palace department,
they did not meet privately unless for public affairs.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Tàicháng
and given the additional title of Jǐshìzhōng.
Since the Dàmíng reign of Sòng,
the music and entertainment that were favored
were mostly licentious tunes of Zhèng and Wèi;
fine music and proper sounds
seldom had enthusiasts.
Huìjī understood music theory
and particularly enjoyed the melodies of the Three Ancestors of Wèi and xiànghé songs.
Whenever they were played,
he would be delighted and unable to stop.
Among the skilled players of the time, Wáng Kàng of Lángxié was considered first-grade,
while Chǔ Sīzhuāng of Wújùn and Xià Chìsōng of Kuàijī were both second-grade.
Chìsōng was quick-witted
and good at grand moves;
Sīzhuāng was slower in thought
but skillful in fighting.
During the reign of Sòng Wéndì,
Yáng Xuánbǎo was Kuàijī Tàishǒu.
The Emperor sent Sīzhuāng to the East to play with Xuánbǎo,
and then had him draw a diagram of the game,
which he reproduced before the Emperor upon his return.
Tàizǔ made Sīzhuāng and Wáng Kàng gamble against each other,
and from mealtime until dusk,
only one game was completed.
The Emperor, tired,
sent them back to the palace department,
and it was not decided until the fifth watch (early morning).
Kàng slept behind the board,
while Sīzhuāng stayed awake until dawn.
Some people at the time said:
"The reason Sīzhuāng's rank was so high
was because his thinking was profound and prolonged,
and no one could match him."
Kàng and Sīzhuāng both reached the position of Jǐshìzhōng.
During the Yǒngmíng reign,
an imperial edict ranked Kàng.
Jìnglǐngwáng Zǐliáng made Huìjī responsible for this matter.
Initially,
Sīhuà had built a residence in Qǔ'ē,
which had a spacious and leisurely charm.
Huìjī often told his close associates:
"After my children are married,
I shall return to my old home to enjoy my retirement."
He maintained a simple and retiring lifestyle,
and the court praised him as a virtuous gentleman.
He died the following year,
at the age of fifty-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His younger brother, Huìxiū 惠休,
in the fourth year of Yǒngmíng 永明 (486 CE),
was appointed Inspector of Guǎngzhōu 廣州.
When his term ended,
he offered his entire assets as tribute.
The Emperor issued an edict to Rú Fǎliàng 茹法亮, the Remonstrance Official of the Central Secretariat, saying:
“You may ask Xiāo Huìxiū 蕭惠休.
I previously had you proclaim an edict telling him not to use his private emoluments to fully cover his offerings.
This time, it is particularly clear that his sincerity is greater than that of those before and after him.
Ask him,
surely he did not infringe upon private property, did he?
I wish to receive a portion of it myself.”
In the eleventh year (493 CE),
he was appointed from General Who Aids the State and Administrator of Nánhǎi 南海
to Inspector of Xúzhōu 徐州.
When Yùlín 鬱林 ascended the throne,
he was promoted to General Who Conquers Armies.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ 建武 (495 CE),
the barbarians besieged Zhōnglí 鍾離.
Huìxiū 惠休 resisted and defended.
The barbarians sent an envoy, Zhòngcháng Wénzhēn 仲長文真, who said to those in the city:
“The sagely ruler is currently cultivating civil virtues,
why do you defend the city and resist orders?”
The Army Supervisor, Yáng Lún 羊倫, replied:
“The Xiǎnyǔn 獫狁 are greatly rampant,
The barbarians attacked the city,
but Huìxiū 惠休 resisted, fought, and defeated them.
He was transferred to Attendant-in-ordinary,
also holding the post of Colonel of Infantry,
and enfeoffed as a Sub-Prefectural Son of Jiàn'ān 建安 County,
with five hundred households.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán 永元 (499 CE),
he was transferred to Administrator of Wúxìng 吳興.
He was summoned to be Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
The deity of Xiàng Yǔ 項羽 in Wúxìng 吳興 Commandery had long been notoriously fierce.
People of the time said,
“Huìxiū 惠休 served the deity diligently,
wishing to obtain a favorable promotion.”
〔三九〕In the second year (500 CE),
he died.
He was posthumously granted Grand Master of Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon with Eminent Rank.
Huìxiū’s 惠休 younger brother was Huìlǎng 惠朗.
He was skilled at horsemanship.
He rebelled with the bandits of Guìyáng 桂陽.
Tàizǔ 太祖 pardoned him,
and reinstated him in service.
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng 永明 (491 CE),
he was appointed Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers Barbarians for the Prince of Xīyáng 西陽,
and acted as Administrator of the Southern Yúnzhōu 雲州 region.
The document manager, Hé Yìsūn 何益孫, was found guilty of embezzlement of a million [coins]
and executed in the marketplace.
Huìlǎng 惠朗 was implicated and dismissed from office.
The court historian says: “A deep bow to the chief minister,
a public remonstrance with the dukes and ministers—
the ancients praised such unyielding integrity;
to admire it is not excessive.
However, if one's roots are isolated and one's position is precarious,
and one's lofty sentiments do not yield,
then although one's principles may prevail,
one's person will be eternally abandoned.
Therefore, many sought a path to leniency,
humbling themselves with modest words.
For those of high standing and established lineage,
there is no need for indirect means;
they can drive straight and gallop forward,
and none can obstruct them.
Wáng Xiùzhī 王秀之 maintained his family traditions throughout his life,
and did not compromise his principles before powerful regents.
How admirable!”
An ode says: “Xiù 秀 resided in the court,
pure in heart and upright in self.
Bóbǎo 伯寶 of an illustrious clan,
honored his family with excellence.
He abided by ancestral traditions,
knew when to advance and when to stop.
Huìxiǎo 慧曉, chaste and bright,
was indeed a gentleman.
Huìjī 惠基 and Huìhé 惠和,
were outstanding scholars of their time.”
Collation Notes
Biography Twenty-eight: Wáng Róng 王融, Xiè Tiǎo 謝朓
Wáng Róng 王融, courtesy name Yuáncháng 元長,
was a native of Línyí 臨沂, Lángyé 琅邪.
His grandfather, Sēngdá 僧達, was Director of the Central Secretariat.
His great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather were both high officials.
Sēngdá 僧達 said to Emperor Xiàowǔ 孝武 of Sòng 宋:
“My deceased father and deceased grandfather
were respectively Minister of Education and Minister of Works.”
His father, Dàoyǎn 道琰,
was Administrator of Lúlíng 廬陵.
His mother was the daughter of Xiè Huìxuān 謝惠宣, Administrator of Línchuān 臨川,
and a discreet and intelligent woman.
She taught Róng 融 calligraphy.
Róng 融 was intelligent and astute in his youth,
widely read and talented in literature.
He was recommended as a Cultivated Talent.
He served as an acting Army Supervisor for the Central Protector of the South, the Prince of Jìn'ān 晉安.
He was dismissed due to official matters.
He became acting Judicial Army Supervisor for the Minister of Education, the Prince of Jìnglíng 竟陵,
and was promoted to Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent.
Róng 融 felt that his father's official career was not distinguished,
and while young, wished to restore his family's prestige.
He memorialized Shìzǔ 世祖, requesting to be tested.
He said:
“Your servant has heard that spring cicadas and autumn crickets
gather and lament according to the season;
dew-laden trees and wind-blown blossoms
delight together at the approach of the year.
If even plants and trees
can have such feelings;
how much more so living beings,
who cannot be unmoved.
Since your servant has been allowed to look upon the imperial palace,
bathe in imperial grace,
be elevated from humble obscurity,
and join the ranks of the eminent,
wearing official attire and sword,
walking in the vermillion court,
returning home yearly,
boasting of honor in the village.
However, to hold office without diligence
was debated by ancient sages;
to receive emoluments without responsibility
is surely ridiculed by the discerning.
That is why your servant feels indignant and restless,
unable to find peace.
Indeed, profound grace is rarely repaid,
a sagely ruler is hard to encounter.
Willows wither before autumn,
time waits for no one.
I covet this glorious era
to fully display my humble efforts,
to repay Your Majesty's unparalleled benevolence.
If my slight sincerity gains trust,
and my limited talent is recognized,
then whether in civil or military administration,
I am at Your disposal.
The ruler's way is broad and accommodating,
the minister's art has no hidden aspects.
Wēng Guī 翁歸 took it upon himself to judge from within,
and Chōngguó 充國 said, 'None is better than this old minister.'
I humbly emulate these former worthies,
daring to tread the path of light commitment.
By risking the impropriety of self-recommendation,
I express my sincerity in serving the public.
Furthermore, when Táng Yáo 唐堯 was on the throne,
he did not participate in the affairs of the Eight Ministers and Eight Worthies;
if Guǎn Yíwú 管夷吾 did so,
your servant will also do so.
May Your Majesty please consider this.”
He was promoted to Aide to the Imperial Secretariat.
His paternal uncle, Jiǎn 儉,
initially received the appointment of Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Róng 融 sent him a poem and a letter.
Jiǎn 儉 greatly admired and feared him,
and said with a smile to others:
“How can the seal of Marquis Ráng 穰侯 be easily relinquished?”
Soon after, he was transferred to Aide to Dānyáng 丹陽,
and Central Secretariat Gentleman.
The barbarian envoy requested books.
The court debated whether to grant them.
Róng 融 submitted a memorial, saying: “Your servant has heard the collective opinion,
doubting whether to give books to the barbarians.
In your servant's humble opinion,
there are indeed points of disagreement.
Indeed, the barbarians have human faces but beastly hearts,
are as fierce as wolves and venomous as bees.
They violate heavenly
principles,
and transgress earthly righteousness.
They hide in dark places,
coming and going between Bīn 豳 and Shuò 朔.
They have persisted through the Zhōu 周 and Hàn 漢 dynasties without repentance,
and through the Jìn 晉 and Sòng 宋 dynasties, they have grown even more defiant.
How can they possess love and respect, benevolence and wisdom,
deference and humility, integrity and cultivation?
They are ashamed of the docile hearts of dogs and horses,
and are like eagles and tigers turning on each other.
Even if they have fodder in storage,
and sufficient bows and arrows,
they will surely steal from border defenses,
and harass
the frontiers.
How can they possibly approach the passes with humble words,
and request tribute?
Your Majesty diligently preserves and nurtures,
not insulting or destroying them in due time.
You permit their sincere kowtows,
and accept their furs
as tribute.
Moreover, they wish to share our culture and written script.
If they are permitted and sent away,
thinking to receive our teachings,
then why cause suspicion and refusal?
This will only cause the scattered remnants of the old territories
to be unsure of where to settle,
and further decay.”
Hú Yújiào,
some may advocate for themselves.
Once tangled weeds are difficult to weed,
and trickling streams cause widespread flooding,
it is not merely a slight itch or minor illness,
but can become a grave internal malady.
Indeed, Sūn Wǔ's words are:
When in distress, impose frequent punishments;
when in dire straits, bestow many rewards.
Are those who are first brutal and then feared by their own people
what are called captives?
Previously, the common folk of the Central Plains,
even when fallen and intimidated by foreign customs,
still wore headcloths and hairpins as a ritual
at the morning of weddings and funerals.
Yet, the prohibitions and edicts were harsh,
and for every move, capital punishment by quartering was added.
At that time, the Xūnzhòu had just
relocated,
and the canine-sheep peoples still formed alliances.
Immediately, resentment arose in their hearts,
and fear in distress led to escape.
Since their generals and soldiers fled and dispersed,
and their resources and supplies dwindled,
they feared the powerful Rú to the north,
and were pressed by the southern
Hú to the west.
The people turned their backs as if a mountain collapsed,
and their strategic defenses were broken.
Thus, they reluctantly conformed to public sentiment,
and falsely usurped the insignia and robes.
Years passed, almost to an end,
and they remained hidden and unheard of.
Those who faced south and
wept
looked forward to it day and night;
those who looked north and departed
stretched from the Jiāng to the Huái.
Their sinister plots were thwarted year by year,
and their shallow calculations had no solution.
Thus, they kowtowed at the suburban gates,
asking for rituals
and seeking music.
If we were to draw them in with refined virtue,
and grant them with copies of documents,
the Hàn imperial system
would once again preside over the Jīfǔ,
the Sīlì would transmit their credentials,
and again enter Guānhé.
There would be no need for an army of eight
hundred,
nor would ten thousand troops be expected.
Certainly, they would hold up drinks and wait,
waving their spears, wishing to fall prostrate.
The three Qín regions would be united,
and the six Hàn states would be integrated.
Moreover, when the captives sent envoys before and after,
they did not exclusively use Hàn people,
but surely included Xiongnú,
to guard against reconnaissance and capture.
And the establishment of officials and division of duties
further revealed their true intentions:
they suppressed
the old stock
and supported their own clansmen and relatives.
For grand tutors and guardians, there was the empress's family Fēng Jìnguó;
for general records, the Guī surname Zhílè Kěhóu;
for the highest officials, Qiūtúi and Gǒu Rénduān;
and for the執政 (prime ministers), Mùlíng and Qián'ěr.
As for the ceremonial attire of the Eastern Capital
and the hairpins and sashes of the Western Capital,
Cuī Xiàobó and Chéng Yúqiú were long in the Cóngzuò bureau,
Lǐ Yuánhé and Guō Jì
yòu were promoted to the Zhōngshū,
Lǐ Sīchōng adorned the captive's clean officials,
and Yóu Mínggēn broadly occupied prominent positions.
Now, the classics have spread far,
and poetry and history flow north.
Those like Fēng and Lǐ
will surely wish to follow and revere them;
those like Zhílè and his ilk
will inevitably cause friction and obstruction.
Why is this?
The Xiongnú use felt-covered cavalry as their bed curtains,
and riding and shooting as their provisions.
When they wear square caps, they
cross sandy dunes and snowy plains;
when they wear left-flapped robes, they soar like the wind and fly like birds.
If they were dressed in scarlet skirts
and crowned with dark (pō)
kuí,
regulated in their bows and greetings,
and taught graceful
steps,
they would surely find it as difficult as shackles,
and be as fearful as a frozen abyss.
They would hesitate
and thus be unable to advance.
And when spring grass and water arise,
hindering the movement of dispersed horses;
when autumn
winds make trees shed their leaves,
cutting off the joy of driving birds;
when the clamor of their lips ceases at the mulberry fields,
and the butter and milk are separated from the Jì customs;
when listening to refined music is like being deaf;
when approaching the square mat is like being perched,
then those like Fēng and Lǐ
would surely achieve their aims,
but what disease would afflict the fierce clans of the captives?
Thus, the deep longing for their homeland would arise,
and rebellious feelings would stir.
Those who shake their robes would join
their sleeves,
and those who draw their blades would form a dense array.
The tribes would contend below,
and the chieftains would be in peril above.
With one move from us, we would conquer and swallow them whole;
the situation would surely be that of Biàn Zhuāng.
Moreover, when Jí Bǎozhào
recommended Yú,
the territory of Jìn became even more prosperous.
When Dà Zhōng offered wisdom,
the Sù family perished.
The emperor's strategy extends far and wide,
with none who do not submit.
The imperial carriage's light visits Dài,
not just in the evening but in the morning.
Your subject requests
to register those in Yī and Chán,
and that these books be managed again.
It would be like taking from the inner treasury
and storing in the outer chest;
it would be reasonable and satisfying,
and would not harm the current affairs.
If these wild words are worth adopting,
please issue
an edict for their implementation.
Shìzǔ replied:
"My thoughts do not differ from yours, sir.
What you have memorialized now
is even more detailed than when we last met."
The matter was ultimately not carried out.
At the end of Yǒngmíng,
Shìzǔ wished to launch a northern expedition,
and ordered Máo Huìxiù to paint a picture of Hàn Wǔ's northern expedition,
and ordered Róng to manage the matter.
Róng was fond of fame and merit,
and therefore presented a memorial, saying: Your subject has heard that feelings arise from within,
and are stimulated when they correspond with events.
When forms are established at the beginning,
the mechanism moves and becomes manifest.
The path of solemn reverence is worthy of respect,
and when greetings and concessions meet, it becomes even more solemn.
Brave
and ardent warriors are to be valued,
and respond to drums and bells with increased thought.
Since the initial establishment of mankind,
its details are already distant.
Coming down to the rise of destiny,
the Way has evidence:
there is nothing that does not
follow a certain course
to ascend to imperial enterprise.
Indeed, when the fertile lands were well-known,
Tiānyǐ knew the wealth of the five directions.
When hides and silks were already arranged,
Dìliú measured the reverence of the four seas.
If the writings of the
Fēngshàn were different,
then the rites of ascending to the center would be widely propagated.
Lamenting the maps of the world,
the mediocrity of sweeping the world was established.
Your subject humbly believes that Your Majesty has exhausted the divine and perfected the sacred,
totaling the extreme and residing in the center.
You embody the transformation of the two primary forces,
and equally illuminate the two luminaries.
You have rescued the profound principle from decay and extinction,
and restored the supreme Way from corruption
to purity.
You can be called the model of the universe,
the first enlightened one among the common people.
Your subject also encountered
and lived in this auspicious time.
Drinking from wells and eating from fields,
I am fortunate to be in the Táng era.
But my knowledge
is obscure and hazy,
and my scholarship superficial.
I am like a fern or a wheel,
how can I be like a bracken or a fiddlehead?
Yet the imperial gaze illuminates the dark,
and heaven's height listens to the lowly.
You appreciate a single good word,
and pity a single thing
when I was out of season,
washed away the dust and grime,
enhanced my value,
lifted me from my humble hut,
and placed me in the imperial court.
Again, I was able to offer congratulations at the New Year,
gazing upon the sun and moon.
This was my heart'0s
desire,
and it has already been fulfilled.
However, a thousand years produce but one such occasion;
a period of enlightened peace is difficult to repeat.
I contemplate using my humble talents,
and am pleased to offer my small contribution.
I secretly studied the arts of battle formation, offense, and defense,
the books of agriculture,
sericulture, and animal husbandry,
the political strategies of Shēn, Shāng, Hán, and Mò,
and the doctrines of Yī, Zhōu, Kǒng, and Mèng.
I often wished to await a summons to the vermilion palace,
to speak directly before the green mat,
to discuss private matters during leisure
banquets,
and to converse about the affairs of the time.
My position is humble and I am insignificant,
so my earnest desire is merely profound.
Currently, the nine regions are tranquil and serene,
the three spirits are harmonious and peaceful.
Trees have branches to cling to,
and wheels have no divergent ruts.
The Dōngdí offer dances,
the Nánbiàn transmit songs.
The Qiāng and Xiǎn cross mountains,
the Qín and Tú traverse seas.
Translators diligently discern the meanings of foreign tongues,
and interpreters are weary of frequent visits.
Indeed, the cassia forests will be opened at Fèngshān,
and golden cities established in the western garrisons.
Yet, these foolish Xūndí,
dare to defy our great nation.
They temporarily reside in Guānhé,
and steal life within Hángǔ.
They have ruined our former capital's pleasant lands,
and transformed our old towns into desolation.
They halt the offering-cup ritual of
Confucian scholars,
and have long left the Yīchuān region with unbound hair.
The remaining populace of Běidì,
and the surviving elders of Dōngdū,
all swallow tears and grief,
listening intently and watching eagerly,
yearning for benevolent governance,
and stretching their necks for
the imperial influence.
If an inch-long letter were dispatched,
fully identifying the soldiers of the enemy,
we could exploit their falling cities,
and accept their surrendered captives.
There would be no need to exert arrows and bows,
nor await spears and shields.
This truly would be the army of a sagely king,
who conquers without fighting.
I beg to take up a spear and lead the vanguard,
to pave the way to the Central Plains,
to clarify the eternal currents of Hánzhǔ,
to sweep away the accumulated fog of
Lángshān,
to tie the Xīyú's neck,
to make the Zuǒxián bend his knee,
to accustomed them to Hūhán's old rituals,
and to bow before the imperial chariot's巡幸.
Then, as the heavens shift and clouds move,
we shall engrave
a tablet on Dàizōng,
emulating the achievements of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
and following the seventy previous sacrifices.
A hundred deities will stand in solemn alert,
and all nations will become subjects.
Jeweled caps will be scattered like stars,
and jade and silk will gather like clouds.
Three
torches will be gathered at the orchid mats,
and the auspicious sound of "Long Live" will be heard.
How magnificent would that not be!
How righteous would that not be!
Of old, Duke Huán of Qí intended to attack Jǔ,
and Guō Yá understood his hidden intention.
Empress Wèi intended to depose the Hàn,
and Dézǔ probed her deep words.
I am foolish and ignorant,
and my judgment
is insufficient to grasp subtleties.
However, I humbly gauge the sagely mind,
and its grand and far-reaching vision.
Since the plan has been recorded,
the achievement is sure to be accomplished.
I cannot contain my joy.
The painting was completed
and hung on the wall of the archery hall in Lángxié city.
Whenever His Majesty traveled there, he would view it.
In the ninth year [of Tiānbǎo],
the Emperor visited the Fānglín Yuán for the spring purification ritual and banqueted his courtiers.
He ordered Róng to compose a poem for the 曲水流觴 (winding water banquet),
which was rich in literary embellishment
and highly praised by contemporaries.
Due to Róng's talent and eloquence,
in the eleventh year,
the Emperor appointed him concurrent Minister of State Reception (Zhǔkè),
to receive the barbarian envoys Fáng Jǐnggāo and Sòng Biàn.
Biàn, seeing Róng's youth,
asked, "How old is the Zhǔkè?"
Róng replied,
"My fiftieth year has long passed its midpoint."
Then Biàn asked,
"I heard at court that the Zhǔkè composed a poem for the 曲水流觴."
Jǐnggāo also said,
"We heard of the Zhǔkè's composition in the north.
It surpasses that of Yán Yánnián.
We truly wish to see it."
Róng then showed it to them.
Some days later,
Sòng Biàn said to Róng in the Yáochítáng (Jade Pond Hall),
"In the past, by reading Xiāngrú's Fēngshàn (sacrifices to Heaven and Earth),
we understood the virtue of Emperor
Wǔ of Hàn;
now, by viewing Lord Wáng's poem,
we perceive the flourishing state of the King of Qí."
Róng replied, "Our royal house's flourishing brilliance
does more than merely match the achievements of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
My humble composition, however,
is ashamed to be compared to Xiāngrú's work."
Since the barbarian tribute horses were unsatisfactory,
the Emperor ordered Róng to ask,
"The regions west of Qín and north of Jì
are truly rich in swift steeds.
Yet the fine horses presented by the ruler of Wèi
are inferior to even mediocre nags.
Judging by reputation and examining the facts,
this is far from trustworthy.
Will the daily solemn vows
sometimes be broken,
and the vast pastures
be unable to continue their lineage?"
Sòng Biàn replied,
"It is not that there is no room for false names;
it is probably due to unfamiliarity with the land."
Róng said,
"King Mù of Zhōu's horse hoofprints were everywhere under heaven.
If the nature of fine steeds
changed with the land,
then Zàofù's driving skill
would sometimes falter."
Biàn said,
"Why is Lord Wáng so concerned about a thousand lǐ?"
Róng replied, "Since your country distinguishes between superior and inferior,
we are merely asking for information.
If a thousand lǐ horse arrived daily,
His Majesty would drive a drum chariot."
Biàn said,
"If there were such intent,
one would certainly not drive a drum chariot."
Róng said,
"Buying the bones of a dead horse
was also for the sake of Guō Kuí."
Biàn could not answer.
Róng, relying on his family background and talent,
hoped to become a high minister within thirty years.
He served in the Central Secretariat,
and once sighed at night,
"Dèng Yǔ would laugh at people like me."
He encountered a large procession
with much noise and could not advance.
Again, he sighed,
"If there are no eight outriders before one's chariot,
how can one be called a true man!"
When the imperial court was suppressing Wáng Huàn, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
Róng again submitted a memorial, saying: "I often read historical records,
and see those who worry about the nation, forget their families,
and sacrifice their lives to repay kindness.
I have never failed to pat the scroll and sigh,
believing that this sentiment is common to both ancient and modern times.
However, some
are moved by a single word,
or a small favor of a meal,
and become worthy of a scholar's regard,
or share the company of commoners.
How could there be someone like me,
who alone was elevated from obscurity,
and excessively promoted
to an unmerited position,
receiving both fame and official titles,
and whose glory and emoluments both increased,
yet who idles away the morning of
peace and enjoys the evening of leisure?
Therefore, I dare to present my sincere foolishness,"
I humbly heard Your Majesty's thoughts.
Now some discussants are concerned about Xī Xià,
but I humbly believe this is not the case.
What is the reason for this?
With Your Majesty's sagacity and brilliance,
and all your officials exerting their full strength,
following this, you can suppress
rebellion.
From above, you govern those below,
indicating words of reward and punishment,
subtly showing the paths of life and death.
People from all regions
will become enemies to each other.
Once military might reaches far,
people cannot protect themselves.
Although a cornered bird will peck,
it is still fated to be like a quails on a beam;
a distressed beast will be startled,
and ultimately hang alongside a deer in the kitchen.
The triumphant army, enjoying their celebratory drink,
certainly won't wait for
dawn.
My humble heart
holds a small wish.
Since the Xiǎnyǔn repeatedly encroached,
brazenly insulting the Yī,
Heaven's Way brings disaster to the wicked,
and peril and demise arrive daily.
The empress dowager faces internal troubles,
and our provisions and strength are externally depleted.
Rumors and public sentiment
are now at a critical juncture.
If we rely on the returning armies from Wū and Hàn,
giving vent to the lingering indignation of our soldiers,
taking Hángǔ Pass would be as easy as turning one's hand,
and scaling the frontier passes like destroying rotten wood.
However, if soldiers are not
prepared beforehand,
they cannot be used immediately;
not training the people for war
is truly abandoning them.
I especially hope to privately gather troops,
and preemptively train and drill them.
If I am granted permission,
I request to be attached to the supervisory
province, to feed these men,
temporarily preparing them for the defense of Shítou.
I, your servant, have valued integrity since youth,
and have long been accustomed to military life.
If I am tested and achieve no merit,
I am prepared to accept the punishment of being openly
shamed;
if I am employed and achieve success,
I will look up and repay the wisdom of one who knows men.
When the northern barbarians moved,
Jìngláng Wáng Zǐliáng recruited men in Dōngfǔ.
He appointed Róng as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Jūzhǔ.
Róng was eloquent and quick-witted in speech and writing,
especially skilled at composing impromptu.
When he had something to write,
he could pick up a brush and complete it immediately.
