Zǐliáng was particularly friendly with him,
their relationship was extraordinary.
In his later years, he became very skilled at horseback riding.
His talent and background were distinguished,
and he also leveraged Zǐliáng's influence.
He devoted himself to entertaining guests,
diligently greeting and conversing with them.
Both civil and military men flocked to him.
He recruited several hundred "cāng chǔ" (rustic southerners) from Jiāngxī,
all of whom were capable.
When Shìzǔ's illness worsened and he temporarily lost consciousness,
Zǐliáng was inside the palace hall.
The grand-prince had not yet entered.
Róng, in military attire and crimson robes,
stood at the entrance of the Zhōngshū Shěng corridor, blocking the Eastern Palace guards from entering,
intending to enthrone Zǐliáng.
When the Emperor recovered,
the grand-prince entered the hall,
and state affairs were entrusted to Gāozōng.
Róng, knowing Zǐliáng would not be enthroned,
removed his military attire and returned to the provincial office.
He sighed, saying:
"Your Highness has ruined me."
Yùlín was deeply resentful and disliked Róng.
A little over ten days after his ascension,
he had Róng arrested and imprisoned in the Tíngwèi prison.
Then he instructed Censor Zhōngchéng Kǒng Zhìguī to compose a memorial, which read:
"Róng's nature is stubborn and dangerous,
his conduct is frivolous and competitive.
His actions shock the multitude,
and his words are unusual.
Recently, when the slight disturbance beyond the frontier
caused him to eagerly seek military leadership,
he then recruited unruly individuals
and incited wild "cāng" (rustic southerners).
He cunningly calculated influence
and unilaterally wielded power and personal gain,
acting with duplicity between lips and teeth,
causing disturbance within his cheeks and tongue.
He dispensed favors and punishments himself,
without any scruples,
slandering court policies
and criticizing princes and dukes.
He considered his talent unparalleled,
deferring to no one.
These matters have been exposed far and wide.
Let Róng answer based on the facts."
Róng replied:
"This prisoner is indeed ignorant and foolish,
with many faults in his conduct.
However, he has long served in a family of
scholars,
and has received instruction from gentlemen.
From his youth
until nearly reaching adulthood,
the people in his district and village
considered him foolish but cautious.
The officials at court considered him faultless.
I was undeservedly favored by the late Emperor,
and also greatly honored by Emperor Wén's recognition and promotion.
Sītú Gōng allowed me to be among the literati,
and Ānlù Wáng showed me special favor and attention.
Since I received national benevolence,
I surely wished to repay it with my life.
The plans for attacking the barbarians that I presented before and after
were also humbly submitted to the previous court.
Now, when the 'dogs and sheep' (barbarians) have recently stirred up trouble,
Jǐ Sēngzhēn conveyed a prior imperial decree,
delivering a message about the movements on the northern frontier,
ordering this prisoner to draft a proclamation.
At that time, I then took the opportunity to petition,
hoping to attend the imperial carriage.

and created the framework of articles.
The concurrently serving Superintendent, Sòng Gōng, and the concurrently serving Judge, Wáng Zhí, were tasked with copying and compiling similarities and differences,
determining what to keep and what to discard.
It was thoroughly discussed with the Eight Dukes and Ministers,
and then rectified and finalized by the Grand
Marshal, Chén Nì.
Among the profound doubts and major deliberations,
where various opinions were contradictory,
the Sagely Insight, with its profound gaze,
made the final decision with the Imperial Brush.
Thus, the legal text was initially established in twenty volumes,
with one volume of records,
totaling twenty-one volumes.
Now it is presented to Your Majesty,
requesting that it be put into effect externally,
and promulgated throughout the four seas.
Your servant also heard Lǎo Zǐ and Zhòng Ní say:
"Those in ancient times who heard legal cases
sought means to preserve life;
those who hear legal cases now
seek means to kill
them."
"Rather than killing the innocent,
it is better to let the guilty escape."
This shows that the duty of judging cases
has been difficult since ancient times.
Although the legal text is now finalized,
it must be applied;
if its application loses fairness,
it is no different from having no laws.
The law books are intricate and detailed,
their text concise but their examples extensive.
Similar cases incline to one side or another,
and thus errors become intertwined.
If the main principle is deviated from even slightly,
grievances and abuses arise
everywhere.
Legal officials, lacking understanding,
often make mistakes and perversions.
Supervising officials, being unfamiliar with the laws,
have no means to judge them.
Then the law books merely shine brightly in their cases,
while wronged souls still linger in prison.
Currently, there are over a thousand prisons in prefectures, commanderies, and counties.
If even one person is wronged each year in one prison,
then within a single year,
over a thousand will die unjustly.
Such deaths from injustice and venom
reach
and disturb the harmonious khí,
which Your Sagely Wisdom urgently considers,
and which must be prevented.
The causes for this
are not merely the fault of the legal officials.
The administrators of various cities
also disrupt the established principles.
Some
rely on leftover influence from military merits,
or on their old age from diligent service.
With uncouth temperament and muddled minds,
[一０] they ruthlessly suppress living beings.
With dim minds and cruel attitudes,
they exploit and devour the common people.
They govern harshly
and take their lives,
twisting the law to inflict guilt.
The accumulation of grievances
also arises from this.
Even if a prison official is good,
they cannot be effective.
This leads to Yú Gōng crying at the border city,
and the filial wife being wronged in a distant land.
Even if Your Majesty wishes to pardon them,
their blood has already stained the Nine Springs.
Upon examining the famous figures of antiquity,
many had expertise in law.
Thus, Shì Zhī and Dìng Guó
had brilliant reputations in the Hàn court;
[一一] Yuán Cháng and Wén Huì
[一二] their achievements shone
in the Wèi court.
[一三]Today's scholars
are unwilling to make it their profession.
Even if some do study it,
they are scorned by public opinion.
This is truly because their efforts are wasted for years
without receiving a single day's reward,
and their accumulated learning, in those years,
ends up being ridiculed by commoners.
I fear that this book will forever fall into the hands of inferiors.
Now, if we expand the system of titles and rewards,
and open avenues for encouragement and admiration,
assess
the performance of officials,
and arrange for the training of noble scions,
select those who have mastered it,
[一四] and place them in internal bureaus,
and choose the talented and good
to serve in external positions,
[一五] if all regional governors select those capable,
and all county magistrates promote those skilled,
then Gāo Yáo's counsel
[一六] can be achieved with ease,
and the achievements of Dù and Zhèng
will not be far off.
Then the wicked will have nowhere
to escape punishment,
[一七] and corrupt officials will be unable to conceal their deceit.
It would be like hands and feet driving each other,
or like a bowstring and arrow nock fitting together.
Your servant, being of limited ability,
was mistakenly put in charge of the Grand Judiciary.
Your Majesty, from your sagely heart,
worries and pities those caught in the legal net,
and in the imperial
court, upholds instructions,
[一八] discerning the people's suffering from afar.
Your servant respectfully reports the will of Heaven,
and humbly presents this to the imperial court.
Regarding the requests deemed appropriate,
it is fitting to transcribe the laws,
establish assistant professors of law in the National Academy,
[一九] following the example of the Five Classics.
Among the students of the National University
who wish to study law,
those who pass the examination with high distinction
should be immediately promoted and employed,
and placed in legal positions,
to encourage scholars.
The edict was reported and accepted,
but the matter was ultimately not implemented.
He was transferred to Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
then promoted to Chief Clerk of the Light Cavalry General (Piàojì Chángshǐ)
and General Who Aids the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he was promoted to General of the Valiant Cavalry (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk of the General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Chángshǐ), and Administrator of Nánjùn.
Zhìguī noted that the barbarians had invaded the south for successive years,
with unending conscription and military campaigns,
causing casualties among the populace.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial, stating: "The Xiongnú have been a menace
since ancient times.
Even the wisdom and courage of the Three Dynasties,
and the exceptional prowess of the Two Hàn,
have only two essential strategies
for calculations:
one is to spur horses
and gallop,
displaying might in the desert;
the other is to send light chariots as envoys,
establishing communications at the barbarian court.
To summarize,
their superiority and inferiority are evident.
Those who debate today
all believe that a man's
spirit
disdains being subordinate to others.
How much more so our celestial majesty?
How can we yield first?
Wú and Chǔ are strong and fierce,
with a million armored soldiers.
Cutting down those leviathans,
where can they not be crushed?
Seeking peace shows weakness,
which is not a national policy.
Your servant believes that the Róng and Dí are beast-like in nature,
fundamentally not human.
Their hooting and wolf-like squatting
are not worth joy or anger;
their bee-like eyes and scorpion-like tails
have
no bearing on beauty or ugliness.
It is only fitting to overcome them with deep strategy,
control them with foresight,
deal with them with magnanimity,
and treat them as mere insect pests.
How can it be worth unleashing the world's wrath,
sacrificing the lives of the common people,
igniting the fury of thunder and lightning,
to contend over the temperament of insects and birds?
A hundred battles, a hundred victories,
are not enough to be called supreme;
corpses strewn for a thousand *lǐ*
do no good to the superior state."
But like ants gathering and silkworms swarming,
〔二０〕endless punitive expeditions could not exterminate them.
The horse-footed hairy hordes
were difficult to contend with.
Emperor Hàn Gāo extended his might across the borders,
but was trapped in a long siege.
Emperor Xiào Wén's state
was prosperous and its laws were clear,
yet his affairs were frustrated and he suffered humiliation.
Emperor Xuān Dì appeased them and brought peace,
and the northern horses were not alarmed.
Emperor Guāng Wǔ used humble words and generous gifts,
and the cold mountains were without mist.
These four
rulers of the two capitals,
who excellently governed the central regions,
offered treasures and goods to secure peace,
and sent imperial clan daughters to foster good relations.
They managed them from afar with a long rein,
and their descendants relied on this.
Was it that they did not want to fight?
They cherished the lives of the people
instead.
Only Emperor Hàn Wǔ, relying on the resources accumulated over five generations,
and inheriting the wealth of the entire realm,
with a proud heart and extravagant ambition,
greatly campaigned against the Xiongnu.
Thus, armies were gathered for successive years,
fighting battles over a thousand *lǐ*,
driving deep into the Hànhǎi,
and watering horses at Lóngchéng.
Although famous kings were captured and slain,
and fierce Jié were slaughtered and put to flight,
nine out of ten Hàn soldiers and armored men perished.
〔二一〕Therefore, when Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbì
went beyond the passes,
a thousand contingents did not return.
When General Èrshī entered the desert,
〔二二〕a hundred battalions suddenly surrendered.
Lǐ Guǎng was defeated at the vanguard,
Lǐ Líng was lost at the rear formation,
and the rest fled
north,
countless in number.
Consequently, the national treasury was depleted,
and the population halved.
As for the achievements of warmongering,
where was their benefit?
Fighting is not as good as peace;
how great is the difference between them?
Since the Western Dynasties lost their order,
and the Eastern Jìn moved its capital,
all the Hú barbarians stirred in chaos,
and the Qiāng and Dí crisscrossed and plundered.
Thorns and brambles grew thick around imperial tombs and temples,
jackals and tigers roared in the palace precincts.
Mountains and ravines
were overturned,
the common people were slaughtered.
They were oppressed and scattered in panic,
a situation unprecedented since the creation of the world.
The gains and losses of that time,
I shall briefly not elaborate.
More recently, in the Yuánjiā era,
there were many years of peace,
but later, failing to assess the situation,
strong enemies were provoked again.
Consequently, city after city fell and people were relocated,
and barbarian horses drank from the Jiāng.
Between Qīng and Xú,
〔二三〕the grass and trees were like human ears.
In the early Jiànyuán
era,
barbarian dust invaded the frontier,
but at the beginning of the Yǒngmíng era,
peace and good relations were re-established,
and for more than ten years,
the border alarms ceased.
Your Majesty commands the heavens and establishes the calendar,
rides the sun and ascends to the throne.
Your voice thunders across the cosmos,
and your power overawes rivers and mountains.
Yet the remnants of the giant boars
have not yet been utterly destroyed,
and the lingering breaths of the long serpents
stealthily peer into the outer territories.
The beacon towers have not been quiet
for five years now.
Last year, the ant-like destruction
festered and consumed Fánchéng and the Hàn River region;
this year, the insect-like poison
continues to spread unchecked.
Raising an
army of one hundred thousand
costs a thousand *jīn* a day.
The expenses over five years,
how can they be estimated?
Why does Your Majesty begrudge a single horse for a courier,
a hundred *jīn* in bribes,
or a few lines of an imperial decree
to entice
these fierce and stubborn enemies,
so that the frontier on the river may rest its shoulders,
and the border regions preserve their lives,
to accumulate armor and nourish the people,
and observe their weaknesses?
If my strategy is implemented,
it will be an unprecedented blessing.
If they do not
obey,
it will be no worse than losing one contingent in battle.
Some say,
"If an envoy is sent but not received,
it will be a humiliation."
Indeed, those who consider the whole world as their scope
do not bother with minor shame.
Those who take responsibility for all within the four seas,
how can they care about trivial matters?
The fall of a single city
is still not worth regretting;
if one envoy does not return,
how can it be a cause for shame?
Moreover, if I gain advantage through
flexibility,
and my strategy is implemented,
why should I dislike the shame?
This is what is meant by a looper caterpillar bending
in order to stretch forth.
I do not say that sending an envoy will certainly achieve peace,
but there is indeed a reason for
peace;
just as one who desires to fight will not necessarily win,
but there is a chance of winning.
Now it is advisable to dispatch a large army early,
and widely display military might.
Levy rhino-hide armor from Mín and Éméi,
and order
tower ships from the Pǔ Hǎi.
Make it so that from Qīng to Yù,
scouting cavalry are spread like stars,
and along the Jiāng and into the Hàn,
armies are arrayed like clouds for ten thousand *lǐ*.
Occupy strategic points to seize their spirit,
cut off their supply routes
to break their courage.
Deploy many deceptive troops
to exhaust their vigilance and confuse their plans.
〔二四〕Firmly establish impregnable defenses
to make their spirits weary and their thoughts yield.
Then, issue a sincere imperial decree,
dispatch fast couriers,
with eloquent words and generous gifts,
and explain the auspicious and inauspicious outcomes.
The northern barbarians are stubborn but appreciate novelty,
greedy and fond of goods.
〔二五〕They fear our might
and like our
bribes.
Fearing our might and liking our bribes,
they will certainly desire peace.
If Your Majesty adopts my suggestion
and implements my plan,
what concern is there that below Yùmén Pass
there will be no Hú barbarians who sue for peace
哉?
Since their arguments for war are earnest,
my arguments for peace are also broad and sound.
I humbly wish Your Majesty would examine the advantages and disadvantages of both paths,
and weigh the pros and cons of these two matters.
With your sagely insight and profound
understanding,
a clear decision can be made.
This humble and mistaken memorial that I have submitted,
I hope it will be sent down to the imperial court
to allow for broad discussion.
I, your servant, have mistakenly received special favor
and serve as an assistant to the Marquis-Duke.
I dare to speak with blunt frankness,
submitting this memorial from a thousand *lǐ* away.
The emperor did not accept it.
He was summoned to be Shìzhōng,
but he did not go,
and remained in his original post.
Zhìguī’s [Wèi Zhìguī 衛稚珪] disposition was pure and detached.
He enjoyed literature and poetry.
He drank seven or eight dòu 斗 of wine.
He shared a close rapport with his maternal cousin Zhāng Róng 張融.
He also formed close friendships with Wáng Sīyuǎn 王思遠 of Lángyá 琅邪, Hé Diǎn 何點 of Lújiāng 廬江, and Diǎn’s brother Yìn 胤.
He took no pleasure in worldly affairs.
He extensively landscaped his residence with mountains and waters.
Leaning on a table, he would drink alone,
with no trivial matters to distract him.
Inside his gate and courtyard,
the weeds were left uncut.
Frogs chirped within.
Someone once asked him,
“Do you wish to emulate Chén Fān 陳蕃?”
Zhìguī smiled and said,
“I consider this to be worth two sets of drums and wind instruments.
Why must I necessarily strive to imitate Zhòngjǔ 仲舉?”
In the first year of Yǒngyuán 永元 [499 CE],
he became the Dūguān Shàngshū 都官尚書.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事 [Grand Steward of the Crown Prince],
and given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 [Palace Attendant].
In the third year [501 CE],
Zhìguī fell ill.
Dōnghūn [Dì 廢帝, also known as Xiāo Bǎojuàn 蕭寶卷] cleared out his attendants [from his sickbed],
and he was transported by palanquin.
His illness consequently worsened,
and he subsequently passed away.
He was fifty-five years old.
He was posthumously granted the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫 [Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, with Gold and Purple Seals].
Liú Huì 劉繪, courtesy name Shìzhāng 士章,
was a native of Péngchéng 彭城.
He was the younger brother of Tàicháng Qūn 太常悛.
His father, Miǎn 勔,
was a powerful and influential figure at the end of the Sòng 宋 dynasty.
Many guests frequented his household.
Miǎn would have Huì converse with them,
and he would respond and engage fluently.
Miǎn joyfully remarked,
“If you ever wear a sash and stand at court later,
you will be able to speak with guests!”
He began his career as Zhùzuò Láng 著作郎 [Secretary in the Bureau of History],
and served as Tàizǔ Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn 太祖太尉行參軍 [Acting Military Advisor to Grand Ancestor, Grand Commandant].
When Tàizǔ 太祖 saw him, he sighed and said,
“Duke Liú 劉公 [referring to his father Miǎn] has not perished [i.e., his legacy continues]!”
When Yùzhāng Wáng Yí 豫章王嶷 became the governor of Jiāngzhōu 江州,
he appointed Huì as Zuǒjūn Zhǔbù 左軍主簿 [Chief Clerk of the Left Army].
He followed Yí to Jiānglíng 江陵,
where he was transferred to Zhèn Xī Wàibīng Cānjūn 鎮西外兵曹參軍 [Military Advisor to the Outer Military Bureau of the General Who Guards the West],
and then Piàojì Zhǔbù 驃騎主簿 [Chief Clerk of the General of Agile Cavalry].
Huì was intelligent, alert, and possessed literary talent.
He was skilled in clerical script.
He was frequently summoned and honored,
and his advanced presentations and responses were brilliant and astute.
Among his colleagues and officials,
no one was treated with such favor.
Wáng Xǔ 王詡 of Lángyá served as Gōngcáo 功曹 [Merit Officer],
and advanced through his administrative abilities.
Yí said to his aides,
“Although I cannot obtain an Yìng Sì 應嗣 [Li Ying 李膺] or a Chén Fān 陳蕃,
you gentlemen certainly have two splendid steeds [talented individuals] here.”
Huì then served as Sīkōng Jìshì Lùshì 司空記室錄事 [Recorder and Clerk to the Minister of Works],
and was transferred to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬 [Attendant to the Crown Prince],
and Dàsīmǎ Zīyì 大司馬諮議 [Consultant to the Grand Marshal],
concurrently holding the position of Lùshì 錄事 [Recorder].
At that time, Yùzhāng Wáng Yí and Wénhuì Tàizǐ 文惠太子 [Crown Prince Wenhui, Xiāo Zhǎngmào 蕭長懋] differed in age and official rank,
and public opinion suggested there was suspicion between the palace and the princely establishment.
Huì earnestly requested to be sent out [from the capital],
and became Nánkāng Xiàng 南康相 [Prefect of Nánkāng Commandery].
During his leisure from local affairs,
he devoted himself to lecturing and expounding [on texts].
One of the emperor’s trusted attendants, Chén Hóng 陳洪, requested leave to return south,
and asked Huì how he was faring in the commandery.
Afterwards, he casually remarked,
“Nánkāng is the throat and tongue of the three prefectures [or commanderies],
and requires capable administration.
How can a young man devoted to scholarship be placed there?”
He was recalled to serve as Ānlù Wáng Hùjūn Sīmǎ 安陸王護軍司馬 [Chief Clerk of the Defender-General for the King of Ānlù],
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎 [Gentleman of the Central Secretariat],
overseeing imperial edicts.
He was ordered to assist Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Hé Yìn 國子祭酒何胤 [Libationer of the Directorate of Education Hé Yìn] in compiling rites and ceremonies.
Towards the end of Yǒngmíng 永明 [493 CE],
the literati in the capital were passionately engaged in writing articles and discussing philosophy,
all converging at the western residence of Jìnglíng Wáng 竟陵王 [Prince of Jìnglíng, Xiāo Zǐliáng 蕭子良].
Huì was a leader among the younger generation,
quick-witted and versatile.
At that time, Zhāng Róng 張融 and Zhōu Yǒng 周顒 were both skilled in rhetoric.
Róng’s tone and delivery were slow and elegant,
Yǒng’s words were ornate and swift.
Huì’s speeches,
however, had a rhythmic pause and a commanding style.
People at the time had a saying for him:
“Liú Huì sticks to the dwelling,
opening another door.”
Meaning he stood between the two [Zhāng and Zhōu] in style.
After Yúfù Hóu Zǐxiǎng 魚復侯子響 [Prince of Yúfù, Xiāo Zǐxiǎng 蕭子響] was executed,
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí wished to arrange his burial.
He summoned Huì to discuss the matter,
and had him compose a memorial.
Huì asked for paper and brush,
and finished it in an instant.
Yí [only] added eight characters,
[二六] saying,
“He raised and nurtured him,
watching him grow into an adult.”
He then sighed, saying,
“How could Mí Héng 禰衡 have surpassed this?”
Later, when envoys from the northern barbarians arrived,
Huì was ordered to receive the barbarian envoys
with his eloquent speech.
After the event concluded,
he was to draft the diplomatic statements.
Huì said to others,
“It’s not just that embellishing is difficult,
but even getting my words [precisely] is hard enough.”
He served his elder brother Qūn 悛 with respect and diligence.
When speaking to others,
he would refer to him as
“Shǐjūn 使君” [My Lord/Governor].
During the Lóngchāng 隆昌 era [494 CE],
Qūn was implicated in a crime and was about to be executed.
Huì knelt before the palace gate, requesting to die in place of his brother.
Gāozōng 高宗 [Emperor Gāozōng, Xiāo Luán 蕭鸞], then regent,
interceded and saved him.
He was appointed Zhènjūn Zhǎngshǐ 鎮軍長史 [Chief Clerk to the General Who Guards the Army],
and then transferred to Huángmén Láng 黃門郎 [Gentleman of the Yellow Gate].
When Gāozōng became Piàojì 驃騎 [General of Agile Cavalry],
he appointed Huì as Fúguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 [General Who Assists the State],
Zīyì 諮議 [Consultant],
concurrently holding the position of Lùshì 錄事 [Recorder],
and overseeing official correspondence.
Upon Gāozōng’s ascension to the throne,
Huì was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 [Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince],
and then sent out to be Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Fǔjūn Zhǎngshǐ 寧朔將軍、撫軍長史 [General Who Pacifies the North, Chief Clerk to the General of the Army].
When Ānlù Wáng Bǎozhì 安陸王寶晊 [King Bǎozhì of Ānlù, Xiāo Bǎozhì 蕭寶晊] became the governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘州,
he appointed Huì as Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ, Chángshā Nèishǐ 冠軍長史、長沙內史 [Chief Clerk to the General Who Leads the Army, Grand Administrator of Chángshā],
concurrently managing the affairs of Xiāngzhōu,
with his general title remaining as before.
Bǎozhì’s consort
was Qūn’s daughter.
Bǎozhì was fond of his concubine.
Huì took her away,
and reported the full matter to the throne.
Bǎozhì resented this,
and he and Huì became estranged.
He left office due to his mother’s death.
He had an extremely filial nature,
observing mourning by his mother’s grave for three years,
eating coarse food.

After the mourning period ended, he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Jìn’ān Wáng Zhēngběi Zhǎngshǐ, Nán Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu 寧朔將軍、晉安王征北長史、南東海太守 [General Who Pacifies the North, Chief Clerk to the General Who Attacks the North for the King of Jìn’ān, Administrator of Southern Dōnghǎi],
concurrently managing the affairs of Nán Xúzhōu 南徐州.
Although Huì was bold and chivalrous,
he always disliked military matters.
He was genuinely skilled at archery,
but never rode a horse.
When his brother Qūn passed away,
the court debated posthumously granting him the titles Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 平北將軍、雍州刺史 [General Who Pacifies the North, Governor of Yōngzhōu].
The imperial edict had already been issued,
but Huì requested Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì 尚書令徐孝嗣 to change it.
When Liáng Wáng Yìshī 梁王義師 [Prince of Liáng, Xiāo Yǎn 蕭衍] raised his righteous army,

the imperial court appointed Huì as Chíjié, Dū Yōng Liáng Nánběi Qín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suíjùn Zhūjūnjì, Fúguó Jiāngjūn, Lǐng Níngmán Xiàowèi, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 持節、督雍梁南北秦四州郢州之竟陵司州之隨郡諸軍事、輔國將軍、領寧蠻校尉、雍州刺史 [Bearer of Imperial Credential, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, North and South Qín Prefectures, Jìnglíng of Yǐng Prefecture, Suí Commandery of Sī Prefecture, General Who Assists the State, concurrently Commander for Pacifying the Barbarians, Governor of Yōngzhōu].
He firmly declined the appointment.
Everyone felt dismayed for him as the imperial court was in chaos.
Huì ultimately did not accept,
and Dōnghūn Dì 東昏帝 instead appointed Zhāng Xīntài 張欣泰.
Huì was transferred to Jiàn’ān Wáng Chēqí Zhǎngshǐ, Xíng Fǔguó Shì 建安王車騎長史、行府國事 [Chief Clerk to the General of Chariots for the King of Jiàn’ān, managing affairs of the princely establishment].
When the righteous army besieged the city,
Nányùnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Jì 南雍州刺史張稷 [Governor of Nányùnzhōu, Zhāng Jì] took overall command of the city’s military affairs.
He and Huì had an extraordinarily close relationship,
and they planned to depose and enthrone.
They conversed secretly for several nights.
When Dōnghūn Dì 東昏帝 was killed,
the city sent Huì and Guózǐ Bóshì Fàn Yún 國子博士范雲 [Erudite of the Directorate of Education Fàn Yún] to deliver the head to Liáng Wáng 梁王 at Shítóu 石頭.
He was transferred to Dàsīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng 大司馬從事中郎 [Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal].
In the second year of Zhōngxīng 中興 [502 CE],
he passed away.
He was forty-five years old.
Huì compiled a list of skilled calligraphers,
and claimed to be good at flying white script.
In his discussions,
he was quite fond of showing off his knowledge.
[二七]
His younger brother was Tián 瑱,
courtesy name Shìwēn 士溫.
He enjoyed literature and drinking,
and was extravagant, not valuing material possessions.
Máo Huìyuǎn 毛惠遠 of Xíngyáng 滎陽 was skilled at painting horses,
and Tián was skilled at painting women.
Both were considered the best of their time.
His highest official position was Lìbù Láng 吏部郎 [Director of the Bureau of Personnel].
He died before Huì.
The Grand Scribe commented: Laws and rites are mutually dependent.
The way of exhortation and admonition,
those with shallow understanding speak of governance,
unable to distinguish precedence.
Thus, they are the embankments for governing the world,
and the reins for controlling the people.
When administering simply,
unity is paramount.
If severity and leniency are changed frequently,
one knows not what to do.
The essence of statutes and ordinances
is concise in wording but broad in meaning.
When penalties are applied according to the classics,
each uses his own judgment.
Since the intent of strictness and leniency differs,
the benefits of severity and mildness also vary.
Words have implications that appear and disappear,
and meanings acquire additions and subtractions.
The affairs of former magistrates,
their governance was not uniform.
What a later lord approved,
became the established practice.
As Zhangshǔ (張薥) replaced one another,
errors gradually crept in.
Thus, punishment opened two doors,
and the law had two paths.
The methods of the scribes became intricate,
and the tendency for manipulation arose.
Seizing opportunities from likes and dislikes,
and exploiting illicit gains worth a thousand pieces of gold,
like cutting chives that grow again,
one would rather err on the side of finding someone guilty.
While those embracing wood (prisoners) in the牢戶 (láohù)
may not necessarily be wronged.
Lower officials reported to their superiors,
dealing with documents.
They observed voices and scrutinized expressions,
but did not use their hearts.
Redressing wrongs and adjudicating cases,
they were not personally urgent.
Following the law and applying the sections,
they fortunately avoided blame or regret.
As for the prefectures and counties that governed the people,
where all affairs originated,
they might pardon offenses based on sentiment,
without even waiting for a trial.
Or they might determine guilt by law,
finding no fault too small.
This was due to the dense net of laws and vexatious regulations,
where the written principles contradicted each other.
Indeed, shame is hard to exhaust,
and bandits are always present.
To seek victory through severity,
is a matter of possibility.
To sweep ancestral tombs of prominent families,
how far off is the profit?
Therefore, the laws of Yǒngmíng (永明)
mostly used leniency and generosity.
Governing things does not fear a benevolent heart,
but is hindered by excessive magnanimity.
It is essential for ordinances to be enforceable,
and their inconsistency and杂乱 (záluàn) are abhorrent.
A eulogy says: Yuán Xùn (袁徇) cherished his relatives,
showing affection as if they were his own sons.
Zhìguī (稚珪) remained aloof,
memorializing to halt military campaigns.
Shìzhāng (士章) was perceptive,
establishing his name by his conduct.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 30: Wáng Huàn (王奐) (cousin Huì (繢)), Zhāng Chōng (張沖)
Wáng Huàn (王奐), courtesy name Yàn sūn (彥孫),
was from Línyí (臨沂), Lángyá (琅邪).
His grandfather, Sēnglǎng (僧朗),
was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left and Minister without Portfolio for Sòng (宋).
His father, Cuì (粹),
was Yellow Gate Attendant.
Huàn (奐) was adopted by his paternal granduncle, Grand Secretary Qiú (球),
hence his courtesy name Yàn sūn (彥孫).
He began his career as Assistant Editor,
then Palace Aide to the Crown Prince,
Chief Clerk to the Prince of Ānlù (安陸), Commander-in-Chief,
then Attendant-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince,
then Administrator of his home province,
then Central Secretariat Director,
then Grand Commandant's Consultant to the Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽),
then Yellow Gate Attendant.
In the first year of Yuánhuī (元徽) (473 CE),
he was appointed Long History of the Prince of Jìnxī (晉熙), General Who Attacks the Barbarians, and Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià (江夏).
He was promoted to Palace Attendant,
concurrently serving as Colonel of Infantry.
He was again appointed Long History of the Prince of Jìnxī (晉熙), General Who Guards the West,
with the added title of General of the Army, and Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng (武昌), Jiāngxià (江夏).
He was summoned to be Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
then transferred to oversee the Ministry of Personnel.
In early Shēngmíng (昇明) (477 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Army and Magistrate of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Earlier,
Wáng Yàn’s (王晏) father, Pǔyào (普曜), was Shěn Yōuzhī’s (沈攸之) Long History.
He often worried that if Yōuzhī (攸之) started an uprising,
he would not be able to return.
At that time, Huàn (奐) was in the Ministry of Personnel,
and transferred Pǔyào (普曜) to an internal position.
Yàn (晏) was deeply grateful for this.
When Yàn (晏) served in Emperor Shìzǔ’s (世祖) household,
Huàn’s (奐) cousin, Yùn (蘊), rebelled.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) said to Yàn (晏),
"Wáng Huàn (王奐) is a maternal relative of the Sòng (宋) imperial family,
and Wáng Yùn (蘊) is a close associate of the rebels.
Since he is a member of their clan,
how can he be without dissenting thoughts?
I intend to report this fully to the emperor."
Yàn (晏) kowtowed and said,
"Wáng Huàn (王奐) is prudent and cautious;
I guarantee he has no rebellious intentions.
My parents are in the capital,
I ask to offer them as collateral."
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) then desisted.
Huàn (奐) was appointed Grand Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興),
with a salary of two thousand piculs,
his generalship remaining as before.
Soon after, he was advanced to General Who Attacks the Barbarians.
In the first year of Jiàn yuán (建元) (479 CE),
he was advanced to General of the Left.
The following year,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
concurrently serving as Tutor to the Prince of Póyáng (鄱陽),
then transferred to Palace Attendant,
then Director of the Imperial Library,
concurrently serving as Colonel of Valiant Cavalry.

He was again promoted to General Who Attacks the Barbarians, Long History of the Prince of Línchuān (臨川), General Who Guards the West, concurrently serving as Colonel of the Southern Man (南蠻), and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡).
Huàn (奐) was promoted three times in one year.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining the position of Southern Man Colonel, stating:
"Now, as heaven and earth have just been opened and
all things are renewed,
Jīngmán (荊蠻) has come to awe,
and Bā Pú (巴濮) are not disturbed.
It is only necessary that the border people live in peace and contentment,
and officials perform their duties.
The former commandery and old province
will daily become prosperous.
I once traveled in the western lands
and saw the fluctuations of prosperity and decline.
Moreover, after the recent military devastation,
the destruction is difficult to restore.
Although it may be rebuilt with good governance,
it has not yet recovered.
Now, to again cut away from the great commandery
and establish a subordinate commandant,
its prestige is not enough to strengthen,
and its reality cannot diminish any hardship.
Furthermore, resources are divided,
and duties are expanded.
The toil of the multitude doubles,
and paperwork becomes more cumbersome.
Not only do I see its difficulty,
but I also secretly believe it is not beneficial for the national plan."
His request was granted.
Thus, the office of Southern Man Colonel was abolished.
He was advanced to General of the Vanguard.
When Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He was then transferred to Envoy with Imperial Insignia, Inspector of Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu (湘州), General of the Vanguard, and Provincial Governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州).
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (484 CE),
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Provincial Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
The military headquarters of Jiāngzhōu (江州) were initially abolished.
In the fourth year (486 CE),
he was promoted to Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and Central Controller of his home province.
Huàn (奐) had no academic learning,
but was valued for his practical ability.
He was promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs,
remaining as Central Controller.
The registrar, Wáng Zhí (王植), asked the Ministry of Personnel Director Kǒng Xiùzhī (孔琇之) to have the registrar-clerk Yú Gōngxǐ (俞公喜) promoted to a drafting position,
falsely claiming it was Huàn’s (奐) intention.
Zhí (植) was dismissed from office for this.
Six years later,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Huàn wished to invite the imperial carriage to his residence.
The Emperor had belatedly embraced Buddhism,
and no longer had animals slaughtered for imperial meals.
He sent Wáng Yàn to tell Huàn:
"I made a vow last year to abstain from killing,
and have decided not to visit ministers anymore.
There is no reason for me to suddenly do so."
When Wáng Jiǎn died,
the Emperor appointed Huàn as Shàngshū Lìng,
and consulted Wáng Yàn about it.
Yàn's position and favor were already considerable,
and he could not yield to Huàn.
He replied to the Emperor:
"Liǔ Shìlóng has great prestige;
I fear it would be inappropriate for him to be after Huàn."
So Huàn was transferred to Zuǒ Púshè,
given the additional title of Gěishì Zhōng,
and sent out as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sì Zhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglín Sīzhōu Zhī Suíjùn Jūnshì, Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Emperor said to Wáng Yàn:
"Huàn is truly devoted to the Śākya clan.
He is genuinely dedicated.
When he is at the frontier, this might hinder his duties.
When you meet him, mention it in conversation,
but do not say it is my idea."
The Emperor, seeing that many of the soldiers in the northern garrisons were in rags,
sent three thousand sets of trousers and tunics,
ordering Huàn to distribute them.
In the eleventh year,
Huàn summarily killed Níngmán Chángshǐ Liú Xīngzǔ.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and ordered Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Kǒng Zhìguī to memorialize on the matter, saying: Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Huàn memorialized that he recorded Xiǎofǔ Chángshǐ Liú Xīngzǔ,
falsely claiming
"Xīngzǔ incited the mountain barbarians,
plotting rebellion,
spreading deceitful rumors,
and using insolent language."
An imperial edict ordered Xīngzǔ to be sent to the capital.
Huàn, fearing that his memorial was fraudulent,
beat Xīngzǔ to death in prison,
and falsely memorialized that he had hanged himself.
Yet his current body
shows injuries, swelling, and putrefaction,
and the matter has been exposed and heard.
When Xīngzǔ's student Liú Ní was brought to the censorate for questioning,
he detailed:
"Xīngzǔ and Huàn worked together,
but could not get along.
Last year, when Zhū Gōng'ēn, the Lǐngjūn, suffered a defeat in the campaign against
the barbarians,
Xīngzǔ memorialized about it.
He presented the memorial to Huàn,
and Huàn became resentful.
If Xīngzǔ had committed a crime,
then the matter should have been known among the people;
but the people are
calm,
and there is no sign of any such incident.
On the eighteenth day of the ninth month, ten years ago,
Huàn sent thirty guards
who claimed to have an imperial edict to arrest Xīngzǔ and imprison him.
The barbarians of Āndìng
Commandery had previously engaged in embezzlement within the commandery.
Xīngzǔ knew about their illicit gains,
and immediately memorialized it.
Huàn did not investigate.
After Xīngzǔ was arrested,
Huàn still ordered the barbarian commander of the guards to watch
him in prison.
Before Xīngzǔ died,
he secretly sent a message to his family from prison, drawn on a lacquer tray,
saying he was innocent,
and asked them to memorialize requesting to be sent to the capital for an appeal.
He would
die without regret."
It also said:
"Huàn strictly forbade Xīngzǔ from communicating,
intending to find a way
to kill him and silence him."
It also said:
"Huàn's intentions were clear.
Huàn's
third son Biāo, who was with Huàn in the province,
interfered in all matters of right and wrong,
and instigated the secret elimination of Xīngzǔ."
It also said:
"Xīngzǔ's family sent porridge,
into which medicine was put.
After two mouthfuls, he noticed it,
and returned it to the jailer's son,
who ate it and suffered severe diarrhea.
Xīngzǔ shouted loudly, 'There's medicine in the porridge!'
Everyone near the prison
heard it."
It also said:
"Huàn's treatment of Xīngzǔ became more urgent daily,
and there was no justice.
On the twenty-first day of the eleventh month,
Huàn sent a prison official to inform Xīngzǔ's family,
saying Xīngzǔ
had hanged himself in prison.
When the body was released,
his family washed him together,
and saw an injury below Xīngzǔ's neck,
his shoulders swollen and putrefied,
and his groin shattered.
It was truly not Xīngzǔ
who hanged himself.
His family and loyal followers all saw it,
it was not just one person."
Further investigation summoned Yōngzhōu Dūliú Tián Wénxǐ,
who's statement matched Ní's.
Xīngzǔ was bitter and longed for relief in prison.
Having received the imperial decree,
his hopes were just being realized.
How could he
possibly, at this point,
hang himself?
The imperial edict arrived on the nineteenth,
and Xīngzǔ died on the twenty-first.
Reasoning from the evidence,
it is clearly a fabrication.
Since the edict ordered him to be sent down,
Huàn summarily defied the decree.
All the accusations he leveled
came from Huàn's
own ideas.
He slandered the former prime minister, Ruò Chén Xiǎndá,
and defamed imperial affairs.
There is nothing deeper than this.
Biāo secretly followed his father to the frontier,
daring to violate royal law.
Their crimes together merit extreme punishment.
The Emperor sent Zhōngshū Shèrén Lǚ Wénxiǎn and Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Cáo Dàogāng, leading five hundred palace guards, to arrest Huàn.
An edict ordered Zhèn Xī Sīmǎ Cáo Hǔ to travel on foot from Jiānglíng to meet at Xiāngyáng.
Huàn's son Biāo was notoriously fierce and violent,
and Huàn could not control him.
His son-in-law Yīn Ruì, fearing disaster,
said to Huàn:
"Cáo and Lǚ are coming now,
but they are not showing a genuine imperial edict.
I fear it is a conspiracy.
It would be appropriate to apprehend them,
and swiftly memorialize to inform the court."
Huàn accepted this advice.
Biāo immediately led over a thousand men from within the province,
opened the garrison arsenal,
took weapons,
distributed armor,
deployed troops in the south hall,
closed the gates, and resisted.
Huàn's student Zhèng Yǔ prostrated himself and implored Huàn,
begging to go out of the city to welcome the imperial envoys.
[Huàn] said:
"I am not a rebel.
I wish to send a memorial first to explain myself.
I am just afraid that lowlifes like Cáo and Lǚ will take advantage of me,
so I will close the gates and defend myself for now."
Biāo then went out to fight Cáo Hǔ's army.
His subordinate Fàn Hǔ led two hundred men to surrender to the imperial army.
Biāo was defeated and fled back.
The locals rose up in righteousness and attacked the west gate of the province.
Biāo ascended the gate to resist and fought them off.
Meanwhile, Huàn's Sīmǎ Huáng Yáoqǐ and Níngmán Chángshǐ Péi Shūyè raised troops inside the city to attack Huàn.
When Huàn heard the troops had entered,
he returned inside to worship Buddha.
Before he could finish,
the soldiers then beheaded him.
He was
fifty-nine years old.
Biāo and his younger brothers Shuǎng and Bì, along with Yīn Ruì, were all captured
and executed.
An imperial edict stated:
"The rebellious traitor Wáng Huàn
possessed a treacherous and perverse nature
from childhood to adulthood.
Outwardly, he feigned integrity and diligence,
but inwardly, he harbored malice and wickedness.
He brought trouble to his village and neighbors,
and was rejected by the literati.
He was deprived of his literary duties,
yet promoted to prominent positions.
He was sent out to govern Fán'ē,
where his administration and punishments were chaotic and disorderly.
His third son, Biāo, defiantly wielded power and authority,
with father and son holding equal sway.
Thus, when the Níngmán Chángshǐ, Liú Xīngzǔ, faithfully served the state,
consistently offering corrections,
Huàn resented his dissent,
falsely accused him of slander,
angrily imprisoned him,
and then reported it.
We, perceiving Huàn's foolish deceit,
issued an edict to send Xīngzǔ back to the capital,
but Huàn, fearing his treacherous plot would be exposed,
secretly murdered him.
Once his deception became evident,
an imperial envoy was dispatched to investigate.
He then took up arms, ascended the battlements,
and rebelliously resisted the imperial command.
Heavenly might swept down like lightning,
righteous men rose in unison,
and within a short period,
the criminal was captured.
The territory was pacified,
and Hannán was cleared.
Apart from those officials who were complicit in the rebellion
or were temporarily coerced,
all others are to be pardoned."
Huàn's eldest son, the Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ Róng,
and Róng's younger brother, the Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng Chēn,
were executed in the market in the capital.
The remaining grandsons were all pardoned.
Yīn Ruì, courtesy name Wénzǐ,
was a native of Chénjùn.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Jìn Tàicháng Róng.
At the end of Sòng Yuánjiā era,
his grandfather, Yuánsù, was executed for his involvement in the Tàichū affair.
Ruì, still in the womb, was also destined for execution,
but his maternal great-grandfather, Wáng Sēnglǎng, petitioned Xiàowǔ to save him,
and he was spared.
Ruì understood literary meanings
and possessed rhetorical skill.
Sītú Chǔ Yuān thought highly of him,
saying to him:
"Among the Yīn clan since the Jingzhōu period,
none surpasses you."
Ruì straightened his posture and replied:
"The Yīn clan has indeed declined and is not as it once was.
If this statement is untrue,
then it is not worthy of being spoken;
if this statement is true,
then it is even more unbearable to hear."
When Huàn was Yōngzhōu,
he requested Ruì to be his Fǔchángshǐ.
Ruì's cousin,
courtesy name Zhāodù,
was, like Ruì, a descendant of Róng.
He was the grandson of Sòng Sīkōng Jǐngrén.
His father, Dàojīn,
both possessed an ancient demeanor,
and for this reason, they were ridiculed by their contemporaries;
there was more than one such incident.
At the beginning of the Sòng Tàishǐ era,
he served as Dùzhī Shàngshū.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities
for frequently citing his father's illness and his own illness.
Emperor Míng issued an edict stating:
"Yīn Dàojīn has been sickly from birth,
and recently has had no other ailments.
Due to his foolish and lazy habits,
he has long obstructed the pure administration.
He is demoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
also holding the position of Xiàowèi."
He held various prominent and clear official positions,
eventually reaching Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he passed away.
Huàn's younger brother Zhòu's daughter was the consort of Chángshā Wáng Huǎng.
Shìzǔ issued an edict stating:
"Huàn himself fell into rebellion,
but the children of the Chángshā Wáng's consort are all grown,
and Huàn was also adopted into his family.
There may be precedents from previous generations.
She may exceptionally not be divorced."
Huàn's cousin was Huì.
Huì, courtesy name Shúsù, was the son of Sòng Chējì Jiāngjūn Jǐngwén.
At the age of twenty,
he served as Mìshūláng,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and then transferred to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Jǐngwén granted him a higher rank for this,
but Huì did not accept it for a year.
Jǐngwén was enfeoffed as Jiāng'ān Hóu,
and Huì inherited his original peerage,
becoming a Wǔděng Nán of Shǐpíng Xiàn.
He was promoted to Mìshūchéng,
and Sītú Yòuchángshǐ.
At the end of the Yuánhuī era,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Jiànpíng Wáng Zhēngběi Chángshǐ,
Nándōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
Huángménláng,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
When Shìzǔ was Fǔjūn,
Lìbù Shàngshū Zhāng Dài selected Huì as Chángshǐ,
and presented the selection document.
Tàizǔ smiled and said to Dài:
"This can be called a fitting choice."
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì
and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He was sent out to serve as Yìxīng Tàishǒu.
He arbitrarily imprisoned the county official Chén Bóxǐ in Yángxiàn prison,
intending to kill him.
The county magistrate Kǒng Guàn, unaware of the crime,
did not follow Huì's instructions,
and Huì was impeached by the relevant authorities,
serving in a civilian capacity.
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
concurrently holding Xiāoqí,
and then transferred to Cháng (Shǐ) concurrently Shìzhōng.
When Shìzǔ went hunting pheasants,
Huì, being a devout Buddhist,
feigned illness and did not accompany the imperial carriage.
He was transferred to Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and requested to resign due to his mother's old age.
He was reassigned as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Dàsīmǎ Chángshǐ, and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
He was sent out to be Xuānchéng Tàishǒu,
with a salary of two thousand shi.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Tàifù Chángshǐ,
but did not accept the appointment.
He continued as Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Yùzhāng Nèishǐ.
His title was advanced to Zhēnglǔ.
He was again dismissed from office for an offense.
He was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn,
Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ,
Sànqí Chángshì,
following the royal army.
He was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
Piāoqí Chángshǐ,
and promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Tàicháng.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he passed away.
He was fifty-three years old.
His posthumous title was Jìngzǐ.
Huì's daughter married Ānlù Wáng Zǐjìng,
a favored son of Shìzǔ.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
she was taken as consort,
and observed the courtesies of an external father-in-law and mother-in-law.
Shìzǔ sent Wénhuì Tàizǐ to accompany her to Huì's home for a feast and music,
where all the high officials arrived in their ceremonial robes,
considering it a great honor.
Zhāng Chōng, courtesy name Sīyuē,
was a native of Wú of Wújùn.
His father, Jiǎn, was Tōngzhíláng.
Chōng was adopted as heir to his paternal cousin, Shìzhōng Jǐngyìn.
Jǐngyìn's childhood name was Zhā,
and his father, Shào,
had the childhood name Lí.
Sòng Wéndì playfully asked Jǐngyìn:
"How does Zhā compare to Lí?"
Jǐngyìn replied:
"Lí is the patriarch of all fruits;
Chōng 亦少有至性,
辟州主簿,
隨從叔 Yǒng 為將帥,
除綏遠將軍、盱眙太守.
Yǒng 征彭城,
遇寒雪,
軍人足脛凍斷者十七八,
Chōng 足指皆墮.
除尚書駕部郎,
Guìyáng Wáng 征南中兵,
振威將軍.
歷驃騎太尉南中郎參軍,
不拜.
遷征西從事中郎,
通直郎,
Wǔlíng Wáng 北中郎直兵參軍,
長水校尉,
除寧朔將軍,
本官如故.
遷左軍將軍,
加寧朔將軍,
輔國將軍.
Chōng 少從戎事,
朝廷以幹力相待,
故歷處軍校之官.
出為馬頭太守,
徙盱眙太守,
輔國將軍如故.
Yǒngmíng 六年,
遷 Xīyáng Wáng 冠軍司馬.
八年,
為假節、監青冀二州刺史事,
〔一六〕將軍如故.
Chōng 父初卒,
遺命曰:
「祭我必以鄉土所產,
無用牲物. 」
Chōng 在鎮,
四時還吳園中取果菜,
流涕薦焉.
仍轉刺史.
Yùlín 即位,
進號冠軍將軍.
Míngdì 即位,
以 Jìnshòu 太守 Wáng Hóng (（軌）)【範】代 Chōng.
〔一七〕除黃門郎,
加征虜將軍.
Jiànwǔ 二年,
虜寇淮泗,
假 Chōng 節,
都督青冀二州北討諸軍事,
本官如故.
虜并兵攻司州,
【詔】(（除）)青【徐】(（右）)出軍分其兵勢.
〔一八〕Chōng 遣軍主 Sāng Xìzǔ 由渣口攻拔虜 Jiànlíng、Yìmǎ、Hòuqīu 三城,
多所殺獲.
又與 Hóng (（軌）)【範】遣軍主 Cuī Jìyán 襲虜 Jìchéng,
據之.
Chōng 又遣軍主 Dù Sēnghù 攻拔虜 Hǔkēng、Féngshí、Jíqīu 三城,
驅生口輜重還,
至 Kěkōu,
虜救兵至,
緣道要擊,
Sēnghù 力戰,
大破之.
其年,
遷 Lúlíng Wáng 北中郎司馬、加冠軍將軍.
未拜,
Fēngchéng Gōng Yáo Chāng 為豫州,
上慮寇【難】未已,
〔一九〕徙 Chōng 為征虜長史、南梁郡太守.
Yǒngtài 元年,
除 Jiāngxià Wáng 前軍長史.
Dōnghūn 即位,
出為 Jiàn'ān Wáng 征虜長史、輔國將軍、江夏內史,
行郢州府州事.
Yǒngyuán 元年,
遷持節、督豫州軍事、豫州刺史,
代 Péi Shūyè.
竟不行.
明年,
遷督南 Yuréng Qīngjì 五州、輔國將軍、南 Yuréng Zhōu Cìshǐ,
持節如故.
會司州刺史 Shēn Xīzǔ 卒,
以 Chōng 為督司州軍事、冠軍將軍、司州刺史.
Péi Shūyè 以壽春降虜,
又遷 Chōng 為督南 Yuréng Qīngjì 五州、南 Yuréng Zhōu Cìshǐ,
持節、將軍如故.
竝未拜.
Cuī Huìjǐng 事平,
徵 Jiàn'ān Wáng Bǎo Yín 還都,
以 Chōng 為督郢司二州、郢州刺史,
持節、將軍如故.
一歲之中,
頻授四州,
至此受任.
其冬,
進征虜將軍.
封 Dìngxiāng Hóu,
食邑千戶.
Liáng Wáng 義師起,
Dōnghūn 遣驍騎將軍 Xuē Yuánsì、制局監 Jì Róngbó 領兵及粮運百四十餘船送 Chōng,
使拒西師.
Yuánsì 等懲 Liú Shānyáng 之敗,
疑 Chōng 不敢進,
停住 Xiàkǒu Pǔ.
聞義師將至,
Yuánsì、Róngbó 相率入郢城.
時 Jìnglín Tàishǒu Fáng Sēngjì 被代還至 Yǐng,
Dōnghūn 敕 Sēngjì 留守 Lúshān,
除驍騎將軍.
Sēngjì 謂 Chōng 曰:
「臣雖未荷朝廷深恩,
〔二０〕實蒙先帝厚澤.
蔭其樹者不折其枝,
實欲微立塵効. 」
Chōng 深相許諾,
共結盟誓.
乃分部拒守.
遣軍主 Sūn Lèzǔ 數千人助 Sēngjì 據 Lúshān Àn 立城壘.
明年二月,
Liáng Wáng 出 Miǎnkǒu,
圍 Lúshān Chéng.
遣軍主 Cáo Jǐngzōng 等過江攻 Yǐngchéng,
未及盡濟,
Chōng 遣中兵參軍 Chén Guāngjìng 等開門出擊,
為義師所破,
Guāngjìng 戰死,
Chōng 固守不出.
Jǐngzōng 於是據 Shíqiáo Pǔ,
連軍相續,
下至 Jiāhú.
Dōnghūn 遣軍主 Bāxī Zǐtóng 二郡太守 Wú Zǐyáng、Guāngzǐ、Lǐ Wénzhāo、Chén Hǔyá 等十三軍援 Yǐng,
至 Jiāhú 不得進,
乃築城舉烽,
城內亦舉火應之.
而內外各自保,
〔二一〕不能相救.
Chōng 病死,
Yuánsì、Róngbó 與 Chōng 子 Zī 及長史 Jiāngxià Nèishǐ Chéng Mào 固守.
Dōnghūn 詔贈 Chōng 散騎常侍、護軍將軍.
假 Yuánsì 子陽節.
江水暴長,
Jiāhú Chéng 淹漬,
義師乘高艦攻之,
Zǐyáng 等大敗散.
〔二二〕Lúshān Chéng 乏粮,
軍人於磯頭捕細魚供食,
密治輕船,
將奔 Xiàkǒu.
Liáng Wáng 命偏軍斷其取路,
防備越逸.
Fáng Sēngjì 病死,
Sūn Lèzǔ 窘,
以城降.
Yǐngchéng 被圍二百餘日,
士庶病死者七八百家.
〔二三〕Lúshān 既敗,
Chéng Mào 及 Yuánsì 等議降,
使 Zī 為書與 Liáng Wáng.
Chōng 故吏 Qīngzhōu Zhìzhōng Fáng Chángyú 謂 Zī 曰:
「前使君忠貫昊天,
操逾松竹.
郎君但當端坐畫一,
以荷析薪.
若天運不與,
幅巾待命,
以下從使君.
今若隨諸人之計,
非唯郢州士女失高山之望,
亦恐彼所不取也. 」
Lúshān 陷後二日,
Yuánsì 等以 Yǐngchéng 降.
Dōnghūn 以 Chéng Mào 為督郢司二州、輔國將軍、郢州刺史,
Yuánsì 為督雍梁南北秦四州郢州之竟陵司州之隨郡、冠軍將軍、雍州刺史,
竝持節.
時郢魯二城 (（以）)【已】降,
〔二四〕死者相積,
竟無叛散.
時以 Chōng 及 Fáng Sēngjì 比 Zāng Hóng 之被圍也.
贈 Sēngjì Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
時 Xīncài Tàishǒu Xí Qiān,
Yǒngmíng 中為中書郎 Wáng Róng 所薦.
父 Gōngmù,
鎮西司馬,
為 Yúfù Hóu 所害.
至是 Qiān 鎮 Pénchéng,
聞義師東下,
曰:
「我家世忠貞,
殞死不二. 」
為 Chén Bózhī 所殺.
The imperial historian says: Shí Què (石碏) abandoned his son,
a great warning against sacrificing one's kin;
Bào Yǒng (鮑永) submitted late,
understanding the principle of serving new masters.
Wáng Huàn (王奐) was truly without duplicity,
his actions confirmed by strict regulations;
Zhāng Chōng (張沖) did not comprehend the heavenly will,
persisting in misguided righteousness.
The reasons for their peril differed,
but the outcome of their downfall was the same.
A eulogy says: The king dwelled in the northern pastures,
his son unable to establish his house.
Ultimately disrupting the imperial order,
overthrowing this illustrious lineage.
Zhāng (張)'s fort was desperately defended,
deaths like tangled hemp.
His awakening came too late,
his understanding still distant.
除青右(疑)校勘記
Biographies Thirty-one: Wén (文) Two Kings, Míng (明) Seven Kings
Crown Prince Wénhuì (文惠) had four sons: Empress Ān (安) bore Yùlín Wáng Zhāo Yè (鬱林王昭業);
Court lady Xǔ (許) bore Hǎilíng Gōng Wáng Zhāo Wén (海陵恭王昭文);
Lady Chén (陳) bore Bālíng Wáng Zhāo Xiù (巴陵王昭秀);
Lady Chǔ (褚) bore Guìyáng Wáng Zhāo Càn (桂陽王昭粲).
Bālíng Wáng Zhāo Xiù (巴陵王昭秀), courtesy name Huái Shàng (懷尚),
was the third son of the Crown Prince.
During Yǒngmíng (永明)'s reign,
he was enfeoffed as Qǔjiāng Gōng (曲江公),
with fifteen hundred households.
In the tenth year,
he became Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) and Jìyáng Tàishǒu (濟陽太守).
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Línhǎi Jùnwáng (臨海郡王),
with two thousand households.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
he became Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Jīng Yōng Yì Níng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Qī Zhōu Jūnshì (都督荊雍益寧梁南北秦七州軍事), Xī Zhōnglángjiàng (西中郎將), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興),
he was summoned to be Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
to guard the capital.
Yǒngjiā Wáng Zhāo Càn (永嘉王昭粲) replaced him.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武) during Míng Dì (明帝)'s reign,
Tōngzhí Chángshì Yǔ Tánlóng (通直常侍庾曇隆) reported:
"When Zhōu (周) established its capital,
the Son of Heaven settled the people within the imperial domain;
when Hàn (漢) made Xiányáng (咸陽) its capital,
the Sānfǔ (三輔) served as guardians of the state.
When the Middle Jìn (晉) moved south,
the circumstances changed and their prestige waned.
Many nearby prefectures and famous states
had their own enfeoffments.
When Sòng Wǔ (宋武) founded the dynasty,
he emulated the classical system,
and within the divine land,
there were no longer separate enfeoffments.
However, in the last years of Xiàowǔ (孝武),
he distributed lands to favored sons,
indulging private affection,
which violated the standards of instruction.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
the nobility of the emperor's younger brothers was specifically established,
which I humbly believe is not ancient.
When a sagely ruler governs the realm,
the old rites are prioritized.
The boundaries of the imperial domain
should follow the former system.
The bestowal of land and appointment
should all be outside the capital."
An imperial edict ordered the Shàngshū (尚書) to deliberate on it.
That winter,
Zhāo Xiù (昭秀) was re-enfeoffed as Bālíng Wáng (巴陵王).
He was killed in the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰),
at the age of sixteen.
Guìyáng Wáng Zhāo Càn (桂陽王昭粲)
was the fourth son of the Crown Prince.
When Yùlín (鬱林) ascended,
he was enfeoffed as Yǒngjiā Jùnwáng (永嘉郡王) as an imperial brother,
and Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史).
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興),
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Jīng Yōng Yì Níng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Qī Zhōu Jūnshì (都督荊雍益寧梁南北秦七州軍事), Xī Zhōnglángjiàng (西中郎將), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
When Míng Dì (明帝) ascended,
he wanted to appoint Wénxǐ Gōng Yáo Xīn (聞喜公遙欣) as Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and transferred Zhāo Càn (昭粲) to be Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍),
and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
he was re-enfeoffed as Guìyáng Wáng (桂陽王).
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Tàicháng (太常),
retaining his generalship.
He was killed in the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰),
at the age of eight.
Míng Dì (明帝) had eleven sons: Empress Jìng (敬) bore Dōnghūn Hóu Bǎo Juǎn (東昏侯寶卷),
Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎo Xuán (江夏王寶玄),
Póyáng Wáng Bǎo Yín (鄱陽王寶寅),
and Hé Dì (和帝);
Consort Yīn (殷) bore Bālíng Yǐnwáng Bǎo Yì (巴陵隱王寶義) and Jìnxī Wáng Bǎo Sōng (晉熙王寶嵩);
Consort Yuán (袁) bore Lúlíng Wáng Bǎo Yuán (廬陵王寶源);
Consort Guǎn (管) bore Shàolíng Wáng Bǎo Yōu (邵陵王寶攸);
Lady Xǔ (許) bore Guìyáng Wáng Bǎo Zhēn (桂陽王寶貞).
The rest died young.
Bālíng Yǐnwáng Bǎo Yì (巴陵隱王寶義), courtesy name Zhì Yǒng (智勇),
was the eldest son of Míng Dì (明帝).
His original name was Míng Jī (明基).
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
he was appointed Chíjié (持節), Dūdū Yáng Nán Xúzhōu Jūnshì (都督揚南徐州軍事), Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史).
He was enfeoffed as Jìn'ān Jùnwáng (晉安郡王),
with three thousand households.
Bǎo Yì (寶義) had a disabling illness from childhood,
making him unfit for public life.
Thus, he was merely given official appointments,
and Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáo Guāng (始安王遙光) replaced him.
Bǎo Yì (寶義) was transferred to Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍),
commanding troops and establishing aides,
stationed at Shítóu (石頭).
In the second year,
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Nán Xúzhōu Jūnshì (都督南徐州軍事), Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (鎮北將軍), and Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史).
When Dōnghūn (東昏) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn (征北大將軍),
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and granted guards.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
he was granted twenty guards with swords.
When Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáo Guāng (始安王遙光) was executed,
he became Dūdū Yáng Nán Xú Èr Zhōu Jūnshì (都督揚南徐二州軍事), Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史),
retaining his Chíjié (持節) status.
The eastern palace suffered from war damage,
its buildings burned and ruined.
The Emperor was busy building new palaces
and had no time for repairs.
Bǎo Yì (寶義) was stationed at Xīzhōu (西州).
In the third year,
he was promoted to Sītú (司徒).
When Hé Dì (和帝)'s Xītái (西臺) was established,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sīkōng (司空),
retaining his Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū (都督), and Cìshǐ (刺史) positions.
When Liáng Wáng (梁王) established the capital,
Empress Dowager Xuāndé (宣德) ordered Bǎo Yì (寶義) to be Tàiwèi (太尉),
also leading Sītú (司徒).
The imperial edict stated:
"The transformation that speaks without words
manifests itself from afar."
People at the time all said this was a true record.
When Liáng (梁) received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Xièmù Xiàn Gōng (謝沐縣公),
and soon after enfeoffed as Bālíng Jùnwáng (巴陵郡王),
to offer sacrifices to the former Qí (齊) imperial house.
He died during the Tiānjiān (天監) reign.
Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎo Xuán (江夏王寶玄), courtesy name Zhì Shēn (智深),
was the third son of Míng Dì (明帝).
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (征虜將軍),
leading the defense of Shítóu (石頭),
and enfeoffed as Jiāngxià Jùnwáng (江夏郡王).
He was then sent out as Chíjié (持節), Dūdū Yǐng Sī Èr Zhōu Jūnshì (都督郢司二州軍事), Xī Zhōnglángjiàng (西中郎將), and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (郢州刺史).
In the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰),
he returned as Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍),
leading the defense of Shítóu (石頭).
Before he could be formally appointed,
Dōnghūn (東昏) ascended the throne,
and he was promoted to Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍).
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
he was further promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
replacing Jìn'ān Wáng Bǎo Yì (晉安王寶義) as Shǐchíjié (使持節), Dūdū Nán Xú Yǔn Èr Zhōu Jūnshì (都督南徐兗二州軍事), and Nán Xú Yǔn Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ (南徐兗二州刺史),
retaining his generalship.
Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) married the daughter of Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì (尚書令徐孝嗣) as his consort.
When Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣) was executed and the marriage dissolved,
the young emperor sent two young women to him.
Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) harbored resentment,
and secretly formed a different plan.
The next year,
Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) raised an army,
returning to Guǎnglín (廣陵),
and sent envoys to declare Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) as their leader.
Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) beheaded his envoy,
and consequently mobilized his officers and soldiers to defend the city.
The Emperor sent cavalry commander Qī Píng (戚平) and external supervisor Huáng Línfū (黃林夫) to assist in defending Jīngkǒu (京口).
When Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧jǐng) was about to cross the river,
Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) secretly conspired with him,
killing Sīmǎ Kǒng Jīn (司馬孔矜), Diǎnqiān Lǚ Chéngxù (典籤呂承緒), and Qī Píng (戚平) and Huáng Línfū (黃林夫),
and opened the gates to welcome Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧jǐng).
He ordered Chángshǐ Shěn Yìzhī (長史沈佚之) and Zīyì Liǔ Chéng (諮議柳憕) to divide the troops,
riding in eight palanquins,
holding crimson banners,
following Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧jǐng) to the capital,
stopping at the East City.
Many common people went to join them.
When Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧jǐng)'s rebellion failed,
the lists of court officials and commoners who joined Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) and Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧jǐng)'s army were seized.
The Emperor ordered them to be burned,
saying:
"If Jiāngxià (江夏) was like this,
how can others be blamed?"
Bǎo Xuán (寶玄) fled for several days before emerging.
The Emperor summoned him into the inner hall,
wrapped him in a screen,
and ordered dozens of lesser officials to beat drums and blow horns, riding around outside it.
He sent someone to tell Bǎo Xuán (寶玄):
"You surrounded me similarly recently."
A few days later, he killed him.
Gāozōng was Yùzhōu,
Shūyè was Right Army Sīmǎ,
additionally Jianwēi Jiāngjūn and Jūnmǔ,
governor of Chénliú Tàishǒu.
In the seventh year,
he was Wáng Jìngzé’s Zhēngxī Sīmǎ,
with the titles Jiāngjūn and Jūnmǔ as before.
He transferred with the administration to Piáojì.
He served as an assistant in Shòuchūn for several years.
In the ninth year,
he was Níngmán Chángshǐ and Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu.
When the matter of the Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Huàn’s rebellion occurred,
Shūyè led his troops in an uprising within the city.
The Emperor, seeing his competence,
retained him as Jìn'ān Wáng’s Zhēngběi Zīyì,
commanding the Zhōngbīng,
Fúfēng Tàishǒu,
then promoted to Jìnxī Wáng’s Guānjūn Sīmǎ.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
he was given the additional title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
with his Sīmǎ position unchanged.
Shūyè had engaged in affairs with Gāozōng early on,
and when Gāozōng became regent,
he heavily relied on Shūyè as a trusted confidant,
sending him to lead troops in surprise attacks against various border garrisons.
Shūyè served wholeheartedly and diligently.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians besieged Xúzhōu.
Shūyè, as a Jūnmǔ, was assigned to Right Guard General Xiāo Tǎnzhī to provide relief.
Shūyè attacked two cities outside the barbarian’s Huái stockade,
capturing them.
Many of the enemy troops drowned themselves in the water.
He was appointed Huángmén Shìláng.
The Emperor, seeing Shūyè’s meritorious loyalty,
enfeoffed him as the Earl of Wǔchāng County,
with five hundred households.
He then became Chíjìe, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xúzhōu, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the fourth year,
the barbarian lord invaded north of Miǎn,
and the Emperor ordered Shūyè to reinforce Yōngzhōu.
Shūyè memorialized:
“The northern people are not keen on distant campaigns;
they only enjoy raiding and attacking the barbarian borders.
Then the bandits in Yōng and Sī [provinces]
will naturally disperse,
without the need to mobilize people for distant travel.”
The Emperor agreed.
Shūyè led his army to attack Hóngchéng,
capturing over four thousand men and women.
He was transferred to Supervisor of Yùzhōu, Fúguó Jiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Chíjìe as before.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
Shūyè, leading Sūn Lìngzhōng, the Tàishǒu of Dōnghǎi, Liú Sīxiào, the Tàishǒu of Xīnchāng, Lǐ Sēnghù, the Tàishǒu of Mǎtóu, and others, a force of fifty thousand men, besieged Wōyáng.
This was the town governed by the barbarian’s Southern Yùnzhōu,
one hundred twenty *lǐ* from Péngchéng.
The false Cìshǐ of Yùnzhōu, Mèng Biǎo, held his ground and resisted.
Shūyè besieged him,
piling up the severed heads to a height of five *zhàng*,
to display to those within the city.
He also sent Jūnmǔ Xiāo Guī and Chéng Bǎozhēn to separately attack Lóngkàng Garrison,
which was the barbarian’s Mǎtóu Commandery.
The barbarians closed their gates and defended themselves.
The false Xúzhōu Cìshǐ, the Prince of Guǎnglíng, leading twenty thousand men
and five thousand cavalry,
arrived at Lóngkàng.
Guī and the others resisted but were no match.
Shūyè, with over thirty thousand men, assisted them,
attacking the barbarians from several directions.
The barbarians had just arrived
and had not yet established their camp,
so they suffered a great defeat.
The Prince of Guǎnglíng fled with several tens of horsemen,
and the government forces pursued and captured his banner.
The barbarians again sent the false generals Liú Zǎo and Gāo Cōng to follow.
Shūyè led his army to meet and defeat them.
In a second battle,
ten thousand heads were cut off,
and three thousand captives were taken.
Weapons, donkeys, horses, silk, and cloth amounted to tens of millions.
When the barbarian lord heard of the defeat of the Prince of Guǎnglíng,
he sent the false Grand Supervisor Wáng Sù and Grand General Yáng Dàyǎn with over one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry to relieve Wōyáng.
Seeing the enemy’s overwhelming numbers,
Shūyè abandoned his army at night and fled.
The next day,
the government forces collapsed and fled.
The barbarians pursued them,
inflicting countless casualties and injuries,
stopping only at dusk.
Shūyè returned to defend Wōkǒu,
and the Emperor sent an envoy to comfort and commend him.
When Gāozōng died,
Shūyè returned to his garrison.
When the Young Emperor ascended the throne,
he executed high officials,
and disturbances repeatedly broke out in the capital.
Shūyè ascended the Shòuchūn city wall, looked north towards the Féishuǐ,
and said to his subordinates:
“Do you wish for wealth and honor?
I say wealth and honor can be achieved.”
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nán Yùn, Qīng, and Jì five provinces, and Nán Yùnzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his Jiāngjūn and Chíjìe titles as before.
Shūyè saw that the times were in chaos
and was unwilling to remain in a close border region.
The imperial court suspected him of wanting to rebel.
Shūyè also sent envoys to inquire about news from the capital.
Thus, dissenting opinions grew stronger.
Shūyè’s nephews, Zhí and Yáng, were both Zhíhé,
serving inside the palace.
Fearing disaster,
they abandoned their mother and fled to Shòuyáng,
persuading Shūyè that the court would certainly launch a surprise attack.
Xú Shìbiāo and others feared Shūyè’s external rebellion,
and sent his kinsman, the Zhōngshū Shèrén Péi Chángmù, to convey an imperial decree,
promising to let him retain his current position.
Shūyè was still uneasy,
and Zhí and others ceaselessly urged him.
Shūyè, anxious and fearful,
asked Liáng Wáng for advice.
Liáng Wáng told him to send his family back to the capital,
and there would naturally be no trouble.
Shūyè then sent his son Fēnzhī and others back to the capital as hostages.
The next year,
he was promoted to the title Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
Reports of Shūyè’s rebellion were ceaseless,
and Fēnzhī became even more fearful,
fleeing again to Shòuchūn.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to suppress Shūyè,
sending Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Cuī Huìjǐng and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Yì to lead a combined land and naval force west to attack,
stopping their army at Xiǎoxiàn.
Shūyè was gravely ill.
Zhí requested aid from the Wèi barbarians,
sending Fēnzhī as a hostage.
Shūyè soon died.
The barbarians sent Grand Generals Lǐ Chǒu and Yáng Dàyǎn with over two thousand cavalry into Shòuchūn.
Initially,
the barbarian lord Yuán Hóng arrived at Shòuchūn in the second year of Jiànwǔ.
His subordinates urged him to attack the city.
Hóng said:
“There is no need to attack;
it will surrender later.”
Zhí and others all returned to Luòyáng.
Cuī Huìjǐng, courtesy name Jūnshān,
was a native of Wǔchéng, Hédōng [Prefecture].
His grandfather Gòu
served as Fèngcháoqǐng.
His father, Xìzhī, was a Zhōu Biéjià.
Huìjǐng first served as a Guózǐ Xuéshēng.
In the Tàishǐ era of Sòng,
he successively held positions up to Yuánwàiláng,
gradually moving to Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
When Tàizǔ was in Huái'yīn,
Huìjǐng and his clansman Zǔ Sī simultaneously allied themselves with him.
Tàizǔ wished to cross north to Guǎnglíng
and had Huìjǐng prepare boats at Táo Jiā Hòuzhǔ.
Although the plan was not realized,
he became close to Tàizǔ because of this.
He was appointed Qiánjūn.
After Shěn Yǒushì’s affair was settled,
he was sent out as Wǔlíng Wáng’s Ānxī Sīmǎ and Hédōng Tàishǒu,
tasked with defending Shǎnxī.
In the third year of Shēngmíng,
when Yùzhāng Wáng was Jīngzhōu,
Huìjǐng was retained as Zhènxī Sīmǎ,
concurrently Zīyì,
with his Tàishǒu position as before.
When Tàizǔ received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Lè'ān County,
with three hundred households.
Yùzhāng Wáng sent Huìjǐng to present a memorial expressing congratulations and return to the capital.
Tàizǔ summoned him,
showing special care and hospitality.
He was transferred to Píngxī Fǔ Sīmǎ and Nánjùn Nèishǐ.
He was then promoted to Nánmán Chángshǐ,
additionally Fúguó Jiāngjūn,
with his Nèishǐ position as before.
Previously, the Man Commandery’s assistants
were of very low rank and emolument.
From this time, their selection began to be highly regarded.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
the barbarians mobilized.
The Prince of Yùzhāng sent Huìjǐng with three thousand men to garrison Fāngchéng,
as an auxiliary force for Sīzhōu.
When the barbarians retreated,
Lǐ Wūnú, a rebel in Liángzhōu, had not yet been pacified.
Huìjǐng was made Chíjíe, Dūdū Liáng Nánběi Qín Shā Sìzhōu Jūnshì, Xīróng Xiàowèi, and Liáng Nánqín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general rank remaining as before.
An imperial edict ordered Jīngzhōu to provide supplies and dispatch him,
assigning a thousand fully armored men,
who marched from Xiāngyáng to the garrison.
Initially,
Wūnú had been repeatedly defeated by government troops,
and fled into the Dī territory.
He took advantage of opportunities to emerge,
harassing Liáng and Hàn,
and occupying Guānchéng.
He sent envoys to Jīngzhōu to request surrender,
but the Prince of Yùzhāng refused.
He then dispatched the Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wáng Túnán to lead the Yìzhōu army from Jiàngé to outflank and attack him,
inflicting a great defeat.
Wūnú returned to hold Wǔxīng.
Huìjǐng mobilized the troops of Hànzhōng,
and advanced to garrison Báimǎ.
He sent a detachment to attack in concert with Túnán,
and Wūnú was utterly defeated,
then fled to Wǔxīng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
While in the province, he accumulated
many precious goods and treasures.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
he returned with his original title.
He was transferred to Huángmén Láng,
and appointed Yǔlín Jiān.
The following year,
he was transferred to Suíwáng Dōngzhōngláng Sīmǎ,
and given the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
He was sent out as Chíjíe, Dū Sīzhōu Jūnshì, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Upon the death of his mother,
an imperial edict ordered him to resume his former post.
Whenever Huìjǐng left a province,
he would invariably [exhaust] his resources to make offerings,
amounting to millions.
Shìzǔ praised him for this.
In the ninth year,
he was recalled with his original title,
transferred to Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài,
and given the additional title of Tōngzhí Chángshì.
The following year,
he was transferred to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and given the additional title of Jǐshìzhōng.
At this time, the barbarian general was about to invade the south,
so the Emperor sent Huìjǐng out as Chíjíe, Dū Yùzhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Xīyáng Sīzhōu Zhī Rǔnán Èrjùn Zhūjūnshì, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Huìjǐng, seeing the young emperor newly enthroned,
secretly colluded with the barbarians,
causing suspicion and fear in the court.
When Gāozōng began to assist in governance,
he sent the Prince of Liáng to Shòuchūn to comfort him.
Huìjǐng sent a secret memorial expressing his loyalty and encouraging the new emperor.
He was recalled,
and made Sànqí Chángshì,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the barbarians raided Xú and Yù.
Huìjǐng, in his current office, was granted a commander's staff to proceed to Zhōnglí,
under the command of Wáng Xuánmiǎo.
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Dùzhī Shàngshū,
and appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài.
In winter,
the barbarian lord attacked the five prefectures north of Miǎn.
Huìjǐng was granted a commander's staff,
and led twenty thousand troops,
and one thousand cavalry,
towards Xiāngyáng.
All the troops of Yōngzhōu were placed under his command.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
Huìjǐng arrived in Xiāngyáng,
but the five prefectures had already fallen.
Huìjǐng was given the additional title of Píngběi Jiāngjūn,
appointed staff,
and had troops detached to assist in garrisoning Fánchéng.
Huìjǐng stationed at Wōkǒucūn,

and advanced to Dèngchéng with the Crown Prince's Zhōngshùzǐ, the Prince of Liáng, and army commanders, the former Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Dǒng Zhòngmín, Liú Shānyáng, Péi Yáng, Fù Fǎxiàn, and over five thousand others.
The forward cavalry returned,
reporting that the barbarian army was about to arrive.
Soon,
tens of thousands of cavalry were seen approaching together.
Huìjǐng held the south gate,
and the Prince of Liáng held the north gate,
ordering all troops to ascend the city walls.
At this time, Huìjǐng and others had eaten a field meal and marched lightly,
all showing signs of hunger and fear.
Three guests from the northern residence in the army,
fled and surrendered to the barbarians,
fully informing them.
The barbarian pseudo-Dūdū Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn Péngchéngwáng Yuán Xié dispatched pseudo-Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Yuán Dǒu to proceed to the southeast of the city,
cutting off Huìjǐng's retreat.
Pseudo-Sīmǎ Mèng Bīn went to the east of the city,
and pseudo-Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Bō Zhèng garrisoned north of the city,
firing arrows into the city.
The Prince of Liáng wanted to sally forth and fight,
but Huìjǐng said:
"The barbarians do not besiege cities at night;
they will naturally leave when dusk falls."
However, the barbarian forces grew stronger.
Huìjǐng withdrew his troops from the south gate.
The various armies did not inform each other,
and retreated in a disorderly rush.
The barbarian army entered from the north gate.
Liú Shānyáng and several hundred of his部曲 fought to the death to cover the rear.
The barbarians sent over a hundred armored horses to charge and seize Shānyáng.
Shānyáng ordered his archers to shoot them,
and three men fell from their horses.
He personally killed over ten men,
but could not hold them back,
and fought and retreated.
Huìjǐng exited southwards past Nàogōu.
The soldiers trampled upon each other,
and all the bridges were broken.
The barbarian army shot at them from both sides of the road.
The army commander Fù Fǎxiàn was killed,
and those who fell into the ditch died, piling up on each other.
Shānyáng took padded staffs to fill the ditch,
and crossed over them to escape.
The barbarian lord led the main force to pursue them.
In the late afternoon,
the barbarian lord reached north of Miǎn,
and surrounded army commander Liú Shānyáng.
Shānyáng held the city and fought fiercely.
By evening,
the barbarians finally retreated.
The various armies were terrified,
and that night, all boarded boats and returned to Xiāngyáng.
When Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
Huìjǐng was reappointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
with Píngběi and his acting commander's staff remaining as before.
He had not yet formally accepted the appointment.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and soon given the additional title of Shìzhōng.
When Chén Xiǎndá rebelled,
Huìjǐng was given the additional title of Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
Dūdū Zhòngjūnshì,
and stationed at Zhōngtáng.
At that time, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Xú Shìbiāo wielded exclusive power and issued commands,
while Huìjǐng merely filled the post.
After the Emperor executed his generals and ministers,
and all the old officials were gone,
Huìjǐng, considering his age and high position,
felt increasingly insecure.
The following year,
Péi Shūyè surrendered Shòuchūn to the barbarians.
Huìjǐng was reassigned Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
with his acting commander's staff, Shìzhōng, and Hùjūn remaining as before,
and led his army by water to conquer Shòuyáng.
His army was stationed at Báixià.
As they were about to depart,
the Emperor's long palanquin cleared the path and he went out of Lángxié City to see him off.
The Emperor, in military attire, sat on the city tower,
and summoned Huìjǐng, who entered the enclosure alone on horseback,
with no one following him.
After exchanging only a few words,
he bowed and departed.
When Huìjǐng was able to leave,
he was very pleased.
His son Jué was Zhíhé Jiāngjūn.
Huìjǐng secretly agreed with him: in the fourth month, when Huìjǐng reached Guǎnglíng,
Jué would immediately flee.
Huìjǐng passed Guǎnglíng by several tens of li,
and summoned all the army commanders, saying:
"I have received the deep favor of three emperors,
and bear the heavy trust of a guardian.
The young emperor is confused and reckless,
and the court is in chaos.
To be in peril and not uphold it,
the responsibility lies with us today.
I wish to jointly achieve great merit with you all,
to secure the imperial ancestral altars.
What do you say?"
Everyone responded in agreement.
Thereupon, he turned his army back to Guǎnglíng.
Sīmǎ Cuī Gōngzǔ, who was guarding Guǎnglíng City,
opened the gates and let them in.
When the Emperor heard of the change,
he appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Zuǒ Xīngshèng as acting commander,
to oversee all the land and water forces in the capital region.
Huìjǐng stayed for two days,
then gathered his troops and crossed the river to Jīngkǒu.
The Prince of Jiāngxià, Bǎoxuán, also acted as an insider,
combining the forces of the two garrisons,
and supporting Bǎoxuán as they advanced towards the capital.
The court dispatched Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Zhāng Fóhù, Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Xú Yuánchēng, Túnqí Xiàowèi Yáo Jǐngzhēn, Xī Zhōngláng Cānjūn Xú Jǐngzhì, Yóudàng 【Jūn】zhǔ Dǒng Bózhēn,
and Qíguān Huán Língfú, among others, to occupy Zhú Lǐ and build several forts.
Bǎo Xuán sent a message to Fóhù saying:
"I am returning to the court myself.
Why do you insist on obstructing me?"
Fóhù replied:
"We, humble men, have received great favor from the state,
and have been ordered to establish small garrisons here.
If Your Highness returns to court,
simply pass through directly;
how would we dare to interfere or block you?"
Thereupon, they shot at Huìjǐng's army,
and a battle ensued.
Huìjǐng's son Jué and Cuī Gōngzǔ led the vanguard,
all of whom were Cáng-Chǔ people skilled in warfare;
they also traveled light and did not cook meals,
carrying wine and meat as provisions on several boats along the river.
Whenever they saw smoke and fire rising from the court army's forts,
