they would attack with full force,
preventing the court army from getting food,
thus starving them.
Yuánchēng and others discussed surrendering,
but Fóhù refused.
On the twelfth day,
Gōngzǔ and others attacked again,
and the fort fell.
Fóhù fled on a single horse,
was pursued, caught, and beheaded.
Xú Yuánchēng surrendered,
and the remaining military commanders all died.
Huìjǐng arrived at Línyí,
ordering Lǐ Yùzhī to open the bridge and cut off the road.
Huìjǐng captured and killed him.
The court dispatched Zhōnglǐngjūn Wáng Yíng to command the various armies,
to occupy Hútóu and build a stronghold,
which stretched up to the western peak of Jiǎng Shān,
comprising tens of thousands of armored soldiers.
Huìjǐng reached Zháchéng.
Wàn Fù'ér of Zhútáng, skilled in archery and hunting,
capable of catching 【tigers】,
presented himself to Huìjǐng, saying:
"Now all the flat roads are blocked by the court army,
making advance impossible.
The only option is to ascend from the Dragon's Tail of Jiǎng Shān,
and catch them by surprise."
Huìjǐng followed his advice,
sending over a thousand men to ascend the mountain in single file,
descending from the western peak at night,
drumming and shouting as they approached the city.
The court army was terrified,
and immediately scattered.
The Emperor also dispatched Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Zuǒ Xīngshèng to lead thirty thousand men from within the palace,
to resist Huìjǐng at Běilí Mén,
but they retreated at the mere sight of him.
Huìjǐng led his army into Lèyóu 【Yuàn】.
〔一０〕 Gōngzǔ led more than ten light cavalry horses and charged into Běiyè Mén,
then came out again,
as the palace gates were all closed.
Huìjǐng led his forces to besiege it.
Thereupon, the cities of Dōngfǔ, Shítou, 〔一一〕 Báixià, and Xīntíng all collapsed.
Zuǒ Xīngshèng fled,
unable to enter the palace,
and hid in a reed boat on the shore of the Huái River.
Huìjǐng captured and killed him.
The palace sent out troops to attack,
but they did not succeed.
Huìjǐng burned the Lántái government offices to create a battlefield.
The garrison commander, Wèiwèi Xiāo Chàng, stationed at Nányè Mén, managed the city's defense,
responding to attacks from all directions,
which gradually stabilized the morale of the populace.
Huìjǐng claimed to have the order of Xuāndé Tàihòu,
and deposed the Emperor as the King of Wú.
At that time, Bá Língwáng Zhāo Zhòu had previously fled among the common people,
and came to surrender to Huìjǐng.
Huìjǐng's intention then shifted towards him,
so he hesitated, unsure of whom to enthrone.
After the victory at Zhú Lǐ,
Jué and Gōngzǔ vied for merit,
which Huìjǐng could not decide.
Gōngzǔ advised Huìjǐng to shoot incendiary arrows to burn Běiyè Lóu.
Huìjǐng considered that the great undertaking was nearing completion,
and if it were to be rebuilt later,
it would require much expense and effort,
so he did not follow his plan.
He was fond of discussing philosophy
and also understood Buddhist principles.
He stayed at Fǎlún Sì,
engaging in high-minded discussions with guests.
Gōngzǔ harbored deep resentment and disappointment.
Previously, Wèiwèi Xiāo Yì was Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
marching from Lìyáng to Shòuyáng.
The Emperor sent a secret envoy to inform him.
Yì led several thousand men, including military commanders Hú Sōng and Lǐ Jūshì, to cross the river from Cǎishí,
encamping at Yuèchéng.
They lit fires,
and inside the court city, drums sounded and shouts of celebration arose.
Gōngzǔ had previously advised Huìjǐng to send two thousand men to cut off the army on the western bank,
preventing them from crossing.
Huìjǐng believed that with the city falling within days,
the external relief would naturally disperse.
Now, Gōngzǔ requested to attack the righteous army,
but was again refused.
Instead, Jué was sent with several thousand elite soldiers to cross to the southern bank.
The righteous army advanced and fought at dawn,
engaging in several clashes.
The soldiers fought to the death,
and Jué was utterly defeated.
Over two thousand people drowned in the Huái River.
Jué retreated on a single horse,
opening the pontoon bridge to block the Huái River.
That night,
Cuī Gōngzǔ and the valiant general Liú 【Líng】yùn went to the city to surrender.
〔一二〕 Huìjǐng's forces' morale disintegrated,
so he took a few trusted confidants and secretly left,
intending to cross the river northwards.
The various armies north of the city were unaware,
and continued to resist.
Troops from within the city sallied out,
killing several hundred people.
When the righteous army crossed the northern bank,
Huìjǐng's remaining forces all fled.
Huìjǐng's siege of the city lasted twelve days in total,
but his troops were scattered throughout the capital,
not forming proper encampments.
When he fled,
his followers gradually dispersed along the way.
He reached Yìpǔ on a single horse,
where he was beheaded by a fisherman.
His head was placed in a loach basket
and carried to the capital.
He was sixty-three years old at the time.
Zhāng Fóhù was posthumously granted the title of Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
Zuǒ Xīngshèng that of Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
both as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
Xú Jǐngzhì and Huán Língfú were Túnqí Xiàowèi,
Dǒng Bózhēn Yuánwàiláng,
Lǐ Yùzhī Jǐshìzhōng,
and others received different ranks.
As for Gōngzǔ,
he was a relative of Huìjǐng,
a brave and powerful warrior skilled with horse and spear,
whose strength surpassed others,
having frequently been in battles.
When suppressing Wáng Jìngzé,
he contended with Zuǒ Xīngshèng's military officer Yuán Wénkuàng for Jìngzé's head.
〔一三〕 He complained to Emperor Míng, saying:
"Gōngzǔ, with a bare horse and crimson robes,
stabbed down the rebel with his own hand.
Thus, Wénkuàng was able to cut off his head.
I risked my life for this merit,
yet it was wrongfully taken from me.
If I lose this merit,
I will surely stab Zuǒ Xīngshèng to death."
The Emperor, recognizing his bravery,
〔一四〕 had someone tell Xīngshèng:
"How could you let Gōngzǔ contend with Wénkuàng for merit?"
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed with two hundred households.
After Huìjǐng was subdued,
Gōngzǔ was imprisoned in Shàngfāng,
and killed shortly thereafter.
Jué fled and became a monk,
but was apprehended and executed.
Before his execution, he wrote to his sister:
"To leave a temporary inn
and return home is considered great joy;
how much more so to be able to follow our late father and wander in Tàiqīng!
Ancient people could lift the Zhōu tripod
yet lamented having no place to stand.
Considering death in this light,
what harm is there?
My usual disposition
is known to all noblemen.
Since I could not attach myself to a swift horse's tail
how could I leave my name to later generations?
The deeds of ancient bamboo and silk that I admired
are now all gone."

dogs,

A foundation already established,

Gradually

Yǎn (Yǎn) soon died in prison.
Zhāng Xīntài (Zhāng Xīntài), courtesy name Yìhēng (Yìhēng),
was a native of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng).
His father, Xīngshì (Xīngshì),
was a General of the Left Guard of Sòng (Sòng).
Xīntài (Xīntài) had aspirations and integrity from a young age,
did not consider military affairs his calling,
and loved clerical script and
reading the Zǐ (Zǐ) and Shǐ (Shǐ) (Master and History classics).
When he was a little over ten years old,
he called upon Chǔ Yuān (Chǔ Yuān), the Minister of Personnel,
who asked him:
"Zhāng Láng (Zhāng Láng), how much do you know of archery and horsemanship?"
Xīntài (Xīntài) replied:
"My nature is timid and I fear horses;
I have no strength to draw a bow."
Yuān (Yuān) was greatly surprised by this.
He was appointed as a Chief Clerk of the prefecture,
and successively served as an aide in various princely mansions.
During the Yuánhuī (Yuánhuī) reign,
Xīngshì (Xīngshì) was at home,
controlling the return of funds from Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu),
and received thirty million cash.
Cāngwú Wáng (Cāngwú Wáng) personally led people to rob him,
and in one night almost everything was gone.
Xīngshì (Xīngshì) worried and fell ill and died.
Xīntài’s (Xīntài) elder brother, Xīnhuá (Xīnhuá), was then serving in Ānchéng Jùn (Ānchéng Jùn),
and Xīntài (Xīntài) sealed all the remaining wealth to await his return.
In the early Jiàn Yuán (Jiàn Yuán) reign,
he successively held the position of General of Níngshuò (Níngshuò),
and was promoted to Department Director of Revenue in the Imperial Secretariat.
Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) had previously befriended Xīntài (Xīntài) early on,
and upon ascending the throne,
appointed him General of the Imperial Guard,
leading the imperial guards.
He was appointed Marshal of the Grand Commandant for the Prince of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng),
and was sent out as Commander of Ānyuǎn (Ānyuǎn) and Administrator of Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng).
Returning, he again became General of the Imperial Guard,
Colonel of Infantry,
and concurrently Supervisor of the Imperial Guards.
Xīntài (Xīntài) was conversant in both refined and popular culture,
and most of his associates were renowned scholars.
After his duty, he would often stroll in gardens and ponds,
wearing a deer-skin cap,
a patched robe, and carrying a tin staff,
with a plain zither tucked under his arm.
Someone reported this to Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ),
and Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) said:
"How dare the son of a general act in such a manner!"
Later, when accompanying the imperial carriage to Xīnlín (Xīnlín),
Xīntài (Xīntài) was ordered to conduct an inspection in full armor.
Xīntài (Xīntài) put down his weapon,
and drank wine and composed poetry under a pine tree.
Lǚ Wéndù (Lǚ Wéndù), the Supervisor of the Imperial Bureau, saw him and
reported it to Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ).
Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) was furious,
and sent him out.
After several days,
his anger somewhat subsided,
and he recalled him,
saying to him:
"You are not happy serving in a military position;
I should assign you a clean office."
He was appointed Regular Palace Attendant.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng (Yǒngmíng),
he was sent out as Marshal of the Central Army for Zhèn Jūn (Zhèn Jūn) and Administrator of Nánpíng (Nánpíng).
When the Prince of Bādōng (Bādōng), Zǐxiǎng (Zǐxiǎng), killed his subordinates,
the Emperor dispatched Hú Xiézhī (Hú Xiézhī), the Central Grand Master, to suppress him in the west,
making Xīntài (Xīntài) his deputy.
Xīntài (Xīntài) said to Xiézhī (Xiézhī):
"Now the Grand Jupiter is in the southwest;
marching against the annual cycle is deeply taboo for strategists,
one must not engage in battle,
for battle will surely lead to danger.
Now in this expedition,
victory would be ignoble,
and defeat would truly be shameful.
Those cunning villains are gathered together,
and those who serve them,
either covet rewards or are coerced by threats,
and thus will not collapse on their own.
If we temporarily station our army at Xiàkǒu (Xiàkǒu),
and declare the consequences of their actions,
they can be captured without battle."
Xiézhī (Xiézhī) did not listen,
and advanced to station troops at Jiāngjīn (Jiāngjīn),
where Yǐn Lüè (Yǐn Lüè) and others were killed.
After the matter was settled,
Xīntài (Xīntài) was transferred to be Marshal of the Western-Pacifying Army for the Prince of Suí (Suí), Zǐlóng (Zǐlóng),
and concurrently Administrator of Hédōng (Hédōng).
Zǐlóng (Zǐlóng) deeply loved and accepted him,
often conversing and feasting with him.
Many official duties in the prefecture and government
were entrusted to him,
and his favor was second only to Xiè Tiǎo (Xiè Tiǎo).
The archivist secretly reported this,
and Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) was angry,
and recalled him to the capital.
He retired to live in a residential alley,
building a house at the foot of Nángāng (Nángāng),
facing Sōngshān (Sōngshān).
Xīntài (Xīntài) carried a crossbow to shoot pheasants,
indulging in leisure and freedom.
He had a good grasp of various arts and crafts,
and was quite proficient in many of them.
Upon Emperor Míng’s (Míng) ascension,
he became Chief Clerk of the Imperial Guard,
and was promoted to Counsellor-in-Chief.
He submitted a memorial proposing twenty advantageous measures,
one of which suggested the demolition and abandonment of pagodas and temples.
The Emperor replied to all with gracious edicts.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the invaders besieged Zhōnglí city.
Xīntài was a military commander,
and he followed Cuī Huìjǐng to rescue it.
Xīntài sent a message to Lǔ Guǎnglíng Hóu of the invaders, saying:
"I hear you are attacking Zhōnglí;
this is your profound strategy,
how can there be no mistake in it!
The Art of War says, 'There are cities that should not be attacked,
and lands that should not be contended for.'
Have you not heard this?
Our state has a million boats and ships,
covering the rivers and crossing the seas,
and the reason we have held back our troops until now is
to exhaust the Wèi soldiers with a border city.
We will transport grain for a thousand *lǐ*,
both travel and stay will be exhausting.
Then, with a period of continuous rain,
the rivers and valleys will overflow,
and then we will sail across the sea,
a million strong advancing together.
What then will you use to resist them?
To order the Wèi sovereign, with the prestige of ten thousand chariots,
to attack this small city,
what does this mean?
If you attack and fail to capture it,
whose shame will it be?
Suppose you can capture it,
and you defend it.
We will line up boats for a thousand *lǐ*,
with prows and sterns connected,
passing Shòuyáng to the west,
and reaching Cānghǎi to the east.
No further requests for weapons,
no more provisions taken.
Soldiers will rest,
and rise to engage in battle.
Then fish and turtles will not pass,
flying birds will be cut off.
With a detached force on the left bank of the Huái River,
that it cannot be defended
is clear as day.
If it is not captured,
I will borrow the law from the Wèi officials
to indict you for your error.
If you suffer military setbacks, and lose many men,
and fail to capture it quickly,
driving soldiers to fill the moats,
or capture it but cannot defend it,
then the esteemed scholars of the Wèi court
must have other profound intentions,
which I cannot yet fathom.
In the past, Wèi Tàiwǔ Fólí
mobilized the entire nation's forces
to attack a city with ten ramparts,
more than half died,
and he barely returned alive.
His wisdom was exhausted at Jīnyǒng,
and even though it was captured, it was not defended.
These were all miscalculations,
and are still ridiculed today.
The previous lesson is not distant,
have you already forgotten it?
Our gates are bustling,
I jestingly convey my thoughts."
The invaders were indeed repelled by the Xúzhōu army,
and further intended to build a city at Shàoyáng Zhōu.
Huìjǐng feared this would be a great disaster.
Xīntài said:
"The reason the invaders are building a city
is to outwardly display their might,
but in reality, they fear us pursuing them.
If we now persuade them that both sides wish to cease hostilities,
then their trouble will naturally subside."
Huìjǐng followed this advice.
He dispatched Xīntài to the invaders' city to fully explain this intention.
When the invaders retreated,
there were still ten thousand soldiers remaining on the island,
who requested to give five hundred horses for passage.
Huìjǐng wanted to cut off their path and attack them.
Xīntài persuaded Huìjǐng, saying:
"Do not obstruct a returning army;
the ancients feared this.
Troops in a desperate situation
should not be underestimated.
Winning them is not enough to show military prowess,
and losing would merely negate previous achievements.
It is better to grant their request."
Huìjǐng then allowed the invaders to pass.
At that time, the military commander Xiāo Tǎnzhī also reinforced Zhōnglí.
Upon returning, he reported to Míngdì, saying:
"There were ten thousand desperate invaders on Shàoyáng Zhōu,
but Huìjǐng and Xīntài let them go instead of taking them."
Because of this, the Emperor did not reward them.
Four years later,
he was sent out as the Administrator of Yǒngyáng.
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán,
he returned to the capital.
When Cuī Huìjǐng besieged the city,
Xīntài entered the city
and led its defense.
After the situation stabilized, he was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Sīmǎ to Lúlíng Wáng Āndōng.
When the righteous army rose,
Xīntài was made Chíjíe, Dūd Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Sì Zhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suí Jùn Jūnjì, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with his general rank remaining as before.
At that time, the Young Emperor was in disarray,
and everyone was looking for an opportunity.

Xīntài, along with his younger brother, the former Shǐ'ān Nèishǐ Xīnshí, secretly conspired with the Crown Prince's Right Commander Hú Sōng, the former Nánqiáo Administrator Wáng Língxiù, the Zhíhé Jiāngjūn Hóngxuǎn, the Hándé Zhǔshuài Gǒu Lì, the Zhíhòu Liú Língyùn, and over ten others,
all agreeing to the plot.
The Emperor sent the Zhōngshū Shèrén Féng Yuánsì to supervise the army and rescue Yǐng,
while Rú Fǎzhēn, Méi Chóng'ér, and the Crown Prince's Right Commander Lǐ Jūshì, the Zhìjú Jiānyáng Míngtài, and over ten others escorted him to Zhōngxīng Táng.
Xīntài and others had men carry knives to the seat and hack Yuánsì,
whose head fell into a fruit platter.
They also hacked Míngtài,
splitting his abdomen.
Chóng'ér was stabbed several times,
and his fingers all fell off.
Jūshì climbed over a wall and escaped,
and Rú Fǎzhēn also scattered and fled back to the palace.
Língxiù then went to Shítóu to welcome Jiàn'ān Wáng Bǎo'yín,
leading several hundred civil and military officials,
shouting 'Jǐngbì!',
and arriving at Dù Mǔzhái.
When Xīntài first heard that the incident had broken out,
he galloped into the palace,
hoping that Fǎzhēn and others were outside,
and that the internal arrangements of the city
would certainly be entirely entrusted to him,
thus responding to the situation and carrying out the deposition and enthronement.
However, Fǎzhēn managed to return,
and ordered the gates closed and guards posted,
not assigning troops to Xīntài.
Hóngxuǎn, who was inside the palace, also dared not act.
The crowd outside soon dispersed.
A few days later, the plot was discovered,
and an imperial edict ordered the arrest of Xīntài, Hú Sōng, and others,
who were all executed.
When Xīntài was young, someone told his fortune that he would attain the rank of the Three Dukes,
but at that time, he was only thirty.
Later, a roof tile fell and injured his forehead.
He again asked the fortune-teller,
who said:
"You no longer have the appearance of a Duke,
but your lifespan will increase,
and you can still become a regional governor."
He died at the age of forty-six.
[二一]
The Historian says: Cuī Huìjǐng, an old general and veteran minister,
concerned about the chaotic times,
turned the power to govern,
raised the army of Jìnyáng,
seized the opportunity and exercised power,
internally attacking the young sovereign,
relying on the people who enjoyed disorder,
and borrowing the plunder from Huáichǔ.
Brave generals surrendered,
and various commanders abandoned their discipline.
Drums and gongs resounded in the palace,
[二二] halberds stood in the city.
Ramparts leaned against doors,
soldiers were exhausted and demoralized.
Though the 'Bronze Tiger' troops were repeatedly dispatched,
there was no aid to relieve the siege.
The situation was like Yìjīng,
rotting fish awaiting their end.
The General who Conquers Barbarians threw himself into the national crisis,
tying up horses and organizing troops,
crossing the river competitively,
sweeping like wind and lightning,
winning victories with ease.
In the battle of Yuèchéng,
flags captured covered the fields.
In the victory at Jīn[⿰耳⿱臼儿],
captives were presented at Xiàngwèi.
Watching dust and observing beacons,
the beleaguered fortresses were reopened.
Slaughtering the Dài and settling Xiāng,
none ever reached this level.
How magnificent,
it was like Huán and Wén in different eras!
The Eulogy says: Shúyè betrayed externally,
Huáiféi lost its strategic advantage.
Huìjǐng turned his spear,
the palace gates were shut in daylight.
Xīntài in haste,
his frosty blade unstained.
Indeed, it arose from the chaos of the times,
as solid ice gradually spreads.

Qiū Língjú,

Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) presented three funeral dirges (wǎngē shī, 挽歌詩),
saying,
"Clouds hang across the wide steps, darkening them;
deep frost chills the high palace halls."
The emperor selected these lines and praised them.
He was appointed to be the North Central Army Staff Officer (Běizhōngláng Cānjūn, 北中郎參軍) for the Prince of Xīn'ān (新安).
He was then sent out to be the magistrate of Shànwūchéng (剡烏程),
but he was not content.
In the early years of Tàishǐ (泰始),
he was implicated in the "eastern rebels" case and impeached for several years.
When Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) was Governor of Wúxīng (吳興),
he said to people:
"The talented scholars in this commandery
are only Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) and Shěn Bó (沈勃)."
He then petitioned to promote him.
Emperor Míng (明帝) ordered him to write a memorial on the grand southern expedition.
After a long time,
he was appointed Grand Commandant Staff Officer (Tàiwèi Cānjūn, 太尉參軍),
then transferred to Anběi Jièshì (安北記室),
and concurrently Administrator of Fúfēng (扶風),
but he did not accept the latter.
He became Shàngshū Sāngōngláng (尚書三公郎),
then Jìankāng Lìng (建康令),
then transferred to Tōngzhíláng (通直郎),
concurrently Zhōngshūláng (中書郎).
During the Shēngmíng (昇明) era,
he was promoted to Zhèngyuánláng (正員郎),
concurrently serving as the Central Rectifier (zhōngzhèng, 中正) of his native commandery,
and concurrently Zhōngshūláng (中書郎) as before.
At that time, the abdication was in progress,
and Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ, 太祖) ordered Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) to participate in managing imperial edicts and pronouncements.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元),
he was transferred to Zhōngshūláng (中書郎),
with Zhongzhèng (中正) as before,
and was ordered to supervise the calligraphy of the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was also put in charge of the National History (guóshǐ, 國史).
The following year,
he was sent out as Zhènnán Zhǎngshǐ (鎮南長史) and Prime Minister (Xiàng, 相) of Xúnyáng (尋陽),
then promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Tōngzhí Chángshì (通直常侍),
and soon concurrently held the position of Jìjiǔ (祭酒) of the Eastern Repository (Dōngguān, 東觀).
Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) said:
"Having held office for a long time, I do not wish for frequent transfers.
If I could remain a Jìjiǔ (祭酒) for the rest of my life,
I would have no regrets."
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he was appointed General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, 驍騎將軍).
Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) was not pleased with a military position,
and said to people:
"I should go back east and dig up Gù Róng's (顧榮) tomb.
The Jiāngnán (江南) region, thousands of li in area,
has scholars of refined style
all originating from here.
Gù Róng (顧榮) suddenly led all those northern barbarians (cāng, 傖) to cross the river,
obstructing our path;
his crimes persist even in death."
He was reassigned to Zhèngyuán Chángshì (正員常侍).
Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) was fond of drinking
and criticizing people.
Once, in Shěn Yuān's (沈淵) presence, he saw a poem by Wáng Jiǎn (王儉).
Shěn Yuān (沈淵) said:
"Master Wáng's (王令) writing has greatly improved."
Qiū Língjū (丘靈鞠) replied:
"How does it compare to mine before I had improved?"
This remark reached Wáng Jiǎn (王儉).
Qiū Língjū's (丘靈鞠) literary fame was very great during the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
but it somewhat diminished after entering Qí (齊).
He had disheveled hair, was unrestrained and untidy,
had no proper decorum,
and did not manage his household affairs.
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) said to people:
"Master Qiū (丘公)'s official career has not advanced,
and his talent has also declined."
He was promoted to Cavalry Commander Staff Officer (Chējì Zhǎngshǐ, 車騎長史) for the Prince of Chángshā (長沙王),
then Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū, 太中大夫),
and died in office.
He authored the Preface to the Record of Jiāngzuǒ (江左) Literature,
beginning with Tàixīng (太興)
and ending with Yuánxī (元熙).
His collected works circulated in the world.
Tán Chāo (檀超), courtesy name Yuèzǔ (悅祖),
was from Jīnxiāng (金鄉), Gāopíng (高平).
His grandfather, Tán Hóngzōng (檀弘宗),
was the Administrator of Nánlángyá (南琅邪) during the Sòng (宋).
Tán Chāo (檀超) was fond of literature from a young age,
uninhibited and assertive.
He began his career as a staff officer in the western division of the province.
He once worked with the Deputy Governor (Biéjià, 別駕) Xiāo Huìkāi (蕭惠開),
and did not defer to him.
He said to Xiāo Huìkāi (蕭惠開):
"You and I both started with one old woman;
what is there to brag about?"
Empress Xiāo (蕭太后),
Xiāo Huìkāi's (蕭惠開) great-aunt,
and the consort of Dàolián (道憐), Prince of Chángshā (長沙王),
was also Tán Chāo's (檀超) great-aunt.
He was recommended as a Xiùcái (秀才).
In the early Xiàojiàn (孝建) era,
he was exiled to Liángzhōu (梁州) due to an incident,
and appointed staff officer of the Xuānwēi Command (宣威府 Cānjūn, 參軍).
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) heard of Tán Chāo's (檀超) literary talent
and ordered him to return and serve in the Eastern Palace,
appointing him as a staff officer to the Commander of Swift Cavalry (Piàojì Cānjūn, 驃騎參軍), Ningmán Zhǔbù (寧蠻主簿),
and Zīyì (諮議) to the Northern General (Zhènběi, 鎮北).
Tán Chāo (檀超) served as a subordinate official in various regional posts repeatedly,
but he was not content.
He was transferred to Shàngshū Dùzhīláng (尚書度支郎),
Chējì Gōngcáo (車騎功曹),
and Administrator of Guìyáng (桂陽 Nèishǐ, 內史).
He entered the court as Diànzhōngláng (殿中郎),
concurrently Zhōngshūláng (中書郎),
Administrator of Línglíng (零陵 Nèishǐ, 內史),
Zhēngběi Piàojì Jièshì (征北驃騎記室),
Guózǐ Bóshì (國子博士),
and concurrently Zuǒchéng (左丞).
Tán Chāo (檀超) was fond of drinking
and reciting poetry.
His demeanor was gentle and graceful.
He compared himself to Xī Chāo (郗超) of Jìn (晉),
becoming known as
"the Two Chāos (二超) of Gāopíng (高平)."
He said to people:
"I still feel I am superior."
Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ, 太祖) admired and cherished him.
He was promoted to General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn, 驍騎將軍),
Chángshì (常侍),
and Right Senior Clerk (Yòuzhǎngshǐ, 右長史) to the Minister of Education (Sītú, 司徒).
In the second year of Jiànyuán (建元),
a historical office was first established,
and Tán Chāo (檀超) and Jiāng Yān (江淹), the Piàojì Jièshì (驃騎記室), were put in charge of historical records.
They submitted a memorial proposing rules and regulations:
the new era name should be used,
and the Sòng (宋) regnal years should not be adopted.
Titles and peerages should be detailed in their respective biographies,
without using fabricated chronological tables.

Ten treatises (zhì, 志) should be established: Treatises on Regulations and Calendar (Lǜlì, 律曆), Rituals and Music (Lǐyuè, 禮樂), Astronomy (Tiānwén, 天文), Five Phases (Wǔxíng, 五行), Suburban Sacrifices (Jiāosì, 郊祀), Punishments and Law (Xíngfǎ, 刑法), and Literature and Art (Yìwén, 藝文) — following Bān Gù (班固);
Treatises on Court Assemblies (Cháohuì, 朝會) and Carriages and Attire (Yúfú, 輿服) — following Cài Yōng (蔡邕) and Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪);
Treatises on Provinces and Commanderies (Zhōujùn, 州郡) — following Xú Yuán (徐爰).
Treatises on Hundred Officials (Bǎiguān, 百官) — following Fàn Yè (范曄),
combined with Provinces and Commanderies.
Bān Gù (班固) included the Five Planets (Wǔxīng, 五星) in the Astronomy treatise and solar eclipses in the Five Phases treatise;
it should be changed so that solar eclipses are included in the Astronomy treatise.
The Jiànyuán (建元) era should be used as the starting point.
Biographies of imperial daughters, as members of the imperial clan,
should be established to honor the importance of the maternal relatives.
Furthermore, biographies of Recluses (Chǔshì, 處士) and Exemplary Women (Liènǚ, 列女) should be established.
An edict was issued for internal and external deliberation.
The Left Minister (Zuǒ Púyè, 左僕射) Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) deliberated:
"The importance of the 'golden grain' (finance and economy)
is foremost among the eight governmental policies.
When finance and commodities are flowing, the country is rich and the people are substantial.
It is fitting to include them in the records
to emphasize fundamental matters.
The treatise on Court Assemblies (Cháohuì Zhì, 朝會志) was not recorded in previous histories.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) mentioned his teacher Hú Guǎng (胡廣)'s account of Han (漢) old rituals,
which was merely the opinion of Bójiē's (伯喈) family,
with trivial and fragmented minor rituals,
overly cumbersome to record.
It is appropriate to establish a Treatise on Food and Commodities (Shíhuò, 食貨)
and omit the Treatise on Court Assemblies.
The Nine Categories of the Grand Plan (Hóngfàn Jiǔchóu, 洪範九疇)
list Five Phases (Wǔxíng, 五行) as the first.
The origin of the Five Phases
precedes the essences of water and fire,
which are the essence of the sun, moon, and Five Phases.
Therefore, it is appropriate to follow previous precedents
without any changes.
Furthermore, establishing biographies for imperial daughters
is also not something that superficial understanding would approve of.
If there are those with high virtue and extraordinary conduct,
they should naturally be recorded in the Biographies of Exemplary Women (Liènǚ, 列女).
If it is merely ordinary beauty,
then the old practice of not recording them should be maintained."
The edict stated:
"Solar and lunar disasters belong to Astronomy.
The rest is as Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) discussed."
Tán Chāo (檀超)'s historical work was not completed
when he died in office.
Jiāng Yān (江淹) completed it,
but it was still not comprehensive.
At that time, Xiōng Xiāng (熊襄) of Yùzhāng (豫章) compiled the Qí Diǎn (齊典),
which started from ten generations prior.
Its preface says:
"The 'Yáo Diǎn' (堯典) in the 'Shàngshū' (尚書),
is called the 'Yú Shū' (虞書).
Therefore, what is attached and described,
is generally called Qí (齊),
and named 'Hé Luò Jīn Kuì' (河洛金匱)."
Biàn Bīn (卞彬), courtesy name Shìwèi (士蔚),
was a native of Yuānqú (寃句) in Jìyīn (濟陰).
His grandfather, Sìzhī (嗣之),
was a Zhōng Lǐngjūn (中領軍).
His father, Yánzhī (延之),
had a resolute character,
and served as the magistrate of Shàngyú (上虞).
Bīn's (彬) talent and conduct were extraordinary,
and his writings often contained critiques and satire.
The province appointed him Xīcáo Zhǔbù (西曹主簿),
then Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and Yuánwàiláng (員外郎).
At the end of the Yuánhuī (元徽) reign of Sòng (宋),
four powerful ministers assisted in governing.
Bīn (彬) said to Tàizǔ (太祖):
"Among the populace, there is a children's rhyme that says: 'Pitiable and lamentable is the corpse in robes;
the filial son is not crying daily in his stead;
the ranks of officials temporarily sounding will lead to annihilation.'
Has Your Excellency heard it?"
At that time, Wáng Yùn (王蘊) was in mourning for his father,
and died with Yuán Càn (袁粲);
hence it says "corpse in robes".
Fú (服) means clothing.
The character Chǔ (褚) has the "clothing" radical on its side.
Removing the character "son" from "filial piety" (孝),
and replacing it with "day" (日),
refers to Chǔ Yuān (褚淵).
"Ranks of officials" (列管) refers to Xiāo (蕭)."
When Bīn (彬) retired,
Tàizǔ (太祖) smiled and said,
"Bīn (彬) made this up himself."
When the Qí (齊) court was first established,
Bīn (彬) again said,
"Who says Sòng (宋) is far away? I stand on tiptoes and look towards it."
Tàizǔ (太祖) heard this,
but did not punish him.
He was appointed Cānjūn (參軍) of the Right Army.
His family was poor,
so he was sent out as the Nánkāng (南康) Commandery丞 (chéng).
Bīn (彬) drank quite a bit,
and discarded all decorum.
In the preface to his "Flea and Louse Rhapsody", he wrote:
"I live in poverty,
wearing plain clothes for ten years without making new ones.
The patched old robe
is where life is nurtured;
I rely on it for warmth and coolness,
and have nothing to replace it with.
As a person of many illnesses,
my daily routines are very lax.
Wrapped in old, worn-out bedding,
I cannot free myself.
Moreover, my nature is lazy and lax,
disinclined to care for my skin.
My washing is not diligent,
my bathing is untimely;
my four limbs are weak and weary,
and I am furthermore foul-smelling.
Hence, between the reed mat and the messy hair,
fleas and lice swarm.
The intense itching covers me like a flood,
giving my flesh no respite;
I scratch, prod, and pinch
without a moment's pause each day.
There is a proverb about lice: 'born in the morning, grandparents by evening.'
As for my lice,
they have no worries of bathing,
and no sorrow of mutual mourning.
They feast and gather on my old collar and rotting cloth garment.
My clothes are never changed,
and biting and gnawing cannot be stopped.
With my casual neglect and laziness,
I am not diligent in hunting them.
Grandchildren and offspring,
for thirty-five years they have been."
His brief remarks are all true records.
He was appointed Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令) of the Nánhǎi (南海) Kingdom,
then Shàngshū Bùbùláng (尚書比部郎),
Anjí Lìng (安吉令),
and Chēqí Jìshì (車騎記室).
Bīn (彬) was fond of drinking,
using a gourd, dipper, and peach pits as dishes.
He wore a silk cap for twelve years without changing it,
and used a large gourd as a hand warmer.
Many of his belongings were strange and unconventional.
He called himself
"Biàn Tiánjū" (卞田居),
and his wife
"Fù Cánshì" (傅蠶室).
Someone advised him,
"My lord, you do not maintain proper conduct at all;
how can your reputation and position be elevated?"
Bīn (彬) said,
"When throwing five wooden dice,
if ten throws all result in the same outcome,
it cannot be due to the thrower's clumsiness.
I enjoy throwing;
that's just how it is."
In the Yǒngyuán (永元) period,
he served as Píngyuè Chángshǐ (平越長史) and Suíjiàn Tàishǒu (綏建太守),
and died in office.
Bīn (彬) also described animals, saying:
"Sheep are lustful and fierce;
pigs are humble and straightforward;
geese are stubborn and arrogant;
dogs are treacherous and unrestrained."
These were all veiled criticisms of the powerful.
His "Frog Rhapsody" says:
"Donning blue and dragging purple,
it is called a frog."
People of the time said this was a metaphor for the Prime Minister.
It also says:
"Tadpoles, yes, yes,
swim in swarms in dark water.
From morning to evening,
they labor like ghosts."
This was a metaphor for the administrative clerks and advisors.
His writings spread among the common folk.
In the Yǒngmíng (永明) period,
Zhūgě Xù (諸葛勗) of Lángyá (琅邪), while a Guózǐshēng (國子生),
composed the "Yún Zhōng Fù" (雲中賦),
which described everyone from the Jìjiǔ (祭酒) downwards,
with descriptions that resembled their actual appearance.
He was imprisoned in Dōngyě (東冶),
and composed the "Dōngyě Tú Fù" (東冶徒賦).
Shìzǔ (世祖) saw it
and pardoned him.
There was also Yuán Gǔ (袁嘏) of Chénjùn (陳郡),
who held his own writing in high esteem.
He told people:
"My poetry needs great talent to keep it down,
otherwise it will fly away."
At the end of the Jiànwǔ (建武) period,
while serving as Zhūjì Lìng (諸暨令),
he was killed by Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則).
Qiū Jùyuán (丘巨源)
was a native of Lánlíng (蘭陵) in Lánlíng (蘭陵).
At the beginning of the Sòng (宋) dynasty, due to land reform, he was assigned to Dānyáng (丹陽),
and later to Lánlíng (蘭陵).
In his youth, Jùyuán (巨源) was nominated as Xiàolián (孝廉) from Dānyáng Commandery (丹陽郡),
and was recognized by Sòng Xiàowǔ (宋孝武).
During Dàmíng (大明) five,
he was ordered to assist Xú Yuán (徐爰) in compiling the national history.
When the emperor passed away,
Yìgōng (義恭), Prince of Jiāngxià (江夏), appointed him as Zhǎng Shūjì (掌書記).
When Míngdì (明帝) ascended the throne,
he made him participate in drafting edicts and proclamations,
and kept him close by.
From Nántái Yùshǐ (南臺御史), he became Wáng Jǐngwén's (王景文) Zhènjūn Cānjūn (鎮軍參軍),
then returned home for mourning.
At the beginning of the Yuánhuī (元徽) period,
Xiūfàn (休範), Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽), was in Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Knowing Jùyuán (巨源) had writing talent,
he sent a boat to fetch him,
and bestowed upon him money and goods.
Jùyuán (巨源) then submitted a petition through Tàizǔ (太祖),
and an imperial edict ordered Jùyuán (巨源) to remain in the capital.
When the Guìyáng (桂陽) incident arose,
he was tasked with drafting official documents and proclamations in the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省).
After the incident was settled,
he was appointed Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請).
Jùyuán (巨源) had hoped for rewards and honors,
but none were forthcoming.
So he wrote to the Shàngshūlìng (尚書令), Yuán Càn (袁粲), saying: "The people believe in reason and offer their hearts,
but are dim in judging affairs.
I had hoped that my sincere loyalty would move and reach (the authorities),
and that rewards would be given beyond expectation;
how could I have expected such desolation, suddenly for three years?
Those who comment will certainly
say that clerical work is a lowly skill,
not something on which life and death depend;
and that encouraging trivial writings
is not where judgment and decisions reside.
However, 'first reputation, then reality'
is an old principle of military and state affairs.
The 'Seven Virtues' and 'Nine Merits'
will make generals famous in their generation.
Looking up at the celestial order,
there are the Right General and the Left Prime Minister;
looking down at the human order,
there are the martial figures of the West and the literary figures of the East.
They are certainly not of the same rank as minor officials and supplicants.
The likes of sorcerers and artisans are peers.
In the past, when an extraordinary force,
arose in an instant,
although the fierce ringleaders were immediately suppressed,
people's minds became even more bewildered.
When Móu Tián opened the city gates,
and Qiān Líng led the rebellion,
at this time,
though hearts and minds were like Hú and Yuè,
those who welcomed the Xīntíng faction
filled the roads,
and those who pledged allegiance to Zhūquè
left their homes empty, whether foolish or wise.
Some people were confused, but the common folk were not confused;
some people were afraid, but the common folk
were not afraid.
This is the first point worth discussing.
When confronted with the Xīntíng faction,
the only one able to draw his sword and slay the rebels
was Zhāng Jìng'ér;
and in the Central Secretariat, the only one able to write vigorously without hesitation
was Qiū Jù
yuán.
As for the civil and military,
there truly were superior and inferior,
but judging success or failure by their deaths,
when facing an enemy that could make the sky collapse,
and resisting unforeseen disaster,
I ask the entire realm,
what
kind of courage was this?
This is the second point worth discussing.
Furthermore, during that period of distress,
when literary scholars were widely summoned,
none from the Imperial Yellow Gate or Central Secretariat failed to gather.
Those who wielded brushes and displayed their literary talent
were not lacking in number.
Why then did the court's
great writers
have to entrust such tasks to ordinary
and lowly people?
If it was because this rebel force was strong
and the outcome was uncertain,
and the various worthies were too timid to pick up a brush,
then the common people should have been rewarded for their bravery;
if it was said that the difficulty of the feathered
dispatch
required a writing master,
and the various worthies deferred, entrusting the task to others,
then the common people should have been rewarded for their talent.
〔一二〕This is the third point worth discussing.
I secretly observed that among the twenty-five people rewarded for their crimes by the Guìyáng rebel,
Lǐ and Zhōng Shuǎng were both in this category.
After the defeat, they came out,
and their crimes were all pardoned.
However, Wú Màiyuǎn was executed with his family.
As for punishment, wielding a brush for a great disaster was harmful, but wielding a spear was even more so.
Judging by the reward categories,
the military men were promoted while the literary men were buried.
This is the fourth point worth discussing.
Furthermore, Màiyuǎn's pronouncements
were perhaps disrespectful and arrogant.
When the common people wrote talismans and dispatches,
they spoke obscenely and insulted.
As soon as the brush was released from hand,
they were immediately destroyed.
If Guìyáng had
succeeded,
and the common people had not been torn apart at the army gates,
they would have been cut in half in the marketplace,
and their infants made into dried meat and mincemeat.
This is something to reflect upon carefully.
This is the fifth point worth discussing.
In the previous year's military campaign,
there were over ten thousand armored soldiers.
Nine-tenths of them
were mere hangers-on,
which can be called numerous.
They climbed the dragon and attached themselves to the qílín,
soaring like clouds.
However,
as for the madmen among the people,
they were truly few.
They merely guarded imperial edicts,
and were vainly submerged in mud.
Could it be that those who bore shields at the dustiest front lines
were all Bái Qǐ,
and those who started by taking up writing tablets
were necessarily not
Lǔ Lián?
The common people were foolish,
but the state's calculations were swift,
employing the opportunity of blazing beacon fires,
and the Emperor chose exceptional talents
to attend the Dǐluó meeting.
Since they were able to overcome the enemy without delay,
and contend
for the lead without failure,
it would be appropriate for them to receive minor rewards,
a little to eat and drink.
Instead, they were discarded in the ditches,
like dragonflies and ants,
and thrown aside,
like dirt and ashes.
Those who were mere retainers and fought in battles,
without strength or courage,
were all promoted according to their rank;
those who participated in the court,
neither literary nor military,
have already sat in the high and pure ranks.
Observing those bodies
thus,
and looking at those examples thus,
since they are not plants or trees,
how can they remain silent?
Jùyuán was ultimately not rehabilitated.
He successively served in various princely mansions,
and was transferred to be the Prefect of the Yǔlín.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (479 CE),
he became Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng,
Commander of the Palace Guards,
and Colonel of the Yuè Cavalry.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng,
but after being installed,
he was unhappy about serving outside the Jiāng region.
Shìzǔ asked him about it.
Jùyuán said:
"The ancients said: 'Rather drink Jiànyè water,
than eat Wǔchāng fish.'
I am already old;
I would rather die in Jiànyè."
He was then made Magistrate of Yúháng.
During Shěn Yōuzhī's affair,
Tàizǔ sent Jùyuán to be the Shàngshū Fú Jīngzhōu.
Jùyuán again expected special rewards for this,
and from then on, his ambition was often unfulfilled.
When Gāozōng was Prince of Wúxīng,
Jùyuán composed a poem about Qiū Hú,
which contained satirical remarks,
and he was consequently put to death.
Wáng Zhìshēn, courtesy name Yúncái,
was from Línyí, Lángyá.
In his youth, he studied composition with Xiè Chāozōng of Chénjùn.
He was fond of drinking,
awkward and lacked grace.
When Sòng Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù was in Nánxúzhōu,
he wrote the "Guānfǎ Piān."
Zhìshēn harmonized with it,
and was appreciated,
appointed as Secretary of the Western Bureau.
Being poor and without clothes,
he had not yet taken office when Jǐngsù was defeated.
Later, he doffed his plain clothes and became Libationer of the Prefecture.
When Tàizǔ was General of the Guards,
Qiū Jùyuán recommended him to Tàizǔ.
He was appointed Aide-de-camp in the mansion,
then Grandee-Secretary of the King of Yùzhāng's state,
promoted to Grand Academician,
Grand Marshal's Aide-de-camp for the King of Yùzhāng,
and concurrently Record Keeper.
Shìzǔ ordered the Crown Prince's Household Steward, Shěn Yuē, to compile the Sòng Shū,
intending to establish a biography for Yuán Càn,
and submitted it to Shìzǔ for review.
Shìzǔ said:
"Yuán Càn was indeed a loyal minister of the Sòng house."
Yuē also included many vulgar and offensive incidents concerning Emperor Xiàowǔ and Emperor Míng.
〔一三〕The Emperor sent his attendants to tell Yuē:
"The deeds of Xiàowǔ should not be so abruptly presented.
I personally experienced events concerning Emperor Míng of Sòng;
you should consider the principle of concealing evil."
Thereupon, much was omitted.
He also ordered Zhìshēn to compile the Sòng Jì.
He was summoned to the Fúróng Táng,
given clothes,
and provided with a residence.
Zhìshēn complained of poverty to the King of Yùzhāng.
The King said:
"When your book is finished,
I will discuss your stipend."
〔一四〕The book was completed in thirty scrolls.
Shìzǔ later summoned Zhìshēn to the Xuánmíng Diàn,
ordering him to present the memorial.
Before the memorial was presented, Shìzǔ died.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
an imperial edict ordered the collection of his book.
Zhìshēn was promoted to Grand Marshal's Aide-de-camp for the King of Jìnglíng,
but was dismissed for an incident.
Jiāngxià Wáng Fēng and Héngyáng Wáng Jūn both treated him well.
Originally,
Zhìshēn was befriended by Grand Marshal Yuán Càn.
When he compiled the Sòng Jì,
his intentions were often to lean towards Càn.
Càn was orphaned young,
and his grandmother named him Mǐnsūn.
Later, admiring Xún Càn,
he changed his name himself.
Hé Qiáo of Kuàijī ridiculed this,
whereupon Zhìshēn wrote a discourse.
His family was poor, and he had no one to serve.
He once starved for five days without food,
and dug up amaranth roots to eat.
Sīkōng Wáng Sēngqián and his son Wáng Zhì shared their clothing and food with him.
[一五]He died at home.
Earlier, Yuán Bǐng from Chénjùn,
whose courtesy name was Shūmíng,
was learned in literature,
and also known to Yuán Càn.
He was writing the Jìnshū but died
before finishing it.
Yǔ Xiǎn from Yǐngchuān
was skilled at composing essays.
He was admired by the King of Yùzhāng
who appointed him to Dàsīmǎ Jìshì Cānjūn.
He died.
Lù Jué, whose courtesy name was Hánqīng,
was a native of Wújùn,
and the son of Yángzhōu Biéjià Xián.
Juéd had a good demeanor in his youth,
and was fond of composing essays.
His five-character poems were very new and innovative in style.
[一六]In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng,
an imperial edict ordered all officials to recommend scholars.
Gù Gǎozhī, Sītú Zuǒxīyuàn of the same commandery, submitted a memorial recommending him.
The province recommended him as Xiùcái.
He served as Shàofù Zhǔbù under Wáng Yàn,
and was promoted to Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn.
Towards the end of Yǒngmíng,
he became celebrated for his writing.
Shěn Yuē of Wúxīng, Xiè Tiǎo of Chénjùn, and Wáng Róng of Lángyá mutually promoted each other due to their similar temperament.
Zhōu Yǒng of Rǔnán was skilled at discerning sounds and rhymes.
Yuē and others used the five notes (gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ) in their compositions,
dividing the tones into four: píng, shàng, qù, and rù.
With these, they formulated rhymes,
which could not be augmented or reduced.
The world called it
"Yǒngmíng Tǐ."
In the biography of Xiè Língyùn in Shěn Yuē's Sòngshū, he again discussed the five notes.
Juéd wrote to Yuē, saying: Fàn Shìzhòng's own preface states,
"I am naturally adept at the five notes,
discerning clear and turbid sounds,
and am particularly skilled at adjusting lightness and heaviness,
and overcoming difficulties.
Many literary figures, ancient and modern,
do not fully comprehend this point.
Even if there are those who grasp it,
it does not necessarily come from a fundamental understanding."
Shěn Shàngshū also said,
"Since Língjūn,
this secret has not been seen."
Or,
"It accords with principle intuitively,
not by deliberate thought.
Zhāng, Cài, Cáo, Wáng had no prior awareness,
and Pān, Lù, Yán, Xiè were even further from it."
The main idea is to make
"gōng and yǔ vary,
and high and low sounds alternate
rhythmically.
[一七]If there is a floating sound in front,
then a sharp sound must follow;
within a single line,
the sounds and rhymes are completely distinct;
between two sentences,
the light and heavy tones are entirely different."
The diction is both beautiful
and
the principles are sound.
But observing the many worthies throughout history,
it seems they were not entirely unaware of this point.
To say,
"this secret has not been seen,"
is close to misrepresentation, is it not?
Considering Fàn Yún's words,
"it does not come from a fundamental understanding."
Shàngshū said,
"not by deliberate thought."
This can be described as inferring emotions incorrectly from profound subtleties,
and pointing out errors in its
melody.
Fàn also said,
"sometimes there are those who grasp this."
Shàngshū said,
"or it accords with principle intuitively."
Then, in beautiful odes and clear songs,
for those with refined diction and harmonious rhymes,
though there may be errors,
there are also agreements.
Extending this,
it can be argued.
As for thoughts having agreements and disagreements,
the ancients were equally not exempt.
As for writings having openness and closure,
it is
unavoidable in actual matters.
This is why Zǐjiàn was criticized by others,
and Shìhéng left regrets at the end of his pieces.
Since it is called "regrets,"
it is not a work of complete beauty;
it can
be criticized.
If a superior person adheres to this criticism,
they might consider the agreement with principle as obscurity.
How could it be like pointing out its agreement with principle and attributing criticism as regrets?
Since the essays of Wèi Wén,
much has been said about clear and turbid sounds.
Liú Zhēn's memorial
greatly elucidated the essence of style and manner,
discussions of roughness and smoothness,
and the idea of "grasping the tip to continue the top."
He elevated profound subtleties in pitch and rhythm,
comparing them to the five colors mutually enhancing each other.
If this secret has not been seen,
what do these discussions refer to?
Therefore, I believe that previous luminaries already
understood the five notes (gōng, zhǐ),
but did not explicitly and precisely
articulate them as the current discussions do.
As for concealing flaws and hiding defects,
or having few agreements and many errors,
that is what Línzī meant by
"When a person
writes,
they cannot be without fault."
It is not that they knew and did not correct,
but to say that if they do not correct, then they do not know.
This is also what Cáo and Lù meant by
"Exhausting one's emotions often leads to regrets;
it cannot be forced."
[一八]Now, to allow for faults and regrets as an argument,
then one must know the place of no regrets and no faults.
To attribute lack of comprehension or agreement as obscurity,
why
misrepresent their clarity in instances of agreement and comprehension?
Perhaps it is also that the quality and ornamentation differ across eras,
and tastes vary between ancient and modern times.
They might prioritize content and substance,
and be less concerned with phrases and sentences.
Content
and substance
are what writing prioritizes,
yet good and bad are still equally balanced.
Phrases and sentences are what intention is less concerned with,
hence fewer agreements and more errors.
The meaning implicitly includes this;
it is certainly not due to ignorance,
that is clear.
Chángmén and Shànglín are probably not the rhapsodies of a single author.
Luòshén and Chíyàn
immediately became works of two distinct styles.
Mèngjiān was precise and upright,
his "Yǒngshǐ" did not detract from the
Eastern Lord.
Píngzǐ was grand and rich,
his "Yǔliè" did not suffer from "Píngxū."
Wáng Càn's initial military campaign,
other writings could not match it.
Yáng Xiū was quick-witted,
yet his "Shǔfù" was not
presented until the next day.
To follow one's inclination with few faults,
then the matter is accomplished in one day.
The more obscure it becomes,
the more distant the principle is from "seven steps."
The thoughts of one person
vary vastly in speed.
The writings of one
family
differ greatly in skill.
Why then must the five notes and pitches
be expected to be perfectly uniform?
The critics can say that its subtlety has not been fully explored,
but they cannot say that there were
no prior discerners.
Yuē replied: There are five notes of gōng and shāng,
and tens of thousands of different characters.
To match the complexity of tens of thousands
with the simplicity of five notes—
the highness, lowness, rising, and falling
are not within the scope of thought or effort.
Moreover, it is not limited to just this.
For a text of ten characters,
arranged and combined in different orders,
though there are no more than ten characters,
even a skilled calculator cannot exhaust all possibilities.
How much more so for something exceeding this?
Hū?
Since Língjūn,
it has not been used in one's bosom;
thus, there is no way to attain even a semblance of it.
If it is such a marvel,
why did the sages not value it?
【Hé】
xié?
This is probably the cleverness of intricate rhymes and sounds,
which are not pertinent to instruction and meaning,
and are not what the sages considered urgent in their writings.
Therefore, Zǐyún likened it to
"carving insects
and engraving seals,"
saying,
"a man of valor does not do it."
Since ancient times, did poets
not know the distinction of gōng and yǔ,
and the difference of shāng and zhǐ?
Although they knew the distinctions of the five tones,
the variations and changes within them
were largely
unknown.
Therefore, my humble opinion is what I call
"this secret has not been seen."
From this, we can infer
that literati of previous generations had not yet understood this point.
If the rhythm and rhyme of an essay
are equated with the sounds and melodies of strings and pipes,
then beauty and ugliness, grace and crudeness
cannot suddenly become contrary to each other.
For example, when Zǐyě plays a tune,
how
can there suddenly be discordant, out-of-tune sounds?
To compare Luòshén with Chénsī's other rhapsodies
is like works by different hands.
Thus, we know that when heavenly inspiration is aroused,
the lǜ and lǚ will naturally
harmonize;
when the six emotions are stagnant,
the musical tones will suddenly clash.
Although Shìhéng said it was
"resplendent like ornate brocade,"
how could there be a piece of Wèi Wén's attire
among the colors washed in the river waves?
This means that Lùshēng's
words
were not entirely comprehensive.
Between rhyming and not rhyming,
there are also fine and coarse distinctions.
Lúnbìan could not express it,
and I, an old man, cannot fully discern this.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (499 CE),
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng rebelled.
His father Xián was executed,
and he was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
Soon, there was an amnesty decree,
but he regretted that his father did not make it in time,
and died of grief,
at the age of twenty-eight.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Yú Yán of Kuàijī,
during the Yǒngmíng period (483-493 CE), was esteemed by Wénhuì Tàizǐ along with Shěn Yuē for his literary talent;
his favor was extraordinary.
His official post reached (Pìao) [Xiāo] Qí Jiāngjūn.
Cuī Wèizǔ, courtesy name Yuèzōng,
was a native of Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
His father, Qìngxù,
was the Inspector of Liángzhōu
during the Yǒngmíng period.
Wèizǔ began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng.
During his father's mourning, he did not eat salt.
His mother said:
"Since you have no brothers,
and no son yet.
Mourning should not destroy life;
you should just refrain from fine dishes.
How can you abstain from salt!
I, too, will not eat it now."
Wèizǔ reluctantly complied.
His father's wealth from Liángzhōu
amounted to ten million,
which he distributed to his relatives.
He inscribed the character 'rì' on lacquerware,
and these 'rì' character vessels
flowed far and wide.
He estimated the amount of loan documents his father had signed,
and told his cousin Hóng: "If they have it,
they will naturally return it;
if they don't,
what can I say!"
He burned them all.
He loved learning and
collected up to ten thousand volumes of books.
Young and eager neighbors would come to borrow them,
dozens of scrolls a day.
Wèizǔ personally retrieved and handed them out,
never refusing.
He served as Fǔjūn Mòcáo Xíng Cānjūn for Shǐ'ān Wáng,
then transferred to Xíngyù,
and concurrently Jìshì.
Yáoguāng liked him
and often summoned Wèizǔ to play games,
but Wèizǔ always declined, citing clumsiness,
and would not see him except on the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month.
During the Jiànwǔ period (494-498 CE),
an imperial edict called for the recommendation of scholars.
His elder cousin Huìjǐng recommended Wèizǔ and Liú Xiàobiāo of Píngyuán,
both being great scholars.
The Emperor wanted to test them with a position of a hundred li,
but Wèizǔ declined to accept.
Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Shěn Yuē and Lìbù Láng Xiè Tiǎo once gathered with guests and friends in the Ministry of Personnel,
and each asked Wèizǔ over ten questions about geography that they did not know.
Wèizǔ stammered,
without eloquent words,
but his answers were precise and thorough,
and the whole assembly was impressed.
Tiǎo sighed:
"Even if Bān and Mǎ were to be reborn,
they could not surpass this."
Wèizǔ sold his residence for four hundred and fifty thousand.
The buyer asked:
"Is there any possibility of a reduction?"
He replied:
"I am truly ashamed compared to Hán Bóxiū;
how can there be two prices?"
The buyer then said:
"You just ask for four hundred and sixty thousand,
and I will give you the one thousand."
Wèizǔ said:
"That would be joining you in deceiving people,
how can that be my intention?"
When young, he was close to Shìzhōng Jiāng Sì.
When Sì became noble,
he often came to visit him,
but Wèizǔ never went in return.
He was always on good terms with Dānyáng Chéng Liú Fēng.
When Yáoguāng rebelled, occupying the Eastern Residence,
Wèizǔ was within the city walls.
One day before the city fell,
Fēng said to him:
"You have an elderly mother;
it is fitting that you leave."
He ordered the gatekeepers to let him out.
Wèizǔ went to the imperial palace to surrender himself.
He was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng
and died of illness.
Wèizǔ authored the Hǎidàizhì,
covering figures from Tàigōng to the Western Jìn dynasty,
in forty scrolls,
half of which were unfinished.
On his deathbed,
he wrote to his cousin Wěi, saying:
"I always wanted to re-annotate the two histories of Qiān and Gù,
and compile more than two hundred omissions from Shǐ and Hàn.
They are in the bamboo basket in the kitchen; you can check and copy them
to preserve the general idea.
The Hǎidàizhì is truly not comprehensive enough;
you can make several copies,
give one copy to each of the Fǔjūn's staff members,
and to my friends Rèn Fǎng, Xú Yín, Liú Yáng, and Péi Kuí."
He also ordered
"to bury the coffin directly in the earth,
without bricks,
and not to set up a spirit seat."
He was thirty-five years old at the time.
Wáng Qūnzī, courtesy name Xuānyuē,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
Both his father and grandfather served as provincial governors.
Qūnzī was learned in rites and widely read from a young age.
He started his career as Chángshì of Jiāngxià Wáng's state,
then Dàsīmǎ Xíng Cānjūn,
Zhāng'ān Lìng,
and progressively rose to Shǐ'ān Nèishǐ.
He did not take up the official post
and was appointed Shānyáng Wáng Píqi Cānjūn,
concurrently Zhìshū Yùshǐ,
Lángzhōng of Ānchéng state,
and Wú Lìng.
In the final years of the Shēngmíng era,
Right Assistant Director Wáng Jiǎn esteemed Confucian arts.
Táo Qūnzī was appointed Assistant Director of the Imperial Library and concurrently Left Aide to the Secretariat,
participating in the establishment of the ceremonial rites of the Qí state.
Initially,
Wáng Jiǎn compiled the Gǔjīn Sāngfú Jí Jì (Collection of Ancient and Modern Mourning Rites).
Táo Qūnzī challenged Wáng Jiǎn on eleven points.
He then compiled five volumes of the Shìxíng (Current Practices).
He was transferred to Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University).
The National University had been defunct for a long time.
In the second year of Jiànwú,
Táo Qūnzī first submitted a memorial to establish a school.
He also concurrently served as Assistant Director of the Imperial Library,
compiling the Yǒngmíng Qǐjū Zhù (Records of Daily Life in the Yǒngmíng Era).
He was transferred to Tōngzhí Chángshì (Director of the Imperial Bureau of Attendants)
and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry),
retaining his positions as Erudite and Assistant Director of the Imperial Library as before.
He was sent out as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) and Nánkāng Xiàng (Grand Administrator of Nánkāng),
with the titles of Tàizhōng Dàfū (Grandee of the Palace) and Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of Splendid Happiness),
and given the added honorific of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
〔二四〕Táo Qūnzī was naturally simple;
his clothes and furs were not washed,
his desk and table were black with dust.
In his old age,
his hand never released a scroll.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he died.
His cousin, Táo Guīzhī,
had a talent for history
and compiled the Qí Zhíyí (Ceremonial Regulations of Qí).
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng,
his son, Zhōngjūn Cānjūn Táo Hào, submitted a memorial, saying:
“My deceased father, the late Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (Commander of Chángshuǐ), Táo Guīzhī,
laid his foundation on simplicity
and cultivated his nature according to Confucianism.
In the second year of Yuánhuī of Sòng,
he was commanded to compile and collect ancient official positions and the division of duties throughout the dynasties.
All that was in the canonical texts
he meticulously investigated.
Thus, the ranks and responsibilities
were all compiled and recorded.
Dismissals, promotions, and appointments
【were all】 comprehensively researched and recorded.
〔二五〕He described the distinctions of ceremonial robes
and the ornaments of caps and pendants.
It happened to be the time of the new dynasty's rise,
when systems and regulations were being renewed.
The late Grand Tutor, your servant Xiāo Yuān, conveyed the imperial decree
to quickly review and correct it.
Before the editing was completed,
misfortune struck my private family.
Disregarding my humble status,
I respectfully venture to submit [the work],
which comprises fifty volumes,
called Qí Zhíyí.
I humbly hope it will be permanently placed in the Imperial Archives
and eternally inscribed in the imperial library.”
An edict ordered it to be deposited in the Imperial Archives.
Zǔ Chōngzhī, courtesy name Wényuǎn,
was a native of Jì, Fányáng.
His grandfather, Zǔ Chāng,
was Dàjiàng Qīng (Minister of the Grand Architect) during Sòng.
His father, Zǔ Shuòzhī,
served as Fèngcháoqǐng (Gentleman-in-Attendance).
From a young age, Zǔ Chōngzhī delved into antiquity
and had an inventive mind.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng appointed him to serve in the Huálín Xuéshěng (Huálín Academy),
and bestowed upon him a residence, carriages, and clothing.
He was released from service and appointed Assistant to the Governor of Nánxú Prefecture,
and subsequently Cānjūn (Staff Officer) in a ducal establishment.
In the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
the calendar devised by Hé Chéngtiān was adopted,
which was considered more accurate than the eleven ancient schools.
Zǔ Chōngzhī, however, considered it still imprecise,
and therefore created a new method.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has extensively consulted ancient texts,
and rigorously investigated past canons.
The Five Emperors' sequences,
the Three Kings' divisions,
the Chunqiu's new moons,
the chronology of eclipses recorded by Tán and Qiān,
the treatises and histories by Biāo and Gù,
the calendrical annotations of the Wèi dynasty,
and the daily records of the Jìn dynasty –
I have explored the differences between ancient and modern,
and observed the essentials of China and the barbarians.
From the time of written characters onward,
over two thousand years,
the phenomena of solar and lunar conjunctions
and separations,
and the verification of star densities and sparsities,
through diligent effort and dedicated thought,
can all be explained.
Furthermore, I have personally measured with gǔi and chǐ,
and personally observed with armillary spheres and clepsydras.
My eyes have exhausted every hair's breadth,
my mind has plumbed every calculation,
and my examination and analysis of changes
are also comprehensively detailed.
However, ancient calendars are crude and erroneous,
generally lacking precision.
Various schools are in conflict,
〔二六〕unable to determine their convergence.
Upon examining what Hé Chéngtiān presented,
his intention was to reform,
but
the methods he established were simplistic
and have now become quite divergent.
According to my verification,
I have observed three major errors:
the positions of the sun and moon
differ by three degrees;
the shadows at the two solstices
are nearly one day
off;
the visibility and invisibility of the five planets
can differ by forty days;
and their retrograde, direct, and stationary motions
may shift by two constellations.
If the solstices and equinoxes are inaccurate,
then the solar terms and intercalary months are not correct;
if the stellar degrees deviate from the heavens,
then observations lack a standard.
Your servant was born in a sagely era,
and consulted those currently in power.
I humbly dare, despite my ignorance,
to create a new calendar.
I respectfully state that there are two reasons for the revision
and three principles for the new method.
For the revisions: First, according to the old method,
in one zhāng cycle (19 years) there are seven intercalary months.
The number of intercalary months
is too many,
causing a one-day error every two hundred years.
Once the solar terms and intercalary months shift,
the method should be revised.
The frequent changes in calendrical records
are indeed due to this point.
Now, I have revised the zhāng method to have one hundred and forty-four intercalary months in three hundred
and ninety-one years,
so that it will align with the Zhōu and Hàn periods,
and be used permanently in the future
without further deviation.
Second: The Yáo Diǎn states:
“On the shortest day,
the star Mǎo culminates,
thereby fixing midwinter.”
Inferring from this,
in the Táng era, the winter solstice sun
was about fifty degrees to the left of its current constellation.
【At the beginning】 of the 【Hàn】 dynasty,
the Qín calendar was used,
〔二七〕and the winter solstice sun was at six degrees in Qiānniú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn reformed and established the Tàichū calendar,
and the winter solstice sun was at the beginning of Niú.
In the Sìfēn
method of the Later Hàn,
the winter solstice sun was at twenty-two degrees in Dǒu.
In the Jìn dynasty, Jiāng Jí used lunar eclipses to verify the sun's position,
knowing that the winter solstice was at seventeen degrees in Dǒu.
Now, comparing it with the culminating stars
and verifying it with
eclipses and full moons,
the winter solstice sun
is at eleven degrees in Dǒu.
In total,
in less than a hundred years,
the difference is two degrees.
Old methods invariably assigned the winter solstice sun a fixed
position.
As the celestial numbers deviated,
the stellar degrees of the seven luminaries
gradually became erroneous.
Once the discrepancies became evident,
it was necessary to revise them.
They were only accurate for a short time
and could not be applied long-term.
Continuous reforms
are also due to this point.
Now, by allowing the winter solstice position to differ slightly year by year,
and re-examining the Hàn annotations,
they are all found to be precise.
It will be used for a long time in the future
without the trouble
of frequent revisions.
Regarding the establishment of the method:
First, by taking Zǐ as the head of the earthly branches,
located due north,
its yáo corresponds to the beginning of the ascending qi of chūjiǔ,
and Xū is the northernmost constellation of the celestial lodge.”
middle.
When the primordial *yuánqì* initially arose,
it ought to be at this time.
The former scholar Yú Xǐ
extensively discussed this principle.
