but due to poverty, it is very difficult to obtain."
The Emperor was very pleased.
Having eaten too much *zhúyí* (逐夷),
his abdomen became swollen and distended,
and his breath was almost gone.
His attendants suggested he drink several liters of sour wine,
and only then did it subside.
His illness grew very severe;
he still consumed three liters of liquid and dregs at each meal.
His dropsy had accumulated for a long time,
and medicine was no longer effective.
On the day he was in his final extremity,
he sat upright,
called for a Daoist priest,
joined his palms, and then passed away.
Because Yuàn (願) had attended the sick for a long time,
he was transferred to Zhèngyuán Láng (正員郎).
He was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jìnpíng (晉平).
While in the commandery, he did not manage production.
The previous administration had engaged in transactions with the people,
and seized their children and wives as pledges.
Yuàn (願) sent people to intercept and retrieve them on the road.
While in the commandery, he established schools and taught.
The commandery previously produced beards of bears,
which could be used as medicine.
When someone presented Yuàn (願) with some,
Yuàn (願) could not bear to kill them [bears],
and released them into the mountains twenty *lǐ* (里) away.
One night, they returned to his bed.
He again sent them to the mountains forty *lǐ* (里) away.
After a night,
they returned to their original spot.
Yuàn (願) then sent them even further away,
and they did not return.
Commentators considered this to be due to his benevolent heart.
By the sea, there was the Yuèwáng Shí (越王石),
often hidden in clouds and mist.
It was said that
"only an incorruptible Grand Administrator could see it."
Yuàn (願) went to observe it,
and it was clear and unobscured.
Later, when Wáng Xiùzhī (王秀之) of Lángyá (琅邪) was Grand Administrator of the commandery,
he wrote to a court official, saying,
"This commandery, succeeding Master Yú (虞公),
still retains good governance,
and the lingering customs are easy to follow,
so I have been somewhat free of trouble."
He resigned due to his mother's old age.
He was appointed as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (後軍將軍).
Chǔ Yuān (褚淵) often visited Yuàn (願).
When Yuàn (願) was not there,
he saw his bed covered in accumulated dust,
with several scrolls of books.
Yuān (淵) sighed, saying,
"Master Yú's (虞君) integrity
has reached such a degree!"
He ordered someone to sweep the floor and dust the bed before leaving.
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎),
and concurrently held the position of Dōngguān Jìjiǔ (東觀祭酒).
His elder brother, Jì (季),
who was the Magistrate of Shàngyú (上虞),
died.
Yuàn (願) walked home from the provincial capital,
returning to the east without waiting for an imperial edict.
He was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍),
then transferred to Tíngwèi (廷尉),
with Jìjiǔ (祭酒) as before.
Yuàn (願) had previously served Emperor Míng (明) of Sòng (宋).
At the beginning of the Qí (齊) dynasty, when the spirit tablets of the Sòng (宋) emperors were moved to Rǔyīn (汝陰) Temple,
Yuàn (願) bowed and bid farewell, shedding tears.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元) (479 CE),
he died,
aged fifty-four.
Yuàn (願) authored "Wǔjīng Lùnwèn" (五經論問) [Discussions and Questions on the Five Classics]
and compiled "Kuàijī Jì" (會稽記) [Records of Kuàijī],
with dozens of pieces of writing.
Liú Huáiwèi (劉懷慰), courtesy name Yàntài (彥泰),
was a native of Píngyuán (平原), Píngyuán (平原).
His grandfather, Fèngbó (奉伯),
during the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
served as Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ (冠軍長史).
His father, Chéngmín (乘民),
was the Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州).
Huáiwèi (懷慰) first served as the Cānjūn (參軍) of the Guīyáng (桂陽) Prince's Zhēngběi Bǎn Xíng (征北板行).
Chéngmín (乘民) died during the Yìjiā (義嘉) incident.
Huáiwèi (懷慰) observed mourning,
did not eat soy sauce,
and did not wear padded clothes in winter.
He raised his orphaned younger siblings
and served his widowed aunt,
all with kindness and righteousness.
He was again appointed as the Cānjūn (參軍) of the Shàolíng (邵陵) Prince's Nán Zhōngláng (南中郎),
Magistrate of Guǎngdé (廣德),
and Shàngshū Jiàbù Láng (尚書駕部郎).
Huáiwèi (懷慰), along with his kinsmen Zōng Cóngshàn Míng (宗從善明) and others,
were trusted confidants of Tài Zǔ (太祖),
and Huáiwèi (懷慰) was also among them.
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) had an old connection,
so Tài Zǔ (太祖) ordered Huáiwèi (懷慰) to write a letter warning and admonishing Yōuzhī (攸之).
Tài Zǔ (太祖) read it and praised its excellence.
He was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉).
When the Qí (齊) state was established,
the Emperor wanted to place Qí Jùn (齊郡) in the capital region.
The discussants argued that the land south of the Yangtze River was fertile,
a place where displaced people resettled.
So, Guābù (瓜步) was governed,
and Huáiwèi (懷慰) was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) and Grand Administrator of Qí Jùn (齊郡).
The Emperor said to Huáiwèi (懷慰),
"The state of Qí (齊) is the foundation of the royal enterprise.
I intend to give you an important post.
The matters of administration
are entirely entrusted to you."
He also gave a handwritten edict, saying,
"One who is skilled in civil affairs
must also be prepared in military matters.
Now I bestow upon you a jade-handled sword."
When Huáiwèi (懷慰) arrived at the commandery,
he repaired the city walls and ramparts,
settled the residents,
reclaimed two hundred *qǐng* (頃) of abandoned land,
and drained a submerged lake for irrigation.
He did not accept gifts or formal visits.
When a commoner offered him one *hú* (斛) of new rice,
Huáiwèi (懷慰) showed him the barley rice he was eating
and said,
"There is more than enough for my morning meal.
Fortunately, I do not need this."
He then wrote "Liánlì Lùn" (廉吏論) [Disquisition on an Incorrupt Official] to express his sentiments.
When Tài Zǔ (太祖) heard of this,
he issued a handwritten edict praising and rewarding him.
He was promoted to supervise the two commanderies of Qín (秦) and Pèi (沛).
As his wife and children were in the capital,
he was granted three hundred *hú* (斛) of rice.
Liǔ Shìlóng (柳世隆), Inspector of Yùnzhōu (⿱六允州), wrote to Huáiwèi (懷慰), saying,
"Jiāodōng (膠東) had profound transforming influence,
Yǐngchuān (潁川) achieved excellence.
Compared with the ancients,
how can one even speak of them?"
After two years in the commandery,
he was promoted to Zhèngyuán Láng (正員郎),
and concurrently led as Zhōngzhèng (中正) of the two provinces of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀).
Liú Huáiwèi 劉懷wèi 懷慰's original name was Wénwèi 聞慰.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 ascended the throne,
because it was the same name as his maternal uncle,
an edict was issued to change it.
He was sent out to supervise Dōngyáng 東陽 Commandery,
and was welcomed by the officials and common people.
He returned to concurrently serve as Southern Middle General Sīmǎ 司馬 for the Prince of Ānlù 安陸.
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng 永明 (491 CE),
he died,
aged forty-five.
When Míngdì 明帝 ascended the throne,
he said to the Imperial Secretary Xú Xiàosì 徐孝嗣:
"If Liú Huáiwèi 劉懷慰 were still alive,
the court would not worry about lacking upright officials."
Huáiwèi 懷慰 was good friends with Jiāng Yān 江淹 of Jìyáng 濟陽 and Yuán Tuàn 袁彖 of Chénjùn 陳郡,
and also authored literary works.
In the early Yǒngmíng 永明 period,
he presented his *Huángdé Lùn* 皇德論.
Péi Zhāomíng 裴昭明 was a native of Wénxǐ 聞喜, Hédōng 河東.
He was the grandson of Péi Sōngzhī 裴松之, Grand Master of the Central Palace in the Sòng 宋 dynasty.
His father, Péi Yǐn 裴駰,
was a Southern Middle General Cānjūn 參軍.
Zhāomíng 昭明 studied the Confucian classics and history from a young age.
During the Tàishǐ 泰始 period (465-472 CE),
he served as a Grand Academy Scholar.
The officials memorialized:
"For the crown prince's wedding,
the 'Nàzhēng' 納徵 (betrothal gifts) used jade bi-discs and tiger skins.
It is unclear what this is based on."
Zhāomíng 昭明 deliberated:
"In the 'Lǐ Nàzhēng' 禮納徵 (Rites of Betrothal Gifts),
'lìpí' 儷皮 (pairs of skins) are used as 'tíngshí' 庭實 (court gifts),
which are deer skins.
The 'Note on the Jin Crown Prince's Betrothal' states 'two tiger skins.'
In the Tàiyuán 太元 period (376-396 CE),
when a princess was betrothed,
one tiger skin and one leopard skin were used.
How can it be said that the wedding rites are unclear?
Due to the differing ranks of princes and dukes,
tiger and leopard skins were chosen for their ornate patterns to dignify the occasion.
Although tigers and leopards are patterned,
they are not mentioned in the 'Zhēnglǐ' 徵禮 (Rites of Betrothal).
Although bears are ancient,
they are not mentioned in the 'Hūnlǐ' 婚禮 (Wedding Rites).
Although gui-tablets and zhang-scepters are beautiful,
their uses may differ.
Now, it is appropriate to adhere to the classics and edicts,
and all irregularities and errors
should be thoroughly corrected."
Thereupon, the officials deliberated,
adding gui-tablets and zhang-scepters,
and two skins each of leopards and bears.
During the Yuánhuī 元徽 period (473-477 CE),
he was sent out as Chancellor of Chángshā 長沙 Commandery.
When his term ended,
the Inspector Wáng Yùn 王蘊 said to him:
"You are upright and poor,
and surely lack funds for your return journey.
Among the gentry of Xiāngzhōng 湘中, if anyone needs a letter of introduction,
I would not begrudge it."
Zhāomíng 昭明 replied:
"Your humble servant, having been honored as a regional assistant,
could not bring glory to the superior prefecture.
How could I trouble your pure reputation with matters of Hóngdū 鴻都 (the imperial capital)?"
He successively served as Sìbù Tōngzhí Láng 祠部通直郎.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng 永明 (485 CE),
he was sent as an envoy to the "barbarians."
Shìzǔ 世祖 said to him:
"Given your talent for fulfilling a mission,
when you return,
I will reward you with a commandery."
He returned to serve as Administrator of Shǐ'ān 始安.
A commoner from the commandery, Gōng Xuánxuān 龔玄宣,
[一０] claimed that a divine being gave him a jade seal and a jade tablet with writing,
and that he didn't need a brush, but could just blow on paper to form characters.
He called himself
"Saint Gōng" 龔聖人,
and used this to delude the masses.
Previous commandery administrators had revered and served him,
but Zhāomíng 昭明 imprisoned him and punished him.
When he returned from his post,
he was very poor.
Shìzǔ 世祖 said:
"Péi Zhāomíng 裴昭明 returned from his commandery post and
had no house.
I am not skilled in writing;
I do not know who among the ancients he can be compared to."
He was promoted to Shèshēng Xiàowèi 射聲校尉.
In the ninth year (491 CE),
he was again sent as an envoy north.
In the early Jiànwǔ 建武 period (494-498 CE),
he served as Wáng Xuánmiǎo's 王玄邈's Ānběi Chángshǐ 安北長史 and Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng 廣陵.
Míngdì 明帝, because he had made no reports while in office,
recalled him and
reprimanded him.
Zhāomíng 昭明 said:
"I simply did not wish to contend for power."
Zhāomíng 昭明 had diligent achievements in all the commanderies he governed.
He often said to people:
"Why does one need to accumulate wealth in life?
Beyond one's own person,
what else is truly necessary?
If one's children and grandchildren are untalented,
my accumulation will be their dissipation.
If they can establish themselves,
then nothing is better than a classic text."
Thus, he never managed any properties throughout his life.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng 中興 (502 CE),
he died.
His cousin from the same ancestral line, Péi Yǐ 裴顗,
courtesy name Yànqí 彥齊,
had unusual conduct from a young age.
During the Tàishǐ 泰始 period (465-472 CE),
while listening to lectures at the Zǒngmíng Guān 總明觀,
he did not yield his seat to Liú Bǐng 劉秉,
who then made him a Cānjūn 參軍.
At the end of Shēngmíng 昇明 (479 CE),
he became a Fèng Cháoqǐng 奉朝請.
When the Qí 齊 dynasty was established,
the Crown Princess Péi 裴妃 needed an 外戚譜 (genealogy of maternal relatives),
but Yǐ 顗 did not provide it,
thus their family registration was separated.
When Tàizǔ 太祖 received the abdication,
Yǐ 顗 submitted a memorial slandering him,
hung up his official hat and departed,
and was executed.
Shěn Xiàn 沈憲, courtesy name Yànzhāng 彥璋,
[一一] was a native of Wǔkāng 武康, Wúxīng 吳興.
His grandfather, Shěn Shuōdào 沈說道,
was the Grand Administrator of both Bāxī 巴西 and Zǐtóng 梓潼 Commanderies.
His father, Shěn Púzhī 沈璞之,
was a Northern Middle General Xíng Cānjūn 行參軍.
Xiàn 憲 initially responded to a provincial summons
and became a Master of Records.
He was capable and organized from a young age.
He successively served as Prefect of Línshǒu 臨首 and Yúháng 餘杭,
[一二] assistant to the Prince of Bālíng 巴陵,
acting Prefect of Xiānglíng 襄令,
[一三] and was appointed as a Jiàbù Láng 駕部郎.
Sòng Míngdì 宋明帝, speaking with Xiàn 憲,
said to him:
"You
have the talent of a Provincial Inspector of Guǎngzhōu 廣州."
He was appointed Prefect of Wūchéng 烏程,
where he achieved significant administrative success.
The Grand Administrator Chǔ Yuān 褚淵 praised him, saying:
"This man is adaptable and can be employed in various capacities."
He was appointed Tōngzhí Láng 通直郎 and
Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě 都水使者 (Commissioner of Waterways).
He excelled in official duties and had achievements in office.
He was appointed Zhèngyuán Láng 正員郎,
then Prefect of Wú 吳,
and Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
In the second year of Shēngmíng 昇明 (478 CE),
when the Western Middle General Huàng 晃 was made Inspector of Yùzhōu 豫州,
Tàizǔ 太祖 promoted Xiàn 憲 to be Huàng's 晃's Chángshǐ 長史,
Grand Administrator of Nánliáng 南梁,
and acting provincial affairs administrator.
He was promoted to Consultative Counselor to the Prince of Yùzhāng 豫章,
but before taking office,
he was dismissed due to an incident.
He was again appointed General of the Army of the Prince of Ānchéng 安成 and Commander-in-chief of the Prince of Wǔlíng 武陵,
and promoted to 少府卿 (Minister of the Lesser Treasury).
The Lesser Treasury managed markets and trade,
interacting with the common people.
Those with administrative ability
all served in this position.
He was promoted to General of the Garrison Army under Wáng Jiǎn 王儉.
When the Prince of Wǔlíng 武陵, Xiāo Yè 蕭曄, became Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽,
Xiàn 憲 was made his Left Army Sīmǎ 司馬.
Tàizǔ 太祖 believed that the numerous households in Shānyīn 山陰 were difficult to govern,
and wanted to divide it into two counties.
Shìzǔ 世祖 memorialized, saying:
"How can a county not be governable?
It's just that the right person hasn't been employed."
Thereupon, Xiàn 憲 was given the concurrent post of Prefect of Shānyīn 山陰,
and his administrative reputation greatly flourished.
Kǒng Zhìguī 孔稚珪 took leave to return east
and said to people:
"Prefect Shěn 沈 has a truly innate talent for assessing matters."
He was granted the title General Who Stabilizes the North.
When Wáng Jìngzé 王敬則 became Administrator of Kuàijī 會稽,
Xiàn 憲 remained as General of the Garrison Army
and continued in his post.
Qiān was made Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General of Resolute Cavalry (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn),
acting Governor (Xíng Shì) of Southern Yùzhōu.
Then Chief Clerk to the Rear General of the Prince of Jìn'ān and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Guǎnglǐng.
The Prince of Xīyáng, Zǐmíng, was deputized as Governor of Nánwǎnzhōu.
Xiàn still remained as Chief Clerk to the General of Resolute Cavalry (Guànjūn Zhǎngshǐ),
and Administrator as before,
frequently acting in matters of the provincial administration.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng (490 CE),
Zǐmíng's clerk (diǎnqiān), Liú Dàojì, took fifty men from the provincial administration for his own service,
and also pressed Zǐmíng's attendants into service,
and embezzled millions from boat equipment and other illicit gains.
This was reported by the officials concerned.
Shìzǔ was enraged
and ordered Dàojì to death.
Xiàn was implicated for failing to restrain him
and was dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) and General Aiding the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
He left office due to illness.
He was appointed Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì),
but before he was invested,
he died.
He was regarded by his contemporaries as an excellent official.
Qiū Zhòngqǐ, from the same commandery as Xiàn,
had previously served as Administrator of Jìnpíng Commandery.
He was clean, incorruptible, and independent.
Chǔ Yuān sighed, saying:
"To see desirable things and yet keep one's heart undisturbed—this is what Duke Yáng (Yáng Gōng) bequeathed to his descendants."
Zhòngqǐ, courtesy name Zǐzhèn,
was known in his youth to Xiàn's paternal cousin, Commander of the Army (Lǐngjūn), Yín.
he served as Chief Clerk to the Commander of the Army for the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ).
His highest office was Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
He died.
Lǐ Guīzhī, courtesy name Kǒngzhāng,
was a native of Zhōngwǔ in Jiāngxià.
Both his father and grandfather served as county magistrates.
【Guīzhī was appointed as an aide (cóngshì) in the province in his youth.
In the early Tàishǐ era of Sòng (465-471 CE),
Cài Xīngzōng was Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
and he appointed Guīzhī as an aide in the Anxī Command (Ānxī Fǔzuǒ),
entrusting him with official duties.
His clean administration became known.
General of the Right Army (Yòu Jūn Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently Supervisor of Rivers and Canals (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě).
Guīzhī was known for his clean and capable service in various posts.
He was appointed General of Roaming Cavalry (Yóují Jiāngjūn),
concurrently keeping his post as Supervisor (shǐzhě) as before.
He was then concurrently transferred to Minor Controller (Shàofǔ).
He died.
Previously,
in the fourth year (486 CE),
Máo Huìsù of Xíngyáng served as Minister of the Minor Controller (Shàofǔ Qīng).
He was strong in official talent and meticulous in managing affairs.
An imperial decree ordered the purchase of 1,200 catties of copper-green (bìqīng) from the market for imperial paintings,
at a cost of 600,000 cash.
Someone slandered Huìsù for taking profit.
Shìzǔ was enraged,
and ordered the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) to assess the price.
It was found to be overpriced by more than 280,000 cash.
The relevant officials reported it,
and he was executed.
After his death, his family was utterly destitute.
The Emperor deeply regretted it.
Kǒng Xiùzhī
was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
His grandfather, Jìgōng,
was Grand Master of Guanglu (Guānglù Dàfū).
His father, Língyùn, was Author (Zhùzuò Láng).
Xiùzhī first became a student of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐ Shēng),
and was recommended as "Filial and Incorrupt" (Xiàolián).
He was appointed Aide (xíng cānjūn) to the General of the Guard (Wèijūn),
then Supernumerary Gentleman (yuánwàiláng),
and Secretary of the Three Ducal Ministries (Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng).
He was sent out as Magistrate (Lìng) of Wūchéng,
where he showed administrative ability.
Upon his return, he was promoted to Palace Gentleman of All Reaching (Tōngzhí Láng),
and appointed Magistrate of Wú County.
There was a child of ten years old
who stole a bundle of rice from a neighbor's field.
Xiùzhī sent him to prison for punishment.
Someone advised against it,
but Xiùzhī said:
"If he can be a thief at ten,
what won't he do when he grows up?"
The entire county was awestruck and disciplined.
He was promoted to Assistant Director of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng),
and again became known for his official duties.
He was transferred to General of the Vanguard (Qián Jūn Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently Minor Controller (Shàofǔ).
He was promoted to General of骁骑 (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
with Minor Controller as before.
He was sent out as General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Commander-in-Chief (Guànjūn Zhēnglǔ) of Gāozōng, and Administrator of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Nèishǐ).
Upon his return, he became Regular Palace Attendant (Zhèngyuán Chángshì),
concurrently Minister of the Left for the People (Zuǒmín Shàngshū) and Grand Judge (Tíngwèi Qīng).
He was sent out as Administrator of Línhǎi (Línhǎi Tàishǒu).
While in office, he was clean and frugal.
When he resigned from the commandery and returned,
he offered twenty catties of dried ginger.
Shìzǔ disliked its small quantity,
but when he learned of Xiùzhī's integrity,
he sighed with admiration.
He was appointed Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General of the Vanguard (Qián Jūn Jiāngjūn) for the Prince of Wǔlíng.
Before he was invested,
he was again sent out as General Aiding the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn),
concurrently supervising Wúxīng Commandery.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu),
and his governance was praised as clean and strict.
When Gāozōng assisted in government,
he imposed restrictions on the various feudal lords,
sending secret decrees to the high officials.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
Xiùzhī was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General of Resolute Cavalry (Guànjūn Zhǎngshǐ) for the Prince of Jìnxī,
acting Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
and Administrator of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Nèishǐ).
Xiùzhī declined,
but it was not permitted.
Before he was invested,
he died.
The court historian says: If a qín or sè is out of tune,
it must be disassembled and re-strung.
In the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, officials
gradually deviated from those of the Hàn.
Although the style of harshness and severity declined,
the sentiment of benevolence and love also diminished.
Confined by strict laws,
restricted by common regulations,
the benevolence of a lifetime had not yet been fully proclaimed and managed,
but after a single month's expectation, governing methods were already sought.
To prioritize public over private interest
is not easy for oneself.
To exploit the people to serve the state
is not difficult for things.
To expect to remedy faults
merely seeks to escape blame.
Furthermore, when desirable things are seen,
appetites and desires flow forth.
Greed leads to the ruin of office,
and taking and giving violates righteousness.
That officials are not good
is invariably due to this.
To expose villainy and discern falsehoods
truly awaits exceptional discernment.
To leave a name and establish achievements
depends solely on integrity and impartiality.
The governance of the people in the present age
has not surpassed this.
The encomium says: The bustling common people,
officials are their long-term guardians.
Disorder must be managed,
obscurity returns to benevolence.
Right and wrong are intertwined,
leniency and severity are displayed in turn.
How then to guide the people?
The value lies in personal integrity.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Volume 35: Eminent Recluses: Chǔ Bóyù, Míng Sēngshào, Gù Huān, Zāng Róngxù, Hé Qiú, Liú Qiú, Yǔ Yì, Zōng Cè, Dù Jīngchǎn, Shěn Língshì, Wú Bāo, Xú Bózhēn
The *Yì* [Classic of Changes] speaks of four paths for a *jūnzǐ*,
which refer to speaking and silence.
Thus, some enter the halls of government and never leave,
while others wander the rivers and lakes, departing forever.
They hide from the hustle and bustle,
their feelings and traces varied in a myriad ways.
If their inner moral principles are sufficient,
and both hope and subtlety are gone,
they conceal their presence in remote cliffs,
obscure their names in foolish valleys,
free themselves from the shackles of benevolence and righteousness,
and forever merge their form and spirit with heaven and earth.
Then, beyond the teachings of fame,
there is another kind of conduct.
Hence, at the time of Yáo's enfeoffment, there were those who were not saints,
and Kǒngmén [Confucius's school] mistakenly entertained guests with chicken and millet.
Secondly, some display the noble virtue of solitary departure,
valuing the empty name of choosing to stay or leave,
inciting competition and avoiding greed,
and being different from the world.
Perhaps they consider avoiding regret later,
and their affairs lead to recognizing danger;
or perhaps their principles are not expounded,
and they wander the mountains and marshes, chanting poems.
All of them use the universe to form their minds,
and borrow wind and clouds as warnings.
If their ambition truly
reaches the Way, it is never otherwise.
They maintain integrity and cultivate simplicity,
adorning it with artistic accomplishments.
Otherwise,
how are they different from woodcutters
in the mountains?
Thus, when Fán Yīng was summoned,
he did not meet Lǐ Gù's expectations;
Féng Huī's humble integrity
was scorned in Zhāng Huá's words.
Expecting them to be outside the尘俗 (common world),
they are able to greatly expand.
As for the dozen or so people today,
they do not seek fame in office,
nor do they criticize customs in retirement.
They preserve themselves in secluded paths,
and follow the Way within the Ruúmén [Confucian school].
These are the principles and conduct of the *yìmín* [hermits].
Therefore, this is compiled as the "Chapter on Lofty Hermits."
Chǔ Bóyù, courtesy name Yuánqú,
was a native of Qiántáng, Wújùn.
His great-grandfather, Hán,
was the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng.
His father, Tì,
was a Counselor to the General Who Subdues Barbarians.
Bóyù was modest and reclusive in his youth,
and had few desires.
At eighteen,
his father arranged a marriage for him.
When the bride entered through the front door,
Bóyù exited through the back door.
He then went to Shàn,
and lived on Pùbùshān.
He was tolerant of cold and heat;
people at the time compared him to Wáng Zhòngdū.
He lived in the mountains for over thirty years,
isolated from people.
When Wáng Sēngdá was the Grand Administrator of Wújùn,
he earnestly invited Bóyù.
Bóyù reluctantly
stayed in the commandery for a night or two,
exchanged only a few words, and then left.
Qīu Zhēnsūn, General of Ning Shuò, wrote to Sēngdá:
"I heard that Mr. Chǔ has come out and is staying at your esteemed residence.
This man has hidden his presence among clouds and dwellings,
does not serve kings or nobles,
holds himself aloof, and eats only plants [lit. 'trees']
for many years now.
If it were not for your bending your principles and valuing the virtuous,
how could you have brought him here?
In the past, Wénjǔ [Kǒng Róng] lived in Yěchéng,
and Āndào [Wáng Xiànzhī] entered Chāngmén.
Now, this is the third such instance.
Indeed, a scholar who abstains from grain,
a person who consumes morning dew,
can be temporarily brought,
but should not be long detained.
You should consider fulfilling his lofty steps
and completing his spiritual transformation.
When he is expected to return to his policy,
may I briefly trouble your pure presence?
I also wish to assist with persuasion."
Sēngdá replied:
"Mr. Chǔ has long been a companion of white clouds.
Ancient hermits
sometimes worried about their children,
or caused Huáyīn to become a market.
But this man is austere,
only befriending pines and rocks.
He has dwelt on isolated peaks and precipitous ridges
for several decades.
Recently, I wanted him to come here,
hoping to comfort him day and night.
We have discussed *zhī* and *guì* [auspicious plants],
and inquired about *lì* and *luó* [vines].
It is as if he has already spied on the misty liquids [of immortality]
and overlooked the azure continent.
I know you wish to see him;
I will certainly arrange a meeting."
In the second year of Sòng Xiàojiàn [455 CE],
Sànqí Chángshì Yuè Xún, while inspecting customs,
memorialized to recommend Bóyù,
who was appointed Aide to the Counselor-in-chief of his home province,
but he did not accept.
When Tàizǔ [Emperor Gāo of Southern Qí] ascended the throne,
he issued imperial edicts to Wú and Kuàijì commanderies,
to respectfully invite and send for him,
but he again declined, citing illness.
The Emperor did not wish to go against his will,
and ordered the establishment of the Tàipíngguǎn on Báishíshān in Shàn for him to reside in.
In the first year of Jiànyuán [479 CE],
he died,
aged eighty-six.
He always lived on the upper floor of a building,
and was buried at the site of the building.
Kǒng Zhìguī received the Daoist teachings from him,
and erected a stele beside his residence.
Míng Sēngshào, courtesy name Chéngliè,
was a native of Píngyuán.
His grandfather, Wán,
was a Judicial Officer of the province.
His father, Lüè,
was a Gěishì Zhōng.
Sēngshào was twice nominated as Xiùcái during the Sòng Yuánjiā era,
and was learned in the Confucian arts.
During the Yǒngguāng era,
he was appointed Registrar by the General of Zhenbei,
but he did not accept either.
He lived in seclusion on Láoshān in Chángguǎngjùn,
gathering disciples and establishing a school.
When Huáiběi was lost to the barbarians,
he crossed the Jiāng [Yangtze River] southwards.
In the sixth year of Míng Dì Tàishǐ [470 CE],
he was summoned as Tōngzhí Láng,
but did not accept.
During the Shēngmíng era,
when Tàizǔ was Grand Tutor,
he issued an order to appoint Sēngshào, Gù Huān, and Zāng Róngxù with banners and silks,
summoning them as Adjutant-Registrars,
but they did not arrive.
Sēngshào's younger brother, Qìngfú,
was the Prefect of Qīngzhōu.
Sēngshào lacked provisions,
so he followed Qìngfú to Yùzhōu,
living on Yǎnyúshān,
at Qíyún Jīngshè.
He delighted in the water and rocks,
and never once entered the prefectural city.
In the winter of the first year of Jiànyuán [479 CE],
an imperial edict stated:
"We set aside our mat, thinking of worthy men,
and harbor thoughts beyond the mundane.
Míng Sēngshào of Qíjùn, with his lofty aspiration and reclusive dwelling,
is immersed in ancient texts and records.
His quiet integrity and conduct
should be honored and adorned."
He was summoned as Zhèngyuán Láng,
but declined, citing illness.
Later, he wrote to Cuī Sīzǔ:
"The aspirations of Resident Míng are commendable.
Did my previous intention not reach him after all?
When it gets a little cooler, I have some matters to discuss.
You may go there,
fully explain my intentions,
and have him return with Qìngfú."
He also said:
"Not eating the millet of Zhōu but eating the wild ferns of Zhōu [a reference to Bó Yí and Shú Qí]
was already debated in ancient times.
Can talk about it cease now?
Let us take it as a joke."
When Qìngfú retired from his post,
Sēngshào followed him home,
and resided at Shèshān in Jiāngchéng.
Tàizǔ said to Qìngfú:
"Your elder brother highly values his principles;
he is also an 'outside minister' to Yáo.
Although We do not interact directly,
there are times when We communicate in dreams."
He presented Sēngshào with a bamboo-root ruyi
and a bamboo-sheath hat.
Sēngshào heard of the virtuous conduct of the śramaṇa Shì Sēngyuǎn
and went to visit him at Dìnglín Sì.
Tàizǔ wished to leave the monastery to see him.
Sēngyuǎn asked Sēngshào:
"If the Son of Heaven comes,
how will you, the recluse, respond to him?"
Sēngshào replied:
"As a person of the mountains and wilds,
I would naturally dig a hole and flee.
(（苦）)【若】If I am unable to decline the command,
then I will follow the precedent of Dài Gōng."
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
Shìzǔ issued an imperial edict summoning Sēngshào,
but he feigned illness and refused to appear.
He was summoned by imperial decree to be a Guózǐ Bóshì,
but he did not take up the post,
and died.
His son, Yuánlín,
courtesy name Zhòngzhāng,
also inherited the family tradition.
Sēngshào's eldest brother, Sēngyìn,
was skilled in xuányán.
During the Sòng dynasty, he served as Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
His younger brother, Sēnggǎo,
also loved learning.
Sòng Xiàowǔ saw him
and praised his name,
which people at the time considered an honor.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
he became Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Qìngfú,
at the beginning of Jiànyuán,
became Huángmén.
Sēngyìn's son, Huìzhào,
during the Yuánhuī era,
served as Tàizǔ's Píngnán Zhǔbù.
He accompanied him in resisting Guìyáng,
and successively rose to Piàojí Zhōngbīng,
jointly leading the zhí with Xún Bóyù.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
he became Bāzhōu Cìshǐ,
pacifying and comforting the Mán and Dàn peoples.
The emperor permitted him to be transferred to Yìzhōu,
but he died
before the transfer.
Gù Huān, courtesy name Jǐngyí,
was a native of Yánguān, Wú Jùn.
His grandfather, Jū,
moved to avoid chaos at the end of Jìn Lóng'ān.
When Huān was six or seven years old, (（晝）)【書】he wrote the cyclical characters,
and had three slips of bamboo.
〔一０〕Huān analyzed and calculated them,
〔一一〕and thus understood the sixty-year cycle.
His family was poor.
His father sent him to drive sparrows from the fields.
Huān composed the *Huáng Què Fù* and returned,
after more than half of the grain had been eaten.
〔一二〕His father was angry
and intended to beat him,
but stopped upon seeing the *fu*.
There was a schoolhouse in his village,
but Huān was too poor to attend.
He would listen by leaning against the wall behind the schoolhouse,
and forgot nothing.
At the age of eight,
he recited the *Xiàojīng*, *Shī*, and *Lún*.
When he grew up,
he was devoted to learning.
His mother was old,
so he personally tilled the fields and recited books,
and at night, he lit chaff to illuminate his studies.
Gù Yǐzhī from the same commandery, upon governing the county,
saw him and was impressed.
He sent his sons to associate with him,
and his grandson Xiànzhī,
all received instruction in the classics.
When Huān was over twenty,
he further consulted Léi Cìzōng of Yùzhāng on various profound Confucian doctrines.
When his mother died,
he did not take food or water for six or seven days.
〔一三〕He built a hut by her tomb
and subsequently lived as a recluse, refusing official positions.
He opened a hall and gathered disciples in Tiāntái Shān in Shàn,
with nearly a hundred students at any given time.
Huān was orphaned early,
and whenever he read the *Shī* to
"Alas for my parents,"
he would grasp the book and weep bitterly.
Scholars consequently ceased lecturing on the *Liáoyí Piān*.
When Tàizǔ assisted in government,
he was pleased with Huān's teachings
and summoned him to be Yángzhōu Zhǔbù,
sending an imperial envoy to welcome Huān.
He arrived only after Tàizǔ ascended the throne.
Huān, styling himself "Your humble servant Gù Huān from the mountains and valleys," submitted a memorial stating:
"Your servant has heard that one lifts a net by its main rope,
and shakes a fur coat by its collar.
When the main rope and collar are in order,
the meshes and hairs will naturally spread out.
Therefore, morality and virtue
are the main rope;
circumstances and power
are the meshes.
If the superior manages the main rope,
then all affairs will proceed in due order;
if the inferior spreads out the meshes,
then no official position will be vacant.
Thus, Tāng and Wǔ, by obtaining power and revering the Dao, prolonged their reigns;
Qín and Xiàng, by neglecting the Dao and relying on power, met their demise.
Indeed, the opening and closing of Heaven's gate
has existed since ancient times;
the four seasons renew themselves,
and gauze and fur clothes alternate in use.
Now, with the positions of fire and swamp exchanged,
the three numinous powers have changed the constitution.
Heaven establishes bright virtue,
nurturing all beings in accordance with the times,
seeking out the hidden and obscure,
so that no words are hidden in the wilds.
Therefore, this foolish man from the remote valleys
dares to reveal his limited perspective.
I have respectfully compiled and edited Lǎozi's teachings,
and present one scroll on the principles of governance.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will examine the hundred kings of antiquity,
and weigh the needs of the present time,
not discarding words because they come from a humble source,
nor abandoning the Dao because the person is insignificant.
If so, it would be a blessing to all within the empire,
and the good fortune of your humble servant.
If you kindly grant a single decree,
〔一四〕then superiors and inferiors will be in perfect harmony.
Even without seeking the people's favor, the people will be pleased;
without praying to Heaven, Heaven will respond.
When Heaven responds and the people are pleased,
then the imperial foundation will be secure.
Your servant's ambition is to delve into the profound,
and not to associate with glory or power.
Clouds and mists are sufficient for me,
and I do not need official stipends.
Since Your Majesty has sought me out from afar,
how dare I not speak my mind fully?
Now that my words are exhausted,
I beg leave to withdraw."
At this time, Aide-de-camp Liú Sīxiào (劉思xiào) presented a memorial with candid words, saying:
"Since the Dàmíng (大明) era, the Sòng (宋) dynasty
has gradually seen decline and decay.
Taxes and levies have increased compared to the past,
and the imperial treasury is even poorer than before.
Moreover, military campaigns have been frequently launched,
and the wounded have not recovered.
Garrisoned soldiers are disabled,
and their provisions are less than half a sù (菽) (a small measure of pulse).
The common people wail in distress,
showing no joy in life.
Yet, those of noble and powerful status,
and those who hoard wealth,
compete in extravagant clothing, carriages, entertainers, and music,
vying for luxury and splendor.
Their pavilions, ponds, and residences
compete in grandeur and magnificence.
As for the people in the mountains and marshes,
they dare not gather or drink their water and grass.
The rich and poor contrast sharply,
and the source of problems has yet to be eliminated.
Your Majesty should issue an enlightened edict,
utter virtuous words,
spread beneficent grace,
forbid邪wèi (邪偽) (evil and falsehood),
lighten taxes,
reduce corvée labor,
stop bribes of exotic treasures,
put an end to the music of Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衞) (licentious music),
change the course of the cosmic cycles,
and respond to the needs for both simplicity and refinement.
Would this not be a great achievement!
Furthermore, Péng (彭) and Biàn (汴) have become nests for owls,
and Qīngqiū (青丘) has become a den for foxes and rabbits.
Their cruel depredations have exceeded a cycle (of twelve years),
and their tyranny grows daily.
Ghosts weep by old springs,
and people mourn over their former lands.
Children feel shame at seeing braided hair (of the barbarians),
and the elderly are humiliated to die seeing garments fastened on the left (barbarian custom).
Your Majesty should look up and respond to the longing expectation of Heaven and men,
and look down and commiserate with the efforts of the common people who crane their necks (in anticipation).
Bestow battle-axes upon generals like Wèi (衞) and Huò (霍),
and send forth strategists like Xiāo (蕭) and Zhāng (張).
Let myriad armies advance,
sweeping through mountains and valleys.
Then Héngshān (恆山) would not be too hard to point at and overturn,
and Bóhǎi (渤海) would not be too much to drink and deplete.
How could it be merely to annihilate the remaining bandits!"
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"From early morning till late,
[一五] I diligently contemplate how to promote good governance.
I long for the dreams of cliff-side hermits,
and devote my energy to supervising the treasury.
I eat late,
[一六] my diligence is extreme.
Gù Huān (顧歡) from Wújùn (吳郡) and Sanqí Láng (散騎郎) Liú Sīxiào (劉思xiào),
one having come from the countryside,
the other holding a minor official post,
both were able to present memorials at the golden gate,
offering their words at the Phoenix Palace.
Their discernment of governing principles
aligns with my heart.
Now I issue their memorials;
the officials outside the court may carefully choose what is appropriate
and present it in due course.
Gù Huān (顧歡) has recently been promoted and honored,
and Liú Sīxiào (劉思xiào) may be assigned to selection and appointment processes,
to make manifest their candid words."
When Gù Huān (顧歡) returned to the east,
the Emperor bestowed upon him a fly whisk and a plain qín (琴).
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (永明) (483 CE),
an edict summoned Gù Huān (顧歡) to be a Tàixué Bóshì (太學博士) (Professor of the Imperial Academy),
and Gù Àn (顧黯) from the same prefecture to be Sanqí Láng (散騎郎).
Gù Àn's (顧黯) courtesy name was Chángrú (長孺).
He had reclusive integrity,
and like Gù Huān (顧歡), he did not accept the summons.
In his later years, Gù Huān (顧歡) consumed medicinal herbs
and did not associate with others.
Every morning when he stepped out of his door,
mountain birds would gather on his palm to eat.
He served the Huáng (黃)-Lǎo (老) (Daoist) doctrines,
understood Yin (陰) and Yang (陽) texts,
and his numerological arts had many verifiable effects.
In the late Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
he went to the capital and temporarily resided in Dōngfǔ (東府).
Suddenly he wrote on a pillar:
"Thirty years, second month, twenty-first day."
He then returned east.
Later, the usurpation and regicide of Tàichū (太初)
indeed occurred in this month and year.
Knowing he was about to die,
he composed a poem to express his aspirations, saying:
"Essence and qi (氣) follow the course of Heaven,
wandering souls transform with all things."
He set a date for his death,
and passed away in Shànshān (剡山).
His body remained soft,
and he was sixty-four years old at the time.
He was buried in his old grave,
and a tree with intertwined branches grew by the tomb.
The county magistrate, Jiāng Shāntú (江山圖), submitted a memorial about this.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) ordered Gù Huān's (顧歡) sons
to compile Gù Huān's (顧歡) literary discussions in thirty volumes.
The two schools of Buddhism and Daoism,
having established different teachings,
scholars mutually criticized and defamed each other.
[一七] Gù Huān (顧歡) wrote the Yíxià Lùn (夷夏論) (Treatise on Barbarians and Chinese), saying: To distinguish right from wrong,
one should rely on sacred scriptures.
Tracing the origins of the two teachings,
I therefore present scriptural passages from both.
The Daoist scripture says:
"Lǎozǐ (老子) entered the pass and went to the Tiānzhú Wéiwèi Guó (天竺維衞國) (Viśāla kingdom in India).
The queen's name was Jìngmiào (淨妙).
Lǎozǐ (老子), while she was sleeping during the day,
rode on the essence of the sun into Jìngmiào's (淨妙) mouth.
Later, on the eighth day of the fourth month, at midnight,
he was born from her left armpit.
Upon falling to the ground, he immediately walked seven steps,
and thus the Buddha-Dao (佛道) arose."
This is from the Xuánmiào Nèi Piān (玄妙內篇).
The Buddhist scripture says:
"Shìjiā (釋迦) (Śākyamuni) achieved Buddhahood
after
innumerable kalpas (塵劫)."
This is from Fǎhuá Wúliàng Shòu (法華𣰋量壽) (Lotus Sutra, Immeasurable Life).
Or,
"(He was) a national teacher and Daoist master,
the patriarch of the Confucian forest."
This is from Ruìyìng Běnqǐ (瑞應本起) (Sutra of the Origin of Auspiciousness).
Gù Huān (顧歡) commented on this, saying: The Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns
all had teachers.
[一八] Among national teachers and Daoist masters,
none surpassed Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊).
Among the patriarchs of the Confucian forest,
who
excelled Kǒng (孔) (Confucius) and Zhōu (周) (Duke of Zhou)?
If Kǒng (孔) and Lǎo (老) were not the Buddha,
[一九] who then would be?
However, what the two scriptures say
fits together like tally halves.
Dao is Buddha,
and Buddha is Dao.
Their holiness
is concordant,
but their manifestations are reversed.
One conceals its brilliance to appear approachable;
the other shines its light to reveal its transcendence.
Dao benefits the world,
thus there is no place it does not enter;
wisdom encompasses all
things,
thus there is nothing it does not do.
Their entry is different,
and their actions must be different.
Each fulfills its nature,
without altering its methods.
Therefore, the ceremonial robes and sashes
are the appearance
of the Chinese;
cut hair and loose clothes
are the attire of the barbarians.
Kneeling, bowing, and bending at the waist
are the respectful manners of the vassal states;
squatting like a fox or dog
is the solemnity of the remote regions.
Coffins and outer coffins
are the customs of Central China;
cremation and water burial
are the customs of the Western Rong (戎).
Preserving the body and adhering to rites
is the teaching of continuing good;
disfiguring the body and changing one's nature
is the learning of eradicating evil.
This applies not only
to humans,
but also to different creatures.
Bird kings and beast chiefs
are often Buddhas;
in infinite worlds,
sages arise in succession.
Some manifest the Five Classics,
some spread the Three Vehicles.
As a bird, it sings like a bird;
as a beast, it roars like a beast.
It teaches the Chinese, and they speak Chinese;
it civilizes barbarians, and they speak barbarian languages.
Although boats and carriages both serve to travel far,
there are distinctions
between water and land.
Though Buddhism and Daoism equally achieve transformation,
there are distinctions between barbarian and Chinese.
If one says that since their purpose is the same,
their methods can be exchanged,
then a carriage could cross a river,
and a boat could travel
lù hū?
Jīn yǐ Zhōngxià zhī xìng,
xiào Xīróng zhī fǎ,
jì bù quán tóng,
yòu bù quán yì.
Xià qì qīnú,
〔二０〕shàng fèi zōng
sì.
〔二一〕Shìyù zhī wù,
jiē yǐ lǐ shēn;
xiàojìng zhī diǎn,
dú yǐ fǎ qū.
Bèi lǐ fàn shùn,
céng mò zhī jué.
Ruò sàng wàng guī,
shú shí qí jiù?
Qiě lǐ zhī kě guì zhě,
dào yě;
shì zhī kě jiàn zhě,
sú yě.
Shě huá xiào yí,
yì jiāng ān qǔ?
Ruò yǐ dào
xié?
Dào gù fúhé yǐ.
Ruò yǐ sú xié?
Sú zé dà guāi yǐ.
Lǚ jiàn kè xián shāmén,
shǒu zhū dàoshì,
jiāozhēng xiǎo dà,
〔二二〕hù xiāng tánshè.
Huò yù dào yǐ wéi liǎng,
huò hùn sú yǐ wéi
yī.
Shì qiān yì yǐ wéi tóng,
pò tóng yǐ wéi yì.
Zé guāi zhēng zhī yóu,
xiáoluàn zhī běn yě.
Xún shèngdào suī tóng,
ér fǎ yǒu zuǒ
yòu.
Shǐ hū wú duān,
zhōng hū wú mò.
Níhuán xiānhuà,
gè shì yī shù.
Fó hào zhèngzhēn,
dào chēng zhèngyī.
Yī guī wú sǐ,
zhēn
huì wú shēng.
Zài míng zé fǎn,
zài shí zé hé.
Dàn wúshēng zhī jiào shē,
wúsǐ zhī huà qiè.
Qiè fǎ kě yǐ jìn qiānruò,
shē fǎ
kě yǐ tuì kuāqiáng.
Fójiào wén ér bó,
Dàojiào zhì ér jīng.
Jīng fēi cū rén suǒ xìn,

Fó Dào
As [the Central Plains] were truly esteemed,
thus the prohibitions and practices could be followed;
as the customs of the *róng* were truly despised,
thus their speech and appearance could be rejected.
Now, the gentlemen and ladies of *Zhū Huá*
have not changed their ethnicity,
〔三０〕yet they expose their heads
and sit askew,
〔三一〕misusing barbarian rites.
It is said that those who cut their hair
are entirely *Hú* people,
and the state has its ancient customs,
so the laws cannot be changed.
Moreover, if one observes the popular doctrines,
their ways must be different.
Buddhism is not the way of *Dōng Huá*,
and Daoism is not the law of *Xī Róng*.
Fish and birds are in different depths,
forever unrelated.
How
can the two teachings of *Lǎo* and *Shì*
be practiced across the eight directions?
Now that Buddhism has flowed eastward,
and Daoism has also advanced westward,
we therefore know that the world has its subtle and crude,
and teachings have their refined and simple.
Thus, the Daoist
teaching grasps the root to lead the branches,
while the Buddhist teaching saves the branches to preserve the root.
May I ask what the difference is?
Where does it ultimately lie?
〔三二〕If cutting hair is considered the difference,
then convicts also cut
their hair.
If erecting statues is considered the difference,
then common shamans also erect statues.
This is not where the ultimate lies;
it lies in the permanent abode.
What is the difference between the phenomena of the permanent abode
and the constant Dao?
The existence of death for immortals
is a provisional teaching.
Immortals is a general term for the great transformation,
not the ultimate name for the profound subtlety.
The ultimate name is nameless;
those with names
are twenty-seven ranks,
immortals transform into *zhēn*,
*zhēn* transforms into *shén*,
or they are called *shèng*,
each having nine ranks.
When the rank reaches its extreme, they enter emptiness and stillness,
without action or name.
If one
consumes *zhī* mushrooms,
extending life for myriad eons,
when life ends, they die.
When the medicine reaches its extreme, it withers.
These are practitioners of longevity,
not of the immortal lineage.
*Míng Sēngshào* in his *Zhèng Èr Jiào Lùn* held that
"The Buddha clarifies his doctrine,
while *Lǎozi* fully preserves his life.
Those who preserve life are obscured;
those who clarify the doctrine are enlightened.
Now, Daoists claim eternal life and immortality,
named as replenishing the celestial bureaucracy,
which greatly contradicts the fundamental principles of *Lǎo* and *Zhuāng*."
Crown Prince *Wénhuì* and Prince *Jìnglíng Zǐliáng* both favored Buddhist Dharma.
*Wúxīng Mèng Jǐngyì* was a Daoist master.
The Crown Prince summoned him into *Xuánpǔyuán*.
Many monks gathered,
and *Zǐliáng* had *Jǐngyì* prostrate to the Buddha.
*Jǐngyì* refused,
so *Zǐliáng* sent him the *Shí Dì Jīng*.
*Jǐngyì* then composed the *Zhèng Yī Lùn*.
Its general idea states:
"The *Bǎojī* says, 'The Buddha preaches the Dharma with one sound.'
*Lǎozi* says, 'The sage embraces the one as the pattern for the world.'
The
subtlety of 'one'
is empty and profound, transcending all realms,
〔三三〕its divine transformations are endlessly abundant.
It acts for myriad things, yet is not acting;
it occupies a single number, yet is numberless.
None can name it;
it is forcibly called 'one.'
In Buddhism, it is called 'true reality';
in Daoism, it is called 'mysterious female.'
The great phenomenon of the Dao
is precisely the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha.
It guards the *dharmakāya* by not guarding,
and grasps the great phenomenon by not grasping.
But there are eighty-four thousand practices for things,
and eighty-four thousand methods are spoken of.
The methods are even countless,
and the practices are also boundless.
〔三四〕Ranks follow conditions;
they must be guided to return to the one.
Returning to the one is called turning towards;
facing the proper means no evil.
Once wrong views are dispelled,
myriad good deeds are renewed daily.
The three, five, four, and six [categories of practice]
are applied as needed.
Standing alone, unchanging,
having no learning, no worries.
Saints throughout countless eons
all follow this 'one.'
*Lǎo* and *Shì* have never been truly separate;
it is the deluded who separate them and have not reunited them.
Myriad good deeds are extensively cultivated;
extensive cultivation leads to Buddhahood.
Although there are ten titles and a thousand epithets,
they ultimately cannot exhaust it.
Since they ultimately cannot exhaust it,
how can it be conceived?"
*Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng Zhāng Róng* wrote *Mén Lǜ*, saying:
"Daoism and Buddhism,
when reaching their ultimate, are not two.
〔三五〕I have seen Daoist masters debate Confucianism and Mohism with Buddhist monks,
〔三六〕and Buddhist monks examine right and wrong with Daoist masters.
〔三七〕In the past, there was a swan flying in the sky,
〔三八〕its great distance making it hard to discern.
The *Yuè* people took it for *yī*,
the *Chǔ* people took it for *yǐ*.
People are from *Chǔ* or *Yuè*,
but the swan is always one."
〔三九〕This was shown to *Tàizǐ Pú Zhōu Yǒng*.
*Yǒng* challenged it, saying:
"Though the emptiness and lack of self-nature
are the same in their stillness,
the methods of attaining this stillness
〔四０〕have different meanings.
The statement 'when reaching their ultimate, are not two'
in your essay,
does it mean that when reaching the ultimate in emptiness,
they are not two in self-nature?
The original thing you venerate is but one, whether it be *hóng* or *yǐ*.
〔四一〕When applying this to Buddhism and Daoism,
you cannot avoid the two distinctions.
〔四二〕I do not know by what lofty insight you discern the root,
and lightly venerate it.
Is there a profound meaning in this?"

*Huān* was not eloquent in speech,
but skilled in writing.
He wrote *Sān Míng Lùn*,
which was very well-crafted,
of the same caliber as *Zhōng Huì*'s four volumes.
He also annotated *Wáng Bì*'s *Yì Èr Xì*,
which scholars passed down.
*Shǐxīng* native *Lú Dù*
also possessed Daoist arts.
When young, he followed *Zhāng Yǒng* on a northern expedition.
After *Yǒng*'s defeat,
the barbarians pursued fiercely,
and they were blocked by the *Huái* River, unable to cross.
*Dù* vowed in his heart:
"If I can escape death,
from now on I will never kill living beings again."
Soon, he saw two shields floating by,
grasped them, and was able to cross.
Later, he retired to *Xīchāng Sāngù Shān*,
and birds and beasts followed him.
One night, a deer bumped his wall.
*Dù* said:
"You are damaging my wall."
〔四三〕The deer left in response.
There was a pond in front of his house where he kept fish,
and he called them all by name.
〔四四〕The fish would come one by one,
take their food, and then leave.
He knew his year and month of death in advance,
and bid farewell to his relatives and friends.
At the end of *Yǒngmíng*,
he died of old age.
Initially,
in the third year of *Yǒngmíng* (485 CE),
*Gù Huìyìn*, then *Piàojì Cānjūn*, was summoned to be *Sītú Zhǔbù*.
*Huìyìn* was
the nephew of *Sòng Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Jì*.
He lived in reclusion, cultivating his aspirations,
and did not respond to official summons.
*Zāng Róngxù*
was a native of *Jǔ*, *Dōngguǎn*.
His grandfather, *Fèngxiān*,
was *Jiànlíng Lìng*;
his father, *Yōngmín*,
was *Guózǐ Zhùjiào*.
*Róngxù* was orphaned young,
and personally cultivated a garden
to provide for sacrifices.
After his mother's death,
he wrote *Dí Qǐn Lùn*,
swept and cleaned the ancestral hall,
set up mats and seats,
and prostrated himself monthly on the first and fifteenth,
〔四五〕never eating precious delicacies before offering them.

Liú Qiú, styled Língyù,
was from Yáng, Nányáng.
His family was of an old clan,
but had migrated to Jiānglíng.
Qiú was unyielding and fond of learning in his youth.
He would live in seclusion once he had earned a living.
During the Tàishǐ reign of the Sòng dynasty,
〔五二〕he served as Píyì Jìshì (Secretary to the General of Agile Cavalry) for Prince Jìnpíng,
and as the Magistrate of Dāngyáng.
After retiring from office and returning home,
he lived in quiet seclusion, abstaining from grains,
and subsisting on the rhizome of largehead atractylodes and sesame seeds.
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán reign,
when the Prince of Yùzhāng was the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
he ordered that Qiú be appointed Biéjià (Associate Inspector).
〔五三〕He sent letters and invitations along with Zōng Cè and Yǔ Yì of the same commandery, and Yǔ Yì of Xīnyě.
〔五四〕Qiú and the others each composed replies to the petitions,
but did not accept the appointments.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
the Inspector, Prince Lúlíng Zǐqīng, memorialized to recommend Qiú, along with Zōng Cè, Zōng Shàngzhī, Yǔ Yì, and Liú Zhāo, all from the same commandery,
requesting that they be granted the honor of a plain carriage and a bolt of silk.
An imperial edict summoned him to be a Tōngzhí Láng,
but he did not accept.
Prince Jìnglíng Zǐliáng sent him a letter to convey his intentions.
Qiú replied:
"Qiú has been ill for all four seasons,
and cultivates and irrigates for three seasons,
enjoying the lingering shade in the mountains and marshes,
entrusting his twilight affections to fish and birds.
Is this not the profound grace of Táng and Yú,
and the grand benevolence of Zhōu and Shào?
When Qiú advances, he does not delve into subtle mechanisms or profound mysteries,
nor does he possess the eloquence of Zhūsì or Jìguǎn;
when he retreats, he does not solidify his mind to transcend worldly burdens,
nor does he possess the integrity of those beneath gravestones or trees.
Since distant benevolence has been bestowed,
and virtuous rules have been established,
I respectfully withdraw from the suspicion of a woodcutter and shepherd,
and humbly accept the courtesy of bowing to a frog. "
Qiú devoutly believed in Buddhism,
wore coarse cloth robes,
and observed a long vegetarian fast for the Buddha.
He annotated the Fǎhuá Jīng (Lotus Sutra)
and personally expounded Buddhist teachings.
Since the western sandbar of Jiānglíng was far from people,
he moved his residence there.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
an imperial edict summoned him to be a Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University),
but he did not accept.
That winter, Qiú fell ill.
At midday, white clouds lingered within the eaves and doorways,
and there was also a fragrant aroma and the sound of a qìng (stone chime).
He died on that day,
aged fifty-eight.
Liú Zhāo was of the same clan as Qiú.
The province appointed him Jìjiǔ Cóngshì (Libationer and Aide),
but he did not accept.
He lived in seclusion in the mountains.
Yǔ Yì, styled Yòujiǎn,
was from Xīnyě, Xīnyě.
He had migrated to the vicinity of Jiānglíng.
His grandfather Méi was the Administrator of Bājùn,
and his father Dàojì was an Aide to the General who Pacifies the West.
Yì's ambition and nature were tranquil and reclusive;
he did not associate with external matters.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
the Inspector, Prince Yùzhāng, appointed him as an Aide to the General of Agile Cavalry,
but he did not accept.
When Prince Línchuān Yìng oversaw the province,
he especially esteemed Yì
and memorialized to recommend him,
sending him one hundred hù (bushels) of wheat.
Yì said to the envoy:
"As a member of the company of wood gatherers and deer,
who wears clothes of untanned fur until the end of his days,
〔五五〕and travels in a carriage of sun and moon,
I have secured the livelihood of self-cultivation.
The grace of the great king
is already profound enough."
He declined and did not accept.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
an imperial edict summoned him to be a Tàizǐ Shèrén (Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince),
but he did not accept.
He found joy in literature and righteousness.
Yuán Tuàn, the Chief Clerk of the General who Pacifies the West, admired his conduct
and sent him a letter and gifts.
Yì reciprocated with a connected-branch table and bamboo writing racks.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
an imperial edict again summoned him to be a Sītú Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works),
but he did not accept.
He died.
Zōng Cè, styled Jìngwēi,
was from Nányáng,
and was the grandson of the Sòng recluse Bǐng.
His family had resided in Jiānglíng for generations.
Cè was quiet and reclusive in his youth,
not enjoying human society.
He sighed, saying:
"My family is poor and my parents are old,
so I do not choose an official position to serve –
the ancient sages considered this a beautiful tale,
but I secretly have doubts.
I truly cannot secretly sense gold from the earth
or mysteriously bring carp from the river;
I can only follow the ways of Heaven
and share in the benefits of the earth.
Who can eat a person's generous salary
and worry about a person's heavy affairs?"
The province nominated him as Xiùcái (Flourishing Talent)
and Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk),
but he did not accept.
Prince Yùzhāng, General of Agile Cavalry, summoned him to be an Aide.
Cè replied to the summons from the princely mansion, saying:
"Why mistakenly injure the sea bird
or cut down the mountain trees?"
When his mother died,
he personally carried soil to plant pines and cypresses.
Prince Yùzhāng again sent a letter to invite him,
appointing him as an Aide.
Cè replied:
"My nature is like that of scales and feathers,
I love to dwell in mountains and valleys,
cherishing pines and bamboos,
lightly straying from human paths.
Wandering freely among rocks and streams,
like a madman,
I suddenly find that old age has arrived,
and my temples are already white.
How can I be expected to demand the impossible and blame the existent,
or limit the fish and admire the bird?"
〔五六〕In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
an imperial edict summoned him to be a Tàizǐ Shèrén (Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Crown Prince),
but he did not accept.
Wishing to travel to famous mountains,
he painted a portrait of Shàng Zǐpíng, originally painted by his grandfather Bǐng, on a screen in his room.
Cè's eldest son, Huàn, was in the capital.
〔五七〕Knowing his father's intention,
he sought office and returned to become Nánjùn Chéng (Assistant Administrator of Nánjùn),
entrusting him with family affairs.
The Inspector, Prince Ānlù Zǐjìng, Chief Clerk Liú Yín, and others all sent him gifts,
but Cè accepted none.
He carried with him the two books, Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ.
When his children and grandchildren bowed and tearfully bade him farewell,
Cè let out a long whistle and did not look,
then went to Lúshān,
residing in his grandfather Bǐng's old dwelling.
The Marquis of Yúfù Zǐxiǎng was the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu
and sent him generous gifts.
Cè said:
"I had a slight madness in my youth,
seeking mountains and gathering herbs,
and came here from afar.
I eat pine and atractylodes according to my stomach's capacity,
and wear clothes of ivy and creepers according to my body's shape.
I am already content with this simple life.
How can I accept these unmerited gifts?"
Zǐxiǎng ordered his carriage to visit him,
but Cè avoided him and refused to be seen.
Later, Zǐxiǎng came unannounced,
suddenly arriving at his residence.
Cè had no choice but
to face him in a cap and coarse robe,
but he did not exchange a single word.
Zǐxiǎng was displeased and withdrew.
The Minister of Personnel, Wáng Jiǎn, sent Cè a rush mat.
After a while,
Cè returned west after his brother's funeral,
and then remained in his old dwelling at Yǒngyè Sì,
cutting off contact with guests and friends,
only communicating and discussing with like-minded Yǔ Yì, Liú Qiú, and his kinsman Shàngzhī.
When the Inspector, Prince Suí Zǐlóng, arrived at his post,
he sent Biéjià Zōng Zhé to convey his regards.
〔五八〕Cè smiled and said:
"The noble and the humble are separated by principle;
how can such a thing reach this far?"
He ultimately did not reply.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was summoned to be Sītú Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works),
but he did not accept.
He died.
Cè was skilled in painting.
He personally painted Ruǎn Jí encountering Sū Mén on a folding screen,
and faced it whether sitting or lying down.
He also painted Yǒngyè Fóyǐng Tái (Buddha Shadow Terrace of Yǒngyè Temple),
all of which were exquisite works.
He was quite fond of musical rhythms
and was good at the Yì Jīng and Lǎozǐ.
He continued Huángfǔ Mì's Gāoshì Zhuàn (Biographies of High-Minded Scholars) in three volumes.
He also once traveled the seven peaks of Héngshān
and wrote the Héngshān and Lúshān Jì (Records of Mount Héng and Mount Lú).
Shàng Zhī
also enjoyed mountains and marshes.
He and Liú Qiú both refused to serve as secretaries to the General of Agile Cavalry.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
the provincial governor, Wǔlíng Wáng, invited him to serve in the secretariat,
and Yùzhāng Wáng invited him to be an assistant governor,
but he declined both.
During the Yǒngmíng reign,
he and Liú Qiú were both summoned to be Tongzhíláng (Court Gentlemen for Transmission of Edicts),
and at the beginning of the revival under Hédi,
he was again summoned to be a Zīyì (Consultant),
but he declined both.
He died of old age.
Dù Jīngchǎn, courtesy name Jǐngqí,
was from Qiántáng, Wú Jùn.
He was a great-great-grandson of Dù Zǐgōng.
His grandfather, Yùn,
served as a military advisor to Liú Yì, General of the Guard.
His father, Dào Jū,
was a provincial official.
He was skilled at playing the qín.
His family had transmitted the Wǔdǒu Mǐ Dào (Five Pecks of Rice Daoism)
down to Jīngchǎn and his son, Qī.
Jīngchǎn was quiet and tranquil in his youth,
and had no interest in officialdom.
He was quite learned in literature and meaning,
and devoted himself to the study of Huáng-Lǎo Daoism.
Kǒng Jì of Kuàijī,
who was upright and had strict principles,
became his close friend at their first meeting.
The commandery summoned him to be a Chief Clerk,
and the province invited him to be an official,
but he feigned illness and left.
He was appointed as Fèngcháoqǐng (Gentleman-in-Attendance),
but did not accept.
He shared a bond with Gù Huān from the same commandery,
and together they opened a school on Dōng Shān in Shǐníng().
〔五九〕During the Jiàn Yuán reign,
when Wǔlíng Wáng Yè was governor of Kuàijī,
Tàizǔ sent the scholar Liú Huán to the east to lecture to Yè.
Jīngchǎn invited Huán to his mountain dwelling to lecture on the classics,
spending all his resources to provide for him.
His son, Qī, personally wore straw sandals
to serve food to Huán's students,
such was his respect for the virtuous.
Kǒng Zhìguī, Zhōu Yǒng, and Xiè Zhēn all wrote letters to maintain their cordial relations.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng,
Zhìguī, along with Guānglù Dàfū Lù Chéng, Cíbù Shàngshū Yú Cóng, Tàizǐ Yòulǜ Shěn Yuē, and Sītú Yòuzhǎngshǐ Zhāng Róng, submitted a memorial recommending Jīngchǎn, saying:
“We humbly observe that Dù Jīngchǎn of Wú Jùn
has a pure and tranquil heart,
and a humble and modest nature.
His gentle disposition comes from his inherent talent,
and his quick understanding is naturally manifested.
He is learned in both Xuan (Daoist) and Ru (Confucian) studies,
and broadly conversant in histories and philosophical treatises.
He delights in literature and arts,
and delves into the profound mysteries of the Dao.
During the Tàishǐ reign,
he hung up his cap and withdrew from the world,
abandoning his family profession,
and lived as a recluse in Tàipíng.
He thatched a hut in a remote ravine,
gathered lingzhi in secluded valleys,
was content with self-sufficient farming,
and had plenty of time for singing while gathering firewood.
He is steadfast and peerless,
indifferent and with few desires.
Wearing hemp clothes and eating wild herbs,
he has lived thus for over twenty years.
Even the determined scholars of antiquity
could not surpass him.
We believe it appropriate to invite him from his secluded valley,
and bring him into court,
so that the ravines will rejoice,
and the vines and creepers will clap their hands.”
There was no reply.
At the beginning of the Jiànwǔ reign,
he was summoned to be Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (Supernumerary Palace Gentleman).
Jīngchǎn said:
“Would Zhuāngzǐ, holding his fishing rod,
be turned back by white jade?”
He declined, feigning illness.
He died at the age of sixty-four
in the first year of Yǒngyuán.
Kǒng Dàozhēng of Kuàijī
〔六０〕maintained his integrity and career, and did not serve as an official.
Jīngchǎn was good friends with him.
During the Yǒngmíng reign,
there was a man named Cài from Zhōng Shān in Kuàijī,
whose given name is unknown.
He kept dozens of mice in the mountains;
they would come when called and leave when dismissed.
His speech was eccentric and wild,
and he was sometimes called
“Zhékxiān” (Banished Immortal).
His end is unknown.
Shěn Línsì, courtesy name Yúnzhēn,
was from Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Yīng【Qī】,
〔六一〕was a Tàizhōng Dàfū (Grandee of the Middle Palace) in the Jìn dynasty.
Línsì was fond of learning in his youth.
His family was poor,
so he wove curtains and recited books,
his hands and mouth never resting.
At the end of the Yuánjiā reign of the Sòng dynasty,
Wéndì ordered Shàngshū Púyè Hé Shàngzhī to compile the Five Classics
and seek out learned scholars.
The county recommended Línsì for selection.
Shàngzhī said to his son, Yǎn:
“There are indeed extraordinary scholars in the east of the mountains.”
〔六二〕After a short time,
Línsì feigned illness and returned to his hometown,
no longer associating with people.
He raised his deceased brother's orphaned son,
and his righteousness was well-known in the local area.
Someone advised Línsì to enter officialdom.
He replied:
“The fish in the trap and the beast in the cage
are one and the same in the world.
The Sages, with their profound understanding,
always walked the path of good fortune first.
I truly cannot yet imitate the practice of 'sitting in forgetfulness,'
so why should I not aspire to 'daily decrease'?”
He then composed the Xuánsàn Fù (Rhapsody of Profound Dispersal) to sever ties with the world.
Tàishǒu Kǒng Shānshì invited him,
but he did not respond.
His clansmen, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Tán Qìng, Shìzhōng Huáiwén, and Zuǒlǜ Bó, came to visit him,
but Línsì never replied.
He lived in seclusion on Wúchā Shān in Yúbù,
〔六三〕lecturing on the classics and teaching.
Several hundred students followed him,
each building their own dwelling
and settling nearby.
Línsì greatly valued Lù Jī's Liánzhū,
and lectured on it to his students frequently.
Zhāng Yǒng, General of the North, became governor of Wúxīng,
and invited Línsì to the commandery.
Línsì heard that there was good scenery behind the governor's hall,
so he went and stayed for several months.
Yǒng wanted to invite him to be a Gōngcáo (Administrator)
and sent someone to convey his intention.
Línsì said:
“Your Excellency's virtue and conduct are pure and simple,
and you care for the mountains and valleys.
Because of this, the common people wear coarse clothes and carry staffs,
forgetting their fatigue and illness.
If you insist on decorating the 'uncarved block' with 'moth eyebrows,'
and crowning a 'guest from Yuè' with an 'official's cap,'
though I am not quick-witted,
I beg to attach myself to your noble principles,
even if it means jumping into the Eastern Sea and dying.”
Yǒng then stopped.
At the end of the Shēngmíng reign,
Tàishǒu Wáng Huàn submitted a memorial recommending him.
An imperial edict summoned him to be Fèngcháoqǐng,
but he did not accept.
In the sixth year of Yǒngmíng,
Lìbù Láng Shěn Yuān and Zhōngshū Láng Shěn Yuē again submitted a memorial recommending Línsì's righteous conduct,
saying:
“Shěn Línsì of Wúxīng
displayed extraordinary character from an early age,
and established stern principles early on.
His integrity and purity are endowed by nature,
and his comprehensive learning comes from diligent study.
His family was poor and solitary,
unable to even afford wild herbs and grains.
He tilled the land with books in his embrace,
without weariness even in old age,
and carried a qín while gathering firewood,
singing without cease.
His elder brother died young,
leaving several orphaned nephews.
He took on the responsibility of raising the young,
enduring hardship and prioritizing their well-being.
He is over seventy years old,
but his conduct and principles remain unchanged.
Since the Yuánjiā reign,
invitations to serve have continuously accumulated,
but his jade-like character has become even purer,
and his frost-like integrity daily more severe.
If he were to speak on policy at the royal court,
and practice the Dao within the imperial precincts,
he would surely spread the court's principles to the border regions,
and propagate the sacred beneficence to distant lands.”
An imperial edict again summoned him to be Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial Academy).
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was summoned to be Zuòzhù Láng (Secretary for Imperial History).
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
but he declined them all.
Línshì carried firewood and drew water,
eating only once every two days,
and maintained his integrity until old age.
He studied diligently without weariness.
When he suffered a fire,
thousands of scrolls of his books were burned.
Línshì was over eighty years old,
but his ears and eyes were still sharp and clear.
〔六四〕He personally recopied the lost texts,
writing in fine script beneath the original fire-damaged pages,
〔六五〕and again completed two or three thousand scrolls,
filling dozens of satchels.
People at the time attributed this to his nourishing his body with quietude and silence.
He authored the *Zhōuyì Liǎng Xì Zhuāngzǐ Nèi Piān Xùn* and
annotated the *Yìjīng*, *Lǐjì*, *Chūnqiū*, *Shàngshū*, *Lúnyǔ*, *Xiàojīng*, *Sāngfú*, and *Lǎozǐ Yàolüè*, totaling several dozens of scrolls.
He considered Yáng Wángsūn and Huángfǔ Mì to have deeply understood life and death,
yet they ultimately adhered to the conventions of ritual, which he found to be hypocritical.
〔六六〕Thus, he composed his own funeral arrangements.
At the age of eighty-six,
he passed away.
Shěn Yǎnzhī of the same commandery,
courtesy name Shìgōng,
son of Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Tánqìng,
also did not serve as an official.
He was summoned to be Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was summoned to be Zhōngshū Láng.
In the third year,
an imperial edict again summoned Shěn Yǐ, formerly Nánjùn Guó Chángshì, to be Zhùzuò Láng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Shèrén.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was summoned to be Tōngzhí Láng.
Yǐ, courtesy name Chùmò,
was the elder grandnephew of Sòng Lǐngjūn Yín.
〔六七〕
Wú Bāo, courtesy name Tiāngài,
was a native of Juànchéng, Púyáng.
He was a Confucian scholar,
skilled in the Three Rites and Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
During the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty,
he crossed the river and gathered students to teach.
He wore a yellow kudzu-fiber turban and
carried a bamboo fly whisk,
eating only vegetables for over twenty years.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
an imperial edict stated:
“The recluse Wú Bāo of Púyáng
has set his aspiration in a remote valley,
maintaining a firm and constant integrity,
immersed in the savor of antiquity,
and his resolve grows stronger with white hair.
Summon him as Tàixué Bóshì.”
He did not accept the appointment.
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng and Yòuwèi Jiāng Shí established a residence for him south of Jiǎngshān.
After Liú Huán's death,
scholars all gravitated towards him.
He died of old age.
Kǒng Sìzhī of Lǔguó,
courtesy name Jìngbó.
During the Sòng dynasty, he and Tàizǔ both served as Zhōngshū Shèrén,
but this was not to their liking.
He resigned his post from Lúlín Jùn
and lived in seclusion on Zhōngshān.
The imperial court appointed him Tàizhōng Dàfū.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
he passed away.
Xú Bózhēn, courtesy name Wénchǔ,
〔六八〕was a native of Tàimò, Dōngyáng.
His grandfather and father were both commandery clerks.
Bózhēn was orphaned and poor in his youth,
practicing writing on bamboo leaves and the ground.
When mountain waters surged violently,
sweeping away homes,
and all his village neighbors fled,
Bózhēn stacked beds to stay,
reading without interruption.
His uncle Fánzhī was a close friend of Yán Yánzhī.
He returned to Qūméngshān to establish a hermitage and lecture,
and Bózhēn went to study under him.
For ten years,
he thoroughly investigated the classics and histories,
and many wandering scholars relied on him.
Tàishǒu Lángyá Wáng Tánsheng and Wú Jùn Zhāng Yān both treated him with respect and invited him to serve,
but Bózhēn would respond to the summons and then immediately withdraw.
This happened a total of twelve times.
The recluse Shěn Yǎn had intimate conversations with him,
establishing a pure friendship.
Gù Huān of Wú Jùn pointed out obscure meanings in the *Shàngshū*,
and Bózhēn's explanations and answers were very clear and well-ordered,
〔六九〕earning him reverence from Confucian scholars.
He was fond of Buddhism and Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
and also understood the arts of Daoism.
Whenever there was a drought,
Bózhēn would divine,
and rain would fall as predicted.
His every action was courteous.
When passing under a crooked tree,
he would hurry to avoid it.
He lost his wife early
and did not remarry in his later years,
likening himself to Zēng Cān.
Nine *lǐ* south of his residence was a high mountain,
which Bān Gù called Jiǔyán Shān.
It was where Lóngqiū Cháng of the Later Hàn dynasty lived in seclusion.
The mountain had many dragon's beard cypresses,
〔七０〕which appeared five-colored when viewed from afar.
People of the time called it Fùrén Yán.
In the second year,
Bózhēn moved to live there.
〔七一〕A catalpa tree grew in front of his gate,
and in one year it grew large enough to be embraced.
One night, a red light suddenly illuminated the stone wall east of his residence,
then quickly vanished.
A pair of white sparrows nested in his door and window,
which commentators regarded as a manifestation of his hidden virtue.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng,
Cìshǐ Yùzhāng Wáng invited him to be Yìcáo Cóngshì,
but he did not accept.
His family was very poor.
He had four brothers,
all with white hair facing each other,
whom people at the time called
“the Four Hoaries.”
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he passed away
at the age of eighty-four.
He had over a thousand students.
Lóu Yòuyú of the same commandery
was also a Confucian scholar.
He authored *Lǐ Jùnyí* in thirty scrolls.
His official position reached Gěishì Zhōng.
Also, Lóu Huìmíng of the same commandery
possessed Daoist arts.
He resided on Jīnhuá Shān,
and all venomous creatures and wild beasts avoided him.
Sòng Míngdì heard of this
and ordered him to live in Huálín Yuán,
appointing him Fèng Cháoqǐng,
but he firmly refused to accept,
requesting to return east.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
he suddenly rode a light boat towards Lín'ān Xiàn,
〔七二〕and no one knew why.
Soon after, the bandit Táng Zhuōzhī attacked and captured the commandery.
〔七三〕Wénhuì Tàizǐ called him out to live on Jiǎngshān,
but he again requested to return,
which was granted.
Shìzǔ ordered a residence to be built for him.
The imperial historian says: Gù Huān (顧歡) discussed the distinction between 'foreign' and 'Chinese' (夷夏),
preferring the Way of the Elders (Daoism) and disparaging Buddhism.
Buddhism,
its principle is quiescent through all ages,
its traces emerged in the middle ages.
Its profound source is vast and boundless,
without beginning or end,
what the universe cannot know,
and what numbers cannot exhaust.
How magnificent!
It is the doctrine established by a true great being (mahāsattva).
It penetrates the subtle mechanism and touches the profound stillness;
where there is a response, there is inevitably a reaction.
It embraces the small with the great,
leaving nothing minute untouched.
As for the teachings of the Rújiā (儒家) (Confucianism):
benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and music (仁義禮樂);
benevolence is love, righteousness is appropriateness,
propriety is compliance, and music is harmony, that is all.
[七四]Now, compassion is the root,
constant joy is the principle,
giving and generosity are the only mechanism,
and bowing and raising become reverence.
The teachings of the Rújiā (儒家)
follow ancestral principles,
using antiquity to prove the present,
and are easy to comprehend in study.
Now, it establishes past causes
and retribution in future effects,
deeds and actions repay each other,
like an endless chain.
The teachings of Yīnyáng (陰陽) (Yin-Yang school)
divine the qi (氣) and observe celestial bodies,
providing the people with seasonal knowledge,
knowing its benefits and harms.
Now, the ears and eyes are completely open,
the mind and intellect are通 (tōng),
the body itself is Kuí-Jǐng (奎井) (a constellation),
why wait for Gān-Shí (甘石) (Gan De and Shi Shen)?
The teachings of Fǎjiā (法家) (Legalism)
originate from penal principles,
prohibiting evil and stopping wickedness,
clearly using rewards and punishments.
Now, the fall into the ten evils,
and the five immediate retributions without interval (uninterrupted suffering),
knife-trees and sword-mountains,
scorching cauldrons and fierce fires.
One creates and receives what one brings upon oneself,
without any deviation or difference.
The teachings of Mòjiā (墨家) (Mohism)
advocate for ultimate frugality and simplicity,
wearing down heels and losing hair on the crown of the head,
and even this is not considered miserly.
Now, the skin is like a broken gourd,
the eyes like well-stars,
giving up sons and abandoning wives,
like protecting a dove from a hawk.
The teachings of Zònghéng (縱橫) (School of Diplomacy)
value strategy and opportunism,
heavenly mouths and linked rings,
[七五]leading to adaptation and change.
Now, one sound brings ten thousand enlightenments,
without needing verbose explanations,
four eloquences and three assemblies,
all receive instruction from our teacher.
The teachings of Zájīa (雜家) (Syncretism)
combine Rú (儒) and Mò (墨).
Now, what was expounded in the five periods (of the Buddha's teaching)
is all-encompassing.
The teachings of Nóngjiā (農家) (Agrarianism)
involve sowing, planting, plowing, and weeding,
skillfully managing the five tasks,
to cultivate the nine grains.
Now, the Udana rice
is already different from Jambudvīpa,
the karmic reward of being born in heaven
is naturally superior food and drink.
The teachings of Dàojiā (道家) (Daoism)
hold to the One and to nothingness,
attaining nature and forgetting emotion,
calming the spirit and not disturbing it.
Now, Prajñā (波若) has no illumination (self-illumination),
all phenomena are empty,
how can there be a Dào (道) that can be named,
how can there be any "One" that can be attained?
When Daoists and Buddhists are compared,
truth and falsehood will be put to the test.
The profound hidden principles of Buddhism
are present everywhere.
If one can skillfully apply them,
then the true is the mundane.
The establishment of the Nine Schools
