was used to borrow from worldly teachings.
The schools of Punishment, Names, Dao, and Mo
had conflicting hearts and differing aims.
If a Rú (儒) does not study,
it does not harm his being a Rú.
But the Buddhist principles are profound and expansive,
with real wisdom and wonderful existence.
If one thing is unknown,
one cannot achieve perfect sainthood.
As for the power of the divine path's manifestations,
the wonder of its responsive interactions and transformations,
it is inconceivable,
and difficult to describe in words or images.
However, the Dao of Zhāng (張) and Mǐ (米) (Zhang Daoling and Mi Heng)
had early verification with talismans and water,
transmitting their master's methods,
originating from Bóyáng (伯陽).
Worldly sentiments ebb and flow,
there are these two teachings.
Monks and nuns, Daoist priests,
clash and contradict each other.
Not only do they revere their own Way,
they also contend for profit.
Upon careful examination of the two teachings,
their principles ultimately converge.
But their traces appear on the left and right,
hence the teachings formed in succession.
Speaking broadly or narrowly,
distinctions of superiority and inferiority naturally arise.
The Dao (道) is fundamentally empty,
not attained through learning.
Discarding sagacity and abandoning wisdom
has already become 'doing' (有為, yǒu wéi).
The nothingness (無) of 'doing' (有為)
is ultimately not the root of the Dao.
If root and branch were both nothingness,
what distinctions of hierarchy would there be?
Buddhism is not like this.
Complete bondage (具縛) is the seed,
transforming darkness into light,
leading the ignorant to sainthood.
Though the path is distant, it can be trodden;
though the karma is vast, it has a definite end.
The way of exhortation and aspiration
has no barrier between self and others.
However, those with narrow sentiments and shallow wisdom
are seldom able to fully accept it.
Worldly considerations measure
the two gates of cause and effect.
One might do good at cock-crow,
but not necessarily receive residual blessings.
One might eat meat from Dōnglíng (東陵),
yet suffer no calamity.
Someone of high and subtle talent may be stifled and not achieve success;
someone of mediocre capacity and dull intellect may live a rich and prosperous life until the end.
Loyalty is met with rejection;
deceit often finds employment.
Judging from this,
there is no immediate retribution of blessings or misfortunes.
However, the uncertainty of karma
is clearly stated in the scriptures;
the three types of retribution establish its principle,
and this doubt is immediately dispelled.
The imperial historian reveres Buddhism,
deeply believing in the obscure karmic connections,
considering this Way to be most noble.
An ode says: Containing truth and embracing simplicity,
treading the Dao and earnestly learning.
Thus, hiding away,
shedding scales and growing horns.
Collation notes:

Biographies Section 36: Filial Piety and Righteousness. Cuī Huáishèn (崔懷慎), Gōngsūn Sēngyuǎn (公孫僧遠), Wú Xīnzhī (吳欣之), Hán Xìbó (韓係伯), Sūn Dàn (孫淡), Huá Bǎo (華寶), Hán Língmǐn (韓靈敏), Fēng Yánbó (封延伯), Wú Dázhī (吳達之), Wáng Wénshū (王文殊), Zhū Qiānzhī (朱謙之), Xiāo Ruìmíng (蕭叡明), Lè Yí (樂頤), Jiāng Mì (江泌), Dù Qī (杜栖), Lù Jiàng (陸絳).
The Master said:
"The Way between father and son
is of Heaven's nature;
it is the righteousness between ruler and minister."
The innate filial piety and righteousness in people
are common by nature,
while purity and meagerness depend on the mind,
not waiting for learning to achieve.
Meeting opportunities for employment late,
not declining the initial methods of the common people,
the proud and arrogant nature
often shames the enjoyment of water and vegetables.
Indeed, to serve parents with a cheerful countenance and exert one's utmost,
to fulfill righteousness by dedicating one's life,
contentedly working in the fields,
not seeking fame or advancement –
this is the essence of Mencius's three joys,
and the sigh of Zhòngyóu (仲由) carrying rice.
It reaches understanding with the spirits and gods;
reason is tied to inspiration and summoning.
When feelings become superficial and the world is thin (morally degenerate),
then filial piety and kindness truly manifest.
Therefore, it is not for those without inner virtue to dwell upon it,
but for those who harbor benevolence to set it as a standard for others.
Those who bury their names and conceal their integrity
are rarely celebrated.
Their deeds are recorded
to be listed in this chapter.
Cuī Huáishèn
was from Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
His father, Xiélì,
was the Administrator of Lǔjùn.
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
he was captured by the barbarians.
Huáishèn and his wife, Fáng Shì, were deeply devoted.
Upon hearing of his father's capture,
he immediately sent his wife away that very day,
wore plain clothes, ate vegetarian food,
and observed mourning rites.
Xiélì later served as the Minister of the Central Secretariat for the barbarians.
He warned Huáishèn not to continue such practices.
When Huáishèn received the letter, he wept even more.
Huáishèn's paternal uncle, Mó, was the Administrator of Xíngyáng
and also fell captive to the barbarians.
Although Mó's sons altered their conduct in captivity,
they did not abandon marriage or official careers.
During the Dàmíng era,
Huáishèn's kinsman, Yuánsūn, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, was sent as an envoy to the north.
The barbarians asked him,
"Cuī Xiélì and Mó both submitted when their strength gave out.
The children and nephews of their two families
have chosen different paths.
Where does righteousness lie?"
Yuánsūn replied,
"Wáng Zūn drove his steeds,
and Wáng Yáng turned back his chariot,
to allow both loyalty and filial piety to flourish,
and for both ministers and sons to be complete."
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era,
Huáinán was conquered.
Many refugees from the border region
had to make choices.
Huáishèn consequently entered the north.
Upon reaching Sānggān,
Xiélì had already passed away.
Huáishèn fainted and then revived.
He carried the coffin back to Qīngzhōu,
barefoot in ice and snow.
The local climate was bitterly cold,
yet his hands and feet remained unharmed.
People at the time considered it a manifestation of filial devotion.
After the mourning period,
because his brother was in the south,
at the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
he escaped back,
but his brother had also already died.
Huáishèn was poor and alone.
His clan and relatives pitied him,
each day collecting and giving him a sheng of rice.
He died during the Yǒngmíng era.
Gōngsūn Sēngyuǎn
was from Shàn, Kuàijī.
He was extremely filial in observing his father's mourning rites
and served his mother and paternal uncle with great diligence.
When the year was lean and grain was expensive,
Sēngyuǎn reduced his own meals and cut down on food
to provide for his mother and uncle.
When his younger brother died
and there was no means for burial,
he personally sold himself to neighbors
to cover the funeral expenses.
He personally carried earth
and planted pines and cypresses with his own hands.
When his elder siblings were unmarried,
he sold himself to arrange their weddings.
His name became known throughout the commandery and county.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he dispatched Yú Yán and other twelve envoys as concurrent Cavalier Regular Attendants to travel throughout the realm.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
they reported Sēngyuǎn and twenty-two others,
and an imperial edict commanded that their doorways be marked
and their taxes remitted.
Wú Xīnzhī
was from Lìchéng, Jìnling.
At the end of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
his younger brother Wèizhī was garrisoned in Wǔjìn County.
He joined Wáng Dàn in an uprising.
Tàizǔ initially sent Military Commander Huá Qīn to suppress them.
The officials and common people all scattered,
but Wèizhī alone remained,
was captured, and was about to die.
Xīnzhī went to Qīn, begging to die in place of his brother.
His words and tears were full of sorrow and urgency,
and both brothers were pardoned.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
〔一０〕an edict was issued to exempt and mark their household.
At the beginning of the Yǒngmíng era,
Zhāng Qǐzhī's two sons from Guǎnglíng committed crimes and were contending to die.
〔一一〕Administrator Liú Qūn reported this to the emperor.
Hán Xìbó
was from Xiāngyáng.
He served his parents with diligence and filial piety.
It was the custom in Xiāngyáng
for neighbors to plant mulberry trees on the border as markers.
Xìbó, believing the mulberry branches shaded his neighbor's land,
moved the border marker back several feet.
His neighbor then encroached again,
and Xìbó would always replant.
After a long time,
the neighbor felt ashamed,
returned the encroached land,
and personally went to apologize to him.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
his taxes were remitted,
and his doorway was marked.
He died of old age.
Sūn Dàn
was from Tàiyuán.
He resided in Chángshā
and was filial to his mother.
When his mother fell ill,
he neither slept nor ate,
taking her recovery as his goal.
His mother pitied him,
so later when she fell ill,
she would not let him know.
The Prince of Yùzhāng, who held the governorship of Xiāngzhōu,
appointed him as a Cavalier Acting Staff Officer.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
his taxes were remitted,
and his doorway was marked.
He died at home.
Huá Bǎo
was from Wúxī, Jìnling.
His father, Háo,
at the end of the Yìxī era,
was garrisoned in Cháng'ān.
Bǎo was eight years old.
Before parting,
Háo said to Bǎo,
"Wait until I return,
and I will perform your capping ceremony."
Cháng'ān fell to the barbarians,
and Háo died.
Bǎo reached seventy years old
without marrying or being capped.
If anyone asked him about it,
he would weep inconsolably for a full day,
unable to answer.
Xuē Tiānshēng, from the same commandery,
ate only vegetables when his mother suffered misfortune.
Tiānshēng also ate only vegetables.
His mother died before her mourning period ended,
and Tiānshēng never ate fish or meat for the rest of his life.
He had kindness and righteousness toward his younger brother.
Also from the same commandery, Liú Huáiyìn and his younger brother Huáizé,
at the age of ten,
suffered their father's death.
They did not wear padded silk
〔一二〕or eat salted vegetables.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
their doorways were all marked.
Hán Língmǐn
was from Shàn, Kuàijī.
He was orphaned early
and, with his elder brother Língzhēn, both possessed filial nature.
Soon after, their mother also died.
Being poor and having no means to arrange the funeral,
the brothers together planted half a mu of gourds.
They would pick gourd seeds in the morning,
〔一三〕and by evening, they would have grown again.
With this, they managed to complete the burial rites.
When Língzhēn died
without a son,
his wife, Zhuó Shì, remained chaste and did not remarry.
〔一四〕Fearing that her family might sway her resolve,
she never requested to return home.
Língmǐn served her like his own mother.
Zhào Shì, wife of Wú Kāngzhī of Jìnling,
lost her father and had a young brother.
During a famine year,
her aged mother was critically ill.
Zhào went to the village to sell herself,
her words full of sorrow and bitterness.
〔一五〕The villagers pitied her,
and each person contributed a sheng of rice to help her,
thus she was spared.
〔一六〕When she married Kāngzhī,
〔一七〕her husband died a short time later.
Her family wanted her to remarry,
but she vowed to die rather than be unfaithful.
Huáng Shì, wife of Jiǎng Jùnzhī of Yìxīng,
did not remarry after her husband's death.
When forced,
she tried to drown herself,
and so they stopped.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
an edict remitted their taxes
and marked their doorways.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
in Huìjī’s Yǒngxìng, the mother of Ní Yìzhī, Lady Dīng,
[一八] lost her husband in her youth.
Her nature was benevolent and loving.
When a famine struck,
she shared her clothes and food to nourish the starving people in her village.
[一九] When neighbors sought loans,
she never refused.
Chén Ráng from the same village lost his parents,
and being orphaned and without relatives,
Lady Dīng took him in and raised him.
When he grew up,
she arranged his marriage.
Also, when Lady Xú, the wife of Wáng Lǐ from the same village,
died as a sojourner in Shānyīn during a famine year,
Lady Dīng bought a coffin and burial articles for her,
and personally went to inter her.
At the end of Yuánhuī,
there was heavy snow,
and merchant travel was cut off.
[二０] Starvation spread house to house in the villages.
Lady Dīng personally provided salt and rice,
distributing them according to the number of mouths.
When Zuǒ Qiáo from the same village suffered four deaths and
had no means to bury them,
Lady Dīng arranged for the coffins.
There were those who failed to pay their three levies,
and she paid them on their behalf.
Lady Wáng, the wife of Lady Dīng’s eldest son, remained a widow and steadfastly refused to remarry.
The commandery and state reported this to the throne,
and an imperial edict honored her household
and exempted them from taxes.
Also, Lady Xú Línglǐ, the wife of Xú Línglǐ from Guǎnglíng, rescued her child from a fire,
and was burnt to death along with the child.
Grand Administrator Liú Qùn reported this.
Furthermore, a woman named Chén from Huìjī,
[二一] had three daughters
but no sons.
Her grandparents were eighty or ninety years old,
senile and unaware of things.
Her father suffered from a severe chronic illness,
and her mother was unfaithful in her marriage.
During a famine year,
the three daughters went together to Xī Hú to gather water caltrops and water shields,
and took turns selling them in the market daily,
never slacking.
The villagers called their household a "righteous gate,"
and many wanted to marry them.
The eldest daughter, grieving her solitary state,
swore she would not marry.
Her grandparents soon died one after another,
and the three daughters personally arranged their funerals and burials,
building a hermitage by their graves.
Also, a daughter of the Wáng family from Yǒngxìng’s Gàizhōng Lǐ,
at the age of five,
[二二] contracted a toxic disease,
losing sight in both eyes.
Her nature was extremely filial.
When she was twenty,
her parents died.
As she cried over their bodies,
blood flowed from both her eyes.
Her younger sister É licked the blood,
and her left eye immediately opened.
People at the time called this a "filial response."
The county magistrate, Hé Tánxiù, did not report it.
Also, a daughter of the Tú family from Zhūjì’s Dōngwū Lǐ,
whose father was blind
and mother suffered from a chronic illness.
Relatives abandoned them,
and the villagers ostracized them.
The daughter moved her parents to live far away in Zhùluó.
[二三] By day, she gathered firewood and wild vegetables;
by night, she spun and wove
to support them.
When both parents died,
she personally arranged their funerals and burials,
carrying earth to build their grave mound.
Suddenly, she heard a voice from the air saying:
"Your utmost filial piety is commendable.
The mountain spirits wish to employ you.
You can cure people's illnesses,
and you will surely become very wealthy."
The daughter thought it was an evil spirit,
[二四] and dared not follow,
so she fell ill.
After some time,
a neighbor was poisoned by a xuè from the stream.
The daughter tried to treat him,
and felt her own illness immediately subside.
She then practiced shamanism to cure people's diseases,
and none failed to be cured.
Her family wealth increased daily.
Many in the village wanted to marry her,
but as she had no brothers,
she swore to guard the graves and refused to marry.
She was later robbed and killed by mountain bandits.
The county magistrate Yú Línzhī fully reported this to the commandery,
but Grand Administrator Wáng Jìngzé did not report it to the throne.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
Yáo Shì, the wife of Chéng Gōngjì from Wúxìng, gave birth to two sons.
However, Gōngjì, his elder brother Gōngyuàn, and Qiánbó all died,
each leaving a son: Xīnzhī and Tiānbǎo.
Yáo raised them,
sold land and houses to arrange their marriages,
and she and her two sons lived as guests in a neighbor's house.
Emperor Míng issued an edict to arrange marriages for her two sons,
honored her household,
and exempted them from corvée labor.
Chǔ Shì, the wife of Fàn Fǎxún from Wújùn,
also diligently performed her wifely duties.
In the Shēngmíng era of Sòng,
Sūn Tán’guàn plotted a rebellion and became a fugitive.
Chǔ said to her son Sēngjiǎn:
"Governor Sūn (Sūn Yuèzhōu) is the son of your paternal aunt's sister,
and thus a maternal cousin to your father, while their friendship surpassed that of ancient worthies.
If he is caught while fleeing, he will surely not escape.
You should take him in."
Tán’guàn was soon executed,
and Chǔ Shì ordered Sēngjiǎn to go and collect his body for burial.
She was over seventy years old
and died in the Yǒngmíng era.
Sēngjiǎn was in the capital;
upon hearing of her illness, he rushed back.
Before he arrived, Chǔ had already died.
As they were about to perform the funeral,
they tried to lift the corpse but could not.
Soon after, Sēngjiǎn arrived.
Fēng Yánbó, courtesy name Zhònglián,
was from Bóhǎi.
He was learned and virtuous,
did not associate with worldly people,
and served his widowed sister-in-law with great care.
The state appointed him as Chief Clerk,
and recommended him as Xiùcái,
but he did not accept.
Later, he served in office.
When Yuán Chóngzǔ was Governor of Yùzhōu,
he requested Grand Ancestor (Emperor Gāo) to appoint Yánbó as Chief Clerk,
concurrently holding the position of Grand Administrator of Liángjùn.
He resigned due to illness,
resided temporarily in Dōnghǎi,
and thus never went to the capital.
Three generations shared wealth,
and he was revered and relied upon by the northern regions.
King Yùzhāng invited him to be Zhongbīng,
but he did not accept,
and died.
In the third year of Jiànkē,
imperial envoys toured the realm.
Chén Xuánzǐ from Yìxīng had four generations and 170 members living together.
Shào Róngxīng and Wén Xiànshū from Wǔlíngjùn had eight generations living together.
Xú Shēngzhī from Dōnghǎi, Fàn Ānzǔ from Wǔlíng, Lǐ Shèngbó, and Fàn Dàogēn had five generations living together.
Tán Hóngbǎo from Línglíng, Hé Hóng from Héngyáng, and Yáng Hēitóu from Huáyáng, distantly related, had four generations living together,
all sharing clothes and food.
An imperial edict honored their households
and exempted them from taxes.
Also, Wáng Xùzǔ from Shǔjùn and Hǎo Dàofú from Huáyáng had several generations sharing a common kitchen.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Míng issued an edict to honor their households
and exempt them from levies and corvée labor.
Wú Dázhī was
a native of Yìxīng.
When his sister-in-law died and he had no means to bury her,
[二五] he sold himself as a servant to ten households
to provide for her tomb and coffin.
During a famine year, his paternal cousin Jìngbó and his wife were captured and sold north of the Jiāng River.
Dázhī had ten *mǔ* of land;
he sold it to redeem them,
and shared his wealth and home with them.
The commandery appointed him as Chief Clerk,
but he firmly declined, yielding it to his elder brother.
He also yielded his ancestral fields to his distant younger cousin,
but the cousin also refused to accept them,
[二六] so the fields remained idle.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
an imperial edict honored his household.
Hénán Xīn Pǔmíng lived as an immigrant in Kuàijī.
From a young age, he shared a single tent with his elder brother.
When his brother died,
he donated the tent to the spirit seat.
During the summer months, there were many mosquitoes,
but Pǔmíng did not show any dissatisfaction with sleeping in the open.
When his brother was about to be buried,
neighbors admired his righteousness
and offered many contributions.
Pǔmíng initially accepted them,
but later returned all of them.
The donors were very surprised.
Pǔmíng said:
“Initially, I was concerned that my brother’s tomb was not complete,
so I did not refuse your kind intentions.
But how can I bear to use the deceased’s remaining belongings as household property now?”
Later, he suffered his mother’s death,
nearly to the point of self-destruction.
The Inspector of Yángzhōu, the Prince of Yùzhāng, invited him to serve as a Counsel to the Gōng Cáo (義) [Yì] Cáo.
[二七]At the age of fifty,
he died.
There was also Hé Bóyú,
and his younger brother Yòuyú.
Both strictly maintained their integrity.
They raised their orphaned nephew,
and when he grew up, arranged his marriage,
giving him all of their family property.
They lived in poverty and withered away,
tirelessly instructing people.
The local people called them “teachers of men.”
When a Grand Administrator arrived in the commandery,
none failed to pay them respects.
In the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng,
Bóyú died.
Yòuyú had been fond of Buddhist dharma since he was young,
[二八]cutting his hair and observing a long vegetarian diet,
practicing with extreme hardship.
He died early in the Liáng dynasty.
Both brothers lived to be over eighty years old.
Wáng Wénshū,
was from Gùzhāng in Wúxīng.
His father was captured by barbarians,
and Wénshū mourned him with tears of blood,
eating vegetables in the mountain valleys for over thirty years.
The Grand Administrator Xiè Dàn invited him to be Gōngcáo,
but he did not accept.
In the eleventh year of Yǒngmíng,
Grand Administrator Kǒng Xiùzhī memorialized, saying:
“Wénshū’s nature embodies the Five Constants,
and his heart accords with the Three Teachings.
Because his father was lost in the land of the Xūn (barbarians),
he carries a lifelong pain,
living in a solitary mat,
bearing grief without end.
He wears hempen clothes year after year,
and eats vegetables and beans awaiting his fate.
The obligation of marriage is extinguished by his natural affection,
and official positions are empty to his simple aspirations.
May your benevolent grace be extended in distinction,
and his hamlet be publicly honored.”
Emperor Yùlín issued an edict to display a plaque at his gate,
changing the name of his residence to
“Xiàoxíng Lǐ” (Filial Piety Hamlet).
Zhū Qiānzhī, courtesy name Chǔguāng,
was from Qiántáng, Wújùn.
His father, Zhāo zhī,
was renowned in the local community for his learning and understanding.
When Qiānzhī was a few years old,
his birth mother died.
Zhāozhī temporarily buried her by a field,
which was later burned by a fire lit by his clansman, Zhū Yòufāng.
His full sister secretly told him about it.
Though Qiānzhī was young,
he grieved as if observing a funeral.
When he grew older, he did not marry.
In the Yǒngmíng period,
he personally killed Yòufāng with a blade,
and went to prison to surrender himself.
The county magistrate, Shēn Língxù, memorialized the throne.

The Assistant Governor Kǒng Zhìguī, concurrently Registrar Liú Jìn, and the Grand Minister of Works' Left Western Clerk Zhāng Róng, submitted a memorial to the Inspector, the Prince of Yùzhāng, saying:
“Rites permit the tradition of avenging wrongs
to express filial piety and righteousness;
Laws establish prohibitions against killing
to demonstrate the system of expediency.
Qiānzhī wielded a blade (軒) [zhǎn] to avenge an injustice,
[二九]thereby fulfilling private rites;
By surrendering himself to death,
he also upheld public law.
If he is still put to death,
he will become a criminal of this age;
If he is pardoned and allowed to live,
he will be a filial son of a glorious dynasty.
Killing one criminal
is not sufficient to promote the law;
Saving one filial son
truly spreads moral virtue.
Zhāng Xù and Lù Chéng,
who are his old acquaintances from the area,
should provide the full details.
Róng and others are not acquainted with Qiānzhī,
but from our humble, limited view,
we feel deep regret.”
The Prince of Yùzhāng reported this to Shìzǔ.
At that time, Wáng Cí, the Grand Administrator of Wújùn, Zhāng Xù, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, and Lù Chéng, the Minister of Personnel, all memorialized discussing this matter.
Shìzǔ praised his righteousness,
but fearing further retaliatory killings,
he ordered Qiānzhī to accompany Cáo Hǔ on a western expedition.
As they were about to depart,
Yòufāng’s son, Yùn [三０], waited at the Jīnyáng Gate to kill Qiānzhī.
Qiānzhī’s elder brother, Xuǎnzhī [三一], then stabbed Yùn to death.
The authorities reported this.
Shìzǔ said:
“These are all acts of righteousness,
and should not be investigated.”
He pardoned all of them.
Shěn Yǐ of Wúxīng heard of this and sighed, saying:
“The younger brother died for filial piety,
the elder brother sacrificed for righteousness.
The virtues of filial piety and brotherly affection
are concentrated in this one family.”
Xuǎnzhī, courtesy name Chǔlín,
had high aspirations and integrity,
and authored a discourse on辯相 (Biànxiāng).
When he was young, Gù Huān saw him and found him extraordinary,
giving him his daughter in marriage.
He rose to the position of Military Advisor to the Prince of Jiāngxià.
Xiāo Ruìmíng
was a native of Nánlánlíng.
He was a cousin of the Commander of the Guards, Chén.
His father, Xiàosūn,
was a General of the Left Army.
Ruìmíng first served as an Aides-de-camp General of the Palace.
From a young age, he possessed extreme natural integrity,
serving his parents with caution and devotion.
When his mother was ill, he personally prayed,
not sleeping at night.
Upon her death,
he succumbed to overwhelming grief and died.
In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
Shìzǔ issued an edict saying:
“Xiāo Ruìmíng, General Longxiáng, Military Advisor of the Commander of the West, and Magistrate of Sōngzī,
had deep and pure love and respect.
His service to his mother exhausted all rites,
and his mourning went beyond sorrow,
leading to his self-destruction.
Although he did not fully comprehend the sagely teachings,
such extreme devotion is pitiable.
He should be granted posthumous honors
to commend a good man.
He is hereby posthumously appointed Grand Imperial Secretary.”
Lè Yí, courtesy name Wéndé,
[三二]was from Nányáng Yáng.
His family had resided in Nánjùn for generations.
From a young age, his words and actions were harmonious and prudent.
He served as a Military Advisor to the Imperial Household.
[三三]When his father fell ill and died in Yǐngzhōu,
Yí suddenly thought of his father and wept,
then requested leave to return home.
Midway, he indeed received the grievous news of his father’s death.
Yí immediately went barefoot, wailing loudly,
emerging at the rear islet of the Táo family.
He encountered a merchant who gave him passage upstream,
and he did not eat or drink for several days.
Once, when he was ill,
he was separated from his mother by a wall.
He endured the pain without speaking,
biting his quilt until it was shredded,
fearing that his mother would grieve for him.
Wáng Sēngqián, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, invited him to be his Master of Records.
Because his colleagues were not proper individuals,
he resigned his office and left.
The Director of the Bureau of Personnel, Yú Gǎozhī, once visited him.
Yí prepared a meal for him,
which consisted only of dried fish and pickled vegetables.
Gǎozhī said:
“I cannot eat this.”
His mother heard this
and personally brought out several kinds of her usual fish soup.
Gǎozhī said:
“You are more extreme than Máo Jìwěi,
but I am not Guō Línzōng.”
He rose to the position of Administrator for Yǐngzhōu,
and then died.
His younger brother, Yù, was also filial.
〔三四〕When their father was on his deathbed,
he held his hand and entrusted him to Wáng Huàn, the Administrator of Yǐngzhōu.
Yù was so grief-stricken that he fainted,
vomiting several sheng of blood,
and subsequently fell ill.
He rose to the office of Registrar for the General of Agile Cavalry.
Towards the end of the Lóngchāng reign,
Yù said to Xú Xiàosì, the Administrator of Dānyáng,
“Rumors are rife outside,
it seems there are affairs like those of Yī [Yǐn] and Zhōu [Gōng].
You, sir, have received the extraordinary favor of Emperor Wǔ,
and bear the heavy burden of his entrustment.
I fear you cannot participate in this endeavor with others.
People laugh at Chǔ Gōng,
and their teeth still ache from the cold to this day.”
Xiàosì was deeply receptive to his words.
During the Jiànwǔ period,
he served as the Magistrate of Yǒngshì,
and the people cherished his virtue.
He died in office.
There was an old woman carrying a basket of vegetables [葉] on her shoulder, going to the market.
〔三五〕Upon hearing of Yù’s death,
she abandoned her load and wept bitterly.
Jiě Zhònggōng from Yànmén,
〔三六〕also resided as an emigrant in Nánjùn.
His family lived in harmony and affection.
Whenever he acquired fields, powerful connections, or wealth,
he would immediately divide it equally with his brothers.
His mother was ill for a long time and did not recover.
He went into the mountains to gather herbs,
and met an old man who told him,
“If you get Dīnggōng téng,
her illness will be immediately cured.
This vine is close by, on the near mountainside, hanging down from a tall tree.”
Suddenly, he disappeared.
Zhònggōng followed his words and found it,
treated the illness,
and his mother immediately recovered.
Even now, people in Jiānglíng still recognize this vine.
Jiāng Mì, courtesy name Shìqīng,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
His father, Liàngzhī,
was a Supernumerary Attendant.
Mì was poor in his youth.
During the day, he would chop firewood,
and at night, he would study,
holding his scrolls by moonlight and ascending to the rooftop.
His character was benevolent and righteous.
When his clothes became worn,
fearing that the lice would starve,
〔三七〕he would take them out and put them back in his clothes.
Within a few days,
he never had lice again for the rest of his life.
After his mother's death,
he regretted not having fully supported her during her life,
and when offered salmon, he could not bear to eat it.
He would eat vegetables but not their hearts,
because they contained the essence of life.
He successively served as Provisional Adjutant in the Central Army of the South.
When the conscripted clerks assigned to him left their posts,
and became ill,
no one would take them in.
The clerks, leaning on staffs, came to Mì.
Mì personally comforted and cared for them.
When a clerk died,
Mì bought a coffin for him.
Having no servants,
he and his brothers jointly carried and buried him.
He held the position of Assistant Instructor for the Imperial Academy.
Riding in a cart pulled by a cow, he was on his way to dye cloth with 'wūtóu' (aconite).
He saw an old man walking,
so he got out of the cart and gave him a ride,
while he himself walked.
Emperor Shìzǔ appointed him tutor to Zǐlín, Prince of Nánkāng.
During the Jiànwǔ period,
after Emperor Míng harmed the various princes,
Mì was worried about Zǐlín,
and went to Zhìgōng dàorén to ask about his fortune.
Zhìgōng overturned the ashes from an incense burner to show him,
saying,
“All gone.
Nothing remains.”
When Zǐlín was indeed harmed,
Mì went to mourn him.
His tears ran dry,
followed by blood.
He personally oversaw the funeral arrangements,
and then departed.
At that time, Yán Huánzhī, tutor to the Prince of Guǎnghàn, also mourned the prince with utmost grief.
Mì soon died.
Mì’s kinsman, Mì, who was the Administrator of Yúnzhōu,
was the son of Huángménláng Yú,
and had the same given name as Mì.
The world referred to Mì as
“Filial Jiāng Mì”
to distinguish him.
Dù Qī, courtesy name Mèngshān,
was a native of Qiántáng, Wú Jùn.
He was the son of the recluse Jīngchǎn.
Zhāng Róng from the same commandery was friends with Jīngchǎn.
Whenever they met to discuss matters,
Qī was always by their side.
Róng pointed to Qī and said,
“In the past, Chén Tàiqiū summoned Yuánfāng,
and Yuánfāng was inferior.
Comparing the present to the past,
what is so precious about the ancients?”
Qī went to the capital,
and studied under the Confucian scholar Liú Huán.
He was skilled in refined conversation,
and could play the qín and drink wine.
Many famous scholars and noble personages respected and treated him well.
Zhōu Yǒng, the Secretariat Director, wrote to Jīngchǎn, saying,
“Your worthy son's scholarship is pure and outstanding,
a talent for later generations.
The affection and admiration I feel,
how can words fully express it?
He is truly an eminent man,
as if he were my own.”
The Provincial Governor, Prince Yùzhāng, heard of his reputation,
and appointed him as an Advisor-Attendant,
then transferred him to Western Secretariat Aide.
Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng, frequently extended courtesies to him.
Hé Yìn, Libationer of the Imperial Academy, who specialized in rites,
also highly esteemed Qī,
and appointed him as a scholar,
in charge of marriage and capping ceremonies.
Because his father was old, he returned home to care for him,
finding joy in farming.
Qī was fat, fair-skinned, tall, and strong.
When Jīngchǎn fell ill,
within ten days, Qī became skin and bones.
When Jīngchǎn died,
Qī did not take water or food for seven days.
He wept incessantly morning and evening,
〔三八〕and ate no salted vegetables.
Each time he arranged to buy items for offerings and memorials,
he personally supervised them,
sobbing uncontrollably.
On the first and fifteenth of the month, and during festivals and at year's end,
he would fast and then resume eating,
vomiting several sheng of blood.
At that time, Hé Yìn and Xiè Fěi were both living in seclusion on Dōngshān.
They sent letters to urge and admonish him,
warning him against self-destruction.
Until the ‘xiángdǎn’ (end of mourning),
he dreamt in the evening that he saw his father,
and cried himself to death.
Initially,
Yìn’s elder brother Diǎn saw Qī and sighed, saying,
“Your charm and demeanor are such that,
though you have gained good repute,
you will not live a long life.”
He died at the age of thirty-six.
Everyone at the time lamented and grieved for him.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
there was a young boy in Shànyǎn county,
eight years old,
who, along with his mother, contracted the red rash disease.
His mother died,
but the family, considering the boy was still very sick,
did not let him know.
The boy suspected it,
and asked,
“Mother often asked about my illness.
Yesterday her voice sounded weak,
and now I don't hear it anymore.
What does this mean?”
Thereupon he threw himself off the bed,
crawled to his mother’s corpse,
and died suddenly.
The villagers reported it to the County Magistrate Zōng Shàncái,
requesting to honor him with a dwelling,
but the matter was ultimately not carried out.
Lù Jiàng, styled Wèiqīng,
was a native of Wújùn.
His father, Xián,
styled Xiáyè,
had a refined demeanor,
and in his dealings with others,
he did not lightly compromise.
In his youth, he was recognized by Zhāng Xù of the same commandery
and rose to the post of Yángzhōu Biejia.
When Emperor Míng died,
Xián said to his close associates:
"The imperial carriage has departed (the emperor has died),
and all officials will henceforth listen to the Grand Tutor.
The ruler of this land holds great power but is weak in talent;
he will surely be unable to rise to the occasion,
and disaster is imminent."
He then suffered a heart ailment
and no longer involved himself in provincial affairs.
When the Inspector, Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng, rebelled,
and the affair failed,
Xián, as a subordinate official, was summoned to Dù Mǔ's residence.
Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì reported that Xián was not involved in the rebellious plot,
but before a reply could be received,
Xú Shìbiāo ordered him killed.
At that time, Jiàng was with Xián
and embraced Xián's neck, begging to die in his place,
and so they were both killed.
The historian says: When a decadent trend arises,
human morality is undermined and diminished.
The teachings of restraint and guidance are heard in vain,
and the unpolished jade of virtue rarely achieves its form.
If one allows loyalty to one's elders to shift,
it might not be a proper conduct;
the pungent and bitter nature of ginger and cassia might change their original qualities.
Yet, merely honoring villages with banners and altering names of neighborhoods,
or inquiring about provisions for the family and preserving their livelihood,
is nothing more than
encouraging the many and the few to boast equally,
and urging diligent farmers alike.
In terms of supporting and promoting the moral teachings,
this is not much.
A eulogy says: Filial piety is the head of all conduct,
and righteousness truly stems from the heart.
White flowers uphold their integrity,
cold trees stand united in spirit.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 37: Favored Officials Jì Sēngzhēn, Liú Xìzōng, Rú Fǎliàng, Lǚ Wénxiǎn, Lǚ Wéndù
When there are celestial phenomena,
there must be human affairs.
The star of the favored official
is arrayed near the Emperor's Seat.
The establishment of teachings through rites
also sets out the attire of close officials.
The meaning of intimacy and favor
has a long history.
From the time of the declining Zhōu dynasty,
where dukes and marquises held exclusive authority,
to the hegemonic lords Huán and Wén,
and down to the Warring States period,
the employment of favored confidants
was not lacking in those times.
Emperor Wén of Hàn favored Dèng Tōng,
who, although his coins circulated throughout the world,
only reached the position of Lángzhōng.
Emperor Wǔ's Hán Yān and Huò Qùbìng
even rose to the rank of Shìzhōng Dàsīmǎ.
Up until Wèi and Jìn,
when the world entrusted heavy power,
and talent and position were somewhat mismatched,
trust and favor were equally applied.
The office of Zhōngshū
was historically responsible for strategic affairs.
Emperor Yuán of Hàn used Lìng Pú to manage affairs,
and Emperor Míng of Wèi allowed Jiān Lìng to wield exclusive power;
when they were in the central court,
they were still considered important appointments.
Chén Zhǔn entrusted responsibilities to superior officials,
and Xún Xù regretted his loss of office.
During the Jìn dynasty, Shèrén ranked ninth grade;
in the south of the Jiāng River, Tōngshìláng was established
to manage imperial edicts and pronouncements.
Thereafter, Láng reverted to Shìláng,
and Shèrén also became known as Tōngshì.
Emperor Yuán employed Liú Chāo of Lángyá,
who held his post with caution and diligence.
In the time of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Qiū Dāng and Zhōu Jiū both came from humble backgrounds.
Since Emperor Xiàowǔ,
officials were selected from both gentry and commoners,
such as Bào Zhào of Dōnghǎi,
who was renowned for his talent and learning.
Also employed was Cháo Shàngzhī of Lǔjùn.
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng considered this an unsuitable choice.
The Emperor sent more than twenty imperial edicts to the Shangshu,
announcing his command and debating the matter.
Yìgōng then sighed, saying:
"The ruler indeed knows people."
And in the time of Emperor Míng,
Húmǔ Hào, Ruǎn Diànfū and others
became entirely devoted to flattery and favor.
At the beginning of Qí, long-serving officials were also employed,
as were trusted confidants.
They handled legal reports and memorials,
and issued imperial edicts and commands.
Those who were somewhat skilled in writing
also drafted imperial documents,
and the bureau of Shìláng
was again encroached upon.
In the Jiànwǔ era,
imperial edicts scarcely passed through the Zhōngshū;
they were exclusively issued by the Shèrén.
There were four Shènèi Shèrén,
who were stationed in the four departments (sìshěng).
Below them were the Zhǔshū Lìngshǐ,
who were formerly military officers,
but Sòng changed them to civil officials,
and their number was not fixed.
All were important and trusted confidants of the emperor,
and all official documents and registers of the realm
were submitted to their departments.
All important and secret state affairs
were like those of the outer bureaus of the Shangshu.
There was a Zhìjújiān
who commanded military officers
and was in charge of weapons, equipment, and military service,
also employing humble people who had received imperial favor.
Now, this chapter on Favored Officials is compiled
to continue the tradition of previous historians.
Jì Sēngzhēn
was a native of Jiànkāng, Dānyáng.
In his youth, Sēngzhēn followed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Xiāo Sīhuà and his son Huìkāi,
and both were appreciated and well-treated.
Huìkāi was harsh by nature,
and Sēngzhēn was once punished for a minor transgression,
but thereafter he was entrusted with duties as before.
When Huìkāi was dismissed from Yìzhōu and returned to the capital,
he was discontented,
but Sēngzhēn served him with even greater diligence.
On his deathbed, Huìkāi sighed, saying:
"Jì Sēngzhēn is destined for wealth and honor,
but I will not live to see it."
He then entrusted Sēngzhēn to Liú Bǐng and Zhōu Yóng.
Previously,
when Huìkāi was in Yìzhōu,
the local people rebelled,
and he was critically besieged.
A Taoist priest said to him:
"The city's siege will soon be lifted.
Your noble family will greatly flourish in the future,
so do not worry about external enemies."
Huìkāi secretly said to Sēngzhēn:
"Among my sons and younger brothers who are currently alive,
none possess extraordinary talent.
It must be the Taoist priest's prophecy coming true."
Sēngzhēn remembered his words
and therefore asked to serve Tàizǔ.
He followed him to Huái'yīn,
and because of his leisurely writing,
he was ordered to reply to letters and memorials from near and far.
From a humble official, he gradually rose to be Tàizǔ's Guànjūn Fǔ Cānjūn and Zhǔbù.
Sēngzhēn dreamt that mugwort grew all over the river,
and, alarmed, he reported it.
Tàizǔ said:
"The poet picks 'xiāo' (mugwort);
'xiāo' is indeed mugwort.
Mugwort grows to block the flow;
you must not speak broadly of this."
Such was his closeness.
At the beginning of Yuánhuī,
he followed Tàizǔ to camp at Xīntíng
to resist the bandits of Guìyáng.
Xiāo Huìlǎng broke into the east gate,
and Sēngzhēn fought alongside his attendants.
When the bandits retreated,
Tàizǔ ordered Sēngzhēn to lead the imperial guards
to patrol the city.
When peace was restored,
he was appointed Nántái Yùshǐ and Tàizǔ Lǐngjūn Gōngcáo.
The Emperor intended to depose and enthrone,
and consulted Yuán Càn and Chǔ Yuān.
Sēngzhēn reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Currently, the court is in chaos,
and people cannot protect themselves.
The hopes of the empire
do not rest with Yuán and Chǔ.
How can Your Excellency remain silent
and passively accept extermination?
The juncture of survival or destruction
awaits your thorough consideration."
Tàizǔ accepted his advice.
Tàizǔ wished to cross the Guǎnglín [River] and raise an army.
Sēngzhēn again advised,
“Although the Emperor is indeed deranged
and has tyrannized the myriad commoners,
the imperial foundation built over generations
is still as solid as a rock.
Now, if we lead a hundred families north,
it is not certain that all will arrive safely.
Even if we take Guǎnglín city,
the Son of Heaven will issue commands from deep within the palace,
denouncing Your Excellency as a rebel.
How can this be avoided?
If we do not succeed,
we would have to flee north to the land of the Hú.
I humbly submit that this is not a foolproof plan.”
The Emperor said,
“You are concerned about your family;
how can you follow me?”
Sēngzhēn prostrated himself, affirming his unwavering loyalty.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
he was appointed Yuánwàiláng
and concurrently held the post of Dōngwǔchéng Magistrate.
Soon after, he was appointed Gěishìzhōng and Shàolíngwáng Cānjūn.
Tàizǔ sat in the high tower of the Eastern Palace,
gazing towards Shítóuchéng,
with Sēngzhēn by his side.
The Emperor said,
“All the generals urge me to execute Yuán and Liú,
but I do not wish to do so immediately.”
When the affair of Shěn Yōubó arose,
he followed Tàizǔ into the court hall.
On the night Shítóu rebelled,
Tàizǔ dispatched all his forces to suppress them.
From within the palace city, the firelight and shouts from Shítóu were very intense,
filling people with foreboding.
Sēngzhēn said to the crowd,
“The continuous shouting
must mean it is being attacked by the government army.
As for the rising firelight,
the rebels would not burn their own city,
so this must mean the government army is victorious.”
Soon after, a report came that Shítóu had been pacified.
The Emperor went out and encamped at Xīntíng,
making Sēngzhēn command a thousand men inside the tent.
Originally,
when the Emperor was in the Commandery Protector’s residence,
he ordered Sēngzhēn to learn to imitate his handwriting for official documents and signatures.
By this time, all replies to memorials
were entrusted to Sēngzhēn.
The Emperor observed them
and laughed, saying,
“Even I can no longer distinguish them.”
Initially,
when the Emperor was building a city in Huái'yīn,
he found a tin
several feet in size,
with篆 script at the bottom,
which no one could recognize.
Sēngzhēn said,
“Why bother identifying these characters?
This is an ancient object,
a sign of the Nine Bestowals.”
Tàizǔ said,
“Do not speak nonsense.”
When the Emperor was about to be appointed Qí Gōng,
the date had already been set.
Yáng Zǔzhī planned to cause trouble during the ceremony at the palace veranda.
Sēngzhēn, however, requested the Emperor to choose an auspicious day.
Soon after, Zǔzhī’s plot was discovered.
The Emperor said,
“Without your words,
I would have suffered a minor setback;
this is no different from calling for ice [and receiving it].”
He was transferred to Qí Guó Zhōngshū Shèrén.
In the early Jiànyuán period,
he concurrently held the post of Dōngyàn Magistrate,
and was enfeoffed as Xīnyáng Xiànnán,
with three hundred households.
He was transferred to Yǔlínjiān,
promoted to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
and then to Shàngshū Zhǔkèláng,
and Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
with his magistracy remaining as before.
He was again appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Shèrén with his original post.
When Tàizǔ was gravely ill,
he ordered Sēngzhēn to manage his last will.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
after mourning,
he was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
then appointed Nántàishān Tàishǒu,
and again Shèrén,
with his original post unchanged.
He was put in charge of the affairs of the princes’ residences.
Sēngzhēn’s appearance and speech
had a refined scholarly demeanor.
Shìzǔ once watched him leave,
and laughed, saying,
“Why must one consider lineage?
Jì Sēngzhēn’s nobility is often unmatched by others.”
Among the powerful figures,
he received the most favorable attention.
He was appointed Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
with his other offices remaining as before.
He was sent out as Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn
and Jiànkāng Magistrate.
Upon his return, he was appointed Zuǒyòulángjiāng
and Tàishān Tàishǒu.
He was also given the command of Xiānqū Shǐ.
Soon after, he was appointed Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
When his mother passed away,
a five-colored two-headed snake was found when her tomb was opened.
When Shìzǔ died,
Sēngzhēn wept loudly and mourned deeply.
Míngdì, seeing that Sēngzhēn had served successive courts,
appointed him Yóujī Jiāngjūn
and concurrent Sīnóng in the first year of Jiànwǔ,
treating him as before.
Wishing to appoint Sēngzhēn to govern a commandery,
Sēngzhēn requested to promote his younger brother Sēngměng
to Zhènmán Hùjūn and Jìnxī Tàishǒu.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
he was appointed Sīnóng Qīng.
When Míngdì died,
he was in charge of the imperial tomb affairs.
He was sent out as Lúlíng
At fifty-five years
he died.
Yáng Fǎchí, a Daoist priest in the Sòng dynasty,
had a long-standing friendship with Tàizǔ.
At the end of Yuánhuī,
he propagated secret plans.
In the Shēngmíng period,
he was made Sēngzhèng.
In the early Jiànyuán period,
he left the Daoist order
and became Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
enfeoffed as Zhōulíng Xiànnán,
with three hundred households.
In the second year [of Jiànyuán],
when the barbarians besieged Qúshān,
Fǎchí was dispatched as
leading a detachment to reinforce them.
In the fourth year of Yǒngmíng,
he was impeached for exploiting his officers and guests,
and confiscating their provisions,
and his enfeoffment was revoked.
He died.
Liú Xìzōng was
a native of Dānyáng.
From a young age, he was skilled in calligraphy and painting,
serving as a calligrapher for Jǐnglì, the son of the Sòng Jìnglíngwáng Dàn.
When Dàn raised an army in Guǎnglín,
everyone in the city died,
but Shěn Qìngzhī was ordered to pardon Xìzōng
and make him a calligrapher for the Eastern Palace.
In the Tàishǐ period,
he became Zhǔshū.
Due to his humble origins, he was repeatedly promoted until he reached the rank of Xūnpǐn.
In the early Yuánhuī period,
he became Fèngcháoqǐng
and concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén
and Yuánwàiláng.
He was enfeoffed as Shǐxīng Nántíng Hóu,
with an income of three hundred seventy households.
He concurrently held the post of Mòlíng Magistrate.
When Tàizǔ deposed Cāngwú,
the next
he called for the upright Shèrén Yú Zhěng,
who was too drunk to get up.
Xìzōng joyfully accepted the command.
Tàizǔ said,
“Today, heaven and earth are reopened;
this is the day for you to exert your full effort.”
He was ordered to copy all administrative edicts
and memorials from various regions.
He was assigned a Zhǔshū
All his work
was done according to the Emperor’s wishes.
He was appointed Yǔlínjiān
and then transferred to Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was then appointed Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn
and sent out as Hǎiyán Magistrate.
When Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn and Jiànkāng Magistrate.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
with his magistracy remaining as before.
Soon after, he was transferred to Yòujūn Jiāngjūn and Huáilíng Tàishǒu,
concurrently holding the post of Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
After his mother’s death, he resigned but was
reappointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn
and restored to his former position.
In the fourth year,
when the bandit Táng Yù rebelled,
the palace guard troops marched east to suppress him.
Liú Xìzōng was dispatched to accompany the army to offer condolences and encouragement,
visiting all the prefectures and counties that had suffered from the bandits.
The common people who had been driven and coerced
were all pardoned without question,
and returned to their civilian ranks.
When Xìzōng returned,
the Emperor said:
"This campaign was one of conquest without battle;
it was pacified in good time,
and the people are settled and peaceful.
This is truly gratifying."
Xìzōng was bestowed money and silk.
The Emperor wished to repair Bái-xià Chéng,
but found it difficult to mobilize labor.
Xìzōng proposed conscripting the eastern commoners who had followed Yù in his rebellion as laborers,
and the Emperor adopted his suggestion.
Later, when the imperial carriage was reviewing military exercises,
the Emperor walked around Bái-xià Chéng and
said:
"Liú Xìzōng obtained this city for the state."
During the Yǒngmíng era,
when barbarian envoys sent letters, Xìzōng was always ordered to draft the replies,
and the Secretarial Bureau was entirely under his command.
He served as Shàofǔ twice,
then was promoted to Yóujī Jiāngjūn and Lǔjùn Tàishǒu.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
and then Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Xuānchéng Tàishǒu.
Xìzōng had served in the court for a long time
and was skilled in official duties.
Emperor Míng said:
"Scholars are incapable of governing the state;
they merely read many books.
One Liú Xìzōng is enough to manage five hundred people of that sort."
His emphasis on administrative matters was thus.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he died in office
at the age of seventy-seven.
Rú Fǎliàng was
a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng.
During the Dàmíng era of Sòng,
he started his career as a xiǎoshǐ,
and successively held positions such as zhāigànfú.
In the last years of Xiàowǔ,
when the regulations on alcohol were enacted,
and flogging punishments were excessive,
during a hunt east of the river,
one hundred and eighty commoners were selected as attendants,
all of whom were handsome and wealthy individuals.
They followed to Nánzhōu,
and more than half of them were flogged.
Fǎliàng was anxious and fearful,
and through connections, he requested and obtained permission to become a Daoist monk.
In the early reign of Emperor Míng,
he renounced monastic life,
allied himself with Ruǎn Diànfū,
and was appointed diǎnqiān to Méng Yáng, the Cìshǐ of Yùnzhōu.
He successively rose to be Xíng Cānjūn in Grand Ancestor's Guānjūn Fǔ.
In the early Yuánhuī era,
he was appointed Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn,
served as diǎnqiān to Jìnxī Wáng Yǐngzhōu,
and was appointed Chángjiān Diànzhōng Yùshǐ.
When Shìzǔ garrisoned Pénchéng,
he needed his former attendants.
Fǎliàng requested to remain as diǎnqiān for Shàngjiāng Zhōudū,
and was appointed Nántái Yùshǐ,
also holding the post of Sōngzī Lìng.
Fǎliàng was amenable and capable,
and skilled at serving others,
thus gradually gaining trust and confidence.
He followed when Shìzǔ returned to Shítou.
In the early Jiànfú era,
he was made Dōnggōng Zhǔshū.
He was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng,
and then Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he remained Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was appointed Yuánwàiláng,
also holding the post of Nán Jìyīn Tàishǒu.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn.
The next year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Rú Fǎliàng, when recently in Pénchéng,
was repeatedly sent with imperial commands,
internally conveying the court's will
and externally comforting the three armies.
His righteous courage spurred everyone on,
making each man hundredfold in spirit.
In difficult and dangerous times,
his heart and strength were fully expended.
He should be granted land
to distinguish his loyal service."
He was enfeoffed as Nán of Wàngcài Xiàn,
with an income of three hundred households.
He was transferred to Jǐshìzhōng
and Yǔlín Jiān.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Línhuái Tàishǒu,
then transferred to Jìnglíng Wáng Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
When Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng killed his subordinates in Jīngzhōu,
the Emperor sent an army westward,
and ordered Fǎliàng to proclaim the imperial will, offer comfort,
and appease Zǐxiǎng.
When Fǎliàng arrived at Jiāngjīn,
Zǐxiǎng called for him,
but Fǎliàng, suspicious and fearful, refused to go.
He also asked to see the bearer of the imperial edict,
but Fǎliàng did not send him.
Therefore, Zǐxiǎng became angry
and sent troops to defeat Yǐn Lüè's army.
After the matter was settled,
Fǎliàng went to Jiānglíng,
and all punishments and rewards were
said to be decided by imperial decree.
When the army returned,
the Emperor regretted executing Zǐxiǎng,
and Fǎliàng was reprimanded.
Soon after,
his trust and favor were restored to old.
When Yùlín ascended the throne,
he was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Yánxīng,
he became Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
Yánchāng Diàn was Shìzǔ's private chamber,
where various imperial garments were stored.
The two young emperors both resided in the West Palace;
when Gāozōng ascended the throne, he lived in Dōngzhāi,
and opened the private chamber, taking out Shìzǔ's white gauze hat and self-defense knife.
Fǎliàng sighed and wept.
He was appointed Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
Few of Gāo Wǔ's old retainers remained;
Fǎliàng, being in charge of clerical affairs,
was not suspected,
and his position and responsibilities remained as before.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
after Wáng Jìngzé's rebellion was quelled,
Fǎliàng again received an imperial edict to offer comfort and encouragement.
Fǎliàng was appointed Dàsīnóng,
a powerful position in the Zhōngshū,
but Fǎliàng was unwilling to leave,
and firmly declined the appointment.
However, his replacement had already arrived,
and Fǎliàng left with tears in his eyes.
He died in office
at the age of sixty-four.
Lǚ Wénxiǎn was
a native of Línhǎi.
Initially, he served as Sòng Xiàowǔ's zhāigàn zhícháng.
In the early Shēngmíng era,
he served as Tàizǔ's Lù Shàngshūshěng Shì,
and successively rose to Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
Yǔlín Jiān,
also holding the posts of Lánlíng Céng and Lìng,
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn,
and Mòlíng Lìng.
He was enfeoffed as Nán of Liúyáng Xiàn.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
he was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
retaining his former office.
Wénxiǎn was known for his strictness and meticulousness in handling affairs.
In the third year,
he also held the post of Nán Qīnghé Tàishǒu.
He and Rú Fǎliàng, among others, successively served as shèrén,
and both enjoyed imperial favor and trust.
Gifts from all directions
amounted to several million per year,
and he built large residences
and created mountains and dug ponds.
In the fifth year,
he served as Jiànkāng Lìng,
then transferred to Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
successively holding the posts of Nán Tàishān and Nán Qiáo Tàishǒu,
then soon Sītú Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
Huáinán Tàishǒu,
and Zhí Shèrén Shěng.
He was successively promoted to Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng,
Nán Dōngguǎn Tàishǒu,
and Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
When Gāozōng assumed regency,
he appointed Wénxiǎn as Shàofǔ,
and he was heavily relied upon.
Throughout the Jiànwǔ and Yǒngyuán eras,
he served as Shàngshū Yòuchéng
and Shàofǔ Qīng.
He died.
Lǚ Wéndù,
was a native of Kuàijī.
During the Sòng dynasty, he was a clerk in the treasury for gold and silver,
and a craftsman in the bamboo workshop.
In the Yuánhuī period,
he became a director of pheasant hunting,
and followed Supervisor Mò Xiūzōng to Yǐng.
When Shìzǔ garrisoned Pénchéng to resist Shěn Yōuzhī,
Wéndù remained behind to serve him,
overseeing various military tasks,
and thus gained his favor.
Upon returning to the capital with him,
he became supervisor of Shítóuchéng,
and also served in the Dōnggōng.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he became Director of the Imperial Workshop (Zhìjújiān),
reaching the rank of Gentleman-in-Attendance (Yuánwàiláng),
and concurrently Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nán Púyáng.
All matters concerning the palace guards and sending people to outer garrisons
were under his purview,
giving him considerable influence.
Thus, it is said that when the post of Yuèzhōu
once became vacant, and the Emperor sought a reliable person to go to Yuèzhōu,
Wéndù recommended Fèi Yánzōng, whom he knew, as suitable for the task,
and the Emperor immediately appointed him Inspector (Cìshǐ).
During the Yǒngmíng period,
an imperial edict stipulated that close attendants were not allowed to make recommendations arbitrarily;
gentlemen who did so would be dismissed from office,
while commoners would receive one hundred lashes.
The Emperor's nature was dignified and stern.
Lǚ Wénxiǎn once coughed loudly by the side of the palace hall;
the Emperor had Rú Fǎliàng reprimand him,
considering it disrespectful.
Therefore, his attendants feared his authority and complied with his will,
and no one dared to speak on matters not under their jurisdiction.
At that time, Rú Fǎliàng was in charge of miscellaneous labor records
and transmitting secret imperial edicts;
Lǚ Wénxiǎn was in charge of grain and silk matters;
other Gentlemen (Shèrén) had no specific assignments.
Pān Chǎng, Commander of the Tiger Guards (Hǔbèn Zhōnglángjiàng), was in charge of supervising construction work.
The Chánlíng Sì
(Temple of Zen Spirit) had just been completed under the Emperor's directive. The imperial carriage visited it,
and the Emperor was very pleased.
Chǎng was delighted
and invited Lǚ Wénxiǎn to privately ascend the temple's southern gate tower.
The Emperor learned of this,
imprisoned Chǎng in the imperial prison,
and exiled Wénxiǎn to Nánqiáo Jùn.
It was a long time before they were reinstated.
Jiāng Qútán of Jìyáng, Shěn Huīfú of Wúxīng, and others,
were gentlemen from gentry families who merely handled communications,
and had no real power.
Huīfú was somewhat skilled in writing.
Many of the imperial edicts during the Jiànwǔ era
were drafted by him.
He rose to the rank of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángménláng).
The historian says: Since the Middle Ages,
those who govern the world,
with countless intricate affairs,
no longer involve the outer bureaus.
The Eight Sections and Five Bureaus of the Department of State Affairs
each have their duties,
linked to the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng) and Six Palaces (Liùfǔ),
with affairs existing as secondary functions.
All are high officials wearing caps and sashes;
their responsibilities are light, yet their status is noble.
The duty of presenting memorials from below has ceased,
and the toil of running errands has also ended.
The matters to be conveyed and entrusted
naturally have their recipients;
they communicate between the inner and outer courts,
directly conveying imperial decrees.
Such officials, with their ceremonial caps and folded tablets,
bow morning and evening,
respectfully attending at the royal tent,
looking up from beside the imperial balustrade,
〔二三〕seeking imperial favor,
accustomed to the Emperor's majestic countenance.
They change from fragrant orchids to smelly salted fish,
growing more trusted with time,
relying on the security of their positions,
and holding the key to opening or blocking access.
Serving their lord for generations,
they grasp the collar to shake the robe.
When rewards and punishments are numerous,
they can avoid exceeding or omitting.
Even the coughs and spittle in the palace and government offices
they are obligated to know first.
Thus they can discern growth and decline from afar,
and obtain the black pearl from the sleeping dragon.
Sitting, they command influence;
lying down, they awe the capital and countryside.
Bribes accumulate daily,
gifts are exchanged annually,
their wealth rivals dukes and marquises,
and their authority extends to provinces and prefectures.
The small bureau of the Imperial Workshop (Zhìjú),
exclusively in charge of military forces,
in the imperial palace,
is interspersed with guard posts.
The elite troops of the Feathered Forest Guards (Yǔlín)
are heavily garrisoned for extensive defense.
As for the Commander-in-chief (Yuánróng) setting out,
and awaiting his return,
clearing the way,
swiftly controlling the reins,
supervising comings and goings,
galloping beside the imperial carriage,
directing various departments,
personally receiving instructions at the imperial desk,
leading and protecting those under their control,
demonstrating complete adherence to regulations.
If troops are conscripted and the populace mobilized for large-scale public works,
the procedures for movement and retention
are in their hands for personal favors.
They cut off and seize official stipends,
display and exploit official documents.
They pursue rebels and fugitives,
assign long garrisons and distant exiles,
so that the army has a thousand-year lifespan
and no family has a hundred-year ghost.
Harming governance and hurting the people,
they are parasites in this regard.
What more when the ruler is young and the times are chaotic?
The extent of their slander and evil
is immeasurable!
The encomium says: Bestowed with grace and made a marquis,
favored by the emperor and old in service.
They manage the Emperor's daily affairs,
both noble and wealthy.
Collation Notes
Biography Thirty-Eight: The Wèi-lǔ
The Wèi-lǔ
were a branch of the Xiōngnú,
with the clan name Tuòbá.
In the sixth year of Jìn Yǒngjiā,
Liú Kūn, Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Bìngzhōu, was attacked by Liú Cōng of the Túgè Hú.
Suǒtóu Yīlú sent his son Yuèlìsūn to lead troops to rescue Kūn in Tàiyuán.
Yīlú then settled in Dàijùn,
also known as Xiānbēi.
They wore their hair loose and fastened their robes on the left,
hence they were called Suǒtóu.
Yīlú's grandson Shíyìjiān,
whose courtesy name was Yùlǜzhān,
later returned to Yīnshān to become Chányú,
leading various Xiōngnú tribes.
In the first year of Tàiyuán,
Fú Jiān sent the false Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Bìngzhōu, Fú Luò, to attack Jiān.
He destroyed Lóngtíng,
captured Jiān, and returned him to Cháng'ān,
where he built a residence for him
and taught Jiān literature.
He divided his tribal followers to rule the four commanderies including Yúnzhōng.
The chiefs of the various tribes would come to court at the end of the year,
and were allowed to see Jiān.
Taxes were levied on the various tribes to provide for him.
Jiān was defeated.
His son, Guī,
whose courtesy name was Shèguī,
followed his maternal uncle Mùróng Chuí and occupied Zhōngshān.
He later took charge of his tribe again,
and gradually grew strong and prosperous.
In the first year of Lóng'ān (397 CE),
Guī defeated Mùróng Bǎo at Zhōngshān,
thus acquiring Bìngzhōu,
and usurped the title of Wèi.
His era name was Tiāncì.
He posthumously honored Jiàn as Lièzǔ Wénpíng Huángdì.
When Guī died,
he was posthumously honored as Dàowǔ Huángdì.
His son Mùmò succeeded him,
with the era name Tàicháng.
When he died,
he was posthumously honored as Míngyuán Huángdì.
His son Táo,
whose courtesy name was Fólí, succeeded him,
with the era name Tàipíng Zhēnjūn.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
the pretender Crown Prince Huǎng was displeased with the high-ranking officials Cuī Shì and Kòu Shì.
Cuī and Kòu slandered him.
The Daoist priest Xuángāo possessed Daoist arts.
Huǎng had him pray for blessings for seven days and seven nights.
Fólí dreamt that his ancestors were both angry,
and pointing a dagger at him, said:
"Why do you believe slander and wish to harm the Crown Prince!"
Fólí awoke in a fright,
and issued a spurious imperial edict saying:
"The great enterprise of a king,
the succession is of grave importance.
The heir apparent's succession
is an ancient custom of all kings.
From now on,
no matter how big or small the matter,
it must first go through the Crown Prince,
and only then be reported to me."
Huǎng later plotted to assassinate Fólí and was himself killed.
When Táo died,
he was posthumously honored as Tàiwǔ Huángdì.
Huǎng's son Jùn,
whose courtesy name was Wūléizhíqín, was enthroned,
with the era name Hépíng.
Huǎng was posthumously honored as Jǐngmù Huángdì.
When Jùn died,
he was posthumously honored as Wénchéng Huángdì.
His son Hóng, whose courtesy name was Wànmín, was enthroned,
with the era name Tiān'ān.
In the ninth year of Jǐnghé (475 CE),
the pretender Crown Prince Hóng was born,
and the era name was changed to Huángxīng.
Shíyìguī first established his capital at Píngchéng,
still following water and pastures,
without cities or walls.
Mùmò first settled down in a fixed abode.
Fólí broke Liángzhōu and Huánglóng,
relocated their residents,
and greatly built up city walls and towns.
He constructed the palace city by sectioning off the west of Píngchéng,
erecting towers at its four corners,
and battlements.
The gates had no roofs,
and the city also lacked them.
Outside the south gate, two earthen gates were erected,
with temples inside.
Four gates were opened,
each corresponding to a cardinal direction's color.
There were five temples in all,
one for each generation,
with tiled roofs.
To their west, the Grand Altar of the Soil and Grain (Tàishè) was erected.
Fólí resided in three halls, including the Yúnmǔ Hall.
He also built a multi-storied building,
and lived on its upper floor.
The dining quarters were named
"Āzhēn,"
located in the west.
Empress Kěsūn would come out from here to seek food.
Initially,
Yáo Xīng appointed the barbarian Hèlián Bóbó from beyond the Great Wall as General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn),
leading five Hú tribes,
stationed at Dàchéng.
After Yáo Hóng's defeat,
he entered Cháng'ān.
Fólí attacked and defeated Bóbó's son Chāng,
and took Bóbó's daughter as his Empress.
During the Yìxī era,
Qíuchí Gōng Yáng Shèng reported,
"The Sūo barbarian Bóbó
is a true descendant of the Xiongnú."
This is correct.
Kěsūn was formerly a concubine.
To the west of the hall, there were over forty rooms for the armor and weapons arsenal,
and to the north of the hall, over ten earthen rooms for silk, cotton, cloth, and fine silk warehouses.
The pretender Crown Prince's palace was in the eastern part of the city,
also with four gates,
tiled roofs,
and towers at its four corners.
The imperial concubines all lived in earthen houses.
Over a thousand maids and servants
wove damask and brocade for sale,
sold wine,
raised pigs and sheep,
herded cattle and horses,
and grew vegetables for profit.
The Grand Provisioner had over eighty cellars,
each holding four thousand hù of grain,
half unhulled grain and half polished rice.
There were also dozens of tiled roof rooms for storing suspended food,
and a Shàngfāng workshop for iron and wood crafts.
Their robes and clothes
were made by palace maids.
The pretender Crown Prince had separate warehouses.
The outer city wall surrounded the south of the palace city,
and was entirely built into wards,
with lanes opening within the wards.
Large wards could accommodate four or five hundred families,
smaller ones sixty or seventy families.
Every southern ward was searched and inspected
to guard against treachery.
Seven *lǐ* to the southwest of the city, near Mount Báidèng,
separate temples for the father and ancestors were erected by the mountain.
To the west of the city was an altar for sacrificing to Heaven,
where forty-nine wooden figures were erected.
They were about a *zhàng* tall,
wearing white turbans, linen skirts, and horsehair cloaks,
standing on the altar.
On the fourth day of the fourth month, cattle and horses were regularly sacrificed,
and a grand display of imperial paraphernalia was arranged.
People raced around the altar and performed music for entertainment.
Three *lǐ* west of the city,
the Five Classics and their national records were carved into stone.
From Yè, sixty stone foundation bases from Shí Hǔ's stone house were taken,
each over a *zhàng* long,
to be used for this purpose.
Within the state, those on the left and right inside were called
"Zhízhēn,"
those on the left and right outside were called
"Wū'ǎizhēn,"
clerks of the bureaus were called
"Bǐdézhēn,"
people who carried clothes were called
"Púdàzhēn,"
armed guards were called
"Húluòzhēn,"
liaison officers were called
"Qǐwànzhēn,"
gatekeepers were called
"Kěbózhēn,"
lowly people who rode post horses for the pretender's court were called
"Fúzhúzhēn,"
post riders from the various prefectures were called
"Xiánzhēn,"
killers were called
"Qìhàizhēn,"
people who went out on behalf of their lord to receive statements were called
"Zhékuìzhēn,"
and people who cooked for nobles were called
"Fùzhēn."
The Three Dukes and nobles
were collectively called
"Yángzhēn."
Fólí appointed Three Dukes, Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Púshè), and Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng),
who deliberated on state affairs together with the Crown Prince.
The Palace Secretary (Diànzhōng Shàngshū) oversaw the palace's military, horses, and warehouses.
The Music Secretary (Yuèbù Shàngshū) oversaw musicians, performers, and military officers.
The Chariot Secretary (Jiàbù Shàngshū) oversaw cattle, horses, donkeys, and mules.
The Southern Secretary (Nánbù Shàngshū) oversaw the southern prefectures and commanderies.
The Northern Secretary (Běibù Shàngshū) oversaw the northern prefectures and commanderies.
There were also the Sīqín Dìhé,
comparable to a Shàngshū;
the Mòdī,
comparable to a Cìshǐ;
the Yùruò,
comparable to a Two-Thousand-Picul official;
and officials who received special appointments, comparable to feudal lords.
All various offices and bureaus with warehouses
had officials of corresponding rank appointed,
all of whom were required to be fluent in both the Hú and Hàn languages,
serving as interpreters for post stations.
The Censorate (Lántái) had Censors-in-Chief (Zhōngchéng Yùshǐ)
who oversaw affairs within the city.
Nine Dòuhé officials were also appointed,
and the households within three *lǐ* of the palace city whose registers were not under any military garrisons
were all placed under their jurisdiction.
Their carriages and clothing:
There were large and small palanquins,
all five layers high.
Beneath, four wheels were fitted.
They were pulled by two or three hundred people.
Four ropes were attached
to prevent overturning.
The lightweight chariots bore dragon banners
and favored black.
Empresses and consorts used canopies of mixed colors,
without banners or decorations.
When the Empress Dowager went out,
women wearing armor rode horses close to the palanquins' sides.
The chieftain of the captives and his empress and consorts often traveled
in silver-inlaid sheep chariots,
without curtains or canopies.
They all sat sideways with their legs dangling in the shafts.
When in the palace hall,
they also sat cross-legged.
The main hall was adorned with tasseled curtains,
golden Bóshān censers,
screens painted with dragons, phoenixes, and vermilion lacquer,
and woven hangings.
Cushions of felt were used for sitting.
In front were placed golden incense burners,
glass bowls,
and golden cups,
holding various eating utensils.
For guests, long platters one *chǐ* long were set out.
For imperial meals, round platters one *zhàng* wide were used.
These were four-wheeled carts.
On the day of the New Year's assembly,
sixty or seventy people pulled them up to the hall.
On the *Là* Day, they performed the exorcism,
and at the year's end,
sacrificed roosters at the city gates,
and placed reed ropes and peach effigies,
following the Hàn rites.
From Fólí to Wànmín,
ornamentation increased with each generation.
To the west of the main hall, an earthen platform was built,
called the Báilóu.
After Wànmín abdicated the throne,
he often roamed and observed from its top.
To the south of the platform was also the Sìxīnglóu.
To the west of the main hall was also a shrine,
with glass tiles.
The palace gates were gradually covered with roofs,
though they were not known as multi-storied buildings.
They were all adorned with painted clay sculptures
depicting Vajra warriors.
The Hú custom favored water,
and they also designed and painted black dragons coiling around
as a talisman against evil.
In the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
Wànmín abdicated to his son Hóng,
and styled himself as Tàishàng Huáng.
Hóng was enthroned,
and his reign was called Yánxīng Yuánnián.
In the sixth year,
Wànmín died,
and was posthumously named Xiànwén Huángdì.
The reign title was changed to Chéngmíng Yuánnián,
which was the fourth year of Yuánhuī.
His paternal grandmother, Fèng Shì,
a native of Huánglóng,
assisted in governing the state.
Initially,
Fólí's mother was a Hàn person,
killed by Mùmò.
Fólí made his wet nurse the Empress Dowager.
From then on,
when a Crown Prince was established,
his mother was invariably executed.
One account says that Fèng Shì was originally from Jiāngdū.
In the twenty-seventh year of Yuánjiā, Fólí invaded the south,
captured Fèng Shì,
and Jùn took her as a concubine,
and she alone was spared.
The next year, *Dīngsì*,
the reign title was changed to Tàihé.
Towards the end of Sòng Míngdì's reign,
they first established peace with the captives.
During the eras of Yuánhuī and Shēngmíng,
envoys from the captives arrived annually.
The first year of Jiànyuán
was also the third year of the pseudo Tàihé.
Hóng, hearing that Tàizǔ had received the abdication,
that winter,
mobilized troops and dispatched Dānyáng Wáng Liú Chǎng as Tàishī,
who raided the two prefectures of Sī and Yù.
The following year,
an imperial edict ordered the dispatch of troops for a northern expedition.
Hóng sent his great generals Yùdòujuàn and Duàn Chángmìng to attack Shòuyáng and Zhōnglí,
but they were defeated by Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Chóngzǔ, Yòu Jiāngjūn Zhōu Pánlóng, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Cuī Wénzhòng, and others.
Hóng again sent the pseudo Nánbù Shàngshū Tuóbá and others towards Sīzhōu,
dividing his forces to advance into the areas of Lùyǔn and Qīng.
A hundred thousand troops besieged Qúshān,
where the garrison commander Xuán Yuándù held the city firmly.
Qīng and Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ Lú Shàozhī sent his son Huàn to lead troops to assist them.
There was no food in the city,
so Shàozhī set up camp at Shítóutíng, south of the prefecture,
and transported food and firewood across the sea to supply the city.
The captives blockaded the sea route
and attacked the city along the coast.
At that time, a great tide arrived,
and the captives were submerged and drowned.
Yuándù led his troops out and attacked fiercely,
greatly defeating them.
The court sent army commanders Cuī Língjiàn, Yáng Fǎchí, and Fáng Língmín, with over ten thousand men, to enter the sea from the Huái River.
At night, each ship lit two fires.
When the captive troops saw them,
they thought a large southern army had arrived,
and immediately retreated in panic.
Initially,
Yuándù claimed to have a "Marquis-sealing mark" on his arm.
During the Sòng dynasty, he showed it to Shìzǔ.
At that time, Shìzǔ was in the Eastern Palace
and wrote to Yuándù, saying:
"Strive to fulfill the destiny on your arm."
After the captives retreated,
the emperor discussed awarding titles and ranks.
Yuándù attributed the success to Shàozhī,
and Shàozhī also declined,
so both awards were shelved.
The emperor then promoted Shàozhī to Huángménláng.
Yùzhōu called Shítóutíng Pínglǔtíng.
Shàozhī, courtesy name Zǐxù,
was from Fànyáng.
He claimed to be a fifth-generation descendant of Lú Chén.
During the Dàmíng era of Sòng,
he participated in the attack on Guǎnglín.
His merits were reported.
Shàozhī distinguished himself and offered his services,
and the emperor appointed him Zhōuzhìzhōng,
entrusting him with a confidential position.
His official rank reached Guānglù Dàfū.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng,
he died.
Three years later,
Lǐ Ānmín, General of the Guard, and Sūn Wénxiǎn, General of the Left Army, fought the captive army at Huáiyáng,
and greatly defeated them.
Initially,
when the captives invaded,
they plundered along the Huái River.
The residents north of the Jiāng River, still remembering the events of Fólí's time,
all fled in panic
and could not be stopped.
Therefore, two armies were stationed at Liángshān,
three armies to the south,
one army at Címǔ,
two armies at Lièzhōu,
two armies at Sānshān,
one army at Báishāzhōu,
five armies at Càizhōu,
three armies at Chánglú,
two armies at Gūpǔ,
and one army at Xúpǔ.
All within and without were awarded ranks and rewards
to display might and discipline.
The pseudo Chānglí Wáng Fèng Shā advanced towards Sīzhōu.
The barbarian Huán Tiānshēng told Shā:
"All the barbarians will respond."
When Shā arrived,
the barbarians remained inactive after all.
Shā was furious
and went hunting by the Huái River before leaving.
After the defeat at Shòuchūn
and the failure to take Qúshān,
the chieftain of the captives came out of Dìngzhōu,
greatly repairing roads,
sounding as if he intended to march south,
but dared not advance.
Then he consulted with the pseudo Liángjùn Wáng, saying:
"The troops sent between Péng and Sì
have no will to fight left.
We must fight one or two battles and then return."
After being defeated at Huáiyáng,
they all fled in panic.
The righteous common people between Qīng and Xú,
who had previously ambushed captive transport carts,
and had also fought and plundered among themselves,
often saw several thousand families return to the south.
The Emperor had not yet been able to expand his territory externally.
Because the barbarians had already been crushed and defeated,
and to demonstrate both might and leniency,
he dispatched Chē Sēnglǎng, the Aide to the Rear Army, on a mission to the north.
The barbarians asked Sēnglǎng, saying:
"The Qí assisted the Sòng for a short time,
why did he ascend to the imperial throne so quickly?"
Sēnglǎng replied:
"Yú and Xià, when they took up their duties,
personally initiated abdication;
Wèi and Jìn, when they assisted (the previous dynasty),
bequeathed it to their descendants.
How could the two saints [Yú and Xià] be so hasty in occupying the imperial throne,
and the two worthies [Wèi and Jìn] be so humble as to act solely for their own good?
The circumstances of the times differ;
how can they be measured by a single standard?
If it is said that the situation demands it,
then one yields oneself to accommodate events."
The barbarians further asked:
"What achievements and deeds does the Qí ruler possess?"
Sēnglǎng replied:
"Our Lord possesses a sacred nature, benevolent and broad-minded,
with heavenly wisdom and far-reaching vision.
From a young age, he was esteemed and favored by Emperor Wén of Sòng,
and entered to participate in the imperial guard.
At the beginning of Tàishǐ,
rebels rose on all sides.
