He pacified Liú Zǐfáng and Zhāng Yān in the east,
campaigning north against Xuē Suǒ'ér,
and also managed military and state affairs,
participating in the formulation of the dying emperor's instructions.
When the two Sòng princes, Guìyáng and Jiànpíng, raised troops and committed internal aggression,
he annihilated them with a single wave of his command.
When the King of Cāngwú violated the Way and corrupted virtue,
exceeding Jié and Zhòu in wickedness,
he followed the distant precedents of Yī and Huò,
carrying out the act of dethroning and establishing a new ruler.
Yuán Càn, Liú Bǐng, and Shěn Yōuzhī, united in their evil, assisted one another.
Again, bearing the banner and wielding the axe,
he greatly pacified the rebellious factions.
He devoted his strength to assisting the times
for over forty years,
managing affairs through peace and peril
for fifteen or sixteen years.
Such achievements and virtue
can be said to be undisputed by all."
The barbarians further asked:
"The southern nation no longer has Qí territory,
why was he enfeoffed as Qí?"
Sēnglǎng replied:
"Yíngqiū, facing the sea,
was indeed a great state.
The Sòng dynasty, when it initiated the opening of its territory,
said it was the ancestral fief of Lǚ Shàng.
Now, between the Huái and the sea,
there are Qīng and Qí on their own,
so it is not without land."
They also asked:
"Why was Cāngwú subjected to execution by beheading?"
Sēnglǎng replied:
"The tyranny of Cāngwú
is unheard of in written records.
King Wǔ beheaded Zhòu,
and hung his head on a yellow battle-axe;
this is a common story,
how does it harm righteousness?"
During Shēngmíng,
the northern envoys Yīn Língdàn and Gǒu Zhāoxiān were among the barbarians.
When they heard that Tàizǔ had ascended the throne,
Língdàn said to the barbarian chief of protocol:
"Sòng and Wèi maintained good relations;
their troubles were shared.
Now Sòng has perished,
and Wèi did not come to its aid;
what is the use of peace and kinship?"
When the barbarians attacked Yùzhōu,
Língdàn then requested to be Sīmǎ for Liú Chǎng,
but was not granted it.
When Sēnglǎng arrived in the north,
the barbarians seated him below Língdàn.
Sēnglǎng stood up and said:
"Língdàn was formerly a Sòng envoy;
now he is a Qí citizen.
I truly hope that the Wèi ruler will treat me with proper rites."
Língdàn spoke against him,
and they began to quarrel and insult each other.
He reported to the barbarians, saying:
"An envoy who cannot uphold integrity for his native court
is truly ashamed and regretful."
Liú Chǎng bribed a guest, Jiě Fèngjūn, to assassinate Sēnglǎng at the assembly.
The barbarians immediately arrested Fèngjūn and executed him,
then prepared Sēnglǎng's coffin and sent his funeral procession south with Língdàn and others,
bestowing generous gifts and condolences.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Zhāoxiān reported everything,
and Língdàn was imprisoned and died.
Sēnglǎng was posthumously granted Sànqí Shìláng.
In the winter of the first year of Yǒngmíng,
General of Galloping Cavalry Liú Zuǎn and General of the Vanguard Zhāng Mó were dispatched as envoys to the barbarians.
In the winter of the following year,
the barbarian envoy Lǐ Dàogù reciprocated the visit.
Shìzǔ conducted a military review of his naval and land forces at Xuánwǔhú,
and received him on the dragon boat.
From then on, envoys exchanged visits annually,
and the borders were peaceful.
In the third year,
it was first ordered that each neighborhood (línlǐ) and district (dǎng) should appoint a head.
Five households formed a lín (neighborhood),
five lín formed a lǐ (village),
and five lǐ formed a dǎng (district).
In the fourth year,
household registers were created.
Zhōu and Jùn were separately established.

Yōngzhōu, Liángzhōu, Qínzhōu, Shāzhōu, Jīngzhōu, Huázhōu, Qízhōu, Hézhōu, Xīhuázhōu, Níngzhōu, Shǎnzhōu, Luòzhōu, Jīngzhōu, Yǐngzhōu, Běiyùzhōu, Dōngjīngzhōu, Nányùzhōu, Xīyǔnzhōu, Dōngyǔnzhōu, Nánxúzhōu, Dōngxúzhōu, Qīngzhōu, Qízhōu, Jìzhōu—twenty-five zhōu were in Hénán;
[一０]Xiāngzhōu,
[一一]Huáizhōu,
Fénzhōu,
[一二]Dōngyōngzhōu, Sìzhōu, Dìngzhōu, Yíngzhōu, Shuòzhōu, Bìngzhōu, Jìzhōu, Yōuzhōu, Píngzhōu, Sīzhōu—thirteen zhōu were in Héběi.
Altogether, the territory of the old Sī, Yù, Qīng, Yǔn, Jì, Bìng, Yōu, Qín, Yōng, Liáng of Wèi and Jìn—ten zhōu—
and the Huáiběi region lost by Sòng became thirty-eight zhōu.
The following year,
the border resident Huán Tiānshēng rebelled.
The barbarians dispatched over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to assist him,
reaching Bǐyáng,
where they were defeated by General Zhēnglǔ Dài Sēngjìng and others.
The wilderness dweller Hú Qiūshēng rose in revolt at Xuánhù,
was attacked by the barbarians,
and, defeated in battle, fled south.
The pseudo-General Ānnán, Duke of Liáodōng, and General Píngnán, Duke of Shànggǔ, again attacked Wǔyīn.
[一三]The Wǔyīn garrison commander, General Fǔguó Yīn Gōngmǐn, resisted and defeated them.
In the sixth year,
the barbarians again sent troops to assist Huán Tiānshēng,
and fought with General Fǔguó Cáo Hǔ,
suffering a great defeat at Géchéng.
By the seventh year,
envoys Xíng Chǎn and Hóu Língshào were dispatched to resume good relations.
Previously, Liú Zuǎn had made two missions to the barbarians,
and Empress Dowager Féng Shì was pleased with him and treated him intimately.
Féng Shì possessed strategies
and composed eighteen chapters of imperial edicts.
The pseudo-Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Lǐ Sīchōng, claimed to have annotated them as a historian.
That year,
Féng Shì died.
In the eighth year,
Shìzǔ returned over two thousand captives taken at Géchéng.
Since Fólí's time,
they had gradually usurped Chinese institutions,
and barbarian customs and national traditions were mixed and confused.
Hóng understood how to discuss righteousness
and could compose literature,
being light-hearted but possessing far-reaching strategies.
He traveled north of the Yellow River to the tomb of Bǐgān,
where he composed an elegy for Bǐgān, saying:
"Were it not for Wǔfā,
who would have caused the tomb to be sealed?
Alas, [一四]why were you not my subject!"
In the Jǐsì year,
Hóng established the circular mound and square altar,
and appointed three Fūrén and nine Pín.
South of Píngchéng, there was the Gānshǔi River,
which originated from the borders of Dìngxiāng,
flowed into the sea,
and was fifty lǐ from the city.
The world called it Suǒgāndū.
[一五]The climate was cold and congealed,
with rising wind and sand,
and snow in June.
There was a discussion about moving the capital to Luòjīng.
In the ninth year,
envoys Lǐ Dàogù and Jiǎng Shàoyóu were sent to return the visit.
Shàoyóu was ingenious
and secretly ordered to observe the architectural styles of the imperial palaces in the capital.
Cuī Yuánzǔ of Qīnghé reported to Shìzǔ, saying:
"Shàoyóu
is my maternal nephew,
and has a particular mind like Gōngshū.
During the Sòng era, when he was captured by the barbarians,
he was given the office of Grand Architect.
Now, as a deputy envoy,
he certainly wishes to model our palaces and gates.
How can we allow the uncivilized people of the felt tents
to take inspiration from the heavenly palaces?
Your subject suggests that Shàoyóu be detained for now,
and the chief envoy be allowed to return to report."
Shìzǔ, deeming this contrary to the spirit of peaceful relations,
did not allow it.
Shàoyóu was from Ānlè.
The architectural system of the barbarian palaces
all originated from him.
Initially,
Bólí (佛狸) attacked the Jié Hú (羯胡) in Cháng’ān (長安)
〔一六〕and killed almost all of the Daoists.
When Yuánjiā (元嘉) launched his southern invasion,
he captured Daoists
and held them in iron cages.
Later, Bólí (佛狸) suffered a serious illness,
and from then on, he revered and feared Buddhism,
establishing stupas and temples.
After Hóng's (宏) father, Hóngchán (弘禪), abdicated,
he wore yellow Daoist robes and plain clothes,
observed precepts, and recited scriptures,
residing in the Shíkū Sì (石窟寺).
In Tàihé (太和) third year of Hóng (宏)
〔一七〕Daoist Fǎxiù (法秀), together with Gǒng'ér Wáng'ārǔguī Wáng (苟兒王阿辱瑰王) and others, plotted a rebellion.
〔一八〕When the plot was discovered,
Fǎxiù (法秀) was imprisoned
and subjected to a cage-head iron [⿰⺡⿱宀⿺元攵] (a torture device).
It inexplicably came loose by itself,
so the captives drilled through his neck bone,
and made a curse saying:
"If there is still a spirit,
it should prevent the drill from penetrating the flesh."
They then drilled through and executed him,
and he died three days later.
The伪Xiányáng Wáng (咸陽王) also wanted to kill all the Daoists,
〔一九〕but Empress Dowager Féng Shì (馮氏) did not permit it.
Hóng (宏) was especially devout,
having a rough understanding of the doctrines,
and erected stupas within the palace.
After Hóng (宏) passed through Gǔluò (古洛),
that year he issued a伪edict to Shàngshū Sīshèn (尚書思慎), saying:
"Indeed, the heavens and earth bestow transformation,
which must rely on the four seasons to accomplish their work;
the sun and moon
also require the five planets to assist their brilliance.
I look up to the Holy Mother,
whose sagacious wisdom is from heaven,
whose achievements surpass antiquity,
who will consult detailed models
to daily renew the imperial standard.
Unexpectedly, sins have invited disaster,
and sudden severe punishment has come.
〔二０〕Remembering the boundless love,
I can never repay it.
Thinking to follow the former decree,
I commanded the construction of a model of the Míngtáng (明堂).
The design you created encompasses the six directions,
surpassing achievements of the middle ages,
its principles are complete and its righteousness is perfect,
it can serve as a model for a thousand years.
It truly is a talent suited for the age,
a vessel of old.
When the officials saw the model,
all unanimously desired its swift construction.
I, being ignorant,
also wish to build this grand ceremony.
You may immediately cease the construction of the palace city this year
to build this structure,
to establish a wondrous system for the imperial era,
to fulfill the former will from afar,
and to satisfy my heart up close."
He also ordered the dukes and ministers to deliberate and finalize the criminal laws.
He also ordered the abolition of the nuó (儺) ceremony before the twelfth month,
allowing only one nuó (儺) per year.
He further decreed:
"For the court congratulations in the last month of winter,
there is no established written regulation.
Wearing short jackets and trousers is not considered respectful;
if winter court robes are provided,
it merely creates unnecessary fuss.
From now on, the Lesser Year's New Year's congratulations are abolished,
and there will be one congratulations at the beginning of the year."
He also decreed:
"The title of Wáng (王) is not to be usurped by common surnames,
the title of Bó (伯) is a regular rank among the five ranks.
The descendants of the Illustrious Ancestor
retain their original Wáng (王) titles,
all other Wáng (王) are to become Gōng (公).
【Gōng (公)】 are to be changed to Hóu (侯),
〔二一〕Hóu (侯) are to become Bó (伯), [82) and Zǐ (子) and Nán (男) remain as before.
Although the names are changed from the original,
their rank is not different from before.
Gōng (公) is the first rank,
Hóu (侯) the second rank,
Bó (伯) the third rank,
Zǐ (子) the fourth rank,
and Nán (男) the fifth rank."
In the tenth year,
the emperor dispatched Sītú Cānjūn (司徒參軍) Xiāo Chēn (蕭琛) and Fàn Yún (范雲) as envoys to the north.
Hóng (宏) went to the western suburbs,
which was the place of the former Altar of Heaven.
Hóng (宏) and the伪dukes and ministers, accompanied by more than twenty cavalry in military attire, circled the altar.
Hóng (宏) circled once,
and the dukes and ministers circled seven times,
which was called 'Tàtán' (蹋壇, stepping on the altar).
The next day,
they again wore military attire, ascended the altar, and offered sacrifices to Heaven.
Hóng (宏) again circled three times,
and the dukes and ministers seven times,
which was called 'Ràotiān' (繞天, circling Heaven).
They used ropes intertwined,
with wooden branches as supports,
covered with blue silk,
shaped flat and round,
large enough for a hundred people to sit underneath,
called a
"sǎn" (繖),
or also
"bǎizǐ zhàng" (百子帳).
They feasted and rested underneath this.
Next, they sacrificed at the temples and the Bùzhèng Míngtáng (布政明堂),
and all court envoys were invited to observe.
Whenever an envoy arrived,
Hóng (宏) personally received them
and engaged them in conversation about principles.
He highly esteemed the people of Qí (齊),
often saying to his subordinates:
"There are many good officials south of the river."
The伪court attendant Lǐ Yuánkǎi (李元凱) replied:
"There are many good officials south of the river,
yet they change their ruler once a year;
north of the river there are no good officials,
yet they have one ruler for a hundred years."
Hóng (宏) was greatly ashamed,
and sent Yuánkǎi (元凱) out as Yōngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ (雍州長史),
but soon recalled him to his post.
At the beginning of Shìzǔ's (世祖) reign,
he governed Báixià (白下) and [132) said to people:
"I want to make this city the upper resting place."
Later, at Shítóu (石頭), he built three thousand [lùchē] (露車, uncovered chariots),
〔二二〕intending to advance on foot to Péngchéng (彭城),
his intentions were quite clear.
Previously, in the eighth year, northern envoys Yán Yòumíng (顏幼明) and Liú Sīxiào (劉思斅) had returned from their mission.
The伪Nánbù Shàngshū (南部尚書) Lǐ Sīchōng (李思沖) said:
"The harmony between our two nations
is for the protection of the people.
We hear that the southern court is extensively building boats and chariots,
intending to invade Huái (淮) and Sì (泗).
Having pledged our hearts,
why should this be so?"
Yòumíng (幼明) replied:
"Our sovereign is now extending great trust to all under heaven,
and does not abandon his subjects.
Since we have agreed to peace,
how can we be disloyal?
Rumors from the borderlands
are somewhat unreliable.
Moreover, if the imperial court were truly [hènù] (赫怒, furiously angry),
〔二三〕and its generals were outside,
it would not be near the Huái (淮) riverbank."
Sīchōng (思沖) said:
"With the strength of our nation,
managing the east of Huái (淮),
what worries us is not conquering the seas and eastern mountains;
it is just a matter of maintaining the vows of trust.
Furthermore, since harmony has been established,
how can there again be disloyalty?
In ancient times, Huá Yuán (華元) and Zǐfǎn (子反),
during a battle,
were still able to speak to each other with sincerity;
this intention is truly admirable."
Yòumíng (幼明) said:
"You do not yet have the urgency of Zǐfǎn (子反),
how can you seek the request to ascend the bed?"
After this, Hóng (宏) also wanted to invade Xú (徐) and Yù (豫) to the south,
and extensively accumulated horse fodder between the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers.
In the eleventh year,
he sent an open letter and a memorial to the throne,
claiming he would invade the south.
Shìzǔ (世祖) mobilized the civilian population of Yáng (揚) and Xúzhōu (徐州)
and extensively called for recruits.
Zhī Yǒu (支酉), a man from the northern regions,
gathered several thousand people and
started an uprising on the Xī Shān (西山) north of Cháng’ān (長安) city.
He sent an envoy to inform the Císhǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州), Yīn Zhìbó (陰智伯).
Wáng Dùrén (王度人) of Qínzhōu (秦州) also rose in rebellion in response to Yǒu (酉),
attacking and capturing the伪Císhǐ (刺史) Liú Zǎo (劉藻).
The people of seven prefectures between Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) all responded with a shockwave,
their numbers reaching a hundred thousand,
each defending their own strongholds,
hoping for the imperial court to send troops to rescue them.
Hóng (宏) sent his younger brother, the伪Hénán Wáng (河南王) Gàn (幹), and Shàngshū (尚書) Lú Yángwū (盧陽烏) to attack the Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) rebel armies.
〔二四〕Gàn (幹) was greatly defeated.
Yǒu (酉) met them in battle,
advancing to Zhuógǔ (濁谷) north of Xiányáng (咸陽),
and besieged the伪Sīkōng Chángluò Wáng (司空長洛王) Miáo Lǎoshēng (繆老生).
〔二五〕They engaged in battle,
and again inflicted a great defeat,
Lǎoshēng (老生) fled back to Cháng’ān (長安).
Yīn Zhìbó (陰智伯), the Císhǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (梁州), sent generals Xí Dérén (席德仁) and Zhāng Hónglín (張弘林) and several thousand men to support Yǒu (酉) and others,
advancing towards Cháng’ān (長安).
They swept away all resistance wherever they went.
When Shìzǔ崩 died,
Hóng聞 heard that Guānzhōng was in a critical situation,
and so he claimed to have heard of the mourning and withdrew his troops.
In the eighth month of the seventeenth year of Tàihé,

the Acting Gāo Zǔ, Grand General of Annán, Governor of the Military Affairs of Xú, Qīng, and Qí Prefectures, Southern Zhonglángjiàng, Inspector of Xú Prefecture, Guǎnglínghóufǔ Zhǎngshǐ, and acting Governor of Huáiyáng, Lù Shùshēng, issued an order to the Zhǎngshǐ of Qíyún Prefecture:
"Having received the Shàngshū Fúténg's imperial edict: 'The imperial army, like thunder,
〔二六〕waves its banners southward,
vowing to clear the impurities from the Jiāng,
and aiming to sweep away the miasma from Héng.
In the latter part of last month,
it crossed the river and reached Luò.
When the former envoys Xíng Luán and others arrived,
we learned of the great affliction there.
According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
upon hearing of mourning, military campaigns are ceased.
Therefore, an order was issued to the officials concerned,
to stop the imperial carriage and halt the wheels,
to rest the horses at Huáyáng,
and sheathe the weapons north of Sōng.
Immediately thereafter, the Zhōu system was established,
to illuminate and inhabit the central region,
to eternally establish the imperial foundation for endless generations,
and to expand the glorious enterprise for ten thousand years.
(（辰）) 【宸】The imperial residence is upright and central,
〔二七〕the grand transformation brings renewal,
the four seas receive blessings,
and none do not inscribe their joy.'
Therefore, what has been conveyed is to be followed like law."
And he also dispatched envoys to mourn the national taboo.
He sent the false Grand Generals Yáng Dàyǎn and Zhāng Cōngmíng, with tens of thousands of men, to attack Yǒu.
Yǒu and Guǎng were both killed.
〔二八〕
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
he sent Sītú Cānjūn Liú Xiào and Chējì Cānjūn Shěn Hóng as envoys to the north.
Hóng claimed his courtesy name was Xuánlǎn.
That summer,
the barbarian Píngběi Jiāngjūn Lǔ Zhíqīng led his forces to surrender.
He was appointed Dūd Luòzhōu Jūnshì,
and held the titles of Píngróng Xiàowèi, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, and Luòzhōu Cìshǐ.
In this year,
Hóng moved his capital to Luòyáng,
and changed his surname to Yuán.
Initially,
a Xiongnú woman named Tuòbá
married Lǐ Líng.
According to barbarian custom, the mother's name was taken as the surname.
Therefore, the barbarians were descendants of Lǐ Líng.
The barbarians greatly tabooed this,
and anyone who said they were descendants of Líng
was immediately killed.
Only now did they change their surname.
Hóng heard that Gāozōng's ascension to the throne was not legitimate.
Having just moved the capital,
he also wanted to display his great power.
That winter,
he personally led a large army to invade the four prefectures of Yù, Xú, Sī, and Liáng.
He sent the false Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Xuē Zhēndù and Shàngshū Xī Qí Āpó to emerge from Nányáng,
heading towards Shā'è.
They built fortresses and dug moats,
but were defeated by Nányáng Tàishǒu Fáng Bóyù and Xīnyě Tàishǒu Liú Sījì.
In the spring of the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Gāozōng sent Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Guǎngzhī to march out through Sīzhōu,
Yòu Púshè Shěn Wénjì through Yùzhōu,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Cuī Huìjǐng through Xúzhōu.
Hóng personally led his troops to Shòuyáng.
Within his army, there was a black felt traveling palace,
large enough for twenty people to sit.
Around the imperial carriage were all Sānláng Hélàzhēn,
many of their spears had white yak-tail plumes,
and the iron cavalry formed groups,
front and rear connected.
The infantry all carried black shields and spears,
connected by black toad banners.
Ox carts and donkeys and camels carried military supplies and female entertainers,
numbering about three hundred thousand people.
He did not attack the city,
but ascended Mount Bāgōng,
recited a poem, and then departed.
Separately, he besieged Zhōnglí City.
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Huìxiū and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Shēn Xīzǔ defended it.
They sent out troops and attacked fiercely.
Hóng's forces were defeated,
many drowned in the Huái River.
He then divided his army to hold Shàoyángzhōu,
blocking the waterway with a stockade,
and building two castles on either side.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Xiāo Tánzhī sent army commander Péi Shúyè to attack the two castles,
and captured them.
Huìxiū also recruited men to sally forth and burn the barbarians' siege engines.
The barbarians' strength was exhausted, and they could not overcome them.
After Wáng Huànzhī was executed,
his son Sù fled to the barbarians.
〔二九〕Hóng appointed Sù as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
He sent Sù and Liú Chǎng, numbering two hundred thousand men,
to besiege Yìyáng.
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Dàn resisted them.
〔三０〕The barbarians built three layers of siege fortifications,
burned all the residents' homes to the ground,
and exerted all their strength to attack the city.
Inside the city, men stood holding shields.
Wáng Guǎngzhī led a relief force.
The barbarians sent over thirty thousand men to intercept and attack Tàizǐ Yòulǜ Xiāo Jìchǎng at Xiàliáng.
Jìchǎng fought unfavorably.
The Sīzhōu city sent urgent pleas for help.
Wáng Guǎngzhī sent army commander Huángmén Shìláng Liáng Wáng to advance by a hidden path.
Together with Tàizǐ Yòulǜ Xiāo Lěi,〔三一〕Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Xú Xuánqìng, and Jīngzhōu Jūnzhǔ Lǔ Xiūliè, they occupied Mount Xiánshǒu,
catching the barbarians off guard.
When the city saw the relief army arrive,
Xiāo Dàn sent Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Bóyú and Jūnzhǔ Cuī Gōngzǔ to sally forth and attack the barbarian stockade.
They set fire with the wind.
Liáng Wáng and the other armies attacked from outside.
Chǎng and Sù abandoned the siege and retreated.
They were pursued, attacked, and defeated.
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Huán Hé marched out of Xīyīnpíng.
The false Lǔjùn Gōng Tánchéng Shùzhǔ Dài Mòlóu and the acting Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu Jiāng Dàosēng set an ambush by the roadside.
Hé engaged them in battle
and utterly defeated them.
Over a hundred households from Qīng and Xú prefectures surrendered.
Qīng and Jì Prefectures Inspector Wáng Hóngfàn sent army commander Cuī Yán to attack and capture the barbarian Jìchéng.
Both were captured.
Hóng had previously sent the false Shàngshū Lú Yángwū and Huázhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Língzhì to attack Zhěyáng City.
〔三二〕Běixiāngchéng Tàishǒu Chéng Gōngqī defended it.
The barbarians attacked the city for over a hundred days,
using siege hooks and rams,
without rest day or night.
Qī killed and wounded several thousand people.
The Court also sent army commanders Yuán Lìshēng,〔三三〕and Cài Dàoguì as relief.
Yángwū and others retreated,
and the government army pursued and defeated them.
In summer,
the barbarians again attacked the two garrisons of Lìchéng in Sīzhōu.
The garrison commanders Wèi Sēngmín and Zhū Sēngqǐ resisted and defeated them.
The false Ānnán Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Wèijùn Wáng Yuán Yīng, with over one hundred thousand men, passed through Xiégǔ,
and raided Nánzhèng.
Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Yì sent army commanders Jiāng Shān'ān and Zhào Chāozōng and other forces, numbering over ten thousand men,
to separately occupy Jiǎonǔ, Báimǎ, and Jǔshuǐ to resist,
but were utterly defeated.
Yīng advanced to besiege Nánzhèng,
using earth mounds and battering rams,
without rest day or night.
Yì led over two thousand men from the eastern army to stoutly defend and resist,
repelling them at every turn.
Yīng attacked the city from spring to summer for over sixty days but could not take it.
Casualties were very numerous,
and the army ran out of provisions.
They pounded yeast into food.
Vegetable leaves cost a thousand coins.
Yì had previously sent army commander Hán Sōng and others to conquer the Láo.
They returned to reinforce the prefectural city,
but at Huángniúchuān,
they were defeated by the barbarians.
Yì sent the Dī man Yáng Yuánxiù back to Qiúchí,
to persuade the Dī to raise an army and cut off the barbarian supply route.
The Dī immediately raised their forces and attacked and captured the six barbarian garrisons of Lìchéng, Yìlán, Luògǔ, Qiúchí, Píngluò, and Sūlè.
The false Shàngshū Běiliángzhōu Cìshǐ Xīn Hēimò died in battle.
Yīng sent his military deputy Qiúchígōng Yáng Língzhēn to occupy Nígōngshān.
Wǔxīng Chéngzhǔ Yáng Jíshǐ sent his younger brother Jíláng, together with the returned Dī Yáng Fùzhī and righteous army commander Xú Yàofǔ, to meet them in battle at Huánggèn,
but they were utterly defeated and fled back.
At that time, the local gentry of Liángzhōu, Fàn Níng and Liáng Jìqún, invited Yīng to a banquet at their home,
and hid soldiers, intending to kill Yīng.
The plot was discovered.
Yīng seized Jìqún and killed him.
Níng fled.
Yīng retreated to protect Zhuóshuǐ.
Hearing that the Dī forces were strong,
he and Yáng Língzhēn both retreated back into Xiégǔ.
There was heavy rain,
and the army's horses were soaked.
They cut bamboo to boil rice,
and cooked and ate it on horseback with torches.
〔三四〕When Yīng reached Xiàbiàn,
Língzhēn's younger brother Póluó Ābǔzhēn rebelled,
and launched a surprise attack.
Yīng's forces scattered,
and he was shot in the cheek.
The false Língjiāng Jiāngjūn Yuè Yángshēng led the iron cavalry to fight to the death and rescue him,
and he managed to escape.
Liáng and Hàn were pacified.
Wǔdū Tàishǒu Dù Língyuàn, Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn Wàng Fǎxǐ, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Wàng Fǎtài, and Zhōu Zhìzhōng Huángfǔ Dān all resisted the barbarians and died in battle.
Língyuàn and Fǎxǐ were posthumously granted the title of Yǔlínjiān,
and Fǎtài was granted Jīshè Jiāngjūn.
At this time, the false Luòzhōu Cìshǐ Jiǎ Yì raided Jiǎkǒu,
but was defeated by Shàngluò Tàishǒu Lǐ Jìng.
In the third year,
the barbarians again attacked Lìchéng in Sīzhōu,
but were resisted and defeated by garrison commander Wèi Sēngmín.
In autumn,
the barbarians sent troops to raid Liánkǒu.
Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu Zhèng Yánzhǐ abandoned the western city and fled,
but the eastern city still held firm.
The Court sent Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Qíyúnzhōu Cìshǐ Xú Xuánqìng as relief.
The barbarians retreated,
and Yánzhǐ was punished for his crime.
Initially,
the two daughters of Fèng Shā, the Prince of Chānglí and elder brother of the false Empress Dowager Fèng Shì,
were as follows: the elder Fèng Měi was beautiful but suffered from an illness,
and became a nun.
The younger Fèng became Empress Hóng,
and gave birth to the false Crown Prince Xún.
Later, when the elder Fèng’s illness improved,
Hóng took her as a Zhāoyí.
When Hóng first moved the capital,
Xún was unhappy,
and yearned to return to Sānggān.
Hóng provided him with clothes and headwear,
but Xún secretly tore and destroyed them,
untied his hair, and wore braided clothing with the left lapel over the right.
The elder Fèng was favored,
and slandered Xún day and night.
Hóng went out of Yèchéng to practice archery on horseback.
Xún took this opportunity to plan a rebellion and return north,
secretly selecting three thousand imperial horses from the palace and placing them on an islet at Héyīn.
When the Empress heard of this,
she summoned and seized Xún,
and sent a swift messenger to inform Hóng.
Hóng moved Xún to Wúbí Chéng,
two *lǐ* north of Héqiáo,
and soon after killed him,
burying him with the rites of a commoner.
He enthroned the elder Fèng as Empress,
and immediately established the false Crown Prince Kè.
This year
was the twentieth year of the false Tàihé reign.
Fú-Lùgū Hèlùhún, the false Commander of the Northern Expedition, Provincial Governor, and Duke of Jùlù, guarded Sānggān.
Hóng’s paternal uncle, Ānshòu, the Prince of Píngyáng, garrisoned Huáizhà,
which was northwest of Sānggān.
Hún, not being one of the Hàn Chinese officials whom Hóng trusted and employed,
conspired with Mùlín, the false Provincial Governor of Dìngzhōu and Duke of Fēngyì, and Tuòbá Āgān'ér, the Duke of Ānlè, to establish Ānshòu,
and divide control of Hébĕi.
Their planned date was delayed and never came to fruition.
Ānshòu, in fear,
informed Hóng.
Hóng killed Hún and several hundred others,
but retained Ānshòu in his position as before.
Previously, Xuē Zhēndù, the false Provincial Governor of Jīngzhōu, and Qiè Qí Āpó, a Shangshū, had been defeated by Fáng Bóyù.
Hóng was enraged,
and, considering Nányáng a small commandery,
vowed to utterly destroy it.
he personally led an army towards Yōngzhōu.
Hóng first arrived at Nányáng.
Fáng Bóyù fortified the city and resisted.
Hóng was accompanied by tens of thousands of cavalry,
shaded by a yellow parasol,
stationed one *lǐ* from the city.
He sent Gōngsūn Yún, the false Zhōngshū Shèrén, to speak to Bóyù, saying:
“I am now sweeping across the Six Directions,
and my approach is different from previous campaigns.
Now, I vow that if I do not achieve victory,
I will never return north,
and will remain here for perhaps three to five years.
Your city is the head of my Six Dragons,
and there is no reason not to attack and capture it first.
At most a year,
at medium no more than a hundred days,
at least no more than a month;
it is not difficult to annihilate.
If you do not change your delusion,
I will cut off your head,
and display it at the army gate.
If the entire city has no second thoughts,
you may fortunately turn disaster into blessing.
However, you have three crimes,
which I will now make known to you.
You first served Emperor Wǔ,
and were privileged to be at his side.
You failed to exert your utmost loyalty to your former lord,
but now exert your utmost loyalty to the current lord;
this is one crime.
Last year, when I sent a detachment under Xuē Zhēndù to temporarily come here,
you then attacked and wounded them;
this is a second crime.
All the descendants of Emperor Wǔ have been executed,
and you have initially made no effort to repay his kindness.
Instead, you strive to serve the current lord,
defying Heaven and harming reason;
this is a third crime.
You cannot be forgiven.
I allow you to consider this three times.
Do not cause the entire city to suffer.”
Bóyù sent his military deputy, Yuè Zhìróu, to reply:
“I understand that you intend to besiege and attack us,
expecting certain victory.
For a humble commoner like me to be able to resist such great might
can truly be called finding a fitting place to die.
Previously, I was favored by Emperor Wǔ,
Even a dog or horse knows gratitude;
how could I be without feeling?
However, Lóngchāng and Yánxīng were
muddled and perverse, deviating from the norm.
A sage and enlightened ruler has now taken over the enterprise;
the family and the state are not different.
Thus, advancing, I do not betray my heart;
retreating, I have no shame in the underworld.
Last year, Xuē Zhēndù instigated the border populace,
and then encroached upon us.
Having received national grace,
I merely made an effort to sweep them away.
Looking at it from my own perspective,
this accusation should be dismissed.”
Hóng led his army and stopped in front of a temple south of the city,
crossing over a ditch bridge at the southeastern corner.
Bóyù had previously sent several brave warriors, dressed in tiger-striped clothing and wearing tiger-head hats,
who suddenly emerged from a hidden dugout.
Hóng’s men and horses were startled and retreated,
killing several men.
Hóng called for the skilled archer Yuán Língdù to shoot them.
They fell at the sound of the bowstring.
Hóng then passed.
At this time, Hóng launched a major southern invasion.

Yuán Xǐ, the false Prince of Xiányáng; Yuán Xié, the Prince of Péngchéng; Wáng Yuánsōng, a Chángshì; Wáng Yuánlì, the Prince of Bǎozhǎng; Yuán Xiè, the Marquis of Guǎnglíng; the Grand Commander of the Dūdū Liú Chǎng; Wáng Sù; Yáng Dàyǎn; Xī Kāngshēng; Chángsūn Zhì; and thirty-six other armies,
followed one after another,
their numbers proclaimed to be a million.
The armies of the princes had crimson drums,
those of the dukes and marquises had green drums,
and those of the counts, viscounts, and barons had black drums.
All had *pí* drums and horns,
their blasts shaking the ground.
Hóng left Yuán Xǐ, the false Prince of Xiányáng, to besiege Nányáng,
and advanced towards Xīnyě.
Liú Sījì, the Administrator of Xīnyě, also resisted.
The court had previously sent Hú Sōng, an army commander and commander of the imperial guards, to assist Chéng Gōngqī, the Administrator of Běixiāngchéng, in defending Zhěyáng Chéng.
Army commander Bāo Jǔ assisted Huáng Yáoqǐ, the Administrators of Xīrǔnán and Běiyìyáng Commanderies, in garrisoning Wǔyīn Chéng.
Hóng besieged Xīnyě Chéng,
fighting incessantly.
He sent someone to tell those in the city:
“Fáng Bóyù has already surrendered.
Why do you alone choose to be ground to pieces?”
“The city still has plenty of soldiers and provisions;
we have no time to talk with you, petty barbarians.”
Cáo Hǔ, the Provincial Governor of Yōngzhōu, sent troops to Jūnkǒu,
but they did not advance.
the city fell.
Sījì was captured and asked:
“Do you wish to surrender now?”
Sījì replied:
“I would rather be a southern ghost
than a northern subject.”
Thereupon he died.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Vanguard and Provincial Governor of Liángzhōu.
At this, the region north of the Miǎnju River was greatly alarmed.

Cài Dàofú, the garrison commander of Húyáng; Chéng Gōngqī, the lord of Zhěyáng Chéng, and army commander Hú Sōng; Huáng Yáoqǐ, the lord of Wǔyīn Chéng, and army commander Bāo Jǔ; and Xí Qiān, the Administrator of Cóngyáng,
all abandoned their cities and fled.
Wáng Sù rallied people to carve and eat his flesh.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Vanguard and Provincial Governor of Yǒuzhōu.
A few days later,
Fáng Bóyù surrendered the city.
Bóyù was
a native of Qīnghé.
After surrendering,
the barbarians made him General of Soaring Dragon,
but Bóyù refused to accept.
Gāozōng, knowing his ambition,
monthly gave his son Xīzhé five thousand coins
and twenty *hú* of rice.
Later, Bóyù sought a southern commandery from the barbarians,
and became Administrator of Fēngyì.
When his son was young,
he taught him to ride horses,
always wishing to return south.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
Xīzhé entered the barbarian territory.
Bóyù was greatly enraged, saying:
“My strength failed to this extent;
I could not die for my principles,
yet I still hoped you would remain in the imperial court to repay the national kindness.
If I followed my heart,
I would also have struggled through difficulties to seek return.
Why did you make such a miscalculation?”
Thereupon, he died among the barbarians.
The barbarians seized the five commanderies north of the Miǎn.
Hóng himself led two hundred thousand cavalry and defeated Crown Prince Shuài Cuī Huìjǐng and others at Dèngchéng.
He advanced to Fánchéng,
reached the Miǎnshǔi, and then departed.
Upon returning to Luòyáng,
he heard that Grand Commandant Chén Xiǎndá was campaigning to recover the five commanderies
and besieging Mǎquān.
Hóng again led a large army south to attack,
defeated Xiǎndá, who died.
When the funeral procession returned,
still over four hundred *lǐ* from Luò,
it was announced as Hóng's imperial edict
to summon the pseudo-Crown Prince Kè to meet at Lǔyáng.
When Kè arrived,
Xié clothed him in Hóng's pseudo-ceremonial attire,
and only then did they begin the mourning.
Upon reaching Luò,
they then announced it to the prefectures and commanderies,
performed the rites of mourning,
and posthumously honored him as Emperor Xiàowén.
That year,
Wáng Sù created for the barbarians a system of official ranks and all government departments,
all modeled after the Central Plains.
There were nine ranks in total,
each with two grades.
When Sù first defected to the barbarians,
he recounted the details of his family's execution,
and Hóng wept for him.
He gave him his sixth younger sister, the pseudo-Princess Péngchéng, in marriage.
Sù was enfeoffed as the Duke of Píngyuán Commandery.
A residence was built for him,
with fragrant plaster on the walls.
He was subsequently trusted and employed.
When Kè ascended the throne,
it was proclaimed as the first year of Jǐngmíng,
which was the second year of Yǒngyuán.
Péi Shúyè, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, surrendered Shòuchūn to the barbarians.
Before this, Shěn Líng, the pseudo-Inspector of Dōngxúzhōu, had led his troops and surrendered.
Líng,
a native of Wúxìng,
had initially fled to the barbarians out of disillusionment.
He was greatly trusted and employed.
After Hóng's death,
he consequently returned south,
and was repeatedly appointed Inspector of Xú and Yuè Prefectures.
At that time, Wáng Sù was the pseudo-General Who Conquers the South and Grand Administrator of Yùzhōu.
[四二]As the imperial court had just lost a major command,
wayfarers came and went,
falsely claiming that Sù wished to return to the state.
The Young Emperor issued an edict appointing Sù as Envoy with Credentials, Palace Attendant, Grand Administrator of Yù, Xú, and Sī Prefectures, General of the Right, Inspector of Yùzhōu,
Duke of Xīfēng,
with an estate of two thousand households.
After the barbarians obtained Huáinán,
that summer,
they sent the pseudo-General of Illustrious Might and Inspector of Nányùzhōu, Xí Fǎyǒu, to attack Hú Jǐnglüè, the Administrator of Běixīncài and Ānfēng Commanderies, at Jiàn'ānchéng.
Over ten thousand people died.
After more than a hundred days,
the imperial court sent no relief,
the city fell,
and the barbarians captured Jǐnglüè and returned.
That winter,
the barbarians again sent General Huán Dàofú to attack Cuī Shìzhāo, the Administrator of Suí Commandery,
and defeated him.
Later, the pseudo-Prince of Xiányáng, Xǐ, considering Kè to be young,
together with the Dī Yáng Jíshǐ, Yáng Língyòu, Qǐfó Mǎjū, and barbarian generals Zhī Hǔ, Lǐ Bóshàng, and more than ten others,
requested a meeting at Hóngchí Pō.
They intended to ambush and kill Kè while he was out hunting on Běimáng.
Xǐ hesitated and could not act,
wishing to set another date.
Mǎjū persuaded Xǐ, saying:
"Your Highness, if you do not go to Běimáng,
you can immediately turn your army around to occupy Luòchéng,
and close the four gates.
When the Son of Heaven hears of this,
he will surely flee to the north of the Yellow River (Héběi) to Sānggān,
[四三]and then cut off the Héquiáo,
making you the Son of Heaven of Hénán.
To rule across the river—
this opportunity must not be missed."
Xǐ again did not follow.
Língyòu suspected Xǐ of betraying him
and immediately rushed to inform Kè.
When Xǐ heard that his plot had failed,
he wanted to escape across the river,
but the rain and darkness obscured his path.
By the time he reached Xiàoyì Post Station,
Kè had already secured Luòchéng.
He sent his younger brother, the Prince of Guǎngpíng, to lead several hundred cavalry into the palace first
[四四]to ensure there was no unrest,
then returned.
He dispatched the Straight Guard's Three Gentlemen with soldiers to attack Xǐ,
[四五]captured and killed him.
According to barbarian law,
those who committed treason were not allowed burial;
their bodies were abandoned on Běimáng.
Wáng Sù died of illness.
The historian says: Qí (Southern Qí) and the foreign invaders (Northern Wèi) divided,
and Jiāngnán became a state, lasting through three dynasties.
Huáxià fragmented and collapsed,
the old capital was torn apart.
Seeing the opportunity and deploying troops,
this matter arose with the Eastern Jìn.
The two Yǔ brothers relied on the prominence of their prime maternal uncle,
claiming the sole right to lead military campaigns.
Yuánguī advanced to Zhūchéng, leading to the defeat of his army,
and Zhìgōng reached Xiāngyáng but turned back his banners.
Chǔ Póu, with strong troops from Xú and Yǎn,
was completely lost at Zōu and Lǔ.
Yīn Hào led the forces from Yáng and Yù,
suffering a great defeat at Shānsāng.
Huán Wēn, displaying heroic prowess in his youth,
capitalized on his reputation and influence from pacifying Shǔ,
marched into Xiánguān,
and fought in the wilderness near Luòyáng and Yèchéng.
Subsequently, the Xiānbēi established themselves securely north of the sea,
and the Qiāng and other foreign invaders carved out Qín and Dài.
They formed their own rival states,
their circumstances perilous and power fragmented.
Emperor Wǔ of Sòng seized the opportunity,
thus he was able to exterminate them one by one.
When the Wèi invaders consolidated their power,
Hénán lost its territory.
Their troops, horses, and land
were no longer as they were in former times.
Emperor Wén of Sòng, though he was self-aware,
could not foresee the enemy's moves.
Therefore, his commanders achieved no merit,
and every battle surely ended in defeat.
During the Tàishǐ era, because border officials defected,
the region north of the Huái River was lost.
His strategies did not revive,
so he discussed peace through marriage alliances.
When Emperor Tàizǔ established his rule,
he had not yet planned for distant goals,
when the dust of war arose first,
invading and ravaging the regional governors.
Victories were won in Huái and Yù,
and forces in Qīng and Hǎi were routed.
He waited at ease for the exhausted enemy,
and achieved a hundred victories effortlessly.
Since the four provinces were lost,
the people longed for their original dynasty.
The national destiny had just been renewed,
and they sang praises for his might and virtue.
Wielding spears and carrying armor,
everyone strived for themselves.
They built deep fortifications and defenses,
eagerly looking forward to the Southern banner.
The Son of Heaven was well-versed in border affairs,
and established military regulations to address the disorder.
If the vanguard forces could have been dispatched promptly,
to sweep afar to Línrú and Péngchéng,
but the supervising generals procrastinated,
and reinforcements arrived late,
〔四六〕those who inclined towards righteousness
had their homes and families utterly destroyed.
Having lost the opportunity,
the court discussions about the north ceased.
They laid down arms and cultivated civilian governance,
and thought of a later opportunity.
In the Yǒngmíng era,
they relied on established policies,
managed border exchanges,
and the passes and borders were peaceful.
The people in the border regions
all lived in peace and ceased to covet (others' lands).
The common people engaged in agriculture and sericulture, without losing their livelihoods;
this was also due to this.
Indeed, where thorns and thistles grow
is the consequence of warfare.
Once invaders attack,
the devastation is difficult to recover from.
Is this not proof of that?
In the early period of the Jiànwǔ era,
the Xūnxióng pressed southward.
The strong garrisons of Yù and Xú provinces,
entrenched in their high walled cities,
stockpiling soldiers,
did not dare to engage them in combat.
The Hu cavalry trampled upon the Huái and Féi rivers' regions,
and often fought on their own territory.
The damage from ladders and battering rams,
and the losses from drum-beating raids,
since the Jiànyuán era,
had never occurred before.
Moreover, the nomadic invaders had moved to the Huá (central plains),
immediately revering the old capital.
The northern parts of Yōng and Sī provinces
were close to Xǔchāng and Luòyáng.
Hundreds of li of flat roads
were connected by postal roads and chariot tracks.
The imperial highways of the Hàn dynasty
extended directly to Zhānglíng,
where their bridle-bits galloped;
they could go in the morning and return in the evening.
The invaders, harboring the ambition to conquer the weak
and the plan to expand their territory,
with strong armies and large forces,
personally harassed and annihilated.
Banners and drums (of war) were constant throughout the year;
arrows and stones (missiles) never ceased.
The court became cowardly and yielding,
unable to rescue or defend.
Thus, the fortifications of Nányáng were destroyed,
the ramparts of Xīnyě crumbled.
People's households and cultivated fields
all became protected by the Dí.
Although generals and soldiers were separately dispatched,
all marching out from south of the Huái River,
they had not yet resolved the crisis north of the Miǎn River,
but had already suffered a deep defeat at Wōyáng.
Taxes and levies were exhausted internally,
the people's lives were depleted externally.
House after house was in turmoil,
and could no longer live peacefully.
Indeed, the calculations of good and ill fortune
〔四七〕truly have a divine mechanism,
but the traces of gain and loss
are each attributed to human affairs.
Is it not because commanders face each other,
greedy for glory and ignoring due rewards,
that in the urgency of victory or defeat,
they did not rescue or yield to each other?
Unclear orders and commands
are indeed a weakness of the Central Plains states.
A eulogy says: Heaven established the mighty Hu,
who usurped imperial ambitions.
They immediately settled the various Huáxià regions,
established their reign and called themselves sovereign.
The common people were gravely ill,
their towns were ravaged and burned.
Collation notes
Biographies, Chapter 39: Mán (Barbarians) and Southeast Yí
The Mán
are diverse in types,
with different languages.
They all reside in mountains and valleys,
scattered across the borders of five provinces: Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yǐng, and Sī.
During the Sòng dynasty, Méi Chóngshēng of the Xīyáng Mán was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāoshān,
Tián Zhìshēng as the Marquis of Wēishān,
and Méi Jiāyáng as the Marquis of Hànshān.
When Emperor Tàizǔ ascended the throne,
officials reported that the Mán enfeoffments should be revoked.
A council discussed, stating:
“Granting peerage to barbarians
is a principle clearly established through successive dynasties.
That tribal chiefs inherit their positions
is clearly documented in previous annals.
Now, with the new imperial reign changing things,
old registers might be diminished.
However, Méi Shēng and others protect their settlements and govern;
their affairs require oversight,
and imperial grace should elevate and commend them
to distinguish them from ordinary ranks.
We believe it is appropriate to retain their titles to instruct the different customs.”
An imperial edict stated:
“They are to be specially retained.”
Zhìshēng was appointed General Who Assists the State and Commandant of the Tiger-Like Braves.
He was later transferred to be Grand Administrator of Jiànníng Commandery,
his general and marquis titles remaining as before.
In the second year of Jiànyuán,
when the invaders attacked Yù and Sī provinces,
it was rumored among the Mán that the invaders were already close,
and it was also heard that the government was conscripting all able-bodied men.
Qín Yuǎn, a Mán from Nán Xiāngchéng, seeing that the commanderies and counties were unprepared,
attacked Tóngyáng.
The county magistrate, Jiāo Wéndù, died in battle.
Mán from Sī Province led invaders to attack Píngchāng garrison.
The garrison commander, Gǒu Yuánbīn, defeated them.
Qín Yuǎn again sallied out and destroyed hundreds of strongholds at Línjǔ,
killing and capturing over a hundred people.
Wén Miǎndé of the Běishàng Huáng Mán raided Wènyáng.
The grand administrator, Dài Yuánsūn, with a solitary and weak city,
feared he could not defend it himself,
and abandoned the garrison to return to Jiānglíng.
The Cìshǐ of Jīng Province, Prince of Yùzhāng, dispatched Staff Officer of the Central Army Liú Pīxù with a thousand men to suppress Miǎndé.
Upon reaching Dāngyáng,
Miǎndé requested to surrender.
His tribe was taken into custody,
and he was ordered to garrison the small city he governed at Wènyáng,
to maintain security for merchants and travelers,
entrusting him with its clear passage.
Qín Yuǎn then fled.
Wènyáng was originally the western boundary of Línjǔ.
Within two hundred *lǐ*,
the water and land were winding and narrow,
requiring people to travel in single file.
There were several places impassable to cavalry,
but the fields by the water were very fertile.
During Huán Wēn's time,
it was carved out and made into a commandery.
To its northwest it bordered Xīnchéng of Liángzhōu,
to its northeast Nánxiāngchéng,
and to its south the two borders of Bā and Wū.
The mountain Mán were all fierce and powerful,
occupying strategic points to act as bandits and rebels.
Since the Tàishǐ era of Sòng,
Xiàng Zōngtóu, a Bājiàn Mán, rebelled.
The Inspector Shěn Yōuzhī cut off their salt and rice,
and repeatedly attacked them without success.
In the third year of Tàixīng of Jìn,
Xiàng Hóng and Xiàng Guī, the Yi kings of Jiànpíng, went to the court to request appointments.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat Zhāng Liàng argued:
"Barbarians should not be granted military titles."
Emperor Yuán decreed that Xiàng Hóng be specifically appointed as Zhéxīn Jiāngjūn and Dāngpíng Xiānghóu,
and also that he be close to Jìn Wáng,
and be granted court robes.
Xiàng Zōngtóu was his descendant.
Tàizǔ established Bāzhōu to pacify them.
When Tián Sīpiāo, a Wǔlíng Yǒuxī Mán, raided and plundered,
the Grand Administrator Wáng Wénhé attacked him.
Leading his army deep into their territory,
the Mán cut off his supplies from the rear.
The Prince of Yùzhāng sent the Zhongbing Cānjūn Zhuāng Míng with five hundred men to lead the Xiāngzhōu garrison troops, totaling one thousand men, to relieve him.
Tián Sīpiāo fought against Wáng Wénhé,
was struck by a crossbow arrow and died.
The Mán surrendered with their city.
At the beginning of Yǒngmíng,
Xiàng Zōngtóu and Tián Dòuqú, a Qiányáng Mán, with five thousand men became bandits.
The Grand Administrator of Bādōng, Wáng Túnán, sent the Adjutant Liú Sēngshòu and others to cut mountains and open roads,
and attacked their fortified camp.
Xiàng Zōngtóu burned his camp at night and retreated.
In the third year,
Chén Shuāng and Lǐ Dá, Xiāngchuān Mán, plundered commanderies and counties.
The Inspector Lǚ Ānguó attacked them without success.
In the fourth year,
the Inspector Liǔ Shìlóng commanded a large force to campaign and attack,
and then pacified them.
In the fifth year,
the Mán of Yōngzhōu and Sīzhōu colluded with the captives,
assisting Huán Tiānshēng, a despoiler, in causing unrest.
In the sixth year,
Tián Sìlù was appointed Dūhù Běisuí'ān Zuǒjùn Tàishǒu, serving temporarily as Běisuí'ān Zuǒjùn Tàishǒu;
the former Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Tián Lǘwáng was appointed as trial serving Yírén Zuǒjùn Tàishǒu;
Tián Hédài was appointed as trial serving Xīnpíng Zuǒjùn Tàishǒu.
All were Yǐngzhōu Mán.
In the ninth year,
the Grand Administrator of Ānlóng, Wáng Sēngxù, raised common men,
and sent Wānchéng Shùzhǔ Wàn Mínhé to assist eight hundred Dīngcūn Mán in attacking one thousand two hundred Dīngcūn Mán.
They were defeated by the Mán.
Wàn Mínhé was wounded,
losing his horse and weapons.
The officials concerned memorialized for his dismissal.
Tián Yìzōng, a Xīyáng Mán,
during Shěn Yōuzhī's time,
gained military command due to his merits.
He then became a bodyguard for the Prince of Línchuān,
but rebelled and defected to the captives.
The captives made him Dōngyùzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
the captives sent Tián Yìzōng to attack Lóngchéng Shù of Sīzhōu.
He was defeated by the Shùzhǔ Zhū Sēngqǐ.
The Mán custom was to wear cloth and go barefoot,
some with coiled topknots,
others with short hair.
Their weapons were decorated with gold and silver,
their shields covered with tiger skins.
They were skilled with crossbows,
and were all violent, fierce, and fond of banditry.
The kingdom of Gāolì in the Eastern Yi,
bordered the Wèi captives to the west.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
Gāolì Wáng, Lèdàng Gōng Gāo Lián was appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Yíng Píng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnfāng, Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóu Sānsī.
In the first year of Tàizǔ's Jiàn Yuán era,
he was promoted to the title of Piáoqí Dàjiāngjūn.
In the third year,
he sent envoys with tribute.
They traveled by sea on ships,
and their diplomatic relations were always maintained.
He also sent envoys to the Wèi captives,
but was strong and prosperous and did not submit to control.
The captives established residences for envoys from various states,
with the Qí envoy first,
and Gāolì second.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng,
Píngnán Cānjūn Yán Yòumíng and Róngcóng Púshè Liú Sīxiào were sent as envoys to the captives.
At the captives' grand assembly,
they were seated consecutively with the Gāolì envoy.
Yán Yòumíng said to the "Acting Zhǔkè Láng" Péi Shūlìng:
"We are entrusted with a mission from the imperial court,
and have come to your country.
Our primary adversary
is Wèi.
As for other foreign barbarians,
they are not logically permitted to expect to follow in our dust.
How much less so the minor Eastern Yi,
who are vassals of the imperial court,
and yet today dare to tread on our heels!"
Liú Sīxiào said to the "Acting Nánbù Shàngshū" Lǐ Sīchōng:
"When our holy dynasty places Wèi envoys,
they are never listed with smaller countries.
You should also know this."
Lǐ Sīchōng said:
"That is indeed so.
But the principal and deputy envoys are not allowed to ascend the hall.
Their seating and rising here are quite high,
sufficient to respond accordingly."
Liú Sīxiào said:
"When Lǐ Dàogù was an envoy in the past,
it was precisely due to their attire that there was a separation.
If the Wèi state were to arrive in proper caps and robes,
how could they be rejected?"
Yán Yòumíng also said to the captive ruler:
"Only Qí and Wèi
are two states of equal standing.
How dare a small barbarian from the borderlands
tread on my heels!"
The Gāolì custom was to wear short trousers
and a single-ribbed 'folding wind' cap,
which they called a 'cè'.
They knew how to read the Five Classics.
When their envoy was in the capital,
the Central Secretariat Director Wáng Róng mocked him, saying:
"Unsuitable clothing
is a misfortune for the person.
What exactly is that thing on your head?"
He replied:
"This is indeed a remnant image of the ancient biàn cap."
Gāo Lián died at over a hundred years old.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
Gāolì Wáng, Lèdàng Gōng Gāo Yún was appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Yíng Píng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnfāng, Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn, Gāolì Wáng, and Lèdàng Gōng.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
