Zhūnóng入朝，
海中遭風溺死，
以其子 Wén Kuǎn為假節、都督緣海軍事、安南將軍、林邑王．
During the Jiànxīng
era of the Jìn dynasty, Fàn Zhìnuwén (范稚奴文), a chieftain of the Rìzhōu (日南) barbarians, often traded as a merchant.
Seeing the institutions of the superior country,
he taught the King of Línyì (林邑), Fàn Yì (范逸), to build city walls, towers, and palaces.
The king wore a heavenly crown like a Buddha crown,
and his body was adorned with fragrant garlands.
The people of the country were fierce and violent,
accustomed to mountains and rivers,
and skilled in fighting.
They blew conch shells as horns.
Everyone went naked.
The four seasons were warm,
without frost or snow.
They valued women and demeaned men,
calling their spiritual masters "Brāhmaṇas" (Póluómén, 婆羅門).
〔一九〕Their relatives intermarried,
with women first sending proposals to seek husbands.
When a woman married,
she wore a Kāsāya (Jiālán, 迦藍) robe, sewn horizontally like a well railing,
and wore flowered jewels on her head.
The Brāhmaṇa would lead the groom and the bride to shake hands and entrust them to each other,
reciting blessings for good fortune.
During mourning, they cut their hair,
which was called filial piety.
They cremated bodies in the wilderness as a burial.
In a distant region, there was a spiritual vulture (Língjiù, 靈鷲) that,
knowing when a person was about to die,
would gather at their home and eat the dead person's flesh completely.
After it flew away,
they would then collect the bones, burn them to ashes, and cast them into the sea for a water burial.
People considered black skin beautiful,
and all southern countries were like this.
At Qūlì (區栗) city, an eight-foot sundial was erected,
and the shadow of the sun passed south by eight inches.
From Línyì (林邑) southwestward for over three thousand Lǐ (里),
one reached Fúnán (扶南).
The kingdom of Fúnán (扶南)
was located south of Rìzhōu (日南) in a great bay to the west of the ocean.
〔二０〕It was three thousand Lǐ (里) in length and breadth,
with a great river flowing westward into the sea.
Originally, a woman was its queen,
named Liǔyè (柳葉).
Then there was Hùntián (混填) from Jī (激) country,
who dreamed that a god bestowed a bow upon him,
〔二一〕instructing him to sail into the sea.
Hùntián (混填) rose at dawn and found the bow under a tree at the god's temple.
He immediately sailed towards Fúnán (扶南).
Liǔyè (柳葉), seeing the ship,
led her people to resist it.
Hùntián (混填) raised his bow and shot from afar,
piercing one side of the ship and striking a person inside.
Liǔyè (柳葉) was frightened
and consequently surrendered.
Hùntián (混填) married her as his wife.
〔二二〕Disliking her naked body,
he folded cloth and made her wear it over her head.
〔二三〕Thus, he governed her country.
His descendants continued the rule.
When King Pánkuàng (槃況) died,
the people of the country established his great general, Fàn Shīmàn (范師蔓).
When Màn (蔓) fell ill,
his sister's son Zhān (篡) usurped the throne,
〔二四〕killing Màn's (蔓) son, Jīnshēng (金生).
Over ten years later,
Màn's (蔓) youngest son, Zhǎng (長), attacked and killed Zhān (篡),
stabbing Zhān (篡) in the belly with a blade and saying:
"You killed my elder brother in the past;
today I avenge my father and elder brother upon you."
Zhān's (篡) general, Fàn Xún (范尋), then killed Zhǎng (長),
and the people of the country established him as king.
This was during the Wú (吳) and Jìn (晉) eras.
During the Jìn (晉) and Sòng (宋) dynasties, they consistently paid tribute.
Towards the end of the Sòng (宋),
the King of Fúnán (扶南), whose surname was Qiáochénrú (僑陳如)
and personal name was Shéyébámó (闍耶跋摩),
sent merchants to trade in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
The Indian monk Nāgā (Nàgāxiān, 那伽仙), who was traveling with them, wanted to return to his country,
but encountered a storm and drifted to Línyì (林邑).
His possessions and goods were all plundered.
Nāgā (那伽仙) found a detour and reached Fúnán (扶南),
fully describing that there was a sage ruler in the central country who had received the mandate.
In the second year of Yǒngmíng (永明) [484 CE],

Shéyébámó (闍耶跋摩) dispatched the Indian monk Śākya Nāgā (Shì Nàgāxiān, 釋那伽仙) to present a memorial, stating: "Your subject, Qiáochénrú Shéyébámó (僑陳如闍耶跋摩), King of Fúnán (扶南), kowtows and respectfully reports:
By heaven's transforming nurture,
spiritual deities are moved,
and the four seasons are in harmony.
I humbly pray that the holy ruler's honored body and daily life may be in good
〔二五〕health, the Crown Prince enjoy myriad blessings,
the six palaces be serene,
all princes, consorts, and internal and external court officials be universally harmonious,
the people of neighboring lands and all nations turn their hearts to you,
the five grains be abundant,
disasters not arise,
the land be pure, and the people be at peace,
with everything tranquil and secure.
Your subject and his people,
with a rich and joyous land,
and harmonious four seasons,
where both clergy and laity are flourishing,
all receive the radiance of Your Majesty's transforming influence,
and universally enjoy peace and stability."
He further stated:
"Previously, your subject sent envoys carrying various goods to Guǎngzhōu (廣州) for trade.
The Indian monk Śākya Nāgā (釋那伽仙) was in Guǎngzhōu (廣州) and took passage on your subject's ship, intending to come to Fúnán (扶南).
In the sea, a storm drifted them to Línyì (林邑),
whose king seized your subject's trade goods
and Nāgā (那伽仙)'s private property.
He fully explained that he came from the central country,
and reverently narrated Your Majesty's sagely virtue and benevolent rule,
discussing in detail the transforming influence,
the flourishing of Buddhist dharma,
the gathering of numerous monks,
the daily growth of dharma activities,
the king's solemn majesty,
the court's prestige and national order,
and compassion for the common people.
The eight directions and six harmonies,
none do not submit.
If one listens to what he says,
then the transformation extends to the devas,
which cannot be described with analogies.
Your subject heard of it,
and his humble heart rejoices.
If I could momentarily behold your honorable presence,
I would look up to your benevolent grace.
Your favor flows to small nations,
and heaven's inspiration descends.
The people of the entire land
will all receive blessings and protection.
Therefore, your subject now sends this monk, Śākya Nāgā (釋那伽仙), as an envoy,
to present a memorial to inquire and offer tribute,
humbly showing your subject's true heart,
and separately conveying our humble sentiments.
However, the offerings are meager and crude,
and I am deeply ashamed and fearful.
I humbly pray for heaven's kind illumination,
to discern my sincere devotion,
and not to blame me."
He further stated:
"Your subject has a slave named Jiūchóuluó (鳩酬羅),
who ran away from your subject
and in another place,
formed a wicked conspiracy,
then broke Línyì (林邑)
and established himself as king.
He never submitted,
betraying grace and forsaking righteousness,
a crime of rebelling against his master
that heaven cannot tolerate.
I humbly recall that Línyì (林邑) was formerly destroyed by Tánhé (檀和)
and has long been civilized.
Heaven's might reaches everywhere,
and the four seas are subdued.
Yet now, Jiūchóuluó (鳩酬羅) maintains a slave's wickedness,
acting independently and stubbornly.
Moreover, Línyì (林邑) and Fúnán (扶南) share a border,
and he is still your subject's slave,
〔二七〕yet he still rebels and departs.
Since the imperial court is distant,
how can he be expected to follow and obey?
This country belongs to Your Majesty,
hence I respectfully present this memorial.
I humbly hear that Línyì (林邑) has ceased its tributes in recent years,
wishing to be forever separated from the imperial court.
How can a lion sit while a big rat remains at ease?
I humbly pray for you to send a military general to attack this wicked rebel.
Your subject will also offer his humble loyalty,
assisting the imperial court in suppressing and eradicating him,
so that all countries along the border and sea
will submit at once.
If Your Majesty wishes to establish another person as king there,
I humbly await your imperial decree.
If you do not wish to openly launch an army to attack Línyì (林邑) for now,
I humbly pray for a special imperial decree to the local authorities,
to assist your subject with a small army as deemed appropriate,
to leverage heaven's might,
destroy these minor bandits,
and punish evil to promote good.
On the day of pacification,
I will present a memorial offering five Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén, 婆羅門) of gold.
I now humbly send this envoy to convey your subject's sincere heart.
The matters stated in the memorial
do not fully express my humble sentiments.
I respectfully entrust Nāgā (那伽仙) and his companions to verbally report in full.
I humbly pray for compassion for what is reported.
I also offer one gilded Dragon King statue,
one white sandalwood statue,
two ivory pagodas,
two pairs of Kapok cloth,
two pieces of glazed glassware,
and one tortoise shell betel nut plate."
Nàjiā Xiān went to the capital.
He said that in his country, it was customary to worship the god Máshǒuluó Tiānshén,
who often descended upon Módān Shān.
The climate there was warm,
and plants and trees did not shed their leaves.
Above it was inscribed a text which read:
"Auspiciously benefiting the human world,
it inspires and unites all beings.
The reason it is so,
is that Heaven's transformative influence is clear.
The immortal mountain is named Módān,
where propitious trees spread their beautiful glory.
Máshǒuluó Tiān,
by this, descends his venerable spirit.
The country is entirely blessed,
and its people are all at peace.
Because of this bestowed grace,
therefore, your vassal pledges his devotion.
Bodhisattvas practice patience and compassion,
their original vows and deeds arise from ordinary foundations.
Once the Bódhī mind is awakened,
the two vehicles are not what is sought.
Throughout countless lives, they accumulate merits and deeds,
practicing great compassion through the Six Pāramitās.
Valiantly surpassing kalpas,
they abandon wealth and life without reserve.
They are not wearied by life and death,
transforming those with karmic connections in the Six Realms.
They fully cultivate the Ten Bhūmis,
leaving fruits of their practice to guide humans and devas.
Once their merits and deeds are established,
their practice complete, they ascend to perfect enlightenment.
All virtues and wisdom are perfectly complete,
the sun of wisdom shines upon the dusty world.
Sentient beings respond according to their connections,
receiving the dharma medicine according to their capacity.
Buddha's transformation spreads throughout the ten directions,
none fail to receive salvation and elevation.
The Emperor is sacred and promotes the Way,
causing the Sān Bǎo to flourish.
He applies his mind to myriad affairs,
his majesty and grace shake the eight quarters.
Countries and cities,
are purified and enlightened by his benevolent influence.
He is also like Shìtíhuányin,
the foremost among all devas.
Your Majesty rules over all people,
the Four Seas universally pledge their devotion,
your sacred compassion flows boundlessly,
deeply covering your vassal's small country."
The edict in reply said:
"That Módān descends his spirit,
and bestows benefits upon that land,
though the customs are different and the transformations varied,
we deeply admire and praise it from afar.
We know that Jiūchóuluó has rebelled there,
secretly occupying Línyì,
gathering villains and plundering,
it is truly fitting to suppress and eliminate them.
Although that place is located in a distant
〔二八〕 remote corner, it traditionally maintained tributary relations.
Since the many difficulties of the Sòng dynasty's latter years,
sea communications have been obstructed,
and Imperial transformation is new, so old confusions have not yet been dispelled.
We
intend to attract distant people with virtuous culture,
and do not yet wish to immediately raise arms.
Since the king has
earnestly expressed his loyalty and sent a request from afar for military might,
we now order the Jiāo Department to respond as appropriate.
Punishing rebels and pacifying the submissive,
this is indeed a national principle.
Strive to achieve extraordinary results,
to meet our expectations.
Nàjiā Xiān has frequently served as a border interpreter,
and is quite familiar with the breadth and depth of the Middle Kingdom,
let him fully explain."
The emperor sent in return five bolts each of crimson-purple ground, yellow-green patterned damask.
The people of Fúnán are clever and skillful.
They plunder neighboring cities and capture disobedient people as slaves,
trading them for gold, silver, and colored silks.
Wealthy men wear a broad strip of brocade wrapped around their waist,
women wear a 'through-head' garment (poncho-like),
and the poor cover themselves with cloth.
They forge gold rings and armlets, and silver utensils.
They fell trees to build houses,
the king resides in a multi-storied building,
with a palisade of wooden stakes as a city wall.
By the sea grow large bamboo leaves,
eight or nine feet long,
which they weave together to cover their roofs.
The people also live in raised dwellings.
They build boats eight or nine *zhàng* long,
and about six or seven *chǐ* wide,
with heads and tails resembling fish.
The king travels by elephant,
and women are also able to ride elephants.
They find amusement in chickens and pigs.
There are no prisons.
When there is a lawsuit,
they take a gold finger ring or a chicken egg and throw it into boiling water,
ordering the accused to retrieve it.
Or they heat a lock until it is red,
and make them hold it in their hands and walk seven steps.
Those who are guilty have their hands scorched and烂烂 (ruined),
while the innocent are unharmed.
They also make them dive into water;
the righteous immediately float without sinking,
while the unrighteous immediately sink.
They have sugarcane, various kinds of cane, pomegranates, and tangerines.
There are many betel nuts.
The birds and beasts are like those in China.
Their nature is good,
they are not adept at war.
They are often attacked and invaded by Línyì,
and cannot communicate with Jiāozhōu,
hence their envoys rarely arrive.
Jiāozhōu is an isolated island across the sea,
controlling foreign countries,
thus relying on its perilous terrain, it often rebels.
In the early years of Sòng Tàishǐ (465 AD),
the Inspector Zhāng Mù died.
Lǐ Chángrén, a native of Jiāozhǐ, killed Mù's northern contingent,
occupied Jiāozhōu, and rebelled.
He died of illness several years later.
His cousin, Shúxiàn, succeeded him,
but his authority was not yet established,
so he sent an envoy to request an Inspector.
The Sòng court appointed Shěn Huàn, the Administrator of Nánhǎi, as the Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
and Shúxiàn as Huàn's Níngyuǎn Sīmǎ and Administrator of the two commanderies of Wǔpíng and Xīnchāng.
When Shúxiàn received the imperial decree,
the people submitted to him.
He then raised troops to defend the strategic passes and refused to admit Huàn.
Huàn remained in Yùlín and died of illness.
In the first year of Tàizǔ Jiànyuán (479 AD),
Shúxiàn was retained as Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
and was pacified.
Shúxiàn received the decree,
but then cut off foreign countries,
and tribute became scarce.
Shìzǔ wished to punish him.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 AD),
Liú Kǎi, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, was made Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
〔二九〕 and troops from Nánkāng, Lúlíng, and Shǐxīng commanderies were dispatched to conquer Jiāozhōu.
Upon hearing this, Shúxiàn
sent an envoy requesting an extension of several years,
offering twelve contingents of pure silver helmets and peacock feather ornaments.
Shìzǔ did not permit it.
Fearing that Kǎi would attack him,
Shúxiàn returned to the court via a secret route from Xiāngchuān.
In the sixth year (488 AD),
Fáng Fǎchéng, the Administrator of Shǐxīng, replaced Kǎi.
When Fǎchéng arrived at the post,
he suffered from illness and did not attend to affairs,
devoting himself solely to reading.
His Chief Clerk, Fú Dēngzhī, therefore usurped power,
changing generals and officials,
without Fǎchéng's knowledge.
The Registrar, Fáng Jìwén, reported this to him.
Fǎchéng was greatly angered and
imprisoned Dēngzhī.
After more than ten days,
Dēngzhī heavily bribed Fǎchéng's brother-in-law, Cuī Jǐngshū, and was released.
He then led his contingent to assault the prefecture and seize Fǎchéng,
saying to him:
"Since the Governor is ill,
he should not exert himself."
He imprisoned him in a separate room.
Fǎchéng, having nothing to do,
again asked Dēngzhī for books to read.
Dēngzhī said:
"Even in quiet seclusion, the Governor might still aggravate his illness,
how can he read books?"
So he did not give him any.
He then reported that Fǎchéng's mental illness had flared up,
rendering him unfit to manage affairs.
Shìzǔ then appointed Dēngzhī as Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
Fǎchéng died upon returning to the mountain range.
Fǎchéng was
a native of Qīnghé.
During Shēngmíng (477-479 AD),
he served as Tàizǔ's Pìqí Zhōngbīng,
rising to Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng.
He was upright and concise by nature,
eight *chǐ* and three *cùn* tall,
standing out among others,
he always humbly bent himself.
Míng Qìngfú, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, was also as tall as Fǎchéng;
there were only these two men in the court.
The imperial historian says: The *Shū*
states, “The Mányí disturb Xia.”
This is a general statement.
As for the various tribes of the Southern Yí,
they established states on divided islands.
Of all the rare and strange things from the four directions,
none surpass these.
Hidden in mountains and concealed by seas,
precious treasures overflow the eye.
Merchant ships arrive from afar,
transporting them to the Southern Provinces.
Thus, Jiāo and Guǎng became rich and substantial,
filling the royal treasuries.
The abundance of goods was quite remarkable,
and the path of moral instruction could reach them.
To use virtue to attract those from afar,
is this not what is meant?
A eulogy says: Sī and Yōng divided their borders,
Jīng and Héngyáng.
The various regions were interspersed,
and the land had Mán regions.
The Eastern Yí were overseas,
at Jiéshí and Fúsāng.
The Southern regions were distant and vast,
extending to the boundless ocean.
They brought tribute without being compelled,
and also came to acknowledge sovereignty.
The extent was vast, and it began to be recorded (doubtful) *Jiàokān Jì*
Biographies 40: Rùiruì Lǔ, Hénán, Dī, Qiāng
The Rùiruì Lǔ
were miscellaneous Hú from beyond the frontier.
They braided their hair and wore robes fastened on the left.
During the Jìn era, after Shíyìguī entered the interior,
the Rùiruì followed water and pasture,
occupying all the former territories of the Xiōngnú,
and awe-inspiring the Western Regions.
The climate was cold early,
and they lived in yurts and felt tents.
They carved wood to record events,
and did not know how to write.
Their horses and livestock were robust,
and their population was numerous and prosperous.
They were constantly at enmity with the Wèi Lǔ.
During the Sòng era, their prime minister, Xīlìyīn, understood astrology and numerology,
and was fluent in Hú and Hàn languages.
He often said that there would be someone in the south with a name similar to “Qí,”
and that person would rise.
In the second year of Shēngmíng,
Great Ancestor (Tàizǔ) assumed regency.
He sent Commander of Agile Cavalry Wáng Hóng (guǐ) Fàn as envoy to the Rùiruì,
setting a date to jointly attack the Wèi Lǔ.
In the eighth month of the first year of Jiànyuán,
the Rùiruì ruler dispatched 300,000 cavalry to invade the south.
They reached seven hundred *lǐ* from Píngchéng.
The Wèi Lǔ defended themselves and dared not fight.
The Rùiruì ruler hunted beneath Yànrán Shān and then returned.
The emperor (shàng) had just ascended the throne
and did not have time to send out an army.
In the second and third years,
the Rùiruì ruler repeatedly sent envoys to offer sable furs and various other goods.
He sent a letter to the emperor (shàng) expressing his desire to attack the Wèi Lǔ,
addressing the emperor (shàng) as
“Your Excellency”
and referring to himself as
He presented a pair of lion-skin trousers,
the skin of which was like tiger skin,
white in color and with short fur.
At that time, a merchant Hú in Shǔ saw it
and said, “This is not lion skin;
it is Fúbá skin.”
The prime minister, Xíng Jīzhīluóhuí, respectfully submitted a memorial, saying: “When the Four Phases govern
and the Two Instruments change their course,
all myriad things are born.
This is indeed due to the alternation of waning and waxing,
a natural progression of the calendar.
In the past, when the Jìn dynasty was about to end,
Chǔ Huán usurped power.
It truly relied on the efforts of Sòng Wǔ to save and rectify the situation,
and thus he was able to support the declining and stabilize the tottering,
turning misfortune into prosperity.
His reign flowed for nine generations,
but the dynastic succession was not continued.
Now,
Heaven has sent calamity upon the former,
and the Sòng dynasty is beset by suspicion and chaos below.
Although I am from a wild and distant land,
I have roughly perused the charts and books.
For several years now,
the stellar patterns have changed their courses.
Fáng and Xīn have undergone transformation,
Xū and Wēi have received blessings.
The fall of Sòng and the rise of Qí—
this is its verification.
The Water Element encountered difficulty,
and the Wood Element responded to the cosmic shift.
The year of Zǐ will be cut short.
Liú Mùzhī recorded
that Mǐn Lǐng has mountains that do not
conform.
Jīng Fáng’s prophecy states,
‘Mǎo Jīn (Liu) will be sixteen (generations),
and the grass (Xiāo) will rise to kingship.’
Having reviewed the charts and omens,
the auspicious signs are not singular.
All say that blessings converge upon the Xiāo clan,
and that Qí
will replace Sòng.
There was an envoy who was adept at law and governance and visited this country.
He inquired about the sagely virtues,
further confirming the heaven-granted disposition.
Therefore, he was able to uphold the majestic imperial lineage,
glorifying
the enterprise of power and stability,
assisting and illuminating heavenly accomplishments,
and rescuing the perverted ruler from calamity.
He established merits in the capital,
his prestige shaking the lands beyond the sea.
His righteous deeds
equaled those of Tāng and Wǔ.
As his unseen
merits became manifest,
the precious mandate naturally returned.
The calendar of receiving the mandate
returned to the virtuous.
Moreover, emperors do not have a constant lineage;
the virtuous are sure to prosper.
The destined moment
is given
only to the divine.
Your Majesty, you have embraced the opportunity for a new beginning,
riding the fortune of the 'ascending dragon.'
Considering that you correspond to the omens and should have transformed the mandate,
you should have long since ascended the throne.
The wild and distant regions incline towards you,
all stretching their necks in anticipation.
If
you have not yet ascended to power,
it is inappropriate to be modest and yield,
as this would go against the will of Heaven and man above,
and thwart the hopes of the common people below.
The imperial Rùiruì succession
originated from the Two Instruments (Heaven and Earth).
Expanding territory and settling the people,
their land crosses the ocean.
One lineage for a hundred generations,
their great enterprise is naturally secure.
Although Wú (Hàn) Mò are in different
regions,
our righteousness is like lips and teeth.
We intend to set a date for the Central Plains
and jointly carry out Heaven’s punishment.
We are preparing our troops and repairing our armor,
awaiting the opportune moment for a grand expedition.
We will brandish our frost-like spears in Bìng and Dài,
and sound our harmonious bells in Qín and Zhào.
We will sweep away the evil and ugly,
and behead the arch-villains.
Then, the imperial chariot will move,
restoring the glory of the Central Plains.
We will forever uphold good neighborly relations,
following the example of Qí
and Lǔ.
May all within the four seas have someone to serve,
and all the common people rely on this.
May the wild and distant regions return and look up to you—
would this not be splendid!”
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
Wáng Hóng (guǐ) Fàn returned to the capital,
having traveled over thirty thousand *lǐ*.
Hóng (guǐ) Fàn
was a native of Línzī, Qí Commandery,
and was trusted by Great Ancestor (Tàizǔ).
During the Jiànwǔ reign,
he served as Inspector of Qīng and Jì Provinces.
He privately occupied territory and encroached upon the enemy’s borders,
suffering a defeat that led to his death from illness.
The Rùiruì king requested a physician, weaving craftsmen, and other items.
Emperor Shìzǔ replied by edict, saying:
“I understand you need a physician, a brocade weaving craftsman, a south-pointing chariot, and a clepsydra.
None of these are things I begrudge.
However, the methods of treating illnesses in the south
differ from those in the north.
Brocade weaving craftsmen
are all women,
unsuited for distant travel.
As for the south-pointing chariot and the clepsydra,
although we possess such instruments,
the skilled artisans who made them have long since passed away,
and to provide faulty ones would be misleading.”
Since the Rùiruì occupied the former territories of the Xiōngnú,
ten years later,
the Dīnglíng Hú again attacked the Rùiruì from the south,
taking their former lands.
The Rùiruì gradually moved southward.
The Wèi Lǔ ruler Yuán Hóng, because of their encroachment,
sent the false King Píngyuán, Jià Lùhún, and General Lóngxiáng, Yáng Yán, with several hundred thousand cavalry to attack the Rùiruì.
There was heavy snow and cold,
and many people and horses died.
First, Liú Qūn (劉悛), the Inspector of Yìzhōu, sent Jiāng Jǐngxuán (江景玄) as an envoy to the Dīnglíng,
to proclaim the nation's power and virtue.
The route passed through Shànshàn and Yútián.
Shànshàn had been destroyed by the Dīnglíng,
its people completely scattered.
Yútián especially believed in Buddhism.
The Dīnglíng usurped the title of Son of Heaven,
received Jǐngxuán (景玄) as an envoy,
and sent him back with a report.
The Ruìruì (芮芮) often traveled from Hénán Dào to Yìzhōu.
Hénán (河南),
was a branch of the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
During the Jiànwǔ (建武) era of the Hàn dynasty,
several thousand Xiōngnú (匈奴) slaves, who had fled and hidden in the border regions of Liángzhōu (涼州), mixed with other peoples.
The barbarians called slaves "zī" (貲),
and one would call them
"zīlǔ" (貲虜) (slave-barbarians).
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾), a half-brother of Mùróng Cuī (慕容廆) of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑), became a Dī (氐) king.
He was in the northwest of Yìzhōu (益州),
spanning several thousand *lǐ*.
His southern border was Lónghé Chéng (龍涸城),
over a thousand *lǐ* from Chéngdū (成都).
There were four large garrisons;
one was in Qīngshuǐ Chuān (清水川),
one in Chìshuǐ (赤水),
one in Jiāohé (澆河),
and one in Tǔqūzhēn Chuān (吐屈真川),
all governed by his sons and younger brothers.
Their king resided in Mùjià Chuān (慕駕川).
They had many livestock,
followed water and grass,
and had no walled cities.
Later, they gradually built palaces and houses,
but the people still used felt tents and "hundred-son tents" as mobile dwellings.
The land was often windy and cold.
When people walked on the flat sands,
sand and gravel would fly up,
and all tracks would be erased.
Fertile land had sparrows and rats sharing burrows,
and grew yellow and purple flowers.
Barren land often had "miasma" (zhàngqì 鄣氣),
which caused people to gasp for breath;
when cattle and horses encountered it,
they became exhausted and sweaty, unable to move.
The Sòng (宋) dynasty initially bestowed titles and appointments.
Towards the end of the Sòng,

Tǔyùhún Shíyín (吐谷渾拾寅), King of Hénán (河南), became Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Palace Attendant, Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xīqín, Hé and Shā three provinces, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Administrator with Rights of the Three Dukes, concurrently Protector-General of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two provinces.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元) era,
Tàizǔ (太祖) promoted his current office to Grand General of Agile Cavalry.
In the Sòng (宋) era, Wáng Shìwǔ (王世武), General of the Palace Guard, was sent as an envoy to Hénán (河南).
That year, he returned with Shíyín's (拾寅) envoy to present tribute.
The imperial edict in response stated:

"The Emperor respectfully inquires of the Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Palace Attendant, Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xīqín, Hé and Shā three provinces, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Administrator with Rights of the Three Dukes, concurrently Protector-General of the Qiāng, Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two provinces, newly appointed Grand General of Agile Cavalry, and King of Hénán: The precious mandate has been renewed and bestowed,
and has gathered upon Our person.
We are unworthily in charge of this great enterprise,
and feel both reverence and apprehension.
Our feelings of gratitude increased this summer.
Wáng Shìwǔ (王世武) has arrived,
and We received your memorial dated the twenty-first day of the fifth month of the fifth year of Yuánhuī (元徽).
Hearing of the humid heat,
We trust you are well.
Moreover, your sincerity extends afar,
protecting and pacifying distant territories.
Now, this edict elevates your noble title,
to reciprocate your loyalty and sincerity.
We send Wáng Shìwǔ (王世武) with this imperial command to formally bestow it upon you.
Furthermore, Wáng Shìwǔ (王世武) and others are also sent to the Ruìruì (芮芮);
We trust you will assist in their dispatch
so they may arrive on time.
Moreover, all the horses and other items presented in your memorial have arrived.
We now send separately a list of ten bolts each of brocade, crimson, purple, blue, green, yellow, and other patterned silks."
Shíyín's (拾寅) son, Yìdùhóu (易度侯), was fond of astrology
and once requested astronomical texts,
but the court council did not grant them.
When Yín (寅) died,
three years later,
his heir apparent, Tǔyùhún Yìdùhóu (吐谷渾易度侯), was appointed Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xīqín, Hé and Shā three provinces,
General Who Guards the West, concurrently Protector-General of the Qiāng, Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two provinces, and King of Hénán.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (永明) era,
an imperial edict stated:
"Yìdùhóu (易度侯) has held his post in the Western Barbarian regions,
pacifying and bringing order,
and his loyal achievements are manifest.
We are pleased with this.
He may be promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry."
Qiū Guānxian (丘冠先), Attendant Gentleman of the Household, was sent as an envoy to Hénán Dào (河南道),
and also escorted the Ruìruì (芮芮) envoy.
He did not return until the sixth year.
He brought back a jade measuring three *chǐ* two *cùn* long,
and one *chǐ* one *cùn* thick.
When Yìdùhóu (易度侯) died,
in the eighth year,
his heir apparent, Xiūliúmào (休留茂), was established as Commissioner with Imperial Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Xīqín, Hé and Shā three provinces,
General Who Guards the West, concurrently Protector-General of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two provinces.
General Who Manifests Martial Might, Qiū Guānxian (丘冠先), was again sent to formally bestow the appointment
and perform the condolence rites.
When Guānxian (冠先) arrived in Hénán (河南),
Xiūliúmào (休留茂) forced him to bow first.
Guānxian (冠先) refused with a stern expression.
Xiūliúmào (休留茂) felt ashamed before his own people,
seized Guānxian (冠先) and pushed him off a sheer cliff into a deep valley, where he died.
Guānxian's (冠先) courtesy name was Dàoxuán (道玄),
a native of Wúxīng (吳興),
and a sixth-generation descendant of Jié (傑), the Director of Personnel of the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Initially, when the Emperor sent Guānxian (冠先),
he showed him to the Grand Tutor Wáng Jiǎn (王儉).
Jiǎn (儉) replied to the Emperor:
"This man is more than capable of the mission."
Thus, he was entrusted with the mission a second time.
When he died,
Shìzǔ (世祖) commanded his son, Xióng (雄), saying:
"Your father, when sent on the mission to Hénán (河南),
upheld loyalty and faced death,
not disgracing the imperial command.
We deeply admire and lament him.
His body lies in a distant land,
and cannot be recovered.
This will not hinder your future career as an official,
and is indeed a lofty example."
He was granted one hundred thousand *qián* and
thirty bolts of cloth.
The Dī (氐) Yáng (楊) clan,
like the Fú Dī (苻氐), originated from Lüèyáng (略陽).
During the Hàn (漢) era, they resided in Qiúchí (仇池),
a place known as Bǎiqǐng (百頃).
During the Jiàn'ān (建安) era, there was a Dī (氐) king of Bǎiqǐng (百頃), who was of this lineage.
During the Jìn (晉) era, there was Yáng Máosǎo (楊茂[⿱艹舀]),
who later grew strong and prosperous;
his deeds are recorded in earlier histories.
Qiúchí (仇池) was surrounded by sheer cliffs on all sides,
naturally forming a defensive structure with watchtowers to repel enemies,
towering several *zhàng* high.
There were twenty-two paths that could be climbed to ascend,
and two gates, east and west,
with winding paths about seven *lǐ* long.
On top were hills and springs.
The Dī (氐) built palaces, fruit orchards, and granaries on the flat ground above.
Both noble and common people lived in plank houses with earthen walls.
The place they governed was named Luògǔ (洛谷).
In the nineteenth year of Yuánjiā (元嘉) of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Péi Fāngmíng (裴方明), General Who Leaps Like a Dragon, and others attacked the Dī (氐),
conquering Qiúchí (仇池).
Later, it was attacked by the Wèi (魏) barbarians
and lost.
Yáng Wéndé (楊文德), a nephew of Dī (氐) king Yáng Nándāng (楊難當), gathered followers in Jiālú (茄蘆).
The Sòng (宋) dynasty bestowed titles and ranks upon him.
After Wéndé (文德) died,
his younger cousin Sēngsì (僧嗣) and Wénqìng (文慶) successively inherited his position.
Yáng Guǎngxiāng (楊廣香), a clan cousin of Nándāng (難當), had previously defected to the barbarians.
During the Yuánhuī (元徽) era, the barbarians attacked and killed Wénqìng (文慶) for him,
appointing him Duke of Yīnpíng (陰平) and Lord of the Jiālú (茄蘆) garrison.
Wénqìng's (文慶) younger cousin, Wénhóng (文弘), was the Administrator of Báishuǐ (白水) and
stationed in Wǔxīng (武興).
The court council appointed him General Who Assists the State, Inspector of Běiqínzhōu (北秦州), and King of Wǔdū (武都) and Duke of Qiúchí (仇池).
Upon Tàizǔ's (太祖) ascension,
he wished to pacify and embrace the foreign peoples.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (建元) era,
an imperial edict stated:
"In the past, distant nations presented tribute,
a beautiful record in former annals;
foreign peoples came to pledge allegiance,
their fame flows through historical records.
The false barbarian's Lord of the Jiālú (茄蘆) garrison and Duke of Yīnpíng (陰平) Commandery, Yáng Guǎngxiāng (楊廣香),
had grievances with his kinsmen
and hostilities arose among his relatives.
During the Sòng (宋) era,
he surrendered his territory to the enemy.
Jiālú (茄蘆) was lost,
and Huáyáng (華陽) was briefly alarmed.
Recently, a lone envoy first sped forth,
proclaiming the imperial might.
Guǎngxiāng (廣香) and others recalled the sincerity of their distant ancestors
and looked up to Our new transformation,
with bared torsos begging to submit,
restoring a thousand *lǐ* of land.
The Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) mixed tribes
all joined in submission.
They should be received in due time
and treated with great kindness and compassion.
Guǎngxiāng (廣xiāng), having abandoned confusion and returned to righteousness,
may be specially granted an appropriate appointment.
His tribal chiefs and strongmen
shall be rewarded according to their names."
Guǎngxiāng (廣xiāng) was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Shāzhōu (沙州), Colonel Who Pacifies the Qiāng, and Inspector of Shāzhōu.
Soon after, he was promoted to General Who Conquers Barbarians.
When the governor of Yǐngzhōu, Fàn Bǎinián, was executed,
his close general, Lǐ Wūnú, fled in fear and rebelled.
Wén Hóng took him in.
Wūnú led over a thousand fugitives to attack Yǐngzhōu,
but was defeated by the governor, Wáng Xuánmiǎo,
and fled back to the Dī territory.
Yùzhāngwáng Yí, the governor of Jīngzhōu, dispatched troops to suppress Wūnú.
He issued a proclamation to Yǐngzhōu, stating that whoever could capture and deliver Wūnú's head
would be rewarded within their own commandery,
and all of Wūnú's fields, dwellings, and properties would be bestowed upon them.
He wrote to Guǎngxiāng, saying: "Indeed, rise and fall are without error,
and compliance and defiance have their consequences,
a truth universally acknowledged since ancient times;
wise and foolish alike perceive it.
Fàn Bǎinián, the governor of Yǐngzhōu, harbored deceitful intentions,
wavering
between two extremes.
Having already been chastised,
[一二] he lingered and delayed obedience.
He then secretly sent Lǐ Wūnú to rebel.
Yáng Wénhóng incited and lured the border regions, making them chaotic and mixed.
Bǎinián has now been
captured and displayed,
and Wūnú has been repeatedly crushed.
We estimate that his remaining embers
will soon extinguish themselves.
Now, we dispatch Administrator Wáng Dàobǎo, acting as the Grand Administrator of Jìnshòu; Ren Shízhī, acting as the Grand Administrator of Běi
Bāxī and Xīnbā Commanderies; and Wáng Ānhuì, acting as the Grand Administrator of Dàngqú, leading three thousand elite soldiers.
They will hasten their march with the speed of wind,
crossing rivers like lightning.
Furthermore,
we order Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Sānbā Xiàowèi Míng Huìzhào, Bājùn Grand Administrator Lǔ Xiūliè, Nán Bāxī Grand Administrator Liǔ Hóngchēng, and Yìzhōu Governor Fù Yǎn
to
mobilize their foot soldiers and cavalry in a race,
selecting their armored troops to vie for speed.
The land and naval forces of Yōngzhōu
will advance to Wèixīng,
and together with the relocated old families from east of the mountains,
will converge at Nánzhèng.
Some will sail boats across Diànjiāng,
others
will fly their banners along the Jiàndào.
They will surge from front and rear like a whirlwind,
striking with thunderous force on the outside and inside.
Wénhóng accommodates rebels and dissenters,
becoming a specialized haven for them.
He insults the imperial authority externally
and abuses the state's people internally.
[一三] Your Lord, whose family has been loyal for generations,
deeply understands what is right and proper.
We imagine you will immediately
rise in righteousness
and respond to the grand army,
forming a pincer movement
to eliminate Wūnú,
thus establishing loyal service
and demonstrating sincere integrity.
Shěn Yōuzhī, relying on ten years of accumulated resources
and the power of a hundred
legions,
saw his cities collapse as his army left the border,
and his troops slaughtered themselves before battle.
The imperial court incurred no expense for arrows,
and the soldiers and common people suffered no wounds.
How much more so for a petty
scoundrel,
who is utterly insignificant in comparison.
His annihilation
will surely not be delayed even for a moment.
Though I am unworthy and ignorant,
I am entrusted with governing this frontier region,
clearing away impurities and sweeping away filth,
which I consider my duty.
This prefecture's
weapons are piled like mountains,
and its banners soar like a forest.
Its soldiers are swift and fierce,
hoarding power and authority.
[一四] To eliminate difficulties and suppress bandits,
why wait for training and practice!
[一五] To cut down sprouting
fungi,
one does not need a mighty axe;
to swat mosquitoes,
one does not need great strength.
His Imperial Majesty, sagacious and wise, meets the times,
and his benevolence spreads widely.
Punishment targets only the chief evil-doers,
the rest are not questioned.
The details of rewards and punishments are
written separately.
I have ordered Dàobǎo to march out to Wèixīng,
and to divide the army to ascend Diànjiāng,
both converging at Jìnshòu."
Because Wénhóng rebelled, Tàizǔ promoted Guǎngxiāng to Chíjié, Dūdū Xī Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Guǎngxiāng's son, Jìng, who was Běibù Zhènjiāngjūn and Jùnshì, was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Wǔdū Tàishǒu.
Yáng Hòuqǐ, Nándāng Zhèngyìn, was appointed Chíjié, Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Běi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, and Wǔdū Wáng,
garrisoned at Wǔxīng.
He was Wénhóng's paternal cousin's son.
In the third year,
Wénhóng surrendered,
and was again appointed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn and Běi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Earlier, Guǎngxiāng had died of illness,
and half of the Dī people fled to Wénhóng,
while the other half went to Cuī Huìjǐng, the governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Wénhóng sent his paternal cousin's son, Hòuqǐ, to advance and occupy Báishuǐ.
Báishuǐ was located upstream from Jìnshòu,
bordered Fú to the west,
was adjacent to the Yì route to the east,
and connected to Yīnpíng and Qiélú to the north,
making it a strategically important location.
Yáng Gōngzé, the Grand Administrator of Jìnshòu, submitted a memorial regarding the appropriate strategy,
to which the emperor replied:
"Wénhóng's crime is unforgivable,
but for the sake of political expediency, he should be granted grace for now.
If you can successfully raid and capture Báishuǐ,
you will certainly be generously rewarded."
Upon Shìzǔ's ascension to the throne,
Hòuqǐ was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Jìng was appointed Shāzhōu Cìshǐ and Yīnpíng Wáng,
retaining his general title.
In the second year,
the eight ministers memorialized that Hòuqǐ's
[勤] loyalty to the frontier was manifest,
[一六] and his fidelity was evident in the border city.
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year,
Hòuqǐ died.
An imperial edict stated:
"Hòuqǐ's sudden demise
fills me with sorrow.
[一七] To pacify and defend the frontier territories,
his successor should be carefully chosen.
Yáng Jíshǐ, acting Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Běi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, and Wǔdū Wáng,
is capable and clear-headed,
and his heart is filled with loyalty.
He will surely be able to secure the borders, pacify the people, and promote culture and education.
He is to be appointed Chíjié, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Běi Qínzhōu Cìshǐ, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Wǔdū Wáng."
Hòuqǐ's younger brother, Hòumíng, was appointed Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn and Báishuǐ Tàishǒu.
Jíshǐ's younger brother, Jílǎng, was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
In the fifth year,
the relevant officials memorialized that Jíshǐ drove out foxes and cleared thorns,
transforming the border regions through his influence.
A mother is honored by her son's nobility,
and should therefore be granted special favor.
Jíshǐ's mother, Lady Jiāng, was appointed Tàifūrén,
and granted a silver seal.
In the ninth year,
the eight ministers memorialized that Yáng Jìng continued his diligent service in the western pasturage,
and his loyalty shone brightly within the empire.
It was fitting to increase his military title
to illuminate the distant regions.
He was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn.
In the tenth year,
Jíshǐ rebelled,
leading a mixed force of Dī and Shǔ people to invade Hànchuān.
Yīn Zhìbó, the governor of Yǐngzhōu, dispatched over a thousand men, including army commanders Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Huán Lúnú, Liáng Jìqún, Sòng [□], and Wáng Shìlóng, to resist him.
[一八] They were unsuccessful
and retreated to defend Báimǎ.
The rebel force of over ten thousand men unleashed their troops, setting fire to and attacking the city's palisades.
Lúnú resisted and fought to the death.
Zhìbó again dispatched several thousand cavalry and infantry, including army commander Yīn Zhòngchāng, to reinforce them.
When they reached Qiānxī Bridge, east of Báimǎ City,
a few li away,
Jíshǐ and his forces attacked with all their might.
The government troops fought fiercely from both inside and outside,
and Jíshǐ suffered a great defeat.
His eighteen camps disintegrated and fled simultaneously,
with several thousand killed or captured.
Jíshǐ fled into barbarian territory.
In the first year of Lóngchāng,
former Qián Jiāngjūn Yáng Jìng was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dū Shāzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Shāzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jíshǐ entered Wǔxīng
and surrendered the city to the barbarians.
The Dī man Fú Yòusūn rose in righteousness and attacked him.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the Dī and Lǔ plundered Hàngzhōng.
The Inspector of Liángzhōu, Xiāo Yì, dispatched Yáng Yuánxiù, a nephew of the former Dī King Yáng Hòuqǐ, to gather a volunteer army.
The Dī masses responded,
cutting off the Lǔ's supply routes.
The Lǔ also sent their pseudo-Inspector of Nánliángzhōu, Gōng Yáng Língzhēn of Chóuchí, to occupy Níshān to resist them.
Yuánxiù died of illness,
and Fú Yòusūn led his forces.
Gāozōng issued an edict saying:
“Gōng Yáng Yuánxiù of Chóuchí,
a scion of the Dī royal line,
was loyal and brave at heart.
When the vile Lǔ pressed aggressively,
his sincere devotion intensified,
propagating the court's authority
and attracting various Rong tribes.
Thousands of li united in agreement,
responding readily and submitting.
His effectiveness was manifest
and truly commendable.
His unfortunate demise
fills me with sorrow.
Indeed, for those who die in service, additional grace is bestowed,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals clarify righteousness.
It is proper to posthumously extend distinguished honors
to greatly encourage and reward.
He is posthumously granted the title of Gōng of Chóuchí.
Let this be brought to his home territory.”
The Dī, led by Yáng Fùzhī, gathered a righteous army and encamped at Jǔshuǐguān,
north of Báimǎ city.
Jí Shǐ initially sent his younger brother Jí Lǎng to lead troops to confront the provincial army at Huánggèng,
where they suffered a great defeat.
Jí Shǐ fled to Xiàbiàn,
while Fùzhī occupied Wǔxīng.
The Lǔ army soon retreated.
Fùzhī left his younger brother Chāngzhī to guard Wǔxīng,
and personally led his troops to occupy Chóuchí.
An edict stated:
“Dī King Yáng Fùzhī
has for generations upheld loyalty and righteousness,
rallied his troops,
achieved meritorious deeds in border cities,
and suppressed wicked villains.
Furthermore, he adheres to the court's laws internally
and pacifies the barbarian wilds externally.
His sincere heart is clearly displayed,
and We greatly commend him.
He is appointed as Chízé, Military Supervisor of Běiqín and Yōng two prefectures, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Běiqínzhōu, and Gōng of Chóuchí.”
The Inspector of Shāzhōu, Yáng Jiǒng, was promoted to the title of Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
In the third year,
Jiǒng died.
Jiǒng's son, Chóngzǔ, was appointed as Jiǎjié, Military Supervisor of Shāzhōu, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Shāzhōu, and King of Yīnpíng.
In the fourth year,
the pseudo-Inspector of Nánliángzhōu, Yáng Língzhēn, with his two younger brothers Póluó and Ābǔzhēn, led over thirty thousand troops and their entire city to surrender and pledge allegiance.
They sent their mother and sons Shuāngjiàn and Āpí to Nánzhèng as hostages.
〔一九〕The Inspector of Liángzhōu, Yīn Guǎngzōng, sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Wáng Sīkǎo to lead troops to reinforce,
〔二０〕but they were captured by the Lǔ. Póluó and Ābǔzhēn died in battle.
Língzhēn attacked Jí Shǐ at Wǔxīng,
killing his two younger brothers Jí Tóng and Jí Zhòng.
Jí Shǐ, in desperate straits,
requested to surrender.
Língzhēn was appointed as Chízé, Military Supervisor of Lǒngyòu, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Běiliángzhōu, [二一〕Gōng of Chóuchí, and King of Wǔdū.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
Jí Shǐ was again appointed as Shǐchízé, Military Supervisor of Qín and Yōng two prefectures, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Píngqiāng Xiàowèi, and Inspector of Běiqínzhōu.
Língzhēn was later killed by the Lǔ.
Since the Lǔ captured Chóuchí,
it was sometimes gained, sometimes lost.
The Sòng regarded Chóuchí as a commandery,
hence the Dī were enfeoffed there.
Dàngchāng
was a Qiāng tribe.
Each had its chieftain
and led its people between Qīan and Lǒng.
At the end of the Sòng,

Liáng Mí Jī, King of Dàngchāng, was appointed as Shǐchízé, Military Supervisor of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, and Gōng of Lǒngxī.
In the first year of Jiànyuán,
Tàizǔ promoted him to the title of Zhènxī Jiāngjūn.
Furthermore, Xiàng Shūpēng, Qiāng King and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Xīliángzhōu, was also promoted to Chízé and Píngxī Jiāngjūn.
He later rebelled and surrendered to the [Lǔ].
〔二二〕In the first year of Yǒngmíng,
the Eight Ministers memorialized, saying,
“The former Shǐchízé, Dūdū of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn,
Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Gōng of Lǒngxī, and King of Dàngchāng, Liáng Mí Jī,
and the former Shǐchízé, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Inspector of Xīliángzhōu, and Qiāng King, Xiàng Shūpēng,
both diligently served on the western frontier
and pacified the border regions.
Their former official titles and ranks should be restored.”
The edict also stated that Liú Luòyáng, the Qiāng King and Grand Commander of Lǒngyòu, could be appointed as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
Mí Jī died.
In the third year,
an edict stated:
“The acting King of Dàngchāng, Liáng Mí Jié,
has sincerely pledged allegiance and attached himself to the court,
achieving meritorious deeds on the western frontier.
It is proper to bestow upon him titles and appointments
to magnify his role as a border protector.
He is appointed as Shǐchízé, Military Supervisor of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Gōng of Lǒngxī, and King of Dàngchāng.”
Mí Jié died.
In the sixth year,

the acting King of Dàngchāng, Liáng Mí Chéng, was appointed as Shǐchízé, Military Supervisor of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Dōngqiāng Xiàowèi, Inspector of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, and King of Dàngchāng.
He requested military ceremonies and various books on performing arts.
The edict replied:
“We understand your need for nine types of military ceremonies, etc.
However, none of these are Our favorites.
Moreover, there are many types of military equipment,
which are not easy to transport.
Internal performing artists are unsuitable for long journeys.
The imperial library's maps and books
are generally not allowed to leave.
However, We now specially bestow upon the King one set each of the Wǔjīng Jízhù and Lúnyǔ. ”
The local custom values tiger skins,
using them in funerals,
and they are used as currency in the kingdom.
The historiographer remarked: The Dī and Hú became strong and prosperous,
rising in succession with changing fortunes.
Qín and Zhào were presumptuous and deviant,
consequently suffering destruction.
Their remaining kin, in their foolishness,
extended across the western border and reached the northern frontier.
The Rùiruì's territory ended in the deep north,
their warhorses separated by heaven.
The Dī Yáng were closely situated,
the Chinese and barbarians sharing a border.
They frequently encroached upon Hàn and Yàng,
gradually pressing upon Láng and Hú.
With border territories in mind,
they observed Our power and virtue.
As Liáng province faced many difficulties,
this became an obstruction.
The remnant Qiāng tribes,
with changing fortunes, began to flourish.
〔二四〕They occupied the entire Lǒng and relied on the river,
communicating far to the southern post stations,
establishing their states and calling themselves vassals,
all receiving official appointments.
When the Jìn clan declined
〔二五〕and the central court collapsed,
exterminating the remaining four barbarians,
it was hoped that the barbarian calamity would be avenged.
They were given weapons
and promoted to military command.
Later generations continued this practice,
greedily expanding their influence and teachings,
pacifying the outer regions and comforting the distant,
prioritizing reputation over reality.
They traded what they had for what they lacked,
opening up border profits for generations.
Feathers, fur, teeth, and hides
were exchanged for what was detrimental to us.
As for the matter of the nine types,
there were reasons [obscured characters] that led to this.
〔二六〕
Eulogy: The Rùiruì and Hénán
both originated from the Hú tribes.
Calling themselves kings and usurping imperial titles,
they seized power and monopolized rule.
〔二七〕The Dī and Qiāng, remnants of evil,
scattered across Hé and Lǒng.
They came as guests and rebelled as traitors,
acting without restraint and yet inheriting traditions.
